It reproves their failure to accept the truth by attributing it to ignorance of what truly benefits them: had they perceived the real and lasting value of faith and piety, they would have chosen them and received a better reward from God in this life and the next.

translation: O you who have believed, do not say "raʿinā" but say "anzurnā" and listen. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse instructs believers to guard their speech and avoid expressions that can be used to show disrespect or be twisted into mockery of the Prophet and the message; instead they must use clear, respectful language and pay heed. By coupling this etiquette with the warning of a painful punishment for disbelievers, the verse underscores both the ethical discipline of precise, reverent speech in religious matters and the serious moral consequences for those who persist in scorn and rejection of divine guidance.

translation: Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord. But Allah confines His mercy to whom He wills; and Allah is the Lord of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the ill will or envy of others cannot obstruct God’s generosity: guidance, forgiveness, and blessings come by God’s sovereign choice, not by human desire. Believers are therefore reassured that opposition from rival communities does not determine God’s favor; instead they should trust in His wisdom, seek His mercy, and recognize that His bounty is vast and distributed according to His wise purposes.

translation: We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten except that We bring forth something better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?
interpretation: The verse teaches that when God withdraws or supersedes a previous ruling or remembrance, He does so from supreme wisdom and purpose — replacing it with a ruling that is better suited or equivalent to what was before — rather than out of error or contradiction. This affirms that changes in divine guidance (legislative or moral adjustments across time) are deliberate, merciful, and context‑sensitive manifestations of Allah’s sovereignty, and it calls believers to trust His wisdom and accept shifts in guidance as expressions of His absolute power and perfect knowledge.

translation:
أَلَمْ تَعْلَمْ أَنَّ اللَّهَ لَهُ مُلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۗ وَمَا لَكُم مِّن دُونِ اللَّهِ مِن وَلِيٍّ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ
“Do you not know that Allah has the dominion of the heavens and the earth? And you have no guardian or helper besides Allah.”
interpretation: The verse emphasizes God’s absolute sovereignty and authority over all creation and denies any independent protector, patron, or ultimate helper apart from Him. It calls people to recognize their dependence on God alone, to refrain from ascribing ultimate power or rescue to other beings or institutions, and to place their trust, allegiance, and supplication solely in the One whose will governs the heavens and the earth.

translation: Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? And whoever exchanges faith for disbelief has certainly gone astray from the right way.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the attitude of persistently testing or doubting prophetic guidance as a way to evade sincere submission: when people demand continual proofs or challenge the messenger in the manner some challenged Moses, it often reflects a refusal to accept guidance. More fundamentally, the verse warns that allowing doubt, obstinacy, or willful rejection to replace true belief is not a neutral change of opinion but a departure from the straight path—apostasy from faith is portrayed as clear misguidance rather than mere intellectual disagreement.

translation: كَثِيرٌ مِّنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ لَوْ يُرِدُونَكُمْ أَن تَكْفُرُوا مِن بَعْدِ إِيمَانِكُمْ حَسَدًا مِنْ عِندِ أَنْفُسِهِمْ مِن بَعْدِ مَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الْحَقُّ ۖ فَاعْفُوا وَاصْفَحُوا حَتَّىٰ يَأْتِيَ اللَّهُ بِأَمْرِهِ ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
interpretation: الآية تنبه إلى أنّ هناك من الناس، حتى من أهل الكتاب، من قد يعرف الحق لكنه يَحسُد ويُرِيد أن يُبعد المؤمنين عن إيمانهم بدافع العداوة أو المصلحة الشخصية. والرد الربّاني على هذا ليس بالمبادَرة إلى التنازع أو الانتقام بل بالرفق والصفح والامتناع عن الردّ السيّئ، مع توكيد الثقة بأن الحكم والجزاء في يد الله وسيأتيه وقت يهيِّئ فيه الأمر ويقيم الحق. فهي دعوة لأخلاق الصبر والعفو والثقة في تدبير الله بدل الانزلاق إلى خصومة تفرّق المجتمع وتُعطي خصم الحق ما يريد.

translation: And establish prayer and give zakāh. Whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is All‑Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse enjoins two fundamental duties—regular worship (prayer) and social responsibility (zakāh)—and links them to the believer’s ultimate investment: deeds performed sincerely and deliberately for God are not lost but preserved as a real, lasting good with Allah. It reassures that every righteous act offered for the sake of God will be returned as reward, because God is fully aware of people’s actions and intentions.

translation: And they say, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Bring your proof, if you are truthful."
interpretation: The verse rejects sectarian exclusivism: claiming that only a particular people or label will attain Paradise is mere wishful hope unless supported by valid proof. By commanding a challenge—"bring your proof"—God exposes the emptiness of unsubstantiated theological certainty and reminds that ultimate judgment rests on submission to divine guidance and truthful, righteous conduct, not on mere communal or ancestral identity.

translation:
بلى من أسلم وجهه لله وهو محسن فله أجره عند ربه ولا خوف عليهم ولا هم يحزنون
“Nay — whoever submits his whole self to Allah while doing good, for them is their reward with their Lord; there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith is wholehearted submission to God combined with ihsān (excellent, sincere conduct). It affirms that when a person genuinely turns their whole self toward God and lives righteously, God Himself will grant the due recompense; that state brings deliverance from fear and sorrow—signifying both inner peace in this life and secure success and absence of regret or punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: قالتِ اليهودُ "لا شيء للنصارى"، وقالتِ النصارى "لا شيء لليهود"، ومَعَ ذلك يَتْلُونَ الكتابَ. كذلك قالَ الذين لا يَعلَمون نفسَ قَولِهم. واللهُ يَحكمُ بينهم يومَ القيامةِ فيما كانوا فيه يختلفون.
interpretation: الآية تندد بالاستعلاء الطائفي والادعاءات الموروثة المبنية على جهل أو تحيّز: كثيرون يَرُدّون حقّ الآخرين لمجرد الانتماء دون محاجّة عادلة أو فهم عميق، ويكرر الجاهلون أقوالهم دون تمحيص. الحكم الحق في الخلافات العقدية والأخلاقية ليس لأهواء الجماعات بل لله وحده يوم الجزاء؛ لذلك تُدعو الآية إلى التواضع والبحث الصادق عن الحق والالتزام بمصداقية الدين بدل التمسك الشكلي بالنصوص أو التعلّق بالهوية الطائفية.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who prevents the name of Allah from being mentioned in His mosques and strives toward their ruin? Those will not enter them except in fear. For them there is disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns any person or group that obstructs communal remembrance of God and actively works to despoil or nullify places of worship. Preventing dhikr in the masjid can be literal (forbidding prayer, closing or converting sacred spaces, attacking their integrity) and moral (silencing guidance, promoting lawlessness where sanctity should be upheld). Such conduct severs the social and spiritual bonds that protect a community; outward access to a mosque becomes hollow—entered only with dread, not with the assurance of faith—and is followed by visible disgrace in life and severe retribution in the next. The passage therefore asserts both a moral principle (the sanctity of communal worship must be defended) and a theological consequence: undermining God’s houses is among the gravest injustices and brings both social ruin and divine punishment.

translation: To Allah belong the east and the west. Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s sovereignty, presence and attention are not confined to any particular place or direction; the imagery of “east and west” and “the Face of Allah” denies any localization of the Divine. Turning in a given direction for worship is a lawful, communal act of obedience, but it does not limit God’s reality: His knowledge, authority and mercy extend everywhere and encompass all circumstances. In short, God is universally present and fully aware, so human orientation or location never confines access to His care, judgment or nearness.

translation:
وَقَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ وَلَدًا ۗ سُبْحَانَهُ ۖ بَل لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۖ كُلٌّ لَهُ قَانِتُونَ
“They say, ‘Allah has taken a son.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly submissive to Him.”
interpretation: The verse rejects the attribution of ‘sonship’ to God by affirming His utter transcendence and self-sufficiency. The exclamation ‘Subḥānahu’ denies any human-like limitation or need in the Divine. By stating that everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God, it emphasizes that nothing can be added to or originate from Him as an offspring; creation is His possession, dependent on Him, not a part of His essence. The phrase ‘kullun lahu qānitūn’ underscores that all beings exist in continuous submission and servitude before God—acknowledging His sole lordship—so the idea of God having a son is incoherent with His unity, independence and perfection.

translation: Originator of the heavens and the earth. And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God alone is the ultimate Creator and Sustainer, whose will is immediate and unconstrained: His divine command brings realities into being without dependence on intermediaries or delay. The phrase “Be and it is” shows the absolute efficacy of His word and the complete reliance of all existence on His sovereign decree.

translation:
وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ لَوْلَا يُكَلِّمُنَا اللَّهُ أَوْ تَأْتِينَآ آيَةٌ ۚ كَذَٰلِكَ قَالَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ ۚ تَشَابَهَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ ۚ قَدْ بَيَّنَّا الْآيَاتِ لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ
"And those who do not know say, 'Why does Allah not speak to us, or why does a sign not come to us?' Thus said those before them — the same was said by them. Their hearts have become alike. We have certainly made the signs clear for a people who are certain."
interpretation: The verse rebukes a recurring attitude: people deprived of true understanding demand spectacular, sensory proof (an audible word from God or a visible miracle) as a condition for belief. Such demands mirror the objections of earlier communities and indicate a common spiritual condition — hearts that are confused, hardened, or seeking pretexts rather than truth. God contrasts this attitude with those whose inner conviction (yaqīn) enables them to recognize and benefit from the clear signs already given. In short, genuine guidance depends on sincere inward certainty, not on insisting upon extraordinary external demonstrations, which often conceal stubbornness, hypocrisy or unwillingness to submit to revealed guidance.

translation: Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner; and you are not to be questioned about the companions of the Blaze.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Prophet’s responsibility is limited to faithfully delivering God’s message — giving glad tidings to those who accept and warning those who reject — and that he is not accountable for the ultimate fate of those who persist in disbelief; their destiny and punishment belong to God’s judgment alone, so the Messenger (and by extension the believers) must focus on conveying the truth rather than being consumed by or held responsible for others’ end.

translation: And never will the Jews nor the Christians be satisfied with you until you follow their religion. Say, “Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the true guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge, then you would have from Allah no protector or helper.
interpretation: This verse teaches that truth and spiritual integrity must not be sacrificed to win the approval of others. The People of the Book will press for conformity, but divine guidance is presented as the objective standard of right direction; a believer’s duty is to adhere to what has been revealed and understood, not to conform to popular or external pressures. Choosing to follow mere desires or the ways of others after receiving clear knowledge severs the bond of trust and dependence on God—one forfeits the special support and guardianship that belong to those who remain faithful to revealed guidance.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture recite it with true recitation; they are the ones who believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it — those are the losers.
interpretation: The phrase “true recitation” points to more than correct pronunciation: it denotes faithful reading with understanding, sincere transmission, and living by the guidance of a revealed book. Those among the People of the Book who engage with their scripture in that manner recognize and accept its divine truth (as confirmed by the Qur’an) and thereby attain faith; by contrast, rejecting the revealed truth results in spiritual loss and failure in the ultimate judgment.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you above the worlds.
interpretation: God calls the Israelites to recall the concrete blessings and distinctions He granted them—prophetic guidance, scripture, deliverance, and special opportunities of covenant—and emphasizes that such divine preference was not merely honor but a trust that carried moral and religious obligations. The verse intends to awaken gratitude and responsible behavior: being chosen implies greater accountability, so remembrance of God’s favors should lead to obedience, upright conduct, and preservation of the covenant rather than complacency or claim to perpetual privilege.

translation: And fear a Day when no soul will avail another in anything, nor will any ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: The verse is a solemn warning that on the Day of Judgment individual responsibility is absolute: family ties, wealth, bargains, and human intercession will not change a person’s accounting unless God wills. Its practical meaning is to turn people away from reliance on others or worldly means for salvation and to urge sincere personal faith, righteous deeds, and seeking God’s mercy now, because each soul will stand by itself before divine justice.

translation: And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with certain words, and he completed them. He said, "Indeed I will make you a leader (imam) for the people." He said, "And of my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine appointment and lasting honor are conditional: God’s promise of leadership is granted in response to sincere submission and tested fidelity, and it is not inherited automatically by lineage. When Abraham asks about his offspring, God’s reply—'My covenant does not include the wrongdoers'—makes clear that descendants share in the promise only insofar as they uphold justice, faith and obedience; those who persist in injustice or reject God’s guidance are excluded from that covenantal favor.

translation: And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a place of security, and said, “Take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer,” and We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael, saying, “Purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and for those who devote themselves to it, and for those who bow and prostrate.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God established the Kaʿbah not merely as a physical structure but as the communal, sanctified center of worship whose upkeep and purity are a prophetic trust. Commanding Abraham and Ishmael to cleanse the House for tawāf, iʿtikāf and prayer emphasizes that sacred space must be kept ritually and morally pure, accessible for varied forms of sincere devotion, and that the rites performed there express and preserve the continuity of monotheistic worship and communal religious identity.

translation: And [remember] when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits — for those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He said, “And whoever disbelieves — I will grant him enjoyment for a little; then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination.”
interpretation: Abraham’s prayer links the well‑being of a community to both material provision and spiritual faith: he asks that the place be safe and that its inhabitants be sustained, specifically highlighting those who hold belief in God and the Last Day. God’s reply establishes a moral and eschatological principle — worldly ease may be allotted even to those who reject faith, but such enjoyment is temporary and will be followed by ultimate accountability. The verse thus teaches that true security and lasting benefit are tied to faith, that temporal blessings are part of God’s wisdom and testing, and that final justice belongs to God alone.

translation: And [remember] when Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations of the House, [saying], “Our Lord, accept [this] from us. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that outward acts of worship and communal religious work acquire true worth only when offered with the sincere hope of divine acceptance. By invoking God as the Hearing and the Knowing, the supplication emphasizes that Allah perceives both visible deeds and hidden intentions, so believers must seek His approval rather than human praise and entrust the outcome to Him. The passage thus models humility, sincerity, cooperative devotion, and reliance on God’s awareness and judgment as the measure of a deed’s real value.

translation: Our Lord, and make us submissive to You and [raise] from our offspring a people submissive to You; and show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Oft-Returning, Most Merciful.
interpretation: This is a humble prayer that links inner faith, communal continuity, correct practice, and repentance: the supplicants ask God to grant them true submission (islām) inwardly and to cultivate a generation that shares that submission, recognizing that faith must be transmitted and embodied. By asking “show us our rites” they seek God’s guidance and clear exemplification so their worship is performed rightly and taught faithfully, while petitioning forgiveness acknowledges human error and dependence on Divine mercy. Invoking God as al-Tawwāb al-Raḥīm underscores trust that God not only guides and corrects but also repeatedly accepts repentance, so the community’s striving, teaching, and return to God remain within the embrace of His mercy.

translation:
رَبَّنَا وَابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِنْهُمْ يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ ۚ إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ
“Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your signs, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise.”
interpretation: This is a plea that genuine guidance be rooted within a people: a leader “from themselves” who, by reciting God’s revelations, instructing in scripture and imparting wisdom, effects both intellectual understanding and moral/spiritual purification. It emphasizes that prophetic guidance is not merely transmission of words but formation of character (tazkiyah) through teaching and practical wisdom, and that such a comprehensive transformation depends on God’s power and wise decree — hence the appeal to His attributes, implying trust that He can and will establish the right guide for true reform.

translation: And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? Indeed We chose him in this world; and indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse indicts abandoning Abraham’s millah (the pure, uncompromising submission to God) as self-deception: turning from that model harms one’s own soul. By stating God chose Abraham in this life and that he will be counted among the righteous in the Hereafter, the text establishes him as the exemplar of true faith and moral conviction—calling believers to emulate his monotheism, sincerity, and steadfast obedience rather than follow innovations, cultural pressures, or short-sighted desires.

translation: When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: It presents true faith as immediate, wholehearted surrender to God's lordship: Abraham’s instant declaration — “I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds” — affirms that Islam is first an inner recognition of God’s sole sovereignty, a readiness to live under that authority, and a model of the monotheistic conviction from which righteous words and deeds flow.

translation: And Abraham advised his sons, and [so did] Jacob: “O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen the religion for you; so do not die except while you are Muslims.”
interpretation: The verse records prophetic parental counsel urging successive generations to preserve the pure way God ordained: submission to Him (Islam) is presented as God’s chosen, guiding arrangement for their lives. It is a charge to teach and maintain sincere monotheism and righteous practice so that one’s life ends in true submission—not a call to force a mere formula at death, but a demand for ongoing belief and conduct that remain steadfast until death, transmitting faith faithfully from parent to child and safeguarding communal identity under God’s guidance.

translation: Or were you witnesses when Jacob was dying, when he said to his sons, “What will you worship after me?” They said, “We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac—one God—and to Him we submit.”
interpretation: The verse affirms the continuity and unity of true faith: Jacob’s sons explicitly endorse monotheism as taught by their forefathers and identify their commitment not with a tribal or sectarian label but with submission to the one God. By recording their declaration—“one God, and we are Muslims (submitters) to Him”—the passage stresses that authentic religion is defined by tawḥīd (God’s oneness) and willing submission, linking the prophetic line (Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob) as witnesses to the same core truth and setting a precedent that faith is measured by submission to God rather than by names or divisions that later arose.

translation: That was a nation that has passed away; for them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn; and you will not be asked about what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse underscores individual and communal moral responsibility: past peoples are accountable for their own deeds and receive their due consequences, while each present community bears responsibility for its own actions. It teaches that one should not claim liability or merit on behalf of previous nations nor expect to be judged for their conduct; instead, focus on one’s own deeds, for each group (and ultimately each person) will be judged and rewarded or punished according to what they themselves have done.

translation: And they said, “Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided.” Say, “Rather, the religion of Abraham — upright (hanīf) — and he was not of the polytheists.”
interpretation: This verse answers those who insist that true guidance can only be achieved by adopting a particular communal label (Jewish or Christian). The Prophet’s correct reply is to affirm allegiance to the primordial faith of Abraham: a single, upright commitment to pure monotheism (hanīf) that rejects idolatry and religious compromise. The statement asserts continuity with Abraham’s uncompromised tawḥīd (Divine unity) as the standard of guidance, not mere affiliation with any later, potentially altered religious community.

translation: Say, "We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the [tribes], and what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit."
interpretation: The verse requires believers to affirm the unity and continuity of divine guidance by accepting God and the revelations sent throughout history to the patriarchs and all prophets, refusing to rank or discriminate among them; it defines the Muslim stance as one of recognizing a single divine source behind these messages and responding with full submission (Islam) to God’s authority.

translation: If they believe in what you believe, then they have been guided; but if they turn away, then they are only in schism. Allah will suffice you against them. And He is the Hearing, the Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that true guidance is acceptance of the same faith: those who embrace it are rightly guided, while those who persistently refuse place themselves in division and rebellion (شقاق). It reassures the Prophet and the community that such opponents cannot ultimately prevail, for God Himself will be their protector and vindicator — believers need not be overwhelmed by fear or seek undue retaliation. The closing attributes, “the Hearing, the Knowing,” stress that God fully perceives both outward deeds and inner intentions and will deal with the matter justly and at the proper time.

translation: The imprint (or dye) of Allah — and who is better than Allah in giving an imprint? — and we are His worshippers.
interpretation: 'صبغة الله' denotes the distinctive mark or identity that God gives through His guidance and way of life; the rhetorical question 'ومن أحسن من الله صبغة' stresses that no one can bestow a truer, purer identity or creed than God. By declaring 'ونحن له عابدون' the speaker affirms complete acceptance of that divine imprint, committing to live and worship wholly according to God’s guidance rather than following altered, mixed, or man-made paths.

translation: Say, “Will you argue with us about Allah while He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds; and we are sincere to Him.”
interpretation: The speaker refuses to be drawn into disputes that would compromise pure devotion: even if God is acknowledged by both sides, what matters is how each lives and worships. By insisting on separate accounts of actions and declaring exclusive sincerity to God, the verse draws a clear line between genuine, uncompromised worship and corrupting practices or doctrines; it affirms that truth is shown through faithful, sincere practice and that each group will be held responsible for its own deeds before God.

translation: أم تقولون إن إبراهيم وإسماعيل وإسحاق ويعقوب والأسباط كانوا هودا أو نصارى ۗ قل أأنتم أعلم أم الله ۗ ومن أظلم ممن كتم شهادة عنده من الله ۗ وما الله بغافل عما تعملون
interpretation: الآية توبخ من يختزلون تراث الأنبياء في تصنيفات طائفية لاحقة، وتذكر أن أحقية المعرفة للحق ليست بيد البشر بل لله وحده؛ ومن يخفي شهادة الحق أو يقمع دلالات الوحي لمصلحة دنيوية يرتكب ظلماً عظيماً، لأن إظهار الحق أو نقله واجب إنساني وديني، وإخفاؤه يضلل الناس ويخالف عدل الله. لذلك تأتي التذكرة بأن الله على علم كامل بكل ما يخبئه الناس ويفعلونه، فلا يغني التكتم أو التحايل عن المحاسبة الإلهية.

translation: That was a people who have passed away; for them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn; and you will not be asked about what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse asserts individual and generational moral responsibility: outcomes belong to those who did the deeds, not to others who come later. It prevents inheriting either guilt or merit from earlier communities and insists that each person and community will be judged on their own actions. Practically this means one cannot justify present conduct by appealing to the behavior or fate of past peoples, nor can one rest on ancestral reputation; each must strive to obtain their own righteous deeds because recompense follows personal responsibility on the Day of Reckoning.

translation:
سَيَقُولُ السُّفَهَاءُ مِنَ النَّاسِ مَا وَلَّاهُمْ عَن قِبْلَتِهِمُ الَّتِي كَانُوا عَلَيْهَا ۚ قُل لِلَّهِ الْمَشْرِقُ وَالْمَغْرِبُ ۚ يَهْدِي مَنْ يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ
"Fools among the people will say, ‘What has turned them away from their qiblah, which they used to face?’ Say: ‘To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path.’"
interpretation: The verse answers those who mock or question the Prophet and the believers for changing the direction of prayer. Its core message is that the physical orientation (qiblah) is subject to God’s will—He owns the entire horizon—so changing it is within His authority and wisdom. More importantly, the verse shifts attention from external signs to divine guidance: true guidance to the straight path is granted by Allah, not determined by which direction one faces. Thus the change of qiblah is a divinely ordained sign and test that distinguishes sincere obedience and submission to God’s command from mere attachment to former conventions.

translation: And thus We have made you a just (middle) nation so that you may be witnesses over the people and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. And We did not make the qiblah which you formerly faced except to know who would follow the Messenger and who would turn back on his heels. And indeed, it is a hard thing except for those whom Allah has guided. And Allah would not let your faith be lost; indeed Allah is Ever Kind, Merciful toward the people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Muslim community is deliberately fashioned as a balanced, moderate exemplar—neither extreme nor marginal—charged with bearing moral and spiritual testimony before humanity, while the Prophet serves as the community’s witness and standard of obedience. The change of qiblah is presented not as an arbitrary shift but as a divinely ordained test to distinguish sincere followers who remain faithful to prophetic guidance from those who retract or abandon it; the difficulty of that change is acknowledged, yet it is surmountable for those whom God guides. Ultimately the passage reassures the believers that God will not allow their commitment to be nullified—His care and mercy preserve the community’s faith and its calling to be a just, witnessing people.

translation: We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. Indeed those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.
interpretation: The verse communicates that the change of the prayer direction was a deliberate, divine measure to shape the Muslim community’s outward unity and spiritual identity: by commanding a visible, shared orientation toward the Kaʿbah, God affirms the Prophet’s guidance, restores the Abrahamic focal point of worship, and places obedience to divine ordinance above prior habits. This alteration serves as a test that differentiates genuine submission — reflected in turning the whole person toward God’s command — from mere intellectual assent: some People of the Book recognize the truth of the change yet their actions may not follow, and God’s complete knowledge of inner motives and outward deeds means that true faith is measured by sincere compliance, not just acknowledgment.

translation: And even if you were to bring to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah; nor are you a follower of their qiblah; nor is each of them a follower of another's qiblah. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse warns that changing religious practice to please others — here the People of the Book — is futile and wrong. It emphasizes that communities and individuals will not uniformly accept another's religious orientation, and that the Prophet (and believers) must not abandon revealed guidance in favor of others' desires. To follow whims or accomodate opposition after receiving clear knowledge is to commit injustice against the truth and oneself.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their own sons; yet indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know [it].
interpretation: The verse indicates that the evidence for the Prophet was present and clear in earlier revelations so that many among the People of the Book apprehended him with the same certainty and familiarity with which one knows one’s own children. That recognition, however, did not always lead to open acceptance: some deliberately hid what they knew—out of fear of losing status, worldly advantage, communal loyalties, or stubbornness—thereby turning clear knowledge into culpable concealment. The passage thus affirms prophetic continuity and condemns the moral responsibility of those who, despite being convinced, suppress the truth for partisan or self-interested reasons.

translation: The truth is from your Lord; so be not among the doubters.
interpretation: This statement affirms that the message just delivered is divinely sourced and therefore unquestionably true; it instructs the believer (and the Prophet as exemplar) to accept and act on that truth with conviction rather than hesitating, wavering, or aligning with skeptics whose doubt stems from self-deception, pride, or heedlessness.

translation: And for every community is a direction to which it turns; so vie with one another in good deeds. Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you together. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse teaches that visible differences in orientation, practice, or communal identity are part of God’s ordering of human life and do not nullify the essential test: moral striving. Rather than fixating on outward distinctions, people are called to ‘compete’ in righteousness and benevolent action, because ultimately God — who has the power to assemble everyone and hold them to account — will judge by what they did. Thus the passage redirects attention from sectarian claims about external directions to the universal responsibility to pursue good deeds everywhere, with the assurance that nothing escapes God’s power and justice.

translation: And from wherever you emerge, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. Indeed, it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The change of qibla is presented as an authoritative divine ordinance meant to orient the community both outwardly and inwardly: fixing a common direction for worship fosters unity, discipline, and visible conformity to God's will, while serving as a measure of sincerity. Calling it “the truth from your Lord” affirms the rule’s divine legitimacy; the reminder that Allah is not unaware of what you do stresses that outward acts and inward intentions are both observed and accountable, so believers must align their hearts with their visible obedience wherever they are.

translation: And from wherever you go forth, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that the people shall have no argument against you except those of them who are unjust. So do not fear them; but fear Me — and that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be rightly guided.
interpretation: The command to face the Sacred Mosque (al‑Masjid al‑Haram) universalizes and seals the Muslim community’s ritual orientation: it is a divinely instituted, unmistakable sign that removes any legitimate excuse or dispute about the direction of worship. By making the qiblah a clear, fixed point, God denies opponents a valid charge and exposes continued objection as mere injustice. The verse therefore shifts the believer’s concern from pleasing or fearing people to fearing God alone (taqwa). The promised completion of God’s favor refers to granting decisive guidance and communal identity (the confirmation of the Prophet’s mission and a distinct way of worship), and the connection to guidance shows that outward conformity to this command is linked to inner guidance and moral steadfastness. In short, the rule secures legal clarity, communal unity, and spiritual orientation toward God rather than human opinion.

translation: Just as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves who recites to you Our verses, purifies you, and teaches you the Book and wisdom, and teaches you that which you did not know.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God appointed a prophet from within the community whose mission is holistic: to transmit divine revelation, reshape moral character and social life (purification), and to convey both the scripture and its practical, ethical understanding (wisdom). By teaching what was previously unknown, the prophet replaces ignorance with authoritative guidance so the community can live by knowledge, virtue, and God’s law.

translation:
فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ وَاشْكُرُوا لِي وَلَا تَكْفُرُونَ
"So remember Me; I will remember you. Be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful to Me."
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere remembrance of God (through invocation, prayer, and continual God‑consciousness) elicits a real, reciprocal regard from Him: when believers turn to God with awareness and gratitude, God ‘remembers’ them by bestowing care, guidance, and the sustaining of their spiritual state. Gratitude (shukr) is not merely thank‑you words but a lived response—heartfelt praise, right use of blessings, and obedience—while ingratitude (kufr) is rejecting or neglecting that relationship and its obligations, which leads to loss of divine favor and spiritual decline. Thus constant remembrance coupled with grateful conduct secures God’s presence and support.

translation: O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.
interpretation: The verse directs believers to make patience (sabr) and prayer (ṣalāh) their primary means of seeking assistance. “Patience” here means steadfast endurance in the face of trials, persistence in obedience, and restraint from hasty or sinful responses; “prayer” denotes both the formal ritual worship that reorients the soul and sincere supplication that turns to God for help. Together they form an active spiritual practice: patience steadies the believer’s character while prayer opens the channel to divine support. The promise that “Allah is with the patient” reassures that God’s guidance, strength, and eventual relief accompany those who persevere and rely on Him, not as passive resignation but as faithful, sustained reliance.

translation: And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, “They are dead.” Rather they are alive, but you do not perceive it.
interpretation: The statement affirms that martyrs are not annihilated by death in the ultimate sense but continue to exist in a higher, unseen reality before God: they are honored, sustained, and receiving reward, so calling them simply ‘dead’ is a limited, worldly view that fails to grasp their ongoing spiritual life and status with Allah.

translation: And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits. And give good tidings to the patient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that hardships—fear, hunger, and losses of property, life, or provision—are divinely permitted tests intended to reveal and refine people’s faith and character. Endurance (sabr) in these trials—remaining steadfast in belief, restraining despair, continuing righteous conduct and seeking God’s help—is the proper response; such patience transforms suffering into a means of spiritual purification and elevation, and it carries God’s glad tidings of reward, mercy and ultimate success.

translation: Those who, when afflicted with a calamity, say, 'Indeed we belong to Allah and indeed to Him we will return.'
interpretation: The verse prescribes a faith-response to loss: by verbally and inwardly affirming that everything belongs to God and that our true destination is His presence, a believer reorients grief into patient submission (sabr), trust in divine wisdom, detachment from worldly attachments, and hope for God's justice and mercy—so trials become occasions for spiritual resilience and reliance on Allah rather than despair.

translation: عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ وَرَحْمَةٌ ۖ وَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ
interpretation: The phrase declares that God confers upon such people His special favor and mercy — described as 'salawāt' (divine blessings and salutations, including forgiveness and the sustaining care of the angels) and 'raḥmah' (tender mercy and protection). This bestowal is not merely a reward after death but a present spiritual reality: by accepting God's decree with faith and patience their hearts are straightened, their affairs are guided, and they are counted among the truly guided (al‑muhtadūn), whose suffering is transformed into means of nearness to God and sound guidance in life.

translation: Indeed, al‑Safa and al‑Marwa are among the rites of Allah. So whoever makes Hajj to the House or performs Umrah, there is no sin upon him in walking between them. And whoever does good of his own accord — then indeed Allah is Appreciative, All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the rites connected with al‑Safa and al‑Marwa are divinely sanctioned parts of worship, removing any social or cultural objection to performing the saʿy (walking between them) during Hajj or ʿUmrah. By saying “no sin” it emphasizes ease and permissibility rather than burden, and by adding that voluntary good deeds are noted, it encourages believers to go beyond the minimum: outward acts done in sincere intention are accepted and valued. The closing attributes — Allah is Shākir (appreciative) and ʿAlīm (all‑knowing) — reassure that God both recognizes and rewards visible deeds and knows inner intentions, so worshippers should perform prescribed rites faithfully and offer additional good deeds with trust in God’s just awareness and recompense.

translation:
إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْتُمُونَ مَا أَنْزَلْنَا مِنَ البَيِّنَاتِ وَالْهُدَىٰ مِن بَعْدِ مَا بَيَّنَّاهُ لِلنَّاسِ فِي الْكِتَابِ ۙ أُولَٰئِكَ يَلْعَنُهُمُ اللَّهُ وَيَلْعَنُهُمُ اللَّاعِنُونَ
“Indeed, those who conceal what We have revealed of clear proofs and guidance after We have made it plain for the people in the Book — those Allah curses, and (so do) those who pronounce curses (against them).”
interpretation: The verse indicts the deliberate suppression of divinely given, decisive guidance by those entrusted with knowledge. When evidence and instruction have been made explicit, hiding them is not merely an error but a breach of trust and a moral crime that merits both divine condemnation and social denunciation. The doubled curse emphasizes heightened responsibility: the clearer the revelation, the greater the obligation to transmit it; concealment for gain or to mislead multiplies culpability and brings both spiritual punishment and the righteous community’s censure.

translation: Except those who repent, reform, and make clear (their case); for those I will accept their repentance — and I am the Oft‑Returning, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God excludes from punishment those whose turning back is genuine and effective: sincere inner repentance accompanied by concrete moral reform and, where appropriate, clarification to remove doubts or harms. Repentance that remains purely verbal or private without corrective action does not fulfill the condition; true repentance manifests in rectifying past wrongs and being transparent when needed. Because God is At‑Tawwab (continually accepting repentance) and Ar‑Rahim (merciful), He promises to receive and forgive those who meet these conditions.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers—upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of all mankind.
interpretation: The verse declares that persistent rejection of God, culminating in death in that state, brings definitive and comprehensive condemnation: 'laʿna' denotes being cut off from God's favor and mercy, and the addition of the angels and all people signals both a divine-spiritual and universal moral denunciation. By specifying death in disbelief the verse emphasizes finality—one’s ultimate spiritual condition is determined at death—while the triple formula underscores the seriousness and totality of the loss suffered by those who persistently refuse guidance (a state that sincere repentance and belief before death would avert).

translation: They will abide therein; neither will the punishment be lightened for them, nor will they be granted respite.
interpretation: The verse conveys the finality and inexorability of divine punishment for those whose condition is described: for them the torment is permanent, with no mitigation and no reprieve. It underscores that divine justice, in this context, will not be relaxed or postponed — a stern warning about the consequences of persistent rejection and moral corruption, and a reminder that mercy requires turning to God rather than assuming automatic relief.

translation: And your God is One God; there is no deity except Him — the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
interpretation: The verse affirms absolute tawḥīd: God alone is the unique, incomparable Lord whose exclusive right it is to be worshiped and obeyed; invoking His names Ar‑Rahmān and Ar‑Raḥīm emphasizes that His sovereign unity is inseparable from all‑encompassing, active mercy, so faith requires both single‑minded devotion to Him and trust that His guidance and judgment flow from compassionate purpose rather than caprice.

translation: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the alternation of night and day, and in the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of people, and in what Allah has sent down from the sky of water by which He revives the earth after its death and disperses therein every living creature, and in the directing of the winds and the clouds made subservient between the sky and the earth — there are signs for a people who reason.
interpretation: The verse declares that the regularity, order, and beneficence observable in nature are deliberate signs intended to lead thoughtful people to recognize God’s existence, power, wisdom, and mercy. By pointing to cosmic design (heavens and earth), cyclical order (night and day), human-directed benefit (ships), providential sustenance (rain reviving dead land and bringing forth life), and governed forces (winds and obedient clouds), it teaches that reflection on these realities should move the intellect and conscience toward faith, gratitude, trust in divine governance, and readiness to accept moral responsibility and the reality of God’s ultimate authority.

translation: And among people are those who take, apart from Allah, equals [to Him], whom they love as they should love Allah; but those who believe are stronger in love for Allah. If only the wrongdoers could see, when they will see the punishment, that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns the displacement of God from the heart: some people attach to created beings or things the same affection and priority that belong to the Creator, effectively making partners with Him in their devotion. True faith, by contrast, produces a deeper, exclusive love for God that governs allegiance and choices. The final image — of the wrongdoers seeing the punishment and realizing that all might and authority belong to God and that His retribution is severe — is meant to awaken conscience: it warns that misplaced love has consequences and will be exposed when reality is unveiled, while also affirming God’s sole sovereignty and ultimate justice.

translation: When those who followed will disown those whom they followed, and they will see the punishment, and all means will be cut off from them.
interpretation: The verse warns that on the Day of Reckoning those who blindly followed others will reject them, realizing too late that their guides led them astray; they will witness God’s retribution and find that no alliances, excuses, or channels of help remain. It underscores individual moral responsibility — that following others does not remove one’s accountability — and the ultimate futility of relying on human patrons when facing divine judgment.

translation: And those who followed will say, “If only we had another turn, then we would disassociate ourselves from them as they have disassociated themselves from us.” Thus Allah will show them their deeds in full — and they will regret them — and they will not be able to escape the Fire.
interpretation: On the Day of Reckoning the followers of corrupt leaders will wish for a second chance to renounce those leaders, but by then Allah will make their own deeds and loyalties plain; their sudden remorse comes too late because their choices have already determined their outcome. The verse warns that following wrongdoing carries personal responsibility and that regret after the fact cannot undo the consequences decreed by divine justice.

translation: O mankind, eat of what is on the earth lawful and wholesome, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan; indeed he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse urges that the material and moral quality of what people take into their lives matters deeply: lawful (halal) and wholesome (tayyib) sustenance fosters physical health, ethical conduct, gratitude, and social justice, while what is illicit or corrupting erodes the self and community. Warning against “following the footsteps of Satan” points to a subtle, incremental strategy of temptation—rationalizations, small concessions, and imitation—that normalizes wrongdoing. Calling Satan a manifest enemy is a call to vigilance: reject the pathways and habits that lead from lawful, beneficial living into compromise and harm, and actively choose means and practices that preserve moral integrity and communal well‑being.

translation: He only commands you with evil and indecency and that you should say about Allah what you do not know.
interpretation: The verse warns that certain guides or impulses—whether satanic suggestions, ignorant leaders, or social pressures—direct people toward immoral behavior and toward asserting things about God without knowledge. Such guidance corrupts both conduct and creed: it normalizes wrongdoing and manufactures false doctrines by encouraging speech about God that is not grounded in revelation or sound understanding. The implication for the believer is clear: reject counsel that promotes sin or unfounded claims about the Divine, seek knowledge before speaking of religious matters, and measure claims by the Qur’an and trustworthy guidance, for one who ascribes to God what one does not know commits a grave moral and theological error and will be held accountable.

translation: And when it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they say, “Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon.” Even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?
interpretation: The verse criticizes the attitude of clinging to ancestral customs as an excuse to reject divine guidance: it condemns prioritizing inherited tradition over what God has revealed, especially when those predecessors lacked sound understanding and guidance. The underlying lesson is that truth must be judged by revelation and reason, not preserved by unexamined loyalty to forebears, because such blind imitation perpetuates error and bars people from guidance.

translation: The example of those who disbelieve is like one who calls out to something that hears nothing but cries and calls — deaf, dumb, and blind; so they do not understand.
interpretation: The verse uses a vivid simile to show that disbelievers are like people who address something incapable of hearing or responding (whether idols, vain pursuits, or hearts closed to truth). Being described as deaf, dumb, and blind emphasizes their inability or refusal to perceive guidance and reason: their words and objections are futile because they cannot apprehend or accept the reality being presented to them.

translation: O you who have believed, eat of the good things with which We have provided you and be grateful to Allah, if you truly worship Him.
interpretation: Believers are enjoined to enjoy what God has lawfully and wholesomely provided, and to let that provision awaken sincere gratitude that goes beyond words: recognizing God as the Source, using blessings in ways that please Him (lawful, generous, and ethical conduct), and expressing thanks through obedience, remembrance, and charity; such thankful living is the practical proof of genuine worship.

translation: He has only forbidden to you dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither seeking it nor transgressing limits, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes both a firm moral-legal boundary and a principle of compassionate exception: certain foods are prohibited because they are impure or linked to devotion to other than God, protecting spiritual and communal integrity; yet the law is not absolutist — when a person faces true necessity (threat to life or survival) and does not take the forbidden thing out of desire or to flaunt disobedience, the burden of prohibition is lifted and no blame attaches. By coupling the concession with conditions (no desire, no transgression) the verse prevents abuse of necessity as an excuse, and by ending with “Allah is Forgiving, Merciful” it reminds believers that divine law aims at preservation of life and conscience, balancing duty with mercy.

translation: Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book and exchange it for a small price — they consume nothing but fire in their bellies. And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them; and they will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse condemns the deliberate concealment, suppression, alteration, or misrepresentation of divine guidance for worldly gain or advantage. Those who do so betray the trust of revelation: their reward is inner corruption and torment (described as fire in their bellies), spiritual exclusion from Allah’s favor (symbolized by His silence toward them on the Day of Resurrection and the withholding of purification), and ultimately a severe and painful punishment. The warning emphasizes both moral responsibility to transmit truth and the grave consequences of sacrificing spiritual integrity for trivial worldly benefits.

translation: Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance and punishment in exchange for forgiveness — how impatient they are for the Fire!
interpretation: The verse castigates people who, by deliberate choice, trade the true path for falsehood and spurn God's mercy in favor of deeds that bring retribution. The commercial imagery of ‘buying’ stresses responsibility and intent: they knowingly prefer what destroys them. The final exclamation — ‘how impatient they are for the Fire’ — is rhetorical, condemning their haste toward self-inflicted ruin and underscoring that rejecting guidance and mercy leads inevitably to deserved punishment.

translation: ذلك بأن الله نزل الكتاب بالحق ۗ وإن الذين اختلفوا في الكتاب لفي شقاق بعيد
interpretation: الله يؤكد أن الكتب السماوية أُنزلت بالحق كمصدر واضح للهدى والبيان؛ ومن يخوض في الاختلاف حول مقاصدها وأصولها—بالتشدد في التمترس بطوائف أو الأهواء أو بتأويلات متعارضة—يكونون قد وقعوا في شقاق عميق يبعدهم عن وحدة الهدى وصدق المقصد الإلهي، فالتنازع هنا ليست مجرد خلافات فكرية بل انقسام يخرج عن مسار الحق ويؤدي إلى التشتت والضلال.

translation: Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the East or the West, but truly righteous is he who believes in Allah and the Last Day and the angels and the Book and the prophets, and gives his wealth, despite his love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, those who ask, and for freeing slaves; and establishes prayer and gives zakah; and fulfills his covenant when he makes one; and is patient in poverty and hardship and at the time of conflict. Those are the ones who have been sincere, and it is they who are the God‑fearing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true piety is not mere external ritual or orientational acts, but a truthful inner conviction manifested in concrete ethical conduct: firm belief in God’s reality and the revealed order, readiness to sacrifice material attachment for the needy (starting with kin and extending to strangers and captives), fulfillment of communal duties (prayer, zakah), trustworthiness in covenants, and steadfast patience under trials. In short, authentic faith is measured by moral responsibility, social justice, and steadfastness, not by outward postures alone.

translation: O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retaliation (qisas) in the matter of the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother anything, then [let there be] follow-up with equitable conduct and payment to him with goodly conduct. That is a mitigation from your Lord and a mercy. But whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of proportionate, legally regulated retribution to protect human life and prevent cycles of private vengeance: equality of status in ruling (free for free, slave for slave, female for female) sets the measure for qisas or its equivalent. At the same time it elevates mercy and social reconciliation by permitting pardon or acceptance of compensation (diyah), encouraging the injured party to forgive or receive payment done in good faith and kindness. Declaring this arrangement a mitigation and mercy shows that God’s law limits blood feuds and offers a path from strict justice toward compassion; but it also warns that anyone who exceeds the permitted bounds after pardon or who wrongfully takes revenge will incur a severe divine punishment.

translation: And there is for you in retribution (al‑qisas) life, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous (attain taqwa).
interpretation: The verse affirms that a system of measured, proportional legal retaliation preserves life and social order by preventing unbounded private vengeance: by limiting responses to what is just and prescribed, it protects human dignity, deters escalation of blood‑feuds, and trains the sensible to accept lawful justice as a means to cultivate God‑consciousness and restraint.

translation:
كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَكُمُ الْمَوْتُ إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا الْوَصِيَّةُ لِلْوَالِدَيْنِ وَالْأَقْرَبِينَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ حَقًّا عَلَى الْمُتَّقِينَ

"It is ordained for you—that when death comes to any of you, if he leaves any wealth, he should make a bequest to parents and close relatives in a fair and proper manner; this is a duty incumbent on the God‑conscious."
interpretation: The verse teaches that arranging one’s posthumous distribution of wealth with justice toward parents and near kin is not merely a private choice but a moral duty linked to piety. By requiring the bequest to be done “bi‑l‑maʿrūf” (in a known, rightful way), the text binds testamentary acts to fairness, social norms and the protection of vulnerable rights, so that property does not become a source of injustice or family discord. In short, planning one’s estate with equity and consideration for close relatives is presented as an outward sign and obligation of God‑consciousness.

translation: So whoever changes it after he has heard it — then the sin is only upon those who change it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that responsibility for distorting or replacing a divinely given judgment, message, or ruling lies with those who effect the change (and with those who coerce or persuade the changer), rather than with the original revelation or its rightful conveyer; Allah, who hears all speech and knows all inward motives, will hold the corrupters answerable.

translation: So whoever fears from his spouse injustice or estrangement, and reconciles between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse permits and even encourages tranquil reconciliation when one fears injustice, ill-treatment, or moral failure in a close relationship: taking steps to restore harmony and settle disputes removes blame, because preserving family unity and preventing greater harm is prioritized. It affirms that sincere efforts to make amends are acceptable before God, who is merciful and ready to forgive human shortcomings when people seek peaceful resolution.

translation: O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may attain God-consciousness (taqwa).
interpretation: The verse makes clear that fasting is not merely a ritual obligation but a purposeful spiritual discipline given across prophetic communities to shape character: by voluntarily restraining the body and its desires, a believer cultivates vigilance before God, moral self-control, empathy for the hungry and needy, and readiness to obey divine commands. In this reading, the institution of fasting functions primarily as a means of internal transformation—training habits of restraint and compassion so that outward practice becomes the foundation for enduring piety and social responsibility.

translation: [Fasting is prescribed] for a limited number of days. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey — then an equal number of days [are to be made up]. And for those who find it difficult (to fast) there is a ransom: feeding a poor person. But whoever does good voluntarily, it is better for him. And if you only knew, fasting is better for you.
interpretation: The verse expresses a law grounded in mercy and purpose: obligations are bounded and adapted to human capacity, and when strict observance would cause real hardship, the community is asked to preserve dignity by providing a humane substitute. Beyond legal flexibility, the text elevates voluntary excellence — extra acts of goodness are preferred to mere minimal compliance — and it points to the deeper aim of the practice: fasting is not only a physical ritual but a training of the soul that brings real benefit (self-discipline, heightened God‑consciousness, and solidarity with the needy). The qualification “if you only knew” invites reflection: the rule exists to shape character and social justice, not to impose needless burden.

translation: The month of Ramadan in which the Qur’an was revealed — a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion. So whoever of you is present in the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey — then an equal number of other days. Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship, and (He desires) that you complete the period and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse presents Ramadan as a concentrated time for internalizing the Qur’anic guidance: the fast is not an end in itself but a disciplined means to make the Qur’an’s light and the moral distinctions it brings real in the believer’s life. The allowance for the sick and travelers shows that the law is guided by mercy and practicality — God’s purpose is facilitation of spiritual growth, not undue burden. Completing the prescribed days and proclaiming God’s guidance through that practice cultivates humility, communal cohesion, and a grateful disposition that aligns one’s behavior with the ethical and spiritual truths revealed in the Qur’an.

translation: And when My servants ask you about Me — surely I am near. I answer the prayer of the one who calls upon Me; so let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that they may be guided.
interpretation: God is assuring that He is intimately close and attentive to His servants: when they sincerely call, He hears and answers. This nearness requires a reciprocal response — not merely uttering words, but turning in trust, obedience and faith toward God — and that turning is the means by which people receive guidance and are rightly led.

translation: It has been made permissible for you the night preceding the fast to have relations with your wives. They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them. Allah knows that you used to betray yourselves, so He turned to you in mercy and forgave you; so now have relations with them and seek that which Allah has decreed for you. And eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread of night; then complete the fast until night. And do not have relations with them while you are in iʿtikāf (seclusion) in the mosques. These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them. Thus Allah makes His ordinances clear to the people that they may become righteous.
interpretation: This verse balances God’s solemn demands with human reality: it legitimizes lawful spousal intimacy during the nights of Ramadan while imposing clear temporal and situational limits so that worship and discipline remain intact. Calling spouses “clothing” emphasizes mutual dignity, protection, closeness, and reciprocal rights rather than mere permission; the reminder that God knew of past lapses and accepted repentance shows divine mercy and the possibility of moral renewal. The instruction to stop at the first light teaches disciplined obedience to divinely appointed boundaries (a visible sign rather than speculative timing), and the prohibition during mosque seclusion underscores sanctity and respect for special forms of worship. Taken together, the verse instructs believers to integrate natural needs and marital rights into a framework of conscious obedience, so that lawful ease does not erode spiritual purpose and people grow in God-consciousness (taqwa).

translation: And do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor present it [as a bribe] to the rulers so that you may consume a portion of the people’s wealth sinfully while you know [it is wrong].
interpretation: The verse forbids not only direct theft or fraudulent appropriation of others’ property but also using corruption—paying off or influencing judges and officials—to obtain someone else’s wealth. It condemns both the active taking and the facilitation of unjust decisions: deliberately manipulating institutions for personal gain makes one complicit in systemic injustice. The clause “and you know” intensifies the reproach, stressing moral culpability when people consciously exploit or enable corruption rather than seeking justice and fair redress.

translation: They ask you about the new moons. Say: “They are fixed times for the people and for pilgrimage.” And righteousness is not that you enter houses by their backs; but righteousness is the one who is conscious of Allah. And enter the houses by their doors. And fear Allah that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine ordinances (like the lunar signs) exist to organize communal worship and lawful practice, and it warns against exploiting legal technicalities or secretive, improper conduct as if that were piety. The image of entering houses by their backs vs. using their doors contrasts illicit, shameful shortcuts with lawful, honorable behavior; true righteousness is rooted in God‑consciousness and outwardly expressed by respectful, lawful actions. Thus religious observance must unite correct external conduct with sincere inner fear of God, for success lies in both.

translation: Fight in the cause of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors.
interpretation: The verse confines legitimate combat to defensive response against those who attack, and places a moral and legal limit on conduct in war: one must not exceed proportional bounds, target innocents, or use fighting as a pretext for aggression. It teaches that warfare, even when necessary, must be governed by restraint, justice, and obedience to God’s ethical limits—because God condemns those who overstep and commit transgression.

translation: واقتلوهم حيث ثقفتموهم وأخرجوهم من حيث أخرجوكم ۚ والفتنة أشد من القتل ۚ ولا تقاتلوهم عند المسجد الحرام حتى يقاتلوكم فيه ۖ فإن قاتلوكم فاقتلوهم ۗ كذلك جزاء الكافرين
interpretation: This verse grants permission for armed resistance against those who wage aggression and persecute the Muslim community: the injunction to “kill them wherever you overtake them” is directed at hostile combatants in the context of warfare and expulsion, not at innocent civilians or as a licence for random violence. It stresses that severe persecution and attempts to force people from their faith or homes (fitnah) can be a harm graver than death and therefore may justify defensive military measures, while also protecting specific sanctities—prohibiting fighting in the Sacred Mosque unless the enemy initiates combat there. In short, the verse should be read as a conditional, wartime ruling that permits proportionate self‑defense against aggressors who violate treaties and persecute believers, bounded by limits (no transgression, protection of sanctuaries, and concern for noncombatants) rather than as a general command to kill.

translation: But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This phrase teaches that the halting of sinful or hostile behavior opens the door to Divine pardon: when people cease their wrongdoing and turn away from it, God’s posture is not perpetual punishment but readiness to forgive and show mercy. It carries both a moral injunction—to accept reconciliation and allow reformation rather than insist on continued retaliation—and a theological principle that repentance and change can restore one to God’s favor.

translation: And fight them until there is no more fitnah and the religion is entirely for Allah. But if they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse confines legitimate use of force to the removal of persecution, coercion, or destructive disorder (fitnah) so that people may freely worship and live under God’s authority; it is not a license for indefinite or expansionist violence. “Fitnah” here means persecution, forced suppression of belief, or destabilizing oppression, and “the religion is for Allah” points to freedom of conscience and rightful submission to God alone. When opponents stop persecuting and cease hostilities, fighting must stop—any further force is only lawful against those who persist in wrongdoing or aggression. In short, the verse frames warfare as defensive, restorative, and morally limited, forbidding transgression and emphasizing restraint.

translation: الشهر الحرام بالشهر الحرام والحرمات قصاص ۚ فمن اعتدى عليكم فاعتدوا عليه بمثل ما اعتدى عليكم ۚ واتقوا الله واعلموا أن الله مع المتقين
interpretation: الآية تأمر برد العدوان بالمثل ضمن ضوابط محددة: تحمي حرمة الأشهر والمواضع المقدسة وتبيّن أن المقابلة تكون قِصاصًا مساويًا لما وقع عليكم لا تعدّياً أو إفراطًا. مقصودها إقامة العدل وردع المعتدين بإعادة الحق إليهم بمقدار ما أخذوه، مع تذكير بوجوب تقوى الله وضبط النفس كي لا يتحوّل الرد إلى ظلم، لأن الله مع الذين يتقون ويعملون بالضوابط الإلهية.

translation: And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw [yourselves] with your own hands into destruction; and do good—indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to use their resources and efforts for God‑pleasing causes (charity, support for the community, and righteous struggle) while warning that selfishness, negligence of duty, or extreme measures that harm oneself or the community lead to ruin. It further requires that giving and actions be done with ihsan—excellence, justice, and kindness—because God loves those who act well and with benevolent intention.

translation: And complete the Hajj and ʿumrah for the sake of Allah. But if you are prevented (from completing them), then [offer] whatever is easy of sacrifice. And do not shave your heads until the sacrifice reaches its place. And whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head—then there is a ransom: fasting or charity or sacrifice. And when you are secure, then whoever performs ʿumrah followed by Hajj (tamattuʿ) — [let him offer] whatever is easy of sacrifice. And whoever cannot find [a sacrifice], then a fast of three days during Hajj and seven when you have returned home—ten days in all. That is for those whose families are not present at the Sacred Mosque. And fear Allah and know that Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes both the sanctity of completing pilgrimage rites for God and the legal principle of mercy and flexibility in worship. It stresses that Hajj and ʿumrah must be offered with sincerity, yet recognises real impediments—illness, harm, being prevented, or inability to procure a sacrificial animal—and provides prescribed compensations (fasting, charity, or a lesser sacrifice) so that obligation does not become an unmanageable hardship. The injunction not to shave until the sacrifice reaches its place preserves the sequence and communal reality of the ritual. The rule for tamattuʿ (performing ʿumrah then Hajj) and the ten-day fast for those unable to offer a sacrifice show that the law accommodates different personal and logistical circumstances while maintaining a framework of accountability. By concluding with the warning to fear God and His severe punishment, the verse ties legal concessions to moral seriousness: ease is granted, but worship must still be undertaken responsibly and reverently.

translation: Hajj is in well-known months. So whoever has made Hajj obligatory upon himself therein, there shall be no obscenity, nor wickedness, nor disputing during Hajj. And whatever good you do, Allah knows it. And take provision, but the best provision is piety. So fear Me, O people of understanding.
interpretation: The verse frames Hajj not merely as a ritual itinerary but as entry into a sanctified temporal and social order: because these months are set apart, pilgrims must suspend base desires, sinful conduct and contentiousness so that the pilgrimage’s purpose—inner purification, communal harmony and sincere worship—can be achieved. The reminder that Allah knows every good deed calls for sincerity rather than ostentation. ‘Take provisions’ acknowledges practical preparedness, yet immediately elevates taqwa as the supreme provision that sustains a traveller spiritually and morally. The closing address to the discerning is a challenge to internalize this balance—prepare outwardly, restrain impulses, cultivate God-consciousness—and so make the pilgrimage (and by extension all sacred practice) transform the heart and the community.

translation: There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord. Then when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at the Sacred Monument; and remember Him as He has guided you, for indeed you were before that among those astray.
interpretation: The verse teaches a balanced approach: permissible, lawful personal needs and gains may be pursued even during sacred rites (there is no sin in seeking your Lord’s bounty), but this must not displace the central duty of conscious remembrance of God. After leaving Arafat the pilgrim should renew sincere invocation at the designated sacred place, carrying out remembrance in the spirit of the guidance they have received—with gratitude, humility, and obedience—since before that guidance they were astray. In short, lawful worldly affairs are allowed, yet worship must be sincere and transformative, reflecting the moral change brought by God's guidance.

translation: Then depart from where the people depart, and ask forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse links an external, communal movement with an inner spiritual task: obedience to the organized, divinely guided sequence of worship should be accompanied by sincere repentance. It teaches that ritual compliance alone is incomplete without turning the heart to God; the promise that “Allah is Forgiving, Merciful” reassures believers that when they leave worldly attachments and submit to the prescribed order while seeking forgiveness, their repentance will be met with mercy and spiritual renewal.

translation: So when you have finished your rites, remember Allah as you remember your forefathers, or with even greater remembrance. And among people are those who say, “Our Lord, give us in this world,” and they will have no portion in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true worship does not end with ritual actions; believers must carry a sustained, heartfelt awareness of God after completing rites—surpassing mere ancestral habit or formality. It also warns that making worldly gain the sole aim (asking only for provisions of this life) severs a person’s tie to the Hereafter: such single-minded attachment to the temporal results in forfeiting the enduring share and rewards to come. The exhortation, therefore, is to orient remembrance and supplication toward what endures, balancing legitimate needs in this world with ultimate concern for the next.

translation: And among them are those who say, “Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good, and in the Hereafter that which is good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.”
interpretation: This verse presents a concise model supplication that teaches a balanced, comprehensive outlook: asking for 'good' (hasanah) in the worldly life and in the Hereafter recognizes that legitimate material, moral, and spiritual well‑being are all desirable, while prioritizing ultimate salvation by explicitly seeking protection from the Fire. It counsels that one’s pursuit of worldly benefits should be lawful and oriented toward the Hereafter, and it expresses humble dependence on God’s mercy for both present needs and final deliverance—combining moderate engagement with the world, moral responsibility, and ultimate concern for eternal fate.

translation: Those — for them is a share of what they have earned; and Allah is swift in reckoning.
