interpretation: The verse warns that every person receives exactly what their deeds merit — whether benefit or retribution — and that God will promptly and precisely settle accounts. “A share of what they have earned” stresses personal responsibility (no one is credited or punished unjustly for another’s deeds), while “God is swift in reckoning” removes any illusion of escaping justice: consequences can follow quickly in this life or will be decisively applied in the Hereafter, so one must act with moral seriousness and heed the accountability that follows every choice.

translation: And remember Allah during the appointed days. So whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him; and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him — for him who fears Allah. And fear Allah and know that you will be gathered to Him.
interpretation: The verse instructs that during the specified sacred days (understood classically as the days of Tashrīq in the pilgrimage season) the primary duty is the remembrance of God, and it grants practical flexibility about a pilgrim’s timing: leaving earlier or staying longer is not sinful provided the person’s conduct is rooted in God‑consciousness. Thus the injunction emphasizes that outward ritual timing is subordinate to sincere piety — the rites are accommodated for those who are mindful of Allah — and closes with a reminder that reverent fear of God and awareness of being ultimately gathered to Him should be the motivating reality behind all observance.

translation: And of the people is he whose speech in the life of this world pleases you, and he calls upon Allah to witness to what is in his heart, while he is the fiercest of opponents.
interpretation: The verse cautions against those who use attractive, worldly rhetoric and even invoke God as a guarantor, yet are inwardly insincere and highly contentious; it teaches that eloquent words and solemn oaths can be tools of deception, and that true character is revealed by consistent conduct and whether one promotes truth or sows dispute for personal ends.

translation: And when he turns away, he strives throughout the earth to cause corruption in it and to destroy crops and offspring. And Allah does not love corruption.
interpretation: This verse characterizes a person who, once freed from restraint or given influence, deliberately works to undermine the common good — whether by literal destruction of land and lineage or by sowing moral, social and economic ruin. “Destroying the harvest and offspring” pictures the annihilation of people’s means of livelihood and their future generations, i.e., attacking what sustains a community. The warning that God does not love corruption emphasizes the severe moral culpability of such behavior and implies that believers must resist and rectify actions that erode society’s welfare and continuity.

translation: And when it is said to him, “Fear Allah,” pride in sin seizes him. Hell will suffice for him — and wretched is the resting-place.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a spiritual pathology: when a person’s self-exaltation is sustained by transgression, admonition to God‑consciousness becomes intolerable and repentance is blocked. That arrogant clinging to sin turns admonition into offense and seals his outcome — Hell is described both as his deserved recompense and the miserable refuge he chooses by refusing humility. The real warning is moral and psychological: arrogance that justifies wrongdoing prevents reform, and only humility before God and acceptance of correction can avert the dire consequence described.

translation: And of the people is he who sells his soul seeking the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is Kind to the servants.
interpretation: The phrase “sells his soul” depicts voluntary, wholehearted self-sacrifice — giving up one’s comfort, rights, reputation, even life — not for fame or worldly return but solely to attain God’s approval. The verse honors such sincere devotion and reassures that Allah, being rā’ūf (tenderly compassionate), recognizes that inner intention, protects and treats these servants with mercy, and grants them what they seek in a manner wiser and kinder than human understanding.

translation: O you who have believed, enter into peace completely and do not follow the footsteps of Satan; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to embrace wholehearted submission to God — a complete turning of heart, conduct, and communal life toward divine guidance so that true peace (silm/islam) prevails. It warns that Satan works by gradual, deceptive steps: small doubts, compromises, and divisions that seem trivial at first but lead away from obedience and unity. By naming him a manifest enemy, the verse urges constant vigilance, immediate rejection of alluring impulses that compromise faith or social harmony, and a deliberate choice of God’s path in every sphere of life.

translation:
فإن زللتم من بعد ما جاءتكم البينات فاعلموا أن الله عزيز حكيم
"So if you go astray after clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty, Wise."
interpretation: This is a warning: turning away or persisting in error after having received unmistakable guidance does not leave one outside God’s power or beyond His wise judgment. Allah’s might means He is fully able to hold people to account and to bring about consequences or correction; His wisdom means that whatever form those consequences take — immediate punishment, delayed retribution, tests, or allowing events to unfold — is just and purposeful. Thus the verse urges sober awareness that rejection of clear truth will meet the fully capable and wise decree of God, not neglect or arbitrary harm.

translation: هل ينتظرون إلا أن يأتيهم الله في ظلل من الغمام ومعه الملائكة ويحكم الأمر؟ وإلى الله تُرجَع الأمور.
interpretation: الآية تُوجه توبيخًا لمن يؤخرون الإيمان أو الطاعة انتظارًا لظهور معجزة ظاهرة أو تدخّل كوني — أن يأتي الله في ظلل من الغمام مع الملائكة ويُقضى الأمر — وتذكّرهم أن السلطان والفصل في كل الأمور بيد الله وحده، وأن الجزاء والحساب والقرارات النهائية تعود إليه، فلا يجوز التراخي أو المماطلة بانتظار منظر خارق قبل الخضوع والالتزام.

translation: Ask the Children of Israel, how many clear signs We gave them. And whoever exchanges the favor of Allah after it has come to him—then indeed Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that receiving unmistakable signs and blessings from God creates an obligation: to accept, preserve and be grateful for His guidance. “Exchanging Allah’s favor” means turning that blessing into ingratitude, denial, distortion, or trading divine guidance for worldly advantage or falsehood. Those who, after being given clear proof, willfully reject or corrupt what they were entrusted with expose themselves to severe divine accountability; the passage thus stresses responsibility, constancy in faith, and the moral danger of repudiating a gift that carried both guidance and duty.

translation: The enjoyment of the life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe. But those who are God-fearing will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah provides for whom He wills without measure.
interpretation: The verse warns that unbelievers are often captivated by and proud of worldly comforts and use those transient advantages to ridicule the faithful; this apparent superiority is temporary and deceptive. True and lasting elevation belongs to the muttaqīn (those who cultivate God-consciousness and righteousness), who will stand in honor above the mockers on the Day of Reckoning. The final clause reminds the reader that provision and bestowal are ultimately in Allah’s hands—He grants sustenance, status, or spiritual bounty to whom He wills without being constrained by human calculations—so one should not be swayed by present mockery but remain mindful of God, seeking His pleasure rather than fleeting worldly applause.

translation: Mankind was [of] one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and He sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between the people concerning that in which they differed. And none differed about it except those to whom it had been given — after the clear proofs came to them — out of mutual envy. Then Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that in which they had differed, by His permission. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human beings share a single primordial orientation toward God and moral order, and when divergence occurred God sent prophets and revealed scriptures to settle disputes and restore guidance. The statement that only those “to whom it had been given” differed — despite clear evidence — points to a moral diagnosis: the rejection or distortion of guidance by some who had prior religious authority arose from envy, partisan interest or attachment to power rather than from lack of evidence. The clause that God then guided the believers to the truth by His permission emphasizes that true resolution of theological and legal disagreement depends on receptivity and sincere submission to the evidence brought by the messengers; divine guidance operates through the teachings and signs God sends but is realized in hearts willing to accept them. The practical lesson is to judge disputes by revealed truth, beware of allowing faction, envy, or tradition to override clear proof, and recognize that guidance ultimately rests with God while human responsibility is to respond honestly to what has been shown.

translation: Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the like of those who passed away before you had not yet come upon you? They were touched by hardship and affliction and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, “When will the help of Allah come?” — Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.
interpretation: The verse teaches that spiritual success and God’s promised reward are not instantaneous or free of trial. It reminds believers that former communities endured severe tests — poverty, suffering and upheaval — which exposed and purified their faith; even the Prophet and his companions felt the strain and cried for divine aid. Far from being a sign of failure, such trials are part of the path: they reveal sincerity, require patience and steadfastness, and prepare people for eventual deliverance. The assurance “Allah’s help is near” turns anxiety into persevering trust: continue to resist, remain obedient and united in the struggle, because relief and victory come after testing and are close at hand.

translation: They ask you what they should spend. Say, “Whatever good you spend is for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor and the wayfarer.” And whatever good you do, Allah is Knowing of it.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when people ask about proper spending, the Prophet is to affirm a broad, humane priority: charity and lawful expenditures directed first to parents and close kin (fulfilling family responsibility and ties), and also to vulnerable groups—orphans, the needy, and travelers. It makes clear that ‘good’ spending is not narrowly confined to ritual dues but includes any sincere, beneficial outlay on these deserving categories, and that such acts are observed and accounted for by God. The ruling both legitimizes support of one’s family and obliges care for wider social weakness, while reminding believers that intention and God’s knowledge of their good deeds determine their moral and spiritual value.

translation:
كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِتَالُ وَهُوَ كَرْهٌ لَّكُمْ ۖ وَعَسَىٰ أَن تَكْرَهُوا شَيْئًا وَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ ۖ وَعَسَىٰ أَن تُحِبُّوا شَيْئًا وَهُوَ شَرٌّ لَّكُمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَأَنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. Perhaps you dislike something and it is good for you; and perhaps you love something and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you do not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches a general moral and theological principle: God may command difficult or unpleasant duties because they serve a greater wisdom beyond our sight. Human tastes and immediate feelings can mislead; what we shun may be beneficial for the community or for our spiritual good, and what we desire may bring harm. Therefore believers must recognize the limits of their knowledge, submit to divinely ordained responsibilities when legitimately prescribed, and trust in God’s wisdom while exercising the moral care and restraint He prescribes.

translation: They ask you about fighting in the Sacred Month. Say, “Fighting in it is a grave matter, but turning people away from the way of Allah, rejecting Him, expelling people from al‑Masjid al‑Harâm and barring them from it, are greater in the sight of Allah; and persecution (fitnah) is worse than killing.” They will keep fighting you until they turn you back from your religion if they can. And whoever of you renounces his religion and dies as a disbeliever—those, their deeds are nullified in this world and the Hereafter; they are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein.
interpretation: The verse sets a moral and legal hierarchy: although fighting during the sacred months is a serious matter, a graver injustice is to prevent people’s access to God—through disbelief, persecution, or the forcible expulsion from a sanctuary. “Fitnah” here denotes the broader corruption and coercion that destroys faith and community more surely than killing does. Thus defensive resistance against those who would bar worship, persecute the faithful, or force apostasy is justified because it prevents a greater evil. The passage also warns that the opponents’ aim is not merely battle but to uproot faith, and it sternly reminds believers that abandoning one’s faith with death in disbelief voids one’s deeds and leads to eternal loss. The practical lesson: preserve the integrity of worship and community even when rules about sanctity are at stake, resist coercion that would extinguish belief, and recognize that inner faith—not merely outward acts—determines ultimate consequence.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and those who emigrate and strive in the cause of Allah — those expect the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine faith is shown by inner conviction and by concrete sacrifices — leaving harmful surroundings (hijrah) and struggling for God’s cause. Such integrated commitment grounds a legitimate hope in God’s mercy: Divine compassion is the proper expectation for those who sincerely believe and act, not despair or fear of inevitable punishment. By naming God “Forgiving, Merciful” the verse reassures the believer that human failings amid effort do not bar God’s pardon; it calls for steadfastness and courageous action while relying on Allah’s mercy rather than presuming automatic reward or condemning oneself for imperfections.

translation: They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: “In them is great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.” They ask you what they should spend. Say: “That which is surplus (beyond your needs).” Thus Allah makes His signs clear to you so that you may reflect.
interpretation: The verse teaches a principle of moral weighting and practical prudence: when a permitted thing carries both benefit and harm, the community should abandon it if the harm outweighs the benefit; likewise, charitable giving should be prudent—given from what remains after legitimate needs (al‑‘afw), not by impoverishing one’s household—so social welfare and individual responsibility are balanced. The closing clause reminds believers that such rulings are meant to guide thoughtful reflection, not blind imitation.

translation: في الدنيا والآخرة. ويسألونك عن اليتامى، قل: إصلاح لهم خير. وإن تخالطوهم فإخوانكم. والله يعلم المفسد من المصلح. ولو شاء الله لأعنتكم. إن الله عزيز حكيم.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد واجب رعاية الأيتام وإصلاح شأنهم كخيار أخلاقي أوليّ، وتحث على إدماجهم ومعاملتهم كإخوة ليزول عنهم وصمة التبعية والاستغلال. كما تذكّر بأن الله وحده يميز بين من ينوي الإصلاح ومن يفسد، فالقوامة والوصاية تتطلب صدق النية وأمانة في العمل. وعبارة أن الله لو شاء لأعنتكم تذكّر بسيادة الله وقدرته وأن عدم تحويل الإنسان إلى عالة هو ابتلاء ومسؤولية؛ لذلك يُحمَّل القادرون واجب العدل والإحسان تجاه اليتيم، لأن ذلك خضوع لحكمة الله ومشيئته، لا مجرد عرف اجتماعي.

translation: And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe. A believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist, even if she pleases you. And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe. A believing slave is better than a polytheist, even if he pleases you. Those (people) invite to the Fire, while Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness by His permission; and He makes His signs clear to the people so that they may take heed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith is the essential criterion in choosing a spouse: a partner who shares and upholds Islam is spiritually and morally preferable to one who does not, regardless of social status, beauty, or worldly attractions. Marrying someone who rejects the faith risks undermining religious practice and leading both partners away from God’s guidance — metaphorically “inviting to the Fire” — whereas God’s invitation through faith leads to Paradise and forgiveness. The passage therefore prioritizes spiritual compatibility and the long-term religious well‑being of the family, and reminds people that God has revealed clear signs so they can reflect and choose rightly.

translation: And they ask you about menstruation. Say: It is harm; so keep away from women during menstruation and do not approach them until they are purified. And when they are purified, then come to them from where Allah has commanded you. Indeed, Allah loves those who turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.
interpretation: This verse instructs believers to refrain from sexual intercourse with women during their menstrual bleeding out of regard for the physical harm and ritual impurity associated with that time. The command to “keep away” and “not approach” preserves women’s bodily integrity and recognizes menstruation as a period that requires distance until the bleeding ends and the woman performs the prescribed purification (ghusl). Once purification is complete, relations may resume “from where Allah has commanded” — i.e., within the lawful, respectful bounds of marital intimacy. The closing clause links this practical ruling to a moral principle: God values both sincere return to Him (repentance) and the maintenance of purity — physical, ritual, and by extension moral — so obedience to these limits is part of spiritual as well as bodily cleanliness.

translation: Your wives are a field for you; so go to your field how and when you wish. And put forward (good) for yourselves; and fear Allah and know that you will meet Him; and give glad tidings to the believers.
interpretation: By likening wives to a cultivated field the verse affirms that lawful marital intimacy is permitted and flexible in manner and timing, but it immediately frames that permission within ethical responsibility: act with God‑consciousness, treat your spouse with care, and live so as to ‘send ahead’ good deeds that will benefit you on the Day you meet Allah. The promise of glad tidings reassures the believers that chastity, faithfulness, and mindful conduct within marriage are integral to one’s moral account and ultimate reward.

translation: Do not make Allah an excuse with your oaths — claiming thereby to be righteous, God-fearing, or to reconcile among people. And Allah is All‑Hearing, All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse warns against invoking God’s name or swearing oaths as a cover or tool to avoid real responsibility or to manufacture a show of piety. Using vows to justify hypocrisy, to dodge duties, or to pretend to bring about reconciliation without sincere effort is condemned; inward intention and actual conduct matter, because Allah hears all and knows what is truly in the heart.

translation: Allah does not take you to task for what is said thoughtlessly in your oaths, but He takes you to task for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that moral and legal responsibility is rooted in inner intent rather than careless words: God will not punish involuntary or idle utterances in oaths, but He will hold people accountable for the deliberate convictions, inclinations, and choices of the heart that lead to actions. The attributes “Forgiving, Forbearing” indicate God’s mercy and patience toward slips and provide scope for repentance, while warning that hidden, persistent malice or resolved intentions will be judged.

translation: For those who pronounce ‘ila’ (an oath of abstention) upon their wives, the waiting period is four months; then if they return [to them], then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse limits and regulates the husband’s practice of declaring total abstention from his wife (ilaʾ) by fixing a definite maximum waiting period of four months, thereby preventing indefinite suspension of marital relations as a means of coercion or punishment; it also makes clear that if the husband retracts the abstention and resumes the marriage bond, this return is permissible and met with God’s forgiveness and mercy, thus encouraging reconciliation and protecting the wife’s rights within the marriage.

translation: And if they decide on divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse underscores that when spouses reach the decisive moment of separating, their words, intentions, and inner struggles are fully within God’s awareness. It serves both as reassurance to those who suffer—that their pleas, pain, and repentance are heard by a compassionate Lord—and as a warning that no hidden motives or injustices escape divine knowledge. Therefore such grave decisions must be approached with humility, justice, and consciousness of accountability before God.

translation: Divorced women shall wait concerning themselves for three menstrual periods. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands have the better right to take them back in that (period) if they intend reconciliation. And for women is a like right to what is owed to them, according to what is equitable; but men have a degree over them. And Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.
interpretation: The verse prescribes the iddah (three menstrual cycles) to protect lineage, clarify paternity and preserve the rights and responsibilities that follow from pregnancy; prohibiting concealment of pregnancy prevents injustice to children, mothers and potential fathers. Granting the husband a stronger right to 'take her back' during this period recognizes that reconciliation remains possible while certain marital ties and mutual obligations persist. The phrase that women have a like right stresses reciprocal, equitable rights and dignified treatment between spouses, while the statement that men have a degree over them indicates a relative difference of authority and duty—rooted in men's assigned responsibilities (such as maintenance and protection)—rather than intrinsic moral superiority. The concluding attributes of Allah (“Mighty, Wise”) affirm that these regulations aim at social order, justice and the welfare of families in accordance with divine wisdom.

translation: Divorce may be pronounced twice; then either keep [her] in an acceptable manner or release [her] with kindness. It is not lawful for you to take back any of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not be able to observe the limits ordained by Allah. But if you fear that they will not observe Allah’s limits, there is no blame on them for what she ransoms herself with. Those are the limits of Allah; so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah — those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse sets a measured legal and moral framework for ending a marriage: divorce is limited (two revocable pronouncements) and, after that, spouses must choose either to reconcile responsibly or to separate honorably. The prohibition against reclaiming what was given (the mahr or gifts) preserves the wife’s material security and dignity, except when both fear that continued union will lead to breaches of God’s commands (in which case the wife may ransom herself — khulʿ — to effect separation without blame). By calling these stipulations “the limits of Allah,” the verse grounds family law in divine boundaries meant to prevent injustice and harm; to transgress them is to commit wrongdoing. The overall purpose is protective: to regulate divorce so as to discourage impulsive breakups, safeguard rights (especially of women), and ensure any separation is conducted with fairness and restraint.

translation: Then if he divorces her (for the third time), she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries another husband; and if he (that other husband) divorces her, there is no blame on them if they reconcile, provided they think they can observe the limits ordained by Allah. And those are the limits of Allah — He makes them clear to a people who know.
interpretation: The verse establishes a safeguard against hasty, irrevocable separation by making a lasting reunion conditional on an intervening lawful marriage: this requirement both deters frivolous use of divorce and ensures the seriousness and social protection of marital bonds. It allows reconciliation after the intervening marriage ends only when both parties genuinely believe they can uphold Allah’s legal and moral boundaries, stressing that these rulings are divinely prescribed limits intended to protect individuals and society; the phrase “limits of Allah” points to a framework of rights and responsibilities clarified for people who understand and will act justly.

translation: And when you divorce women and they reach their prescribed term, either retain them in kindness or release them with kindness; and do not retain them to cause harm so as to transgress. And whoever does that has indeed wronged himself. And do not take the signs of Allah as a mockery, and remember the favor of Allah upon you and what He has revealed to you of the Book and wisdom by which He exhorts you. And fear Allah and know that Allah is, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse insists that divorce must be governed by justice and dignity: once a woman’s waiting period ends, the husband should either resume the relationship honorably or let her go honorably, never using the legal form of divorce as a means to hurt, coerce, or deprive. Such abusive manipulation is described as self‑injury and a violation of divine limits. The admonition not to mock Allah’s signs forbids treating religious rulings or sacred procedures as tools for personal revenge or social pressure. Remembering God’s favors and the revealed guidance is offered as the moral discipline that prevents injustice, and the final reminder to fear God and that He knows all things underlines accountability for both outward actions and inner intentions.

translation: And when you divorce women and they have reached their term, do not prevent them from marrying their (former) husbands if they mutually agree among themselves in a fair way. That is an admonition for those of you who believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is purer for you and cleaner; and Allah knows while you do not know.
interpretation: The verse forbids using divorce to trap or oppress women after their prescribed waiting period (ʿiddah) by blocking a lawful reconciliation; when both spouses freely consent and settle matters honorably, they should be allowed to remarry. It teaches that respecting mutual consent and lawful, decent conduct in family affairs is not merely pragmatic but spiritually purifying and ethically superior, and it reminds believers that God’s guidance about social justice and personal dignity surpasses their limited judgments.

translation: Mothers shall breastfeed their children for two full years for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. For the father is the provision and clothing of them in a fitting manner. No person is burdened except to the extent of his capacity. No mother should be harmed because of her child, nor should the child be harmed because of his mother. And upon the heir is [a duty] like that. But if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them. And if you wish to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, there is no blame on you as long as you pay what is given in a proper manner. And fear Allah and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse lays down a moral-legal principle that balances care, responsibility and compassion within the family: breastfeeding for two years is honored but not coercively imposed; financial responsibility lies with those able to provide; obligations are limited to each person’s capacity; neither mother nor child should be subjected to harm or neglect; heirs share similar duties; family decisions (such as early weaning) require mutual consent and consultation; hiring a wet-nurse is permissible when fairly compensated. All these social rules are anchored in the wider ethical demand to be God‑conscious and mindful that God observes people's conduct, so justice, mercy and mutual agreement govern intimate family relations rather than harsh compulsion.

translation: And those of you who die and leave behind wives — those wives shall wait concerning themselves four months and ten days; then when they have fulfilled their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in a lawful (or decent) manner. And Allah is, of what you do, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse prescribes the widow’s iddah of four months and ten days as a fixed, respectful interval—serving to honor the deceased, allow grieving, and remove doubt about pregnancy and lineage—and makes clear that once that period is complete the woman is free to pursue lawful personal decisions (including remarriage) without blame attaching to others; the closing phrase underscores that outward observance must align with God‑aware sincerity, since Allah fully knows people’s deeds and intentions.

translation: There is no blame upon you for that which you announce of an offer for marriage to women, or for that which you keep in yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them; but do not make a secret promise to them except that you speak a proper word. And do not resolve upon the tying of the marriage knot until the prescribed term of the Book has come to an end. And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so fear Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse regulates intentions and proposals regarding marriage—especially while a woman is still in the prescribed waiting period—allowing a man to express or to harbour a desire to marry but prohibiting secret, binding promises or concluding the marriage contract before the revealed waiting-term (al-‘iddah) is complete. Its legal instruction safeguards women’s rights and social order by preventing covert commitments that could create confusion or injustice; its moral teaching reminds believers that inner thoughts are not hidden from God, so one must act with honesty, speak honorably rather than deceive, and restrain oneself until the proper time. The closing attributes — that God knows hearts and is Forgiving and Forbearing — both admonish accountability and offer hope for mercy when people err.

translation: There is no blame upon you if you divorce women before you have touched them or assigned for them a prescribed dower. And provide for them a provision: the rich according to his capability and the poor according to his capability — a provision in a decent manner. This is a right upon the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse permits ending a marriage that was not consummated (no sexual contact and no fixed dower) without moral blame, but it immediately imposes a compensatory, humane obligation: the husband must still give the woman a fair financial provision (mutʿah) proportionate to his means. The ruling balances legal latitude in such divorces with a clear ethical duty to protect the woman’s dignity and livelihood; generosity and justice in carrying out this provision are described as the mark of the righteous. In short, freedom to divorce in this specific circumstance is limited by a requirement of equitable, compassionate treatment tailored to the husband’s ability.

translation: And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have assigned for them a prescribed (dower), then half of what you assigned — unless they remit it, or the one in whose hand is the marriage contract remits it. And to remit is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget the kindness between you. Indeed, Allah is, of what you do, Seeing.
interpretation: The verse lays down a fair, measured rule for divorce that occurs before consummation: the wife is entitled to half the agreed dower, ensuring she is not left without some compensation. At the same time it urges mercy and generosity by allowing the dower to be forgiven — an act described as closer to piety — so that legal entitlement does not preclude gracious treatment. The phrase about the one “in whose hand is the marriage contract” denotes the party with authority over the marital bond (traditionally the husband or guardian) who may choose to relinquish the claim; the broader principle is that law and rights should be exercised with compassion. The final reminder — not to forget the favour between you and that God is aware of your deeds — calls believers to preserve mutual kindness and gratitude even amid separation, so that legal strictness is tempered by moral responsibility before God who sees all.

translation: Guard strictly the prayers — and (especially) the middle prayer — and stand before Allah in devout humility.
interpretation: This command calls for disciplined preservation of the prayer life: to protect the obligatory prayers from neglect, giving particular emphasis to the ‘‘middle’’ prayer (commonly understood as the prayer that maintains the believer’s spiritual balance), and to perform them with inward submission and reverence. “حافظوا” implies vigilance against lateness, carelessness, and distractions; “قانتين” stresses that worship must be sincere, humble and obedient before God, not merely outward ritual — a practice meant to sustain personal piety, moral steadiness, and communal order.

translation: But if you fear [an enemy], [then pray] on foot or on horseback; and when you are secure, remember Allah as He has taught you what you did not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the external forms of worship can be adapted in circumstances of danger: what matters is preserving the bond with God. In exigency prayers may be performed while moving or riding, yet this flexibility does not negate the duty to return, when safe, to the fuller, taught forms and to deepen remembrance of God — showing that divine guidance balances strict ritual with compassion for human hardship and aims to instill knowledge and practice believers previously lacked.

translation: And those of you who die and leave wives behind — a bequest to their wives: maintenance for a year without (their) being expelled. But if they go out (leave), there is no blame on you for what they do of themselves in a reasonable/good manner. And Allah is Mighty, Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes a protective rule for widows: when a husband dies, his wife is entitled to be provided for from his estate as a form of bequest or maintenance for one year, and she should not be driven out of the home during that time. This corrects unjust customary practice of evicting widows and ensures their economic and social security immediately after bereavement. At the same time the verse recognizes the widow’s agency — if she chooses to leave (for example to remarry or to take other lawful steps for her welfare), there is no sin or blame on the heirs or community for her independent, proper actions. The closing clause affirms that this ruling is both an exercise of God’s authority and of wise, compassionate legislation.

translation: And for divorced women is provision in a fair manner; a right upon the God‑fearing.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divorced women are entitled to reasonable, dignified maintenance (mutā bi‑l‑maʿrūf) and that ensuring this support is an ethical and communal duty incumbent on the God‑fearing. It links legal obligation to moral consciousness: providing for women after divorce is not optional charity but a just responsibility that preserves their dignity and measures true piety; the phrase “in a fair manner” bounds this right to what is customary, humane, and just rather than to excess or neglect.

translation: Thus Allah makes His signs clear to you, so that you may understand (use reason).
interpretation: God is saying that He presents clear signs—in scripture, in the world, and in life’s events—not to coerce belief but to invite deliberate reflection; the purpose is to engage human intellect and moral judgment so people can discern truth, learn lessons, and choose rightly, thereby bearing responsibility for their response to the guidance offered.

translation: Have you not seen those who went forth from their homes — thousands — fearing death? Then Allah caused them to die, then He gave them life. Indeed Allah is Ever-Bountiful to the people, but most people are not grateful.
interpretation: The verse describes how, in the midst of overwhelming fear and apparent defeat, God allowed those believers to experience a state of death (understood as actual death, temporary prostration/fainting, or utter hopelessness) and then restored them to life and deliverance. The point of the account is to show that such reversals — from terror to apparent end, then to revival and rescue — are manifestations of Allah’s mercy and bounty designed to test and teach reliance on Him; despite receiving such clear favors, most people nevertheless fail to recognize and thank God.

translation:
وَقَاتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ
“Fight in the cause of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”
interpretation: The verse enjoins believers to actively strive—up to and including armed resistance when legitimately required—for the defense of God’s cause, justice, and the community, while warning that Allah hears every voice and knows every intention; therefore such striving must be sincere, lawful, and morally constrained, since God assesses both outward actions and inner motives.

translation: Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him many times over? And Allah withholds and grants (provision), and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to spend in God’s cause by framing charity as a ‘loan’ to Allah: though given by people, it is treated by God as an investment that He will repay manifold. It reassures the giver that generosity is not loss but will be multiplied in reward, while also reminding that sustenance and provision are ultimately in God’s hands—He expands or restricts wealth as He wills—and that everyone will be held accountable before Him. Thus the passage both encourages selfless giving with trust in divine multiplication and humbly acknowledges human dependence on God’s provisioning and final judgment.

translation: Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, “Appoint for us a king that we may fight in the cause of Allah”? He said, “Would you perhaps, if fighting were prescribed for you, not fight?” They replied, “And why should we not fight in the cause of Allah, when we have been driven out of our homes and from our children?” But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And Allah is knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse condemns the inconsistency of those who demand leadership and promise to struggle when it suits their grievances but shrink from duty when real obligation and sacrifice are required. It exposes the difference between rhetorical commitment and actual readiness to bear responsibility, warning that moral accountability rests not on words or complaints but on willingness to endure hardship for what one claims to support; God, who knows inner states, will judge those who falsely claim causes while avoiding their obligations.

translation: And their prophet said to them, “Indeed, Allah has appointed Talut as a king over you.” They said, “How can he have kingship over us when we are more worthy of kingship than he, and he has not been given abundance of wealth?” He said, “Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him in knowledge and in bodily stature. And Allah grants His sovereignty to whom He wills. And Allah is Vast, All-Knowing.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that legitimate leadership is ultimately a matter of divine wisdom rather than popular expectations or material wealth. People may judge suitability for rule by lineage, status or riches, but God’s choice can rest on less visible yet essential qualities—sound knowledge, competence and the capacity to fulfill responsibilities. The passage calls for humility before God’s wisdom, readiness to accept appointed authority when it serves the common good, and a reminder that God, who knows all circumstances and intentions, gives power to whom He wills according to wisdom beyond worldly judgments.

translation: وقال لهم نبيهم: إن آية ملكه أن يأتيكم التابوت فيه سكينة من ربكم وبقية مما ترك آل موسى وآل هارون تحمله الملائكة. إن في ذلك لآية لكم إن كنتم مؤمنين.
interpretation: الآية تشرح أن مجيء التابوت المحمّل بـ "السكينة" وبآثار آل موسى وآل هارون هو علامة إلهية تُثبت شرعية الملك الذي اختاره الله؛ التابوت هنا ليس مجرد صندوق تاريخي بل تجسيد لحضور الله ودوام عهده ومصدر طمأنينة للناس، وحمل الملائكة له يبيّن أنه تكليف وتأييد من السماء. لذلك المطلوب من المؤمنين هو أن يعترفوا بسلطة الله في نصب القادة وأن يقيموا حكم الحق اعتماداً على الدليل الإلهي لا على الاعتبارات الدنيوية وحدها.

translation: When Talut set out with the troops he said, “Indeed Allah will test you at a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me—except whoever takes a handful with his hand.” So they drank from it, except a few of them. When he and those who believed with him had crossed it, they said, “We have no strength today against Goliath and his soldiers.” But those who were certain that they would meet Allah said, “How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah.” And Allah is with the patient.
interpretation: This passage teaches that trials and imposed disciplines (here the river test) are means God uses to distinguish genuine commitment and self-restraint among followers; true readiness for a mission is shown not by numbers or immediate confidence but by disciplined obedience, conviction of meeting God, and patience—qualities by which a small, steadfast people can prevail, for victory comes by God’s permission and He sustains the patient.

translation: And when they confronted Goliath and his forces, they said, “Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”
interpretation: The verse teaches a paradigm of spiritual struggle: true triumph in overwhelming trials combines three things — God-given patience (an enduring inner calm and perseverance), steadfastness in action (firmness of stance and resolve), and divine assistance (victory that ultimately comes from God). It shows that patience is not passive resignation but a grace one asks God to 'pour' into the heart, and that inward endurance must be joined with outward constancy; sincere supplication and reliance on God are therefore essential components of moral courage and successful resistance to injustice and falsehood.

translation:
فَهَزَمُوهُمْ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ وَقَتَلَ دَاوُودُ جَالُوتَ وَآتَاهُ اللَّهُ الْمُلْكَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ وَعَلَّمَهُ مِمَّا يَشَاءُ ۗ وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ النَّاسَ بَعْضَهُمْ بِبَعْضٍ لَّفَسَدَتِ الْأَرْضُ ۖ وَلَـٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ ذُو فَضْلٍ عَلَى الْعَالَمِينَ

“So they defeated them by the permission of Allah. And David killed Goliath, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom and taught him of that which He willed. And if Allah had not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but ever is Allah, Possessor of bounty for the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that human victories, authority, and knowledge are ultimately gifts granted by God’s will: David’s triumph over Goliath is an example of God enabling the weak or few to overcome stronger foes by His permission, and the subsequent bestowal of kingship and wisdom shows that political power and insight are divine trusts and guided provisions. The phrase about Allah’s repelling people by some through others points to a moral and social balance God maintains—periodic rises and falls of groups, leaders, or nations serve to check oppression and prevent the earth’s corruption; they are not mere historical accidents but aspects of divine governance. The closing affirmation that Allah is “possessor of bounty” reminds us that these changes, rewards, and disciplines are expressions of God’s encompassing grace and purposeful management of human affairs.

translation: These are the signs of Allah which We recite to you in truth; and indeed you are of the messengers.
interpretation: The statement functions as divine authentication: by calling the recited passages 'signs' and declaring their truthful revelation, it establishes the Qur'an as an objective, God-originated criterion that confers legitimate authority on the Prophet. The practical implication is that the message is not human opinion but a tested, binding guidance whose acceptance or rejection determines one’s moral and spiritual standing.

translation: Those are the messengers — We preferred some of them over others. Among them are those to whom Allah spoke, and We raised some of them in degrees. And We gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the Spirit of Holiness. And if Allah had willed, those who came after them would not have fought among themselves after the clear proofs had come to them; but they differed, so among them are believers and among them are disbelievers. And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought; but Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the varying ranks and special honors granted to prophets, and the giving of clear signs, are part of God’s wise ordaining rather than indications of injustice or randomness. By stating that God could have prevented later disputes but allowed them, the passage teaches a balance between divine sovereignty and human moral responsibility: Allah’s power and knowledge encompass all possibilities, yet He permits human freedom so that belief becomes a conscious, accountable choice and the consequences of people’s actions are real. Thus the apparent contingency of history — discord after clear guidance — serves God’s purposes for testing, distinguishing sincere faith from rejection, while underscoring that every outcome nonetheless occurs within God’s will.

translation: O you who have believed, spend of what We have provided for you before there comes a Day in which there will be no trading, no intimate friendship to avail, nor intercession; and the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: God commands the faithful to give from their lawful provision now because on the Day of Reckoning worldly mechanisms that people rely on — buying off punishment, relying on close ties, or seeking others’ intercession — will be ineffective. The verse urges charity and righteous spending as an investment whose benefits endure when social and economic avenues are closed, and it warns that rejecting God’s guidance is an act of injustice: those who deny the truth wrong themselves and forfeit any hope of protection by worldly relations or bargains on that Day.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what will be after them, and they encompass not a thing of His knowledge except for what He wills. His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation tires Him not. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s absolute, self-sufficient sovereignty and the transcendence of His attributes: He alone is eternal and sustains all existence without need of rest or weakness. The restriction on intercession underscores that all mediation, mercy or advocacy depends entirely on His will and authority, not on any independent power of creatures. His knowledge is complete and encompassing — nothing past, present or future is hidden from Him except insofar as He chooses to veil it — which places human beings in a posture of humility and accountability. The image of the Kursi denotes God’s sovereign dominion and sustaining governance over the entire cosmos, and the declaration that its upkeep does not fatigue Him stresses that God’s lordship is effortless and absolute. Taken together, the verse calls for reliance, reverence and submission to a single, all-powerful God whose knowledge, authority and mercy are exercised freely according to His will.

translation: There is no compulsion in religion. Verily, the right way has become distinct from error; so whoever rejects Taghūt and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold that will never break. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse establishes that faith cannot be genuinely produced by force: belief must arise from free conviction because God’s guidance and error are presented clearly enough for people to choose. ‘Taghūt’ denotes any authority, idol, or corrupt power that claims ultimate authority or leads people away from God; to disbelieve in Taghūt and believe in Allah means to renounce false claims to ultimate sovereignty and to turn to God’s sovereignty and guidance. Describing this commitment as the “firmest handhold” emphasizes that sincere submission to God and adherence to His guidance provide enduring moral and spiritual security that will not fail, while God’s being All‑Hearing and All‑Knowing assures that choices are seen and judged with perfect knowledge.

translation: Allah is the Protector (wali) of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve—their protectors are Taghut, who bring them out of light into darkness. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein.
interpretation: The verse sets up a moral and spiritual taxonomy of allegiance: true security and transformation come from being under Allah’s guardianship, which is an active liberation from ignorance, moral bondage and inner turmoil (the “darkness”) into clarity, guidance and upright life (the “light”); by contrast, rejecting God makes one dependent on taghut—false authorities, idols, tyrannical powers, or one’s own corrupt desires—that reverse that movement, leading from clarity into deeper blindness and moral ruin. The promise and threat are existential and eschatological: turning to God effects real change in a person’s state and destiny, while aligning with false lords results in perdition and eternal loss.

translation: ألم تر إلى الذي حاج إبراهيم في ربه أن آتاه الله الملك إذ قال إبراهيم ربي الذي يحيي ويميت قال أنا أحيي وأميت ۖ قال إبراهيم فإن الله يأتي بالشمس من المشرق فأت بها من المغرب فبهت الذي كفر ۗ والله لا يهدي القوم الظالمين
interpretation: الآية تبرز أن السيادة الحقيقية على الحياة والموت والنظام الكوني هي لله وحده، وأن ادعاء البشر لصفات إلهية لا يصمد أمام اختبار العقل والواقع. موقف إبراهيم يوضح منطقًا قرآنيًا: من يدّعي القدرة الإلهية يجب أن يتمكن من تغيير سنن الطبيعة، فإذا عجز تبين محدوديته واهتدى الناس لحقيقة التفرّق بين الربّ والخلق؛ وفي المقابل تُبيّن الخاتمة أن العنجهية والظلم والإصرار على الكفر تُحرّم الهداية، لأن القلوب التي تختار الطغيان تصير أعمي عن إدراك الحق.

translation: Or [consider] the one who passed by a town that had fallen into ruin; he said, “How will Allah bring this to life after its death?” So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. He said, “How long have you remained?” He said, “I remained a day or part of a day.” He said, “Rather, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink; they have not decayed. And look at your donkey; and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones—how We bring them together and clothe them with flesh.” And when it became clear to him, he said, “I know that Allah is Able to do all things.”
interpretation: The story functions as a corrective to human skepticism and a demonstration of divine sovereignty: what appears impossible under human reasoning — reviving a dead town, preserving food across a century, reconstituting bones — is entirely within God’s power. Its purpose is to humble presumptuous doubt, to show that temporal perception and natural assumptions do not limit God’s ability, and to provide a concrete sign intended to transform incredulity into firm conviction that Allah is capable of resurrecting life.

translation: And when Abraham said, “My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead,” He said, “Do you not believe?” He said, “Yes, but [I ask] only that my heart may be reassured.” He said, “Take four birds, then (cut them) and arrange them for yourself, then place a portion of them on every hill, then call them — they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Mighty, Wise.”
interpretation: This passage teaches that even the greatest believers may seek experiential certainty in addition to conviction of the heart. God’s reply turns Abraham’s request into a lesson: belief is not judged solely by words, and God provides a visible sign through obedient action. By commanding Abraham to take, dismember, disperse and then call the birds, God shows that life and resurrection are by His sovereign decree — what appears impossible to human agency is restored at His command. The concluding attributes (“Mighty, Wise”) emphasize that the demonstration both manifests divine power over life and is given with wisdom to strengthen faith rather than to prove it for its own sake.

translation: The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a seed that produces seven ears; in every ear there are a hundred seeds. And Allah multiplies [the reward] for whom He wills. And Allah is Vast, All‑Knowing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that sincere giving for God’s cause, however small it may seem, is transformed by Allah into abundant, multiplying good: the image of one seed becoming many ears and hundreds of grains shows that divine reward and benefit are exponential, not limited to our apparent calculation. The multiplication is by Allah’s will and wisdom, so the promise is both an assurance to the giver and a reminder that God—being Vast and All‑Knowing—sees intentions and bestows increase accordingly, producing widespread material and spiritual effects beyond what the giver can foresee.

translation: Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow up what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury — for them is their reward with their Lord; there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the value of charitable giving is determined by the giver’s sincerity and behavior after the gift: true charity is given without seeking praise, without reproaching or shaming the receiver, and without trying to reclaim credit. Such selfless giving is accepted by God and entrusted to His recompense; as a consequence the giver is freed from anxiety and sorrow — both the worldly fear of loss or ingratitude and the eschatological fear of being deprived of reward. Thus the passage emphasizes inner intention, trust in God’s justice, and respect for the dignity of recipients as essential components of morally acceptable charity.

translation: “A kind word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the moral quality and effects of our acts determine their worth: gentleness, respectful speech, and pardoning others preserve human dignity and build relationships, and these are spiritually superior to giving material aid that humiliates, burdens, or harms the recipient. It warns that outward charity can be counterproductive if it causes pain or seeks praise, and it reminds us that God does not need our gifts but values righteous intent and compassionate conduct; His forbearance means He is patient with human failings while ultimately holding people to account for how they treat others.

translation: يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تبطلوا صدقاتكم بالمنّ والأذى. كَالَّذِي يُنْفِقُ مَالَهُ رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ وَلَا يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ ۖ فَمَثَلُهُ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌ فَأَصَابَهُ وَابِلٌ فَتَرَكَهُ صَلْدًا ۖ لا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَى شَيْءٍ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا ۗ وَاللَّهُ لَا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الْكَافِرِينَ
interpretation: This verse warns that acts of giving lose their spiritual worth when motivated by showing off or accompanied by belittling the recipient. True charity requires sincerity before God and respect for those helped; if one gives to be seen by people or then reminds, insults, or harms the beneficiary, the outward gift becomes spiritually barren — like a stone whose dust is washed away by rain so nothing of value remains. The passage teaches that faith and humility are integral to righteous deeds: without belief and pure intention, the actions yield no lasting reward and do not lead to guidance.

translation: And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and to steady their souls is like a garden on high ground: when a heavy rain falls upon it, it yields its produce twice over; and if heavy rain does not fall upon it, then light rain (dew) suffices. And Allah is Seer of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere giving — done purely for God and to steady one’s own heart — brings both outward increase and inner firmness. The garden on elevated land represents a soul positioned to receive God’s grace: when abundant mercy (the ‘heavy rain’) comes, its returns are multiplied, yet even a little mercy (‘light rain’ or dew) will still make it fruitful. Thus genuine charity or piety does not depend on quantity to be effective; its sincerity assures spiritual benefit and multiplied outcomes in ways seen and unseen. The closing reminder that God sees what you do underscores that the true measure of deeds is their inward motive, not public display.

translation:
أَيُوحِبُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن تَكُونَ لَهُ جَنَّةٌ مِن نَّخِيلٍ وَأَعْنَابٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهَارُ لَهُ فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ وَأُصِيبَ بِهِ كِبَرٌ وَهُوَ ضَعِيفٌ لَهُ ذُرِّيَّةٌ ضُعَفَاءُ فَأَصَابَهَا إِعْصَارٌ فِيهِ نَارٌ فَاحْتَرَقَتْ ۗ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمُ الْآيَاتِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَفَكَّرُونَ

"Would any of you like to have a garden of date-palms and vines beneath which rivers flow, having therein of every fruit, while he is stricken with old age and has weak offspring, and then a whirlwind with fire strikes it so that it is burned? Thus Allah makes clear His signs to you so that you may reflect."
interpretation: This parable warns that worldly abundance is fragile and can fail to benefit its owner if misused or if circumstances change. The picture of a rich garden destroyed while its owner is incapacitated and his heirs are unable to preserve it teaches that wealth by itself is not a secure good: one must convert transient blessings into enduring moral and spiritual value—by using them responsibly, spending for good, educating and preparing successors, and attaching one’s heart to what remains beyond sudden loss. Allah presents such vivid examples to awaken reflection so people act now to safeguard what truly matters.

translation: O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned and from that which We have produced for you from the earth. And do not select the bad of it to spend, while you yourselves would not take it except with closed eyes. And know that Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse instructs believers to give generously from what is pure, lawful and valuable—both from their rightful earnings and from the bounty of the earth—rather than handing over inferior, spoiled or questionable items out of stinginess or hypocrisy. It condemns offering to others what you would refuse to accept for yourself (except out of embarrassment), emphasizing that charity must be dignified, sincere and made from goodness, not from contempt or negligence. Finally, by reminding that Allah is self-sufficient and praiseworthy, the verse teaches that giving benefits the giver’s heart and moral standing, not God’s need, so withholding quality in charity only harms the giver’s spiritual account and the social purpose of compassion.

translation: Satan threatens you with poverty and bids you to immorality, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that whispers of fear and shame—exemplified by Satan’s warning about poverty and his urging toward indecent behavior—are tools to block moral action (especially giving, patience, and upright conduct). Believers are to recognise such tactics as lies meant to make them cling to wealth or lower their ethical standards. In contrast, God’s promise of forgiveness and increase calls for trusting Him, acting generously and morally despite apparent risk, and relying on His vast provision and knowledge: He sees true need and intention and is able to replace what is spent and forgive shortcomings. Thus the practical lesson is to resist fear-driven selfishness and pursue charity and righteousness with reliance on God’s mercy and sufficiency.

translation:
يؤتي الحكمة من يشاء ۚ ومن يؤت الحكمة فقد أوتي خيرا كثيرا ۗ وما يذكر إلا أولو الألباب
"He grants wisdom to whom He wills; and whoever is granted wisdom has certainly been given abundant good. And none will take heed except those endowed with understanding."
interpretation: Here “al‑hikmah” (wisdom) denotes a divinely bestowed capacity to discern, internalize and rightly apply God’s guidance—not mere information but sound insight that shapes belief, judgment and conduct. The verse teaches that this inner gift is an abundant spiritual good given by God to whom He chooses; it produces righteous action and benefits both the individual and society. Only those with reflective, sincere hearts and intellects (“ulo al‑albab”) recognize, retain and live by this wisdom, so true remembrance and reform are the fruit of God’s gracious bestowal rather than of empty learning or heedlessness.

translation: Whatever you spend of expenditure or whatever vow you make, Allah knows it; and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every act of spending for God’s cause and every vow—whether done openly or in secret—is fully known and recorded by Allah, so believers should act with sincerity and trust that divine knowledge and judgment will recompense them rightly; simultaneously it warns that those who persist in injustice or opposition to the truth have no ultimate protector or rescuer who can avert Allah’s judgment or secure them a share of His favor.

translation: If you disclose your charities, that is well; and if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you. It will wipe away some of your sins. And Allah is Ever Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that giving in charity is praiseworthy whether done openly or secretly, but concealing one’s giving and delivering it directly to the needy is spiritually superior because it protects sincerity. Public charity can have social benefits (encouraging others, meeting communal needs), yet private giving safeguards the giver from ostentation (riya) and attachment to praise. The promise that charity expiates some sins emphasizes its moral and purifying effect: sincere generosity repairs spiritual failings. Underlying all this is the reminder that God fully knows the reality of people’s deeds and intentions, so one should act for His sake rather than for worldly recognition.

translation: It is not for you to guide them; but Allah guides whom He wills. And whatever good you spend is for yourselves. And you do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah. And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you, and you will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse separates human responsibility from divine sovereignty: a person’s duty is to call, teach and give, not to compel hearts — true guidance is granted by God alone. At the same time it reframes charity and good deeds as investments in the giver’s own moral and spiritual well‑being when done with the sincere intention of seeking Allah’s pleasure. Because intention determines value, acts performed for God are never lost: Allah will give full recompense without injustice. Practically, this teaches perseverance in righteous action without seeking worldly recognition or guaranteeing others’ acceptance, relying instead on God’s justice and decree.

translation: For the poor who have been constrained in the way of Allah and cannot travel through the land — the ignorant may think them self-sufficient because of their restraint. You will recognize them by their marks; they do not ask people persistently. And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.
interpretation: The verse teaches that there is a special category of needy people whose dignity and restraint hide their want: they are prevented from working or moving about in the path of God, do not beg insistently, and may appear outwardly self-sufficient. The community is therefore warned not to judge need by appearance and is urged to identify and aid such people compassionately and respectfully; charity toward them — even if unseen or unsolicited — is noticed and recorded by God, so giving should be sincere and responsive to real need rather than to outward displays.

translation: الَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ أَمْوَالَهُمْ بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ سِرًّا وَعَلَانِيَةً فَلَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ وَلَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن البذل المستمر والصادق، سواء أُعطي خفية أو علانية وفي أي ظرف، هو علامة إيمان وتوكّل على الله؛ من يفعل ذلك لا يخسر شيئًا بل ينال جزاءً إلهيًا يضمن له الطمأنينة والأمن ويخلّصه من الخوف والحزن، أي أن الإيثار يثمر أمانًا قلبياً ونجاةً في المقابل الإلهي.

translation: Those who consume interest cannot stand [on the Day of Resurrection] except as one stands who is being driven insane by Satan’s touch. That is because they say, “Trade is but like interest.” Yet Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest. So whoever receives admonition from his Lord and desists may keep what has passed; and his case is for Allah. But whoever returns to it — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein.
interpretation: The verse condemns riba (usury) as a spiritually and socially corrupt practice: likening its victims to the one struck by Satan emphasizes that engaging in or defending riba is the result of moral delusion and demonic misguidance, not sound ethical reasoning. By contrasting permitted trade with forbidden riba the text highlights a principled distinction: legitimate commerce involves mutual consent, reciprocity and risk-sharing, whereas riba guarantees gain at another’s expense and thus undermines justice and social solidarity. The allowance that one who repents may keep past transactions while his ultimate reckoning is left to God reflects a balance of divine justice and mercy — wrongs should be abandoned and corrected, but sudden retrospective punishment for past dealings is not imposed when one sincerely reforms. The warning that persistent return to riba leads to dire accountability underlines the seriousness of economic ethics in the Qur’anic moral vision: economic rules are integral to spiritual responsibility and communal well‑being.

translation: Allah destroys usury and increases the returns of charity, and Allah does not love any sinful disbeliever.
interpretation: The verse asserts a moral and economic principle: God will nullify and punish wealth gained by exploitative interest (riba) while He blesses and multiplies what is given in sincere charity. It emphasizes that wealth purified by generosity endures and grows in God’s sight, whereas unjustly acquired gains will be wiped away, and it warns that God does not favor those who persist in disbelief and sinful, exploitative behavior—thereby linking true faith with just, charitable conduct.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds and establish prayer and give zakah — for them is their reward with their Lord; and there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse is a promise that true security before God comes from the integrated life of faith: inner conviction, upright conduct, regular worship, and social responsibility. Saying the reward “is with their Lord” stresses that ultimate justice and recompense are in God’s hand—perfect, everlasting and not subject to worldly loss—so believers are relieved of existential fear about judgment and deep grief over final outcomes. Thus the passage teaches that personal peace and freedom from anxiety are fruits of a balanced commitment to devotional closeness and ethical action, and it frames charity (zakah) and prayer (salat) not as mere rituals but as means by which a believer's trust in God is actualized into social justice and assured divine recompense.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and leave whatever remains of interest, if you are believers.
interpretation: The verse is a stern moral imperative: true faith requires abandoning all remaining dealings in riba (usury/interest). By coupling ‘fear Allah’ with relinquishing ‘what remains’ of riba, it makes leaving any outstanding or ongoing usurious arrangements an act of piety and a test of sincerity—continuing to cling to unjust gain contradicts the claim of belief. Practically this means repentance, ceasing exploitative contracts, rectifying affairs where possible, and trusting God rather than relying on prohibited profit; thereby economic behavior is shown to be inseparable from genuine submission to Allah.

translation: But if you do not [desist], then be forewarned of a war from Allah and His Messenger. But if you repent, you shall have your principal — you shall not wrong and you shall not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse functions as a stern legal and moral injunction: persistent refusal to abandon a clearly forbidden practice (classically understood as usury/riba) invites the full withdrawal of divine and communal protection — described as “war” — meaning both a severe spiritual sanction and the loss of normal legal and social safeguards. Repentance restores one to the lawful order: creditors may recover only the original capital (no illicit gain), and transactions must be governed by equity so that neither party is unjustly enriched or harmed. The passage therefore emphasizes the seriousness of violating economic justice and the corrective consequence of returning to fair, principal-only dealings under God’s law.

translation: And if he is in hardship, then grant him respite until he is eased; and if you remit it (as a charity), that is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: The verse urges creditors to let compassion and communal well‑being guide their dealings: delaying payment for someone in difficulty or forgiving the debt is not merely an economic concession but a morally superior act that purifies one’s wealth, prevents harm and enmity, and wins greater spiritual reward. The phrase “if you only knew” points to unseen benefits and divine wisdom — forgiving and showing patience produce long‑term social and spiritual good that outweighs short‑term material advantage.

translation: And fear the Day when you will be returned to Allah. Then every soul will be repaid in full for what it has earned, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse is a moral summons: awareness of the inevitable return to God should govern conduct now, because accountability is personal and exact—each person will receive the just consequence of their deeds. That certainty both warns against wrongdoing and reassures the believer that divine justice is perfectly fair: no good will be lost and no one will suffer unjustly, so one must live with God-consciousness, seeking repentance and doing what is right.

translation: O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a fixed term, write it down. And let a scribe write between you in justice. And let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him; so let him write, and let the one who owes dictate, and let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything of it. But if the one who is indebted is of limited understanding or weak or unable to dictate, then let his guardian dictate with justice. And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men. And if there are not two men, then one man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the two errs, the other can remind her. And the witnesses should not refuse when they are called. And do not be weary to write it down, whether it is small or large, to its term. That is more just in the sight of Allah and more solid as testimony and closer to preventing doubt between you. Except when it is a present trade which you conduct among yourselves — then there is no blame on you if you do not write it down. And take witnesses when you make a contract. And let not the scribe nor the witness be harmed. For if you do so, it is an act of wickedness in you. And fear Allah. And Allah teaches you. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse uses the specific case of written debts to teach a general moral and legal principle: economic dealings must be structured to protect rights, prevent disputes, and safeguard the vulnerable. Requiring clear documentation, impartial scribes, and witnesses institutionalizes fairness and accountability so that transactions do not become a source of injustice; provisions for guardianship and special measures for those unable to speak show a priority to defend weak parties. At the same time the text recognizes practical needs (a narrow exemption for immediate retail exchanges), balancing justice with social convenience. The repeated appeals to fearing God, honoring witnesses and scribes, and the warning against harming them root contractual honesty in spiritual responsibility—making truthful, careful record‑keeping both a civic duty and a form of piety—while affirming that God, who teaches and knows all, is the ultimate guarantor of justice.

translation: And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge held in hand is sufficient. But if one of you trusts another, let the one who is entrusted return the trust, and let him fear Allah his Lord. And do not conceal testimony; and whoever conceals it—indeed his heart is sinful. And Allah is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse balances legal flexibility with moral responsibility: when formal written contracts are impractical (e.g., during travel), a tangible pledge may serve as temporary security, but this exception does not excuse failing moral duties. Trustworthiness and the prompt return of what is entrusted are insisted upon as acts tied to God-consciousness; withholding testimony to gain advantage or protect someone is condemned as a moral corruption of the heart and an injustice to others. By closing with God’s awareness, the verse reminds people that outward allowances do not remove inner accountability—transactions and testimonies must protect rights, preserve social trust, and be governed by honesty and fear of God.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it; He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse asserts Allah’s absolute sovereignty and knowledge: all creation — outward realities and inner states — belongs to Him and nothing of a person’s thoughts or intentions is beyond His scrutiny. Thus moral responsibility extends to inward motives as well as outward acts; concealment of one’s inner life does not remove one from divine judgment. The mention that He forgives or punishes “whom He wills” emphasizes that mercy and retribution proceed from God’s wise and sovereign will, so believers are urged to purify intentions, seek God’s pardon, and live with awareness of an all-powerful, just, and merciful Lord.

translation: The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and [so have] the believers. Each one has believed in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers; we make no distinction between any of His messengers. And they say, “We hear and we obey. [We seek] Your forgiveness, our Lord; and to You is the final return.”
interpretation: This verse encapsulates the heart of faithful posture: absolute assent to revelation together with readiness to submit. By affirming belief in God, angels, scriptures and messengers and refusing to distinguish between messengers, it emphasizes the unity and continuity of God’s guidance, rejecting selective acceptance. The phrase “we hear and we obey” indicates a moral disposition of obedience even amid incomplete understanding, while the plea for forgiveness and the reminder of eventual return acknowledge human fallibility and frame obedience within humility and dependence on God’s mercy.

translation: Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. It will have [the consequence of] what it has earned, and upon it will be what it has deserved. Our Lord, do not punish us if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord, and do not place upon us a burden like that which You placed upon those before us. Our Lord, do not impose upon us that which we have no strength to bear; and pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse affirms a moral theology in which Divine commands and dispensations are measured by human capacity: accountability is real but bounded by God’s justice and mercy. It counsels a posture of humble responsibility—striving and accepting the moral consequences of one’s actions—while simultaneously recognizing human frailty and turning to God for relief, forgiveness, and support.
