The petition portion models how believers should relate to Divine sovereignty: honest about weakness, mindful of communal history, asking that tests not exceed ability, seeking pardon and compassion, and invoking God as protector who empowers the faithful in the face of opposition. Together the statements encourage balanced ethics: faithful effort without despair, repentance without excusing wrongdoing, and reliance on God’s mercy alongside personal responsibility.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif Lam Meem.
interpretation: The disjoined letters “Alif Lam Meem” are a divine sign meant to arrest the listener’s attention and to point to the Qur’an’s miraculous character: though formed from ordinary alphabetic elements, its meaning, eloquence and authority transcend human composition. Their precise import is known ultimately to God; their presence humbles the reader and invites reflection on the transcendent source of the revelation.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer (Self-Subsisting).
interpretation: The verse declares God’s absolute oneness and ascribes to Him two complementary attributes: al‑Ḥayy (the Ever‑Living), meaning His life is eternal and independent of time or decay, and al‑Qayyūm (the Sustainer/Self‑Subsisting), meaning He alone upholds, maintains and governs all existence. From this it follows that all creation is contingent and wholly dependent on Him for its existence and preservation, while He is in no need of anything.

translation:
نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَأَنزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ وَالْإِنجِيلَ
“He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it; and He revealed the Torah and the Gospel.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur’an is a genuine divine revelation delivered to the Prophet as a confirmation of the same divine guidance contained in earlier scriptures. It signals continuity in God’s message—validating the essential truths of the Torah and Gospel—while also implying that the Qur’an is the culminating, decisive scripture that restores and preserves God’s guidance where earlier texts or understandings had been altered or misunderstood.

translation: من قبل هدى للناس وأنزل الفرقان ۗ إن الذين كفروا بآيات الله لهم عذاب شديد ۗ والله عزيز ذو انتقام
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن الله قد أمن للناس هدى متصلًا — وتكلّل ذلك بإرسال الفرقان (الذي يميز بين الحق والباطل) كمعيار قاطع للهدى. من يصرّ على تكذيب آيات الله لا يكون تحركه مجرد اختلاف فكري، بل رفض لوسيلة الهداية التي تمنح الإنسان الاختيار والمسؤولية؛ لذلك ثَمَّ عقوبة شديدة، ليست تعبيرًا عن نزعة انتقامية عاطفية بل عن تحقق عدل إلهي لا يُهدر حقوق الناس ولا يُترك الظلم بلا جزاء. وصف الله بالعزّة وذو الانتقام يبيّن أنه قوي قادر على إقامة الحق وأخذ الجزاء بحق من أشاع الباطل، فالتذكير بالعقاب هنا وظيفة تربوية تحث على قبول الهدي والتزامه حفاظًا على النظام الأخلاقي والعدل الإلهي.

translation: Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah in the earth or in the heavens.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute and perfect knowledge of all realities—external events and inner states, seen and unseen, past, present and future. Nothing anyone conceals—intentions, private deeds, or hidden circumstances—escapes His awareness. The practical implication is moral and spiritual: humans are ultimately accountable before an all-knowing Lord, should cultivate sincerity and conscience in actions and worship, and can trust in God’s just and wise handling of matters since nothing is overlooked or beyond His knowledge.

translation: He is the One who forms you in the wombs as He wills. There is no deity except Him — the Exalted in Might, the All‑Wise.
interpretation: The verse asserts that every aspect of human formation — body, sex, constitution, and the conditions accompanying birth — is brought into being by God’s sovereign choice. By adding “there is no god but He” and the attributes al‑'Aziz (Mighty) and al‑Hakim (Wise), it rejects any competing power over creation and teaches that what is decreed is both uncontestable in power and grounded in wisdom, even when its reasons are not apparent; the proper response is humility, trust in God’s plan, and recognition that life’s particulars serve a purposeful, wise design.

translation: He is the One who has sent down to you the Book. Among it are verses that are precise in meaning — they are the foundation of the Book — and others that are allegorical. As for those whose hearts are crooked, they follow what is allegorical seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. And none knows its true interpretation except Allah. Those firmly rooted in knowledge say, “We believe in it; all is from our Lord.” And none will take admonition except people of understanding.
interpretation: This verse sets a principle for reading revelation: some Qur’anic passages are clear and foundational, while others are deliberately ambiguous or layered. The presence of ambiguity is not a flaw but a test: those with crooked intent seize uncertain passages to foment division or to force speculative meanings that suit their aims, whereas the truly knowledgeable respond with trust and restraint, recognizing that ultimate knowledge of inner meanings belongs to God alone. The proper posture toward ambiguous texts, then, is epistemic humility combined with fidelity to the clear teachings — affirming what is known, refraining from reckless conjecture, and allowing established, sound principles to govern understanding. Only those who discipline their intellects and hearts (“people of understanding”) will benefit from this balance and be protected from discord.

translation: Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from Yourself; indeed, You are the Bestower.
interpretation: This is a communal supplication recognizing that initial guidance is a gift from God but is fragile unless sustained by His ongoing mercy. The petitioner acknowledges human weakness and the danger of spiritual backsliding even after receiving guidance, and therefore asks God — described by the attribute al‑Wahhāb, the Generous Bestower — to preserve steadfastness and to grant the merciful support that alone can keep hearts firm. Implicitly it teaches reliance on divine grace alongside personal vigilance, and frames moral and spiritual constancy as a continuing gift rather than a one‑time achievement.

translation: Our Lord, indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.
interpretation: This invocation expresses firm conviction that a final divine reckoning is certain and that God’s promises are unfailing; that conviction reshapes how one lives now — it brings solace to the sincere by affirming ultimate vindication and justice, and it serves as a solemn admonition to the heedless. By anchoring hope and accountability in God’s certainty rather than transient worldly measures, it calls the believer to moral seriousness, unity, and trust in divine recompense.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve — never will their wealth or their children avail them against Allah at all; and those — they are the fuel of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning material means and kinship cannot intercede or provide protection for persistent unbelievers. Describing them as “fuel of the Fire” shows that the very things people trust and cling to in this life (wealth, status, offspring) can be transformed into sources that intensify their punishment—either because those attachments diverted them from faith or because they will have no efficacy before God. The underlying exhortation is to place ultimate reliance on sincere faith and righteous deeds rather than on transitory worldly securities.

translation:
كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ ۚ كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ

"Like the fate of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins; and Allah is severe in punishment."
interpretation: The verse invokes the example of Pharaoh and earlier nations to teach that persistent rejection of God's revelations and habitual wrongdoing brings about a decisive, deserved divine response. The phrase "أَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ" stresses that the calamity that befell them was the consequence of their accumulated sins and obstinate refusal to repent, not an arbitrary act. "وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ" emphasizes the certainty and gravity of that retribution as a moral warning: communities that persist in denial, corruption, and oppression risk bringing ruin upon themselves unless they turn back to God and reform their ways.

translation: Say to those who disbelieve, “You will be overcome and gathered into Hell — and wretched is the resting-place.”
interpretation: The verse functions as a stern prophetic warning and theological assertion: persistent rejection of God's guidance leads inevitably to divine overpowering and final accountability, and the phrase “wretched is the resting‑place” emphasizes that the ultimate end of such obstinacy is not merely punishment but the utter ruin and loss of any true security, dignity, or repose.

translation:
قد كان لكم آية في فئتين التقتا: فئة تقاتل في سبيل الله وأخرى كافرة يرونهم مثليهم رأي العين، والله يؤيد بنصره من يشاء؛ إن في ذلك لعبرة لأولي الأبصار.
"There was for you an example in the two groups that met: one fighting in the cause of Allah and the other disbelieving; they beheld them as twice their number with the eye. But Allah grants victory by His support to whom He wills. Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have sight."
interpretation: The verse teaches that outward appearances and numerical advantage do not determine outcomes; when two forces confront each other, fear, perception, and circumstances can make an opponent seem greater than they are, yet ultimate success rests on God's support. It calls the believer to draw the lesson—do not be swayed merely by what the eye counts or by intimidation, but cultivate trust in divine assistance, steadfastness, and right cause; God may grant victory to the seemingly weaker party according to His wisdom, so discernment and reliance on Him are the true factors in triumph.

translation: زُيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ حُبُّ الشَّهَوَاتِ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ وَالْبَنِينَ وَالْقِنَاطِيرِ الْمَقْنُطَرَةِ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَالْخَيْلِ الْمُسَوَّمَةِ وَالْأَنْعَامِ وَالْحَرْثِ ۗ ذَٰلِكَ مَتَاعُ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا ۖ وَاللَّهُ عِنْدَهُ حُسْنُ الْمَآبِ
interpretation: God is warning that He has made sensual pleasures and wealth attractive as a test: affections for spouses and children, vast hoarded riches, fine horses, livestock and cultivated land are legitimate comforts but fundamentally transient. If they become people’s ultimate aim they distract from moral responsibility and preparing for the everlasting return to God, which is far superior. The verse therefore calls for keeping worldly enjoyments in their proper place — enjoyed lawfully but subordinated to deeds and priorities that secure the good, eternal outcome with Allah.

translation: قُلْ أُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِخَيْرٍ مِّن ذَٰلِكُمْ ۚ لِلَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ جَنَّاتٌ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهَارُ خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا وَأَزْوَٰجٌ مُطَهَّرَةٌ وَرِضْوَٰنٌ مِّنَ اللَّهِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ بَصِيرٌ بِالْعِبَادِ
interpretation: الآية تدعو إلى إعادة ترتيب قيمة الخير: ما يُعدّ خيرًا حقًا هو قرب الله ورضاه الذي يمنحه لمن تقوى—ليس النِعم الزائلة بل نِعَم باقية ذات كمال روحي واجتماعي. تصوير الفردوس بالحدائق والأنهار والزوجات المطهّرة لا يقتصر على لذّة مادية، بل يشير إلى دوام الحياة المطمئنة والتطهر والكمال الأخلاقي والاجتماعي الذي يناله المتقيون؛ و"الرضوان من الله" يعبّر عن أعلى منزلة لا تُقاس بالمنافع الدنيوية. ختم الآية بأنّ الله بصير بالعباد يطمئن أن ما في الظاهر أو ما يُخفى من نوايا الثواب والعقاب بيد الله، فالمقصد بالعمل الصالح هو التقرب إلى الله وإحقاق الحق داخليةً وخارجيةً، لا مجرد تحقيق مصالح دنيوية أو سمعة مؤقتة.

translation: Those who say, “Our Lord, indeed we have believed; so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.”
interpretation: This verse presents the posture of true believers: a firm, confessed conviction (“we have believed”) coupled with sober awareness of human failure. Rather than claiming perfection, they turn to God with a humble communal supplication asking first for forgiveness of their sins and then for deliverance from the Fire. The prayer links genuine faith to dependence on divine mercy — faith is an inner certainty that nevertheless must be sustained by repentance, seeking pardon, and asking God’s protection from ultimate punishment.

translation: Those who are patient, and truthful, and devoutly submissive, and those who spend (in charity), and those who seek forgiveness in the early hours (before dawn).
interpretation: The phrase points to the inner structure of genuine faith: enduring patience that trusts God amid hardship, integrity that makes truthfulness a constant practice, humble and attentive devotion in worship, generous self-giving with one’s wealth, and the habit of returning to God in the quiet pre-dawn for repentance. Together these traits indicate a spiritually disciplined life—one that seeks purification of the heart, relies on God’s mercy, and manifests belief both inwardly (in worship and repentance) and outwardly (in conduct and charity).

translation: Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and [so do] the angels and those endowed with knowledge—standing firmly for justice. There is no deity except Him, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the oneness of God (tawḥīd) is attested not only by Allah Himself but by the highest, impartial witnesses—angels and the people of true knowledge—whose testimony is rooted in justice rather than whim or desire. “Qāimān bil-qisṭ” signals that this witness is upright and fair, removing any pretext for doubt: the claim of God’s uniqueness rests on authoritative, dispassionate recognition. The repetition and the attributes al‑ʿAzīz (Almighty) and al‑Ḥakīm (All‑Wise) underscore that God’s unity is both powerful and wisely ordered, so submission to Him is grounded in both strength and wisdom.

translation: Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam. And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual envy. And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah — then indeed, Allah is swift in account.
interpretation: This verse declares that what is truly acceptable to God is submission to Him (Islam) — a fundamental orientation of faith and obedience that corresponds to the original message of the prophets. The clause about the People of the Book explains that their divisions arose not from lack of evidence but from after clear knowledge had reached them, motivated by partisan envy and self-interest that led to distortion and rupture of unity. The warning that God is “swift in account” underscores the moral consequence: denying or rejecting God’s clear signs is a serious act that will be judged promptly and decisively. Taken together, the verse calls believers to return to sincere submission, to value authentic knowledge over factionalism, and to remember that denial of divine guidance entails real and immediate accountability before God.

translation: So if they dispute with you, say, “I have submitted my face to Allah, and so have those who follow me.” And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, “Have you submitted?” If they submit, then they have indeed been rightly guided; but if they turn away, then your duty is only to convey [the message]. And Allah is Seer of the servants.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet (and by extension any caller to God) to respond to argumentation by declaring wholehearted submission to Allah — a turning of the whole self and community toward Him — and then to invite others (both People of the Book and the unlettered) to the same submission. The question “Have you submitted?” is both an open invitation and a test of sincerity: if people accept, true guidance has reached them; if they refuse, the messenger’s responsibility is fulfilled by conveying the truth, not by forcing acceptance. The final clause, “And Allah is Seer of the servants,” reassures the caller that God observes inner states and outward deeds and will judge accordingly, so one should focus on clear, sincere proclamation and leave outcomes and hidden motives to God’s knowledge and justice.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets unjustly and kill those who enjoin justice among the people—give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse treats the extermination or suppression of divine guidance and of those who call to equity as a fundamental crime against the moral order: such behavior expresses a collective turning away from God and a corrosive social corruption that cannot go unanswered. The warning of a “painful punishment” underscores both the inevitability of divine justice (which may appear as worldly downfall or retribution in the Hereafter) and the moral imperative to defend prophets and proponents of justice, to oppose systems of impunity, and to recognize that power founded on injustice is ultimately transient and accountable.

translation: Those are the ones whose deeds have been rendered void in this world and in the Hereafter, and they will have no supporters.
interpretation: The verse warns that outward acts lose all spiritual value when detached from true faith, sincere submission to God, and rectitude of intention. People who persist in disbelief, associate others with God, act hypocritically, or perform good works for show rather than for God's sake will find those deeds produce no benefit here or in the Hereafter; having forfeited divine favor, they will have no intercessors or protectors to rescue them from accountability.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They call to the Book of Allah that it should judge between them; then a party of them turns away, and they are averse.
interpretation: The verse criticizes people of earlier revelation who invoke God’s Book as the standard of judgment—often to gain legitimacy or to test others—but when its clear ruling goes against their interests they deliberately avoid it. It exposes a hypocrisy: using divine authority when convenient yet rejecting it when inconvenient, and warns that true submission requires accepting God’s judgment even when it upends personal or communal preferences.

translation: That is because they said, “The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days,” and what they were fabricating in their religion deceived them.
interpretation: The verse criticizes those who, through arrogance and false religious inventions, minimized divine punishment by claiming they would only suffer briefly and then be spared. Their self‑made doctrines and rationalizations produced complacency and delusion, leading them to underestimate divine justice and to persist in wrongdoing; ultimately their own fabrications became the cause of their misguidance and loss.

translation:
فَكَيْفَ إِذَا جَمَعْنَاهُمْ لِيَوْمٍ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ ۖ وَوُفِّيَتْ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ مَّا كَسَبَتْ ۚ وَهُمْ لَا يُظْلَمُونَ
"Then how (will it be) when We gather them on a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul will be fully repaid for what it has earned, and they will not be wronged."
interpretation: The verse is a solemn reminder of the absolute, incontrovertible reality of the Last Day: when all people are assembled before God, earthly statuses, alliances, and pretenses will be powerless, and divine justice will be executed with exactness. The rhetorical question amplifies the gravity of that gathering—no ambiguity will remain—so that each soul receives precisely what its deeds warrant. The phrase “they will not be wronged” affirms God’s perfect fairness: no one will be deprived of their due—reward for good, consequence for wrongdoing—and thus the passage functions both as a warning to the arrogant and comfort to the oppressed that ultimate justice rests with God alone.

translation: Say, “O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty! You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will; You honor whom You will and You abase whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are over all things competent.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that authority, honor, and humiliation are not inherent human rights but contingent gifts or withdrawals by God’s will; thus political fortunes and social standing are transient and subject to Divine wisdom. It teaches believers to ground their trust in God rather than in worldly power, to exercise any given authority with responsibility and justice, and to accept losses with patience, since true good and the final outcome rest with God alone, who is fully able to change circumstances for good.

translation: You make the night enter into the day and make the day enter into the night; You bring forth the living from the dead and bring forth the dead from the living; and You provide for whom You will without account.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty and power to reverse and govern all states of existence. The regular alternation of night and day, the emergence of life from what appears lifeless, and the distribution of provision beyond human reckoning are presented as signs that destiny, sustenance, life and death are ultimately determined by Divine will. The moral consequence is to cultivate trust and humility: one should not be arrogant in prosperity nor despair in hardship, for changes and reversals are within God’s control and His wisdom transcends human measures.

translation: Let not the believers take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Whoever does that has nothing to do with Allah, unless you cautiously fear them (and act in self‑defense). And Allah Himself warns you; and to Allah is the eventual return.
interpretation: The verse commands that the fundamental bonds of trust and loyalty for a believing community should not be replaced by reliance on those who oppose its core commitments. ‘‘Awliyā’’’ here denotes close protectors, patrons, or partners whose interests and loyalties one relies upon; taking such ties with disbelievers in preference to fellow believers undermines communal solidarity and the moral-religious identity that defines the Muslim community. The phrase ‘‘has nothing to do with Allah’’ signals that such conduct is incompatible with the spirit of allegiance demanded by faith — it severs or corrupts the believer’s effective relationship to the community and the ethical responsibilities that flow from it. The clause of exception — ‘‘unless you cautiously fear them’’ — permits prudential, protective measures when facing real danger or deception (for example, concealing one’s position, making tactical arrangements, or temporarily cooperating to avoid harm), but only as a guarded, defensive expedient, not as a transfer of loyalty or dependence. The warning that ‘‘Allah Himself warns you’’ and the reminder that ‘‘to Allah is the return’’ place the rule within the framework of ultimate accountability: outward actions that substitute hostile alliances for communal duty will be judged, and believers must weigh immediate safety against long‑term fidelity to their covenant and moral obligations.

translation: Say, ‘Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or disclose it, Allah knows it. He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and Allah is over all things competent.’
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine knowledge reaches both outward deeds and inward motives, so moral responsibility extends to what is hidden inside the heart as well as to visible actions. Because nothing is truly secret from God, hypocrisy and covert wrongdoing cannot escape final reckoning, and sincerity of intention becomes the essential measure of faith. At the same time, God’s encompassing knowledge and power offer consolation: the oppressed and sincere may trust that God sees reality and is fully able to bring about justice, reform hearts, and effect outcomes in the heavens and the earth.

translation:
يوم تجد كل نفس ما عملت من خير محضراً، وما عملت من سوء تود لو أن بينها وبينه أمداً بعيداً؛ ويحذركم الله نفسه، والله رؤوف بالعباد.

"The Day when every soul will find what it has done of good presented before it, and as for what it has done of evil, it will wish that there were a great distance between it and that; and Allah warns you concerning Himself—and Allah is Kind to the servants."
interpretation: The verse teaches that accountability is immediate and unavoidable: deeds will stand revealed on the Last Day, and those who persisted in wrong will experience crushing regret they cannot undo. The clause "Allah warns you of Himself" should be read as an act of mercy and justice—God cautions people about the real consequences of their choices (His own retribution) so they may refrain, repent, and reform while there is still time. Thus divine warning and divine compassion are not contradictory: warning is part of God's care to guide people away from ruin, emphasizing personal responsibility, the urgency of turning back to God, and that mercy does not negate the certainty of moral consequences.

translation:
قُلْ إِن كُنتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ فَاتَّبِعُونِي يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ وَيَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ ذُنُوبَكُمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ
"Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.’"
interpretation: True love of God in this verse is defined not as mere feeling but as practical conformity to His guidance embodied in the Prophet. To ‘follow’ the Messenger means to accept and live by the revelation and prophetic example; doing so is the means by which God bestows His love and grants forgiveness. The promise underscores that divine affection and pardon are not automatic but are given to those whose loyalty to Allah is proven by obedience to His path, while the final clause comforts believers that God’s disposition toward them is characterized by forgiveness and mercy.

translation: Say, 'Obey Allah and the Messenger.' But if they turn away — then indeed, Allah does not love the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that submission to divine guidance and the Prophet’s authority defines one’s relationship to God: the duty to call people to obedience rests with the messenger, while those who willfully reject that guidance make a free moral choice that places them outside God’s favor. It therefore functions both as an instruction to the community to accept revealed guidance and as a warning that persistent, deliberate turning away is a disqualifying sign of disbelief and estrangement from God’s love.

translation: Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Imran above the worlds.
interpretation: The statement of divine “selection” signals that these persons and households were singled out by God for special favor and entrusted with unique roles: they were purified, entrusted with guidance and revelation, and set as exemplary models and custodians of prophetic leadership. This chosenness denotes an honor and responsibility granted by God for the welfare and direction of creation—qualifying them to be paradigms whose faith, conduct and progeny would preserve and transmit guidance—not an assertion of intrinsic worth apart from God’s will, but a declaration of their appointed status in the history of guidance.

translation: Descendants, some of them from others. And Allah is All-Hearing, All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The phrase underscores the continuity and interconnection of human generations—people and communities are born out of earlier ones—and it reminds us that these familial and social ties, along with whatever transpires within them (debts, rights, grievances, or blessings), are fully known and heard by Allah; nothing escapes His awareness, so lineage and its consequences are subject to divine knowledge and accountability.

translation: When the wife of Imrān said, “My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb to be dedicated (muharraran); so accept it from me. Indeed, You are the All‑Hearing, the All‑Knowing.”
interpretation: The verse portrays a believer’s wholehearted consecration and dependence upon God: offering what is most dear as a vow is an expression of surrender, but its spiritual value rests not in the outward act alone but in seeking God’s acceptance. The term “muharraran” implies dedicating the child to a pure, devoted service or sanctuary life, and the closing invocation — “You are the Hearing, the Knowing” — teaches that vows must be accompanied by humble trust that God perceives intent and will accept what is sincerely offered; true devotion combines outward commitment with inner sincerity and reliance on Divine wisdom.

translation: فَلَمَّا وَضَعَتْهَا قَالَتْ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَضَعْتُهَا أُنثَىٰ ۖ وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتْ وَلَيْسَ الذَّكَرُ كَالْأُنْثَىٰ ۖ وَإِنِّي سَمَّيْتُهَا مَرْيَمَ وَإِنِّي أَعِيذُهَا بِكَ وَبِذُرِّيَّتِهَا مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ
interpretation: الآية تكشف موقف الأمّية التي تقابل واقعة لم تكن في انتظارها — ولادة بنت بدلاً من ذكر كانت تظنّ أنه أنسب للخدمة المخصّصة — فتعترف بتفوق علم الله وحكمته («والله أعلم بما وضعت») وتبيّن الفرق الاجتماعي أو الوظيفي بين الذكر والأنثى دون إنقاص قيمة الفتاة («وليس الذكر كالأنثى»)، لكنها مع ذلك تكرّس المولودة لغاية مقدّسة بتسمّيتها مريم وتلتمس من الله حفظها وحفظ نسلها من وسوسة الشيطان وطغيانه. في معنى أعمق، الآية تبرز مزيجاً من السجود لإرادة الله، والوعي بالحقائق الاجتماعية، والرغبة في الحماية الروحية كي تُنمو المولودة في طهارة وقداسة تخولها أداء دورها الإلهي المميّز.

translation: So her Lord accepted her with a gracious acceptance, caused her to grow up a beautiful growth, and entrusted her to Zakariya. Whenever Zakariya entered upon her in the sanctuary he found with her provision. He said, “O Mary, from where is this for you?” She said, “It is from Allah.” Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account.
interpretation: The verse depicts God’s special favor toward Mary: He accepted and raised her in purity and excellence, placed her under the guardianship of Zakariya, and supplied her with sustenance in a way that exceeded ordinary means. The “provision” found with her is presented as a sign of divine generosity — provision that comes directly from God’s will and mercy, not tied to human expectation or lineage. The phrase “Allah provides for whom He wills without account” stresses that God’s giving is sovereign, abundant, and beyond numerical reckoning; it reassures that sincere devotion and God’s selection can result in extraordinary support and honor, and it affirms God’s power to sustain His servants in ways that transcend normal causality.

translation: Then Zakariya called upon his Lord, saying, “My Lord, grant me from Yourself a goodly offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication.”
interpretation: Zakariya’s plea models asking Allah for a divinely granted, morally sound legacy rather than merely biological progeny: by saying “from Yourself” he acknowledges that true blessing and the formation of a righteous child are ultimately acts of God’s grace, and by calling Allah “the Hearer of supplication” he affirms confident reliance on divine response. The verse therefore teaches that believers should turn directly to God for what truly benefits them—especially spiritual and moral good—trusting His power to accomplish what human means cannot and humbly seeking a lasting, praiseworthy outcome.

translation: Then the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: “Indeed, Allah gives you glad tidings of a son whose name will be Yahya; he will confirm a Word from Allah, and will be a leader, chaste, and a prophet — among the righteous.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s response to sincere devotion is not only personal consolation but the raising of a moral exemplar who sustains divine truth: Yahya’s mission to “confirm a word from Allah” signifies continuity and validation of God’s revelation, while the titles (leader, chaste, prophet among the righteous) indicate that true prophetic authority combines spiritual integrity, purity of life, and steadfast commitment to righteousness — so the miracle promised to Zakariya is ultimately the establishment of principled spiritual leadership that preserves and embodies God’s message.

translation:
قَالَ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي غُلَٰمٌ وَقَدْ بَلَغَنِيَ الْكِبَرُ وَامْرَأَتِي عَاقِرٌ ۖ قَالَ كَذَٰلِكَ اللَّهُ يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ
(He said, “My Lord, how can I have a son when I have reached extreme old age and my wife is barren?” He said, “Thus [it will be]; Allah does what He wills.”)
interpretation: The verse underscores that God’s creative power and decree are not constrained by ordinary causes or human expectations: what appears impossible (a son despite old age and barrenness) can occur by God’s will. It teaches reliance and humility before divine wisdom — human doubts and natural reasons do not limit God’s ability to bring about His plan, and His promises are fulfilled according to His sovereign will and timing.

translation: He said, “My Lord, make for me a sign.” He said, “Your sign is that you shall not speak to the people for three days except by gesture.” And remember your Lord abundantly and glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning.
interpretation: The passage teaches that God’s answers may come as formative, non-verbal signs that shift a believer from seeking outward proof to cultivating inner trust and disciplined devotion. A temporary silence can be a means of purification and focus—restraining speech so attention turns to prayer, gestures, and reliance on God—and it humbles the heart while making the eventual blessing more manifest. The accompanying exhortation to constant remembrance and glorification in the evening and morning frames such signs: faithful, regular dhikr and worship are the proper response to divine favors or trials and the spiritual practices that prepare one to receive and recognize God’s gifts.

translation: And [remember] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you, purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse affirms that God bestowed a special, divinely ordained status on Mary: He selected her for a unique role, endowed her with spiritual and moral purification, and raised her in rank above all women of the worlds. The terms indicate both an appointment to a particular trust (her role as the mother of Jesus) and an inner sanctification that made her a paradigm of chastity, devotion, and submission to God — an exemplary honor given by God's wisdom and grace.

translation: O Mary, be devoutly submissive to your Lord; prostrate and bow with those who bow.
interpretation: The command stresses that true piety combines inner submissiveness (iqnaʿ) with outward acts of worship: humility before God, regular physical devotion (rukuʿ and sujud), and participation in the worshipping community. Addressing Mary—though honored and the recipient of a miracle—emphasizes that spiritual greatness is shown not by privilege but by steadfast obedience, humility, and communal devotion, making her a model for believers.

translation: That is from the tidings of the Unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they cast their pens as to which of them should be the guardian of Mary, nor were you with them when they disputed.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Prophet’s knowledge of that private, past incident (the drawing of lots over Mary’s guardianship and the ensuing dispute) did not come from observation or hearsay but from divine revelation. By stating that he was not present, God removes any basis for accusing the Prophet of inventing the story and emphasizes that Allah alone knows hidden affairs and may disclose them to His Messenger to establish truth, vindicate the Prophet’s trustworthiness, and correct people’s misunderstandings.

translation: When the angels said, “O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him; his name will be the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary — honored in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah].”
interpretation: The verse records the angelic announcement to Mary that God will bring forth a son by His creative command — “a word from Him” — signifying a miraculous origin by God’s decree. The titles given — al‑Masīḥ (the Messiah) and ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary) — identify his prophetic mission and human lineage, while wa‑jīhan fī l‑dunyā wal‑ākhirah (honored in this world and the Hereafter) emphasizes both his distinguished status during his earthly ministry (miracles, guidance and respect) and his exaltation in the life to come. Being “min al‑muqarrabīn” (among those brought near) indicates a special closeness to God and high spiritual rank among righteous servants, affirming his honored station without implying divine sonship but rather a unique, God‑ordained dignity and mission.

translation:
وَيُكَلِّمُ النَّاسَ فِي الْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًا وَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
"And he will speak to the people while in the cradle and in maturity, and [he will be] among the righteous."
interpretation: The phrase points to divine authentication of a prophetic mission: extraordinary signs that transcend normal human development (speech in infancy and later authoritative speech) serve to vindicate the person and establish his trustworthiness and divine commission. By coupling these signs with the description “of the righteous,” the verse teaches that prophetic authority is not merely miraculous spectacle but is inseparable from moral integrity and exemplary conduct—God validates a messenger both by supernatural confirmation and by the righteous life that gives lasting ethical and spiritual authority.

translation: She said, “My Lord, how can I have a son when no man has touched me?” He said, “Thus [it will be]; Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”
interpretation: The passage affirms God’s absolute creative sovereignty: He is not limited by ordinary causes, and His will alone brings things into existence. What appears impossible from a human perspective can be effected by God’s command — He decrees and it immediately comes to be.

translation: “And He will teach him the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel.”
interpretation: This verse affirms that God endowed Jesus (ʿĪsā) with divinely bestowed knowledge: not merely the specific scripture revealed to him but also deep, practical wisdom and understanding of the earlier revealed books (the Tawrāh) and the Injeel, thereby validating his prophetic role, his capacity to teach and judge rightly, and the continuity of God’s guidance across earlier revelations.

translation: “And (I am) a messenger to the Children of Israel: I have come to you with a sign from your Lord — that I will create for you out of clay the likeness of a bird, then I will breathe into it and it will be a bird by Allah’s leave; and I will heal the blind and the leper, and I will raise the dead by Allah’s leave; and I will inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses. Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the extraordinary acts attributed to Jesus function as divinely granted signs to establish his prophethood and to point people to God’s power. By highlighting that these works occur “by Allah’s leave,” the passage stresses God’s sole sovereignty over creation, life, healing, and knowledge of the unseen; miracles authenticate a messenger’s mission and call people to faith, but they remain manifestations of God’s authority rather than proof of any partner to Him.

translation: And [it is] confirming what was before it of the Torah, and I have made lawful for you some of what had been forbidden to you. And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord; so fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Prophet’s message is a continuation and confirmation of earlier revelation, and that God — not human tradition — determines legal rulings, sometimes permitting what was previously restricted. The mention of a divine ‘sign’ both validates the Prophet’s authority and calls for a response: true religious life requires God‑consciousness (taqwa) and submission to the messenger because he faithfully communicates God's guidance and legal adjustments for the community’s welfare.

translation: Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The statement affirms the single, shared lordship of God over the prophet and the people, repudiating any notion that a prophet is divine or that different deities rule different communities. By commanding “worship Him,” it makes exclusive submission to God—obedience, devotion, and following His guidance—the essential religious response. Calling this “a straight path” indicates that pure monotheistic worship and living according to God’s guidance is the clear, correct way to moral and spiritual truth, in contrast to deviations such as idolatry, ascribing partners to God, or innovations that divert people from authentic guidance.

translation: When Jesus perceived their disbelief, he said, “Who will be my helpers to (the cause of) Allah?” The disciples said, “We are Allah’s helpers; we have believed in Allah and bear witness that we are Muslims.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true support for a prophet (or for God’s message) is rooted in inner conviction and active submission: Jesus’s call for “helpers to Allah” is answered not by mere allegiance or numbers but by companions who accept tawhīd, declare their faith, and commit to living under God’s guidance. The disciples’ reply frames assistance as spiritual and ethical—believing in God, testifying to that belief, and adopting the stance of Islam (submission)—so that being a helper of God means embodying belief, witness, and obedience in the face of opposition.

translation:
رَبَّنَا آمَنَّا بِمَا أَنزَلْتَ وَاتَّبَعْنَا الرَّسُولَ فَاكْتُبْنَا مَعَ الشَّاهِدِينَ
“Our Lord, we have believed in what You revealed and we have followed the Messenger; so record us among the witnesses.”
interpretation: The phrase is a devotional petition in which believers, having acknowledged the truth of divine revelation and committed to follow the Prophet, ask God to enroll them among those who bear witness to that truth — meaning both to be publicly identified with and to actively testify for God’s guidance in this life and to be counted among the righteous who will attest to the message on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: And they plotted, and Allah planned; and Allah is the best of planners.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human conspiracies, however cunning, are encompassed and outweighed by God’s sovereign wisdom. God’s “planning” is not deceit but perfect knowledge and authority: He foresees, permits, redirects, or frustrates human schemes so that they ultimately serve His just purpose—often turning plots meant for harm into causes of good for the righteous and ruin for the wrongdoers.

translation: When God said, “O Jesus, indeed I will take you (mutawaffīka) and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve, and make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection.” Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse announces divine intervention on behalf of Jesus: God promises to remove him from the harm of hostile disbelievers by taking him in a way that secures him (understood as his being saved from humiliation or death at their hands and/or being raised bodily), to elevate his rank before God, and to vindicate and distinguish his true followers from their opponents. The making of his followers “superior” indicates a moral and religious ascendancy—God’s support for the faithful believers and the ultimate vindication of the prophetic message—lasting until the Resurrection. The final clause reminds that all parties return to God for the ultimate adjudication: longstanding disputes about Jesus’ status and related theological disagreements will be settled by God’s judgment, not by human contention.

translation: As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse asserts a principle of divine justice: persistent rejection of God’s guidance and active hostility toward the truth brings both tangible consequences in this life (loss of guidance, social or moral downfall, humiliation) and ultimate retribution in the Hereafter. The phrase “they will have no helpers” emphasizes that no allies, protectors, or intercessors will be able to avert God’s decree for those who persist in disbelief. The warning is meant to deter arrogance and obstinacy and to remind people of the grave consequences of turning away from Divine guidance.

translation:
وأما الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات فيوفيهم أجورهم ۗ والله لا يحب الظالمين
“As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their due rewards; and Allah does not love the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The verse affirms God's justice and mercy: genuine faith joined with righteous action will be fully recompensed by God—no rightful reward will be lost—while God disapproves of injustice and oppression (whether committed against others or against oneself), and such wrongdoing excludes one from His love and favor.

translation: That is what We recite to you of the verses and the Wise Reminder.
interpretation: The statement affirms that the words given to the Prophet are divinely revealed material—clear signs (verses) paired with a ‘wise reminder’—and that their purpose is not merely information but formative guidance: to correct hearts, establish truth, warn and instruct people in belief and conduct. Because they come from God’s wisdom, they demand reflection, acceptance, and obedience rather than casual dismissal.

translation: Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam. He created him from dust; then He said to him, "Be," and he was.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Jesus (ʿĪsā), like Adam, came into existence solely by God's creative command — his miraculous origin does not imply divinity but illustrates that life and extraordinary events result from Allah’s sovereign power to create by His word; thus prophets and human beings remain created dependents of God, and miracles point to God’s authority rather than to the intrinsic divinity of those through whom they occur.

translation: The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the revelation is a definitive, divine reality and issues a command to abandon vacillation: the Prophet (and by extension the sincere believer) must accept and act on this guidance with certainty, not be swayed by speculative skepticism or hesitant indecision that rejects clear evidence; it calls for firm conviction, trust in God's message, and decisive transmission of it rather than remaining in paralyzing doubt.

translation: So if anyone disputes with you concerning him after the knowledge that has come to you, say: Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then we will pray and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars.
interpretation: The verse establishes mubahala — a solemn, prayerful appeal to God to judge between parties — as a last resort for resolving a theological dispute when clear evidence has already been presented but denial persists. By proposing to bring their children, women and themselves, the Prophet both underscores the gravity of the challenge and signals the moral courage and special standing of his household, who are willing to stake their honor before God rather than engage in rhetorical contest. Thus the passage teaches that when persuasion by reason and signs fails, truth may be entrusted to God’s judgment, and it affirms the Prophet’s and his family's readiness to be validated directly by divine decree rather than by mere argument.

translation: Indeed, this is the true account. There is no god but Allah, and indeed Allah — He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the narrative is a truthful, divinely-willed account meant to confirm tawhîd (there is no deity except God); by naming God al-ʿAzīz (the All‑Mighty) and al‑Hakīm (the All‑Wise) it teaches that the events related—however painful or puzzling—occur under God’s sovereign power and wise purpose, so the proper response is trust in God, patience under trial, and submission to His wisdom.

translation: But if they turn away, then indeed Allah is All‑Knower of the corrupters.
interpretation: If people reject guidance and persist in causing corruption or spreading mischief, their turning away does not put them beyond Divine awareness; Allah fully knows their actions, motives and schemes and will hold them accountable or frustrate their wrongdoing. This is a warning that apparent success of corrupters is temporary because God observes and will respond justly.

translation: Say, “O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you — that we will not worship except Allah, and will not associate anything with Him, and will not take one another as lords besides Allah.” But if they turn away, then say, “Bear witness that we are Muslims.”
interpretation: This verse is an invitation to sincere, principled dialogue grounded in the common, irreducible core of faith: exclusive worship of God and the rejection of any form of association with Him — including elevating other human beings to the status of lords or ultimate authorities. It calls for resolving disputes by returning to that shared testimony of pure monotheism as the basis for mutual recognition and moral unity. At the same time it sets a clear boundary: if the other side persists in rejecting that foundational principle, the believers are to state their identity as submitters to God and cease attempts to compromise core doctrine — offering witness respectfully rather than forcing agreement. The verse thus balances outreach and firmness: it promotes honest interfaith engagement on a minimal, theologically decisive common ground while safeguarding the uncompromising ethical and spiritual meaning of tawhid (the oneness of God).

translation: O People of the Scripture, why do you dispute about Abraham, when neither the Torah nor the Gospel was revealed until after him? Will you not then use reason?
interpretation: God rebukes the People of the Book for debating Abraham’s identity and faith while appealing to scriptures that came later; the verse insists that one cannot fairly judge Abraham by texts revealed after his time and calls for sound reason — pointing to Abraham’s primordial stance of pure monotheism (hanīf) and submission to God, which predated and was later affirmed (not created) by the Torah and the Gospel.

translation: ها أنتم هؤلاء: لقد جادلتم فيما كان لكم به علم، ولم تُجادلوا فيما ليس لكم به علم. والله يعلم وأنتم لا تعلمون.
interpretation: الآية توبخ قومًا يتعاملون بالمنافع والأهواء: يجتهدون ويرتفعون في الخصام حول ما يمتلكون دليلاً أو مصلحة فيه، لكنهم يغضون الطرف أو يتهربون من الجدال والتقصي في المسائل التي يجهلونها أو التي تتطلب استقامة ضمائرهم. الرسالة دعوة للصدق والمنهج العلمي والأخلاقي في الحوار—أن يُبنَى الكلام على علم وتحقيق لا على جهل أو تحيّز، مع تذكير أن المعرفة الحقيقية عند الله وحده، وعلى الناس أن يطلبوا العلم ويتواضعوا أمام حكمته.

translation: Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; but he was a hanif — a Muslim — and he was not of the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Abraham’s true identity rests not in later communal labels but in his pure, unadulterated submission to God (tawḥīd). Calling him a “hanif” and “muslim” emphasizes his rejection of idolatry and his upright turning toward one God; thus the model of faith presented is sincere surrender to God’s will rather than adherence to an inherited sectarian identity.

translation: Indeed, the most deserving of people in relation to Abraham are those who followed him — and this Prophet and those who believe; and Allah is the Protector of the believers.
interpretation: The verse asserts that true closeness to Abraham is not a matter of bloodline but of following his way of wholehearted submission to God (monotheism, trust, righteous conduct). It includes the Prophet Muhammad and all sincere believers among those who share Abraham’s spiritual legacy, thereby overturning any claim that ancestry alone confers religious superiority. By adding that Allah is the Wali (protector, guardian, ally) of the believers, the verse consoles and affirms that God supports and defends those who adopt Abraham’s faith and conduct, making spiritual commitment the criterion of honor.

translation: A faction among the People of the Book wish that they could lead you astray; but they do not lead astray except themselves, and they do not perceive it.
interpretation: This verse diagnoses a covert hostility: some among the People of the Book desire to divert the Muslim community out of envy or resistance to the new message, yet their schemes cannot change who is truly guided by God. In seeking to mislead others they only increase their own spiritual loss, remaining blind to the moral and religious consequences of their conduct. The passage therefore warns believers to be watchful of such covert opposition, to judge by truth rather than by hostile intent, and it affirms that ultimate responsibility for misguidance lies with those who choose falsehood, not with God’s protectiveness over the rightly guided.

translation: O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while you yourselves bear witness?
interpretation: God reproaches those among the People of the Book who, despite having scriptures, knowledge and internal testimony that point to Divine signs and truth, nonetheless reject them. The verse highlights the moral and intellectual contradiction of denying what one’s own testimony or revealed sources confirm—implying that such rejection is not from ignorance but from obstinacy, misinterpretation, or self-interest, and calls for them to reconcile their denial with the evidence they themselves possess.

translation: O People of the Scripture, why do you mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?
interpretation: This verse reproaches those among the People of the Book who knowingly corrupt or obscure divine guidance: they take what is true from revelation yet blend it with falsehood, distort it, or withhold clear truths for ulterior motives (such as preserving authority, social advantage, or avoiding inconvenient consequences). The admonition emphasizes moral responsibility to transmit and uphold the truth plainly and not to adulterate or suppress it for personal or communal gain, since concealment and mixture of truth with falsehood betray knowledge and invite accountability before God.

translation: وقالت طائفةٌ من أهلِ الكتابِ: "آمنوا بالذي أُنزِلَ على الذين آمنوا في وجهِ النهارِ، واكفروا بآخرِه؛ لعلهم يرجعون".
interpretation: الآية تشير إلى تكتيك بعضِ أهلِ الكتاب الذين يقبلون أجزاءً من الوحي تُوافقُ مذاهبهم أو تفيدهم، ويرفضون الأجزاء الحاسمة التي تثبّت رسالة الإسلام، وذلك على أملِ استدراج المؤمنين للعودة إلى معتقداتهم السابقة. عبارةُ "وجه النهار" تعبّر مجازاً عن القَبول الظاهري أو الجزئي لما يوافقهم، بينما "آخره" يعنى المتصل بالحقيقة الكاملة التي يَحاولون التنكّر لها؛ فالآية تفضح النية الماكرة والقبول الانتقائي كوسيلة للتشويش والإرجاع عن الحق.

translation: “And they say, ‘Do not believe except in those who follow your religion.’ Say, ‘Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah: that someone be given the like of what you were given, or that they dispute with you before your Lord.’ Say, ‘Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of Allah; He grants it to whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.’”
interpretation: The verse rejects religious exclusivism and places ultimate authority for guidance and favor with God alone. It teaches that possession of a scripture, lineage, or claim to truth does not guarantee exclusive entitlement to guidance; Allah may grant similar signs or resolve disputes before Him, and He distributes bounty and guidance according to His wisdom. Believers are therefore to reject claims of inherent superiority and trust that God — vast in mercy and fully knowing — is the final arbiter who gives guidance to whom He wills.

translation: He singles out with His mercy whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: This affirms that mercy is ultimately an act of God’s sovereign grace, allotted according to His perfect knowledge and wisdom rather than as a debt owed to anyone. It invites humility and trust: one should seek God’s mercy through right conduct and sincere turning, while recognizing that receiving it depends on God’s will. The phrase “Possessor of great bounty” emphasizes that whatever mercy and favors are granted flow from God’s abundant, generous nature—far beyond human merit—and that apparent withholding of particular favors does not imply injustice but the exercise of divine wisdom.

translation: And among the People of the Scripture are some who, if you entrust them with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them are some who, if you entrust them with a dinar, will not return it to you except while you stand over them. That is because they say, “There is no obligation on us concerning the unlettered,” and they utter against Allah that which is false, while they know.
interpretation: The verse exposes a moral and legal hypocrisy: some individuals manipulate religious technicalities to evade duties toward others, using alleged exemptions (here, “no obligation concerning the unlettered”) as a pretext for shirking trust and fairness. The lesson is twofold—do not paint entire communities with one brush (there are trustworthy and untrustworthy people everywhere), and beware of those who knowingly distort religious rules to justify dishonesty, for such distortion is tantamount to lying about God and corrupts social relations and mutual obligations.

translation:
بلى من أوفى بعهده واتقى فإن الله يحب المتقين
“But indeed, whoever fulfills his covenant and is conscious of Allah — then Allah loves the God‑fearing (the pious).”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true piety (taqwa) is shown not merely by ritual acts but by moral integrity: keeping promises and covenants. Fulfilling what one has committed to—toward God or people—together with God‑consciousness, is a core mark of the righteous; those who combine trustworthiness with fear/respect of God attain His love and favor.

translation: Indeed, those who buy a small gain at the cost of the covenant of Allah and their oaths—those will have no share in the Hereafter; Allah will not speak to them, nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them; and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that exchanging sacred commitments to God—whether pledges of faith, moral duties, or sworn promises—for petty worldly profit (bribery, hypocrisy, or betrayal) destroys a person’s claim to divine mercy. The vivid consequences (no speech from God, no divine gaze, no purification) indicate a total severing of relationship with Allah: loss of guidance, loss of acceptance of one’s deeds, and loss of spiritual rehabilitation, to be followed by severe recompense. Its practical lesson is the absolute sanctity of covenants and oaths and a stern admonition against sacrificing integrity and religious duty for fleeting material advantage.

translation: And indeed among them is a party who twist their tongues with the Book so that you would think it is from the Book, while it is not from the Book; and they say, “It is from Allah,” while it is not from Allah; and they utter against Allah what is false, and they know it.
interpretation: The verse criticizes those who deliberately manipulate revealed texts—altering words, phrasing, or presentation—to make inventions or biased readings appear as if they were part of divine scripture, and then assert that these alterations come from God. It denounces this conscious deception as a moral and theological corruption: by falsifying divine speech to serve their own aims (social, political, or doctrinal), they mislead others and bear culpability for knowingly attributing lies to God. The warning is both about the act (twisting language to pass off human additions as revelation) and about the culpability of those who do so with full awareness.

translation: It is not fitting for any human that Allah should give him the Book, wisdom and prophethood, and then he would tell the people, “Be servants to me instead of Allah.” Rather, be rabbāniyyīn (devoutly devoted to the Lord) in what you teach of the Book and in what you study.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those entrusted with divine revelation and religious authority must not turn that trust into demands for personal worship or worldly power; their proper role is to cultivate humble, God-centered scholarship and piety—to teach, study, and form a community of learned, obedient servants of God (rabbāniyyīn)—so religious leadership is defined as service, instruction, and moral example, not self-exaltation or authoritarian rule.

translation: And He does not command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He command you to disbelieve after you have submitted?
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s exclusive right to be worshipped and rejects any notion of deifying prophets or angels: God would not instruct people to ascribe partners or lords besides Him, because that would be tantamount to commanding disbelief after one has accepted submission. Thus prophets and angels are to be honored as God’s servants and messengers, not worshipped or given ultimate authority—worship and obedience belong to God alone.

translation: And [remember] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: “Whatever I give you of the Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and help him.” He said, “Do you agree, and will you accept this obligation upon you?” They said, “We agree.” He said, “Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that God bound the line of prophets to a single, ongoing commitment: when a later messenger appears who confirms the earlier revelation, the earlier prophets (and by implication their communities) are required both to believe in that confirmer and to support him. The covenant stresses the continuity and unity of divine guidance—scripture and wisdom given earlier point forward to a confirming prophet—and makes acceptance of truth, even when it comes later, an essential part of prophetic responsibility. God’s statement “I am with you among the witnesses” underlines the solemn, divine guarantee of this pledge and frames belief in successive messengers as part of the consistent, witnessed plan of revelation.

translation: So whoever turns away after that—then those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse warns that when a person knowingly rejects or abandons clear guidance, covenant, or truth after it has been made plain, that deliberate turning away marks them as a fāsiq: someone who habitually breaks God’s moral limits and repudiates rightful guidance, thereby placing themselves in a state of rebellion with attendant spiritual and communal consequences.

translation: Are they seeking a religion other than Allah’s? To Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse confronts any attempt to establish a rival way to God by affirming Allah’s exclusive and universal sovereignty: every creature ultimately yields to His rule—some by conscious faith, others by necessity—so human beings are morally obliged to recognize that ultimate authority, choose genuine submission rather than inventing alternative creeds, and live in awareness that all will return to God for judgment.

translation: قُلْ آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَمَا أُنزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَمَا أُنزِلَ إِلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطِ وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَىٰ وَعِيسَىٰ وَالنَّبِيُّونَ مِن رَّبِّهِمْ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِّنْهُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ
interpretation: الآية تُكْتَبُ مبدَأً عقائدياً أساسياً: الإيمان بوحدة الرسالة الإلهية واستمرارها عبر الأنبياء والكتب، ورفض التمييز الانتقائي بينهم. هي دعوة للاعتراف بأن الهداية جاءت متعاقبة من رب واحد، وأن المؤمن الحق يلتزم الاستسلام لله بإقرار كل نبي وما أنزل عليه كجزء من حكمة إلهية متصلة، لا بتجزئتها أو استثنائها.

translation: And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted of him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s acceptance of a person rests on sincere submission to His guidance — here called “Islam” (surrender to God and adherence to the revelation He sent). Those who knowingly turn to a different system of belief or way of salvation, rejecting or abandoning the divinely prescribed path, cannot expect their deeds to be accepted by God; consequently they incur loss in the Hereafter. The statement stresses that true religious legitimacy and the efficacy of actions are determined by God’s criterion of submission and faith, not by human preferences or invented rites, and it serves as a warning to align one’s creed and practice with God’s guidance out of genuine surrender.

translation: How can Allah guide a people who disbelieved after they had believed and had borne witness that the Messenger was true, and clear proofs had come to them? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance is tied to a sincere, receptive heart: when people knowingly reject the truth after witnessing clear evidence and affirming the Messenger, their persistent choice reveals a hardening and injustice against their own souls. Because guidance requires openness and acceptance, Allah does not grant guidance to those who willfully persist in denial and wrongdoing — not as a denial of His power, but as the consequence of their deliberate rejection which renders further guidance ineffective.

translation: Their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of all people together.
interpretation: The verse pronounces a comprehensive repudiation: those guilty of the condemned behavior incur a threefold condemnation—divine punishment from Allah, enforcement or testimony of that judgment by the angels, and collective rejection by people. The triple phrasing stresses total loss of divine favor, absence of protection or intercession, and social ostracism; it functions as a stern warning that persistent, deliberate transgression (especially against God’s ordinances or His Messenger) brings irrevocable spiritual and communal consequences both in this world and the Hereafter.

translation: They will abide therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be granted respite.
interpretation: This verse asserts the irrevocable finality of divine retribution for those who persist in rejection and grave wrongdoing: their torment in the Hereafter will be continuous and uncompromised—neither reduced nor deferred—underscoring the seriousness of persistent sin and the ultimate certainty of divine justice.

translation: Except those who repent after that and amend (their deeds); for Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s mercy is available to those who genuinely turn back: sincere repentance accompanied by concrete reform erases prior culpability before God. It emphasizes that true return to Allah involves both inner remorse and outward change, and that through such repentance one may attain divine pardon because Allah is ever-forgiving and compassionate.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief—never will their repentance be accepted; and they are the ones astray.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a willful, persistent turning away from truth after having embraced it is a moral and spiritual condition of hardened rejection: such sustained apostasy shows an entrenched refusal of guidance that frustrates sincere repentance, and therefore those who remain in that state are rightly described as being misguided.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers — never will the earth, were it filled with gold, be accepted from any of them, even if he offered it as ransom. For them there is a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate accountability before God is based on faith and repentance, not on wealth or worldly bargaining; no amount of riches—even the earth filled with gold—can atone for persistent denial of the truth at the time of death, so those who die in disbelief face inevitable punishment and find that neither material means nor human allies can rescue them.

translation: You will never attain righteousness until you spend [in charity] from that which you love. And whatever you spend — indeed Allah is Knowing of it.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true piety is proven by generous sacrifice: giving only surplus or what is easy does not complete moral excellence. To reach ‘‘al‑birr’’ one must give from what one holds dear, because such giving demonstrates sincere trust in God and detachment from worldly attachments. The reminder that God is fully aware of what and how much one gives underscores that outward acts are inseparable from inner value and intention, and that God will judge and reward accordingly.

translation: All food was lawful for the Children of Israel, except what Israel (Jacob) had forbidden to himself before the Torah was revealed. Say, “Then bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful.”
interpretation: The verse challenges reliance on ancestral or private prohibitions by showing that religious law must be rooted in revealed scripture. It exposes claims based on undocumented custom (or individual vows) and demands documentary proof — asking opponents to produce and read the Torah — thereby asserting that valid communal rules come from the revealed text, not from unauthorised personal restrictions or later oral accretions.

translation: So whoever invents a lie against Allah after that—those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse warns that falsely attributing words, rulings, or revelations to God once His guidance has been made clear is a severe moral crime: such fabricators commit injustice by corrupting the truth, misleading people, and thereby earn culpability and accountability for leading others away from God’s guidance.

translation: Say, “Allah has spoken the truth.” So follow the religion of Abraham, upright; he was not of the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse commands acceptance of the divine message to be followed by concrete return to the pure, uncompromised monotheism exemplified by Abraham (hanīf). It means that once one affirms the truth of God’s revelation, one must reshape belief and practice to match Abraham’s orientation: sincere inner turning to God, moral integrity, and rejection of idolatry, cultural compromises or sectarian distortions. The verse stresses that true faith is not mere verbal assent but a living commitment to the singular, upright way of Abraham.

translation: Indeed, the first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah — blessed and a guidance for the worlds.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God chose a specific, divinely-sanctified sanctuary (the Kaʿbah in Bakkah/Mecca) as the inaugural, communal locus of worship for humanity. Its being “blessed” signals special sanctity and divine favor, while calling it “guidance for the worlds” shows that its purpose is universal: to serve as a lasting spiritual axis and visible sign that draws people toward monotheism, communal unity, ritual orientation (prayer, pilgrimage), and moral order beyond tribal or temporal boundaries.

translation: In it are clear signs: the Station of Abraham. And whoever enters it shall be safe. And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people who are able to find a way to it. And whoever disbelieves — then indeed, Allah is free of need from the worlds.
interpretation: The verse designates the Kaʿbah and its precincts as loci of divine, tangible signs (exemplified by Maqām Ibrāhīm), affirming their sacredness and the special security afforded to those who enter them; it establishes ḥajj as a binding act of worship and a communal obligation upon every person who has the physical, financial and safe access to perform it, so that the community manifests submission to God and remembrance of the prophetic legacy. The closing clause reminds that rejection of this duty or of faith does not diminish God’s self-sufficiency—loss and accountability fall upon the disbeliever, not upon Him.

translation: Say, “O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah? And Allah is a witness over what you do.”
interpretation: The verse challenges those who claim attachment to earlier revelation but deny the clear signs brought by God’s final message, calling them to honest self-examination: their rejection is not merely a theological disagreement but a moral inconsistency that God, who fully knows both outward deeds and inner motives, testifies to and will hold accountable.

translation: Say, “O People of the Scripture, why do you prevent from the way of Allah those who believe, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And Allah is not unaware of what you do.”
interpretation: The verse indicts religious custodians among the People of the Book who, despite their position as guardians of revelation and therefore bearing witness, actively obstruct sincere seekers of God by twisting doctrine, erecting social or legal barriers, or promoting distortions that make the straight path seem wrong. It emphasizes that such gatekeeping is an abuse of their entrusted role: their witness increases their responsibility, and their maneuvers—motivated by prejudice, fear of losing authority, or envy—do not escape divine knowledge. The warning is moral and juridical: preventing guidance through theological or institutional manipulation is a grave sin for which they will be held accountable.

translation: O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will turn you back after your faith, into disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against submitting to or following a group among the People of the Book when that obedience would override or compromise Islamic belief and practice. It means that allowing such a faction to dictate religious matters, allegiances, or doctrines can draw Muslims away from the faith they embraced and lead them into disbelief; therefore believers must remain committed to the revealed guidance and not let external parties determine their creed or community identity in ways that undo their iman.

translation: And how can you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are being recited to you and His Messenger is among you? And whoever holds fast to Allah has indeed been guided to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who reject faith despite direct access to divine signs and the Prophet’s presence, and teaches that true guidance is obtained by ‘holding fast to Allah’—an active, sincere clinging expressed through firm belief, obedience, reliance, and conformity to the Qur’an and the Messenger; whoever truly grasps this ‘rope of God’ is delivered onto the straight way.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah as He ought to be feared, and do not die except while you are Muslims (in submission).
interpretation: This command calls believers to a deep, continual God‑consciousness (taqwa) — not a mere ritual fear but reverence, sincere obedience, and constant awareness of Allah’s rights and commands — such that one’s whole life is oriented toward submission. The warning “do not die except as Muslims” stresses the importance of maintaining and preserving that inner state until death: one must keep faith alive by repentance, upright actions, truthfulness, and avoidance of hypocrisy and major sins, so that one’s final state at death is genuine surrender to God.

translation: And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you — when you were enemies He brought your hearts together, so by His favor you became brothers; and you were on the edge of a pit of the Fire and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse enjoins communal fidelity to the single bond that truly unites believers — the revelation and covenant of God — warning that authentic religious life requires collective adherence rather than factionalism. Calling it the “rope of Allah” emphasizes that unity must be rooted in what God has revealed and in mutual submission to His guidance; it is not merely a political or social alliance. The reminder of God’s prior favor — turning hostility into brotherhood and rescuing people from spiritual ruin — is given so believers recognize unity as a divine gift that demands gratitude expressed through steadfastness, mutual support, and the rejection of schism. In short, the passage ties moral responsibility (holding fast to revealed guidance together) to historical grace (being saved from division and peril) and presents God’s clear signs as means by which communities are both formed and kept rightly guided.

translation: And let there be from among you a community who invite to goodness, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong; and those are the successful.
interpretation: The verse obliges the community to cultivate a committed minority whose task is to shape society’s moral direction: success is not merely private faith but the collective responsibility to promote what is good and to resist harm. This duty implies organized, persistent moral engagement—through teaching, example, and fair action—carried out with knowledge, wisdom and patience, so that communal life reflects ethical principles rather than leaving reform to individuals alone.

translation: And do not be like those who split and differed after clear proofs had come to them; for those there will be a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse admonishes the community to safeguard unity by submitting to the clear guidance God has given; when people let personal desires, pride, or partisan interests override that guidance and they fracture into factions and disputes despite having clear evidence, they commit a serious breach that brings divine accountability.
