translation: For men is a share of what parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what parents and close relatives leave — whether it be little or much; a share prescribed.
interpretation: The verse establishes that inheritance entitlements are divinely ordained for both men and women from the estates of parents and near kin. These shares are mandatory and guaranteed regardless of the size of the estate, serving to protect heirs (including socially vulnerable persons) from arbitrary disinheritance and to ground family wealth distribution in fixed, just rules rather than personal or customary preference.

translation: And when the distribution (of inheritance) is to be made, let those nearest in kin, the orphans and the needy come, and give them from it, and speak to them words of kindness.
interpretation: The verse enjoins that inheritance must be distributed with fairness and compassion: those who have a rightful claim—relatives, orphaned heirs and the poor—must be included and given their due share promptly, not overlooked or deprived. Beyond the legal duty to allocate shares, it stresses preserving human dignity by addressing beneficiaries gently and respectfully, thereby preventing injustice, exploitation and discord when dividing an estate.

translation: Let those be mindful who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them; so let them fear Allah and speak a just/upright word.
interpretation: The verse warns those whose death would leave vulnerable heirs (young, incapable, or defenseless) to act with godly caution: they must protect those dependents by observing Allah’s commands and by making clear, lawful declarations — for example a fair will, appointment of trustworthy guardians or administrators, and plain truthful testimony — so that the rights and welfare of the weak are secured and no injustice befalls them.

translation: Indeed, those who unjustly consume the property of orphans only eat fire into their bellies, and they will enter burning fire.
interpretation: This is a stern moral and legal warning: misappropriating an orphan’s wealth is not merely a crime against people but a spiritual self-destruction. The metaphor “eating fire into their bellies” signifies that the illicit gain will bring no benefit—it will be the source of one’s torment—so that what was seized as profit becomes fuel for punishment. Beyond the literal punishment in the Hereafter, the verse implies immediate moral consequences: loss of blessing, corrosion of conscience, social breakdown, and certain divine accountability. Therefore those entrusted with others’ rights (guardians, judges, officials) must protect and return orphan’s property, for trustworthiness is fundamental and violation guarantees ruin rather than reward.

translation: Allah enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, a share equal to that of two females. If there are two or more females, they shall have two thirds of what is left; but if there is only one, she shall have the half. For the parents, each of them is entitled to one sixth of what the deceased leaves, if he had a child; but if he had no child and his parents are his heirs, then for his mother is one third; and if he has brothers (i.e. siblings), then for his mother is one sixth — all this after any bequest he may have made or any debt. You do not know which of your parents or your children are nearer to you in benefit. This is an ordinance from Allah. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes a precise, divinely mandated inheritance scheme intended to translate social and financial responsibilities into fixed shares so that family needs and rights are protected and disputes are minimized. By allocating a male’s share equal to that of two females, the law recognizes and compensates for the social duty—primarily financial maintenance—that men traditionally bear, while different shares for a mother reflect whether other heirs will also support the deceased’s dependents. Requiring distribution only after settling debts and any legitimate bequest preserves moral and contractual obligations. The reminder that you cannot know which of your parents or children will be most beneficial warns against ad hoc favoritism and justifies fixed, impartial rules: they are a measured, communal solution rooted in God’s knowledge and wisdom to ensure fairness, economic stability, and the protection of vulnerable relatives.

translation: And to you (men) belongs half of what your wives leave if they have no child; but if they have a child, then for you is one fourth of what they leave, after any bequest they may make or any debt. And for them (the wives) is one fourth of what you leave if you have no child; but if you have a child, then for them is one eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you may make or any debt. And if a man or a woman leaves neither descendants nor parents but has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth; but if they are more than that, they share in one third, after any bequest to be given or any debt — an ordinance from Allah. And Allah is Knowing, Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse prescribes fixed, proportionate shares to ensure just distribution of a deceased person’s estate among spouses and certain collateral relatives. It balances the economic needs of surviving spouses with the claims of children (reducing the spouse’s share when there are descendants) and provides specific shares for sole or multiple siblings when there are no direct descendants or parents. The phrase “after any bequest or debt” establishes the legal order: valid debts and permissible bequests (limited so as not to harm the heirs’ ordained shares) must be settled before distributing the prescribed shares, protecting both creditors and the heirs. Declaring this rule as an ordinance from Allah and noting that He is Knowing and Forbearing stresses that these measurements are divinely wise and equitable, intended to prevent disputes, protect vulnerable family members, and preserve social stability through clear, divinely mandated limits.

translation: These are the limits (hudūd) of Allah. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger—He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the great attainment.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the divine rules just mentioned are Allah’s established boundaries designed to preserve justice and well‑being; accepting and living by them—sincere obedience to God and the Prophet—is the path to ultimate success. Rather than mere ritual conformity, this obedience means submitting one’s life to God’s guidance (including moral and legal norms), and the promised consequence is eternal admission into Paradise. Thus the passage teaches that honoring God’s limits secures both social order in this world and the supreme, everlasting reward in the hereafter.

translation: And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits — He will admit him to a Fire, wherein he will abide; and he will have a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that deliberate, persistent rejection of divine authority and prophetic guidance — whether through disbelief, shameless transgression of the moral and legal boundaries God has set, oppression, or open rebellion — severs one from God's mercy and leads to just retribution. ‘‘Entering a Fire’’ and ‘‘abiding therein’’ convey both the reality and enduring nature of that consequence, while the ‘‘humiliating punishment’’ stresses the loss of honor and standing before God. The statement functions as a both theological assurance of divine justice and a practical deterrent, calling people to remain within God’s ordained limits to preserve spiritual dignity and social order.

translation: And those of your women who commit illicit sexual intercourse—bring against them four (witnesses) from among you; and if they testify, confine them to the houses until death takes them or Allah makes for them a way.
interpretation: This verse addresses a measured legal response to proven sexual immorality by women: it requires a high evidentiary standard (four witnesses) and prescribes confinement in the home as a custodial, deterrent and protective measure rather than an immediate corporal punishment. The phrase “until death or Allah makes for them a way” shows the rule is not absolute; it allows for eventual relief through death, genuine repentance, reconciliation, change of legal status (e.g. divorce or other lawful remedy), or Divine mercy. The underlying aims are to protect family and community dignity, to guard against false accusations by demanding strict proof, and to leave room for rehabilitation and God’s clemency.

translation: And as for the two of you who commit it with her, then punish them. But if they repent and make amends, then leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse prescribes both a disciplinary response to a proven sexual transgression and a clear path for restoration: when an illicit sexual act involving a married woman is established, the offenders are to be punished to uphold justice and deter harm; yet if those offenders sincerely repent and repair the wrong (by ceasing the sin, seeking forgiveness, and restoring what was damaged), the communal punishment is to be set aside and they are to be left in peace. The ruling balances social order and moral accountability with the primacy of sincere repentance and God’s readiness to forgive — showing that legal deterrence and compassionate reintegration coexist under divine guidance.

translation: Repentance is only for Allah — for those who do evil in ignorance, then promptly repent; for them Allah will accept repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine forgiveness from God is granted especially to those whose wrongdoing sprang from ignorance, error, or weakness rather than from hardened, persistent rebellion; when such people recognize their fault, feel sincere remorse, cease the sin and quickly turn back to God with a firm resolve not to return, Allah — who fully knows their hearts and the circumstances — accepts their repentance. The emphasis on prompt, sincere turning and on God’s knowledge and wisdom warns that true repentance requires inner transformation, not merely words, and that acceptance rests with God’s wise judgment.

translation: Repentance is not (accepted) of those who continue to commit evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, “I now repent,” nor of those who die while they are disbelievers. For them We have prepared a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that mere last‑moment professions of repentance by people who have persistently lived in sin and disbelief are not accepted: true tawbah requires sincere remorse, an actual break from sinful behavior, and a firm resolve not to return to it, made while one is able to live accordingly. Those who persist in rejection and die in that state cannot reverse their condition after death, and will face the prescribed punishment.

translation: O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will. And do not coerce them in order to take back part of what you gave them — except that they may commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. But if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes therein much good.
interpretation: This verse forbids treating women as property or inheriting them without their consent, and it prohibits husbands from mistreating or pressuring wives to reclaim gifts or dowries; only a clearly proven major sexual misconduct could justify severe legal action. Instead, spouses are commanded to behave with kindness and fair conduct in marriage, and to exercise patience and restraint when they feel aversion, since what one dislikes may contain unforeseen good ordained by God. The ruling affirms the dignity and agency of women within marital relations and emphasizes ethical, compassionate treatment rather than coercion.

translation: And if you intend to exchange one wife for another and you have given one of them a qintar (a large sum), do not take from it anything. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?
interpretation: This verse forbids a husband from recovering the bridal gift (mahr) already given to a wife when he divorces her in order to marry another. Even if the gift was very large (qintar), it must not be reclaimed; to try to do so is condemned as calumny and an obvious moral wrongdoing. The instruction protects the financial rights and dignity of women, warning that using divorce or false accusations as a pretext to deprive a wife of her lawful due is both unjust and sinful.

translation:
وكَيْفَ تَأْخُذُونَهُ وَقَدْ أَفَاضَ بَعْضُكُمْ إِلَىٰ بَعْضٍ وَأَخَذْتُمْ مِيثَاقًا غَلِيظًا
"And how could you take it back, when some of you have already been intimate with one another and you have taken from them a solemn, binding covenant?"
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who seek to reclaim what they gave to their spouses (for example a dowry or other rights) after marriage has been consummated. Intimacy and the marriage contract create a grave, binding covenant (ميثاق غليظ) of mutual rights and obligations; once that covenant has been entered and the marital relationship established, it is unjust and impermissible to seize back what was given or to treat the spouse’s rights as revocable. The phrase "solemn covenant" emphasizes the legal and moral weight of the marital bond, forbidding retroactive retrieval of gifts or privileges that would violate that trust.

translation: And do not marry women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed that was a depravity and detestable and an evil way.
interpretation: The verse prohibits entering into marriage with any woman who was or is married to one’s father, condemning the practice as morally corrupt and socially harmful; the exception “except what has already passed” refers to marriages that occurred before this ruling was revealed, and the moral language underscores the law’s purpose to protect family integrity, lineage, and social order by forbidding a relation seen as indecent and destructive.

translation: Forbidden to you [for marriage] are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts and your maternal aunts, the daughters of your brothers and the daughters of your sisters, your foster-mothers who nursed you, your milk‑sisters, the mothers of your wives, and your step‑daughters who are in your guardianship from the wives with whom you have consummated intercourse — but if you have not consummated, there is no sin upon you — and the wives of your sons who are of your own loins, and that you marry two sisters simultaneously, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse lays down specific marital prohibitions to protect clear lines of kinship, family integrity, and social order. It treats both blood relationships and established foster‑relationships (through nursing) as creating permanent prohibitions, showing that social bonds formed by care carry the same legal and moral weight as biological bonds. The clause about stepdaughters hinges on the factual reality of consummation, demonstrating that the law is sensitive to actual relational status rather than mere formal ties. The prohibition against taking two sisters at once aims to prevent intra‑family rivalry and preserve harmony among close relatives. By adding “except what has already passed” and ending with God’s forgiveness and mercy, the verse both recognizes the binding force of these rules going forward and reassures that past mistakes or situations occurring before the rule’s establishment may be forgiven, emphasizing divine compassion alongside the establishment of ethical limits.

translation: And [forbidden to you are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess. That is the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful to you are (all) others — that you may seek them with your wealth, desiring chastity, not lewdness. So for whatever you enjoy of them, give them their due compensation as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree beyond the obligation. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse lays down a legal and moral framework for sexual relations and marriage: it forbids intercourse with married women while acknowledging, in the historical context of warfare and captivity, the exceptional status of women “whom your right hands possess.” Beyond those prohibitions, men may lawfully form marital bonds with free women by offering a marital gift (mahr) with the purpose of chastity rather than illicit sex; the gift is an obligatory right of the woman and must be given, and spouses may lawfully arrange additional mutually agreed terms after this obligation. The ruling aims to regulate relationships, protect the woman’s financial and dignitary rights, and ensure consensual, honorable contracts — all under God’s knowing and wise judgment.

translation: And whoever among you cannot afford to marry the chaste believing women, then (let him marry) from those whom your right hands possess — of your believing slave girls. And Allah is most knowing of your faith; you are one another. So marry them with the permission of their people and give them their due compensation in a fair manner, the chaste — not the immoral and not those who take secret lovers. But once they are chaste, if they commit indecency, they will receive half the punishment prescribed for free, married women. That is for those among you who fear hardship; and if you are patient, it is better for you. And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse permits men who cannot lawfully marry free, chaste believing women—because of financial, social, or other constraints—to take believing slave-women as lawful partners, while laying down safeguards to protect those women and the moral fabric of society: their faith and mutual humanity are affirmed, consent of their guardians is required, they must be given a proper due (a mahr) and treated as chaste partners rather than as objects of secret or licentious relations. The stipulation that a chastened slave-wife who later commits indecency bears half the legal consequence of a free married woman reflects the verse’s concern with different social and legal statuses in that context, not a licence for mistreatment; overall the aim is to regularize relationships, prevent illicit behavior, secure rights and dignity, and encourage patience and self-restraint as a preferable option, with Divine mercy and forgiveness held out as supreme.

translation: الله يريد أن يبين لكم ويهديكم سنن الذين من قبلكم ويتوب عليكم، والله عليم حكيم.
interpretation: الآية تشير إلى أن مقصود الله من التشريع والبيان ليس مجرد فرض قواعد بل توضيح مسارات حياة أمم مضت—سنن مجربة توضح ما يؤدي إلى صلاح أو فساد المجتمع—لكي يهتدي الناس ويصححوا مسارهم ويقبل منهم التوبة؛ وبما أن هذه العملية تتم بقدرةٍ علمية وحكمة إلهيتين، فالتغيير في أحكام أو البيان أو التاريخ التعليمي للمجتمع هو جزء من حكمة ربانية تهدف إلى بناء أمة واعية تتعلم من تجارب السابقين وتصلح نفسها تحت هدايةٍ واعية ورحمةٍ إلهية.

translation:
وَاللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَن يَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ وَيُرِيدُ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ الشَّهَوَاتِ أَن تَمِيلُوا مَيْلاً عَظِيماً
"And Allah wishes to accept your repentance; but those who follow their desires wish that you should deviate greatly."
interpretation: The verse highlights a moral contrast: God’s disposition toward the believer is mercy and restoration—He seeks their return to right conduct—while people driven by base desires aim to lead others far from the truth. Practically, it warns believers to turn sincerely to God for forgiveness and to be vigilant against influences whose self-serving passions would pull the community into serious error.

translation: Allah intends to lighten your burden; and mankind was created weak.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s rulings are fashioned with human limitations in mind: because people are inherently frail—physically, emotionally and morally—Divine law contains concessions, mitigations and allowances (for illness, necessity, fear, error, hardship, etc.) so that religion does not impose unbearable strain. In short, God’s guidance aims at ease and practical mercy compatible with human weakness.

translation: O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except by trade by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves [or one another]. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.
interpretation: This verse sets a foundational ethical principle: property and life are sacred and must be protected. Illicitly taking another’s wealth—by fraud, coercion, deception, usurpation, or any unjust means—is forbidden; the only legitimate transfer of wealth is consensual, honest exchange. Closely linked to that economic injunction is the prohibition against destroying life, including suicide or killing others, which underscores that desperation, dishonor, or material gain never justify harming oneself or another. Taken together the commands require a social order based on justice, mutual consent, and care for human dignity, reminding believers that God’s mercy accompanies these obligations and that lawful livelihood and the preservation of life are integral to spiritual responsibility.

translation: And whoever does that out of aggression and injustice, We will make him enter a Fire; and that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those who act with wanton aggression and injustice will inevitably be held to account by God and subjected to severe punishment; it serves as a sober warning that transgression against God’s limits and the rights of others will not go unpunished, because bringing about that retribution is entirely within God’s effortless power—therefore justice and restraint are demanded by divine accountability.

translation: If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will expiate for you your (other) sins and admit you to a noble entrance.
interpretation: This verse promises that deliberate avoidance of serious, prohibited transgressions is the key that unlocks God’s mercy: by refraining from major sins believers receive divine pardon for their lesser faults and are granted an honorable admission (understood as a dignified place in the hereafter). It stresses responsibility and prioritization in moral conduct—God’s forgiveness is available, but it is conditioned on turning away from the gravest offenses, showing that mercy and accountability go together.

translation: Do not wish for what Allah has favored some of you with over others. For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse warns against envy of others’ advantages by reminding that God’s distributions relate to individual efforts, roles and responsibilities: each person — man or woman — is entitled to the portion tied to what they acquire or are responsible for, and ultimate provision and honor come from Allah. Rather than coveting what others possess, believers should petition God for His grace and trust His perfect knowledge and wisdom in allotting outcomes.

translation: And to each We have appointed heirs of what parents and close relatives leave, and those whom your oaths have bound — give them their due. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, a Witness.
interpretation: The verse affirms that inheritance and the distribution of a deceased’s estate are divinely ordained rights: Allah specifies rightful beneficiaries (parents, kin) and also includes those to whom one has made binding commitments (for example, persons tied by pledges or contractual obligations). The practical lesson is a moral-legal injunction to honor and dispense exactly what is due to both familial heirs and those bound by one’s oaths or agreements, because Allah is watching and will hold people accountable for fulfilling these obligations.

translation: Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because Allah has given the one more (strength) than the other, and because they spend out of their wealth. So the righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding what Allah would have them guard. As for those from whom you fear rebellion, admonish them, then forsake them in bed, and (as a last resort) lightly strike them; but if they obey you, do not seek a way against them. Indeed Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes a regulated, hierarchical responsibility (qiwamah) in marriage grounded in the duty of men to provide and care, not as a license for unilateral domination. Its practical guidance for dealing with serious, persistent marital discord (nushūz) is graduated and remedial: first counsel, then withdrawal of intimacy as a nonviolent corrective, and only as an absolute last resort the measure expressed by the verb daraba — which the prophetic practice and many scholars limit to a symbolic, non‑injurious action aimed at awakening conscience and restoring harmony, never causing harm or humiliation. The immediate reinstatement of normal relations when obedience and reconciliation occur, and the warning that God is Most High and Great, together curtail any abuse and place the entire procedure within moral, ethical, and legal bounds.

translation: And if you fear a breach between them, then appoint an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people; if they both desire reconciliation, Allah will bring them together in harmony. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse prescribes a structured, fair means of settling serious marital discord by appointing respected, impartial mediators from each spouse’s circle so that disputes are handled with knowledge of each side’s context and rights. It makes clear that successful restoration depends first on the genuine willingness of both partners to repair the relationship; when that sincere intention exists, Allah—who knows hearts and circumstances—can align hearts and circumstances to produce reconciliation. Thus the passage emphasizes procedural justice, communal responsibility to protect the marriage, the centrality of sincere intent, and the ultimate dependence on God’s guidance rather than on coercion or mere formality.

translation: Worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him; and show kindness to parents, to relatives, to orphans, to the needy, to the near neighbor, to the distant neighbor, to the companion at your side, to the wayfarer, and to those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allah does not love the arrogant, the boastful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true devotion to God is inseparable from concrete ethical responsibility: sincere worship of Allah requires exclusive monotheism and is validated by compassionate action toward every human relation — from closest kin to distant neighbors, dependents and travelers, even those under one’s authority. By listing a wide spectrum of social bonds it makes faith’s moral scope comprehensive, showing that religious commitment is measured not by rites alone but by how one treats the vulnerable and the other. The closing warning — that God dislikes the proud and boastful — ties the whole command to inner disposition: humility and modest conduct are essential signs of authentic belief, while arrogance undermines both worship and the social duties it demands.

translation: الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ وَيَأْمُرُونَ النَّاسَ بِالْبُخْلِ وَيَكْتُمُونَ مَا آتَاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ ۗ وَأَعْتَدْنَا لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَذَابًا مُهِينًا
interpretation: الآية تضع البخل ليس مجرد قلة إنفاق بل موقف أخلاقي: من يبخل على نفسه ويشجع غيره على البخل ويُخفي نعم الله عنه ليتهرب من حقٍّ أو ليخفي فضله، يكون قد أبدى جحودًا وفسادًا اجتماعياً ودينياً. ذلك السلوك يهدم التضامن ويستبدل الرحمة بالأنانية، ولهذا تُعرض عليه العقوبة المهينة كتحذير من استمراره في إنكار الحقوق والامتنان وإخراج حق المحتاجين.

translation: And those who spend their wealth to show off to people and do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day; and whoever has Satan as a companion—how evil a companion he is.
interpretation: The verse condemns charitable or pious acts done for public acclaim rather than from true faith. When giving is motivated by ostentation instead of belief in God and accountability in the Hereafter, the deed becomes spiritually bankrupt and aligned with Satan’s influence. Calling Satan a “companion” indicates that hypocrisy and show turn a person’s closest moral guide into a deceiver who corrupts good acts, turning them into sources of loss rather than of reward; the verse therefore urges sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and consciousness of God and the Hereafter as the proper basis for righteous action.

translation: فَمَا لَهُمْ إِنْ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَأَنفَقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقَهُمُ اللَّهُ ۚ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ بِهِمْ عَلِيمًا
interpretation: الآية توبِّخ أولئك الذين يعطلون خلاصهم بأنفسهم: لو آمنوا بالله وباليوم الآخر وتحرّكوا عملاً بالعطاء مما أنعم الله عليهم لزالت أسباب الانحراف والذنب عنهم. السؤال البلاغي يدل على أن العائق ليس نقصاً في الوسائل بل موقفهم القلبي، وأن الله مطّلع على نواياهم وأعمالهم وسيجازي كل واحد بحسب حقيقته.

translation:
إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَظْلِمُ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ ۖ وَإِنْ تَكْ حَسَنَةً يُضَاعِفْهَا وَيُؤْتِ مِن لَّدُنْهُ أَجْرًا عَظِيمًا
"Indeed, Allah does not wrong even by the weight of an atom; and if there is a good deed He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward."
interpretation: The verse emphasizes God's perfect justice and abundant mercy: He will not oppress anyone even by the smallest measure, so no loss or injustice at the final reckoning will occur, while every good act—however small—is valued beyond its apparent size and is multiplied by God, who grants an immense reward from His own bounty. Practically, this teaches that believers should neither despair over minor shortcomings nor belittle small righteous deeds, because divine accountability is exact yet paired with overwhelming generosity.

translation: So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these?
interpretation: The verse emphasizes inevitable, universal accountability on the Day of Judgment: God will appoint from each people a witness to attest to their acceptance or rejection of guidance, and the Prophet will stand as a witness over his own community. This arrangement removes any excuse of ignorance or denial and serves to establish clear, impartial testimony to each group's moral and religious responsibility before God's judgment.

translation: On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were levelled with them, and they will not be able to hide a word from Allah.
interpretation: The verse teaches that at the Resurrection the remorse and dread of those who rejected the Message will be so overwhelming that they would prefer annihilation rather than face judgment; simultaneously it affirms God’s absolute knowledge and justice — no speech, excuse, or inward intention can be concealed — which serves as a warning to take the Prophet’s guidance seriously and as a reminder that accountability is unavoidable.

translation: O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor in a state of major ritual impurity—except those passing through—until you have washed. And if you are ill or on a journey or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself or you have contacted women and do not find water, then seek clean earth and wipe over your faces and your hands. Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse sets a principle that prayer requires both conscious presence of mind and ritual cleanliness, because worship is an attentive, dignified encounter with God and cannot be properly offered when one’s faculties are clouded or one remains in a state that ritual law treats as major impurity. At the same time it embodies a merciful legal balance: it forbids praying while intoxicated and requires ghusl after sexual impurity to preserve the sanctity of prayer, but it also makes concessions for real human hardship—travel, illness, recent discharge, lack of water or situations where washing is impractical—by permitting tayammum (striking clean earth and wiping the face and hands) or delaying full ablution. Framed by the reminder that God is Pardoning and Forgiving, the ruling shows that the purpose of the rules is not to burden believers but to protect the integrity of worship while granting ease and accommodation when strict compliance is impossible.

translation:
ألم تر إلى الذين أوتوا نصيبا من الكتاب يشترون الضلالة ويريدون أن تضلوا السبيل
“Do you not see those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They buy misguidance and wish that you be led astray from the way.”
interpretation: The verse censures certain individuals among the People of the Book who, despite possessing part of divine revelation, willfully adopt and promote error. The phrase “يشترون الضلالة” is metaphorical: it denotes a conscious choice to exchange truth for falsehood — often for worldly advantage, pride, factional interest, or to weaken a rival community — rather than mere ignorance. Their conduct is intentional (“يريدون أن تضلوا السبيل”): they aim to divert others from the straight path by twisting texts, imposing corrupt interpretations, or spreading misleading claims. The passage therefore warns believers to be discerning, not to accept religious guidance uncritically simply because it comes from recognized authorities, and to remain attached to the authentic message so as not to be led astray by those who exploit scripture for ulterior motives.

translation: And Allah is most knowing of your enemies. And sufficient is Allah as a protector (wali), and sufficient is Allah as a Helper.
interpretation: The verse reassures believers that God alone fully knows the reality, intentions and capabilities of those who oppose them; therefore true security lies in turning to Allah — His knowledge, guardianship and support are enough to neutralize plots, to be a protector when human allies fail, and to grant victory or relief, so believers should place their trust in Him rather than be overwhelmed by fear of adversaries.

translation: Among those who are Jews are men who distort words from their places and say, “We hear and we disobey,” and “Hear us” — yet they do not listen; and “Look to us” — twisting their tongues and attacking the religion. And if they had said, “We hear and we obey,” and “Hear and look upon us,” it would have been better for them and more upright; but Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they believe only a little.
interpretation: The verse condemns the deliberate manipulation of revelation and the hypocrisy that accompanies it: some profess to receive divine teaching while altering its meanings to suit their interests, instructing others to accept their distortions, and using rhetoric to undermine true guidance. True “hearing” in the Qur’anic sense requires submission and action — saying “we hear and we obey” — whereas claiming to hear while choosing disobedience reveals bad faith. The passage teaches that corrupting scripture and employing deceptive speech leads to moral and communal decay and divine disapproval, and that humble acceptance and obedience would have restored uprightness and a sound community.

translation: O you who were given the Scripture, believe in what We have revealed, confirming that which is with you, before We obliterate faces and send them back on their heels, or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath. And the command of Allah is always done.
interpretation: This verse admonishes the People of the Book to accept the Qur'an as the confirmation and continuation of earlier revelation: rejection is not a mere intellectual stance but risks a decisive reversal of status and blessing. The images of faces being obliterated or turned back on their heels and of a curse like that inflicted on those who violated the Sabbath signify public humiliation, loss of honour and the withdrawal of divine favour that follows persistent denial. The mention that God’s command is inevitably accomplished underlines that salvation depends on timely acceptance and sincere obedience, while stubborn refusal brings moral and communal consequences ordained by God.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly invented a tremendous sin.
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute centrality of tawḥīd (the oneness of God) in Islam: making partners with God is a unique and ultimate transgression because it denies or dilutes the very attribute that defines the Divine. Such association, if one dies upon it without sincere repentance, cuts off the possibility of God’s forgiveness in the sense intended here, because it annihilates the foundational relationship on which acceptance rests. By contrast, other sins — however grave — remain within the scope of God’s mercy and may be forgiven according to His will. The phrase “has indeed fabricated a tremendous sin” underscores that shirk is not merely a wrong action but a falsehood and injustice against God and oneself: it ascribes to created things what belongs to the Creator and thus distorts reality and moral responsibility. The practical lesson: preserve pure monotheism, understand God’s forgiveness is vast yet founded on His sovereignty, and seek sincere repentance from any deviation before it becomes final.

translation: أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى الَّذِينَ يُزَكُّونَ أَنفُسَهُمْ ۚ بَلِ اللَّهُ يُزَكِّي مَن يَشَاءُ وَلا يُظْلَمُونَ فَتِيلًا
interpretation: الآية توبخ من يفتخرون بتزكية أنفسهم ويدّعون أنهم أنقوا وملائكة بأفعالهم، وتذكر أن التطهير الحقيقي والتغيير القلبي منحة إلهية يمنحها الله لمن يشاء بحكمته؛ فالإصلاح البشري لا يلغي حاجة الإنسان إلى رحمة وتوفيق الله. وفي الوقت نفسه تؤكد عدل الربّ: لا يُظلم أحد بأصغر قدر — لا يُحال أحد إلى فقدان حقه أو أجره ظلماً — فالموقف المطلوب هو التواضع والطلب المستمر لزكاة الله لا التكبر على الناس باعتبار النفس مُطهّرة بذاتها.

translation: See how they invent lies against Allah; and sufficient is that as a manifest sin.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who knowingly fabricate falsehoods about God—attributing to Him words, laws, partners, or intentions that He has not revealed—and declares that such fabrication is by itself a clear and sufficient sin; it stresses that inventing doctrines or statements in God’s name is a grave theological and moral offense that corrupts guidance, misleads people, and merits condemnation.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in al‑jibt and al‑taghūt, and say to those who disbelieve, “These are more rightly guided than the believers.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes some among the People of the Scripture who, despite possessing revealed guidance, accept falsehoods—represented by al‑jibt (idolatry/superstitions/false cults) and al‑taghūt (false authorities, tyrants, or systems that divert from God)—and thereby align with and praise outright disbelievers, claiming they are better guided than the true believers. It diagnoses a moral and spiritual failure: preference for corrupt allies, self‑interest, prejudice, or political advantage over fidelity to the truth of revelation, and warns the community to recognize and resist the corrupting influence of false creeds and power structures.

translation: Those are the ones upon whom Allah has pronounced a curse; and whoever Allah curses, you will never find for him any protector or helper.
interpretation: When God’s curse is mentioned here it signifies withdrawal of divine favor and guidance: a person so condemned is spiritually and morally isolated, deprived of true legitimacy and inner support, so that no protector — whether worldly ally or false authority — can avert the consequences. The statement emphasizes that ultimate security comes from God’s approval, and without it apparent assistance is powerless to change one’s standing before Him.

translation: Or do they have a share of sovereignty? If so, they would not give the people even the smallest thing.
interpretation: The verse points out the impotence of those who are claimed to possess divine authority: had they truly held any real rule or power, they would control resources and withhold even the tiniest favor from people. Their inability to benefit or harm others proves they are not truly sovereign and thus unworthy of worship.

translation: Or do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? Indeed We gave the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We granted them a mighty kingdom.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the attitude of envying others' blessings and reframes divine distribution as purposeful rather than arbitrary. By citing the family of Abraham—who were endowed with revelation, deep insight, and great authority—it shows that God’s favors encompass both spiritual guidance and worldly responsibility, given according to His wisdom and plan. Thus envy misconceives blessings as mere personal advantage; true honor and benefit come through God’s chosen guidance and rightly used responsibilities, so one should seek God’s favor by faith, knowledge, and righteous conduct rather than coveting what others possess.

translation:
فَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ آمَنَ بِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ صَدَّ عَنْهُ ۚ وَكَفَىٰ بِجَهَنَّمَ سَعِيرًا
"Among them are some who believed in it and among them are some who turned away from it; and Hell is sufficient as a blazing torment.",
interpretation: The verse underlines that when divine guidance is presented people exercise free will and respond differently; acceptance and rejection are therefore moral choices for which each person is accountable. Describing Hell as “a sufficient blaze” emphasizes the seriousness and completeness of divine retribution for persistent rejection: God’s warning is not empty, and ultimate justice will fully vindicate the truth and punish obstinate denial.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs — We will drive them into a Fire. Whenever their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so that they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.
interpretation: The verse employs vivid, bodily imagery to assert the certainty and continuity of recompense for persistent rejection of divine guidance. The recurring renewal of skin stresses that the sufferers will remain conscious of and repeatedly experience retribution, not that God delights in pain but that He has the power to enact complete, unmistakable justice. Coupled with the attributes “Exalted in Might and Wise,” the passage signals that such consequences serve a wisdom-based purpose — as a stern warning to deter wrongdoing, to affirm the seriousness of denying God’s signs, and to demonstrate that divine authority and justice are absolute and purposeful rather than arbitrary.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds — We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to an expanded shade.
interpretation: The verse assures that true faith coupled with righteous conduct yields an enduring, multifaceted divine reward: the garden imagery (rivers, shade) conveys continual, overflowing sustenance, peace, and protection rather than merely physical luxuries, while “purified spouses” signals relationships purified of malice and moral defect — a condition of spiritual harmony. Emphasizing eternal habitation underscores God’s just and merciful response to sincere moral commitment, so the description functions both as a comforting promise of perfected, lasting felicity and as an incentive to live a life of faith expressed through good works.

translation: Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people to judge with justice. Indeed, Allah exhorts you with that which is best. Indeed, Allah is Ever-Hearing, Ever-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse establishes that social integrity and legitimate authority are divine obligations: “trusts” encompass not only deposited property but any responsibility, right, office or power entrusted to a person, and must be handed back or exercised for its rightful beneficiaries; likewise any adjudication must be impartial and governed by equity regardless of personal ties or interests. The statement that Allah “exhorts you with that which is best” signals that these commands promote human welfare and moral excellence, while “Allah is Hearing and Seeing” reminds that every fulfillment or breach of trust and every judgment is observed by God and will be held to account, making ethical fidelity both a social duty and a matter of spiritual responsibility.

translation: O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.
interpretation: The verse enjoins a hierarchy of allegiance rooted in faith: ultimate obedience belongs to God and His Messenger, and obedience to communal leaders (ulū al-amr) is valid only insofar as it accords with divine guidance. When disagreements arise, the believer’s duty is to submit the matter back to the primary sources — the Qur’ān and the authentic teachings/practice of the Prophet — because doing so manifests genuine belief in God and the Last Day and yields the most sound, just, and lasting resolution. Implicitly the verse limits obedience to human authorities: they are followed as custodians of God’s law, not as sources of independent legitimacy; if their directives conflict with God’s commandments, believers must return to scripture and prophetic example.

translation:
ألم تر إلى الذين يزعمون أنهم آمنوا بما أنزل إليك وما أنزل من قبلك يريدون أن يتحاكموا إلى الطاغوت وقد أمروا أن يكفروا به ويريد الشيطان أن يضلهم ضلالا بعيدا
“Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They wish to refer matters to the Taghūt (false authorities/tyrants/idols), although they were commanded to reject it; and Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”
interpretation: The verse condemns a hypocrisy in which people verbally affirm belief in divine revelation yet prefer to submit disputes, laws, or ultimate authority to illegitimate powers (taghūt—idols, tyrants, corrupt courts, or unlawful custom) instead of God’s guidance. Such referral to false authority shows a turning away from the command to disown and resist taghūt; it is rooted in self-interest, fear of loss, or attachment to worldly positions. Satan exploits those motives to divert sincere-sounding believers from true submission, guiding them far from divine guidance. Thus the passage teaches that true faith requires rejecting illegitimate rulers and judgments and accepting God’s law, because nominal profession without that inward and practical commitment is precisely the pathway of deception.

translation: When it is said to them, “Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,” you see the hypocrites turning away from you in aversion.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a recurrent behavior of hypocrites: when faced with a sincere call to submit to God’s revelation and to follow the Prophet, they do not merely decline quietly but actively recoil and obstruct. Their turning-away is a sign of inner hostility and calculation—protecting worldly ties, pride, or interests—while outwardly avoiding clear commitment. The passage thus warns believers to recognize that some opposition is not ignorance but deliberate resistance, to persevere in calling to the truth, and to expect that such duplicity will be exposed and judged by God.

translation: So what will it be when a calamity befalls them because of what their hands have done, and then they come to you, swearing by Allah, “Had we so intended, we would only have done good and been rightly guided”?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, after suffering the consequences produced by their own deeds, try to escape responsibility by oaths and protestations of good intent; it teaches that outcomes are a result of actions and that mere claims of having only meant well cannot undo or excuse wrongful conduct—sincere intention must be matched by righteous behavior, and accountability before God is real and unavoidable.

translation: أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ مَا فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ، فَأَعْرِضْ عَنْهُمْ، وَعِظْهُمْ، وَقُل لَهُمْ فِي أَنفُسِهِمْ قَوْلًا بَلِيغًا
interpretation: الله مطلع على نياتهم وخفايا صدورهم، فالمعنى العملي للنهي عن التقرّب إليهم هنا هو عدم منحهم ثقة ومكانة داخل الجماعة أو الانخراط معهم كأنهم مؤمنون صادقون؛ ومع ذلك لا تُهمل الدعوة والتحضير الداخلي لهم — بل واجبُك أن تبعد عن معاشرتهم الموطّدة، وتؤنّبهم وتوجّه إليهم كلمة قاطعة ومؤثرة تصيب ضمائرهم (“قولا بليغا في أنفسهم”) تهدف إلى كشف نفاقهم وإيقاظ ضميرهم وإعطائهم فرصة للتوبة، لا إلى مداعبتهم أو مدحهم ظاهريًا.

translation: And We did not send any messenger except that he should be obeyed by permission of Allah. And if, when they wronged themselves, they had come to you and sought forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had sought forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of Repentance, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the authority of the prophets rests on Allah’s sanction: following a messenger is, ultimately, obeying God. It also summons wrongdoers to immediate, sincere return to God—seeking His forgiveness—and indicates that the Prophet’s intercession in prayer on behalf of repentant people is a legitimate means toward restoration. The promise that Allah is “Accepting of Repentance, Merciful” reassures that genuine repentance, approached directly to God (and supported by the Prophet’s supplication), can overcome past sins; it stresses personal responsibility to repent and the compassionate readiness of God to forgive.

translation: No — by your Lord, they will not truly believe until they take you as judge concerning what they differ about among themselves, then feel no reluctance in their souls about what you have decided and submit completely.
interpretation: True faith is not merely outward profession but includes wholehearted acceptance of divine guidance as conveyed by the Prophet. The verse teaches that believers must not only seek the Prophet’s judgment in disputes but must also relinquish personal prejudices, preferences, or tribal loyalties that conflict with that judgment. ‘No reluctance in their souls’ signifies inner assent — a sincere, unreserved conviction that the decision is right — accompanied by full, willing compliance. Thus iman requires both internal acceptance and external submission to God’s law as implemented by the Prophet.

translation: And if We had prescribed for them, “Kill yourselves” or “Leave your homes,” they would not have done it except a few of them. And if they had done what they are admonished with, it would have been better for them and would have made them more firmly established.
interpretation: This passage confronts the moral weakness and lack of sincere commitment among those who claim guidance: even if God had commanded them to make the ultimate sacrifice, most would not comply. The stark hypothetical serves to reveal their unwillingness to undertake difficult obligations and to show that steadfast obedience to God’s counsel — not merely words or selective observance — is what leads to true benefit and a firmer, more stable faith. The verse therefore warns that real spiritual strength comes from acting on admonition, embracing difficult duties when required, and not shrinking from the demands of sincere devotion.

translation: And when We grant them from Us a great reward.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that the ultimate recompense for the faithful is a direct bestowal from God — an immense, gracious reward originating in His mercy and will. It underscores that the highest blessings in the Hereafter (the joy, honors, and nearness to God) are not merely the outcome of measurable deeds alone but are God’s own generous gift, exceeding worldly expectations and given in accordance with His justice and compassion.

translation: And We would have guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: It affirms God’s ability and willingness to lead people by His revelation to the correct way of belief and conduct (the ‘straight path’ of sincere monotheism, righteous practice and balance), while implying that such guidance is effective only insofar as people accept and follow the message — guidance is granted but not forced, respecting human choice.

translation: And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger—those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.
interpretation: The verse promises that sincere obedience to God and His Messenger elevates a believer’s spiritual status so that in the Hereafter they will be counted among the honored ranks—prophets, the truthful, martyrs and the righteous. It means not literal identity with those categories but real nearness to Allah attained by adopting their qualities: faithfulness to divine guidance, truthfulness, readiness to sacrifice for the cause of God, and consistent righteousness. Thus following Allah and the Messenger yields the highest companionship and reward, and calls believers to emulate the moral and spiritual virtues exemplified by those exemplary figures.

translation: That is the bounty from Allah; and sufficient is Allah, the All‑Knower.
interpretation: The verse affirms that any favor, success or advantage ultimately comes from God’s grace, and that God’s knowledge is fully sufficient as a vindication and guide. It teaches reliance on divine wisdom: God alone truly knows causes, intentions and outcomes, so attributing results to Him, accepting His decree, and trusting His judgment are the proper responses rather than seeking human credit or allowing envy, suspicion or accusation to unsettle one’s faith.

translation: O you who believe, take your precautions; then advance in detachments, or advance all together.
interpretation: This is a directive calling the community to constant vigilance and organized readiness in the face of danger: take precautions, and when action is required either send out composed, steady detachments (for reconnaissance, defense or to avoid sudden defeat) or mobilize the whole community at once. It emphasizes prudence, discipline, and collective responsibility—adapting posture and formation to the situation so the community can meet threats effectively.

translation: And among you are those who lag behind; and if an affliction befalls you, he will say, 'Allah has favored me in that I was not among them a witness.'
interpretation: This verse condemns the selfish, cowardly attitude of people who avoid communal responsibility (such as confronting danger or participating in a struggle) and then, when the community suffers, feign gratitude for having been absent. It exposes a corrupt conscience that values personal safety over solidarity and moral duty, showing hypocrisy rather than genuine faith; true faith and upright character demand standing with the community in hardship, not taking pleasure in others’ trials to excuse one’s own avoidance.

translation:
وَإِنْ أَصَابَكُمْ فَضْلٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ لَيَقُولَنَّ كَأَنَّ لَمْ تَكُنْ بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَهُ مَوَدَّةٌ ۖ يَا لَيْتَنِي كُنْتُ مَعَهُمْ فَأَفُوزَ فَوْزًا عَظِيمًا
"And when a bounty from Allah befalls you, he will say, 'It is as if there had been no affection between you and him.' 'Oh, that I were with them — then I would attain a mighty success.'"
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrite’s opportunism: when believers endure hardship for God their loyalty is real, but when God grants success the hypocrite pretends there was never close feeling and expresses regret and a desire to join them only to share in the triumph. It teaches that true faith and fellowship are proven by steadfastness in adversity, not by attaching oneself to people merely at the moment of their victory.

translation:
فَلْيُقَاتِلْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ الَّذِينَ يَشْرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا بِالْآخِرَةِ ۚ وَمَن يُقَاتِلْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ فَيُقْتَلْ أَوْ يَغْلِبْ فَسَوْفَ نُؤْתِيهِ أَجْرًا عَظِيمًا
“So let those fight in the cause of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter; and whoever fights in the cause of Allah and is killed or gains victory—We will surely give him a great reward.”
interpretation: The verse privileges inner intention and self‑sacrifice: it summons those who truly renounce transient worldly benefit for eternal good to engage in struggle for God’s cause, and it affirms that divine recompense is guaranteed for sincere commitment regardless of outward outcome—death as a martyr or victory. Its core lesson is that God values the heart’s readiness to sacrifice and promises a great reward to those whose actions are motivated by that sincere, otherworldly orientation.

translation: And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the cause of Allah and for the oppressed among men, women and children who say, “Our Lord, take us out of this city whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a guardian and appoint for us from Yourself a helper?”
interpretation: The verse reproaches the community for failing to act on behalf of the weak and persecuted, framing assistance to them as a duty ‘‘in the way of God’’ rather than optional charity. By naming men, women and children and recording their plea, the verse exposes the moral urgency: these are innocent people crying to God to be freed from a society ruled by tyranny, and they ask for divine guardianship and support. The rhetorical question—“what is wrong with you that you do not fight…?”—turns the failure to intervene into a spiritual failing, implying that true faith requires standing up to oppression by whatever legitimate means are necessary (moral advocacy, material aid, sanctuary, and, when ethically justified, organized struggle), always within the bounds of God’s law. The promise of divine support is linked to human commitment: God’s aid is invoked for those who respond to the oppressed rather than remain passive observers.

translation: Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of Taghut. So fight against the allies of Satan; indeed the plot of Satan has ever been weak.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the underlying loyalties that drive human conflict: true believers struggle to uphold God’s guidance and justice, whereas disbelievers serve false authorities and oppressive systems (taghut). The injunction to “fight the allies of Satan” calls for active opposition to those who promote falsehood, corruption, tyranny, or lead people away from divine guidance—whether by legitimate defensive combat or by moral, intellectual and social resistance as circumstances require. The concluding assurance that “Satan’s plot is weak” reassures the faithful that deceptive and oppressive schemes are ultimately fragile before God, encouraging courage, steadfastness, and reliance on God in confronting injustice.

translation:
ألم تر إلى الذين قيل لهم كفوا أيديكم وأقيموا الصلاة وآتوا الزكاة فلما كتب عليهم القتال إذا فريق منهم يخشون الناس كخشية الله أو أشد خشية ۚ وقالوا ربنا لم كتبت علينا القتال لولا أخرتنا إلى أجل قريب ۗ قل متاع الدنيا قليل والآخرة خير لمن اتقى ولا تظلمون فتيلا
"Have you not seen those to whom it was said, ‘Hold back your hands, establish prayer, and give zakah’? Then when fighting was prescribed for them, a party of them feared people as they should fear Allah—or even more—and they said, ‘Our Lord, why has fighting been enjoined upon us? Why were we not delayed for a short while?’ Say: ‘The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who are conscious of Allah. And you will not be wronged in the least.’"
interpretation: The verse rebukes a spiritual failing: preferring safety, reputation or comfort in this life over obedience to God’s ordained duty. It exposes how fear of people (social censure, loss, danger) can masquerade as piety when in fact it reveals attachment to fleeting worldly benefits and a lack of true reliance on God. The divine response reframes values—temporal enjoyment is insignificant compared with the lasting good of the Hereafter for the God‑conscious—and reassures that fulfilling God’s command, even at personal cost, will not result in injustice or loss of what truly matters. The practical lesson: genuine taqwa is shown by readiness to obey God despite hardship; reluctance motivated by worldly fear disqualifies such pretence of righteousness and forfeits the superior, eternal gain.

translation: Wherever you are, death will overtake you, even if you are within high towers. If good befalls them they say, “This is from Allah,” and if evil befalls them they say, “This is from you.” Say, “Everything is from Allah.” So what is the matter with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over life and events and rebukes the inconsistent, shallow mindset of those who acknowledge God for blessings but blame the Prophet (or others) for misfortunes. By commanding “Say, ‘Everything is from Allah,’” it teaches a core theological point: both ease and hardship occur within God’s providence and wisdom. The rebuke—“what is the matter with these people…”—points to a failure of understanding and faith: true submission requires recognizing divine authorship of all outcomes, accepting trials as part of God’s decree, and not shifting blame out of short-sighted emotion.

translation: Whatever good befalls you is from Allah; and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. And We have sent you, [O Muhammad], to the people as a messenger, and sufficient is Allah as a Witness.
interpretation: The verse teaches that blessings are gifts of God's grace while harms usually stem from a person’s own choices or sins; it thereby affirms human moral responsibility. It also clarifies the Prophet’s role as a messenger whose duty is to convey guidance—not to cause people’s fortunes or misfortunes—and concludes by stressing that Allah alone is the ultimate, sufficient Witness and Judge over actions and outcomes, calling for gratitude, accountability, and reliance on God.

translation: Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; but if they turn away, We have not appointed you as a guardian over them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that following the Prophet is, in effect, following God because the Prophet faithfully communicates God's guidance; at the same time it makes clear that the Prophet’s role is to convey the message, not to coerce or supervise people’s beliefs—he is not responsible for forcing acceptance or policing hearts. Acceptance or rejection is an individual duty for which people themselves will be held accountable, while the Prophet is accountable only for conveying the revelation.

translation: And they say, “Obedience.” But when a party of them leaves you, they go about with a purpose other than what you say. And Allah records what they conceal. So turn away from them and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses the hypocrisy of those who profess submission outwardly while nursing contrary designs in private; it stresses that God knows their hidden intentions and will hold them to account. The instruction to the Prophet to turn away and trust in God is a leadership principle: do not be distracted or governed by the show of obedience when actions and motives betray it. Trust in Allah’s knowledge and management of affairs rather than attempting to be swayed, controlled, or unduly entangled with people whose inner resolve contradicts their words; reliance on God and distancing from deceitful counsels preserves the integrity of the community and the mission.

translation:
أفلا يتدبرون القرآن ۚ ولو كان من عند غير الله لوجدوا فيه اختلافا كثيرا
"Do they not then reflect upon the Qur’an? If it had been from any other than Allah, they would surely have found in it much inconsistency."
interpretation: This verse functions as both an invitation and a challenge: by calling people to ponder the Qur’an’s words, it asserts that the remarkable unity, coherence and internal harmony of its teachings—despite being revealed gradually over many years and addressing diverse events, laws and audiences—cannot be the product of human authorship. The absence of pervasive contradictions is presented as evidence of divine origin and as a reason for sincere reflection that leads one away from dismissing the book as mere human composition.

translation: وَإِذَا جَاءَهُمْ أَمْرٌ مِّنَ الْأَمْنِ أَوِ الْخَوْفِ أَذاَعُوهُ ۖ وَلَوْ رَدُّوهُ إِلَى الرَّسُولِ وَإِلَى أُولِي الْأَمْرِ مِنْهُمْ لَعَلِمَهُ الَّذِينَ يَسْتَنْبِطُونَهُ مِنْهُمْ ۗ وَلَوْلَا فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ وَرَحْمَتُهُ لَاتَّبَعْتُمُ الشَّيْطَانَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
interpretation: The verse reproaches a communal habit of spreading unverified reports of safety or danger instead of referring them to legitimate sources of judgment (the Messenger and those in authority). It teaches that proper consultation with qualified leaders would have allowed those capable of sound judgment to discern the truth and prevent confusion. At the same time it reminds that the community’s resistance to deception is ultimately a gift of God’s grace and mercy—without that divine restraint most people would have been led astray by misleading impulses. The practical lesson: verify information, consult rightful authority and knowledgeable interpreters, and recognize dependence on God’s mercy to avoid collective error.

translation: So fight in the way of Allah; you are responsible only for yourself. And urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve; and Allah is more severe in might and more severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse is instructing that when struggle (including armed struggle in the context of defense or a just cause) becomes necessary, each person must fulfil their own duty without being burdened for others’ obligations, and leaders should exhort and motivate believers rather than compel or carry others’ responsibilities. It emphasizes that human effort is paired with reliance on God’s will: sincere striving may lead God to curtail the enemy’s power without overwhelming loss, and ultimate protection and justice belong to God, whose power to punish or restrain is far greater than human power. Thus the passage regulates fighting by personal accountability, moral encouragement, trust in divine support, and the reminder of God’s severe but just retribution.

translation:
من يشفع شفاعة حسنة يكن له نصيب منها ۖ ومن يشفع شفاعة سيئة يكن له كفل منها ۗ وكان الله على كل شيء مقيتا
"Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share of it; and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a burden of it. And Allah is, over all things, a Disposer (or Controller)."
interpretation: The verse teaches that using one’s influence—whether by pleading, recommending, mediating or enabling—carries real moral consequence: such acts do not vanish neutrally but become part of the moral accounting. If your intercession contributes to good, God counts you among its beneficiaries; if it furthers harm, you bear part of its responsibility. Beyond this ethical principle, the statement that God is “over all things a Disposer” affirms that ultimate acceptance, measurement and distribution of reward or blame rest with Him alone: intercession is meaningful but neither arbitrary nor independent of divine oversight, so believers must exercise care and responsibility in whom and what they support.

translation: When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with one better than it or at least return it. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, a Reckoner.
interpretation: The verse enjoins elevating interpersonal courtesy: respond to another’s salutation not with indifference but with equal or greater warmth so as to strengthen social bonds and spread goodwill. Because God is fully aware and will account for deeds, even small acts of politeness carry moral weight; believers are therefore urged to turn routine exchanges into opportunities for sincere generosity, reconciliation and communal harmony rather than letting them lapse into coldness or neglect.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him. He will surely assemble you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?
interpretation: The statement establishes God’s exclusive divinity and absolute sovereignty over life and death, asserting that the resurrection and final gathering of all people is an inevitable, certain event rooted in divine decree. By asking rhetorically who could be more truthful than God, it emphasizes that God’s promises and warnings are the ultimate standard of truth and reliability; therefore human hopes, fears, denials or assurances are ultimately subordinate, and believers are called to orient their trust, conduct, and accountability to God’s reality rather than to transient worldly claims.

translation: What is [the matter] with you that you are two groups regarding the hypocrites? And Allah has made them fall back for what they earned. Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has led astray? And whoever Allah sends astray – you will never find for him a way.
interpretation: This verse reproaches division in the community over how to deal with those whose hypocrisy has become manifest. Its core lesson is theological and practical: true guidance is a gift from God, and when persistent wrongdoing has hardened a heart so that God withdraws His guidance, human efforts to reform that person will be fruitless. Believers are therefore warned not to splinter themselves trying to salvage the irreformable; instead they should protect the community, apply wise and just measures toward harmful conduct, entrust ultimate judgment to God, and concentrate their energy on those still open to guidance.

translation: They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved so that you would be equal. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper.
interpretation: This verse addresses the problem of people who feign belief while actively siding with the community’s enemies. It functions as a security ruling in the context of war and treachery: Muslims are warned not to trust or form protective alliances with those who remain aligned with hostile forces until they demonstrate genuine commitment (symbolized by emigrating to the Muslim community). If, after being given that opportunity, they persist in hostility and act as enemies, they are to be treated as combatants — subject to lawful military action — and not accepted as allies or supporters. The command is therefore conditional and contextual, aimed at preserving communal safety and responding to active betrayal, not a blanket, extra‑judicial license to harm peaceful non‑Muslims or dissenters.

translation: Except for those who reach a people between you and whom there is a covenant, or who come to you whose breasts are constricted so that they cannot fight you or fight their own people. And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you and they would have surely fought you. So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them.
interpretation: The verse explains that some who appear at the border or among you are not genuine enemies: they may be refugees or members of a third party bound by a treaty, or they may be inwardly prevented by fear, conscience, or circumstance from fighting either you or their own people. Their inability or unwillingness to engage is ultimately by God’s will—He could have enabled them to fight but did not. Therefore, when such people withdraw, refrain from hostility, and genuinely offer peace, believers have no legitimate grounds to pursue or attack them; the duty is to accept the cessation of hostilities and honor the boundary of peace rather than press aggression.

translation: You will find others who wish to feel secure from you and to make their people secure; whenever they are returned to persecution (fitnah) they plunge into it. So if they do not withdraw from you, nor offer you peace, nor restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you catch them. And those — We have given you over them clear authority.
interpretation: This verse addresses the rules of engagement toward groups who repeatedly betray safety: it permits decisive force against those who persistently return to hostility and treachery despite options to withdraw, conclude peaceful terms, and cease aggression. The permission to “seize” and “kill” is framed as a specific, limited sanction in the context of active, repeated aggression (fitnah) and is balanced by the clear injunction to accept withdrawal, peaceful settlement, and restraint when they are genuinely offered; the phrase that God has granted “clear authority” indicates a sanctioned prerogative to defend the community and deter further treachery, not a blanket endorsement of violence outside that concrete wartime or security context.

translation: And it is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then the freeing of a believing slave and a blood-money (diya) paid to his family as accepted compensation — unless they remit it —; but if he was from a people hostile to you while he was a believer, then the freeing of a believing slave is required; and if he was from a people with whom you have a treaty, then a diya paid to his family and the freeing of a believing slave. Whoever does not find (a slave to free) must fast two consecutive months as repentance to Allah. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse lays down a moral-legal principle: the killing of a fellow believer is categorically forbidden except in the accidental case, and such an error demands concrete acts of atonement aimed at restoring justice, honour, and social harmony rather than mere punishment. The prescribed expiation—freeing a believing slave and providing blood-money to the victim’s heirs (unless they forgive it)—serves both to acknowledge the sanctity of life and to compensate the bereaved, while the distinctions between a believer from an enemy people and one from a treaty community reflect concern for the wider political and contractual context of wrongdoing. The alternative of fasting two consecutive months for those unable to perform the primary expiation underscores repentance and spiritual reform when material means are lacking. Overall the ruling balances deterrence and mercy, enjoins reparation and reconciliation, and emphasizes that these measures are based on God’s knowing wisdom rather than arbitrary retaliation.

translation: And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell — he will abide therein eternally; and the wrath of Allah is upon him and He has cursed him and prepared for him a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse asserts that the deliberate taking of a fellow believer’s life is among the gravest violations of God’s ordinance: it is an assault on the divine gift and the communal trust that binds believers. The graphic language — eternal abode in Hell, God’s wrath and curse, and a great prepared punishment — signals that such an act causes a fundamental spiritual rupture, alienating the perpetrator from God’s mercy and from the moral order of the community; thus the verse functions as the strongest moral and legal deterrent to protect life and uphold justice.

translation: O you who have believed, when you set out in the cause of Allah, be sure to verify and be cautious; and do not say to one who greets you with peace, “You are not a believer,” seeking the goods of this worldly life — for with Allah are abundant spoils. Thus you were before; then Allah bestowed His favor upon you, so be discerning. Indeed Allah is, of what you do, Ever Aware.
interpretation: The verse commands moral restraint and careful investigation in moments of conflict: believers must not hastily judge or declare another’s disbelief—especially out of greed for worldly gain such as spoils or property—but must verify facts and avoid using suspicion as a pretext for injustice. By recalling God’s past favors and God’s complete knowledge of actions, the verse insists on sincerity, fairness, and protection of others’ rights even under the pressures of warfare or expedition.

translation: Not equal are those of the believers who sit [at home]—except those who are disabled—and the mujahidin in the cause of Allah, striving with their wealth and their lives. Allah has preferred the mujahidin with their wealth and their lives over those who sit by degrees. And to each Allah has promised the good; and Allah has preferred the mujahidin over those who sit with a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine assessment distinguishes between passive believers and those who actively sacrifice their wealth and lives for God's cause: genuine incapacity excuses a person from action, but for those able to strive, engagement and self-sacrifice raise one’s spiritual rank and yield greater reward. At the same time, God promises good to all sincere believers, so the grading of merit underscores both divine justice and the moral imperative to translate faith into committed, risking service when one is able.

translation: (He grants) degrees from Him and forgiveness and mercy; and Allah is Ever-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that God, by His grace, elevates believers to higher spiritual stations, pardons their faults, and bestows His compassionate care; it reminds us that true honor and ultimate success come not from human effort alone but from Allah’s forgiving nature and merciful favor, so hope and reliance should be placed on His mercy.

translation: Indeed, those whom the angels take [in death] while they are wronging themselves will say, “In what [condition] were you?” They will say, “We were oppressed in the land.” The angels will say, “Was not the earth of Allah spacious for you to emigrate therein?” For those, their refuge is Hell — and evil it is as a destination.
interpretation: The verse teaches that claiming to have been ‘weak’ or ‘oppressed’ is not automatically accepted as an excuse if one had real, practicable means to leave oppression and preserve one's faith or safety.
