God (through the angels’ questioning) distinguishes genuine incapacity from avoidable neglect: when viable opportunities or routes of migration and refuge existed, remaining by choice or from unreasonable attachment or fear is a culpable failure. Thus responsibility is judged in light of what was realistically possible, and refusing lawful means to protect one’s faith or life when able incurs grave accountability.

translation: Except the weak among men, women, and children — who are unable to devise a plan and cannot find a way.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes those who are genuinely powerless — vulnerable men, women, and children who lack the means, agency, or opportunity to escape, resist, or seek guidance — and treats them as exempt from the ordinary burdens of responsibility; it affirms Divine consideration and mercy toward people whose incapacity prevents them from acting or finding a way out.

translation: As for those, it may be that Allah will pardon them; and Allah is Ever Pardoning, Oft-Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse expresses a hope in God’s mercy toward the people just described: Allah may, in His wisdom, remit their wrongdoing. The word “عسَى” (it may be) indicates possibility rather than guarantee, while pairing “عَفْو” (pardon/erasure of the fault) with “غَفُور” (covering and forgiving) emphasizes two complementary aspects of divine mercy. Ultimately forgiveness is God’s prerogative—so one should neither despair of His mercy nor presume upon it, but turn to Him seeking pardon.

translation: And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many refuges and abundance. And whoever leaves his home emigrating to Allah and His Messenger and then is overtaken by death — his reward has become incumbent upon Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse assures that sincere migration for God’s cause—whether physical relocation or leaving behind what obstructs obedience—will be met by God’s facilitation and provision: He opens many places of refuge and space for the emigrant. Crucially, the verse affirms that the believer’s intention is what secures divine recompense; if one departs home with the purpose of serving Allah and His Messenger but dies before reaping worldly results, God nonetheless guarantees the reward because He values the sincere motive. The concluding clause (“Allah is Forgiving and Merciful”) frames this promise within divine compassion: God not only rewards but also forgives and shows mercy to those who sacrifice for His cause, so believers may act in trust rather than fear of worldly loss.

translation: And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: This verse conveys a general principle: Divine law permits easing ritual requirements when genuine danger or hostile circumstances threaten the community or individuals. The concession to shorten prayer is not a weakening of worship but a pragmatic measure that prioritizes preservation of life, safety, and communal continuity; it shows that obligations can be lawfully adapted under real threat. By describing hostile opponents as a “clear enemy,” the text limits the concession to contexts of evident hostility rather than making it a blanket rule, and it teaches prudence—religious duties are served best when balanced with measures that protect people and the mission of the community.

translation: And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their arms. And when they prostrate, let them be behind you; and let another group come forward which has not yet prayed, and let them pray with you and take their precaution and carry their arms. Those who disbelieve wish that you would neglect your arms and your baggage so they could come down upon you in one single attack. And there is no blame upon you if there is any harm to you because of rain or you are ill that you should put down your arms; but take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that religious devotion must be practised with practical care and communal responsibility in times of danger: worship is not to be separated from security. It prescribes a concrete arrangement—rotating groups so some guard while others pray and keeping weapons at hand even in prayer—to prevent vulnerability to enemy surprise. At the same time it allows humane flexibility (putting down arms when genuinely hindered by weather or illness) while insisting on vigilance. The underlying principle is trust in God combined with wise, collective precautions; neglect born of false reliance or carelessness plays into the enemy’s hands, and those who exploit such negligence will face divine humiliation.

translation: And when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides. Then when you are secure, establish the prayer. Indeed, prayer has been prescribed for the believers at appointed times.
interpretation: The verse teaches a twofold principle: ritual prayer is a binding, time‑specified obligation that structures the believer’s life, yet true worship is continuous and not limited to the formal moment. In conditions that prevent full performance (for example fear, travel, or danger) believers are commanded to maintain God‑consciousness in whatever posture they are in; once safety and stability return they must resume the regular, appointed prayers. Thus the verse balances flexibility for real circumstances with the firmness of prayer’s ordained times, emphasizing both constant remembrance and disciplined communal duty.

translation:
وَلَا تَهِنُوا فِي ابْتِغَاءِ الْقَوْمِ ۖ إِن تَكُونُوا تَأْلَمُونَ فَهُم يَأْلَمُونَ كَمَا تَأْلَمُونَ وَتَرْجُونَ مِنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَرْجُونَ ۗ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا
"Do not lose heart in striving for the cause of the people; if you suffer, they too suffer as you suffer, yet you hope from Allah what they do not hope for. And Allah is All‑Knowing, All‑Wise."
interpretation: The verse commands steadfastness: believers must not grow faint or abandon collective struggle (moral, social, or defensive) simply because it is hard. Shared hardship with opponents does not make the effort pointless, because believers possess a trust in God’s support and purposes that their adversaries lack. That trust gives meaning to suffering and distinguishes the believer’s endurance as purposeful rather than futile; since God fully knows the realities and acts with wisdom, perseverance grounded in reliance on Him is both justified and morally required.

translation: Indeed We have sent down to you the Book in truth so that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you; and do not be an advocate for the treacherous.
interpretation: The verse instructs that the revealed scripture is the authoritative standard for judging disputes and that the appointed judge (here the Prophet, and by extension any arbiter) must apply it impartially; one must refuse to defend, excuse, or align with those who betray trusts or corrupt the truth—personal ties, fear, or favoritism must not lead one to become a partisan for the untrustworthy, because doing so would pervert justice and betray the purpose of the revelation.

translation: And seek forgiveness of Allah; indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: This exhortation calls the believer to turn back to God in sincere repentance whenever they err, assuring them that repentance is effective because forgiveness and mercy are essential attributes of God. Seeking God’s forgiveness is both a means of removing sin’s burden and of renewing one’s relationship with Him: it opens the door to pardon, softens the heart, averts consequences, and restores hope, since Allah’s mercy outweighs His punishment and is available to those who sincerely return to Him.

translation: And do not argue on behalf of those who betray their own selves; indeed, Allah does not love one who is treacherous and sinful.
interpretation: The verse warns against defending or excusing people who have violated trusts or persisted in wrongdoing. “Betraying their own selves” denotes actions that harm one’s soul—treachery, injustice, hypocrisy—and standing up for such people implicates you in their guilt. Believers are therefore urged to uphold truth and justice even against friends or kin, for God does not approve of treachery and persistent sin.

translation: They try to hide themselves from people, but they do not hide from Allah; and He is with them when they spend the night planning words that are displeasing. And Allah encompasses what they do.
interpretation: The verse warns against self-deception in hypocrisy: concealing vile speech or secret plots from other people offers no refuge because Allah is ever‑present and fully aware of private thoughts and nocturnal schemes. Since God’s knowledge and power encompass all actions, outward secrecy and appearances are worthless; true accountability depends on inner sincerity and fear of God, not on having deceived other humans.

translation: Here you are — these are the ones you argued for in the life of this world; so who will argue with Allah for them on the Day of Resurrection? Or who will be a guardian over them?
interpretation: الآية تحذّر من الاستدلال والدفاع عن الظالمين أو الباطل في الدنيا وتؤكد أن ما يوفّره الدفاع أو السلطة الدنيوية لا يقي صاحبه يوم القيامة؛ إذ لا يكون لهم من يردّ عنهم قضى الله ولا وكيلاً يحمِيهم إلا برضى الله وإذنه. المعنى العملي: لا يغترّ المرء بدعم الناس أو المنافع الدنيوية، فإن النجاة والحماية في الآخرة بيد الله وحده، والموقف الحقيقي هو التزام الحق وعدم تأييد الباطل.

translation: And whoever does a wrong or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness of Allah, he will find Allah Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Divine mercy is available to those who sincerely repent: committing an evil or harming oneself through sin does not place one beyond God’s pardon if one turns back to Him. True repentance (tawbah) entails genuine remorse, immediate cessation of the wrongdoing, a firm resolve not to return to it, and—when others were harmed—making restitution and seeking their pardon; fulfilling these conditions, the sinner will meet Allah’s attributes of forgiveness and mercy, transforming failure into a renewed moral opportunity rather than final despair.

translation: And whoever earns a sin does so only against himself; and Allah is, indeed, Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that moral accountability is ultimately personal: wrongful acts are borne by the doer and their inner self, not by God or by Divine injustice. Even if a sin seems to bring advantage outwardly, its true burden — spiritual harm, impaired conscience, and eventual reckoning — rests on the actor. That God is “Knowing” underscores that hidden motives and private deeds are fully observed, so no one can escape divine awareness; that He is “Wise” reassures that outcomes and recompense are measured with justice and wisdom, even if delayed or inscrutable. The practical call is to recognize personal responsibility, fear the inward consequences of wrongdoing, and turn to repentance, since ultimate judgment is both comprehensive in knowledge and balanced in wisdom.

translation: And whoever earns a sin or offence and then lays it upon an innocent person, has indeed borne a calumny and a manifest sin.
interpretation: The verse condemns the compounded injustice of committing a wrong and then shifting the blame onto someone innocent: such conduct is not merely a private failing but an added crime of false accusation and slander. It emphasizes personal accountability before God, the moral weight of injuring another to hide one’s own fault, and the social damage that false charges cause to trust and reputation. The proper response demanded by this teaching is sincere repentance, rectifying the wrong by exonerating and, where possible, restoring the harmed person, and cultivating honesty and restraint in speech so that one does not multiply sin by harming others to conceal one’s own mistakes.

translation: And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, a faction of them would have plotted to mislead you; but they do not mislead except themselves, and they will not harm you at all. And Allah has revealed to you the Book and the wisdom and taught you what you did not know; and the bounty of Allah upon you is great.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s grace and mercy preserved the Prophet and his mission against the designs of certain people who sought to confuse or mislead him. Divine protection came through the revelation of the Scripture and the imparting of wisdom and knowledge that completed what he lacked, so human schemes could neither change the truth nor harm the Messenger; those who attempted to mislead only harmed themselves. The passage therefore teaches reliance on divine guidance, recognition that legitimate guidance is a gift from God (not the product of human manipulation), and gratitude for the safeguarding of the community and the authenticity of the message.

translation: There is no good in much of their private talk except for one who enjoins charity or that which is right or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah — We will give him a great reward.
interpretation: The verse condemns secretive, idle, or self‑serving scheming among people while affirming that private counsel is praiseworthy when it aims to promote tangible benefit for others — giving, enjoining moral good, or mediating disputes. The decisive criterion is intention: when such counsel is offered purely to seek God’s pleasure (not to gain status, harm others, or stir faction), it transforms otherwise dubious secrecy into a morally valuable act deserving a great reward; thus Muslims are guided to make their hidden talks constructive, focused on public good, and free from personal malice or hypocrisy.

translation: And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has been made clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers — We will give him what he has taken and drive him into Hell; and evil is that destination.
interpretation: The verse warns that knowingly rejecting or opposing the Prophet and deliberately abandoning the path of the believing community is a grave, culpable choice. Divine response here is twofold: God allows such a person to pursue and receive the consequences of the course he has chosen (whether apparent worldly gain or the fruits of his deviation), and ultimately he will be consigned to Hell as the just outcome. In other words, after clear guidance has been presented, willful schism is treated as self-chosen misguidance whose inevitable end is a terrible abode.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly gone far astray.
interpretation: The verse teaches that attributing partners to God (shirk) is uniquely grave because it contradicts the very basis of worship and acceptance by God; if a person dies entrenched in such association it bars forgiveness, whereas other sins remain within the realm of God’s mercy and may be pardoned according to His will. Thus the statement underscores both the centrality of pure monotheism (tawḥīd) as the condition for ultimate forgiveness and the vastness of divine mercy toward those who repent or whose sins are not of that defining, incurable character — and it warns that choosing to associate others with God is a profound, far-reaching misguidance.

translation: They invoke besides Him nothing but females; and they invoke nothing but a rebellious Satan.
interpretation: The verse criticizes the pagan practice of ascribing female deities or ‘daughters’ to God and shows that such cultic attachments do not come from true guidance but from a corrupt, obstinate satanic influence. By saying they call upon “only females” it exposes the baselessness and cultural prejudice behind their idol-worship, and by calling the source a “rebellious Satan” it explains that their false beliefs are the result of deliberate, persistent misleading rather than divine truth.

translation: May Allah curse him. He said, “I will surely take from among Your servants a share appointed (for myself).”
interpretation: The verse depicts Satan’s condemned arrogance and his declared strategy: after being cursed for rebelling, he vows to appropriate certain human beings as his ‘portion’ — not literally owned, but those he will mislead and draw away from God. Calling them a “share appointed” reflects his presumptuous claim that he can lay hold of people as if they were allotted to him; the deeper meaning warns believers that Satan will persistently seek adherents through temptation, deception and subtle inducement, so they must seek God’s protection, remain mindful, and resist his plots.

translation: “And I will mislead them, and I will instill in them vain desires, and I will command them so that they will mark (or mutilate) the ears of the livestock, and I will command them so that they will change the creation of Allah. And whoever takes Satan as a patron instead of Allah has indeed suffered a clear loss.”
interpretation: The verse exposes Satan’s method: he turns people away from God not only by open rebellion but by seeding false hopes, encouraging superstitious or corrupt practices, and promoting changes to what God has established (the phrase about ‘altering God’s creation’ symbolizes moral, legal or social innovations that violate divine intent). Taking Satan as one’s guide—i.e., accepting those temptations and innovations in place of God’s guidance—leads to profound, manifest loss: moral decay, social disorder, and ultimate ruin in the hereafter.

translation: He promises them and inspires them with false hopes; and Satan promises them nothing but delusion.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the enticements offered by Satan and those who follow his ways are outwardly attractive but essentially deceptive—appealing to desire with promises of easy gain, status, or comfort to breed complacency and mislead people from God’s guidance; such assurances are illusory and ultimately harmful, so one must resist being seduced by them.

translation: Their abode is Hell, and they will find no escape from it.
interpretation: This declares the irrevocable and final outcome for those whom God has condemned: Hell will be their permanent dwelling and no plea, intercession, or means of evasion will avail them. The wording stresses both the certainty and permanence of divine judgment, serving as a stern warning to abandon disbelief and hypocrisy before the opportunity for repentance is gone.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds — We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever; the promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful in word than Allah?
interpretation: The verse functions as a solemn assurance and a moral principle: genuine faith expressed through righteous action leads to an enduring, perfected state of well‑being (symbolized by gardens with flowing rivers), and this reward is guaranteed by God’s unfailing truthfulness. The imagery emphasizes lasting spiritual fulfillment rather than merely temporal pleasure, while the rhetorical question underscores that God’s promises are the ultimate standard of trustworthiness—intended to inspire hope, steady resolve, and reliance on divine justice rather than on fleeting worldly claims.

translation: It is not according to your wishes nor the wishes of the People of the Scripture. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find besides Allah any protector or helper.
interpretation: The verse stresses that human hopes, affiliations, or claims to privilege do not determine divine judgment; accountability is grounded in one’s deeds. Those who commit wrong cannot evade consequence by relying on wishes, communal identity, or supporters—there is no ultimate protector or intercessor apart from God. The passage therefore warns against complacency, false assurance, or dependence on others to overturn moral responsibility, and calls each person to fear God and act righteously because only God’s justice and mercy ultimately prevail.

translation: And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while he is a believer—those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged in the least.
interpretation: The verse affirms that sincere faith combined with righteous action is the sole criterion for attaining Paradise, without discrimination between men and women; God’s judgment is perfectly just, so every believer’s good deeds will be fully recognized and rewarded and no one will be denied even the smallest due nor be treated unjustly.

translation: And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good, and follows the way of Abraham, inclining toward truth? And Allah took Abraham as a close friend.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the ideal religious standing is not mere profession but total, sincere surrender to God (the image of submitting one’s face denotes whole‑person devotion), united with moral excellence in conduct ('muhsin'). True religion imitates Abraham’s upright, uncompromising monotheism—an inner disposition turned outward in righteous action—and Allah’s naming of Abraham as 'khalīl' (close friend) both honors that model and holds it up as the exemplar toward which believers should orient their faith and behavior.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is encompassing of all things.
interpretation: The statement declares God’s absolute sovereignty and ownership over all existence and emphasizes that His knowledge, power, authority and care fully encompass every aspect of reality; nothing is independent of Him, nothing escapes His awareness or control, which grounds human responsibility under divine rule and offers both accountability and reassurance that all affairs rest within God’s just and comprehensive governance.

translation: And they ask you about women. Say, “Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning orphan girls whom you do not give what has been decreed for them and whom you desire to marry, and the weak among children, and that you should stand up for the orphans with justice. And whatever good you do—indeed Allah is Knowing of it.”
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet to answer questions about women not by human opinion but by reference to the divine legislation in the Qur'an, which chiefly seeks to protect the vulnerable—especially orphan girls and weak children—against being deprived of their due or being exploited through marriage or guardianship. The rulings mentioned are meant to ensure that those who cannot protect their own rights receive what is prescribed for them, and that guardianship and inheritance are carried out with equity. By concluding with “whatever good you do—Allah is Knowing of it,” the verse both consoles that sincere efforts to do right are seen by God and reminds people that true obedience is measured by implementing the Book’s justice toward the weak rather than by selfish desires.

translation: And if a woman fears from her husband hostility or turning away, there is no blame on them if they make reconciliation between them — reconciliation is better. And the souls have been made greedy. But if you do good and guard yourselves (with piety), then indeed Allah is, of what you do, All‑Aware.
interpretation: This verse permits and encourages amicable settlement when a wife fears ill‑treatment, rebellion, or withdrawal by her husband: restoring harmony through mutual compromise is preferable to prolonged conflict. It acknowledges that human souls are often driven by selfish desires (for more material gain, legal advantage, or pride), which can impede fair agreement; therefore the law allows flexibility—even if the settlement departs from strict legal formulas—to achieve peace. The concluding admonition links the moral quality of such settlements to sincerity and God‑consciousness: if the parties act justly and piously, Allah knows their deeds, and their reconciliation will stand as morally valid.

translation: And you will never be able to be equitable between the women, even if you should desire it; so do not incline completely (toward one) and leave another hanging as if suspended. And if you amend and fear (Allah), then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse acknowledges the human impossibility of distributing equal love or emotional inclination among multiple wives, but commands fairness in treatment of their rights and obligations. It warns against obvious favoritism that abandons a wife’s legal, financial or emotional needs (‘leaving her suspended’) and instructs husbands to strive for impartiality in actions—maintenance, time, respect and duties—even if inner feelings cannot be perfectly balanced. It also reassures that sincere correction and God‑consciousness, when one seeks to restore justice, are met with Allah’s forgiveness and mercy.

translation: And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them out of His bounty; and ever is Allah, All-Encompassing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches reliance on God’s sufficiency and providence: if people or groups part ways, it is not ultimately detrimental because Allah can and will provide for and make independent each party according to His generous resources; what unfolds is governed by His comprehensive capacity and wise decree, so believers should trust His provision and judgment rather than fear division.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We certainly instructed those to whom the Scripture was given before you and you [O People of the Scripture and believers] to fear Allah. And if you disbelieve — then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And ever is Allah Free of need, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty and ownership over all creation and uses that truth to urge piety: both earlier recipients of revelation and the present community are reminded to live in God-consciousness and obedience. The warning that even if some disbelieve, God’s dominion remains unchanged underlines that human rejection does not diminish Divine authority or need; rather, God is self-sufficient (ghaniyy) and worthy of praise (hamid). The passage therefore calls for humility, accountability, and steadfastness in faith grounded in the recognition of God’s ultimate control and worthiness.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute sovereignty and self-sufficiency: all resources, authority and outcomes ultimately belong to and are managed by Him. Its practical implication is a call to relinquish ultimate dependence on people or possessions and to place trust (tawakkul) in God’s wisdom and justice—knowing He alone can truly protect, provide and settle affairs—while continuing to act responsibly, ethically and justly within the means He has entrusted to us.

translation: If He wills, He will remove you, O people, and bring others [in your place]; and Allah is fully able to do that.
interpretation: This verse warns that the continuance of any people, status, or authority is not guaranteed—everything rests on God’s will. If a community persists in ingratitude, disbelief or corruption, God can replace them with others who are more faithful or worthy; conversely, those who obey and remain humble should not take their position for granted. The statement underscores divine sovereignty and power, urging humility, accountability, and readiness to reform, since worldly standing is transient and subject to God’s decree.

translation:
من كان يريد ثواب الدنيا فعند الله ثواب الدنيا والآخرة ۚ وكان الله سميعا بصيرا
"Whoever seeks the reward of this world — then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing."
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate recompense is determined by God’s wise knowledge and will: even when people pursue merely worldly gains, Allah may grant them both temporal benefits and eternal reward according to His judgment. It underlines divine sovereignty over outcomes, reminds us that God fully knows hearts and deeds (He hears and sees everything), and thus calls for trust in His justice and mercy while encouraging sincerity—since results are not confined to human intent but are dispensed by God’s all‑aware wisdom.

translation: O you who believe, be steadfast in upholding justice, and be witnesses for Allah — even if it is against yourselves or your parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah has greater claim upon them; so do not follow desire and thereby depart from justice. And if you distort (the truth) or turn away, then indeed Allah is fully aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to embody divine justice as a moral identity: to testify and act impartially even when truth conflicts with self‑interest or family ties. Being “witnesses for Allah” means making God’s standard of fairness the criterion for judgment, refusing favoritism toward wealth, status, or lineage, and resisting personal desires that would twist evidence or silence the truth. The reminder that Allah is fully aware of actions and inner motives is both a warning against corruption and an appeal to cultivate God‑consciousness so that justice becomes principled practice rather than a convenience.

translation: O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger, and the Book which He sent down before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day — then indeed he has gone far astray.
interpretation: The verse demands a comprehensive, coherent faith: true belief is not partial but embraces the whole framework of divine guidance — God’s existence and authority, the prophetic messenger, the Qur’an revealed to him, the scriptures revealed earlier, the angels as God’s agents, the succession of messengers, and accountability on the Last Day. It warns that rejecting any of these foundational realities is not a minor mistake but a grave deviation from the straight path. In other words, iman (faith) requires accepting the unity and continuity of revelation and the unseen realities it presupposes; denial of any pillar of that creed severs one from the guidance that leads rightly and causes one to stray far.

translation: Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, and increased in disbelief — never will Allah forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way.
interpretation: It describes people whose profession of faith was insincere and unstable — repeatedly embracing belief when advantageous and reverting to denial until their rejection becomes entrenched; that persistent, deliberate hardening of heart (not a single sincere repentance) places them beyond Allah’s forgiveness and guidance as a consequence of their ongoing, escalated disbelief.

translation: Give the hypocrites tidings that for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The command to “give tidings” is rhetorical: it expresses the Prophet’s duty to warn and the certainty of what follows. The term “hypocrites” denotes those who feign faith while secretly denying or undermining the community; describing their lot as a “painful punishment” emphasizes both the severity and justice of the consequence that awaits such duplicity. The verse thereby underlines God’s knowledge of hidden states, affirms that hypocrisy destroys trust and merits fitting retribution, and serves as a stern deterrent calling people to inner sincerity rather than outward show.

translation: Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers — do they seek honor through them? Verily, all honor belongs entirely to Allah.
interpretation: This verse censures those who prefer political, social, or military alliance with nonbelievers over solidarity with the believing community, suggesting they do so to obtain power, status, or security. It affirms that true honor, sovereignty and decisive power belong solely to God, not to transient human patrons; therefore seeking lasting dignity by aligning with opponents of the faith is misguided and vain. Believers are thus reminded that real honor comes from God and from fidelity to the community of faith, not from reliance on worldly allies who oppose or undermine that community.

translation: And it has been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and mocked at, do not sit with them until they engage in some other discourse; for then you would be like them. Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them.
interpretation: The verse issues a social and spiritual safeguard: believers must not tacitly legitimize or normalize ridicule of God’s revelations by remaining passive in gatherings where such mockery occurs, because continued association can erode conviction and make one resemble the mockers. The allowance to remain once the topic changes shows the aim is preservation of faith, not needless isolation; the final warning ties persistent complicity or alignment with ridicule to a shared moral fate, stressing personal responsibility to protect one’s belief and the integrity of the community.

translation: Those who lie in wait for you: if there is for you a victory from Allah they say, “Were we not with you?” And if the disbelievers gain a share [of success] they say, “Did we not prevail over you and prevent you from the believers?” But Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers.
interpretation: The verse condemns opportunistic people who alter their posture to claim credit or assert dominance according to changing fortunes; it teaches that such human posturing is ultimately hollow because divine justice will expose true motives and adjudicate claims on the Day of Resurrection. Believers are therefore reassured that transient boasts or betrayals matter less than God’s final judgment, and that God will not allow the disbelievers to have ultimate authority over the faithful—so trust in divine justice, not in the shifting rhetoric of self‑interested parties.

translation: Indeed the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them. And when they stand for prayer they stand lazily, showing off to the people, and they remember Allah only a little.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses hypocrisy as a self-defeating posture: those who feign faith try to manipulate God and people for advantage, yet because God’s knowledge and sovereignty are absolute He frustrates their schemes and lets their deceit rebound on them. The external signs—sluggishness in prayer and ostentation—reveal an inner spiritual vacancy: their worship is performance for human applause rather than sincere remembrance of God, so it carries little worth. The lesson is that religion reduced to appearance is hollow and will be exposed and nullified by God; true value lies in heartfelt presence, humility, and genuine remembrance, not in outward show.

translation: Wavering between the two — neither toward these nor toward those. And whoever Allah leads astray, you will never find for him a way.
interpretation: It speaks of people whose hearts are unstable and indecisive, oscillating between truth and falsehood without sincerely committing to guidance; such vacillation often stems from lack of sincere seeking, hypocrisy, or persistent heedlessness. Guidance is bestowed by Allah, and when He allows a person to be led astray, no amount of external argument or urging will find a lasting path to rectify him, because his heart has become closed, unsettled, and unable to receive or hold true guidance.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do you wish to place over yourselves a clear authority from Allah?
interpretation: This verse forbids giving the role of intimate protector, trustee, or decisive ally to those whose commitments oppose the Muslim community, especially when doing so replaces reliance on fellow believers. "Awliya" here means those in whom one places trust, protection, or decisive influence. The warning is that preferring hostile or indifferent outsiders for support, leadership, or confidential matters weakens communal solidarity, exposes the community to betrayal and harm, and thereby risks bringing about an obvious divine consequence (a "clear authority") — i.e., loss of moral autonomy, social security, or an imposed subjugation that follows from abandoning rightful loyalties. The injunction does not prohibit ordinary peaceful relations or fair dealings with non‑believers, but it prohibits forming alliances or dependencies that compromise the integrity, safety, and shared obligations of the believing community.

translation: Indeed, the hypocrites are in the lowest depths of the Fire, and you will not find for them any helper.
interpretation: The verse warns that hypocrisy — professing faith outwardly while denying or betraying it inwardly — is met with the gravest moral and eschatological consequence: those who undermine trust from within will occupy the most humiliating station in the afterlife and be utterly cut off from support. ‘You will not find for them any helper’ signifies that no intercession, ally, or righteous deed will avail them to avert that fate; their duplicity nullifies claims to protection and renders them isolated before divine judgment. The passage thus emphasizes the seriousness of inner faith and the social danger of concealed disbelief.

translation: Except those who repent and amend and hold fast to Allah and make their religion sincere for Allah — those will be with the believers. And Allah will surely give the believers a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that people who may have been in error, sin, or hypocrisy are not permanently excluded if they undertake four things: sincere repentance (turning away from past wrongs), genuine reform of their conduct, firm reliance and attachment to God (iʿtisam bi‑llāh), and purifying their religion from ostentation so that it is for God alone. When these conditions are met, they are counted among the true believers and will share in God’s generous recompense; mercy and acceptance follow real inner change and steadfast, sincere commitment to God rather than mere words or past labels.

translation:
ما يفعل الله بعذابكم إن شكرتم وآمنتم ۚ وكان الله شاكرا عليما
"What would Allah do to you for punishment if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Most Appreciative, All‑Knowing."
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical challenge: sincere gratitude (shukr) combined with true faith (iman) removes the very grounds for divine punishment, because God’s dealing with people is governed by mercy and justice rather than whim. Gratitude here is more than lip‑service—it includes inner acknowledgment of God’s favors and outward obedience—while faith denotes genuine trust and submission. Describing Allah as Shākir (appreciative) and ʿAlīm (knower) underscores two truths: God abundantly rewards even small acts of thankfulness and He perfectly perceives inner states and intentions. Thus genuine thankfulness and belief attract God’s forgiveness and increase rather than provoke retribution.

translation: Allah does not love the public utterance of evil words except by one who has been wronged; and Allah is Ever-Hearing, Ever-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse counsels restraint in airing faults and speaking ill aloud: ordinarily one should not broadcast harmful speech, insults, or accusations because that spreads harm and discord. An exception is recognized for a person who has been oppressed and must speak openly to defend themselves, expose an injustice, or seek redress — in such a case public complaint is permitted. The closing phrase, “Allah is Hearing, Knowing,” reminds that God perceives intentions and circumstances, so what matters is the truthfulness and necessity behind the speech and not malice or desire to humiliate others.

translation: If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an offense, then indeed Allah is Ever‑Forgiving, All‑Powerful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that actions and responses should be guided by trust in God’s attributes: whether you make a good deed public or keep it private, or whether you choose to forgive someone instead of seeking revenge, do so with confidence that Allah forgives and has the power to rectify and recompense. Believers are therefore encouraged to act with sincerity and mercy—to conceal good when appropriate and to pardon wrongs—relying on God’s ability to reward what is hidden and to administer justice when needed.

translation:
إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُكْفِرُونَ بِاللَّـهِ وَرُسُلِهِ وَيُرِيدُونَ أَن يُفَرِّقُوا بَيْنَ اللَّـهِ وَرُسُلِهِ وَيَقُولُونَ نُؤْمِنُ بِبَعْضٍ وَنَكْفُرُ بِبَعْضٍ وَيُرِيدُونَ أَن يَتَّخِذُوا بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ سَبِيلًا
“Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, and say, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ and desire to take a way in between —”
interpretation: The verse reproves the stance of selectively accepting revelation and messengers in order to escape full submission: treating prophetic authority as divisible is not a neutral compromise but a form of repudiation. By trying to pick and choose which messengers or teachings to accept, people undermine the unity of divine guidance and reveal a disingenuous, self‑serving posture that amounts to disbelief rather than a legitimate middle path; true faith requires recognizing the integrity and collective authority of God’s messengers, not fragmenting or relativizing it.

translation: Those are indeed the disbelievers; and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse affirms that persistent rejection of divine guidance constitutes a settled state—one that brings inevitable divine response. The “humiliating punishment” emphasizes not just physical suffering but the loss of honor, protection, and God’s favor: a degradation that manifests in social disgrace, spiritual ruin, and final accountability. Announcing this punishment underscores both God’s justice toward persistent wrongdoing and a moral warning to deter arrogance and heedlessness while consoling the faithful that injustice will not go unaddressed.

translation: And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make any distinction between any of them — to those He will give their reward; and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: True faith means affirming the unity of divine guidance by accepting all prophets and their messages without elevating or dismissing any of them; such comprehensive acceptance merits God’s due recompense. The promise of reward coupled with God’s attributes of forgiveness and mercy teaches that sincere belief — even when accompanied by human shortcomings — is met with divine generosity, and it warns against sectarian selectivity that fragments the community of believers.

translation: The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down upon them a book from the heavens. Indeed they had asked Moses for something even greater than that, saying, “Show us Allah outright,” and the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf after clear proofs had come to them, and We pardoned that; and We gave Moses manifest authority.
interpretation: The verse warns against demanding spectacular, visible miracles as a precondition for faith—such demands stem from arrogance and test God rather than sincere seeking. It shows that clear signs alone do not guarantee right conduct: people can see proofs and still fall into disobedience. Divine response balances justice and mercy: wrongdoing is not without consequence, yet God’s pardon and the conferral of legitimate prophetic authority can follow when guidance and repentance are possible. The practical lesson is to accept guidance on its own terms—humble submission and moral accountability matter more than insisting on extraordinary displays.

translation: And We raised above them the Mount in confirmation of their covenant, and We said to them, “Enter the gate prostrating,” and We said to them, “Do not transgress concerning the Sabbath,” and We took from them a stern covenant.
interpretation: This verse teaches that God can employ unmistakable, external signs and solemn oaths to make His covenant binding and evident; the command to enter “prostrating” shows that true acceptance of divine instruction requires humble submission, not mere lip assent, while the Sabbath injunction exemplifies a concrete rule meant to discipline communal conduct and test obedience. Describing the covenant as “stern” stresses the gravity of the responsibility and the moral accountability incumbent on a people who have been given clear guidance.

translation: بِسَبَبِ نَقْضِهِم مِيثَاقَهُمْ وَكَفْرِهِم بِآيَاتِ اللَّهِ وَقَتْلِهِمُ الأَنْبِيَاءَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ وَقَوْلِهِم «قُلُوبُنَا غُلُفٌ» ۚ بَلْ طَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهَا بِكُفْرِهِم فَلَا يُؤْمِنُونَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
interpretation: الآية تفسّر حالة الجمْع المذكور بأن عِقَابهم الروحي هو حصيلة أفعالهم المستمرة: نَقْضُ العَهْد، وَكَفْرُهُم بِالآيات، وَقَتْلُ الأَنْبِيَاءِ بِظُلْم، وَادِّعاءُهُم أن قلوبهم محجوبة عن التأثر («قلوبنا غلف») — وهذا ادعاء تَغَيُّبٍ وغياب إدراك حقيقي. فـ«طبع الله عليها» تُفهم هنا باعتبارها قَدَرًا قضائيًا أو نتيجة إلهية لتماديهم في العناد: الله جَعَلَ تَجَلُّداً في قلوبهم لا يتيح لها القبول الكامل للحق، فلا يبقَى منهم إلا القليل المؤمن. بعبارة أخرى، الختم ليس مجرد تصفية عشوائية، بل نتيجة طبيعية لعصيانهم المتكرر وإصرارهم على رفض الهداية، فتتحول قلوبهم إلى حالة من القسوة والجمود الروحي، ويُتاح للحق الدخول إلا لعدد قليل.

translation:
وَبِكُفْرِهِمْ وَقَوْلِهِمْ عَلَى مَرْيَمَ بِهْتَانًا عَظِيمًا
"And because of their disbelief and their saying about Mary a tremendous lie."
interpretation: The verse condemns certain false claims made out of disbelief—specifically the attribution to Mary (and thereby to her son) of what is untrue—and labels such assertions as a grave slander. It underscores that inventing or ascribing divinity, sonship, or other falsehoods regarding Mary and her child contradicts tawhīd (Islamic monotheism) and is a serious moral and theological offense.

translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but it was made to appear to them. And indeed, those who differ about it are in doubt concerning it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the popular claim that Jesus was killed and crucified is mistaken: by God's will the apparent event was an illusion or substitution, so Jesus was not actually slain by people. It also censures those who insist on his death without true knowledge, exposing such assertions as mere conjecture; the passage therefore underscores divine sovereignty over outcomes, warns against relying on speculation rather than knowledge, and affirms that reality may differ from what appears outwardly.

translation: Nay—Allah raised him up to Himself; and Allah is Mighty, Wise.
interpretation: This clause affirms that what appeared to be human triumph over a righteous servant was overturned by God: He removed that servant from the hands of his enemies and elevated him in rank and preservation. The verb “raised” conveys both protection from the supposed disgrace and a real exaltation before God, while the attributes “Mighty” and “Wise” emphasize that this outcome flows from divine power and purposeful wisdom—no human plot can thwart God’s will, and what seems like defeat may, by God’s wise design, become vindication and honor, with the preserved servant held by God until the time He wills.

translation: And there is not one of the People of the Scripture but will surely believe in him before his death; and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.
interpretation: The verse indicates that ultimately the People of the Book will come to acknowledge ʿĪsā (Jesus) before the end of his life—a reading commonly understood as the recognition that will occur at his return—and that this eventual affirmation does not cancel the moral and spiritual consequences of their earlier rejection: on the Day of Resurrection Jesus will testify concerning their prior denial, so their belated belief will be weighed in the context of their earlier stance and deeds.

translation:
فَبِظُلْمٍ مِّنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا حَرَّمْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ طَيِّبَاتٍ أُحِلَّتْ لَهُمْ وَبِصَدِّهِمْ عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ كَثِيرًا
“So, because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jewish, We forbade them good things that had been lawful to them, and (because of) their turning many away from the way of God.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that when a community persistently abuses revelation and justice—by altering divine guidance, forbidding what God made lawful, or actively diverting people from the path of God—God may withdraw certain blessings and impose legal or social restrictions on them. This is presented both as a consequence of their injustice and as a corrective measure that exposes the moral cause-and-effect: misuse of religious authority and obstructing guidance leads to loss of privileges and serves as a warning to others to preserve faithful obedience rather than corrupting the law.

translation: Interest has seized them although they were forbidden from it, and they consume people’s wealth unjustly. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse indicts those who, despite knowing the prohibition, allow themselves to be overtaken by riba (usury/abusive interest) and thereby perpetrate economic injustice; this conduct is portrayed not merely as a legal fault but as a moral corruption—greed and hypocrisy that violate the rights of others and unravel social trust. The declaration that God has prepared a painful punishment for the disbelievers among them stresses divine accountability: persistent, knowing transgression of financial and moral bounds brings both inevitable worldly harm (social disorder, loss of blessings) and severe recompense in the Hereafter, and thus serves as a stern warning to uphold justice and refrain from exploiting people’s wealth.

translation: ولكن الراسخون في العلم منهم والمؤمنون يؤمنون بما أنزل إليك وما أنزل من قبلك ۚ والمقيمين الصلاة ۚ والمؤتون الزكاة والمؤمنون بالله واليوم الآخر أولئك سنؤتيهم أجرا عظيما
interpretation: الآية تميّز فئة من الناس — «الراسخون في العلم» ومن آمنوا — الذين يدركون عبر العلم الصحيح واستيعاب النصوص أن ما أُنزِل إلى النبي محمدٍ متصل بما أُنزل قبلَه، فإيمانهم ليس كلاماً فقط بل يظهر في الالتزام العملي: إقامَة الصلاة وإيتاء الزكاة والإيمان بالله واليوم الآخر. الرسالة أن المعرفة الراسخة لا تتناقض مع الخشوع العملي، وأن اتحاد العلم الصحيح مع الإيمان والعمل هو معيار للقبول عند الله، ولذلك يُوعَدون بأجر عظيم؛ بمعنى أن الاعتراف بالهدية الإلهية التاريخية المتصلة والعيش وفق المبادئ الإيمانية يؤدي إلى التكريم الإلهي.

translation: Indeed, We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him; and We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the (twelve) tribes, and to Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon — and to David We gave the Psalms.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the revelation given to Muhammad is part of a single, continuous divine guidance bestowed upon a succession of messengers. It affirms the common origin and moral-purpose of prophetic messages across generations, legitimizing Muhammad’s mission by linking it to earlier prophets and scriptures, and calls believers to recognize the unity of God’s guidance while respecting the distinct forms that revelation took for different peoples and times.

translation: And messengers — some of whom We have already related to you, and some of whom We have not related to you — and Allah spoke to Moses in direct speech.
interpretation: The verse reminds that God has sent many prophets, and He chooses which of their stories to make known; this underscores Divine wisdom in what is revealed and what is withheld, so believers should not judge the completeness of history by what is recounted. The mention that God “spoke to Moses” highlights that revelation can take different forms — including an extraordinary, direct communication — as an affirmation of Moses’ prophetic status and of the authentic, varied ways God communicates with His servants, without implying human likeness to God; the overall lesson is trust in God’s authority to disclose guidance as He wills and to validate His messengers.

translation: Messengers [were sent], bearing glad tidings and warnings, so that the people may have no argument against Allah after the messengers; and Allah is Ever Mighty, Ever Wise.
interpretation: By dispatching prophets who both encourage and admonish, God removes any legitimate excuse for ignorance — making human responsibility and accountability inevitable. This arrangement exemplifies divine justice and wisdom: guidance is offered clearly and fairly, and God’s sovereignty and prudence underlie the moral order in which acceptance brings reward and rejection brings consequence.

translation: But Allah bears witness to what He has revealed to you — He sent it down by His knowledge — and the angels bear witness. And sufficient is Allah as a Witness.
interpretation: The verse affirms the revelation's absolute divine authority and authenticity: its source is God's knowing will, not human invention, and it is verified by the witnessing of the angels; therefore no further human testimony is necessary and the declaration of Allah (with the angels as corroborators) is conclusive proof against those who deny or question the message.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and avert [others] from the way of Allah have gone far astray.
interpretation: The verse warns that rejecting God’s message and actively preventing others from following it is not a mere error but a compound, enduring deviation: such people are cut off from true guidance, their moral and spiritual perception becomes corrupted, and their actions increase their distance from truth—bringing progressive misguidance in this life and exposing them to loss in the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong — Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to any way.
interpretation: The verse teaches that persistent rejection of faith together with continued injustice places a person beyond the scope of Allah’s pardon and guidance: forgiveness and right guidance are mercies granted to those who accept truth and turn from wrongdoing, so one who obstinately chooses disbelief and oppression, refusing repentance, brings upon themselves the just consequence of being deprived of divine forgiveness and direction.

translation: Except the path to Hell — they will abide therein forever; and that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse teaches that for those who persistently reject God and choose the way of error the only ultimate outcome is the road that leads to Hell, with permanence as its characteristic; the clause “and that is easy for Allah” emphasizes that enforcing this just consequence and carrying out divine judgment is effortless for God, underlining both the inevitability of moral accountability and the futility of trying to escape or thwart God’s ordained retribution.

translation: O people, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord; so believe — it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse addresses all humanity to show that the Prophet’s message is a divinely given, beneficial guidance: accepting it leads to what is truly good for people, while rejecting it does not diminish God’s absolute sovereignty over creation. The warning is both an invitation and a reminder of responsibility — belief is urged because it aligns human life with the wisdom and knowledge of God, whereas disbelief leaves people to bear the moral and spiritual consequences; God’s knowledge and wisdom ensure the message is purposeful and just.

translation: O People of the Scripture, do not overstep the bounds in your religion and do not say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He conveyed to Mary and a spirit from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers; and do not say “Three” — desist; it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is only one God; exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse admonishes the People of the Scripture (Jews and Christians) against theological excesses that elevate human beings into divine status. It affirms that Jesus (‘Isa), while singular and miraculously born, is principally a messenger and a created manifestation of God’s command, not God’s son in any ontological sense. The prohibition of saying “Three” targets the Christian doctrinal formulation of a triune God, urging a return to uncompromising monotheism: God is one, transcendent, and does not beget nor is begotten. By insisting that all that exists belongs to God and that He alone is sufficient as guardian, the verse calls for correct belief (recognizing all prophets and not elevating any to divinity), theological humility, and trust in God’s exclusive sovereignty and care.

translation: The Messiah will never be reluctant to be a servant of Allah, nor the angels who are close [to Him]. And whoever is disdainful of His worship and arrogant—He will gather them all to Him.
interpretation: This verse upholds strict monotheism by showing that true honor is servitude to God, not exemption from it; it rejects any notion that the Messiah or others near God are above worship. The passage teaches a moral and eschatological lesson: pride and refusal to submit lead to being brought before God on the Day of Gathering for judgment, so humility and submission to Allah are the required stance for rightly ordered belief and conduct.

translation: As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will fully grant them their rewards and will increase them out of His bounty; but as for those who were disdainful and arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find for themselves besides Allah neither a guardian nor a helper.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith manifested in good deeds not only earns exact divine justice but also opens one to additional, gracious increase from God—reward as both right and gift. By contrast, an attitude of pride and contempt cuts a person off from that mercy and brings inevitable retribution; such arrogance results in spiritual isolation so complete that no worldly ally or intercessor can avert the consequence. Thus humility and active righteousness are portrayed as the means to receive God’s multiplying favor, while self-exaltation leads to loss and abandonment before divine judgment.

translation: O people, a conclusive proof has come to you from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light.
interpretation: The verse declares that God has provided humanity with decisive, unmistakable evidence of His guidance: a messenger and revelation that together function as the 'burhān' (decisive proof) and the 'nūr mubīn' (manifest light). This proof is not merely intellectual argument but a living, illuminating guidance that exposes error, clarifies moral and spiritual truths, and opens the heart to right conduct. Addressing “people” underscores its universal scope — it is meant to dispel doubt for all humanity and to bring practical, inward transformation; acceptance leads to guidance and reform, while rejection leaves one without that illuminating criterion to distinguish truth from falsehood.

translation: As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty, and will guide them to Himself on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse promises that sincere faith combined with clinging to God — trusting Him, adhering to His guidance, and seeking refuge in Him — results in divine compassion and favor: God grants forgiveness, spiritual blessings, and the means of growth. That mercy and bounty reshape the believer’s life by directing their heart and affairs toward righteous conduct and nearness to God; the “straight path” denotes both a morally upright way of living under God’s guidance in this world and the destined return to Him in the hereafter.

translation: They ask you for a legal ruling. Say, “Allah gives you a ruling concerning al-kalālah: if a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, then for the sister is half of what he leaves; and he inherits her if she has no child. But if there are two sisters, they shall have two-thirds of what he leaves. And if there are brothers and sisters, the male shall have the share of two females. Allah makes clear to you [His ordinances] so that you do not go astray. And Allah is Knowing of all things.”
interpretation: This verse functions as a divine clarification of inheritance law intended to remove dispute and uncertainty in delicate family situations. Rather than a mere social custom, the prescribed shares are legal measures designed to protect the rights of heirs (including women who might otherwise be neglected), to ensure orderly transfer of wealth, and to prevent conflict that would harm family and community. The difference in male and female portions reflects the social and financial responsibilities placed upon men in that legal framework (primarily their duty to provide and maintain dependents), so the rule addresses obligations and outcomes rather than intrinsic worth. The concluding phrase emphasizes that these detailed rules come from God’s knowledge and aim to keep the community rightly guided, not to demean any party.

translation: O you who have believed, fulfill your covenants. Lawful for you are the grazing animals, except what is recited to you (as prohibited); and hunting is not lawful for you while you are in a state of consecration (ihram). Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills.
interpretation: The verse insists on the moral necessity of honoring agreements and recognizes that God’s generosity (permitting lawful sustenance) operates within divinely set limits; some permissions may be temporarily suspended for higher religious purposes (e.g., the prohibition on hunting during ihram). Thus true obedience combines faithful fulfillment of contracts with submission to specific divine rulings, acknowledging that God’s determinations are authoritative and purposeful.

translation: O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah, nor the sacred month, nor the sacrificial animals, nor the garlands, nor those who come to the Sacred House seeking the bounty and pleasure of their Lord. And when you have exited (the state of) ihram, then hunt. And let not the hatred of a people for having kept you from al‑Masjid al‑Haram lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches a single integrated principle: sacred symbols, times, rites and those devoted to worship must be protected and not profaned, because holiness is grounded in submission to God; lawful exceptions (for example, hunting) depend on proper ritual status (leaving ihram). Even when people wrong you—such as by preventing access to a sacred place—you must not allow resentment to justify reciprocal transgression. Instead social bonds are to be organized around mutual help in goodness and God‑consciousness and to refuse any cooperation in wrongdoing or aggression. The command to fear Allah and the warning of severe punishment underline that this restraint and cooperative ethic are moral obligations backed by divine accountability.

translation: Prohibited to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, and that which has been strangled, or beaten to death, or fallen to death, or gored to death, and that which wild beasts have eaten—except what you are able to slaughter—and that which is sacrificed on stone altars, and that you seek decision by divining arrows. That is transgression. Today those who disbelieve have despaired of [defeating] your religion; so do not fear them, but fear Me. This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion. But whoever is forced by severe hunger with no inclination to sin—then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse sets clear boundaries for lawful nourishment and communal conduct to protect spiritual integrity and social identity: it forbids foods and methods of killing that carry ritual impurity, idolatrous dedication, or superstition, and it condemns divination as a form of shirk and moral disorder (fasq). By doing so the law distinguishes the community’s relationship to God from surrounding practices and strengthens trust in divine guidance. The declaration that unbelievers have despaired and that the religion is perfected signals that these stipulations are not temporary cautions but part of the completed divine ordinance for a Muslim way of life. At the same time, the concession for one in dire necessity—who takes prohibited food solely to survive without desire for sin—reveals the moral principle that intent and compulsion mitigate culpability: the sharʿa aims to preserve life and conscience, and where survival demands, divine mercy and forgiveness apply. In short, the verse balances firm religious boundaries and communal identity with a humane, intent-sensitive exception rooted in God’s mercy.

translation: They ask you what is lawful for them. Say, “Lawful for you are the good (tayyibāt).” And [lawful is] what you have trained of hunting animals, training them by what Allah has taught you—so eat of what they catch for you and mention the name of Allah upon it—and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God permits what is wholesome and lawful (tayyibāt) and specifically allows the meat taken by trained hunting animals when those animals are trained according to the means God has provided. The command to “mention the name of Allah” when taking that prey and to “fear Allah” links lawful provision to conscious obedience: permission is not a blank check to ignore God’s guidance. Rather, permissible sustenance must be taken with remembrance of God and moral restraint, because people remain accountable—God’s judgment is prompt. In short: lawful provision includes what your trained animals catch, but consumption must be done within God’s framework of remembrance and reverent responsibility.

translation: Today I have made lawful for you the good things. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And (lawful for you are) chaste women from the believing women and chaste women from those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their due dowries, seeking chastity, not committing fornication nor taking them as secret lovers. And whoever disbelieves in the faith — his deeds are rendered vain, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse establishes a regulated opening of social and familial relations between Muslims and People of the Book: it permits mutual consumption of lawful foods and permits marriage with chaste women among both believing women and women of earlier revealed communities, but only within legitimate marriage (the giving of the due mahr) and with the intention of chastity, explicitly forbidding illicit sexual relations and clandestine liaisons. This framing makes clear that permissibility is conditional — lawful integration and family life are allowed but must observe moral, legal, and contractual boundaries — and it closes by reminding that rejection of true faith nullifies one’s deeds, so legal allowances do not replace the central requirement of sincere belief.

translation: O you who have believed, when you stand for prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe your heads, and (wash) your feet up to the ankles. And if you are junub (in a state of major ritual impurity), then purify yourselves. But if you are ill or on a journey or one of you comes from relieving himself or you have touched women and you do not find water, then perform tayammum with clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to place difficulty upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful.
interpretation: The verse establishes ritual purity as the immediate preparation for standing before God in prayer while showing that religious obligations are balanced by divine compassion: specific practices (wudu, ghusl, tayammum) are prescribed to make worship orderly and bodily-spiritual cleanliness achievable, and exceptions (illness, travel, lack of water, recent impurity) are allowed so that obligation does not become undue hardship. The underlying aim is inner and communal purification and the completion of God’s blessing, cultivating gratefulness rather than legalistic burden.

translation:
واذكروا نعمة الله عليكم وميثاقه الذي واثقكم به إذ قلتم سمعنا وأطعنا ۖ واتقوا الله ۚ إن الله عليم بذات الصدور
"And remember the favor of Allah upon you and His covenant by which He bound you when you said, ‘We hear and we obey.’ And fear Allah. Indeed Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts."
interpretation: The verse urges believers to take to heart that God’s past mercies and the pledge they gave to obey His guidance are not mere words but moral obligations. Saying “we hear and we obey” creates a binding responsibility that must be borne out in conduct and inner sincerity; hence the command to fear Allah — live with reverence, vigilance, and integrity. The reminder that God knows “what is in the breasts” warns that outward conformity is insufficient: true faith requires purified intentions, because God evaluates both visible actions and hidden motives.

translation: O you who believe, be steadfast witnesses for Allah in justice. And let not the hatred of a people make you avoid being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah; surely Allah is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to occupy the role of moral and civic guardians on God’s behalf: to stand firm in upholding justice wherever they act—legally, socially and personally—so that their testimony and conduct reflect divine standards rather than private interests. “Do not let hatred of a people” warns that personal bias, tribal loyalty or enmity must never corrupt judgment; true obedience requires correcting feelings that would lead to partiality. The verse also teaches that impartial justice is itself an expression of piety—being fair draws one nearer to God—while the injunction to fear Allah reminds believers that accountability is both external (to others) and internal (before God), since God knows motives and deeds; this awareness is the safeguard that preserves integrity in difficult situations.

translation: God has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse asserts that true faith must be lived through righteous action; God’s promise links inner belief with outward conduct, assuring that sincere believers who act rightly will receive comprehensive pardon (the removal and healing of sin) and an immeasurable, enduring recompense — understood ultimately as nearness to God and the bliss of the Hereafter. This both comforts believers with God’s mercy and motivates continuous moral striving.

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse warns that persistent, willful rejection of God’s revelations and the clear evidences He has sent leads to moral and spiritual ruin and to just, final retribution; calling such people “companions of the Hellfire” affirms that denial of God’s guidance has real consequences in the hereafter, underlining divine justice and serving as a deterrent to heedfulness and sincere acceptance of the signs.

translation: O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when there were people about to stretch out their hands against you, but He restrained their hands from you. And fear Allah; and let the believers put their trust in Allah.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to cultivate gratefulness and God-consciousness by recalling that God intervened to avert harm intended by others. That memory should produce taqwa (reverence and obedience) and a reliance on God rather than self-sufficiency or dependence on worldly powers; true security and success come from Allah’s protection, so believers should live in humility, obedience, and trust in Him.

translation: And Allah had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We appointed from them twelve leaders. And Allah said, “Indeed I am with you. If you establish prayer and give zakah and believe in My messengers and support them and loan Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow.” But whoever of you disbelieves after that has certainly gone astray from the soundness of the way.
interpretation: This verse presents a conditional divine promise tied to communal and personal responsibility: the appointment of twelve leaders among Israel and God’s assurance are paired with concrete duties—regular prayer, almsgiving, sincere faith in and support for God’s messengers, and generous spending ‘as a loan to God.’ The reward promised (forgiveness of sins and admission to gardens beneath which rivers flow) underscores that spiritual standing is secured through active obedience and social solidarity in upholding revelation. Conversely, turning away after these clear commitments amounts to self-diversion from the straight path: the moral is that divine favor is not automatic but given in response to faith lived out through worship, charity, and defense of the prophetic mission; neglect or repudiation after receiving guidance constitutes serious misguidance.

translation: So because they broke their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard. They distort words from their proper places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of. You will continually find treachery among most of them, except for a few of them. So pardon them and forgive. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse teaches that persistent breach of God’s covenant produces inner hardening and leads people to twist truth and neglect their obligations; yet in the face of widespread failing the proper leadership response is restraint and magnanimity — pardoning and overlooking faults rather than responding with vindictiveness. Such forbearance is part of moral excellence (ihsan), aimed at preserving what good remains and inviting reform, and it accords with God’s love for those who do good.

translation: And of those who said, “We are Christians,” We took their covenant; but they forgot a part of what they were reminded of, so We set enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that abandoning or neglecting parts of a divinely entrusted teaching undermines communal integrity: such neglect brings about persistent social division and mutual hostility as a consequence allowed by God, and it serves as a moral sign whose ultimate resolution will be divine accountability. In other words, fidelity to the covenant is not merely formal — altering or discarding obligations damages the community’s moral fabric and will be made manifest and judged by God.

translation: O People of the Scripture, our messenger has come to you making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much. A light from God has come to you and a clear Book.
interpretation: The verse declares that God has sent a final messenger to rectify the record and provide a decisive standard: the Prophet exposes doctrines and practices that had been hidden or altered, while mercifully overlooking many past faults, and presents the Qur’an as a divine ‘light’ and explicit criterion. Its practical thrust is that a transparent, authoritative revelation has arrived to correct misunderstandings, settle disputes, and guide people back to the true, uncorrupted knowledge of God.

translation:
يهدي به الله من اتبع رضوانه سبل السلام ويخرجهم من الظلمات إلى النور بإذنه ويهديهم إلى صراط مستقيم
"By it — (the Book) — Allah guides those who seek His good pleasure to ways of peace; He brings them out from darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path."
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance, centered in the Revelation, works when a person sincerely orients their intention toward God’s approval: such readiness opens the heart to a transformative guidance that produces inner peace, moral clarity and orderly communal life. The phrase “by His permission” reminds us that guidance is ultimately a gift from God, not merely a human achievement, yet this gift is received and realized only through a free, responsive turning toward what pleases God. The promised movement from “darkness” to “light” describes both an inward change (from ignorance, error and spiritual distress to knowledge, truth and serenity) and an outward reordering of conduct; the “straight path” signifies a balanced, consistent way of living—ethical, devotional and social—that leads to lasting well‑being and accountability before God.

translation: Those who say, “Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary,” have certainly disbelieved. Say, “Then who could prevent anything from Allah if He willed to destroy the Messiah, the son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on the earth?” To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. He creates what He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute uniqueness and sovereign power, rejecting any attribution of divinity to the Messiah.
