By posing the rhetorical question—who could stop God if He intended to destroy Jesus, his mother, and everyone on earth—it stresses that no created being shares God’s authority over life, death, and creation. The point is theological: claiming Jesus as God contradicts the reality that dominion, creative power, and ultimate control belong solely to God, who acts according to His will and is capable of all things.

translation: And the Jews and the Christians said, “We are the children of Allah and His beloved.” Say, “Then why did He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are only human beings of those He has created. He forgives whom He wills and He punishes whom He wills. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and to Him is the return.”
interpretation: The verse corrects a claim of spiritual privilege: asserting the title “children of God” or special beloved status does not exempt anyone from moral responsibility or Divine justice. God answers such claims by pointing to the obvious — people who are punished for their wrongdoing cannot be outside the moral order — and reminds that all humans are His created beings, subject to His will. Mercy and punishment are dispensed by God according to His knowledge and wisdom, and ultimate authority over the universe and final return belong solely to Him.

translation: O People of the Book, there has come to you Our Messenger to make clear to you — as a succession of messengers — so that you do not say, “No bearer of good tidings nor warner has come to us.” Indeed, there has come to you a bearer of good tidings and a warner. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse addresses Jews and Christians who rejected the Prophet by claiming they had received no true bringer of glad tidings or warner. It asserts that Muhammad is part of the same prophetic succession and that his mission clarifies and fulfills what earlier revelation pointed toward, removing their pretended excuse of no messenger’s coming. By calling him both "busher" (bearer of good news) and "nadhir" (warner), the verse affirms the dual role of guidance and warning that prophets perform and reminds the addressees that God’s power guarantees that the truth and accountability conveyed by this messenger cannot be nullified.

translation: “And when Moses said to his people, ‘O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given to any of the worlds.’”
interpretation: The passage serves to transform divine bestowals into moral obligations: unique favors—especially guidance and authority—are entrusted to a people not for self-exaltation but as responsibilities that demand gratitude, righteous conduct, and faithful stewardship. The reminder warns that privileges are conditional on upholding the covenant (obedience, justice, preservation of revealed guidance); misuse, ingratitude, or rejection of that trust risks forfeiture of the blessing and accountability before God.

translation: “O my people, enter the sacred land which Allah has decreed for you, and do not turn back (in retreat), lest you return as losers.”
interpretation: The verse admonishes believers to take hold of the opportunity and responsibility God has granted them—whether a literal promised territory or any God‑ordained goal—and to act with trust and resolve rather than letting fear, hesitation, or disobedience drive them to withdraw. Turning back in the face of the test forfeits the blessing and renders one a failure; success requires courage, collective resolve, and faithful obedience to God’s command.

translation: They said, “O Moses, indeed in it are a people of great might, and we will never enter it while they remain there; but if they leave, then we will enter.”
interpretation: This remark reveals a failure of faith and moral resolve: the people prefer to wait for the removal of obstacles by others rather than trust God and their leader to face difficulty. Their demand that the strong inhabitants depart first is an excuse to avoid struggle and responsibility, reflecting cowardice, reliance on safety over covenantal duty, and thereby forfeiting the promise that required courageous obedience.

translation: Two men of those who feared [Allah], upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, said, “Enter upon them through the gate; and when you enter it, you will surely be prevailing. And put your trust in Allah, if you are believers.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that true piety coupled with God’s favor enables decisive, courageous action: ‘entering the gate’ represents taking the necessary step into a difficult or risky situation, and the promise of being ‘prevailing’ is grounded not in human boldness alone but in reliance on God. The injunction to ‘put your trust in Allah’ emphasizes active tawakkul—plan and act with resolve while trusting that God will grant success to those who believe and are conscious of Him.

translation:
قالوا: "يا موسى إنا لن ندخلها أبداً ما داموا فيها؛ فاذهب أنت وربك فقاتلا؛ إنا هاهنا قاعدون".
They said, “O Moses, we will never enter it while they are in it; so go, you and your Lord, and fight — indeed we are sitting here.”
interpretation: This statement reveals the people's cowardice and failure of faith: instead of trusting God's promise and fulfilling their collective duty, they refuse to confront the inhabitants, shift responsibility onto Moses (and ostensibly God), and adopt passivity. It exposes moral weakness — avoidance of commanded struggle, reliance on excuses, and a relinquishing of responsibility that brings divine displeasure and consequences.

translation:
قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي لَا أَمْلِكُ إِلَّا نَفْسِي وَأَخِي ۖ فَافْرُقْ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَ الْقَوْمِ الْفَاسِقِينَ
He said, “My Lord, I have no power except over myself and my brother; so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people.”
interpretation: The verse teaches humble reliance on God: the speaker recognizes that human influence is limited and that he cannot compel or reform a corrupt people by his own strength, so he asks God to intervene decisively — to distinguish and protect him and his companion from the transgressors, securing a clear separation in fate, guidance, and consequences rather than depending on human coercion.

translation: قَالَ: «فَإِنَّهَا حَرَامٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أَرْبَعِينَ سَنَةً يُتَاهُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ» ۚ فَلَا تَأْسَ عَلَى الْقَوْمِ الْفَاسِقِينَ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن العقوبة الإلهية قد تُترجَم إلى سلب النعم والطمأنينة فترةً محددة كوسيلة لتأديب وتنقية الجماعة عن معصيتهم؛ والوصية بعدم الأسى تذْكر النبيّ والمؤمنين بأن لا يبدّلوا إحباطهم وتعاطفهم المعتادين إلى تشغّل وانهزامية تجاه من أصرّوا على الفسق، لأن حكم الله وعدالته هي التي تجري، والواجب مواصلة الدعوة والصبر بدل الانغماس في الحزن على أولئك الذين اختاروا طريق التمرد.

translation: And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth: when they both offered a sacrifice, it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. The latter said, “I will surely kill you.” The former said, “Indeed, Allah only accepts from the righteous.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s acceptance of deeds is determined by inner righteousness and God-consciousness (taqwa), not merely by outward actions or social standing. The accepted brother’s calm reply — that Allah accepts only from the righteous — points to sincerity, humility, and moral rectitude as the real criteria for divine approval, while the rejected brother’s jealousy and threat illustrate how spiritual corruption (envy, pride, impatience) leads to grave wrongdoing. The incident warns believers to cultivate piety and restraint rather than seek validation through envy or violence.

translation: If you were to stretch out your hand to kill me, I would not stretch out my hand to kill you; indeed I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The speaker declares a moral refusal to retaliate against threatened violence, grounding that restraint in fear of God and trust in divine justice—choosing piety and patient reliance on Allah over personal vengeance.

translation: “Indeed, I intend that you bear my sin and your sin, and that you be among the companions of the Fire. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The verse portrays a malicious intention—someone seeking to make another person carry both their own guilt and the speaker’s guilt so that they together suffer the punishment of Hell. It warns that oppressors or corrupters who enlist others in their wrongdoing attempt to spread and multiply culpability, but such collusion only increases accountability; the ultimate and fitting outcome for those who wrongfully burden others with sin is punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: So his soul urged him to kill his brother; he killed him and thus became among the losers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that surrendering to the lower self — driven by envy, anger or base desire — can lead one to commit the gravest wrongs against a fellow human. ‘نفسه طوعت له’ shows the temptation arose from within and therefore was subject to choice and restraint; the result, becoming ‘من الخاسرين,’ denotes moral and ultimate loss — the forfeiture of integrity and true success in this life and the hereafter. The warning is to guard the soul, practice self-control and not let inner impulses justify destructive acts.

translation: فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُ كَيْفَ يُوَارِي سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ ۚ قَالَ يَا وَيْلَتَىٰ أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَـٰذَا الْغُرَابِ فَأُوَارِيَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِي ۖ فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ النَّادِمِينَ
interpretation: The verse teaches that God can instruct and awaken human conscience through the signs in His creation, prompting a moral recognition that may come even after a grave wrong. It highlights the shame and remorse that ought to follow unjust actions, condemns the destructive roots such as envy that lead to violence, and implies that guidance and mercy can move the sinner to humility; yet it also points to the ethical requirement that remorse be accompanied by corrective, respectful behavior toward the harmed (and by genuine reform), not merely regret.

translation:
من أجل ذلك كتبنا على بني إسرائيل أنه من قتل نفسا بغير نفس أو فساد في الأرض فكأنما قتل الناس جميعا ومن أحياها فكأنما أحيا الناس جميعا ۚ ولقد جاءتهم رسلنا بالبينات ثم إن كثيرا منهم بعد ذلك في الأرض لمسرفون
"Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul — except for a soul or for corruption in the land — it is as if he killed all mankind; and whoever saves a life, it is as if he saved all mankind. And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs, yet many of them thereafter were transgressors in the land."
interpretation: The verse establishes a fundamental moral principle: each human life bears universal value so great that unjust killing amounts morally to annihilating all humanity, while preserving a single life is like preserving the whole human community. By framing the rule in this stark, almost hyperbolic way, the text seeks to cultivate empathy, social responsibility and restraint, to justify strict limits on violence (permitting killing only in narrowly defined cases such as just retribution or removing grave public corruption), and to warn that rejecting clear guidance from the messengers leads society into excess, bloodshed and disorder.

translation: Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth [to cause] corruption is that they be killed or crucified or that their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides or that they be exiled from the land. That is for them a disgrace in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse is read as establishing a legal principle that violent, organised attacks which threaten public safety, order and the social fabric—classically understood as armed brigandry, rebellion or terrorism—may be met by the authority of the polity with severe, proportionate penalties intended to protect society and deter further corruption. Classical and later jurists limit the verse to such violent crimes (not to peaceful dissent), insist on strict proof and due process, allow alternatives (exile, pardon, restitution) and emphasize opportunities for repentance; the underlying purpose is safeguarding life, property and communal order rather than endorsing private vengeance or indiscriminate brutality.

translation: Except those who repent before you have power over them; so know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The clause narrows the preceding legal ruling by exempting a person who truly repents before the community or its representatives are able to apprehend or enforce punishment. Sincere, timely repentance — accompanied by remorse and a resolve to reform — removes the liability for the prescribed sanction, and those in authority should accept such repentance rather than proceed to retribution. The closing attributes, ‘Forgiving, Merciful,’ console and remind believers that God’s predominant disposition toward those who turn back to Him is pardon and compassion, encouraging people to seek repentance rather than despair.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means of nearness to Him and strive in His cause; perhaps you will be successful.
interpretation: The verse links inner piety to deliberate effort: taqwa (God‑consciousness) must be lived, and believers are urged to pursue whatever legitimately draws them nearer to Allah — sincere faith, repentance, worship, following the Prophet’s example, righteous deeds and lawful forms of mediation — while actively struggling against inner inclinations and for justice and truth in His way. True success (falah) is presented as the hoped‑for outcome of this combined inward reform and outward striving, not as something attained without effort.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve — if they were to possess all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves therewith from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection; but what they intend will not be accepted of them, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly wealth and means are powerless before divine justice: no amount of riches can buy forgiveness or avert the consequences of rejecting God's guidance. It warns that on the Day of Reckoning regret and attempts to bribe away punishment will be futile, and that true deliverance depends on sincere faith, repentance, and God's acceptance rather than material bargaining.

translation: They long to get out of the Fire, but they will not be able to get out of it; and for them is an abiding punishment.
interpretation: The verse underscores the irrevocable consequence of having persistently rejected guidance: at the time of reckoning the sufferers’ intense wish to escape will be futile because their earlier choices and the established divine judgment leave no room for reversal. It is a moral admonition that true escape from punishment depends on timely acceptance and sincere turning, not on belated regret when the sentence has been fixed.

translation: As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned — a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Mighty, Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes a severe, emblematic penalty aimed at protecting property and deterring theft, but it must be understood within the wider Islamic legal and moral framework: the punishment is prescribed only for proven, deliberate theft that meets strict conditions (clear proof or confession, a minimum threshold of value, absence of necessity or coercion, and proper custodial procedures), and it functions as part of a system intended to preserve communal order, justice, and prevention rather than gratuitous cruelty. Invoking Allah as “Mighty, Wise” signals that the measure serves a considered objective—balancing deterrence and social welfare—while leaving room for mercy, repentance, and legal safeguards in its application.

translation: So whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, then indeed Allah will accept his repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine forgiveness is available to anyone who not only feels remorse but actively turns away from injustice and repairs the harm done; sincere tawbah requires inner repentance plus concrete reform of behavior and relations, and when these conditions are met Allah responds with pardon and mercy — a guarantee that encourages moral responsibility and hope rather than despair.

translation: Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse underscores divine sovereignty as the basis for both moral responsibility and spiritual hope: because God alone holds ultimate authority over the world, His decisions about punishment and forgiveness are neither arbitrary nor constrained by human power. Believers are therefore called to live with a balance of reverent fear (awareness of accountability) and confident hope (reliance on God’s mercy), to seek repentance and righteous action, and to trust that whatever God wills flows from His complete power, wisdom, and justice.

translation: O Messenger, let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you—among those who say, “We believe” with their mouths but do not believe in their hearts—and among the Jews: they are listeners for falsehood, listeners to other people who did not come to you, twisting the words after their places, saying, “If you are given this, take it; and if you are not given it, then beware.” And whoever Allah intends to put to trial, you will have no protector for him against Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has not willed to purify; for them is disgrace in this world, and a great punishment in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This address reassures the Prophet and the believing community that outward professions and the manipulations of opponents do not overturn divine reality: some people may profess faith while remaining inwardly estranged, and others will distort revelation and follow deceitful leaders for their own ends. Their behavior and the trials they face are signs of a spiritual condition that only God ultimately determines—He allows trials to reveal and delimit who is open to moral and spiritual purification and who is not. The passage therefore counsels detachment from being unduly troubled by such hypocritical show or by opponents’ sophistry, affirms that final judgment and reform of hearts rest with God alone, and warns that persistent refusal of genuine guidance brings disgrace in this life and severe accountability in the next.

translation: Those who are quick to listen to lies, who devour unlawful gains. So when they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them; and if you turn away, they will not harm you at all. And if you judge, then judge between them with equity — indeed, Allah loves the equitable.
interpretation: This verse warns against people who eagerly accept falsehood and live by illicit gain (such as bribery or fraud) and instructs a leader—especially the Prophet—to refuse to be drawn into their schemes or to adjudicate their disputes when they present themselves. It reassures that withdrawing from dealing with such corrupt individuals does not threaten the integrity or mission of the leader, and it commands that if one does judge, one must do so with strict impartiality and fairness. The broader moral is a prohibition of complicity with corruption and a firm obligation on officials and judges to uphold justice, since God loves those who act equitably.

translation: And how will they judge you while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah, yet they turn away after that? And those are not believers.
interpretation: The verse censures people who possess God’s revealed law (the Torah) and therefore have access to divine guidance and criteria for judgment, yet when faced with clear rulings they refuse to submit, turn away, or reject the ordained decisions. Their possession of scripture makes their rejection culpable: having the law should have led them to accept rightful judgment, so their deliberate abandonment demonstrates hypocrisy and proves that they are not genuinely faithful.

translation: Indeed We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light. The prophets who submitted judged by it for the Jews, as did the rabbis and the scholars by what they were entrusted of the Book of Allah; and they were witnesses thereto. So do not fear the people, but fear Me, and do not exchange My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed — then those are the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that revealed scripture is the divinely appointed standard for law and guidance, and that religious leaders are entrusted with safeguarding and applying that standard. Their authority and testimony depend on fidelity to the revelation; therefore judges and teachers must fear God rather than public opinion or personal gain, and must not barter away divine commands for worldly advantage. To abandon Allah’s criterion in favor of other measures is not merely a policy error but a fundamental rejection of the basis of faith and community order.

translation: And We ordained for them therein: life for life, eye for eye, nose for nose, ear for ear, tooth for tooth, and wounds equal for equal. But whoever pardons it by way of charity, it shall be an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes the principle of qisās (proportional retribution) as a means of just restraint—measuring punishment to fit the harm to prevent excessive revenge and to protect human life and dignity. At the same time it commends mercy: if the injured party forgives or accepts a charitable remission, that act of pardon serves as spiritual expiation and moral elevation for the forgiver. Thus the law balances justice and compassion, and the verse closes with a warning that those who refuse to rule according to God’s revealed measure—either by taking law into their own hands or by rejecting just limits—are the real wrongdoers.

translation:
وَقَفَّيْنَا عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمْ بِعِيسَى ابْنِ مَرْيَمَ مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ ۖ وَآتَيْنَاهُ الْإِنجِيلَ فِيهِ هُدًى وَنُورٌ وَمُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ وَهُدًى وَمَوْعِظَةً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ
"And following in their footsteps We sent Jesus, son of Mary, confirming what came before him of the Torah; and We bestowed on him the Gospel — in it was guidance and light, confirming what preceded it of the Torah, and a guidance and admonition for the righteous."
interpretation: The verse affirms the continuity and unity of divine guidance: Jesus is presented not as an isolated figure but as a link in the prophetic chain who validates the earlier revelation (the Torah) and brings a new scripture whose purpose is ethical and spiritual illumination. Describing the Gospel as “guidance and light” stresses its function to clarify God’s will and to enlighten hearts, while calling it a “confirmation” of the Torah emphasizes that true revelation does not negate but fulfills and completes prior guidance. The final clause — that it is “a guidance and admonition for the muttaqin (the God‑conscious)” — signals that scriptures bear fruit when received by receptive, God‑fearing souls; revelation serves as a means to form piety and moral integrity rather than as mere historical text. In short, the verse teaches prophetic continuity, the confirmatory relationship between successive scriptures, and the transformative aim of revelation toward those who heed it.

translation: And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it; and whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed — then those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse affirms that communities entrusted with a revealed scripture (here called the People of the Gospel) have the duty to shape their judgments and communal laws by the divine guidance contained in that scripture; the legitimacy to judge others is therefore conditional on fidelity to revelation. Refusal or neglect to apply what God revealed — whether through deliberate rejection, distortion, or practical disregard — is characterized as fusuq (open transgression), signifying a breach of the covenant and a public departure from moral order. In short, the passage emphasizes that religious authority and social justice require adherence to genuine revelation, and it censures those who claim spiritual leadership while abandoning the revealed standard.

translation: And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Scripture and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their inclinations away from what has come to you of the truth. To each of you We prescribed a law and a clear way. And if Allah had willed, He would have made you a single community; but [He intended] to test you in what He has given you. So compete in good deeds. To Allah is your return all together, and He will inform you concerning that over which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the Quran is revealed as a truthful confirmation of earlier scriptures and as an overseeing criterion: it restores and guards the divine guidance that preceded it. The practical requirement is that disputes must be settled by what God has revealed, not by human desires, because following whims undermines the truth entrusted to the Prophet. The diversity of laws and ways among peoples is presented as deliberate divine wisdom — not a mistake — intended as a moral test: differences are allowed so that individuals and communities are tried in how they use their God-given guidance. The proper response to that test is not sectarian triumphalism but striving to outdo one another in righteous deeds. Ultimately all will return to God, who alone will resolve the matters in which people disagreed; therefore believers should judge by revelation, avoid following vain passions, recognize the purpose behind diversity, and focus on moral striving and accountability rather than on asserting absolute superiority.

translation: “And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires; and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. And if they turn away, then know that Allah only intends to afflict them with some of their sins. And indeed many of the people are defiantly disobedient.”
interpretation: This verse instructs those who are entrusted with ruling or guiding (especially the Prophet and judges) to apply God’s revelation impartially and resist popular pressures or personal inclinations. It warns that opponents may try to divert the guide from revealed truth through persuasion, flattery or intimidation, so vigilance is required. If people persistently reject the divine guidance, God may allow the consequences of their own wrongdoings to befall them as a form of just retribution and exposure of their error; the closing reminder that many are openly rebellious explains why firmness and adherence to revelation are necessary.

translation: Do they then seek the judgment of the Age of Ignorance? And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain (in faith)?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who prefer to return to the customs and legal judgments of the pre-Islamic ‘jahiliyyah’ instead of accepting God’s guidance. It affirms that Allah’s rulings are supremely just and fitting, and that anyone who truly possesses firm conviction and certainty in the truth of revelation will recognize and accept His judgment as superior; choosing the ways of ignorance is therefore a rejection of what certainty demands and a surrender to inferior, unjust standards.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies (awliya’). They are allies of one another. And whoever among you takes them as allies is [one] of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse warns believers not to place their primary loyalty, protection, or political dependence in Jews and Christians insofar as those relationships would subordinate the Muslim community or involve supporting actions contrary to Muslim interests and justice. “Awliyā’” here is read as bonds of alliance and trust that determine allegiance; the prohibition targets alliances that would make a Muslim effectively part of an opposing party or enable injustice. Read in its historical and legal context, the injunction aims to safeguard communal autonomy and faith, not to forbid ordinary social interaction, trade, or fair and kind treatment of non‑Muslims.

translation: You will see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening among them, saying, “We fear that a calamity may befall us.” Perhaps Allah will bring about a victory or a matter from Him, and they will awaken to what they had concealed in their souls, regretful.
interpretation: The verse describes people whose inner corruption—doubt, hypocrisy or malice—is reflected in their conduct: they hasten to avoid danger and voice feigned fears to excuse shirking responsibility. Their outward anxiety masks hostile intent or lack of trust in God. God, however, can either grant a clear victory (vindicating the sincere) or send an affair that exposes and resolves the situation; when that happens their true motives will be laid bare and they will be left remorseful. In short, private cowardice or hypocrisy cannot escape God’s decree, and apparent safety‑seeking will turn to regret when the divine outcome reveals what lay in their hearts.

translation: And those who believed say, “Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their strongest oaths that they were certainly with you?” Truly they are (only outwardly) with you; their deeds have been made void, so they have become losers.
interpretation: The verse expresses the believers’ dismay at people who gave solemn oaths of loyalty yet proved insincere; because their profession of faith and pledges were hypocritical, the moral and spiritual value of their actions is nullified. It warns that outward association and verbal oaths without true inner faith and fidelity render deeds worthless before God, resulting in real loss in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: O you who have believed, whoever among you turns away from his religion — Allah will bring forth a people whom He will love and who will love Him, humble toward the believers, stern against the disbelievers, who strive in the cause of Allah and do not fear the reproach of any critic. That is the bounty of Allah; He grants it to whom He wills. And Allah is Vast, Knowing.
interpretation: This verse assures that God, in His sovereignty, will preserve and advance the way of truth even if some current believers abandon it. The “people” God may raise are characterized not merely by ritual piety but by a deep reciprocal love with God, inward humility and support within the faithful community, resolute firmness against forces opposing the faith, committed struggle for God’s cause, and moral courage to act rightly despite criticism. The passage teaches that such collective qualities are a divine gift — granted according to God’s will and wisdom — and that fidelity to God’s cause depends ultimately on His sustaining grace rather than on human numbers or reputation.

translation:
إنما وليكم الله ورسوله والذين آمنوا الذين يقيمون الصلاة ويؤتون الزكاة وهم راكعون
“Your guardianship (walaa) is only Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe — those who establish prayer and give zakah while they are bowing.”
interpretation: The verse means that true authority and allegiance belong to God, His Prophet, and sincere believers whose faith is proven by steadfast worship and selfless giving. The phrase “while they are bowing” underscores that their devotion and readiness to support others arise from genuine humility before God, so rightful leadership and trustworthiness in the community are to be measured by piety and charitable commitment rather than by worldly status or power.

translation: And whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies—then indeed, the party of Allah are the ones who will be victorious.
interpretation: The verse affirms that true allegiance — making God, His Messenger, and the believing community one’s guiding protectors through sincere faith, obedience, and solidarity — places a person within “the party of Allah,” who receive divine support and ultimate triumph; it calls for wholehearted loyalty to divine guidance and communal unity rather than reliance on rival worldly factions.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take those who take your religion for mockery and amusement—from among those who were given the Scripture before you—and the disbelievers as allies. And fear Allah, if you are truly believers.
interpretation: Believers are warned against forming intimate alliances, entrusting protection, or placing their dependence on people—whether among some of the People of the Book or among outright disbelievers—who treat the Muslim faith with contempt, jest, or trivialization. Allowing such persons to become 'awliyāʾ' (protectors, patrons, or those given authority and trust) risks moral and political compromise, erosion of communal religious integrity, and exposure to hostile influence. The injunction to "fear Allah" links upright belief to preserving the community’s independence and sincerity of worship; this should not be read as forbidding ordinary just dealings with non‑Muslims, but as prohibiting close alliances, leadership roles, or loyalties that would empower those who demean the religion to undermine it.

translation: And when you are called to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a play. That is because they are a people who do not reason.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who respond to the summons to worship with ridicule and amusement; this outward levity signals a deeper moral and intellectual failing—an inability or refusal to apprehend the gravity and significance of divine obligation. Their mockery is not mere laughter but a symptom of spiritual deafness and corrupt priorities: preferring diversion and contempt over reverence and accountability, which shows they lack the right understanding and conscience required to recognize and submit to moral truth.

translation:
قُلْ يَا أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ هَلْ تَنقِمُونَ مِنّا إِلّا أَنْ آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَمَا أُنْزِلَ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَأَنَّ أَكْثَرَكُمْ فَاسِقُونَ
"Say, O People of the Scripture: Do you take offense at us only because we have believed in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and in what was revealed before, and because most of you are transgressors?"
interpretation: The verse confronts the real motive behind the hostility of some among the People of the Book: it is not a neutral theological disagreement but a reaction to a faith that recognizes divine guidance both in the Prophet’s message and in earlier scriptures, a stance that implicitly condemns widespread moral and religious failings among them. By framing the charge as a rhetorical question, Allah exposes their resentment as rooted in self-defense of corrupt practices, authority, or identity rather than in honest debate, and invites them to self-examination rather than blind rejection.

translation: Say, “Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a retribution from Allah? It is for whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has taken His wrath, and whom He has made of them apes and swine and made them worshippers of Taghut. Those are worse in position and further astray from the straight way.”
interpretation: The verse warns that the most terrible consequence is not merely a physical punishment but spiritual and moral ruin: when divine displeasure falls on a people, God may abase them so that their reason, ethics and social standing are corrupted — described figuratively as being made into “apes and swine” — and they come to serve false powers (Taghut). This condition of being cursed, morally degraded and turned toward idolatry is the worst possible state and the farthest removed from guidance.

translation: And when they come to you, they say, 'We believe,' while they have entered with disbelief and they have certainly gone out with it. And Allah is most knowing of what they were hiding.
interpretation: The verse condemns hypocrisy: some people pretend faith outwardly to gain trust or safety while their inner conviction remains unbelief. True iman is a settled inward reality that shows itself in consistent behavior, not mere words. The passage warns believers not to be deceived by professions alone and reminds that Allah alone knows hidden intentions and will hold people accountable for what they conceal.

translation: And you will see many of them hastening into sin and transgression and consuming what is unlawful. How evil indeed are the deeds they do.
interpretation: The verse indicts a pervasive moral attitude: people who rush toward wrongdoing and overstep limits out of eagerness for immediate gain, especially by taking what is forbidden, are not merely committing isolated sins but embodying a corrupt disposition that destroys justice and spiritual integrity. ‘Hastening’ underscores a willful, impatient pursuit of forbidden profit or power; ‘eating the unlawful’ points to economic and social practices that stain the heart and community. By calling their deeds ‘evil,’ the verse warns that such conduct produces real harm — moral decay, social injustice, and divine disapproval — and urges vigilance to resist greed, curb aggressive transgression, and preserve lawful, upright behavior.

translation: Why do not the rabbis and the scholars forbid them from saying what is sinful and from devouring unlawful gain? Wretched indeed is what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse condemns religious authorities who fail in their duty to enjoin right and forbid wrong: by remaining silent or tolerating sinful speech and illicit gain, they become complicit and corrupt their communities. It holds that possessing sacred knowledge without moral responsibility — especially when one benefits from others’ wrongdoing — is a grave failing and deserving of rebuke.

translation: And the Jews say, “The hand of Allah is chained.” Their hands are chained and they are cursed for what they say. Rather, both His hands are spread out; He spends as He wills. And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will only increase many of them in transgression and disbelief, and We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it; and they strive throughout the land seeking corruption, and Allah does not like the corrupters.
interpretation: The verse rebukes a claim made by some among the People of the Book that God is stingy or restricted (“His hand is chained”) and answers by asserting God’s unlimited generosity and power (“both His hands are spread out; He spends as He wills”). It then explains a moral and spiritual dynamic: repeated rejection, distortion, or misuse of divine guidance can harden people’s hearts so that subsequent revelation becomes, for many of them, a cause of greater wrongdoing and denial rather than guidance. As a consequence of persistent disobedience and corrupt behavior, God permits social fractures—hostility and mutual hatred—among them as a form of chastisement and consequence. Their plots of aggression are foiled by God’s will (“whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it”), and their continual pursuit of worldly mischief and corruption is condemned: such corrupters are not beloved by God. The passage thus combines theological correction about God’s nature with an ethical lesson: misusing revelation and choosing transgression brings internal discord, frustrated schemes, and divine disapproval.

translation: And if the People of the Book had believed and been conscious of Allah, We would surely have removed from them their sins and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine mercy and salvation are conditional on sincere belief and God‑conscious conduct rather than birthright or possession of scripture: God affirms He is ready to forgive and admit into Paradise those from earlier communities if they truly embrace faith and righteousness. The conditional wording (‘if they had believed and feared’) emphasizes human responsibility — the withholding of that mercy is the consequence of their failure to accept faith and live righteously, not an inherent exclusion based on lineage — and the phrase about wiping away sins signals God’s willingness to expiate past wrongs when people turn to Him with genuine piety.

translation: وَلوْ أَنَّهُمْ أَقامُوا التَّوْرَاةَ وَالإِنْجِيلَ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْهِم مِن رَّبِّهِم لَأَكَلُوا مِن فَوْقِهِم وَمِن تَحْتِ أَرْجُلِهِم ۚ مِنْهُمْ أُمَّةٌ مُقْتَصِدَةٌ ۖ وَكَثِيرٌ مِّنْهُمْ سَاءَ مَا يَعْمَلُونَ
interpretation: If the People of the Book had sincerely upheld and implemented the Torah, the Gospel and the revelations given to them — not merely held them in name but lived by their commands — they would have received God’s plentiful provision both from above (heavenly blessings, signs, and favor) and from beneath their feet (the earth’s sustenance). The verse acknowledges that among them there is a balanced, rightly-guided group, yet many others departed from that path and committed wrongful deeds; their neglect and disobedience are presented as the reason they were deprived of the full blessings that faithful observance would have brought.

translation: O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to deliver the revelation fully and without omission, even if doing so exposes him to opposition or danger; it absolves him of responsibility for others’ rejection by affirming that guidance is ultimately from God, and it comforts him with the promise of divine protection against the efforts of people to thwart the mission. The core lesson is that the duty to transmit God’s message takes precedence over concern for personal consequence, while outcomes of belief remain in God’s hands.

translation: Say, “O People of the Book, you are not rightly guided until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.” Yet many of them will, with respect to what was revealed to you from your Lord, increase in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that religious identity alone (being 'People of the Book') does not guarantee true guidance; true legitimacy before God requires living by and implementing the revealed Scriptures. It rebukes those who, instead of submitting to renewed revelation, respond with greater arrogance, distortion, neglect or outright rejection—thereby increasing in transgression and disbelief—and instructs the Prophet not to be consumed by sorrow over their obstinate denial, since their rejection springs from their own willful misconduct rather than any deficiency in the message.

translation: Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Sabians and the Christians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds—no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s acceptance and security before Him are grounded in core faith and moral conduct, not simply in communal labels: sincere belief in God and the Hereafter combined with righteous action is what removes fear and grief. Thus people from different religious communities who genuinely hold these convictions and live righteously share the same spiritual hope and protection, emphasizing a universal criterion of accountability based on faith plus deeds rather than inherited identity alone.

translation: Indeed We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent messengers to them; whenever a messenger came to them with something their souls did not desire, a party of them denied him and a party of them killed [him].
interpretation: The verse teaches that communities can fall into the pattern of embracing only that guidance which flatters their inclinations while resisting, rejecting, or even persecuting messengers who demand moral or social reform. It warns that desire and self-interest can blind people to truth and lead to culpable rejection of divine guidance, making sincere submission to God — not selective acceptance based on convenience — the true test of faith.

translation: And they considered that there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf; then Allah accepted their repentance; then they again became blind and deaf — many of them. And Allah is Ever‑Seer of what they do.
interpretation: The verse criticizes people whose fear of social disturbance or temptation led them to shut their hearts and senses to guidance (described as becoming 'blind and deaf'). Some of these people genuinely repented and were forgiven, but many lapsed back into willful heedlessness. The passage warns against self‑deception—thinking one can avoid moral responsibility by withdrawing or by pretending not to see—and reminds that repentance must be real and lasting, for God fully observes both outward deeds and inward states.

translation: لقد كفر الذين قالوا إن الله هو المسيح ابن مريم ۖ وقال المسيح يا بني إسرائيل اعبدوا الله ربي وربكم ۖ إنه من يشرك بالله فقد حرم الله عليه الجنة ومأواه النار ۖ وما للظالمين من أنصار
interpretation: الآية ترفض صراحة اعتقاد الألوهية للمسيح وتؤكد موقفه النبوي الداعي إلى عبادة الله وحده — فقول إن الله هو المسيح يعد كفرًا لأنه يلغى وحدانية الله. كما تبيّن شدة ونتيجة الشرك: من يشرِك بالله يُحرم من دخول الجنة ويكون مصيره النار، ولا يجد الظالم أولياء أو نصيرين ينقذونه من عقاب الله. المقصود رسالة توحيدية واضحة وتحذير حازم بأن إدراك مكانة عيسى عليه السلام يجب أن يكون في إطار النبوة والعبادة لله وحده، وإلا كانت العواقب أخروية بالغة السوء.

translation: Indeed, those who say, "Allah is the third of three," have certainly disbelieved. There is no deity except the One God. And if they do not desist from what they are saying, a painful punishment will surely touch those among them who disbelieve.
interpretation: The verse rejects any doctrine that divides or associates partners with God—specifically the claim that God is one of three persons—as constituting disbelief because it contradicts tawhīd (the absolute, indivisible unity of God). By asserting “there is no deity except One,” it affirms that God cannot be partitioned or equated with created persons. The warning of a painful punishment underscores the seriousness of persisting in such a belief and, implicitly, calls for abandoning that claim and returning to correct monotheistic belief to avert divine retribution.

translation: Will they not turn to Allah in repentance and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke and invitation: it highlights that people who persist in sin without seeking reconciliation are choosing to ignore the open door of divine mercy. God’s attributes—Ghafūr and Raḥīm—assure that sincere repentance (true remorse, turning away from the wrong, and resolving not to return to it) will be met with forgiveness and compassion; therefore refusal to repent is not mere human weakness but a deliberate spurning of God’s readiness to pardon, with spiritual consequences for those who persist in that choice.

translation: The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. And his mother was a woman of truth. They both used to eat food. See how We make clear the signs to them; then see how they are turned away.
interpretation: This verse functions as a theological correction: it rejects any claim of divinity for Jesus by reaffirming his role as a human messenger within the line of prophets, upholds Mary’s integrity as a truthful, devout witness, and uses the ordinary humanity of both to dismantle deification. By stressing that God’s signs are plainly shown yet people still persist in error, the passage warns against inventing partners for God and exhorts acceptance of the clear monotheistic truth.

translation: Say, “Do you worship besides Allah that which neither possesses power to harm you nor to benefit you? And Allah — He is the Hearing, the Knowing.”
interpretation: The verse confronts the folly of directing worship to powerless beings by asking believers and idolaters to reflect: those other deities cannot control what truly matters in human life — harm or benefit — so worshiping them is baseless. True allegiance belongs to God alone, who hears every voice and knows every intention and circumstance; worship must therefore be oriented toward the One who has real authority over people's affairs and who is fully aware of their needs and motives.

translation: Say, “O People of the Scripture, do not exceed bounds in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before and have led many into error and have strayed from the straight way.”
interpretation: The verse is an admonition to Jews and Christians not to practice ghuluww (exaggeration or distortion) by adding to or elevating religious beliefs beyond what God revealed—examples include deifying prophets, fabricating obligations, or reshaping scripture to suit partisan aims. It also warns against imitating prior groups driven by whims and self-interest who corrupted guidance and misled many; the practical demand is to cling to authentic revelation and the straight path, rejecting innovations and personal desires that divert communities from divine truth.

translation: Cursed were those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved, by the tongue of David and of Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.
interpretation: The verse indicates that certain Israelites who rejected God’s guidance were condemned — a condemnation attested through the words or scriptures associated with the prophets David and Jesus. It teaches that persistent disobedience and habitual transgression against divine commands lead to divine disfavor; the mention of these prophets’ tongues underscores that their own revealed teachings or testimony made clear that such rebellious conduct deserved censure and loss of God’s favor.

translation: They did not forbid one another from an evil they committed. How wretched indeed was what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse condemns a people’s moral failure when they tolerate and even participate in wrongdoing without reproach: by refusing to enjoin good and forbid evil, they become complicit and entrenched in corruption. It teaches that communal responsibility requires preventing and correcting sin, and that silence or mutual encouragement of vice is itself blameworthy and leads to divine disapproval.

translation: You will see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieve. Evil is that which their souls have sent forth for them — that Allah’s wrath is upon them, and they will abide in the punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that when people deliberately align themselves with unbelievers—choosing loyalties and actions against the way of God—they are effectively the authors of their doom; their own choices (‘what their souls have sent ahead’) earn them God’s anger and an enduring punishment. It is a moral admonition that loyalties and conduct matter: siding with injustice or disbelief against the covenant of faith is a grave spiritual failure whose consequence is divine displeasure and lasting harm.

translation: And if they had believed in Allah and in the Prophet and in what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies; but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine faith — accepting God, His Messenger, and the revealed guidance — shapes loyalties and conduct: true belief would prevent people from forming protective ties with those who undermine divine guidance or oppose the community of the truthful. The fact that many nevertheless ally with such parties is a sign not of mere ignorance but of moral rebellion (fusuq): a willful turning away from the guidance that should govern their social and political choices.

translation:
لَتَجِدَنَّ أَشَدَّ النَّاسِ عَدَاوَةً لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا ۖ وَلَتَجِدَنَّ أَقْرَبَهُم مَوَدَّةً لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إِنَّا نَصَارَىٰ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّ مِنْهُمْ قِسِّيسِينَ وَرُهْبَانًا وَأَنَّهُمْ لَا يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ
"You will surely find the most hostile of people to the believers to be those who associate others with God, and you will surely find the nearest in affection to the believers those who say, ‘We are Christians.’ That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant."
interpretation: The verse explains a social-psychological pattern observed in the Prophet’s environment: hostility or friendliness toward the Muslim community tends to follow spiritual orientation and moral character rather than mere communal labels. Polytheists, invested in religious structures and social orders opposed to the new message, were often most resistant; some Christians, by contrast, showed sympathy because their religious life included devout guides (priests and monks) and an ethos of humility. The underlying point is an ethical criterion for relations — piety, religious responsibility, and lack of arrogance foster trust and goodwill — and believers are encouraged to recognize and deal with people according to those moral realities rather than by blanket assumptions about groups.

translation: And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth. They say, “Our Lord, we have believed; so register us among the witnesses.”
interpretation: The verse shows that true recognition of divine truth moves the heart deeply: tears are a sign of spiritual conviction, humility, and remorse for past error, not mere sentiment. Those who are thus convinced do not stop at inward feeling; they pray to be recorded “with the witnesses,” asking God to count them among those whose faith is both sincere and outwardly testified — people who will bear witness to the truth in word and deed and stand as proof of it before God and creation.

translation:
وما لنا لا نؤمن بالله وما جاءنا من الحق ونطمع أن يدخلنا ربنا مع القوم الصالحين

"And what reason is there for us not to believe in Allah and in that truth which has come to us? We hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous."
interpretation: The verse conveys that when people encounter clear, divinely-sent truth, there is no rational or moral justification to reject it; true response entails embracing faith in God and the revealed guidance and placing humble trust in His mercy, hoping to be counted among the righteous—thus linking sincere acceptance of the truth with hopeful expectation of inclusion among the pious.

translation: فَأَثَابَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِمَا قَالُوا جَنَّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهَارُ خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا ۚ وَذَٰلِكَ جَزَاءُ الْمُحْسِنِينَ
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن ثواب الله للمؤمنين مرتبط بإخلاص الأقوال والامتثال العملي لها: «بما قالوا» تشير إلى الإيمان الصادق والاعتراف به خصوصًا عند الابتلاء، ولا تُنفَكّ هذه الأقوال عن الأعمال الصالحة التي تثبتها. وعدُ «جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار» تصوير للنعيم الدائم والاكتمال الروحي والمادي في الآخرة، وكلمة «خالدين فيها» تؤكد بقاء هذا الجزاء بلا انقضاء. بتسمية هذا الجزاء لِـ«المحسنين» تؤكد الآية أن الكمال الإيماني يُقاس بالإحسان — أي الإخلاص، والصدق في القول، والعمل الصالح، والصبر — وأن الله يجازي المحسنين جزاءً كاملاً ومؤبداً.

translation: And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs—those are the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that deliberate rejection of God’s revelations and the conscious denial of the clear signs by which guidance is offered marks a moral posture that severs one from mercy; such obstinate unbelief is not a neutral state but an active refusal that shapes one’s ultimate destiny, and thus those who persist in this denial are described as destined companions of the Fire — a consequence of their sustained turning away from the truth and responsibility to respond to it.

translation: O you who have believed, do not make unlawful the good things which Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like the transgressors.
interpretation: الآية تنهى المؤمنين عن فرض تحريمات ذاتية أو مبالغات دينية تتجاوز ما أباحه الشرع؛ تحذّر من الغلو والافتئات على حدود الله في العبادة والمعاملات، وتدعو إلى الاعتدال وعدم إنكار أو تجريد الحلال من طيبته أو حرمان الناس منه، لأن من يتعدى الحدود يصبح ظلماً ومقصوداً مكروهاً عند الله.

translation: Eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good; and fear Allah, in Whom you are believers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that faith must be reflected in ordinary acts: believers are to take only provisions that are both permitted (halal) and wholesome (tayyib), because legality alone is not enough without moral and spiritual purity. By linking this command to taqwa—“fear Allah, in Whom you are believers”—the verse makes dietary choices a matter of accountability, gratitude, and obedience, so that consuming sustenance becomes an expression of sincere faith and ethical responsibility.

translation: اللَّهُ لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمْ بِالْلغْوِ فِي أَيْمَانِكُمْ وَلَكِن يُؤَاخِذُكُم بِمَا عَقَدتُّمُ الْأَيْمَانَ ۖ فَكَفَّارَتُهُ إِطْعَامُ عَشَرَةِ مَسَاكِينَ مِنْ أَوْسَطِ مَا تُطْعِمُونَ أَهْلِيكُمْ أَوْ كِسْوَتُهُمْ أَوْ تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ ۖ فَمَنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ فَصِيَامُ ثَلَاثَةِ أَيَّامٍ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ كَفَّارَةُ أَيْمَانِكُمْ إِذَا حَلَفْتُمْ ۚ وَاحْفَظُوا أَيْمَانَكُمْ ۚ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ آيَاتِهِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ
interpretation: The verse teaches a moral principle: God distinguishes inadvertent speech from deliberate commitment and, rather than mere punishment, requires remedies that repair social trust and shape the believer’s character. By converting broken or serious vows into acts that benefit others or into self-discipline, the law channels responsibility into compassion and restraint, encouraging careful speech, accountability, and gratitude for divine guidance.

translation: O you who believe! Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificial] stone pillars and divining arrows are but an abomination, the handiwork of Satan — so avoid them that you may succeed.
interpretation: This verse teaches that certain practices — those that impair reason (intoxicants), promote chance and greed (gambling), and rely on idol worship or superstition (stone idols and divination) — are instruments through which Satan weakens faith, fractures social bonds, and diverts people from mindful obedience to God. The command to ‘avoid them’ is therefore a preventative injunction: by removing sources of moral confusion, addiction, exploitation, and discord, believers preserve clear judgment, justice, and communal harmony, which are prerequisites for true success in this life and the hereafter.

translation: Satan only desires to sow enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?
interpretation: The verse explains the deeper wisdom behind the prohibition of intoxicants and gambling: they are not merely personal sins but means by which satanic influence fractures social bonds and diverts people from spiritual life. By stirring anger, mistrust and conflict, these vices weaken families and communities and blunt the conscience so that remembrance of God and regular worship are neglected. The rhetorical question invites sober self-examination and decisive restraint; the principle extends beyond the specific acts named—anything that breeds enmity and pulls people away from God’s remembrance and prayer functions as a satanic stratagem and must be avoided to preserve both communal harmony and spiritual health.

translation: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and be wary; but if you turn away, then know that upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery (of the message).
interpretation: The verse commands believers to submit to God and to follow the Prophet, with a warning against turning away; at the same time it limits the Prophet’s responsibility to faithfully conveying God’s revelation. If people reject the guidance, the Prophet is not accountable for their refusal — his duty is to make the message clear, while acceptance and the consequences of rejection rest with each person.

translation: There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds concerning what they have eaten, when they feared (Allah), believed and did righteous deeds; then afterwards feared, believed; then feared and excelled. And Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse removes culpability for past actions (specifically what one ate) once a person sincerely turns to God — embraces faith, develops God‑consciousness (taqwa), and lives by righteous deeds. The repeated sequence (fear, belief, righteous action, then again fear and belief, then fear and doing good) indicates a progressive, enduring commitment: genuine repentance and sustained moral reform erase prior unintentional or ignorant faults. The ultimate criterion is ongoing righteousness and striving for excellence (ihsan), for which Allah’s love is promised.

translation: O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with some of the game that your hands and your spears may reach, so that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen. So whoever transgresses after that — for him is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when lawful gains or opportunities (symbolized by game taken by hand or spear, e.g. in hunting or on the battlefield) come within reach, Allah uses that situation as a test to reveal who truly fears Him inwardly, even when no one else observes. The permission or ease exposes inner character: a person of sincere taqwa will restrain themselves from exceeding God’s limits and will act justly; one who seizes more than is permitted or persists in wrongdoing after the opportunity has been given demonstrates lack of God‑consciousness and will face severe consequences. In short, outward availability of benefit does not remove inner accountability — genuine faith shows itself by self‑restraint and obedience even in private."}

translation: O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in a state of ihram. And whoever of you kills it intentionally — the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed of the sacrificial animals, to be decided by two just men among you: an offering brought to the Kaʿbah, or expiation in the form of food for the poor, or an equivalent of that as fasting — so that he may taste the consequence of his act. Allah has pardoned what is past; but whoever repeats (such wrongdoing), Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution.
interpretation: This verse teaches a principle that sanctity, responsibility, and restorative justice coexist: when a person knowingly violates a committed sacred condition, the harm is not merely private but damages the communal and spiritual order, so the remedy must both repair that harm and cultivate remorse. The prescribed penalties are not punitive in isolation but restorative options — ritual restitution toward the sanctuary, feeding those deprived, or disciplined fasting — judged by upright members of the community so that consequence is measured, equitable, and publicly accountable. At the same time God’s forgiveness for past mistakes encourages sincere repentance, while the promise of retribution for repeated deliberate transgression affirms that mercy does not nullify accountability; persistent defiance of sacred obligations brings divine response. Overall the verse balances compassion with firmness, urging mindfulness of sacred commitments, communal adjudication, and tangible acts that restore relationships with God, people, and the sanctified space.

translation: Lawful for you is the catch of the sea and its food as provision for you and for the travelers, and forbidden to you is hunting on land while you are in a state of ihram. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse delineates a specific legal and ethical balance: during sacred consecration (ihram) outward restraints are required (no hunting on land) to cultivate discipline and respect for the sanctity of the state, yet God permits necessary provisions (sea game and its food) for pilgrims and travelers — showing compassion and practical flexibility in religious law. The final admonition to fear Allah and remember the hereafter ties these rulings to inner accountability: ritual prohibitions are not mere formalities but practices meant to shape piety and prepare the believer for standing before God.

translation: Allah has made the Kaʿbah the Sacred House, an establishment for the people, and [has made] the sacred months and the sacrificial animals and the garlands. That is so you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth; and that Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: By designating specific places, times and rites as sacred, God provides a public, divinely sanctioned framework that organizes communal worship, limits violence and private appropriation, and channels human devotion into prescribed acts. These sanctities function not merely as legal rules but as social and spiritual markers that foster unity, protect the weak, and regulate relations among people; their ultimate purpose is to remind individuals that nothing—outer actions or inner motives—escapes God’s knowledge, and therefore sincerity, reverence, and obedience within that framework are required.

translation: اعلموا أن الله شديد العقاب وأن الله غفور رحيم — "Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful."
interpretation: The phrase pairs warning with consolation to shape moral behavior: the awareness of Divine severity deters persistent wrongdoing and underscores accountability, while the assurance of forgiveness and mercy invites sincere repentance and reform. Together they teach that one must neither presume immunity from consequence nor despair of pardon; true moral life responds to both fear of justice and hope in God’s readiness to forgive, prompting continual self-examination, repentance, and striving to correct one’s course.

translation: The Messenger's duty is only to convey [the message]. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.
interpretation: The verse relieves the Prophet of responsibility for people’s acceptance: his sole obligation is to transmit God’s guidance faithfully, not to compel belief or control outcomes. At the same time it affirms God’s absolute knowledge of both outward deeds and inner intentions, so moral accountability rests on what people both disclose and hide; sincerity and inward states matter before God even when others cannot see them.

translation: قُلْ لَا يَسْتَوِي الْخَبِيثُ وَالطَّيِّبُ وَلَوْ أَعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَ الْخَبِيثِ ۚ فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ يَا أُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ
interpretation: الآية تذكّر بأن القيمة الأخلاقية والشرعية للأشياء لا تُقاس بشعبيتها أو بكثرتهما؛ ما هو رديء أو محرم لا يصبح حسنًا لمجرد أن كثيرين يرضون به. مَن عنده عقل ونُبلٌ (أولي الألباب) مدعو لأن يستند إلى تقوى الله في تمييز الحلال من الحرام والحق من الباطل، ويصون نفسه عن الإنجرار وراء ما يبهركك بكثرته، لأن التقوى والاختيار على أساس الحق هما طريق الفوز والنجاح الحقيقيين.

translation:
يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تسألوا عن أشياء إن تبد لكم تسؤكم وإن تسألوا عنها حين ينزل القرآن تبد لكم عفا الله عنها ۗ والله غفور حليم
“O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they are made plain to you, will distress you. And if you ask about them while the Qur’an is being revealed, they will be made plain to you. Allah has pardoned that which is past; and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.”
interpretation: The verse cautions believers against pursuing needless, speculative or provocative questions—especially about matters not yet settled—because having definitive answers might impose burdens, cause distress, or lead to division. It calls for restraint and trust in the timing and wisdom of divine guidance, while comforting that past erroneous or excessive questioning has been pardoned, reflecting God’s mercy, forgiveness, and patient forbearance.

translation: Some people before you asked about it, and then they became disbelievers because of it.
interpretation: The verse warns that previous communities who pressed for proofs or questioned the message from a stance of obstinate skepticism ended up rejecting it; their persistent doubting and refusal to accept clear guidance turned into disbelief, and the address cautions the hearers not to follow that same pattern of rebellious questioning.

translation: Allah did not make [any animal] a bahīrah, nor a sā’ibah, nor waṣīlah, nor ḥām. But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason.
interpretation: The verse condemns the practice of inventing sacred prohibitions and then attributing them to God: the specific tribal categories named are human superstitions, not divine rulings. Its core teaching is theological and ethical—lawfulness and prohibition belong to God and must not be fabricated by people; to ascribe such invented customs to Allah is a deliberate falsehood and a sign of spiritual and intellectual negligence. Believers are therefore warned to discern revelation from inherited superstition and not to let blind tradition override divine guidance.

translation: And when it is said to them, “Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,” they say, “Sufficient for us is that upon which we found our fathers.” — Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?
interpretation: This verse condemns blind adherence to ancestral custom as an excuse to reject God's revelation and the Prophet’s guidance: it teaches that tradition is not a legitimate defense when it contradicts divine truth, and each person bears responsibility to follow guidance rather than repeat the ignorance or misguidance of their forebears.

translation: O you who have believed, take care of yourselves. No one who goes astray will harm you if you are rightly guided. To Allah is your return all together; then He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse charges believers with personal responsibility for their own faith and conduct: hold fast to guidance and cultivate your own righteousness rather than relying on others or blaming them for their errors. Others’ deviation cannot imperil you if you remain firmly guided; still, you are accountable before God — everyone will return to Him and be shown their deeds — so concentrate on maintaining sincerity, correcting your own state, and fulfilling your duties rather than excusing yourself by pointing to other people’s misguidance.

translation: O you who have believed, (take) testimony among you: when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest, let there be two just men from among you or two others from outside your community. And if you are traveling in the land and death overtakes you, then let them be detained after the prayer and let them swear by Allah, if you have any doubt, “We will not sell our testimony for any price, even if it concerns a near relative; nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah, for then indeed we would be among the sinners.”
interpretation: The verse prescribes both a practical procedure and a moral principle to protect the integrity of testamentary testimony: require reliable witnesses (even if they are not from one’s own group), allow testimony to be taken while traveling, and bind witnesses by an oath to refuse bribery or concealment—even to spare kin. At its core the verse elevates truth and justice above familial or material pressures, making clear that bearing honest testimony is a duty before God and that compromising it is a communal and individual sin.

translation: فإن عُثرَ عليهما أنهما استحقّا إثماً فآخران يقومان مقامهما من الذين استحق عليهم الأوليان فيقسِمان بالله لشهادتنا أحقُّ من شهادتهما وما اعتدينا إنا إذا لمن الظالمين
interpretation: الآية تُبيّن إجراءً قضائياً وأخلاقياً: إذا تبَيّن أن الشاهدَين الأصليين فاسدان أو مستحقّان للذمّ فلا يُعتمدان، بل يُستبدلان بشاهدين آخرين من بين الذين كانت لهما علاقة بالواقعة، فيُحلّان محلّهما ويُقسمان بالله لتأكيد أن شهادة من قامت عليهما الدعوى أصحّ وأوْلى من شهادة الأولَين. المقصود أن العدالة تتطلب استبدال الشهادات الملوَّثة وإقرار الحقّ بما يشهد له الأدلة واليمين، وأن من اتّبع هذا الطريق لم يَتجاوز حدّه أو يَظلم؛ بل إنّ التصرّف المخالف للحقّ وحده هو الظلم.

translation: That is more fitting: that they should bring testimony in its proper form, or that they should fear that oaths will be retracted after their oaths. So fear Allah and heed; and Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse calls for moral firmness and legal integrity: witnesses and those involved in judicial or familial affairs must present honest, unambiguous testimony rather than holding back or later retracting under pressure or collusion. This ethical demand is grounded in God‑consciousness — fearing Allah and paying heed to His commands — because persistent rebelliousness and moral corruption cut a people off from divine guidance; social justice and rightful outcomes rely on sincere testimony upheld by piety.

translation: يوم يجمع الله الرسل فيقول: «ماذا أُجِبتم؟» قالوا: «لا علم لنا، إنك أنت علام الغيوب».
interpretation: في هذا البيان تبرز حقيقة أن مهمة الرسل كانت إيصال الحقّ وبيان الحكم، أما معرفة ما في القلوب ونهاية الأمور فمخصصة لله وحده. عند الجمع في القيامة يُسأل الرسل عن كيفية استقبال أقوامهم للدعوة، فيقرّون بأن نتيجة القبول أو الإعراض وما حملته القلوب من أسرار ليس من علمهم، بل هو علم الله المطلق بالغيوب. المقصود توكيد مسؤولية الرسول في البلاغ وعدم إدعاء السيطرة على النتائج، وتأكيد سيادة الله ومعرفته الكاملة بما كان وسيكون، مما يحثّ على التواضع عن ادعاء علم الغيب والاعتماد على حكم الله العادل.

translation: When Allah said, “O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother: when I strengthened you with the Pure Spirit, so that you spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught you the Book and Wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel; and when you fashioned from clay the likeness of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission; and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission; and when you brought forth the dead by My permission; and when I kept the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, yet those among them who disbelieved said, ‘This is nothing but obvious magic.’”
interpretation: God’s address to Jesus serves to clarify that the extraordinary gifts and miracles given to him — speech as an infant, knowledge, healing, raising the dead, and creating life from clay — were acts made possible by God’s granting and authority, not signs of Jesus’ own independent divinity. The passage emphasizes two linked truths: the absolute sovereignty of God, who bestows knowledge and power to chosen servants, and the human tendency to reject clear signs out of obstinacy—so miracles are meant as proofs pointing people back to God’s lordship, not to aggrandize the prophet. Thus the proper response is recognition of God’s favor and obedience to His guidance, while rejection of such signs is shown to be culpable denial rather than rational appraisal.

translation: And when I inspired to the Disciples, ‘Believe in Me and in My Messenger.’ They said, ‘We have believed; bear witness that indeed we are Muslims.’
interpretation: The verse reports that God revealed to the followers of Jesus an invitation to believe both in God and in the Messenger appointed in God’s plan, and the disciples’ reply—“We have believed; bear witness that we are Muslims”—affirms that true discipleship is submission to divine guidance and acceptance of the continuity of prophetic revelation. Their response models sincere faith as both affirmation of tawhīd (God’s unity) and willing submission (Islam), showing that genuine followers of earlier prophets recognized and embraced the broader unfolding of God’s message.

translation: When the disciples said, “O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table [spread] from heaven?” He said, “Fear Allah, if you are believers.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that spiritual certainty must rest on God‑consciousness and sincere inner commitment rather than on the spectacle of miracles. The Prophet’s admonition “Fear Allah, if you are believers” functions as a moral challenge: asking for a sign without true piety is misplaced, for a miracle can confirm faith but also serves as a test that imposes responsibility. True belief is shown by reverence, obedience, and self‑examination, not by demanding extraordinary tokens.

translation: قالوا: "نريد أن نأكل منها وتطمئن قلوبنا ونعلم أن قد صدقتنا ونكون عليها من الشاهدين." — "They said, 'We wish to eat of it so that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have told us the truth, and that we may be among those who witness it.'"
interpretation: The people ask for a direct, tangible demonstration so that their inner doubts are settled and they can be certain of the messenger’s truth and testify to it publicly. The verse highlights a common human need for experiential confirmation to attain inner peace and communal certainty: witnessing a sign can transform suspicion into firm conviction and enable people to bear truthful testimony.

translation: Jesus, son of Mary, said, “O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread from heaven that it may be for us — for the first of us and the last of us — and a sign from You; and provide for us, for You are the best of providers.”
interpretation: The plea expresses a request for a visible, enduring miracle — a heavenly banquet — meant to serve both as tangible sustenance and as a lasting sign for believers across generations: to strengthen faith, answer doubt, and create a communal occasion of gratitude. It highlights complete reliance on God for provision and presents miracles as instruments appointed by God to confirm belief and unify the community rather than as ends in themselves.

translation: قال الله: «إني منزلها عليكم؛ فمن يكفر بعد منكم فإني أعذبه عذاباً لا أعذبه أحداً من العالمين».
