interpretation: الآية تحذر أن الله أنزل أمراً أو عقاباً واضحاً على قومٍ كإنذارٍ بيّن، وأن مَنْ يستمر في الكفر والإعراض بعد تبيّن الحقّ وإظهار العذاب سيُلاقى عقاباً فريداً وشديداً لا يُلحقه بالآخرين. المقصود أن العناد على الباطل بعد ظهور الدليل يستوجب جزاءً استثنائياً يبيّن جدّية الحساب الإلهي وكون التمادي في الكفر بعد البيان خطيئة لا تُغتفر بسهولة، فتكون عقوبته خاصة ومتميّزة بين سائر العوالم.

translation: And when Allah will say, “O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, ‘Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah’?” He will say, “Glory be to You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within my soul, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.”
interpretation: This verse underscores the Quranic doctrine of strict monotheism (tawhid) and exonerates Jesus from any claim to divinity: prophets do not and cannot claim divine status, and any such attribution will be exposed and judged. Jesus’ emphatic denial and his appeal to God’s perfect knowledge emphasize human limitation before the Divine—God alone knows the unseen and the inner realities of beings—so ultimate accountability will reveal and rectify false deifications, affirming Allah’s absolute transcendence and sole right to worship.

translation: I did not tell them anything except what You commanded me: ‘Worship Allah—my Lord and your Lord.’ And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them. But when You caused me to be taken away, You were the Watcher over them; and You are, over all things, Witness.
interpretation: The verse affirms the prophetic role as confined to delivering God’s command and testifying to its delivery: the messenger declares he faithfully called his people to worship the one God and served as a living witness that he fulfilled his duty while present. He makes clear he cannot force guidance or guarantee their response; once he is removed (by death or absence), God alone continues to observe, preserve, and hold people accountable. The passage underscores divine sovereignty in oversight and judgment—prophets are conveyors and witnesses, whereas ultimate knowledge, supervision, and responsibility belong to God alone.

translation: If You punish them, then they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, then indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.
interpretation: A humble submission to divine sovereignty: the speaker acknowledges that every outcome—discipline or pardon—is fully within God’s authority. Punishment would only confirm their status under His rule, while forgiveness arises from His overpowering might and prudent wisdom; therefore one entrusts both justice and mercy to God, recognizing His right and ability to judge and to pardon.

translation: قَالَ اللَّهُ: "هَذَا يَوْمٌ يَنْفَعُ الصَّادِقِينَ صِدْقُهُمْ ۚ لَهُمْ جَنَّاتٌ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهَارُ خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا أَبَدًا ۚ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ الْفَوْزُ الْعَظِيمُ"
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن حقّ النجاح يوم الحشر مرهون بالصدق — ليس فقط صدق اللفظ بل صدق الإيمان والنية والعمل والوفاء بالمقاصد. "ينفع الصادقين صدقهم" يعني أن صدقهم يصبح سبب نجاتهم وقبول أعمالهم، فيُؤْتَوْن الجزاء المقصود: جنات دائمَة تجري من تحتها أنهار، أي نعيم سرمدي وحياة مطمئنة بلا انقطاع. رضا الله عنهم ورضاهم عنه يدلّ على بلوغ المقام الأعلى من القبول الإلهي والاطمئنان الباطني، فهذه الرضاوية هي المقصود الأسمى للعبد، وكونها "الفوز العظيم" يشير إلى أن النجاة بالصدق والبلوغ إلى سرور الربّ أعظم انتصار يمكن أن يطلبه الإنسان.

translation: To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is within them; and He is over all things All‑Powerful.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s exclusive, comprehensive sovereignty and omnipotence: every part of existence is under His authority and subject to His will. Practically this teaches that human power and worldly arrangements are limited and contingent, so believers should combine responsible effort with trust and humility before God, knowing that events and outcomes ultimately depend on His control and wisdom.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darkness and the light; yet those who disbelieve set up equals to their Lord.
interpretation: The verse intends to show that the manifest signs in creation—such as the originating of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of darkness and light—point decisively to Allah’s sole authority and wisdom; therefore to deny Him or to ascribe partners to Him is an unjust and unreasonable response that ignores clear evidence of His oneness and lordship.

translation: He is the One who created you from clay, then decreed an appointed term — and an appointed term is with Him — yet you are in doubt.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, despite the clear sign of God’s power in creating humans and the certainty that God alone determines life’s span and the time of meeting Him, persist in doubting the reality of the hereafter, divine judgment, or God’s sovereign control. Such doubt is portrayed not as honest uncertainty but as willful heedlessness or arrogance; the intended moral consequence is to awaken recognition of mortality, prompt gratitude and submission to God, and compel preparation for the inevitable appointed meeting and accountability.

translation: And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your public, and He knows what you earn.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's sole sovereignty over every realm and His absolute, intimate knowledge of both inner intentions and outward deeds. It teaches that nothing—hidden thoughts, spoken words, or acquired actions—escapes His awareness, so moral responsibility rests not only on external behavior but on the sincerity and content of the heart; this offers reassurance that unseen good is known to God and a warning that concealment cannot evade His judgment.

translation: And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them but they turn away from it.
interpretation: The verse describes a persistent moral and spiritual disposition: when clear evidence or guidance from God is presented, these people deliberately avoid engaging with it—out of pride, heedlessness, or attachment to falsehood—so they refuse to reflect, accept, or be guided, thereby hardening themselves against truth and losing the opportunity for rectification.

translation: They indeed denied the truth when it came to them; so the tidings of what they used to mock will surely come to them.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who rejected and mocked the divine message will one day be presented with the actual events and realities they scoffed at—above all the Resurrection and God’s judgment—and when these truths arrive they will be forced to acknowledge their error, face the consequences, and feel regret.

translation: Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established in the earth more firmly than We have established you? We sent down the sky upon them in abundant rain and caused rivers to flow beneath them; then We destroyed them for their sins and raised up after them another generation.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly stability, prosperity, and natural bounty are not guarantees against divine judgment: despite being firmly settled and well-provided for, previous peoples were punished because of their persistent transgressions. It is a warning that God’s power and justice can remove a community and replace it with another if its members persist in wrongdoing and ignore guidance, so believers must not be complacent but remain morally and spiritually responsible.

translation: And if We had sent down to you a written scripture on parchment and they had touched it with their own hands, those who disbelieve would say, "This is nothing but clear magic."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the core reason for rejection is willful obstinacy and hostile motives, not an absence of external proof: even the most tangible, hands‑on evidence would be dismissed by those determined to deny, showing that guidance is ultimately a matter of the heart and God’s opening, not something that can be forced by mere sensational signs.

translation:
وَقَالُوا لَوْلَا أُنزِلَ عَلَيْهِ مَلَكٌ ۖ وَلَوْ أَنزَلْنَا مَلَكًا لَّقُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ ثُمَّ لَا يُنظَرُونَ
“And they say, ‘Why was an angel not sent down to him?’ Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been settled, and then they would not have been granted respite.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who demand a spectacular, external miracle (an angel) as a way to avoid sincere moral choice. God’s point is that sending an angel would have made the truth unmistakable and compelled immediate judgment — there would be no further delay for self-deception or excuses. Their request therefore exposes stubbornness and a desire to evade responsibility: asking for ever-greater signs does not excuse disbelief, and when the decisive outcome comes those who insisted on such demands will not receive lenient postponement.

translation: And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have obscured to them what they invent.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the rejection of the message is rooted in the hearers’ own stubbornness and propensity to fabricate excuses; changing the outward form of the messenger (angel or man) would not alter their attitude. God points out that their objections are not a valid objection to the truth but a product of self-deception and deliberate distortion, so blame rests with those who invent and persist in falsehood, not with the nature of the messenger.

translation: And already messengers before you were ridiculed, and that which the mockers used to ridicule overtook them.
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet and warns the scoffers: derision of God’s messengers is a recurring pattern, but apparent freedom to mock is temporary. Historically, those who mocked the truth were ultimately overtaken by the very outcome they scorned—so the passage affirms divine justice and timing, counsels perseverance for the sincere, and cautions that mockery leads to eventual humiliation or punishment like what was derided.

translation:
قُلْ سِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ انظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الْمُكَذِّبِينَ
"Say, ‘Travel through the land and then observe how was the end of those who denied (the truth).’"
interpretation: God enjoins people to examine history and the world as evidence: by observing the ruined fates of past communities that rejected divine guidance and called the messengers liars, one can see the real consequences of persistent denial and be warned to repent and follow the truth.

translation: Say, “To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?” Say, “To Allah.” He has prescribed mercy for Himself. He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection—there is no doubt about it. Those who have ruined their own souls—they will not believe.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s sovereign ownership of all things is inseparable from a self‑declared attribute of mercy, and that the final gathering on the Day of Resurrection is an inevitable reality anchored in His will. At the same time it points to a moral and spiritual truth: some people, by persistent rejection and corrupt choice, have so damaged and closed their own hearts and consciences that they are incapable of sincere belief even when faced with clear truth. Thus God’s mercy is real and fundamental, yet human responsibility and the hardening effect of deliberate rejection mean mercy does not become effective for those who have willfully ruined themselves.

translation: And to Him belongs whatever dwells by night and by day, and He is the All-Hearing, the All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s continual, comprehensive sovereignty and awareness: everything and everyone, in every state and at every hour, ultimately belong to Him and are within His perception. By calling Him the Hearing and the Knowing it stresses that no speech, deed, internal state or hidden circumstance escapes His attention. The practical thrust is twofold — comfort for the faithful in God’s unceasing care and oversight, and a sober reminder to act with humility and moral responsibility because secrecy and evasion are impossible before divine knowledge.

translation: Say, “Shall I take as a guardian other than Allah—Creator of the heavens and the earth—while He alone gives provision and is not in need of any provision?” Say, “Indeed I have been commanded to be the first to submit (to Allah).” So do not be among the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse reproves entrusting anyone or anything with the role of protector or Lord apart from God, because only God—as the Creator and self-sufficient Sustainer—truly possesses authority and the power to provide; created things cannot be relied on for ultimate guardianship. By commanding the Prophet to be foremost in submission, it establishes prophetic leadership by personal example and calls believers to mirror that wholehearted surrender. The final injunction against being among the polytheists is a decisive theological and practical warning: do not ascribe partners to God in lordship, dependence, or worship, and make exclusive reliance on Him the core of one’s faith and conduct.

translation: Say, "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day."
interpretation: The speaker expresses a deep God-consciousness and moral restraint: a sincere fear that any act of disobedience exposes one to severe, inescapable recompense on the Day of Judgment. This sentiment is meant to show humility before divine authority, to justify refusal to comply with demands that would violate duty to God, and to serve as a deterrent—reminding both the speaker and the audience that human freedom is framed by ultimate accountability and God's just sovereignty.

translation:
من يصرف عنه يومئذ فقد رحمه ۚ وذلك الفوز المبين
"Whoever He averts from it on that Day, then He has shown him mercy; and that is the manifest victory."
interpretation: The verse teaches that being preserved from God's retribution or trial at the decisive reckoning is itself an expression of divine mercy, and that receiving that mercy — protection from punishment and being granted God’s favor in the final accounting — is the true, unmistakable success beyond all worldly gains.

translation: “And if Allah should touch you with harm, there is no remover of it except He; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.”
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s unique and sovereign authority over both harm and benefit: ultimately no one can avert affliction or confer good except Allah, even though He may employ means and agents to do so. The appropriate response is to combine practical effort with trust in God—be patient and seek lawful remedies when tested, be grateful when blessed—and to recognize that relief, healing, and prosperity are granted by God’s will and power alone.

translation: And He is the Subduer over His servants; and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.
interpretation: God’s name al‑Qāhir affirms that His sovereignty is absolute and irresistible — nothing in creation can frustrate His will or escape His control — while His names al‑Ḥakīm and al‑Khabīr show that every exercise of that power is governed by perfect wisdom and complete knowledge of realities; thus whatever He imposes, allows, or withholds on His servants is not arbitrary but purposeful, rooted in comprehensive awareness of what is ultimately good, just, and fitting for them.

translation: Say, “What thing is greatest in testimony?” Say, “Allah; He is a witness between me and you. And He has revealed to me this Qur’an to warn you thereby and those it reaches. Do you indeed bear witness that with Allah there are other gods?” Say, “I do not bear witness.” Say, “He is only one God, and indeed I am free from what you associate [with Him].”
interpretation: The verse asserts that God’s testimony is the ultimate standard of truth and that the Qur’an is a divine warning; it uses a direct challenge to expose the emptiness of polytheistic claims and makes clear that the Prophet will not lend his assent to falsehood. In essence it declares uncompromising monotheism—affirming God’s singular sovereignty, placing the burden of proof on those who claim other deities, and formally dissociating the messenger from all forms of shirk.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their own children; those who have harmed/lost themselves — they do not believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that people of earlier revelation can perceive the prophetic confirmation in the scriptures with as much clarity and familiarity as they have for their own offspring, yet recognition does not automatically lead to true faith. “They have lost themselves” indicates a moral and spiritual ruin brought on by willful refusal, pride, attachment to worldly interests, or deliberate concealment of the truth; having closed themselves off, they remain unbelieving despite clear knowledge.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper.
interpretation: The verse condemns as the gravest injustice those who fabricate lies about God or reject His clear signs: such behavior distorts truth and misleads people. By attributing falsehoods to the Divine or denying revelation out of pride, desire, or ignorance, a person wrongs his own soul and cuts himself off from guidance; therefore those wrongdoers are doomed to failure in both this world and the Hereafter.

translation: And on the Day We will gather them all together; then We will say to those who associated others (with Us), “Where are your partners which you were asserting?”
interpretation: The verse warns that on Resurrection the illusion of partners or intermediaries will be exposed: every claim that someone or something shared in God’s divinity, power, or intercession will be put to the test and found false. Those who practiced shirk will stand judged and will have no reliable allies to answer for them — their supposed partners will be absent, silent, or will deny them — demonstrating both the utter futility of associating others with God and the absolute sovereignty and exclusive right of God to be worshipped and relied upon.

translation: Their trial was nothing except that they said, “By Allah — our Lord — we were not polytheists.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes those whose only defense when exposed was a verbal oath of monotheism; it highlights that mere words and convenient professions of faith cannot hide the reality of shirk or hypocrisy. Sincerity of heart and consistency of deed are what matter before God, so a late or insincere declaration — however solemnly sworn — avails nothing against the true state of one’s belief and will not avert divine judgment.

translation: Observe how they have lied against themselves; and the things they used to fabricate have abandoned them.
interpretation: The verse warns that inventing falsehoods—whether about God, His message, or religious truth—is self‑destructive: such fabrications will be uncovered and will not benefit their inventors, leaving them exposed, deprived of guidance and support, and responsible for the consequences of their deceit.

translation: And among them are those who listen to you; but We have placed coverings over their hearts so that they do not understand it, and deafness in their ears. And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. And when they come to you to argue with you, those who disbelieve say, 'This is nothing but tales of the former peoples.'
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a spiritual condition: some people outwardly attend the message yet remain impervious to its truth because, through persistent rejection and moral obstinacy, God has allowed layers of veiling and dullness to settle upon their perception. This sealing is presented not merely as punishment but as the consequent hardening that follows willingly closing one’s heart to guidance; it produces intellectual and emotional resistance so that even clear signs fail to move them. Their dismissive retort — branding revelation as ancient tales — is a defensive strategy to avoid moral accountability and to preserve their prior commitments. The passage thus emphasizes both human responsibility (the choice to accept or reject) and the Divine response that legitimizes the consequences of that choice, while warning believers against hypocrisy and the self-protective rationalizations that prevent true understanding.

translation: And they forbid (people) from it and keep away from it; in truth they only destroy themselves, yet they perceive it not.
interpretation: The verse indicates that those who oppose and repel the message—seeking to bar others from it and distancing themselves—do not harm the truth or its recipients; rather their rejection and obstinacy bring loss and ruin upon themselves. Their hostility is ultimately self-destructive, though out of heedlessness they fail to recognize the consequences of their own turning away.

translation: And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire, they will say, “Oh, that we might be returned [to life on earth] and not deny the signs of our Lord and be among the believers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the desperate regret of the condemned shows guidance was available and that their denial was a culpable, deliberate choice; their wish to return illustrates that sincere faith and obedience must be realized in this life, because repentance after death is too late — a warning to accept and act upon God’s signs now, and an affirmation of divine justice and accountability.

translation: But what they had been hiding before has now become apparent to them; and if they were returned [to life], they would indeed revert to that from which they were forbidden, and they are surely liars.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses the moral and spiritual reality of insincere people: their private disbelief or corrupt inclinations eventually come to light, and the fact that—if given another chance—they would repeat the same forbidden actions shows their lack of genuine repentance or conviction. Their outward claims are therefore exposed as falsehoods, demonstrating habitual hypocrisy and untrustworthiness.

translation: And they said, “It is nothing but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a mindset that confines human existence to the visible, fleeting world and denies any final accountability. That denial is not merely a doctrinal claim but a moral stance: by insisting there will be no resurrection, people remove the prospect of ultimate judgment and so justify indifference to divine guidance and ethical responsibility. The Qur’an here points to this attitude—rooted in heedlessness, attachment to immediate gains, and often arrogance—as the barrier that leads people to reject prophets and signs, a self-deception that will ultimately be shown false.

translation: And if you could see when they stand before their Lord—He will say, "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "So taste the punishment for that you used to deny."
interpretation: The verse conveys that God's truth and judgment are ultimately self-evident, and that persistent, willful rejection of guidance is a moral choice that carries real consequences. When the reality becomes undeniable, a late admission of truth cannot reverse what has been done; divine punishment is presented as the just outcome of sustained denial, and the passage serves as a warning to accept guidance while one still can, since acknowledgment after the fact cannot avert the due consequences.

translation: Truly ruined are those who denied the meeting with Allah; until when the Hour comes upon them unexpectedly, they will say, “O woe to us for what we neglected of it,” while they bear their burdens upon their backs. How evil is what they bear.
interpretation: The verse warns that denying accountability before God brings ultimate loss: those who treated the prospect of resurrection and judgment as unreal will be overtaken unprepared, and their belated regret will not alter the outcome. Their “burdens on their backs” signify the personal weight of their deeds and responsibilities that cannot be shifted to others; in the end they must shoulder the consequences of what they ignored or omitted. The passage therefore teaches that acknowledging the reality of the Hereafter and acting accordingly—before the Hour arrives—is essential, for postponement or dismissal of moral duty leads to irrevocable harm.

translation: And the life of this world is nothing but play and diversion, while the home of the Hereafter is better for those who are God-fearing. Will you not then use reason?
interpretation: The verse admonishes that the temporal pleasures and distractions of this world are ultimately insignificant; true and lasting good is the eternal life to come, which is attained by God-conscious conduct. It urges people to reflect and apply reason so they prioritize what endures—righteousness, accountability, and preparation for the Hereafter—over fleeting amusement and worldly excess.

translation: We certainly know that what they say grieves you; indeed, it is not you they reject, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah.
interpretation: God is consoling the Prophet: the hurt caused by their accusations stems not from any flaw in his message but from the moral blindness and injustice of his opponents. Their opposition is rooted in stubbornness, pride, or self-interest that leads them to refuse the clear signs and guidance from God; thus their rejection is ultimately a rejection of divine evidence, not of the Prophet’s sincerity or truthfulness.

translation: And indeed messengers before you were denied, yet they remained patient over being denied and harmed until Our help came to them. And there is no changer of the words of Allah. And indeed there has come to you news of the messengers.
interpretation: This verse functions as a consoling principle and theological rule: prophets who are rejected and persecuted must respond with steadfast patience and trust, because God’s promises and decrees are unchangeable and will realize in their appointed time. The histories of earlier messengers — their suffering followed by divine support and vindication — are presented not merely as past events but as a pattern and assurance: perseverance under trial, rooted in faith in God’s immutable word, is the proper response to denial and hostility, since ultimate help and justice belong to God alone.

translation: And if it is hard for you that they turn away, then if you could, seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder to the heavens and bring them a sign. And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them all upon guidance. So be not among the ignorant.
interpretation: This verse comforts and corrects: it acknowledges the Prophet’s pain at people’s rejection but rejects the idea that he can—or must—compel belief by extraordinary means. The image of digging a tunnel through the earth or climbing a ladder to the heavens is deliberate hyperbole: even miraculous, impossible feats would not guarantee guidance, for guidance is ultimately a matter of God’s will and the turning of hearts. The practical lesson is twofold: continue to convey the message faithfully without demanding signs or trying to force outcomes, and trust God’s sovereignty over guidance. ‘So be not among the ignorant’ warns against failing to recognize these limits—against blaming oneself or resorting to vain attempts to control belief instead of showing patience, wisdom, and reliance on Allah.

translation: Only those who hear respond. And the dead — Allah will resurrect them, then to Him they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse is teaching that true acceptance of God’s call is an inward, attentive hearing that leads to response and conduct; those who are ‘dead’ in heedlessness (and the physically dead) will nevertheless be brought back to life by Allah, and ultimately everyone will be returned to Him for reckoning. Thus it links moral responsibility — be the kind of listener who truly responds — with the certainty of resurrection and final accountability before God.

translation: And they say, “Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?” Say, “Indeed, Allah is Able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know.”
interpretation: The verse answers skeptics who demand a miraculous proof by asserting that God’s power to send a sign is not in question; rather, their demand exposes their ignorance or obstinacy. God may withhold a sign because such spectacles often do not lead the hard‑hearted to true faith—their refusal is rooted in disposition and lack of understanding, not in any inability of God. Thus the point is that belief depends on the state of the heart and insight, and not merely on visible wonders produced on demand.

translation: There is no creature on the earth nor a bird that flies with its wings but they are communities like you. We have not omitted anything in the Record. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all living beings exist as organized communities with their own natures and purposes, not mere isolated objects; Allah’s knowledge and decree encompass every detail of creation (nothing is left out of the Divine Record), and ultimately every creature will be brought before its Lord. Practically, this counsels humility and responsible stewardship: humans are not the sole owners of moral significance, must recognize the created order and limits of their authority, trust in God’s perfect knowledge and justice, and prepare for the universal gathering before God.

translation: And those who deny Our signs — they are deaf and mute, wandering in darkness. Whomsoever Allah wills He leads astray, and whomsoever He wills He places on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse explains a moral and spiritual consequence: persistent rejection of God’s evidences hardens the heart so that a person becomes incapable of receiving guidance — described metaphorically as being 'deaf and mute' and lost in darkness. The clauses about God’s will ("whomsoever He wills...") do not cancel human responsibility but state the Divine principle that guidance and misguidance are ultimately administered by God in accordance with His knowledge and justice: those whose inner disposition is fixed against truth are left to the consequences of their choice, while those whom God bestows guidance upon are enabled inwardly to recognize and follow the straight way.

translation: Say, "Have you considered: if the punishment of Allah were to come upon you or the Hour were to come upon you, would you call upon besides Allah — if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The verse confronts those who rely on or worship other beings by exposing the futility of expecting them to avert divine punishment or to control the Last Day; it affirms that ultimate power and judgement belong to Allah alone and uses a rhetorical question to show that in moments of true need people will find that their supposed helpers cannot save them, thereby calling listeners to recognize God’s sole sovereignty and to abandon reliance on false intercessors.

translation: بل إياه تدعون فيكشف ما تدعون إليه إن شاء وتنسون ما تشركون — Nay, it is Him alone Whom you call upon; He will remove (or expose the impotence of) whatever you call upon besides Him, if He wills, and you will forget those partners you associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true power and response belong solely to God: whatever other beings, idols, or intermediaries people invoke have no independent efficacy unless God permits. By His will He can strip away or expose the uselessness of those supposed helpers, and in doing so people will abandon or forget the false partners they had set up — a warning that reliance on anything besides God is ultimately futile because He alone decides what will be effective.

translation: And certainly We sent to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and affliction so that perhaps they might humble themselves and supplicate.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine trials are deliberate, pedagogical measures meant to awaken hearts and remove arrogance: hardships (external calamities and inner distress) are used by God as a compassionate means to lead people to reflection, sincere supplication, and repentance. The phrase “so that perhaps” expresses God’s hope that suffering will produce humility and return to Him; if a people respond, the trial fulfills its corrective purpose, but if they persist in denial and pride, the trials remain as both warning and consequence.

translation: Why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves and plead for mercy? Rather their hearts had grown hard, and Satan made what they were doing seem fair to them.
interpretation: The verse warns that divine chastisement is meant to prompt sincere repentance and softening of the heart, but when people respond with stubbornness and callousness—further aided by Satan’s deception that makes sins look appealing—they miss the chance for reform; the true remedy is humble return to God, not persistence in self‑justifying wrongdoing.

translation: So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the doors of everything; then, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and behold — they were brought low.
interpretation: The verse warns that abandoning divine guidance can lead God to grant abundant worldly ease—which appears as open doors to every comfort—as a trial that increases negligence and pride. Their rejoicing in material gain marks spiritual forgetfulness; consequently, divine retribution can come unexpectedly, stripping away that apparent success and leaving them humiliated and powerless. The lesson: worldly prosperity is not proof of God’s approval and can itself be the means of one’s downfall if it fosters forgetfulness of obligation and dependence on God.

translation:
فَقطَعَ دَابِرَ الْقَوْمِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا ۚ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
“So He cut off the end (the continuity) of the people who did wrong; and all praise is due to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God, in His justice and wisdom, terminates the enduring power or lineage of persistent oppressors so that their wrongdoing does not continue to corrupt society; this divine action is to be received with thankful recognition of Allah’s sovereignty, as a reassurance to the faithful that tyranny is not permanent and a warning to those who persist in injustice.

translation: Say, “Have you considered: if Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight and seal over your hearts — which god other than Allah could restore them to you? Observe how We present the signs, yet they still turn away.”
interpretation: The verse is a sharp rhetorical admonition: ultimate control over human faculties and inner guidance belongs to God alone, so no idol, prophet, or intermediary can reverse God’s decree if He withdraws hearing, sight, or seals the heart. The “sealing” signals a spiritual hardening that often follows persistent rejection; it is both a consequence of heedlessness and a warning that delay in responding to God’s signs risks permanent loss of receptivity. By saying “see how We present the signs,” the text stresses God’s repeated, varied efforts to call people, while “they turn away” indicts human stubbornness — therefore the proper response is immediate reflection, humility, and submission before God’s mercy is withdrawn.

translation: Say, “Have you considered: if the punishment of Allah were to come to you suddenly or openly, would He destroy anyone except the unjust people?”
interpretation: The verse underscores God’s moral justice: when divine punishment arrives — whether unexpectedly or manifestly — it is not arbitrary but falls on those who persist in oppression and wrongdoing; this both comforts the upright that they will not be wrongfully destroyed and serves as a warning that continued injustice leads to deserved ruin unless one repents and reforms.

translation: We send not the messengers except as bringers of good tidings and as warners. So whoever believes and does righteous deeds—there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: God’s purpose in sending prophets is twofold: to proclaim the glad news of mercy and reward to those who accept guidance, and to warn of the consequences of rejection. True security—‘no fear and no grief’—is promised to those who both embrace faith inwardly and translate it into upright conduct outwardly. ‘Faith’ here is not merely assent but commitment, and ‘reform’ (أصلح) denotes moral and social rectitude—purifying the heart, fulfilling obligations, and restoring justice. Those who combine sincere belief with practical righteousness are released from existential anxiety about divine judgment and from the sorrow that follows moral failure and loss, in this life and in the hereafter.

translation: And those who denied Our signs — punishment will touch them for what they used to commit of transgression.
interpretation: The verse asserts that rejecting God’s revelations is not a mere intellectual error but a willful, habitual rupture from divine guidance; the resulting punishment is presented as a just consequence proportional to their ongoing disobedience and moral corruption (the ‘fisq’ they practiced), emphasizing accountability rather than arbitrary suffering.

translation: Say, “I do not say to you that I have with me the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say about myself that I am an angel; I only follow what is revealed to me.” Say, “Are the blind and the seeing equal? Will you not then reflect?”
interpretation: The verse asserts the Prophet’s humility and limits—he disavows claims of secret power, hidden wealth, or angelic status—and grounds his authority solely in revelation; by contrasting the ‘blind’ and the ‘seeing’ it urges people to use reason and inner perception to distinguish true guidance from error and to accept the message based on its evidence rather than on myth, spectacle, or false attributions.

translation: And warn, by it, those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord. They have no guardian or intercessor besides Him; perhaps they will attain God‑consciousness.
interpretation: This verse directs the Prophet to address those whose hearts are already uneasy about being presented before God, using the Qur’an as a reminder to awaken their responsibility. It stresses that on the Day of Gathering no worldly protector or independent intercessor will avail them — every defense or intercession is ultimately subject to God’s will — so the warning is meant to move these people to cultivate taqwa: to reform their behavior, strengthen sincere reliance on Allah, and live in mindful obedience so they stand rightly when they are brought before their Lord.

translation: And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. You have no responsibility over them in the least, nor do they have responsibility over you; so do not expel them and thus be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse admonishes the Prophet (and by extension the community) to be patient and tolerant toward people who quietly and sincerely turn to God at dawn and dusk seeking His pleasure. It emphasizes that judgment and accountability belong to God, not to fellow humans—so one should not police, exclude, or persecute sincere worshippers because of social differences, weakness, or different status. Forcing them out of a place of devotion or rejecting them for outward reasons would be an unjust act; true piety is measured by intent before God, and excluding such people makes the excludeer among the wrongdoers.

translation: And thus We tested some of them by others, so that they might say, “Are these the ones upon whom Allah has favored from among us?” Is not Allah Most Knowing of the grateful?
interpretation: God ordains differences in people’s conditions as a moral and spiritual test: visible advantage can provoke envy and false judgments about divine favor, but true merit is an inward reality—gratitude, righteousness, and sincere devotion—which only God fully knows. The verse warns against equating outward blessings with God’s approval and reminds believers that ultimate appraisal rests with Allah, who alone discerns who is truly thankful.

translation: And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say, “Peace be upon you.” Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: that if any of you does evil out of ignorance and then repents afterwards and reforms, indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that mercy is a foundational, self‑imposed principle of God’s dealing with people: believers are to be received with the greeting of peace as an expression of trust in that mercy. Wrongdoing committed in ignorance does not bar one from God’s compassion if it is followed by sincere repentance and concrete efforts to set things right; God’s forgiveness is thus available but is linked to remorse and moral repair. Socially, this teaches both a disposition of welcoming and trust toward repentant believers and a moral requirement that repentance be accompanied by corrective action—balancing divine grace with personal responsibility.

translation: And thus We expound the verses in detail, that the way of the criminals may become clear.
interpretation: God makes His revelations explicit and unfolded so that the moral trajectory and consequences of those who persist in wrongdoing are exposed; by clarifying the signs He reveals the true nature, methods and ultimate ruin of the guilty, both warning people to avoid that path and demonstrating that their course is evident and deserving of judgment.

translation: Say, “I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides Allah.” Say, “I will not follow your desires; you have gone astray, then, and I am not among the guided.”
interpretation: The verse asserts a foundational criterion for true guidance: obedience to God’s command over conformity to popular wishes. It explains that following divine revelation may require rejecting communal pressures, customs or passions that legitimize false objects of worship, and that such resolute refusal is itself the mark of staying on the straight path while those who give in to vain desires are led astray.

translation: Say, “Indeed I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, yet you have denied it. I do not possess for you anything to hasten [your demand]. The judgment belongs only to Allah; He relates the truth, and He is the best of deciders.”
interpretation: The speaker affirms that his message rests on unmistakable divine evidence and that rejection lies with the people, not with him. He cannot coerce belief or accelerate God’s timing—neither miracles nor immediate retribution are under his control. Ultimate authority to pronounce and realize judgment belongs solely to God, who alone reveals the truth and is the fairest arbiter; therefore one must accept the limits of human agency, submit to divine timing, and trust God’s final, just resolution.

translation: Say, “If I had what you are hurrying for, the matter between me and you would have been settled; and Allah knows best who are the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to rebut those who demand immediate outcomes (whether punishment, signs, or recompense) by reminding them that he does not control God’s decree; if he possessed the power they seek to force a resolution, he would settle the dispute at once. The deeper point is that ultimate judgment, knowledge of guilt, and the timing of consequences belong to Allah alone — human impatience, accusations, or attempts to compel a verdict change nothing of Divine justice, which will be exercised by God in His wisdom against the wrongdoers.

translation: And with Him are the keys of the Unseen; none knows them except Him. He knows what is in the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, but it is (all) in a clear Book.
interpretation: The verse declares God’s absolute and exclusive knowledge and sovereignty: He alone holds the ‘keys of the Unseen,’ meaning He controls what is hidden and what will be revealed, and nothing—whether on land or in the sea, whether the tiniest falling leaf, a seed buried in darkness, or any living or withered thing—occurs outside His knowledge. That every detail is inscribed “in a clear Book” emphasizes precise, unambiguous divine record and decree. The passage therefore teaches that providence and accountability are comprehensive: nothing is accidental or lost to God’s awareness, which comforts the believer in God’s care and underpins moral responsibility and ultimate judgment.

translation: And He is the One who takes your souls by night and knows what you have done by day; then He will resurrect you therein so that an appointed term may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return, and then He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s absolute sovereignty over life, death and time ensures that hidden and apparent deeds alike are known and will be judged. The seeming delay of recompense is not neglect but part of God’s wise timing to complete appointed terms; therefore nothing escapes divine accountability. This is both a warning to abandon secret wrongdoing and a reassurance to the wronged that ultimate justice and full disclosure of deeds rest with God.

translation: And He is the Dominant (Overwhelming) over His servants; and He sends guardians over you. Until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect [their duty].
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s sovereignty is total and precise: the angels assigned to human beings both protect and administer what God wills, yet when the appointed moment of death arrives they carry out that decree with absolute fidelity. The phrase “they do not neglect” stresses that divine providence and the execution of destiny are exact and unavoidable—no creature can evade or postpone what God has fixed. The practical implication is to live with humble awareness of accountability: trust in God’s protection, but use life to prepare spiritually and morally for the inevitable meeting with Him, since death will occur exactly as decreed.

translation: Then they will be returned to God, their true Lord. Surely to Him belongs the judgement, and He is the swiftest of those who take account.
interpretation: The verse reminds that the ultimate reality of human existence is return to God, who alone has rightful authority over people’s affairs. “Their true Lord” emphasizes that any worldly masters or claims of sovereignty are transient compared with God’s permanent dominion. Declaring that the judgement belongs to Him stresses that final decisions about justice, reward and punishment rest with God alone, not with fallible human judgment. Saying He is “the swiftest of those who take account” underlines that God’s reckoning is inevitable, exact, and can come without delay: deeds are known and will be rightly weighed. The practical implication is both a warning and an incentive — to live with moral seriousness, to seek God’s mercy, and to orient one’s trust and obligations toward the One whose judgment is final and unavoidable.

translation: Say, “Who can save you from the darknesses of land and sea?” — whom you call upon in supplication, humbly and secretly — “If He were to save us from this, then indeed we would surely be among the grateful.”
interpretation: The verse confronts human inconsistency and the futility of relying on powerless deities: the imagery of ‘darknesses of land and sea’ denotes dire danger, confusion and helplessness in which people instinctively turn in private to whoever they believe can help. It exposes that such appeals are driven by need, not conviction, and that the vow of gratitude uttered in extremity is often hollow if it is not coupled with steady recognition of the One who alone has power to deliver. The theological lesson is twofold: affirm God’s exclusive ability to rescue, and call people to translate their conditional promises into constant, faithful gratitude and obedience rather than transient, self-serving vows.

translation: Say: “Allah will save you from it and from every distress”; yet you still associate partners (with Him).
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that deliverance and relief come solely from God; persisting in associating partners after witnessing His power is a sign of ingratitude, superstition, and moral blindness. It shows the futility of relying on or worshiping others as protectors, and calls for a proper response to God’s favors: exclusive trust, gratitude, and recognition of His sole authority.

translation: Say, “He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to cause you to be divided into factions and let some of you taste the violence of others.” See how We alternate the signs so that perhaps they will understand.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s complete sovereignty over both natural and social orders and explains that the shifting of circumstances—calamities from the sky or the earth, or the breaking up of societies into hostile groups—can serve as deliberate, educative measures. By allowing fortunes to rise and fall and by permitting internal strife, God exposes the moral consequences of peoples’ choices, disrupts complacency, and creates occasions for reflection and repentance; the alternation of signs is therefore a purposeful method to awaken insight and moral responsibility so that people may come to true understanding.

translation: And your people denied it, while it is the Truth. Say: “I am not over you a guardian.”
interpretation: The verse instructs the Messenger to make clear that his responsibility is to convey the truth, not to coerce belief or to shoulder the moral consequences of people’s choices; he cannot function as their keeper, protector, or enforcer of guidance—each person is accountable for accepting or rejecting the message, and ultimate judgment belongs to God.

translation: For every matter there is an appointed place of settlement; and you will come to know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every event, decree, or announcement has a fixed, divinely ordained outcome or culmination—nothing is random or without its appointed time and place. It warns that the realities promised or warned about (notably the Day of Reckoning and the consequences of people's deeds) will be realized unmistakably, so people will ultimately witness and acknowledge the fulfillment of God’s decree; this calls for awareness that actions have inevitable consequences and that God’s timing and judgment are certain.

translation: When you see those who engage in vain disputation about Our signs, then turn away from them until they enter into another conversation; and if Satan makes you forget, then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse instructs believers to withdraw from gatherings or debates where people mock, belittle or engage in frivolous talk about God’s signs, not by arguing further but by removing oneself until the topic changes. This withdrawal is a protective measure for one’s faith and conscience: continued presence can desensitize and normalize disrespect toward divine guidance. The verse also acknowledges human weakness—Satan may cause a momentary lapse that leads one to remain—so upon remembering one must not continue to sit among the wrongdoers. In short, it prescribes prudent avoidance of company and conversation that undermines belief, and requires corrective action if one is momentarily led astray.

translation: And there is nothing of burden concerning their reckoning for those who fear [Allah]; but it is a reminder — perhaps they will become mindful (of God).
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine taqwa (God‑consciousness) shields a person from the oppressive fear of divine accounting: sincere piety and upright conduct mean one need not dread condemnation. At the same time the proclamation functions as a warning and admonition aimed at others — its purpose is to awaken people to cultivate that same fear of God and reform, so they too may be secure before the Day of Reckoning.

translation: Leave those who have taken their religion as play and diversion and whom the life of this world has deceived. And remind [them] with it, lest you cause a soul to perish for what it has earned — it will have no protector or intercessor besides Allah. And if it were to offer every compensation, it would not be accepted from it. Those are the ones whose deeds have failed them; for them is a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment for what they used to deny.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Messenger to disengage from people whose hearts are captivated by worldly amusements and who treat faith as a joke: his responsibility is to convey the warning, not to compel belief or to rescue those who persist in heedlessness. It emphasizes personal moral accountability — when someone chooses disbelief and clings to worldly deception, their deeds become ineffective, no human protector or intercessor can avert divine judgment, and no ransom can purchase acceptance. The graphic image of boiling drink and painful torment underscores the real and irreversible consequences of a life lived in neglect of God, and it serves as both a warning to the heedless and a reassurance that ultimate justice rests with God alone.

translation: Say, “Shall we call upon besides Allah that which will neither benefit us nor harm us, and turn back on our heels after Allah has guided us? Like the one whom the devils led astray on the earth — bewildered — and he has companions calling him to guidance, ‘Come to us.’ Say, ‘Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance.’ And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke of turning away from divine guidance in favor of powerless alternatives and a moral diagnosis of relapse into error: guidance from God is the only true, effective direction for life, so abandoning it after receiving it is not mere mistake but a spiritual capitulation comparable to being enthralled by corrupting influences (described as devils). The imagery of a bewildered person urged by others toward guidance shows that external invitations are not enough if inner conviction is lost; steadfastness requires sincere submission (Islam) and resistance to social pressures and false authorities. Thus the passage commands personal and communal commitment to God’s way, warning that reverting to useless objects of worship or to prior ignorance negates the benefit of prior guidance and leaves one morally and spiritually ruined.

translation: And establish prayer and fear Him; and it is He to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse ties together two pillars of a believer’s life—regular, disciplined worship (ṣalāh) and inner God‑consciousness (taqwā)—to teach that true religion is both outward devotion and inward restraint. Establishing prayer disciplines the self and community rhythm, while fearing God shapes moral choices in every situation; together they prepare one for the inevitable return and accountability before God, since all people will ultimately be gathered to Him. Thus the command is not merely ritualistic, but a directive to live with constant awareness of divine presence and responsibility.

translation: He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in truth. And when He says, “Be,” it is. His word is the truth. To Him belongs the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown. Knower of the unseen and the seen; and He is the Wise, the All‑Aware.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute sovereignty: creation and resurrection occur by His instant, truthful command, so ultimate authority and judgment belong to Him alone. Because He knows both what is hidden and what is manifest and governs with perfect wisdom and awareness, human claims to power or hidden assurances are unreliable; the proper response is humble submission to God’s decree, trust in His justice, and readiness to be accountable before Him.

translation: And when Abraham said to his father Azar, “Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error.”
interpretation: The verse shows the prophetic conviction that authentic faith must confront inherited falsehood: Abraham’s address is not merely a denunciation but an appeal to reason and conscience, exposing idolatry as irrational and morally wrong. By calling his people’s condition a “manifest error,” the verse legitimizes clear, principled opposition to entrenched practices and frames prophetic guidance as a duty to challenge collective misguidance with moral clarity and rational argument.

translation: And thus We showed Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among the certain in faith.
interpretation: God made Abraham witness, by vision and by reflection on the order and signs in creation, the reality of divine sovereignty over heavens and earth. This direct showing was meant to transform intellectual assent into firm, experiential certitude: Abraham’s certainty is not merely inherited or speculative but rooted in the clear perception of God’s absolute dominion and providential wisdom.

translation: فلما جنَّ عليه الليل رأى كوكبًا قال هذا ربي فلما أفل قال لا أُحبُّ الآفلين
interpretation: الآية تبرز منهج إبراهيم في التمييز بين الخالق والمخلوقات: بدلاً من قبول آلهةٍ مبنية على العادة أو الخرافة، ينظر بعين التأمل في طبيعة الظواهر ويستبعد ما يفتقد للثبات والاستقلال. لأن ما يطلع ويغيب ليس مستمرًا ولا قادراً على الحكم أو الإيجاد، فهو لا يصلح أن يكون معبودًا؛ ومن هنا تتأسس دعوته للتوحيد بالاستدلال على صفات الديمومة والاستقلال لله مقابل حالة العجز والاعتماد لدى المخلوقات.

translation: When he saw the moon rising, he said, “This is my Lord.” But when it set, he said, “Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray.”
interpretation: The verse portrays Abraham’s contemplative rejection of celestial objects as deities: he initially points to the bright moon as if it could be a lord, but when its setting reveals its transience he immediately abandons that claim. His concluding admission — that without his Lord’s guidance he would be among the misguided — emphasizes that true faith is reached not by following fleeting signs or appearances but by seeking and receiving divine guidance; it expresses humility, reasoned reflection, and the conviction that guidance is a gracious gift from God rather than something guaranteed by mere observation.

translation: So when he saw the sun rising he said, “This is my Lord; this is greater.” But when it set he said, “O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate (with Allah).”
interpretation: The verse illustrates Abraham’s rational rejection of idol-worship: by observing that heavenly bodies rise and set, he recognizes that anything transient and subject to change cannot be the Eternal Lord. His declaration therefore affirms God’s absolute transcendence above created phenomena and serves as a moral and theological disavowal of his people’s polytheism—showing that true faith rests on recognizing God’s permanence and uniqueness, not on venerating impermanent created things.

translation: Indeed, I have turned my face toward the One who created the heavens and the earth, devoutly upright; and I am not of the polytheists.
interpretation: This is a resolute affirmation of exclusive devotion to the Creator: to “turn the face” means to direct one’s whole intention, worship and conduct toward God alone, while “ḥanīf” denotes an original, unwavering monotheism that breaks with inherited idolatry. The speaker thereby rejects all forms of shirk and asserts that true faith requires single-minded submission to Allah, even in the face of communal or familial pressure.

translation: وَحَاجَّ قَوْمَهُۚ قَالَ أَتُحَاجُّونَنِي فِي اللَّهِ وَقَدْ هَدَانِي ۖ وَلَآ أَخَافُ مَا تُشْرِكُونَ بِهِۦٓ إِلَّآ أَن يَشَاءَ رَبِّي شَيْئًا ۗ وَسِعَ رَبِّي كُلَّ شَيْءٍ عِلْمًا ۗ أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ
interpretation: الآية تظهر موقف النبي واطمئنانه إلى هدايته الإلهية فرفض أن يُرهب أو يُرغم على الانصياع لعبادة غير الله بسبب محاججة قومه. قولُه «ولا أخاف ما تشركون به إلا أن يشاء ربي شيئاً» يعبر عن تواضع المؤمن أمام مشيئة الله مع ثقة بأن النتائج بيدٍ عليا، وعبارة «وسع ربي كل شيء علماً» تؤكد مبدأ سيادة العلم الإلهي وشمول معرفته لكل حال ومآل. الدعوة النهائية «أفالَ لا تتذكرون» هي نداء للتأمل والتفكر: تذكّروا حقيقة الهداية والحق بدل التمسك بالجاهليات والعادات الباطلة.

translation: And how should I fear what you associate [with Allah] while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority? So which of the two parties is more entitled to security, if you know?
interpretation: The verse rejects the idea that the Messenger should be intimidated by the idols or threats of the polytheists. It points out the real fault lies with those who ascribe partners to God without any revealed proof or sanction (سلطان); that baseless attribution, not the Prophet’s call, removes divine protection and exposes them to accountability. The rhetorical question makes plain that true security—both moral certainty and ultimate safety before God—belongs to those guided by divine authority, not to those who invent gods without evidence.

translation: Those who believe and do not mix their faith with injustice — for them is security, and they are rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse affirms that genuine faith must remain pure and untainted by ظلم (injustice), which encompasses both wronging others through oppression and falsehood and doing injustice to oneself by corrupting belief (e.g., associating partners with God). When a person’s conviction is sincere and not compromised by sinful conduct or shirk, God grants them true security — relief from fear and ultimate safety — and keeps them on the straight path; sincerity coupled with justice yields inner peace, moral rectitude, and guidance toward salvation.

translation: And that was Our proof which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s revelations and proofs given to prophets serve to distinguish truth from rejection, and that God, in His perfect wisdom and knowledge, elevates people by ranks according to His counsels and the realities of their hearts. “Raising degrees” reflects God’s sovereign, purposeful assignment of honor, understanding, and station (in this life and/or the hereafter) — not arbitrary promotion but a raising measured by insight, faithfulness, and God’s just and all‑knowing assessment.

translation: And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob; each of them We guided. And Noah We had guided before, and among his descendants [were] David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We recompense the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s granting of righteous offspring and of guidance is a direct divine favor and form of recompense. By naming prophets from different generations (including Noah and Abraham’s lineage) it emphasizes the continuity of God’s guidance across time and that guidance and prophetic honor are bestowed by God’s will, not by human pedigree alone. The closing clause, “Thus do We reward the doers of good,” indicates that such blessings—righteous progeny, moral excellence, and access to divine guidance—are among the ways God rewards those who act with excellence (ihsan), making spiritual consequence and God’s grace the ultimate measure of true honor.

translation: And Zakariya and Yahya and 'Isa and Ilyas — each of them was among the righteous.
interpretation: By mentioning these exemplary prophets, the verse teaches that God’s true honor is given to moral integrity and steadfast devotion. Their lives illustrate that righteousness—sincere faith, obedience, humility, and service to others—is the lasting criterion for divine favor, and believers are called to emulate their inner purity and constancy rather than seek status or worldly gain.

translation: And Ishmael and Al-Yasa‘ and Jonah and Lot — and each of them We preferred above the peoples.
interpretation: The verse asserts that God bestowed a special, divinely granted elevation upon each of these prophets: they were distinguished above ordinary people by being chosen as messengers and by receiving guidance, moral excellence, steadfastness, and signs. The phrase indicates not mere worldly prestige but a religious and ethical superiority in God’s sight and record, marking them as exemplary guides and recipients of particular divine favors.

translation:
وَمِنْ آبَائِهِمْ وَذُرِّيَّاتِهِمْ وَإِخْوَانِهِمْ ۖ وَاجْتَبَيْنَاهُمْ وَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ
"And from among their fathers, their offspring and their brothers — We chose them and guided them to a straight path."
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance is an act of God's free choice and mercy that can touch members across family lines: being related to pious people does not automatically confer guidance, nor is lineage the cause of right guidance; rather Allah selects and directs whom He wills — sometimes among fathers, children, or siblings — and it is His selection and guidance that leads people onto the straight path.

translation: That is the guidance of Allah; He guides with it whom He wills of His servants. And had they associated others (with Him), whatever they were doing would have been rendered void.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true guidance is a divine gift given according to Allah’s wisdom and will — human effort cannot by itself guarantee spiritual guidance. It also affirms that shirk (associating partners with God) undermines the moral and religious value of one’s actions: acts of worship or obedience lose their intended purpose when directed at or compromised by partners beside God, because sincere tawḥīd (the oneness of God) and correct intention are prerequisites for deeds to be accepted and bear fruit.

translation: أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ آتَيْنَاهُمُ الْكِتَابَ وَالْحُكْمَ وَالنُّبُوَّةَ ۚ فَإِن يَكْفُرْ بِهَا هَؤُلَاءِ فَقَدْ وَكَلْنَا بِهَا قَوْمًا لَّا هُمْ بِهَـٰذَا بِكَـٰفِرِينَ
interpretation: الآية توضح أن الله سبحانه وتعالى منَّ على أمم بعينها بالكتاب والسلطة للحكم وهبة النبوة، لكن حفظ الحق وكيْله وعماد استمراره مشروطان بالإيمان والصدق في الالتزام؛ فإذا أبوا بعض هؤلاء على قبول الحق ونقضوا عهد الرسالة، يختار الله لمن يخلفهم أمة تفي بهذه الأمانة ولا تكفر بها. المقصود أن شرعية حفظ النقل الإلهي وتأويله وقيادته لا تقوم على النسب أو الانتماء التاريخي وحده، بل على الإيمان والعمل، والله يوكّل الرسالة لمن يستحقها بالثبات والإخلاص.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance. Say, “I do not ask you for any reward for it; it is only a reminder for the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true guidance is a gift from God embodied in certain people (the prophets and the righteous exemplars), and the proper response is to emulate their way of faith and conduct because their example reflects divinely‑ordained truth. The Prophet’s mission is not driven by worldly gain—he seeks no payment—but by conveying a universal admonition: the revelation is a timeless reminder addressed to all peoples, intended to reform hearts and societies; therefore acceptance means internalizing and following the moral and spiritual model presented, not merely acknowledging words.

translation: And they did not appraise Allah with true appraisal when they said, “Allah did not reveal anything to any human.” Say, “Then who revealed the Book which Moses brought— a light and guidance for the people? You make it into parchments that you show and conceal much, and you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew.” Say, “It is from Allah;” then leave them in their idle contention, playing.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who deny that God can or did communicate with human beings by pointing to the obvious contradiction: the Torah came through the human prophet Moses as a source of light and guidance. It also condemns the hypocrisy of manipulating sacred texts—exposing some parts while hiding others—for advantage, and of claiming knowledge beyond one’s legitimate learning. The prescribed response for the Prophet (and believers) is to affirm plainly that the revelation is from God and then disengage from their vain disputes and diversions rather than be drawn into futile contention; the passage thus teaches both a reaffirmation of divine revelation given to prophets and a measured, dignified withdrawal from those who corrupt or deny it.

translation: This is a Book which We revealed, blessed, confirming what was before it, so that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they faithfully preserve their prayers.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qurʾān as a divinely sanctioned, auspicious confirmation of earlier revelations whose purpose is both particular and universal: to warn the spiritual center (the “Mother of Cities,” classically understood as Mecca) and its surrounding peoples, and thereby to call humanity to accountability. Calling the Book “blessed” emphasizes that its guidance produces growth, mercy and moral benefit; calling it a confirmer stresses continuity with previous scripture rather than rupture. The link drawn between belief in the Hereafter and acceptance of this revelation shows that true assent is not merely intellectual but eschatological — belief in final reward and accountability makes people receptive to the message. Finally, the phrase about safeguarding prayer indicates that genuine faith manifests in disciplined, protected worship: believers do not treat ritual as mere formality but guard its times, integrity and inward presence, so worship becomes both a sign and a means of holding fast to the Qurʾān’s teachings.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or says, “It has been inspired to me,” while nothing has been inspired to him; or who says, “I will reveal like what Allah has revealed”? And if you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the pangs of death and the angels stretch forth their hands, [saying], “Discharge your souls; today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say against Allah other than the truth, and because you were arrogant concerning His signs.”
interpretation: The verse warns that fabricating divine authority or claiming revelation to serve one’s own ends is among the gravest injustices, because it corrupts truth and misleads people. By portraying the wrongdoer in the helpless final moment—when human pretensions fall away and the angels assert divine judgment—the passage teaches that such falsehoods will be exposed and judged; the promised “punishment of humiliation” is not merely physical pain but the stripping of the honor, authority and dignity the false claimant sought. The spiritual lesson is clear: arrogance that elevates personal desires above God’s truth and rejects His signs leads inevitably to disgrace and accountability, and no worldly claim of revelation can avert that ultimate reckoning.

translation: And you will surely come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you will leave behind whatever We bestowed upon you. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners [with Us]; it has been severed between you, and lost from you is what you used to claim.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Gathering every person will stand before God in the same singular, dependent state as at first creation: no wealth, privilege, or supposed allies accompany them, and any claimed intercessors or partners — whether idols, patronage, or trusted supporters — will be absent and powerless. Its moral is that ultimate responsibility and recompense are individual and cannot be transferred; reliance on worldly supports, false deities, or assumed intermediaries is futile, so true preparation is to cultivate sincere faith and righteous deeds before God alone.

translation: Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?
interpretation: This verse points to God’s manifest power over life and death by citing natural, observable signs: the splitting of a seed (or date-stone) that yields a living plant and the cycle by which life issues from what appears lifeless while the living return to death. These processes are offered as evidence that the One who controls such transformations is fully capable of raising the dead on the Day of Judgment. The rhetorical question at the end rebukes those who, despite these clear signs, allow themselves to be misled into denying divine sovereignty or the reality of resurrection; it underscores human dependence on God’s will for giving life and bringing about death.

translation: He is the One who splits the dawn, and made the night a resting place, and made the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the regular alternation of dawn, night, sun and moon is not random but a deliberate, measured ordinance from God: these cosmic rhythms have appointed roles (rest, markers and means of calculation) and thereby manifest divine sovereignty, wisdom and precise knowledge. By describing this order as God’s “tqdeer” (measure), the verse calls people to recognize the purposeful governance behind nature, to trust in the Creator’s planning, and to see the celestial order as a sign that affirms monotheistic belief and guides human timing, worship and conduct.

translation: And He is the One who made for you the stars so that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea. We have certainly explained the signs for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God fashioned the stars as practical aids for human navigation and, more broadly, as clear signs of divine order and guidance. By saying “We have explained the signs,” it emphasizes that these natural phenomena are deliberately manifest and intelligible so that people who reflect and seek knowledge can use them for both worldly benefit (finding one’s way through literal darkness and difficulty) and spiritual recognition of God’s wisdom and sovereignty.

translation:
وهو الذي أنشأكم من نفسٍ واحدةٍ فمستقرٌّ ومستودعٌ ۚ قد فصلنا الآيات لقوم يفقهون
“And He is the One who created you from a single soul, and [made for it] a dwelling and a place of deposit. We have fully explained the signs for a people who understand.”
interpretation: The verse affirms humanity’s common origin to teach unity, equality and total dependence on God; by saying He made for that one soul both a temporary dwelling and a place of deposit the text points to the successive stages God ordains (our life and our eventual resting-place), reminding the reflective person that worldly existence and the grave are both under Divine providence. The repeated offering of “signs” is thus an invitation to thoughtful moral responsibility: recognizing our shared origin should erase grounds for pride and compel awareness of accountability before God.

translation: And He is the One who sends down water from the sky; with it We bring forth every kind of vegetation; from it We bring forth greenery, and from that greenery We bring forth grains piled one upon another; and from the palm trees, from their spathes come clusters hanging low; and gardens of grapevines, olives and pomegranates, alike and different. See their fruit when they bear fruit and their ripening. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse invites believers to read the cycle and diversity of plant life as deliberate signs of divine wisdom and providence: the ordered stages of growth and the variety of fruits reveal God’s sustaining power, exact coordination, and beneficent design. Rather than being merely botanical facts, these processes are meant to prompt reflection, gratitude, trust in God’s care, and recognition that the manifest order and purposeful variety in creation point to a Creator worthy of faith.

translation: They set up partners for Allah — the jinn and their creations — and attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glory be to Him and exalted above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse condemns the human tendency to invent partners and offspring for God: some people turned to the unseen jinn as objects of worship or co‑deities and fancied that God has sons and daughters. Such claims are made ignorantly and stem from superstition, myth or conjecture. The statement ends by affirming God’s absolute transcendence and purity from these false ascriptions — He is exalted above being joined with partners or limited by human notions of lineage.

translation: Originator of the heavens and the earth. How could He have a son when He has no consort? He created everything, and He is, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the belief that God could have humanlike offspring or partners by affirming His unique, self-sufficient status as the Uncaused Originator: because God alone brought the heavens and the earth into existence without need of precedent or help, and because He created every thing and possesses complete knowledge of all, the ascription of a son or consort to Him is a projection of human assumptions, not a possible attribute of the Divine.

translation: That is Allah—your Lord. There is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things; so worship Him. And He is, over all things, an Agent/Protector.
interpretation: The verse grounds the duty to worship in God’s unique unity and creative sovereignty: because God alone is the Maker and Sustainer of everything, exclusive worship and submission to Him are required. Calling Him wakīl (Agent/Protector) reassures the believer that God not only created the world but also governs, sustains, and is fully competent to manage every affair; therefore true devotion combines obedience with trust in His wisdom and care, freeing one from reliance on idols, intermediaries, or fear of created powers.

translation: No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision; and He is the Subtle, the All‑Aware.
