interpretation: The verse teaches that God is utterly transcendent beyond human sight and sensory comprehension, yet He is intimately and precisely aware of everything the eyes perceive and far beyond; ‘اللّطيف الخبير’ emphasizes that His knowledge penetrates the finest, most hidden realities with gentle care, so we must recognize that the Divine cannot be confined to physical perception while trusting in His attentive, subtle providence.

translation: Clear proofs have come to you from your Lord; so whoever has insight does so for the good of his own soul, and whoever is blind (to them) does harm to himself; and I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has delivered unmistakable guidance, but the moral and spiritual outcome rests on each person’s reception of it: recognizing and acting on the signs benefits one’s own soul, while obstinate rejection brings liability only upon the rejecter. It also defines the Prophet’s role — his duty is to convey the message, not to compel belief or to bear others’ responsibility — underscoring personal accountability and the principle that guidance is granted and realized through one’s own inner insight.

translation:
وَكَذَٰلِكَ نُصَرِّفُ الْآيَاتِ وَلِيَقُولُوا دُرِسْتُمْ وَلِنُبَيِّنَهُ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْلَمُونَ
"And thus We turn away the signs so that they may say, 'You have been taught,' and (so) We may make it clear to a people who know."
interpretation: God sometimes ordains that His signs be received in different ways: the stubborn and hostile will seize on what they hear to accuse the Messenger (saying he was merely 'taught' by others), while those endowed with true understanding will perceive the clear truth. This varying reception exposes people’s inner states, distinguishes sincere insight from wilful rejection, and thereby makes the guidance manifest to the rightly aware.

translation: Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord; there is no deity except Him. And turn away from the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse commands that the divine revelation be the sole standard for faith and conduct: affirm uncompromising monotheism and withdraw from adopting or accommodating the beliefs, practices, or argumentative frameworks of those who associate partners with God — not as a call to unjust hostility, but as a directive to preserve the purity of the message, avoid compromising truth to win approval, and refuse to be led astray by polytheistic influences.

translation:
وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ مَا أَشْرَكُوا ۗ وَمَا جَعَلْنَاكَ عَلَيْهِمْ حَفِيظًا ۖ وَمَا أَنْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِوَكِيلٍ
"And if Allah had willed, they would not have associated [others with Him]. And We did not appoint you over them as a guardian, nor are you a disposer over them."
interpretation: This verse teaches that the acceptance of faith is ultimately determined by God's will, and He could have prevented people from committing shirk but allows human beings to act and be tested. It reminds the Prophet that his duty is to convey the message, not to coerce or control people's hearts: he is not their 'ḥafīẓ' (one who can make or protect them from disbelief) nor their 'wakīl' (an agent who manages or forces their choices). Responsibility for belief and its consequences rests with individuals and with God, so the Prophet is to continue calling to truth, entrusting outcomes to God rather than seeking to impose them.

translation: And do not insult those they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah out of spite and ignorance. Thus We have beautified for every people their own deeds; then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them about what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches restraint and wise conduct in religious debate: insulting others’ gods or beliefs only provokes retaliation and hardens hostility, so believers are commanded to avoid abusive attacks and allow God to judge. It recognizes that people naturally find their own practices attractive, and therefore correction should be carried out with patience and moral integrity rather than provocation, trusting that ultimate accountability and clarification of deeds belong to God alone.

translation: They swore by Allah their strongest oaths, “If a sign comes to us, we will surely believe in it.” Say, “The signs are only with Allah.” And what makes you know that, when it comes, they will not believe?
interpretation: The verse shows that people often demand spectacular proofs and vow they would believe if shown, but such vows expose insincerity or arrogance; signs belong to God alone and do not guarantee acceptance. Even a clear miracle can be rejected by hearts already closed by pride, habitual denial, or attachment to falsehood, so one cannot assume that presenting a sign would necessarily produce faith—guidance and true conviction are given by God, not compelled by outward wonders.

translation:
وَنوَلِّيَنَّ أَفْئِدَتَهُمْ وَأَبْصَارَهُمْ كَمَا لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهِ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ، وَنَذَرَهُمْ فِي طُغْيَانِهِمْ يَعْمَهُونَ
"And We will turn their hearts and their eyes away, just as they did not believe in it the first time; and We will leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly."
interpretation: The verse conveys that persistent, willful rejection of clear guidance brings about a divine withdrawal of inner receptivity: when people repeatedly refuse to accept the truth, God ‘turns’ their hearts and sight so that they lose the spiritual sensitivity and insight they once had. This is presented not as arbitrary cruelty but as the consequence of obstinacy — their refusal hardens their faculties, making them even less able to perceive the truth than before. The final clause—leaving them in their transgression to wander—describes the resulting state: abandoned to their own arrogance and error, they continue in confusion and misguidance, unable to find the straight way because they rejected the means that would have opened their understanding.

translation: And if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered together before them every [created] thing, they would not have believed unless Allah willed; but most of them are ignorant.
interpretation: The verse means that faith cannot be compelled by external spectacle alone: even the most extraordinary signs would not produce true belief in people whose hearts are closed or whose rejection is rooted in arrogance, habit, or heedlessness. Guidance is a grant from God — He gives faith to whom He wills — and many remain unbelieving despite clear manifestations because their inner disposition and ignorance prevent them from receiving guidance.

translation: And thus We made for every prophet an enemy — devils from among mankind and jinn — who whisper to one another adorned speech as deception. And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it; so leave them and what they fabricate.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God, in His wisdom, allows each messenger to face persistent opponents — both human and jinn — who collaborate by framing falsehood in attractive language to mislead people. Their persuasive, ornamented speech (زخرف القول غرورا) is a deliberate tactic to deceive, yet it does not imply independent power: God could have prevented their actions but permits them as part of a divine test and to make clear who chooses truth. The Prophet is therefore instructed not to be swayed by or obsessed with their fabrications; rather, leave their false claims to God’s judgment and continue in conveying the message.

translation: “And so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may be inclined toward it, and that they may be pleased with it and continue in what they are doing.”
interpretation: Those who reject the reality and consequences of the Hereafter become emotionally and morally attached to the transient comforts and excuses of this life; God therefore allows their hearts to be drawn toward that temporary satisfaction so that they remain content with their choices and persist in wrongdoing. This verse explains a spiritual consequence of unbelief: the hardening or misdirection of the heart, which deepens self-deception and makes people continue in the actions that led them away from guidance.

translation:
أَفَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أَبْتَغِي حُكْمًا وَهُوَ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ إِلَيْكُمُ الْكِتَابَ مُفَصَّلًا ۚ وَالَّذِينَ آتَيْنَاهُمُ الْكِتَابَ يَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّهُ مُنْزَلٌ مِنْ رَبِّكَ بِالْحَقِّ ۖ فَلَا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الْمُمْتَرِينَ

“Or should I seek a judge other than Allah? He is the One who has sent down to you the Book, explained in detail. And those to whom We gave the Scripture know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth; so do not be among the doubters.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes any appeal to authorities or laws other than God for final judgment, asserting that the Qur’an is a clear, detailed revelation whose truth is already recognized by People of earlier Scripture; therefore believers must not waver or treat divine guidance as doubtful. In practical terms it affirms the exclusive moral and legal authority of God’s revealed guidance, grounding obedience and judgement in the divinely delivered Book rather than personal preference, partisan interests, or spurious traditions.

translation: And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice. None can change His words, and He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms the finality and reliability of God’s decree and revelation: what He has spoken — His promises, warnings, laws and judgments — will come to pass with perfect truth and justice. Human hopes, schemes, or objections cannot alter divine decision, so accountability and recompense are inevitable. By calling God Ṣamiʿ (All‑Hearing) and ʿAlīm (All‑Knowing), the verse underscores that nothing escapes His awareness and that His fixed word rests on full knowledge and awareness of circumstances; therefore believers are to trust His justice and heed His guidance, while those who reject it are reminded that evasion or distortion of divine truth is impossible.

translation: And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah. They follow nothing but conjecture, and they do nothing but lie.
interpretation: The verse warns that conformity to the popular majority is dangerous in matters of guidance: most people act on assumptions, hearsay, or self-interest rather than knowledge and truth, so following them tends to divert one from God’s way. Therefore a believer must prioritize divine guidance, sound evidence, and sincere moral judgment over mass opinion or social approval, and leaders must not trade truth for popularity.

translation: Indeed, your Lord knows best who goes astray from His way, and He knows best the [rightly] guided.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate knowledge of guidance and misguidance belongs solely to God: whether hearts are receptive or sealed is known to Him alone. For the Prophet and believers this means their duty is to convey truth sincerely, not to assume they can effect guidance by force or become despondent when people reject the message; the final turning of a soul toward or away from God rests in God’s wise, unseen judgment and decree.

translation: So eat of that upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are truly believers in His signs.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine faith is shown in how one accepts God’s provisions: invoking Allah’s name over food and consuming what He has permitted are practical expressions of belief in His revelations. True believers manifest their submission and trust by honoring the lawful limits God set for sustenance, allowing recognition of His lordship to guide their actions rather than mere verbal profession of faith.

translation: And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat of that upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned, while He has explained to you what He has forbidden you—excepting that to which you are compelled? And indeed many lead [others] astray by their desires without knowledge. Indeed, your Lord — He is most knowing of the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who, through unnecessary scruples, cultural taboos, or blind imitation of leaders, refuse what God has made lawful when His name is pronounced over it. It emphasizes that God has clearly delineated prohibitions, so adding extra bans is unjustified except in genuine necessity, and it warns that many people mislead others by following their whims rather than sound knowledge. Ultimately, God alone truly knows who has transgressed and will hold them to account.

translation: And abandon the outward and inward aspects of sin. Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.
interpretation: الآية تنهى عن الإثم بصيغتين: الظاهر من الأفعال والسلوك، والباطن من النوايا والأهواء. المقصود أن الإنكار أو الامتناع الظاهري وحده غير كافٍ إذا بقيت القلوب والمشاعر متعلقة بالإثم، لأن الجزاء عند الله على ما يكسبه الإنسان — من أفعال ونيات — فالمؤمن مطلوب منه تطهير السرائر واجتناب مصادر الإثم لا الاقتصار على المظاهر فقط.

translation: And do not eat of that upon which Allah’s name has not been mentioned; indeed that is defiance. And surely the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you; and if you obey them, then you are surely polytheists.
interpretation: The verse links a concrete ritual act (eating without mentioning God) to a deeper spiritual stance: neglecting God’s name over what one consumes is not merely a lapse in etiquette but a symptom of rebellion against divine authority. It warns that Satanic influence works by co-opting people and leaders who argue to normalize such neglect, turning social pressure and clever argumentation into a means of eroding obedience. The stern clause “if you obey them, you are mushrikun” teaches that placing human desires, customs, or authorities above God’s commands effectively assigns to them the role that belongs to God alone — a form of spiritual partnership. Thus the verse calls for vigilance about both the provenance and ritual status of what we accept, and resistance to popular or persuasive forces that would lead us to subordinate God’s guidance to human interests.

translation: Is the one who was dead — and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among people — the same as the one whose likeness is in darkness, unable to come out of it? Thus We have made attractive to the disbelievers what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance is a divine, transformative gift: God revives the spiritually dead and gives them a luminous faculty that clarifies truth, directs conduct, and enables moral engagement with others. Those without that light remain imprisoned in layers of ignorance and self-deception, unable to find the way out, and God allows their wrongful deeds to appear pleasing to them — both revealing His sovereignty in granting guidance and explaining why persistent rejection leads people to remain blinded and accountable for their choices.

translation: And thus We placed in every town its foremost criminals so that they might plot within it; but they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive it.
interpretation: God permits prominent wrongdoers to emerge in communities so that their schemes, however grand they seem, reveal the consequences of moral decay and ultimately rebound on their makers. Their plotting produces discord, injustice and instability that destroy their own standing and welfare—whether by social collapse, loss of trust, exposure, or divine judgment—even though they remain blind to the fact that they are crafting their own ruin. The verse therefore explains a divine principle: apparent power of the wicked is transient and self-defeating within God’s just order, and communal tolerance or empowerment of such figures brings harm back upon the community and its leaders.

translation: And when a sign comes to them they say, “We will never believe until we are given like what the messengers of Allah were given.” Allah knows best where to place His message. The guilty will be struck with humiliation before Allah and a severe punishment for what they used to plot.
interpretation: The verse reproves those who demand extraordinary miracles as a pretext to refuse faith: such demands reveal obstinacy, not genuine pursuit of truth. God, who alone bestows prophethood and revelation, will not be compelled by their contrivances; He places guidance where He wills. As a consequence of their scheming and rejection, they will be deprived of honor—made low in God’s reckoning—and will suffer a severe retribution both as a moral outcome of their plots and as divine justice for their wrongdoing.

translation: So whoever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whoever He wills to send astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight, as if he were ascending into the sky. Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance is experienced inwardly: when God grants guidance He makes the heart receptive — enlarged, calm, and capable of embracing faith and submission — so the person can understand, accept, and live by truth. Conversely, when guidance is withdrawn as a consequence of persistent rejection, arrogance, or attachment to falsehood, the heart becomes spiritually cramped and distressed, like someone gasping and unable to breathe while climbing; this inner constriction makes receiving truth difficult or impossible. The final clause indicates that this state is not merely psychological but has moral-spiritual consequences: disbelief and persistent resistance leave a stain or impurity on a person’s moral perception and actions, increasing their distance from the clarity and purity that allow guidance to take root.

translation: And this is the path of your Lord, straight. We have detailed the verses for a people who remember.
interpretation: The verse conveys that Allah’s revealed way is a clear, upright guidance intentionally made explicit; God has spelled out signs, rulings and reminders so that those whose hearts are attentive and who practice sincere remembrance (dhikr and reflection) can discern the truth, follow the moral and spiritual course set by Him, and thus bear responsibility for their response—clarity is given, but acceptance requires an engaged, remembering heart.

translation: For them is the Home of Peace with their Lord, and He is their Protector because of what they used to do.
interpretation: The phrase signals that the righteous attain an enduring condition of safety, fulfillment, and freedom from fear — a state of perfect well‑being in the company of God. Calling God their wali (protector/guardian) shows that He becomes their intimate patron and defender, securing and honoring them on the basis of their consistent good conduct; their deeds are the means by which they are recognized and admitted to this divine intimacy. At the same time the structure of the statement points to divine mercy: human responsibility (faithful action) is affirmed, yet the final bestowal of lasting peace and guardianship is God’s gracious response to those deeds, combining personal effort with God’s benevolent reward.

translation: And the Day He will gather them all together, [it will be said], “O company of the jinn, you have led many of mankind astray.” And their allies among mankind will say, “Our Lord, some of us enjoyed the company of others and we have reached the term which You appointed for us.” He will say, “The Fire is your dwelling, wherein you will abide, except for what Allah wills.” Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing.
interpretation: This verse depicts the mutual responsibility and accountability of both jinn and the humans who followed or aided them: on the Day of Gathering they will be confronted together, and the jinn are charged with having led many people into error. The human allies’ protest — that they mutually benefited one another and merely lived until the term God appointed — is presented as a self-justifying excuse that cannot overturn the moral facts of their choices. God’s response (that the Fire is their abode except by His will) affirms that the outcome follows divine justice and wisdom: punishment corresponds to their deeds, yet ultimate dispensation rests with God’s knowledge and mercy. The closing affirmation that the Lord is “Wise and Knowing” emphasizes that the judgments, exceptions, and decrees are neither arbitrary nor ignorant but founded on perfect knowledge and wise purpose.

translation: And thus We give some of the wrongdoers authority over others because of what they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when people persist in injustice and reject guidance, God permits some wrongdoers to prevail over others as a consequence of their own deeds — a form of retributive consequence and trial that manifests the outcomes of their choices, serving both as punishment and as a warning to turn back to righteousness.

translation: O company of jinn and mankind! Did there not come to you messengers from among you who recite to you My verses and warn you of the meeting of this, your Day? They will say, “We bear witness against ourselves.” But the life of this world deceived them, and they will bear witness that they were disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate accountability is rooted in individual choice: people (and jinn) are confronted with clear guidance but may be led astray by the allurements of worldly life, and when the truth becomes unavoidable they themselves acknowledge their prior rejection. It affirms divine justice — that rejection was a consequence of their own will and distraction, not arbitrary punishment — and warns that temporary worldly deception will lead to self-condemnation when one faces the Day of Reckoning.

translation:
ذلك أن لم يكن ربك مهلك القرى بظلم وأهلها غافلون
"That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns in injustice while their people are heedless (unaware)."
interpretation: The verse emphasizes divine justice and deliberate moral causality: God does not annihilate communities out of arbitrary cruelty or while their inhabitants remain ignorant and unwarned. When destruction comes it is the consequence of sustained wrongdoing, rejection of guidance, and persistent corrupting behavior after ample warning and opportunity for repentance; thus the statement reassures that punishment is justly grounded and affirms human responsibility rather than fatalistic, unjust divine action.

translation: And for everyone there are degrees according to what they did; and your Lord is not unaware of what they do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God dispenses moral order with fine gradations: people will be placed in ranks proportionate to the sincerity, quality and consequence of their actions and inner dispositions. ‘Degrees’ indicate that reward and spiritual status are not uniform but measured — even small sincere deeds earn their due, and greater sacrifices and righteousness yield higher stations — while the affirmation that the Lord is not unaware removes all doubt: nothing of intention or action is overlooked. Thus it comforts those who strive with hope of just recompense and warns that no deed, good or ill, will be lost or go unaccounted for.

translation:
وَرَبُّكُمُ الغَنِيُّ ذُو الرَّحْمَةِ ۚ إِنْ يَشَأْ يُذْهِبْكُمْ وَيَسْتَخْلِفْ مِن بَعْدِكُمْ مَا يَشَاءُ كَمَا أَنشَأَكُم مِّن ذُرِّيَّةِ قَوْمٍ آخَرِينَ
"And your Lord is Self-Sufficient, Possessor of Mercy. If He wills, He can cause you to perish and replace you with whomever He wills, just as He produced you from the offspring of other peoples."
interpretation: Although God is independent and full of mercy, His mercy does not annul His sovereign power to give or withdraw worldly standing; human communities and their privileges are contingent on His will. The verse warns against complacency, arrogance, or reliance on lineage, numbers, or past status by reminding people that God can remove a disobedient people and raise another in their stead. Its moral thrust is to cultivate humility, gratitude, and obedience to God, recognizing that temporal continuity and honor are gifts granted or withdrawn by divine wisdom and decree.

translation: Indeed, what you are promised will surely come, and you will not be able to avert it.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute inevitability of God’s promise—primarily the final reckoning—and the impotence of human power to delay, deny, or escape it; its purpose is to warn that temporal strength, plots, or disbelief cannot nullify divine decree, urging recognition of ultimate accountability and a corresponding reorientation of conduct (repentance, justice, and sincere worship).

translation:
قُلْ يَا قَوْمِ اعْمَلُوا عَلَى مَكَانَتِكُمْ ۖ إِنِّي عَامِلٌ ۖ فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ مَن تَكُونُ لَهُ عَاقِبَةُ الدَّارِ ۗ إِنَّهُ لَا يُفْلِحُ الظَّالِمُونَ
“Say, ‘O my people, act according to your station; indeed I am working (too). Soon you will know who will have the final abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.’”
interpretation: The verse teaches that moral exertion and trust in God must go together: each group or individual should do what is within their capacity and proper role, while ultimate judgment and the final outcome belong to God. It is a reassurance that present appearances of power or advantage do not determine eternal success; injustice and oppression are ultimately self-defeating, and those who persist in wrongdoing will not attain lasting felicity.

translation: And they apportioned to Allah out of what He produced of the tillage and the cattle a share, and they said, “This is for Allah” — by their claim — “and this is for our partners.” But that which is for their “partners” does not reach Allah, and that which is for Allah — it reaches their partners. Evil is the judgment they make.
interpretation: The verse condemns a common form of polytheistic hypocrisy: people arbitrarily divide their produce and livestock into portions they claim are for God and portions for their idols or trusted associates, yet their division is vain and unjust. They think by saying “this is for Allah” they have fulfilled a religious duty while actually privileging idols or selfish interests; idols have no power to share in divine rights, and God neither needs nor is bound by such human allocations. By framing a portion as ‘for God’ they often give the best to their worldly partners and the worse to the name of God, or otherwise render their rites meaningless. The passage exposes the contradiction and moral failure of that practice and declares their judgment—using religion to justify such divisions—wrong and blameworthy.

translation: And thus it was made attractive to many of the polytheists — by their partners (their false gods or allies) — to kill their children, in order to turn them away and to confuse their religion. And if Allah had willed, they would not have done it. So leave them and what they invent.
interpretation: The verse warns that polytheism corrodes moral sensibilities so severely that adherents come to justify even infanticide under the influence of their false partners; it affirms Allah’s supreme will (such evil happens only by permitting human choice, not by God’s desire) and instructs the Prophet to disengage from and leave people to their falsehoods and fabrications rather than be consumed by disputation.

translation: And they say, “These are cattle and crops reserved (hajr); none may feed from them except whom we will,” by their claim; and some cattle are forbidden because of their backs; and there are cattle upon which they do not pronounce the name of Allah—an invention they fabricate against Him. He will requite them for what they used to invent.
interpretation: The verse reproves the practice of inventing pseudo‑religious rules to serve personal interests—declaring certain animals or produce ‘set aside’ or forbidden, manipulating rites (e.g., omitting God’s name at sacrifice), and thus ascribing falsehoods to God. Such customs corrupt worship, justify selfish control of resources, and evade moral obligations; the warning is that God will hold those who fabricate and propagate these lies accountable and punish them for their false attributions.

translation: And they say, “What is in the bellies of these animals is reserved exclusively for our males and forbidden to our women.” But if it dies, then they are partners in it. He will surely recompense them for what they have said. Indeed, He is Wise and All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse condemns the human tendency to invent or attribute unjust rules to God in order to preserve male privilege and exclude women; it exposes the hypocrisy and self-interest behind such prohibitions and warns that these fabrications will be judged and requited by God, who understands people’s true motives and acts with perfect wisdom and knowledge.

translation: Indeed, lost are those who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, and who declared unlawful what Allah had provided for them — fabricating a lie against Allah. Truly they have gone astray and were not guided.
interpretation: The verse condemns practices rooted in ignorance and superstition that overturn moral and divine order: attributing false prohibitions to God or inventing religious pretexts to justify violence and to deny God’s provisions reveals spiritual ruin. It teaches that claiming religious sanction for harmful customs (such as depriving others of sustenance or destroying life) is a grave falsehood that severs people from guidance and leads to real, lasting loss; believers must therefore reject such invented traditions, recognize provision and authority as belonging to God, protect the vulnerable (especially children), and ground their rules in true divine guidance rather than ignorance or social habit.

translation: And He is the One who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised, and the date-palms, and crops of different shapes and tastes, and the olive and the pomegranate — alike and unlike. Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest; and do not be wasteful. Indeed He does not love the wasteful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s abundant and varied provision is entrusted to humans not merely for private enjoyment but for responsible stewardship: one may consume from what God has produced, yet must fulfill the moral and social duty to give the rightful share (e.g., charity, due rights at harvest) and must refrain from extravagance. The core lesson is moderation and social justice—appreciation of blessings combined with obligation toward others and avoidance of waste, because God disapproves of those who squander what has been entrusted to them.

translation: And among the cattle are (some) for burden and (some) for slaughter. Eat of what Allah has provided for you and do not follow the footsteps of Satan; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse warns against rejecting or corrupting God’s lawful provision through heedlessness or piety turned into needless restriction. “Do not follow the footsteps of Satan” means refuse the gradual whispers and tactics that lead one to invent prohibitions, indulge desire, waste blessings, or make small compromises that accumulate into disobedience. Recognizing Satan as an obvious enemy calls for vigilance, grateful acceptance of what is permitted, and moderation in using God’s gifts.

translation: Eight pairs — of the sheep two, and of the goats two. Say: “Are the two males forbidden, or the two females? Or is it that their wombs enclose them both? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful.”
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who nitpick the Quran’s brief phrase about creatures being created in “eight pairs.” By posing pointed questions (are the males forbidden, or the females, or do their wombs encompass them both?), God exposes the questioners’ lack of real knowledge and their intent to sow doubt through pedantry. The intended lesson is that ultimate knowledge of creation and its laws belongs to God alone; empty quibbling over technicalities cannot overturn divine speech, and those who claim superior certainty must produce actual, verifiable knowledge rather than raise sophistical objections.

translation: وَمِنَ الْإِبِلِ اثْنَيْنِ وَمِنَ الْبَقَرِ اثْنَيْنِ ۗ قُلْ هَلِ الْذَّكَرَانِ حَرَّمَتْ أَمِ الْأُنْثَيَيْنِ ۖ أَمْ أَلْحَقَ بِهِمَا رَحِمُ الْأُنْثَيَيْنِ ۖ أَمْ كُنتُمْ شُهَدَاءَ إِذْ وَصَّاكُمُ اللَّهُ بِهَٰذَا ۚ فَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنِ افْتَرَىٰ عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا لِيُضِلَّ النَّاسَ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الظَّالِمِينَ
interpretation: The verse condemns those who fabricate religious rules and attribute them to God by clever but empty distinctions (e.g., arguing about ‘the two males’ vs ‘the two females’ or the wombs), showing that such casuistry is a cover for inventing prohibitions without true authority or witness. It indicts the moral gravity of falsely ascribing law to Allah to mislead others—calling it one of the worst injustices—and asserts that God does not guide those who persist in such wrongful innovation.

translation: Say, “I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden for a person who wishes to eat it, except that it be a dead animal, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine—for indeed it is unclean—or that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.”
interpretation: The verse defines specific dietary prohibitions—carrion, flowing blood, pork, and meat sacrificed to other than God—as matters of ritual and moral boundary, while explicitly prioritizing intention and need: when a person is coerced or compelled to consume forbidden things without desire or deliberate transgression, they are not held culpable because divine law balances clear prohibitions with compassion and forgiveness for those acting under necessity.

translation: And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with a claw; and of the cattle and the sheep We forbade to them their fat, except what their backs carry, or the entrails, or that which is mixed with bone. That was because of their transgression, and indeed We are truthful.
interpretation: This verse explains that God, as a response to the Israelites’ disobedience, imposed specific dietary prohibitions on them: broad bans on certain animals and on most of the fats of cattle and sheep, with limited, defined exceptions. The restriction is presented as a punitive, law-bearing measure linked to their wrongdoing, and the closing phrase affirms that this judgment and its stipulations are a truthful, divinely authoritative ruling rather than an arbitrary decree.

translation:
فَإِن كَذَّبُوكَ فَقُلْ رَبُّكُمْ ذُو رَحْمَةٍ وَاسِعَةٍ وَلَا يَرُدُّ بَأْسَهُ عَنِ الْقَوْمِ الْمُجْرِمِينَ
"So if they deny you, say: 'Your Lord is Possessor of vast mercy, yet His punishment will not be turned back from the guilty people.'"
interpretation: The verse teaches a balance between divine compassion and justice: in the face of rejection one should proclaim God’s overwhelming mercy as the primary attribute, yet also affirm that mercy does not erase accountability. It consoles the faithful and instructs the Messenger to respond with trust in God’s benevolence while warning that persistent wrongdoing and obstinate denial place people outside the protection of that mercy and bring just consequences.

translation: سيقول الذين أشركوا: «لو شاء الله ما أشركنا ولا آباؤنا ولا حرمنا من شيء.» كذلك كذب الذين من قبلهم حتى ذاقوا بأسنا. قل: «هل عندكم من علم فتخرجوه لنا؟ إن تتبعون إلا الظن وإن أنتم إلا تخرصون.»
interpretation: The verse exposes the polytheists’ hollow excuse that if God had willed they (and their forebears) would not have committed shirk or forbidden what God permitted. It shows this claim to be mere speculation — the same unfounded reasoning used by earlier peoples who denied the truth until they suffered God’s punishment — and places the burden on them to produce any real knowledge or proof. The underlying message is that invoking a hypothetical divine will cannot absolve people of responsibility: beliefs and actions must be supported by evidence, not by conjecture or self‑serving assertions.

translation: Say, “For Allah is the decisive, overpowering proof; if He had willed, He would have guided you all.”
interpretation: The verse asserts that ultimate proof and authority belong to God alone: He has presented clear, compelling evidence (through revelation and signs) so that no one can claim ignorance as an excuse. Guidance, however, is granted by His will; He could have made everyone accept the truth yet chooses—within His wisdom—to allow human choice and to test hearts. For the Prophet, this relieves any burden of forcing belief: his responsibility is to convey the message, not to compel outcomes. For people, it affirms moral accountability—those who persist in rejection do so despite the decisive proof God has provided, and thus bear responsibility for their refusal.

translation: قُلِ ٱھْلِمْ شُهَدَآءَكُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَشْهَدُونَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ حَرَّمَ هَـٰذَا ۖ فَإِن شَهِدُوا۟ فَلَا تَشْهَدْ مَعَهُمْ ۚ وَلَا تَتَّبِعْ أَهْوَآءَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا۟ بِـَٔايَـٰتِنَا وَٱلَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ وَهُمْ بِرَبِّهِمْ يَعْدِلُونَ
interpretation: The verse establishes two linked moral-legal principles: first, the burden of proof lies with those who accuse — they must produce witnesses if they claim that Allah forbade something; without valid testimony their claim is null and must not be endorsed. Second, believers must not be guided by the desires or social pressures of people whose judgment is corrupted by denial of God’s signs and of the Last Day, and who equate others with their Lord. Practically, this teaches firm reliance on evidence and revealed guidance, refusal to sanction falsehood even under communal pressure, and avoidance of moral conformity to those whose worldview has undermined truth and accountability.

translation: قُلْ تَعَالَوْا أَتْلُ مَا حَرَّمَ رَبُّكُمْ عَلَيْكُمْ: أَلَّا تُشْرِكُوا بِهِ شَيْئًا، وَبِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا، وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا أَوْلَادَكُم مِنْ إِمْلَاقٍ — نَحْنُ نَرْزُقُكُمْ وَإِيَّاهُمْ — وَلَا تَقْرَبُوا الْفَوَاحِشَ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْهَا وَمَا بَطَنَ، وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ. ذَٰلِكُم وَصَّاكُم بِهِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ.
interpretation: This verse presents a concise code of fundamental ethical duties meant to order personal and social life: affirm exclusive devotion to God by rejecting all forms of idolatry; treat parents with kindness and respect as a primary social obligation; protect children’s lives by forbidding infanticide motivated by poverty, coupled with the assurance that provision ultimately comes from God; avoid sexual immorality in both its outward manifestations and inward inclinations; and respect the sanctity of human life, permitting its taking only for a legitimate, just cause (i.e., lawful retribution or due legal right). Together these injunctions emphasize God’s sovereignty, the dignity and protection of vulnerable human beings, sexual and moral purity, and justice in the application of punishment — all given so people may reflect, use reason, and build a moral, stable society.

translation: Do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best way until he reaches maturity. And give full measure and weight in justice. We do not burden any soul except to its capacity. And when you speak, be just—even if [the person] is a near relative. And fulfill the covenant of Allah. That is what He enjoins upon you so that you may remember.
interpretation: The verse binds together a set of ethical duties aimed at protecting human dignity and social balance: guardians must not misuse an orphan’s wealth and must manage it only for the child’s good until maturity; economic transactions require honest weights and measures so the weak are not cheated; divine law recognizes human limits and does not impose impossible burdens; speech and judgment must be impartial even toward kin; and commitments to God must be honoured. Taken together, these injunctions establish a coherent moral principle—restraint out of responsibility and accountability to God—designed to prevent exploitation, preserve trust in social and economic relations, and cultivate justice and mercy in communal life.

translation: And know that this is My straight path; so follow it, and do not follow other ways, for they will scatter you away from His way. That is what He has enjoined upon you so that you may become righteous.
interpretation: The verse asserts that the revealed guidance — Islam’s way of sincere monotheism and the moral-legal teaching brought by the Messenger — is the single straight road to God. Believers are commanded to adhere to it wholly rather than chasing alternative courses born of personal desires, cultural fashions, false doctrines or innovations; such divergent routes fragment communities and pull people away from God’s intended guidance. The injunction is therefore both a call to fidelity to prophetic teaching and a warning against syncretism and division, given so that the community may cultivate God-consciousness (taqwa) and live in accordance with the Divine purpose.

translation: Then We gave Moses the Book in full, completing Our favor upon the one who did right, and as an explanation of everything, and as guidance and mercy, that perhaps they might believe in the meeting with their Lord.
interpretation: The giving of the Scripture to Moses is presented as the culmination of God’s beneficence: it was delivered completely and with detailed clarity so that people would have unmistakable guidance and a merciful framework for living. Its purpose is not merely ritual or law, but to form conviction about ultimate accountability — to lead hearts to believe in the inevitable encounter with their Lord and to orient conduct accordingly; rejection of that clear, detailed guidance therefore amounts to a refusal of the favor meant to awaken faith and moral responsibility.

translation: And this is a Book which We have revealed, blessed — so follow it and be conscious (of Allah), that you may be shown mercy.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur’an as a divinely blessed guide whose benefit depends on human response: only by actively following its teachings and cultivating taqwa (God‑consciousness, reverent obedience) do people open themselves to Allah’s mercy — understood as forgiveness, guidance, and well‑being both spiritually and in life’s affairs — making adherence and inner piety the condition for receiving the Book’s promised blessings.

translation:
فَتَقُولُوا۟ إِنَّمَا أُنۢزِلَ ٱلۡكِتَـٰبُ عَلَىٰ طَآئِفَتَيۡنِ مِّن قَبۡلِنَا وَإِنَّا لَعَنۢدَ دِرَاسَتِهِمۡ لَغَـٰفِلُونَ
"So that you might say, ‘The Book was revealed only to two groups before us, and indeed we were unaware of their study.’"
interpretation: The verse rebukes the tactic of dismissing a current revelation by claiming it concerned only earlier communities and pleading ignorance of prior scriptures. It means people cannot absolve themselves of responsibility by saying revelation was meant solely for others or that they were oblivious to earlier teachings; the admonition is that truth and guidance address every generation, and one must seek and reckon with it rather than use supposed unfamiliarity as an excuse to reject or neglect it.

translation: Or do they say, “If only a Book had been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than they”? But indeed there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord, and guidance and mercy. So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of Allah and turns away from them? We will surely recompense those who turn away from Our signs with a severe punishment for their turning away.
interpretation: The verse confronts a common excuse — claiming one would accept guidance only if a written book were shown — by pointing out that the real gift (clear proof, guidance, and mercy) has already been given. Its thrust is ethical and theological: culpability lies not in the form of revelation but in the heart’s response. Those who knowingly reject or invent falsehood about God’s signs and deliberately avert themselves from them are morally wronged by their own choice; their punishment is presented as the just consequence of persistent, willful refusal rather than a failure of evidence. The passage therefore emphasizes human responsibility for accepting guidance when it is plainly offered and warns that obstinate turning away merits accountable recompense.

translation: Are they waiting for anything other than that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord should come, or that some of the signs of your Lord should come? On the day that some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will profit by its faith if it had not believed before or had not earned good through its faith. Say, “Wait; indeed, we are waiting.”
interpretation: This verse reproaches those who delay or withhold faith until they receive spectacular, unmistakable proofs (angels, the direct coming of God, or visible signs). It warns that when God unleashes decisive signs at the End, a last‑minute profession of belief — unless it grew earlier into genuine faith and righteous deeds — will not avail. The command “Say, ‘Wait; indeed, we are waiting’” expresses the Prophet’s and true believers’ patient resolve: they will not bow to demands for extraordinary signs as a precondition for belief, and they accept God’s timing and judgment, knowing that sincere faith is proved by prior conviction and moral action, not by reaction to final, overwhelming wonders.

translation: Indeed, those who have divided their religion and become sects — you are not (to be) of them in anything. Indeed, their affair is [left] to Allah; then He will inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse absolves the Prophet of responsibility for those who splinter the faith into rival groups and affirms that such fragmentation is a deviation that does not bind the messenger. It emphasizes that judgment over divided communities belongs solely to God, who will disclose and judge their motives and deeds; thus believers are urged to avoid sectarianism, to remain committed to the core guidance entrusted by God, and to leave the final accounting of innovations and divisions to divine justice rather than human endorsement or retaliation.

translation: من جاء بالحسنة فله عشر أمثالها، ومن جاء بالسيئة فلا يجزى إلا مثلها وهم لا يظلمون.
interpretation: الآية تصوغ مبدأ عدل ورحمة إلهيتين في ميزان الأعمال: الخير يُجزى بسخاء (هنا بتسعة عشر ضعف المثل حرفياً عشر أمثال)، بينما السوء يُقابَل بمقداره فقط — مما يظهر أن الجزاء لن يكون مبالغاً في العقاب. عبارة «وهم لا يظلمون» تؤكد أن الحساب عادل ومحايد؛ كل عمل يُؤخذ بحقّه، والله لا يجور في المثوبة أو الجزاء. من ذلك استنتاج تحفيزي عملي: لا تستهِن بصغائر الخير لأن الله يضاعفها، ولا يغرّك اليأس من الذنب لأن العدل الإلهي لا يزيد في العقاب ولا يظلم التائب.

translation: Say, “Indeed my Lord has guided me to a straight path — a sound/established religion — the way of Abraham, upright, and he was not of the polytheists.”
interpretation: The verse asserts that the Prophet’s guidance is not his own invention but God’s gift: a single, uncompromising way that combines correct belief and moral-legal integrity. “Straight path” denotes a clear, divinely marked orientation toward pure monotheism and ethical uprightness; “deen qayyim” signals a complete, balanced system of faith and practice that sustains human life. By invoking Abraham as “hanif,” the text places Islam in direct continuity with his uncompromising monotheism and rejects all forms of idolatry and syncretism — affirming that true religion is both inner conviction and outwardly consistent conduct rooted in God’s guidance.

translation: Say, "Indeed, my prayer, my rites, my life, and my death are for Allah, Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: This is a concise declaration of exclusive devotion: the believer rejects divided loyalties and consecrates not only formal acts of worship but the whole of personal existence and destiny to God alone. By linking ritual practice (nusk) with everyday living and with death, the verse teaches that true worship in Islam is comprehensive—uniting outward rites, inner intention, moral conduct, and acceptance of fate under the single sovereignty of Allah, requiring sincerity, consistency, and relinquishment of competing attachments.

translation: He has no partner; and thus I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims.
interpretation: The verse asserts uncompromising tawḥīd (God’s unique, sole divinity) and frames the Prophet’s mission as obedient example: he affirms that worship belongs to God alone because this is the command he must both submit to and convey, and by calling himself ‘the first of the Muslims’ he exemplifies that true leadership is being foremost in surrender to God’s will. It therefore repudiates any claim to share God’s lordship and places moral and spiritual precedence in humble, active submission rather than in worldly rank.

translation: قُلْ أَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أَبْغِي رَبًّا وَهُوَ رَبُّ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ ۚ وَلَا تَكْسِبُ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ إِلَّا عَلَيْهَا ۚ وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ ۚ ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَيُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ
interpretation: الله وحده هو الربّ الحقيقي والمتصرف في كل موجودات الوجود، فلا يجوز أن يختار المؤمن غيره إلهاً أو رباً. كل نفس مسؤولة عن أعمالها مباشرة؛ لا تُنْقَل ذنوبٌ أو حسناتٌ من إنسان إلى إنسان آخر بحيث يثقل أحدٌ على حساب آخر، فكلٌ سيحصد ما عمل. وفي نهاية الأمر الرجوع كلّه إلى ربّكم فَيُحْكَم بالقسط ويُبَيِّن للناس الحقّ بشأن ما كانوا يختلفون فيه—فالتذكير هنا دعوة للتفكير في حقيقة التوحيد، ولتحمل المسؤولية الفردية، ولترك التبريرات التي تُحمّل الآخرين أو تُسوّي بين المحسن والمسيء.

translation: And He is the One who made you successors upon the earth and raised some of you above others in degrees, to test you in what He has given you. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human life on earth is a delegated stewardship: differing ranks, wealth, or status are not mere accidents but deliberate conditions placed to test moral responsibility. Those who are elevated are charged to exercise justice, generosity and humility rather than arrogance or oppression; those who are less advantaged are tested in patience, trust and upright conduct. The closing clause balances warning and hope: God’s readiness to punish wrong is real and demands seriousness and accountability, yet His forgiveness and mercy remain open to repentance and reform, so the proper posture is both fear of wrongdoing and confident return to God through ethical behavior.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif‑Lam‑Mim‑Sad.
interpretation: The invocation 'Bismillah ar‑Rahman ar‑Rahim' frames what follows as undertaken under God’s authority and compassion, indicating that the message is to be received within the context of divine mercy. The disconnected letters 'Alif‑Lam‑Mim‑Sad' are one of the muqaṭṭaʿāt; their precise meaning is known to God alone, and they function to arrest the listener’s attention, mark the Qur’an’s miraculous and inimitable speech, and humble human certainty before the transcendent source of the revelation.

translation: A Book revealed to you — so let there be no distress in your breast because of it — that you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur’an is a divinely sent scripture and its revelation removes any hesitation or inner burden from the messenger about proclaiming it. His task is to deliver the message — to warn of consequences and to offer a lasting reminder — while guidance and acceptance are ultimately for those who believe; the passage both consoles the messenger and defines his responsibility to present the truth faithfully so that it can awaken, correct, and strengthen the faithful.

translation: Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord, and do not follow guardians (awliyā’) besides Him; little do you remember.
interpretation: The verse demands that the believer make revealed guidance the ultimate criterion for belief and action, rejecting any persons, traditions, desires, or authorities treated as substitute protectors or sources of law. Calling others “awliyā’” besides God is a warning against outsourcing one’s conscience and judgment to leaders, customs, or whims that divert from divine guidance. The final phrase—“little do you remember”—is a rebuke: people habitually neglect this priority, so the verse urges conscious, continual commitment to the revelation as the sole reliable guide and protection against error.

translation: And how many a town have We destroyed — Our punishment came upon it by night or while its people were sleeping.
interpretation: The verse warns that persistent wrongdoing and heedlessness can bring sudden, inevitable divine retribution, often when people feel most secure (by night or in sleep); the destruction of past communities is given as a moral lesson to prompt timely repentance and reform, showing that routine safety or complacency does not shield a people from accountability.

translation: But their supplication when Our punishment came to them was only that they said, "Indeed, we were wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse highlights that many people only acknowledge their wrong and seek forgiveness when confronted with unavoidable punishment; this belated admission, made at the point of no escape, shows the inadequacy of last‑minute remorse and emphasizes the Quranic lesson that sincere, timely repentance and consistent righteousness are required before accountability arrives.

translation:
فَلْنَسْأَلَنَّ الَّذِينَ أُرْسِلَ إِلَيْهِمْ وَلْنَسْأَلَنَّ الْمُرْسَلِينَ
"So let us ask those to whom they were sent, and let us ask the messengers."
interpretation: The verse directs that when assessing claims about revelation or contested matters one should consult the primary, authoritative witnesses — those to whom the message was delivered and the messengers themselves. It urges relying on direct testimony and testimony of prophets rather than on conjecture or secondhand reports, highlighting that truth is best established by questioning those nearest to it.

translation: So We will relate to them [the story] with knowledge; and We were not absent.
interpretation: God promises that He will make clear to people, with complete and exact knowledge, the reality of their deeds and the matters about which they differed. Nothing of their actions, intentions or conversations escaped Him; He was fully present in awareness and witnessing. On the Day of Reckoning He will therefore recount and judge with perfect knowledge and justice, leaving no ambiguity or omission.

translation: And the scales on that Day will be the truth. So whoever's scales are heavy — they are the successful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that on the Day of Judgment God will measure deeds by an objective, infallible standard; those whose record of righteous actions and sincere intentions outweighs their misdeeds (their scales are heavy) will attain true success — salvation and God's pleasure. ‘Weight’ here implies not merely quantity but the authenticity and moral worth of actions, showing that ultimate success depends on sincere obedience, ethical conduct, and inner sincerity rather than worldly rank or appearance.

translation:
وَمَنْ خَفَّتْ مَوَازِينُهُ فَأُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ خَسِرُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ بِمَا كَانُوا بِآيَاتِنَا يَظْلِمُونَ
"And whoever's scales are light — those are the ones who have ruined themselves, because they were unjust toward Our signs."
interpretation: The verse teaches that in the final reckoning people’s deeds are weighed; if a person’s moral account is deficient (‘light scales’), that loss is self-inflicted. The phrase about being unjust to God’s signs points to attitudes and actions — denying, ignoring, corrupting, or failing to respond faithfully to divine guidance — which both diminish one’s righteous deeds and constitute injustice against oneself. In short, neglect or rejection of God’s revelations leads to a scarcity of good deeds and thus to ruin on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We have certainly established you on the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood; little are you grateful.
interpretation: The verse admonishes that the blessings of settled life and provision are granted by God and therefore require genuine gratitude. That gratitude is not mere words but practical: recognizing God through worship, moral obedience, stewardship of the earth, and right use of resources. The common failure to show such thankfulness — manifesting as heedlessness, abuse of provisions, or neglect of duty — undermines the moral purpose of those gifts and invites divine accountability or the withdrawal of blessings.

translation: And We have certainly created you, then We fashioned you; then We said to the angels, “Prostrate to Adam,” so they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not of those who prostrated.
interpretation: The verse affirms that humanity is a deliberate, dignified creation and that God’s command to prostrate to Adam functioned as a defining test: the angels’ obedience contrasts with Iblis’s proud refusal. Iblis’s rejection—rooted in arrogance and willful disobedience—establishes him as the prototype of rebellion and deception, while the episode simultaneously underscores human worth and responsibility: dignity granted by God is not a license to pride but a trust that requires humility and submission to divine guidance.

translation:
قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ إِذْ أَمَرْتُكَ ۖ قَالَ أَنَا خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ خَلَقْتَنِي مِن نَّارٍ وَخَلَقْتَهُ مِن طِينٍ
“He (Allah) said, ‘What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?’ He (Iblis) said, ‘I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay.’”
interpretation: This reply reveals that Iblis’s refusal was driven by arrogance and a false sense of superiority based on origin. By elevating his fiery nature above Adam’s clay, he puts a created distinction above God’s command—showing pride as the root of disobedience. The verse warns that valuing one’s perceived status or nature over submission to divine will leads to rebellion and moral corruption; differences in creation do not justify defiance of God’s explicit orders.

translation: He said, “Get down from it; for it is not for you to be arrogant therein. Get out — indeed you are of the humiliated.”
interpretation: God’s command to expel Iblis illustrates a moral principle: nearness to God, honor, and office are conditional on submission and humility, not on pride or self-exaltation. By refusing obedience, Iblis loses his place and is reduced to humiliation; the verse teaches that arrogance severs one’s standing before God and brings degradation, while true dignity lies in humble obedience to Divine command.

translation: قَالَ أَنظِرْنِي إِلَى يَوْمٍ يُبْعَثُونَ — He said, “Delay me until the Day when they will be resurrected.”
interpretation: The verse depicts the desperate plea of someone at death asking for a reprieve to be returned until the Day of Resurrection. Its meaning is to highlight the futility of such hopes and to teach that this life is the sole arena for accepting guidance; once death comes there is no postponement or second worldly chance, and the certainty of resurrection and accountability makes any request for a delayed return ineffectual.

translation: قال: «إنك من المنظرين» — “He said, ‘Indeed you are among those who grant a respite.’”
interpretation: This describes the person as one who postpones decisive action or judgment—someone who gives others a reprieve or delay, thereby deferring accountability; it criticizes the effect of allowing transgression or expectation to continue by withholding timely resolution.

translation: He said, “Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.”
interpretation: The verse shows Satan’s announced strategy: blaming God for his own fall, he vows to lie in wait along the straight path to mislead people. His method is persistent, covert interception — whispering, tempting, planting doubts, and encouraging distractions and vain pursuits — with the aim of diverting hearts from God's guidance rather than confronting them openly.

translation: Then We will come upon them from before them and from behind them and on their right and on their left; and you will not find most of them grateful.
interpretation: The verse conveys that when divine recompense arrives it will overtake those who have persisted in ingratitude from every direction, because their lack of thankfulness has severed them from perceiving and receiving God's guidance and mercy; thus ingratitude not only forfeits blessings but leaves people vulnerable to being overwhelmed by the consequences of their heedlessness.

translation: He said, “Get out of it, disgraced and driven away. Whoever of them follows you — I will surely fill Hell with you all.”
interpretation: The verse conveys that defiant pride and deliberate disobedience bring decisive exclusion from God’s mercy and a just outcome within the moral order: Satan’s expulsion is both humiliation and a sign that those who freely choose his path will share in that doom. The promise to “fill Hell” stresses the seriousness and inevitability of the consequences for persistent turning away from guidance, serving as a stern warning about the communal and lasting effects of following evil and as an affirmation of God’s sovereign justice.

translation:
وَقُلْنَا يَا آدَمُ اسْكُنْ أَنْتَ وَزَوْجُكَ الْجَنَّةَ فَكُلا مِنْ حَيْثُ شِئْتُمَا وَلا تَقْرَبَا هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةَ فَتَكُونَا مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ
"And We said, ‘O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise; eat from it wherever you will, but do not approach this tree, lest you become of the wrongdoers.’"
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s mercy gives humans ample provision and freedom, yet couples this with clearly defined limits as a test of moral responsibility. The single prohibition is meant to distinguish lawful enjoyment from transgression: obedience preserves the blessings granted, while violating the boundary makes one culpable—‘among the wrongdoers’—by turning freedom into self-harm and injustice. In short, human liberty is meaningful only when exercised within God‑set limits, which cultivate accountability and moral maturity.

translation: فَوَسْوَسَ لَهُمَا الشَّيْطَانُ لِيُبْدِيَ لَهُمَا مَا وُورِيَ عَنْهُمَا مِن سَوْآتِهِمَا وَقَالَ مَا نَهَاكُمَا رَبُّكُمَا عَن هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةِ إِلَّا أَن تَكُونَا مَلَكَيْنِ أَوْ تَكُونَا مِنَ الْخَالِدِينَ
interpretation: The verse illustrates Satan’s method: he manipulates human emotion and reason by exposing vulnerability and offering grand but false promises (becoming angels or immortal) to justify disobedience. Rather than confronting God’s command directly, he stirs shame, curiosity, and ambition so that people doubt divine wisdom and seek status or permanence. The lesson is that temptation often combines emotional provocation with ideological lies, and moral failure comes from yielding to that deception—not from the created thing itself.

translation: And he swore to them, “Indeed, I am to you both of those who give sincere advice.”
interpretation: This phrase reflects the use of an oath to establish trust and to present oneself as acting from genuine concern; its lesson is that true counsel is proven by sincere intention and by consistent, caring conduct toward those advised, not merely by the verbal claim of being well‑intentioned.

translation: So they were both led astray by deception. When they tasted of the tree, their nakedness became apparent to them, and they began to fasten together upon themselves the leaves of Paradise. Then their Lord called to them, "Did I not forbid you that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?"
interpretation: The verse teaches that temptation works through deception: succumbing to it brings an immediate loss of innocence and dignity, prompting attempts to hide and repair the damage. It also shows God’s corrective calling — reminding humans of prior warning and identifying Satan as a manifest enemy — which highlights two poles of the moral situation: human vulnerability and responsibility to heed divine guidance, and the need to recognize and resist Satan’s deceit while turning to God’s guidance and mercy.

translation: They said, “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”
interpretation: This verse exemplifies sincere repentance and the theological truth that human beings cannot reverse the harm of their sins by will alone: one must acknowledge personal wrongdoing, turn humbly to God, and urgently seek His forgiveness and mercy. It teaches that ultimate success depends not merely on human effort but on God’s pardon; without His forgiving mercy a person remains spiritually ruined, so true return to God requires admission of fault, dependence on divine compassion, and trust that mercy, not mere self-justification, is the remedy for loss.

translation:
قَالَ اهْبِطُوا ۖ بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ ۖ وَلَكُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَى حِينٍ
“He said, ‘Descend: some of you will be enemies to others, and for you on earth there is a dwelling-place and provision for a time.’”
interpretation: God’s command to ‘descend’ signals that the earthly life is a temporary, appointed abode where human beings will be given sustenance but also tested. The warning that “some of you will be enemies to others” points especially to the hostile role of Satan and his allies who will seek to mislead human offspring, producing opposition to God’s guidance; as a result human life will be marked by struggle, temptation and conflict. The phrase “a dwelling-place and provision for a time” emphasizes that this worldly existence is transient and instrumental — not the ultimate home — so people must seek God’s guidance and remain conscious of accountability while living amid trials and enmities.

translation:
قَالَ فِيهَا تَحْيَوْنَ وَفِيهَا تَمُوتُونَ وَمِنْهَا تُخْرَجُونَ
He said, “In it you will live, and in it you will die, and from it you will be brought forth.”
interpretation: The statement affirms that life, death and the final re-emergence are entirely governed by God’s will; its purpose is to strip away human self-sufficiency, cultivate humility and accountability, and urge living with awareness of the temporary nature of worldly status so one prepares morally and spiritually for the inevitable resurrection under divine judgment.

translation: O children of Adam, We have bestowed upon you garments to cover your private parts and as adornment; but the garment of piety is best. That is among the signs of Allah, that they may take heed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that while physical clothing serves modesty and social adornment, the superior and most protective 'garment' is taqwa — God-consciousness and moral integrity; inner righteousness preserves dignity and governs behavior more fundamentally than cloth, and this contrast is presented as a sign from God meant to prompt reflection and ethical reform.

translation:
يا بني آدم لا يفتننكم الشيطان كما أخرج أبويكم من الجنة ينزع عنهما لباسهما ليريهما سوآتهما ۗ إنه يراكم هو وقبيله من حيث لا ترونهم ۗ إنا جعلنا الشياطين أولياء للذين لا يؤمنون
“O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he caused your parents to leave the Garden, stripping off their garments to expose to them their private parts. Indeed he and his hosts see you from where you do not see them. Indeed We have made the devils allies to those who do not believe.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that temptation is an ongoing, deceptive strategy aimed at undermining both inner faith and outward moral dignity: Satan operates subtly, together with unseen companions, to normalize shameful acts and sever people’s relation with God. Those who turn away from belief become susceptible to these influences and effectively align themselves with such forces. The practical lesson is vigilance—seeking God’s protection, preserving the ‘garments’ of faith, modesty and obedience, and resisting the social and internal pressures that make sin seem natural or harmless.

translation: And when they commit an indecency they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah commanded us to do it." Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality. Are you inventing about Allah that which you do not know?"
interpretation: The verse rebukes the common human tactic of defending immoral or unjust practices by appealing to ancestral custom and falsely claiming divine approval. It affirms that God cannot be the source of what is morally reprehensible, and it exposes as a grave lie any attribution of such practices to God made without knowledge. The instruction thereby shifts responsibility back to individuals and societies: tradition does not sanctify wrongdoing, and one must measure customs against true divine guidance and conscience rather than hide behind ‘our fathers did it.’

translation: Say, “My Lord has commanded justice; and set your faces toward every mosque, and call upon Him, devoting the religion sincerely to Him — just as He began you, you will return.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that the fundamental duty God requires is justice — fairness in belief, worship and dealings — and calls believers to orient their lives toward God by engaging sincerely in communal and private worship (symbolized by the mosque) without hypocrisy or association of partners. By reminding them that their life began by God’s creative act and will end in return to Him, it ties ethical conduct and pure devotion together: true religion is impartial justice expressed through wholehearted, exclusive worship of God in all places and situations.

translation: Some He guided, and for a group misguidance has become incumbent upon them; indeed they took the devils as allies instead of Allah, and they think that they are rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that ultimate guidance or misguidance rests with God: those who persistently reject truth and cling to false, misleading influences find misguidance settled upon them. By “taking the devils as allies” it characterizes their attachment to deceptive impulses, false leaders, or corrupt ideas that protect and justify their deviation in place of God’s guidance; yet because of self-deception and the flattering counsel of these allies, they mistakenly believe themselves to be rightly guided.

translation: O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but do not be extravagant. Indeed He does not love the extravagant.
interpretation: The verse teaches a balanced ethic: approach worship with dignity and cleanliness (taking appropriate outward adornment when coming to the masjid or to prayer) and lawfully enjoy God’s provisions, while avoiding excess in consumption, display, or spending. ‘Do not be extravagant’ (lā tusrifū) is a moral injunction against wastefulness and extremes—whether in personal consumption, ostentatious dress, or excessive displays of piety—because such excess harms oneself and others and runs counter to God’s will; moderation, respect in worship, and responsible stewardship of blessings are what God loves.

translation: Say, “Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?” Say, “They are for those who believe, in the life of this world exclusively — on the Day of Resurrection.” Thus We make the signs clear for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse challenges those who arbitrarily condemn or prohibit the lawful, beautiful bounties God has provided. It affirms that wholesome adornments and provisions are part of God’s provision for His servants and are intended to be enjoyed lawfully in this life; ultimately, on the Day of Recompense true possession and reward will belong to the believers. The rhetorical question exposes false austerity and illegitimate claims of prohibition, stresses God’s sole authority over what is lawful, and reminds thoughtful people that clear guidance distinguishes legitimate enjoyment from wrongful prohibition.

translation: قُلْ إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ رَبِّيَ الْفَوَاحِشَ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْهَا وَمَا بَطَنَ وَالْإِثْمَ وَالْبَغْيَ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ وَأَنْ تُشْرِكُوا بِاللَّهِ مَا لَمْ يُنَزِّلْ بِهِ سُلْطَانًا وَأَنْ تَقُولُوا عَلَى اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
interpretation: الآية تضبط معايير الشرع والأدب الإلهي بربط الأخلاق بالعلم والحق: تحرم كل قبيح لا يقتصر على المظهر بل يشمل النوايا والميول الباطنة، وتدين الذنب والظلم باعتباره تعدٍ على حقوق الخلق، وتُحذر من اختراع أصول عبادة أو أسانيد شرعية لا أذن الله بها — أي الاعتقاد أو العمل باسم الدين بلا سندٍ إلهي — كما تدين الادعاء على الله بالقول أو الحكم بلا علم. من ذلك يستخلص مبدأان مهمان للممارسة الدينية والاجتماعية: أن الشرع يقيّم النيات والأفعال معاً ويطالب بالعدل، وأن كل تصرف أو عقيدة تُنسب إلى الله يجب أن تقوم على علم وسُلطة شرعية، فلا مكان للتكهنات والاستبداد العقدي أو للادعاءات اللامسؤولة باسم الدين.

translation: For every people there is an appointed term; and when their term arrives they cannot delay it by a single hour, nor can they bring it forward.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Allah determines a precise, fixed term for the life, fate, or reckoning of every people and event; that divine timing is absolute and cannot be altered by any human effort. This doctrine underscores God’s sovereignty, the limits of human power to evade or hasten what has been decreed, and calls people to humility, responsibility, and reliance on God’s wise timing rather than vain attempts to control destiny.

translation: O children of Adam, there will come to you messengers from among you who recite My signs to you; so whoever fears Allah and reforms, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s guidance reaches humanity through human messengers, and that true safety—freedom from divine punishment and inner sorrow—comes from two linked dispositions: taqwa (God‑consciousness and reverent obedience) and islah (active moral and social reform). Those who cultivate reverence for God and correct their own behavior and relationships attain both outward protection and inner peace, a state in which they need not fear judgment nor suffer regret.

translation: And those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejecting God's revealed guidance out of pride is not a merely intellectual error but a moral stance that cuts one off from mercy; “آياتنا” (Our signs) denotes the revelations and clear indications of truth, and “استكبروا عنها” describes an obstinate, haughty refusal to accept them. Such persistent, unrepentant denial rooted in arrogance leads to being designated among the inhabitants of Hell—signifying a lasting consequence for a settled rejection of guidance, unless one abandons pride and returns to submission before it is too late.

translation: Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Those — their portion (of consequence) from the Record has come to them. So when Our messengers come to take them, they will ask, “Where are those you used to invoke besides Allah?” They will answer, “They have failed us,” and they will bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that falsely attributing words or attributes to God, or rejecting His revealed signs, is the gravest injustice and carries inevitable accountability: the record (al‑Kitāb) already contains the consequences of such choices. At the moment of reckoning the delusions and substitutes people trusted will prove powerless, and the very acts of misguidance will testify against their doers. The deeper lesson is moral and existential: claiming or inventing religious authority relieves no one at the last hour, and human responsibility before God is inescapable — one’s beliefs and claims have real consequences, and false deities or invented doctrines cannot intercede for those who knowingly embraced falsehood.

translation: قَالَ ادْخُلُوا فِي أُمَمٍ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِكُم مِّنَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنْسِ ۖ فِي النَّارِ ۖ كُلَّمَا دَخَلَتْ أُمَّةٌ لَّعَنَتْ أُخْتَهَا ۖ حَتَّىٰ إِذَا أَدْرَكُوهَا جَمِيعًا قَالَتْ أَخِرُهُمْ لِأُولَاهُمْ رَبَّنَا هَؤُلَاءِ أَضَلُّونَا فَآَتِهِمْ عَذَابًا ضِعْفًا مِّنَ النَّارِ ۖ قَالَ لِكُلِّ ضِعْفٌ ۖ وَلَـٰكِن لَّا تَعْلَمُونَ
interpretation: الآية تبيّن قضاء الله العادل على مستوى الجماعات: من استمرّوا في الضلال يدخلون النار، وتنكشف فيه سلاسل التأثير والتبعية بين الأمم — فالذين أضلّوا غيرهم يتحمّلون وزر ما نقلوه من ضلال، فيُثاب عليهم بعقوبة مضاعفة باعتبار الضرر الواسع الذي أحدثوه. الحيرة والتشاجر بين الطوائف يوم القيامة لا يغيّران قضاء الله، وعبارة «ولكن لا تعلمون» تذكّر بأن الناس في الدنيا لا يدرون حق قدر وعاقبة تضييع الهداية ولا حجم المسؤولية عن إضلال الآخرين، وأن الجزاء الحقّ موضوع عند الله وحده.

translation: And the earlier ones said to the later ones, “You had no superiority over us; so taste the punishment for what you used to earn.”
interpretation: This verse affirms that on the Day of Reckoning no group will be granted special privilege or exemption: accountability is personal and based solely on one’s deeds. Any claim of precedence, favoritism, or transfer of merit is denied; each person will ‘taste’ the recompense that their own actions have earned, underscoring the absolute justice and individual moral responsibility in divine judgment.

translation: Indeed, those who deny Our signs and are arrogant toward them — the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of a needle. Thus do We recompense the criminals.
interpretation: The verse employs a stark, impossible image to teach that persistent denial of God’s revelations combined with pride closes one off from divine mercy and ultimate reward. ‘Gates of heaven’ stands for access to God’s guidance and favor; the camel‑through‑the‑needle metaphor stresses absolute impossibility rather than a literal event. Calling them ‘criminals’ frames their rejection as moral injustice whose consequences are a just and certain recompense unless they abandon their arrogance and repent.

translation: For them are couches from Hell, and above them coverings; and thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse employs paradoxical imagery—“couches” and “coverings”—to show that the fate of the unjust is total, inescapable engulfment in torment. What sounds like resting-places becomes instruments of punishment: they are laid upon and overlaid by the layers of Hell, emphasizing confinement, suffocation and inescapability.
