The phrase “thus do We recompense the wrongdoers” points to the moral logic: persistent injustice brings a fitting, inevitable retribution from God; apparent worldly advantage for the wrongdoer will be turned into its opposite in the hereafter.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds — We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse teaches a basic principle of divine justice and mercy: God’s demands and judgments are measured to each person’s ability, taking into account their circumstances, knowledge and strength. It reassures the believer that obligations and trials are not oppressive but tailored, so that sincere faith paired with righteous action leads to the ultimate, lasting reward. This principle also shapes moral and legal attitudes toward others—calling for compassion, lenience in judging people’s shortcomings, and hope rather than despair in the face of struggle.

translation: And We removed whatever rancor was in their breasts; rivers flow beneath them. They will say, “Praise be to Allah Who has guided us to this; we would never have been guided had Allah not guided us. Certainly the messengers of our Lord brought the truth.” And they will be called, “Is this not the Paradise which you were made to inherit for what you used to do?”
interpretation: The verse shows that Paradise brings an inner cleansing granted by God: He removes hatred, envy and grudges from the hearts of the believers so that relations there are free from the moral distortions of this life. The inhabitants recognize that their guidance and entry into this state are entirely by divine grace—while their deeds made them eligible—so they respond with humble gratitude and affirm the truth brought by God’s messengers. Thus the verse teaches the balance of God’s mercy (the purifying and guiding action that makes real goodness possible) and human responsibility (acts that earn the inheritance), and it points to the spiritual fruit of guidance: inward peace, mutual goodwill, and thankfulness to God.

translation: And the companions of Paradise called out to the companions of the Fire, “Indeed we have found that which our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found that which your Lord promised you to be true?” They said, “Yes.” Then an announcer proclaimed among them, “The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The verse affirms the certainty of God’s promise and the reality of final accountability: when the divine decree is fulfilled, denial or delay cannot alter outcomes. The scene emphasizes that the believers’ trust is vindicated, while the wrongdoers’ belated admission only confirms the justice of their punishment. The public proclamation of God’s curse underscores both the moral consequences of oppression and the irrevocable nature of the hereafter, serving as a solemn warning that choices in this life carry real, ultimate consequences.

translation: Those who turn people away from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, while they, concerning the Hereafter, are disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who deliberately obstruct or pervert God's path—by corrupting teachings, misleading others, or using influence to bend guidance to their own desires. Such conduct stems from an inner denial or neglect of the Hereafter: because they reject ultimate accountability, they feel free to derail others from the straight course, and so their outward misguidance is an expression of their inward disbelief and moral corruption.

translation: And between them is a partition, and on the Heights are men who will recognize each [person] by their marks. And they will call to the inhabitants of Paradise, “Peace be upon you!” — they have not entered it, though they long for it.
interpretation: The Aʿrâf are understood as an elevated boundary where people whose deeds are closely balanced stand. From that vantage they can discern the true moral character of those on either side by visible signs (their “marks”). Their greeting to the people of Paradise and their yearning to enter express the interplay of hope and accountability: they are not yet admitted despite their longing, showing that ultimate admission is by God’s sovereign judgment and mercy, and that some souls remain suspended between reward and punishment until Allah’s final decision.

translation: And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they will say, "Our Lord, do not make us among the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: The verse teaches that when people see the real outcome of injustice, the righteous will earnestly implore God to be kept away from the company of the oppressors. This plea reflects two truths: that final salvation is ultimately a matter of God’s mercy (so one must humbly seek protection), and that true faith includes a decisive moral stance — a rejection of oppression of others and of one’s own soul — because being counted among the ظالمين (wrongdoers) is the fate believers dread and therefore seek to avoid by repentance, righteous conduct, and reliance on Divine mercy.

translation: And the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying, “What has your assembly availed you, and that you were arrogant?”
interpretation: This verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning worldly alliances, numbers, lineage, and pride are meaningless — no collective status or arrogance can avert divine judgment. True accountability is individual: outward gatherings or social power cannot substitute for inner righteousness, and the realities of one’s deeds become evident to those with insight.

translation: أَهَٰؤُلَٰءِ الَّذِينَ أَقْسَمْتُمْ لَا يَنَالُهُمْ اللَّهُ بِرَحْمَةٍ ۚ ادْخُلُوا الْجَنَّةَ لَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْكُمْ وَلَا أَنْتُمْ تَحْزَنُونَ
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن مشيئة الله ورحمته لا تُقيَّد بأيمان البشر أو أحكامهم؛ الناس قد يحكمون بالنفي والحرمان لكن الله وحده يقرر من ينال رحمته ودخول الجنة، ومن يدخل بعفو الله يُطمئن بلا خوف ولا حزن. العبرة: لا نتعالى في إصدار أحكام نهائية على الآخرين لأن الله أرحم وأعدل من أحكام البشر.

translation: And the companions of the Fire will call to the companions of Paradise, "Pour upon us some water or of what Allah has provided you." They will say, "Indeed, Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the blessings of the Hereafter are allocated according to people's moral choices: those who persisted in disbelief and rejection will find relief denied, not out of arbitrary cruelty but as the fulfillment of divine justice and the consequence of their own decisions. It underscores the finality of the Day of Judgment—once the temporal opportunity for belief and repentance is passed, the distribution of mercy and provision is fixed—serving as a warning to take guidance seriously while there is still time.

translation: Those who took their religion as play and diversion, and whom the life of this world deceived—today We will forget them, as they forgot the meeting of this, their Day; and they used to deny Our signs.
interpretation: The verse warns that treating faith lightly and being seduced by worldly distractions leads to a decisive loss: God will withdraw His favor and leave such people to the consequences of their own neglect. “We will forget them” signifies divine abandonment — removal of guidance, protection, and acceptance — reflecting the moral principle that persistent disregard or denial of God’s signs results in spiritual oblivion and inability to avail oneself of mercy or intercession on the Day of Reckoning, precisely because they themselves ignored and forgot the reality of that meeting while they lived.

translation: And indeed We brought them a Book which We have made clear in detail through knowledge — a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’an is a divinely articulated revelation whose deliberate clarity and measured detail come from God’s comprehensive knowledge; its purpose is not merely information but transformative direction and compassionate support — it corrects error, shapes moral life, heals spiritual brokenness, and opens a path to God for those who accept it in faith.

translation: هل ينظرون إلا تأويله؟ يوم يأتي تأويله يقول الذين نسوه من قبل: قد جاءت رسل ربنا بالحق، فهل لنا من شفعاء فيشفعوا لنا، أو نرد فنعمل غير الذي كنا نعمل؟ قد خسروا أنفسهم وضل عنهم ما كانوا يفترون.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Day of reckoning is unavoidable and that those who ignored or denied God’s messages will then recognize the truth but find their pleas for intercession or a second chance futile; their ruin is self-caused — having trusted in falsehoods and delayed repentance, they lose any benefit from excuses or invented allies, for divine justice responds to deeds, not belated desires.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself upon the Throne. He wraps the night over the day, seeking it swiftly; and the sun, the moon and the stars are subjugated by His command. To Him belongs creation and command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse asserts God's absolute oneness and sovereign governance: the precise alternation of night and day and the obedience of celestial bodies are signs of a single, wise authority who ordains and sustains the universe. “Established on the Throne” denotes the affirmation of His supreme rule and management of affairs, not a physical confinement, and the phrase that creation and command belong to Him emphasizes that all existence and law derive from His will. The intended takeaway is trust in Divine wisdom, recognition that the cosmos manifests purposeful order under God’s administration, and a summons to submit to His authority and praise His perfection.

translation: Call upon your Lord with humility and in private; indeed He does not love the transgressors.
interpretation: God instructs that supplication should be sincere, humble and often made away from ostentation — a private, lowly turning to Him rather than loud display — and pairs this ethic of worship with a moral warning: God does not favor those who exceed bounds by oppressing, wronging others, or behaving arrogantly. The verse teaches that true relationship with God requires both inward humility in prayer and outward restraint in conduct, implying that spiritual petitions are hollow if one persists in injustice or transgression.

translation: And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation, and call upon Him with fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse warns believers not to undo the moral and social order God has restored through guidance and righteous reform — refraining from injustice, exploitation, and destructive behavior once things have been set right. It instructs a balanced spiritual posture toward God: supplicate Him with both fear of His displeasure and hope for His bounty. That balanced reliance is linked to practical conduct: God’s mercy is close to those who practice ihsān — sincere excellence and benevolence in worship and dealings with others — so inner piety must be matched by outward good action to receive divine mercy.

translation: And He is the One who sends the winds as good news announcing His mercy; then when they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and with it We send down water, and thereby bring forth every kind of fruit. Thus We bring forth the dead so that you may take heed.
interpretation: The verse draws a lesson from a natural, observable process: God deploys winds as a means to bring rain that revives lifeless land and produces abundant sustenance. This concrete example serves as an analogy and proof of divine power and wisdom—if God can restore physical life to barren earth by ordinary means He has ordained, He is likewise fully capable of restoring human life after death. The intended effect is to awaken reflection, humility, and readiness to acknowledge God's authority, mercy, and the reality of resurrection.

translation: And the good land brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord; but that which is corrupt does not bring forth except in meagre, distressing fashion. Thus We set forth the signs for a people who are grateful.
interpretation: The verse employs the image of fertile versus barren soil to teach a moral-spiritual law: Allah’s blessings and guidance take root only where hearts and societies are receptive and rightly oriented, and even natural provision depends ultimately on His will. Where moral corruption or spiritual hardness prevails, results will be poor or harmful despite outward effort. By alternating clear signs, abundance and hardship, God distinguishes and trains people so that those who are grateful recognize, preserve and benefit from His favors while ingratitude and corruption yield sterility and loss.

translation: Indeed We sent Noah to his people, and he said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a terrible Day.”
interpretation: The verse emphasizes the prophetic role as a compassionate warning meant to avert collective ruin: calling to exclusive worship of God (tawḥīd) is both a moral summons and a preventative measure, and the prophet’s expressed fear of a “terrible Day” signals that divine justice will ultimately hold communities accountable—so guidance depends not only on the truth of the message but on people’s willing acceptance of it.

translation: قال الملأ من قومه: "إنا لنراك في ضلال مبين" — "The chiefs of his people said, ‘Indeed, we see you to be in manifest error.’"
interpretation: The verse portrays how community leaders instinctively reject and stigmatize a messenger whose message threatens their authority and entrenched beliefs. By calling him 'in manifest error' they are not neutrally assessing evidence but defending their position—their accusation of 'clear misguidance' exposes their moral and intellectual blindness and the social mechanism whereby truth is dismissed out of pride, fear, or vested interest.

translation: He said, “O my people, there is no misguidance in me; rather I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: The speaker emphasizes that his words are not the product of personal error or whim but the transmission of a divinely commissioned office: he affirms his trustworthiness and the objective, sacred origin of his message, thereby confronting those who dismiss him as deluded and holding his audience morally responsible to consider and respond to the guidance he brings.

translation: I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I give sincere counsel to you, and I know from God what you do not know.
interpretation: The speaker grounds his moral and spiritual authority in a divine mandate and in knowledge granted by God; his admonition is not mere personal opinion but guidance informed by insight into realities and consequences beyond ordinary awareness, so accepting his counsel is presented as submitting to God’s will and protection, while rejecting it is portrayed as rejecting a divinely warranted source of truth and care.

translation: Are you astonished that a reminder from your Lord has come to a man among you, to warn you, so that you may be conscious (of Allah) and perhaps be shown mercy?
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who are surprised that divine guidance would be delivered through an ordinary human: the messenger’s humanity does not diminish the revelation’s authority. Its purpose is corrective and formative — to awaken fear of God (taqwa) and thereby open the way to God’s compassion. The proper response is humility and receptivity to the warning, cultivating God‑consciousness so one may earn mercy, rather than rejecting the message because it came by a fallible person.

translation: They denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs; indeed they were a people who were blind.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد مبدأً أخلاقياً وتكوينيًا واحدًا: النجاة والهلاك ليسا محض حدثين ماديين، بل نتيجة لحالة روحية وأخلاقية. إنقاذ المخلصين هنا يعكس رحمة الله ومكافأته لمن استجاب للدلالة والإيمان، بينما إغراق المكذبين يرمز إلى محو نظام اجتماعي قائم على العناد والعمى الأخلاقي — وصفهم بـ«قوماً عمين» ليس وصفًا طبيًا بل إشارة إلى جهل متعمد وحجب للقلب والعقل عن إدراك الحق. من ذلك يستخلص القارئ درسًا تحذيريًا وزاجيًا: التمرد على البينات والتمادي في التكذيب يؤديان إلى الفناء الجماعي، وأما الثبات على الهدي فهو بفضل الله ورحمة منه لا بقدرة بشرية فحسب.

translation: And to 'Aad We sent their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be conscious (of Him)?"
interpretation: The verse underscores that true religion rests on exclusive devotion to God and an inner disposition of taqwa (God‑consciousness). It teaches that no human strength, lineage, or idol can warrant being worshipped, and that communal wellbeing depends on humble submission to divine authority; pride and power cannot excuse turning away from God, and failing to cultivate fear/reverence of Him leads a people toward moral ruin and divine accountability.

translation:
قال الملأ الذين كفروا من قومه: «إنا لنراك في سفاهةٍ وإنا لنظنك من الكاذبين».
"The chiefs among those who disbelieved of his people said, 'We see you in clear folly, and indeed we regard you as one of the liars.'"
interpretation: The verse exposes a common social reaction: powerful opponents, seeking to protect their status and avoid accountability, dismiss a truthful caller by attacking his character—branding him foolish and a liar—rather than addressing the substance of his message. Such denunciations are defensive tactics that reveal arrogance and moral resistance, not proof against the truth; the passage therefore warns the sincere to judge by evidence and character, not by the loud condemnations of entrenched interests.

translation: قال: "يا قومي، ليس بي سفاهةٌ؛ ولكني رسولٌ من ربِّ العالمين."
interpretation: العبارة تؤكّد أن دعوى النبوة ليست حالة نفسية أو طيشًا بل مهمة مُنَزَّهَة عن السفه والدوافع الذاتية، وأن مصدرها سلطة برّانية تتجاوز المصالح القَبَليّة والآراء البشرية. إن نفي السفه مع تأكيد الرسالة من «ربِّ العالمين» يطالب السامعين بتمحيص الحُجج والأخلاق والنتائج لا بهتافات الرفض: الحكم على المرسل يجب أن يكون بقيمة دعوته وأدلتها ومظهرها الأخلاقي، لأن الحق يأتي من سلطةٍ كونيةٍ ورؤيا شاملة تتخطى حدود الأهواء.

translation: I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am for you a sincere, trustworthy advisor.
interpretation: The speaker (a messenger) is asserting his integrity: he faithfully transmits God’s revelations without distortion or personal agenda and seeks only the good of his people. By calling himself “ناصح أمين,” he emphasizes both moral sincerity (seeking others’ welfare) and reliability (preserving and delivering the message accurately), inviting listeners to trust the guidance because it comes from someone whose intention and conduct are upright.

translation: Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you? And remember when He made you inheritors after the people of Noah and increased you in stature in creation. So remember the favors of Allah, that you may prosper.
interpretation: The verse reproves those who are astonished that guidance and warning should arrive by means of one of their own: a prophet raised from among them. It reminds them that divine generosity has already placed them in privileged positions—made them heirs after earlier peoples and bestowed upon them ease, capacity, and multiplied means in creation—and therefore acceptance of the reminder and gratitude are required. Remembering Allah’s favors is presented not as mere sentiment but as the moral obligation that grounds true success: to acknowledge God’s gifts, respond to the messenger’s warning, and live responsibly so those favors do not become occasions for ingratitude and ruin.

translation: They said, “Have you come to us so that we may worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you promise, if you are among the truthful.”
interpretation: The verse highlights a recurrent human posture of resisting transformative guidance by clinging to inherited customs and demanding spectacular proof or promised consequences before accepting change; it exposes a mindset that makes faith conditional on external demonstrations rather than sincere inward conviction.

translation: He said, "A scourge and wrath from your Lord has indeed come upon you. Are you disputing with me about names that you and your fathers have given — for which Allah has sent down no authority? So wait; indeed I am with you among those who wait."
interpretation: The speaker refuses to be drawn into petty disputes over human-made labels and traditions that have no sanction from God, warning that divine punishment and anger have already come upon the people; rather than contest their invented terms, he entrusts the matter to God's judgment, adopts patient forbearance, and stands as a witness who will await the inevitable outcome of God's decree.

translation:
فأنجيناه والذين معه برحمة منا وقطعنا دابر الذين كذبوا بآياتنا ۖ وما كانوا مؤمنين
“So We saved him and those with him by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the remnant of those who denied Our signs; and they were not believers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that deliverance is ultimately by God’s mercy, not by human means: prophets and sincere followers are preserved by divine compassion, while the apparent strength or continuity of those who reject God’s signs is severed by God’s judgment. The phrase “قطعنا دابر” indicates the ending of their power and legacy, and “ما كانوا مؤمنين” explains that their outward position or temporary success did not amount to true faith—hence their ruin. The passage therefore comforts the faithful that genuine belief determines final destiny and warns that persistent denial leads to decisive divine retribution.

translation: And to Thamud We sent their brother Salih. He said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has come to you a clear proof from your Lord. This is the she-camel of Allah — a sign for you. So let her graze in Allah’s earth and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God sent a prophet with an unmistakable miracle (the she‑camel) as both confirmation of his mission and a test of the people’s obedience. Salih’s message affirms God’s exclusive sovereignty and commands respect for what God has set apart; harming the camel would not be merely an offense against an animal but a deliberate rejection of divine authority and of clear evidence, thereby inviting severe divine retribution. In short, the miracle functions to expose whether a community will acknowledge God’s signs and abide by limits He prescribes or will transgress and bring ruin upon itself.

translation: And remember when He made you successors after the ʻĀd and settled you in the earth so that you might build palaces in its plains and carve houses out of the mountains. So remember the favors of Allah and do not spread corruption on the earth.
interpretation: The verse reminds a people that their social position, comfortable settlement, and technical ability to build are not merely their own achievements but trusts (khilāfah) granted by God. Being God’s vicegerents on earth carries the duty of grateful remembrance — recognizing divine gifts in conduct and worship — and the moral obligation to use resources, power and knowledge without transgressing: not to become arrogant, oppress others, exploit the land, or cause social or environmental corruption. Prosperity, therefore, is presented as a test that requires humility, justice and responsible stewardship rather than license to spread mischief.

translation: The chiefs among his people, those who were arrogant, said to those whom they considered weak, "Do you know that Salih has been sent by his Lord?" They said, "Indeed, we are believers in what he has been sent with."
interpretation: The verse exposes a power dynamic: proud leaders pose a rhetorical, shaming question to pressure and isolate the humble, treating belief as a mark of foolishness, while the weak answer with sincere conviction. It teaches that true faith often resides with the lowly and is not determined by social status or public opinion, and it condemns the use of prestige and intimidation to suppress guidance and truth.

translation: قال الذين استكبروا: «إنا بالذي آمنتم به كافرون» — "Those who were arrogant said, 'Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed.'"
interpretation: The verse depicts the stance of proud, obstinate people who, driven by arrogance and refusal to submit, openly renounce the faith of others; their denial stems not from sincere inquiry but from pride and hostility, illustrating how arrogance hardens the heart against guidance and motivates rejection of truth out of spite rather than conviction.

translation: So they hamstrung the she-camel and acted insolently toward the command of their Lord, and said, “O Ṣāliḥ, bring upon us what you threaten us with, if you should be of the messengers.”
interpretation: The verse illustrates a deliberate, defiant rejection of God’s sign: by maiming the miraculous camel they not only violated a divine ordinance but also mocked the messenger, demanding the threatened punishment as if to test or trap him. Their act represents moral arrogance and vested-interest resistance to truth—destroying a clear sign when it conflicts with their desires or authority—and serves as a warning that such willful contempt for divine guidance inevitably leads to ruin.

translation: So the convulsion seized them, and they awoke in their homes crouching.
interpretation: The verse warns that when divine retribution arrives it can come suddenly and utterly overwhelm those who felt secure in their dwellings; their presumed safety is abolished, leaving them humiliated, powerless, and on their knees—a reminder of the fragility of worldly refuge and the consequences of ignoring warning and accountability.

translation: So he turned away from them and said, “O my people, indeed I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you sincerely, but you do not love those who give sincere advice.”
interpretation: The speaker is affirming that he has done his duty—faithfully delivering God’s revelation and offering heartfelt counsel—but recognizes that people may reject guidance not because it lacks truth but because they are unwilling to be admonished; the verse stresses the moral responsibility to convey truth and counsel while accepting that acceptance lies with the listeners, whose resistance often stems from pride, attachment to their ways, or dislike of correction.

translation: And [mention] Lot when he said to his people, “Do you commit indecency such as none among the worlds has committed before you?”
interpretation: The verse is a prophetic rebuke that condemns the people’s deliberate, public pursuit of a grave, unprecedented immorality. It emphasizes that their behavior was not a private failing but a conscious, transgressive abandonment of the moral order—so exceptional in its perversity that it merits special condemnation—and implies that such arrogant persistence in clear wrongdoing invites divine judgment.

translation: Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are an excessive (transgressing) people.
interpretation: The verse condemns the practice of pursuing sexual relations with men in place of women as an expression of illicit desire; it portrays such conduct not merely as a private preference but as a moral transgression that exceeds the bounds set by God, disrupting the intended social and moral order and warranting strong reproach.

translation:
وما كان جواب قومه إلا أن قالوا أخرجوهم من قريتكم ۖ إنهم أناس يتطهرون
"And the reply of his people was only, ‘Expel them from your town; indeed they are people who purify themselves.’"
interpretation: The verse portrays how a community rejects callers to reform by labeling them as separatist or self-righteous; calling them “people who purify themselves” is a pejorative meant to mark them as outsiders who set themselves apart (ritually or morally), thereby justifying their expulsion. It highlights the social mechanism of stigmatizing moral reformers—framing their commitment to purity as a threat to communal norms so the community can avoid engaging with their message.

translation: So We saved him and his family — all of them — except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.
interpretation: The verse teaches that familial relation to a prophet does not secure salvation: Noah’s wife, though closely related, was excluded because she persisted in disbelief or hypocrisy. ‘Those who remained behind’ denotes those who rejected guidance and so were left to divine judgment; the decisive criterion for deliverance is sincere faith and obedience, not kinship or proximity to a righteous person.

translation: And We rained upon them rain; so observe how was the end of the criminals.
interpretation: The verse serves as a warning that persistent, conscious wrongdoing and rejection of guidance do not go unaddressed: the ‘‘rain’’ symbolizes a sudden, overwhelming divine response brought upon those who persisted in injustice, and the command to “observe” invites reflection on these historical outcomes as proof that moral transgression has real, inevitable consequences — a lesson to abandon arrogance and heed guidance before it is too late.

translation: And to Madyan (We sent) their brother Shu‘ayb. He said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord. So give full measure and full weight, and do not deprive people of their due, and do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set right. That is better for you, if you are believers.”
interpretation: This verse presents Shu‘ayb’s message as a unity of faith and practice: true belief in the one God must be demonstrated by upright social and economic conduct. The “clear proof” legitimizes his call, and the specific commands—honest measures and weights, giving people their rights, and refraining from corrupting a previously orderly society—make belief concrete and communal rather than merely private. The warning not to “spoil the earth after its reform” implies that divine blessings and social stability can be undone by greed, fraud, and injustice; therefore obedience to God and integrity in daily dealings is not only morally required but also pragmatically beneficial for the whole community, a sign of authentic iman (faith).

translation: And do not station yourselves on every path by which you might prevent and turn away from the way of Allah those who believe in Him, seeking to make it crooked. And remember when you were few and He increased you; and see how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: The verse condemns the behavior of those who set themselves up as obstacles to guidance—deliberately blocking, diverting, or distorting the path of God so that believers are led astray. It warns against using influence, positions, or rhetoric to make the straight way seem crooked, and reminds such people of their humble origins and of God’s power to increase or diminish communities. The moral is: do not arrogantly monopolize or pervert guidance for your own ends; remain humble, refrain from obstructing others’ access to truth, and heed the example of past corrupters whose schemes brought them ruin.

translation: And if a party of you believe in what I was sent with and a party do not believe, then be patient until Allah judges between us; and He is the best of judges.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet and the believers to exercise restraint when the community is divided over the message: rather than forcing a verdict, exacting immediate punishment, or breaking fellowship, they are to wait for God’s adjudication. It underlines that ultimate vindication and justice belong to Allah alone, so believers should practice patience, avoid rash reprisals, and trust God’s perfect judgment and timing.

translation: قالَ المَلأُ الَّذين استَكْبَروا مِن قَومِهِ: «لَنُخرِجَنَّكَ يا شُعَيْبُ وَالَّذينَ آمَنوا مَعَكَ مِن قَرْيَتِنا، أَوْ لَتَعودُنَّ في مِلَّتِنا»؛ قالَ: «أَوْلو كُنّا كارِهِينَ»
interpretation: الآية تصوّر صمود شُعيب وقوة موقفه أمام تهديد زعماء قومه الذين استكبروا: لقد عرضوا عليه خيارين قسريين — إما الطرد من بلدهم أو الرجوع إلى عقائدهم — فكان ردُّه رفض الخضوع حتى لو كان مبغوضاً عليه (أي حتى لو اضطرّ إلى الأمر وكان ذلك مُكْرَهًا عليه). هذا يعبّر عن مبدأ أن الحق والرشد لا يُسلَّم به لِضغوط السلطة أو المجتمع، وأن المؤمن الصادق يفضل الثبات على الحق وتحمل الطرد والشدائد على أن يتخلى عن رسالته أو يزاوج بين الحق والباطل إرضاءً للمتكبرين.

translation: We would indeed have fabricated against Allah a lie if we were to return to your way after Allah has saved us from it. And we would never return to it except that Allah, our Lord, wills. Our Lord’s knowledge encompasses all things. Upon Allah do we rely. Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who decide.
interpretation: The speaker declares a principled, faith‑driven refusal to revert to the people’s false practice after being delivered—such a return would be a falsehood against God. He affirms that guidance and outcomes are subject only to God’s will and knowledge, places full trust in God’s providence, and asks God to render a just, decisive judgment between them and their people; thus the plea combines steadfastness, reliance on divine sovereignty, and an appeal to God as the ultimate arbiter and source of true victory.

translation:
وَقَالَ الْمَلَأُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ قَوْمِهِ لَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتُم شُعَيْبًا إِنَّكُمْ إِذًا لَخَاسِرُونَ
“And the prominent among those who disbelieved of his people said, ‘If you follow Shu‘ayb, then indeed you will surely be among the losers.’”
interpretation: The verse exposes how self-interested leaders oppose moral reform by framing obedience to a prophet as social and economic ruin; their warning reflects fear of losing wealth, status, and corrupt advantages, not an honest judgment of truth, and shows how vested interests use intimidation to preserve injustice.

translation: So the convulsion seized them, and they lay prostrate in their homes.
interpretation: The verse warns that when a people persist in denying the truth, divine punishment can overtake them suddenly and decisively in the very safety of their homes; it teaches that worldly security and delay in responding to clear warning do not protect one from God’s swift retribution, so one must heed the messenger and repent before destruction arrives.

translation: الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا شُعَيْبًا كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنُوا فِيهَا ۚ الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا شُعَيْبًا كَانُوا هُمْ الْخَاسِرِينَ
interpretation: من أنكروا دعوة شعيب ورفضوا هدايته أُبْطِلَتْ عليهم مصالحهم ودُرِّسَتْ منافعهم؛ ما ظنوا أنه انتفع بهم باطل عند العقاب الإلهي فكانوا خاسرين فعلًا — خسارة مادية حين فُقِدَت النِّعَم ومجتمعية حين انتهى وجودهم، وخسارة أخروية بالحرمان من رحمة الله ونتيجته الأزلية.

translation:
فَتَوَلَّى عَنْهُمْ وَقَالَ يَا قَوْمِ لَقَدْ أَبْلَغْتُكُمْ رَسَالاتِ رَبِّي وَنَصَحْتُ لَكُمْ ۖ فَكَيْفَ أَسَىٰ عَلَىٰ قَوْمٍ كَافِرِينَ
“So he turned away from them and said, ‘O my people, I have indeed delivered to you the messages of my Lord and have given you sincere counsel; so how should I grieve for a people who are disbelievers?’”
interpretation: The speaker affirms that once he has faithfully fulfilled his duty—conveying God’s revelations and offering honest advice—his moral responsibility is complete; he must not be overwhelmed by sorrow over those who deliberately reject the truth. This expresses the prophetic stance of compassionate duty combined with resigned trust in God’s judgement: guidance is to be offered sincerely, but acceptance or rejection rests with people and their hearts, not on the messenger.

translation: We did not send a prophet to any town but We afflicted its people with hardship and adversity, so that perhaps they might humble themselves (and supplicate).
interpretation: This verse explains a recurring divine method in prophetic history: when communities persist in heedlessness or rejection, God permits trials and hardships to befall them not merely as retribution but as a corrective, purifying measure intended to jolt hearts into humility, sincere supplication, and return to God. Such afflictions test and expose true faith, provide an opportunity for repentance and reform, and — if taken to heart — serve as a means of mercy; if ignored, they may be followed by sterner consequences.

translation: Then We replaced the bad with good for a time, until they desisted; and they said, “Our fathers were touched by hardship and ease.” So We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God may lift a punishment and grant relief or blessings as a temporary respite and test, not as an unconditional pardon. Such reprieve is intended to reveal whether people will turn to God and amend their ways or persist in heedlessness. Relying on ancestral precedent—claiming that one’s forebears experienced both hardship and prosperity and therefore one is excused—is a false justification; it reflects stubbornness rather than genuine guidance. Consequently, when heedlessness continues, the apparent ease can be withdrawn abruptly and a people may be overtaken by sudden punishment while they remain unaware. The passage warns that fluctuations in worldly condition are not proof of divine approval and that responsibility before God cannot be evaded by citing one’s lineage or history.

translation: وَلَوْ أَنَّ أَهْلَ الْقُرَىٰ آمَنُوا وَاتَّقَوْا ل_fَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِم بَرَكَاتٍ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَلَـٰكِن كَذَّبُوا فَأَخَذْنَاهُم بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine blessing and societal flourishing are linked to collective faith and God-conscious behavior: when a community embraces belief and piety, God opens for it both material and spiritual favors, but persistent rejection of guidance and continued sinful conduct lead to blessings being withheld and to accountability — consequences that correspond to the community's own deeds.

translation: Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them overnight while they are asleep?
interpretation: The verse warns against communal complacency and the illusion of invulnerability: entire communities that live in comfort and disregard God’s guidance may suddenly be overtaken by divine retribution without warning, even at night when they are unaware. It calls for humility, vigilance, and moral reform, reminding people that worldly security is not proof of divine favor and that consequences can arrive unexpectedly for heedlessness and persistent wrongdoing.

translation:
أَوْ أَمِنَ أَهْلُ الْقُرَىٰ أَنْ يَأْتِيهِمْ بَأْسُنَا ضُحًى وَهُمْ لَا يَلْعَبُونَ
“Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the forenoon while they are at play?”
interpretation: The verse warns against complacent security derived from worldly comfort and distraction: communities who ignore God's guidance and indulge in heedless amusements may be struck suddenly and unexpectedly. “ضحى” (forenoon) stresses the swiftness and unanticipated timing of divine retribution, and “يلعبون” (playing) symbolizes moral negligence and preoccupation with trivial pleasures instead of repentance, justice, and the prophetic call. The lesson is ethical and practical: temporal ease does not guarantee immunity from accountability; believers must remain conscious, humble, and ready to correct their course rather than assuming safety because they are comfortable or busy with leisure.

translation: Do they then feel secure from the plan (makk) of Allah? No one is secure from the plan of Allah except the people who are losers.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who presume they can escape or outwit divine retribution are deluding themselves. “Makk” here denotes Allah’s decisive scheme or intervention that overturns the arrogance, plots, and apparent triumphs of wrongdoers. Only the truly foolish or spiritually ruined — the ‘losing’ people who are heedless, proud, and reject guidance — would imagine they are safe; their sense of security is itself a sign of ultimate loss, for God’s plan to establish justice will overtake those who oppose Him.

translation: Has it not been made clear to those who inherit the earth after its people that, if We willed, We could surely strike them for their sins, and seal their hearts so that they do not hear?
interpretation: The verse warns that occupying the land after former peoples does not guarantee immunity from God’s judgment: He could punish successors for the same sins and cause a spiritual shutting—‘sealing’ of the heart—so they no longer receive or respond to guidance. What appears as continued prosperity is therefore conditional and temporary; persistent rejection of truth brings a divinely‑wrought hardness of heart as a consequence, not mere arbitrary whim, calling for humility, vigilance, and moral responsibility.

translation: Those towns — We recount to you some of their stories. And indeed their messengers came to them with clear proofs, yet they would not believe in what they had previously denied. Thus Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse explains that when communities repeatedly reject the clear signs and messengers sent to them, their persistent refusal becomes a moral and spiritual hardening: God ‘seals’ their hearts not as an arbitrary punishment imposed first, but as the consequence of their own consistent denial. The sealing signifies that guidance is withdrawn and their receptivity to truth is progressively blocked, leaving them entrenched in disbelief and blind to the very proofs they once rejected.

translation: And We did not find for most of them any covenant; indeed We found most of them to be transgressors.
interpretation: The verse conveys that when God inspected the moral and spiritual state of people, He found that the majority had not honored the covenant incumbent upon them—whether the primordial pledge to recognize and serve God or the obligations tied to prophetic guidance and moral duties. Their failure to keep this covenant shows itself in persistent disobedience and immoral conduct; hence they are called fāsiqīn (those who break bounds). The passage warns that mere affiliation or profession is insufficient: fidelity to the covenant—manifested in righteous conduct, truthfulness, and obedience to God’s guidance—is the measure that prevents communities from falling into widespread transgression.

translation: Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they were unjust toward them. So observe how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God repeatedly sends clear guidance and signs through His messengers, yet powerful leaders who benefit from oppression often reject and mistreat that guidance; such rejection is not a mere difference of opinion but active corruption and injustice. The downfall of Pharaoh and his circle is presented as a moral and historical example: those who persist in denying truth, suppressing the weak, and spreading corruption will ultimately face divine consequences. The passage thus warns contemporaries to avoid following tyrants and corrupters and invites reflection on the inevitability of justice and the protection promised to the oppressed.

translation: And Moses said, “O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: Moses is directly confronting Pharaoh and grounding his authority not in human power but in a divine commission. By calling himself a “messenger” he asserts that his words and demands come from God, and by naming God “the Lord of the worlds” he emphasizes the Creator’s universal sovereignty over all beings and realms—thus challenging Pharaoh’s claim to absolute rule and calling him to recognize and submit to God’s authority.

translation: حَقيقٌ علىَّ أن لا أقول على الله إلا الحقّ؛ قد جئتكم ببينةٍ من ربّكم فَأرسِلْ مَعي بَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أمانة النبي في نقل الوحي ووجوب التمسك بالصدق في شأن الله حتى أمام السلطة الظالمة، وتبيّن أن العلامات والبينات الإلهية تعمل كتصديق للرسالة وتمنح الحقّ بالمطالبة بالحرية والإنصاف لقضية المضطهدين؛ بمعنى أعمّ، أن الوحي يفرض على رسل الله الصدق والمطالبة بالعدل، ولا يقبل التهوين أو التحريف بدافع الخوف أو المصلحة.

translation: قال: «إن كنت جئت بآية فأت بها إن كنت من الصادقين»
interpretation: هذه عبارة تحدٍّ من جانب من يكذب الرسول، تدل على ميل كثيرين إلى مطالبة بآياتٍ ظاهرة كشرط للاعتراف بالرسالة، وتبيّن أن المطلوب منهم ليس برهانًا علميًا محايدًا بل فخٌ لردّ الرسالة؛ كما تذكّر أن قبول النبوة لا يعتمد فقط على العروض العجائبية بل على علامات الثبات والصدق في القول والعمل، وأن الآيات تُعطى بقدر الله لا لتحقيق نزوات المشككين.

translation:
فَأَلْقَى عَصَهُ فَإِذَا هِيَ ثُعْبَانٌ مُّبِينٌ
So he cast down his staff, and behold, it became a clear/manifest serpent.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that by God's will the ordinary can be turned into an unmistakable sign: the staff’s transformation into a “manifest serpent” functions to authenticate Moses’ mission and to confront proud, unbelieving authority. It teaches that divine power supersedes human appearances and argumentation, presenting an obvious, undeniable phenomenon so people cannot just dismiss the truth on grounds of rhetoric or status.

translation: And he drew out his hand; behold, it was white to the onlookers.
interpretation: The verse relates a miraculous sign granted to Moses: when he revealed his hand it became strikingly white or luminous for those watching, a clear supernatural manifestation intended to authenticate his prophetic mission and to overpower the deceptions of the magicians. The whiteness signifies an unmistakable, divinely caused transformation — not an ordinary ailment — meant to convince witnesses of God’s power and to distinguish true revelation from mere trickery.

translation: The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people said, “Indeed, this is a skilled/knowledgeable magician.”
interpretation: The verse highlights how rulers and elite groups, when faced with unmistakable signs, may admit the competence behind them yet refuse their truth by labeling them as sorcery; calling him “a skilled magician” both concedes the apparent power and provides a pretext to dismiss the divine source, protecting the elites’ authority and avoiding moral accountability.

translation: He intends to drive you out of your land; so what do you command?
interpretation: The verse exposes an adversary’s aim to expel the community and, by asking a pointed question, urges the believers to deliberate and determine a deliberate response. It calls for collective counsel and decisive, principled action—whether that means firm defense of one’s rights, seeking lawful refuge, changing alliances, or relying on God—rather than passive submission; the emphasis is on responsibility, unity, and wise resolve when faced with aggression.

translation: قالوا: «أرْجِهِ وأَخاهُ وأرسِل في المدائنِ حاشِرين» — They said, “Turn him back along with his brother, and send into the towns people to summon/assemble (the populace).”
interpretation: The verse depicts opponents who refuse the message and try to silence it by removing its bearer and mobilizing others to rally against him; it illustrates a common hostile tactic—expelling inconvenient truth and calling the community to suppress or reject guidance rather than engaging with its content.

translation: They will bring to you every skilled magician.
interpretation: The phrase signifies that opponents will marshal their most practiced deceivers—experienced magicians or rhetoricians—to confront the messenger, relying on craft and apparent know‑how to dazzle and mislead people; it warns that expertise in trickery or eloquence does not make a falsehood true and that such artifice will ultimately be judged against the reality of the message.

translation: And the magicians came to Pharaoh and said, "Indeed, we will have a reward if we are the ones who prevail."
interpretation: This verse highlights a moral dynamic: people often bind their allegiance to whoever promises benefit or prestige, placing material gain and social standing above truth and justice. Such contingent, mercenary loyalty reveals spiritual weakness and willingness to compromise principles for reward — a human tendency that is exposed and judged in moments of public trial.

translation: He said, “Yes; and indeed you are among the near [ones].”
interpretation: This is an affirmative declaration granting the addressed a sure rank of intimate proximity to God. The term “المقربين” does not merely mean physical closeness but denotes a spiritual status: those specially favored, elevated and admitted to God’s presence and mercy because of faith, obedience and sacrifice. The phrase stresses certainty (إنكم) and privilege (لمن المقربين), assuring the believers that they will be counted among the elect who enjoy nearness, honor and fellowship with the Divine.

translation: قالوا: "يا موسى إما أن تلقي وإما أن نكون نحن الملقين" — "They said, ‘O Moses, either you throw [first], or we will be the ones to throw.’"
interpretation: The verse reveals the challengers’ attempt to control the terms of confrontation: through insistence on sequencing they expose a strategy of arrogance and manipulation, seeking to frame the contest so they can imitate or respond and thus defend their authority rather than submit to evidence of a higher truth.

translation:
قَالَ أَلْقُوا ۖ فَلَمَّا أَلْقَوْا سَحَرُوا أَعْيُنَ النَّاسِ وَاسْتَرْهِبُوهُمْ وَجَاءُوا بِسِحْرٍ عَظِيمٍ
“He said, ‘Cast down.’ So when they cast down, they bewitched the eyes of the people, terrified them, and brought forth a mighty magic.”
interpretation: The verse points to a common mechanism of deception: powerful showmanship that manipulatively targets people’s senses and emotions. The phrase “they bewitched the eyes of the people” signifies deliberate creation of an overwhelming sensory illusion that makes falsehood appear real; “they terrified them” shows the companion tactic of intimidation to silence doubt; and “a mighty magic” denotes a spectacular performance designed to win popular assent by appearance alone. The lesson is moral and epistemic: do not let dazzling displays or fear determine what you accept as true—discernment, reason, and attention to genuine signs (and ultimately God’s judgment) are needed to see through impressive but deceptive outward forms.

translation: And We revealed to Moses, “Cast down your staff.” And behold, it swallowed up what they were fabricating.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when God empowers His messenger, the ordinary is made into a clear sign that decisively nullifies human deceit; miracles function as divine confirmation of truth and expose the futility of contrived falsehoods against God’s will.

translation:
فوقع الحق وبطل ما كانوا يعملون
"Then the truth came to pass, and what they were doing was rendered void."
interpretation: When divine truth is made manifest and established, any practices, arguments or deeds grounded in falsehood lose their validity and efficacy; actions that rest on error or denial of God's guidance carry no standing before God, so those actors’ works are nullified despite their effort.

translation: So they were defeated there and returned humiliated.
interpretation: The verse signifies that those who opposed the truth were overpowered at that place and forced to withdraw in disgrace; it underscores that divine support frustrates the plots of the arrogant, and that apparent worldly strength without justice or faith ultimately leads to dishonor.

translation: And the magicians fell down prostrate.
interpretation: Upon witnessing the unmistakable miracle shown by Moses, the magicians were moved to immediate submission: they abandoned their sorcery, acknowledged the truth and the Lordship of Allah, and physically prostrated as an act of sincere belief and repentance — a demonstration that clear divine signs can overturn prior deception and compel people to recognize and submit to the truth even at great personal risk.

translation: قالوا: "آمنا بربِّ العالَمينَ" — "They said, 'We believe in the Lord of the Worlds.'"
interpretation: A concise profession of faith affirming God’s exclusive sovereignty and lordship over all realms and creatures; it expresses wholehearted acceptance of divine authority and guidance, recognizing that true belief entails submission to the Creator who governs and sustains all that exists.

translation: The Lord of Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This phrase affirms that the same one God is sovereign over both Moses and Aaron, emphasizing the unity and continuity of divine authority and mission—showing that their prophetic roles, guidance, and support come from the one Lord rather than separate or competing powers.

translation: Pharaoh said, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed this is a scheme you have devised in the city to drive its people out of it; but you will soon know."
interpretation: The verse reveals the typical tactic of a tyrant: an arrogant ruler who cannot tolerate loyalty or truth that emerges without his approval, so he brands sincere belief as a subversive plot to justify repression. By turning faith into an alleged crime and threatening retribution ('you will soon know'), Pharaoh exposes both his fear of losing control and his willingness to criminalize and punish dissent. The passage thus interprets the incident as an example of how power corrupts judgment and seeks to silence conviction by reframing it as treason, while implicitly foreshadowing that such threats will be shown false or judged by a higher justice.

translation: I will cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all.
interpretation: This line records the cruel, boastful threat of the oppressors toward those they intended to punish; it exposes their barbarity and arrogance by describing a vow of mutilation and public crucifixion, and the Qur'ān cites it to condemn such brutality and to set the moral scene for the divine judgment that follows.

translation: They will say, "Indeed, to our Lord we are returning."
interpretation: A declaration of the inescapable reality that every person will stand before God for reckoning; it expresses a late realization of divine sovereignty and accountability, acknowledging that earthly attachments and deceptions cannot prevent the final return and judgment.

translation:
وما تنقم منا إلا أن آمنا بآيات ربنا لما جاءتنا ۚ ربنا أفرغ علينا صبرا وتوفنا مسلمين
"They bear us no hatred except because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they reached us. Our Lord, pour out on us patience and let us die as Muslims."
interpretation: The speakers explain that the hostility they face is solely due to their acceptance of God’s revelations; rather than retaliating, they beseech God for abundant, sustained patience to endure persecution and for a final end in true submission. The petition reflects a request for inner steadfastness and a dignified, faithful death — trusting God’s decree and seeking endurance rather than vengeance.

translation: And the chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said, “Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land and to leave you and your gods?” He said, “We will kill their sons and spare their women, and we will be dominant over them.”
interpretation: The verse illustrates how entrenched power disguises its self-preservation as defense of order and religion: by labeling Moses’ movement “corruption,” the rulers justify brutal measures—systematic killing of male children and subjugation of women—to extinguish future resistance. It exposes the moral bankruptcy and arrogance of tyrants who dehumanize their opponents to retain dominance.

translation: Moses said to his people, “Seek help from Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He grants it as an inheritance to whom He wills among His servants. And the final outcome belongs to the righteous.”
interpretation: The verse instructs believers that in moments of oppression and uncertainty they must couple active reliance on God with steadfast patience: seek divine aid, pursue what is right, and endure trials without despair. It affirms that possession and authority over the earth are ultimately determined by God’s wisdom and choice, not merely by force, lineage, or immediate circumstances. Therefore true and lasting success—ownership, dignity, and decisive outcomes—comes to those who maintain piety, trust in God, and perseverance rather than to those who rely on transient power or haste.

translation: They said, “We were harmed before you came to us and after you have come to us.” He said, “Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors on the earth so that He may see how you will act.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the overturning of a people's fortunes — the defeat of oppressors and the elevation of the formerly oppressed — is itself a divine test. God may grant power and dominion not simply as reward but to observe whether those raised up will govern with justice and gratitude or repeat the injustices they suffered. Thus patience and moral readiness are required: the prospect of becoming ‘successors on the earth’ is a responsibility and trial, and true worth is shown by right conduct when power is attained.

translation: And certainly We seized the people of Pharaoh with years and a decrease of fruits so that they might remember.
interpretation: The verse indicates that God can impose prolonged, tangible hardships (e.g., years of scarcity and diminished harvests) as both consequence and corrective: by removing comforts that conceal wrongdoing, these trials are meant to awaken conscience, expose false self‑sufficiency and corrupt leadership, and provide an opportunity for repentance and reform. The prolongation (‘years’) gives time for a sincere return, while the loss of blessings (‘fruits’) clarifies dependence on God; if people persist in stubbornness despite such signs, their guilt becomes manifest and further accountability follows.

translation: And when a good thing came to them they said, “This is for us.” But if an evil befell them, they turn away, blaming Moses and those with him. Unquestionably, their evasion/shift of blame will avail them nothing against Allah, yet most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse reproves those who arrogantly claim credit for blessings while seeking scapegoats when misfortune strikes. Instead of acknowledging God’s will and facing accountability, they dismiss or blame the messenger and his followers. Such deflection is ultimately futile before God — their attempts to escape responsibility or to redirect blame do not change divine judgment — yet most remain ignorant of this reality.

translation: And they said, “Whatever sign you bring to us to bewitch us with, we will not believe in you.”
interpretation: The verse depicts a willful, prejudiced rejection of truth: people who, rather than examine evidence, dismiss every miracle as sorcery to protect their stance and privileges—showing that their refusal is rooted in hardened hearts and intent to oppose guidance, not merely in lack of proof.

translation: So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood — distinct signs — but they were arrogant, and they were a people given to crime.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the decisive factor is not merely the occurrence of miraculous signs but the moral response to them: God may provide clear, repeated warnings out of mercy, yet if people meet those warnings with pride and obstinacy they render themselves culpable and subject to judgment. Humility and readiness to reform, not the number or severity of signs, determine whether one is guided or condemned.

translation: And when the scourge befell them, they said, “O Moses, call upon your Lord by that which is promised with you; if You remove from us the scourge, we will surely believe you and will send with you the Children of Israel.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a bargaining, insincere response: under affliction they demand Moses invoke God's promised aid in return for a verbal profession of faith and the release of the Israelites, revealing opportunism and conditional, unreliable submission rather than genuine conviction.

translation: But when We removed from them the scourge (punishment) until an appointed term they were to reach, behold, they broke (their covenant).
interpretation: The verse teaches that when God lifts a visible punishment for a fixed respite, many people treat that relief as license rather than mercy: instead of reforming they return to previous wrongdoing and violate their commitments to guidance. The lifting of chastisement therefore functions as a test of sincerity—true faith shows in using the reprieve to repent and remain steadfast, while breaking the covenant exposes ingratitude and guarantees that the cycle of warning and punishment may resume.

translation:
فانتقمنا منهم فأغرقناهم في اليم بأنهم كذبوا بآياتنا وكانوا عنها غافلين
"So We took vengeance on them and drowned them in the sea because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them."
interpretation: The verse conveys that persistent denial of clear divine guidance combined with heedlessness brings inevitable accountability: the drowning figure expresses both a historical punitive outcome and a metaphor of being overwhelmed by the consequences of rejecting God's signs. It emphasizes God’s moral sovereignty—signs demand a response, and ignoring them leads to decisive ruin rather than impunity.

translation: And We made the people who had been made weak inherit the eastern and western regions of the earth which We had blessed. And the fair promise of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of what they patiently endured; and We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been making and the things by which they had boasted.
interpretation: The verse affirms a moral and historical reversal ordained by God: those who suffered long under oppression (the Children of Israel) were ultimately granted widespread, blessed inheritance as the fulfillment of God’s righteous promise, a result earned through steadfast patience. In contrast, the power, constructions and proud pretentions of the oppressor (Pharaoh and his people) were ruined and rendered null. The underlying lesson is that divine justice overturns unjust dominance—endurance and trust in God lead to eventual vindication, while tyranny and self-aggrandizing achievements are transient and will be undone.

translation: And We caused the Children of Israel to cross the sea, and they came upon a people who were devout toward their idols. They said, “O Moses, make for us a god like theirs.” He said, “Indeed you are a people who do not know.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human weakness: even after witnessing divine deliverance, people can be swayed by the visible trappings of other communities and seek tangible objects of devotion. Their demand that Moses produce a ‘god like theirs’ reflects a preference for imitation and concrete symbols over grasping the unseen unity of God and trusting revealed guidance. Moses’ rebuke — calling them ignorant — stresses that turning to outward idols or copying corrupted practices is a failure of understanding and faith; true commitment requires steadfastness to the principle of tawḥīd rather than conforming to surrounding falsehoods.

translation:
إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ مُتَبَرٌ مَا هُمْ فِيهِ وَبَاطِلٌ مَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ
"Indeed, these people are astray in what they are in, and null are the deeds they used to perform."
interpretation: The verse affirms that the group described is fundamentally misguided about their present state—their beliefs and position are wrong—and because their beliefs are false, the actions they built upon them carry no true value; their deeds will not avail them before God since they were grounded in error or lacked the correct orientation (truth and sincerity) required for acceptance.

translation: He said, “Do you desire for yourselves a god other than Allah — while He has bestowed His favor upon you above all the worlds?”
interpretation: The verse reproaches the absurdity and ingratitude of turning to other gods despite Allah’s clear benevolence and superiority: it insists that choosing a deity besides God contradicts the evidence of His unique favors and lordship, and thus calls people to abandon false objects of worship, acknowledge Allah’s exclusive right to be worshipped, and respond with humility and gratitude.

translation: And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who were afflicting you with the worst torment—killing your sons and keeping your women alive—and that was a severe trial from your Lord.
interpretation: The verse presents the Exodus as both an act of divine mercy and a moment of spiritual testing: the extreme cruelty of Pharaoh (infanticide and the seizure of women) illustrates how worldly tyranny can assault a community’s very survival, while God’s intervention is meant to expose, purify and strengthen faith. Believers are reminded that deliverance is not merely escape from suffering but a sign that trials are purposeful—meant to awaken reliance on God, engender gratitude, and impose a moral responsibility to live righteously after rescue. It also affirms that oppression will be judged and that God’s protection comes in response to the community’s plight and as part of His broader plan to test and elevate them.

translation: And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten; thus the term appointed by his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Moses said to his brother Aaron, “Take my place among my people, act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters.”
interpretation: This verse highlights two linked lessons: first, the forty nights represent a divinely ordained period of seclusion and instruction in which Moses was prepared and tested—its completion signals God’s perfect decree and the seriousness of prophetic preparation. Second, Moses’ charge to Aaron shows the weight of entrusted leadership: in the prophet’s absence a trusted steward must preserve justice and religious integrity and resist the temptations and practices of those who corrupt the community. The warning against following the ‘way of the corrupters’ teaches that moral vigilance and firm guidance are essential to prevent a people from slipping into idolatry, division, or imitation of corrupt models when their primary guide is absent.

translation: And when Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, “My Lord, show me that I may look at You.” He said, “You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it should remain in place, then you will see Me.” But when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it collapse, and Moses fell unconscious. And when he recovered, he said, “Exalted are You; I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s true essence transcends created perception: human senses cannot behold the Divine directly. God answers Moses with a sign suited to creation rather than granting literal vision; the overwhelming effect on the mountain and on Moses shows that the Divine presence, when manifested, surpasses the capacity of created things. The appropriate human response to encountering God’s majesty is humility, repentance, and faith—accepting limits of perception while affirming God’s sovereignty and turning to Him in submission.

translation: He said, “O Moses, indeed I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speaking; so take what I have given you and be among the grateful.”
interpretation: God’s address to Moses affirms that his selection was not for honor alone but because God entrusted him with revelation and direct communication; this election carries a duty — accept the divine law and guidance granted to you, apply and transmit it faithfully to the people, and remain humble and thankful to God. Gratitude here is shown through obedience, stewardship of the revealed message, and using God’s favor to serve others rather than to boast.

translation: And We inscribed for him on the tablets an admonition of everything and a detailed explanation of all things. So take them firmly and enjoin your people to take the best of it. I will show you the dwelling of the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance given to Moses was comprehensive and clear, meant to be grasped and held with resolve; a prophet’s role is to adhere firmly to that guidance and to direct his people toward its best, most beneficial principles rather than insisting on every peripheral detail. The promise to “show you the dwelling of the defiantly disobedient” is a warning: persistent rejection of the core moral guidance brings ruin. Thus the passage emphasizes responsible leadership (firmness and wise selection), prioritizing what truly benefits the community, and the real consequences of persistent opposition to God’s message.

translation: سَأُصْرِفُ عَن آيَاتِي الَّذِينَ يَتَكَبَّرُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ ۖ وَإِن يَرَوْا كُلَّ آيَةٍ لَا يُؤْمِنُوا بِهَا ۚ وَإِن يَرَوْا سَبِيلَ الرُّشْدِ لَا يَتَّخِذُوهُ سَبِيلًا ۖ وَإِن يَرَوْا سَبِيلَ الْغَيِّ يَتَّخِذُوهُ سَبِيلًا ۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا وَكَانُوا عَنْهَا غَافِلِينَ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن رفض الحق المتأصل في التعالُب والتكبر يُفضي إلى فقدان القدرة على الاستجابة للهداية: عندما يغلِق الإنسان قلبه بعنادٍ وكبرياء، تتحول آيات الهداية إلى محض وقائع لا تؤثر فيه، ويصبح الميل إلى الضلالة خيارًا عمليًا مُكرَّسًا. بهذا تبرز الآية مبدأ جزائي قائم على المسؤولية الإنسانية — أن الله يبعد آياته عن من أصرّ على إنكارها وغفل عنها، ليس غضبًا أعميًا فحسب بل نتيجة حتمية لاختيارات النفس: ليتبين أن الهداية تحتاج خضوعًا ووعيًا، وأن التمادي في العناد يجعل المصير روحياً خسارةً ذاتية.

translation: And those who deny Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter — their deeds have been rendered void. Will they be recompensed for anything except what they used to do?
interpretation: The verse asserts that denial of God's clear signs and of the final meeting with Him (resurrection and judgment) strips outward acts of their spiritual worth: without right belief and recognition of accountability, deeds do not earn divine acceptance or eternal reward. “Their deeds have been rendered void” means that what appeared as good actions are deprived of salvific value because they were disconnected from faith and sincerity; the rhetorical question underscores that such people will receive no compensation beyond the mere external results of their worldly actions — they will not gain the moral or eternal fruits of righteous conduct on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: And the people of Moses, after him, took from their ornaments a calf — a body that lowed. Did they not see that it did not speak to them nor guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse condemns the substitution of living, divinely revealed guidance with lifeless symbols: despite the calf’s outward sound and shape it had no power to speak, instruct, or lead, yet people clung to it and thereby committed injustice. It warns against seeking tangible signs or idols in place of faith and obedience, showing idolatry arises from heedlessness and a readiness to trust appearances rather than truth.

translation: And when it fell into their hands and they saw that they had gone astray, they said, “If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.”
interpretation: The verse shows that once people confront the consequences of their deeds and recognize their deviation, they realize that worldly gain or belated awareness cannot by itself secure them — what ultimately rescues is God’s mercy and pardon. It teaches that sincere repentance and seeking Allah’s forgiveness are essential: without divine mercy, one remains truly ruined despite any outward success or regret.

translation: And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieving, he said, “How evil is what you have put in place of me after me! Did you hasten the matter of your Lord?” And he threw down the Tablets and seized the head of his brother, drawing him toward him. He said, “O son of my mother, indeed the people made me weak and were about to kill me; so let not my enemies gloat over me and do not place me among the wrongdoing people.”
interpretation: The verse communicates that a true leader’s deep anger and sorrow at his community’s betrayal of divine guidance are morally grounded: such righteous indignation—and even forceful, unmistakable acts—serve to repudiate corruption and defend the sanctity of revelation. The appeal to his close companion reveals the leader’s human vulnerability and legitimate desire to avoid humiliation or association with wrongdoing, teaching that upholding truth may require resolute, sometimes solitary, action to prevent the triumph of injustice and the mockery of enemies.

translation: He said, “My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy; indeed, You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”
interpretation: The speaker models profound humility and dependence on God by seeking forgiveness not only for himself but also for his companion, recognizing that ultimate safety and honor lie in being encompassed by Divine mercy. By invoking God’s attribute as “the Most Merciful of the merciful,” the plea affirms that human effort and status are insufficient for true success; salvation and vindication come through God’s compassion, so one should turn to Him collectively and hope in His clemency rather than relying on pride or self-sufficiency.

translation: Indeed, those who took the calf will receive the wrath of their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators (of falsehood).
interpretation: The verse teaches that turning from God to fabricated objects of worship—or inventing false doctrines—brings immediate and divine consequences: God’s anger and actual disgrace or loss in worldly affairs. The punishment is both spiritual and practical (social, political, material), showing that rejecting divine guidance and promoting falsehood leads to one’s own ruin; “thus do We recompense the fabricators” stresses that their downfall is a just outcome of their invention and deception.

translation: And those who committed evil deeds, then repented afterward and believed — indeed, your Lord thereafter is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere repentance combined with true faith restores a person to God's mercy: repentance must include remorse, turning away from the sin, and a firm resolve not to return, and when it is genuine and followed by belief, God accepts it and forgives. The phrase “afterward” stresses that forgiveness follows real moral change rather than empty words, affirming both Allah’s readiness to pardon and the believer’s responsibility to reform.

translation: And when Moses’ anger subsided, he took up the tablets; and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine revelation (the written law) functions primarily as guidance and a manifestation of God’s mercy for those who approach Him with reverence and humility; it implies that spiritual receptivity (tempering anger and submitting to God’s way) enables one to benefit from the moral and salvific direction contained in the commandments rather than experiencing them merely as punishment or constraint.

translation: And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time; and when the quake took them, he said, “My Lord, if You had willed You could have destroyed them before and me as well. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done? It is but Your trial by which You send astray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us; and You are the best of the merciful.”
interpretation: Moses’ words show a leader who, confronted with a collective calamity visited on a delegation he selected, recognizes God’s absolute sovereignty while pleading for mercy on behalf of his people. He refuses the notion that the whole community should be punished for the faults of a few, framing the disaster as a divinely-ordained test that distinguishes who is guided and who is led astray according to God’s wisdom. By calling God their Protector (mawla) and asking forgiveness and mercy, Moses both submits to God’s prerogative and appeals to His compassion, teaching that responsible leadership combines humility before divine judgment, intercession for others, and reliance on God’s mercy rather than retribution or despair.

translation: “And decree for us in this world good and in the Hereafter; indeed we have turned to You.” He (Allah) said, “My punishment — I will inflict it upon whom I will, and My mercy encompasses all things; so I will decree it for those who fear Me, who give zakāh, and who believe in Our signs.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God alone determines reward and punishment: His wrath may be visited on whom He wills, but His mercy is vast and He chooses to bestow it particularly on those who cultivate taqwa (God‑consciousness), fulfill their social and religious obligations (exemplified by zakāh), and have sincere faith in His signs; thus seeking both good in this life and the hereafter requires turning to God with piety, rightful conduct, and trust in His merciful decree.

translation: Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written in what is with them — in the Torah and the Gospel — who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them from what is wrong, and makes lawful for them the pure things and prohibits for them the impure, and removes from them their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him, honor him, help him, and follow the light which was sent down with him — those are the successful.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد دور النبي محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم كنبي متمّم لسلسلة الرسالات: أنه مذكور في الكتب السابقة، وأن رسالته عملية وأخلاقية وتشريعية معاً. وصفه بالأُمِّيّ يشير إلى أنه لم يكن من المتعلمين بالكتب البشرّية، ما يبرز صفة إعجاز القرآن وصدق النبوة، ويشير أيضاً إلى أن الناس لا يحتاجون إلى وسائط بشرية ليتحقق الهداية. المهم في الرسالة أنها تأمر بالمعروف وتنهى عن المنكر — أي أنها تهدف إلى إصلاح القيم والسلوك — وتبيح الطيبات وتحرم الخبائث، فتضع حدوداً بين الحلال والحرام تنظّم حياة الأفراد والمجتمعات. إزالة الإصرّ والأغلال تعني تخفيف الأثقال الدينية والاجتماعية والتقليدية التي كانت تقيّد الناس، سواء كانت عبادات مشدّدة بلا أساس أو قيود ظالمة. الخلاص والنجاح هنا مرتبطان بالقبول العملي: الإيمان بالنبي، تعظيمه، نصرة دعوته، واتباع النور (الوحي) الذي أنزل معه؛ أي أن النجاة ليست مجرد اعتراف لفظي بل التزام عملي بنوره وتعاليمه.
