translation: Do not perform the funeral prayer for any of them who dies, nor stand at his grave; indeed they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger and died while they were defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Muslim community to withhold public rites of honor (funeral prayer and standing at the grave) from those among their ranks who have openly rejected God and His Messenger and persisted in rebellious wickedness until death. The ruling reflects a communal and legal consequence: ritual gestures that recognize a person as part of the believing community are denied to those whose deliberate disbelief and persistent dissidence place them outside that community; the prohibition both manifests disassociation from their stance and serves as a deterrent, underscoring that spiritual allegiance, not merely social ties, determines entitlement to communal religious honors.

translation: And let not their wealth and their children astonish you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in this worldly life and to cause their souls to depart while they are disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse warns that outward prosperity—riches and many children—does not prove Allah’s pleasure and can itself be a means of divine punishment: such blessings may distract people, harden their hearts, or elevate their pride so that they persist in unbelief and thus meet death spiritually lost. Believers should not be deceived by appearances or let worldly success of others sway their certainty about what leads to true guidance; ultimate judgment belongs to God.

translation: And when a surah was revealed, ‘Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger,’ some of those among them who had excuses came to you asking permission and said, ‘Let us remain with those who sit [behind].’
interpretation: الآية تنتقد من يتذرعون بأعذار شخصية ليحرموا أنفسهم من واجب جماعي عندما تُؤمر الأمة بالإيمان والجهاد؛ تكشف عن ميلهم للبقاء مع القاعدين والامتناع عن المشاركة العملية. المقصود أن الإيمان لا يكتمل بالقول وحده بل يتطلب انخراطاً ومسؤوليّة مشتركة، وأن السماح المتكرر للأعذار يضعف قوة الجماعة ويخالف روح التكافل والالتزام.

translation: They are content to be among the laggards, and a seal has been set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.
interpretation: The phrase condemns those who willingly accept being counted with the ‘laggards’ or those left behind from guidance and the community of the rightly guided. Because of repeated rejection, stubbornness, or hypocrisy, God places a ‘seal’ on their hearts — a divine withholding that hardens their inner receptivity. This sealing is described not as arbitrary cruelty but as the consequence of their chosen complacency with error: their disposition and actions close them off from spiritual perception, insight, and moral understanding, so they remain unable (or unwilling) to grasp the truth.

translation: But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives; for them are the good things, and it is they who will prosper.
interpretation: The verse affirms that genuine commitment to God is measured by active sacrifice — offering both one’s resources and oneself in the cause of truth — and that such wholehearted striving transforms ordinary actions into lasting blessings. “Al-khayrāt” (the good things) encompasses both material support, spiritual growth, and the manifold rewards God grants in this life and the next, while “al-mufliḥūn” (the truly successful) denotes those who attain ultimate felicity and salvation. The statement thus commends sincere, risk-taking devotion and promises that self-giving perseverance, not mere words or outward appearance, yields divine favor and real success.

translation: Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow; they will abide therein forever. That is the great success.
interpretation: The verse should be understood as a divine assurance that the ultimate reward for faith and righteous conduct is an enduring reality — Paradise pictured with gardens and streams as symbols of complete, perpetual well‑being, provision, and peace. Calling it “the great success” reframes true victory not as temporal pleasures or achievements but as eternal security, spiritual fulfillment, and proximity to God’s mercy, the decisive and final triumph over hardship and transience.

translation: And those of the Bedouins who were excused came asking permission [to be absent], and those who had lied to Allah and His Messenger remained sitting. A painful punishment will strike those among them who disbelieved.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes sincere, legitimate excuses from fraudulent refusal. “The excused among the Arabs” are those who genuinely could not join the expedition and properly sought permission; they are permitted to stay. By contrast, “those who lied to Allah and His Messenger” refers to people who pretended reasons or openly rejected the obligation—their remaining behind is an act of repudiation, not a valid excuse. The warning that a painful punishment will befall those who disbelieved underscores that deliberate evasion of communal duty tied to faith and open rejection of God’s command entail serious divine accountability, both in worldly consequences (dishonor, loss of support) and ultimate retribution.

translation: There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who do not find (the means) to spend, if they are sincere toward Allah and His Messenger. There is no blame on the doers of good. And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine accountability is measured by capacity and inner intention: inability—whether physical, medical, or financial—absolves one from outward obligations when accompanied by sincere loyalty to God and His Messenger. True moral worth is assessed by effort and intention rather than mere external participation, and God’s forgiveness and mercy cover those whom circumstances prevent from acting.

translation:
وَلَا عَلَى الَّذِينَ إِذَا مَا أَتُوكَ لِتَحْمِلَهُمْ قُلْتَ لَا أَجِدُ مَا أَحْمِلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ تَوَلَّوْا وَأَعْيُنُهُمْ تَفِيضُ مِنَ الدَّمْعِ حُزْنًا أَلَا يَجِدُوا مَا يُنفِقُونَ
"There is no blame on those who, when they were called to be carried (to join), said, 'I do not find anything to carry you on.' They turned away, and their eyes overflowed with tears out of sorrow that they found nothing to spend."
interpretation: The verse absolves sincere poverty: it teaches that Allah does not hold accountable those whose true desire to join a communal religious effort (such as a military expedition or other collective duty) is thwarted by genuine lack of means. Their overflowing tears demonstrate heartfelt longing and faith, so outward inability is excused; moral responsibility is measured by intention and capability, not mere aspiration. Implicitly this ruling also calls the community to recognize such hardship and support the needy so they may participate when able.

translation: Indeed, the fault is only with those who ask your permission while they are wealthy; they are content to be among those left behind, and Allah has set a seal upon their hearts, so they do not know.
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who, motivated by comfort and attachment to their wealth, seek to be excused from communal religious obligations (for example, joining the community in struggle or migration). Their request reveals a settled preference for the safe, affluent company of the laggards rather than commitment to collective duty. As a result of their persistent choice and inward hardness, Allah has ‘sealed’ their hearts — meaning their receptivity to guidance and moral perception is dulled — so they remain oblivious to the spiritual and moral reality of their conduct.

translation: They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say, “Do not make excuses; we will not believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. And Allah will see your deeds, and His Messenger; then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.”
interpretation: The verse warns against being swayed by the smooth apologies of those whose hypocrisy has been exposed: once inner disposition and motives have been divinely disclosed, outward words cannot undo the reality. The command to refuse their excuses teaches communal prudence — trust and membership are not restored merely by verbal contrition when the evidence of conduct and intent contradicts it. By stating that Allah and His Messenger have witnessed their deeds and that ultimately they will be returned to the All‑Knower, the verse affirms that accountability is both already recorded and will be decisively established on the Day of Reckoning; thus moral truth and responsibility transcend immediate social reconciliation, and sincere reform must be proven by consistent, observable change, not just apologies.

translation: They will swear by Allah to you when you return to them so that you will turn away from them. So turn away from them; indeed they are filth, and their abode is Hell — a recompense for what they used to earn.
interpretation: The verse warns that some people will employ false oaths and outward professions to manipulate believers and draw them away from the community of truth. The command “turn away from them” is an instruction to refuse their influence and not be deceived by perfunctory promises; their outward words conceal inner corruption (described as rij's — impurity), and because their actions reflect persistent hypocrisy and wrongdoing, they will face just recompense in the hereafter. The passage thus upholds vigilance against deceptive companions, prioritizes moral integrity over polite concession, and affirms divine justice for those who persist in dishonest, corrupt behavior.

translation: They swear to you so that you may be pleased with them. If you are pleased with them, then indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse warns that some people use oaths and flattery to gain the approval of others while concealing their rebelliousness; even if those they target are appeased, such human approval cannot secure God’s pleasure. It teaches that endorsing or overlooking clear disobedience for the sake of pleasing people is wrong — divine approval depends on fidelity to God’s commands, not on being won over by promises or social convenience, and those whose behavior remains defiantly sinful will not attain Allah’s satisfaction.

translation: The Bedouins are the severest in disbelief and hypocrisy and are more likely to be ignorant of the limits which Allah has revealed to His Messenger. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: The verse is explaining a social-dynamic reason for why certain desert tribes resisted and misunderstood the newly revealed laws and teachings: their isolation, strong attachment to pre‑Islamic customs, and weaker integration into the Muslim community made them more prone to outward unbelief or hypocritical behavior and to neglect or misapply the Prophet’s ordinances. The final clause affirms that God fully knows people's inner states and deals with them with wisdom, implying that guidance and corrective measures must take account of differing backgrounds and readiness to accept change.

translation: And among the Bedouins are some who take what they spend as a loss and await for you the ambushes (or misfortunes); upon them is a grievous punishment. And Allah is All‑Hearing, All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse criticizes people who outwardly give or participate but do so grudgingly and with hostile intent—counting their spending as a loss while secretly hoping for the believers’ downfall and plotting against them. Their apparent acts are spoiled by malice and calculation; what matters is inner disposition, and hidden schemes and resentment will not go unnoticed or unpunished. The warning affirms that Allah hears and knows the true motives of hearts, so sincerity and uprightness, not mere outward appearance, determine moral and spiritual accountability.

translation: And among the Bedouins are some who believe in Allah and the Last Day and take what they spend as a means of nearness to Allah and as acts in conformity with the Messenger’s teachings. Indeed, that is a means of nearness for them; Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the moral worth of actions depends on inner intent and adherence to prophetic guidance: even humble, peripheral people who sincerely spend and act to draw near to God—and who align themselves with the Messenger’s way—have their deeds accepted and will be brought into God’s mercy. It warns against judging by outward status and affirms that sincere devotion and right intention secure divine forgiveness and compassion.

translation: And the foremost — the first to embrace faith — among the Muhājirīn and the Anṣār and those who followed them in goodness: Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great attainment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the highest form of success is attaining Allah’s pleasure through sincere faith, sacrifice, and upright conduct exemplified by the early believers; their eternal gardens are both the reward and the confirmation of divine approval, and Muslims are called to emulate their faith and moral commitment so as to secure this ultimate, everlasting triumph.

translation: And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those who have persisted in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice, then they will be returned to a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God alone perceives hidden hypocrisy and will not leave it unaddressed: He brings measured chastisements—here described as two successive punishments (understood as repeated trials or afflictions in this life that expose and warn)—and after these will be a decisive, severe punishment in the Hereafter. The passage underscores divine omniscience, the moral consequence of persistent hypocrisy, and the use of worldly trials by God as both warning and purification before final accountability.

translation: And others admitted their sins — they mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad — perhaps Allah will accept their repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that acknowledging one’s faults and not concealing wrongdoing, even when one’s life contains both good and bad actions, opens the way to divine pardon: sincere admission, remorse, and continued effort toward good allow a person to hope for Allah’s turning to them in forgiveness. By naming God as ‘Ghafūr Rahīm’ it reassures believers that human imperfection does not bar mercy, so one should repent honestly, seek reform, and trust in God’s compassion rather than despair.

translation:
خذ من أموالهم صدقة تطهرهم وتزكيهم بها وصل عليهم ۖ إن صلاتك سكن لهم ۗ والله سميع عليم
“Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray over them. Indeed, your prayer is a source of reassurance for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to take charitable contributions from believers not as punishment but as a means of moral and social purification: the gift cleanses the giver’s heart and wealth and fosters spiritual and communal growth. The Prophet’s role includes both administering that charity and invoking God’s blessing over those who give; his prayers comfort and strengthen the community, reinforcing trust and cohesion. By ending with “Allah is Hearing, Knowing,” the verse underscores that the inward intention behind giving matters and that God is fully aware of both outward acts and inner motives, so the charity serves ethical, spiritual, and practical purposes within the community.

translation: Do they not know that Allah is the One who accepts repentance from His servants and receives the charities, and that Allah—He is the Oft-Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s disposition is to welcome sincere return and to accept the outward signs of repentance (such as giving charity) as means of spiritual reform. By naming God At‑Tawwab and Ar‑Rahim it reassures believers that forgiveness and restoration are provided by Divine mercy, not by human approval; therefore people should turn humbly and repeatedly to God in hope and sincerity, trusting that He alone evaluates and accepts repentance and righteous deeds.

translation: And say, “Work; for Allah will see your work, and His Messenger and the believers; and you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.”
interpretation: This verse exhorts believers to continue doing righteous deeds with sincerity and steadfastness: every action is observed by God, witnessed by His Messenger and the believing community, and will ultimately be brought before God—the One who knows both hidden motives and outward acts—who will make plain the reality of what people did. It calls for inner integrity (doing good for God's sake, not merely for show), perseverance in obedience despite opposition or indifference, and trust in final divine accountability rather than seeking only worldly approval.

translation: And others are left to the decree of Allah — He will either punish them or accept their repentance. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the ultimate determination of certain people's fate is suspended to God's sovereign judgment: whether they will be dealt with by punishment or by forgiveness is not for people to finalize but for God, whose perfect knowledge and wisdom ensure a just balance between recompense and mercy. This should restrain human pronouncements of absolute condemnation, foster reliance on divine justice, and sustain both a sober fear of wrongdoing and hopeful reliance on the possibility of God's pardon for those who turn back to Him.

translation: And those who took a mosque to cause harm and disbelief and to create division among the believers and to spy on those who had fought against Allah and His Messenger previously — and they will surely swear, “We intended nothing but good” — and Allah bears witness that indeed they are liars.
interpretation: The verse denounces the hypocrisy of those who exploit a sacred place for political and hostile ends: building a mosque not for sincere worship but as an instrument of mischief, schism, and collusion with enemies. It teaches that outward claims of good intent (even sworn oaths) cannot conceal malicious inner motives; God, who knows hearts and hidden facts, exposes such duplicity. The broader moral is that religious institutions and symbols must not be used to undermine communal unity or to shelter adversaries, and that hypocritical pretense is a grave moral failing subject to divine judgment.

translation: Do not ever stand [to pray] in it. A mosque founded on righteousness from the first day is more worthy that you should stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.
interpretation: The verse warns against participating in or legitimizing a place of worship whose origin or purpose is corrupt or hypocritical, and urges attachment to communities and institutions established on taqwa (God-consciousness) from the outset. It teaches that the worth of communal worship is tied to the sincerity and moral character of its founders and members: one should prefer to lead and join in gatherings that foster both outward ritual purity and inward moral purification. By highlighting that there are people who love to purify themselves and that God loves the purified, the text elevates the pursuit of spiritual and ethical cleansing as a central criterion for belonging, leadership, and genuine worship.

translation: Is one who has founded his building upon piety toward Allah and seeking His pleasure better, or one who has founded his building upon the edge of a crumbling precipice so that it collapses with him into the Fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the unjust people.
interpretation: The verse contrasts two spiritual foundations: a life and deeds rooted in taqwa (God-consciousness) and sincere intention to please God — which are firm and rightly guided — versus a life built on unstable motives (hypocrisy, worldly ambition, injustice, or flimsy beliefs) that will inevitably collapse and lead to ruin in the Hereafter. It warns that persistent wrongdoing and falsehood remove divine guidance, so true security and success come only from sincere faith, righteous conduct, and seeking Allah’s approval.

translation: The structure they built will continue to sow doubt in their hearts until their hearts are severed. And Allah is All‑Knower, All‑Wise.
interpretation: When people construct their lives or systems on falsehood, hypocrisy, injustice or schemes that breed suspicion, that very edifice keeps generating inner unease and moral corrosion; over time this persistent doubt hardens and severs the heart from truth, compassion and guidance. The verse warns that such self‑made structures bring about spiritual ruin, and reminds that ultimately God alone has full knowledge and wisdom regarding people’s states and the consequences of their deeds.

translation: Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their possessions [in exchange] for Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah; they kill and are killed. [It is] a true promise binding upon Him in the Torah and the Gospel and the Qur'an. And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in your transaction which you have contracted with Him — and that is the great attainment.
interpretation: This verse presents a spiritual covenant: sincere believers voluntarily offer their selves and wealth in obedience and struggle for God, and in return God guarantees them Paradise. The phrase “they fight… kill and are killed” expresses their readiness to confront oppression and to risk or give life itself for the cause of truth, not as wanton violence but as part of committed struggle tied to moral and communal obligations. The promise is affirmed as consistent with earlier scriptures, underscoring God’s perfect faithfulness to His covenant. The command to rejoice transforms sacrifice into hopeful assurance: those who accept this divine bargain should take comfort in its certainty, since true success is the spiritual victory of trusting God and striving for what He ordained.

translation: التائبون العابدون الحامدون السائحون الراكعون الساجدون الآمرون بالمعروف والناهون عن المنكر والحافظون لحدود الله ۗ وبشر المؤمنين
interpretation: The verse names a cohesive set of qualities that constitute true faith: continual turning to God (repentance), devoted worship and thankful praise, active striving (whether traveling for God's cause, seeking knowledge, or serving the community), humble submission expressed in bowing and prostration, social responsibility to enjoin good and forbid evil, and careful observance of the limits God has set. Read together these traits portray a balanced believer whose inner renewal and devotional life are inseparable from outward ethical conduct and legal/communal restraint; the injunction to "give good news to the believers" indicates that embodying these qualities brings divine favor, moral firmness, and reassurance to the faithful.

translation: It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists — even if they are their relatives — after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse establishes a limit on intercessory supplication: when people have openly and persistently embraced disbelief and their fate as inhabitants of the Fire is manifest, the Prophet and the believing community must not seek God’s forgiveness on their behalf. This prohibition protects the moral and doctrinal integrity of the Muslim community, signals that mercy and intercession are appropriate only while genuine hope of guidance or repentance remains, and affirms that religious truth and accountability take precedence over tribal or familial ties.

translation: And Abraham’s seeking forgiveness for his father was only because of an appointment he had made with him; but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to Allah, he disowned him. Indeed Abraham was forbearing, compassionate.
interpretation: The verse teaches the ethical balance between family devotion and fidelity to God: Abraham patiently upheld a promise to pray for his father out of mercy and hope, but when his father’s hostility to God became undeniable he formally distanced himself to uphold divine truth. This conduct is presented as forbearance — compassion coupled with principled firmness: one should strive gently for loved ones’ guidance, yet decisively break ties with open enmity to God when reconciliation is impossible.

translation: And Allah would never cause a people to go astray after He had guided them, until He makes clear to them what they should fear (or guard against). Indeed, Allah is, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance is accompanied by clarification of duties and limits: God does not leave a community misguided after granting them guidance without first making plain what constitutes piety, forbidden conduct, and the duties that preserve faith. Therefore if a people later stray, responsibility rests on their refusal to observe the explanations and warnings already given, for Allah has made the path and obligations known and is fully aware of every state and choice.

translation: Indeed, Allah — to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have no protector or helper besides Allah.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty and sole authority over existence: He alone controls creation, bestows life and takes it away, and therefore no person, power, or idol can ultimately protect, sustain, or intercede independently of Him. The intended effect is to ground the believer’s trust, reliance, and worship in God alone, to diminish misplaced dependence on worldly authorities or allies, and to remind people that true help, refuge, and ultimate authority rest with the Divine.

translation: Indeed Allah has accepted the repentance of the Prophet and the Muhajirun and the Ansar who followed him in the hour of hardship, after a party of them had nearly gone astray; then He accepted their repentance. Indeed, He is to them, Most Compassionate, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine mercy embraces sincere return: even when believers’ hearts briefly waver under severe trial, what determines their standing with God is repentance and recommitment. It reassures the Prophet and the community that human frailty in moments of hardship does not permanently estrange one from God’s favor, provided one turns back sincerely — a theme that emphasizes God’s compassion and the corrective, restorative power of repentance.

translation: And [He accepted the repentance] of the three who were left behind — when the earth became narrow for them though it is vast, and their souls grew constricted, and they thought that there was no refuge from Allah except in Him; then He turned to them (accepted their repentance) so that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Ever-Acceptor of Repentance, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that true repentance arises from an inward realization and distress: when a person’s conscience makes the world feel tight despite its breadth and they acknowledge that there is no shelter except with God, sincere turning to Him is born. God’s acceptance follows that genuine remorse, recognition of wrong, and return to right conduct; He responds with forgiveness and mercy. The passage thus emphasizes both the human condition that leads to repentance (felt contrition and dependence on God) and God’s compassionate readiness to receive those who sincerely return to Him.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to cultivate taqwa (God‑consciousness) — a constant awareness of Allah that restrains wrongdoing and guides moral choice — and to choose companionship and alignment with those who are sincere and truthful in belief, speech, and conduct. It implies that true faith is lived out through honesty and steadfastness, that company influences a person’s faith and character, and that believers should seek association with people who uphold truth and righteousness, supporting them and following their example rather than siding with falsehood or hypocrisy.

translation: It was not for the people of Medina and those around them of the Bedouin that they should turn back from following the Messenger of Allah, nor should they prefer their own selves over him. That is because they do not suffer thirst, fatigue, hunger, distress in the cause of Allah, nor do they tread a place that angers the disbelievers, nor strike the enemy with any blow, except that it is recorded for them as a righteous deed. Indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.
interpretation: The verse explains why the Ansar and allied Arabs stood faithfully with the Prophet: their hearts were fully committed so that every hardship endured or risk taken in God’s cause—thirst, exhaustion, hunger, exposing themselves to enmity or provoking the enemy—was counted as a righteous deed. The principle taught is that sincere sacrifice and struggle for the mission of God, even when it brings suffering or provokes opposition, is neither overlooked nor wasted; Allah records and recompenses every genuine act of goodness and self-giving, independent of outward success.

translation: They do not spend—whether a small or a large amount—nor do they cross a valley, except that it is recorded for them, so that Allah may recompense them with the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every act of spending or exertion made for God’s sake, even if outwardly small or burdensome, is noticed and recorded by God; reward is not measured merely by apparent size but by God’s knowledge of intention and effort, and He will recompense the doer with the best possible reward. This encourages believers to give and strive without counting only worldly magnitude, trusting that nothing sincere is lost.

translation: And it was not for the believers to go forth all at once. And why should there not be from every group among them a party who remain to gain deep understanding in the religion and to warn their people when they return to them — that they might be mindful?
interpretation: The verse sets a principle of communal responsibility: public action must be balanced with the cultivation and retention of knowledgeable people within each subgroup so the community’s religious understanding, guidance, and moral vigilance are maintained. By leaving trained individuals to study, teach, and admonish their people upon return, the community preserves its conscience and continuity, prevents error and neglect, and ensures that decisions and campaigns are rooted in sound religious knowledge.

translation:
يا أيها الذين آمنوا قاتلوا الذين يلونكم من الكفار وليجدوا فيكم غلظة ۚ واعلموا أن الله مع المتقين
“O you who believe, fight those of the disbelievers who are near you, and let them find in you firmness; and know that Allah is with the righteous.”
interpretation: This verse enjoins the community, in conditions of hostility and threat, to mount a firm, disciplined resistance against nearby hostile non‑believers so as to deter aggression and protect the community. The word غلظة (ghalẓa) denotes resolute strength and sternness in action—not cruelty or wanton harm—and is to be exercised within the bounds of piety and moral restraint, for the promise "Allah is with the muttaqīn" ties legitimate use of force to righteousness, justice, and God‑conscious conduct. Classical readings therefore treat the command as contextual to defensive/wartime circumstances rather than a general license for oppression of non‑Muslims.

translation: Whenever a chapter is revealed, some of them say, “Which of you has this increased in faith?” But as for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.
interpretation: The verse contrasts two responses to divine revelation: the mockingly skeptical posture of some—who claim the message changes nothing for them, often to mask their rejection—and the sincere reception of the faithful, for whom each revelation deepens conviction, brings spiritual reassurance, and elicits gladness. It teaches that true guidance is recognized inwardly and yields real growth and joy in the heart, while feigned indifference betrays hardness or hypocrisy rather than genuine understanding.

translation: As for those in whose hearts there is a disease, it has added filth to their filth, and they died while they were disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse is speaking of an inner spiritual sickness—hypocrisy, resentment, stubborn denial, or moral corruption—that makes a person resistant to guidance; rather than being purified by signs and admonition, their heart becomes further defiled and hardened, so they grow more entrenched in rejection and ultimately die without accepting faith.

translation:
أَوَلَا يَرَوْنَ أَنَّهُمْ يُفْتَنُونَ كُلَّ سَنَةٍ مَرَّةً أَوْ مَرَّتَيْنِ ثُمَّ لَا يَتُوبُونَ وَلَا هُمْ يَذَّكَّرُونَ
“Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice, yet they do not repent and they do not take heed?”
interpretation: The verse teaches that recurring hardships or setbacks are divine warnings and opportunities for moral correction; God allows such trials repeatedly as a merciful means to awaken people to their faults, so persistent failure to repent in the face of these signs reveals willful heedlessness and moral obduracy, risking the withdrawal of mercy and the imposition of sterner consequences.

translation: And whenever a surah is revealed, some of them look at one another, “Does anyone see you?” then they turn away. Allah has turned their hearts away because they are a people who do not understand.
interpretation: The verse points to hypocrisy’s spiritual consequence: those who perform religion for show rather than from conviction habitually seek witnesses and withdraw when sincerity is lacking. Because they persist in insincerity and refuse to open themselves to guidance, God withdraws their inner receptivity — their hearts are diverted and they cannot truly comprehend or benefit from the revelation.

translation: There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer; he is eager for your welfare — toward the believers he is kind and merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Prophet is one of the community who is emotionally and morally invested in their wellbeing: he feels the pain of their troubles, which demonstrates that his mission is motivated by compassion rather than self‑interest. His being “eager for your welfare” (حريص عليكم) expresses an intense, active concern to secure their guidance and good — even when that requires stern warnings or sacrifices — while “kind and merciful” (رءوف رحيم) qualifies the manner of his care as tender and forgiving. Together the phrases portray a model of leadership that is intimate, self‑sacrificing, vigilant for the good of others, and ultimately grounded in mercy.

translation: But if they turn away, say: “Sufficient for me is Allah; there is no deity except Him. In Him I have placed my trust, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne.”
interpretation: When people reject guidance or withdraw their support, the believer is directed to fortify themselves by affirming divine sufficiency and absolute oneness: declaring “Allah is sufficient for me” is an inner stance of tawakkul that recognizes God alone as protector, helper, and final arbiter. Naming Him as Lord of the Mighty Throne underscores His supreme authority and guardianship over all affairs, so the faithful find peace, resolve, and continued responsibility in trusting God rather than seeking validation from those who turn away.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Alif‑Lam‑Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book.
interpretation: The disjoined letters “Alif‑Lam‑Ra” function as an attention‑drawing divine signature whose full import belongs to God; immediately calling what follows “the verses of the Wise Book” affirms that the Qur’an’s statements are not human conjecture but purposeful, coherent divine guidance—each verse shaped by wisdom to instruct, warn, and adjudicate, and thus to be received with humility and acted upon as part of a unified, wise revelation.

translation:
أَكانَ لِلنّاسِ عَجَبًا أَنْ أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى رَجُلٍ مِّنْهُمْ أَنْ أَنْذِرِ النّاسَ وَبَشِّرِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنَّ لَهُمْ قَدَمَ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ ۚ قَالَ الْكَافِرُونَ إِنْ هَذَا لَسَاحِرٌ مُبِينٌ
“Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them: ‘Warn the people and give glad tidings to those who believe that for them is a firm, true standing before their Lord’? The disbelievers said, ‘This is clear sorcery.’”
interpretation: God here rebukes those who are astonished that revelation would be granted to an ordinary human; prophets are deliberately human so the message is accessible and the responsibility rests with people’s response. The verse highlights the dual purpose of revelation—stern warning to the heedless and comforting assurance to the believers that they will have a verified, enduring standing before their Lord (qadam ṣidq, i.e. a truthful, established position on the Day of Reckoning). The charge of “sorcery” by the disbelievers is presented as a predictable tactic of denial: instead of confronting the moral and spiritual claims of the message, they dismiss it as magic to avoid being convicted by its truth.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself upon the Throne; He manages all affairs. There is no intercessor except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord—so worship Him. Will you then not take heed?
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute oneness and sovereignty of God: He is the sole Creator of the cosmos, and His “establishing on the Throne” expresses His supreme authority and governance over creation (not a limitation but the affirmation that divine rule is established). By stating “He manages all affairs” and that no one may intercede except by His leave, the verse emphasizes that all power, judgment, and means of access to God belong to Him alone. The practical demand that follows—worship Him and remember Him—flows from that theological reality: recognizing God’s exclusive lordship obliges human beings to submit, single out Him for devotion, and live in continual consciousness of His authority and mercy.

translation: إليه مرجعكم جميعا. وعد الله حقٌّ. إنّه يبدأ الخلق ثم يعيده ليجزي الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات بالقِسْطِ. والذين كفروا لهم شرابٌ من حميمٍ وعذابٌ أليمٌ بما كانوا يكفرون.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد يقين البعث والجزاء: العودة إلى الله أمر حتمي للجميع، ووعده بالجزاء قائم لا يَخْلُف. ذكر أنّه «يبدأ الخلق ثم يعيده» يستدل منه على قدرة الخالق المطلقة؛ لأن من يَؤصل الخلق أصلًا قادر على إعادته حيًا للجزاء، فلا محالة في تحقيق الحساب. كلمة «بالقسط» تبين أن الجزاء سيكون بمقياس عدل تام، يُؤتى كلٌّ حقّه بلا زيادة ولا نقصان؛ وبذلك يصبح الإيمان والعمل الصالح السبيل إلى نيل الجزاء المستحق. أما مشروعية وعنف الجزاء الوارد بمنظور «شراب من حميمٍ وعذاب أليم» فهي تعبير عن نتيجة إنكار الناس للحق وإصرارهم عليه، فتأتي العقوبة مبدأً مترتبًا على رفض الأدلة وتحمل تبعاته في القيامة.

translation: He is the One who made the sun a radiant light and the moon a reflected light, and ordained for it stages so that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth; He sets forth the signs for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse points to the sun and moon as purposeful, lawful signs: their light and ordered phases serve practical human needs (timekeeping, calendars, navigation) and simultaneously manifest God’s deliberate wisdom and measure in creation. Saying it was created “in truth” rejects randomness and asserts a coherent, purposeful order governed by God; the final clause calls on thoughtful people to observe these regularities, infer divine authorship, and let that recognition inform their understanding of God’s power, providence, and the moral seriousness of existence.

translation: Indeed, in the alternation of night and day and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth are signs for a people who are God‑conscious.
interpretation: The regular cycle of night and day and the variety observed throughout the heavens and earth are not random but deliberate manifestations of God’s wisdom, power and order; for those who are God‑conscious these phenomena serve as prompts to reflect, recognize divine sovereignty, correct heedlessness, and orient their lives toward humble worship, moral responsibility, and trust in God’s providence.

translation: Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us and are pleased with the life of this world and feel secure in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs.
interpretation: This verse diagnoses a spiritual condition: when people cease to live with the awareness of meeting God (whether by denying the Hereafter or by failing to prepare for it), they grow content with fleeting worldly comforts and develop a false sense of security. That complacency produces and reflects heedlessness toward God’s signs—revelation, moral guidance, and reminders—so the heart is dulled, the urgency to repent and act rightly is lost, and the person becomes increasingly cut off from guidance and readiness for ultimate accountability.

translation: Their abode will be the Fire because of what they used to earn.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes divine justice: those addressed will be consigned to Hell as the direct result of their own deliberate actions and choices. The verb “يكسبون” conveys that they accumulated sinful deeds or persistent rejection through their behavior, and therefore their final dwelling is a just consequence of what they themselves brought about — a warning that moral responsibility and the outcome in the Hereafter are determined by one’s deeds, not by birth, wealth, or claims.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds — their Lord will guide them by their faith; rivers flow beneath them in the Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: The verse indicates that sincere faith joined with virtuous action makes a person receptive to God’s guidance: faith is not merely belief but the inner instrument through which God steers the heart, choices and circumstances toward rightness. The promise that rivers run beneath them in the Gardens of Bliss portrays the reward as both certain and continuously life-giving—an enduring state of spiritual and material ease that flows from the alignment of inner conviction and outward conduct. In short, inward faith that bears outward good works attracts divine direction in this life and yields the abiding blessing of the hereafter.

translation: Their invocation therein will be, “Glory be to You, O Allah,” and their greeting therein will be, “Peace.” And the last of their invocation will be, “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse conveys the spiritual posture of the redeemed: confronted with God's absolute perfection they first proclaim His transcendence, they dwell in the certainty and safety expressed by peace, and their ultimate response is universal praise. The ordered sequence—glorification, reception of peace, then triumphant praise—teaches that awe of God leads to inner restoration and culminates in wholehearted gratitude that recognizes God’s sovereignty and mercy over all existence.

translation: And if Allah were to hasten for the people the evil as they hasten for the good, their appointed term would have been ended for them; so He leaves those who do not hope to meet Us in their transgression, wandering blindly.
interpretation: God delays immediate punishment despite people’s impatience for blessings and their swift pursuit of worldly good; this delay is deliberate wisdom — it preserves the chance for repentance, allows God’s timing and justice to be fulfilled, and exposes people’s true choices. Those who deny the meeting with God and persist in arrogance and sin are left to continue in their misguided course — their bewilderment and blind wandering are the consequence of rejecting guidance and of God’s withholding of the immediate retribution that would have otherwise cut their term short.

translation: And when harm touches a person, he calls upon Us — whether lying on his side, sitting, or standing. But when We remove from him his harm, he goes on as if he had never called upon Us to avert a harm that had touched him. Thus We have made pleasing to the extravagant what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse reproves a common, unstable human response: people urgently seek God in distress but forget Him and fail to show gratitude, obedience, or steadfast reliance once relief comes. By saying God makes their past excesses appear attractive, the text explains that ease and removed hardship can be a trial that conceals the moral ugliness of their conduct, encouraging repetition of neglect and transgression. The passage therefore calls for constant faithfulness — not conditional invocation in crises only — and warns that prosperity which makes wrongdoing seem beautiful is itself part of the test and a consequence of one’s prior heedlessness.

translation: And indeed We destroyed generations before you when they did wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, yet they would not believe. Thus do We recompense the guilty people.
interpretation: The verse teaches a moral and theological principle: divine punishment in history is portrayed not as arbitrary wrath but as the outcome of a community’s persistent injustice and deliberate rejection of manifest guidance. The messengers’ “bayyînât” are presented as sufficient opportunity for understanding and reform; when a people collectively harden themselves in wrongdoing and refuse the evidence given, their moral corruption closes the path to repentance and brings about just recompense. In short, the passage warns that sustained oppression and rejection of clear truth lead to inevitable accountability, and it functions both as an explanation of past events and a deterrent exhortation for present and future communities to heed guidance and abandon transgression.

translation: Then We made you successors on the earth after them, so that We might see how you will act.
interpretation: The verse asserts that God has placed humanity as stewards or vicegerents on earth following earlier peoples, framing human life as a trial of responsibility: being a khalīfah entails preserving creation, establishing justice, and living according to God’s guidance. “To see how you will act” indicates divine scrutiny and moral accountability—our conduct on earth (either care and obedience or corruption and injustice) determines our standing before God and the consequences that follow.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say, 'Bring a Qur'an other than this one or change it.' Say: 'It is not for me to change it of my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me. Indeed I fear, if I were to disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.'
interpretation: The verse uncovers the nature of rejection: people who refuse the meeting with God ask that the divine message be altered to suit themselves, revealing bias and self-interest rather than genuine inquiry. It affirms the Prophet’s role and restraint—he cannot fabricate or amend revelation but conveys solely what is revealed—and presents his motivating conscience: a reverent fear of accountability before God on the Day of Judgment. Thus the passage teaches that true guidance is not a matter of personal preference, that prophetic integrity rests on obedience to revelation, and that ignoring or demanding to change divine guidance carries severe spiritual consequences.

translation: Say, “If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you aware of it. I had sojourned among you a long while before it—will you not then use reason?”
interpretation: The Prophet here rebuts accusations of fabrication by pointing out two realities: revelation occurs by God’s will, not human invention, and he had lived among his people long before the message yet gained no worldly advantage from it. Thus the verse invites listeners to reflect—if he were seeking gain or inventing this, it would have been evident long before; their persistent rejection therefore rests on obstinacy or failure to reason rather than on credible evidence.

translation: So who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse condemns attributing falsehoods to God or rejecting His revealed signs as the gravest injustice; such behavior corrupts guidance and moral order. Those who fabricate doctrines, ascribe false attributes to Allah, or willfully deny clear evidence place themselves among the ‘‘criminals’’, and their schemes will be frustrated—they lose true success in this life and the hereafter and face divine retribution and nullification of their claims.

translation: And they worship besides Allah that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, “These are our intercessors with Allah.” Say, “Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?” Exalted and transcendent is He above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse condemns the belief that powerless created things—idols, images, or other beings—can serve as real intermediaries with God. Claiming such intercession effectively amounts to instructing or limiting God’s knowledge and authority, as if He needed to be told who may approach Him. The rhetorical question exposes the absurdity: God’s knowledge of the heavens and the earth is perfect and complete, and He alone decides and grants intercession; any attribution of independent mediatory power to others is a form of false association and a denial of God’s transcendence and sovereignty.

translation: And mankind were but one community, then they differed. And if not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, it would have been decreed between them concerning that in which they differ.
interpretation: The verse teaches that humanity began in a fundamental unity but, through free choice, split into differing beliefs and communities. The “word that had already gone forth from your Lord” is understood as God’s prior decree to postpone immediate, final judgment (and to allow the unfolding of history and the sending of guidance). In other words, God permitted the divergence as part of a measured plan — to test people, to give them opportunity to receive guidance and choose, and to let the truth be distinguished from error — with ultimate resolution reserved for His appointed time.

translation: And they say, “Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?” Say, “The unseen is only for Allah — so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait.”
interpretation: The verse answers those who demand spectacular miracles as proof: the knowledge and timing of the unseen belong solely to God, not to human expectation. The Prophet’s role is to convey the message and stand among people in patience, not to grant skeptics’ demands on their schedule. By telling them to ‘wait,’ the text both rebukes arrogant impatience and affirms that ultimate judgment and the clear manifestations of truth occur by God’s will and timing; accountability rests on how people respond now, not on their insistence for immediate prodigies.

translation: And when We make mankind taste mercy after hardship has touched them, behold, they devise plots against Our signs. Say, “God’s plotting is swifter.” Indeed, Our messengers record what you plot.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human gratitude is fragile: when hardship is relieved some people grow presumptuous and begin to scheme—to deny, manipulate, or ignore divine guidance—thinking they can evade consequence. But God’s wisdom and management of events surpass and overtake their designs; what they plot is observed and recorded by His messengers (the recording angels), and will be accounted for or reversed according to His sovereign plan. The passage thus warns against trusting temporary ease, urges humility and thankfulness, and affirms that apparent worldly machinations cannot outstrip divine justice and decree.

translation: He is the One who makes you travel on land and sea. Then when you are in the ships and they sail with them by a favorable wind and they rejoice in it, a stormy wind comes upon it and the waves come at them from every direction, and they think that they are surrounded; they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion, saying, “If You save us from this, we will surely be among the grateful.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God alone governs life’s ease and peril, directing human movement and circumstance. Prosperity often breeds complacency, while sudden disaster strips away self-sufficiency and reveals true dependence on God; people then pledge sincere devotion in hope of deliverance. The passage warns against conditional, crisis-only faith and calls believers to constant, genuine reliance and gratitude toward God rather than vows that arise only in distress.

translation:
فَلَمَّا أَنقَذَهُمْ إِذَا هُم يَبْغُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ ۗ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنَّمَا بَغْيُكُمْ عَلَى أَنفُسِكُمْ ۖ مَتَاعُ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا ۖ ثُمَّ إِلَيْنَا مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَنُنَبِئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ

“When He saved them, immediately they began to transgress on the earth without right. O people, your transgression is only against yourselves — [it is] the enjoyment of the life of this world; then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that Divine deliverance does not free one from moral responsibility: those who, after being rescued, resume injustice are only harming themselves. Their excuse — pursuing the transient comforts of this worldly life — is short‑sighted; such gains do not remove the inevitable return to God, where every action will be disclosed and judged. In short, sin ultimately injures the sinner, and temporary worldly benefit cannot remove final accountability.

translation: The example of the life of this world is but like water which We send down from the sky; then it mingles with the produce of the earth, of which people and livestock eat. And when the earth has taken on its adornment and is embellished and its people think that they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it a harvested field, as though it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We expound the signs for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly prosperity is temporary and deceptive: God’s mercy (likened to rain) produces visible growth that leads people to feel secure and self-sufficient, but that apparent control is an illusion because God’s will can remove those blessings suddenly. It is a warning against pride and complacency, calling people to recognize dependence on God, to be grateful and humble, and to reflect on the deeper, lasting realities beyond transitory material success.

translation: And Allah invites to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: The phrase depicts God’s active call toward ultimate safety and perfection — an abode free of fear, discord and loss (often understood as the final dwelling of the rightly guided and the inner peace of submission). Guidance is presented as a divine gift: God directs whom He chooses to a clearly upright way — a consistent life of sincere monotheism, moral balance and righteous practice that leads toward that promised peace. The verse thus affirms both God’s merciful initiative in calling people to salvation and the reality that receiving guidance involves God’s will together with the seeker’s sincere turning and effort.

translation: For those who do good is the best [reward] — and an increase besides. No gloom nor humiliation shall cover their faces. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere righteous conduct earns not merely a fitting recompense but additional blessing: those who uphold goodness are granted honor and dignity so complete that neither spiritual darkness (despair, alienation from God) norsocial disgrace will touch them. Their worth is preserved and elevated, and they are promised an honored, everlasting abode in Paradise — a state of permanent dignity, security, and closeness to God as the ultimate consequence of true goodness.

translation: And those who have earned evil — the recompense for an evil deed is its like, and abasement will cover them; they will have no protector from Allah. Their faces are as if covered with fragments of night — dark. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein.
interpretation: This verse affirms divine justice: wrongdoing brings its appropriate consequence, both in moral loss and in humiliation. “Recompense of an evil deed is its like” stresses that harmful actions ultimately return to the doer, not necessarily by human retaliation but by results and divine judgment. The humiliation and absence of a protector from God indicate both the social and spiritual ruin of those who persist in evil and reject guidance — they are stripped of honor, help and the light of guidance. The image of faces wrapped in pieces of night conveys the inner state of despair, confusion and shame that accompanies being cut off from God’s mercy; it also signals alienation from truth and from the community of the guided. Calling them “companions of the Fire” with permanence underscores that such consequences are real and lasting unless one turns to sincere repentance and reform.

translation: And the Day We will gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated partners, “Place your partners; you and your partners.” Then We will set a barrier between them, and their partners will say, “You did not worship us.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Resurrection the reality and futility of shirk will be exposed: those who chose partners for God will be forced to summon them but the supposed partners — idols, false gods, or fabricated intercessors — will be powerless and will disown any claim to being worshipped. The “barrier” signifies the irrevocable severance between human beings and their false objects of reliance, showing that accountability rests with the people’s choice and that ultimate authority and support belong solely to God.

translation:
فكفى بالله شهيدا بيننا وبينكم إن كنا عن عبادتكم لغافلين
"Let Allah be a sufficient witness between us and you: that we were heedless concerning your being worshipped."
interpretation: The speakers invoke God as the ultimate witness to affirm that any failure in honoring or recognizing the addressee’s elevated status was not born of malice but of ignorance and negligence. By calling on Allah’s testimony they both assert their claim of sincere unawareness and submit the truth of their statement to God’s judgment, acknowledging that only He can rightly judge intentions and settle disputes between people.

translation: هناك تُبْلَى كل نفس بما أسلفت، ويُرَدُّون إلى الله مولاهم الحق، وتَخْذُلُهم ما كانوا يفترون.
interpretation: الآية تحذر من يوم الحساب حيث تُقاس النفوس على أعمالها ونيّاتها؛ في ذلك اليوم لا ملجأ حقيقي إلا الله – هو المولى الحق الذي يُردّ إليه الناس – وكل أوهام البشر وادعاءاتهم واختراعاتهم (آلهتهم الزائفة، أعذارهم، سمعتهم، أو أي سند دنيوي اعتقدوا أنه ينقذهم) ستتخلى عنهم. بهذا تؤكد الآية مبدأ المسؤولية الفردية بأن ما أعدّ الإنسان من عمل وإخلاص هو وحده الذي يفيد عند الحكم الإلهي، بينما الزيف والادّعاء لا قيمة لهما.

translation: Say, "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Or who possesses hearing and sight? And who brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living? And who directs the affair?" They will say, "Allah." Say, "Then will you not fear [Him]?"
interpretation: By pointing to concrete realities—sustenance, the faculties of perception, the cycle of life and death, and the governance of events—the verse demonstrates that these ultimate functions belong to one Lord alone. Its rhetorical questions elicit the admission “Allah,” then confront that admission with a demand for its ethical consequence: acknowledging God’s sole sovereignty must lead to taqwa (God‑consciousness, reverent fear, grateful dependence, and moral accountability) rather than mere verbal assent.

translation: That is Allah — your Lord, the Truth. So what is there after the Truth except error? How then are you being turned away?
interpretation: The verse underscores that God’s guidance is the definitive reality: once the truth of divine guidance is presented, anything offered in its place is true deviation. The rhetorical questions are a moral rebuke and reminder — they point to the human responsibility to recognize and submit to that final truth, and they expose turning away as a conscious or culpable choice rooted in desire, pride, ignorance, or heedlessness; thus the passage calls for sincere acceptance of God’s guidance and warns of the spiritual consequence of preferring falsehood over what is clearly right.

translation: Thus has the word of your Lord been fulfilled concerning those who transgressed: that they will not believe.
interpretation: It teaches that persistent transgression and deliberate rejection of God's guidance lead to a just outcome: by repeatedly turning away, people bring about a hardening of heart and spiritual incapacity to accept faith, so the divine decree that they remain in disbelief is the just consequence of their own continued choices rather than an arbitrary punishment.

translation:
قل هل من شركائكم من يبدأ الخلق ثم يعيده ۚ قل الله يبدأ الخلق ثم يعيده ۖ فأنى تؤفكون
“Say, ‘Is there among your partners any who begins creation and then repeats it?’ Say, ‘Allah begins creation and then repeats it.’ So how are you deluded?”
interpretation: The verse presents a logical criterion for true divinity: the power to originate life and to bring it back. By affirming that Allah alone begins creation and will re-create it, it nullifies the claims of any purported partners (who show no such power) and rebukes those who persist in following them — exposing their error and affirming God’s exclusive sovereignty over creation and resurrection.

translation: Say, 'Is there among your partners anyone who guides to the truth?' Say, 'Allah guides to the truth.' Then is he who guides to the truth more deserving of being followed, or he who cannot guide unless he is guided? So what is wrong with you — how do you judge?'
interpretation: This statement emphasizes that true guidance belongs to God alone and sets a criterion for legitimate authority: the ability to lead people toward truth. It exposes the irrationality of following powerless beings or idols that have no independent capacity to guide, and it calls people to reassess their standards for whom they obey. The final question confronts moral responsibility — urging reflection on how one forms judgments and prompting a return to principles of reason and accountability in choosing leaders and objects of devotion.

translation: And most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture avails not against the truth at all. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse warns that many people base their beliefs and actions on speculation, assumptions, or popular opinion rather than on sound knowledge and evidence. Such conjecture cannot change reality or the truth and will not stand in place of proper proof; ultimately, God alone knows the inner motives and the actual consequences of people’s deeds. The practical lesson is to seek certainty through sincere investigation and revelation rather than be led astray by rumors, surface impressions, or fashionable claims, because ultimate judgment and accountability rest with God’s all‑knowing awareness.

translation: And it was not conceivable for this Qur'an to be invented by anyone other than Allah; rather it is a confirmation of what preceded it and a detailed exposition of the Book — there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse functions as a rebuttal to claims that the Prophet fabricated scripture: it affirms the Qur’an’s divine origin and authoritative status by linking it to prior revelations and describing it as a clear, doubt‑free explanation. Consequently the Qur’an is presented as the decisive standard for belief and practice — a revelation to be accepted and followed, and a vindication of the Prophet’s role as transmitter, not inventor, of God’s message.

translation: Or do they say, “He invented it”? Say, “Then bring a surah like it and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.”
interpretation: The verse issues a decisive, testable challenge to those who accuse the Prophet of fabricating the Qur’an: if the claim were true, they should be able to produce a comparable chapter or obtain comparable support from any force they worship. Its purpose is not merely rhetorical provocation but to expose the impotence of human artifice and false deities and to defend the Qur’an’s divine origin by setting an open standard — creative, rhetorical, and spiritual — that opponents repeatedly fail to meet. The phrase “if you are truthful” places moral responsibility on the challengers: their refusal or inability to meet the test is evidence of the Qur’an’s authenticity and of the truthfulness of the Prophet’s claim.

translation: But rather they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and when its clarification came to them. Thus did those before them deny. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the habit of rejecting divine guidance from a place of ignorance and arrogance — refusing what one does not fully understand and demanding immediate proof or interpretation. It warns that this attitude is not new: past communities behaved the same way and met ruin. The implicit lesson is to approach revealed truth with humility and openness, because persistent denial born of pride or impatience leads to the same destructive outcome that befell earlier wrongdoers.

translation:
وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُؤْمِنُ بِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَا يُؤْمِنُ بِهِ ۚ وَرَبُّكَ أَعْلَمُ بِالْمُفْسِدِينَ
"And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it; and your Lord knows best the corrupters."
interpretation: The verse teaches that human responses to divine guidance will be mixed—some accept it, some reject it—but the true measure of who corrupts or causes harm is known only to God. It calls for humility in human judgment: we should recognize the diversity of reception, avoid presumptuous labels or punishments based on outward appearances, and trust God’s perfect knowledge and justice in distinguishing and holding accountable the real corrupters.

translation: And if they deny you, say: ‘To me my deeds and to you your deeds; you are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do.’
interpretation: The verse teaches a principle of separation of accountability: when faced with rejection, the right response is to dissociate from others’ choices and leave each person to bear the consequences of their own actions. It affirms the prophet’s duty as conveying the message without coercion and insists that moral responsibility rests individually, placing ultimate judgment in God’s hands while preserving dignity and restraint in dealing with opponents.

translation:
وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَسْتَمِعُونَ إِلَيْكَ ۚ أَفَأَنتَ تَسْمَعُ ٱلصُّمَّ وَلَوْ كَانُوا۟ لَا يَعْقِلُونَ
"And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?"
interpretation: The verse underscores that outward listening does not equal inward reception: some who seem to attend to the Prophet are spiritually 'deaf' and lack the faculty or willingness to grasp guidance. The rhetorical question stresses the Prophet’s human limitation — he cannot force comprehension or faith upon those whose hearts and minds are closed; true understanding and guidance are granted by God and require the listener’s openness and reason.

translation: And among them are those who look toward you. Would you then guide the blind, even though they will not see?
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that guidance is ultimately a matter of God and of inner receptivity: outward attention to the Messenger does not guarantee spiritual perception, and no human—however earnest—can make those whose hearts are closed truly ‘see’ faith; readiness of heart and God’s granting of insight are required for real guidance.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people in the least; but it is the people who are wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes God’s absolute justice: He does not oppress or punish anyone without just cause. When individuals experience loss, punishment, or moral failure, this is attributed to the consequences of their own choices—disbelief, injustice, corruption, or ignoring divine guidance—rather than to any unfairness on God’s part. In other words, responsibility and accountability lie with human beings; divine outcomes reflect people’s deeds and moral consequences, not arbitrary divine injustice.

translation: And the Day He will gather them, it will seem as if they had not remained but an hour of the day; they will recognize one another. Indeed, those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost, and they were not guided.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the worldly life is fleeting and will be perceived as vanishingly brief when people stand before God; in that moment all pretenses fall away and true realities — who believed, who denied, who was rightly guided — become plain. The real loss is not merely death or worldly failure but the forfeiture of guidance and the eternal good: those who denied meeting with God wasted their opportunity to be guided and thus suffer ultimate ruin and regret.

translation: And perhaps We will show you some of those whom We have warned, or We will cause you to die; then to Us will be their return. And Allah is a Witness over what they do.
interpretation: This address to the Prophet reassures and cautions: God may allow him to witness a portion of the punishment promised to the wrongdoers or may take him away before that occurs, but in every case their ultimate return is to God, Who fully observes and is witness to all their deeds. The verse teaches that apparent delay, evasion, or temporary success of transgressors does not negate accountability; final judgment belongs to God alone, so the Prophet’s duty is steadfast perseverance and trust in divine justice rather than anxiety over immediate outcomes.

translation: ولكل أمة رسولٌ؛ فإذا جاء رسولهم قُضي بينهم بالقسط وهم لا يُظلمون.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد مبدأ العدالة الإلهية: الله يبعث لكل قوم مبينًا للحق، ومجيء الرسول يضع معيارًا واضحًا يُقاس به سلوك الناس، فتصير مسؤوليتهم مبنية على ما عُرف إليهم من الهداية. هكذا يكون الفصل بينهم إما بالتصديق واتباع الحق أو بالرفض وتحمل تبعاته، وفي كل حال يكون الحكم عادلاً لا ظلم فيه لأن الجزاء يُعطى بحسب ما وُجّهت إليه عقولهم وقلوبهم وما اختاروه.

translation: And they say, "When will this promise be, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The utterance reflects a dismissive tactic, not sincere inquiry: doubters demand the exact timing of God's promised outcome to cast doubt on the messenger and to postpone responsibility. The verse thus exposes the arrogance and procrastination of those who reject warning, and implicitly reminds that the knowledge and timing of God's decrees belong to God alone, not to human skeptics.

translation: Say, “I do not possess for myself any harm or benefit except what Allah wills. For every people is a term; when their term comes, they cannot delay it for an hour, nor can they bring it forward.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate control over benefit, harm, life and death belongs solely to God and that human agency — even that of the Prophet — is limited; every community has an appointed term ordained by God that cannot be hastened or postponed. The practical implication is moral: cultivate reliance on God (tawakkul), humility about human power, and responsibility in preparing for the appointed term rather than seeking to control outcomes beyond God’s decree.

translation: قُلْ أَرَأَيْتُمْ إِنْ أَتَاكُمْ عَذَابُهُ بَيَاتًا أَوْ نَهَارًا مَا يَسْتَعْجِلُ مِنْهُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ
interpretation: The Prophet is told to confront the deniers: whether God's punishment comes by night or by day, the guilty will be powerless to avert or hasten against it. Their arrogance and attempts to evade reckoning are futile; the verse emphasizes the inevitability of divine justice and aims to humble and warn those who presume they can escape it.

translation: Is it a fault that, when it has come to pass, you believe in it? Now — when before you had been hastening its coming?
interpretation: The verse censures those whose professed belief arrives only after they have long desired and even urged divine punishment: such delayed faith reveals hypocrisy and insincerity. Belief born solely from witnessing the consequence does not erase earlier rejection or the moral responsibility attached to it, and therefore is spiritually deficient despite its outward declaration.

translation: Then it will be said to those who did wrong, “Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you recompensed with anything except for what you used to earn?”
interpretation: The verse emphasizes divine justice and personal responsibility: the inhabitants of Hell are told that their eternal suffering is the direct and fitting consequence of their own deeds and choices. The rhetorical question underscores that no one will be treated unfairly or spared without cause—each soul receives only what it has earned, so hope for escape or blaming others is vain.

translation: وَيَسْتَنبِئُونَكَ أَهُوَ ۖ قُلْ إِنَّ رَبِّي إِنَّهُ لَحَقٌ ۖ وَمَا أَنتُم بِمُعْجِزِينَ
interpretation: الآية تردّ على من يسألون عن حقيقة الرسالة بأنها أمراً قابلاً للشك: يأمر النبي أن يؤكد بقَسَمٍ بربّه أن هذا القول حقٌ ثابت، ويذكّر أن مشكّكيْن لا يملكون أن يبطِلوا هذا الحقّ أو يوقفوا تنفيذ مشيئة الله؛ الحقّ قائمٌ بما هو عليه رغم أحقاد المنكرين.

translation: And if every soul that did wrong had whatever is on earth, it would surely offer it as ransom; and they will conceal their remorse when they see the punishment. And it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse teaches that no accumulation of worldly riches can undo persistent wrongdoing or buy salvation at the moment of reckoning: people would gladly give the whole world to escape punishment, yet too-late remorse and attempts at ransom will not avert divine justice. It stresses the need for timely, sincere repentance and righteous action, and it affirms that God’s judgment is perfectly fair — everyone will receive what is due and no one will be treated unjustly.

translation: Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute ownership of all existence and, on that basis, stresses that His promises—most importantly the coming of judgment and recompense—are certain and will be fulfilled. Its warning is that many people remain heedless or deluded by worldly concerns or arrogance, failing to recognize God’s sovereignty and the moral consequences that follow; therefore it calls for sober awareness, humility before Divine authority, and preparation for the assured Divine reckoning.

translation: He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This asserts God’s exclusive sovereignty over life and death; realizing that every soul ultimately returns to Him is meant to awaken humility, trust in His decree, and a readiness for accountability that shapes righteous conduct and detaches one from worldly arrogance.

translation: O mankind, there has come to you a reminder from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts and guidance and mercy for the believers.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a universal divine admonition whose immediate effect is inward: it cures spiritual maladies — doubt, confusion, anxiety, moral sickness — by clarifying truth and awakening the conscience. Its role as guidance steers those who accept it onto the straight path, and as mercy it effects inward transformation and consolation for believers; addressed to all, its restorative power requires sincere reception to take effect.

translation: Say, “In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy — in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they amass.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true joy and ultimate benefit lie in recognizing and relying on God’s grace and mercy — which confer guidance, forgiveness, inner peace and lasting good — and therefore believers should value and rejoice in divine favor above the fleeting accumulation of worldly wealth.

translation: Say, "Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision and then you have made of it unlawful and lawful?" Say, "Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent against Allah?"
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who, without divine authorization, assert that certain of God’s provisions are forbidden or permitted; it exposes the arrogance of inventing religious rulings and attributing them to Allah. By highlighting that sustenance and its lawful status come from God, the verse challenges human claims to legislate for God, warns against fabricating commandments and misrepresenting divine will, and calls people to submit to what Allah has revealed rather than to their own contrivances.

translation:
وما ظن الذين يفترون على الله الكذب يوم القيامة ۗ إن الله لذو فضل على الناس ولكن أكثرهم لا يشكرون
"And what will be the fate of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed Allah is Possessor of bounty toward the people, yet most of them do not give thanks."
interpretation: The verse functions as a stern moral warning: fabricating falsehoods about God is a grave transgression that will be exposed and judged on the Day of Resurrection.
