It also reminds that God’s abundant favors and guidance toward humanity make human ingratitude and dishonest speech especially blameworthy — the proper response to divine bounty is recognition, gratitude, and truthful conduct.

translation: And you are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite any portion of the Qurʼān, nor do you perform any deed, but We are witnesses over you when you are engrossed in it. And not the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heaven, nor anything smaller or greater than that, escapes your Lord’s knowledge—everything is in a clear record.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s continuous, intimate knowledge and witnessing of every human inner state, speech, and action: nothing is private in the sense of being unknown to the Lord. The mention of reciting the Qurʼān, being involved in affairs, and performing deeds emphasizes that both outward acts and inward preoccupations are observed; “witnesses” implies God’s awareness (and the recording agents He appoints) accompany people even while they are immersed in what they do. By adding that not even the weight of an atom—smaller or greater—escapes Him and that all is preserved in a clear Book, the verse teaches two connected lessons: accountability (every detail will be brought to account) and reassurance (nothing is omitted from divine justice or mercy). Practically, it calls for conscious sincerity and moral responsibility in private and public life, and it comforts the oppressed that their condition is seen and documented by One who is just and precise.

translation:
أَلَا إِنَّ أَوْلِيَاءَ اللَّهِ لَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ
"Behold, truly the friends (awliyā’) of God—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve."
interpretation: The verse assures that those who are genuinely allied with God—those who live in sincere faith, obedience and trust—are granted a deep, abiding security: they are spared ultimate fear and sorrow because of God’s protection, guidance and promised reward. This does not mean they will be free of everyday trials, but that their inner state and final outcome are secure: fears that stem from loss, condemnation or abandonment are removed, and grief is replaced by certainty and hope through nearness to God.

translation: Those who believed and were conscious (mindful) of God.
interpretation: It refers to people whose faith is coupled with taqwa — a sustained God‑consciousness that shapes both inner disposition and outward behavior: sincere obedience, avoidance of sin, moral vigilance, humility before God, and reliance on Him in conduct and choices.

translation: For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. There is no changing in the words of Allah. That is the great success.
interpretation: The verse asserts the certainty and permanence of God’s promises: those who are rightfully entitled to God’s favor will receive genuine good—both as ripening consequences in this world (guidance, inner peace, beneficial outcomes) and as ultimate reward in the Hereafter. By stating that God’s words do not change, the text emphasizes divine reliability and the unassailable nature of His decrees and promises; human doubts, delays, or oppositions cannot nullify what God has affirmed. Thus “the great success” refers to attaining God’s pleasure and the eternal felicity guaranteed by His unchangeable word, and it calls believers to trust and live by that sure promise rather than seek transient or illusory securities.

translation:
وَلَا يُحْزِنْكَ قَوْلُهُمْ ۘ إِنَّ الْعِزَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا ۚ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ
“Do not let their words sadden you. Indeed, all honor and might belong entirely to Allah; He is the All‑Hearing, the All‑Knowing.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that a believer’s dignity and hope must rest on God’s sovereign honor rather than on human approval or reproach. Because true power, status and ultimate vindication are wholly in Allah’s hands—and He fully hears and knows what is hidden—one should not be emotionally undone by others’ speech. This grounding in God calls for patience, trust, and restraint: respond with steadfastness and reliance on divine justice instead of seeking immediate worldly vindication or being crushed by slander.

translation: Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those whom people invoke besides Him are not partners [with Allah]; they follow nothing but conjecture, and they are only uttering falsehood.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over every being in heaven and earth and rejects any real power or partnership for the beings people worship beside Him. It teaches that these supposed deities or intermediaries neither control outcomes nor deserve reliance; devotion to them rests on mere assumptions, inherited opinions, or idle talk rather than knowledge. Thus the passage warns that turning to anything other than God is basing faith and trust on conjecture and falsehood, and calls for recognizing and submitting to the One who truly owns and governs all existence.

translation: He is the One who made the night for you that you may rest in it, and the day to give you sight. Indeed in that are signs for people who listen.
interpretation: The verse directs attention beyond physical description to purpose: the alternation of night and day is a deliberate, wisdom-filled ordinance from God that aligns with human needs—night for repose, inwardness and renewal; day for clarity, work and social life. Because this cycle is regular, beneficial and finely suited to human life, it serves as an āyah (a sign) intended to awaken thoughtful, attentive people to God’s providential design, urging them to reflect, be grateful, and recognize divine authority and wisdom.

translation: They say, “Allah has taken a son.” Exalted is He! He is free of need; to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. You have no authority for this—do you attribute to Allah what you do not know?
interpretation: The verse condemns the attribution of human familial relations to God and affirms His absolute transcendence and self-sufficiency: claiming that Allah has a son is a baseless, anthropomorphic projection that imposes created categories on the Creator. By stating that everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Him and that those who assert such a thing have no authority or proof, the text warns against speaking about the Divine without knowledge and insists that legitimate claims about God must be supported by evidence, not by conjecture or cultural imagination.

translation: Say, “Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah will not succeed.”
interpretation: The verse warns that deliberately attributing falsehoods to God—whether by inventing doctrines, claiming false revelations, ascribing partners or attributes to Him that are not true, or otherwise misrepresenting His will—results in spiritual and moral failure: such fabricators are cut off from true guidance, lose Divine favor, and will not attain success in this life or the Hereafter.

translation: A provision (enjoyment) in the life of this world; then to Us is their return, and We will make them taste the severe punishment for what they used to disbelieve.
interpretation: الآية تشير إلى حكم أعمق من مجرد وصف حالة دنيا: النعم الدنيوية التي ينعم بها الكافرون هي متاع زائل وابتلاء يختبر قلوبهم، والاعتماد عليها أو التمادي في إنكار الحق لا يغيّر حكم الله. «ثم إلينا مرجعهم» تؤكد حتمية الحساب والقيامة، وعبارة «نذيقهم العذاب الشديد بما كانوا يكفرون» تربط العقاب بعلة واضحة — الكفر المتكرر والمقصود — فتجعل الجزاء مستحقاً ومتناسباً مع الرفض المتمادي للهدى. بعبارة أخرى الآية تذكر بأن التمتع بالدنيا لا يبرئ من المسؤولية الأخروية، وأن الجزاء على الكفر واقع لا محالة إذا استمر الإنسان في إنكاره.

translation: And recite to them the story of Noah when he said to his people, “O my people, if my remaining among you and my reminding you of the signs of Allah is burdensome upon you, then upon Allah I have relied. So assemble your plan and your partners, and let not your plan be a cause of grief to you; then carry out your plan against me and do not give me respite.”
interpretation: The verse teaches the prophetic stance toward persistent rejection: after faithfully delivering the message, the prophet places his trust in God rather than clinging to people’s approval, challenges opponents to act on their hostility, and thereby exposes that human plotting cannot thwart divine will. It affirms both the moral integrity of refusing to compromise truth for acceptance and the reliance on God’s judgment when people persist in disbelief.

translation: So if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any reward; my reward is only from Allah. And I have been commanded to be of those who submit (Muslims).
interpretation: This statement emphasizes the prophet’s absolute sincerity and reliance on God: his mission is not motivated by worldly gain or personal advantage but by obedience to God, who alone will dispense recompense. It teaches that calling others to truth must be done without seeking payment or coercion, accepting people’s response with trust in divine justice, and embodying submission to God as the fundamental orientation of the messenger’s life and conduct.

translation: But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ark, and made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So observe how was the end of those who were warned.
interpretation: The verse affirms that when a messenger (here, Noah) was rejected, God intervened to preserve the obedient — rescuing the believers in the ark and establishing them as 'khulafā’' (successors) who inherit the earth and continue human life and God’s mandate — while bringing decisive punishment on those who denied the clear signs. The lesson is both historical and moral: God vindicates His truth and protects the faithful, and the visible fate of past communities serves as a concrete warning that rejection of divine guidance leads to ruin; therefore listeners are urged to learn from that outcome and take the warning seriously.

translation: Then We sent after them messengers to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs; yet they would not believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.
interpretation: God repeatedly sends messengers bearing clear evidence, but when a people persistently reject and cling to the falsehoods they once embraced, their refusal becomes entrenched. “Sealing the hearts” here means that, as a direct consequence of prolonged obstinacy and wrongdoing, their capacity to perceive and accept guidance is blunted or withdrawn: they are left to the moral and spiritual state they have chosen. This sealing is therefore both a just consequence of persistent transgression and the final stage in a process that begins with deliberate rejection of truth.

translation: Then We sent, after them, Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs; but they grew arrogant, and they were a people given to crime.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring moral truth: when clear guidance and evidence are presented, persistent rejection arising from pride and attachment to power becomes culpable wrongdoing. Arrogance before the truth — especially by rulers and their inner circles who oppress others — converts disbelief into criminality in God’s sight. The passage warns that miracles and signs are meant to remove excuses, so stubborn refusal grounded in pride carries full responsibility and invites divine accountability.

translation: But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, “This is plain sorcery.”
interpretation: When God sends clear, divine guidance, some people refuse it and instead call it “magic” to discredit it; this verse highlights a common defensive reaction—labeling the revelation as trickery to avoid acknowledging its divine source and the moral responsibility that acceptance would entail, revealing their stubbornness, arrogance, and spiritual blind spot.

translation: Moses said, “Do you (now) call this the truth after it has come to you? Is this man a magician? Indeed the magicians will not succeed.”
interpretation: Moses' rebuke teaches that clear divine truth cannot legitimately be dismissed as mere sorcery; those who insist on calling God’s manifest signs trickery are motivated by blindness, pride, or self-interest, and though deceit may appear to prevail briefly, such falsehood and the people who practice it will ultimately fail and be exposed, while God’s message endures and triumphs.

translation: They said, “Have you come to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon, and to be arrogant in the land? We will not believe you.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a common human resistance to reform: people reject a prophetic call by appealing to ancestral custom and by accusing the caller of seeking worldly prestige. Their refusal is rooted not in an impartial assessment of truth but in attachment to inherited practices and fear of losing status or honor—using tradition and the charge of ambition as defenses against accepting change.

translation: وقال فرعون: «ائتوني بكل ساحر عليم»
interpretation: الآية تكشف كيف يستجيب الطاغية بالاستعانة بكل مهارة دنيوية وخداع لصدّ الحقيقة: يساوي بين العلم الحقيقي ومهارة الخداع ويحشد الخبرات البارعة لإثبات سلطته ودرء ما يهدد موقعه، مما يظهر غطرسة قلبه وخوفه من فقدان السيطرة.

translation: So when the magicians came, Moses said to them, "Cast down whatever you are going to cast."
interpretation: Moses deliberately invites the magicians to perform their act in full view so that their trickery will be exposed and God’s clear sign can be distinguished from mere sleight of hand; his command creates a public test intended to reveal truth, demonstrate reliance on divine support, and enable people to judge between falsehood and a genuine miracle.

translation: When they cast (down), Moses said, “What you have brought is sorcery; indeed Allah will annul it. Indeed Allah does not set right the deeds of the corrupters.”
interpretation: The verse teaches a general principle: God exposes and nullifies deception and will not bless or make successful actions rooted in corruption and mischief. It affirms trust in divine justice over impressive outward displays—what depends on fraud cannot stand where God wills truth and reform.

translation: وَيُحِقُّ اللَّهُ الْحَقَّ بِكَلِمَاتِهِ وَلَوْ كَرِهَ الْمُجْرِمُونَ
interpretation: Allah will bring the truth to prevail by His own decrees and revelations—through His words, the sending of messengers, the guidance revealed and the unfolding of events—and the hostility or hatred of wrongdoers cannot prevent or overturn that divine establishment of truth; ultimately falsehood will be exposed and defeated despite their dislike.

translation:
فما آمن لموسى إلا ذرية من قومه على خوف من فرعون وملئهم أن يفتنهم ۚ وإن فرعون لعال في الأرض وإنه لمن المسرفين
"But none of the people believed in Moses except a few of his descendants, out of fear of Pharaoh and his chiefs that they would be persecuted. Indeed Pharaoh was arrogant in the land, and indeed he was of the transgressors."
interpretation: The verse highlights how the reality of oppressive power can suppress sincere acceptance of truth: when rulers are violent and proud, many will conceal or reject belief out of self-preservation, so only a courageous minority will openly embrace the message. It also characterises tyrants like Pharaoh as arrogant and excessive, whose pride and transgression justify warning and moral condemnation rather than accommodation.

translation: وقال موسى: «يا قوم، إن كنتم آمنتم بالله فعليه توكلوا إن كنتم مسلمين»
interpretation: الآية تأكيد على أن الإيمان الحقيقي لا يقتصر على القول بل يُعرَف بتجسيده في التوكل على الله؛ توكيل الله يعني أن يضع المؤمن ثقته في حمايته وقدره ويعتمد عليه في الشدائد مع مواصلة العمل والطاعة. بالقول «إن كنتم مسلمين» يُشير النبي موسى إلى أن الاستسلام لله يظهر في هذا الاتكال، وأن الوقوف بثقة أمام الخوف والاعتماد على الحيل الدنيوية دليل على صدق الإيمان.

translation: فقالوا: "على الله توكلنا. ربنا لا تجعلنا فتنةً للقوم الظالمين."
interpretation: العبارة تعبّر عن إقرار المؤمنين بتوكّلهم الكامل على الله وطلبهم الحماية منه من أن يُصبحوا سببًا أو موضوعًا لفتنة لدى الظالمين — أي ألا تَجعل حالهم، ثباتهم على الحق، أو ظروفهم سببًا لامتحان يزيد من ظلم الآخرين أو مبررًا لتعنيفهم، ولا أن يُستغل وجودهم ليُغرَق الناس في الظلم أو لتزداد محنتهم بالاضطهاد والابتلاء الذي يهدد إيمانهم أو سلامتهم.

translation: And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.
interpretation: A humble plea that true rescue from those who reject and oppose the truth comes not by human effort but by God’s compassion; it expresses reliance on divine mercy as the means of protection from spiritual and worldly harm inflicted by the disbelieving, and affirms trust that only God’s mercy can effect deliverance.

translation: And We revealed to Moses and his brother, “Establish dwellings for your people in Egypt, and make your houses places of worship, and keep up the prayer.” And give glad tidings to the believers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance combines practical community care with spiritual discipline: when relocating or reorganizing a people, leaders must also ensure that ordinary domestic life is sanctified by regular worship. Turning homes into places of devotion and maintaining the prayer preserves the community’s covenant with God during upheaval, and the promise of glad tidings reassures believers that steadfastness in these duties secures God’s mercy and support.

translation: Moses said, “Our Lord! Indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs beauty and wealth in the life of this world, [so that] they may lead people astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts so that they do not believe until they see the painful punishment.”
interpretation: Moses is observing that God’s giving of splendor and riches to Pharaoh and his circle becomes the means by which they and those around them are seduced away from the path of truth. His prayer asks God to remove the material power that sustains their arrogance (“obliterate their wealth”) and to let their stubborn rejection stand exposed (“harden their hearts”) so that no insincere or opportunistic profession of faith will neutralize the lesson. In this reading the request is not a capricious desire for endless punishment but a plea for manifest justice: that the pretence of worldly success not shelter oppressors from the consequences of their rejection, and that the truth be made unmistakable by the eventual appearance of the painful retribution.

translation: "He said, ‘Your prayer has been answered; so be steadfast, and do not follow the way of those who do not know.’"
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine forgiveness or acceptance is not merely a return to the previous state but a mandate for enduring transformation: استقيما (be steadfast/upright) implies sustained obedience, moral firmness and continuous vigilance rather than a momentary act. The warning not to follow those who “do not know” cautions against imitating desires, heedless customs, or leaders guided by ignorance (including satanic promptings); such imitation perpetuates error. In short, acceptance by God obliges one to cultivate knowledge, resist misleading examples, and maintain a steady, principled path.

translation: And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his hosts pursued them in tyranny and enmity; until when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims."
interpretation: This verse teaches that a last‑moment verbal profession of faith, made when one’s life and choices have already placed one under God’s judgment, cannot substitute for sincere, sustained submission and righteous conduct. Pharaoh’s declaration, uttered at the point of drowning, shows recognition of the truth but not genuine repentance or prior acceptation by God; Allah’s assessment rests on the reality of the heart and the consistency of one’s deeds, and divine justice and decree are realized — salvation is by true, accepted faith and submission, not merely desperate words at the brink of death.

translation: الآن وقد عصيت قبل وكنت من المفسدين: "Now — I have disobeyed previously and was among the corrupters."
interpretation: The phrase functions as a candid admission and turning point: the speaker acknowledges a prior pattern of rebellion and harmful conduct, implying awareness of responsibility and the need for repentance and moral reform rather than denial or justification.

translation: So today We will save you with your body so that you may be a sign for those who come after you; and indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs.
interpretation: God’s intervention in preserving or restoring the physical person functions as an unmistakable, tangible demonstration of His power over life and death meant to serve as a lasting proof for later generations; the verse teaches that such concrete signs are intended to remove doubt about resurrection and prophecy, yet it warns that despite these manifest proofs many people remain inattentive or indifferent to divine evidence.

translation: And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a secure abode and provided them with good things, and they did not differ until knowledge came to them. Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they used to differ.
interpretation: This verse reminds that God bestowed security, provision and revealed guidance to a people, yet after the arrival of that knowledge they began to split into disputing groups; the lesson is that mere possession of revelation or learned status can become a source of division when pride, partisan interest, or misapplied reasoning override sincere submission. Ultimate justice and the resolution of such disputes belong to God on the Day of Judgment, so true knowledge must lead to humility and obedience rather than factionalism.

translation: So if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so never be among the doubters.
interpretation: Addressing the Prophet (and by extension believers facing skepticism), the verse says that if questions arise about the revelation, one should consult the knowledgeable readers of earlier scriptures — not to accept their authority over God's message but to seek confirmation and clarification from those familiar with the prior revelations. This consultation underscores the continuity and corroboration between the Quran and earlier revelations and serves primarily as reassurance: the message given is true, divinely sourced, and therefore should remove hesitation and doubt.

translation: And do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.
interpretation: The verse warns against rejecting God’s revelations and the clear signs—whether in Scripture or in creation—and explains that such denial is not a neutral error but a turning away from guidance that results in true loss: loss of divine mercy, right guidance, moral integrity, and ultimate success in the Hereafter. It therefore exhorts the listener to humility and acceptance of God’s proofs, since persisting in denial leads to spiritual and existential ruin.

translation:
إِنَّ الَّذِينَ حِقَّتْ عَلَيْهِم كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ
"Indeed, those upon whom the Word of your Lord has come to pass will not believe."
interpretation: It indicates that when God’s decisive judgment (a consequence pronounced because people persistently rejected the truth) has taken effect upon certain people, their hearts become closed and they will not accept faith — a moral consequence of their persistent denial and stubbornness, serving as a warning that continued rejection of guidance leads to a final state in which belief is withheld.

translation: And even if every sign were to come to them, until they see the painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns the stubborn refusal of those whose hearts are closed: they demand the spectacle of punishment itself as a condition for belief, showing that their rejection is not from lack of evidence but from willful obstinacy. It teaches that faith requires sincere acceptance of guidance, not merely waiting for miraculous punishments to be convinced, and warns that insisting on such a sign will only hasten the very ruin they mock.

translation: Had there not been a town that believed — and whose belief benefited it — the punishment would have seized the wrongdoers; but We spared the people of Jonah: when they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and granted them enjoyment for a while.
interpretation: God’s mercy and wisdom sometimes delay or avert collective punishment because the presence and faith of some believers benefit their community; the example of the people of Jonah shows that sincere turning to God can lift public humiliation and bring a temporary reprieve in worldly life, underscoring both the power of repentance/faith to avert immediate calamity and the transitory nature of worldly relief.

translation:
وَلَوْ شَاءَ رَبُّكَ لَآمَنَ مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًا ۚ أَفَأَنتَ تُكْرِهُ النَّاسَ حَتَّىٰ يَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ
“And if your Lord had willed, all who are on the earth would have believed — all of them. So are you to compel people until they become believers?”
interpretation: The verse underscores that God’s omnipotence coexists with human moral responsibility: although God could have caused universal belief, He permits human freedom and the moral test that entails. It thus reminds the Prophet (and the community) that guidance is ultimately granted by God’s will, not by human coercion; the Prophet’s role is to convey the message and invite, not to force conviction. The persistence of unbelief in some people is therefore part of God’s sovereign wisdom and the arena of human accountability, and believers should respond with patient preaching, trust in God’s judgment, and rejection of compulsion in matters of faith.

translation: And it is not for any soul to believe except by permission of Allah; and He places the filth (al-rijs) upon those who do not use reason.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith ultimately comes by God’s allowing and enabling rather than merely by accidental choice or sheer human whim; receptive hearts are opened only with Divine permission. At the same time it ascribes the condition of rejection to those who refuse to reflect and exercise their intellect: because they persist in heedlessness or stubbornness, God sets upon them ‘al-rijs’—a spiritual stain or abasement that manifests as misguidance, moral corruption, and humiliation, rendering them unable or unwilling to perceive the truth. Thus the statement both affirms God’s sovereign role in granting guidance and indicates that deliberate neglect of reason and reflection brings about one’s own spiritual downfall.

translation: Say, “Observe what is in the heavens and the earth.” Yet neither the signs nor the warnings will avail a people who do not believe.
interpretation: The verse calls people to reflect on creation as testimony to God and to heed prophetic admonitions, but it also teaches a hard truth: evidence and warnings cannot effect guidance in hearts that are closed by arrogance, desire, or entrenched refusal. It shifts responsibility—showing that the messenger’s role is to present clear signs and cautions, while acceptance depends on inner receptivity. Thus true guidance requires not merely external proofs but a humble, open will to recognize and respond to them; without that openness the clearest signs and sternest warnings remain fruitless.

translation: So do they await anything except the (same) days as those who passed away before them? Say, “Then wait; indeed I am with you among those who who wait.”
interpretation: The verse confronts those who demand immediate, spectacular proof by pointing to the historical pattern: communities that rejected their messengers faced the consequences of their refusal. The Prophet’s reply—“Then wait; I am with you among those who wait”—is not a retreat but a stance of patient trust. It teaches that divine judgment unfolds in God’s timing, not by human insistence; the warning is real and inevitable, yet the Prophet stands in solidarity with people, exercising restraint and entrusting outcome to God while continuing to call them. The moral: one should not expect to force God’s signs on demand, but submit to divine timing, heed the warning from past nations, and cultivate patience and steadfastness in the face of rejection.

translation:
ثم ننجي رسلنا والذين آمنوا ۚ كذلك حقا علينا ننج المؤمنين
"Then We save Our messengers and those who believe. Thus it is incumbent upon Us to save the believers."
interpretation: The verse declares a divine guarantee: God, by His will and wisdom, will ultimately deliver and vindicate His messengers and the sincere believers. "Thus it is incumbent upon Us" is not a human‑legal obligation but an affirmation of God’s unchanging promise and responsibility — that through preservation, support in trials, and final salvation He will protect and establish the faithful according to His decree.

translation: Say, O people, if you are in doubt about my religion, then I do not worship those whom you worship instead of Allah; rather I worship Allah, He who takes your souls, and I have been commanded to be among the believers.
interpretation: The verse confronts doubt by shifting the criterion of true divinity to God’s sovereign power over life and death: the Prophet’s worship is not tribal habit or blind imitation but a response to the One who controls existence and will hold people accountable. It therefore calls listeners to judge faith by the reality of God’s authority and the moral duty to submit to the Divine command, rather than by inherited or powerless idols.

translation: And set your face toward the religion, upright; and do not be of the polytheists.
interpretation: A command to align the whole person—belief, worship, intentions and conduct—steadfastly with pure monotheism (hanīfiyyah). It calls for an upright, sincere orientation to God that preserves the primordial fitrah, requires perseverance and integrity in faith despite social pressure, and rejects any compromise, syncretism or association of partners with God.

translation: And do not call upon, besides Allah, that which will neither benefit you nor harm you; and if you do, then indeed you are of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse forbids directing worship, supplication, or ultimate reliance to anything other than God—powers, idols, people, or objects that have no real ability to affect your final good or harm. Treating powerless things as sources of ultimate help or protection is a misplaced trust and constitutes an injustice (shirk) against the true order of divine sovereignty; by doing so one wrongs oneself and stands among the unjust.

translation: And if Allah touches you with harm, then none can remove it except He; and if He intends for you good, then none can repel His bounty. He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants, and He is the Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s exclusive sovereignty over suffering and blessing: no created cause can ultimately lift a hardship or grant a benefit except by God’s will. It teaches that trials and gifts come under divine wisdom — trials may serve as purification, discipline, or a means to draw a person back to God, while blessings are bestowed according to His knowledge and mercy. Believers are therefore called to respond with patient reliance, sincere supplication and repentance in adversity, and grateful, responsible use of God’s favors in prosperity, always holding hope in His forgiveness and compassion.

translation: Say, O people, the Truth has come to you from your Lord; whoever is guided does so for the benefit of his own soul, and whoever goes astray does so to its harm — and I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God has delivered clear guidance, but acceptance of that guidance is an individual moral act: guidance and misguidance are consequences that accrue to each person’s own soul. The messenger’s function is to convey the truth, not to coerce belief or to bear others’ responsibility; ultimate accountability and judgement rest with God. Thus the passage emphasizes human free will, personal responsibility before divine law, and the limits of the prophet’s authority as a caller rather than a guardian.

translation: And follow what is revealed to you and be patient until Allah gives judgment; and He is the best of judges.
interpretation: The verse commands steadfast adherence to divine guidance and counsel, paired with patient forbearance when faced with injustice, slander, or delay, entrusting ultimate vindication and decision to Allah alone—because His wisdom and justice surpass human judgment—so one should refrain from rash retaliation and rely on God’s timing and fair decree.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then explained in detail — from One Who is Wise, All‑Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is a divinely authored, coherent guidance: its statements are deliberately established with authority and then unfolded in ways suited to human comprehension. The disjointed letters signal that aspects of revelation transcend immediate human conventions, while the description “from One Wise, All‑Acquainted” reassures that every formulation, gradation, and specification in the text serves a wise, knowing purpose; therefore apparent brevity, repetition, or gradual clarification in the scripture is intentional and grounded in divine wisdom and intimate knowledge of people’s needs and capacities.

translation: Worship none but Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of glad tidings.
interpretation: This verse is a clear exhortation to exclusive devotion to God (tawḥīd) and a statement about the Prophet’s office: his message is not personal opinion but divine mandate. By commanding worship of Allah alone, it calls for full spiritual and practical reliance on God, abandoning all forms of idolatry or substitutes; by identifying himself as a warner and a bringer of good news, the Prophet emphasizes that his role is twofold—he warns of the consequences of disbelief and sin, and gives hope of God’s mercy and reward to those who repent and obey—so that people are motivated both by fear of wrongdoing’s consequences and by hope for divine grace, leading them toward moral reform and sincere faith.

translation: وَأَنْ تَسْتَغْفِرُوا رَبَّكُمْ ثُمَّ تُوبُوا إِلَيْهِ ۚ يُمَتِّعْكُمْ مُتَاعًا حَسَنًا إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مَّسْمُوعٍ وَيُؤْتِي كُلَّ ذِي فَضْلٍ فَضْلَهُ ۚ وَإِن تَوَلَّوْا فَإِنِّي أَخَافُ عَلَيْكُمْ عَذَابَ يَوْمٍ كَبِيرٍ
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أنّ الاستغفار والتوبة الصادقة يفتحان باب رحمة الله الذي قد يمنح من يستغفرون متاعاً حسناً في الدنيا ولمدة محددة، وأنّ الله يقيم عدله فيعطي كل ذي فضل جزاءه. لكنها تحذّر أيضاً أن هذه النِعَم الدنيوية ليست ضماناً نهائياً فمتى أصرّ الناس على الرفض والتولّي عن الحق فإنّ الخوف الحقيقي هو عذاب يوم الحساب؛ بمعنى آخر: ادخلوا التوبة بصدق لبلوغ رحمته ونوال الجزاء، وإلا فالعقاب في الآخرة قادم لا مفرّ منه.

translation: Your return is to Allah; and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse asserts that every person will ultimately be returned to God, who alone possesses absolute power and authority over all affairs; this undercuts any reliance on worldly security or injustice by affirming that deeds and intentions are within His purview and will be accounted for, so believers are called to live with awareness of divine accountability, to seek justice and repentance, and to trust in God’s sovereign ability to right wrongs and administer final judgment.

translation: Behold, they draw up their breasts as if to hide themselves from Him; and when they wrap their garments about them, He knows what they conceal and what they declare. Indeed He is Knower of the innermost hearts.
interpretation: The verse teaches that outward concealment—drawing in one’s chest, wrapping one’s clothes, or any external show of hiding—cannot shield a person from God’s knowledge. Allah sees both secret intentions and public actions; therefore hypocrisy and attempts to deceive divine scrutiny are futile. Moral accountability is ultimately tied to the sincerity of the heart, since nothing of the innermost thoughts and feelings is hidden from Him.

translation: And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah; and He knows its dwelling-place and its repository. All is recorded in a clear Book.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God is the ultimate provider and knower of every living being’s needs, habitats, and outcomes: “rizq” embraces the means and circumstances that sustain life, while knowledge of each creature’s “mustaqar” and “mastawdaʿ” (place of rest and place of storage) shows God’s oversight of both immediate circumstances and ultimate ends. That all is kept in a manifest Record emphasizes divine planning and accountability. The practical implication is to cultivate trust in God’s provision, humility in relation to His all-encompassing knowledge, and responsible stewardship of creation rather than anxiety or arrogance.

translation: And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water — that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed. And if you say, ‘Indeed you will be resurrected after death,’ those who disbelieve will say, ‘This is nothing but clear magic,’
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that creation is a deliberate act under God’s sovereign authority and serves a moral purpose: life is a trial to reveal who excels in righteous conduct. The image of the Throne ‘upon the water’ signals God’s preeminent mastery even over the primeval elements, not a material limitation, and the ‘six days’ denote ordered stages of making rather than weakening His power. Mentioning the disbelievers’ charge of ‘magic’ shows a recurrent human response—rejecting the reality of resurrection and judgment out of prejudice or inability to accept moral accountability—so the passage both grounds the purpose of existence in divine wisdom and explains why prophetic warnings encounter stubborn denial.

translation: And if We were to withhold the punishment from them until an appointed term, they would surely say, “What is detaining it?” Nay — on the Day it comes to them it will not be turned away from them, and what they used to mock will encompass them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Divine delay is not denial: when God postpones punishment for a measured time, the disbelievers mistake that for permanent escape and mockingly ask what holds it back. The interpretation is that such postponement serves God’s wisdom (for warning, for testing, or to complete a term), but it does not annul accountability; when the appointed Day arrives there will be no avoidance and those very things they ridiculed — the signs, the warnings, the consequences of their deeds — will overtake and surround them, exposing the futility of their mockery and the certainty of divine justice.

translation: And if We grant a person a mercy from Us and then take it away from him, indeed he is ever despairing, ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse points to a typical human reaction: when God bestows blessings and then withdraws them, people often respond with despair and ingratitude rather than patience or recognition of the mercy’s purpose. The withdrawal functions as a test or reminder, exposing the instability of the heart and revealing reliance on worldly comforts; the passage therefore warns against attaching one’s hope solely to fleeting favors and calls for steadfastness, gratitude, and trust in God whether in ease or in trial.

translation: And if We grant him blessings after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, “Evil has departed from me.” Indeed, he is (one) who rejoices and boasts.
interpretation: The verse condemns the human tendency to treat relief as proof of personal innocence or permanent exemption from consequences: when God lifts a trial and gives comfort, some people immediately assume their faults or divine displeasure are gone and become self-satisfied and proud. The intended lesson is that blessings are not automatic absolution but a test and trust from God, calling for humility, gratitude, and continued righteousness rather than complacent boasting.

translation: Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; for them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The clause draws a clear line: divine punishment announced earlier does not apply to those who combine steadfast patience in faith and trial with consistent righteous conduct. ‘Patience’ implies perseverance in belief, restraint from sin, and endurance through trials; ‘righteous deeds’ denotes sincere worship and ethical, beneficial actions. Together these qualities open the way to God’s mercy — the removal of sins — and an abundant, elevated recompense in the hereafter, showing that moral perseverance plus right action are the means to attain pardon and a significant reward.

translation: Perhaps you would abandon some of what is revealed to you, and your breast would be constricted by it, lest they say, “Why was a treasure not sent down to him, or an angel come with him?” You are only a warner, and Allah is, over all things, a Disposer.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet’s natural human anxiety about conveying difficult revelations in full: he might be tempted to omit or soften parts out of fear of rejection or mockery, especially when people demand spectacular signs (treasure or angels) as proof. The instruction and consolation here are twofold—first, to deliver the message faithfully without withholding what was revealed, and second, to recognize his proper role: he is a warner and messenger, not the guarantor of people’s belief or their worldly incentives. Ultimate authority, support, and management of outcomes belong to God alone, so the Prophet should remain steadfast in transmission and trust God’s oversight of affairs.

translation: Or do they say, “He invented it”? Say, “Then bring ten surahs like it that are fabricated, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah—if you are truthful.”
interpretation: This verse is a divinely posed challenge aimed at exposing the impossibility of fabricating the Qur’an and thereby proving its divine origin. By demanding that the objectors produce ten chapters like it and enlist any helpers they trust, the address both raises the standard of proof beyond mere assertion and makes their failure publicly evident: if their claim that the Prophet ‘invented’ the revelation were true, they should be able to replicate it or obtain comparable support from their deities or allies. Their inability to meet the challenge demonstrates that the Qur’an’s linguistic, rhetorical, moral and prophetic qualities are not the product of human fabrication, and that rejection stems from denial and vested interests rather than lack of evidence.

translation: But if they do not respond to you, then know that what has been revealed is by Allah’s knowledge alone, and that there is no god but He — so will you submit (be Muslims)?
interpretation: The verse instructs the believers that when others reject the prophetic message they must not doubt its origin or truth: the revelation comes from Allah’s own knowledge and embodies the affirmation of tawḥīd (there is no deity but Him). Faced with refusal, the proper response is not to compromise the message to win approval but to recognize its divine source and internalize it — i.e., to become true Muslims by sincere submission to God rather than seeking validation from those who reject the truth.

translation:
من كان يريد الحياة الدنيا وزينتها نُوفِّيْهِمْ أَعْمَالَهُمْ فِيهَا وَهُمْ فِيهَا لَا يُبْخَسُونَ
"Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornments — We will fully give them their deeds in it, and therein they will not be wronged."
interpretation: The verse means that those whose aim is solely the fleeting pleasures and honors of this world will receive the full, immediate fruits and enjoyments of their actions in this life — that is all their recompense. It is not a commendation but a warning: their reward is limited to the temporal realm and they will be excluded from the higher, eternal rewards of the Hereafter; in other words, God will give them what they sought, but their share will end with the world and they will ultimately suffer loss in the final reckoning.

translation: Those are the ones for whom there will be nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire; what they did therein has been nullified, and vain are the deeds they used to do.
interpretation: The verse speaks of people whose rejection of God’s guidance or whose actions were rooted in falsehood will render their deeds spiritually worthless. Though they may have acted and achieved in this life, those works lack the valid intention, righteous belief, or submission required for acceptance, so in the judgment their efforts are annulled (حبط) and shown to be inherently void or ineffective (باطل); their ultimate recompense, therefore, is only punishment.

translation: Is then he who is upon clear proof from his Lord — and a witness from Him recites it — and before it was the Book of Moses as a guide and mercy — are those who believe in it? And whoever disbelieves in it among the parties, the Fire is his destined abode. So be not in doubt about it; indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur’an comes with unmistakable divine evidence and a direct witnessing of its truth (understood as the angelic confirmation of revelation or an obvious, verifiable sign). It places this new revelation in continuity with the earlier scripture given to Moses, showing that God’s guidance is consistent across prophets: the earlier Book served as leadership and mercy, and the Qur’an confirms and completes that guidance. Accepting this chain and its clear proofs is the mark of true belief; rejecting it—especially in organized opposition—brings the warning of final punishment. The injunction “do not be in doubt” is a corrective to scepticism: the message is not a matter of opinion but the plain truth from the Lord, even though, lamentably, most people fail to accept it.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, “These are the ones who lied against their Lord.” Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that inventing false claims about God—whether by ascribing to Him attributes He has not revealed, fabricating revelation, or propagating doctrines that distort His oneness and justice—is the gravest form of injustice. Such falsehoods will not remain hidden: on the Day of Reckoning the truth will be made manifest and objective witnesses (whether the record of deeds, the messengers, creation, or appointed angels) will expose those who lied about God. The pronouncement of Allah’s curse underscores both the moral seriousness of corrupting divine truth and the inevitable accountability that deters people from inventing or defending falsehood about the Divine.

translation: Those who divert people from the way of Allah and strive to make it appear crooked — and in the Hereafter they are the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who, out of malice, ambition, or self-interest, intentionally obstruct divine guidance and twist religion so others are led astray; such behavior reveals a repudiation of the truth and will result in being judged as disbelievers in the final reckoning.

translation:
أولئك لم يكونوا معجزين في الأرض وما كان لهم من دون الله من أولياء ۘ يضاعف لهم العذاب ۚ ما كانوا يستطيعون السمع وما كانوا يبصرون
"Those — they had no power on earth, and besides Allah they had no protectors; for them the punishment will be doubled. They could not hear, nor could they see."
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who rely on false sources of security or who arrogantly imagine themselves invulnerable will find, at the time of divine reckoning, that they possess neither true power nor allies to avert God’s decree. Their punishment is intensified because their rejection was wilful: their inability to “hear” and “see” is moral and spiritual—deliberate deafness and blindness toward guidance and truth—so they are incapable of perceiving signs or escaping the consequences of their choices.

translation:
أُولَـئِكَ الَّذِينَ خَسِرُوا أَنفُسَهُمْ وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ
"Those are the ones who have ruined themselves, and what they used to fabricate has departed from them."
interpretation: The verse warns that those who cling to falsehood—whether false beliefs, vain hopes, or self-deceptions—and turn away from guidance bring about their own spiritual ruin. In the decisive moment their inventions and excuses prove worthless and abandon them; the loss is not an accident but the necessary consequence of choosing illusion over truth.

translation: Indeed, they — in the Hereafter — are the greatest losers.
interpretation: The verse declares that those who persisted in denial, heedlessness, or the pursuit of fleeting worldly gains at the expense of faith and righteousness will suffer the ultimate loss in the life to come: deprivation of God’s mercy and eternal felicity. What seemed like success in this world will be exposed as vain and worthless, and their final ruin will be absolute and irreversible.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord—those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true salvation is not mere profession of faith but a holistic condition: heartfelt submission to God, manifested in moral, devotional and social good. The word translated “humbled themselves” (akhbaṭu) denotes deep, reverent humility and turning wholly to the Lord — an inward disposition that excludes pride, ostentation and self-reliance. Righteous deeds that flow from this sincere humility are the visible fruit that associates a person with the “companions of Paradise,” and the phrase “they will abide therein” stresses that this attainment is final and enduring. In short, faith, humble surrender to God, and ethically consistent action are inseparable markers of those who attain everlasting felicity.

translation: The example of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in example? Will you not then remember?
interpretation: The verse uses a vivid metaphor to contrast those who receive and live by divine guidance with those who reject or are resistant to it: the ‘seeing and hearing’ symbolize spiritual perception and responsiveness to God’s signs, while the ‘blind and deaf’ symbolize spiritual insensitivity and refusal to perceive truth. It asserts that these states are not morally or epistemically equal — one group is enabled to recognize and act upon guidance and thus bears responsibility, while the other remains closed off and therefore separated in consequence and standing. The rhetorical question urges the listener to reflect, recognize the difference, and choose the receptive stance of insight and accountability.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah to his people, saying, “Indeed, I am to you a clear warner.”
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that God dispatches messengers with an unmistakable, lucid warning so that people are given a fair opportunity to recognize the truth; the manifestness of the prophet’s message removes excuse, frames guidance as an act of mercy, and thereby makes acceptance or rejection a deliberate moral choice for which people are accountable.

translation:
أن لا تعبدوا إلا الله؛ إني أخاف عليكم عذاب يوم أليم
"That you worship none but Allah; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful Day."
interpretation: A solemn admonition urging exclusive devotion to God: the speaker warns that turning away from true monotheism and persisting in idolatry or false worship will lead to severe recompense on the Day of Judgment, combining compassionate concern for the people’s salvation with a stern reminder that genuine security and deliverance are found only in worshiping Allah alone.

translation: فقال الملأ الذين كفروا من قومه: "ما نراك إلا بشراً مثلنا، وما نراك اتبعك إلا الذين هم أراذلنا بادي الرأي، وما نرى لكم علينا من فضل، بل نظنكم كاذبين".
interpretation: The verse highlights how entrenched, proud leaders respond to a moral or spiritual challenge: instead of engaging on the merits, they protect their status by denying the messenger's authority (reducing him to 'just a man'), disparaging his followers as socially or intellectually inferior to delegitimize the movement, and rejecting any claim that would diminish their privilege—ending by branding the caller a liar to maintain their power and self-conception rather than seeking truth.

translation: He said, “O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear proof from my Lord and He has granted me mercy from Himself—should I compel it upon you while you are averse to it?”
interpretation: The verse teaches that a messenger’s role is to present clear evidence and embody God’s mercy, not to force belief. Genuine guidance must be accepted freely; coercion would nullify its moral and spiritual worth. Thus responsibility for accepting the truth lies with the people, while the prophet’s duty is to convey the message and leave the outcome to God’s judgment and mercy.

translation: O my people, I do not ask you for it any wealth; my reward is only from Allah. And I will not drive away those who have believed — indeed they will meet their Lord — but I see that you are a people who are ignorant.
interpretation: The speaker is asserting prophetic integrity and a principle of non-coercion: he does not seek material gain from his mission and leaves recompense to God, refuses to exclude sincere believers, and thus distinguishes his role as a guide from any worldly ambition or coercive authority. His rebuke of the people's ignorance points to the moral failing behind their rejection—closed minds and failure to recognize truth—while reminding them that ultimate accountability belongs to God, not to the messenger.

translation: “O my people, who will defend me against Allah if I were to expel them? Will you not then take heed?”
interpretation: A stern rhetorical warning: the speaker reminds his people that human alliances or actions cannot avert God’s will or judgment. By asking who could protect him from Allah if he were to cast people out, he underscores that ultimate authority and protection belong to God alone, urging his listeners to abandon pride, recognize divine sovereignty, and heed the warning before it is too late.

translation: وَلَا أَقُولُ لَكُمْ عِندِي خَزَائِنُ اللَّهِ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ الْغَيْبَ وَلَا أَقُولُ إِنِّي مَلَكٌ وَلَا أَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ تَزْدَرِي أَعْيُنُكُمْ لَنْ يُؤْتِيهِمُ اللَّهُ خَيْرًا ۖ اللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا فِي أَنفُسِهِمْ ۖ إِنِّي إِذًا لِمِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد وضوح موقف الرسول في الإنكار على نفسه أية ادعاءات تفوق أو خصوصية إلهية — ليس عنده كنوز الله ولا علم الغيب، ولا يدّعي كونه ملكاً أو ملاكاً — وتُحذّر من الحكم الظالم على الناس بناءً على المظاهر أو الاحتقار؛ العلم بحقائق النفوس والقدر والمنة بيد الله وحده، وأي ادعاء بالعلم أو الحكم المطلق يكون ظلماً وخطأً. باختصار: هي دعوة إلى التواضع والصدق في تبليغ الرسالة ورفض الاجتهاز المتعجرف في محاسبة الناس، لأن ذلك تحول إلى ظلم إن ادعيه المُبلّغ.

translation: They said, “O Nūḥ, you have disputed with us and increased your disputing; bring upon us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful.”
interpretation: The verse reveals the obstinate, mocking stance of Nūḥ’s people: rather than accept his moral warnings they accuse him of excessive argument and demand the promised punishment as a public proof. Their challenge exposes pride and willful rejection—shifting the burden of proof onto the prophet and postponing repentance until a visible, often catastrophic sign appears—illustrating a recurrent pattern of denial faced by messengers.

translation: He said, “It is only that which Allah brings to you, if He wills, and you will not be able to avert it.”
interpretation: The speaker affirms that the occurrence in question is entirely subject to God’s will and cannot be produced or stopped by human effort; whatever sign, judgment or provision Allah decrees will come to pass if He so wills, and people are powerless to frustrate or repel that divine decree.

translation: وَلَا يَنفَعُكُمْ نُصْحِي إِنْ أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَنصَحَ لَكُمْ إِنْ كَانَ اللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يُغْوِيَكُمْ ۚ هُوَ رَبُّكُمْ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن الهداية حق إلهي لا تُحسم بمجرد النصح البشري: إذا أقدم الإنسان على رفض الحق واستمر في إغلاق قلبه، قد يجعل الله حاله بحيث لا يُجدي عنده أي موعظة. بذلك تبرز الآية سيادة الله في إعطاء الهداية وسير الأمور، وفي الوقت نفسه تحذر من عواقب الإصرار على الباطل، لأن الخلود في الرفض يهيئ للمرء أن تُحجب عنه النعمة. الخاتمة «هو ربكم وإليه ترجعون» تذكير بالمساءلة النهائية أمام الله، فالنصح يجب أن يُؤخذ على محمل الجد قبل فوات الفرصة.

translation: أم يقولون: افتراه؟ قل: إن افتريته فعلي إجرامي، وأنا بريء ممّا تجرمون
interpretation: الآية تردّ على اتهام المشركين للنبي بأنه اخترع الكلام الإلهي؛ فتأخذ موقفاً مزدوجاً: إن كان ما يقوله مُفترى فهو خطيئته وحده ويتحمّل عاقبته، لكنه يعلن براءته من آثام وإثاماتهم. بمعنى آخر، الرسول يبرهن على أمانته وصدق دعوته لا بالاحتجاج النفعي فحسب، بل بإظهار أن اختلاق الوحي لو كان كذلك لكان خطأً على عاتقه، أما ما يقدمونه من معاصٍ واتهامات فهو مسؤوليتهم وحدهم—فتبعات رفض الحق وتحميل الاتهامات لا تلغي ذمّة النبي ولا تبرّر سلوكهم.

translation: And it was revealed to Noah, 'None of your people will believe except those who have already believed; so do not grieve over what they have been doing.'
interpretation: God is informing Noah that the widespread rejection of his message is part of the divine decree: only the few who have truly embraced belief already will remain firm, and no further persuasion will change the outcome. The command not to grieve relieves the prophet of personal responsibility for their obstinacy and teaches that guidance and acceptance are ultimately determined by God. Practically, the verse consoles and steadies the messenger—calling him to continue his duty without despair—and reminds believers that truth may be rejected by many, yet the prophet’s role is to convey the message, not to secure every heart.

translation: And build the ark under Our eyes and by Our revelation, and do not plead with Me concerning those who have wronged—indeed, they are to be drowned.
interpretation: God commands Noah to carry out the ark’s construction under divine supervision and guidance (’Our eyes’ = vigilant oversight; ’Our revelation’ = inspired instruction), and at the same time forbids interceding on behalf of the persistent wrongdoers whose punishment is already decreed. The verse emphasizes two truths: obedience to God’s command in the face of mockery, and the inevitability of divine justice when people persist in rejection and corruption—human pleading cannot avert a judgment that has been determined by God’s wisdom and decree.

translation: And he constructed the ark; and whenever a group of his people passed by him they ridiculed him. He said, “If you mock us, then we will (mock) you just as you mock.”
interpretation: The verse conveys a moral-theological principle: derision of Divine guidance and of its messengers will be met by a corresponding reversal — humiliation or loss — as part of God’s justice. It also highlights the prophet’s steadfastness: rather than abandoning his duty in the face of ridicule, he warns that persistent contempt will bring its own consequences, so arrogance toward truth inevitably invites a fitting response and ultimate accountability.

translation: Soon you will know who will be visited by a punishment that disgraces him, and upon whom will descend an abiding punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that persistent denial and rejection of God’s guidance will not go unexposed or unpunished: those who persist in arrogance and opposition will be publicly shamed (a humiliating chastisement that strips away their pretensions) and will ultimately suffer a lasting, decisive punishment. It reassures the faithful that apparent worldly advantage for the deniers is temporary, and affirms the certainty of final accountability and the distinction between transient disgrace in this life and enduring retribution in the Hereafter.

translation: “Until when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, We said: ‘Load into it of each (species) two, and your family — except those for whom the decree had already passed — and those who believed.’ And only a few believed with him.”
interpretation: The verse underscores the primacy of God’s sovereign decree in deliverance while affirming human responsibility: when divine judgment arrives, rescue occurs only by God’s command and for those whose fate has not been sealed and who responded in faith. The mention of exceptions points to God’s foreknowledge and justice, and the provision to take pairs of creatures and household members shows God’s intent to preserve life so creation can be renewed after trial. The contrast between the few believers saved and the many who did not believe serves as a moral warning that accepting guidance before the decree is both necessary and consequential.

translation: He said, “Board it; in the name of Allah its course and its anchorage. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.”
interpretation: By invoking “In the name of Allah” over the ark’s sailing and mooring, the speaker teaches that lawful effort and provision of means should be accompanied by entrusting their outcome to God; the addition “my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful” expresses a humble hope in God’s compassion rather than reliance on one’s own power, affirming that success, safety, and final reconciliation ultimately lie in God’s control and mercy.

translation: And it sailed with them on waves like mountains, and Noah called to his son — and he was apart — “O my son, embark with us and be not with the disbelievers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation is a matter of individual choice, not family lineage: even the closest kin of a prophet may persist in disbelief. Noah’s urgent appeal shows the prophet’s human care and the moral responsibility to warn, but it also makes clear the limit of prophetic power—belief cannot be compelled. The son’s withdrawal and refusal illustrate how personal allegiance to error can endure despite clear warning, and the image of waves like mountains underscores the overwhelming and decisive nature of divine judgment when the appointed time arrives.

translation: He said, “I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.” He said, “There is no protector today from the decree of Allah except for whom He shows mercy.” And the waves came between them, and he was among the drowned.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true deliverance rests solely with Allah’s will and mercy; when divine judgment unfolds, no human refuge, plan, or apparent stronghold can avert it. It warns against relying on worldly escapes or false hopes instead of seeking Allah’s guidance and mercy, and affirms the absolute sovereignty of God over all means of escape.

translation: فقالوا: «يا أرضِ ابلعي ماءَكِ، ويا سماءُ أقلعي». فاضمحلّ الماءُ وقضي الأمرُ، واستوت السفينةُ على الجودي. وقيل: «بعداً للقوم الظالمين».
interpretation: الآية تبيّن كيفية تنفيذ حكم الله: حين يشأ يغيّر أبعاد الخلْق ليُنجِي من أرادهم ويُهلك من استمرّ في الظلم. الأمر لِابتلاع الأرض للماء ولتوقّف السماء يرمز إلى السيادة الإلهية الكاملة على الطبيعة ولامكانية المقاومة أمام قضائه، واستواء السفينة على الجودي علامة حفظ الناجين ونهاية الابتلاء، أما عبارة «بعداً للقوم الظالمين» فتعبر عن الطرد والندم اللاحق بالظالمين وضمنَتْها تحذيرٌ صارم بأن الإصرار على الجور يؤدي إلى الخسران الدائم.

translation: And Noah called upon his Lord and said, “My Lord, indeed my son is of my family; and indeed, Your promise is true; and You are the most just of judges.”
interpretation: The verse records Noah’s heartfelt appeal, revealing how a prophet can both plead for a loved one and recognize God’s absolute truthfulness and justice. It teaches that compassionate intercession for kin is natural, yet it affirms that ultimate outcomes rest with God’s wise and just decree—so believers may hope and petition, but must submit to divine judgment.

translation:
قَالَ يَا نُوحُ إِنَّهُ لَيْسَ مِنْ أَهْلِكَ ۖ إِنَّهُ عَمَلٌ غَيْرُ صَالِحٍ ۖ فَلَا تَسْأَلْنِ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ ۖ إِنِّي أُنذِرُكَ أَنْ تَكُونَ مِنَ الْجَاهِلِينَ
He said, “O Nuh, he is not of your family; indeed his deed was not righteous. So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. I warn you lest you be among the ignorant.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that true belonging before God is defined by faith and righteous conduct, not by blood ties. Allah rejects Noah’s plea for his disbelieving son to show that persistent rejection or sinful conduct severs one’s claim to spiritual kinship; prophets and believers must submit to divine knowledge rather than plead from emotion or ignorance. It underscores divine justice and the proper limits of intercession: love for relatives cannot override God’s judgment, and one must not demand what one does not know, lest one fall into ignorance.

translation: He said, “My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge; and unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will surely be among the losers.”
interpretation: This is a humble plea that models two linked attitudes: caution before claiming or demanding what one does not know, and total reliance on God’s pardon and compassion. Rather than engaging in presumptuous questioning or asserting things beyond his knowledge, the speaker retreats to God, recognizing that human fallibility makes divine forgiveness and mercy essential to avoid spiritual ruin.

translation: It was said, 'O Nuh, descend in peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations among those with you.' And (as for) nations, We will give some of them enjoyment for a time, then from Us a painful punishment will touch them.
interpretation: God is affirming two complementary realities: a promised deliverance and blessing for the obedient — here Noah and the communities associated with him — and a deferred but certain recompense for those who persist in rejection. The phrase “descend in peace” denotes salvation and ongoing well‑being bestowed by God, while the promise that some peoples will be allowed temporal enjoyment before a painful punishment highlights divine patience and testing; delay of punishment is not pardon but a measured, wise allowance for choices to unfold. The verse thus teaches that God’s mercy secures the faithful, His forbearance gives scope to human freedom, and His justice ultimately vindicates moral consequences.

translation: Those are among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you. You and your people did not know them before this. So be patient; indeed, the final outcome belongs to the God‑fearing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that prophetic knowledge comes directly from Divine revelation rather than human learning, grounding the Prophet’s authority; its practical message is pastoral and moral — to endure opposition with steadfast patience and trust in God’s justice, since apparent setbacks do not determine ultimate success, which is reserved for those who live in God‑consciousness and righteousness.

translation: And to the people of ʿĀd We sent their brother Hūd. He said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. You are only fabricators (of falsehood).”
interpretation: Hud’s address is a summons to pure monotheism and a rebuke of the social-religious habit of inventing gods and traditions. Calling them “your brother” shows he speaks from kinship and moral concern, while labelling them muf'tarūn (fabricators) indicts their worship as human-made falsehood—rooted in imitation, desire, and misleading leaders rather than in evidence or truth. The verse therefore condemns idolization of created beings as unjustified innovation and warns that relying on such inventions severs people from rightful accountability to the One God.

translation: O my people, I do not ask you for any payment for it; my recompense is only from the One who created me. Will you not then understand?
interpretation: The speaker (a prophet) affirms that his mission is not motivated by worldly gain and he seeks no material reward from his community; his true recompense is with God, his Creator. By invoking his origin from the One who fashioned him, he grounds his authority and accountability in the Divine, not in human patronage, and thus appeals to his listeners to use reason: if the message stands on truth and comes from God, they should recognize it independently of any personal benefit to the messenger and submit to what is right.

translation: “O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance; He will send the sky upon you in continuous showers and will increase you in strength in proportion to your strength. Do not turn away, you criminals.”
interpretation: The prophet urges his people to seek God’s pardon and sincerely repent, promising that such repentance will bring God’s mercy manifested as sustaining rain and an increase in their collective capacity—whether in livestock, crops, wealth, or social strength. The phrase “increase you in strength to your strength” indicates augmentation of what they already possess rather than arbitrary favor. The warning “do not turn away, you criminals” stresses that this promise is conditional: if they relapse into persistent wrongdoing and reject obedience, they forfeit the promised mercy.

translation: They said, “O Hūd, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods because of what you say, and we will not believe you.”
interpretation: This reply reflects stubborn, self‑protective rejection rather than a reasoned critique: by claiming there is no “bayyina” (clear proof) they set an impossible evidential standard or demand a different kind of sign, while simultaneously refusing the moral and social cost of abandoning ancestral idols. Their words reveal willful blindness and attachment to tribal identity and tradition—an obstinate refusal to be guided even when guidance is offered—illustrating the Quranic theme that some reject truth out of pride, habit, and fear of losing communal belonging.

translation: "We will only say that some of our gods have befallen you with harm." He said, "I bear witness to God; and (you) bear witness that I am free from what you associate (with Him)."
interpretation: The speaker emphatically disavows the attempt to blame idols for events and instead publicly upholds tawhīd: he testifies to Allah alone and summons witness to his innocence of shirk, teaching that true faith requires openly rejecting false deities, refusing to ascribe divine agency to created things, and making one’s repudiation of idolatry unmistakable before others.

translation:
من دونه ۖ فكيدوني جميعا ثم لا تنظرون
"Who is there besides Him? So conspire against me, all of you, and then you will not be able to see."
interpretation: The verse expresses the utter futility of human plots against divine will: people may band together and scheme, but their machinations cannot avert what God has decreed nor bring them the outcome they seek; their united plotting will prove powerless and will yield no visible advantage.

translation: إني توكلت على الله ربي وربكم؛ ما من دابة إلا هو آخذ بناصيتها؛ إن ربي على صراط مستقيم.
interpretation: القول هنا يعبر عن توكل مطلق على رب واحد واعتراف بسيطرته الكاملة على كل مخلوق: تشبيهُ أخذِ النفس بقبضتها على النُّصبة يدل على أن الله يوجّه مسارات المخلوقات ويهيمن على مصائرها بدقة. هذا التوكل ليس استسلامًا سلبيًا بل ثقة واعية بالربط بين العمل والطاعة والاعتماد على حكمة الله، مع اليقين بأن طريقه مستقيم — أي قائم على الحق والعدل والهداية — فتتبدد الآمال بغيره ويستقر الأطمئنان في الاعتماد على حكمته وتدبيره.

translation:
فإن تولوا فقد أبلغتكم ما أرسلت به إليكم ۚ ويستخلف ربي قوما غيركم ولا تضرونه شيئا ۚ إن ربي على كل شيء حفيظ
"So if they turn away, then indeed I have conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you; and my Lord will appoint in your stead people other than you, and you will not harm Him in the least. Indeed, my Lord is, over all things, a Guardian."
interpretation: The verse affirms that the prophet’s responsibility is limited to faithfully delivering God’s message; once that duty is fulfilled, the moral burden for acceptance rests on the people themselves. Their persistent rejection cannot thwart God’s purpose—He can and will bring forth another people who receive guidance—and nothing they do diminishes or harms God. Thus the passage teaches both a release for the messenger from culpability for others’ rejection and a solemn warning that communal obstinacy may lead to being replaced, all under the watchful sovereignty and protection of God.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that deliverance is ultimately a manifestation of divine mercy and occurs according to God’s sovereign timing: human repentance and acceptance of prophetic guidance make one eligible for rescue, but the actual saving is an unearned gift from God rather than a guaranteed outcome of effort. It also serves as a warning that persistent rejection of truth leads to inevitable, severe consequences, so reliance should be placed on God’s mercy, prompt obedience to guidance, and trust in His decrees rather than on human means alone.

translation: And those were the 'Ād — they denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every proud, obstinate tyrant.
interpretation: The verse points to the people of ʿĀd as an instructive example: they did not merely fail to recognize God’s signs but willfully rejected them (جحدوا بآيات ربهم), actively resisted the guidance brought by the messengers (عصوا رسله), and instead surrendered to the dictates of domineering, self-willed leaders (اتبعوا أمر كل جبار عنيد). This combination — deliberate denial of divine truth, rebellion against prophetic guidance, and uncritical obedience to tyrannical authority — explains why their society fell into moral and social ruin. The passage warns that pride and submission to oppressive, stubborn leadership in place of submission to God produce corruption and bring about divine accountability.

translation:
وَأُتْبِعُوا فِي هَذِهِ الدُّنْيَا لَعْنَةً وَيَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ۚ أَلَا إِنَّ عادًا كَفَرُوا رَبَّهُمْ ۚ أَلَا بُعْدًا لِعَادٍ قَوْمِ هُودٍ
"They were overtaken in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Know then: 'Aad denied their Lord. Woe, then, to 'Aad — the people of Hud."
interpretation: The verse interprets the ruin of the people of ʿĀd as both an immediate divine stigma in history and an assured reckoning in the hereafter: their denial of God, despite clear admonition through Hud, turned their worldly might into the instrument of their disgrace. The doubled admonitory particles (ألا) heighten the warning — their fate is not merely historical fact but a paradigmatic lesson: arrogance, pride in material power, and rejection of prophetic guidance bring divine repudiation, loss of honor among peoples, and ultimate punishment. Thus the passage is intended to make listeners heed the moral cause–and–effect: persistent disbelief and insolence toward God’s messengers lead inevitably to ruin.

translation: And to Thamud We sent their brother Salih. He said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He created you from the earth and settled you in it, so ask His forgiveness and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive.”
interpretation: The verse presents Salih’s core admonition: because God alone is the Creator and Sustainer — having brought you into existence from the earth and established you in it — you stand under a trust and moral obligation to worship Him. That origin and settlement are offered as evidence that human dignity and provision are gifts tied to duty; therefore the proper response to human frailty and failure is to seek God’s forgiveness and turn back to Him, for God is close and ready to answer sincere repentance. The passage thus links ontology (your origin), responsibility (worship and stewardship), and hope (God’s nearness and responsiveness) to urge immediate moral correction.

translation: They said, “O Ṣāliḥ, you were indeed one we used to hope for among us before this. Will you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Truly we are in doubt about that to which you invite us — it is something strange.”
interpretation: The people are using two defensive moves to reject the prophet’s call: appealing to past trust and to ancestral custom while professing ‘doubt’ as a pretext. Rather than a sincere intellectual uncertainty, their words function to preserve the social order, identity, and vested interests tied to inherited practices. The verse highlights a common human reaction to moral reform — discrediting the messenger by invoking familiarity and tradition, and masking resistance with feigned skepticism so as to avoid changing settled ways of life.

translation:
قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ أَرَأَيْتُمْ إِن كُنتُ عَلَى بَيِّنَةٍ مِن رَبِّي وَآتَانِي مِنْهُ رَحْمَةً فَمَنْ يَنصُرُنِي مِنَ اللَّهِ إِنْ عَصَيْتُهُ فَمَا تَزِيدُونَنِي غَيْرَ تَخْسِيرٍ
“He said, ‘O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear proof from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who will help me against Allah if I were to disobey Him? So you would add to me nothing but loss.’”
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that genuine support and validation come only from God: even if a messenger stands on clear evidence and receives God's mercy, his ultimate duty is obedience to God, and no one can shield him from God's judgment should he betray that duty. Thus rejecting a divinely guided messenger is self-defeating—opposition to revealed truth only brings loss to those who persist in it, while the messenger’s proper stance remains submission to God alone.

translation: “O my people, this is the she‑camel of Allah — a sign for you. So leave her to graze in Allah’s land and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.”
interpretation: The camel is presented as a deliberate, visible miracle and a communal trust: God has set it as a test of obedience and restraint.
