The command to let it graze and not to harm it means that when God establishes a clear sign and prescribes respectful treatment, deliberate violation of that injunction is a direct refusal of divine authority and the social covenant; such transgression invites immediate collective consequences. Thus the verse teaches that respecting God’s signs and limits protects the community, while arrogantly abusing or destroying them brings swift punishment.

translation: So they hamstrung it and said, “Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days.” That is a promise not to be belied.
interpretation: The verse shows that God sometimes grants transgressors a brief, apparent respite or safety — an appointed period during which they may indulge — but this allowance is itself part of God’s decree and will be fulfilled: the temporary enjoyment is not an everlasting escape, and the ultimate outcome (reward or punishment) follows the fixed promise of God.

translation: So when Our command came, We saved Ṣāliḥ and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that day. Indeed, your Lord — He is the Strong, the Exalted in Might.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when God’s decisive judgment arrived He intervened to rescue Prophet Ṣāliḥ and the faithful by His mercy, sparing them the public humiliation and ruin that befell the transgressors. “Our command” denotes the moment of God’s implementing judgment, while “mercy from Us” emphasizes that deliverance is granted by divine compassion, not by human power. The phrase “from the disgrace of that day” points to both immediate worldly humiliation and ultimate recompense, and the final clause—“your Lord is the Strong, the Exalted in Might”—affirms God’s absolute ability to enforce justice and to grant mercy according to His wisdom, reassuring believers that protection and vindication rest solely with Him.

translation: And those who did wrong were seized by the blast, and they awoke in their homes crouching.
interpretation: The verse conveys that divine punishment can come suddenly and decisively: الصيحة signifies an overwhelming, God‑sent catastrophe (a compendious cry or calamity) that overtakes the wrongdoers without warning, and جاثمين — found collapsed or crouched in their own dwellings — stresses their helplessness and inability to escape. The passage warns that oppression and persistent denial of God’s guidance lead to abrupt, unavoidable accountability, showing that worldly refuge and arrogance cannot shield one from divine justice.

translation:
كأن لم يغنوا فيها ۗ ألا إن ثمود كفروا ربهم ۗ ألا بعدا لثمود
“As if they had never prospered there. Indeed, Thamud denied their Lord. Woe then to Thamud!”
interpretation: The verse teaches that material comforts and settled life cannot save a people who reject divine guidance; the fate of Thamud shows that disbelief renders worldly gains meaningless and brings inevitable punishment, serving as a stern warning to prioritize faith and obedience over reliance on prosperity.

translation: And certainly Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings; they said, 'Peace.' He said, 'Peace.' And he did not delay in bringing a roasted calf.
interpretation: The verse points to Abraham’s immediate, heartfelt response to divine reassurance: the angels’ greeting of ‘peace’ embodies blessing and security, and Abraham’s swift preparation of a roasted calf manifests his joyful faith, generous hospitality, and readiness to honor God’s messengers. It teaches that genuine belief expresses itself in prompt, tangible acts of devotion and service rather than mere words.

translation: When he saw their hands not reaching him, he perceived their denial and was seized with fear for them. They said, “Do not fear; indeed, We have been sent to the people of Lot.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that natural fear in the face of hostile, rejecting people is understandable, but God’s mission is supported: divine messengers reassure the righteous and carry out God’s decree, showing that human aggression cannot ultimately frustrate Divine protection and judgment.

translation:
وَامْرَأَتُهُ قَائِمَةٌ فَضَحِكَتْ فَبَشَّرْنَاهَا بِإِسْحَاقَ وَمِن وَرَاءِ إِسْحَاقَ يَعْقُوبَ
“And his wife, standing by, laughed; so We gave her the glad tidings of Isaac and, after Isaac, Jacob.”
interpretation: The verse highlights how God overturns human expectation and physical limits: the woman’s laughter expresses astonished disbelief at news of a child in old age, and God’s reply is not argument but a promise fulfilled—first Isaac, then Jacob—showing both the immediacy of divine mercy and the unfolding of a divinely ordained lineage. “من وراء إسحاق يعقوب” indicates succession and continuity of blessing and prophecy, teaching that God’s plans may exceed our imagination, that apparent impossibilities can become realities by His will, and that God’s assurances transform doubt into hope and a single miracle into an ongoing legacy.

translation: She said, “Woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman, and this my husband is an old man? Indeed, this is a strange thing.”
interpretation: An expression of human astonishment and incredulity before a divine miracle: the speaker voices the apparent impossibility of the situation (using age and social expectations as markers of natural limitation), and by calling it “a strange thing” acknowledges that what is about to happen transcends ordinary cause and effect. The statement both reveals sincere humility and fear of social consequence and prepares the listener to recognize the forthcoming birth as an unmistakable sign of God’s power that overrules natural norms.

translation: قالوا: «أَتَعْجَبِينَ مِنْ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ؟ رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ عَلَيْكُمْ أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ، إِنَّهُ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ»
interpretation: الآية ترد على دهشة أو استغراب بشر لأمرٍ إلهيّ فتصوّره خطأً، فتنبّه إلى أن الاستغراب لا يناسب حكمة الله المطلقة؛ فكلمة الرحمة والبركات على أهل البيت تأتي تطميناً بأن التدبير الإلهي يتخلّله رعاية ونعمة للعائلة المؤمنة، وخاتمة «إنه حميد مجيد» تؤكد أن ما يصدر من الله يستحق الثناء والإجلال حتى لو بدا للناس غير مألوف أو مدهشًا.

translation: So when the dread had departed from Abraham and the glad tidings came to him, he pleaded with Us concerning the people of Lot.
interpretation: The verse portrays Abraham, after the immediate fear subsided and he received the good news, interceding with God on behalf of the people of Lot. “جَادَلَنَا” here is best understood as pleading or bargaining rather than hostile disputation: Abraham compassionately asks God to show mercy and to spare the communities if some righteous remain. The episode highlights prophetic mercy and advocacy, the practice of seeking God’s clemency, and at the same time affirms that such intercession occurs within God’s ultimate authority and justice.

translation:
إِنَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ لَحَلِيمٌ أَوَّاهٌ مُنِيبٌ
“Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, often invoking [God], and constantly turning back [to Him].”
interpretation: The verse highlights three complementary moral-spiritual qualities of Abraham: ‘lahīm’ (forbearing) means he restrained anger, showed long-suffering and gentleness toward people despite opposition; ‘awwāh’ conveys an intense, recurring heartfelt calling or longing — frequent supplication and yearning for closeness to God; and ‘munīb’ denotes steady turning back in repentance, submission and devotion. Taken together the phrase portrays a prophet who pairs patient conduct with persistent inner devotion: he endures trials with calm restraint, repeatedly pours out his soul in prayer, and continually reorients himself toward God, offering a model of dignified patience combined with constant spiritual return.

translation:
يا إبراهيم أعرض عن هذا ۖ إنه قد جاء أمر ربك ۖ وإنهم آتيهم عذاب غير مردود
“O Abraham, turn away from this; indeed the command of your Lord has come, and a punishment will surely come upon them — a punishment that will not be averted.”
interpretation: The verse instructs Abraham to cease pleading or debating on behalf of the people because God’s decision has been finalized; their persistent wrongdoing has reached the point where divine judgment is inevitable. It teaches that prophets must submit to God’s decree and withdraw when the time for mercy has passed, trusting that ultimate justice rests with God and that human intercession cannot overturn a decision He has decreed.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt constrained by them, and he said, "This is a hard day."
interpretation: Lot’s exclamation conveys deep anguish and a prophetic awareness: confronted with a society whose members openly violated moral bounds and threatened the safety and sanctity of his guests, he felt trapped and powerless. Calling it “a hard day” signals both the immediate crisis—danger to the visitors and to what is right—and the nearness of a severe, divinely‑ordained reckoning for the community’s persistent corruption.

translation: And his people came to him rushing, and before that they used to commit evil deeds. He said, 'O my people, these are my daughters — they are purer for you; so fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a right-minded man?','
interpretation: The verse portrays Prophet Lūṭ’s desperate moral appeal to a society steeped in persistent vice: he invokes the sanctity of hospitality and lawful relationships by offering his daughters as a lawful alternative, thereby highlighting the corruptness of their intent. By calling them to fear God and asking rhetorically if any sensible person remains among them, he shames their behavior, stresses communal responsibility to protect guests and uphold decency, and exposes that their rejection is not a matter of legal ambiguity but of moral blindness and outright rebellion against God’s guidance.

translation: They said, “Indeed you know that we have a right over your daughters, and you surely know what we intend.”
interpretation: The verse exposes how corrupt people appeal to supposed social ‘rights’ to justify injustice and sexual coercion: by claiming an entitlement to the Prophet’s daughters they mask their real, immoral intent toward his guests. It condemns the arrogance of using custom or alleged entitlement to override hospitality, family protection, and moral law, and highlights the need to resist such abusive claims rather than accede to them.

translation: قَالَ: «لَوْ أَنَّ لِي بِكُمْ قُوَّةً أَوْ آوِي إِلَى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ»
interpretation: This expresses the speaker’s vain longing either to have the power to dominate and punish others or to shelter himself in an impregnable refuge; it reveals reliance on worldly strength and alliances instead of submitting to truth and shows how people, when confronted by what they cannot overcome, wish for force or escape—wishes that are ultimately futile before divine decree.

translation: They said, “O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So flee with your family during a portion of the night and let not any of you look back — except your wife; indeed, what will strike them will strike her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?”
interpretation: The passage teaches that divine deliverance for the obedient is immediate and requires decisive, trustful action: when God’s messengers warn, one must depart without hesitation or sentimental attachment to a corrupt past. The prohibition on looking back is not merely physical caution but a moral injunction against clinging to sinful ties that would endanger salvation; the exception of Lot’s wife shows that inner allegiance matters—outward departure alone does not save one who remains complicit. The reference to the coming morning underscores the imminence and inevitability of God’s judgement, urging prompt obedience and complete severance from wrongdoing.

translation: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ أَمْرُنَا جَعَلْنَا عَلِيَهَا سَافِلَهَا وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهَا حِجَارَةً مِن سِجِّيلٍ مُنْدَدٍ
interpretation: The verse communicates that when God’s ordinance for judgment is executed, it is decisive and irreversibly effective. The vivid images (the overturning and the rain of ‘sijjīl’ — hard, baked stones set in layers) emphasize that divine justice is neither accidental nor weak: persistent collective corruption and rejection of guidance bring about a complete reversal of worldly order and a concrete, incontrovertible punishment. The account functions as a theological warning about the certainty and seriousness of God’s retribution and as an affirmation of His absolute power to enforce His decree.

translation: مَسْوُمَةٌ عِندَ رَبِّكَ ۖ وَمَا هِيَ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ بِبَعِيدٍ
interpretation: الآية تفيد أن الجزاء أو الحِساب المتعلق بالظالمين مثبت ومكتوب عند الله تعالى؛ ليس أمراً محتملاً أو مرهوناً بالمصادفات، بل هو قضاء إلٰهي مؤكد، وكونه «ليس ببعيد» يبيّن قربه من حيث اليقين والوقوع — إما بوقوعه في الدنيا لمن يستوجب ذلك أو بوقوعه حتماً في الآخرة — فتعمل كتحذير جازم بأن الظلم لا يظل من دون محاسبة وأن عدل الله لا يتأخر عن أهله.

translation: And to Madyan (Midian) We sent their brother Shuʿayb. He said, “O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale. Indeed I see you in prosperity, but I fear for you the punishment of a Day that will encompass (you).”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true submission to God demands both exclusive worship and just social conduct: Shuʿayb condemns economic dishonesty (shortening weights and measures) as a moral failure that contradicts faith. Apparent worldly prosperity is not proof of divine approval and can mask corruption; unchecked injustice invites an inevitable, all-encompassing divine reckoning. Thus genuine piety must be reflected in honest transactions and social fairness to avert collective punishment.

translation:
ويا قوم أوفوا المكيال والميزان بالقسط ۖ ولا تبخسوا الناس أشياءهم ولا تعثوا في الأرض مفسدين
“O my people, give full measure and weight with justice; do not deprive people of what is theirs, and do not spread corruption on the earth as corrupters.”
interpretation: The verse enjoins economic and social justice: it demands honesty and fairness in transactions (accurate measures and weights), protection of others’ rights and property (no shortchanging or unjust deprivation), and forbids conduct that harms the social order (corruption, violence, exploitation). It connects individual integrity in daily dealings to the health of the community and implies moral and divine accountability for those who cheat or spread corruption.

translation: بَقِيَّةُ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ إِن كُنتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ ۚ وَمَا أَنَا عَلَيْكُمْ بِحَفِيظٍ
interpretation: Here "بقيتُ الله" denotes the lasting remainder of God’s grace, guidance or sacred trust — the enduring, spiritual good that God leaves behind — and the speaker is asserting that this divine, eternal benefit is far better for you than any temporary worldly advantage, provided you truly believe. The clause "وما أنا عليكم بحفيظ" is a disclaimer: the speaker will not act as your keeper or guardian to force faith or protect you from the consequences of rejecting that good; acceptance and responsibility rest with each person.

translation: They said, “O Shu‘ayb, does your prayer command you that we should leave what our fathers worshipped, or that we should not do as we please with our property? Indeed you are the forbearing, the right-minded.”
interpretation: The verse records a sarcastic rebuttal by Shu‘ayb’s people: they reject his call to abandon ancestral worship and to reform their economic conduct, framing his religious admonition as an improper personal imposition. By praising him as “forbearing” and “right-minded” ironically, they dismiss the moral and social implications of his message while insisting on the freedom to maintain customary beliefs and to use their wealth as they wish; the passage thus exposes how tradition and self-interest are used to resist prophetic reform and to neutralize ethical demands by reducing them to private preference.

translation: He said, “O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear proof from my Lord and He has granted me a good provision from Himself, and I do not intend to differ with you in what I forbid you; I only intend reform as much as I am able — and my success is only by Allah. In Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.”
interpretation: The speaker is asserting that legitimate guidance rests on divine confirmation and upright conduct rather than personal ambition; the outward blessing he received is presented as a sign that his message is not self‑made. He emphasizes that his aim is to reform and enjoin good within the limits of his capacity, refusing coercion or imposition, and he grounds all achievement in reliance on God while exemplifying humility through repentance. The verse, therefore, teaches that true leadership and reform are characterized by evidence, moral restraint, dependence on God, and continual returning to Him.

translation: O my people, let not my hostility toward you lead you to that you should suffer what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih; and the people of Lot are not far from you.
interpretation: The speaker (a prophet) warns that rejecting or opposing his message out of spite or stubbornness will not shield the community from God’s punishment; he disavows personal animosity and urges them to abandon the sinful conduct that brought destruction on earlier peoples, stressing that similar sins (like those of Lot) are present among them and therefore divine retribution is a real and imminent possibility—so they must repent, humble themselves, and accept guidance to avoid the same fate.

translation: And ask forgiveness of your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Most Merciful, Ever‑Loving.
interpretation: The verse teaches that seeking God’s forgiveness must be accompanied by a true turning away from past wrongs: repentance is an inward reorientation and outward change. It reassures believers that God’s response is not distant judgment but compassion and affectionate readiness to accept and draw close to the repentant; because He is both merciful and 'Wadud' (deeply loving), sincere penitence is met with pardon and renewed relationship rather than rejection.

translation: قالوا: «يا شعيبُ، ما نفقه كثيرًا ممّا تقول، وإنا لنراك فينا ضعيفًا، ولولا رهطك لرجمناك، وما أنت علينا بعزيز».
interpretation: هذه كلمات تكشف عن سلوك الناس حين تُهدّد مصالحهم وأعرافهم: بدلاً من مناقشة الرسالة بالمنطق أو الاعتبار، يختارون إقناع أنفسهم بأنها غير مفهومة، ويهاجمون المبلّغ شخصيًا بوصفه «ضعيفًا» ثم يلجأون إلى الترهيب والتهديد مستندين إلى روابط القرابة لحماية مصلحتهم. الآية تبيّن كيف تجمع الغطرسة، المحافظة على الوضع القائم، والخوف من التغيير ليدفعوا إلى قمع الحقيقة بالقول والتهديد بدلًا من التعامل معها بنزاهة.

translation:
قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ أَرْهْطِي أَعَزُّ عَلَيْكُم مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَاتَّخَذْتُمُوهُ وَرَاءَكُمْ ظِهْرًا ۖ إِنَّ رَبِّي بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ مُحِيطٌ
“He said, ‘O my people, is my kin (my clan) more dear to you than Allah? You have taken them as a support behind you. Indeed, my Lord encompasses (is fully aware of) whatever you do.’”
interpretation: The speaker reproves his people for letting family or tribal allegiance override duty to God and for relying on human backing as if it could protect them from divine accountability; he warns that such social protection is futile because God fully knows and surrounds all their deeds and will judge accordingly.

translation: O my people, act according to your positions; indeed I am acting. Soon you will know who will be visited by a punishment that will disgrace him and who is a liar. And wait—indeed I am with you, watching.
interpretation: The speaker asserts that he has done his duty in warning and will not compel belief; he warns that truth will be vindicated by the consequences God brings—those who persist in rejection will be publicly disgraced by punishment—while the messenger remains among them as a patient, observing witness to their choices and to the impending divine judgment.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Shuʿayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us; and the blast seized those who had wronged, so they awoke in their homes prostrate.
interpretation: The verse teaches that deliverance and destruction are ultimately acts of God’s will: the faithful are rescued not by their own strength but by God’s mercy (نجينا... برحمة منا), while persistent wrongdoers are overtaken suddenly by a decisive punishment (الصيحة) that leaves them helpless and humiliated in their own dwellings (أصبحوا في ديارهم جاثمين). The contrast underscores both divine compassion for those who submit and the inevitability of accountability for those who persist in injustice and rejection of guidance; salvation comes as a gift, and punishment comes swiftly when the divine decree is executed.

translation: كأن لم يغنوا فيها: As if they had never prospered there. أَلَا بَعدًا لِمَدْيَنَ كَمَا بَعَثَتْ ثَمُودَ: Woe to Madyan — just as Thamud were destroyed.
interpretation: The verse warns that worldly prosperity is no safeguard against divine retribution: when a people persist in corruption and reject the message, their fortunes can be erased so completely that it is as though they had never flourished. By invoking Madyan and the prior doom of Thamud, the text signals that a community facing divine judgment will suffer sudden, total ruin unless it heeds the warning and turns back to right conduct.

translation: And indeed We sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God equipped Moses with unmistakable divine proofs and a manifest mandate: the “signs” are the miracles and revealed guidance that demonstrated God’s backing, and the “clear authority” (sulṭān mubīn) is the decisive, authoritative proof and commission given to him to establish his mission, confront oppression and falsehood, and leave people’s acceptance or rejection as a matter of their free choice rather than lack of evidence.

translation: إلى فرعون وملئه — فاتبعوا أمر فرعون، وما أمر فرعون برشيد
interpretation: الآية تبيّن خطر الطاعة غير المشروطة للسلطان الظالم: إن اتباع الجماعة لأوامر فرعون لم يجعل تلك الأوامر صالحة أو موجهة إلى الحق، فتذكّر أن الشرعية والهدى يُقاسان بمعيار الله والعدالة لا بسلطةٍ قاهرة أو إجماعٍ فاسد.

translation: He will present his people on the Day of Resurrection and will drive them into the Fire — and evil is the resting-place provided.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who, by their words or leadership, mislead others away from guidance: on the Day of Judgment such a leader will be held accountable and will bring his followers to ruin, all of them exposed to the punishment of Hell. It emphasizes collective responsibility — the danger of following corrupt guidance and the grave responsibility of those who influence others — and it stresses the utter horror and finality of that fate by calling it an evil and deplorable place of return.

translation: And they followed — in this [life] — a curse, and (it will be) on the Day of Resurrection. How wretched is the aid that is given!
interpretation: The verse warns that those who follow falsehood, their passions, or misleading allies will bring upon themselves God’s curse both in this world and on the Day of Judgment; the help or companionship they relied on will prove to be a miserable, harmful support that brings humiliation rather than benefit.

translation:
ذلك من أنباء القرى نقصه عليك ۖ منها قائم وحصيد
"That is among the accounts of the towns which We relate to you; some of them still stand, and some have been reaped (harvested)."
interpretation: The verse indicates that God recounts past communities to the Prophet not merely as history but as moral instruction: the varying destinies—some towns preserved as lasting signs, others swept away—express divine wisdom and accountability. Preservation or ruin function as means to warn, remind, and prompt reflection that worldly permanence is transient and that communities are judged according to their faith and conduct.

translation: وَمَا ظَلَمْنَاهُمْ وَلَـكِن ظَلَمُوا أَنفُسَهُمْ ۖ فَمَا أَغْنَتْ عَنْهُمْ آلِهَتُهُمُ الَّتِي يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ مِن شَيْءٍ لَمَّا جَاءَ أَمْرُ رَبِّكَ ۖ وَمَا زَادَهُمْ غَيْرَ تَتَبِيبٍ
interpretation: الله يعلن براءته من الظلم؛ ما لَم يحصل لهم من عذاب إلا نتيجة ظلمهم لأنفسهم عبر الكفر والشرك والمعاصي. آلهتهم وأوثانهم التي كانوا يرجون منها نفعًا لم تنفعهم شيئًا حين جاء قرار الله وحلول الجزاء، بل جعلت منهم سببًا في زيادة تفسخ أو هلاكٍ لحالهم — أي أن التمسك بالأوثان والضلال لم يزدهم إلا ضياعًا وعمقًا في البلى. المعنى العملي: المسؤولية الفردية والنتيجة الحتمية للأفعال؛ من يختَر الباطل ويعاند الحق يورث نفسه الهلاك، ولا شفيع لما يحاولون من دون الله.

translation: And thus your Lord seized (punished) when He seized the towns while they were wrongdoers. Indeed, His seizure is a painful, severe [punishment].
interpretation: The verse teaches that when a community persists in injustice and rejection of God’s guidance, divine justice can intervene decisively: the destruction of such towns is presented as an inevitable, severe retribution intended both as recompense and as a warning to others. The description “a painful, severe” punishment emphasizes the intensity and certainty of that consequence, while implicitly urging repentance and moral reform before divine judgment arrives.

translation: Indeed in that is a sign for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day when the people will be gathered for their Lord; that is a Day witnessed.
interpretation: The verse functions as a solemn admonition: the certainty and public nature of the Day of Gathering should reshape a believer’s priorities — prompting sincere repentance, vigilance against complacency, and consistent righteous conduct — because ultimate accountability before God is unavoidable and makes transient worldly concerns irrelevant.

translation: وما نؤخره إلا لأجل معدود — And We delay it only for an appointed (counted) term.
interpretation: The postponement mentioned is a deliberate, limited respite from divine retribution: God defers the punishment for a specifically appointed, finite period—not out of inability or forgetfulness but as part of His wisdom and mercy—so that people are tried and given an opportunity to repent; when the appointed term arrives the decree will be executed.

translation: A Day will come when no soul will speak except by His permission; among them are the wretched and the blessed.
interpretation: The verse affirms that on the Day of Reckoning every human's ability to speak and be heard will depend entirely on God’s will: ‘speech’ there signifies the public manifestation of a person’s true moral state—testimony, pleas, intercession or confession. That divine permission will divide people into two clear destinies: the shaqi (wretched) whose words will only confirm their loss and exclusion from mercy, and the saʿeed (blessed) whose permitted speech will witness their salvation and thankfulness. The point is to stress God’s absolute sovereignty in judgment and that ultimate felicity or ruin is determined by His decree in accordance with people’s deeds and God’s mercy.

translation: As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire; for them therein is sighing and gasping.
interpretation: The verse tells of the fate of those who choose the path of injustice and rejection: they will inhabit Hell, and the words زفير (exhalation/sighing) and شهيق (inhalation/gasping) portray continual, agonized breathing—sighs of despair and choking gasps. This imagery stresses the severity, relentless nature, and humiliating helplessness of their torment (physically felt as heat, suffocation and thirst and spiritually as utter degradation), showing the inevitable consequence of persistent turning away from guidance.

translation: They will abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure—except as your Lord may will. Indeed, your Lord is ever an accomplisher of what He wills.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the described permanence of that abode is vast—lasting for the duration of the created cosmos—while immediately qualifying it by reminding us that nothing persists except by God’s will. The phrase “except as your Lord may will” removes any absolute necessity from created things and places all duration under divine prerogative; and “your Lord is ever an accomplisher of what He wills” emphasizes that God’s will is effective, decisive, and capable of bringing about whatever He intends. In short, the passage underscores both the seriousness and endurance of the outcome described and, at the same time, the absolute sovereignty and efficaciousness of God over all events and destinies.

translation: And as for those who are made to prosper, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure — except as your Lord wills — a gift not cut off.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the felicity granted to the righteous is a divinely secured, enduring reality: their enjoyment in Paradise is portrayed as continuous and inexhaustible (a gift “not cut off”), signifying God’s boundless generosity. The phrase “except as your Lord wills” does not undermine that promise but reminds that the duration and manner of all outcomes rest with God’s wisdom and sovereignty; in other words, believers are assured of perpetual, unfading blessings whose timing and ultimate unfolding are under Allah’s wise authority.

translation: So be not in doubt concerning what these people worship. They worship nothing but what their fathers used to worship before, and indeed We will grant them their due portion — not diminished.
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet that the idolaters’ persistence is rooted in ancestral habit rather than ignorance of the Prophet’s sincerity; God will not be unjust or forgetful but will assign to each people what they deserve. Thus the responsibility of the Messenger is to convey the truth, while the ultimate outcome — reward or consequence for following inherited error — rests with God, who will give every group its exact, undiminished reckoning.

translation: And certainly We gave Moses the Book, yet they disputed over it. And had it not been for a decree that had gone forth from your Lord, the matter between them would have been decided; and indeed they are in perplexing doubt about it.
interpretation: God reminds that despite giving clear scripture to Moses, people quarreled over its meaning; rather than immediately enforcing judgment He allowed the dispute to continue by a prior divine decree so that His wisdom and plan could unfold. The verse therefore indicts those whose disagreements reveal unstable, suspicious doubt — an inward moral and intellectual confusion — and teaches that apparent delay in divine settlement is purposeful (to test, warn, and complete guidance), not a sign of God’s neglect.

translation: And indeed, every person — your Lord will surely give them their deeds in full; indeed He is, concerning what they do, Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse teaches that final justice is certain: God will apportion recompense exactly according to each person’s actions and inner states. Because He is fully aware of both outward deeds and hidden intentions, no one will be wronged or over‑rewarded; worldly inequalities do not determine ultimate judgment. The practical consequence is to live with sincere responsibility — seeking God’s pleasure, avoiding reliance on human judgment, and neither despairing over apparent injustice nor becoming heedless because of passing success.

translation:
فَاسْتَقِمْ كَمَا أُمِرْتَ وَمَن تَابَ مَعَكَ وَلَا تَطْغَوْا ۚ إِنَّهُ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ
"So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and those who have repented with you; and do not transgress. Indeed, He is, of what you do, Seeing."
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet and the community to persistently uphold the straight, divinely prescribed path with steadiness and consistency; it extends the same call to those who have repented and rejoined the community, emphasizing that repentance must be accompanied by sustained upright conduct. The prohibition 'do not transgress' warns against excess—whether arrogance, injustice, moral laxity, or religious extremism—and calls for moderation and respect for limits in belief and behavior. The reminder that God is Seeing affirms that actions (and the intentions behind them) are observed and will be reckoned, so steadfastness, sincerity, and avoidance of transgression are required both for communal order and personal accountability.

translation:
وَلَا تَرْكَنُوا إِلَى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا فَتَمَسَّكُمُ النَّارُ ۖ وَمَا لَكُم مِّن دُونِ اللَّهِ مِنْ أَوْلِيَاءَ ثُمَّ لَا تُنصَرُونَ
"Do not lean toward (give favor or ally yourselves with) those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you; you will have no protectors besides Allah, and then you will not be helped."
interpretation: The verse warns believers against forming sympathies, alliances, or dependence on oppressors—whether out of fear, kinship, social advantage, or political expediency—because closeness to injustice tends to corrupt one’s own conduct and makes one complicit, exposing one to divine punishment. It also reminds that no human patron can ultimately substitute for God’s protection: siding with tyrants severs true reliance on Allah and leaves one without help in the final reckoning. The moral teaching is to preserve independence of conscience, refuse complicity in wrongdoing, and prioritize obedience to God over transient worldly ties.

translation: And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approaches of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.
interpretation: The verse teaches that regular, timely worship—structured throughout the day and into the night—is a practical discipline that continually purifies the soul: by returning frequently to God in prayer and righteous actions, a believer’s good deeds counterbalance and wipe away past faults. It frames worship not as mere obligation but as a merciful, restorative means of moral renewal and sustained mindfulness for those who heed it.

translation: And be patient; indeed, Allah does not let the reward of the doers of good be lost.
interpretation: This verse commands steadfast patience amid hardship or delay, assuring believers that sincere, excellent conduct (al‑ihsan) will not go unrewarded by God. It means one should persevere in righteous action and moral excellence even when immediate results are absent or injustice seems to prevail, trusting that Allah — in His perfect knowledge and justice — preserves and grants the due recompense, whether in this world or in the hereafter; thus patience is both an active endurance and continued commitment to good, rooted in reliance on divine justice.

translation: Had there not been, among the generations before you, men of perseverance who would forbid corruption on earth—except for a few of those We saved—those who did wrong would have followed what they enjoyed of luxury, and they were criminals.
interpretation: The verse asserts that the moral health of a community often rests on a small number of steadfast people who actively resist injustice; without such remonstrators the wealthy and powerful would pursue their comforts unchecked, leading society into widespread wrongdoing. It is both a consolation—that God preserves a remnant who restrain corruption—and a warning that neglecting the duty to oppose evil and surrendering to ease and luxury enables criminality to prevail, so believers must strive to be among those who forbid corruption.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers.
interpretation: The verse affirms Divine justice and responsiveness: God does not annihilate communities arbitrarily; destruction comes as a measured consequence of persistent collective corruption and rejection of guidance. The presence of sincere reformers — those who work to restore moral and social order and call people back to right conduct — is a cause for mercy and protection, so communal salvation depends on sustained reform and responsibility rather than random punishment.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind a single community; yet they would continue to differ.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human religious and social diversity is by Divine allowance: God could have made everyone uniform, but He permits difference so that human freedom, moral responsibility, testing, and the manifestation of His mercy and justice can occur. In other words, disagreement and variety among people serve a wise purpose—to distinguish those who seek truth and to make the granting of guidance and mercy meaningful—rather than indicating a defect in God's command.

translation: Except those upon whom your Lord bestows mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord is bound to be fulfilled, "I will fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s creation of jinn and humans involves both His justice and His mercy: many will follow error and face punishment as part of the unfolding of divine decree, yet God’s mercy remains the real exception that saves some. The “except” underscores that mercy is a gracious, sovereign choice by God, and the announcement that Hell will be filled emphasizes the seriousness of misguidance—so believers are called to recognize human vulnerability, urgently seek God’s mercy, and live in awareness of both divine justice and mercy.

translation: And thus We relate to you some of the tidings of the messengers so that We may strengthen your heart thereby. And in this [revelation] has come to you the truth and a reminder and admonition for the believers.
interpretation: The verse explains that God intentionally presents selected stories of earlier prophets to the Prophet Muhammad not as mere historical report but as an instrument to confirm and fortify his conviction, patience, and resolve in the face of denial. By framing those accounts within the Qur'an’s message, God makes them signs of the same divine truth and practical lessons: they console and counsel the community, teach believers to recognize recurring spiritual patterns (faith, trial, rejection, consequence), and urge steadfastness and moral learning so that believers may avoid past errors and remain committed to guidance.

translation:
وقُل لِلَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ: «اعْمَلُوا عَلَى مَكَانَتِكُمْ ۖ إِنَّا عَامِلُونَ»

"And say to those who do not believe, ‘Do as you will; surely we are working (as well).’”
interpretation: A resolute reply to opponents: let them pursue their courses and schemes, for the Prophet and the faithful will persist in their divinely commanded work—worship, calling to truth, and implementing justice—confident in God’s support. It declares steadfastness, reliance on God’s plan, and the implicit warning that opposing efforts cannot frustrate what God has ordained; each party will ultimately bear the consequences of its actions.

translation: And wait; indeed, we are waiting.
interpretation: A defiant taunt by the rejecters of the message: they refuse to heed the warning and arrogantly tell the Messenger to wait, declaring that they themselves will remain and watch — a statement that exposes their stubbornness, mockery, and determination to postpone repentance while expecting to see what will befall others.

translation: To Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him returns all affairs. So worship Him and place your trust in Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate knowledge and authority lie solely with God — He alone knows what is hidden and ultimately governs every outcome — and from that reality it draws moral and spiritual consequences: believers should dedicate worship to Him and practice sincere reliance (tawakkul) instead of anxious self-reliance, while recognizing that every action is seen and will be accounted for, which requires integrity, patience in trials, and trust in God’s wise management of affairs.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Alif‑Lam‑Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.
interpretation: The disconnected letters (الر) are presented as a sign of the Quran’s miraculous, divine origin—something beyond human composition that draws attention to the speech that follows. By calling what follows “the verses of the Clear Book,” the text asserts that these passages are manifest signs and guidance: they are meant to be understood as decisive evidence, to teach, warn, and reform communities. Placing the revelation under “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate” frames even stern guidance and judgment within God’s mercy, indicating the purpose of the disclosure is ultimately to guide people toward moral and spiritual recovery rather than arbitrary punishment.

translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse signals that the Qur’an’s linguistic form is part of its means of guidance: revealed in Arabic to be immediately clear, rhetorically powerful, and intelligible to its first audience, it invites active reasoning and reflection (taʿaqqul) rather than passive reception. By linking language to comprehension, the verse emphasizes that understanding—using one’s intellect to weigh its arguments, perceive its signs, and allow insight to transform belief and conduct—is an essential step in responding to the message.

translation: We relate to you the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, and indeed before it you were surely among the heedless.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur'an presents selectively chosen, exemplary narratives whose primary function is moral and spiritual instruction, consolation, and guidance rather than mere recital of events. Calling them “the best of stories” stresses their didactic and transformative value: they reform hearts, correct prior heedlessness, and demonstrate that the Prophet’s knowledge and the community’s guidance come through divine revelation, thereby establishing the Qur’an’s authority and purpose.

translation: “When Joseph said to his father, ‘O my father, indeed I have seen eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.’”
interpretation: The dream is a true, divinely inspired omen: the eleven ‘stars’ signify his eleven brothers and the ‘sun’ and ‘moon’ represent his parents (commonly taken as father and mother), and their prostration symbolizes their future recognition, honor and submission to Joseph’s God‑given rank—foretelling his rise, reconciliation with his family, and the unfolding of Allah’s plan, rather than literal worship.

translation: He said, "O my sons, do not relate your vision to your brothers lest they devise against you a plot. Indeed Satan is to man a manifest enemy."
interpretation: The verse counsels prudence: evident favors or visions can provoke jealousy, and Satan exploits human weakness to turn that jealousy into harmful scheming. Jacob’s warning teaches that one should be cautious about whom one discloses intimate or exalted insights to, because Satan can inflame envy and lead people to betray or harm what God intended; trust in God and exercise discretion to protect blessings from being twisted into causes of harm.

translation: And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of narratives, and He will complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Yaʿqūb, just as He completed it upon your fathers before — upon Ibrāhīm and Isḥāq. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: God’s bestowal of special knowledge and of a prophetic role is deliberate and serves a broader, wise plan that unfolds across generations. Exceptional gifts (like insight into hidden meanings) are instruments in God’s governance to bring about justice, guidance and the completion of His favor; believers are therefore called to trust that apparent misfortunes and later vindications are means by which God, in His knowledge and wisdom, accomplishes His purposes for individuals and their communities.

translation: Indeed in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask.
interpretation: The narrative of Joseph and his brothers functions as a set of divine signs for sincere seekers: it demonstrates how God’s wisdom and providence operate in human affairs—turning injustice into eventual vindication, transforming hatred into reconciliation, rewarding patience and integrity, and exposing the moral consequences of envy—so that those who inquire and reflect may recognize God’s guidance and respond in faith and submission.

translation: When they said, “Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we are, although we are a company; indeed our father is in clear error.”
interpretation: The verse illustrates how envy warps perception and reasoning: those who feel slighted convince themselves that the favored one is unduly preferred and that the father's judgment is plainly wrong, using resentment to justify hostile actions; it warns that jealousy produces moral blindness and self‑justifying accusations rather than objective assessment.

translation: Kill Joseph or throw him into some remote land; then your father's attention will be for you alone, and you will thereafter be a righteous people.
interpretation: The brothers, driven by jealousy, propose removing Joseph so that their father’s affection and attention would fall solely upon them; they justify this wrongdoing by expecting that without Joseph they will regain favor and be seen as a virtuous, united family. The phrase about the father’s “face” refers to his care or regard, and “becoming a righteous people” is their self‑serving rationalization for an act motivated by envy rather than true piety.

translation: قال قائل منهم: «لا تقتلوا يوسف، وألقوه في غيابات الجب؛ يلتقطه بعض السيارة إن كنتم فاعلين».
interpretation: الآية تُظهر خطة أحد الإخوة ليتخلصوا من يوسف دون إظهار القتل العلني، فبدلاً من استحقاق القتل يقترح إلقاءه في بئر على أمل أن تصادفه قافلة وتستغله أو تبتاعه، وبذلك تتبدد مسؤوليتهم الظاهرة. في تفسير أوسع: الحكاية تكشف قساوة الحسد الذي يدفع الإنسان إلى التآمر والتبرير الأخلاقي لإيذاء آخرين (التركيز على الحل العملي الذي يوفر مخرجاً معويّاً للذنب)، وفي الوقت نفسه تبيّن كيف تعمل الحكمة الإلهية على تحويل مساعي البشر الخبيثة إلى مسار يقود إلى خير أسمى ليوسف — درس عن خطورة الحسد، ووسائل البشر الملتوية لتفادي المسؤولية، وثقة في أن مقاصد الله قد تتكشف على نحو معاكس لنيات الظالمين.

translation: They said, “O our father, why do you not entrust Joseph to us? Indeed, we are sincere counselors for him.”
interpretation: The brothers’ words are a piece of persuasive rhetoric: they present themselves as caring and trustworthy to gain permission to take Joseph, masking jealousy and harmful intent. The verse thus cautions against judging solely by comforting words—true intent is shown by character and past behavior—and illustrates how people may cloak wrongdoing in the language of care to achieve selfish ends.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow; he will frolic and play, and indeed we will be his guardians.
interpretation: This line exposes the hypocritical, deceptive stance of those who opposed the truth: they propose sending a seemingly innocent emissary under the pretext of harmless play while concealing an investigative or hostile intent, and they cloak that intent with a boastful assurance of ‘guardianship.’ The verse points to the moral failing of disguising malice as care and the arrogance of claiming control over another’s fate while rejecting sincere guidance.

translation: He said, “It grieves me that you should take him away, and I fear that the wolf may eat him while you are heedless of him.”
interpretation: The words reflect Yaʿqūb’s deep, anguished vigilance: his sorrow is not mere sentimentality but a perceptive awareness of vulnerability and of destructive forces that prey on the weak. The “wolf” functions both literally and symbolically for treachery, envy or neglect, and the warning against being “heedless” admonishes caregivers to exercise responsibility and watchfulness. At the same time the verse shows a prophet’s human grief lived within surrender to God’s will—teaching that heartfelt fear and sorrow for the vulnerable are legitimate and morally active feelings that call for protection, not passive acceptance.

translation: They said, “If the wolf were to eat him while we are a company, then indeed we would be losers.”
interpretation: The phrase is a disingenuous excuse: instead of admitting their envy and violent intent, the brothers invent an external cause and feign remorse to escape blame. It illustrates how wrongdoers often construct plausible stories that shift responsibility onto fate or accident to protect their reputation, revealing hypocrisy and moral cowardice rather than genuine contrition.

translation: So when they had gone away with him and agreed to put him in the bottom of the well — and We inspired to him, “You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs while they do not perceive.”
interpretation: God is assuring the one wronged by implanting in him a sure inner knowledge that, in God’s appointed course, the truth of the wrongdoing will become known to the perpetrators through events and his presence even if they are unaware at the time; the verse teaches that divine consolation, vindication, and justice often unfold subtly and in God’s timing, requiring patience and trust rather than immediate human retaliation.

translation: And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.
interpretation: The description of them 'weeping' portrays a calculated display of sorrow intended to elicit sympathy and conceal wrongdoing — their tears function as an emotional mask to manipulate their father and hide their guilt.

translation: They said, “O our father, indeed we went racing and left Joseph with our belongings, and a wolf ate him. And you would not believe us, even if we were truthful.”
interpretation: This statement exposes the brothers’ attempt to hide their guilt by inventing an implausible story and shifting blame; it reveals moral corruption—jealousy leading to betrayal, cowardice in facing responsibility, and the use of deceit to preempt scrutiny—while the narrative framework signals that truth and justice will ultimately be vindicated despite such temporary concealment.

translation: And they brought upon his shirt false blood. He said, “Rather, your souls have enticed you to something. So patience is most fitting. And Allah is the One sought for help against what you describe.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that when confronted with slander or fabricated evidence, one should recognize such wrongdoing as the result of people’s misleading desires, respond with ‘sabr jameel’ — composed, dignified patience rather than impulsive retaliation — and entrust one’s cause to God, seeking His help and justice rather than relying solely on worldly means.

translation: A caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, “Good news — a boy!” So they concealed him as merchandise. And Allah was, of what they did, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse points to the moral sickness of treating a human being as a commodity and concealing wrongdoing for short‑term advantage; it also affirms that such secret schemes are never beyond God’s knowledge. In other words, apparent success from sinful actions is both ethically condemnable and ultimately encompassed by divine knowledge and wisdom, so hidden evil will be accounted for and may serve within God’s larger plan toward justice and eventual vindication.

translation: And they sold him for a paltry price— a few coins— and they were, concerning him, of those who were indifferent.
interpretation: The phrase portrays the sellers’ moral indifference: they treated their kin with callous detachment and accepted a trivial sum, showing that their hearts had become numb to compassion and justice so that they could betray him for little gain.

translation: And the man from Egypt who bought him said to his wife, “Honor his lodging; perhaps he will be of benefit to us, or we will adopt him as a son.” Thus We established Joseph in the land and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse shows that what appears to be human planning and chance — the purchaser’s kindness and decision to keep Joseph in his household — was woven into a larger divine design. God mounted Joseph into a position in Egypt not merely for worldly comfort but to prepare him with the special knowledge (the interpretation of dreams and events) necessary for his future role. The phrase that God is “predominant over His affair” reminds us that behind human choices and intentions there is Allah’s sovereign wisdom and purpose, which people usually fail to perceive; acts of mercy, provision, and even apparent misfortune can thus be instruments in God’s unfolding plan to educate, elevate, and use His servants for a greater good.

translation: And when he reached full strength, We granted him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: When a servant matures and God finds in him earnestness and righteousness, God bestows on him the inner faculties (sound judgment, discernment) and the outward means (knowledge, authority) needed to act justly and benefit others; this verse teaches that divine reward often comes as empowerment to do good—wisdom and capacity entrusted to those whose conduct merits it, so they may rule rightly and serve as examples for others.

translation: And the woman in whose house he was sought to make advances toward him and she locked the doors and said, “Come on.” He said, “I seek refuge in Allah! Indeed, He is my Lord who has made my dwelling good; indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true moral strength in moments of temptation comes from immediately seeking God’s protection and recognizing that one’s honorable circumstances are a gift and trust from Him; this awareness empowers steadfast resistance to wrongdoing and reminds that those who act unjustly will not ultimately prosper.

translation: And indeed she had set her heart on him, and he would have inclined to her — had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus We averted from him evil and immorality; indeed, he was of Our sincere devoted servants.
interpretation: The verse teaches that moral victory over temptation is produced by the combination of an immediate awareness of God (the “proof” or barāhīn) and sincere devotion. The “proof” is not merely external coercion but a clear, conscience‑stirring sign—whether revelation, inner conviction, or a witnessing of divine authority—that makes sin unacceptable; together with Yusuf’s genuine devotion, this awareness mobilized his will and brought God’s protection, turning away corruption. The passage therefore emphasizes that purity of conduct depends both on divine assistance and on an earnest, heartfelt commitment to God.

translation: And they raced toward the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her husband at the door. She said, “What is the recompense for the one who intended evil toward your wife, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?”
interpretation: The verse highlights how someone in a position of influence can manipulate outward signs and legal language to reverse guilt and protect their reputation: by posing a rhetorical question about the proper punishment for one who ‘intended evil,’ the accuser frames the situation to demand severe sanction while presenting herself as the injured party. The passage warns against accepting appearances or rhetorical force as proof, stresses the vulnerability of the innocent to slander when power and social norms favor the claimant, and points to the moral requirement that judgment be based on truth rather than on expedient accusations—ultimately affirming that divine justice will reveal the reality behind human deceit.

translation: He said, “She sought to seduce me away from myself.” And a witness from her household testified, “If his shirt is torn in front, then she speaks the truth and he is surely one of the liars.”
interpretation: This verse exposes how appearances and biased testimony can be used to decide guilt or innocence: the accused declares his resistance and innocence, while someone close to the accuser interprets a physical sign in a way that would support her claim. It warns that human witnesses often see what fits their loyalties and that outward indications can be misread; the passage thus calls for caution in accepting partial testimony and for reliance on fuller evidence and divine justice to reveal the true situation.

translation:
وإن كان قميصه قد من دبر فكذبت وهو من الصادقين
“If his shirt has been torn from the back, then they have lied — he is indeed among the truthful.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that outward signs can be manipulated to support a false accusation, yet such contrived evidence does not alter the moral reality: the accused’s integrity remains intact and is recognized as truthful. It warns against trusting manufactured appearances and affirms that truthfulness is not negated by deceitful testimony.

translation: When he saw his shirt had been torn at the back, he said, “It is from your plot — indeed your plot is great.”
interpretation: Yūsuf, confronted with the torn shirt as staged evidence, immediately recognizes and condemns the women's contrivance; by calling their stratagem “great” he both asserts his innocence and highlights the seriousness and deliberateness of their deceit, teaching that moral integrity, clear perception, and swift refusal of temptation expose manipulative schemes even when outward appearances are arranged to incriminate the innocent.

translation: “Yūsuf, turn away from this; and seek forgiveness for your sin—you were indeed of the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a tactic of the guilty who, to hide their own fault, demand repentance from and accuse the innocent; it warns against manipulative shifting of blame and urges firmness against coerced confessions while trusting God’s justice.

translation: And the women in the city said, “The wife of al-ʿAzīz is attempting to seduce her slave for himself; indeed, he has captivated her with love. Verily, we see her in manifest error.”
interpretation: This verse exposes how public opinion and gossip form quickly from appearances and desire: the women of the town, observing the situation and moved by Yusuf’s beauty, hastily cast moral blame on the lady and label her as clearly misguided. Their words show the human tendency to interpret passion as wrongdoing and to spread a condemning narrative without full knowledge—foreshadowing the social injustice and slander that will surround Yusuf’s trial and illustrating the Quranic lesson to beware of rash judgments, envy, and the destructive power of rumor.

translation: So when she heard of their plot, she sent for them and prepared for them a seat and gave each of them a knife, and said, “Come out before them.” But when they saw him, they were amazed at him and cut their hands and exclaimed, “Glory be to Allah! This is not a man; this is nothing but a noble angel.”
interpretation: The verse illustrates how God’s truth can abruptly expose human contrivances: the women’s spontaneous, physical reaction and their invocation of God show that Yusuf’s presence transcended ordinary attraction and struck them as extraordinary—so much so that they recoiled and declared him other than a mere man. Their behavior both signals the powerful, disorienting effect of Yusuf’s chastity and beauty and serves to undermine the charge that he acted corruptly, demonstrating that divine integrity vindicates the innocent and overturns human plots.

translation: قالت فذلكن الذي لمتنني فيه ۖ ولقد راودته عن نفسه فاستعصم ۖ ولئن لم يفعل ما آمره ليسجنن وليكونا من الصاغرين
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring moral pattern: when a person in power is refused, they may resort to slander and threats to secure compliance, weaponizing authority to punish the upright. It also highlights the cost and moral strength of steadfastness—guarding one's integrity can provoke injustice and worldly humiliation, yet believers are taught to remain firm in righteousness despite such threats, trusting that true judgment and recompense rest with God.

translation: He said, “My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me; and if You do not turn away their scheme from me, I shall incline toward them and be of the ignorant.”
interpretation: Yusuf expresses that preserving faith and honor is worth hardship: he would rather endure imprisonment than submit to a sinful temptation that would betray God’s trust. By asking God to avert their plot he acknowledges both reliance on divine protection against seductive forces and his own vulnerability; without that protection he fears yielding and thus falling into spiritual ignorance and disgrace. The verse therefore teaches prioritizing moral integrity over worldly ease and seeking God’s help to resist temptation while humbly admitting human weakness.

translation:
فاستجاب له ربه فصرف عنه كيدهن ۚ إنه هو السميع العليم
"So his Lord responded to him and turned away their plot from him. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing."
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere turning to God elicits His active protection: He can frustrate hidden schemes and avert harm without needing to display a public miracle. The divine attributes “All‑Hearing” and “All‑Knowing” reassure the believer that God perceives both spoken pleas and inward realities and that ultimate vindication and safety rest with Him when one seeks refuge in Him.

translation: ثُمَّ بَدَا لَهُمْ مِن بَعْدِ مَا رَأَوْا الْآيَاتِ لِيَسْجُنّنَهُ حَتَّى حِينٍ
interpretation: الآية تبيّن حقيقة نفسية واجتماعية: أن الناس قد يصرّون على الظلم رغم مشاهدة البراهين الواضحة، فيختارون سجنَ الصادق مؤقتًا ليكتموا قضيته أو يخففوا إحراجهم، ليس لأن الحجة ضدّه صحيحة بل لأسبابٍ مثل الحسد أو حفاظًا على مصالحهم. عبارة «حتى حين» تؤكد أن الحبس كان إجراءً زمنيًا متدنّياً ومؤقتًا، وتذكّر بأن الابتلاء بالحبس أو التأجيل قد يكون جزءًا من تدبير إلهي لتمحيص الصبر وإظهار الحق لاحقًا.

translation: And two young men entered with him into the prison. One of them said, “Indeed, I see myself pressing wine,” and the other said, “Indeed, I see myself carrying upon my head bread, from which the birds eat.” “Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you to be of the doers of good.”
interpretation: The dreams function as divinely sent signs whose images point to concrete future states: the act of pressing wine symbolises restoration to the former office of cupbearer and a return to freedom and service, while carrying bread on the head with birds eating from it depicts a humiliating death or public exposure of the body (commonly understood as execution or crucifixion) after which scavengers will feed on it. The men’s appeal — “we see you to be of the doers of good” — explains why they seek Yusuf’s interpretation: they judge him truthful and pious, and thus a fitting channel through whom God reveals the meaning of these portentous dreams.

translation: He said, “No food will come to you except that I will tell you its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed I have abandoned the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who are, concerning the Hereafter, disbelievers.”
interpretation: Yusuf is asserting that his insight into forthcoming events (here, the meaning behind the food/dreams) is a divinely granted gift, not mere conjecture, and he invokes that gift to benefit others; by declaring he has left the faith of his former people he emphasizes that true religion is defined by belief in God and the Hereafter rather than by inherited customs, signalling his moral and spiritual separation from a community he judges to be in error.

translation: And I followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. It was not fitting for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the favor of Allah upon us and upon mankind, but most people do not give thanks.
interpretation: The speaker affirms a continuous, inherited commitment to pure monotheism as handed down by prophetic ancestors, presenting the rejection of idolatry (shirk) not as mere custom but as a principled obligation; this fidelity is described as a merciful gift from God that enables a people to recognize and preserve true guidance, and the verse warns that failing to acknowledge and be grateful for that divine favor is common — ingratitude often leads people away from the clear path despite the blessing they have received.

translation: O my fellow prisoners, are the many, scattered lords better, or Allah — the One, the All‑Subduer?
interpretation: The speaker forces a rational comparison: worship of multiple, fragmented 'lords' implies reliance on competing, powerless authorities, whereas Allah’s description as al‑Wāḥid (the One) and al‑Qahhār (the Overwhelming/Subduer) affirms unique, absolute sovereignty and effective control over all affairs. By highlighting unity and overwhelming power, the verse urges rejection of divided, impotent deities and directs trust and worship to the single, omnipotent Creator who alone truly deserves to be called Lord.

translation: What you worship besides Him are nothing but names which you and your fathers have invented, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Sovereignty belongs to Allah alone. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse is a critique of inherited idolatry and cultural practices that lack divine sanction: names, titles or rituals passed down through families do not confer legitimate religious authority unless God has revealed and authorized them. True authority and the right to legislate belong solely to Allah, and therefore genuine religion consists in recognizing His sole sovereignty and worshiping Him alone. The warning is both theological and ethical: cling not to ancestral customs simply because they are familiar, but submit to the command of God; failure to do so is widespread because many remain unaware or negligent of this foundational truth.

translation: O my two fellow prisoners, as for one of you, he will give his lord to drink wine; and as for the other, he will be crucified, and the birds will eat from his head. The matter about which you both inquired has been decided.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty and finality of God’s decree: human conjecture and pleading cannot alter what God has ordained. The phrase “قضي الأمر” underscores that once God’s judgment is set, events unfold according to His wise purpose—serving as a test, a vindication of truth, and a warning—revealing that outcomes are ultimately determined by divine wisdom rather than by human expectation.

translation: And he said to the one whom he thought would be delivered, "Mention me to your Lord." But Satan caused him to forget to mention him to his Lord, and Joseph remained in prison for several years.
interpretation: This verse teaches that human intentions and assurances are fragile and can be undermined by inward negligence or satanic prompting; when the cupbearer failed to speak up, it was not merely a social lapse but an instance of how Satan obstructs timely good by inducing forgetfulness or complacency. The passage calls believers to avoid relying solely on others’ promises, to seek God’s help against such subtle derailments, and to view delays and setbacks (like Joseph’s prolonged imprisonment) as part of divine wisdom that tests patience, preserves ultimate justice, and makes God’s deliverance more manifest.

translation: And the king said, "Indeed I see [in a dream] seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears and others withered. O chiefs, inform me of my vision if you are able to interpret dreams."
interpretation: The vision symbolizes a coming cycle of seven years of abundance followed by seven years of devastating scarcity; the king's appeal for an explanation underscores the necessity of sound counsel and that true interpretation of signs is granted by God (as later demonstrated through Joseph).

translation: قالوا: «أضغاث أحلام، وما نحن بتأويل الأحلام بعالمين» — They said, “Confused, nonsensical dreams; and we are not people who know how to interpret dreams.”
interpretation: The men are expressing honest humility and refusal to claim authority over the unseen: dreams can be obscure and their true meanings are not accessible by mere conjecture but only to those whom God grants understanding. The verse therefore cautions against pretending expertise in matters beyond ordinary knowledge and prepares the reader for divine gifting of interpretation rather than human boastfulness.

translation: وقال الذي نجا منهما: «اذكروني عند سيدك» — «أنبئكم بتأويله» — فأرسلوا به.
interpretation: الآية توضّح كيف اعتمد الناس على وساطة البشر لتحقيق مخرج: السجين الذي نجا طلب من رفيقه أن يذكره عند الملك لعلّ ذلك يفتح له باب الخلاص، ووعدهم بأنه يستطيع كشف سرّ الرؤيا؛ والنتيجة أن السلسلة البشرية (الذكر لدى السلطان وإرساله) صارت وسيلة لتحقيق حكمة إلهية أوسع. بعبارة أخرى، تخبرنا أن الله قد يجعل وسائل بشرية — تذكر لدى ذي سلطان، كلمة واحدة في الوقت المناسب — سبباً لبيان الحقّ وإخراج قدر المظلوم، وهذا يتطلب مبادرة إنسانية مع توكّل على تدبير الله.

translation: يا يوسف أيها الصدِّيق، أفِتنَا في سبع بقرات سِمانٍ يأكلهنَّ سبعٌ عجاف، وسبع سُنبُلات خُضر وأُخر يابسات، لعلي أرجع إلى الناس لعلهم يعلمون.
interpretation: الآية تُظهِر أن الرؤى يمكن أن تحمل إشارات إلهية عن دورات من الرِزق والفتن، وأن الحكمة الإلهية تُمنَح لبعضَ الناس ليحوِّلوا هذه العلامات إلى تبصير عملي؛ طلب المفسِّر هنا يبيّن حاجة المجتمع إلى تفسيرٍ موثوق ليتخذ إجراءاتٍ استباقية تحميه من المحن وتُعدُّه للأعوام القادمة.

translation: قال: تزرعون سبع سنين دأبًا، فما حصدتم فذروه في سنبله إلا قليلا مما تأكلون.
interpretation: الآية تُظهر حكمة التخطيط والتدبير الحضري: أثناء سنوات الوفرة يجب تكوين مخزون محفوظ (ترك الحبوب في سنابلها) والاقتصار في الأكل على قدر يسير، كي يُحفظ ما يكفي لمواجهة سنوات القحط المقبلة؛ وهذا درس في إدارة موارد المجتمع والوقاية من الأزمات بالالتزام والتأدب في الإنفاق.

translation:
ثم يأتي من بعد ذلك سبع شداد يأكلن ما قدمتم لهن إلا قليلا مما تحصنون
"Then after that will come seven severe years that will consume what you have prepared for them, except a little of what you store."
interpretation: الآية تفيد تنبؤاً بدورة رزق وإفتقار: بعد سنوات من الرخاء ستعقبها سبع سنين قحط وشدة تلتهم غالب ما جُمِعَ خلال الفترات الطيبة، ويبقى من الحفظ والادِّخار سوى قليل. المعنى العملي والروحي هو دعوة إلى حسن التدبير والحفظ في زمن الزيادة والاعتراف بحدود القدرة البشرية أمام قضاء الله — فالتخزين والتخطيط مطلوبان، لكنه اختبار للثقة والاعتماد على الله لأن الإنسان لا يضمن منع الفقد إلا جزئياً.

translation:
ثم يأتي من بعد ذلك عامٌ فيه يُغاث الناسُ وفيه يُعصرون
"Then after that will come a year in which the people are given relief (rain) and in which they press (their produce)."
interpretation: The verse teaches that God, in His wise ordering, alternates between hardship and blessing: following a period of scarcity or trial comes a year of rain and agricultural abundance so that people are relieved and able to press their fruits (e.g., olives or grapes). It is a reminder that provision and respite are granted by God’s will, turning difficulty into opportunity and calling for gratitude, proper stewardship of the bounty, and recognition that ease may follow hardship by divine decree.

translation: وقال الملكُ: «ائتوني به». فلما جاءَه الرسولُ قالَ: «ارجع إلى ربِّك فاسأله ما بالِ النِّسوةِ اللاتي قَطَعنَ أيديهنَّ؛ إنَّ ربي ببَكيدِهنَّ عليمٌ».
interpretation: الآية تؤكد مبدأين أخلاقيين وتعليميين: الأول هو الحفاظ على العرض والابتعاد عن مواطن الفتنة أو الموقف الذي قد يوحي بضعف الأدب والبراءة، والثاني هو التوكّل على علم الله بالنيات والدسائس؛ فالحق لا يعلو عليه سِتر ولا مخادعة، والله مطلع على ما يضمره الناس وسيكشف الحق ويؤخذ على من تدبَّر الشر. من ذلك استنتاج واجبِ التقوى والحكمة في التعامل مع المواقف، والاعتماد على قضاء الله وعدله بدلاً من المناورات البشرية.

translation: قَالَ مَا خَطْبُكُنَّ إِذْ رَاوَدْتُنَّ يُوسُفَ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ ۚ قُلْنَ حَاشًا لِلَّهِ مَا عَلِمْنَا عَلَيْهِ مِن سُوءٍ ۚ قَالَتِ امْرَأَةُ الْعَزِيزِ الْآنَ حَصَّحَ الْحَقُّ أَنَا رَاوَدْتُهُ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ وَإِنَّهُ لَمِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ
interpretation: This passage records the moment the falsehood is exposed: after the women initially reject blame, the wife of al‑Aziz publicly confesses that she sought to seduce Joseph and, by doing so, affirms his innocence and veracity. The verse teaches that truth will ultimately surface despite attempts to conceal wrongdoing, vindicating the upright and revealing the hypocrisy of the guilty.

translation: ذلك ليعلم أني لم أخنه بالغيب وأن الله لا يهدي كيد الخائنين
interpretation: الآية تؤكد مبدأ أخلاقيٍّ وتصوّريّ: الثقة والبراءة ستُظهرها الحقيقة في نهاية المطاف، لأن الله لا يجعل طريق الهداية موفقاً لمؤامرات الخيانة؛ أي أن المخططات الخبيثة التي تقوم على الخيانة سيُحبطُها الله، فتُنكشفُ الظلمات ويُنتصر الحق، مما يطمئن المؤمنين على أن العدالة الإلهية تمنع نجاح مكائد الخائنين.

translation: And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is surely inclined to evil, except those whom my Lord has mercy upon. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The speaker confesses human weakness and warns that moral purity is not the result of self-sufficiency but of God's mercy; without divine compassion the nafs (self) tends toward wrongdoing, so true righteousness rests on humility, repentance, and reliance on God's forgiveness and mercy rather than on pride in one’s own rectitude.

translation: And the king said, “Bring him to me so that I may appoint him exclusively for myself.” But when the king spoke to him, he said, “Indeed, today you are established and entrusted with us.”
interpretation: The verse indicates that Yusuf’s proven character and gift (especially his sound judgment and insight shown in interpreting the dream and managing crises) moved the ruler to place him in a position of authority. ‘Makin’ (established) denotes a settled, honored status with real power, and ‘amin’ (trusted) emphasizes moral responsibility; together they teach that true leadership in society comes from being both competent and trustworthy, so God’s favor is manifested in people’s recognition and lawful commission to serve the public good.

translation: He said, “Appoint me over the storehouses (treasuries) of the land; indeed I am a vigilant, knowing guardian.”
interpretation: The verse presents a model of legitimate leadership: one asks not for power for its own sake but for the duty of stewardship, grounding the request in two complementary qualifications — trustworthiness (حفيظ) and knowledge (عليم). It teaches that management of public resources requires moral integrity to protect and preserve them and practical competence to plan and administer them wisely; authority is justified when offered as service for collective welfare rather than personal gain, and competent, upright stewardship is a means by which Divine providence can be realized in society.

translation: And thus We established Joseph in the land so that he might settle wherever he wished. A provision by Our mercy for whom We will; and We do not let the reward of the doers of good be lost.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Joseph’s rise and secure position were acts of God’s wise mercy rather than merely human achievement: God places people in stations and grants sustenance according to His will. ‘‘Provision’’ and ‘‘establishment’’ are presented as divine gifts, and the promise that the reward of the muhsinīn (those who do good) will not be lost reassures that sincere righteousness is recorded and recompensed by God even if worldly outcomes seem delayed or obscured. In short, worldly standing and provision are ultimately dispensed by divine wisdom, and faithful goodness will receive its due.

translation: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are conscious (of Allah).
interpretation: The verse teaches that true, lasting benefit is found in the life to come rather than in fleeting worldly gains; those whose faith is sincere and who cultivate taqwa — a steady God‑consciousness that governs intentions and behavior — will attain a superior, enduring recompense. It therefore calls believers to prioritize moral integrity, patience, and obedience to God over short‑term advantages, trusting that steadfast righteousness yields the ultimate and better reward.

translation: And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him; and he recognized them, while they did not recognize him.
interpretation: The verse points to God-given insight and the moral architecture of testing and reconciliation: Allah endows the upright with subtle knowledge that sees beneath appearances, placing them in a position to observe whether others’ hearts have changed. Rather than immediate exposure or vengeance, this grants the favored person the opportunity to respond with measured justice and mercy, turning past injury into a means for repentance, family restoration, and moral teaching. It also reminds that outward power or presence does not equal inner awareness—true recognition is granted by God.

translation: And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, “Bring me your brother from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?”
interpretation: The verse teaches that legitimate authority pairs generous provision with a clear expectation: genuine munificence is itself a form of persuasion and proof of fairness. By giving openly and claiming equitable treatment, a leader both reassures those under his care and summons their cooperation; generosity thus functions strategically to encourage trust, reveal true intentions, and test the sincerity of others, because authentic giving is accompanied by rightful demands and just conduct.

translation: If you do not bring it to me, then you will have no claim before me and you will not come near me.
interpretation: The speaker is asserting that absence of the required proof or evidence strips opponents of any standing or right to argue; in the context of divine judgment it means their case will be rejected and they will be denied nearness, intercession, or access to mercy — lack of proof results in exclusion and final repudiation.

translation: They said, “We will surely entice his father concerning him, and indeed we will be doers (of it).”
interpretation: The verse reveals how envy and desire lead people to engineer deceit by weaponizing family affection—seeking to inflame a father’s feelings to bring about an unjust outcome—and emphasizes the conspirators’ firm resolve to carry out their scheme; it teaches that such manipulation of love for wrongful ends is a moral corruption and a test for the innocent, calling for vigilance against exploiting relationships and for reliance on God’s justice.

translation:
