وقال لفتيانه: "اجعلوا بضاعتهم في رحالهم لعلهم يعرفونها إذا انقلبوا إلى أهلهم لعلهم يرجعون".
"And he said to his young men, 'Put their merchandise into their saddlebags—perhaps they will recognize it when they return to their people; perhaps they will [then] come back.'"
interpretation: The speaker is scheming: by secretly placing the money among the travelers’ goods he creates a pretext that they will discover it at home and therefore have reason to return. The verse exposes a deliberate manoeuvre to bring those men back—an act of calculated deception intended to produce a desired future encounter (to gain advantage or resolve an unfinished matter).

translation:
فَلَمَّا رَجَعُوا إِلَىٰ أَبِيهِمْ قَالُوا يَا أَبَانَا مَنَعَ مِنْنَا الْكِيلَ فَأَرْسِل مَعَنَا أَخَانَا نَكْتُلْ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ
"So when they returned to their father they said, ‘O our father, a ration has been withheld from us; so send with us our brother that we may obtain measure, and indeed we will be his guardians.’"
interpretation: The verse exposes a piece of human behavior: people sometimes cloak self‑interested or culpable intentions in plausible, dutiful language to persuade those in authority. By promising to guard their brother and invoking necessity (the withheld ration), the speakers seek to legitimize their request and relieve suspicion, turning a demand into an appeal to responsibility. The passage thus highlights both the power of rhetorical framing to win trust and the moral danger when such appeals are used to conceal prior wrongdoing and to manipulate a parent’s care.

translation: قال: «هل آمنكم عليه إلا كما أمنتكم على أخيه من قبل؟ فالله خير حافظًا، وهو أرحم الراحمين.»
interpretation: الآية توبخ الثقة الفارغة في العهود والبشر وتحول النظر إلى الحماية الحقيقية: الأمن الحقيقي لا يقوم على وعودٍ عرضية أو سلوك مكررٍ عالق في الخطأ، بل على حفظ الله ورعايته. ثِقَلها تأكيد أن الله هو الحافظ الأعلى الذي يردّ الحقوق ويُعطف أكثر من أي رحمة بشرية، فالمؤمن ينبغي أن يعتمد على رعاية الله وعدالته بدل أن يضع ثقته المطلقة في ضمائر ضعيفة وقابلة للخطأ.

translation: And when they opened their belongings, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. They said, “O our father, what more shall we desire? This is our merchandise returned to us; we will take our families home, protect our brother, and add to the camels’ load — that is a small measure.”
interpretation: The verse exposes the brothers’ practical, conciliatory stance: reassured by the restoration of their goods, they present a plan aimed at repairing the situation — bringing their family, ensuring Benjamin’s safety, and offering a modest additional payment to smooth relations. It highlights their concern for family welfare and willingness to make a small material concession to avert conflict, reflecting both genuine care and a pragmatic attempt to restore trust and settle the crisis.

translation: قال: «لن أرسله معكم حتى تؤتونني موثقا من الله أن تأتوني به، إلا أن يحاط بكم». فلما آتوه موثقهم قال: «الله على ما نقول وكيل».
interpretation: الآية تبرز قيمة العهد واليمين عندما يُستحكمان باسم الله: طالب الحافظ ضمانًا راسخًا قبل المجازفة بما يحب، ونصّ شرط الاستثناء ('إلا أن يحاط بكم') اعتراف بضعف الإنسان أمام الإكراه والحرب. بقولِه «الله على ما نقول وكيل» يُحطّ الأمر بالمسؤولية الإلهية، فالإيمان بكون الله شهيدًا ووكيلًا للقول يجعل اليمين عهدًا أخلاقيًا وقانونيًا يُحاسَب عليه، ويذكّر بأن تعويل الناس على عهود بعضهم محدود، وأن الضمان الحقيقي في التزامٍ مراقبٍ من قبل الله الذي يراعي النيات ويحاسب على الأقوال والأفعال.

translation: وقال: «يا بني، لا تدخلوا من باب واحد، بل ادخلوا من أبواب متفرقة؛ وما أغني عنكم منّي ضدّ الله شيئاً. إن الحكم لا يختصّ إلا بالله. عليه توكّلت، وعليه فليتوكّل المتوكّلون.»
interpretation: الآية تجمع بين الحثّ على الاحتياط العملي والاعتراف بحدود القدرة البشرية أمام مشيئة الله: فالتوجيه العملي (الدخول من أبواب متفرقة) يبيّن أهمية اتخاذ الأسباب والحذر، بينما التذكير بأن لا فائدة لما يملكه أو يفعله الإنسان أمام حكم الله يؤكد أن النتيجة النهائية بيد الله وحده. من ثمّ توكّل الرجل ليس امتناعاً عن الأخذ بالأسباب، بل وضع الأسباب ثم الاعتماد الخالص على الله والقبول بحكمه، مع توجيه الناس إلى أن يجعلوا توكّلهم على الله بعد القيام بما في وسعهم.

translation: And when they entered to their father at the time he had appointed, their presence availed them nothing against Allah — except that there was a need in Yaʿqūb’s heart which he fulfilled. And indeed he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human scheming cannot overturn God’s decree: the sons’ fabricated evidence did not change divine reality. What it did do was soothe a deep emotional need in Jacob — an outward consolation he allowed himself — while Jacob himself retained inward, divinely granted insight. He exercised wise restraint, accepting the apparent proof to satisfy his soul without exposing the deeper certainty God had given him. The passage thus contrasts surface appearances with true inner knowledge and honors prophetic patience and submission that most people lack.

translation: And when they entered in to Joseph, he took his brother aside and said, “Indeed I am your brother; so do not be distressed about what they used to do.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that true kinship and prophetic wisdom first seek to heal fear and shame: Joseph affirms his bond and comforts Benjamin so that past sins and humiliations will not crush hope or trust. Rather than retaliate or escalate blame, he models mercy and psychological care—removing despair, restoring dignity, and directing the heart away from fixation on others’ wrongdoing toward patience, reconciliation, and reliance on God’s just ordering of events.

translation: So when he had furnished them with their supplies, he placed the drinking vessel in his brother’s saddle; then a caller cried, “O caravan, you are surely thieves!”
interpretation: This verse illustrates how God can bring about a greater good through a believer’s discreet, patient planning: what outwardly appears as an accusation or misfortune may serve to uncover truth, restore ties, and establish justice. It warns against judging by appearances and commends prudent, morally bound measures coupled with reliance on God to achieve righteous ends.

translation: قالوا وأقبلوا عليهم: "ماذا تفقدون؟"
interpretation: العبارة تُصوّر مواجهة عدائية: خصوم يندفعون نحو أصحاب الرسالة ويستجوبونهم بقصد الاستفزاز والبحث عن ذريعة للتشكيك أو الإيقاع بهم؛ فهي تعكس نبرة رفض واستعلاء ورغبة في مساءلة الآخرين بقوة بدلاً من السعي للفهم.

translation: They said, “We have lost the king’s drinking-cup; whoever brings it will have a camel-load [as reward], and I will vouch for him.”
interpretation: The verse exposes how greed and desire for gain can drive people to fabricate or seize on false charges and to organize deception. Offering a large material reward and someone’s willing pledge to act as guarantor reveal a calculated readiness to exploit symbols of authority (the king’s goblet) and to assume culpability in order to achieve selfish ends—a moral warning about how covetousness corrodes honesty and solidarity.

translation: They said, “By Allah! Surely you know that we did not come to cause corruption on the earth, nor were we thieves.”
interpretation: This is an oath of denial offered by those accused: they appeal to God to assert that their purpose was not to spread corruption or to steal. The verse highlights that people may use solemn oaths to defend their innocence, but true intent and guilt are known only to God; therefore outward protestations cannot substitute for objective judgment and God’s knowledge of the heart.

translation: They said, “So what will be its recompense if you are liars?”
interpretation: The words convey a scoffing challenge: the listeners treat the prophet’s claim as a bargainable claim and demand to know what punishment or loss would follow if he were false. Their question exposes cynicism and attempts to reduce a moral‑truth claim to a question of personal gain or consequence, thereby evading responsibility to examine the truth of the message.

translation:
قالوا: "جزاؤه من وجد في رحله فهو جزاؤه"، كذلك نجزي الظالمين.
"They said, 'Its due is: let whoever finds it on his journey — that shall be his due.' Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse depicts a community trying to shirk responsibility by decreeing that a burden (or its penalty) be borne by whoever happens to encounter it in transit; their attempt to pass the obligation onto others reveals their injustice. The warning is that such scheming does not avert divine justice—God will recompense the wrongdoers with the fitting consequence of their evasion and wrongdoing.

translation: فَبَدَأَ بِأَوْعِيَتِهِم قَبْلَ وَعَاءِ أَخِيهِ ثُمَّاسْتَخْرَجَهَا مِنْ وَعَاءِ أَخِيهِ ۚ كَذَٰلِكَ كَدَنَا لِيُوسُفَ ۖ مَا كَانَ لِيَأْخُذَ أَخَاهُ فِي دِينِ الْمَلِكِ إِلَّا أَنْ يَشَاءَ اللَّهُ ۚ نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَاتٍ مَنْ نَشَاءُ ۗ وَفَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عِلْمٍ عَلِيمٌ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن الظواهر والأحداث التي تبدو نتيجة لخطط بشرية تخضع في حقيقتها لمشيئة الله وتدبيره؛ نجاح يوسف وإثبات الذنب على أخيه لم يكن ليتم بما يغير سلطان الملك إلا بإذن الله، والله يرفع درجات من يشاء حسب حكمته، ومعرفة البشر محدودة أمام العلم الإلهي الأعلى. من هذا يستلزم أن نعزو النصر والمقام والحكمة إلى تدبير الله وأن نَعتبر حدود الفهم البشري أمام علمه المطلق.

translation: They said, “If he steals, then a brother of his stole before.” But Joseph kept it to himself and did not disclose it to them. She said, “You are in the worse position,” and Allah knows best what you describe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that in disputes people often deflect guilt by pointing to past faults of others, while the innocent may choose silence out of integrity and to avoid lowering themselves; the woman’s rebuke—calling them ‘the worst in position’—is an attempt to shift blame and shame onto the accusers, and the final clause reminds that outward claims and appearances are not decisive—only God fully knows the realities of people’s hearts and actions.

translation: They said, “O esteemed one, he has a father who is an old man; take one of us in his place — indeed we see you among the doers of good.”
interpretation: The verse highlights how people seek mercy by appealing to a ruler’s reputation for kindness: out of familial solidarity they offer themselves as substitutes and employ praise to persuade the authority to show clemency. It therefore exposes both sincere concern for an elderly parent and the human tendency to use flattery as a means to obtain compassion from those in power.

translation: قال: «معاذَ الله أن نأخذ إلا من وجدنا متاعنا عنده، إنا إذا لَظالمون»
interpretation: القول يعبّر عن مبدأ أخلاقي واضح: يحرم أخذ مال الآخرين بغير حق، ويجوز فقط استرداد ما هو لنا عندما نجده عند غيرنا؛ ومن يفعل خلاف ذلك يكون ظالماً، والعبارة تظهر تمسك المتكلم بالعدل وضميره حتى في مواقف القوة.

translation: When they despaired of finding him, they withdrew to confer privately. Their eldest said, “Did you not know that your father exacted from you a solemn pledge by Allah? And before that you were heedless concerning Joseph. I will not leave this land until my father permits me, or Allah judges for me — and He is the best of judges.”
interpretation: This verse signals a moral turning point: the eldest brother invokes the sacredness of the oath and their prior wrongdoing toward Joseph to prevent a repeat injustice, refusing to evade responsibility. His stance—seeking either rightful parental permission or submitting the matter to God’s judgment—expresses repentance, the restoration of accountability within the family, and a trust that ultimate justice belongs to God, who is the best and fairest Judge.

translation: Go back to your father and say, “O our father, indeed your son has stolen; and we testify only to what we know, and we were not guardians of the unseen.”
interpretation: The brothers are using a rhetorical device—admitting only what is observable and disavowing knowledge of the hidden—to cloak a deliberate falsehood. The verse indicts attempts to manipulate testimony by feigning limited knowledge: claiming ignorance of the unseen does not excuse bearing false witness or shirking moral responsibility. It thus warns that partial truths and disclaimers can be used to perpetrate injustice, while ultimate knowledge and judgment belong to God.

translation: And ask the town in which we were and the caravan in which we came; indeed we are truthful.
interpretation: The words assert that the claim being made is not mere assertion but verifiable by public witnesses and circumstances; they stress that guidance comes with observable signs and testimony, so rejection is a conscious refusal rather than ignorance, and thus moral responsibility rests with those who deny what the evidence corroborates.

translation: He said, "Nay—your own selves have suggested this to you. So patience is beautiful; perhaps Allah will bring them all back to me. Indeed He is the All‑Knowing, All‑Wise."
interpretation: The verse teaches that apparent wrongdoing often springs from the whisperings and desires of people's own souls, and the proper response is 'beautiful patience'—a composed, dignified endurance that avoids hasty accusation or revenge, entrusts the matter to God's knowledge and wisdom, and holds hope that He may rectify and restore what has been lost.

translation: وتولى عنهم وقال: «يا أسفى على يوسف!» وأبيضت عيناه من الحزن؛ فهو كظيم.
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن يعقوب كان مثقلاً بحزن شديد على يوسف إلى حد أثر ذلك على جسده (شحوب أو ضعف بالبصر)، ومع ذلك كان حزيناً مكبوتاً متحمّلاً مصابه بصبر كظيم؛ فهي إشارة إلى عمق العلاقة الإنسانية مع الأنبياء، وإلى صبرهم الداخلي وتحمّل البلاء بدل الانفجار به أو اليأس.

translation: They said, “By God, you will surely continue to mention Joseph until you become consumed by grief or until you are among the perishing.”
interpretation: The brothers’ words reveal hypocritical malice: by swearing to God they feign righteous certainty while exposing their wish to end Jacob’s perpetual lament—either by driving him into illness or causing his death. The verb تفتأ (you keep mentioning) stresses the relentless grief they resent, and حرضًا (being consumed/ruined) signals the total ruin they hope to bring about. The verse thus condemns the use of pious language to disguise envy and a plan to silence or destroy what one cannot bear.

translation: قال: "إنما أشكو بثّي وحزني إلى الله، وأعلم من الله ما لا تعلمون"
interpretation: يُعبّر هنا يعقوب عن توجه قلبه الكامل إلى الله في محنة فقده: لا يلملم أمره عند الناس بل يفرغه في الدعاء والتوكل، مع يقين أن لله علماً وأقداراً لا تظهر للناس. العبارة تصف موقف الإيمان بالصبر والاعتماد على حكمة الله في ما يبدو كابتلاء، وتؤكد أن الاطمئنان الحقيقي ينبع من معرفة أن الله أعلم بالمآل مما يفوق فهم البشر.

translation: O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother, and do not lose hope in the mercy of Allah. Indeed no one despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse teaches a rule of faith and practice: combine active effort with unwavering trust in God. “Rūḥ Allāh” here is best understood as God’s sustaining mercy, relief, provision or help; believers must not abandon hope in that mercy even in long hardship. Despairing of God’s aid is presented not merely as pessimism but as a posture linked to denial—those who wholly give up hope thereby resemble the disbelieving—whereas hope keeps one open to Divine support and grace.

translation:
فَلَمَّا دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ قَالُوا يَا أَيُّهَا الْعَزِيزُ مَسَّنَا وَأَهْلَنَا الْضُّرُّ وَجِئْنَا بِبِضَاعَةٍ مَّزْجَاةٍ فَأَوْفِ لَنَا الْكَيْلَ وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنَا ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُجْزِي الْمُتَصَدِّقِينَ
"And when they entered upon him they said, ‘O Aziz, distress has touched us and our family, and we have come with deficient goods. So give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.’"
interpretation: The verse illustrates the proper attitude and rhetoric of those in need toward those in authority: they combine a claim to justice (requesting the full, rightful measure) with an appeal to mercy (asking for charity), and they remind the wealthy that generosity is rewarded by God. It teaches a social ethic in which fair commercial dealings are demanded even from the powerful, while voluntary compassion toward the needy is both a moral duty and spiritually rewarded—thus encouraging rulers and merchants to be just in trade and liberal in almsgiving.

translation: قال: «هل علمتم ما فعلتم بيوسف وأخيه إذ أنتم جاهلون؟» — “He said, ‘Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?’”
interpretation: A sharp reproach that aims to awaken moral responsibility: the question exposes that their actions stemmed from blind jealousy and negligence, reminding that ignorance does not excuse injustice and that one must recognize the wrong, repent, and accept responsibility for harm done.

translation:
قالوا أإنك لأنت يوسف ۖ قال أنا يوسف وهذا أخي ۖ قد من الله علينا ۖ إنه من يتق ويصبر فإن الله لا يضيع أجر المحسنين
"They said, ‘Is it truly you, Joseph?’ He said, ‘I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah (is conscious of Him) and is patient — then indeed, Allah does not let the reward of the doers of good be lost.’"
interpretation: The verse teaches a theological and moral principle: deliverance and success are ultimately gifts of God, but they are enacted in human life through inner piety (taqwa) and steadfast patience (sabr). It reassures that sincere righteousness and endurance amid trial are not wasted — God preserves and recompenses true goodness. The practical implication is to cultivate God-consciousness and patience in adversity, trusting that divine mercy will transform suffering into vindication and lasting reward.

translation: قالوا تالله لقد آثرك الله علينا وإن كنا لخاطئين — “They said, ‘By God! God has indeed favored you over us, and truly we were in the wrong.’”
interpretation: A statement of humble admission and recognition: the speakers acknowledge that God has bestowed a clear blessing on the newcomer, confess their prior error in judgement, and thereby model sincere repentance, gratitude for divine provision, and readiness to rectify one’s attitude when evidence of God’s favor becomes manifest.

translation: He said, “There is no blame upon you today; Allah forgives you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.”
interpretation: This declaration teaches that divine pardon can override human condemnation: when God chooses forgiveness, legal or social guilt is lifted and the harmed relationship is restored. It emphasizes that ultimate authority over accountability belongs to God, whose mercy does more than withhold punishment — it rehabilitates and dignifies the forgiven. The verse thus invites hope and repentance, reminding believers to rely on God’s compassion while also prompting communities to accept divine pardon and move toward reconciliation rather than persistent recrimination.

translation: Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face; he will regain his sight. Then bring to me all your family together.
interpretation: The verse shows that God can bring healing and the recognition of truth through humble, concrete means entrusted to Him; the shirt acts as an instrument by God's will to restore sight, and that restoration serves as the turning point for forgiveness and the reunification of the family—teaching trust in God's power, the reality of divine signs, and the moral outcome of reconciliation and mercy.

translation: And when the caravan had departed, their father said, “Indeed I perceive the scent of Joseph; were it not that you would deny me.”
interpretation: Yaʿqūb (Jacob) experiences a subtle, hopeful intuition — he 'smells' Joseph, a sign that his son may still be alive — yet he holds back from announcing it because he fears his sons will dismiss or mock him. The verse emphasizes his restrained, dignified hope and spiritual sensitivity: he recognizes evidence of reunion but chooses patience and discretion rather than speaking publicly and risking further hurt.

translation:
قالوا تالله إنك لفي ضلالك القديم
"They said, 'By God, you are surely in your former, longstanding error.'"
interpretation: The verse records the opponents’ emphatic rejection: by swearing “By God” they assert with moral certainty that the messenger remains entrenched in his old misguidance. The wording exposes their stubbornness and unwillingness to consider the message on its merits—preferring to dismiss it as mere continuation of what they already knew—so the statement functions less as an objective verdict and more as a rhetorical, self‑serving refusal to acknowledge guidance.

translation:
فَلَمَّا أَتَى الْبَشِيرُ أَلْقَاهُ عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ فَارْتَدَّ بَصِيرًا ۖ قَالَ أَلَمْ أَقُل لَّكُمْ إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
"So when the bringer of good news came, he threw it upon his face and he recovered his sight. He said, 'Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?'"
interpretation: The verse stresses that prophetic knowledge and divine signs can reverse human blindness — when God manifests the truth unmistakably, the one who had warned is vindicated. It teaches that what may seem improbable to people can be real by God’s decree, that insight and authority granted by God surpass ordinary human understanding, and that dismissal of divinely bestowed knowledge is exposed when the reality appears.

translation:
قالوا: «يا أبانا استغفر لنا ذنوبنا، إنَّا كُنَّا خاطِئين».
"They said, 'O our father, ask forgiveness for us of our sins; indeed we have been wrongdoers.'"
interpretation: This utterance exemplifies true tawba (repentance): an honest admission of guilt, humility in seeking mercy, and turning to God through the supplication of a righteous elder. It teaches that forgiveness begins with recognizing one’s wrong, submitting in remorse, and relying on God’s mercy (sometimes through intercession by the pious), which together open the way to moral reform and reconciliation.

translation: قال: «سأستغفر لكم ربي؛ إنه هو الغفور الرحيم.»
interpretation: الآية تعبّر عن موقف رحمة وأملٍ ينبع من اليقين بصفة الله: أن يسعى المرء بالتوسّل والاستغفار للآخرين بدلاً من اليأس أو العقاب، مع الإقرار بأن المغفرة بيد الله وحده الذي تتجلى فيه صفتا الغفران والرحمة. هذا يعلّم أن الدعاء والشفاعة بالاستغفار عملٌ محمود يُظهر التواضع والاعتماد على رحمة الله، مع قبول أن ثمرة هذا الجهد متروكة لحكمه ورحمته.

translation: So when they entered upon Yusuf, he took his parents to himself and said, “Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, safe and secure.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s providence brings restoration when mercy and responsibility meet submission to His will. Joseph’s act of sheltering his parents and his gentle invitation—qualified by “in shāʾa Allāh”—models humility before divine decree, while “āminīn” indicates provision of real safety from fear, want, and dishonor. Thus true reunion and stability require both compassionate, protective action by people and trust in God’s guidance and timing.

translation: And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. He said, “O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true. He has been kind to me when He took me out of prison and brought you here from the desert after Satan had caused discord between me and my brothers. Indeed my Lord is subtle in what He wills; indeed He is the Knowing, the Wise.”
interpretation: The verse expresses a theology of providence and moral transformation: Joseph recognizes that his rise and his family’s restoration are not merely human achievements but the unfolding of God’s wise and subtle plan. ‘Subtle’ (latīf) indicates that God works through hidden, gradual, and sometimes unexpected means—turning injustice, imprisonment, and fraternal betrayal into reconciliation, authority, and mercy. By attributing every good to God’s kindness and by naming Satan’s role in the earlier rupture, Joseph models patient trust, grateful humility, and moral clarity: evil human actions can be real yet limited, and God can redirect their consequences toward forgiveness, healing, and the fulfillment of divine wisdom. The passage therefore teaches reliance on God’s timing, the hope that suffering can serve a greater purpose, and the duty to respond to restored power with gratitude and justice rather than revenge.

translation: “My Lord, You have surely granted me of sovereignty and taught me the interpretation of dreams/utterances. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my Patron (wali) in this world and the Hereafter; cause me to die a Muslim and join me with the righteous.”
interpretation: Joseph’s words model the believer’s response to God-given success: he recognizes that authority and knowledge are gifts from the Creator, refuses to claim credit for them, and therefore directs his gratitude into complete submission and reliance on God. By addressing God as Fāṭir (Creator) and wālī (Protector/Patron) he affirms that ultimate power and guardianship belong to God alone in both worldly life and the life to come; worldly elevation becomes a motive to seek spiritual safety, a good end (dying in Islam), and fellowship with the righteous rather than self-exaltation. The verse teaches that true honor is measured by dependence on God, upright conduct, and the hope for final companionship with the pious.

translation: That is from the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you; and you were not with them when they agreed upon their affair while they were scheming.
interpretation: God is telling the Prophet that the information given to him about hidden matters is divine revelation, not knowledge acquired by human means. The statement reminds that the Prophet did not witness the conspirators’ secret plotting and therefore cannot be blamed for knowing their plans; rather, God discloses what is unseen to confirm the Prophet’s mission, to expose the scheming of those who plot in secret, and to reassure the community that human intrigues do not escape divine knowledge and will be accounted for.

translation: And most of the people — even if you were to strive — will not be believers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the majority will not accept true faith despite the Messenger’s utmost efforts; it reminds us that guidance is ultimately rooted in the disposition of people’s hearts and the divine decree, so the Prophet’s duty is to convey and strive while recognizing that convincing every soul is beyond human control. The practical lesson is to persist sincerely in calling to truth, entrust the outcome to God, and not measure success solely by numbers or expect universal acceptance.

translation:
وما تسألهم عليه من أجر ۚ إن هو إلا ذكر للعالمين
“You do not ask them any payment for it; it is but a reminder for all the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse affirms the Prophet’s sincere, non‑commercial mission: the revelation is offered freely as a moral and spiritual admonition, not as a commodity to be bought. Its aim is universal—to awaken consciences and call all people (and creation) to account—so acceptance depends on hearts and choices rather than any material incentive; the message’s authority and value are intrinsic and will stand as testimony before God.

translation: And how many signs there are in the heavens and the earth which they pass by while they turn away from them.
interpretation: The verse reproves human heedlessness: countless clear indications of God’s existence, power, wisdom and guidance appear in the created world and in revelation, yet people routinely ignore or avoid reflecting on them out of distraction, pride, or unwillingness to submit; the statement calls for attentive contemplation so that those signs become means of guidance rather than proofs overlooked to their own detriment.

translation: Most of them do not believe in Allah without ascribing partners to Him.
interpretation: The verse warns that apparent belief among many people is defective because it is mixed with shirk: they acknowledge God yet attach partners to Him in worship, reliance, or attributes. True iman requires exclusive devotion and the negation of partners; when belief coexists with associating others with God, it is not genuine tawḥīd but a corrupted faith that undermines salvation and accountability.

translation: Do they then feel secure that a covering (overwhelming) of Allah’s punishment will not come upon them, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?
interpretation: The verse censures the complacency of those who, because of apparent ease or success, presume they are immune to God’s retribution or that the Day of Judgment will never catch them. It warns that divine punishment or the Hour can descend unexpectedly and decisively, so presumptuous security or postponing repentance is dangerously mistaken—one must remain conscious, humble, and ready, since unseen accountability can arrive at any moment.

translation:
قُلْ هَـٰذِهِ سَبِيلِي أَدْعُوٓا إِلَى اللَّهِ ۚ عَلَىٰ بَصِيرَةٍ أَنَا وَمَنِ ٱتَّبَعَنِي ۖ وَسُبْحَانَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَآ أَنَا مِنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ

“Say: ‘This is my way; I call to Allah — with clear insight — I and those who follow me. Glory be to Allah; and I am not of the polytheists.’”
interpretation: The Prophet is commanded to present his mission as a clear, public method of calling to the one God: it is based on discernment and evidence rather than coercion or secret persuasion. By saying “I and those who follow me” he highlights that true guidance is lived communally and visibly, not merely asserted in words. The phrase “Subhan Allah” affirms God’s absolute transcendence and serves as a firm repudiation of any form of associating partners with Him; in short, the verse defines the principles of sincere invitation — clarity, integrity, communal witness, and uncompromising monotheism.

translation: And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed — men from among the people of the towns. Do they not travel through the land and see how was the end of those before them? And the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then understand?
interpretation: God reminds people that prophets are ordinary members of their communities who receive divine revelation, so their humanity cannot invalidate their message. He urges people to reflect — by traveling, observing, and learning from the fates of past nations who rejected guidance — to see that attachment to transient worldly life led to ruin, whereas the eternal provision of the Hereafter belongs to the God‑conscious. The verse thus calls for sober, historical reflection and rational apprehension: accept the message on its merits, cultivate piety, and prioritize the everlasting over the ephemeral.

translation: Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been rejected, Our help came to them, and We saved whom We willed; and Our punishment cannot be averted from the guilty people.
interpretation: This verse teaches that apparent defeat and despair in the face of persistent rejection do not determine the outcome: deliverance and vindication come by God's will and in His timing. It emphasizes divine sovereignty in granting rescue (in this world or the next) and the inevitability of divine justice — those who persist in wrongdoing cannot prevent God’s punishment — and so calls for patient trust in God rather than relying on immediate human success.

translation: Indeed in their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding. It is not a fabricated narration; rather it is a confirmation of what was before it, a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’anic accounts of past events are deliberate pedagogical instruments: they are meant to awaken reflection, confirm and clarify earlier revelation, and exhibit the unity and wisdom of God’s governance. By calling the stories neither fanciful nor superfluous but detailed confirmations, the verse affirms the Qur’an’s divine authority and presents its narratives as transformative guidance and compassion—meant to shape the hearts, beliefs, and actions of those who truly reflect and believe.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Alif‑Lam‑Ra. These are the verses of the Book; and that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe.
interpretation: The verse affirms the Qur’an’s divine authority and truth—signaled even by the enigmatic disjoined letters (المر) as a mark of the scripture’s miraculous, unmatchable language—and warns that despite clear, truthful revelation many will refuse to accept it out of stubbornness, pride, or attachment to falsehood, so believers are given both assurance of the message’s certainty and a sober awareness of widespread rejection.

translation: Allah is the One who raised the heavens without any visible pillars that you see, then He established Himself over the Throne; and He has made the sun and the moon subservient — each runs for an appointed term. He commends and manages every matter and expounds the signs so that you may be certain of meeting your Lord.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute creative power and sovereign governance: the heavens are sustained not by observable supports but by God’s will, underscoring the unseen, transcendent cause behind creation. “Establishing Himself on the Throne” signals His supreme authority and lordship over all affairs (not a likeness to created beings), while the sun and moon being made subservient and running each for an appointed term point to an orderly, measured cosmos governed by divine decree. By saying He arranges matters and explains His signs, the verse teaches that the regularity and intelligibility of the universe are evidence intended to awaken human reflection and moral responsibility, guiding people toward firm conviction in the eventual meeting with their Lord and accountability before Him.

translation: And He is the One who spread out the earth and placed firm mountains and rivers in it; and of every fruit He made pairs, two; He causes the night to cover the day. Indeed in that are signs for people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse intends to move the listener from observation to conviction: the consistent, balanced order of the world — its stability (expressed by mountains), its provision (rivers and fruits), the complementary ordering of living things (pairs), and the regular alternation of night and day — are not accidental but purposeful manifestations of a single Wise Creator. These natural arrangements function as indicators of divine sovereignty and care; when contemplated thoughtfully (lil-qawmin yatafakkarun) they point to trust in God’s providence, recognition of His design, and the moral responsibility to respond to that recognition rather than attributing existence to chance.

translation: And on the earth are adjacent tracts and gardens of vines and crops and palm trees — some single, some clustered — all watered by one (source); and We make some of them excel others in the fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason.
interpretation: The passage invites reflection on a purposeful order: diversity of provision and gradation of excellence arise from a single source, indicating deliberate wisdom rather than chance. By highlighting unity of sustenance alongside variation in outcomes, it teaches dependence on a single Provider, calls for gratitude rather than envy, and urges people to employ reason to recognize divine wisdom and to act responsibly as stewards of shared resources.

translation: And if you are amazed, then their saying is more astonishing: “When we are dust, will we indeed be brought into a new creation?” Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord; and those are the fetters upon their necks, and those are the companions of the Fire — they will abide therein.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the scoffing of those who deny resurrection: their rhetorical question about being recreated from dust reveals an obstinate blindness to God’s demonstrated power to originate life and to bring it back. The Qur’anic response makes clear that this denial is not a mere intellectual error but a moral rejection of their Lord whose consequences follow: in the Hereafter they will be humiliated and bound (the “fetters” symbolize the restraint, disgrace and accountability that result from their choices) and will be consigned as companions of the Fire, with the permanence of that fate stressed to warn of the grave outcome of persistent disbelief. The passage thus connects wrong belief about God’s power with inevitable spiritual bondage and just recompense.

translation: They urge you to hasten the evil before the good, though before them examples have already passed away. And indeed, your Lord is Oft‑Forgiving to the people for their wrongdoing; and indeed, your Lord is Severe in punishment.
interpretation: People demanded that the Prophet bring immediate retribution to prove his truth, failing to recognize that past communities already bore clear examples of how warning and punishment unfolded. The verse teaches that God’s apparent delay in punishing is not weakness but mercy: He prolongs opportunity for repentance and guidance, forgiving much of human wrongdoing. At the same time this mercy does not remove divine justice—when people persist in injustice and reject guidance, God’s severity will ultimately be manifested. Thus the passage balances hope (reliance on God’s forgiveness and the occasion to reform) with sober warning (inevitability of accountability), calling both the disbelieving rush for spectacle and the complacent believer to proper trust, patience, and moral responsibility.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, “Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?” You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the unbelievers’ demand for an extraordinary miracle as a precondition for faith, and clarifies the Prophet’s role: he is a warner who delivers God’s message, not someone who can compel belief by producing signs on demand. ‘For every people there is a guide’ indicates that guidance is dispensed by God according to His wisdom—each community is given the means and messenger suited to it—and that insisting on a special sign reflects obstinacy rather than a genuine openness to guidance; ultimately acceptance or rejection rests with people and with God’s will.

translation: Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs decrease and what they increase; and everything with Him is by a measure.
interpretation: The verse affirms Allah’s complete knowledge and sovereign determination over conception, pregnancy and lineage: He knows every embryo and what a womb will lose or gain (miscarriage or birth), and all outcomes—timing, number, life and death—occur according to His precise, measured decree and wisdom; nothing of these matters is random or beyond His awareness.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Great, the Most Exalted.
interpretation: This phrase affirms that God’s knowledge embraces every hidden reality and every manifest thing, and that His majesty transcends all creation; nothing—inner states, future events, or outward deeds—is beyond His awareness, and His absolute greatness calls for humble submission, trust in His wisdom where human sight fails, and recognition of ultimate accountability to One who is exalted above all.

translation:
سَواءٌ مِنكُم مَّن أَسَرَّ القَولَ وَمَن جَهَرَ بِهِ، وَمَن هُوَ مُستَخِفٌّ بِاللَّيلِ وَسَارِبٌ بِالنَّهارِ
"It is all the same among you—whether someone conceals a word or utters it openly, whether one hides by night or goes about by day."
interpretation: The verse teaches that outward secrecy or publicity does not alter moral responsibility: whether a person keeps thoughts or accusations hidden or proclaims them, whether they act furtively at night or openly by day, their intentions and deeds remain known and accountable. Secrecy cannot erase the reality of what one intends or the consequences that God (and ultimately people) will discern; therefore sincerity and upright conduct are required both inwardly and outwardly, and one cannot rely on concealment to escape truth or judgement.

translation:
لَهُ مُعَقِّبَاتٌ مِن بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِ يَحْفَظُونَهُ مِنْ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ ۗ وَإِذَا أَرَادَ اللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍ سُوءًا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُ ۚ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِ مِنْ وَالٍ

“For him are guardians before him and behind him who preserve him by the command of Allah. Indeed Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves. And when Allah intends evil for a people, there is no repeller of it; and there is none besides Him to protect.”
interpretation: The verse teaches a twofold principle: divine guardianship and human responsibility. The “guards before and behind” (often understood as angels) show that God’s protection and decree surround people, yet this protection operates under His command and wisdom. The decisive clause—God will not change a people’s condition until they change what is in themselves—makes human agency central: moral, spiritual and practical reform from within is the necessary condition for God’s mercy and transformation to manifest. At the same time, when persistent wrongdoing brings God’s punitive will, no created power can avert that decree; there is ultimately no protector or intercessor independent of God. Thus the verse calls believers to sincere inner reform and effort while recognizing that outcomes finally rest with God’s will—so one must act responsibly, seek God’s aid, and trust that genuine change from within opens the door to divine alteration of a people’s state.

translation: He is the One who shows you the lightning — to inspire fear and to kindle hope — and who brings forth the heavy clouds.
interpretation: The verse teaches that natural phenomena are not meaningless: God deploys signs like lightning to provoke two complementary responses in people — awe and fear of His power (which disciplines and cautions against arrogance) and hope for His mercy and provision — while the raising of heavy clouds points to His sovereign control over the processes that deliver sustenance. Together these prompt recognition of human dependence, motivate moral humility and trust in God, and call people to respond in faith and gratitude.

translation: And the thunder glorifies His praise, and the angels [do so] out of fear of Him. He sends the flashes and strikes therewith whom He wills; yet they argue about Allah, while He is severe in retribution.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every element of creation — even violent phenomena like thunder — participates in God’s glorification, and the angels respond in reverent awe. The mention of God sending lightning and striking whom He wills underscores His absolute sovereignty over the forces of nature and over life and death; such events are manifestations of divine power, not random happenstance. Against this background, human disputes about God reveal ignorance and misplaced pride: to argue over Him while signs of His dominion are manifest is misguided. The phrase “He is severe in retribution” warns that God’s power can be exercised as just punishment or decisive intervention, so the proper human response is humility, recognition of divine authority, and submission rather than contention.

translation: To Him belongs the true call; but those whom they invoke besides Him do not respond to them at all, except like one who stretches his hands toward water that it may reach his mouth, but it does not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine supplication and help belong solely to God; invoking other beings is futile and illusory. The simile of a person stretching toward water that never reaches his mouth shows the impotence of what people call upon and the fruitlessness of relying on them — those calls produce no real response, guidance, or benefit, and therefore are signs of misguidance rather than true help.

translation: And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly; and their shadows, morning and evening.
interpretation: The verse affirms the universal and inescapable sovereignty of God: every being and every aspect of creation—whether by conscious choice or by its very nature—manifests submission to Him. The contrast between willing and unwilling submission highlights that while nature and fate demonstrate God’s lordship inevitably, humans are morally called to transform involuntary acknowledgment into intentional, heartfelt surrender; the repeated reference to morning and evening emphasizes that this recognition is continuous and all-encompassing.

translation: Say, “Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?” Say, “Allah.” Say, “Then have you taken, besides Him, guardians who possess for themselves neither benefit nor harm?” Say, “Is the blind equal to the one who sees? Or are darkness and light equal? Or have they set up for Allah partners who have created like His creation, so that the creations appear similar to them?” Say, “Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the All‑Dominating.”
interpretation: The passage confronts polytheism by exposing its logical and empirical impossibility: true lordship requires the power to create, to benefit or harm, and to govern reality, none of which idols or invented partners possess. Through sharp contrasts (blind vs. seeing, darkness vs. light) and the challenge of comparable creators, it underscores that apparent similarities in creation cannot make false gods equal to the One who brought everything into being. The repeated command “Say” trains the believer to answer such doubts plainly: affirm Allah’s exclusive sovereignty and creative authority. Calling God al‑Qahhār (the All‑Dominating) stresses that ultimate control over existence and events rests with Him alone, so trust, worship, and reliance belong to Him and not to powerless substitutes.

translation: He sends down water from the sky; then valleys flow according to their measure, and the flood carries along foam, scum, rising up. And of what they ignite in the fire, seeking ornament or merchandise, is a similar foam. Thus Allah sets forth the example of the truth and the falsehood. As for the foam, it is swept away as worthless; but that which benefits the people remains on the earth. Thus Allah sets forth the parables.
interpretation: المثل يبيّن أن الله يفرّق بين الحق والباطل بمقارنةٍ ساطعة: الباطل مثل الزبد البراق — مظهر خاوي وزينة زائلة تُحمل وتزول بلا منفعة — بينما الحق مثل الماء الذي ينفع الأرض ويستقر فيها ويثمر نفعاً للناس (علمًا، هدىً، أعمالًا صالحة). الإشارة إلى ما يُصهر في النار ابتغاء زينة أو متاع تأكد أن المطالب السطحية والمظاهر الفارغة لا تدوم، أما قيمة الحق والنفع الحقيقي فتبقى وتؤثر في الناس. دنبالٌ لذلك: اعرفوا ما يبقى من منفعة حقيقية ولا تُغرّكم المظاهر العابرة.

translation: “For those who answered their Lord with the best (response), and for those who did not answer Him — if all that is on earth, and an equal portion with it, were theirs, they would offer it as ransom. Those will have a bad reckoning, and their abode will be Hell — an evil resting‑place.”
interpretation: The verse contrasts two kinds of people: those who accept God’s guidance and submit (receiving the ‘best’—a good end and reward), and those who reject it. It warns that no amount of worldly wealth could redeem the latter on the Day of Reckoning; their attempts to buy salvation would be useless because moral choice, sincere faith and righteous deeds — not material possessions — determine final outcome. “سوء الحساب” (a bad account) and “جهنم… وبئس المهاد” (Hell, an evil resting‑place) underscore the certainty and severity of the consequences for those who persist in denying the truth.

translation: أفمن يعلم أنما أنزل إليك من ربك الحق كمن هو أعمى؟ إنما يتذكر أولو الألباب.
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن إدراك حقيقة الوحي يفرّق بين حالين روحيتين: فالمعرفة الحقّة بالرسالة الإلهية تلزم القلب بالعناية والتغيير، وهي ليست مساوية لـ'العمى' الروحي الذي يبقى جامدًا بلا فكر ولا إحساس. فثمار الوحي لا تظهر إلا عند من يجمع بين العلم والتفكّر—أولو الألباب—الذين يتدبّرون، يتركّب لديهم الإيمان عملاً وسلوكًا، فيستفيدون حقّاً من الهداية، بينما يبقى مجرد الاطلاع أو الإقرار الظاهري بلا تأثير.

translation: Those who fulfill the covenant with Allah and do not break the pledge.
interpretation: This phrase praises those whose faith is shown by steadfastness and integrity: they honor the commitments tied to their relationship with God (obedience, duties, and trust in Him) and likewise uphold promises, treaties, and trusts among people. True devotion therefore appears in constancy — not abandoning obligations, not betraying trusts, and living consistently with the pledges they have made before God and others.

translation: And those who join that which Allah has commanded to be joined, and fear their Lord and dread the evil of reckoning.
interpretation: The verse praises believers who actively preserve the ties and obligations God prescribed—especially kinship, covenants and social duties—not from mere sentiment but out of God‑consciousness. Their reverence for their Lord and fear of the Day of Account restrain them from cutting off relationships or committing injustice; this inner awareness of accountability is the motive that sustains mercy, responsibility and the maintenance of communal and familial bonds.

translation: And those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord, and establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them, secretly and publicly, and repel evil with good — for them is the best outcome of the home.
interpretation: The verse presents a spiritual ethic: true success before God combines inward resolve and outward responsibility. Patience here is purposeful endurance aimed at God’s approval, not passive suffering; it is joined to steadfast worship and to generous giving both privately and publicly, showing sincerity alongside social responsibility. Responding to harm with goodness is a moral strategy that breaks cycles of retaliation and transforms relationships. Together these dispositions cultivate personal holiness, social harmony, and therefore the assured, lasting reward in the final abode.

translation: They will enter Gardens of Eternity, and whoever among their fathers, their spouses, and their offspring was righteous — and the angels will enter upon them from every gate.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the companionship of Paradise extends to those relatives who themselves attained righteousness, emphasizing that reunion in the hereafter is not automatic by kinship but is conditioned on personal faith and good conduct; at the same time it reassures the believer that righteous families may enjoy communal companionship in bliss. The image of angels entering from every gate underscores the fullness, honor, and continual blessing of that state — angels come to greet, congratulate, and usher the blessed into all the manifold joys and safety of Paradise, indicating abundance, ease of access, and the public witness of divine favor.

translation: “Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; and excellent is the final home.”
interpretation: God’s greeting to the faithful in the Hereafter highlights that patient perseverance in the face of trials — steadfast faith, perseverance in obedience, and endurance of suffering without abandoning God’s path — is the cause of their reception into divine peace; the verse therefore teaches that true success lies not in worldly ease but in enduring faithfully so as to attain the supreme, everlasting reward of the final abode.

translation: And those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and spread corruption on the earth — those are the ones for whom is the curse, and they will have a wretched abode.
interpretation: The verse warns against people who, having accepted God’s covenant (their duty toward God and society), betray it by violating promises, tearing apart the bonds God ordained (primarily kinship ties and social/trust relationships), and perpetrating injustice and disorder in the community. Such conduct destroys the moral and social fabric ordained by God; it not only merits divine curse but also leads to ruinous consequences in this life and the Hereafter, showing that faith must be matched by fidelity to obligations toward God and fellow human beings.

translation: الله يبسط الرزق لمن يشاء ويقدر ۚ وفرحوا بالحياة الدنيا وما الحياة الدنيا في الآخرة إلا متاع
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن الرزق بيد الله يوزعه بقدرته وحكمته، وأن ازدياد الناس في مالٍ ونعمة لا يثبت لهم منزلة أخروية؛ فمن يفرح بالحياة الدنيا ويغتر بها فقد انطبع على اعتبار الزينة واللذة العابرة، وأما في الآخرة فمباهج الدنيا ستكون مجرد متاع زائل لا يقاس بثواب الله الباقي. لذلك تذّكر الآية أن الاغتراف من نعم الدنيا يجب أن يكون مصحوبًا بالوعي بأن هذه النعم امتحان وفرصة للذكر والطاعة، لا غاية مطلقة تؤمن من حساب الآخرة.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, “Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?” Say, “Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns (in repentance).”
interpretation: The verse answers the demand for spectacular proof by showing that true guidance is ultimately a divine gift tied to the moral and spiritual state of people: God does not grant guidance merely by displaying signs to unwilling hearts. “Leading astray” should be understood largely as the withdrawal or withholding of guidance as a just consequence of persistent rejection and self‑chosen blindness, while “guiding to Himself” is bestowed upon those who sincerely turn, repent and humble themselves. Thus faith is not produced by miracles alone but by an inner turning toward God for which He, in His wisdom, grants guidance.

translation: Those who have believed and whose hearts are reassured by the remembrance of Allah — indeed, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are reassured.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true inner calm is not merely an emotional state but a spiritual condition produced when faith is actively lived through turning the heart toward God. “Remembrance of Allah” here means sustained awareness and engagement with God — through prayer, Qur’anic reflection, invoking His names, and trusting His wisdom — and this ongoing orientation dissolves fear, disperses restlessness, and grounds moral resolve. The phrasing underscores a principled truth: authentic tranquility of the heart is achieved principally by keeping God present in one’s consciousness and relying on Him.

translation: Those who believed and did righteous deeds — glad tidings for them and an excellent return.
interpretation: The verse asserts that true salvation lies in the union of inner faith and outward righteous action: God promises those who combine belief with moral deeds a special felicity (ṭūbā) and a noble, enduring outcome (ḥusn maʾāb) in the Hereafter — not merely transient blessings but forgiveness, honor, nearness to God, and everlasting reward as the rightful consequence of their faith lived through righteous conduct.

translation: Thus We have sent you to a people to whom other peoples had passed before them, so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you — while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: “He is my Lord; there is no deity except Him. In Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn.”
interpretation: The verse reassures the Messenger that his duty is to convey God’s revelation even when his community repeats the pattern of previous nations in rejecting divine mercy. It teaches that true response in the face of denial is not coercion or despair but a settled spiritual posture: steadfast affirmation of God’s oneness, reliance upon Him (tawakkul), and continuous turning back to Him. Success is thus defined by faithful obedience and trust, leaving outcome and judgment to God alone.

translation: And even if a Qur’an were made to cause the mountains to move by it, or to split the earth, or to make the dead speak — to Allah belongs the affair entirely. Will those who have believed then be despondent? If Allah had willed, He would have guided all people. And those who disbelieve will continue to be overtaken by the consequences of what they have done — a calamity, or it will draw near to their homes — until the promise of Allah comes. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Quran’s authority does not lie in coercive, spectacle-making wonders but in God’s sovereign will and the moral responsibility of people. It rejects the notion that compelling, world-shattering miracles would be the proper means to force belief; guidance is a divine gift granted according to God’s wisdom, not something the Prophet can impose. Believers are therefore urged not to despair when many reject the message, since universal guidance rests with God alone, and the apparent delay in recompense does not mean injustice — the consequences awaiting the rejecters are real and certain because Allah’s promise will be fulfilled in His timing.

translation: وَلَقَدْ اسْتُهِزِئَ بِرُسُلٍ مِّن قَبْلِكَ فَأَمْلَيْتُ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا ثُمَّ أَخَذْتُهُمْ ۖ فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عِقَابِ
interpretation: الآية تبيّن حكمة تأخير العقاب: الله يتروى ويمنح مهلة لاختبار القلوب وفرصة للتوبة، لكن هذه المهلة ليست تبريراً للاستمرار في الكفر أو السخرية من الحق. النبرة الاستفهامية تشير إلى حتمية العدالة الإلهية وشدتها على من أصرّ على الضلال، فتكون العبرة للمؤمنين بالثبات وللمعرضين دعوة إلى الاستفادة من الرحمة قبل أن يصير الجزاء حاسماً.

translation: Is then He Who is established over every soul according to what it has earned? And they have set up partners for Allah. Say, “Name them.” Or will you inform Him of what is on the earth, or is it an outward saying? Nay — He has made their plotting attractive to those who disbelieve and has turned them away from the way. And whoever Allah leads astray — for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse confronts the folly and danger of ascribing partners to God: such claims neither add to God’s knowledge nor affect His judgment, and the challenge to “name” these partners exposes their baselessness. More broadly, it teaches that guidance is a divine trust — when people persist in rejection, God may allow false beliefs to appear attractive to them as a consequence of their choice, and if God withdraws guidance from someone there remains no true guide. Thus the passage affirms God’s sole authority over recompense and guidance and warns that clinging to false deities results in spiritual misguidance from which there is no remedy except turning back to the One God.

translation: For them is a punishment in the life of this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe; and they will have no protector from Allah.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who persist in rejection, corruption or injustice will taste consequences already in this worldly life, but those are only a foretaste: the real and more grievous retribution lies in the Hereafter. It emphasizes the inevitability and finality of divine justice — no wealth, kinship, power, idols or human allies will be able to shield such people from God’s decree. The passage thus calls readers to abandon false reliance on worldly supports and to heed the moral responsibility that will be judged definitively before God.

translation: The example of Paradise which the righteous were promised: beneath it rivers flow; its fruit is perpetual and its shade. That is the ultimate outcome for those who feared [Allah]; and the ultimate outcome for the disbelievers is the Fire.
interpretation: The verse uses the imagery of enduring rivers, everlasting fruit and permanent shade to signify that the reward for taqwa is not fleeting worldly pleasure but continuous, dignified sustenance, security and honour rooted in God’s favour. By calling this the ‘عقبى’ (ultimate end) of the pious, the verse affirms a moral economy in which conscious God‑fear and righteous conduct lead to a fitting, eternal consummation, while denial and rejection lead to a correspondingly just and final punishment; the language thus both consoles the faithful with the certainty of divine recompense and warns of the seriousness of moral choice.

translation: And those to whom We gave the Scripture rejoice in what has been revealed to you; and among the factions are some who reject part of it. Say, “I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not to associate anything with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return.”
interpretation: The verse notes that some People of the Book recognize and welcome the Prophet’s message, while other groups—driven by factional interests or prejudice—refuse parts of it. The Prophet is therefore instructed to remain steadfast in the fundamental duty: pure worship of God alone, free from all forms of association. His role is to call people to God, not to enforce belief; ultimate judgment and return belong to God alone. The passage thus emphasizes the unity of the prophetic message (tawhīd), the reality of human division and selective acceptance, and the Prophet’s trustful reliance on God as the one to whom both his invite and his destiny are directed.

translation:
وَكَذَٰلِكَ أَنزَلْنَاهُ حُكْمًا عَرَبِيًّا ۚ وَلَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتَ أَهْوَاءَهُم بَعْدَ مَا جَاءَكَ مِنَ الْعِلْمِ مَا لَكَ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِن وَلِيٍّ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ
“And thus We have sent it down — a decisive Arabic ruling. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have from Allah no protector and no helper.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur’an was revealed in clear, native Arabic so its judgments and guidance are unmistakable; it warns the Prophet (and by extension those entrusted with guidance) not to abandon revealed truth to accommodate popular whims. To follow people’s desires after receiving clear knowledge is to forfeit divine legitimacy and support — one would lose God’s protection, authority, and assistance — therefore fidelity to the revealed message, not compromise for acceptance, is required for true leadership and success.

translation: And certainly We sent messengers before you, and We made for them spouses and offspring; and it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by Allah’s permission. For every appointed term there is a written decree.
interpretation: The verse teaches that prophets were ordinary human beings with families, so their moral and social lives are part of God’s wisdom, and that any miracle or clear sign attributed to a prophet occurs only by God’s permission — not by the prophet’s independent power — while every event, lifespan, and appointed occurrence takes place according to God’s predetermined and recorded timing; thus people should neither demand signs on their own terms nor imagine prophetic power apart from divine will, but should trust God’s authority and timing.

translation:
يَمْحُو اللَّهُ مَا يَشَاءُ وَيُثْبِتُ ۖ وَعِنْدَهُ أُمُّ الْكِتَابِ
"Allah erases what He wills and confirms (what He wills); and with Him is the Mother of the Book."
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty over revelation and decree: He alone decides which injunctions, signs, or people He will remove and which He will establish. ‘Erasing’ and ‘confirming’ point both to the abrogation and confirmation within revealed law and to changes in worldly conditions; nothing contradicts His wisdom because every change is rooted in the eternal, archetypal record—’Umm al-Kitâb’ (the Mother of the Book, understood as the Preserved Tablet or the divine, immutable source of knowledge). Thus believers are reminded to trust divine wisdom when laws or circumstances shift, recognizing that such dispensation stems from God’s comprehensive, perfect knowledge and purpose.

translation: And whether We show you some of what We have promised them or We cause you to die, it is only for you to convey [the message], and upon Us is the accounting.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet that his sole obligation is to deliver God's message; he is not responsible for enforcing belief, proving every promise, or securing visible punishment for rejecters. God alone determines the timing of events, the prophet’s life and death, and will administer ultimate justice and recompense. The teaching is a release from the burden of controlling outcomes: trust in God’s wisdom, persist in the duty of proclamation, and leave the judgment and consequences to God’s authority.

translation:
أَفَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّا نَأْتِي الْأَرْضَ نَنقُصُهَا مِنْ أَطْرَافِهَا ۚ وَاللَّهُ يَحْكُمُ لَا مُعَقِّبَ لِحُكْمِهِ ۚ وَهُوَ سَرِيعُ الْحِسَابِ
"Do they not see that We will come to the earth and diminish it from its outskirts? And Allah judges; there is no reversing His judgment; and He is swift in accounting."
interpretation: The phrase about coming to the earth and lessening it from its edges is a description of the last things — the earth will be altered, contracted or stripped of its familiar bounds when the Hour approaches so that no refuge or concealment remains. This picture underlines divine sovereignty: God alone determines the course of events and issues the final verdict, a decree that no one can annul or delay. Coupled with “He is swift in accounting,” the verse warns that people will be promptly held to account for their deeds, so worldly security or power cannot avert the inevitable judgment.

translation: And those before them schemed, but to Allah belongs all scheming; He knows what every soul earns, and the disbelievers will come to know for whom is the final abode.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human plotting, however clever or successful it may seem, is ultimately subordinate to God’s sovereign plan and knowledge: God records every deed and will, in the end, make manifest the true outcome. Those who deny or take comfort in temporary gains will discover that divine justice—not worldly schemes—determines who truly attains the everlasting abode.

translation: ويقول الذين كفروا: «لست مرسلا». قل: «كفى بالله شهيداً بيني وبينكم، ومن عنده علم الكتاب».
interpretation: الآية ترشد إلى أن إنكار الكافرين لرسالة النبي لا يزيح عن الحقيقة شيئاً، إذ تكفي شهادة الله وعلمه المطلق ليثبت صدق الرسالة؛ عبارة «من عنده علم الكتاب» تؤكد أن الحكم النهائي والمعرفة الصحيحة للحق في الكتاب والسُنة بيد الله وحده، فالمؤمن مأمور أن يعتمد على برهان الله وشهادته ويترك إنكار الناس للحكم الإلهي.

translation: Alif-Lam-Ra. A Book We have revealed to you so that you may bring people out of darkness into light by the permission of their Lord, to the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur’an as a divinely given means of transformation: it is sent to move people out of spiritual and moral ‘darkness’—ignorance, error, bondage to false beliefs and corrupt habits—into ‘light,’ namely knowledge of God, ethical clarity, and liberated worship. Saying this comes “by the permission of their Lord” stresses that guidance is ultimately a gift from God and that the Prophet’s role is to convey the message while God enables its effect. The destination, “the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy,” defines the goal as a life ordered toward God’s sovereignty and worthiness of praise—submission, justice, and conduct befitting the divine Majesty.

translation: Allah — to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty and ownership of all existence: nothing in the heavens or on earth belongs to anyone apart from Him. Because He is the sole Lord and ultimate authority, persistent denial and rejection of that reality bring inevitable accountability; the warning of “woe” and a “severe punishment” underscores the seriousness and certainty of consequence for those who stubbornly disbelieve, intended to awaken awareness, humility, and repentance before that judgment.

translation: Those who prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter and who turn people away from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked — those are in far-away error.
interpretation: The verse condemns a moral posture that elevates transient worldly gain above eternal accountability; this preference not only corrupts the chooser but leads them to obstruct and distort God’s guidance for others. Such behavior reflects deliberate spiritual blindness and active misguidance, placing the doers — and those they lead astray — in a profound, remote state of error with adverse moral and eschatological consequences.

translation:
وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِن رَّسُولٍ إِلَّا بِّلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ ۖ فَيُضِلُّ اللَّهُ مَن يَشَاءُ وَيَهْدِي مَن يَشَاءُ ۚ وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ
"We sent no messenger except in the language of his own people, that he might make [the message] clear to them. Allah causes to stray whom He wills and guides whom He wills; and He is the Exalted in Might, the All-Wise."
interpretation: God’s practice of commissioning prophets in the tongue of their people underlines His mercy and concern that the guidance be intelligible and accessible; the clause about God misguiding or guiding indicates His ultimate sovereignty over the moral/spiritual outcome, yet this sovereignty is exercised through means — clear speech, signs, and appeals to conscience — so that responsibility and response remain real. Calling God “Al‑Aziz, Al‑Hakim” affirms that whatever outcome (guidance or deviation) ensues is by a power that is both effective and wise: God gives people a fair, lucid offer of guidance and, in wisdom, allows consequences to follow from their reception or rejection of it.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs: “Bring out your people from the darknesses into the light and remind them of the Days of Allah.” Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful one.
interpretation: The verse means that God raised up Moses with clear proofs to free his people from spiritual and social darkness — ignorance, falsehood and oppression — and lead them into moral and religious clarity (the light). Reminding them of the “Days of Allah” refers to recalling the moments when God’s help, judgment, favors or trials are manifest in history so people learn and reform. These occurrences are not mere stories but ethical and theological signs: they teach and confirm God’s power and purpose to those who respond with sabr (steadfast patience in trials and obedience) coupled with shukr (recognition and grateful return in obedience). In short, the events of prophetic deliverance are meant to convert historical memory into present guidance for the steadfast and thankful believer.

translation: “And when Moses said to his people, ‘Remember the favor of Allah upon you when He delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who were inflicting upon you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women for themselves — and in that was a great trial from your Lord.’”
interpretation: Moses reminds his people to recognize that their escape from Pharaoh was not merely a change of circumstances but a clear divine favor and a severe test: the cruelty they endured exposed the depth of oppression, and God’s deliverance was both mercy and an occasion to prove gratitude and steadfastness. Remembering such a rescue should cultivate humble thankfulness, vigilance against repeating moral failures, and a resolve to live by justice and faith, for God’s salvations carry the responsibility to respond rightly rather than fall into ingratitude or complacency.

translation: “And when your Lord declared: ‘If you are grateful, I will surely give you more; but if you are ungrateful, My punishment is indeed severe.’”
interpretation: The verse states a general divine principle: genuine gratitude — recognizing God’s gifts, speaking thanks, and using blessings rightly (through obedience, charity, and moral conduct) — invites further bounty and elevation from God, whereas ingratitude or denial (refusing to acknowledge or using blessings to disobey) brings severe consequence. It functions as both encouragement and warning, linking human moral response to God’s merciful increase or His just retribution.

translation: And Moses said, “If you — and all who are on the earth — were to disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.”
interpretation: Moses’ remark emphasizes that God’s essence, power, and worth do not depend on human recognition or acceptance; disbelief neither diminishes His sovereignty nor adds to His worth. The statement is meant to correct a human-centered attitude that imagines God needs people’s belief or praise. Its practical lesson is to show that faith and submission are ultimately for people’s own good and accountability, not to fulfill any deficiency in God, and thus to warn listeners that rejecting guidance harms themselves while leaving God unaffected.

translation: Has there not come to you the report of those before you — the people of Nūḥ and ʿĀd and Thamūd and those after them? None knows them except Allāh. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they thrust their hands to their mouths and said, “Indeed we reject that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in suspicious doubt as to that to which you invite us.”
interpretation: This verse diagnoses a recurrent moral disposition: when confronted with unmistakable guidance, some people will reject it not because of genuine doubt but from a willful, performative refusal—masking their rejection as ‘‘doubt’’ while their true motives are pride, attachment to corrupt habits, or fear of social loss. The image of putting hands to the mouth signals sham astonishment and suppression of conscience; the passage warns that such hypocritical skepticism is culpable and that repeating it leads nations to ruin.

translation: Their messengers said, “Is there any doubt concerning Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth? He calls you so that He may forgive you your sins and grant you respite until an appointed term.” They said, “You are nothing but humans like us; you intend to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship. Then bring us a clear authority.”
interpretation: The verse contrasts the messengers’ appeal to God’s unique authority and merciful invitation to repentance with the people’s reflexive rejection rooted in inherited habit and demand for spectacular proof. It teaches that refusal often comes not from lack of reason but from attachment to ancestral practices and the expectation that truth must arrive with visible, extraordinary signs; meanwhile, genuine guidance invites moral change and trust in God’s authority and mercy even when the proofs presented are conveyed through ordinary human agents.

translation: Their messengers said to them, “We are nothing but human beings like you, but Allah bestows His favor upon whom He wills among His servants. And it was not for us to bring you a proof except by the permission of Allah. So let the believers put their trust in Allah.”
interpretation: The verse points to a theological principle: prophets are human instruments, not self-exalted beings, and the real authority of a message comes from God’s granting of signs and support. ‘Sulṭān’ (a manifest proof or power) is not producible by human effort alone but is given by God’s will, so acceptance of truth cannot be enforced by status or force. Consequently true reliance (tawakkul) belongs to believers who trust in God’s wisdom and timing—acknowledging that guidance, vindication, and success are ultimately Allah’s prerogative rather than the outcome of human prestige or coercion.

translation: Why should we not put our trust in Allah, since He has guided us to our ways? We will surely be patient with whatever harm you inflict upon us. And upon Allah—let those who trust, trust (in Him).
interpretation: Because God has shown the believers the right path, they have no legitimate excuse for doubting or abandoning reliance on Him; instead their appropriate stance in the face of hostility is steadfast patience and reliance on Allah alone. The verse links divine guidance with a moral obligation: guidance calls for trust, and trust manifests in enduring harm without resentment, while true reliance means placing one’s ultimate dependence on God rather than on human power or immediate relief.

translation: And those who disbelieved said to their messengers, "We will surely drive you out of our land, or you must return to our religion." So their Lord inspired to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."
interpretation: God reassures the prophets that threats and temporary expulsions by the unjust do not determine ultimate justice: although oppressors may boast of driving out or forcing believers to renounce their way, God has revealed to His messengers a sure promise that the tyrants’ power is transient and that the wrongdoers will be brought to ruin — a message of patient steadfastness for the faithful and a warning of inevitable divine accountability for the oppressors.

translation: And We will cause you to dwell in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing and fears My warning.
interpretation: God is promising to restore and settle the faithful in the land after the removal or defeat of those who wronged them; but this assurance is not automatic — it is tied to inner piety. “Fearing My standing” means being conscious of standing before God (accountability on the Day of Reckoning) and living with that awareness, and “fearing My warning” means taking God’s threats of punishment seriously so one refrains from transgression. Thus the verse links a future, outward deliverance with an inward moral responsibility: divine favor and security in the earth are granted to those who fear God, heed His warnings, and shape their conduct by that reverent awareness.

translation: They sought to gain a decisive victory, but every arrogant, obstinate tyrant was thwarted.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who, from pride and stubbornness, demand triumph by force and oppression will ultimately be disappointed; apparent might and tyranny cannot secure success against God's decree, and arrogance leads to ruin rather than lasting victory.

translation:
من ورائه جهنمٍ، ويسقى من ماءٍ صديدٍ
"Behind him is Hell, and he will be made to drink of corrosive/boiling water."
interpretation: الآية تصف نتيجة من يعرض عن هدى الله: جهنم تلازمه كقضاء محتوم لا مهرب منه، وما يُسقى له من «ماء صديد» رمز لمعاناة مؤلمة ومذلة — ماء يحرق ويقوّض الجسد ويُظهر خزي المبتعد عن الحق. المعنى الأخلاقي أن الإنكار والعناد لا يقتصران على خسارة دنيوية بل يجران صاحبه إلى عذاب قاسٍ في الآخرة، جسدياً وروحياً.

translation: يتجرعه ولا يكاد يسيغه ويأتيه الموت من كل مكان وما هو بميت ۖ ومن ورائه عذاب غليظ
interpretation: الآية تصف حالة من يعاقبه الله نتيجة كفره أو عصيانه: كأنّه يتذوق عذابًا مؤلمًا لا يطيقه، ويشتد حوله الموت من كل جانب فلا يُنقذه، ثم لا يختم الأمر بالموت كراحة بل يتبعه عذاب شديد في الآخرة — تأكيد على استمرار العذاب وحرمان المخالف من خلاص أو مهلة تُنقذه.
