translation: The example of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day; they cannot retain any of what they have earned. That is the distant misguidance.
interpretation: The verse means that actions severed from true faith and right intention have no lasting weight or benefit: though they may appear as deeds, they are insubstantial—like ashes scattered and wasted by a fierce wind—and on the Day of Reckoning will yield nothing. The image emphasizes the futility of worldly works without sincere belief and the grave, far-reaching nature of being cut off from guidance (الضلال البعيد).

translation: Do you not see that Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth? If He wills, He can do away with you and bring about a new creation.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty and creative authority: the entire cosmos exists by His purposeful truth, and human existence is contingent on His will. It serves as a solemn warning that persistence in unbelief or corruption is not beyond God’s power to remove—He can abolish a people and replace them with a new creation that will fulfill His purpose—thereby calling for humility, obedience, and awareness of inevitable accountability before the Creator.

translation: And that is not difficult for Allah.
interpretation: A succinct affirmation of divine omnipotence: whatever action or outcome is under discussion — be it resurrection, judgment, guidance, reward or punishment — is entirely within God’s power and is accomplished without difficulty; human doubts about possibility do not constrain the Sovereign, for nothing is beyond His capacity.

translation: And they will all be presented before Allah. Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant, “We were indeed your followers; can you avail us anything against the punishment of Allah?” They will say, “If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same to us whether we show anxiety or patience; for us there is no escape.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment worldly rank and followers will not shift responsibility: those who once led others but lacked true guidance will disown their followers and admit they had no power to secure salvation for anyone. Guidance is a gift from God, not a transferable social privilege; arrogance that substitutes status for righteousness becomes exposed when accountability comes, and the proud are reduced to helpless resignation. The moral is that personal responsibility and sincere faith, not reliance on influential patrons or on outward dominance, determine one’s standing before God.

translation: وقال الشيطان لما قضي الأمر: «إن الله وعدكم وعد الحق، ووعدتكم فأخلفتكم. وما كان لي عليكم من سلطان إلا أن دعوتكم فاستجبتم لي. فلا تلوموني ولوموا أنفسكم. ما أنا بمصرخكم وما أنتم بمصرخي. إني كفرت بما أشركتمون من قبل. إن الظالمين لهم عذاب أليم.»
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن الشيطان ليس سوى مُغرٍ وداعٍ لا مُكرِّه؛ عندما ينكشف الحق في القيامة سيعترف بأنه خدَع الناس بخداع ووعودٍ كاذبة وأنه لم يكن له سلطان إكراه عليهم، فالمسؤولية تبقى على من استجابوا له. المقصود علميًا وأخلاقيًا أن الجزاء على الشرك والمعاصي هو نتيجة اختيارٍ بشري واستسلامٍ للغواية، وأن تبرئة الشيطان في الموقف الأخير تُنزِل المسؤولية إلى الإنسان، وتُبرز كذلك حقيقة وعد الله الحق مقابل وعد الشيطان الكاذب وعاقبة الظالمين.

translation: And admit those who believed and did righteous deeds to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by permission of their Lord; their greeting therein will be, "Peace."
interpretation: The verse promises that ultimate reward for true faith coupled with righteous action is entry into a permanent, blessed state — Paradise pictured with flowing rivers to convey sustained spiritual and physical good. Saying this occurs “by permission of their Lord” reminds that such felicity is granted by God’s grace rather than as an automatic right, and the greeting “Peace” expresses the complete security, inner tranquillity, and absence of fear or regret that characterize that state. Thus the passage ties sincere belief and moral conduct to divine generosity, encouraging seekers to combine faith with deeds while relying on God’s mercy.

translation:
ألم تر كيف ضرب الله مثلا كلمة طيبة كشجرة طيبة أصلها ثابت وفرعها في السماء
“Have you not seen how Allah sets forth an example? A good word is like a good tree—its root is firm and its branches reach into the sky.”
interpretation: The ‘‘good word’’ symbolizes a truthful, sincere conviction or teaching (and the righteous deeds that flow from it) that is firmly rooted in sound belief, knowledge, and guidance. Like a tree with a deep, stable root, such a faith/word provides inner steadiness; like branches reaching toward the sky, it grows, spreads benefit to others, and attains high moral and spiritual outcomes. The image stresses lasting stability, continuous growth, wide-reaching influence and enduring fruitfulness that come when a person’s conviction and practice are rightly founded.

translation: It brings forth its fruit every season by permission of its Lord. And Allah sets forth examples for people so that they may take heed.
interpretation: The recurring yielding of produce is offered as a tangible sign of God’s continual sustenance and governance: life’s cycles and provision occur not by chance or solely by human effort but by the will and decree of the Lord. By pointing to such natural processes as a parable, God intends to awaken human reflection, gratitude and humility, so that people recognize their dependence on Him, abandon arrogance, and let that remembrance shape their conduct and faith.

translation: And the example of an evil word is like that of an evil tree: it is uprooted from the surface of the earth — it has no stability.
interpretation: The verse likens corrupt or false speech (or deeds and beliefs rooted in falsehood) to a diseased, worthless tree that has been torn from the soil and therefore has no firm root or lasting hold. Such words lack grounding in truth and guidance, produce no enduring good or beneficial fruit, are easily swept away, and lead those who rely on them to instability and ruin in this life and the next.

translation: Allah makes firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter; and Allah leads astray the wrongdoers; and Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: The phrase “the firm word” refers to the divine support that anchors a believer’s conviction and conduct; God’s firming of the faithful means He grants them an inner steadiness and outward perseverance so that their belief endures through trials and bears fruit in the Hereafter. By contrast, persistent injustice brings the withdrawal of that stabilizing guidance, resulting in misguidance for the wrongdoers—not merely as arbitrary punishment but as the natural consequence of their rejection of truth. The closing clause affirms divine sovereignty: outcomes of guidance or error are realized within God’s wise will, combining human moral responsibility with ultimate dependence on God’s decree.

translation: ألم تر إلى الذين بدلوا نعمت الله كفرا وأحلوا قومهم دار البوار
interpretation: The verse censures those who, having received Allah’s favors and guidance, willfully exchange them for disbelief; by abandoning gratitude and truth they not only forfeit their own salvation but, when they influence others, lead their people into moral and spiritual ruin — a ruin that manifests in corrupt, collapsing societies in this life and final loss in the Hereafter.

translation: They will enter Hell, and what an evil resting-place it is.
interpretation: The verse affirms the sure and terrible consequence for persistent rejection and wrongdoing: entering Hell is depicted as an unavoidable, collective outcome (يصلونها conveys being driven into it), and وبئس القرار stresses its utter misery and permanence as a dwelling. Its purpose is to warn and to urge people toward repentance and righteous conduct to avert that final, dreadful fate.

translation: And they set up equals to Allah to lead [people] astray from His way. Say, “Enjoy yourselves; for indeed your final destination is the Fire.”
interpretation: The verse indicts those who fabricate partners for God as instruments to divert people from guidance and places the burden of judgment on their own choice: the Prophet is told to leave them to their present indulgence because such pleasures are temporary and cannot avert the inevitable outcome—divine recompense. It is both a warning that false deities and corrupt paths are futile and a statement of divine justice: persistent rejection of truth bars one from salvation and leads to punishment.

translation: قُل لِعِبَادِي الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَأَنْفِقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ سِرًّا وَعَلَانِيَةً قَبْلَ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ يَوْمٌ لَا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ وَلَا خِلَالٌ
interpretation: الخِطاب هنا توجيه عملي ومُلحّ للمؤمنين: ثبّتو صلتكم بالله بالصلاة واظهروا أثر إيمانكم بإخراج النفقة من رزقكم، سواءً على العلن لتُعينوا المجتمع وتكونوا قدوة، أو سرًّا لتنقوا النفوس وتطلبوا أجر الله الخالص. والآية تضيف عامل الزمن والتحذير—افعلوا ذلك الآن لأن يوم القيامة لا تنفع فيه التعاملات الدنيوية ولا الصلات الاجتماعية كضمان أو بديل عن العمل الصالح؛ لا بيع ولا صداقة ستُبدّل الحال أمام الحساب، فالمصلحة الحقيقية هي استثمار الوقت والمال في العبادة والعمل الصالح قبل زوال الفرصة.

translation: Allah — He who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water from the sky; by it We produced for you fruits as provision, and He made the ships subservient to you so that they may sail through the sea by His command, and He made the rivers subject to you.
interpretation: The verse aims to awaken awareness that the everyday means of life and movement (rain, crops, ships, rivers) are not merely natural accidents but manifestations of Divine sovereignty given to humanity as provision and trust; this recognition calls for humility, gratitude, and responsible stewardship rather than pride or claiming independent mastery over what ultimately comes by God’s will.

translation: And He has made the sun and the moon subservient to you, each running [its course] constantly; and He has made the night and the day subservient to you.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has ordered the cosmos — the steady motion of sun and moon and the alternation of night and day — to serve human needs (light, timekeeping, seasons, rest and labor). Their regularity (دائبين) both facilitates human life and stands as a sign of divine wisdom and providence, calling people to acknowledge their dependence on God and to use these blessings responsibly in gratitude and obedience.

translation: And He has given you from all that you asked of Him. And if you were to count the favors of Allah, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, man is surely most unjust and ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God providentially grants human needs and answers requests in abundant ways beyond full human accounting; yet, because people often fail to recognize, properly use, or acknowledge these blessings, they tend toward wrongdoing and ingratitude. It is therefore a moral admonition: to cultivate awareness of God’s continual gifts, to respond with gratitude and justice, and to correct the habitual tendencies of denial or misuse that betray one’s dependence on the Divine.

translation:
وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ: «رَبِّ اجْعَلْ هَٰذَا الْبَلَدَ آمِنًا وَٱجْنُبْنِي وَبَنِيَّ أَنْ نَعْبُدَ ٱلْأَصْنَامَ»
"And [remember] when Abraham said, 'My Lord, make this city secure and keep me and my children from worshipping idols.'"
interpretation: The verse reflects Abraham’s dual concern for both the communal and the spiritual well‑being of his line: he asks God to preserve the sanctity and safety of the place (so that true worship can be practiced undisturbed) and to protect his descendants from falling into shirk. It teaches that establishing a secure social environment and safeguarding the faith of future generations are united duties—parents and leaders should seek divine help to create conditions where monotheism can endure and where children are guarded against corrupting influences.

translation: My Lord, indeed they have led astray many people. So whoever follows me among them—then indeed he is of me; and whoever disobeys me—indeed, You are Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse speaks to the moral dynamics between corrupting influences and personal responsibility: when certain actors mislead the community, those who willingly attach themselves to and imitate them become complicit and are, in effect, counted as part of that misguidance; conversely, those who resist or disobey that course are not beyond hope, for God’s forgiving and merciful nature remains available. It is both a warning against unreflective following of harmful leaders and an assurance that repentance and turning away from error can restore one to God’s mercy.

translation: Our Lord, indeed I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House. Our Lord — that they may establish prayer — so make among the people hearts incline toward them and provide for them from the fruits that they might be grateful.
interpretation: Ibrāhīm’s supplication shows reliance on God when he places his family in a harsh place near the Kaʿbah: he asks not only for material provision but for social acceptance so his descendants can maintain regular worship. The prayer teaches that sustaining a community of faith requires both inward support (hearts inclined toward them, i.e., goodwill and protection from others) and outward provision (fruits, livelihood), and that these gifts enable steadfast prayer and produce gratitude to God. It models prudent planning coupled with trust in God’s provision for both spiritual and worldly needs.

translation: Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal and what we declare; and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heavens.
interpretation: This phrase is a believer’s affirmation that God’s knowledge embraces both inward intentions and outward deeds, so that sincerity cannot be feigned nor secret suffering remain unnoticed; grounded in that conviction one seeks God’s help, forgiveness and justice, lives with conscience before His presence, and finds reassurance that what humans overlook or conceal is fully known to the Divine Judge.

translation: Praise be to Allah who granted me, in my old age, Ismaʿil and Ishaq; indeed my Lord is the Hearer of prayer.
interpretation: The speaker acknowledges that what appeared humanly unlikely—children at an advanced age—came by Allah’s grace, and by calling God “the Hearer of prayer” he affirms that sincere supplication is noticed and answered according to God’s wisdom; the verse therefore teaches gratitude for divine favors, trust in God’s attentive response, and patience in awaiting outcomes beyond human expectation.

translation: My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer and [make] of my descendants [who establish prayer]. Our Lord, and accept my supplication.
interpretation: A humble plea by Abraham asking God to root steadfast, sincere worship in himself and to secure that same commitment in his progeny; it expresses the responsibility to leave a living religious legacy, the importance of cultivating devotion across generations, and the believer’s dependence on God’s acceptance — not merely outward performance — for that prayer to be effective.

translation: Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the account will be established.
interpretation: This plea expresses the believer’s humble dependence on divine mercy at the final reckoning: rather than relying on deeds alone, the supplicant asks Allah to remit shortcomings for himself, for his parents (highlighting enduring filial duty and the spiritual link between generations), and for the wider community of believers—acknowledging that ultimate salvation is a gift of God’s forgiveness when people stand before Him to be judged.

translation:
وَلَا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ غَافِلًا عَمَّا يَعْمَلُ الظَّالِمُونَ ۚ إِنَّمَا يُؤَخِّرُهُمْ لِيَوْمٍ تَشْخَصُ فِيهِ الْأَبْصَارُ
“Do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do; He merely delays them until a Day when the eyes will stare (in horror).”
interpretation: The apparent postponement of punishment is not negligence but deliberate divine wisdom: God fully knows every act of injustice and will bring the oppressors to account at the decisive Day of Reckoning. That Day will be one of shock, exposure and helplessness—the perpetrators’ power and deeds will be laid bare, and they will be unable to avert or deny what they did. The verse comforts the afflicted with the promise of ultimate justice and warns wrongdoers that temporary success is fleeting and will be overturned when true accountability comes.

translation: Hastening on, with their heads covered; their glances do not turn back to them, and their hearts are like air.
interpretation: The verse portrays people who rush blindly toward their fate — outwardly hurried and veiled (signifying shame, humiliation, or obstinate haste), incapable or unwilling to look back for repentance or counsel. Their inner states are insubstantial and empty—devoid of sincere faith, conviction, or remembrance of God—so their actions carry no true guidance or benefit.

translation: And warn the people of the Day when the punishment will come upon them; and those who did wrong will say, “Our Lord, delay us for a short term — we will answer Your call and follow the messengers.” [Allah] will say, “Did you not swear before that for you there would be no return?”
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning the guilty may beg for respite and promise obedience, but such last‑minute pledges cannot erase a lifetime of denial and false oaths. Their earlier rejection of the truth — even oaths asserting that there would be no return — exposes their insincerity and removes any claim to postponement; divine judgment weighs consistent belief and conduct, not desperate promises at the moment of punishment.

translation: وَسَكَنْتُمْ فِي مَسَاكِنِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا أَنفُسَهُمْ وَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمْ كَيْفَ فَعَلْنَا بِهِمْ وَضَرَبْنَا لَكُمُ الْأَمْثَالَ
interpretation: الآية تشير إلى أن إيواء الناس في بقايا مساكن أقوامٍ سابقين كانوا قد «ظلموا أنفسهم» (بكفرهم أو بإصرارهم على المعاصي) يجعل من تلك الأنقاض درساً واضحاً عن سنن الله في الجزاء: كيف أزاح عنهم العزّة والنعمة نتيجة فسادهم. الله يوضح مصائر هؤلاء القوم ويضرب الأمثال حتى يرى الورثة علامات العبرة، فيتدبّروا، ويتجنبوا تكبُّرًا وفجورًا يوديان بهم إلى زوالٍ مماثل.

translation: And they devised their plot, and with Allah is their plot; and if their plot were to make the mountains move from their place...
interpretation: The verse teaches that human scheming, however elaborate and seemingly powerful—even imagined as able to overturn mountains—is ultimately subordinate to God’s sovereign will; plots against the truth cannot succeed except by God’s leave, and what the plotters fancied as mighty will come to nothing and return upon them under Allah’s control.

translation:
فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ مُخْلِفَ وَعْدِهِ رُسُلَهُ ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ ذُو انْتِقَامٍ
“So do not suppose that Allah will fail in His promise to His messengers. Indeed, Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution.”
interpretation: This verse affirms that the assurances conveyed through God’s messengers—whether promises of support, vindication, reward for the patient, or punishment for the defiantly unjust—will surely come to pass because God’s sovereignty and power are absolute. Calling God “Mighty, Owner of Retribution” stresses that He is fully capable of executing justice; any apparent delay is not negligence but part of His wisdom, and ultimately He will recompense actions appropriately. The statement comforts the sincere and warns the insolent: divine promises are certain, and accountability is inevitable.

translation: The Day the earth will be changed into a different earth, and the heavens [will be changed], and they will all emerge before Allah, the One, the All-Subduing.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the Resurrection’s utterly transformative and decisive hour: the present created order will be replaced or radically altered, and every creature will be made to stand forth before God. It stresses two truths — first, the radical renewal of creation to receive final judgment (the existing earth and skies will not remain as they are), and second, the absolute sovereignty of God as the singular, overpowering Lord before whom all are helpless. The image is meant to humble human pride, to warn that worldly certainties will be overturned, and to affirm that ultimate power and judgment belong solely to Allah, the One who subdues all things.

translation: And you will see the criminals that Day, bound together in fetters.
interpretation: The verse portrays the scene of the Day of Judgment where wrongdoers are rendered powerless and publicly exposed: they will be physically restrained in chains as a manifestation of divine justice, humiliation, and incapacity to escape. Being “linked together” (مقرنين) indicates that their corrupt alliances, mutual encouragement in sin, or collective deeds now bind them together in consequence, showing that worldly partnerships that served injustice offer no protection before God.

translation: Their garments will be of tar, and the Fire will cover their faces.
interpretation: The verse uses the stark images of tar and a fire that covers faces to convey the inward reality of divine retribution: tar—black, adhesive, suffocating—symbolizes how sinful choices cling to and constrict the wrongdoer, intensifying their pain and cutting them off from relief, while the fire over the face signifies utter humiliation, the loss of honor and light (inability to behold guidance), and an overwhelming, inescapable suffering that corresponds to and is sealed by their own actions.

translation:
ليجزي الله كل نفس ما كسبت ۚ إن الله سريع الحساب
"So that Allah may recompense every soul for what it has earned. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning."
interpretation: The verse asserts the certainty and precision of divine justice: every individual’s actions are observed and will be requited by God in exact measure. Describing God as “swift in reckoning” underscores that moral consequences are real and will be brought to account without undue delay or omission, thereby imposing serious responsibility on one’s choices and deterring negligence or injustice.

translation: This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned thereby, and that they may know that He is but one God, and that those endowed with understanding may take heed.
interpretation: The verse presents the revelation as a universal proclamation meant to provoke inner change: its warnings aim to awaken moral responsibility, its declaration of God’s oneness confronts divided loyalties and false securities, and its true audience are those who use reason and self-reflection. Guidance therefore requires both the clear call of revelation and the willing, thoughtful response of hearts that ponder, recognize, and act upon the truth.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Alif, Lam, Ra. Those are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.
interpretation: The opening invocation frames the revelation as rooted in divine mercy; the disjointed letters (Alif‑Lam‑Ra) point to the Qur’an’s miraculous, divine origin and call attention to what follows. Calling the statements 'the verses of the Book' and 'a clear Qur’an' affirms that the scripture provides explicit, decisive guidance and signs — both linguistic and real‑world proofs — intended to distinguish truth from falsehood, confirm prophetic authority, and lead sincere hearers to reflection and submission.

translation:
ربما يود الذين كفروا لو كانوا مسلمين
"It may be that those who disbelieve wish that they had been Muslims."
interpretation: The verse warns that at the moment of confronting reality—death, judgment, or clear evidence of the truth—those who rejected faith will long to have submitted to God. That belated desire, however, cannot erase the moral consequences of the choices they made; genuine submission must be embraced sincerely and in time, not as a late wish born of regret. The verse therefore urges prompt, wholehearted acceptance of faith rather than postponement or obstinacy.

translation: Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let false hope distract them — soon they will come to know.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet (and by extension the believers) to refrain from being consumed by attempts to force the recalcitrant to accept the truth; God allows them to pursue worldly pleasures and be deluded by vain expectations for a time. Their present ease and hopes are temporary distractions that conceal the inevitable reality: in due course they will be made to see the outcome of their choice — the truth of God’s message and the consequences of rejecting it — so the proper response is patient trust in God’s timing rather than anxious intervention.

translation: And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree (a written record).
interpretation: The verse teaches that the downfall of any community is neither arbitrary nor sudden but occurs according to God’s predetermined, recorded decree; destructions are the realization of a just, purposeful plan tied to peoples’ conduct, serving both as evidence of divine justice and as a warning to those who persist in wrongdoing.

translation: No nation can bring forward its appointed term, nor can they delay it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the span and appointed end of every people are fixed by God’s decree; no human power or collective effort can hasten or postpone the moment God has set. It teaches that history and the fate of communities are governed by divine timing, warning against arrogance, false security, or attempts to evade accountability, and urging people to recognize their limits, act righteously, and use the time granted to them responsibly.

translation:
وَقَالُوا يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِي نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ الذِّكْرُ إِنَّكَ لَمَجْنُونٌ
"And they said, 'O you upon whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad.'"
interpretation: This verse presents the reaction of opponents who, unable or unwilling to engage with the truth of the divine message, attack the character of its bearer by calling him insane; it reflects a common strategy of denial—delegitimizing the messenger to dismiss the message—revealing not the weakness of the revelation but the psychological and social resistance of those who refuse to accept its guidance.

translation: If you were to bring the angels to us, we would not believe you — even if you were among the truthful.
interpretation: This statement expresses the stubborn refusal of some people to accept Divine guidance: they demand a spectacular sign yet would reject it even if shown. It points to hypocrisy and closed-heartedness — their unbelief is not cured by external proofs because acceptance requires inner readiness and sincere submission, not merely visible miracles or verbal assertions of truth.

translation: We send down the angels only with the truth, and they are never made to wait.
interpretation: The verse asserts that God dispatches angels solely to fulfill true, decisive divine purposes (e.g., revelation, judgment, succor), and when He sends them they execute His command promptly and without delay—teaching that angelic intervention occurs according to God’s wise timing and is not subject to human whims or procrastination.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will surely preserve it.
interpretation: The verse expresses God’s assurance that the Qur’an will be divinely protected from distortion, loss, or corruption—a promise that secures its authentic wording and enduring authority (understood traditionally as preservation both on the Preserved Tablet and through trustworthy transmission), so that its guidance remains intact and reliable for all generations.

translation:
وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا مِن قَبْلِكَ فِي شِيَعِ الْأَوَّلِينَ
“And truly We sent before you to groups of former peoples [messengers].”
interpretation: The verse places the Prophet’s mission within an ongoing divine pattern: God has repeatedly dispatched guidance to past communities, so this message is neither unprecedented nor isolated. Its purpose is to establish prophetic legitimacy, to counter claims of novelty or singularity, and to prompt the audience to learn from history—recognizing that denying revealed guidance has been the path to moral and communal ruin in earlier peoples, and therefore to respond with humility and obedience rather than repetition of their errors.

translation: And no messenger comes to them except that they ridicule him.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurrent social and spiritual pattern: communities that are attached to their own interests and pride reflexively dismiss and mock divine guidance rather than engage with its truth. Mockery here functions as a defensive tool—an attempt to preserve reputation, power, or ease by reducing a prophetic warning to a joke—revealing moral blindness and obstinacy. The passage therefore warns that habitual scorn toward a messenger is not mere speech but a symptom of deeper rejection that prevents sincere reflection and ultimately brings spiritual and communal ruin.

translation: Thus We insert it into the hearts of the criminals.
interpretation: It signifies that God allows or ordains a harmful disposition—a hardness, delusion, or disease of the heart—to take root in the hearts of wrongdoers, making them resistant to guidance and further entrenching them in their evil as a just consequence of their choices.

translation: They do not believe in it, while the precedent (sunnah) of the former peoples has already passed.
interpretation: The verse points out that those who reject the revelation are merely repeating a long-standing human pattern: despite clear warnings and the historical record of earlier communities who denied their messengers and suffered the consequences, they persist in unbelief. The phrase "sunnah al-awwalin" refers to God’s established way of dealing with persistent rejection — a consistent divine procedure shown in history — so their denial is neither new nor excusable, and they are subject to the same moral and eschatological implications as those who came before them.

translation: And if We were to open for them a gate in the heaven and they continued to ascend through it,
interpretation: The verse teaches that stubborn rejection of truth is rooted in a closed heart: even if God were to show the most extraordinary, unmistakable sign (a gate opened in the heavens and their ascent through it), those determined to deny or arrogantly reject guidance would remain unconvinced, demonstrating that true acceptance depends on inner receptivity and divine guidance rather than merely on witnessing miracles.

translation: They will say, "Our eyes were only made dim; rather, we are a people bewitched."
interpretation: The verse exposes a defensive excuse of the rejecters: faced with undeniable truth, they shift blame onto an external cause (darkened sight or bewitchment) to avoid admitting their own willful rejection. Spiritually, this language points to self-inflicted moral and intellectual blindness—choices and habits that closed their hearts and eyes—yet they portray it as something done to them. The statement therefore reveals both their attempt to escape responsibility and the inward consequence of persistent denial: a state in which one can no longer recognize truth and prefers to call that inability a supernatural affliction rather than own it as the fruit of one’s own refusal.

translation: And indeed We have placed in the heaven constellations and adorned it for the beholders.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God arranged the heavens with stars and constellations as a deliberate manifestation of His power and order. Their placement both beautifies the sky and functions as clear signs for people to observe—inviting reflection, guiding practical needs (like navigation and timekeeping), and prompting recognition of the Creator’s wisdom and sovereignty, thereby fostering faith and humility.

translation: And We have preserved it from every accursed devil.
interpretation: This asserts a divine guarantee of the Qur’an’s integrity: Allah prevented any satanic interference in its revelation and transmission so that its wording and guidance remain pure and trustworthy. The statement underwrites the Qur’an’s authoritative status as an uncorrupted criterion for belief and practice, assuring believers that its message has been safeguarded from distortion, interpolation, or misleading influence.

translation: Except him who steals away a hearing, so he is pursued by a clear flaming meteor.
interpretation: This refers to rebellious jinn or devils who try to eavesdrop on the heavenly assembly to learn of the unseen; when they attempt to 'steal' a hearing they are driven off by a manifest, blazing shihāb, which signifies God’s protection of divine revelation and the prevention of corrupt beings gaining access to celestial knowledge.

translation:
والأرض مددناها وألقينا فيها رواسي وأنبتنا فيها من كل شيء موزون
"And the earth — We have spread it out, and cast into it firm mountains, and caused to grow therein of every (kind) a measured thing."
interpretation: The verse affirms that God intentionally fashioned and ordered the earth: He extended its surface for habitation, set mountains that stabilize and shape it, and brought forth a balanced, measured diversity of life. This measured harmony in physical structure and living variety points to Divine wisdom and provision, showing that creation is purposeful, sustaining, and meant to be recognized and responsibly maintained by humanity.

translation: And We have made for you therein means of livelihood, and you are not their providers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that sustenance and the resources people use are ultimately granted and sustained by God; human effort may be the immediate means, but humans are not the ultimate givers. This reality calls for humility, trust in God, gratitude for His provision, and responsible use of the means bestowed rather than pride in self-sufficiency.

translation: And there is not a thing but with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every resource, capacity, or provision ultimately belongs to God's custody and is dispensed by Him according to deliberate measure and wisdom. Nothing is distributed randomly or beyond His knowledge; what reaches creation—whether sustenance, natural phenomena, opportunities, or favors—is given in the amount and timing He has ordained. The practical implication is to place trust in divine providence, recognize that apparent scarcity or abundance is part of a wise allocation, and maintain moral responsibility in how one seeks, uses, and shares what is received.

translation: And We sent the winds as fertilizing agents, then We sent down water from the sky and gave it to you to drink — yet you are not its keepers.
interpretation: The verse underscores God's sovereign provision through the natural order: winds play a role in fertilization and in the formation and movement of clouds, and rain is sent down by God to sustain life. By stating that people are not the keepers of that water, the verse teaches humility and dependence — human beings benefit from and must responsibly use Divine provision but have no ultimate control or ownership over the forces and resources that sustain them. It calls for gratitude, trust in God’s wisdom, and warns against arrogance or claiming mastery over what is by God’s ordinance.

translation: And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritors.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over existence: He alone bestows life and appoints death, and when beings perish everything they possessed reverts to Him — He is the ultimate inheritor of creation. It reminds that human life and possessions are transient, that control over beginning and end rests with God, and points forward to His power to restore life (resurrection) and to take up what remains when creatures pass away.

translation: And We certainly know those of you who are foremost, and We certainly know the ones who are left behind.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s exhaustive, precise knowledge of people’s spiritual posture and timing: He perceives who eagerly presses forward in faith and righteous action and who lingers behind. This distinction is not merely observational but bears moral and eschatological consequence—ranks and recompense will reflect whether one was among the forerunners or the latecomers. Thus the passage both comforts that no effort is unseen and admonishes to strive to be among the foremost, for God’s judgment will take into account not only deeds but the heart’s urgency and commitment.

translation: And indeed your Lord—He it is Who will gather them; truly He is Wise, All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate assembly and accounting of people is solely under God's governance; His attributes of Wisdom and Knowledge mean that the timing, manner, and measures of that gathering are purposeful and perfectly just, with every intention and circumstance fully known and accordingly judged — so reliance on His providence and trust in the rectitude of His final adjudication are required.

translation: And indeed We created man from sounding clay, from black, molded mud.
interpretation: The verse affirms that human beings were brought into existence out of lowly, earthly substances — the dry, ringing clay (صلصال) and the dark, malleable mud (حمإ مسنون) — to stress both our humble origin and God’s deliberate craftsmanship. The specific words convey contrast and care: the “sounding” clay points to a solid, formed substance while the “molded” mud indicates a worked, shaped material, underscoring that humanity was purposefully fashioned rather than arising by chance. From this follows a moral and spiritual lesson: our dignity does not come from an exalted material origin but from God’s intentional act of creation and from the responsibilities and capacities He gave us; therefore humans should respond with humility, gratitude, and accountable conduct toward their Creator.

translation: And the jinn — We created them before from a smokeless flame of fire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the jinn are a pre‑human creation made of a different, subtle element (a smokeless, intense fire), which explains their unseen, luminous and mobile nature; yet despite this different origin they share with humans the gift of moral choice and will be judged for their responses to God's guidance, so their fiery origin denotes a distinct ontological species and capacities, not exemption from responsibility.

translation: And when your Lord said to the angels, "I will create a human being from clay, from sounding clay, from moulded mud."
interpretation: The phrase stresses that human existence is a deliberate, measured act of divine workmanship: though fashioned from humble, inert material, the descriptors (“salsal,” “ham’ masnūn”) point to careful shaping and order. The verse therefore highlights a moral and ontological lesson — human dignity and responsibility do not derive from lofty material origin but from God’s intentional creation and the faculties and duties He confers, making humanity both humble in origin and accountable in purpose.

translation: When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit, then fall down to him in prostration.
interpretation: God’s command that the angels prostrate to Adam signifies the unique dignity and entrusted role given to human beings through the divine “breath” — a bestowal of life, consciousness and moral responsibility. The prostration is an act of honor and recognition of that God‑given capacity (not an act of worship to Adam), intended to show that humanity’s worth comes from God’s gift and to mark humans as bearers of knowledge and accountability before God.

translation:
فَسَجَدَ الْمَلَائِكَةُ كُلُّهُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ
"So all the angels prostrated, every one of them."
interpretation: The phrase emphasizes the angels’ complete, unanimous and immediate obedience to God’s command; their prostration symbolizes humble submission to divine will and recognition of the honoured status God willed to confer, offering a paradigm of humility and acceptance of God’s decree in contrast to prideful refusal.

translation: Except Iblis refused to be among those who prostrated.
interpretation: The verse uses Iblis’s refusal as a moral exemplar: pride and unwillingness to humble oneself before God’s command (symbolized by prostration) lead to spiritual ruin and exile from divine favor. It teaches that true righteousness requires submission and humility, while self-exaltation breeds rebellion and enmity toward guidance.

translation: He said, “O Iblis, what prevented you from being among those who prostrate?”
interpretation: The divine question exposes Iblis’s refusal as a deliberate, pride-driven choice rather than mere error; by asking why he did not join the prostrators, the verse spotlights arrogance and disobedience as fundamental moral failings and warns that rejecting God’s command from exalted self-regard leads to exclusion from rightful submission and spiritual ruin.

translation: He said, “I would never prostrate to a human whom You created from sounding clay, from dark, altered mud.”
interpretation: The utterance reveals Iblis’s arrogant rationale for disobedience: he judges worth by physical origin and claims superiority, using that supposed superiority to refuse God’s command. The verse thus exposes how pride and a false hierarchy (valuing one’s substance over obedience) corrupt moral judgment and lead to rebellion, teaching that spiritual worth before God is not determined by material composition but by submission and humility.

translation: قال: "فَاخْرُجْ مِنْهَا فَإِنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ" — He said, “Get out of it; indeed you are accursed.”
interpretation: The phrase signals a definitive divine condemnation: because of arrogant disobedience the being is expelled from God’s presence and labeled 'rajīm'—rejected, cast out and deprived of divine favor. 'Rajīm' thus denotes not merely physical removal but an ontological loss of status and protection, a permanent severing that justifies his subsequent enmity and role as a corrupter.

translation: And indeed the curse is upon you until the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: The verse pronounces that the addressee has incurred a divinely decreed curse that endures up to the final reckoning; it signifies irrevocable divine disapproval for persistent wrongdoing or rejection, marking the person as deprived of God's favor in this life and subject to adverse judgment and consequences at the Day of Resurrection.

translation: He said, “My Lord, then let me see the Day on which they will be resurrected.”
interpretation: Uttered at the point of death, this plea exposes a last‑minute yearning for certainty and a desire to witness divine justice. It often reflects not true repentance but the human temptation to postpone accountability until one can see the outcome; the verse thus teaches that the Hour is fixed and cannot be summoned on demand, and that genuine readiness consists in sincere belief and righteous action before that moment arrives rather than demanding proof at death.

translation: قَالَ فَإِنَّكَ مِنَ الْمُنْظَرِينَ — He said, “Then indeed you are among those who are given respite.”
interpretation: To be called one of the munẓarīn means being accorded a postponement of immediate punishment — a temporary reprieve until an appointed time. This delay is not forgiveness but part of God’s wisdom: it allows His plan to unfold (testing people, giving opportunity for repentance, or completing decreed consequences) while reserving final judgment for the set hour.

translation: Until the Day of the appointed time.
interpretation: This phrase points to the fixed, divinely appointed Day of Reckoning known only to God; it reminds believers that ultimate judgment and the settlement of all affairs are certain and set by God's wisdom, calling for patience, trust in His timing, and continued righteous conduct while awaiting that inevitable hour.

translation: قَالَ: «رَبِّ، بِمَا أَغْوَيْتَنِي لَأُزَيِّنَنَّ لَهُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَأُغْوِيَنَّهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ» — "He said, ‘My Lord, because You have caused me to go astray, I will surely make [evil] appear attractive to them on earth, and I will mislead them all.’"
interpretation: The utterance displays Iblis’s conscious strategy and arrogance: he intends to corrupt by beautifying wrongdoing and by systematic deception so that people are drawn away from uprightness. It teaches that temptation typically works through attraction and allure—presenting what is harmful as desirable—and therefore faith requires discernment, vigilance, and reliance on God; it also shows that such corruption operates within a divine permission that serves as a trial separating sincere obedience from yielding to seduction.

translation: Except Your servants among them — the sincere.
interpretation: This phrase signals that, within a broader group facing a general rule or punishment, God makes an exception for those who are truly devoted to Him. Their inner sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and exclusive devotion distinguish them from others and secure divine protection or exemption; the clause emphasizes that God’s judgment attends to the state of the heart and honors genuine, selfless worship by sparing and favoring the faithful.

translation: He said, “This is a straight path for me.”
interpretation: The speaker affirms that the way shown is the correct, divinely guided course he must follow and uphold. The phrase “for me” indicates a personal responsibility and commitment to walk and embody that path, while “straight” signals moral and spiritual rectitude—clarity between right and wrong, freedom from deviation or extremes, and a balanced, purposeful conduct that leads to true guidance and success.

translation: “Indeed, My servants — you shall have no authority over them, except those among the astray who follow you.”
interpretation: God is asserting that Satan’s power is not absolute but contingent on human choice: he cannot dominate the faithful whom God protects, and only those who willingly pursue error and heed his whispers—the 'ghaawin'—place themselves under his influence. The statement both reassures believers of divine safeguarding and assigns responsibility to individuals, showing that yielding to temptation, not an irresistible external force, is what grants the tempter authority.

translation:
وَإِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمَوْعِدُهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ
"And indeed Hell is surely their appointed place — all of them."
interpretation: The verse affirms that for those described (the condemned), Hell is their predetermined and unavoidable abode; the phrase “all of them” stresses the completeness and certainty of this fate for that group, underscoring divine justice and the inevitability of recompense for persistent rejection of guidance.

translation: It has seven gates; for each gate there is a distinct, apportioned group.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the punishment in Hell is arranged with precise order and proportion: there are seven entrances, each reserved for a particular class of wrongdoers, so that people are assigned to a gate according to the nature and measure of their deeds, underscoring divine justice and the fitting, measured recompense for actions.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs.
interpretation: The verse promises that those who feared God and lived in obedience and moral restraint (al-muttaqīn) will be granted the tranquil, abundant rewards of Paradise — pictured as shady gardens and flowing springs. This imagery conveys both spiritual repose and bodily delight: their lives in the hereafter will be free from want, anxiety and sin, sustained by pure, life-giving blessings that reflect God’s mercy and the lasting consequences of piety.

translation: Enter it in peace, safe and secure.
interpretation: This phrase is a divine assurance and promise of final deliverance: those who have fulfilled God’s guidance are told they will be admitted into their ultimate abode with complete safety — freed from fear, grief, and punishment — experiencing perfect tranquility and certainty of God’s mercy. The words express both the external security of being preserved from harm and the inner peace of certainty and contentment, affirming that the culmination of the believer’s struggle is restful, protected fellowship with God and the fulfilment of His promise.

translation: And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts — [they will be] brothers, seated on couches facing one another.
interpretation: The verse conveys that God will cleanse the hearts of the faithful from all resentment and envy so that in the life to come their relationships will be purified and restored. The image of ‘brothers on facing couches’ signifies intimate, equal, and peaceful companionship: inward hostility is eradicated by Divine mercy, leaving sincere affection, mutual accord, and tranquil social intercourse among the believers in Paradise.

translation: No fatigue will touch them there, nor will they be expelled from it.
interpretation: The verse affirms the certainty and permanence of the believers’ reward in Paradise: its inhabitants will experience no weariness or distress from the pleasures they enjoy, and they face no possibility of being driven out or losing that abode—their comfort is continual, free from toil and fear of expulsion.

translation: Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: God commands that His servants be told that His primary disposition toward them is forgiveness and mercy: this reassures those who have erred that sincere repentance will meet with pardon, it encourages hope rather than despair, and it shapes the believer’s relationship with God as one in which mercy is the norm—calling people to return, reform, and trust in God’s compassionate forgiveness while still striving for righteousness.

translation: And that My punishment is indeed the painful punishment.
interpretation: This declares that God’s retribution for persistent rejection and transgression is real, severe, and certain; it is meant to uphold divine justice, to deter entrenched wrongdoing, and to urge people toward repentance and reform before they meet that painful consequence.

translation: And inform them about the guest of Abraham.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to recount the episode of Abraham’s visitors (the divinely sent guests) as a demonstrative proof: Abraham’s immediate hospitality, his recognition of their divine mission, and the outcome of that encounter are presented to contrast true faith with rejection, to validate prophetic revelation, and to warn that acceptance of God’s messengers brings guidance while persistent denial brings consequence.

translation: إذ دخلوا عليه فقالوا: «سلامٌ». قال: «إِنَّا مِنْكُمْ وَجِلُونَ»
interpretation: When strangers enter someone's presence and offer the customary greeting of peace, the one addressed replies by confessing his own timidity and belonging to them — a humble, vulnerable response that acknowledges human fear and dependence. The verse teaches that people may honestly show fear and modesty before others (especially when they feel exposed or powerless), and that such humility is a truthful stance that can temper interactions and elicit mercy rather than arrogance or false confidence.

translation: They said, “Do not be afraid; indeed We give you glad tidings of a knowledgeable/wise boy.”
interpretation: The statement reassures that what seems impossible can be brought about by God and that the promised son will possess divinely granted understanding and wisdom. The term “عَلِيم” here denotes more than ordinary learning—it signals a gift of insight, sound judgment, and guidance from God that equips the child for a special, God‑ordained role and protects him from the ignorance and weakness of ordinary human life.

translation: قَالَ أَبَشَّرْتُمُونِي عَلَىٰ أَن مَسَّنِيَ الْكِبَرُ ۖ فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ
interpretation: الآية تصور ردة فعل إبراهيم عليه السلام على تبشير الملائكة بولادة ولد له وهو في سنٍ متقدم، وتدل ظرفيًا على عقلانية النبي: إنه لا يقبل البشارة بلا تدبر، بل يستعلم عن أسسها، وفي الوقت نفسه تؤكد مبدأً إيمانيًا أعمق — أن ما يبدو بعين البشر مستحيلاً أو غير متناسق مع القوانين الطبيعية ليس مقيدًا بقدرة الله، وأن التسليم للتقدير الإلهي يجتمع مع سؤال رشيد وطلب بيان من المؤمن، لا مع قبول أعمى.

translation: قالوا: "بشّرناك بالحق، فلا تكن من القانطين"
interpretation: القول يطمئن المتلقي أن البشارة ليست مجرد كلام بل حقُ مؤكد، ويأمر بالابتعاد عن اليأس: لأن اليأس ينافي الإيمان والثقة بوعود الله والرحمة، فالمطلوب الثبات والصبر والرجاء في تحقق ما بشر به الحق رغم الشدائد.

translation: He said, “And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the truly lost?”
interpretation: This verse teaches that despairing of God’s mercy is itself a mark of being misguided: true faith balances fear of sin with confident hope in God's forgiveness, while complete despair—abandoning hope in mercy—reflects a hardened, erring heart that has cut itself off from repentance; only those who are spiritually lost would deny the vastness of Divine mercy.

translation: قال: "فَما خَطْبُكُم أَيُّهَا الْمُرْسَلُونَ" — "He said, 'So what is the matter with you, O messengers?'''
interpretation: A sharp rebuke directed at those entrusted with a mission: it confronts their unexpected hesitation, confusion, or failure and demands explanation for their lapse. The verse highlights accountability for those sent to convey a message or carry out duties, insisting that responsibility requires clarity, resolve, and action rather than silence or dereliction.

translation: They said, “Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals.”
interpretation: This statement identifies the addressees as morally and spiritually culpable: the messengers declare their mission is to a community entrenched in unjust, sinful conduct and in rejection of divine guidance. Calling them "mujrimīn" emphasizes that their behavior is not merely mistaken but culpable, justifying urgent warning, summons to repentance, and — if they persist — the prospect of lawful divine consequence; it highlights the responsibility of people to respond to clear guidance and the legitimacy of prophetic admonition toward those who persist in wrongdoing.

translation:
إلا آل لوط إنا لمنجوهم أجمعين
"Except the family of Lot — indeed We will save them all."
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that God's judgment is precise and His mercy discriminating: when a community is punished for its corruption, He can and does rescue the righteous within it (as He did for Lot’s household). Salvation is thus presented as a divine decree granted to those who are saved by faith and obedience, not as automatic protection for an entire people.

translation: “Except his wife — We had ordained [it]; indeed she is of the erring.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the woman’s role in the incident was not merely incidental but unfolded within God’s measure so that her true moral state would be exposed: her uncontrolled passion, insistence and subsequent wrongdoing mark her among those who go astray. It emphasizes both divine knowledge and human responsibility — God allows circumstances to bring inner dispositions to light, and those who yield to desire and falsehood become culpable and lose their right standing.

translation: So when the messengers came to the people of Lot…
interpretation: The phrase marks a decisive moment of divine outreach: God sent His messengers as a final warning and summons to repentance, making the community morally accountable—acceptance would bring mercy, persistent rejection would bring judgment; it exemplifies the prophetic pattern that a people’s response to clear guidance determines their fate.

translation: قال: "إنكم قوم منكرون" — He said, "Indeed, you are a people who deny (the truth)."
interpretation: This is a categorical rebuke that characterizes the addressed as people whose defining posture is willful rejection of evident guidance; it diagnoses a hardened, obstinate disposition rather than mere occasional doubt, serves to expose their moral responsibility for denial, and functions rhetorically to warn them of the consequences and to justify the speaker’s rejection or admonition.

translation: They will say, “Nay — we have brought you what they were doubting about.”
interpretation: On the Day of Reckoning the wrongdoers will defiantly claim that the very reality people once disputed has now been presented to them; their words attempt to shift responsibility and to boast that the consequences and proofs they once scoffed at have come to pass, thereby exposing their prior doubt and hypocrisy while vainly trying to justify themselves.

translation: And We have brought you the truth, and indeed We are truthful.
interpretation: God is affirming that the revelation given to the Prophet is genuine and authoritative, assuring that its content is from a truthful, trustworthy Source whose promises and warnings will not fail — therefore the message must be accepted and relied upon, and the Prophet’s claim of conveying divine guidance is vindicated.

translation:
فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ وَاتَّبِعْ أَدْبَارَهُمْ وَلَا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنكُمْ أَحَدٌ ۚ وَامْضُوا حَيْثُ تُؤْمَرُونَ
“So secretly take your family during part of the night, follow their tracks, let none of you look back, and go where you are commanded.”
interpretation: The verse commands a prudent, disciplined withdrawal from danger: leave covertly in stages at night to avoid detection, follow the safe route others have taken so as not to stumble or be exposed, and forbid any backward glance that would reveal hesitation, attachment, or risk the group’s safety. At a deeper level it teaches decisive trust in God and in appointed guidance—putting the protection of family and community above sentimental ties to a place, obeying the plan given, and avoiding the fatal paralysis that comes from looking back.

translation: And We decreed concerning that matter to him: that the end of these people be cut off by morning.
interpretation: The verse declares a divine decision that the posterior outcome — the descendants, power and future prospects — of those wrongdoers will be completely severed and brought to nothing by dawn. “Dārِبُ” here denotes what comes after (lineage, aftermath, or lasting influence), and “مقطوع مصبحين” stresses both totality and suddenness: their legacy and strength will be decisively terminated as morning breaks, signifying swift, irrevocable divine judgment rather than a gradual decline.

translation: And the people of Medina came, rejoicing.
interpretation: The phrase depicts the believers of Medina entering with hopeful gladness—an emotional and spiritual response rooted in trust in God and solidarity with the Prophet. Their rejoicing reflects how divine reassurance and communal unity replace fear with confident expectation, motivating them to support the mission and accept whatever outcome with joyful submission.

translation: قال: «إنَّ هؤلاء ضيفي، فلا تفضحون»
interpretation: المراد أن المتكلم يعلن أن هؤلاء الأشخاص تحت كفالته وضمانه، فيطلب من الحاضرين أن يحفظوا لهم كرامتهم ولا يكشفوا عوراتهم ولا يفضحوهم؛ تأكيد على حرمة الضيافة ووجوب حماية أهل البيت والضيوف من السخرية والإهانة أو الكشف الذي يجرح شرفهم.

translation: Fear Allah, and do not be put to shame.
interpretation: The verse instructs that cultivating taqwa — reverent God-consciousness and obedience — protects a person from moral and spiritual disgrace: by fearing Allah one refrains from sinful, dishonorable actions and reliance on vain sources of honor, thereby preserving true dignity in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: قالوا: «أولَمْ نَنْهَكُمْ عَنِ الْعَالَمِينَ» — They said, “Have we not forbidden you regarding the worlds?”
interpretation: The phrase reflects the stance of those who reject the messenger: they speak as if human or tribal prohibitions can silence the call to God. By asking “Have we not forbidden you…,” they assert a self‑made authority to exclude and intimidate, treating guidance as something to be suppressed rather than considered. The verse thus exposes the arrogance and illegitimacy of such objections — it is a rhetorical move by deniers to delegitimise prophetic admonition, demonstrating how people often resort to prohibitions and social pressure to avoid facing moral responsibility. The underlying lesson is that human bans cannot override Divine truth, and that resistance to guidance frequently takes the form of silencing and marginalizing its bearers.

translation: He said, “These are my daughters, if indeed you are going to act.”
interpretation: The speaker points to his daughters and makes the outcome contingent on the listeners’ intention: he is neither imposing nor deciding unilaterally but placing responsibility on others. The phrase ‘إن كنتم فاعلين’ highlights human agency — what will be done regarding his daughters depends on the choice and conduct of those addressed, signaling conditional consent and entrusting them with the moral responsibility for their action.

translation: By your life, indeed they are, in their stupor, groping blindly.
interpretation: The verse, sworn by the Prophet’s life, describes those who are so intoxicated by their worldly pleasures, pride, or heedlessness that they are in a figurative swoon (سكرتهم) and therefore wander (يعمهون) without clear sight or direction. The image conveys moral and spiritual blindness: their inner disorientation prevents them from recognizing guidance and reality, leaving them confused, misled, and unable to find the straight path.

translation: So the single terrifying blast seized them while they were facing the east (toward the rising sun).
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine retribution can come suddenly upon those persisting in misguidance—caught in the very posture of their false devotion (facing the sunrise or idols). It emphasizes the impotence of created things to protect or save, and that relying on rites, directions or false objects of worship cannot avert God’s decree; heedlessness of true guidance can bring abrupt and decisive ruin.

translation: So We made its upper part its lower part, and rained upon them stones of baked clay.
interpretation: The verse conveys that when a community persists in denying God's guidance and transgressing bounds, God can decisively reverse their fortunes — what was lofty is brought low — and execute a clear, tangible punishment. The turning of the high into the low signifies total overthrow and loss of status, while the raining of 'stones of baked clay' (sijjīl) underscores the firmness, inevitability and preordained nature of that judgment, serving as a warning and lesson to others about the consequences of obstinate rejection.

translation: Indeed in that are signs for those who seek to learn.
interpretation: The verse means that the occurrences just mentioned constitute clear evidence for reflective, enquiring people — those who actively look for guidance and draw lessons. “المتوسّمون” are not the heedless but those who scrutinize events and seek tokens of God’s wisdom and truth; for them these signs point decisively to divine power and call them to belief and moral reform.

translation: And indeed it is surely a firm, established path.
interpretation: The pronoun “it” denotes the Divine message just mentioned (the Qur’ān/this judgment); calling it a “sabeel muqīm” affirms that this guidance is steady, enduring and divinely founded—not a transient opinion or vague impulse—but a clear, unshakable way ordained by God for rightly orienting belief and conduct, to be followed as a permanent criterion for life.

translation: Indeed, in that there is surely a sign for the believers.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that the phenomena or events referenced are not mere accidents but intentional manifestations—āyāt—through which God reveals His power, wisdom, mercy and truth. For those who truly believe, these signs call for reflection and remembrance: they confirm Divine attributes, deepen conviction, inspire gratitude and trust, and serve as reasons to live righteously. In short, the verse asserts that believers recognize and are spiritually transformed by such signs, using them as evidence of God’s guidance and as motivation for steadfast faith and obedience.

translation: And indeed the companions of the thicket were surely wrongdoers.
interpretation: This pronouncement classifies the people of al‑Aykah as morally culpable: their persistent rejection of prophetic guidance and their systemic injustices (social, economic and spiritual) amounted to ظلم—wrongdoing against God and fellow humans—and therefore justified divine retribution; the verse warns that communal, entrenched transgression that resists correction leads to accountable consequences.

translation: So We took vengeance on them, and indeed it was a clear and manifest lesson.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s punishment of the wrongdoers was not arbitrary but a deliberate, visible retribution that served as an unmistakable lesson: their fate was the just consequence of their rejection and corruption, made manifest so that others might recognize the truth, heed the warning, and understand the reality of divine justice and accountability.

translation: And indeed the companions of Al-Ḥijr denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse functions as a warning: the denial of God's messengers—born of pride, attachment to familiar customs, and refusal to submit to clear signs—precipitated the downfall of that people. It teaches that rejecting truthful guidance for arrogance or worldly complacency risks divine judgment, while humility and readiness to heed guidance open the way to mercy.

translation: And We gave them Our signs, yet they turned away from them.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that divine guidance—whether through observable signs in creation or revealed verses—can be presented clearly, but acceptance requires an open, humble heart; when people respond with willful turning away (out of pride, heedlessness, or attachment to worldly interests) the evidence no longer benefits them, making their rejection a morally accountable choice that brings spiritual blindness and eventual consequence.

translation: And they would hew out houses from the mountains, secure.
interpretation: The verse highlights both human skill and misplaced confidence: people could cut dwellings into rock and make them appear safe and impregnable, yet this image is used to criticize their complacency and arrogance—relying on material fortifications and feeling immune to harm while ignoring God's guidance; such seeming security ultimately cannot ward off divine decree or moral accountability.

translation: So the blast overtook them at dawn.
interpretation: The verse signifies that divine punishment fell suddenly and decisively at an unexpected moment—while the people were beginning their day—showing that persistent rejection of God's warnings can invite an overwhelming, unavoidable decree; it emphasizes God's absolute authority and the futility of worldly complacency or reliance on routine when faced with divine judgment.

translation: So what they used to earn did not avail them.
interpretation: It declares that the things people accumulated — their wealth, status, or the deeds they took pride in (especially when contrary to God's guidance) — proved useless at the time of reckoning; worldly gains and wrongful achievements cannot avert punishment or secure true success, for ultimate benefit depends on sincere faith and righteous conduct rather than mere accumulation.

translation: And We did not create the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them except in truth; and indeed the Hour is surely coming. So pardon with a beautiful (gracious) pardon.
interpretation: God affirms that the cosmos is created with purpose and reality and that the Day of Reckoning is inevitable; in light of this, believers are urged to exercise noble forbearance — to overlook others’ faults, refrain from vindictive responses, and respond to wrongs with dignified, generous forgiveness — trusting that ultimate judgment belongs to God and that patient, gracious conduct better preserves moral integrity and communal harmony.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the All‑Knowing.
interpretation: This affirms God’s two complementary attributes: as al‑Khallāq He is the unique, ongoing originator who not only brings things into being but fashions them with wisdom and varied forms; as al‑ʿAlīm He knows fully and perfectly—every outward event, inward intention, cause and consequence, seen and unseen. Together these names mean that nothing in existence is accidental or beyond God’s awareness, so human life must be approached with humility, trust in His wisdom, and accountability before His comprehensive knowledge.

translation: And indeed We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur’an.
interpretation: The phrase highlights two complementary gifts given to the Prophet: a concise, central formula of praise and petition (commonly understood as the seven-verse Fātiḥah, repeatedly used in worship) and the expansive, weighty revelation of the Qur’an. Together they show that God provided both an immediate, liturgical guide that orients daily prayer and experience, and a comprehensive scripture that carries authoritative guidance for belief, law, and moral life—underlining the completeness and sufficiency of the divine message entrusted to him.

translation: Do not extend your eyes toward that with which We have granted enjoyment to some of them, nor grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers.
interpretation: The verse warns against covetous longing and sorrow over the fleeting worldly favours granted to others; it teaches emotional restraint and trust in God’s wisdom rather than envy or despair when wrongdoers appear to prosper. At the same time it commands a posture of humility, gentleness and compassion toward fellow believers—'lower your wing' meaning to soften one’s demeanor, protect and console the community, promote unity, and show patient, modest leadership rather than arrogance or resentful attachment to worldly gain.

translation: And say, "Indeed, I am the clear warner."
interpretation: The command is to present the Prophet’s role as openly and unmistakably warning people of the moral and spiritual consequences of rejection; his duty is to convey the truth plainly and warn, not to compel belief, leaving acceptance or rejection as each person’s responsibility.

translation: كَمَا أَنزَلْنَا عَلَى الْمُقَسِّمِينَ — "Just as We revealed to those who divide (share the spoils)."
interpretation: This phrase signals that the ruling being stated follows an established, divinely revealed precedent concerning the allocation of communal gains: God prescribes how shared resources are to be apportioned so that distribution is equitable, prevents concentration of wealth, secures the community’s needs, and is carried out according to divine instruction rather than human caprice.

translation: Those who have made the Qur'ān into fragments (as if something to be chewed and spat out).
interpretation: It describes people who treat the Book with contempt and selectivity—tearing it into pieces by taking whatever fragments suit their desires and discarding the rest, thereby abandoning its comprehensive guidance.

translation: By your Lord, We will surely question them all.
interpretation: A solemn divine oath asserting the certainty of universal accountability on the Day of Judgment: every person — without exception — will be summoned and examined before God about their beliefs, intentions and deeds; the statement functions as a warning to uproot complacency and to instill moral responsibility, since nothing will remain hidden or unaccounted for.

translation: concerning what they used to do
interpretation: The phrase emphasizes that people’s actions are noted and will be brought to account before God: nothing done—openly or secretly—escapes divine knowledge, so individuals are morally responsible for their past deeds and will face the consequences.

translation: Proclaim openly what you are commanded, and turn away from the polytheists.
interpretation: A directive to proclaim God’s message clearly and courageously without diluting it to win over opponents, while withdrawing from futile engagement with persistent rejecters—prioritizing faithful delivery and trust in God over seeking the approval or entanglement with those who deny the truth.

translation: Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers.
interpretation: God reassures the Prophet that He Himself is enough to counter those who mock him: their scorn will not undermine the Prophet or the mission because God will protect, uphold, and ultimately vindicate him—rendering their ridicule powerless either by preventing harm, turning hearts away from mockery, or dispensing justice and support in God’s wisdom.

translation: Those who set up with Allah another god—soon they will know.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those who commit shirk (ascribing partners to God) will inevitably be made aware of the truth: the impotence of the idols or partners they trusted and the sole sovereignty of Allah. The phrase “فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ” conveys certainty and impending reckoning—either by experiencing the consequences (punishment or loss) or by being confronted with unmistakable evidence—so that their error is exposed and they must answer for it.

translation: And indeed We know that your breast is constricted by what they say.
interpretation: This statement is a divine assurance that Allah is intimately aware of the Prophet’s inner anguish caused by the mockery, rejection, and accusations of people. Its purpose is both consolatory and normative: it legitimizes the Prophet’s natural emotional pain while reminding him that such feeling is seen by God and will be met with His support and justice. In practical terms it calls for steadfast patience and trust in God’s awareness and timing, not despair or retaliation, because the hurt is acknowledged and will be compensated or redressed by divine wisdom.

translation: So glorify the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate.
interpretation: The verse urges that true devotion combines verbal glorification of God with humble bodily submission: praise should be expressed not only in words but concretely by joining the worshippers in prostration. Together, tasbih (glorifying God) and sajdah (prostration) shape a believer’s life—cultivating humility, obedience, and closeness to the Lord rather than mere lip service.

translation: Worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.
interpretation: An exhortation to unremitting, lifelong devotion: sustain sincere worship, obedience, and righteous conduct continuously until “al‑yaqīn” — understood by the classical commentators as the inevitable certainty of death — arrives. Worship here is comprehensive (rituals, remembrance, ethical behavior, patience in trials) and must not be abandoned once faith is established or after past deeds; the believer is urged to persevere in spiritual growth so as to meet death in a state of servitude to God.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The command of Allah has come; so do not hasten it. Exalted is He and far above what they associate [with Him].
interpretation: The verse declares that Allah’s decree — the fulfillment of His promise or the execution of His judgment — is set and will occur according to His wisdom, so people should not try to force, demand, or accelerate what God has appointed. It rebukes human impatience and the expectation that signs or outcomes must be produced on human terms, while affirming God’s transcendence over any partners or misconceptions people attach to Him; thus trust in divine timing and submission to His sovereign plan are required rather than urging or disputing it.

translation: He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants, [saying], “Warn that there is no deity except Me, so fear Me.”
interpretation: God, by His sovereign will, dispatches heavenly messengers—notably the Spirit (Gabriel)—to chosen servants to convey His revelation and warning. The verse teaches that guidance and admonition originate from God, are delivered through angelic intermediaries to His appointed servants (prophets or inspired people), and center on the fundamental call to pure monotheism and God‑consciousness: acknowledge that there is no deity but God and live in reverent awareness of Him.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth; exalted is He above what they associate (with Him).
interpretation: The statement affirms that creation was done deliberately, with measure, wisdom and purpose (بالحق), so it points to a single, sovereign originator whose action alone warrants ultimate authority. By adding that He is ‘exalted above what they associate,’ the verse rejects attributing partners or divine status to anything in creation: those supposed partners are part of the created order and lack the sovereignty, knowledge and power that belong to the Creator, so worship and obedience rightly belong to Him alone.

translation: He created man from a drop (of fluid), and then behold — he becomes an open, manifest disputant.
interpretation: The verse points to the contrast between man's humble origin and his later attitude: though fashioned from a mere drop, people become bold in disputing and rejecting divine guidance and favours. It is a rebuke of human arrogance and ingratitude — a reminder that our beginnings should temper our presumptuousness when we argue against clear signs and truth.

translation: And the cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and (many) benefits, and from them you eat.
interpretation: The verse prompts recognition that material provisions are intentional signs of divine care and therefore come with ethical expectations: humans must respond with gratitude, use what is given responsibly (avoiding waste and cruelty), and share resources justly. It frames human dominion as stewardship rather than absolute ownership, directing reflection on God’s wisdom in creation and shaping personal and social conduct around mercy, moderation, and thankfulness.

translation:
وَلَكُمْ فِيهَا جِمَالٌ حِينَ تُرِيحُونَ وَحِينَ تُسَرِّحُونَ
“And for you in them are fine camels (beauties) — when you make them rest and when you drive them forth.”
interpretation: The verse points to God’s gifts that combine usefulness and beauty in ordinary life: animals (here rendered as camels) are not only means of work and transport but also objects of aesthetic pleasure in both repose and motion.
