This dual character is a sign to be recognized — prompting gratitude, mindful stewardship, and an awareness that divine provision pervades both our labor and our leisure rather than being confined to lofty or exclusively religious moments.

translation:
وَتُحْمَلُ أَثْقَالُكُمْ إِلَى بَلَدٍ لَمْ تَكُونُوا بَالِغِيهِ إِلَّا بِشَقِّ الأَنْفُسِ ۚ إِنَّ رَبَّكُمْ لَرَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ
"And your burdens will be carried to a land which you would not have reached except with the greatest difficulty. Indeed, your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful."
interpretation: The verse reassures that what lies beyond human capacity—the final good, relief, or attainment—is made possible by God's mercy: He bears or eases the heavy loads of His servants and conveys them to a place or state they could not have reached by ease alone. Thus divine compassion transforms unbearable struggle into achievable hope, promising that God will not abandon people to their burdens but will facilitate and recompense their striving with gentle care and mercy.

translation: And (He created) horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride and as an adornment; and He creates what you do not know.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God has provided visible, practical blessings—beasts for transport, labor and beauty—while also reminding us that His creative power and wisdom extend beyond what we perceive. “He creates what you do not know” calls for humility: many purposes, benefits, laws and creatures remain hidden from human understanding, and God’s provision and design may include uses and realities that will only be discovered later. The passage invites trust in divine wisdom, reflection on the limits of human knowledge, and gratefulness for both the manifest and the unseen bounty of creation.

translation: And with Allah is the straight course, and from it there is deviation. And if He had willed, He would have guided you all.
interpretation: This verse teaches that ultimate guidance and misguidance rest with God: He has established a clear, upright way, yet some turn away from it. That He could have guided everyone but did not highlights divine sovereignty and wisdom — guidance is a bestowed mercy given according to God’s will and in harmony with human receptivity and responsibility; people are therefore accountable to seek and adhere to the straight path, while recognizing that success in guidance is ultimately a gift from God.

translation: He is the One who sends down water from the sky; from it you have drinking, and from it grows vegetation in which you pasture (your animals).
interpretation: The verse points to rain as a clear sign of God’s sustaining mercy: what we take for granted—our drinking water and the fodder that supports our livelihoods—comes only through His provision and ordinance. It calls us to recognize our dependence on Divine grace, to respond with gratitude and trust, and to behave as responsible stewards of the resources God gives.

translation:
ينبت لكم به الزرع والزيتون والنخيل والأعناب ومن كل الثمرات ۗ إن في ذلك لآية لقوم يتفكرون
"By it He causes for you the crops, the olives, the date‑palms, the grapevines, and every kind of fruit. Indeed in that is a sign for people who reflect."
interpretation: The verse calls attention to the ordered, life‑giving provision in creation as evidence of a wise, sustaining Lord: the regular emergence and variety of useful plants are not random but manifestations of deliberate care and governance. For those who reflect, these ordinary blessings become prompts to recognize dependence on Divine mercy, to give thanks, and to align their trust and conduct with the reality that the world’s provisions are purposeful signs pointing to God’s power and wisdom.

translation: And He has subjected to you the night and the day and the sun and the moon, and the stars are subdued by His command. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason.
interpretation: The verse invites reflection on the ordered, purposeful regularity of the cosmos: these celestial cycles are arranged so that humans can live, measure time, navigate, and worship, and their disciplined functioning testifies to a single wise Creator. For people who think, this ordered system is not merely useful but evidential—calling them to recognise divine sovereignty, to be grateful, and to align their conduct and responsibilities with the moral and practical lessons derived from that order.

translation: And whatever He has produced for you on the earth of various colours — indeed in that is a sign for people who remember.
interpretation: The verse points to the observable diversity in creation (different plants, fruits, animals, soils, landscapes and even peoples’ appearances) as deliberate evidence of God’s wisdom, care and creative order. That variety is meant to prompt reflection, gratitude and recognition of divine authorship: those who ‘remember’ (take heed and reflect) will see in the richness and balance of the world a clear sign leading them toward faith, humility and mindful dependence on God.

translation: And He is the One who subjected the sea for you, so that you may eat from it fresh meat and extract from it ornaments which you wear, and you see the ships cleaving through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s subjugation of the sea is both provision and sign: the sea supplies lawful sustenance (fresh flesh), raw materials (pearls, shells, etc.), and means of commerce and travel (ships), all enabling human livelihood. These tangible blessings are presented to awaken recognition of God’s power, to prompt responsible use of resources and reliance on Him, and ultimately to foster sincere gratitude rather than pride — gratitude being the intended moral and spiritual response to divine bounty.

translation: And He cast into the earth firm anchors (mountains) so that it would not sway with you, and [He placed] rivers and pathways — that you might be guided.
interpretation: The verse indicates that God arranged the world’s physical order (mountains as stabilizers, rivers and routes) not merely as conveniences but as intentional, providential means: they preserve life and enable human society while serving as visible signs meant to awaken people to God’s wisdom and lead them to recognize and follow His guidance.

translation:
وَعَلاماتٍ ۚ وَبِالنَّجْمِ هُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ
"And (these are) signs; and by the star they are guided."
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has placed clear, useful signs in creation—landmarks and the stars—which people use to find their way physically; mentioning the star emphasises that these created things reliably facilitate human navigation while pointing to a deeper truth: guidance ultimately comes from God, who made those signs for our benefit.

translation: Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?
interpretation: الآية تدعو للتأمل العقلي والوجداني في اختلاف الرب المطلق عن المخلوقات المحدودة: لا يجوز مساواة الخالق بالمخلوق لأن الخلق عجز وحاجة وتبدّؤ، بينما الله تعالى هو الباديء القادر الثابت والرازق. بهذا يُناهض النصّ الشرك ويحضّ على تذكّر الربوبية والاعتماد والشكر، فتكون الاستجابة توحيدًا عمليًا في الإيمان والسلوك.

translation: And if you were to count the favors of Allah, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The statement points to the limitless, multifaceted nature of God’s blessings—so numerous that human accounting cannot exhaust them—and pairs that reality with God’s ready forgiveness and mercy. The implication is twofold: it humbles us by showing our inability to fully repay or tally what we receive, and it consoles and motivates us because God’s mercy covers our shortcomings; rather than licensing neglect, this mercy should prompt sincere gratitude, repentance when we fail, and responsible use of the gifts entrusted to us.

translation: And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal.
interpretation: The verse asserts that God’s knowledge embraces both inner intentions and outward actions, so moral responsibility depends not only on visible deeds but on hidden motives as well — a warning that nothing secret escapes divine awareness and a reassurance that unseen good or bad will be reckoned.

translation: And those whom they call upon besides Allah do not create anything, while they themselves are created.
interpretation: The verse exposes the irrationality of associating partners with God by pointing out that these putative deities lack the essential attribute of divinity — the power to create — and are themselves contingent, created beings; therefore worshiping them is unjustified, and true sovereignty and worthy worship belong solely to the One who alone brings things into existence.

translation: Dead, not alive; and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.
interpretation: The verse characterizes those who reject guidance as spiritually dead—though outwardly alive, their hearts and minds are unresponsive to truth, so they remain in a state of heedless incapacity and have no awareness of the time or reality of resurrection until God raises them on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Your God is One God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are in denial and they are arrogant.
interpretation: The verse affirms uncompromising monotheism and then diagnoses why some reject ultimate accountability: their inner disposition, not mere lack of evidence, drives their denial. Describing their hearts as “munkirah” indicates an active refusal or suppression of truth—an emotional and moral deadening that blocks acceptance—while calling them “mustakbirun” shows this denial is rooted in pride and a refusal to submit. In other words, rejection of the Hereafter is presented as a willful, proud turning away that neutralizes conscience and responsibility, rather than a neutral intellectual position.

translation: There is no doubt that God knows what they hide and what they declare; indeed He does not love the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that God's knowledge embraces both private intentions and public actions, so inner motives are morally consequential and cannot be concealed from divine judgment. It condemns pride—refusing truth, exalting oneself, or looking down on others—as a spiritual defect that alienates one from God's favor; therefore the believer must cultivate sincerity and humility, since outward piety without humble, honest intent is unacceptable.

translation: And when it is said to them, “What has your Lord sent down?” they say, “Tales of the former peoples.”
interpretation: The verse describes how certain people respond to revelation by dismissing it as mere ancient stories—labeling the Prophet’s message as recycled myths to avoid accepting its authority. Calling it “أساطير الأولين” is not a neutral description but a defensive tactic that masks prejudice, intellectual inertia, and refusal to engage with the text on its own terms; it exposes an attitude that substitutes ridicule or preconceived disbelief for sincere inquiry or moral responsibility.

translation: They will carry their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and (they will carry) the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. How evil indeed is that which they bear.
interpretation: The verse teaches that accountability on the Day of Judgment is not only personal but also relational: those who lead others astray bear, in addition to their own sins, the moral weight of the consequences their misguidance produces. ‘Without knowledge’ condemns negligent or irresponsible influence—claiming ignorance does not remove responsibility when one’s words or actions cause others to err. Thus the passage warns especially against abusing positions of influence (as teacher, leader, parent, or exemplar) and stresses the duty to seek truth, act conscientiously, and avoid misleading others, for such misguidance multiplies one’s culpability and will be judged severely.

translation: Indeed those before them plotted, but Allah caused their buildings to topple from their foundations; the roof fell upon them from above, and the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive.
interpretation: The verse warns that human schemes and conspiracies against truth and divine guidance are ultimately futile: God can unravel and overturn what seemed secure, bringing sudden and unexpected ruin from angles the plotters never anticipated. It teaches that arrogance, hidden plotting, and reliance on apparent strength lead to unforeseen destruction, serving as a warning that divine justice can come swiftly and from the most vulnerable points of one’s supposed foundations.

translation: Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and will say, "Where are My partners which you used to claim?" Those to whom knowledge was given will say, "Indeed, disgrace and evil are upon the disbelievers today."
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment God will expose the futility of all claimed partners and humiliate those who ascribed divinity or authority to others; the supposed partners will be powerless to help or answer. Those endowed with true knowledge — who recognize divine unity and the consequences of error — will plainly acknowledge that the blame, shame and dire outcome belong to the disbelievers and those who persisted in shirk, thereby affirming that honor belongs only to God and that false objects of trust bring only humiliation.

translation: Those whom the angels take [in death] while they are wronging themselves — when asked, 'What did you used to do?' they will say, 'We did not do evil.' Nay; indeed Allah is fully aware of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who die having oppressed their own souls by sin or rejection will attempt to deny or minimize their wrongs when confronted, but such protestations will not erase reality: God’s knowledge encompasses every deed and intention, and at the moment of accountability excuses and self-justifications will fail.

translation: So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein; and wretched is the residence of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse announces the inevitable consequence for those whose pride led them to reject Divine guidance: their exaltation in this world is reversed into everlasting humiliation. The command to “enter the gates of Hell” and to remain there emphasizes the certainty and permanence of divine justice, while calling their end “wretched” highlights the moral lesson that arrogance, which causes one to refuse truth and mercy, results not in honor but in permanent disgrace and loss.

translation: And it will be said to those who were God‑conscious, “What has your Lord sent down?” They will say, “Good.” For those who do good, in this world is good, and the home of the Hereafter is better; and excellent indeed is the dwelling of the righteous.
interpretation: The verse affirms that true piety recognizes God’s revelations and decrees as wholly beneficial: the faithful, when asked about what God has sent, answer that it brings goodness. That goodness is twofold — upright conduct and obedience yield real, positive outcomes in this life (peace, moral integrity, lawful provision, social harmony), but the ultimate and superior reward lies in the Hereafter. The phrase “excellent indeed is the dwelling of the righteous” stresses that the final abode granted to those who live in God‑awareness (their guiding principles, patience, and good deeds) surpasses any worldly good; thus believers are called to pursue righteous action now with the confident expectation of a far better eternal home.

translation: Gardens of Eden — they will enter them, with rivers flowing beneath them; therein they will have whatever they wish. Thus Allah recompenses the God‑conscious.
interpretation: The verse promises that those who live in God‑consciousness (al‑muttaqīn) will be admitted to an eternal, pure realm whose ever‑flowing rivers symbolize unending, wholesome provision and tranquility; the assurance that they will have “what they wish” indicates complete, fitting fulfillment of their righteous needs and longings. In short, the passage presents Paradise as both God’s just recompense and a lasting state of spiritual and physical sufficiency, meant to reassure and motivate upright conduct.

translation: Those whom the angels take at death while they are in a state of purity and goodness — the angels will say, “Peace be upon you; enter Paradise for what you used to do.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that a death reached in a state of righteousness, witnessed and affirmed by the angels, is met with a greeting of ‘peace’ that signals deliverance and God’s approval. Admission to Paradise is presented as the fitting recompense for a life of righteous deeds: the angels’ salute confirms the believer’s upright end and the moral accountability by which their past actions are rewarded, while the tone of welcome also reflects divine mercy that receives those who died ‘tayyibīn’ (pure/virtuous).

translation: Are they waiting except that the angels should come to them or that the command of your Lord should come? Thus did those before them. And Allah wronged them not, but they were themselves wrongdoers.
interpretation: الآية توجه إنذاراً لمن يؤخرون الإيمان ويطالبون بعلامة خارقة (كقدوم الملائكة أو حكم ربّي ظاهر) قبل أن يقبلوا بالرسالة: هذا تأجيل مخلّ بالفعل الإيماني ومسؤولية الاختيار، وقد سبق أن فعلت أقوام قبلهم فكانت نهايتهم جزاءً لخياراتهم. ثم تؤكد العدل الإلهي: ما ظلمهم الله بإهلاكهم، بل هم ظلموا أنفسهم بإصرارهم على الإنكار ورفض البينات، فالعقاب نتيجة حتمية للاختيار الباطل لا ظلماً من الله.

translation:
فَأَصَابَهُمْ سَيِّئَاتُ مَا عَمِلُوا وَحَاقَ بِهِم مَّا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ
“So the evils of what they had done befell them, and that which they used to mock encompassed them.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that people ultimately reap the consequences of their own wrongful deeds: the harms they brought upon others and themselves return to strike them, and the very thing they scorned—God’s warning, the truth, or the punishment they ridiculed—arrives and surrounds them with no escape. Their mockery becomes the cause of their humiliation and ruin, illustrating divine justice and the certainty that denial and ridicule do not avert the outcome of one’s actions.

translation: And those who associate others with Allah say, “Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him—neither we nor our fathers—and we would not have forbidden anything besides Him.” Thus did those before them. So is there upon the messengers except the clear delivery?
interpretation: The verse criticizes the common excuse of polytheists who invoke a hypothetical divine will to justify inherited idol-worship and man-made prohibitions: they claim that if God had intended otherwise they would have worshipped only Him, thereby shifting responsibility from their choices and traditions to an imagined divine decree. The Lord points out that this rationalization was the same pattern shown by earlier peoples, and emphasizes that the prophets’ duty is limited to conveying the clear message; acceptance or rejection—and the moral responsibility that follows—rests with the people themselves.

translation: And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], “Worship Allah and avoid Taghût.” Then among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error became justified. So travel through the earth and see how was the end of the deniers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s prophetic message is universal and simple: true religion consists in sincere worship of God and rejection of any false lordship or oppressive falsehood (taghût — idols, tyrants, corrupt systems). Human communities differ by their response: guidance is granted to those who accept and act upon the message, while persistent rejection leads to entrenched error as a consequence. The injunction to ‘travel the earth’ urges people to examine history and the visible outcomes of those who denied the truth, showing that divine warning and human responsibility are both real — guidance is offered to all, but people’s choices determine their end.

translation: If you were to strive eagerly to guide them, then indeed Allah does not guide whom He causes to go astray, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate guidance is a divine grant, not the result of human effort: one may endeavor earnestly to show the way, but if people persistently reject guidance and God withdraws His guidance as a consequence, no amount of human urging can force true guidance upon them, and they will be left without protectors or rescuers. Thus responsibility lies in doing what is required of the caller, while recognizing that the acceptance of guidance is granted by God alone.

translation: And they swear by Allah with their strongest oaths, “Allah will not resurrect the one who dies.” Nay — a true promise rests with Him; yet most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse censures those who, in arrogance, use vehement oaths to deny resurrection, and it affirms that such human assertions cannot alter God’s sure promise to raise the dead. The statement underscores that belief in resurrection is an objective reality grounded in God’s truth, while the widespread rejection of it arises from ignorance, heedlessness, and attachment to worldly life; the warning is to recognize divine accountability rather than be comforted by vain human claims.

translation: So that He may make clear to them that wherein they differ, and that those who disbelieve may know that they were liars.
interpretation: The verse indicates that God sent revelation to resolve contested points and remove ambiguity: by exposing the true position He intends that disputes over belief, law, or guidance be settled. Once the truth is made manifest, those who denied or opposed it are shown to have been speaking falsely — their claims and objections are unmasked, removing any excuse and establishing accountability.

translation: His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: The verse underscores God's absolute, effortless sovereignty over existence: created realities are contingent on His will, so what we perceive as causes and processes operate within His decree. Recognizing that everything comes into being by God's single command fosters humility, trust in Divine providence, and the understanding that ultimate power and authority belong solely to God.

translation: And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged — We will certainly grant them a good place in this world, and the reward of the Hereafter is far greater, if they only knew.
interpretation: This verse consoles and guarantees divine justice to those who leave their homes out of faith because of persecution: Allah will provide them relief, status or well-being in this life as a sign of His care, but the true and supreme recompense lies in the Hereafter. It calls believers to persevere and prioritize the eternal promise over immediate losses, trusting that worldly hardships borne for God will be compensated and that the ultimate outcome far surpasses present comforts.

translation: Those who are patient and place their trust in their Lord.
interpretation: This phrase characterizes a spiritual stance in which endurance and active reliance on God are inseparable: patience (sabr) means persevering through trials, restraining wrongful impulses, and continuing righteous effort, while trusting in the Lord (tawakkul) means consciously entrusting outcomes to God’s wisdom and decree even as one takes legitimate means. Together they describe a disciplined, trusting believer whose calm perseverance invites God’s support and ultimate vindication.

translation: And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know.
interpretation: The verse teaches that prophecy is a function of revelation bestowed upon human messengers rather than an intrinsic divine nature of the messenger; it therefore cautions against elevating the messenger beyond his human role or inventing religious knowledge. When questions remain, one should turn to the 'people of the Reminder'—those versed in the revealed scriptures and their transmission—recognizing the necessity of learned, transmitted guidance, communal responsibility for preserving knowledge, and humility before the established sources of religious understanding.

translation: with clear proofs and written records. And We have sent down to you the Reminder so that you may make plain to the people what has been revealed to them, and perhaps they will reflect.
interpretation: The verse stresses that divine guidance arrives supported by unmistakable signs and by prior recorded revelations, and that the prophet’s role is primarily to elucidate and teach that guidance so people can recognize its meaning and implications. It implies a twofold responsibility: God provides objective evidence and preserved texts, while the messenger translates and applies them to people’s circumstances; the hoped-for result is sincere reflection and moral change rather than mere hearing. Thus true acceptance requires both sound proof and thoughtful engagement.

translation: Are then those who plot evil secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them up, or that a punishment will not come upon them from where they do not perceive?
interpretation: The verse warns that those who scheme and commit evil should not assume they are safe: God can bring sudden, total ruin on them or strike from unexpected directions. It emphasizes that human plotting cannot evade divine justice — apparent security is fragile and can be overturned by unforeseen consequences or a decisive intervention from God.

translation:
أو يأخذهم في تقلبهم فما هم بمعجزين
"Or He may seize them in their comings and goings, so they are not able to avert [it]."
interpretation: The phrase indicates that God can suddenly take wrongdoers in the midst of their activities or schemes; their movement, plotting, or hopes of escape will be powerless to prevent His decree. It emphasizes that human maneuvering cannot frustrate divine judgment, and when God decides to seize, no one can rescue or delay what He wills.

translation: Or He may seize them while they are in fear; indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that God’s dealing with people balances justice and mercy: ordinarily He delays punishment, warns and gives chances to repent, but if people persist in wrongdoing He can overtake them abruptly — yet even that overtaking occurs within His mercy and wisdom. ‘Seizing them in fear’ can be a swift, decisive consequence that prevents greater harm, serves as a clear admonition, and limits continued wrongdoing; describing God as ‘rūʾūf raḥīm’ emphasizes that His actions, even punitive ones, are tempered by compassion, aimed ultimately at restraint, instruction, or the preservation of moral order rather than wanton cruelty.

translation: Do they not see what Allah has created—whose shadows extend to the right and to the left—prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?
interpretation: The verse teaches that the whole of creation, even apparently inert phenomena, operates in constant, obedient submission to God’s will; this natural order—likened to prostration—is a sign of divine sovereignty intended to confront human pride and to call people to recognize God’s authority and live in humble submission rather than heedless arrogance.

translation: And to Allah prostrate whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels — and they are not arrogant.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s sovereignty is absolute and that every part of creation—living beings and even the angels—fulfills its created purpose by submitting to Him. This submission is not merely external ritual but a reality rooted in humility: angels are given as exemplars of obedience because they possess no pride to resist God’s will. The implicit admonition to humans is that arrogance obstructs true worship and relationship with God; genuine prostration requires inner surrender and recognition of divine lordship rather than vain self-exaltation.

translation: They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.
interpretation: The verse describes the true believer whose awareness of God’s transcendent authority and constant watchfulness (expressed as fearing their Lord “from above them”) fosters reverent fear and accountability, and that inward conviction manifests in steadfast obedience to divine commands whether or not others are watching.

translation: وقال الله: «لا تتخذوا إلهين اثنين؛ إنما هو إله واحد، فإياي فارهبون.»
interpretation: الآية تأمر بتوحيد العبادة والولاء لله وحده: تحذر من تقسيم الإيمان أو نسب السلطة الإلهية لغير الله (أي اتخاذ «إلهين») وتبرز أن الله واحد لا شريك له، ولذلك ينبغي أن يكون الخوف والخشية والطاعة موجهة إليه وحده، لأن أي إخلال بهذا التوحيد يهدّم المقصود من العبادة ويضع صاحبه تحت محاسبة الرب الواحد.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him belongs the religion firmly established. Will you then fear anyone other than Allah?
interpretation: The verse affirms Allah’s absolute sovereignty and that rightful allegiance and judgment belong solely to Him. Its practical thrust is ethical and spiritual: recognizing God as the ultimate owner and arbiter should remove the misplaced fear and submission to other beings, authorities, idols, or worldly powers. True piety is to orient one’s fear, obedience and trust toward Allah alone, refusing to let transient rulers, social pressures, or superstitions dictate one’s conscience.

translation: And whatever blessing there is in you — it is from Allah; then when harm touches you, to Him you cry aloud.
interpretation: The verse confronts a common moral and spiritual failing: people receive blessings from God yet often behave as if those gifts are their own, neglecting gratitude and recognition of dependence. Only when suffering comes do they urgently seek God’s help. The proper response, implied here, is inward consistency — to acknowledge God as the source of every good, cultivate constant thankfulness and reliance in times of ease, and not reserve turning to Him for crisis alone. This fosters humility, corrects ingratitude, and aligns belief with conduct by making remembrance and supplication a continuous habit rather than an emergency recourse.

translation:
ثم إذا كشف الضر عنكم إذا فريق منكم بربهم يشركون
"Then when He removes the hardship from you, behold, a party among you begins to associate partners with their Lord."
interpretation: The verse reproaches a recurrent human failing: some people sincerely turn to God in distress, but when relief comes they revert to attributing causes, authority, or worth to other things or persons — social habits, idols, worldly powers, or false beliefs — thereby denying God’s exclusive lordship. It teaches that true faith is proven by constancy and gratitude, not only by supplication in need; deliverance exposes whether reliance on God was real or merely circumstantial.

translation:
ليَكفُروا بما آتَيناهم؛ فَتَمَتَّعوا؛ فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمونَ
"[Do] so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves [for a little]; soon you will know."
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who reject God’s gifts and guidance: it records their boastful indulgence in worldly pleasures as if free from consequence, but warns that this enjoyment is temporary and deceptive—sooner or later they will learn the reality of God’s authority and will be held to account, whether by punishment, by the collapse of their apparent advantage, or by the disclosure of truth in the Hereafter.

translation: And they assign to that of which they have no knowledge a portion of what We have provided them. By Allah, you will surely be asked about what you used to fabricate.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the practice of attributing parts of God’s provision, authority, or revelation to things or claims for which there is no true knowledge—whether false deities, invented rites, or fabricated teachings—and warns that such assertions are sinful fabrications. It affirms that those who make or promote these unfounded claims will be held to account and questioned by God for the lies they devised.

translation: And they ascribe to Allah daughters — exalted is He — while for themselves is what they desire.
interpretation: The verse reproves the human habit of projecting our social biases onto God: by claiming God has 'daughters' the polytheists reduce the Divine to human family roles, yet they hypocritically keep for themselves the favoured and desirable things. The interjection 'سبحانه' (exalted is He) stresses God's absolute transcendence and negates any such anthropomorphic ascription; the passage thus exposes both theological error and moral self-deception — inventing divine relations to justify one's own prejudices and preferences.

translation: And when one of them is given the news of a female, his face darkens and he suppresses his grief.
interpretation: The verse condemns a social prejudice that treats the birth of a daughter as misfortune: the visible shame and hidden sorrow reveal a cultural devaluation of female life rooted in economic, honor, and lineage concerns. By highlighting that reaction, the Qur’an criticizes such misogynistic attitudes and calls for abandoning inherited customs that regard daughters as a calamity, affirming that girls are of equal moral worth and deserving of gratitude and justice rather than reproach.

translation:
يتوارى من القوم من سوء ما بشر به ۚ أيمسكه على هون أم يدسه في التراب ۗ ألا ساء ما يحكمون
"Some among the people shrink away from the evil of that with which they were warned. Will He hold him back in humiliation, or bury him in the dust? How bad are the judgments they make."
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, when warned of divine consequence, try to evade or minimize the warning by imagining easy outcomes—either a mere humiliation or a temporary reprieve—rather than facing true accountability. Through rhetorical questions it exposes the folly of their reasoning: their assessments of God’s will and of their own fate are deeply mistaken and morally ruinous.

translation:
لِلَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآخِرَةِ مَثَلُ السُّوْءِ ۖ وَلِلَّهِ الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَىٰ ۚ وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ
“For those who do not believe in the Hereafter, the example is an evil one; and for Allah is the highest example — and He is the Almighty, the All‑Wise.”
interpretation: The verse is asserting that the outlook of those who deny the Last Day is fundamentally defective: the standards, comparisons and goals by which they live are corrupt, short‑sighted and lead to loss (an ‘evil’ likeness). By contrast, Allah’s ‘highest example’ is the perfect, enduring model of truth, justice and ultimate reckoning; His way, attributes and judgments are supremely reliable. The clause ‘He is the Almighty, the All‑Wise’ underscores that God’s power and wisdom guarantee the justice and soundness of His example, unlike the flawed measures of the disbelievers.

translation: And if Allah were to punish the people for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it (the earth) any creature; but He postpones them to an appointed term. And when their term comes, they will not delay it an hour, nor will they bring it forward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s restraint toward widespread injustice is deliberate mercy and part of His sovereign plan: He withholds immediate annihilation to allow a prescribed period for testing, for people to change, and for His purposes to be fulfilled. That delay should not be mistaken for absence of justice, because the time God has fixed for consequence is certain and inescapable — when the appointed term arrives no one can hasten or postpone it. Thus the postponement is both an opportunity for repentance and a solemn warning that ultimate accountability is inevitable.

translation: وَيَجْعَلُونَ لِلَّهِ مَا يَكْرَهُونَ وَتَصِفُ أَلْسِنَتُهُمُ الْكَذِبَ أَنَّ لَهُمُ الْحُسْنَىٰ ۖ لَا جَرَمَ أَنَّ لَهُمُ النَّارَ وَأَنَّهُمْ مُفْرِطُونَ
interpretation: الآية توبخ المنافقين أو المكذبين الذين يلوّعون الحق بحسب أهوائهم: ينسِبون لله ما يكرهون أو يرسمون لإرادته صورًا تخدم مصالحهم، وتخرج على ألسنتهم أكاذيب تزعم لهم حسن المصير، لكن هذه التصريحات الباطلة لا تغيّر الحقيقة — جزاؤهم النار لأنهم تجاوزوا حدود الحق وأهملوا الواجبات الإلهية، فكانوا مفرِطين (غافلين ومتعدِّين للحدود).

translation: تالله لقد أرسلنا إلى أممٍ من قبلك فزين لهم الشيطان أعمالهم فهو وليهم اليوم ولهم عذاب أليم
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن سابقى الأمم حين أرسل اليهم الرسل رفضوا أو أعرضوا، فقام الشيطان بتجميل الأعمال السيئة لهم وإظهارها مقبولة، فصار لهم ناصراً ووليّاً في طريق الضلالة — أي أتاح لهم الاستمرار في أفعالهم وشجّعهم عليها في الحياة الدنيا — لكن تلك المرافقة لا تنقذهم بل تؤدي إلى حساب وعذاب شديد عند الله؛ فالمسألة تحذير من خداع الشيطان وأن مظهرية الخير الذي يمليه على القلوب مجرد وسيلة تقود إلى عاقبة أليمة.

translation: We did not send down the Book to you except to make clear to them that in which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’an’s central role is corrective and clarifying: it was revealed to settle disputes and remove confusion about matters of belief, law and conduct by making the truth plain, rather than to legitimize every competing claim. In doing so it functions as practical guidance and a source of mercy for those who accept it—promising that those who believe and follow its clarity will be guided and receive God’s compassion. It therefore casts the Prophet’s mission primarily as that of a communicator who resolves disagreements by bringing the revealed standard, and it links the attainment of guidance and mercy to the community’s receptive faith and obedience.

translation: And Allah has sent down from the sky water and brought the earth to life thereby after its death; indeed in that is a sign for a people who listen.
interpretation: The verse points to the routine, observable event of rain reviving barren land as a deliberate, accessible proof of divine sovereignty and power over life and death. Its purpose is not merely to describe a natural cycle but to provoke attentive reflection: if God can restore lifeless earth, He can likewise raise mankind and hold them to account. Thus the passage functions as both a rational argument for belief in resurrection and a moral summons—addressed to those who truly listen—to recognize God’s mercy and authority and to let that recognition transform their faith and conduct.

translation: And indeed for you in the cattle is a lesson: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies — between excrement and blood — pure milk, palatable to the drinkers.
interpretation: The verse is a sign of divine wisdom and providence: God’s creative power transforms what is, by outward appearance, impure into wholesome, pure nourishment. This natural process — milk emerging from within animals despite its proximity to waste and blood — demonstrates that the Creator alone governs life’s hidden workings, turns apparent filth into benefit, and therefore calls people to reflect, recognize their dependence on God’s sustaining care, and respond with gratitude and trust.

translation: And from the fruits of the palm trees and the grapevines you make intoxicants and wholesome provision. Indeed in that is a sign for people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse points to a deeper lesson: God’s creation contains things that can serve as both benefit and trial, and this duality is deliberate so that reflective people may recognize divine wisdom and their own moral responsibility. That the same sources yield ‘good sustenance’ and an intoxicant invites sober contemplation about human choice, gratitude, moderation, and the recognition that provision and temptation alike are signs of the Creator’s power and purpose.

translation: And your Lord inspired the bee, saying, “Take for yourself dwellings in the mountains, in the trees, and in what people construct.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God endows even small creatures with divinely-instilled guidance—here directing the bee to suitable habitats—so that their lives are ordered, protected, and purposeful; it is a sign of God’s wisdom and care in creation and a call for humans to reflect on and learn from the orderly, providential way God governs all beings, including the harmony between natural habitats and human-made structures.

translation: Then eat of every fruit and follow the ways of your Lord made easy. From their bellies comes a drink of varying colors, in which there is healing for the people. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s wise provision and ordered processes in creation: bees, guided by instinct and the paths God has eased for them, gather from many fruits and produce a varied, wholesome drink (honey) whose beneficial, sometimes medicinal, effects benefit humans. The command to 'follow the ways of your Lord made easy' frames this natural economy as both a literal facilitation for creatures and a moral lesson for people—what passes from creation to us as benefit is a sign (āyah) inviting reflection on divine providence, interdependence in creation, and the duty to recognize and be grateful to the Creator.

translation: And Allah created you, then He will take you in death; and among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit age so that he knows nothing after having known anything. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Powerful.
interpretation: The verse reminds that human life, vigour and intellect are granted by God and can equally be withdrawn—sometimes returning a person to helplessness and loss of memory after a time of knowledge. That reversal is meant to humble people, to warn against pride in one’s faculties, and to urge the prudent use of youthful strength and understanding in preparation for God’s reckoning. At the same time it reassures that even when human capacities fail, nothing leaves God’s knowledge or power: He is fully aware of people’s states and able to do as He wills, so accountability and divine wisdom remain intact despite human frailty.

translation: And Allah has preferred some of you over others in provision. But those who have been favored with provision do not give of their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they may be equal therein — then do they deny the favor of Allah?
interpretation: The verse teaches that the unequal distribution of wealth is by God’s design as a test and responsibility: those who receive more are morally obliged to share with those under their care (dependents, servants, captives, the needy). Refusing to use God’s gift to relieve inequality is a form of ingratitude and denial of God’s bounty; the proper response to being favored is generosity, support, and social responsibility, not hoarding what has been entrusted to you.

translation: And Allah has made for you from yourselves mates, and has made for you from your mates sons and grandchildren, and has provided you with good things. Will they then believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?
interpretation: The verse uses the intimate and continuous blessings—spouses formed from your own nature, offspring and descendants, and lawful, wholesome provisions—as clear signs of God’s deliberate care and mercy. Its rhetorical question exposes the contradiction of accepting falsehood or idolatry while refusing to acknowledge or be grateful for these evident favors: such disbelief is moral and spiritual blindness. The intended lesson is that recognition of God’s providence should lead to faith, gratitude, and right conduct rather than to denial and ingratitude.

translation: And they worship, besides Allah, that which possesses for them no provision from the heavens and the earth and is not able [to do so].
interpretation: The verse teaches a fundamental theological point: provision (rizq) and control over sustenance belong solely to God, so directing worship or trust toward other beings or idols is a profound misplacement of reliance. Worship implies entrusting one’s needs and destiny to the object of worship; since these false gods have neither ownership nor power to grant provision, devotion to them is irrational and spiritually misleading. True reliance and worship must be directed to Allah alone, who alone ordains and distributes sustenance.

translation: So do not set up comparisons for Allah; indeed Allah knows, and you do not know.
interpretation: The verse warns against trying to explain or define God by likening Him to created things or forcing human analogies onto the Divine. Such comparisons arise from limited human understanding and risk distorting belief; we are urged to adopt humility before God’s transcendence, accept the limits of our knowledge, and rely on God’s own knowledge rather than presume to fully grasp or equate His essence by our imperfect models.

translation: Allah sets forth an example: a slave who is powerless and cannot do anything, and one whom We have provided from Us with good provision — and he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to Allah. Nay, most of them do not know.
interpretation: The parable teaches that God’s bestowal of means and ability creates a real moral and practical distinction: someone endowed by God with provision can act, give, and fulfil obligations both privately and publicly, whereas the powerless cannot; to claim they are equal is a failure to recognize God’s wise distribution of capacity and responsibility, and the phrase “Al‑hamdu lillāh” affirms God’s sovereignty and justice in that ordering.

translation: And Allah presents an example of two men: one of them is dumb, unable to do anything, and he is a burden on his guardian — wherever he directs him he brings no good. Is he equal to the one who enjoins justice, and he is on a straight path?
interpretation: The verse uses a parable to contrast impotence and dependence with active moral agency. The “dumb” man represents someone who cannot benefit himself or others, who is passively carried by another and produces no good; the other man represents a person who follows divine guidance, acts rightly, and calls others to justice. The point is not merely physical ability but moral capacity and responsibility: those who are guided and who strive to establish justice occupy a far higher and more trustworthy position than those who are incapable of doing good or leading; therefore authority, trust, and moral weight rightly belong to those who are on the straight path and promote justice, not to the impotent or negligent.

translation: To Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is but like the twinkling of an eye—or even nearer. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse teaches that only God possesses knowledge of the unseen, including the precise time of Resurrection; the Hour will arrive with absolute suddenness from human perception—faster than a blink—so people cannot rely on forecasting or delay of accountability. This immediacy, coupled with the affirmation that God is fully powerful over everything, means believers must live in constant moral awareness and readiness, trusting God’s sovereign control while acting responsibly because the final reckoning may occur at any moment.

translation: “And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing, and He made for you hearing, sight and hearts so that you may be grateful.”
interpretation: The verse teaches humility and responsibility: our initial ignorance and dependence underscore that hearing, sight and the heart are divinely granted capacities meant to enable perception, reflection and moral choice; true gratitude is therefore an active response—recognizing God’s favors through understanding, remembrance and upright conduct rather than mere sentiment.

translation: ألم يروا إلى الطير مسخرات في جو السماء ما يمسكهن إلا الله ۗ إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يؤمنون
interpretation: الآية تدعو إلى التفكر في نظام الطير وحركته كدليل على سيادة الله وعنايته المستمرة بالمخلوقات: أن طيرانها، ثباتها في الجو، وتوجيهها ليست أمورًا عشوائية أو نتيجة لقوى موازية بل هي بقوة وتقدير الله وحده. لذلك تكون هذه الظواهر آيات تُقوّي إيمان المؤمنين، وتذكّرهم بالاعتماد على الخالق وفهم أن وراء انتظام الكون حكمة ومشيئة إلهية تستوجب الاعتراف بربوبيته وشكرها.

translation: And Allah has made for you from your homes a dwelling, and He has made for you from the skins of the cattle tents which you find light when you travel and when you stay; and of their wool, their fur and their hair He has made furnishings and goods for a time.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes God’s providential design: He supplies both permanent dwellings and portable shelters, and transforms animal materials into textiles and furnishings so human life is accommodated in varying conditions (traveling or settling). This demonstrates divine wisdom and care in fitting creation to human needs, while the phrase “to a time” reminds us that such comforts are temporary—prompting gratitude, reliance on God, and reflection on these signs of His power.

translation: And Allah has made for you from what He has created shadows, and has made for you from the mountains shelters, and has made for you garments to protect you from the heat and garments to protect you in battle. Thus He completes His favor upon you, that you might submit.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s material provisions — relief (shades), stability (mountains as shelters), and clothing (for comfort, dignity, and defense) — are not accidental but purposeful favors. By removing physical hardships and providing security and social order, these gifts create the conditions in which people can live, choose rightly, and recognize their dependence on the Creator. Describing this provision as the completion of His favor emphasizes that worldly benefits are signs of divine mercy meant to lead humans toward safety, moral responsibility, gratitude, and ultimately submission to God’s lordship.

translation: If they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance (of the message).
interpretation: The verse teaches that the messenger’s (or believer’s) duty is limited to delivering God’s clear message faithfully; if people reject it, the responsibility for acceptance or rejection lies with them and with God, not with the one who conveyed the truth—therefore one must fulfill the duty of honest, unambiguous communication without coercion and without bearing blame for others’ refusal.

translation: They recognize the favor of Allah, then they deny it; and most of them are disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse indicts those who are conscious of God’s gifts yet refuse to acknowledge Him as their Giver—either through ingratitude, attributing blessings to chance or other causes, or by rejecting God’s rights—and shows that such denial of divine providence amounts to a spiritual rejection (kufr), explaining why ingratitude and repudiation of God’s sovereignty commonly lead people into disbelief.

translation: And the Day We will resurrect from every nation a witness; then it will not be permitted for those who disbelieved to make excuses, nor will they be granted a respite.
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment God will bring forth for each people the messenger or witness who conveyed God’s message to them, so that every soul’s acceptance or rejection will be publicly established; at that point the disbelievers can no longer claim ignorance, invent excuses, or ask for more time—their accountability is final and their denial is nullified.

translation: And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lessened for them, nor will they be granted delay.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine justice is final and uncompromising: oppressors and transgressors will find no mitigation, intercession, or postponement of their punishment. It serves as a warning that accountability is inevitable, urging people to abandon injustice and seek repentance before it is too late.

translation: And when those who associated others with Allah see their partners, they will say, “Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to invoke beside You.” And they will cast toward them the word, “Indeed you are liars.”
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection the polytheists will stand before the beings or idols they had worshipped and, recognizing them, will confess that they had relied on them in life; but those supposed partners will disown any help or claim, and the worshippers will hurl accusations of falsehood at them. The verse highlights the ultimate impotence and injustice of shirk: what was worshipped as a helper proves to be nothing, the relationship is exposed as a lie, and the culprits’ regret and the partners’ denial together make clear that invocation of anyone besides God was both futile and false.

translation: And they will cast toward Allah on that Day the salām (their submission/appeasement), and what they used to invent will fail them.
interpretation: The verse means that at the Resurrection the wrongdoers will, in desperation, present to God whatever outward gestures or offerings of surrender and peace they have—seeking to placate Him—but their prior fabrications, excuses and false beliefs will abandon them and prove worthless; their last-minute attempts at appeasement cannot undo the consequences of their earlier deeds and deceptions.

translation: Those who disbelieved and hindered (people) from the way of Allah — We increased for them punishment upon punishment because of the corruption they were spreading.
interpretation: The verse means that disbelief combined with actively blocking others from God’s way carries multiplied culpability: God’s punishment is intensified “above the punishment” because such behavior does not merely affect the individual but propagates misguidance and social disorder. Preventing people from guidance magnifies the harm and therefore warrants greater retribution, reflecting the communal consequences of their corruption and the proportional justice of God in this world and the Hereafter.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will raise among every nation a witness over them from themselves. And We will bring you as a witness over these. And We have sent down to you the Book as clarification for all things and as guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that ultimate accountability will be measured against the specific guidance each people received — their own witnesses (prophets, scriptures, or consciences) — while the Prophet is a witness to how his community responds. Calling the Qur’an a clarification of everything affirms its role as the comprehensive criterion that distinguishes truth from error, directs moral and legal life, and embodies God’s mercy and glad tidings for those who submit. The practical thrust is personal responsibility: one will be judged by the light and testimony given to one’s own community, and embracing the Qur’an’s guidance is thus decisive for one’s standing before God.

translation: Indeed, Allah commands justice, good conduct (ihsân), and giving to kin, and He forbids indecency, evil and transgression. He admonishes you so that you may take heed.
interpretation: This verse summarizes the core of divine ethical instruction: to establish a balanced society by insisting on fair treatment (justice), active goodness and excellence in behavior (ihsân), and the preservation of family ties (giving to kin), while prohibiting personal immorality (fahshâ), socially or morally reprehensible actions (munkar), and oppressive transgression (baghy). The final clause—He admonishes you so that you may take heed—frames these commands as a moral reminder meant to transform both individual conduct and communal structures, urging conscious responsibility rather than mere ritual observance.

translation: And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you make a covenant, and do not break oaths after their confirmation, while you have made Allah over you a surety. Indeed, Allah knows what you do.
interpretation: The verse stresses that promises and pledges—especially those made invoking God—are not mere words but moral and religious obligations. Calling Allah as guarantor increases the weight of a commitment, so reneging after affirming an oath is a breach of trust, hypocrisy before God and people, and undermines social bonds; since Allah is the witness of all actions, one must be sincere, avoid frivolous oaths, and honor agreements to maintain justice and communal reliability.

translation: And do not be like the woman who unraveled her yarn after it had become strong, taking your oaths as a means of deceit among yourselves so that one people might be (treated) like another. Allah only tests you by it; and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that over which you used to differ.
interpretation: The verse warns against using formal words, promises or oaths as tools to evade duties or to undo settled rights. The image of undoing a well-spun thread rebukes those who deliberately reverse what is firm for private advantage. Such manipulative behaviour is a moral test: it exposes who is sincere and who will sacrifice justice for gain. The practical lesson is to honor covenants, protect the rights of the vulnerable, refuse legalistic tricks that equalize the unequal, and remember that ultimate judgment and clarification of disputes belong to God on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: And if Allah had willed, He would have made you a single community; but He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse affirms that religious and doctrinal diversity exists not from incapacity but by Divine will and wisdom: God could have made everyone uniform in belief, yet allows varied paths as part of the moral and spiritual landscape in which human beings are tested. Guidance and misguidance are presented as outcomes within God’s sovereign will that interact with human disposition and choices—those who sincerely seek truth and submit are guided, while those who persist in arrogance or rejection are left to stray. Despite this divine dispensation of diversity, the verse closes by reminding that individual responsibility remains decisive: every person will be held accountable for their actions and intentions on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: And do not make your oaths a means of deception among yourselves, causing your feet to slip after they were firm; and you will taste the evil for having turned [people] away from the way of Allah — and for you is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns treating solemn vows as instruments of manipulation or exclusion: when people invoke oaths to justify breaking duties, to mislead, or to bar others from guidance, that cynical use of religious commitment corrodes moral firmness, undermines communal trust, and leads both to spiritual decline and to harming others’ access to God’s way; such behavior thereby incurs serious divine retribution.

translation: And do not sell the covenant of Allah for a small price. Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: This warns against abandoning or compromising one’s pledge to God—faith, obedience, justice and moral integrity—in exchange for fleeting, trivial worldly gain (wealth, status, ease, or protection). To “sell” the covenant means to trade eternal duties and principles for immediate benefits; the verse stresses that God’s reward, mercy and the long‑term well‑being He offers far surpass any short‑lived advantage. The phrase “if you only knew” urges sober reflection: had people realized the true value of what they relinquish, they would not barter away what leads to lasting good for ephemeral profit.

translation: What you have will perish, and what is with Allah will remain. And We will surely reward those who are patient their reward with the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly possessions and status are temporary while what Allah grants — His mercy, guidance, and the lasting reward — endures. It therefore calls believers to value steadfastness and righteous patience in the face of trials, promising that such endurance will be recompensed by Allah with a reward that reflects and surpasses their best deeds; in short, prioritize permanent, God‑won rewards over fleeting worldly gain and trust in divine justice.

translation: Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer—We will surely grant them a good life, and We will surely recompense them according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere faith combined with righteous action is the true basis for God's favor, without distinction between men and women. "A good life" (حياة طيبة) points to dignified, secure, and spiritually balanced well‑being in this world, and the promise of a just, abundant recompense in the Hereafter. By saying He will reward them "with the best of what they used to do," the text emphasizes that divine recompense corresponds to the quality and sincerity of deeds and is often perfected or multiplied by God beyond mere human accounting, so believers receive holistic, fitting good both now and in the final reckoning.

translation: So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.
interpretation: The verse instructs that before engaging with the Qur'an one should consciously invoke Allah’s protection to block satanic whisperings and interference; this prepares the heart and mind to receive the revelation with presence, sincerity and correct understanding, guarding against distraction, doubt, misinterpretation and the corrupting influences that would prevent the Qur’an’s guidance from taking effect.

translation: Indeed, he has no authority over those who have believed and who rely upon their Lord.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Satan possesses no real dominion over sincere believers whose hearts are rooted in faith and who place their trust in Allah; their reliance on God — expressed by turning to Him, seeking His protection, adhering to His guidance, and resisting whispers — nullifies Satan’s power to compel or mislead them, so his influence is limited to vain suggestions that faith and trust can repel.

translation: His authority is only over those who take him as their guardian and those who are, with him, polytheists.
interpretation: The verse teaches that whatever power or influence evil (often understood as Satan or false authority) appears to have is not universal but depends on human choice: it reaches only those who willingly entrust themselves to it — people who turn away from God, accept that power as their protector, or commit shirk by associating others with God. In short, misguidance and subjugation occur because people choose to follow and ally themselves with that power, not because it has independent, absolute control over all souls.

translation: And when We replace one verse with another — and Allah knows best what He reveals — they say, “You are only a fabricator.” Nay, most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse explains that changes in revealed rulings or the issuance of new guidance are actions of Divine wisdom, not signs of fabrication by the Prophet; those who accuse him misunderstand the nature of gradual or adjusted revelation and reveal their ignorance or obstinacy in judging God’s law rather than acknowledging that Allah, who knows best, may substitute earlier directives with later ones for wisdom and changing circumstances.

translation:
قُلْ نَزَلَهُ رُوحُ الْقُدُسِ مِن رَّبِّكَ بِالْحَقِّ لِيُثَبِّتَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَهُدًى وَبُشْرَىٰ لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ
“Say: It was sent down by the Spirit, the Holy, from your Lord in truth — that He may make firm those who believe, and as a guidance and glad tidings for the Muslims.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur’ān came by means of the trustworthy Divine Messenger (the Spirit, understood as Gabriel) from God, and emphasizes the purpose of that revelation: not merely to convey information but to work inwardly and practically — to strengthen and steady the faith of believers, to serve as a clear moral and spiritual guide, and to bring reassurance and glad tidings to those who submit. In short, it underlines both the divine origin and the transformative, consoling function of the revelation in the lives of the faithful.

translation: And We certainly know that they say, “He is taught only by a human.” The tongue of the one to whom they incline is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue.
interpretation: This verse answers the slander that the Prophet’s knowledge of the Qur’an came from a human teacher. God says He knows their charge and points out its contradiction: the person they cite speaks a non‑Arabic tongue, whereas the Qur’an is manifestly and precisely Arabic. That linguistic fact undermines the accusation — the Qur’an’s idiom, rhetorical mastery and insight into Arab realities could not plausibly have been produced by instruction from a foreign‑language source — and therefore serves as evidence of the Qur’an’s divine origin and of the falsity of those who attribute it to mere human teaching.

translation: Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah—Allah does not guide them, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse conveys that persistent rejection of God’s clear signs (whether the revealed message or evident truths in creation) results in God withdrawing guidance from such people: their stubborn denial hardens their hearts and leaves them stranded spiritually. Guidance is presented as a divine gift that requires receptive faith; when individuals obstinately refuse, the withholding of guidance becomes a just consequence, and they will face the painful repercussions of that persistent rejection.

translation: Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah invent falsehood; it is they who are the liars.
interpretation: The verse teaches that fabricating untruths—whether by falsely ascribing statements to God, twisting revelation, or inventing doctrines to reject clear evidence—is the outcome of rejecting Allah’s signs (the revealed verses and the manifest proofs in creation). It identifies such fabrication as a moral and epistemic failing: unbelief leads people to distort reality to suit their purposes, and this deliberate distortion, not mere error or doubt, is what the Qur’an calls true lying.

translation: Whoever disbelieves in Allah after having believed—except one who is coerced while his heart remains reassured in faith—but whoever willingly opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is the wrath of Allah, and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes coerced denial from voluntary apostasy: outward words or actions under compulsion do not break a person’s accountability if their heart remains firm in belief, whereas a believer who freely and willingly embraces and manifests disbelief bears divine anger and severe consequences. It emphasizes the primacy of inner conviction, moral responsibility for freely chosen rejection of faith, and Allah’s justice in judging intentions and voluntary choices.

translation: That is because they preferred the life of this world over the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse explains a causal relationship: when people knowingly choose the transient gains and comforts of this worldly life as their priority, they cultivate an inner disposition that resists spiritual truth and moral responsibility. Divine guidance requires a receptive, sincere heart; persistent preference for the dunya hardens the will and closes one off to signs and guidance. Thus Allah’s withholding of guidance from such disbelieving people is not arbitrary but the fitting consequence of their settled choice — He allows them to follow the inclinations they have embraced, resulting in further misguidance and loss.

translation: Those are the ones upon whom Allah has set a seal over their hearts and over their hearing and over their eyes; and those are the heedless.
interpretation: The verse teaches that persistent rejection and deliberate turning away from divine guidance can result in a spiritual sealing: God, in His justice, makes the faculties of understanding (heart), receptivity (hearing) and perception (sight) closed to truth. This sealing is both a consequence of people’s own stubbornness and a divine withholding of guidance, so they remain unable or unwilling to grasp signs and reminders and thus remain heedless of what they were warned about.

translation: لا جرم أنهم في الآخرة هم الخاسرون — Undoubtedly, they will be the losers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who persist in disbelief and sinful heedlessness, even if they appear to prosper now, will suffer ultimate loss: deprivation of God’s mercy, the rewards of righteous deeds, and true eternal felicity. ‘Loss’ here is existential and final — it makes any temporary worldly advantage meaningless — and thus the verse urges valuing final accountability and aligning life with what leads to lasting success before God.

translation:
ثم إن ربك للذين هاجروا من بعد ما فتنوا ثم جاهدوا وصبروا إن ربك من بعدها لغفور رحيم
"Then indeed your Lord — for those who emigrated after they had been tested, then strove and were patient — indeed your Lord thereafter is Forgiving, Merciful."
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s pardon and mercy are promised to those whose faith is demonstrated by a clear moral turn: leaving behind a harmful situation for the sake of God (hijra), actively striving in His cause, and enduring hardship with patience. The sequence — being tested, then emigrating, then striving and bearing patiently — shows that sincere change and persevering commitment transform one’s standing before God: past failings are not an obstacle when they are followed by genuine effort and forbearance, and in such cases Divine forgiveness and mercy are assured.

translation: On the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself, and every soul will be fully recompensed for what it did, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse teaches individual accountability and God’s absolute, precise justice: on the Resurrection each person stands alone to answer for their actions—social ties or excuses will not avert the reckoning—and everyone will receive exactly what their deeds merit, with no one being treated unjustly (neither deprived of their due nor punished unfairly).

translation: And Allah sets forth an example: a town that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it in abundance from every direction. But they denied the favours of Allah, so He made them taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing.
interpretation: This verse warns that communal prosperity and security are gifts dependent on gratitude and right conduct; when a people become ungrateful and engage in wrongful behaviour, the blessings they took for granted can be withdrawn and transformed into pervasive hardship—symbolized by a ‘garment’ of hunger and fear—so that the consequences they face are the direct result of their own actions.

translation: And indeed there came to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse warns that when truthful guidance arrives embodied in someone from one’s own community, rejecting it is a culpable, willful act; the phrase “from among them” underscores the messenger’s closeness and sincerity, so their denial is not innocent error but wrongdoing, and Divine punishment follows as just consequence of persistent refusal and injustice — a lesson about responsibility to accept sincere guidance and the moral accountability that follows its persistent rejection.

translation: So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the favor of Allah, if indeed you worship Him.
interpretation: The verse ties rightful living to true worship: believers are required not only to accept what God has made lawful, but to seek what is wholesome and to acknowledge these blessings through gratitude. Genuine worship is shown in practical obedience and thankfulness—choosing lawful, pure means of livelihood and manifesting recognition of God’s providence in one’s actions—so claiming to worship Allah while neglecting gratitude and the ethical use of His provisions is inconsistent with sincere faith.

translation: Only forbidden to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been invoked in the name of any other than Allah. But whoever is forced [by necessity], neither desiring it nor transgressing [its limit]—then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse sets clear dietary prohibitions to safeguard spiritual and communal purity—carrion, blood, pork and meat dedicated to other deities are unlawful—but it immediately qualifies this rule with a principle of necessity: when a person faces real compulsion to preserve life or avoid harm, and does not seek the forbidden thing out of desire nor exceeds what is necessary, the prohibition is lifted and Allah’s mercy covers the concession. The ruling therefore balances strict moral law with practical compassion, making intention and restraint central: lawful exceptions exist in emergencies, but deliberate transgression or excess remains blameworthy.

translation: And do not say about what your tongues describe falsely, “This is lawful and this is forbidden,” inventing a lie against Allah. Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse warns that declaring religious rulings or moral categories by personal whim, idle speech, or falsehood—attributing to God what He has not revealed—is a grave offense. To pronounce something “halal” or “haram” without divine authority or sound knowledge is to fabricate against Allah; such fabrications corrupt guidance, mislead people, and bring spiritual and social ruin. Thus believers must refrain from careless judgments, seek the revealed guidance and verified knowledge, and be humble in making legal or ethical declarations, for those who knowingly ascribe falsehoods to God will not prosper.

translation: A brief enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The phrase warns that the pleasures of this world granted to those who turn away from guidance are transient and insignificant compared with the consequences to come: they enjoy a little here, but in the afterlife they will face severe, enduring punishment. It cautions against being deceived by short-lived material comforts and reminds that true accountability and lasting outcome depend on one's faith and conduct, not on temporary worldly gain.

translation: And as for those who became Jews, We forbade for them what We had not forbidden you before; and We did not wrong them — rather they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse answers a charge that God unfairly deprived them: it teaches that God did not oppress the Jewish people by arbitrarily forbidding lawful things; instead, by introducing extra restrictions, misrepresenting divine rulings, and persisting in disobedience and innovation, they brought harm upon themselves and incurred the consequences of their own wrongful actions.

translation: Then indeed, your Lord — for those who did evil out of ignorance, then repented afterwards and reformed — truly your Lord thereafter is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah’s mercy extends to people whose wrongdoing stemmed from ignorance when they respond with sincere repentance and concrete reform. It highlights that genuine tawbah — remorse for the fault, immediate cessation, making amends where possible, and a firm resolve not to return to the sin — can transform past errors into forgiven deeds under God’s forgiveness and compassion. Thus divine justice is balanced by mercy: mistakes are not eternally held against one who truly turns back and repairs the harm, but this forgiveness presumes real accountability and change rather than casual reliance on God’s grace.

translation: Indeed, Abraham was a nation — devoutly submissive to Allah, upright in faith, and he was not of the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham as an autonomous exemplar whose life embodies pure, inward submission to God rather than conformity to ancestral or social norms. Calling him “a nation” signals that his steadfast obedience (qanūt) and his decisive turning away from idolatry (hanīf) form a complete model of faith for others to follow: a religion rooted in sincere, personal devotion and moral integrity, not in tribal identity or majority practice. Thus the passage emphasizes that true religiosity is defined by sincere monotheism and upright conduct, even if that sets one apart from prevailing communal beliefs.

translation: Grateful for His favors; He chose him and guided him to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse teaches that being thankful for God’s blessings is the fitting human response to divine grace: God, in His bounty, selects and grants guidance to a person, and that gift of guidance must be met with heartfelt gratitude expressed in humble recognition and obedient, steadfast conduct on the straight way. It also implies that guidance and status are gifts from God rather than purely human achievements.

translation: And We gave him in this world a good [portion], and indeed he will be among the righteous in the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse indicates that when God grants someone comfort or success in this life, those blessings—if met with sincere faith and upright conduct—are a sign of divine favor that can lead to acceptance in the Hereafter; worldly good is therefore neither proof of moral failure nor an end in itself, but a trust and a test whose true worth is shown by whether a person remains among the righteous.

translation: Then We revealed to you: “Follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth; he was not of the polytheists.”
interpretation: God instructs the Prophet to adhere to and revive the pure, upright monotheism exemplified by Abraham — a heartfelt turning to God (hanif) that rejects all forms of association and tribal religious compromise. The verse frames Islam as a restoration and continuation of Abraham’s uncorrupted way: genuine submission to God rooted in inner conviction, moral integrity, and exclusive worship, rather than adherence to pagan customs or divided loyalties.

translation: Indeed, the Sabbath was prescribed only for those who differed concerning it; and indeed your Lord will surely judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they used to differ.
