interpretation: The verse indicates that the special ruling about the Sabbath was imposed in response to a community’s disputes and transgressions regarding that ordinance: it became a pointed legal restriction on those who quarreled over and violated it, serving as both a test and a consequence of their behavior. Ultimately, God will be the final arbiter — on the Day of Resurrection He will judge between the parties and settle who was right or wrong in the matters they contested, reminding that human controversies over rites and laws are subordinate to divine judgment.

translation: Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good exhortation, and argue with them in that which is best. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has gone astray from His way, and He is most knowing of the rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse sets out an ethic for calling others to God: prioritize wise, context-sensitive methods and kind, sincere admonition rather than force or contempt, and engage disagreements with calm, respectful, and constructive argumentation aimed at opening hearts not humiliating opponents. It also places the outcomes beyond human control—God alone knows the state of hearts and who will be guided—so the believer’s duty is to attend to the manner and integrity of the invitation, to avoid harshness or arrogance, and to trust God with the result.

translation: And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished; and if you are patient, it is better for the patient.
interpretation: The verse sets a limit on retaliation—any response to harm must be proportionate, forbidding excessive vengeance—and simultaneously commends forbearance as the higher ethical course: choosing patience over exacting equal retribution preserves justice and social order, prevents escalation, and accrues spiritual benefit and divine approval for the one who endures.

translation: And be patient; and your patience is only by Allah. Do not grieve over them and do not be distressed by what they plot.
interpretation: The verse commands steadfast endurance rooted in reliance on God: true patience is a Divine gift, not merely human willpower. It instructs the Prophet (and believers) not to let opponents’ schemes provoke sorrow or anxious turmoil, because their plotting is limited and Allah’s ordinance prevails. Practically this means maintaining inner calm, trust in God’s support, and continuing one’s duty without being consumed by fear or bitterness over others’ machinations.

translation: Indeed, Allah is with those who are conscious of Him (the righteous) and those who do good (the doers of excellence).
interpretation: The verse promises divine companionship — not merely distant approval but active nearness: guidance, support, protection, and strengthening — for people who combine inner God‑consciousness (taqwa) with outward excellence and sincerity in action (ihsan). By linking both states, it teaches that lasting help from God comes when one cultivates a reverent, watchful heart and translates that awareness into upright, exemplary conduct; such a fusion attracts God's assistance in enduring trials, achieving perseverance, and receiving ultimate reward.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Exalted is He who transported His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose precincts We have blessed, that We might show him some of Our signs; truly He is the Hearing, the Seeing.
interpretation: The verse presents the Night Journey as a divinely willed revelationary event whose purpose was not only physical relocation but the disclosure of heavenly signs to strengthen the Prophet’s mission and to locate him within the continuum of prophetic history. By calling the destination “blessed” it ascribes spiritual and historical sanctity to that place and to the prophetic link it represents. The closing affirmation “He is the Hearing, the Seeing” serves as a theological guarantee: God fully perceives the outward occurrence and its inner wisdom, so the miraculous nature and purposive lessons of the journey are anchored in Divine knowledge and authority, inviting trust in God’s testimony beyond ordinary perception.

translation: And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: “Do not take any protector besides Me.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Torah was revealed as a clear moral and spiritual guide and that a central demand of that guidance is exclusive trust and allegiance to God. It warns against elevating anyone or anything—idols, false deities, worldly powers, or presumed intermediaries—to the role of ultimate protector, trustee, or authority. True security, decision, and dependence belong to God alone; making others one’s ‘wakīl’ replaces divine guidance with reliance on created beings and thus leads away from the path indicated by the Scripture.

translation: A progeny whom We carried with Noah; indeed he was a grateful (thankful) servant.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes two truths: God’s mercy in preserving a righteous remnant through Noah’s ark, and the moral quality that marked Noah himself. “A grateful servant” (ʿabdan shākuran) does not mean mere feeling but active, humble thankfulness expressed in steadfast obedience, patience in trial, and continual praise and reliance on God. The description links Divine deliverance with the servant’s grateful disposition, presenting gratitude as both a sign of true faith and a cause of God’s favor and protection.

translation:
وَقَضَيْنَا إِلَىٰ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ فِي الْكِتَابِ لَتُفْسِدُنَّ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَّتَيْنِ وَلَتَعْلُنَّ عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا
"And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: ‘You will surely spread corruption on the earth twice, and you will surely reach a great height (of power/arrogance).’"
interpretation: The verse signals a recurring moral pattern: when a community is granted strength or success it can become proud and unjust, resulting in two major episodes of corruption and dominance among the Children of Israel. The phrase “twice” denotes two distinct historical peaks of worldly power accompanied by wrongdoing, and the warning teaches that worldly elevation without justice and humility leads to divine discipline and eventual humiliation; thus authority is a trust that must be exercised righteously, or it will be removed as a consequence of corruption.

translation: When the first of the two appointed terms came, We sent against you Our servants of great strength; they swept through the dwellings, and it was a promise fulfilled.
interpretation: The verse explains that God’s warning about an initial chastisement was realized when He allowed powerful hostile forces to overpower and penetrate the community’s homes. It teaches that collective moral failure brings real, divinely-permitted consequences: historical defeats and exile are not mere accidents but instruments of God’s judgment and reminders that worldly security and sovereignty are under His control. The fulfilment of the warning underscores accountability, the seriousness of communal corruption, and the need to return to God’s guidance to avoid such outcomes.

translation: Then We turned the assault back upon them for your sake, and We reinforced you with wealth and children, and made you greater in numbers when you marched forth.
interpretation: The verse explains that God overturned the enemy’s intended blow so that it fell upon them instead, and He supplied the believers with material and human reinforcements — wealth, offspring, and greater numbers ready for mobilization. The meaning is that victory and strength in conflict are granted by God’s support: when He wills, He can reverse enemies’ plans and multiply resources and people for His servants, so their success depends on divine aid rather than merely their own effort.

translation: إن أحسنتم أحسنتم لأنفسكم ۖ وإن أسأتم فلها ۚ فإذا جاء وعد الآخرة ليسوءوا وجوهكم وليدخلوا المسجد كما دخلوه أول مرة وليتبروا ما علوا تتبيرا
interpretation: الآية تذكر حقيقة روحية وأخلاقية واحدة: ما يناله الإنسان من خير أو شر يعود عليه بالأساس، وأي تزييف للحق أو استكبار على المسجد أو على المجتمع سيُكشف ويُقابل بالهوان عند الحساب. يوم القيامة تُقلب مقاييس الدنيا—يُبدَل زيف الوجوه بمقتٍ وذل، وتُعاد الناس إلى حالة الدخول الأولى للمسجد من حيث الضعف أو الخزي، وتُهدَم وتُبطل كل مظاهر العلو والرياء التي بنوها؛ فكل مجدٍ دنيوي قائم على الظلم أو الرياء يزول ولا ينفع صاحبه حين يأتي وعد الآخرة.

translation: Perhaps your Lord will have mercy on you; but if you return (to wrongdoing), We will return (to punishment). And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.
interpretation: This statement balances hope and warning: Divine mercy remains possible for those who reform, yet persistence in rejecting guidance will provoke a just response. It urges firmness in faith and repentance by making clear that God's patience is not limitless — turning back to disbelief brings consequences — and that Hell is prepared as an inescapable confinement for those who obstinately reject the truth.

translation: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ وَيُبَشِّرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ الصَّالِحَاتِ أَنَّ لَهُمْ أَجْرًا كَبِيرًا
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن القرآن ليس مجرد نص معرفي بل عامل هادٍ فعّال يقود إلى «الأقوم» — الطريق الأعدل والأقوم أخلاقياً وروحانياً — وما يجعله ناجحاً هو تجسيده في حياة المؤمنين، فالإيمان وحده لا يكمل التأهيل للثمرة الإلهية إلا إذا تجلى في أعمال صالحة مستمرة. البشارة بـ«أجر كبير» تعمل كضمان إلهي لاستمرارية الجهد والصبر على التزام القيم القرآنية، وتدل أيضاً أن المقصود بالهداية قرآناً هو تغيير القلب والسلوك وإقامة عدل واستقامة في المجتمع، لا مجرد اطلاع نظري على النص.

translation:
وَأَنَّ الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآخِرَةِ أَعْتَدْنَا لَهُمْ عَذَابًا أَلِيمًا
"And as for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment."
interpretation: The verse conveys a grave warning: rejection of the Hereafter severs a person from the moral horizon of ultimate accountability, and God — in His knowledge and justice — has reserved a severe chastisement for such denial. It affirms both Divine foreknowledge and the moral consequence that persistent denial of accountability leads to ruin; the punishment is presented as a just response to the spiritual and ethical blindness that disbelief produces.

translation: And man calls for evil as he calls for good, and man has always been hasty.
interpretation: The verse points to a deep tendency in human nature: because our knowledge is limited and our desires immediate, we often pray for or pursue what seems good without discerning its true consequences, and at times, in haste or despair, we even call for things that bring harm. The warning is that hastiness and short-sightedness lead to misjudgment in our wishes and decisions; we must cultivate patience, reflection, and trust in God’s wisdom about what is genuinely beneficial or harmful.

translation: And We have made the night and the day two signs. We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day clear, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. And everything We have explained in detail.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the alternation of night and day is a purposeful divine order designed to serve human life and accountability: by making the day manifest and the night subdued, God provides visible time and opportunity for work, provision-seeking and communal activity, while the regular cycle furnishes a dependable measure for counting years, organizing worship and recording deeds. In this way the cosmic rhythm both facilitates practical needs (sustenance, social organization, calendars) and underpins moral and eschatological responsibility—signs made clear so people can reflect, act and be judged accordingly.

translation: And every human being — We have fastened to him his record (ṭā’irahu) upon his neck; and on the Day of Resurrection We will bring out for him a book which he will find open.
interpretation: The verse teaches that each person is inseparably bound to the consequences of their own deeds: God preserves a record that accompanies the individual like a visible, inescapable sign ('upon his neck'), and on the Day of Judgment that record will be presented as an open book. This emphasizes personal responsibility and divine justice — nothing done is lost or hidden, and people will meet the clear, accountable truth of their actions when their own book is shown.

translation: Read your record. Sufficient against you this Day is your own self as accountant.
interpretation: At the final reckoning each person is confronted with their own documented deeds and cannot shift blame: the self will serve as the decisive witness and reckoner. The command to “read” emphasizes a direct, undeniable confrontation with one’s actions, underscoring personal responsibility and the inevitability and exactness of divine justice.

translation:
من اهتدى فإنما يهتدي لنفسه ۖ ومن ضل فإنما يضل عليها ۚ ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى ۗ وما كنا معذبين حتى نبعث رسولا
"Whoever is guided, then he is guided for the benefit of his own soul; and whoever goes astray, then he goes astray to its detriment. No bearer of a burden will bear the burden of another. And We would not punish until We have sent a messenger."
interpretation: The verse affirms a principle of individual moral responsibility and divine justice: guidance and misguidance are principally the consequences of a person's own choices and affect their own soul; nobody will be held accountable for another's sin, and God does not enact punishment without first sending a messenger to warn and explain — thereby preserving human free will, ensuring fair warning, and making each person answerable for their own conduct.

translation:
وَإِذَا أَرَدْنَا أَنْ نُهْلِكَ قَرْيَةً أَمَرْنَا مُتَّرَفِيهَا فَفَسَقُوا فِيهَا فَحَقَّ عَلَيْهَا الْقَوْلُ فَدَمَّرْنَاهَا تَدْمِيرًا
"And when We intend to destroy a town, We first command its affluent ones, and they act defiantly therein; so the decree becomes due upon it, and We destroy it with complete destruction."
interpretation: The verse teaches that communal ruin often begins with those who possess wealth and influence: when the well‑to‑do misuse their means and lead in open transgression, their example makes the community ripe for divine judgment. The phrase “We command” reflects God’s allowing a trial in which the choices of the affluent are exposed, and “the word becomes due” means that once moral accountability is established by their manifest rebellion, punishment follows inevitably. Thus the passage warns that privilege brings responsibility, and the corruption of leaders or elites precipitates collective destruction.

translation: How many generations did We destroy after Noah. And your Lord is fully aware and all‑seeing of the sins of His servants.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s past punitive actions against corrupt nations are not arbitrary anecdotes but demonstrations of a principle: God knows perfectly what people do—both outward deeds and hidden motives—and His knowledge justifies eventual accountability. The warning of previous destructions is meant to deter persistent wrongdoing and to reassure the faithful that injustice and secret sins are not overlooked; ultimate judgment rests with an omniscient, attentive Lord whose awareness makes moral responsibility genuine and inescapable.

translation: Whoever seeks the immediate (things of this world) — We hasten for him therein whatever We will for whom We please; then We make for him Hell in which he will burn, disgraced and driven away.
interpretation: The verse warns that pursuing only short‑term, worldly gains in preference to God’s guidance can be met, by God’s will, with temporary ease or success — not as approval but as part of His sovereign plan and a test. Such provision can deceive a person into thinking they have God’s favor, yet if it accompanies rejection of faith and right conduct it leads to ultimate humiliation and punishment: the person is cast into Hell ‘madhmūman madhhūrā’ (blamed and driven off). The passage therefore teaches that worldly prosperity is not the criterion of true success; one must measure life by obedience, moral responsibility, and concern for the Hereafter rather than by immediate gratification.

translation: And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he ought while he is a believer — those, their striving is truly appreciated.
interpretation: The verse affirms that genuine faith combined with purposeful, rightly-directed effort toward eternal good will not be lost: ‘striving as it ought’ means exertion with correct intention, method and measure (sincere belief, obedience, patience, righteous deeds and sacrificing immediate gains for the everlasting). “Their striving is appreciated” (mashkūra) indicates divine recognition and reward — such labor is recorded, honored, and compensated by God, even if its full fruits are delayed or hidden.

translation: No — We will extend to both these and those from the bounty of your Lord; and the bounty of your Lord is never forbidden.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Allah’s gifts and provisions are vast and freely bestowed according to His wisdom, not confined to a single group or limited by human notions of entitlement. It reassures that Divine mercy and sustenance can reach different people in different ways, and that God is not stingy or bound by human restrictions in distributing His favors.

translation: Consider how We have favored some of them over others; and for the Hereafter there are higher ranks and greater preferment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly inequalities (wealth, status, abilities) are part of God’s dispensation and not the ultimate measure of a person’s worth. True and lasting superiority lies in the Hereafter—greater ranks and favors there are earned by faith and righteous conduct. Therefore one should neither be prideful because of transient worldly advantage nor despair because of its absence, but should strive for the eternal degrees granted by God through piety and good deeds.

translation: Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.
interpretation: The verse warns that making anything an equal or rival to God — whether idols, other beings, or ultimate trust placed in wealth, desires, or leaders — severs the relationship of dependence and favor with the Divine; as a result, one is left deprived of God’s support and honor. The image of “sitting reproached and forsaken” expresses the spiritual and social outcome of such association: loss of guidance, withdrawal of mercy and protection, and exposure to blame and humiliation in this life and at the reckoning.

translation: And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you show kindness to the parents. If either or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them “uff” (a word of irritation) and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word.
interpretation: This verse teaches that absolute devotion to God coexists with a solemn duty of compassionate care toward parents: even when their age brings weakness, ingratitude, or burdens, believers must not show the slightest contempt or impatience (the terse ‘uff’), nor push them away. Instead they must maintain respectful, gentle, honorable speech and behavior. The command emphasizes both outward conduct and inner disposition—patience, dignity, and mercy toward parents are part of serving God—while setting a clear limit on permissible responses to frustration, replacing harshness with kindness and honor.

translation: And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say, “My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small.”
interpretation: The verse commands believers to show parents profound humility, tenderness, and deference—the metaphor of “lowering the wing” evokes protective, gentle care toward those who raised you. It obliges respectful, patient, compassionate behavior (even if parents are imperfect) and couples that behavior with a heartfelt prayer asking God to grant them mercy comparable to the care they gave in childhood, linking moral duty (gratitude and gentle conduct) with supplication for their well‑being.

translation: Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then He is, to those who turn back (in repentance), Most Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse reminds believers that only God fully knows hidden intentions, so outward appearances cannot substitute for inner sincerity. It therefore urges continual self-correction: pursue genuine righteousness, and when you err return to God in sincere repentance — for He is especially forgiving toward those who repeatedly turn back to Him — while also warning against self-deception and judgment of others based on externals.

translation: And give the near of kin his due, and the poor and the wayfarer; and do not squander wastefully.
interpretation: This command frames giving as a disciplined moral obligation: one must prioritize the rights of relatives and the vulnerable rather than indiscriminate or showy largesse. Caring for kin secures social bonds and justice, supporting the needy and travelers preserves communal welfare, and the prohibition of prodigality warns that even charitable acts lose moral value when they become wasteful or undermine one’s own responsibilities. The balance demanded is between generous support for legitimate claimants and prudent stewardship of resources so that obligations are met and harm avoided.

translation: Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse links extravagant, irresponsible squandering of resources with the moral character of the devils: such behavior reflects the same ingratitude, excess and rebellion that characterize Satan. Calling squanderers “brothers of the devils” asserts a likeness of disposition and consequence (harm to self and society), while describing Satan as “kafūr” (extremely ungrateful/denying) underscores that wastefulness stems from failure to acknowledge God’s blessings and to honor one’s duties; the practical implication is to practice grateful, responsible stewardship of what God grants and to avoid the selfish excesses that lead one toward spiritual ruin.

translation: And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle (or gracious) word.
interpretation: The verse counsels that when one must withdraw from people — whether because of their rejection, corruption, or to protect one’s own relationship with God — the distancing should be coupled with gentleness in speech. Retreating for the sake of Allah does not permit harshness; rather, one should remain courteous and conciliatory so as to preserve dignity, keep the door open for guidance, and trust in the mercy one seeks from the Lord.

translation:
وَلَا تَجْعَلْ يَدَكَ مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ وَلَا تَبْسُطْهَا كُلَّ الْبَسْطِ فَتَقْعُدَ مَلُومًا مَحْسُورًا
“And do not make your hand chained to your neck (i.e., be miserly), nor stretch it out with all force (i.e., be extravagant), lest you sit down blamed and destitute.”
interpretation: The verse counsels financial and moral moderation by warning against two harmful extremes. The image of a hand ‘chained to the neck’ criticizes parsimony that withholds rightful support from others and from one’s duties, choking social and spiritual obligations; the image of stretching the hand ‘to the utmost’ warns against reckless prodigality that exhausts resources and leads to reproach and ruin. The proper path is measured generosity — giving according to means while preserving what is needed for one’s responsibilities — so that one neither becomes a source of oppression through hoarding nor falls into shameful want through wasteful excess.

translation: Indeed, your Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]. Indeed He is, concerning His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah distributes sustenance by His wisdom: He can broaden provision for some and limit it for others, not out of caprice but in a manner that suits His knowledge of each person’s inner states and outward needs. The pairing of “bast” (expansion) and “qadr” (measurement) indicates that abundance and restriction are both measured, purposeful realities that serve tests, trials, moral development, and the functioning of social responsibility. Because God is “khabeer” (fully informed of realities) and “baseer” (observing conditions), apparent inequalities are not evidence of divine neglect or injustice; rather they occur within God’s comprehensive awareness and plan. The implication for the believer is to balance trust in divine wisdom with responsible effort and to respond to others’ differing provisions with gratitude, patience, and generosity rather than envy or despair.

translation: And do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for them and for you. Indeed, killing them is a great sin.
interpretation: The verse condemns the practice of killing children born into hardship and frames it as both a moral crime and a failure of trust in God's provision: economic fear does not excuse injustice against the innocent, and believers are urged to rely on God's sustaining care rather than commit a grave transgression against human life.

translation: And do not come near zina (adultery or fornication); indeed, it is a shameful deed and an evil way.
interpretation: The command not merely forbids the act but warns against anything that leads to it—intentions, situations, and behaviors that make transgression likely. Calling zina “a shameful deed” and “an evil way” indicates both its moral corruption and its practical harms: it damages trust and families, spreads injustice and social disorder, and pulls people away from upright conduct and God-consciousness. Thus the verse enjoins preventive measures (guarding the gaze, modesty, lawful relationships, avoiding seclusion or temptation) and a societal stance that protects dignity and social order, aiming to preserve individuals’ spiritual and communal well‑being.

translation:
وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ ۗ وَمَنْ قُتِلَ مَظْلُومًا فَقَدْ جَعَلْنَا لِوَلِيِّهِ سُلْطَانًا فَلَا يُسْرِفْ فِي الْقَتْلِ ۖ إِنَّهُ كَانَ مَنْصُورًا
"And do not kill the soul which Allah has made sacred, except by right. And whoever is killed unjustly—we have given his heir authority [to demand retribution]; so let him not exceed bounds in taking life; indeed he will be supported."
interpretation: The verse establishes that human life is a trust from God and must not be taken except under lawful, measured circumstances (such as a just legal penalty, legitimate self-defence, or other divinely sanctioned exceptions). When a wrongful killing occurs, the family of the victim is granted a legal and moral standing to seek redress (retribution, pardon, or compensation), but that authority is limited: vengeance must be proportional and restrained. The law thus balances the private right to justice with a clear prohibition on excess, preventing cycles of revenge and asserting that true justice operates within divinely ordered limits—those who act within those limits are under God’s protection and support.

translation: And do not approach the property of the orphan except in that which is best, until he reaches maturity. And fulfill the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned (or held accountable).
interpretation: The verse frames the orphan’s wealth as a trust that demands restraint, care, and fiduciary responsibility: guardians and those in charge may not exploit or treat it as their own but must manage or use it only in ways that truly benefit the orphan and only until he attains maturity. By immediately coupling this with the command to “fulfill the covenant,” the text generalizes the ethic of trustworthiness to all promises, contracts and custodial duties — stressing that honoring trusts is a core moral duty and that every broken or fulfilled covenant will be held to account before God. Practically, this obliges transparency, lawful fair treatment, and accountability in all relations where one is entrusted with another’s rights or property.

translation: And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance. That is better and best in outcome.
interpretation: The verse enjoins absolute honesty and equity in dealings: use accurate measures and impartial standards literally in trade and figuratively in all judgments and obligations. Doing so is morally superior and brings the best results — harmonious social relations, trust, and righteous reckoning before God — for ‘أحسن تأويلا’ indicates that upright fairness yields the truest and most beneficial outcome in this world and the next.

translation: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart — all of those will be questioned about.
interpretation: The verse warns against acting, judging or spreading information without proper knowledge, and reminds that our faculties — what we hear, what we see and what we intend in our hearts — carry moral responsibility before God; therefore one must verify, restrain careless speech and sight, and purify intentions, because each sensory impression and inner disposition will be held accountable.

translation: And do not walk upon the earth with arrogance. Indeed, you will never pierce the earth, nor will you attain the height of the mountains.
interpretation: The verse is a moral admonition against arrogance and ostentation: human grandeur is illusory and powerless. Striding proudly through life, looking down on others or claiming exaggerated importance, does not alter the created order nor elevate one above natural limits. True dignity is found in humility, restraint and just conduct; arrogance only blinds a person to their dependence on God and leads to oppression and moral decline.

translation: كلُّ ذلك كانَ، عِندَ رَبِّكَ، شيئًا سيئًا مكروهًا.
interpretation: الآية تصف أن الأعمال والأحوال المشار إليها ليست مجرد سيئات في نظر الناس بل هي محقَّقة الكراهة والرفض عند الله؛ أي أن قيمتها الأخلاقية ضارة ومرفوضة إلهيًا، فلا يُقاس قبولها بما يظنّه البشر من نفع أو نجاة بل بحكم الله الذي يراها شرًّا ويقابلها بالإنكار والجزاء.

translation: ذَٰلِكَ مِمَّا أَوْحَىٰ إِلَيْكَ رَبُّكَ مِنَ الْحِكْمَةِ ۗ وَلَا تَجْعَل مَعَ اللَّهِ إِلَٰهًا آخَرَ فَتَلِقَىٰ فِي جَهَنَّمَ مَلُومًا مَدْحُورًا
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن ما وُحِيَ به إلى النبي هو حكمة إلهية تُلزِم القبول والعمل، وتُشدِّد على مركزية التوحيد: عدم إشراك شيء مع الله. تحذيرها من الشرك ليس مجرّد تهديد شعري بل بيان لنتيجة حقيقية ومُحْكَمَة—الضياع الأبدي في النار مع ذِمّة واندِحار—مما يبيّن أن إشراك غير الله يقطع رابط الإنسان بالخالق ويُفضي إلى هلاك روحي وأخلاقي واجتماعي. الآية إذًا تجمع بين إثبات سلطة الوحي كمرشد للحياة وبين دعوة عملية للثبات على التوحيد، لأن مخالفة ذلك تُفضي إلى الخزي والنبذ والعقاب.

translation: Did your Lord appoint for you sons and take from the angels daughters? Indeed you utter a grave (or monstrous) statement.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the belief that God can have offspring or familial relations like humans—especially the pre-Islamic claim that angels are God’s daughters. It asserts God’s absolute transcendence and unity (tawḥīd) by showing that ascribing human-like lineage or gender to the Divine is theologically and conceptually absurd, a serious and offending claim that misconstrues the Creator–creation relation and diminishes divine majesty.

translation: And indeed We have set forth in this Qur'an (its message) so that they may remember, yet it only increases them in aversion.
interpretation: God is saying that the Qur'an has been made clear and arranged to awaken memory, conscience and guidance in people, but clarity by itself does not guarantee acceptance: for many it only strengthens their repulsion and drive to turn away. The verse teaches that divine guidance is offered openly and meant to transform hearts, yet whether it succeeds depends on people’s inner states — pride, attachment to prior commitments, or hostile disposition can make the clear message provoke rejection rather than acceptance.

translation: Say, ‘If there were gods with Him, as they claim, then they would surely seek a way to the Possessor of the Throne,’
interpretation: The verse rejects polytheism by pointing out that any supposed gods would themselves have to seek access, favor, or authority from the true Lord of the Throne; they would not be independent powers. This shows the incoherence of attributing divinity to others and affirms God’s absolute sovereignty — He alone is the one who grants approach, intercession, and control.

translation: Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they say—exalted in greatness.
interpretation: The phrase affirms God’s absolute transcendence: every claim, misattribution, or description that people make about Him—whether ascribing partners, offspring, likeness to creation, or other false notions—is beneath His majesty and cannot touch His essence; human words cannot encompass or define the Divine, who is exalted far above all that is said about Him.

translation: The seven heavens and the earth and all who are in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing but celebrates His praise; yet you do not comprehend their glorification. Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Oft‑Forgiving.
interpretation: All of creation continually manifests God’s perfection and praise through its ordered existence and functioning; this ‘tasbih’ is often nonverbal and beyond human perception, so people may fail to recognize these signs. The verse therefore calls for humility before the signs of God and reassures that, despite human ignorance and shortcomings, God is patient and merciful, withholding immediate punishment and offering forgiveness.

translation: And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier.
interpretation: The verse means that at the proclamation of the Qur'an God interposes an unseen partition between the Prophet (or the reciter) and those who deny the Last Day: their ears and hearts are veiled so the message does not penetrate them. This “hidden barrier” both protects the reciter from the corrupting influence and hostility of the deniers and signifies a divine sealing of the deniers’ faculties as a consequence of persistent rejection, rendering them incapable of receiving guidance from the recited revelation.

translation: And We have placed coverings over their hearts so that they do not understand it, and deafness in their ears; and when your Lord is mentioned alone in the Qur'an, they turn away in aversion.
interpretation: The verse describes a moral-spiritual blockage: persistent rejection and hardness of heart lead to veils ('akinnah') and a dullness ('waqra') that prevent people from perceiving and receiving guidance. ’When your Lord is mentioned alone’ refers to clear, uncompromising proclamation of God and His message; those attached to falsehood or worldly desires shrink back in repulsion. The passage thus portrays both the internal state produced by stubborn denial and the consequence that God allows — a protective covering and deafness — which manifest as willful turning away rather than open engagement with the truth.

translation: We are best acquainted with what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they confer secretly; when the wrongdoers say, "You follow nothing but a bewitched man."
interpretation: The statement underscores that God knows both public words and private counsels of those who reject the messenger; labeling him “bewitched” is exposed as a vain tactic of slander and self-justification. Rather than proving the message false, that secret accusation reveals the speakers’ hostility, envy, and refusal to engage with the truth—things that cannot be concealed from Divine knowledge and for which they will be held accountable.

translation: Observe how they set forth parables for you; they have gone astray and cannot find a way.
interpretation: The verse calls the Prophet’s attention to how opponents invent and offer analogies about the message. Those analogies, stemming from rejection and misplaced reasoning, do not illuminate truth but instead betray their misguided state; their attempts to explain or oppose the revelation only expose their spiritual confusion and inability to find the straight path.

translation: وقالوا: "أإذا كنا عظامًا ورفاتًا، أإنا لمبعوثون خلقًا جديدًا؟"
interpretation: الآية تبرز اعتراض المكذبين المبتنين على المشاهدة الحسية — أنهم يرون الجسد متحللاً إلى عظم وتراب فَيستخلصون استحالة البعث — وتؤكد بالعكس أن الانحلال المادي ليس قياسًا على قدرة الخالق؛ فالله الذي خلقنا أولًا قادر على إحيائنا مرة أخرى أو إحداث صورة جديدة منا، والآية تذكِّر بأن البعث أمر إلهي يتجاوز قيود الفهم والحدود المادية التي يراها الناس.

translation: Say, “Be you stones or iron.”
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke: the Prophet is told to challenge those who demand miraculous signs by saying that even if they could turn him into inert matter (stones or iron) it would not undermine God’s power or excuse their refusal. The verse exposes the impotence of human claims and false deities versus God’s sole authority over creation, life and resurrection, and thus rebukes those who insist on visible wonders instead of accepting the message.

translation: Or [is it] a creation of what grows in your breasts? They will say, “Who will restore us?” Say, “The One who produced you the first time.” Then they will cast down their heads toward you and say, “When will that be?” Say, “Perhaps it will be near.”
interpretation: The verse confronts scepticism by pointing to God’s demonstrated power: those who doubt resurrection do so from limited imagination or pride, yet the same Lord who brought human life into being once can bring it back. The mocking questioners expose their incredulity, but are reminded that the reality they deny is under divine control and may arrive suddenly—so the passage calls for humility before God’s sovereignty and urgent readiness for return and accountability.

translation: The Day He will call you, and you will respond to Him with praise, and you will think that you had only stayed a little.
interpretation: At the Resurrection God’s summons will expose the truth of divine sovereignty so that people instinctively glorify Him and see how fleeting their worldly life was; the verse therefore teaches that earthly pursuits and perceptions of time are ephemeral and urges humility and preparation for the eternal accountability that will make this life seem negligibly brief.

translation: And say to My servants that which is best; indeed Satan incites between them. Indeed Satan is to man a manifest enemy.
interpretation: God commands believers to adopt speech that is beautiful and constructive as a means of preventing and healing social rifts, because the primary method by which Satan undermines human relations is to sow discord through hurtful words, insults, and provocations. The verse thus warns that many quarrels and enmities are not merely human failings but the result of a deliberate, visible strategy by Satan to divide people; resisting that strategy requires self-restraint of the tongue, choosing kind or silence over retaliation, and cultivating words that restore dignity and harmony so communities remain united in obedience to God.

translation: Your Lord knows you best; if He wills, He will have mercy on you, or if He wills, He will punish you. And We did not send you over them as a guardian.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s exclusive knowledge and sovereignty over people’s fate — mercy and punishment occur by His will — and reminds that the Prophet’s role is limited to conveying the message, not to control, protect, or enforce outcomes for others; therefore responsibility and ultimate judgment lie with God, and people must respond to the guidance rather than expect the Prophet to alter divine decrees on their behalf.

translation: And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth. And We have certainly favored some of the prophets over others; and We gave David the Zabur (the Psalms).
interpretation: The verse emphasizes God's exclusive, comprehensive knowledge of all creatures and events, reminding listeners that ultimate appraisal belongs to Him alone. It explains that prophets were assigned differing ranks and gifts by divine wisdom—not as a basis for human arrogance or envy—but to suit each prophet’s mission and role; the specific mention that David was given the Zabur illustrates how God equips chosen servants with particular revelations and means of guidance appropriate to their responsibilities, so believers should accept divinely ordained differences as just and purposeful.

translation: Say, “Call upon those whom you claim besides Him; they do not possess the power to remove harm from you nor to change it.”
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to challenge the worshippers of other deities by inviting them to invoke their chosen beings and see that those beings cannot avert calamity or alter people’s condition. It emphasizes that ultimate control over harm, relief, and the course of events belongs to God alone; supposed intermediaries or partners have no real agency to protect, cure, or redirect fate. The intended lesson is theological and practical: reliance, supplication, and worship must be directed to God, since turning to powerless idols or intermediaries is futile and cannot change one’s plight.

translation: Those whom they call upon seek a means to their Lord — which of them is nearest — and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is to be dreaded.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the beings people invoke as intermediaries are themselves seeking nearness to God, hoping His mercy and fearing His chastisement; this undercuts any claim to independent divinity and shows that access to God and His mercy belong ultimately to Him alone. It is therefore a warning to abandon trust in idols or supposed intercessors and to turn directly to Allah with sincere faith and reverence, mindful that His punishment is real and to be feared.

translation: And there is no town but We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection or punish it with a severe punishment; that was recorded in an inscribed Book.
interpretation: The verse affirms the inevitability of divine justice: communities that persist in disbelief and corruption will not escape consequences—either they are removed in this world or held to account on the Day of Judgment—and this certainty, documented in the Divine Decree, is meant as a warning to turn from wrongdoing and not rely on transient worldly power.

translation: And We did not withhold [sending] the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she‑camel as a manifest sign, but they wronged her. And We send the signs only as a warning.
interpretation: The verse explains that divine signs and miracles are not meant to coerce belief but to expose the condition of people’s hearts and to warn them. Because preceding nations repeatedly rejected clear proofs, such visible signs function as tests whose violation reveals arrogance and injustice (as in Thamud’s mistreatment of the she‑camel). Therefore God sends signs primarily to remove excuses and to warn — to make the truth evident so that acceptance is a free, responsible choice and rejection carries moral and consequential accountability.

translation: واذْ قُلْنَا لَكَ: إنَّ رَبَّكَ أَحَاطَ بِالنَّاسِ. وما جَعَلْنَا الرُّؤْيا الَّتِي أَرَيْنَاكَ إلا فِتْنَةً لِلنَّاسِ، وَالشَّجَرَةَ المَلْعُونَةَ فِي القرآنِ. وَنُخَوِّفُهُمْ فَما يَزيدُهُمْ إلا طُغْيانًا كبيرًا.
interpretation: الآية تهدئ النبي وتوضّح حكمة ما أُري له من رؤى والذكر التأديبي: أن ما يُعرض من رؤى وتحذيرات ومثال الشجرة «الملعونة» وضع في القرآن كابتلاء وبيان لتحقّق قلوب الناس، لا كوسيلة لإكراه الناس على الإيمان. فالمقصود أن الله محيط بعلم الناس وتصرفاتهم، وأن الوسائل التحذيرية قد تُميّز المؤمنين عن المستكبرين، لكنها لا تُجدي مع من عزّت عليه الطغيان والبغض؛ تلك الفئة تزداد تثبيتًا في معصيتهم رغم التحذير، وعلينا أن نفهم أن الاختبار والإنذار جزآن من تدبير الله لابتلاء الأنفس وبيان مواقفها.

translation: And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he said, "Shall I prostrate to one You created from clay?"
interpretation: The verse exposes Iblis’s pride and contempt: his refusal is not about a physical fact but about valuing his own perceived purity above obedience to God. It teaches that God’s honor upon Adam derived from divine choice—knowledge and role—not from material origin, and that true dignity before God is shown by submission to His command. Thus arrogance that elevates created distinctions over divine authority leads to rebellion and ruin.

translation: قال: «أرأيتك هذا الذي كرَّمتَ علىَّ؟ لئن أخرَتَّني إلى يوم القيامة لأحتنكنَّ ذريَّته إلا قليلاً»
interpretation: الكلام يُظهر غيظ الحسد وإصرار العدو على نسج سياسة لإضلال البشر عبر الأجيال؛ نواياه ليست عابرة بل منهجية تهدف إلى اقتناص النفس البشرية وإفساد السلالة، بينما عبارة «إلا قليلاً» تبيّن أن قدرته واسعة لكنها ليست مطلقة، وأن النجاة والثبات على الحق منتجع من رحمة وحماية إلهية وكذلك من يقظة الإنسان وإصراره على الصلاح.

translation: He said, “Go, and whoever of them follows you — then indeed Hell will be your recompense, an abundant recompense.”
interpretation: The verse exposes Satan’s vindictive strategy: he commissions spreading misguidance and regards the sharing of others’ damnation as his ‘reward.’ Calling the torment a “جزاء موفور” (abundant, fully deserved recompense) emphasizes that the punishment will be ample and fitting for the wrongdoing; thus the passage warns that succumbing to satanic temptation does not bring advantage but only multiplies ruin, and that Satan’s apparent triumph is in truth the expansion of collective loss and retribution.

translation:
وَاسْتَفِزَّ مِمَّنِ اسْتَطَعْتَ مِنْهُمْ بِصَوْتِكَ وَأَجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِمْ بِخَيْلِكَ وَرِجْلِكَ وَشَارِكْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْأَوْلَادِ وَعِدْهُمْ ۚ وَمَا يَعِدُهُمُ السَّيْطَانُ إِلَّا غُرُورًا
"Rouse against them whomever you can with your voice; and bring upon them your cavalry and your foot-soldiers; and share with them in wealth and children, and make them promises. And Satan promises them nothing but deception."
interpretation: The verse warns that opponents of truth — aided by satanic influence — mobilize people through stirring speech, show of force, and material inducements (wealth and offspring) and by promising them safety or gain. Its lesson is not to glorify those outward tactics or to be seduced by worldly promises: such inducements are ultimately delusive (غرور) and lead people away from what is right. Therefore believers must see through rhetoric, resist corrupt bargains, prepare prudently for justice and defense, and place their trust in God rather than in the empty promises of Satan or those he inspires.

translation: Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them; and sufficient is your Lord as a guardian (disposer of affairs).
interpretation: This verse teaches that Iblis (and satanic whispering generally) has no coercive dominion over those who truly belong to God: his influence is limited to suggestion, not compulsion. “My servants” denotes those who are committed to God through faith, seeking His guidance and protection; for them, divine guardianship is decisive. By declaring “your Lord is sufficient as a guardian,” the verse reassures believers that God alone manages their affairs, repels and restrains the enemy’s schemes, and will bring about justice and guidance — so reliance on God, sincere obedience, and seeking refuge in Him neutralize the apparent power of evil.

translation: Your Lord is the One who propels the ships for you through the sea so that you may seek of His bounty; indeed He has been, toward you, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the practical means by which people obtain sustenance and opportunity (exemplified by ships crossing the sea) are not merely human achievements but manifestations of God’s facilitating mercy: He provides the conditions, forces, and openings that enable travel, trade and provision. Recognizing this should engender humility and gratitude, a reliance on God alongside using available means responsibly, rather than prideful self-sufficiency.

translation: And when distress touches you at sea, you call upon Him alone; then when He brings you safely to land, you turn away — and man is, indeed, ever ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse criticizes the habitual fickleness of people who recognize God’s power only in moments of acute need because all other supposed helpers fail them in crisis; once safety is restored they revert to neglect, reliance on false supports, or forgetfulness. It is an admonition to constant gratitude and steadfast trust in the One whose help is real, rather than situational, and a reminder that true faith should not be contingent on hardship alone.

translation: Do you feel secure that the earth will not be made to swallow you up from one side, or that He will not send against you a shower (of stones), and then you will find for yourselves no protector?
interpretation: The verse warns against complacent self‑sufficiency and arrogance: apparent worldly safety is fragile and contingent on God’s will. Those who trust in their material position or reject divine authority may be overturned suddenly—by natural catastrophe or divine chastisement—and then will have no advocate to save them. The passage calls for humility, awareness of God’s power, and reliance on Him rather than on transient worldly means.

translation:
أَمْ أَمِنْتُمْ أَنْ يُعِيدَكُمْ فِيهِ تَارَةً أُخْرَىٰ فَيُرْسِلَ عَلَيْكُمْ قَاصِفًا مِنَ الرِّيحِ فَيُغْرِقَكُمْ بِمَا كَفَرْتُمْ ثُمَّ لَا تَجِدُوا لَكُمْ عَلَيْنَا بِهِ تَبِيعًا
“Or do you feel secure that He will return you to it a second time, and then send against you a violent wind and drown you because of your disbelief? Then you will find no ransom for yourselves against Us.”
interpretation: The verse warns against complacency after a reprieve: apparent safety is a test, not a guarantee. Those who persist in denial or hypocrisy, assuming mercy will be indefinitely renewed, risk invoking a decisive, divine punishment from which no bribery, negotiation, or intercession can save them. It emphasizes that repeated rejection of God’s guidance can lead to an irreversible outcome rather than endless forbearance.

translation: And We have certainly honored the children of Adam, and We carried them on land and sea, and provided them with good things, and preferred them over many of those We created, with [definite] preference.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God elevated human beings by granting them dignity and faculties (intellect, speech, senses), means of mobility and livelihood (‘carrying them on land and sea’), and lawful, wholesome provisions. This honor is a divine bestowal that places humans in a privileged position among creatures—enabling moral and spiritual development—but it is a gift tied to responsibility and accountability before God, not an inherent or unconditional superiority.

translation: The Day We will call each people with their leader. Then whoever is given his record in his right hand — those will read their record, and they will not be wronged even as much as a thread.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on Resurrection God will summon every community together with the leaders who guided or represented them so that witness and responsibility are clear. Receiving the record in the right hand is a Qur’anic symbol of divine acceptance and salvation: those people will read their deeds with certainty and rejoice in the just outcome. The phrase “not wronged even as much as a thread” emphasizes God’s perfect justice and precision — no righteous act will be overlooked and no one will be deprived or punished unjustly; each soul receives exactly what it earned.

translation: And whoever is blind in this [life]—he will be blind in the Hereafter and more astray in way.
interpretation: Here “blind” is metaphorical for spiritual insensitivity or a heart closed to God’s guidance. The verse means that persistent refusal or heedlessness toward truth in this world reflects a hardness of heart that will not be remedied automatically after death: such a person will enter the Hereafter deprived of spiritual vision and deviating even further from the right path. It underscores human responsibility — guidance requires a receptive heart, and continued rejection in this life leads to a graver, more irreversible loss in the next.

translation: And indeed they were about to try to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you, so that you might invent against Us something else; and if they had taken you as a close friend...
interpretation: The verse explains that the Prophet’s opponents plotted to lead him away from God’s revelation—pressuring him to fabricate a different message to serve their interests—and even contemplated making him their partisan to secure his allegiance. This shows both the malicious intent of the disbelievers to corrupt the message for their own ends and, implicitly, the divine safeguarding of the Prophet’s honesty and the integrity of the revelation.

translation: And if We had not made you firm, you would surely have almost inclined toward them a little.
interpretation: God is saying that without His strengthening the Prophet’s heart and resolve, the Prophet might have been lightly swayed toward the people in question—showing sympathy, softening his stance, or being influenced by their arguments. The phrase “a little” stresses that even a seemingly small inclination can be dangerous if not checked; divine support prevented a minor tendency from becoming compromise. The passage teaches that human leaders and servants of truth are naturally vulnerable to subtle concessions, and they need God’s steadiness, reassurance, and guidance to preserve firmness in their mission.

translation: If We were to make you taste a double portion of the trials of life and a double portion of the trials of death, then you would find for yourself no helper against Us.
interpretation: The verse intends to highlight God’s absolute power and human helplessness before His decree: were God to intensify both the hardships experienced in this life and the severity (or recurrence) of death’s torment, no one — no ally, protector, or intercessor — could avert or lessen that divine chastisement. It is a warning against trusting in apparent protectors or denying God’s authority, and a reminder of our total dependence on His will and mercy.

translation: And indeed they were about to try to provoke you out of the land to drive you from it, and they would not have remained in your stead except for a little.
interpretation: The verse reassures that hostile schemes to unsettle the Prophet and his community — to provoke them into abandoning their rightful place or mission — are both malicious and ultimately short‑lived. It teaches reliance on God rather than reacting to provocations, patience in the face of plots, and the conviction that transient gains made by aggressors cannot displace what is ordained and sustained by divine support.

translation: It is the established way (sunnah) of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers; and you will never find any change in Our way.
interpretation: God is declaring that the pattern by which He has dealt with earlier messengers—the sending of guidance, the testing of communities, and the ultimate outcome (support for the truthful and accountability for persistent rejection)—is a fixed, divine ordinance. This 'sunnah' is not subject to alteration or exception: the principles and consequences set by God remain constant, so one should expect the same divine procedure to apply rather than any change or special dispensation.

translation: Establish prayer from the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and [recite] the Qur'an of dawn. Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.
interpretation: The verse enjoins regular observance of the prescribed prayers through the day and night and singles out the dawn recitation as specially 'witnessed' — meaning it is observed and recorded by the angels (and accepted by God). By highlighting Fajr as continually witnessed, the text stresses its spiritual importance: performing the dawn prayer is a visible sign of sincere submission, opens the believer to divine attention at a liminal, spiritually charged hour, and carries a distinct testimony and reward before God and the heavenly witnesses.

translation: And from [part of] the night, then pray with it an extra (prayer) for you; perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.
interpretation: The verse enjoins rising in part of the night for voluntary worship (tahajjud) as a means of spiritual discipline and nearness to God; it links such devoted, voluntary prayer to divine elevation. The phrase “maqam mahmud” is understood here as a unique, commendable rank granted by God—commonly interpreted as the honored position of praise and recognition granted to the Prophet (and, by implication, to those who sincerely strive), especially on the Day of Judgment—showing that extra, sincere devotion can lead to special honor, closeness to God, and intercessory status by God’s leave.

translation:
وَقُل رَّبِّ أَدْخِلْنِي مُدْخَلَ صِدْقٍ وَأَخْرِجْنِي مُخْرَجَ صِدْقٍ وَاجْعَل لِّي مِنْ لَدُنْكَ سُلْطَانًا نَصِيرًا
"And say: My Lord, admit me by a truthful (sincere/upright) entrance and let me depart by a truthful exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority (a decisive, victorious help)."
interpretation: The speaker asks God to make every beginning and ending of his affairs free from falsehood, hypocrisy, and error—so that his entry into situations (tasks, communities, stages of life) and his departure from them are marked by sincerity, integrity, and truth. He also implores a direct, decisive assistance from God—an empowered support or authority that vindicates the right, protects him from opposition, and enables him to carry out what is right. In short, it is a plea for moral uprightness in action and for spiritual and practical divine backing to ensure truth prevails.

translation: And say, “The Truth has come and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.”
interpretation: The verse functions as both a proclamation and a theological principle: divine guidance (al‑Haq) once revealed establishes a reality that falsehood cannot endure. The verb zahq conveys not merely disappearance but being driven away, crushed or snuffed out — falsehood is inherently transient and self‑defeating when confronted by truth. Practically, this reassures believers that unjust ideas, corrupt systems, and vain claims, however imposing they seem, will ultimately collapse; it therefore calls for steadfastness in proclaiming and living by the revealed truth, trusting that truth’s triumph is inevitable and that patience and clarity, not accommodation of falsehood, are the proper response.

translation: And We send down of the Qur’an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, but it increases the wrongdoers only in loss.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’an functions as therapeutic guidance and compassionate aid for those who accept it: its teachings cure spiritual maladies (doubt, moral corruption, despair), restore the heart to faith and upright conduct, and bring consolation and communal well‑being. For those who persist in injustice and rejection, however, the same clear truth brings no benefit — their refusal only multiplies their culpability and loss, because they close themselves off from the very remedy and moral correction the scripture offers.

translation: And when We bestow favor upon man he turns away and distances himself; and when evil touches him, he becomes despairing.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a moral-spiritual failing: many people let blessings make them heedless and withdraw from gratitude and duty, yet when calamity strikes they lose patience and hope. It is a critique of faith that depends on circumstances and an implicit call to cultivate steadfast gratitude, patience, and trust in God regardless of fortune.

translation: Say, “Everyone acts according to his own disposition, and your Lord knows best who is most rightly guided.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that people's outward behavior flows from their inward dispositions—belief, understanding, upbringing and inclinations—so each person follows the likeness of what is within. At the same time it reminds believers that ultimate knowledge of who is truly guided belongs to God alone, who sees the heart and its sincerity; therefore our duty is sincere effort in conveying and living the truth while leaving the final judgment of guidance to Allah’s all‑knowing wisdom.

translation: And they ask you about the soul. Say: “The soul is from the affair (command) of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that the rūḥ (soul/spirit) belongs to God’s domain—its origin, essence and working are matters of Divine command and not fully accessible to human investigation. By instructing the Prophet to answer this way, God places a boundary around speculative metaphysics: humans may study effects and symptoms, but the inner reality of the soul is ultimately sustained, bestowed and taken by God’s will. The reminder “you have been given of knowledge except a little” calls for epistemic humility—accepting revealed truth about life and death, recognizing God’s sovereignty over existence, and avoiding arrogant claims of complete understanding where only Divine knowledge is decisive.

translation: And if We willed, We could surely remove that which We revealed to you; then you would not find for yourself, concerning it, any protector against Us.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute authority over revelation: He could withdraw the message given to the Prophet, and if He did there would be no human defender or advocate able to intercede for him before God about that removal. It emphasizes that the reality, preservation and authority of the revelation depend solely on God’s will, not on human support or argument, and thus warns those who challenge or demand to control divine signs.

translation: Except as a mercy from your Lord; indeed His bounty toward you was great.
interpretation: The verse teaches that whatever benefit, protection, authority or relief the Prophet experienced was not from his own merit but purely a gift of God’s mercy; Allah’s generosity toward him was immense, so one must ascribe all good to Divine grace, respond with gratitude and humility, and avoid claiming personal credit for blessings that are ultimately bestowed by God.

translation: Say, “If mankind and jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur’an, they could not produce the like of it, even if some of them were helpers to others.”
interpretation: The verse asserts the Qur’an’s inimitability: no amount of combined human and jinn effort can reproduce its linguistic eloquence, coherence, depth of meaning, prophetic knowledge, moral guidance, and spiritual effect. By framing this as an open challenge—one that remains unmet even with full cooperation—it points to the Qur’an’s status as a revelation beyond created capacities and serves as evidence of its divine origin and the truth of the prophetic message.

translation: And indeed We have presented to the people in this Qur’an from every kind of parable; yet most of the people refused [to accept] except disbelief.
interpretation: The verse conveys that God, out of wisdom and mercy, furnished the Qur’an with a wide variety of examples and analogies so that people of different minds and circumstances could grasp its guidance. The fact that “most people” nonetheless respond with kufr is not because the message is lacking but because many hearts remain closed by stubbornness, attachment to worldly desires, pride, or moral blindness; thus the verse emphasizes both the completeness of the divine effort to guide and the human responsibility (and culpability) for rejecting that guidance.

translation: And they said, "We will not believe in you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth."
interpretation: The verse exposes people who demand an ostentatious, physical miracle as a precondition for belief; it teaches that such conditions reveal insincerity and a reliance on spectacle rather than genuine moral and spiritual conviction, and that faith cannot be coerced or purchased by visible wonders alone.

translation: Or perhaps you have a garden of date-palms and grapevines, and you cause rivers to gush through it, gushingly.
interpretation: The verse uses the vivid image of a cultivated garden with flourishing trees and flowing rivers to teach that apparent worldly prosperity—even when it seems produced by human labour and skill—is ultimately a blessing and sign from God. Such visible bounty is meant to prompt gratitude, humility and recognition of divine providence rather than prideful self-sufficiency; it reminds the believer that sustenance and the means to enjoy it are gifts that carry a moral demand to acknowledge and thank their Source.

translation: أَو تَسْقُطَ السَّمَاءُ كَمَا زَعَمْتَ عَلَيْنَا كَسْفًا أَوْ تَأْتِيَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْمَلَائِكَةِ قُبَيْلًا
interpretation: يبيّن النص موقف المشككين الذين يطالبون بعلامةٍ خارقةٍ لا يمكن دحضها — سقوط السماء أو ظهور الله والملائكة أمام الناس — ويفسّر هذا الطلب كدليل على عنادهم وغطرستهم: إذ يريدون إيماناً قهريّاً مبنياً على منظرٍ مسرحيٍّ بدل قبول هدىٍ يتطلب إرادة وصحوة قلب. الرسالة الأساسية أن الله يُهدي بحسب حكمته، وأن طلب الإعجاز الظاهر كشرط للإيمان يعكس جحوداً روحياً لا يبرّر صاحبه يوم المحاسبة.

translation: “Or that you should have a house of gold, or that you should ascend into the heaven — We will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a Book that we may read.” Say: “Glory be to my Lord! Was I aught but a human messenger?”
interpretation: The verse teaches that prophetic authority rests on divine appointment and revelation, not on ostentation or spectacular signs demanded by skeptics. It exposes the habit of those who set ever‑changing, impossible conditions for belief and affirms the prophet’s humility: he is a human chosen to convey God’s message, not someone seeking worldly glory or celestial status. The proper response to demands for sensational proof is to glorify God, uphold the truth of revelation, and refuse to be judged by the shifting standards of unbelievers.

translation: And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has Allah sent a human being as a messenger?"
interpretation: The verse condemns the rejection of revelation simply because its bearer is a human. It shows that the real obstacle was not a defect in the message but prejudice and pride: people could not accept that God would choose an ordinary human to convey divine truth. That choice is intentional — prophets are human so they can exemplify submission, be tested, and make guidance accessible and relatable — and refusing them on the grounds of their humanity reveals arrogance, attachment to status, and an unwillingness to submit to God's free wisdom.

translation: Say, “If there were on the earth angels walking about in peace, We would have sent down to them from the heavens an angel as a messenger.”
interpretation: The verse answers those who demanded an angel as a visible sign by showing that God’s choice of messengers corresponds to the nature of the recipients: angels are inherently obedient and therefore do not need the same kind of prophetic admonition given to free‑willed humans. It also rebukes the unreasonable demand—if the inhabitants of earth were angels, God could and would send a suitable messenger to them; the fact that He sends human prophets to humans reflects wisdom in matching the form of guidance to the moral and existential condition of the people being guided.

translation: Say, “Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. Indeed He is, concerning His servants, All‑Knower, All‑Seeing.”
interpretation: The Prophet is told to appeal to God’s own testimony as the decisive proof: Allah’s knowledge and sight encompass both outward deeds and inner intentions, so His witness supersedes any human accusation or demand for additional proof. This statement reassures the messenger that he need not manufacture worldly witnesses or be shaken by deniers, and it serves as a warning that ultimate judgment rests with the One who fully knows and sees His servants.

translation: And whoever Allah guides — then he is the rightly guided; and whoever He sends astray — you will not find for them any guardian besides Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces: blind, dumb and deaf. Their refuge will be Hell — and whenever it subsides, We will increase for them the blaze.
interpretation: The verse affirms that true guidance is a gift from God and ultimately dependent on His will; human effort apart from divine opening cannot secure ultimate guidance. Persistent rejection of truth hardens a person’s state so thoroughly that no protector can save them from divine judgement. The image of people raised “on their faces — blind, dumb and deaf” describes their total impotence before reality: spiritually deprived of insight (blind), unable to speak truth or intercede (dumb), and unable to hear or accept guidance (deaf). Their final abode is Hell, and the phrase about increasing the blaze emphasizes that the punishment is not static but proportionate and intensifies as a just recompense for continual denial and moral corruption.

translation: That is their recompense because they disbelieved in Our signs and said, “When we have become bones and scattered dust, will we indeed be resurrected as a new creation?”
interpretation: The verse teaches that denying God’s signs and mocking the possibility of resurrection is a culpable attitude that brings its own consequence: such skepticism reveals moral blindness and places one in a posture of rejection that earns divine recompense. It also affirms the absolute power of God to recreate what has perished, and warns that persistent, contemptuous denial of this truth leads to spiritual ruin and just consequences in the hereafter.

translation: Do they not see that Allah — He who created the heavens and the earth — is able to create their like? And He has appointed for them an appointed term, of which there is no doubt; yet the wrongdoers refuse except to disbelieve.
interpretation: The verse stresses that God’s original creative power over the heavens and the earth logically guarantees His power to recreate or resurrect people; He has already fixed a certain, unquestionable time for what He decrees (death, resurrection and final reckoning). Despite this evident ability and the certainty of His decree, those who persist in injustice and pride willfully reject faith and deny the reality that must follow — their refusal is not from ignorance but from obstinate ingratitude and rebellion against clear signs.

translation: قُل لَوْ أَنْتُمْ تَمْلِكُونَ خَزَائِنَ رَحْمَةِ رَبِّي إِذًا لَأَمْسَكْتُمْ خَشْيَةَ الْاِنْفَاقِ ۚ وَكَانَ الْاِنْسَانُ قَتُورًا
interpretation: الآية تبرز ميل الإنسان الفطري إلى البخل والخوف من الإنفاق حتى لو تُوفِّرت له نعم الرحمة كلها؛ بمعنى أن رفض الناس أو طلبهم لآيات بينة ليس دائماً ناتجاً عن غياب الدليل، بل عن صفة نفسية تميل إلى التمسك بالموجودات وتحفّظها، فتُفضي إلى قسوة القلب ونقص الشكر والكرم—فتكون الدعوة إلى الاعتماد على الله والعمل بالرحمة والإنفاق علاجاً لتلك النفسية.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel when he came to them — but Pharaoh said to him, “Indeed I think, O Moses, that you are affected by magic.”
interpretation: Despite God’s granting of unmistakable miracles to Moses as proof, the ruler (Pharaoh) rejects them by branding them as sorcery; the verse illustrates how those entrenched in power, pride, or vested interest can deny even clear evidence by attributing it to deception, thus exposing a common psychological and political pattern of rejecting truth to protect authority and avoid accountability.

translation: He said, “I certainly know that what these people have been sent with is from the Lord of the heavens and the earth — clear proofs — and I truly think, O Pharaoh, that you are about to be brought to ruin.”
interpretation: The speaker declares conviction grounded in the manifest signs of the revelation: because its proofs are clear, he affirms its divine source and, with moral certainty, pronounces Pharaoh’s imminent overthrow. The verse teaches that recognizing God’s truth imposes the duty to denounce arrogant wrongdoing and trust that God will bring just retribution; the word “مثبورا” conveys decisive ruin or expulsion as the inevitable consequence for the tyrant.

translation: So he intended to drive them out of the land, so We drowned him and all who were with him.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when a tyrant seeks to dispossess or persecute people by force, God frustrates such oppressive schemes and delivers decisive punishment; it affirms divine protection for the oppressed and the inevitable retribution awaiting arrogance and wrongful aggression.

translation: And We said after him to the Children of Israel, “Dwell in the land.” And when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth as a gathered assembly.
interpretation: The verse conveys that worldly residence and privileges are temporary and granted by God for a set period; the ‘‘promise of the Hereafter’’ denotes the resurrection and final reckoning when people will be raised together. It underscores God’s absolute power over life and death, the inevitability of collective accountability, and serves as a warning against complacency—no matter how secure or settled one seems in this world, ultimate return and judgement before God are certain and unavoidable.

translation: And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended. And We did not send you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.
interpretation: The verse asserts the revelation’s divine authenticity and certainty — it is implanted and communicated 'with the truth' as a decisive criterion that corresponds to reality and justice — and it defines the Prophet’s role: not to compel belief but to faithfully convey God’s message, offering glad tidings to those who accept guidance and warnings to those who persist in rejection, leaving the moral choice and ultimate outcome to people and to God’s judgment.

translation: And [this is] a Qur'an which We have divided into parts so that you may recite it to the people at intervals, and We have sent it down gradually.
interpretation: The verse indicates that God revealed the Book in measured portions and arranged its delivery over time to make the Prophet’s recitation and the community’s learning, memorization and implementation manageable, to allow guidance to respond to unfolding circumstances, and to strengthen belief by gradual repetition and consolidation rather than overwhelming people all at once.

translation: Say, “Believe in it or do not believe.” Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in prostration.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to leave belief as a free choice, but it highlights a telling sign: those truly endowed with prior, sincere knowledge (righteous scholars and seekers of truth among the earlier communities) respond to the Qurʾān not with argument or pride but with immediate humility and submission. Their falling down in prostration signifies recognition that the Qurʾān confirms and completes divine guidance they knew, and it shows that authentic knowledge leads the heart to worship and to acknowledge God’s authority rather than to dispute or reject His message.

translation: And they will say, “Glory be to our Lord! Truly the promise of our Lord will surely be fulfilled.”
interpretation: The verse depicts the belated realization and praise of God when the consequences of His promise (judgment or recompense) become manifest: people will acknowledge God’s perfection and admit that His decree cannot be escaped. The phrase “Subhan Rabbina” expresses stunned recognition and regret, while “إن كان وعد ربنا لمفعولا” affirms the absolute certainty and inevitability of God’s promise—serving as a condemnation of prior denial and a warning that human disbelief or delay cannot prevent what God has decreed.

translation: They prostrate with their faces to the ground, weeping; and that increases them in reverent humility.
interpretation: The verse depicts sincere believers whose awareness of God moves them into bodily abasement (prostration) and inward sorrow (tears); the outward posture and the inner emotion reinforce one another, so that genuine fear, love, and repentance before God deepen their khushūʿ (reverent humility) rather than diminish them — true spiritual elevation is shown in humble submission accompanied by heartfelt contrition and attentive devotion.

translation: Say, “Call upon Allah or call upon ar‑Rahmān.” Whichever name you call, to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names. And do not make your prayer a loud display, nor a whispering concealment; seek a middle way between them.
interpretation: The verse affirms the unity of God despite different names and enjoins moderation in worship: invoking Allah by any of His beautiful names is valid because they point to the same Divine Reality, and religious practice should avoid extremes — neither ostentatious exhibitionism nor overly secretive withdrawal. True devotion balances inward humility and reverent awareness of God with outward propriety and consideration for others, seeking a measured, sincere path in speech, supplication, and ritual.

translation: And say: “Praise be to Allah who did not take a son, and who has no partner in (His) dominion, and who has no protector out of weakness; and magnify Him with great magnification.”
interpretation: The verse proclaims God’s absolute oneness and self-sufficiency: He is free from human attributes of lineage or need, has no co-ruler or rival in His sovereignty, and requires no protector who might be weak or humiliated. The command to magnify Him calls for wholehearted recognition and exaltation of that unique transcendence—rejecting any beliefs that ascribe offspring, partners, or dependence to God and responding instead with sincere praise and glorification.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down upon His Servant the Book and has not made therein any crookedness.
interpretation: The verse declares the Qur'an’s divine authorship and unimpaired integrity: God emphasizes that He revealed a straight, clear, and consistent guidance to His Servant (the Prophet), free from error, contradiction or distortion.
