Saying the Book has “no crookedness” reassures believers of its moral and linguistic purity—that its directives are balanced, coherent, universally applicable, and therefore worthy of trust, submission and adherence.

translation: A revelation, upright, from the Most Merciful, to warn of a severe punishment from Him and to give glad tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that for them is a good reward.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur’an as an authoritative, life‑setting revelation whose function is moral correction and assurance: its origin “from Him” and description as قَيِّمًا (upright/establishing) stress that it has the power to set affairs straight, to awaken conscience by warning people of real and consequential divine accountability, and at the same time to strengthen and encourage the faithful by promising a genuine, beneficial recompense. In short, it frames guidance as both deterrent and hope — a means to reform hearts and societies by combining the sober prospect of God’s just punishment for persistent wrong with the consoling certainty of reward for sincere, righteous action.

translation: They will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The phrase asserts the absolute, unending permanence of the condition just mentioned—those referred to will dwell in that place with no end, underscoring the finality of divine judgment and the everlasting nature of the recompense (whether reward or punishment).

translation: وَيُنذِرَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ وَلَدًا — "And [to] warn those who say, 'Allah has taken a son.'"
interpretation: This verse issues a divine admonition against the claim that God has offspring: it treats such an assertion as a serious theological error (shirk) rooted in misunderstanding and misattribution. By warning those who hold it, the verse affirms God's absolute transcendence — He neither begets nor is begotten — and signals that asserting otherwise carries moral and eschatological consequences.

translation:
ما لهم به من علم ولا لآبائهم ۚ كبرت كلمة تخرج من أفواههم ۚ إن يقولون إلا كذبا
"They have no knowledge of it, nor did their forefathers; an odious/grievous word has gone forth from their mouths — they utter nothing but lies."
interpretation: The verse condemns the very act of asserting grave claims without any legitimate knowledge or inherited authority: when speech is born of ignorance and pride it becomes a serious moral wrong. Rather than conveying truth, such statements perpetuate falsehood, mislead others, and corrupt both belief and communal trust, so the speaker’s words are judged harshly because they rest on arrogance and unfounded tradition rather than evidence.

translation: Perhaps you would be on the verge of killing yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this discourse—out of sorrow.
interpretation: This verse consoles and cautions the Prophet: it acknowledges his deep distress at people’s rejection yet warns that such compassion must not overwhelm him. The language of ‘killing oneself with grief’ is metaphorical—Allah reminds him that guidance is ultimately God’s affair, and his responsibility is to convey the message patiently and trust in God’s judgment rather than be consumed by despair or self-reproach when people refuse to believe.

translation: Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the beauty, wealth, and pleasures of this world are intentionally placed as a temporary adornment to serve as a test: human beings will be tried by how they respond to these gifts. True success is not measured by possession or display but by how one uses what one has — whether for obedience, charity, restraint, and righteous conduct — so that those who channel worldly means toward good and keep their priorities on moral and spiritual duties are the ones who excel in deed.

translation: And indeed, We will surely make whatever is upon it a barren, hard plain.
interpretation: God asserts His power to strip the earth of its growth and turn fertile ground into bare, parched land as a manifestation of His control over creation; this serves as a warning and reminder that what appears permanent can be rendered lifeless by divine will—implying both the reality of coming upheaval (and judgment) and His ability to reverse the order of things (for example, to bring the dead back), so people should not be heedless of His signs.

translation: Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a marvel?
interpretation: The verse rebukes an attitude of treating the story as a mere sensational oddity; it teaches that this account is one of many divine signs meant to prompt sober reflection, strengthen belief in God’s power over sleep, life and death, and lead people from idle astonishment to submission and moral guidance rather than to consume it as a curious spectacle.

translation: إذ أوى الفتية إلى الكهف فقالوا ربنا آتنا من لدنك رحمة وهيئ لنا من أمرنا رشدا
interpretation: دعاء يعلّم كيفية التوجّه إلى الله في الشدّة: أن نطلب منه رحمته ـ شمول الحماية، الغفران والسعة ـ ومعها أن يهيّئ لنا في شأننا رشداً، أي هدىً عمليّاً وثباتاً على القرار الصائب؛ فالتوكل الحقيقي يجمع بين طلب العناية الإلهية وطلب التنوير في اختيار المسلك الصحيح.

translation: So We sealed up their hearing in the cave for a number of years.
interpretation: The phrase signifies that God caused their auditory perception and sensory responsiveness to be suspended during the prolonged sleep — not merely a physical plugging of ears but a divinely effected unawareness — in order to protect and conceal them for a decreed number of years; the wording highlights the miracle of God altering normal human faculties and frames their long sleep as a sign of His power and providence.

translation:
ثم بعثناهم لنعلم أي الحزبين أحصى لما لبثوا أمدا
"Then We raised them (from sleep) so that We might know which of the two parties was most accurate in reckoning how long they had remained."
interpretation: It signifies that God brought about this event as a decisive sign to resolve human disagreement and to demonstrate that ultimate knowledge and authority over time, life and historical truth belong to Him; divine manifestations are used to correct human error, humble speculative claims, and reorient people to trust God's wisdom rather than rely solely on their own calculations.

translation: We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wholehearted faith is met by divine augmentation of guidance and steadfastness: God presents the true account of the young believers not merely as history but as a moral demonstration—when people place their trust in God He deepens their inner light, resolve, and protection in trials, so their example becomes a living lesson and source of reassurance for others.

translation: And We steadied their hearts when they stood up, and they said, “Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will never invoke any god besides Him — indeed we had spoken before in excess.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true firmness of faith is a gift from God at decisive moments: He steadies hearts so people can renounce former errors and arrogances, confess pure monotheism, and repent for having previously gone beyond bounds. It emphasizes that sincere belief involves both a divinely supported inner resolve and the humble admission of past excesses rather than mere words or habit.

translation:
هؤلاء قومنا اتخذوا من دونه آلهة ۖ لولا يأتون عليهم بسلطان بين ۖ فمن أظلم ممن افترى على الله كذبا
"These are our people who have taken gods besides Him. Why do they not bring upon them a clear authority? Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?"
interpretation: The verse censures the practice of assigning partners to God by pointing out that those who worship other deities cannot produce any genuine, demonstrable authority or proof for them. It underscores that invoking or inventing false claims about God — attributing to Him rivals, mandates, or revelations that do not belong to Him — is not merely error but a profound injustice and fabrication. Thus the moral is twofold: theological — there is no legitimate divine sanction for idols or partners, and ethical — to lie about God’s nature or decree is among the gravest wrongs a person can commit.

translation: And when you withdrew from them and from what they worship besides Allah and took refuge in the cave — your Lord spread over you His mercy and prepared for you from your affair an ease.
interpretation: This verse reassures that when the believers in the story separated themselves from a corrupt, idolatrous society to protect their faith and sought refuge (in the cave), God surrounded them with His mercy and arranged their circumstances so as to ease their burden and provide a way of relief and accommodation. The promise is general: sincere withdrawal from practices that threaten one’s faith and trusting in God does not leave one abandoned; rather God intervenes — granting spiritual and practical support, protecting believers and ordering events toward their preservation and eventual release.

translation: And you would have seen the sun, when it rose, incline away from their cave to the right, and when it set, pass them by on the left, while they lay in an open space within it. That is among the signs of Allah. Whomever Allah guides, then he is truly guided; and whomever He lets go astray — you will never find for him a protector who guides him aright.
interpretation: The verse points to two linked truths: first, that God’s sovereignty extends even to the regular motions of the heavens and He may, for wise purposes, alter or present those motions in a way that safeguards His servants without fanfare. The description of the sun’s apparent change of course is not merely a historical detail but a demonstration that God can protect and conceal the faithful by manipulating natural appearances, reminding listeners that what seems fixed in creation is ultimately subject to His will. Second, the closing sentence draws a theological lesson: guidance is a gift from God, not merely the result of human effort or clever argument; true guidance comes from His directing, and when He allows a soul to stray, no human guardian or guide can reverse that condition. Together these elements teach humility before God’s power, trust in His providence, and the recognition that ultimate guidance and protection rest with Him alone.

translation: وَتَحْسَبُهُمْ أَيْقَاظًا وَهُمْ رُقُودٌ ۚ وَنُقَلِّبُهُمْ ذَاتَ الْيَمِينِ وَذَاتَ الشِّمَالِ ۖ وَكَلْبُهُمْ بَاسِطٌ ذِرَاعَيْهِ بِالْوَصِيدِ ۚ لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِرَارًا وَلَمَلَئْتَ مِنْهُمْ رُعْبًا
interpretation: الآية تظهر معجزة حفظ الله لأصحاب الكهف: هم في نوم عميق بإرادة الله، لكن مظهرهم يوحي باليقظة، وهذا يدل على قدرة الله على تعليق وتسخير أحوال الطبيعة لحِفظهم وإخفائهم. قلبهم إلى اليمين واليسار تكريم ووقاية لأبدانهم من التلف وإظهار لمقتضى الرحمة الإلهية، ووضع الكلب باسط ذراعيه عند المدخل علامة رعاية وحراسة غير عادية. وأن من يطالعهم ليفزّ ويمتلئ رعبًا يبرز غرابة حالتهم الخارجة عن المعتاد لتكون آية تدحض الشبهات وتطمئن المؤمنين إلى أن الله قادر على أن يخرج من قعر التاريخ عظامًا أو نفوسًا مصونَة حين يشاء.

translation: And thus We raised them (from sleep) so that they might question one another. A speaker among them asked, “How long have you tarried?” They replied, “We tarried a day or part of a day.” They said, “Your Lord knows best how long you tarried; now send one of you with this (money) of yours to the city, let him see which food is purest, and bring you provision from it; and let him act gently and discreetly, and let no one be aware of you.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God may arrange outward circumstances to prompt wise human responses: even while affirming that ultimate knowledge of hidden matters belongs to God, believers are expected to consult one another, take prudent practical measures, and move with humility and discretion in the world to protect themselves and obtain lawful sustenance. It thus balances trust in divine knowledge with responsible, modest action.

translation: Indeed, if they were to gain power over you, they would stone you or force you back into their religion, and you would never succeed at all.
interpretation: The verse warns that when hostile opponents recover dominance they will resort to violent coercion—both murder and enforced reversion—to eradicate the community’s faith and identity. By saying ‘you would never succeed,’ it teaches that under such oppression genuine spiritual or communal success is impossible: freedom of conscience and communal integrity are conditions for true success. The implication is a call to avoid conditions of vulnerability, to protect the community and its freedom to practice its faith, and not to submit to coercion that would nullify moral and religious standing.

translation: And thus We caused them to be overtaken (by punishment) so that they might know that the promise of Allah is true and that there is no doubt about the Hour, when their affairs were being disputed among them. They said, “Build over them lofty structures.” Their Lord knows best about them. Those who had prevailed in their matter said, “Let us take over them a mosque.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine chastisement was permitted as a manifest proof of Allah’s promise and the certainty of the Last Day; the reactions of the people after being struck—arguing among themselves and proposing to raise monuments or turn the sites into places of worship—reveal human self-deception: some seek to memorialize pride, others to sanctify ruins to claim legitimacy or erase culpability. The clause “Their Lord knows best about them” underscores that ultimate knowledge and judgment rest with God, and that human efforts to reframe or commemorate a condemned people do not overturn divine decree or substitute true moral accountability.

translation: They will say, “They were three, and their dog was the fourth.” And others will say, “They were five, and their dog was the sixth” — conjecturing about the unseen. And others will say, “They were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog.” Say, “My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few.” So do not dispute about them except in a way that is obvious, and do not ask any of them about it.
interpretation: The verse rebukes confident speculation about matters of the unseen and establishes a principle of epistemic humility: God alone knows hidden realities, and human claims beyond verified knowledge are mere conjecture. It instructs restraint in argument — limiting debate to what is manifest and evident rather than quarrelling over trivia — and forbids prying or pressing the righteous for hidden details. The practical teaching is to prioritize clear, moral lessons over idle curiosity, avoid asserting or arguing about what one cannot know, and defer to divine knowledge with humility.

translation: And do not say about anything, “Indeed I will do that tomorrow.”
interpretation: The verse warns against asserting absolute certainty about future actions; it teaches humility before God’s decree by reminding the believer that the future is ultimately under Allah’s control, so one should avoid presumptuous promises or claims and instead speak with dependence on and acknowledgement of God’s will.

translation: Except as Allah wills. And remember your Lord when you forget, and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer than this to right conduct."
interpretation: The phrase corrects rigid self-assertion by reminding us that outcomes are ultimately subject to Allah’s will; when you realize you have erred or a plan falls through, the proper response is not stubbornness or despair but to bring God to mind, seek His guidance, and express hopeful submission. Saying “perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer than this to right conduct” is both an acknowledgment of human limitation and an act of trust — it turns forgetfulness or retraction into an opportunity for repentance and for Allah to direct one toward a better, more fitting course.

translation: And they remained in their cave three hundred years and (added) nine.
interpretation: The precise wording stresses God’s exact knowledge and answers an apparent numerical discrepancy: the formula reconciles different ways of counting years (for example, solar versus lunar reckoning), so that what looks like inconsistency to humans is resolved when the calendars are accounted for. Its purpose is not merely to report a number but to point to divine preservation and the limits of human reckoning—showing that temporal details belong to God and that apparent contradictions disappear under proper understanding.

translation: قُلِ ٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثُوا۟ ۖ لَهُۥ غَيْبُ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٲتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۖ أَبْصَرُ بِهِۦ وَأَسْمَعُ ۚ مَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِّن وَلِىٍّ وَلَا يُشْرِكُ فِى حُكْمِهِۦٓ أَحَدًا
interpretation: The verse asserts that knowledge of hidden realities belongs solely to God and that He alone possesses full sight and hearing over the heavens and the earth; therefore no one can properly serve as a divine protector or share in His authority. The intended lesson is both epistemological and devotional: we must acknowledge the limits of human certainty about unseen matters, trust in God’s exclusive knowledge and governance, and refrain from attributing partners, intercessory sovereignty, or ultimate authority to any being besides God.

translation: Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord. There is no changer of His words, and you will not find besides Him any refuge.
interpretation: The verse commands steadfast proclamation of the revealed text and simultaneously affirms its Divine preservation: God’s words are immutable and cannot be altered or superseded by any human authority or power. It reassures the Prophet and the community that the Scripture’s authority is secure and that ultimate protection, guidance, and recourse belong to God alone, so believers must trust in Him, preserve and transmit the message faithfully, and not seek an alternative guardian or source to undo or replace His word.

translation: And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. And let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornments of the worldly life. And do not obey the one whose We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his desire, and whose affair has become excessive (ruined).
interpretation: This verse counsels the believer — addressed especially to the Prophet as a model for the community — to remain steadfast in the company of sincere worshippers whose aim is God’s pleasure, guarding oneself against distraction by worldly show and status. It warns against taking guidance from people whose hearts have been turned away from remembering God and who merely follow their passions: such leaders are spiritually deprived and lead matters into error. Practically, the verse teaches fidelity to pious companions, inward sincerity of intention (“seeking His face”), vigilance against the lure of worldly prestige, and refusal to follow those whose inner heedlessness makes their advice spiritually corrupt or ruinous.

translation: And say: “The truth is from your Lord; so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.” Indeed We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose curtains will encompass them; and if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten copper that scalds faces. Evil is the drink and evil the resting place.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine guidance is presented plainly and that human beings are granted genuine freedom of choice—belief cannot be coerced. It warns that moral responsibility carries real consequences: those who persist in injustice and rejection of the truth will face a just and severe recompense. The graphic imagery (a surrounding fire and a scalding, viscous water) underscores both the intensity and inevitability of that consequence and the futility of pleading for reprieve after one’s deeds; it functions as a moral deterrent, calling listeners to accept truth and act righteously while they still can.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds — We will never let the reward of anyone who does good be lost.
interpretation: This verse is a solemn assurance of God’s perfect justice: every sincere act rooted in faith and righteousness is recorded and preserved, and will be recompensed by God — nothing done well for His sake is wasted. It calls believers to steady hope and perseverance, trusting that even small or unseen good deeds will receive their due reward in God’s accounting.

translation: Those will have Gardens of Everlasting Bliss beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein on couches — what an excellent reward and what a beautiful resting-place.
interpretation: The verse uses rich, familiar imagery (gardens with flowing rivers, gold bracelets, green silk and brocade, couches) not merely to promise sensual pleasures but to symbolize the full, dignified, and permanent fulfilment of the righteous. “Gardens beneath which rivers flow” signifies continuous, unbroken provision and life—an existence free from the instability and toil of worldly life. The ornaments and fine garments mark divine honor and purification rather than mere display: they indicate restored dignity, spiritual status, and the community of the saved. Reclining on couches conveys perfect rest, peace of heart, and contemplative enjoyment rather than aimless indulgence. The closing phrase (“excellent reward… beautiful resting-place”) stresses that these blessings are the fitting outcome of patient faith and moral steadfastness: both outward bliss and inward serenity, together constituting the ideal, permanent home for those who attained God’s pleasure.

translation: And present to them the parable of two men: We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines, and We encircled them with palm trees and placed between them fields.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of luxuriant gardens as a parable to show that material blessings are a divine gift and a test: abundant provision can incline a person to self-sufficiency, pride and forgetfulness of God rather than to gratitude and stewardship. The lesson is that worldly prosperity is transient and conditional—true moral and spiritual success depends on recognizing God as the source, acting with humility and thankfulness, and not taking blessings as absolute proof of one’s righteousness.

translation: Both of the gardens brought forth their fruit and did not fail in any of it; and We caused a river to gush forth between them.
interpretation: The verse presents the gardens and the flowing river as symbols of God’s gratuitous, complete provision: their full, unblemished yield and the continuous stream signify blessings that are plenary and sustained by Divine will. It teaches that abundant, uninterrupted prosperity is not solely the fruit of human effort but a gift from God, and it invites recognition that such bounty is contingent on His favor rather than an inherent, deserved right.

translation: And he had fruit; so he said to his companion, as he conversed with him, “I am richer than you and more honored in people.”
interpretation: The verse highlights the man's proud reliance on wealth and social standing as proof of superiority—an attitude of arrogance and ingratitude that mistakes temporary material abundance and influential followers for true worth. It serves as a moral rebuke: equating worldly riches and status with lasting value is spiritually myopic and precedes the loss of those transient blessings.

translation: And he entered his garden while he was unjust to himself. He said, “I do not think that this will ever perish.”
interpretation: The verse exposes the self-delusion of one who, through pride, ingratitude and reliance on worldly possessions, wrongs his own soul by imagining those blessings are permanent; this moral blindness — denying contingency, accountability and the sovereignty of God — is itself an injustice that leads to downfall.

translation: And I do not think the Hour will be established; and if I were returned to my Lord, I would surely find something better than it as a return.
interpretation: These words reflect the stance of someone who denies or downplays the Last Day: they claim they do not expect the Hour to occur, and even imagine that if they were 'returned' to their Lord they would gain a better outcome. The verse exposes arrogant self‑deception—a refusal to accept inevitable accountability—by equating return to God with imagined advantage, when in truth 'return' means facing divine judgment and recompense rather than escaping consequences.

translation: "His companion said to him while disputing with him, 'Have you disbelieved in the One who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then fashioned you into a man?'"
interpretation: The speaker shames the denier by showing the logical inconsistency of rejecting resurrection while acknowledging God’s creative power: if God can bring you into being from dust and a tiny drop and shape you into a living human, then raising you again is not impossible. The verse therefore confronts arrogance and ingratitude, calling for humility and recognition of God’s authority over both origin and ultimate return.

translation: Indeed, He is Allah, my Lord, and I will not associate anyone with my Lord.
interpretation: A clear, unambiguous profession of tawḥīd: the speaker affirms that God alone is Lord and vows to reject shirk (assigning partners to God). It expresses absolute loyalty and reliance on Allah, refusing idols, intermediaries or any competing sources of ultimate authority, and signals that one’s identity, worship and decisions must be rooted solely in the exclusive oneness of God.

translation: And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, “What Allah has willed; there is no power except with Allah”? For perhaps you would then not say, “I am less than you in wealth and children.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes pride and failure to acknowledge Allah when enjoying worldly blessings. Saying “ما شاء الله لا قوة إلا بالله” is an expression of recognition that blessings are given by Allah and human power is limited; neglecting this remembrance leads to boasting, comparison, and reliance on one’s own ability, which in the Qur’anic account precedes loss. The passage teaches humility, gratitude, and tawakkul (trust in God): by attributing success to Allah rather than to oneself, one avoids arrogance and the false security that invites ruin.

translation: Perhaps my Lord will give him something better than your garden and will send upon it a downpour from the sky so that it becomes a smooth, slippery plain.
interpretation: The verse expresses trust that God can reverse apparent fortunes: He may replace one's worldly blessings with something superior and, at the same time, abase the proud by turning their possessions into ruin through divine intervention. It teaches that reliance on status or wealth is precarious because God alone controls sustenance and outcome, so humility and trust in God are the proper responses to worldly abundance.

translation: Or its water becomes a deep chasm, so you will not be able to reach it.
interpretation: The image shows that when a blessing, opportunity, or source of support withdraws and sinks beyond reach, human effort cannot recover it; thus the verse admonishes urgency in seizing what is good while it is accessible, humility before limits of human power, and reliance on God, for some losses are irreversible except by God’s will.

translation: ثم أحاطت به أضرار أجّجت ثماره، فأصبح يقلب كفيه على ما أنفق فيها، وهي خاوية على أعراجها، ويقول: «يا ليتني لم أشرك بربي أحدًا».
interpretation: الآية تحذر من الاعتماد على الدنيا والكبر والشرك: من يعتز بثروته ويجعلها ملاذه أو يشرك مع الله في اعتقاده أو عمله قد يفاجأ بفناء نعمه فجأة، فيبقى عاجزًا تائهًا يبكي على ما أنفقه ويأسف علانية. عبارة «يقلب كفيه» رمز للعجز والندم، و«خاوية على أعراجها» تشير إلى خلو ما كان متينًا من ثماره. عبرتها أن الأمان الحقيقي في التوحيد والاعتماد على الله، وأن من يغترّ بالمال أو المنزلة قد يجد خسارته كامنة في غروره لا في عجز القدر عن العطاء.

translation: And he had no party to help him besides Allah, and he was not ever helped.
interpretation: The verse affirms the utter helplessness of any being or supposed ally apart from God: no idol, leader, or coalition can truly defend or secure anyone against divine will. Claims to independent power or protectors other than Allah are illusions; ultimate support and victory come only by God’s will, and those who rely on other ‘parties’ will find themselves unsupported.

translation: There the guardianship belongs to Allah, the Truth; He is the best in reward and the best in final outcome.
interpretation: The verse affirms that at the decisive moment—when all other supports are removed and affairs are finally settled—real authority, protection, and care belong solely to God. “Wilāyah” here means true sovereignty and guardianship: any worldly protectors or idols are powerless then. Therefore only God can grant the genuine recompense and the best ultimate end; those who placed their trust in Him will receive His supreme reward and the best final outcome, while reliance on false guardians yields no lasting benefit.

translation:
وَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلَ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا كَمَاءٍ أَنزَلْنَاهُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَاخْتَلَطَ بِهِ نَبَاتُ الْأَرْضِ فَأَصْبَحَ هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ ۗ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مُّقْتَدِرًا
"Present to them the example of worldly life: it is like water We send down from the sky; the plants of the earth mingle with it, then become dry stubble which the winds scatter. And Allah is over all things competent."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the pleasures, gains, and adornments of this life are transient and dependent: God’s provision produces growth and beauty, but without enduring purpose it can quickly turn to worthless stubble scattered by winds (calamity, loss, death). Therefore attachment to ephemeral worldly benefits is misplaced; one must remember God’s ultimate sovereignty over provision and outcomes and orient one’s aims and deeds toward what endures beyond the fleeting world.

translation: Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world; but the enduring righteous deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better as an object of hope.
interpretation: The verse contrasts transient worldly attractions (wealth and offspring), which beautify and occupy human life, with the lasting moral and spiritual deeds that endure beyond this life. “Al-baqiyyāt al-ṣāliḥāt” refers to righteous acts whose effects remain—sincere faith, ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, righteous upbringing of children, supplication, and any good whose impact persists. These lasting deeds are presented as superior because God values and rewards them more fully (“khayr ʻinda rabbika thawāban”) and they provide a truer, more reliable hope for the future (“khayr amalan”). The practical import is not to despise legitimate worldly blessings, but to treat them as means to perform and cultivate enduring goodness rather than as ultimate ends.

translation: And the Day when We will move the mountains and you will see the earth laid bare, and We will gather them — and We will not leave any one of them behind.
interpretation: The verse points to the inevitable Day of Resurrection when God’s sovereignty will be unmistakably displayed: the upheaval of mountains and the exposure of the earth symbolize the removal of every refuge and the collapse of what seemed permanent, so that nothing can be hidden. The assurance that “We will not leave any one of them” stresses universal, individual accountability — every person will be brought forth and judged without exception. The intended practical effect is to awaken moral seriousness and humility before God’s power and justice, reminding listeners that worldly securities do not exempt anyone from responsibility on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: And they will be presented before your Lord in ranks. "You have indeed come to Us as We created you the first time." Nay! But you had supposed that We would never appoint for you an appointed time.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Resurrection people will be brought before God in orderly ranks, returned to a state of utter dependence like their original creation, which exposes the futility of worldly status and power. It overturns the denial or complacency of those who imagined there would be no appointed meeting with God, affirming God’s absolute power to recreate and His sure appointment of a Day of account; thus the passage calls for humility, awareness of accountability, and recognition that human presumption cannot alter divine decree.

translation: And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it; and they will say, "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great but it has recorded it?" And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone.
interpretation: The verse affirms that on the Day of Reckoning every deed—no matter how trivial—will be brought to light and serve as clear, undeniable evidence. For the wrongdoer this summons produces dread and regret; for the believer it is a reminder to live with moral awareness, seek repentance, and prepare for accountability. At the same time the statement that God "does not wrong anyone" reassures that the final judgment is perfectly just: nothing is overlooked, and no one will be treated unfairly—each person’s recompense corresponds precisely to their deeds.

translation: And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblīs; he was of the jinn and so he disobeyed the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, while they are enemies to you? Evil indeed is the exchange for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rank before God is determined by submission, not by created status: Iblīs’s refusal—born of pride—made him a transgressor despite his origin. The rhetorical question condemns those who accept Satan and his followers as protectors in place of God: doing so is self‑destructive because these allies are actually enemies who lead to loss and corruption. Thus the passage warns against misplaced loyalty and following sources of temptation instead of adhering to God’s guidance, a choice that is a ruinous and unjust exchange for the wrongdoer.

translation:
ما أشهدتهم خلق السماوات والأرض ولا خلق أنفسهم وما كنت متخذ المضلين عضدا
“I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of themselves; nor was I one to take the misleaders as supporters.”
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s exclusive sovereignty and rejects any human claim to share in His creative authority or to serve as His appointed witnesses. It is a rebuke of those who, through arrogance or persuasion, present themselves as having special access to divine power or truth: they were neither present at creation nor authorized to testify about it, and God does not rely on or take the misguided as allies. The practical implication is to distrust claims of deified leaders or self‑appointed guides and to recognize human limitations before Divine knowledge and authority.

translation: And the Day He will say, "Call upon those whom you claimed as partners." So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning the futility of shirk will be publicly exposed: those who relied on other gods, powers, or sources of help will find them powerless and inaccessible. The “partners” will neither answer nor intercede, and God will set a barrier—literal or metaphysical—so there can be no transfer of support or escape. The scene underscores that ultimate assistance, authority, and judgment belong solely to God; dependence on anything besides Him was a delusion that will be revealed when accountability comes.

translation: And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are to fall into it, and will find for it no diversion.
interpretation: The verse captures the moment when those who rejected guidance are suddenly confronted with the undeniable reality of divine punishment: all their prior hopes—of being spared, delayed, or diverted by excuses, status, or intercession—collapse. It teaches that persistent denial and moral arrogance make the consequences inevitable and irreversible, so true safety lies only in sincere submission and timely repentance before that decisive moment arrives.

translation: And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an examples of every kind; yet man has ever been, most of anything, given to disputation.
interpretation: The verse means that God has presented the Qur'an in many forms—stories, parables, legal rulings, signs—so people of different temperaments can recognize guidance; nevertheless human nature tends toward quarreling and clinging to preconceived desires. In practice this verse diagnoses why clear guidance often fails to transform: people prefer arguing, defending ego or habit, or disputing to avoid sincere submission. The implicit call is to overcome that disputatious tendency by humble reflection on the examples, prioritizing truth over argument.

translation: And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them and they sought forgiveness of their Lord, except that the precedent of the former peoples came upon them or the punishment overtook them beforehand?
interpretation: The verse teaches that when clear guidance reaches a community, two realities can block its acceptance: either the established divine pattern (sunnah) whereby previous peoples who persisted in denial were dealt with in a fixed way now befalls them, or God’s punishment occurs before they are moved to repent. It emphasizes both the certainty of God’s justice in dealing with peoples who persist in rejection and the urgent need to respond to guidance quickly, since delay may mean being overtaken by consequences before one can seek forgiveness.

translation: We send not the messengers except as bearers of glad tidings and as warners. Yet those who disbelieve argue with falsehood to overturn the truth, and they have taken My signs and what they were warned of in derision.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the prophetic mission is limited to conveying guidance—promising reward and warning of consequences—and that rejection of revelation is often not the result of sincere inquiry but of deliberate sophistry and contempt. When people argue “with falsehood” and mock the signs and warnings, they reveal an attachment to pride, vested interests, or habitual error that leads them to use rhetoric to suppress truth rather than to seek it; the passage therefore calls attention to the moral condition behind denial (not merely intellectual debate) and implies that believers should recognize such tactics, remain steadfast, and understand that ridicule and fallacious argument cannot alter the reality of divine guidance or the accountability it brings.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord yet turns away from them and forgets what his own hands have sent before? Indeed We have set covering upon their hearts, lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears; and even if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who, when confronted with God's clear signs, willfully avert attention and become heedless of the consequences of their own actions. Their persistent rejection and moral negligence lead to a spiritual hardening—described metaphorically as coverings on the heart and deafness in the ears—which diminishes their capacity to perceive and accept truth. This state is not portrayed as arbitrary removal of responsibility but as the inward consequence of repeated turning away: having closed themselves to guidance, even sincere invitations thereafter cannot reach them.

translation: And your Lord is the Oft‑Forgiving, Full of Mercy. If He were to requite them for what they have earned, He would hasten for them the punishment; but for them is an appointed time from which they will find no refuge.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s delay in punishing the wrongdoers is an expression of His mercy and forbearance, not indifference. By restraining immediate retribution He provides people time and opportunity for repentance, moral reform, and the fulfillment of His wisdom in testing and calling. Yet this mercy coexists with inevitable divine justice: there is a fixed, unavoidable appointed hour of reckoning when escape will be impossible. Thus God’s patience should be understood as both an invitation to return and a solemn warning — it is a grace to be responded to, not a license for complacence.

translation: And those towns — We destroyed them because they were unjust, and We appointed for their destruction a fixed time.
interpretation: This verse teaches that God’s response to persistent communal injustice is both just and measured: He does not punish arbitrarily or instantly but sets an appointed term, giving people opportunity for warning and repentance; yet when a society persists in transgression and rejects guidance, ruin becomes inevitable. The statement underscores divine justice (wrongdoing is not left unaddressed), divine mercy (a delay permitting reform), and a moral lesson that collective immorality and obstinacy carry definite, God‑willed consequences.

translation: And [recall] when Moses said to his servant, “I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas, or I will go on for a long time.”
interpretation: Moses’ declaration expresses determined perseverance in the pursuit of guidance and knowledge: he is willing to endure long travel and hardship to attain the meeting with truth, exemplifying single‑minded resolve, patient striving, and readiness to submit effort to God’s direction while acknowledging that attainment ultimately depends on God’s will.

translation: But when they reached the junction between them, they forgot their fish, and it took its course into the sea.
interpretation: The verse implies that what appears as human negligence can serve God's purpose: the forgotten fish, by escaping, became the divinely appointed sign that led to the destined meeting and lesson. It teaches humility before God's wisdom, showing that ordinary, unintended events may be the means by which God reveals hidden guidance and corrects human presumption.

translation: So when they had gone on, he said to his young companion, “Bring us our meal; indeed we have met with fatigue on this journey of ours.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that even in the pursuit of lofty aims one must acknowledge human limits and care for basic needs: admitting fatigue and pausing for sustenance is not weakness but prudence. It models humility and practical responsibility during a demanding spiritual or educational journey, reminding the seeker that physical care and patient reliance on God accompany true striving.

translation: قَالَ أَرَأَيْتَ إِذْ أَوَيْنَا إِلَى الصَّخْرَةِ فَإِنِّي نَسِيتُ الْحُوتَ وَمَا أَنْسَانِيهِ إِلَّا الشَّيْطَانُ أَنْ أَذْكُرَهُ ۚ وَاتَّخَذَ سَبِيلَهُ فِي الْبَحْرِ عَجَبًا
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن الإنسان، حتى من أعطاه الله علماً وفضلاً، معرض للزلات والنسيان ولتأثير الوساوس الشيطانية، لكن ذلك لا يعرقل حكم الله وحكمته: فالأحداث التي تبدو هفوة أو ضياعاً قد تُستثمر في مسار إلهي أوسع لتكون علامة أو سبباً لآفاق جديدة. منها درس تواضع عن مدى محدودية علمنا، يقظة من وساوس الشيطان التي تلهينا، وثقة بأن لحكمة الله غايات خفية قد تتضح لاحقاً عبر ما ظاهره ضعف أو خطأ.

translation: قالوا: «ذلك ما كنا نبغ». فارتدّوا على آثارهما قصصًا.
interpretation: الآية تبيّن حالة النفس البشرية تجاه الاكتشاف والاهتداء: حين يعثر الساعي على ما كان يقصده يقرّ به ويستجيب بسرعة، فيتبع الآثار والدلائل الواضحة بلا تردد—وترمز لذلك إلى الالتزام الفوري بالطريق المستدلّ عليه والثقة بالعلامات التي تقود إلى المراد.

translation: So they found one of Our servants to whom We had granted mercy from Us and whom We had taught knowledge from Our presence.
interpretation: The verse indicates that God singled out a servant and endowed him by divine choice with both mercy and special, God‑bestowed knowledge. This teaches that true insight and the authority to act in ways that may exceed ordinary human understanding are gifts from God, meant to serve His wisdom; believers should therefore recognize the limits of their own knowledge, accept that some guidance comes as a divine endowment, and respond with humility and trust in God’s greater plan.

translation: Mûsā said to him, “Shall I follow you so that you teach me of the sound judgment (rashad) that you have been taught?”
interpretation: Humility before deeper, divinely‑granted wisdom: even the most gifted acknowledge limits and seek a teacher to transmit practical, inner guidance. True rashad is not only theoretical knowledge but lived insight that often transcends immediate reason; acquiring it requires willingness to follow, patience with methods one may not yet understand, and trust in a guide through lessons that reveal hidden purposes.

translation: He said, “You will not be able to be patient with me.”
interpretation: A cautioned recognition of human limits: the speaker warns that the seeker will lack the endurance to accept actions whose wisdom is hidden, teaching that humility, restraint, and trust are required when confronted with events that seem unjust or inexplicable before their deeper purpose is revealed.

translation: And how can you be patient concerning that of which you have no knowledge?
interpretation: The verse points out the human limitation of expecting calm acceptance of matters one does not understand: genuine patience rests on some degree of knowledge, certainty, or trust. When people are confronted with events or losses they cannot comprehend, it is natural to struggle; the verse therefore urges humility about our ignorance, the pursuit of understanding where possible, and turning to God for reassurance and guidance rather than blaming others or pretending serene acceptance without conviction.

translation: He said, “You will find me, if God wills, patient, and I will not disobey any of Your commands.”
interpretation: The speaker is making a firm pledge of endurance and complete submission: he commits to bear hardship with steadfast patience while affirming he will obey God's command, yet he qualifies his resolve with “insha'Allah” to acknowledge that true perseverance depends on God's support. The verse teaches that righteous firmness combines personal determination with humility and reliance on God, so obedience and patience are offered sincerely but with recognition of divine will.

translation: قال: «فإن اتبعتني فلا تسألني عن شيء حتى أحدث لك منه ذكرا»
interpretation: الآية تعبر عن توجيه يقوم على التسليم والاحتكام لزمن ومراحل التعليم والوحي: من يتبع قائداً أو مرشداً يُطلب منه أن يصبر ولا يزحم السؤال قبل أن يُعرض له ما يجب أن يُعرض، لأن الدلالة والتذكير ستأتي بوقتها من عنده. المعنى العملي: ثقة في ترتيب الحق ومراحله، والامتناع عن الفضول المسبق الذي يشتت عن تلقي الحكمة في وقتها.

translation:
فانطلقا حتى إذا ركبا في السفينة خرقها ۖ قال أخرقتها لتغرق أهلها لقد جئت شيئا إمرا
“So they set out, and when they boarded the ship he made a hole in it. [Moses] said, ‘Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a reprehensible thing.’”
interpretation: The verse highlights that divine wisdom can operate beyond immediate human perception: actions that appear harmful or blameworthy to limited minds may serve a greater purpose ordained by God. It calls believers to humility about their knowledge, to patience in the face of seemingly unjust acts, and to trust that ultimate judgment and outcomes rest with God, who can avert greater harm or bring mercy through means that at first seem wrong.

translation: He said, “Did I not tell you that you would not be able to remain patient with me?”
interpretation: A rebuke that teaches humility before deeper knowledge: when one confronts actions grounded in wisdom beyond their understanding, impatience leads to premature judgment and disruption of guidance. The verse warns that human beings often overestimate their capacity to bear unexplained hardship or to follow a teacher whose insight they do not possess, so the proper stance is trust, restraint, and recognition of one's limited perspective in matters governed by divine wisdom.

translation: قَالَ: «لا تُؤَاخِذْنِي بِمَا نَسِيتُ وَلا تَرْهَقْنِي مِنْ أَمْرِي عُسْرًا»
interpretation: مبدأٌ أخلاقي وشرعي يبرز ضعف الإنسان واحتياجه إلى رحمة الله: عند الخطأ الناشئ عن النسيان يُلتمس التخفيف وعدم المحاسبة الصارمة، ولا ينبغيُ تحميل الناس أعباءً تفوق طاقتهم؛ وبذلك تُفصل المسؤولية بين الزلّ غير المقصود والعمد، وتُؤكَّد سمة التسامح والاعتدال في التدبير الإلهي للعباد.

translation: So they set out, and when they met a boy, he killed him. Moses said, “Have you killed an innocent, pure soul for other than a soul? Indeed you have brought forth a deplorable/strange thing.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a clash between immediate human moral intuition and hidden divine wisdom: Moses reacts from a natural, absolute sense that killing an innocent life is reprehensible, while the broader story shows that actions which seem unjust to limited human perception may serve a greater divine purpose beyond apparent harm. The lesson is to recognize the limits of our judgment, temper instant condemnation with humility, and trust that God's knowledge of consequences and intent can justify measures that appear inexplicable or abhorrent to us.

translation: ألم أقل لك إنك لن تستطيع معي صبرا؟ — Did I not tell you that you would not be able to be patient with me?
interpretation: The verse teaches that readiness for deep, hidden wisdom requires disciplined patience and humility; impatience reveals a spiritual immaturity and an inability to receive explanations that are given gradually, so one must restrain curiosity, trust the guide, and submit to the process if one hopes to benefit from higher knowledge.

translation: He said, “If I ask you about anything after this, do not accompany me; indeed I have been granted an excuse from my Lord.”
interpretation: The speaker is drawing a clear boundary: the journey of sharing hidden wisdom has a limit, and further questioning will terminate the relationship because he acts under a special mandate or dispensation from God. The verse teaches that certain actions are undertaken by divine instruction and are not open to continual human interrogation; pressing beyond the established limit undermines the trust and access to that higher knowledge, so one must respect the restraint given and accept that some divine reasons may remain concealed.

translation: So they set out, and when they came to the people of a town they asked its people for provisions, but they refused to provide them lodging. There they found a wall that was about to collapse, so he repaired it. He said, "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."
interpretation: The verse highlights the moral of sincere, selfless service: a righteous person may perform helpful deeds without seeking or accepting worldly payment, preferring the unseen reward from God. By refusing to charge for his help, he demonstrates humility, trust in divine provision, and the principle that true goodness is offered for God's sake rather than for material return.

translation: قال: "هذا فراق بيني وبينك. سأنبئك بتأويل ما لم تستطع عليه صبرا."
interpretation: المتكلم يعترف بواقع الفراق الوشيك ويوضح أنه سيُزيل عن الآخر شاغله ببيان معنى ما كان قد أشغل ذهنه — دلّ ذلك على أن الكشف عن الحقائق يخفف عن النفس التي لا تطيق الجهل، وأن طلب التفسير من ذيّ علم قبل الفراق وسيلة للحصول على الطمأنينة وترتيب الأمور وفق قضاء الله.

translation: أما السفينة فكانت لمساكين يعملون في البحر فأردت أن أعيبها وكان وراءهم ملك يأخذ كل سفينة غصبا
interpretation: الآية تبيّن حكمة الله في تسيير أمور الناس بأن يَجعل ضرراً يسيراً في سفينة الفقراء بدل أن يقع عليهم ضرر أعظم من جهة طاغٍ يستولي على كل سفينة بالقوة؛ أي أن الإفساد الظاهر للسفينة كان مقصودًا رحمةً بهم لحمايتهم من مصادرةٍ أوسع، وهو مثال على أن ما يبدو شراً قد يكون تدبيرًا إلهيًّا لحماية العباد ودرء ظلم أعظم.

translation:
وأَمَّا الغُلامُ فَكانَ أَبَواهُ مُؤْمِنَيْنِ فَخَشْنَا أَن يُرهِقَهُما طُغْيانًا وَكُفْرًا
"And as for the boy — his parents were believers, and We feared that he would burden them with transgression and unbelief."
interpretation: The phrase expresses God's wise and protective planning: by His foreknowledge He perceived that leaving the child with his parents would expose them to grave trial — either the child’s circumstances or others’ pressures would bring hardship, provoke rebellion or force them into denial of their faith. Thus God’s decision to remove and redirect the child’s fate is an act of mercy and preservation for the believing parents and for the unfolding of a greater plan. The wording “We feared” should be understood as divine precaution based on knowledge of likely harm, not human weakness; it highlights God’s care in averting trials that would overwhelm the faithful and ensuring outcomes that serve justice and guidance.

translation:
فأردنا أن يبدلهما ربهما خيرا منه زكاة وأقرب رحما
"So We desired that their Lord would replace them with something better than them — purer and nearer in kinship."
interpretation: The verse indicates that God, displeased with those who were deficient in faith or in maintaining family and social ties, intends to substitute them with people of higher moral and spiritual quality: 'زكاة' here conveys purified, righteous character or faith that cleanses, and 'أقرب رحما' denotes a closer commitment to kinship and compassionate relationships. Thus the promise is of a replacement by believers whose conduct purifies the community and strengthens familial bonds.

translation: وأَمَّا الْجِدَارُ فَكَانَ لِغُلَامَيْنِ يَتِيمَيْنِ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ وَكَانَ تَحْتَهُ كَنْزٌ لَهُمَا وَكَانَ أَبُوهُمَا صَالِحًا فَأَرَادَ رَبُّكَ أَن يُبْلِغَا أَشُدَّهُمَا وَيَسْتَخْرِجَا كَنْزَهُمَا رَحْمَةً مِنْ رَبِّكَ ۚ وَمَا فَعَلْتُهُ عَنْ أَمْرِي ۚ ذَٰلِكَ تَأْوِيلُ مَا لَمْ تَسْتَطِعْ عَلَيْهِ صَبْرًا
interpretation: The verse instructs that what may look like odd or harsh events are often unfolding from divine wisdom to preserve and bring about greater mercy, especially for the vulnerable; it also clarifies that prophetic actions occur under God’s command, not personal whim. The broader lesson is to trust God's hidden purposes, refrain from judging by outward appearances, and recognize that patience and reliance on revelation are required because God's plans can protect rights (e.g., of orphans) and reveal benefits only at the appointed time.

translation: They ask you about Dhul‑Qarnayn. Say, ‘I will recite to you a remembrance of him.’
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to answer curiosity not with mere facts for entertainment but by presenting the story as a purposeful ‘dhikr’—a moral and spiritual reminder. Its aim is to make listeners reflect on how God appoints and limits worldly authority, to show the responsibilities and dangers of power, and to turn hearts toward reliance on God rather than indulging idle speculation about historical detail.

translation:
إِنَّا مَكَّنَّا لَهُ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَآتَيْنَاهُ مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ سَبَبًا
"Indeed, We established him on the earth and gave him, of everything, a means."
interpretation: God is saying that He empowered that person with legitimate authority and supplied the practical means—knowledge, skills, resources, favorable circumstances and routes of access—by which he could govern, provide, decide and accomplish what was required; his power and success are thus presented as a divine grant enabling him to fulfill his role rather than as something he achieved entirely by his own effort.

translation: فأتبع سببا — "So he followed a path (a course of action)."
interpretation: It expresses the idea of deliberately taking up and pursuing a particular course or method in life: once a person decides on a way (whether righteous or misguided), they set themselves on that direction and thus become responsible for the consequences it brings.

translation:
حتى إذا بلغ مغرب الشمس وجدها تغرب في عين حمئة ووجد عندها قوما ۗ قلنا يا ذا القرنين إما أن تعذب وإما أن تتخذ فيهم حسنا
"Until, when he reached the place where the sun set, he found it setting in a muddy spring, and he found by it a people. We said, ‘O Dhul‑Qarnayn, either punish them or treat them with kindness.’"
interpretation: The verse recounts Dhul‑Qarnayn’s encounter at the westernmost point as it appeared to him (the sun seeming to set into a muddy spring) and then focuses on God’s grant of responsibility to him toward the people he found there. The phrase about punishment or taking them kindly sets out a principle of legitimate authority: a ruler or agent acting for God must judge between corrective force against persistent wrongdoing and compassionate engagement that seeks reform and reconciliation. The Qur’an’s report is phenomenological in language (describing how things appeared) and its theological emphasis is on the balance of justice and mercy in governance and on the need to choose the means that will rightly bring people to guidance or restrain oppression.

translation: He said, “As for whoever has wronged, We will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a grievous (odious) punishment.”
interpretation: The verse warns that wrongdoing will not go unavenged: the unjust will suffer punishment (whether in this life or by means allowed in the world), and ultimately will be brought back before God to receive a further, severe and humiliating penalty (ʿadhābun nakīr). It affirms the certainty of resurrection and final accountability and underscores divine justice — punishment can be both immediate and decisive in the Hereafter, exposing the humiliation and severity reserved for persistent oppressors.

translation: As for the one who believes and does righteous deeds, for him is the best reward; and We will say to him from Our command, ‘Be at ease.’
interpretation: The phrase “جزاء الحسنى” denotes the complete, highest good — ultimate felicity, nearness to God, and the eternal blessings of Paradise — rather than a mere temporal benefit. “سنقول له من أمرنا يسرا” expresses God’s active mercy: by His decree He will remove burdens, lighten the reckoning, welcome the believer with ease and honor, and facilitate the believer’s entry into that good. Thus the verse affirms that genuine faith coupled with righteous action earns not only deserved recompense but God’s gracious initiative to make the final outcome comfortable, dignified, and free of hardship.

translation: Then he followed a way (a course/means).
interpretation: It denotes taking deliberate steps along a particular path or employing an intermediary cause to achieve an aim — emphasizing human initiative in pursuing means or a course of action (while implying that such means remain subordinate to God’s will).

translation: Until, when he reached the place where the sun rises, he found it rising upon a people for whom We had provided no shelter against it.
interpretation: The verse reports, in the traveler’s perspective, that Dhu al-Qarnayn came to a place where the sun appeared to rise over a people who had no protection from it; the phrase “We had not made for them any covering” should be understood theologically rather than as an astronomical claim. It emphasizes God’s sovereignty over provision and that those people were left exposed—physically and symbolically—because no protective provision had been ordained for them, thereby highlighting human vulnerability and the limits of any ruler’s power before God’s decree.

translation: Thus — and indeed We have encompassed in knowledge whatever is with Him.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute, all‑encompassing knowledge: everything that exists, the seen and unseen, past, present and future, and all inner realities are fully within His awareness. It affirms that nothing is hidden from Him and that His knowledge is perfect and complete, a truth that grounds both reassurance for believers and accountability for those who deny or ignore that reality.

translation: ثم أتبع سببا — "Then he followed a course/way (a means)."
interpretation: The phrase describes turning away from the straight guidance and pursuing some other course or worldly means—choosing a path motivated by desire, habit, or false reasons rather than by divine guidance, with the consequence of drifting from the truth.

translation: Until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found on the farther side of them a people who could scarcely understand a word.
interpretation: The verse indicates that human communities differ in their capacity to receive guidance: encountering people who “could scarcely understand a word” signifies not only linguistic distance but a deeper spiritual or intellectual insensitivity to truth. It underscores the messenger’s effort to reach even remote, uncomprehending groups and teaches that understanding and guidance are ultimately bestowed by God, so the duty is to convey the message while leaving the result to Divine will.

translation: They said, “O Dhu al-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are causing corruption in the land; so shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you erect between us and them a barrier?”
interpretation: The verse illustrates a social and political principle: when a community faces systemic disruption and threat, it may lawfully entrust authority with resources to secure public safety. “Corruption in the land” conveys more than isolated crime — it denotes pervasive social and political breakdown that calls for collective protection. The offer of kharaj (tribute) in return for a barrier frames a pragmatic social contract—people consenting to support a just leader’s defensive work—while the episode also points to the limits of human remedies and the ultimate sovereignty of God over what such measures can achieve.

translation: قَالَ مَا مَكَّنِي فِيهِ رَبِّي خَيْرٌ فَأَعِينُونِي بِقُوَّةٍ أَجْعَل بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَهُمْ رَدْمًا
interpretation: الآية تكشف مبدأ أخلاقي وقيادي: القوة الحقيقية والتمكين مصدرها الله، فعندما يَقرّ القائد بذلك يرفض تحويل منصبه إلى منفعة شخصية ويطلب بدلًا من ذلك مساهمة عملية من الجماعة لخدمة مصلحة مشتركة. هي دعوة لدمج التوكّل على الله مع السعي العملي والتعاون الجماعي — النعمة الإلهية تهيئ الإمكانات، لكن ترجمتها إلى حماية وبناء تتطلب مشاركة بشرية وجهد مادي من المجتمع.

translation: “Bring me plates (or ingots) of iron.” Then, when he had set them between the two anvils, he said, “Blow.” When he had made it (red) hot like fire, he said, “Bring me that I may pour over it molten copper.”
interpretation: This verse recounts God’s endowment to Prophet Dawud (David) of practical skill and authority over material craft: the smithing process is described to show that the ability to shape and strengthen iron was a gift from God. It emphasizes that technical knowledge and power (here exemplified by making and tempering metal) are divinely granted means by which a righteous leader can build, defend and order society; the scene also underlines that such worldly crafts require human labor and skill (the blowing, the anvils) but are ultimately enabled by God’s favor and should be used responsibly under His guidance.

translation:
فما استطاعوا أن يظهروه وما استطاعوا له نقبا
"But they were unable to bring it forth, nor could they make any breach in it."
interpretation: The verse indicates the utter powerlessness of those who denied the sign or sought to frustrate God's decree: their efforts could neither prevent or nullify what God had ordained nor find any opening to escape or undermine it. Human plotting and attempts to avert divine will proved futile.

translation: Say, “This is mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it dakkāʼ (pulverized dust). And the promise of my Lord is true.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the prophetic mission is fundamentally an act of God’s mercy intended to guide and reform, yet it carries a solemn warning: Divine justice will inevitably arrive and utterly eradicate falsehood and oppression. The word dakkāʼ conveys total pulverization—no remnant of the unjust order will remain—and this certainty should encourage trust in God’s promise and prompt people to respond to the mercy offered before the final, unavoidable reckoning.

translation: And that Day We left some of them to surge against others in confusion; and the Horn was blown, and We gathered them all together.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of Resurrection when, as a sign of Divine judgment, God permits people to be thrown into chaotic, frantic contact with one another—a visible expression of their helplessness, mutual reproach and disorder—only to end that turmoil abruptly by the blowing of the trumpet, which gathers every soul under God’s control for final reckoning; it underscores both human disarray without guidance and the absolute, sovereign organization of the Resurrection.

translation: And We will present Hell that Day to the disbelievers, openly on display.
interpretation: The verse signifies that on the Day of Judgment God will make the reality and consequences of Hell unmistakably visible to those who denied the truth; their prior denial and arrogance will be futile, their excuses removed, and the warnings they ignored will stand as clear evidence of divine justice and the truth of the messages they rejected.

translation: Those whose eyes were covered from My remembrance, and who were unable to hear.
interpretation: The verse characterizes people who are spiritually blind and deaf: their “covered eyes” signify an inability or refusal to perceive and acknowledge God’s reminders and signs, and their inability to “hear” denotes a closed, unreceptive heart and ear — not mere physical impairment but moral and spiritual insensitivity caused by heedlessness, arrogance, or persistent sin. As a result, reminders, proofs, and guidance do not reach them and they remain estranged from guidance.

translation:
أَفَحَسِبَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أَن يَتَّخِذُوا عِبَادِي مِن دُونِي أَوْلِيَاءَ ۚ إِنَّا أَعْتَدْنَا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكَافِرِينَ نُزُلًا
"Do those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants besides Me as allies? Indeed We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as an abiding place."
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who, out of unbelief, place their trust or allegiance in others—idols, worldly leaders, base passions, or any created beings—instead of God. It teaches that such ‘allies’ are powerless to save or intercede, and that rejecting God’s lordship leads to His just recompense: Hell prepared for those who persist in disbelief. The passage affirms God’s exclusive sovereignty and warns against the futility of seeking protection or ultimate support anywhere except with Him.

translation: قُلْ هَلْ نُنَبِّئُكُم بِالأَخْسَرِينَ أَعْمَالًا — Say, “Shall We inform you who are the greatest losers in their deeds?”
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical summons that exposes who truly comes out worst when their deeds are weighed: not those who lack wealth or status, but those whose lives were devoted to transient desires and who rejected or ignored guidance, so that their apparent accomplishments are rendered void. It warns that sincere faith and moral responsibility give eternal weight to actions, whereas worship of worldly gain, heedlessness of God’s commands, or hypocrisy make one’s deeds futile—so what seemed like success becomes the source of final loss.

translation: Those whose efforts are lost in the life of this world, while they think that they are doing good.
interpretation: This warns that outwardly successful or seemingly righteous activity can be spiritually null if it is directed by wrong ends or devoid of sincere submission to God. People who orient their striving toward selfish, worldly gains, status, or mere show — or who reject God’s guidance — may believe their actions are praiseworthy, yet those deeds carry no lasting value before God. True "good" in the Qur’anic sense requires correct belief, right intention, and alignment with divine guidance; without these, labor that looks admirable in this life is ultimately wasted.

translation: Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in the meeting with Him, so their deeds have become worthless; We will not assign to them any weight on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rejection of God’s revelations and of the reality of standing before Him nullifies one’s moral and religious claims: outward actions by those who deny the truth lose their spiritual validity and will not be accepted or counted for reward on the Day of Judgment. Sincere faith is the condition that gives deeds their weight before God, and without it actions are spiritually void.

translation: That is their recompense: Hell — because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.
interpretation: The verse asserts that deliberate unbelief together with contemptuous treatment of God's revelations and prophets brings a fitting and severe consequence. Mocking the signs and messengers is presented not as mere intellectual doubt but as willful scorn that closes the heart to guidance; it aggravates guilt and leads to spiritual ruin, so God’s pronouncement of Hell functions as both a declaration of divine justice and a warning to respect and heed the truth conveyed by the signs and the messengers.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds — for them are the Gardens of Al-Firdaws as an abiding lodging.
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate success in the hereafter is granted to those whose inner faith is alive and expressed through continued righteous conduct. By naming the reward 'Jannat al-Firdaws' the text points to the highest, most honored degree of Paradise, and by calling it a 'nuzlan' (lodging) it emphasizes that this favor is a permanent, dignified gift from God. The passage thus teaches that sincere belief and consistent moral action are inseparable: true iman must be manifested in good deeds, and through that integrated life believers receive assurance of God’s mercy and an enduring, elevated abode in the next world.

translation: Abiding therein forever; they will not desire any change from it.
interpretation: The phrase portrays the inhabitants of Paradise as enjoying permanent, unshakable felicity: their stay is eternal and their satisfaction so complete that they have no wish to leave, alter, or exchange that condition for anything else. “لا يبغون عنها حولا” stresses the absence of restlessness, longing for worldly life, or any craving for change—hearts and desires are fully fulfilled in an unchanging, perfect reward from God.

translation: قُلْ إِن كَانَ الْبَحْرُ مِدَادًا لِكَلِمَاتِ رَبِّي لَنَفِدَ الْبَحْرُ قَبْلَ أَن تَنفَدَ كَلِمَاتُ رَبِّي وَلَوْ جِئْنَا بِمِثْلِهِ مَدَدًا
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute, inexhaustible knowledge, speech and wisdom: no matter how vast the means used to record or enumerate divine words, they cannot be fully contained. The metaphor teaches human humility before the infinite scope of God’s guidance and the futility of trying to encompass divine reality, calling believers to rely on and continually seek what God reveals rather than presume they can exhaust it.

translation: Say, “I am only a human being like you; it has been revealed to me that your God is One. So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord.”
interpretation: The passage insists that prophetic authority rests on revelation, not divinity, and sets the test of true faith: sincere, exclusive devotion to God (no partners in worship) joined to concrete righteous action. Hope of meeting God is meant to motivate moral responsibility — belief must be expressed in unalloyed monotheistic worship and in deeds that reflect that commitment.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.
interpretation: The disconnected letters «كهيعص» function as a divine signful preface: their phonetic elements are presented without an ordinary lexical meaning in order to arrest the listener’s attention and to point to the miraculous nature of the Qur’an — that from these same elemental letters God produced speech and guidance beyond human composition. Their precise significance is known to God alone, and their presence serves as both an invocation to heed what follows and a challenge to human claims about language and authorship.

translation: A reminder of the mercy of your Lord toward His servant Zakariyya.
interpretation: The verse frames the upcoming narrative as a lesson in divine compassion: it calls readers to recognize that God’s mercy actively intervenes in the lives of humble, devoted servants—reversing despair, answering sincere prayer, and prompting trust and gratitude in the One who bestows unexpected blessings.

translation: When he called upon his Lord with a low, private call.
interpretation: The phrase indicates a humble, intimate supplication — a quiet, inward plea offered with reverence and sincerity rather than for public display. It highlights the believer’s private turning to God in deep need and trust, spoken softly out of modesty and awe while depending wholly on God’s response.

translation:
قال رب إني وهن العظم مني واشتعل الرأس شيبا ولم أكن بدعائك رب شقيا
"He said, ‘My Lord, indeed my bones have become weak and my head has been filled with white [hair], and never have I been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord.’"
interpretation: The verse conveys Zakariya’s humility and awareness of physical frailty in old age combined with firm confidence in God’s mercy: though his body has weakened and he has aged, he continues to hope and to pray because his life’s experience has shown that sincere supplication to God is not in vain. It teaches that bodily weakness does not invalidate spiritual hope or the expectation that God responds to steadfast, faithful prayer.

translation: “And I feared the successors after me, and my wife is barren; so grant me from Yourself an heir.”
interpretation: The speaker expresses a deep concern for the continuity of righteous stewardship and turns to God alone for a divinely appointed successor; the plea reflects reliance on God’s power to provide a legitimate, pious heir who will preserve the speaker’s responsibilities and spiritual legacy despite seemingly impossible natural circumstances.

translation: Let him inherit me and inherit from the family of Jacob; and, my Lord, make him pleasing [to You].
interpretation: This is a prayer for a legitimate spiritual and moral successor: one who will carry on the petitioner’s own devotion and the prophetic/covenantal heritage of Jacob. Asking God to “make him pleasing” expresses the request that God form the child’s character, grant him guidance and righteousness, and accept him as a faithful continuator of the religious legacy—beloved by God and beneficial to the community.

translation: “O Zakariya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not given that name to anyone before.”
interpretation: The verse signals that the child’s identity and mission are God‑given: the name Yahya is divinely appointed to mark him as unique and specially honored. That the name had not been used before emphasizes God’s sovereign choice and the exceptional role this son will play—bringing spiritual renewal, confirming prophetic succession, and manifesting divine favor and miracle in his birth and life.

translation:
قَالَ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي غُلَٰمٌ وَكَانَتْ امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا وَقَدْ بَلَغْتُ مِنَ الْكِبَرِ عِتِيًّا
“He said, ‘My Lord, how can I have a son when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?’”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith combines humble recognition of human limitation with trust in God’s unlimited power: what appears impossible by natural conditions (barrenness, extreme old age) can be accomplished by God’s will. It thus calls believers to sincere reliance and supplication, showing that divine decree can overturn human impossibilities as a response to trust and prayer.

translation: قال: «كَذٰلِكَ قَالَ رَبُّكَ: هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ، وَقَدْ خَلَقْتُكَ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَلَمْ تَكُ شَيْئًا.»
interpretation: الآية تذكير بأن قدرة الله على الخلق والتغيير سهلة ومطلقة: ما دام قد أخرجك من عدمٍ إلى الوجود من قبل، فليس هناك ما يعسر عليه الآن؛ لذا تُرشد الآية إلى الاتكال على قدرة الله وعدم اليأس من تبدُّل الأحوال بقدرته ورحمته.

translation:
قَالَ رَبِّ اجْعَل لِّي آيَةً ۖ قَالَ آيَتُكَ أَلَّا تُكَلِّمَ النَّاسَ ثَلَاثَ لَيَالٍ سَوِيًّا
“He said, ‘My Lord, grant me a sign.’ He said, ‘Your sign is that you shall not speak to the people for three consecutive nights.’”
interpretation: God granted Zakariya a sign in the form of temporary, uninterrupted silence to confirm divine promise and to serve as a visible demonstration of God’s power. The muteness—though not an illness—was both a proof for others of the truth of what was coming (the miraculous answer to his prayer) and a means of training patience, trust, and reliance upon God; it shows that God’s signs may take unexpected, restrained forms (even silence) that strengthen faith and attest to His control over human conditions.

translation: So he came out to his people from the chamber of worship and inspired to them: “Glorify [your Lord] morning and evening.”
interpretation: الآية تصف زكريا عليه السلام وهو يخرج من محرابه، مكان الانقطاع للعبادة، ليقود قومه إلى ذكر الله. قول الله «أوحى إليهم أن سبحوا بكرة وعشيا» يفهم منه أن الدعوة إلى الله تُعرض بالوحي واللطف الإلهي، وأن المطلوب ذكرٌ منظّم ومستمر — صباحًا ومساءً — لأن المواظبة على التسبيح تُحيي القلوب وتثبت الإيمان. كما تبرز الآية توازن رسالة النبي بين الخلوة والعبادة الخاصة والخروج لتعليم الناس وتوجيههم عمليًا نحو التقوى.

translation: “O Yahya, take the Scripture firmly. And We gave him judgement while he was yet a youth.”
interpretation: Allah’s command to ‘take the Scripture with firmness’ calls Yahya to internalize, protect and practically uphold divine guidance with resolve — not merely to possess knowledge but to live it, teach it and apply it in judgment. Granting him “al‑hukm” while still a youth highlights that God endowed him with spiritual maturity, discernment and lawful authority beyond his years so he could adjudicate, guide the community and distinguish right from wrong; it emphasizes that true authority and wisdom are gifts from God manifested through steadfast adherence to the revealed Book.

translation: وَنِعْمَةً مِنَّا ورِقَّةً وَتَطْهِيرًا، وَكَانَ تَقِيًّا
