interpretation: الآية تُظهر أن صلاح وتورع المذكور ليس ثمرة فحسب لجهود نفسه وحدها بل هبة إلهية: الله منحه قلبًا رقيقًا ورحمة ووسيلة للزكاة/التطهّر الروحي، فانبنت تقواه وسلوكه التقيّ على هذه النعمة الإلهية، أي أن الكمال الأخلاقي هنا مردّه فضل رباني يُهيئ النفس للخشية والالتزام.

translation: and dutiful to his parents, and he was not arrogant or rebellious.
interpretation: The verse presents filial piety as part of a coherent moral character: true devotion to one’s parents is inseparable from humility and submission to right conduct. It condemns any posture of domineering pride or willful disobedience that would undermine compassion and duty; in other words, honoring parents must be accompanied by an inner meekness and obedience to God’s guidance, not by oppressive or rebellious behavior.

translation: And peace be upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.
interpretation: The formula bestows divine honor and tranquility on Jesus at the defining milestones of his existence, affirming both his genuine humanity (subject to birth and death) and his eschatological vindication by God; it thus elevates his prophetic dignity and calls for reverent recognition of his status as a chosen servant of God without implying divinity.

translation: And mention in the Book Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east.
interpretation: The verse highlights Mary as a model of devout withdrawal and reliance on God: her deliberate seclusion signifies sincere devotion, moral purity, and a turning away from social pressures so she could seek God’s presence. By commanding that she be remembered “in the Book,” the passage elevates her example as spiritually exemplary and teaches that humble, intentional retreat and trust in God prepare the soul for divine support and extraordinary grace.

translation:
فَاتَّخَذَتْ مِنْ دُونِهِمْ حِجَابًا فَأَرْسَلْنَا إِلَيْهَا رُوحَنَا فَتَمَثَّلَ لَهَا بَشَرًا سَوِيًًّا
“So she withdrew from them and took a screen; We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a well-formed man.”
interpretation: Mary separated herself in modest seclusion, and God sent His Spirit—understood in the Qurʾanic context as the angel Gabriel acting by God’s command—who assumed the appearance of an ordinary, well-proportioned man in order to address her respectfully and gently. The verse emphasizes both Mary’s chastity and the wholly divine origin of the coming conception: the angel’s human form facilitated communication without implying any human sexual contact, and the phrase “Our Spirit” highlights that this was an act of God’s will carried out through His created messenger.

translation: قَالَتْ: "إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِالرَّحْمَٰنِ مِنْكَ إِنْ كُنْتَ تَقِيًّا" — "She said, 'I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are a righteous (one).'"
interpretation: Mary's words express an immediate turning to God for protection and a demand that any person approaching her prove their trustworthiness by manifesting God-consciousness; she refuses to accept or be intimate with a stranger unless he shows himself to be truly pious, combining modesty, prudence, and reliance upon God.

translation: He said, “I am only a messenger of your Lord to grant you a pure (chaste, righteous) boy.”
interpretation: The phrase frames the conception as an authoritative, divine intervention rather than a natural occurrence: the angel identifies himself as a messenger from God to reassure Mary and to declare that the child is bestowed by God's will. Describing the child as zakiya (pure) indicates more than physical innocence—it marks him out for moral and spiritual elevation, preservation from ordinary moral blemish, and a special, sanctified role in God’s plan.

translation: قَالَتْ: «أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي غُلَٰمٌ وَمَا مَسَّنِيَ بَشَرٌ وَلَمْ أَكُ بَغِيًّا»
interpretation: مريم هنا يعبر عن دهشته ويدرأ عن نفسه أي اتهام بالفجور؛ بتأكيدها أنها لم يمسّها بشر ولم تكن بغيًا، تبرز الآية أنها معصومة عن مقياس الفجور وأن الحمل معلومة خارقة للعادة، فالمعجزة تُنسب إلى قدرة الله تعالى على الخلق بلا علّة بشرية، وتعمل هذه الواقعة دفاعًا عن شرفها ودلالة على سيادة مشيئة الله التي لا تحتاج إلى الأسباب العادية.

translation: He said, "So it will be." Your Lord says, "It is easy for Me; and We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us; and it was a matter decreed."
interpretation: The phrase 'it is easy for Me' asserts God's absolute power to bring about what seems impossible to human reasoning, showing that miracles do not contradict divine sovereignty. Presenting the event as both a 'sign' and a 'mercy' indicates its dual purpose: as evidence pointing people to God's authority and as a channel of spiritual and compassionate benefit—guidance, healing, and mercy—bestowed by God. Calling it an 'appointed/decreed matter' stresses that this occurrence is intentional and wise within God's predetermined plan, inviting trust in His will even when it transcends ordinary causes.

translation: So she conceived him, and she withdrew with him to a remote place.
interpretation: The verse indicates Mary’s chastity and prudence: after conceiving by God’s decree, she quietly removed herself to a distant place to preserve her dignity, avoid public scandal, and rely on God’s protection. Her seclusion reflects the behavior of the righteous when faced with an extraordinary circumstance—seeking privacy and trust in God rather than exposing herself to judgment.

translation: Then the pangs of childbirth drove her to the trunk of the palm tree. She said, “Oh, would that I had died before this and had become a thing utterly forgotten.”
interpretation: The verse expresses Mary’s immediate, human despair in the face of overwhelming pain and the likely social shame she feared; her wish to have died and to be “utterly forgotten” (the doubled phrase intensifying erasure) is a cry of vulnerability and escape, not moral failure. It highlights that even the most chosen and pious can experience terror and hopelessness in extreme moments, thereby preparing the reader to understand subsequent divine consolation as a merciful response to natural human anguish.

translation:
فَنَادَاهَا مِن تَحْتِهَا أَلَا تَحْزَنِي قَدْ جَعَلَ رَبُّكِ تَحْتَكِ سَرِيًّا
"Then a voice called to her from beneath her, ‘Do not grieve; indeed your Lord has placed beneath you a stream.’"
interpretation: The verse conveys that when a believer faces distress, God’s help may come unexpectedly and immediately: the calling from beneath and the ‘stream beneath you’ symbolize divine consolation and provision. It teaches that Allah arranges both tangible relief and inner reassurance in times of trial, transforming apparent loneliness into sustained support.

translation: And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.
interpretation: The verse shows that God’s assistance often arrives through a simple, divinely guided action: by obeying the command and taking a small physical step, one receives immediate sustenance and relief. It emphasizes reliance on God’s mercy—that provision and ease can come unexpectedly and directly when one turns to Him and follows His guidance.

translation: So eat and drink and cool your eye. And if you see any among the people, say, 'Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak to any human today.'
interpretation: God directs Mary to care for her physical needs and to adopt a sacred silence as a means of protection and devotion: by framing her refusal to speak as a vow to the Most Merciful she transforms a potentially embarrassing silence into an act of worship, deflects accusation, and entrusts the resolution of the situation to God—allowing the miraculous truth to emerge without her having to debate or defend herself.

translation: So she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, “O Mary, you have certainly brought something strange.”
interpretation: The verse highlights how the community responds to an extraordinary event by condemning and suspecting the woman involved: calling Mary’s birth “fariyā” (a strange, unprecedented, even scandalous thing) shows they interpret what they cannot explain as moral transgression, reflecting human tendency to turn wonder into accusation and to slander what upends social norms.

translation: “O sister of Aaron, your father was not a bad man, nor was your mother unchaste.”
interpretation: The phrase reflects a Semitic, honorific use of kinship: people address Mary as ‘sister of Aaron’ to link her to a revered, pious lineage and to insist on her family’s honor and chastity. It conveys their astonished rebuke to the idea of immorality, using a familiar formula that praises her background rather than asserting literal siblinghood with Aaron.

translation: So she pointed to him. They said, “How can we speak to one who is, in the cradle, a child?”
interpretation: The people’s question expresses their natural skepticism at a miraculous claim made by a vulnerable young woman; it highlights the human tendency to judge possibilities by outward appearance (age, weakness). The verse prepares for the divine overturning of such expectations — God can grant speech, wisdom, and signs to whom He wills — and thus it underscores that apparent incapacity (a child in a cradle) does not limit God’s power or the truth of His signs, nor does it imply guilt or wrongdoing on the part of the one accused.

translation: He said, "Indeed I am a servant of Allah; He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet."
interpretation: This statement is Jesus’s affirmation of total submission to God and the source of his authority: God entrusted him with revelation (the Book) and appointed him a prophet. The verse emphasizes his human, prophetic role and that his mission, knowledge, and miracles derive from God’s commissioning, affirming continuity with the prophetic line and countering any claim that his status is independent of or equal to God.

translation:
وَجَعَلَنِي مُبَارَكًا أَيْنَ مَا كُنتُ، وَأَوْصَانِي بِالصَّلَاةِ وَالزَّكَاةِ مَا دُمْتُ حَيًّا
"And He has made me blessed wherever I may be, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakāh as long as I remain alive."
interpretation: The verse conveys that God has granted the speaker (in context, the prophet) a life that brings divine blessing and benefit wherever he goes, and has entrusted him with enduring duties of worship and social responsibility. Being “made blessed wherever I am” signifies that his presence carries divine favor and contributes good to others, while the command to maintain prayer and alms-giving “as long as I live” emphasizes the continuous, inseparable link between personal devotion and caring for the community: prophetic leadership consists not only in receiving divine support but in practising and promoting constant spiritual discipline and tangible justice.

translation: He has made me dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me arrogant or wretched.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that God shaped the prophet’s moral character: he is marked by dutifulness, humility and compassion toward his mother, and God prevented him from becoming proud, oppressive, or morally ruined—so the verse stresses that true prophetic dignity lies in humble service and freedom from arrogance or corrupt domination.

translation: And peace be upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.
interpretation: The speaker invokes God’s peace and blessing upon himself at three decisive points — his miraculous entry into life, his departure from it, and his future raising — signifying that his person and mission are under God’s protection and vindication from beginning to end, and pointing to God’s sovereignty over birth, death, and resurrection.

translation: That is Jesus, the son of Mary — the truthful statement concerning which they dispute.
interpretation: God here affirms unequivocally that Jesus is the son of Mary and calls that identification a divine, incontrovertible truth. By describing it as "the word of truth" which people argue about, the verse emphasizes that human doubts and controversies cannot overturn what God has declared; it is a corrective to misconceptions (whether denying his human birth, denying his prophethood, or ascribing divinity to him) and a reminder to accept revealed fact rather than follow speculation.

translation: It is not for Allah to take a son; glory be to Him! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and it is.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute transcendence and unity by rejecting any notion that He begets or has offspring—an anthropomorphic attribute incompatible with His divine nature—and it highlights the immediacy and sovereignty of His creative will: existence and events do not come about by biological or temporal processes but solely by God’s command, so that all being is contingent on His single, unfettered decree and there is no need for partners, causes, or intermediaries in His creative act.

translation: And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord; so worship Him. This is a Straight Path.
interpretation: The verse insists that acknowledging Allah’s exclusive and universal lordship—and responding with wholehearted worship and obedience—is the essential criterion of true guidance. It rejects any elevation of intermediaries to divine status, unites the speaker and the audience under one Sovereign, and defines ‘the Straight Path’ as the lived reality of sincere monotheism: ritual devotion coupled with moral submission to God’s guidance, which alone leads to spiritual soundness and communal harmony.

translation: So the confederates fell into dispute among themselves; then woe to those who disbelieved at the sight of a Great Day.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly coalitions and plans can collapse through internal division, and it turns that historical occurrence into a moral warning: those who reject God will, on the Day of Judgment, be struck by overwhelming remorse and terror when they see the reality of that Day. Their disputes, alliances and power will be exposed as futile, leaving them to face a humiliating and grievous reckoning from which there is no refuge.

translation: I hear of them and I behold — the Day they will come to Us; but the wrongdoers today are in clear error.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s complete hearing and seeing of what the deniers say and foretells their inevitable return to Him for judgment. It exposes the present condition of the unjust: whatever power or speech they wield now does not hide them from divine knowledge, and their apparent confidence is actually a manifest misguidance. The passage thus stresses the certainty of accountability and the futility of worldly arrogance in the face of God’s awareness and ultimate justice.

translation: And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be concluded while they are in heedlessness and they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse is a solemn admonition: there will come a final, irrevocable hour when God’s judgment is carried out (‘the matter is concluded’), and those who lived in ghaflah—heedless, preoccupied with worldly concerns and rejecting faith—will be overtaken by remorse too late for effective repentance. It teaches that persistent unbelief and neglect of guidance produce irreversible consequences, urging immediate attention to faith and righteous action before the decisive Day arrives.

translation: Indeed, it is We who will inherit the earth and whoever is on it; and to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: The statement affirms God’s absolute, enduring sovereignty: earthly ownership and power are temporary and ultimately revert to God. “We inherit the earth” does not mean a human-style succession but that when creation’s allotted time ends—through death, divine judgment, or the end of this order—control and dominion belong solely to God. The return to God denotes final accountability and the inevitability that every person and being will be brought back before God, so worldly status and possessions have no permanent claim against divine authority.

translation: And mention in the Book Abraham; indeed he was a truthful (siddiq), a prophet.
interpretation: God commands that Abraham be cited in the revealed scripture to single him out as a moral and spiritual exemplar: the title “siddiq” affirms his absolute sincerity and trustworthiness in accepting and living by God’s guidance, while “prophet” affirms his role as one who received and transmitted divine truth. The verse therefore locates Abraham as a decisive link in the prophetic chain whose character—unwavering faith, integrity, rejection of idolatry, and total submission to God—serves as a model for believers and as confirmation that the Qur’an continues and affirms the same monotheistic message conveyed by earlier revelation.

translation: “When he said to his father, ‘O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, and will not avail you anything?’”
interpretation: The verse exemplifies the prophetic approach of gentle, rational admonition: true worship belongs to a Being who perceives and can benefit or harm, so devotion to mute, sightless idols is irrational and spiritually futile. It teaches that persuasion should combine logic (pointing out the impotence of false deities) with familial compassion (addressing one’s parent respectfully), urging a return to reliance on the Living, Hearing, and Seeing Lord rather than on powerless objects.

translation: O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you; so follow me — I will guide you to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse exemplifies how one who has received true guidance should approach loved ones: with respect and humility, offering clear evidence and a sincere invitation rather than force or insult. It legitimizes correcting inherited practice when one possesses new, reliable insight, yet models a compassionate method of daʿwah that preserves familial bonds—presenting the way and the promise of guidance while leaving acceptance to the other’s choice and to God’s final judgment.

translation:
يا أبت لا تعبد الشيطان. إن الشيطان كان للرحمن عصيا.
“O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed Satan has ever been, toward the Most Merciful, disobedient.”
interpretation: Ibrāhīm is urging his father to abandon idol-worship because following Satan means following one who has openly rebelled against God’s mercy; Satan’s disobedience demonstrates his enmity, deceit, and inability to lead to salvation, so one must reject his influence and turn to sincere submission to the Most Merciful.

translation: O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful may seize you, and that you would become an ally of Satan.
interpretation: Ibrāhīm’s words express a moral and spiritual warning: persistent rejection of God’s guidance exposes a person to divine retribution and at the same time places them under Satan’s influence. To “become a wali of Satan” means to be turned into a companion and servant of evil—one whose choices, loyalties and protections are governed by misguidance rather than by God—so the plea urges repentance to avert both punishment and spiritual enslavement to falsehood.

translation: Ar-Rāghib said, “Are you turning away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you; so be gone from me for a while.”
interpretation: The verse illustrates how those entrenched in inherited falsehoods respond to a call to truth: instead of examining their beliefs they resort to coercion and social ostracism. The threat of stoning and the command to leave show two complementary tactics—violence and exclusion—used to silence reformers, revealing that their commitment is to custom and power rather than to justice or reason; the passage thus highlights the moral courage required to persist in upright conviction when faced with communal intimidation.

translation:
قَالَ سَلَامٌ عَلَيْكَ ۖ سَأَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكَ رَبِّي ۖ إِنَّهُ كَانَ بِي حَفِيًّا
He said, “Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you; indeed He has been ever gracious to me.”
interpretation: The verse teaches a model of faith-filled conduct toward a rejecting kin: instead of forcing belief or responding with anger, the believer greets with peace, withdraws from fruitless contention, and entrusts the matter to God by seeking His forgiveness for the wrongdoer. Abraham’s confidence that God had been gracious to him expresses reliance on divine mercy as the true means of guidance, showing that patience, dignified disengagement, intercession, and trust in God’s compassion are the proper response when one’s message is rejected.

translation: And I will withdraw from you and from those you invoke besides God, and I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be wretched by calling upon my Lord.
interpretation: The speaker decisively breaks with idolatry and the company of those who worship other than God, choosing instead to entrust his affairs to God alone; this expresses both a moral separation from false deities and a deep reliance on sincere prayer, with the hope that turning to God will preserve him from misery, ruin, or spiritual perdition.

translation: So when he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah, We granted him Isaac and Jacob; and each of them We made a prophet.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Abraham’s conscious break with his people’s idolatry — a moral and spiritual disengagement from false objects of devotion — was met by God’s gracious bestowal of both blessed offspring and a continuing line of guidance. It signals that true turning toward God often requires renouncing prevailing errors, and that divine favor can take the form of progeny entrusted with responsibility: prophethood is a gift and appointment from God given to those chosen to carry forward the mission of monotheism rather than a mere hereditary entitlement.

translation: And We granted them of Our mercy, and We made for them a lofty tongue of truth.
interpretation: By His mercy God not only favored those people but endowed them with elevated, sincere speech — a noble, truthful eloquence (and by extension a high, truthful status) that authenticated their character and enabled their words to testify to divine guidance.

translation: And mention in the Book Moses; indeed he was truly devoted, and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Moses was specially singled out by God—his life combined inner sincerity and exclusive devotion to the Divine with the public role of conveying God’s message. Calling him both a messenger and a prophet emphasizes that true prophetic authority rests on moral purity, trustworthiness, and submission to God’s will: Moses is presented as the exemplar of one who is inwardly purified and outwardly commissioned to guide and reform his people.

translation: And We called him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near, and made him one of those brought near.
interpretation: The verse portrays God’s intimate, privileged communication with His servant: being called from the “right side” of the mountain and “brought near” signifies not a mere physical location but a bestowed honor and spiritual elevation—selection for direct revelation, trust, and closeness to God that distinguishes the recipient from ordinary listeners.

translation: And We granted him, from Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s mercy can come as concrete support for a messenger: by appointing Aaron—his close kin—as a prophet to assist him, God strengthened the prophetic mission, provided mutual corroboration and companionship in facing opposition, and showed that divine help may be given through trusted, familial partners who uphold and testify to the same revelation.

translation: And mention in the Book Ismāʿīl. Indeed, he was true to the promise and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: This verse directs the reader to remember Ismāʿīl as an exemplar of faithful devotion: he faithfully fulfilled the covenant and promise entrusted to him and carried the divine mission as a messenger-prophet. It highlights two linked virtues for believers to emulate — steadfastness in fulfilling commitments to God and others, and sincere submission to God’s guidance in mission and worship — showing that prophetic authority is validated by moral integrity and reliable action.

translation: And he used to enjoin upon his family prayer and almsgiving, and he was pleasing in the sight of his Lord.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true righteousness is not limited to private devotion but is shown by guiding those under your care toward regular worship and social responsibility; a person whose life centers on establishing prayer and charity within his household earns God’s acceptance—God’s pleasure is thus presented as the fruit of both personal piety and the formative, ethical influence one has on others.

translation: And mention in the Book Idrīs; indeed he was a truthful one, a prophet.
interpretation: The verse elevates Idrīs as an exemplar of spiritual integrity: calling him ṣiddīq stresses his inward truthfulness and trustworthiness before God, while nabbī affirms his receipt of divine guidance. By preserving his memory in the Scripture the Qurʾān places him within the continuum of authentic prophetic witnesses so that believers recognize and emulate his steadfast devotion, moral sincerity, and the authority of the prophetic way he embodied.

translation: And We raised him to a lofty station.
interpretation: It signifies that God exalted the one referred to (the Messenger) to an elevated, honored status—a special nearness to God and distinguished public rank that confers authority, protection, and dignity so he could receive, manifest and lead by the revealed guidance.

translation: Those are the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favor: from among the prophets, from the offspring of Adam, and of those We carried [in the ship] with Noah, and from the offspring of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down prostrate and weeping.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true reception of divine guidance effects an inner transformation: it produces immediate humility, surrender, and heartfelt emotion before God. Divine favor and guidance operate across human history and lineages, and the unmistakable sign of being genuinely guided is not pedigree or outward status but the soul’s response—prostration, tears, repentance and awe—when confronted with God’s words.

translation: Then came after them successors who neglected the prayer and followed their desires; so they will surely meet ruin.
interpretation: The verse warns that when a people — especially their leaders or succeeding generations — abandon the discipline of prayer and prioritize base appetites, they sever the connection to God that provides moral guidance and restraint; that spiritual neglect breeds collective misguidance, social decay and ultimately brings loss, humiliation or divine punishment (the “ghāyah”) as the inevitable consequence of turning away from obedience.

translation: Except those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds—those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged in the least.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's mercy is open to those who sincerely turn away from sin: true repentance combined with genuine faith and consequent righteous action erases the moral debt and restores one’s standing before God, resulting in admittance to Paradise. The phrase “they will not be wronged” emphasizes that God will neither deny them their due reward nor treat them unjustly—their repentance is accepted, their good deeds are fully counted, and past sins do not continue to condemn them.

translation: Gardens of Eden which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen; indeed, His promise is certain to come.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the everlasting reward described as the 'gardens of Eden' is not mere metaphor or human hope but a real, divinely guaranteed outcome known in the unseen. By framing it as a promise from the Most Merciful and stressing that it will surely come, the text emphasizes God’s absolute faithfulness, the reality of resurrection and recompense, and the moral consequence that believers should trust in God’s justice, endure trials, and orient their lives toward righteousness rather than transient worldly gains.

translation: They will hear therein no vain talk — only “Peace!” — and for them will be their provision therein morning and evening.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moral and existential quality of Paradise: speech there is purified of all frivolity, slander and discord, reduced to salutations of peace that reflect perfect security, mutual goodwill and inner tranquility. The phrase about provision “morning and evening” emphasizes continual, effortless sustenance and blessing — not the intermittent, anxious provision of worldly life but an assured, regularly renewed bounty (material and spiritual) bestowed without toil, underscoring the completeness and constancy of the recompense for the righteous.

translation:
تِلكَ الجَنَّةُ الَّتي نُورِثُ مِنْ عِبادِنَا مَن كَانَ تَقِيًّا
"That is the Paradise which We grant as an inheritance to those among Our servants who are pious (God‑fearing)."
interpretation: The verse teaches that Paradise is not a mere reward transaction but a divine bestowal: God bequeaths eternal habitation to those whose lives were marked by taqwa (God‑consciousness, reverence, and righteous conduct). Describing it as an ‘inheritance’ emphasizes permanence, honor, and that this gift comes from God’s generosity to the rightly guided, confirming that true, lasting felicity belongs to those shaped by piety rather than to worldly status or deeds performed for show.

translation: And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between them, and your Lord is never forgetful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine action—especially the sending of revelation and the movement of angels—occurs solely by God’s deliberate command, not by chance or independent will. By saying all that is before, behind, and between belongs to Him, it stresses God’s absolute sovereignty over past, present and future and His complete governance of every realm. The declaration that God is never forgetful denies any negligence or lapse in His care: He is always fully aware, attentive and dependable. Together the passage reassures believers that guidance, mercy and the unfolding of events are purposeful, controlled by an all-knowing, ever-present Lord, so reliance on Him and trust in prophetic guidance are warranted.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them — so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of any name for Him?
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over all creation, commands wholehearted worship and patient perseverance in that worship, and then poses a rhetorical challenge to human presumption: no one can truly give God a fitting, limiting label, partner, or equivalent. It calls believers to humility before the transcendent Lord and to resist attempts to define, confine, or ascribe equals to Him.

translation: And man says, “When I am dead, will I then be brought back to life?”
interpretation: The verse records and critiques a common, dismissive attitude: people who confine reality to their immediate senses and therefore find the idea of resurrection absurd. This skepticism is presented as stemming from short‑sightedness and heedlessness, not from sound reasoning; the passage thus challenges listeners to reconsider God’s proven power over life and death and to recognize that denying resurrection is morally and intellectually mistaken.

translation: Has man not considered that We created him before, when he was nothing?
interpretation: The verse is a call to humility and recognition of dependence on God: by reminding humans that their existence began from nothing by God's creative will, it demands they abandon arrogance, be grateful and obedient, and live with awareness of the One who bestowed their life and will hold them accountable.

translation:
فَوَرَبِّكَ لَنُحْشِرَنَّهُمْ وَالشَّيَاطِينَ ثُمَّ لَنُحْضِرَنَّهُمْ حَوْلَ جَهَنَّمَ جِثِيًّا
"By your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils, then We will surely bring them and set them around Hell, prostrate (on their knees)."
interpretation: The verse stresses the absolute certainty of divine resurrection and judgment and the resulting public humiliation of those who opposed truth. Being ‘‘gathered with the devils’’ signifies that the moral and spiritual company one keeps will be manifest at the Reckoning: those who followed corrupt influences will be identified with them. Being brought ‘‘around Hell on their knees’’ symbolizes complete powerlessness, loss of dignity, and exposure before God’s justice. The passage functions as a solemn warning that choices have inevitable consequences, that false guides and their followers will be publicly shown for what they are, and that no one can evade accountability when Divine judgment is enacted.

translation: Then We will surely extract from every group those among them who were most insolent toward the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse warns that on the Day of Reckoning God will single out from each community the most stubborn, arrogant deniers of His mercy and guidance—often the leaders or most defiant members—and present them as accountable exemplars. It means persistent rebellion against God does not remain anonymous or consequence‑free: the most obstinate will be exposed and held responsible for their rejection, demonstrating to all the moral and communal cost of proud opposition to the Most Merciful.

translation: Then indeed We are most knowing of those who are more deserving of it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate knowledge of who truly deserves a right, honor, or outcome belongs to God alone. Human judgments about who is entitled are limited and can be mistaken because people do not see inner motives, hidden circumstances, or long‑term consequences. Therefore one should not insist on claiming ultimate fairness on the basis of outward appearances or resent God's distribution; trust in God’s wise and just assessment, which will rightly allocate what people merit even if human perception differs.

translation: And there is not one of you but will surely come to it; that is an inevitable decree of your Lord.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every human being will unavoidably be brought to the place of reckoning—commonly understood as the threshold or reality of Hell—on the Day of Resurrection; this confrontation is a fixed, divine decree, and while some may be spared actual torment by God’s mercy, the fact of being brought to account is certain and serves as a warning to take one’s deeds and reliance on God seriously.

translation: Then We will save those who feared Us, and leave the wrongdoers therein prostrate.
interpretation: The verse teaches that salvation on the Day of Reckoning is the consequence of taqwa: those who lived in God‑consciousness will be delivered from punishment, whereas the unjust will be abandoned to a state of utter collapse and humiliation. The word “جثياً” evokes physical helplessness—kneeling, prostrate, powerless—so the image underscores both God’s mercy toward the righteous and the complete, deserved degradation of the wrongdoers as the manifest outcome of divine justice.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say to those who believe, “Which of the two parties is better in standing and better in speech?”
interpretation: Faced with unmistakable divine proof, the rejecters deflect by turning the issue into a contest of worldly standing and eloquence; their question is a mocking tactic meant to belittle the believers and avoid engaging with the evidence, revealing arrogance and a preference for social prestige and rhetorical dominance over sincere acceptance of truth.

translation: And how many generations before them did We destroy who were better furnished and more splendid in appearance.
interpretation: The verse warns that worldly comfort, luxury, and outward splendor are not signs of divine favor or protection; past communities that enjoyed superior material conditions were nevertheless removed because their prosperity failed to translate into righteousness, humility, or obedience. The intended lesson is that material success can be a test, and ultimate judgment rests on moral conduct and submission to God rather than on visible wealth or status.

translation: Say, “Let whoever is in error be granted respite by the Most Merciful—until when they see what they were promised, whether it be the punishment or the Hour—then they will know who is worse in position and weaker in forces.”
interpretation: God’s postponement of punishment is not endorsement but part of His wisdom: He allows the wrongdoers a temporary respite so that their false confidence and apparent strength become manifest. When the promised event comes—either the chastisement or the final Hour—those who seemed secure will be exposed as occupying a far worse, humiliated state, and their numbers, allies and resources will prove powerless to protect them.

translation: And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance. And the enduring righteous deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in their return.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance is not a one‑time gift but something God increases in the sincere seeker: guidance deepens into firmer faith, clearer understanding and steadfast conduct. “Al‑bāqiyāt al‑ṣāliḥāt” (the enduring righteous deeds) are those lasting acts—sincere belief, continual worship, steadfast good character, beneficial knowledge and charity that persists—which carry superior worth before God because their reward is enduring and they determine one’s final outcome. Therefore the verse urges prioritizing lasting, sincere righteousness over fleeting worldly gains, since such deeds bring multiplied divine reward and a better ultimate return in the Hereafter.

translation: أَفَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي كَفَرَ بِآيَاتِنَا وَقَالَ أُوتِيتُ مَالًا وَوَلَدًا؟
interpretation: الآية تصف موقفًا نفسياً ودينياً: إنكار الآيات لا يقوم على دليل عقلاني بل على طمأنينة زائفة تُستمد من النِعَم الدنيوية — المال والذرية — فيظن المنكر أن الرفاهية المؤقتة تكفل له الإعفاء من المساءلة والجزاء، وهو سوء فهم يُظهر الغرور ويدل على أن النعم لا تُبرهن على الحق ولا تُضعف من حجية الآيات الإلهية.

translation:
أَأُطْلِعْتَ الْغَيْبَ أَمِ اتَّخَذْتَ عِندَ الرَّحْمَٰنِ عَهْدًا؟
"Have you been shown the unseen, or have you taken from the Most Merciful a covenant?"
interpretation: A reproach to those who arrogantly claim certainty about hidden matters or assert a private, binding arrangement with God: it denies the legitimacy of human pretensions to exclusive knowledge or divine commission, reminding that mastery of the unseen and the authority to bind others belong only to the Most Merciful, so people must not base claims, judgments, or leadership on self-appointed revelations.

translation: Nay — We will record what he says, and We will prolong for him the punishment.
interpretation: This verse is a stern warning that God’s knowledge and justice are inescapable: every word of denial, mockery or rebellion is being faithfully recorded, and divine retribution will be meted out in a deliberate, enduring manner. Its purpose is to remind listeners that temporal boldness or attempts to evade responsibility are futile — accountability is certain, and persistent rejection of the truth can bring a prolonged, fitting consequence.

translation:
وَنَرِثُهُ مَا يَقُولُ وَيَأْتِينَا فَرْدًا
"And We will take as inheritance what he utters, and he will come to Us alone."
interpretation: The verse indicates that on the Day of Reckoning a person’s own words and claims—especially false assertions or theologies that deny or rival God—become evidence taken up against them; their speech will not benefit them and they will stand alone before God with no partners or supporters to intercede, so what they spoke will return as testimony in Allah’s hand.

translation: وَاتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ آلِهَةً لِيَكُونُوا لَهُمْ عِزًّا
interpretation: الآية توبخ من جعلوا لغير الله آلهةً ليس لانقياد قلبٍ إلى حقٍّ بل للحصول على هيبةٍ ومكانةٍ ودعمٍ اجتماعي أو قبلي؛ أي أن العبادة والشركة استُخدمت كأداة لرفع القدر والاعتزاز الباطل، فبدل أن يكون التوكّل والاعتزاز بالله صاروا يقصدون أصنامًا أو زعماءً كوجاهة ومصدر قوة.

translation: No! They will disown those who worshipped them and will become hostile toward them.
interpretation: This verse warns that whatever was set up as a false object of worship—idols, imagined deities, or worldly things people relied upon—will on the Day of Reckoning repudiate the claim that it deserved devotion and will offer no help; instead it will stand as an adversary to its worshippers. The passage teaches that created things have no power to intercede or save, exposing the futility and danger of putting trust in anything other than God.

translation: Have you not seen that We sent the devils against the disbelievers, inciting them vehemently?
interpretation: The verse implies that when people persist in rejecting divine guidance, God allows devils to inflame and incite their hearts—so their rejection is intensified, exposed, and turned into open hostility and wrongdoing; this increase of misguidance is both a consequence of their choice and a form of divine retribution and distinction.

translation:
فَلا تَعْجَلْ عَلَيْهِمْ ۖ إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ نُعِدُّ لَهُم عَدًّا
“So do not hasten against them; indeed, We are only keeping count for them.”
interpretation: The verse counsels patience: do not rush to bring about people’s punishment or to demand immediate retribution, for God is meticulously recording their deeds and will administer justice in His appointed time — therefore one should refrain from precipitous judgment or action and trust in Divine timing.

translation: The Day We will gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation.
interpretation: On the Day of Resurrection God will assemble those who were God‑conscious and present them before the Merciful as a chosen delegation — not as accused ones but as honoured, vindicated people brought near to receive God’s mercy, favour and recompense; the word “وفدًا” stresses their collective, distinguished status and proximity to the Compassionate.

translation: And We will drive the criminals to Hell in throngs.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those who persistently reject guidance and transgress God’s limits will inevitably be brought to their appointed punishment; the word "ردًا" stresses their forced, undignified procession and the certainty of divine retribution—serving both as a warning about the consequences of injustice and as a reminder of God’s absolute justice and control over fate.

translation:
لا يملكون الشفاعة إلا من اتخذ عند الرحمن عهدا
"Intercession will not be possessed except by those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful."
interpretation: The verse teaches that intercession on the Day of Judgment is not an automatic right anyone can claim; it is granted only to those whom Allah Himself has authorized by a special pledge or commission. In other words, intercession occurs solely by the will and appointment of the Most Merciful — certain persons (e.g., prophets, angels, or chosen servants) will be allowed to intercede because Allah has made a covenant or given them permission, and no one may intercede independently of that divine mandate.

translation: And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."
interpretation: The verse records and condemns the false assertion that God has offspring; it exposes the theological error of ascribing human familial relations to the transcendent, underlining God’s absolute uniqueness, self-sufficiency, and the falseness and ignorance inherent in attributing a child to the Divine.

translation: Indeed you have come with something, then.
interpretation: The speaker is affirming that the addressees have presented an action, claim, or offering and is signaling that this presentation will be examined and held to account; it carries a tone of admonition that mere arrival with something—without truth, righteousness, or proper intent—does not excuse one from judgment or consequence.

translation: The heavens are almost splitting apart from it, and the earth is cracking open, and the mountains are collapsing into dust.
interpretation: The verse is a depiction of the cosmic upheaval that will attend God's decisive judgment: it emphasizes the absolute power and reality of the Hour (or of the divine consequence) by portraying nature itself as unable to withstand it. Its purpose is to confront human arrogance and denial—reminding listeners that what they dismiss as merely rhetorical will in fact overturn the created order, thereby urging sincere recognition, accountability, and submission to God's warning.

translation: that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son
interpretation: The phrase condemns the claim that God (the Most Merciful) has offspring: it highlights the theological error of attributing human relationships and dependence to the transcendent Creator. Ascribing a son to God implies partners, need, and human likeness — all incompatible with divine unity, self-sufficiency, and transcendence — and thus represents a fundamental misunderstanding and rejection of the true nature of God.

translation: And it is not fitting for the Most Merciful that He should take a son.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s absolute transcendence and self-sufficiency: to ascribe a son to the Most Merciful would imply need, dependence, temporal generation or partnership—attributes incompatible with divine unity (tawḥīd). It rejects anthropomorphic or familial language when taken literally and warns against elevating any created being to share in God’s unique, uncaused, and eternal nature.

translation: There is not one being in the heavens or on earth but will come to the Most Merciful as a servant.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every created thing—angels, jinn, humans and whatever exists—will ultimately be brought before God in a posture of servitude and dependence. “Coming to the Most Merciful as a servant” stresses universal subjection: no being retains independent lordship or exemption from God’s authority. It points to the eschatological reality of standing before God for reckoning and mercy, emphasizing both His absolute sovereignty and the inevitable humility and accountability of all creations.

translation: Indeed He has numbered them; their reckoning has been counted.
interpretation: It affirms that God precisely records and reckons every individual and every deed — nothing is overlooked, and the promised accounting and recompense are exact and unavoidable.

translation:
وَكُلُّهُمْ آتِيهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ فَرْدًا
"And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, each one alone."
interpretation: The verse emphasizes individual moral responsibility and the absolute sovereignty of God: on the Day of Judgment every soul will stand separately before God and receive its own recompense or punishment, so neither kinship, rank, nor collective identity can transfer responsibility or guarantee mercy — accountability is personal and determined solely by God’s just assessment.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will bestow upon them affection.
interpretation: The phrase indicates that Allah, out of His mercy, will cause such people to be loved and held dear — a gift that manifests both as Divine favor and as hearts being drawn toward them. In other words, sincere faith paired with righteous action earns not only Allah’s closeness, acceptance, and mercy, but also attraction and goodwill from others (angels and people), resulting in spiritual intimacy, protection, and harmonious social ties.

translation:
فإنما يسرناه بلسانك لتبشر به المتقين وتنذر به قوما لدا
“We have only made it easy in your tongue so that you may give glad tidings to the righteous and warn by it a stubborn (haughty) people.”
interpretation: God fashioned the message in the Prophet’s language and in clear terms so it could fulfill its two complementary purposes: to console and encourage those who fear and obey God with the promise of good, and to confront and admonish those whose hearts are hardened by pride and persistent rejection. The phrase “لدا” points to moral obstinacy—a resistance rooted in arrogance—so the verse emphasizes both divine mercy (making guidance accessible) and the necessary warning to those who refuse it.

translation: And how many generations have We destroyed before them! Do you perceive any one of them, or hear for them any trace?
interpretation: The verse warns by example: God has so utterly removed many past peoples that none remain to be seen or to speak for themselves, showing that disbelief and persistent rejection of divine guidance can lead to complete, irreversible eradication. It underscores human fragility and the futility of relying on ancestry, monuments, or argument once divine judgment has taken its course, urging heedfulness and humility before God’s sovereignty.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta‑Ha.
interpretation: Ta‑Ha are among the Qurʾanic muqaṭṭaʿāt (disjoined letters); their exact meaning is known only to God, and they function as a solemn, attention‑calling formula that signals the miraculous, weighty revelation and invites the listener to heed what follows.

translation:
ما أنزلنا عليك القرآن لتشقى
"We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed."
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet (and believers) that the Qur'an's purpose is mercy, guidance and ease—not to inflict misery or unbearable burden. Its rulings and admonitions aim to promote human flourishing within attainable limits and to comfort and steady the community amid trials; it calls for reform and obedience without making religious life an instrument of needless hardship.

translation: إلا تذكرة لمن يخشى — Only as a reminder for those who fear (Allah).
interpretation: The phrase restricts the immediate, practical effect of the message to hearts already endowed with taqwa — a reverent fear and God-consciousness. It means the revelation functions as a wake-up call: those who approach it with humility and awareness of God will heed it, reflect, repent, and change, whereas the heedless will receive it without inner response. The word "تذكرة" emphasizes that the text’s power lies in its ability to stir conscience in those prepared to be guided.

translation: A revelation sent down from the One who created the earth and the highest heavens.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that the message is a direct sending from God, identified as the Creator of both the earth and the loftiest heavens; by linking the revelation to the Maker of all realms it emphasizes His absolute sovereignty, knowledge and authority to guide creation, and thereby legitimizes the message as coming from One who sustains, knows, and governs every sphere of existence.

translation: The Most Merciful established Himself upon the Throne.
interpretation: The phrase affirms God’s absolute sovereignty, authority and governance over all that exists: “istawā” conveys perfect mastery and rule over the highest realm (the ‘Arsh) in a manner befitting His majesty, without implying physical bodily rest, spatial confinement, or likeness to creation.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute, all-encompassing sovereignty: every existent—those in the skies, on the earth, in the space between, and hidden beneath the ground—belongs to Him. It emphasizes that no realm or thing, whether visible or unseen, elevated or subterranean, is independent of His ownership and control, underscoring divine omnipotence and the reliance of all creation upon His will.

translation: And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.
interpretation: This statement teaches that God’s knowledge encompasses not only outward speech but the innermost intentions and concealed realities that no one else perceives. Its moral demand is that believers attend to the state of their hearts as much as to their words: outward professions or loud declarations cannot substitute for inner sincerity, nor can private motives be hidden from divine judgment. Awareness of this complete knowledge should produce humility, conscientiousness, repentance for what is wrong within, and trust that God’s justice and mercy attend to what lies deepest in the soul.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him; to Him belong the most beautiful names.
interpretation: The phrase affirms absolute tawḥīd: God alone is the true God and uniquely possesses the perfect, sublime names that express His essential attributes. Those “most beautiful names” are not mere labels but indicators of divine perfections (knowledge, mercy, power, life, justice, etc.); recognizing and invoking God by them shapes correct belief, reliance, worship, and ethical conduct while preventing attribution of divine qualities to created things.

translation: Has the account of Moses reached you?
interpretation: A rhetorical summons to invoke Moses’ precedent: the verse points to the recurring divine pattern that supports and vindicates true messengers, comforts the faithful amid opposition, calls for steadfast trust in God, and serves as a warning that tyrannical power will be overturned.

translation: إِذْ رَأَى نَارًا فَقَالَ لِأَهْلِهِ امْكُثُوا إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا لَعَلِّي آتِيكُمْ مِنْهَا بِقَبَسٍ أَوْ أَجِدُ عَلَى النَّارِ هُدًى
interpretation: Moses’ movement toward the fire illustrates the posture of a sincere seeker: motivated by a simple, practical need (to fetch a flame for his family) yet open to a higher, spiritual outcome (finding guidance). The verse shows that ordinary aims, pursued with humility and attentiveness, can become the occasion for divine encounter — God meets those who seek, turning a mundane act into the moment of revelation and guidance.

translation: فَلَمَّا أَتَاهَا نُودِيَ يَا مُوسَىٰ — "So when he came to it, he was called, 'O Moses!'"
interpretation: The verse signifies that God takes the initiative in appointing and initiating prophetic mission: when Moses approached the miraculous sign, God addressed him directly, marking Moses’s selection, the intimate and authoritative nature of divine guidance, and the moment when ordinary seeking becomes a covenantal commissioning requiring attentiveness, humility, and readiness to receive responsibility.

translation: “Indeed, I am your Lord; so remove your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley, Ṭūwa.”
interpretation: God’s command to remove the sandals is a directive to enter a state of reverence, purity and humility: Moses must set aside ordinary, worldly trappings and prepare inwardly and outwardly to stand in the sanctified presence and receive revelation. The location—“the sacred valley, Ṭūwa”—underscores that this encounter is not ordinary but transformative, marking Moses’ transition into prophetic responsibility under divine authority.

translation: “And I have chosen you, so listen to what is being revealed.”
interpretation: The words express that God’s selection is both an honour and a responsibility: being chosen for the prophetic role requires the recipient to receive revelation with full attentiveness, humility and obedience, setting aside personal inclinations so that the divine message can be faithfully heard, internalized and conveyed to others.

translation: Indeed, I am Allah—there is no deity except Me; so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.
interpretation: God’s statement asserts His unique sovereignty and demands exclusive devotion: worship here means wholehearted submission in belief and action, not mere external ritual. The command to establish prayer “for My remembrance” shows that the regular, disciplined worship of prayer is intended to cultivate continual God-consciousness (dhikr) in the heart, anchoring one’s life in tawḥīd, guiding moral conduct, and transforming outward acts into sincere, sustained devotion and accountability to God.

translation: “Indeed the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives.”
interpretation: God’s withholding of the exact time of the Last Day serves a moral and spiritual purpose: by keeping the Hour indistinct He preserves human responsibility and freedom, preventing people from acting only because they know the deadline or from abandoning effort out of despair. Signs and warnings may be given, but the precise moment is hidden so that each person’s choices and endeavors remain sincere and undetermined by certainty; ultimately every soul will receive a just recompense proportionate to its striving and intentions.

translation:
فلا يصدنك عنها من لا يؤمن بها واتبع هواه فتردى
"So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his own desire turn you away from it, lest you perish."
interpretation: A warning to remain firm on divine guidance: do not be swayed by someone who rejects the truth and follows his passions, for if you adopt his course you will be led into ruin—moral and spiritual loss and ultimately destruction.

translation: And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?
interpretation: God draws attention to the ordinary object (Moses’ staff) to show that miraculous efficacy belongs to God’s will, not to the object itself; the verse teaches that the Divine can make common means into clear signs and instruments of authority, so the wonder lies in God’s power acting through humble things rather than in the thing or person alone.

translation: He said, “It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I use it to drive my sheep, and I have other uses for it.”
interpretation: Moses’ description stresses the staff’s ordinary, utilitarian character—a walking‑stick, a shepherd’s tool, and a thing of everyday use—expressing his humility and lack of pretension. The verse prepares the theological lesson that God does not need inherently wondrous objects to manifest His signs: by His will the commonplace can become a miracle. Thus the staff’s true efficacy will be shown not in its own nature but in God’s power, and Moses’ modest account highlights human limitation and reliance on the Divine when the ordinary is transformed into a sign.

translation: He said, “Throw it, O Moses.”
interpretation: The command to throw the staff teaches that miraculous efficacy lies in obedience to God’s will rather than in the object itself: by carrying out God’s instruction Moses becomes the agent through whom a clear sign is shown, so believers are prompted to trust and act on divine commands even when the means appear ordinary or frightening.

translation: So he threw it, and behold — it was a living snake that moved swiftly.
interpretation: The verse teaches that by God's will the ordinary can be transformed into a clear sign to confront disbelief and reveal divine authority: the miracle is meant not merely to astonish but to overturn reliance on appearances, test the firmness of people's hearts, and demonstrate that sovereignty over nature belongs to God alone.

translation: He said, “Take her, and fear not; We will return her to her former state.”
interpretation: The verse conveys a reassurance from God (or His angelic messenger) that what appears irreversible—loss, barrenness, aging, or a change in circumstance—can be restored by divine power; therefore one should not be overwhelmed by fear when entrusted with a difficult duty, for God is able to reinstate people or situations to their previous condition and vindicate His promise.

translation: وَاضْمُمْ يَدَكَ إِلَىٰ جَنَاحِكَ تَخْرُجْ بَيْضَاءَ مِنْ غَيْرِ سَوْءَ ۚ آيَةً أُخْرَىٰ
interpretation: The verse signifies that God provided Moses with a clear, visible miracle so that the extraordinary alteration of his hand would authenticate his prophetic claim; the supernatural whiteness—free from disease—functions as divine endorsement meant to dispel doubt and show that the message he brings is from God, not a human fabrication.

translation: لَنُرِيَكَ مِنْ آيَاتِنَا الْكُبْرَىٰ — We will surely show you some of Our greatest signs.
interpretation: A promise that God will make manifest decisive, unmistakable demonstrations of His power and judgment—through extraordinary events, clear worldly consequences, or profound revelations—so that the truth becomes evident, the faithful gain strengthened certainty, and the deniers are confronted with undeniable proof.

translation: Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.
interpretation: The description of Pharaoh as having “transgressed” (طغى) presents him as the archetype of willful, boundless tyranny — a conscious rebellion against moral, social, and divine limits. The command to confront such a figure legitimizes active resistance to oppressive power: messengers (and by implication sincere believers) are obliged to challenge injustice and falsehood with clear evidence, moral courage, and reliance on God, because tyranny is not mere error but deliberate violation of rightful bounds that must be opposed.

translation:
قالَ رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي
"He said, 'My Lord, expand for me my breast.'"
interpretation: Moses asks God to enlarge his inner capacity — to remove anxiety and constriction of heart and grant tranquility, courage, clarity of mind, and eloquence — so he can receive guidance, bear the burden of his mission, and speak firmly and wisely before his people.

translation: And make my affair easy for me.
interpretation: A concise prayer asking God to remove obstacles and grant facilitation, clarity, and the needed ability to carry out a responsibility successfully—expressing reliance on divine support so one’s task becomes manageable and effective.

translation: And loosen the knot from my tongue.
interpretation: A prayer asking God to remove whatever blocks clear expression—whether a physical impediment, fear, hesitation, or confusion—so that one may speak fluently, confidently, and in a manner that others can understand and receive the intended message.

translation: أن يفهموا قولي (so that they may understand My speech)
interpretation: دعاء وثناء على أن الفهم الحق لكلام الله هو هبة إلهية تتجاوز العلم اللفظي: المراد هنا إدراك المعنى والمراد والآثار العمليّة لكلام الله—تمييز حكمه وحكمته، واستيعاب ما يلزم منه في القلب والسلوك—إذ الفقه في هذا السياق هو بصيرة تؤدي إلى تطبيق سليم لا مجرد حفظ أو تعليق كلامي.

translation: And appoint for me a minister from among my family.
interpretation: Zakariya is asking God to grant him a faithful helper and successor from his own household — a trustworthy deputy who will assist him in worship and religious duty, inherit and continue his spiritual mission, and support him in his old age; the term “minister” (wazīr) here denotes a devoted helper/deputy rather than merely a political office.

translation: “Hārūn is my brother.”
interpretation: By naming Aaron as his brother, Moses stresses that he is not solitary in his mission but has a close, trustworthy partner who will share his prophetic responsibility—providing familial legitimacy, support in confronting Pharaoh, and practical help (especially in speech and representation) in carrying the divine message.

translation: Strengthen my back with it.
interpretation: A prayer asking God to make the thing just mentioned (understood in classical exegesis as divine support—whether faith, offspring, or a specific grant) into a firm support for the supplicant: to fortify his strength, resolve and endurance so he can bear trials and sustain his responsibilities.

translation: and has associated him in My affair
interpretation: This rebukes those who attribute to another person or thing a share in God’s exclusive authority and governance — treating a created being as if it were a partner in matters of legislation, judgment, guidance, or control of affairs that belong solely to God. The phrase condemns the notion of conferring divine prerogatives on others and affirms God’s sole sovereignty.

translation: so that We may glorify You abundantly
interpretation: This expresses a purposeful resolve to respond to God’s grace by repeatedly and profusely declaring His perfection: it frames praise as an ongoing, intentional practice—collective or individual—rooted in humility and constant remembrance rather than occasional acknowledgment.

translation: And We remind you often.
interpretation: God is saying that He will repeatedly bring to the Prophet’s mind and to the community the truths, warnings, promises and lessons of revelation so that hearts remain firm, heedlessness is checked, and people are continually admonished and guided.

translation: Indeed, you were seeing us.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the addressee had direct perception and intimate awareness of the speakers—their presence, condition, or actions were plainly visible to him, highlighting his clear insight and knowledge of their state.

translation: He said, "Indeed, your request has been granted, O Moses."
interpretation: The verse shows that God answers sincere petitions, but does so according to His wisdom and transcendence; Moses’ plea to ‘see’ God was fulfilled not by ordinary human sight but by a manifestation of divine signs that revealed God’s power while preserving His incomparability—teaching that God grants requests in ways that both fulfill the petitioner and uphold divine majesty, calling for trust and humility.

translation: وإنّنا قد منّنا عليك مرةً أخرى — And indeed We have bestowed upon you a favor once more.
interpretation: The phrase conveys that God is reminding the recipient (classically the Prophet) that divine grace has been renewed or added to earlier blessings; it emphasizes God’s continuing care and intervention in the believer’s life, calling for recognition of recurring mercy, increased gratitude, and trust in ongoing guidance rather than seeing prior favor as a one‑time occurrence.

translation: When We revealed to your mother that which was revealed.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the birth and status of the child were not accidental but set by God's direct communication: the mother received a divine inspiration that framed the child's destiny, indicating that certain people and events are initiated and sanctified by God's will communicated through revelation rather than by ordinary human planning.

translation: «اقذفيه في التابوت فاقذفيه في اليم؛ لعلّ اليم يبلعه فيلقيه الساحل فيأخذه أحدهم — عدوّ لي وعَدُوٌّ له. وألقيت عليك محبّةً مني، ولتصنعي على عيني.»
interpretation: الآية تظهر أن ما يخطّطه الناس بقصد الإيذاء قد يتحوّل بقدر الله إلى طريق للخلاص والرفعة؛ إنّ الله يسيّر القلوب والظروف فتتحوّل مكرات البشر إلى وسائط لنعمةٍ وحماية، ويمنح مَن شاء من فضله ومحبة الآخرين ليُربَى وينال منزلةً أعظم مما كان يُتوقّع. بمعنى آخر، المشيئة الإلهية أقوى من خطط البشر: ما ظنّوه هلاكًا كان سببًا في حفظ يوسف ورفعه.

translation: When your sister walked by and said, “Shall I show you someone who will take care of him?” So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul — We rescued you from distress and tried you with trials. You remained for years among the people of Madyan, then you came at the appointed time, O Moses.
interpretation: The verse teaches that what appear as accidents, mistakes, or hardships are woven by divine wisdom into a process of preservation, purification, and preparation: God’s mercy redirects and protects, trials refine character and dependence on Him, and a person’s readiness and mission unfold only at the time appointed by God. Human choices and sufferings are thus integrated into a larger, purposeful guidance that readies the servant for his destined role.

translation: And I have fashioned you for Myself.
interpretation: It signifies that your creation is oriented toward belonging to God: you were made to be directed toward His presence and purpose—to worship, reflect His attributes, and fulfill the role He willed for you. This is not to imply any need in God, but to place your existence within a divinely ordained meaning and responsibility.

translation: Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not grow weak in remembering Me.
interpretation: God commands Moses to proceed with Aaron bearing the divine proofs, and at the same time warns them to remain steadfast in God‑consciousness and reliance: do not let fear, discouragement or busyness cause you to neglect prayer, dhikr, or trust in Me. The paired injunction links outward demonstration (the signs as evidence before a hostile audience) with inward perseverance (continual remembrance of God), showing that successful prophetic action requires both clear proof and unbroken reliance on God.

translation: Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed.
interpretation: The command frames Pharaoh’s condition with the verb ṭaghā — to exceed limits — so the verse is directing the messengers to confront a ruler whose pride, injustice and usurpation of divine authority have put him beyond moral and religious bounds. It legitimizes speaking truth to power: prophets must warn and challenge tyrants, exposing their oppression and false claims, because such transgression invites divine accountability and a response aimed at restoring justice.

translation:
فَقُولا لَهُ قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشَىٰ
"So speak to him a gentle word; perhaps he will take heed or fear."
interpretation: The verse teaches a principle of prophetic wisdom: when confronting arrogance or wrongdoing, use measured, kindly speech rather than harshness. Gentle, respectful admonition has a better chance to soften the heart, prompt genuine reflection (tadhakkur), or awaken a restraining fear—whether of God, of conscience, or of consequences—thereby opening the door to change or at least tempering harmful behavior.

translation: قالا: "رَبَّنَا إِنَّنَا نَخَافُ أَنْ يَفْرِطَ عَلَيْنَا أَوْ أَنْ يَطْغَى" — "They said, 'Our Lord, indeed we fear that he may wrong us or become tyrannical toward us.'"
interpretation: This is a plea expressing anxiety about entrusting oneself or one's affairs to another whose power could be abused. The speakers recognize the real risk that a person in authority might transgress limits—either by failing in duty toward them or by oppressing them—and therefore turn to God for protection and justice. The verse highlights human vulnerability before unequal power, the moral danger of unchecked authority, and the believer’s recourse to God as the safeguard against injustice and tyranny.

translation: قال: «لا تخافا، إنني معكما؛ أسمع وأرى.»
interpretation: هذه كلمة تطمين من الله لموسى وهارون تُذكرهم بأن مصدر الأمان والنجاة ليس في المناعة البشرية أو مظهر القوة، بل في حضور الله الذي يسمع دعاءهم ويبصر أحوالهم. إعلان السمع والبصر هنا يؤكد علمه التام بما يقع من ظلم وخطر وبما في صدور عباده، فالثقة به تدفع إلى الجرأة على مواجهة الظلم والاعتماد على النصرة الإلهية بدلاً من الخوف من العدو.

translation: فَأْتِهِ فَقُولآ إِنَّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ فَأَرْسِل مَعَنَا بَنِيٓ إِسْرَائِيلَ وَلَا تُعَذِّبْهُمْ ۖ قَدْ جِئْنَٰكَ بِآيَةٍ مِّن رَّبِّكَ ۖ وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَىٰ مَنِ اتَّبَعَ الْهُدَى
interpretation: الآية تبرز منهج الدعوة الربّانية إلى الحق: المرسلون يحملون تفويضاً إلهياً يقترن بالآية والدليل، فيطلبون رفع الظلم عن المظلومين بلطف وحزم دون انتقام، ويؤكدون أن النجاح الحقيقي هو اتباع الهدى الذي يورث السلام الروحي والنجاة. في هذا تذكير بأن المواجهة مع الجور ينبغي أن تكون مدعومة بالأدلة، مقرونة بالرحمة والإنصاف، مع الثقة بأن الله يمنح السلام لمن يلتزم بالهدي.

translation: Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away.
interpretation: The statement functions as a revealed warning that divine justice will overtake those who knowingly reject the truth and willfully abandon guidance; it emphasizes moral accountability and serves to urge sincere acceptance or repentance rather than stubborn refusal.

translation: قال: «فَمَنْ رَبُّكُمَا يَا مُوسَىٰ» — He said, “Then who is your Lord, O Moses?”
interpretation: The question is a confrontational challenge aimed at eliciting from Moses an explicit affirmation of ultimate authority: it forces him to distinguish the one true Lord from false powers or rulers, to assert divine sovereignty, and to demonstrate firm faith and clarity in the face of opposition.

translation: He said, “Our Lord is the One who gave everything its creation and then guided it.”
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s comprehensive sovereignty: He does not merely bring things into existence but also ordains their natures, dispositions and the guidance by which they fulfill their purpose. Creation and its right orientation (fitra, laws, means of guidance) both originate from Him, so nothing is accidental; ultimate direction and providence come from God, and human responsibility is to recognize that guidance and align one’s will to it.

translation: قال: فما بالُ القرونِ الأولىِ؟
interpretation: هذا سؤال بلاغي يوجهه المتكلم ليذكر سامعه بحقيقة التاريخ: الأمم السابقة التي جحدت بالرسل وارتكبت المعاصي لم تَهْلِكَ عبثًا، وإنما كان مصيرها عبرة وعقابًا مَنْ جَاوز حدَّه؛ إذًا المقصود تذكير الناس بأن يستخلصوا العظة من حال القرون الأولى ويعتبروا بتصرفاتهم قبل أن يلاقيهم مثل ما لاقتها، فلا يكون السؤال عن مصيرها مجرد فضول بل تحذير يدعو إلى التوبة والالتزام.

translation: He said, “Its knowledge is with my Lord—in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets.”
interpretation: It affirms that ultimate knowledge—especially of unseen matters, precise timings, and the exact accounting of affairs—belongs solely to God and is preserved in His Record; God is free from error or lapse, so we must rely on His decrees, trust that nothing will be omitted from His justice or mercy, and refrain from attributing uncertainty or negligence to divine wisdom.

translation: He who made the earth a resting place for you and made paths for you in it, and sent down water from the sky — and with it We produced diverse pairs of plants.
interpretation: The verse points to the ordered provision and purposeful design of creation as signs meant to awaken recognition of God’s wisdom and mercy; by making the world hospitable, sustaining life through rain, and producing diverse vegetation, God calls humans to gratitude, trust in His providence, and responsible stewardship of the resources entrusted to them.

translation: Eat and pasture your cattle; indeed in that are signs for those endowed with understanding.
interpretation: The command links lawful enjoyment of God’s provision with responsible stewardship: by consuming permissible food and tending your animals with care you both meet needs and observe a divinely ordered system. Such everyday practices are meant to prompt reflection on God’s wisdom and mercy, to foster gratitude, ethical treatment of creation, moderation, and insight into the moral and providential signs that guide sound judgment.

translation: From it We created you, and into it We shall return you, and from it We will bring you forth once again.
interpretation: The verse affirms a deliberate threefold sequence—origin from the earth, return to the earth at death, and a later emergence from it—as a theological proof of resurrection. By pointing to the same matter as both the source and the repository of the human body, it shows that God who fashioned us from the earth can surely gather and recreate us from it; the statement thus undercuts skepticism about life after death, stresses God’s sovereign control over life and death, and serves as a moral reminder that present life leads to a future accountable resurrection.

translation: And certainly We showed him all Our signs, yet he denied and persisted in refusal.
interpretation: The verse depicts a case where divine evidence—both outward signs in creation and inward moral-revelatory proofs—was made clear to a person, but his reaction was not merely intellectual doubt; it was a willful rejection and stubborn refusal to submit. Linguistically, كَذَّبَ indicates denying the truth, while أَبَى denotes a proud, deliberate turning away. The passage teaches that seeing or being shown signs does not compel guidance: acceptance requires humility and moral choice, and persistent, prideful denial in the face of clear evidence brings spiritual ruin and moral responsibility for that choice.

translation: He said, “Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Moses?”
interpretation: This reflects how those whose power or livelihood is threatened by a call to justice react: they dismiss the messenger as a magician and portray reform as a dangerous plot to seize their possessions. It reveals a pattern—refusal of truth motivated by self‑interest and fear of losing status—where accusations (e.g., of sorcery) are used to delegitimize guidance rather than engage its substance; the verse warns that opposition often springs from vested interests, not from sincere evaluation.

translation: فَلَنَأْتِينَكَ بِسِحْرٍ مِّثْلِهِ فَاجْعَل بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِدًا لَا نُخْلِفُهُ نَحْنُ وَلَا أَنتَ مَكَانًا سِوَىٰ
interpretation: The speakers are proposing a formal, public contest—asking for a set time and a different venue—to present their magic as an equal rival to the miracle offered; this reveals a tactic common to opponents of truth: seeking regulated spectacles and conditions that lend credibility to deception and aim to sway the crowd by appearance and procedure rather than by seeking genuine guidance.

translation:
قالَ مَوْعِدُكُمْ يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ وَأَنْ يُحْشَرَ النَّاسُ ضُحًى
“He said, ‘Your appointed time is the Day of Adornment, and that the people will be gathered in the forenoon.’”
interpretation: This points to the Day of Resurrection as a moment when all outward shows and pretensions are exposed: the ‘Day of Adornment’ is not a celebration but the unveiling of what people once used to display, and the assembling ‘in the forenoon’ emphasizes a public, unmistakable and unavoidable gathering in broad daylight. The imagery underlines that on that appointed day no disguise or delay will avail—deeds will be laid open and every soul will face its true state.

translation: So Pharaoh turned away; he gathered his plot, then he came.
interpretation: The verse depicts Pharaoh’s willful malice: instead of repenting or yielding, he withdraws to deliberate and marshal a calculated scheme, then returns to execute it. It highlights the character of tyrants who, when challenged, do not soften but intensify their machinations—showing that a temporary retreat can precede a more determined attempt to enforce oppression.

translation: Moses said to them, “Woe to you! Do not fabricate lies against Allah, lest He destroy you with a punishment. Truly ruined is the one who invents falsehood.”
