interpretation: The verse condemns the act of ascribing false statements or authority to God — whether by inventing spurious revelations, excusing injustice in God’s name, or attributing to Him what He has not said — and warns that such fabrication is a grave moral and spiritual failure. The stern “woe” and the threat of divine punishment underline that falsely invoking God corrodes communal trust and personal responsibility; the final phrase (“ruined is he who invents falsehood”) declares that the fabricator brings about his own destruction both ethically and ultimately before God.

translation: Then they disputed their affair among themselves and held secret counsels (whispered to one another).
interpretation: The verse describes people who, instead of resolving matters openly and honestly, fall into factional bickering and private plotting; such secret whispering signals avoidance of accountability, lack of sincere commitment to truth, and an intent to manipulate outcomes. It functions as a moral warning: clandestine counsel breeds division, hypocrisy, and misguidance, whereas righteous conduct requires frank consultation, transparency, and obedience to divine guidance.

translation:
قالوا: إن هذان لساحران يريدان أن يخرجاكم من أرضكم بسحرهما ويذهبا بطريقتكم المثلى
"They said, 'These two are surely sorcerers who intend, by their magic, to drive you out of your land and to change your best way of life.'"
interpretation: The verse reveals how opponents of reform cast truthful, challenging voices as dangerous and illegitimate by accusing them of sorcery; the charge masks a deeper motive—fear of losing land, status, or the established social and religious order. It teaches that resistance to a prophetic or moral message often stems not from its falsity but from threatened interests and attachment to familiar ways, prompting people to dismiss guidance by labeling it harmful rather than examining its truth.

translation: So assemble your schemes, then come forward in ranks. Today has indeed prospered whoever was arrogant.
interpretation: The verse exposes the smugness of the proud who, by pooling their plots and advancing together, imagine themselves victorious; that ostensible “success” is presented ironically — it is a worldly, superficial triumph of arrogance, not true moral or spiritual success, and does not absolve them from ultimate divine reckoning.

translation: They said, “O Moses, either you throw [your staff], or we will be the first to throw.”
interpretation: The speakers—the magicians—are asserting control of the confrontation out of pride and calculation: by insisting on who should act first, they aim to stage the event so their conjuring can best deceive the crowd and undermine Moses’ miraculous sign, revealing their desire to manipulate perception rather than seek truth.

translation: قَالَ بَلْ أَلْقُوا فَإِذَا حَبَالُهُمْ وَعِصِيُّهُمْ يُخَيَّلُ إِلَيْهِ مِن سِحْرِهِمْ أَنَّهَا تَسْعَى
interpretation: الآية تبرز حقيقة نفسية وأخلاقية: كيف أن البهرجة والمهارة في الخداع تبدلان الإدراك فتمنح الظواهر المصطنعة قوة تأثيرٍ تفوق الحقيقة لدى من يعشق السلطة أو الكبر. منها عبرة أن المظاهر الخادعة تستطيع أن تضلّ جماعةً أو قائداً متجبّراً لأن العناد والرغبة في التشبث بالسلطة يجعلان النفس تميل إلى تصديق ما يروّج له السحرة بدلاً من التمييز بين الحق والوهم، وما يتطلبه ذلك من تواضع واعتراف بالآيات الحقيقية.

translation: So Moses felt a fear in his soul.
interpretation: The phrase conveys Moses’ immediate inward apprehension—a mingling of awe, humility, and alarm—arising when he faced a divine sign or grave responsibility, showing that even a prophet can be overwhelmed by reverence and the weight of God’s command.

translation:
قُلْنَا لا تَخَفْ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ الْأَعْلَى
“We said, ‘Do not be afraid; indeed, you are the Highest.’”
interpretation: This is God’s comforting assurance to His servant: do not fear adversity or apparent weakness, for God will raise your rank and grant you superiority in honour and outcome. “The Highest” signifies being exalted in status and vindicated—both in people’s regard and ultimately before God—so the trust and courage shown in trial will be rewarded with elevation and triumph.

translation: And cast what is in your right hand; it will devour what they have made. They have only devised the plan of a sorcerer, and no sorcerer will prosper wherever he comes.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God equips His messenger with a real, divinely commanded sign that will instantly neutralize the opponents’ fabricated tricks; what appears as power on their part is merely artifice and cunning, and such sorcery—being dependent on deception rather than truth—cannot succeed in the presence of God’s manifest truth, so falsehood is exposed and ultimate victory belongs to the righteous.

translation: So the magicians threw themselves down in prostration and said, we believe in the Lord of Aaron and of Moses.
interpretation: When confronted with the clear sign of God carried by Moses, those who had been experts in deception abandon their craft, physically prostrate, and openly confess faith. Their act shows that true recognition of God comes from witnessing divine truth and responding with sincere submission (symbolized by prostration), even at great personal risk. Calling God 'the Lord of Aaron and of Moses' affirms both the prophetic authority of Moses and the divine lordship that empowers his signs; it illustrates that guidance is granted by God’s will, can reach the most unlikely hearts, and that power exercised by sorcery collapses before genuine divine authority.

translation: قَالَ: «آمِنْتُمْ لَهُ قَبْلَ أَنْ آذِنَ لَكُمْ ۖ إِنَّهُ لَكَبِيرُكُمُ الَّذِي عَلَّمَكُمُ السِّحْرَ ۖ فَلَأَقْطَعَنَّ أَيْدِيَكُمْ وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ مِنْ خِلَافٍ وَلَأُصَلِّبَنَّكُمْ فِي جُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ أَيُّنَا أَشَدُّ عَذَابًا وَأَبْقَى»
interpretation: القول يكشف عن أسلوب الطاغية في مواجهة الحقيقة: بدلاً من مناقشة الحجة يصف القائل صاحبها بالساحر ويستخدم التهديد بالعقاب البدني والمهانة العامة لاستعادة الخضوع والخوف لدى الناس. هذه العبارة تدل على استبداد يقوم على التشويه الإعلامي والعنف كوسيلة للسيطرة، وعلى مغالطة باعتبار دائمته أقوى من محقِّق الحقائق؛ لكنها في ذاتها شهادة على ضعف موقفه الأخلاقي ونهاية حكمه المحتومة، وتذكير بأن التهديدات الأرضية لا تصنع الحق ولا تديم السلطة أمام حكم الله والواقع التاريخي.

translation: قالوا: "لن نؤثرك على ما جاءنا من البينات والذي فطرنا؛ فاقض ما أنت قاضٍ — إنما تقضي هذه الحياة الدنيا".
interpretation: The words record a stubborn refusal to accept the messenger’s claim: the interlocutors insist they will not set him above the clear proofs already given to them and above the Creator, and they dismiss his authority by confining its effect to this present worldly life. The verse thus exposes a mindset that clings to its own premises, minimizes the messenger’s role to a mere temporal judge, and rejects the wider, ultimate accountability and truth the messenger brings — revealing obstinacy, short‑sightedness, and a refusal to be guided by evidence of a transcendent judgment.

translation: Indeed, we have believed in our Lord so that He may forgive us our sins and what you compelled us to of the magic. And Allah is better and more enduring.
interpretation: The words express a repentant turn to God in which coerced wrongdoing is acknowledged yet not excused: true repentance seeks divine pardon, and the speaker affirms that God's goodness, mercy and permanence far surpass any fleeting power or reward of a worldly ruler—placing conscience and trust in God above fear of temporal authority.

translation: Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a wrongdoer — for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.
interpretation: The verse warns that anyone who stands before God in a state of unrepented wrongdoing—having persisted in injustice, denial, or rebellion—will suffer everlasting punishment: Hell is described as a condition from which there is no death to end the torment and no true life or relief to be had. It expresses that such a destiny is continuous conscious suffering, devoid of mercy or the living blessings associated with proximity to God.

translation: And whoever comes to Him a believer having done righteous deeds — those will have the highest ranks.
interpretation: The statement teaches that ultimate nearness to God and the loftiest stations in the Hereafter are granted to those whose inner conviction (iman) is matched by sincere, consistent righteous action. “Coming to Him” points to the final meeting with God (death or standing before Him), and “the high degrees” signify elevated status, honor, and closeness to God in reward; thus faith without righteous deeds will not by itself secure the highest ranks, and believers are urged to couple true belief with moral and religious practice to attain those lofty stations.

translation: Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever — and that is the reward of the one who purifies himself.
interpretation: The verse teaches that eternal paradise is the recompense for genuine spiritual purification (tazakkā). Here tazakkā primarily means an inward transformation — cleansing the heart of selfishness, hypocrisy and sin, cultivating sincere repentance, God‑consciousness and morally upright action — rather than mere external ritual. The promise of gardens with flowing rivers and perpetual dwelling emphasizes the continuous, abundant and lasting nature of God’s reward, linking inner moral reform directly to ultimate success in the hereafter.

translation: And indeed We revealed to Moses: “By night take My servants away, then strike for them a dry path through the sea. Do not fear being overtaken, nor be afraid.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that when God commands a righteous undertaking, believers must act decisively and trust Him: He can transform insurmountable obstacles into a path of deliverance and will protect those who obey. The reassurance “do not fear being overtaken, nor be afraid” emphasizes that divine care removes the paralysis of fear and pursuit, so faithful action under God's guidance brings salvation even when circumstances appear impossible.

translation: So Pharaoh pursued them with his hosts, and the sea overwhelmed them completely.
interpretation: This verse describes the decisive divine judgment by which God thwarted Pharaoh’s arrogant pursuit: despite his military might, Pharaoh and his forces were swallowed by the sea. It teaches that worldly power cannot resist God’s decree; the drowning of the oppressors vindicates the oppressed and demonstrates that deliverance and punishment occur by God’s direct intervention when arrogance and persecution reach their limit.

translation: And Pharaoh led his people astray, and he was not guided.
interpretation: The verse indicts Pharaoh as a ruler who, by pride, coercion and false pretension to truth, actively turned his people away from God’s guidance; it emphasizes that his authority produced collective deviation while he himself lacked any true guidance, illustrating how corrupt leadership corrupts a community and that such leaders are themselves spiritually bereft.

translation: O Children of Israel! Indeed We saved you from your enemy, and We made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount, and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails.
interpretation: By recalling those past favors the verse is asserting a theological and moral claim: divine deliverance, the covenantal meeting at the mountain, and the miraculous provision are not mere historical gifts but signs establishing God's authority and the community’s obligations. Such blessings were meant to elicit gratitude, obedience and fidelity to the covenant; failure to respond appropriately shows ingratitude and a breach of the responsibilities that accompany God’s mercies.

translation:
كُلُوا مِن طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ وَلا تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي ۖ وَمَنْ يُحِلْ عَلَيْهِ غَضَبِي فَقَدْ هَوَى
"Eat of the good (lawful, wholesome) things with which We have provided you, and do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you; and whoever My wrath descends upon has indeed fallen."
interpretation: الآية تأمر باستقلال النعم وحسن الانتفاع بها: يُباح التمتع بالرزق إذا كان حلالاً وطَيِّبًا، لكن تحذّر من التجاوزات — كالإسراف، والظلم، واستعمال الرزق في المعاصي أو في إيذاء الآخرين — لأن ذلك يوقِعُ صاحبَه تحت غضب الله. ووقوع الغضب الإلهي يُفهم هنا كسقوط روحي وأدبي وحرمان من الهداية والبركة؛ فالإنسان الذي يُحلّ عليه غضب الله قد فقد مقام الحفظ والرشاد ووقع في الخسران.

translation:
وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَن تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى
"Indeed, I am Ever-Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, then is rightly guided."
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s readiness to forgive repeatedly but sets forth a moral and spiritual sequence: sincere turning back from sin (tawbah), firm belief (īmān), and the outward fruit of that faith in righteous action. The closing phrase, “then is rightly guided,” indicates that true forgiveness is not a one-time legal pardon but is realized when repentance and faith lead to a settled state of guidance — a continued orientation toward God’s way. “Laghaffār” (I am Oft-Forgiving) stresses God’s abundant mercy, yet the promise is not detached from responsibility: mercy meets sincere effort and transformation. In short, God’s forgiving nature invites return and change; those who genuinely repent, embrace faith, and live righteously will find their repentance consummated in lasting guidance and the mercy of God.

translation: “And what made you hasten away from your people, O Moses?”
interpretation: God’s question gently reproves Moses for leaving his people in haste: it draws attention to how even well‑intended urgency can have harmful consequences when it removes a leader’s oversight. The verse teaches that prophetic zeal must be balanced with responsibility, and that human actions — even by chosen servants — are accountable when they produce openings for error among those left behind.

translation: He said, “They are the ones entitled to my legacy, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased.”
interpretation: The speaker relinquishes personal attachment to worldly claims—acknowledging that others rightly inherit what remains of him—and immediately turns to God, hastening in supplication and submission so that his ultimate aim is God’s approval. The verse teaches priority of seeking divine pleasure over clinging to possessions or status, trusting God with the welfare of those left behind and accepting loss with humble devotion.

translation: قال: «فإِنَّا قَدْ فَتَنَّا قَوْمَكَ مِن بَعْدِكَ وَأَضَلَّهُمُ السَّامِرِيُّ»
interpretation: الله يخبر موسى أن قومه قد تعرضوا لابتلاء واغراء خلال غيابه، وأن السامري كان سبب انحرافهم وقيادتهم إلى الشرك؛ يُظهر هذا أنّ الفتنة هنا ليست مجرد مصاب عارض بل اختبار لثبات الإيمان، وأن مسؤولية الضلال تقع على من يقود الناس إلى الخطأ كما على الذين اختاروا اتباعه، بينما تنفي الآية عن موسى أي ذنب في ذلك وتؤكد حكمة الله في امتحان الناس وبيان الخالصين منهم.

translation: Then Moses returned to his people, angry and deeply distressed. He said, “O my people, did not your Lord promise you a good promise? Has the appointed time of that promise become lengthy for you, or did you wish that the wrath of your Lord should descend upon you, so that you would break my appointment?”
interpretation: The verse reproaches a community whose impatience or deliberate turning away from God led them to violate their covenant with His messenger. It teaches that divine promises require steadfast trust and obedience; expecting God’s favor while abandoning the commitment that secures it is self‑defeating and exposes a people to deserved consequences. The passage also affirms the prophet’s role in calling the community back to responsibility and highlights collective moral accountability: blessings depend not only on hope but on faithful conduct.

translation: قالوا: "ما أخلنا بعهدك فيما يتعلق بملكنا، ولكننا كنا نحمل أوزار زينة القوم فقمنا بإلقائها"، فكذلك ألقى السامري.
interpretation: القول هنا يعكس تبريراً وتهرُّباً من تحمل المسؤولية: قوم موسى يُنكرون أنهم نقضوا عهدهم ويصغِّرون فعلهم، فيحيلونه إلى اضطرارهم لحمل "أوزار زينة القوم" ثم إلقائها، ويحوِّلون ذنب الابتداع والعبادة إلى فعل طارئ سببه السامري. الآية تبيّن ميل الناس إلى تحميل الفاعل الأصلي كل اللوم وادّعاء أن مشاركتهم كانت مجرد استجابة للضغوط أو لحظات ضعف، بدلاً من اعترافٍ صريح بالخطأ والندم الحقيقي.

translation: So he produced for them a calf — a body that made a lowing — and they said, “This is your god and the god of Moses.” Then he forgot.
interpretation: The verse indicts the ease with which a community can be led from divine guidance into idolatry: under the pressure of a persuasive fabrication and social conformity, people replace knowledge with conjecture. “He forgot” signals a moral lapse (whether in a leader who failed to restrain them or in the people’s collective failure) born of fear and weakness, showing that abandoning principled conviction for the avoidance of conflict allows falsehood to take the place of revealed truth.

translation: Do they not see that no word will return to them, nor will they have power to harm or to benefit?
interpretation: The verse teaches the finality of Divine reckoning: when God's decree is carried out human speech and argument become powerless—no excuses or pleas will avail, and no one will possess the ability to cause harm or bring benefit. It emphasizes God’s exclusive sovereignty and the need to live rightly now, for thereafter human agency and rhetoric will be impotent.

translation: And indeed Aaron had already said to them before, “O my people, you have only been tested by it; and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that apparent popular demands for tangible substitutes for God's guidance are often trials that reveal and deepen spiritual weakness; the proper response — exemplified by Aaron — is to recognize the situation as a fitna, to appeal to God’s mercy, and to return to trusted prophetic guidance and lawful obedience so the community can be led back from temptation rather than capitulate to it.

translation: قالوا: "لن نبرح عليه عاكفين حتى يرجع إلينا موسى" — "They said, ‘We will not leave [the mountain]; we will remain there devoted in worship until Moses returns to us.’"
interpretation: The phrase conveys a communal vow of continuous, focused devotion and expectation: the people bind themselves to patient, disciplined waiting for prophetic guidance rather than scattering or acting on their own. At the same time it implicitly exposes a test of steadfastness—such promises reveal sincere trust and obedience when maintained, but also the difficulty of sustaining communal faith under prolonged uncertainty, a vulnerability that can lead to failings if resolve weakens.

translation: Moses said, “O Aaron, what prevented you when you saw them going astray?”
interpretation: The verse is a sharp moral rebuke that underscores the duty of those with spiritual or communal responsibility to intervene when people deviate from the right path; remaining passive out of fear of discord or desire for popularity is not an acceptable excuse—leaders must courageously uphold and protect truth even when doing so risks confrontation.

translation: Will you not follow? Have I then disobeyed my command?
interpretation: A sharp, rhetorical rebuke asserting the speaker’s rightful authority and treating the listener’s refusal as willful disobedience—intended to shame, challenge, and compel submission by exposing the moral gravity of defiance.

translation: قالَ يا ابنَ أمٍّ: «لا تَأخُذ بِلَحْيَتي ولا بِرأسي، إني خِشيتُ أن تَقولَ: فرَّقتَ بينَ بني إسرائيل، ولم تُرَقِّب قَولي»
interpretation: The verse warns that even truthful or necessary actions must be taken with prudence because appearances and accusations can distort them; leaders and those correcting others should avoid harshness or visible force that can be portrayed as oppression or causing division, for people may seize on outward conduct and ignore sincere intent — so preserving unity and credibility requires sensitivity to how one’s actions will be perceived and the danger of slander.

translation: He said, "So what is the matter with you, O Samiri?"
interpretation: A sharp rebuke and demand for accountability: Moses confronts the Samaritan, calling him to explain and own his wrongdoing for misleading the people—highlighting individual responsibility for corrupting others and the need to acknowledge and repent for one’s misdeed.

translation: She said, “I perceived what they did not perceive; so I seized a handful from the messenger’s effects and threw it away. Thus my soul suggested (this) to me.”
interpretation: The speaker admits that, acting on her own desires, she claimed a special perception and tampered with or discarded a piece of evidence connected to the messenger in order to shape others’ impressions. Her statement—“thus my soul suggested to me”—is a candid confession that her action sprang from inner temptation or impulse rather than from truth or right judgment.

translation: He said, “Then go — for you in the life of this world may have the power to say ‘no harm will touch [us],’ and indeed you have an appointed time which you will not miss. And look to your god at whom you remained bent; We will burn him, then We will pulverize him and scatter him into the sea as dust.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the temporary licence given to deniers or to idols (or to Satan acting through them) to boast and promise immunity in this life is deceptive: it is only a brief respite before an inevitable appointed reckoning. It emphasizes God’s absolute sovereignty — the objects of human devotion are powerless and will be utterly destroyed — and warns against being swayed by worldly threats or false security, for ultimately false gods and the delusion they inspire will be annihilated and divine justice will be fulfilled.

translation: Your God is only Allah; there is no deity except Him. He encompasses all things in knowledge.
interpretation: The verse affirms exclusive monotheism — that the only true object of worship is Allah — and links that claim to His comprehensive omniscience. By saying "إنما" it confines divinity to Allah alone, rejecting every rival or partner, and by stating that He "encompasses all things in knowledge" it depicts God as fully aware of every hidden and manifest reality (past, present and future). This total knowledge is the ground of His authority and justice, the reason human actions are accountable to Him, and the source of a believer’s trust and reliance on Him.

translation: Thus We recount to you some of the reports of what has gone before, and We have given you a Reminder from Us.
interpretation: God informs the Prophet that the narratives of earlier peoples are being presented not as mere stories but as chosen lessons to be used for guidance and admonition; the “Reminder” given “from Us” (al‑dhikr) is a divinely sourced message (the Qur’an) meant to confirm previous truths, console and strengthen the Prophet, warn the community, and teach by example the consequences of belief and disbelief — thereby demonstrating that the revelation is God’s, not the Prophet’s personal invention.

translation: من يعرض عنه—فإنه يحمل يوم القيامة وزرًا.
interpretation: الآية تحذر أن من يتعمد تجاهل أو الانصراف عن هدى الله لن يفلت من المحاسبة؛ في يوم القيامة سيُحمّل ثِقَل مسؤولية رفضه ومعصيته—حِمْلٌ أخلاقي وروحي يُجابه به جزاءً وندماً على اختياره الابتعاد عن الحق.

translation: They will abide therein forever; and wretched indeed for them is the return on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those deserving punishment will dwell eternally in Hell, and that the moment of return to God's judgment (the Day of Resurrection) will be an overwhelmingly dreadful, burdensome ordeal for them — a final, unavoidable confrontation with the consequences of their deeds from which there is no relief.

translation: The Day the Trumpet will be blown; and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-black.
interpretation: When the final Trumpet (the signal of Resurrection) is sounded, God will personally assemble the wrongdoers to be judged; “blue-black” (زَرْقًا) depicts their altered, shameful, terror-stricken appearance—discolored by fear, humiliation and the consequence of their deeds—so the verse emphasizes both the certainty of collective resurrection and the utter disgrace and accountability that will overtake those who persisted in wrong.

translation: يتخافتون بينهم: «إن لبثتم إلا عشراً» — They whisper among themselves, ‘If you remain, you will stay only ten (days).’
interpretation: The verse exposes the secret, cynical self-reassurances of opponents who, instead of confronting openly, mutter to one another to belittle and shorten the commitment of others; it highlights a tactic of undermining perseverance by framing steadfastness as temporary and thereby seeks to warn the faithful against yielding to such covert demoralization and to remain firm despite whispered discouragement.

translation: نحن أعلم بما يقولون إذ يقول أمثلهم طريقة إن لبثتم إلا يوما
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that God fully knows even the rhetoric used by a group's spokesman who, to dismiss a truth, adopts a polished formulation—here claiming the visitors or claims were only brief. It points out that apparent eloquence and calculated ridicule serve to minimize and rally opposition, but such rhetorical posturing neither hides inner rejection nor escapes God's knowledge; those who cloak stubborn denial in clever words remain accountable.

translation: They ask you about the mountains. Say, “My Lord will scatter them into dust, scattering.”
interpretation: The verse signals that on the Day of Resurrection God will dismantle even the most solid, seemingly permanent parts of creation (the mountains) to manifest His absolute power. That cosmic upheaval removes worldly supports and refuges, humbles human pride in apparent stability, and exposes everyone to equal accountability before God.

translation: فَيَذَرُّهَا قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا — He will leave it a bare, level plain.
interpretation: The words describe how, at the resurrection, God will strip the earth of its features and reduce it to a smooth, flattened expanse; this image signifies the removal of worldly distinctions and concealments so that every deed and reality is exposed and all people stand equally before divine judgment.

translation: You will see therein neither crookedness nor any defect.
interpretation: The phrase affirms the absolute perfection and uprightness of the place being described (commonly understood as Paradise): nothing there is bent, perverse, unjust or degraded. ‘عوج’ denotes any crookedness or deviation from the straight, upright moral or structural order, and ‘أمْتًا’ denotes any defect, baseness or dishonor. Together they emphasize that every person, relation and thing in that realm will be straight, pure and free from fault, injustice, shame or moral distortion.

translation: That Day they will follow the Caller whose call will have no crookedness; and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper.
interpretation: On the Day of Gathering everyone will be irresistibly drawn to the single, straight summons appointed by God—a call that is just, clear and without deviation—and in the overwhelming presence of the Merciful human speech will be crushed into hushed murmurs. The image shows both the absolute authority and truth of the divine call and the complete humility, awe and helplessness of people: no proud or noisy protest remains, only quiet confession, fear and submission as creation stands before its Lord.

translation: On that Day intercession will not benefit except the one for whom the Most Merciful grants permission and whose word He approves.
interpretation: Intercession on the Day of Judgment has no independent power; it operates only by Allah’s sovereign leave and acceptance — only those whom the Merciful permits and whose plea He is pleased with may intercede, showing that all mediation before God depends solely on His will.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass any of His knowledge.
interpretation: The words affirm God’s absolute, boundless knowledge — of people’s past and future, their outward deeds and hidden states — and contrast it with human finitude: no one can fathom or possess any part of that divine knowledge. The practical implication is epistemic humility and restraint: humans must acknowledge their limited sight, refrain from claiming certainty about the unseen, and depend on God’s guidance for truths beyond their capacity to know.

translation:
وَعَنَّتِ الْوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ الْقَيُّومِ ۖ وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظِلْمًا
“And faces will bow down before the Ever‑Living, the Sustainer, and ruined is whoever bears (commits) injustice.”
interpretation: This affirms that ultimate reality is God’s sovereign life and sustenance, before whom every being must humble itself; moral failure — persisting in oppression or carrying injustice — brings spiritual ruin, so true safety lies in humility before God and in living justly rather than clinging to power or wrongdoing.

translation:
وَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصَّالِحَاتِ وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ فَلَا يَخَافُ ظُلْمًا وَلَا هَضْمًا
"And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer — he will have no fear of injustice nor of any diminution [of reward]."
interpretation: The verse promises that when faith is paired with sincere righteous action, God guarantees just and full recompense: the believer need not fear being wronged, overlooked, or having their reward lessened. It affirms divine justice and protection, assuring the faithful that their good deeds will not be deprived or unfairly diminished, and thus calls for perseverance in goodness despite apparent worldly setbacks.

translation: And thus We have sent it down — an Arabic Qur'an — and We have set forth therein warnings so that they might attain God‑consciousness, or that it might bring them a reminder.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’an’s language and rhetorical design intentionally employ warnings and reminders as moral instruments: God presents clear admonitions to awaken conscience and prompt voluntary change, but their effect is not automatic—guidance is offered and hoped for (لعل) while human hearts must freely respond to become truly God‑conscious.

translation: So exalted is Allah, the Sovereign, the True. And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge.”
interpretation: The verse establishes an epistemic and ethical posture: recognizing God’s supreme authority, one must adopt patience and humility in receiving and conveying religious guidance—avoid rushing to judgments, rulings, or explanations before the full evidence is given—and maintain a continual, prayerful seeking of deeper knowledge so that belief and practice rest on complete, God‑given understanding rather than haste or speculation.

translation: And indeed We had taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We found not in him determination.
interpretation: The verse indicates that Adam’s lapse arose from human forgetfulness and a lack of steadfast resolve rather than irredeemable malice; it teaches that humans are naturally fallible and in need of continual divine guidance and inner firmness, so that moral responsibility is understood in the light of human weakness while leaving room for correction and mercy.

translation: And when We said to the angels, “Prostrate to Adam,” they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.
interpretation: The verse signifies that God conferred a unique dignity on Adam — an honor acknowledged by the obedient angels — and used the command to prostrate as a clear test distinguishing submission from pride. Iblis’s refusal, born of arrogance and self-exaltation, reveals that true worth before God rests on obedience and humility rather than on rank or origin, and it also shows that moral responsibility and the capacity to choose (even to disobey) exist for some created beings.

translation: So We said, “O Adam, indeed this one is an enemy to you and to your wife; so let him not drive you both out of Paradise, that you should be miserable.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that Satan’s posture toward humanity is fundamentally hostile: his aim is to entice people away from God’s command and thus deprive them of the state of Divine felicity. God’s warning to Adam is a prescriptive reminder to recognize that hostility, to refuse the tempter’s whisperings, and to remain obedient and vigilant—because yielding to Satan’s deceit results in spiritual exile and ensuing suffering.

translation: Indeed, therein for you will be that you neither hunger nor are unclothed.
interpretation: This verse promises divine provision and dignity: addressed chiefly to the Prophet (and by extension to the faithful), it assures that in the intended abode of God’s mercy there will be no want (hunger) and no humiliation or exposure (nakedness). Metaphorically it signifies both material sufficiency and preservation of honor and security as part of God’s reward and care.

translation: And that therein you will neither be thirsty nor be exposed to the noonday heat.
interpretation: It signifies that Paradise removes all bodily want and hardship: physical needs such as thirst and the exhausting heat are abolished, pointing to a fuller reality of absolute provision and inner ease—believers there will lack nothing, free from toil, anxiety, and all forms of privation by virtue of God’s complete mercy.

translation: Then Satan whispered to him, saying, 'O Adam, shall I show you the tree of immortality and a kingdom that does not perish?'
interpretation: The verse illustrates Satan’s method of temptation: he offers deceptive, irresistible promises—eternal life and undying dominion—to exploit human longing for permanence and status. By couching falsehood as guidance, Satan seeks to induce disobedience to God; the passage warns that such appeals play on human vulnerability and are a test of trust in divine command versus seductive but misleading counsel.

translation: So they both ate of it, and their nakedness became apparent to them, and they began to fasten together over themselves leaves of Paradise to cover themselves. And Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred.
interpretation: The verse signals the shift from primordial innocence to moral consciousness: by disobeying, Adam and Eve gained awareness of shame and the need to cover themselves, symbolizing how sin brings self-knowledge, vulnerability, and social norms. The wording stresses human fallibility—Adam’s act is described as disobedience that led him astray (ghawā), not as eternal depravity—teaching that error and its consequences are part of the human condition and point to the need for repentance, guidance, and God’s corrective mercy.

translation: ثم اجتباه ربه فتاب عليه وهدى
interpretation: الآية تعني أن الله اختار هذا الرجل لفضله ورعايته الخاصة، وبعد توبته قبل الله منه وأظهر له طريق الهدى. التأويل هنا: اختيار الرب لا ينافي خطأ الإنسان، بل قد يأتي بعد الضعف والتوبة—فالتوبة الصادقة تُستجاب فيُكفر الله الذنب ويمنح المؤمن هداية ثابتة، دالّة على رحمة الله وقدرته على إصلاح حال العبد ورفعه.

translation: He said, “Descend from it, all of you. Some of you are enemies to others. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be miserable.”
interpretation: The verse describes the human condition after leaving the garden: separation from the immediate, protected state brings rivalry, temptation and moral risk, yet God simultaneously provides a remedy — ongoing guidance (through revelation, prophets, conscience and signs). The core teaching is that the availability of divine guidance makes right conduct a real choice: those who sincerely follow God’s guidance are preserved from spiritual error and ultimate misery, while rejecting that guidance exposes one to misguidance and suffering. It therefore frames exile as a test paired with a clear, practical means of salvation: following God’s guidance.

translation: وَمَنْ أعْرَضَ عَن ذِكْرِي فَإِنَّ لَهُ مَعِيشَةً ضَنْكًا وَنَحْشُرُهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ أَعْمَى
interpretation: من أعرض عن ذكر الله — أي تجاهل تعاليمه وعبادته وتمعنه في هدايته — يُعاقَب في حياته بضيق وحرج: فقدان الطمأنينة والقدرة على التمييز الأخلاقي وسوء العاقبة في أموره الدنيوية، ثم يُبعث يوم القيامة أعمى كناية عن فقدان البصيرة والقدرة على إدراك الحق والارتكاز عليه؛ أي أن الحرمان من النور والبصيرة يوم الجزاء نتيجة طبيعية لاختياره المستمر للابتعاد عن مصدر الهدي والنور.

translation: قَالَ رَبِّ لِمَ حَشَرْتَنِي أَعْمَىٰ وَقَدْ كُنتُ بَصِيرًا
interpretation: يُصوِّرُ الآية احتجاجَ الكافر يوم القيامة لِما يُبصرُه من عقاب، لكنه في باطنها معنىً أعمق: «العمى» هنا علامة على العمى الروحي وفقدان البصيرة الإيمانية نتيجة إعراض صاحبها عن الحق، فالمشتكي لا يَحملُ اللهُ المسؤولية فحسب بل يجهل أن فقدانه للبصيرة هو نتيجة اختياره وإهماله للهدى في حياته؛ فالمشهد تذكير بأن النظر الحسي وحده لا يكفي، وأن تضييع حقائق الإيمان يؤدي إلى التقييد بالعمى الأخروي والمحاسبة.

translation: He said, “Thus Our signs came to you and you forgot them; and likewise today you will be forgotten.”
interpretation: This is a warning that deliberate neglect or rejection of God's clear signs brings a reciprocal loss: by casting off guidance in life one incurs the withdrawal of divine favor and remembrance. The “forgetting” promised on the Day points to being abandoned, deprived of honor, witness and intercession — a state where past claims, merits and ties bear no weight and the heedless are left unheard and unremembered as the consequence of their earlier heedlessness.

translation: Thus We recompense whoever transgressed and did not believe in the signs of his Lord; and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more enduring.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s justice addresses both moral excess and disbelief: those who live beyond moral bounds—through arrogance, oppression or heedless indulgence—and refuse the clear signs face ultimate accountability. ‘Recompense’ here is measured but inevitable, and the warning that the Hereafter’s punishment is ‘more severe and more lasting’ stresses that final consequences outweigh any temporary worldly gain; the passage therefore urges humility, acceptance of divine guidance, and repentance to avoid an enduring outcome.

translation: Have they not been shown how many generations We destroyed before them, who walked in their dwellings? Indeed in that are signs for people of sound understanding.
interpretation: The verse points to historical destructions as deliberate warnings, not mere chronicles: the fact that entire communities once secure in their homes were removed teaches that worldly stability does not protect against moral decay and divine accountability. Those who truly use reason and conscience (āwliyū al-nahā) should read these events as signs prompting inner reform, humility, and readiness to respond to guidance rather than as curiosities or proof of inevitability; the purpose of such signs is to awaken ethical responsibility and deter persistent rejection of truth.

translation: And if not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, it would have been binding and an appointed term.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that God had already issued a prior decree fixing the timing and conditions of what might otherwise have been immediate enforcement; the “word” is God’s settled ordinance or measure, and because of that prior decree He permits events to follow the appointed term and wisdom rather than taking instant, unavoidable action.

translation: So be patient over what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting; and during some hours of the night glorify [Him] and at the ends of the day — that you may be content.
interpretation: The verse counsels that in the face of reproach one’s proper response is patient endurance coupled with a regulated practice of remembrance. By repeatedly praising God at the daily turning points (dawn and sunset), in the quiet watches of the night, and at the edges of the day, the servant shapes an inner rhythm that resists reactive anger and nurtures spiritual steadiness; this disciplined dhikr both sustains the prophetic mission and leads the heart toward contentment and alignment with God’s will (the sense of “لعلك ترضى” being the attainment of inner satisfaction and ultimately God’s approval).

translation: And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to some of them — the splendor of the life of this world — in order to test them therein. And the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting.
interpretation: The verse cautions against coveting the bright, transient pleasures and status some people possess, because these worldly enjoyments are a trial; fixating on them breeds envy and distracts from what truly endures. Believers are urged to cultivate contentment, seek what pleases God, and trust that Allah’s provision — His guidance, real sustenance, and the eternal reward — is superior and everlasting.

translation: Command your family to observe prayer and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the final outcome is for the God‑conscious (the righteous).
interpretation: God is instructing the Prophet to take responsibility for guiding his household in continual worship and to remain patient and consistent in that duty. The assurance “We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you” removes the concern that preaching or maintaining the community should be done for worldly reward or sustenance; provision and support come from God so the Messenger’s task is sincere teaching and perseverance. The promise that the outcome belongs to the righteous underlines that true success — both moral influence and ultimate recompense — depends on God‑consciousness and steadfastness in worship, not on immediate material gain or visible results.

translation: And they say, “Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?” Has there not come to them clear evidence in what is in the earlier scriptures?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who demand a fresh miraculous sign even though the earlier revealed scriptures already contain manifest proofs and confirmations of the prophet’s truth. It stresses that the demand is not a genuine search for guidance but an expression of obstinacy or insincerity—since the ‘scrolls of old’ provided clear, sufficient evidence (prophecies, teachings, and testimonies) that should have been accepted instead of insisting on another visible wonder.

translation:
وَلَوْ أَنَّا أَهْلَكْنَاهُمْ بِعَذَابٍ مِّن قَبْلِهِ لَقَالُوا رَبَّنَا لَوْلَا أَرْسَلْتَ إِلَيْنَا رَسُولًا فَنَتَّبِعَ آيَاتِكَ مِن قَبْلِ أَن نُذِلَّ وَنُخْزَى
"And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, ‘Our Lord, why did You not send a messenger to us so that we might have followed Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?’"
interpretation: The verse rebukes the human tendency to offer excuses and express belated regret after punishment. It points out that clamoring for a messenger as a post‑factum justification does not absolve persistent refusal to heed prior warnings and signs; accountability is real, and repentance or complaints after disaster cannot undo the consequences of willful rejection — people are therefore urged to accept guidance while it is offered rather than postpone belief until it is too late.

translation: Say, “Each of you may wait — so wait; soon you will know who are the companions of the Straight Path and who has been rightly guided.”
interpretation: A confident challenge to opponents: allow them to wait, for the passage of time and God’s judgment will make clear who truly follows the straight way and who is misguided. The verse affirms that truth will be vindicated and ultimate outcomes will distinguish the guided from the deluded, calling the believers to patience and trust in God’s final reckoning.

translation:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. اقترب للناس حسابهم وهم في غفلة معرضون
"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The time of the people's reckoning has drawn near, while they remain heedless and turn away."
interpretation: The verse functions as an urgent admonition: accountability before God is inevitable and near in reality even if not felt, yet most people are distracted by worldly concerns and deliberately avert their attention. Its purpose is to awaken conscience — to compel immediate self-examination, repentance, and reordering of priorities toward moral responsibility and preparation for the Hereafter before the moment of judgment arrives.

translation: There does not come to them any reminder from their Lord that is newly revealed, but they listen to it while they are at play.
interpretation: The verse criticizes those who receive divine revelation only as a form of amusement: although fresh guidance reaches them, they give it mere surface attention and treat it as entertainment rather than letting it move their hearts or change their conduct. “Listening while they play” signals heedlessness and diversion — hearing without acceptance, so the message fails to achieve its purpose in them.

translation:
لَاهِيَةٌ قُلُوبُهُمْ ۗ وَأَسَرُّوا النَّجْوَى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا هَلْ هَذَا إِلَّا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ ۖ أَفَتَأْتُونَ السِّحْرَ وَأَنتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ
"Their hearts are distracted; and those who did wrong whispered among themselves, ‘Is this nothing but a man like yourselves? Will you be deceived by magic while you see?’"
interpretation: The verse describes the moral condition behind rejection of the Prophet: the rejecters’ hearts are preoccupied and closed to guidance, so they conspire in secret and reduce the messenger to ‘just a man’ to avoid facing the truth. By calling the clear signs ‘magic’ despite witnessing them, they expose a willful self-deception — not ignorance but stubborn prejudice and an unwillingness to submit their reason and conscience to the evident message.

translation:
قالَ ربي يعلمُ القولَ في السماواتِ والأرضِ، وهو السميعُ العليمُ
"He said: ‘My Lord knows what is spoken in the heavens and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.’
interpretation: The statement affirms God’s absolute, intimate knowledge of every utterance and intention across the entire created realm: nothing said aloud, whispered, imagined, or inwardly intended in heaven or on earth escapes Him. By naming Him as As‑Samīʿ (the All‑Hearing) and Al‑ʿAlīm (the All‑Knowing), the verse emphasizes that God not only perceives sounds but understands meanings, contexts, motives and consequences; this both consoles those wronged—since secret injustices are known—and warns believers to guard their speech and inner states because all are within divine awareness and accountability.

translation: They say, "Confused dreams!" No indeed; he has fabricated it. No indeed; he is a poet. Let him bring us a sign like those sent to the former peoples.
interpretation: This verse records the dismissive accusations of those who rejected the Prophet: they reduce the revelation to mere delusion ("confused dreams"), accuse him of inventing it, and label him a poet to deny its divine origin, then demand a sensational miracle like those previously given to past nations. The passage exposes the hardness of their hearts and the insincerity of their demand — they require external spectacle while refusing to judge the message on its coherence, moral guidance, prophetic testimony and its own inimitable nature. Their challenge repeats a recurrent pattern in history: people ask for signs as a pretext to reject, instead of submitting to truth; thus the criterion of truth is rightly the surrender to God's guidance, not the mere satisfaction of those who set impossible conditions for belief.

translation: There was not a single town that believed before We destroyed it. Will they then believe?
interpretation: The verse warns that historically, communities who persisted in denial and were struck by God’s punishment did not genuinely embrace faith before their end; it teaches that last‑minute claims or hopes of escape are futile—sincere acceptance of guidance must come beforehand, and people should heed the warnings now rather than assume they can defer belief until a moment of crisis.

translation:
وما أرسلنا قبلك إلا رجالا نوحي إليهم ۖ فاسألوا أهل الذكر إن كنتم لا تعلمون
“We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s messengers are human beings who received divine revelation, not supernatural beings, and instructs those who lack knowledge about religious matters to consult the ‘people of the Reminder’ — i.e., those versed in the revealed scripture and its meaning (scholars/People of the Book) — as the proper source for authoritative understanding.

translation: And We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they ever immortal.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those being spoken of were fully human—subject to hunger, need, and death—so their authority derives from God’s revelation, not from any divine or angelic status; their human condition teaches humility, shows that guidance came through ordinary people, and refutes attributing immortality or divinity to them.

translation: Then We fulfilled Our promise to them; so We saved them — and whomever We willed — and We destroyed the transgressors who exceeded the bounds.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes Divine fidelity and justice: when God’s promise of deliverance is fulfilled for the obedient, He rescues them, while those who persist in excessive wrongdoing and arrogance bring about their own ruin. It teaches that ultimate salvation is granted by God’s will in response to faith and righteous conduct, and that persistent transgression leads to deserved destruction.

translation: We have indeed sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder; will you not then use reason?
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur’an as a divinely revealed reminder tailored to human concerns—recalling their origin, duties, ethical guidance, and the consequences of their deeds. Calling it “your remembrance” stresses that its aim is to awaken what people have neglected: moral accountability, correct belief, and right conduct. The rhetorical question “will you not then use reason?” presses listeners to engage intellectually and reflectively with the message rather than remain heedless or bound to unexamined customs; true acceptance requires thoughtful understanding and practical reform.

translation: And how many a town have We destroyed while it was oppressive, and afterwards We produced other peoples.
interpretation: This verse warns that collective injustice brings inevitable divine intervention: God removes corrupt, oppressive social orders and raises up different communities in their stead. It underscores the moral law governing nations — that power grounded in wrongdoing is transient, that communities will be held accountable for systemic injustice, and that such change can be both a warning to oppressors and a reassurance to the wronged that God can restore justice by transforming people’s fortunes; hence societies must reform and avoid arrogance.

translation: So when they perceived the severity of Our punishment, behold, they began to run away from it.
interpretation: The verse illustrates that people often remain heedless until the reality of God’s punishment becomes unmistakable; only then do they try to escape. It criticizes faith or compliance that is only superficial and reactive—recognition of truth that comes too late, prompted by fear of consequences rather than sincere conviction or prior moral reform.

translation:
لا تركضوا وارجعوا إلى ما أترفتم فيه ومساكنكم لعلكم تسألون
"Do not rush away; return to the comforts and dwellings in which you were indulged — perhaps you will be questioned."
interpretation: The verse warns against frantic, thoughtless flight from one’s accustomed life and possessions; it calls people to return to their familiar homes and the comforts they enjoyed as a reminder that these blessings and how one acted toward them will be the subject of questioning. In other words, it urges sober reflection on worldly ease, accountability for one’s responsibilities and use of blessings, and warns that one cannot escape divine scrutiny simply by running away.

translation: They will say, “O woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers.”
interpretation: At the moment of judgment the guilty openly confess that they lived in injustice—rejecting truth, harming others, and disobeying God—and recognize that their remorse comes too late; the verse warns that acknowledgment after the consequence is inevitable does not undo the moral responsibility one neglected while there was still time to repent and reform.

translation: Their pleas continued until We made them like reaped grain—extinguished.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when God’s decree of ruin comes, human cries and appeals avail nothing: those who persisted in wrongdoing are abruptly cut down and rendered powerless, likened to harvested stalks (حصيد) emptied of life and benefit and described as extinguished (خامدين), emphasizing the completeness and finality of divine judgment and the futility of too‑late supplication.

translation: And We did not create the heavens and the earth and all that is between them for play.
interpretation: This affirms that the cosmos is a deliberate, wise act of God: creation is purposeful and meaningful, manifesting signs, order, and governance that point to divine wisdom and require a corresponding human response of recognition, responsibility, and moral accountability rather than treating existence as random or frivolous.

translation:
لو أردنا أن نتخذ لهوا لاتخذناه من لدنا إن كنا فاعلين
"If We had willed to make it a mere diversion, We could have done so from Our own side, if We chose to act."
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that God’s revelations and actions are not frivolous or done for amusement; He stresses His absolute power and sovereignty — had He wished to treat matters as play He certainly could have, but He does not act without purpose or wisdom, so His decrees and the sending of guidance are deliberate and meaningful.

translation: But We cast the truth upon falsehood, and it crushes it; and behold, it vanishes. Woe to you for what you ascribe.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine truth — the revealed guidance and the power of God — is decisively set against falsehood so that false beliefs and fabrications are overwhelmed and ultimately obliterated; it warns those who invent or attribute untruths (especially about God, His names, or His acts) that their fabricated claims will be exposed and bring them ruin, for falsehood cannot withstand the force of God’s truth.

translation: To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they become weary.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute ownership of all creation and explains the spiritual condition of those brought close to Him: true proximity to God produces humility and tireless devotion. Those who truly recognise His sovereignty cannot be arrogant in worship, nor do they find worship burdensome—because sincere servitude, born of knowledge and love of God, removes pride and transforms continual worship into a sustaining act rather than a weary duty.

translation: They glorify [Allah] night and day, never growing weary.
interpretation: The phrase describes a spiritual disposition in which God's servants keep their hearts constantly oriented toward God: their praise and remembrance are not occasional rituals but a sustained, heartfelt state that persists through all circumstances. “Night and day” signifies unbroken constancy, and “never growing weary” emphasizes perseverance born of sincere devotion—worship that becomes an enduring way of life rather than a fleeting effort.

translation: أم اتخذوا آلهة من الأرض هم ينشرون — “Or have they taken gods from the earth who themselves bring forth?”
interpretation: The verse condemns the worship of created, earthly things by pointing out the absurdity of assigning deity to what is itself produced and dependent; those ‘gods’ come from the earth and possess no independent power to originate, sustain or benefit — their apparent influence is only a product of human attribution, whereas true creative and sustaining power belongs solely to God.

translation: If there were in them (the heavens and the earth) other gods besides Allah, they both would have been corrupted. So exalted is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they ascribe.
interpretation: The verse offers a logical proof against polytheism: the orderly, sustained functioning of the heavens and the earth shows that a single, unified sovereign manages them; if multiple deities truly governed, their conflicting wills would have produced chaos and ruin. By naming God “Lord of the Throne” the text affirms His absolute, uncontested authority and then repudiates the pagan attributions and imaginative projections of partners, offspring or incarnations — God is transcendent and free from those descriptions.

translation: He is not questioned concerning what He does, while they will be questioned.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty and self-sufficiency: God does not stand in need of explanation or inquiry about His actions, because His wisdom and authority are beyond human measure; by contrast, human beings are accountable and will be called to answer for their deeds, so they must bear responsibility and seek guidance rather than presume to judge divine conduct.

translation: Or have they taken besides Him gods? Say, “Bring your proof.” This is a reminder — from those with me and a reminder from those before me. Nay, most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.
interpretation: The verse functions as a rational and moral rebuttal to idolatry: by demanding that rivals to God be substantiated with evidence, it exposes the emptiness of unproven objects of worship and insists that the Qur’anic message belongs to a continuous prophetic tradition rather than being a novel invention. Its remark that “most do not know the truth” locates the cause of rejection not in the absence of guidance but in ignorance or willful avoidance, thereby assigning moral responsibility to those who refuse to seek or accept evidence.

translation: And We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him: ‘There is no deity but I, so worship Me.’
interpretation: The verse affirms that the core, unchanging message brought by every prophet is tawhīd — the exclusive oneness and sovereignty of God — coupled with the command to direct all worship, allegiance, and obedience to Him alone. It stresses continuity in divine guidance, rejects polytheism and dependence on intermediaries, and implies that ‘worship’ encompasses both inward faith and outward devotion to God’s laws and commands.

translation: And they say, “The Most Merciful has taken a son.” Exalted is He! Rather, they are honored servants.
interpretation: The verse rejects the claim that God (al‑Rahmān) has offspring: it affirms His absolute transcendence and denies any filial or anthropomorphic relationship. The phrase “سبحانه” (Glory be to Him) underscores God’s utter incomparability, while “بل عباد مكرمون” corrects the error by identifying those whom people exalt as children of God instead as honored, noble servants (classically understood as angels or chosen servants) whose function is worship and obedience—not divinity. The statement thus defends tawhīd (God’s oneness) and warns against elevating created beings to a divine status.

translation: They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those in God’s presence—primarily the angels—have no independent initiative in word or deed: they neither speak of their own accord nor act except under God’s instruction. It emphasizes divine sovereignty and perfect submission, showing that all authority for speech and action rests with God and that even exalted beings operate only as He wills.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them. They do not intercede except for one whom He approves, and they are apprehensive out of fear of Him.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute knowledge and authority and teaches that intercession is not an independent right but a privilege granted by God alone. Those who may intercede—whether angels, prophets, or the righteous—do so only with His permission and do so in humility and trembling reverence, which underscores both God’s sovereign control over mercy and the solemn, awe‑filled nature of standing before Him.

translation: And whoever among them says, “Indeed I am a god besides Him,” We will recompense him with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse warns that anyone who arrogantly claims divinity or divine status in place of God commits the gravest form of injustice and falsehood; such a claim is treated as a major transgression (shirk/ظلم) and will be met with just retribution in Hell, underscoring God’s punishment for those who usurp His unique lordship and lead others astray.

translation: Have not those who disbelieve considered that the heavens and the earth were once joined together, and We separated them? And We made from water every living thing. Will they not then believe?
interpretation: The verse points to the cosmic acts of God as clear signs meant to awaken recognition: the Creator who brought the heavens and earth into being and then set them in their ordered relation, and who made all life to arise from water, displays unmatched power, wisdom, and control over existence. Its rhetorical question exposes that refusal to believe is not due to a lack of evidence but a deliberate turning away; the proper response to these manifest signs is submission to God’s oneness and lordship, for they demonstrate both His creative authority and His sustaining mercy.

translation: And We placed firm mountains in the earth so that it would not shake with them, and We made in it wide paths, perhaps they may be guided.
interpretation: The verse presents the geological order — mountains as stabilizers and wide routes across the land — as purposeful provisions from God: these features sustain human life and enable travel, trade and contact, and are therefore signs meant to prompt reflection. By observing how creation is arranged to support and direct human affairs, people are invited to recognize divine wisdom and so be led toward right belief and conduct.

translation: And We made the sky a guarded ceiling, yet they turn away from its signs.
interpretation: Calling the sky a “guarded ceiling” highlights its purposeful, protective and ordered nature as evidence of God’s sustaining power and governance; the verse admonishes that this visible preservation and cosmic order are clear signs of divine mercy and authority, and that failing to heed them — turning away in denial, heedlessness, or ingratitude — reveals spiritual blindness to God’s sovereignty.

translation: And He is the One who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; each swims in its orbit.
interpretation: This affirms God’s exclusive sovereignty and the deliberate, law‑bound order of the universe: the steady, governed motions of night, day, sun and moon are manifestations of His power and wisdom, meant to refute any divinization of celestial bodies and to call people to reflect, trust in His design, and submit to His rule.

translation: And We did not grant to any human before you immortality. So if you die, will they be the ones to live forever?
interpretation: God reminds the Prophet that mortality is the human condition and that no messenger was made eternal; his death therefore does not negate the truth of his message nor confer immortality or ultimate authority on others. Permanence and true life belong only to God, and the coming or passing of any human does not change divine purpose or judgment.

translation: Every soul will taste death. And We will surely test you with evil and with good as a trial; and to Us you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse teaches that mortality is universal and that earthly life is a purposeful trial: both suffering and prosperity are means by which God tests people's inner states and conduct, so believers are called to patience, gratitude and uprightness, conscious that all deeds will be judged when they return to God.

translation: And when those who disbelieve see you, they only take you in ridicule: “Is this the one who mentions your gods?” Yet in the remembrance of the Most Merciful they are disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse exposes a common defensive posture of the rejecters: they deride the Prophet as if he were merely pandering to their idols to dismiss his challenge, but this mockery actually betrays their spiritual blindness — they prefer ridicule to confronting the true remembrance of the Merciful, using scorn to avoid responsibility for their persistent rejection of guidance.

translation: Man was created of haste. I will show you My signs, so do not be impatient.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a natural human weakness—impatience—and admonishes against forcing God’s hand by demanding immediate proofs or outcomes. It teaches that divine matters unfold in God’s appointed time, not according to our urgency; therefore the faithful should cultivate patience, trust God’s wisdom, and refrain from pressing for instant signs or judgments beyond human control.

translation: And they will say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The verse illustrates the cynical stance of those who, confronted with warnings of the Last Day, demand a precise timeframe as a way to evade moral responsibility. Their question is not an earnest request for knowledge but a rhetorical challenge intended to mock and postpone belief: by insisting on exact dates they try to reduce the divine promise to a negotiable, empirical demand. The passage exposes such questioning as a tactic of denial—it reveals stubborn refusal to accept consequences until the moment of reckoning arrives, when their prior taunts will be shown as vain.

translation: If only those who disbelieve knew—when the Fire will not be kept off their faces nor off their backs, and they will receive no help.
interpretation: The verse teaches that disbelief leads to an absolute, unavoidable divine judgment in which human efforts, alliances, or attempts to flee will be powerless. Its purpose is to awaken the conscience: to show the futility of relying on worldly means against God’s decree and to urge timely recognition of the truth, repentance, and submission before the moment of reckoning becomes irreversible.

translation: But it will come upon them suddenly and stun them, so they will not be able to repel it nor will they be granted a respite.
interpretation: The verse warns that when the decisive moment of divine judgment or punishment arrives unexpectedly, those who denied or resisted the truth will be overwhelmed and powerless to avert it, and they will not be given time or opportunity to delay, escape, or reconsider their ways.

translation: And indeed messengers before you were mocked, but those who mocked them were overtaken by that which they used to mock.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ridiculing God’s messengers is a recurring human failing that ultimately leads to the mockers’ own humiliation or punishment; it reassures the faithful that present scorn does not alter God’s support for the truth, and warns those who taunt divine guidance that their apparent triumph is temporary and will be reversed by consequences attested by history.

translation:
قُل مَن يَكْلَؤُكُم بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ مِنَ الرَّحْمَٰنِۖ بَلْ هُمْ عَن ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِم مُعْرِضُونَ
"Say: ‘Who protects or shelters you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?’ — Nay, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord."
interpretation: The verse rebukes the false reliance on anything or anyone other than God by highlighting that continuous, vigilant care belongs to the Merciful alone; yet people persist in neglecting His remembrance. Their turning away is both an expression of ingratitude and the root of spiritual blindness: by refusing to remember and acknowledge the One who truly sustains and guards them, they cut themselves off from the source of real protection and guidance and are left trusting transient, inadequate supports.

translation: Or do they have gods who can protect them from Us? They cannot even help themselves, nor can they be companions with Us.
interpretation: The verse asserts the utter powerlessness of any being worshipped besides God: such 'gods' lack independent ability to defend their own existence or to interpose against God’s will. It teaches that relying on created things for protection or mediation is futile because they neither possess self-sustaining strength nor can they stand as partners or allies alongside the Divine; ultimate authority and the capacity to decree and avert are God's alone.

translation: Rather, We granted enjoyment to these and their fathers until their lives were prolonged for them. Do they not see that We come to the earth and diminish it from its outermost edges? Are they then the prevailing ones?
interpretation: The verse warns that worldly comfort and long life are not signs of immunity from God's judgment. God reminds the heedless that He can, if He wills, curtail their prosperity and shrink their dominion—removing people or possessions from the remotest parts of the earth—so they should not imagine themselves to be the ultimate victors or secure against divine decree. The passage calls for humility and recognition that power and permanence belong to God alone.

translation:
قُلْ إِنَّمَا أُنذِرُكُم بِالْوَحْيِ ۚ وَلَا يَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ الدُّعَاءَ إِذَا مَا يُنذَرُونَ
"Say: I only warn you by revelation; and the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Prophet’s duty is to convey God’s revelation and warnings, not to compel belief; many who are described as “deaf” are spiritually or morally closed off, so despite clear admonition they fail to respond. Thus guidance’s acceptance depends on people’s readiness to hear, not on the messenger’s effort.

translation: And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord were to touch them, they would cry, “O woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers.”
interpretation: This portrays people who only acknowledge their injustice when overwhelmed by divine chastisement; their exclamation is a belated, desperate realization born of suffering rather than sincere repentance, showing that mere late admission of guilt cannot undo the consequences of persistent denial and wrongdoing and warning that true reform and submission must occur before punishment, not only after it.

translation: And We will set up the balances of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And if there is (anything) the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it. And sufficient are We as Reckoners.
interpretation: The verse affirms that on the Day of Judgment God will establish perfect, impartial measures to weigh every deed, ensuring absolute justice: nothing — not even an action as tiny as a mustard seed — will be omitted or treated unfairly. The promise “We will bring it” underlines God’s complete knowledge and power to account for every secret and visible act, and “sufficient are We as Reckoners” declares that God alone is fully competent to judge. Thus the passage calls people to recognize that all their deeds, however small, are recorded and will be justly recompensed or held to account.

translation: And We indeed gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion, and a light, and a reminder for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God bestowed upon Moses and Aaron a revealed guidance (الفرقان) that distinguishes truth from falsehood, described as a luminous source (ضياء) and a cautioning reminder; its true effect is realized in the hearts of the muttaqīn (the God‑fearing), who accept, act on, and are guided by that revelation — implying that scripture and prophetic guidance function both as an objective criterion and as a spiritual light whose benefit depends on the righteousness and receptivity of the hearers.

translation: Those who fear their Lord in the unseen, and they are apprehensive of the Hour.
interpretation: The verse describes believers whose reverence for God is inward and constant — a fear rooted in faith rather than in visible signs — so that even unseen accountability shapes their hearts and actions. Their anxiety about the Hour (the Day of Judgment), whose timing is hidden, keeps them vigilant, humble, and morally restrained: this sober fear is not despair but a motivating consciousness that leads to repentance, restraint from sin, and steady readiness for final reckoning.

translation: And this is a blessed Reminder which We have revealed. Are you then denying it?
interpretation: Calling the Book a “blessed reminder” and asserting “We revealed it” emphasizes both its divine origin and its role as a source of real benefit—guidance, moral healing, and mercy—for those who accept it. The rhetorical question exposes denial as an unjustifiable rejection of something meant to bring good; it frames refusal not merely as a different opinion but as a moral and intellectual failing (born of pride, heedlessness, or attachment to falsehood) that deprives people of the blessings promised and makes them accountable. The verse therefore presses for sober reflection, humble acceptance, and gratitude toward what God has sent.

translation: And indeed We had already granted Abraham his right guidance, and We were well acquainted with him.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Abraham’s soundness of judgment and steadfast faith were a direct gift from God given to him prior to his public role; it emphasizes that his monotheism and moral uprightness were rooted in divine guidance and that God knew his inner disposition and sincerity—thereby validating Abraham’s prophetic integrity and presenting him as a model whose true guidance originates from God, not from mere human convention.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, “What are these statues that you are devoted to?”
interpretation: Ibrahim here confronts the practice of idolatry by directly questioning his father and community about their persistent devotion to lifeless images; the verse portrays him calling them to reflect on the futility and irrationality of worshipping powerless objects and to reconsider the proper object of reverence — the One Creator.

translation: They said, 'We found our fathers worshipping it.'
interpretation: A defensive appeal to tradition: people excuse persisting in error by pointing to ancestral practice, preferring inherited customs and social conformity over independent inquiry and the pursuit of truth, thereby resisting correction or reform.

translation: He said, “Indeed you and your fathers have been in manifest error.”
interpretation: A categorical rebuke that ascribes an enduring, obvious misguidance to a people and their forebears; the phrase “ضلال مبين” stresses that their deviation was clear and unmistakable, not a subtle misunderstanding, which implies collective and inherited responsibility for persisting in false beliefs and practices despite available guidance — thus removing excuses and calling for conscious recognition, repentance, and return to the straight path.

translation: قالوا: "أجئتنا بالحق أم أنت من اللاعبين؟" — "They said, ‘Have you come to us with the truth, or are you one of those who play?’"
interpretation: The verse depicts the dismissive stance of opponents who refuse to engage sincerely with a messenger’s claim; by asking whether he brings truth or is merely jesting, they aim to belittle the message and evade its moral challenge, treating revelation as either deliberate deception or frivolity rather than confronting its demands.

translation: قَالَ بَلْ رَبُّكُمْ رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ الَّذِي فَطَرَهُنَّ وَأَنَا عَلَى ذَٰلِكُم مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد توحيد الربوبية: أن صفّة الربوبية الثابتة لله تستند إلى كونه خالق السماوات والأرض، فالفطر هنا يعني الابتداء والإيجاد الذي يجعل للمتصف به سلطاناً وحقّاً في الربوبية. كلمة «بل» تعمل تصحيحاً لما قبِلَه السامعون من افتراضات خاطئة، وعبارة «وأنا على ذلكم من الشاهدين» تدل على موقف الشهادة والشجاعة في إعلان الحقّ أمام المخالفين، وتذكّر بأن الاعتراف بالخلق يستلزم الخضوع لله والإنكار لكل شرك أو مزاعم لغيره.

translation: By Allah, I will surely overthrow your idols after you have turned away fleeing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the apparent power and legitimacy of idols rest solely on human support; once people abandon them they will be exposed and brought low. It conveys the inevitability of the collapse of false deities and the ultimate triumph of divine truth, emphasizing that idol-worship is transient and powerless compared with God’s authority.

translation: So He left them few and scattered, except for an old man for them, that perhaps they might return to him.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God, in His wisdom, reduced a people’s numbers yet left an elderly man among them as a living point of reference; this was so they would have someone to whom they could turn and thereby be guided back. It emphasizes God’s mercy in preserving means of counsel and leadership as a way for communities to repent, regroup, and restore guidance rather than being cut off utterly.

translation: قالوا: «من فعل هذا بآلهتنا؟ إنه لمن الظالمين» — “They said, ‘Who has done this to our gods? Indeed he is among the wrongdoers.’”
interpretation: The verse highlights a common social reaction: when entrenched beliefs or symbols are challenged, the community reflexively brands the challenger as a wrongdoer. Calling the destroyer ‘one of the unjust’ is a moral inversion — it reveals how people defend false comforts and vested interests by labeling reform or truth-telling as oppression, thereby protecting the status quo rather than examining the justice of their own attachment.

translation: They said, "We heard a young man mentioning them; he is called Ibrahim."
interpretation: The verse highlights how his people sought to dismiss Abraham’s admonition by reducing it to the talk of “a youth.” By naming him and stressing his age, they acknowledge his words but try to delegitimize the warning—a common social reaction to reformers: reject the message by belittling the messenger rather than addressing the truth of what he says.

translation:
قالوا: فأتوا به على أعين الناس لعلهم يشهدون
"They said, 'Bring him out before the eyes of the people; perhaps they will bear witness.'"
