interpretation: The verse highlights how people resort to public display to manufacture or secure validation: by presenting someone openly they hope to create witnesses or exert social pressure so that testimony will be produced. It points to the use of spectacle—either to establish apparent truth or to humiliate and coerce—showing how communal observation and opinion can be summoned to serve an agenda rather than to seek sincere justice.

translation: قالوا: «أأنت فعلت هذا بآلهتنا يا إبراهيم» — “They said, ‘Did you do this to our gods, O Abraham?’”
interpretation: The line exposes a common defensive tactic: instead of engaging with the critique of idolatry, the community seeks to displace blame onto the critic to protect their beliefs and social order. It shows how people, when faced with uncomfortable truth, often accuse and vilify reformers to avoid examining the underlying error and to justify persecution.

translation: He said, “No; this was done by their chiefs. So ask them, if indeed they can speak.”
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who evade responsibility by blaming prominent leaders or idols for what has occurred; it exposes the hollow excuse of shifting guilt onto others and challenges the claim by pointing out the impotence of those so-called authorities — if they could speak or answer they would, but their silence or inability undercuts the followers’ defense and reveals their culpability.

translation:
فَرَجَعُوا إِلَى أَنْفُسِهِمْ فَقَالُوا إِنَّكُمْ أَنْتُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ
"Then they turned to one another and said, ‘Indeed, you are the wrongdoers.’"
interpretation: The verse exposes a common moral failing: when confronted with guilt people often refuse to admit it and instead shift blame onto others. Rather than sincere self-examination and repentance, each person accuses the other as the transgressor, revealing hard-heartedness and an attempt to escape responsibility; the implication is that true reform requires inward acknowledgment of one’s own fault, not mutual recrimination.

translation: Then they bowed down upon their heads. Indeed, you knew what these were uttering.
interpretation: The verse shows that when opponents or hypocrites are confronted their shame becomes visible — they lower their heads — while the addressee (understood in context as the Prophet or one aware of the matter) already knew their secret words and intentions. The statement emphasizes that outward silence or embarrassment does not erase culpability, since inner speech and motive are known to the one addressed (and ultimately to God); it underlines certainty of prior knowledge and the exposure of hypocrisy.

translation: قال: «أَفَتَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَنفَعُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَا يَضُرُّكُمْ؟»
interpretation: الآية تفضح عبثية توجيه العبادة إلى غير الله ببيان عجز تلك المعاقين عن أن يأتوا نفعًا أو ضَرًّا؛ فتُظهِر أن تخصيص التبعية والعبادة لمن لا يملك أصلاً تأثيرًا على المصائر أمر غير عقلاني، وتدعو إلى إقرار توحيد الله وحده كمصدر الحَقّ والقدرة والاعتماد، وترك عبادة الأصنام والشركاء الذين لا حول لهم ولا قوة.

translation: Is it for you and for what you worship besides Allah? Will you not then use reason?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge to those who associate others with God: it exposes the absurdity of imagining any share, authority, or worth in created things alongside Allah. By calling for reason, the verse urges people to reflect on reality — that idols or partners have no independent power to give, sustain, or account for existence — and therefore to recognize the impossibility of treating them as equals to the One Sovereign.

translation: قالوا: 'حرقوه وانصروا آلهتكم إن كنتم فاعلين' — They said, 'Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act.'
interpretation: This utterance reveals the posture of those clinging to falsehood: instead of engaging in reason, they resort to intimidation and spectacle, daring others to make their supposed gods manifest by rescuing the accused. It exposes their impotence and moral corruption — relying on coercion and public bravado to uphold a position they cannot defend spiritually — and serves as a test that separates sincere conviction from mere social pressure or violent obstinacy.

translation: “We said, ‘O fire, be coolness and safety for Abraham.’”
interpretation: The verse conveys that by God’s command the very element meant to destroy became harmless and comforting to Abraham; it illustrates God’s power to suspend natural consequences to protect and honor a righteous believer, turning a trial into a manifest sign of divine vindication and support for faith.

translation: And they devised a plot against him, but We made them the greatest losers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when hostile parties conspire to harm God’s chosen servant, God frustrates their machinations and turns the outcome into their own ruin; “الأخسرين” denotes ultimate loss—humiliation, failure of their worldly schemes, and spiritual defeat in the Hereafter—so deceitful plotting brings self-defeat rather than success.

translation: And We saved him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for the worlds.
interpretation: The verse conveys that God intervened to protect Abraham and Lot and established them in a divinely chosen, fertile land. This placement is not merely personal favor but part of a providential plan: the land is described as 'blessed for the worlds,' meaning its fertility, safety, and moral-spiritual significance are intended to benefit succeeding peoples and generations. Thus the passage emphasizes divine care that combines deliverance from danger with the entrusting of a blessed environment whose good consequences extend beyond the immediate protagonists to humanity at large.

translation: And We granted him Isaac and Jacob as a bounteous gift, and We made each of them righteous.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God bestowed Isaac and Jacob upon Abraham as an extra, gracious favor (nafla) and that their uprightness was a divine endowment; it emphasizes that virtuous descendants and the continuity of prophetic guidance are gifts from God, given out of His generosity rather than as something earned solely by human effort.

translation: And We made them leaders who guide by Our command, and We inspired in them the doing of good deeds, the establishing of prayer, and the giving of zakah; and they were, to Us, devoted worshippers.
interpretation: The verse explains that true leadership in the community is conferred by God upon those whose authority rests on obedience to His guidance and whose lives exemplify it. Such leaders are shaped inwardly—God inspires them toward concrete moral action, regular communal worship, and care for the needy—so their guidance is not mere rhetoric but embodied practice. Their legitimacy comes from servitude to God: they lead to bring people back to divine ways, prioritizing worship and social responsibility over personal gain, and thus embody the model others are to follow.

translation: And Lot — We gave him judgment and knowledge, and saved him from the town that was committing abominations. Indeed, they were a wicked, rebellious people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God grants His messenger Lot both sound judgment and true knowledge so he can discern and enforce right from wrong; yet when a community persists in gross immorality and open rebellion (described here as al-khabāʻith and as a “qawm suʼ fāsiqīn”), prophetic guidance alone cannot salvage them. The passage thereby underscores two linked truths: divine bestowal of authority and insight to the righteous, and the moral consequence that entrenched communal corruption, attended by refusal of guidance, leads to ruin while God delivers those who remain obedient.

translation: And We admitted him into Our mercy; indeed, he was of the righteous.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that when a person truly belongs to the ranks of the righteous through sincere faith and conforming deeds, God envelops him in His mercy — a mercy that here means pardon, elevation of status, and admission into Paradise. It emphasizes that divine favor is both a response to genuine righteousness and an honor granted by Allah’s will.

translation:
وَنُوحًا إِذْ نَادَى مِن قَبْلُ فَاسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُ فَنَجَّيْنَاهُ وَأَهْلَهُ مِنَ الْكَرْبِ الْعَظِيمِ
“And [mention] Noah, when he called before; so We responded to him and saved him and his family from the great distress.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere, timely supplication elicits God’s direct mercy: when the prophet turned to God in earnest before the coming calamity, God answered and delivered him and his household. It affirms both divine responsiveness to true faith and the principle that turning to God can avert or relieve imminent doom, while also implying divine justice toward those who persist in rejection.

translation: And We saved him from the people who denied Our signs; indeed they were an evil people, so We drowned them all.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God intervenes to protect the righteous (here the messenger or true believer) from a community that stubbornly rejects divine guidance; their persistent, collective wrongdoing made them deserving of severe punishment, and their drowning is presented as both just recompense for entrenched disbelief and a warning that God preserves the faithful and brings decisive judgment on persistent, systemic rejection of His signs.

translation: And (remember) David and Solomon when they judged concerning the field — when the people's sheep had grazed therein — and We were witnesses to their judgment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that rightful adjudication is rooted in divine guidance and moral wisdom: God’s witnessing of the prophets’ judgment both legitimizes and protects just decisions, so disputes should be settled by measured, principled reasoning guided by God rather than by force or partiality.

translation: So We taught Solomon its interpretation. And to each [of them] We gave judgment and knowledge. And We made the mountains to glorify [Us] with David, and the birds; and We were the doers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God endows His chosen servants with specific, fitting gifts—Solomon was granted the ability to apprehend and resolve what others could not, and David was supported by signs in creation—so rulership and judgment are validated by divine wisdom and by God’s sovereign power to subordinate nature in support of the righteous. This underlines that true authority and sound judgment come from God’s appointment and the bestowal of insight, not merely human effort.

translation: And We taught him a craft — garments for you — to shield you from your own force. So will you be grateful?
interpretation: The verse presents the making of clothing (and by extension protective gear) as a divinely granted技術: God endowed humans with practical knowledge that shelters them from physical harm, the harshness of the world, and the disruptive consequences of unchecked aggression. That gift is not merely utilitarian but a sign that human ability and social order depend on God’s providence; the rhetorical question at the end summons grateful acknowledgement and responsible use of these gifts — employing skills to preserve life and dignity rather than to foster pride or oppression.

translation: And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind — a tempestuous wind that ran at his command to the land which We had blessed; and We were, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God, by His will, granted Solomon miraculous authority over a powerful wind so it would carry out his orders and serve practical ends in the fertile, divinely favored region; this gift both demonstrates God’s sovereignty over nature and underlines that such powers are granted and measured according to God’s perfect knowledge and purpose, not by the servant’s independent power.

translation: And among the devils are those who plunge (or dive) for him and carry out other deeds besides that; and We were guardians over them.
interpretation: The phrase points to organized agents of temptation — some devils are sent out to seek, gather and transmit means of misleading speech and actions for their chief (Iblīs) and to carry out various deceptive operations. This activity is real but not free: God watches over and restrains them, permitting their mischief only within limits He has set, so their influence can mislead people yet remains ultimately under divine supervision and accountability.

translation: And [remember] Ayyub (Job), when he called upon his Lord, “Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”
interpretation: The verse presents Ayyub’s prayer as a paradigm of faithful reliance: he names his pain honestly yet places his trust in God’s unique mercy. It teaches that sincere turning to God in hardship—acknowledging suffering while affirming divine compassion—is the proper posture for seeking relief and healing.

translation: So We answered him; We removed the harm that afflicted him, and We restored his family to him and gave them their like along with them — a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere supplication and steadfastness draw a real divine response: God can lift suffering, restore what was lost, and even increase blessings as an act of mercy. Such deliverance is not merely a reversal of fate but a purposeful sign meant to awaken gratitude, trust, and attentive worship in the hearts of believers, showing that patient reliance on God is met by His compassion and serves as a lesson for the faithful.

translation: And Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and Dhū l-Kifl — all were of the patient.
interpretation: The verse singles out these righteous servants as exemplars of ṣabr: they withstood personal trials, carried out their duties, and remained steadfast in worship and trust in God despite hardship and opposition. By naming them the text teaches that patient perseverance in obeying God, bearing loss or trial without complaint, and persisting in one’s mission are essential moral qualities for believers to emulate.

translation: And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were of the righteous.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God, by His gracious mercy, admitted those sincere and upright believers into His favor (forgiveness and Paradise). Their inward faith and outward righteous conduct made them worthy, yet their final acceptance and reward are ultimately an act of Divine compassion rather than merely the result of deeds alone.

translation: And (remember) Dhū’n-Nūn when he went off in anger and thought that We would not appoint (anything) over him; then he cried out in the darknesses, “There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that when Jonah left his duty in resentment, thinking God would not hold him accountable, he was brought low and only sincere turning to God rescued him. His brief, humble invocation — pure affirmation of God’s oneness, glorification of Him, and an explicit admission of wrongdoing — is presented as the model of true repentance: one should not presume escape from divine power or mercy, and in moments of utter helplessness a heartfelt confession and exclusive reliance on God open the way to forgiveness and deliverance.

translation:
فَاسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُ وَنَجَّيْنَاهُ مِنَ الْغَمِّ ۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نُنجِي الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
“So We answered him and delivered him from distress. And thus We deliver the believers.”
interpretation: The verse affirms a general divine principle: when a believer turns to God in sincere need, humility and repentance — calling from real anguish like Jonah did — God responds and brings rescue. That rescue is not limited to an immediate, visible removal of danger but includes any form of relief God, in His wisdom, bestows (release from sorrow, inner relief, changed circumstances, or ultimate salvation). The statement “thus We deliver the believers” universalizes the promise: genuine supplication combined with trust in God is met by His mercy and deliverance according to His wisdom and timing.

translation: And [mention] Zakariya, when he called to his Lord, “My Lord, do not leave me alone [without an heir], while You are the best of inheritors.”
interpretation: Zakariya’s plea expresses a deep human need for continuity and for a righteous successor, and it models how one turns to God when worldly means fail. By saying “do not leave me alone” he seeks someone to carry on his worship and legacy; by calling God “the best of inheritors” he acknowledges that ultimate provision, succession, and the disposal of affairs belong solely to God. The verse thus teaches reliance on God’s mercy, humility in asking for what we lack, and trust that God — who alone truly manages inheritance and legacy — gives or withholds according to His wisdom.

translation: So We answered him, and We granted him Yahya, and We made his wife righteous for him. Indeed they used to hasten to do good deeds and used to call upon Us, seeking (Our favor) with hope and with fear, and they were humble before Us.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God responds to sincere, humble supplication that is accompanied by active righteousness: those who hasten to do good, pray to God with a balanced attitude of hope and fear, and remain humble before Him will find their requests answered and their affairs rectified—God grants the sought blessing and reforms what is needed (for example making a spouse suitable or granting righteous offspring) as a result of such faithfulness and humility.

translation: “And [the one] who guarded her chastity — so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds.”
interpretation: This verse refers to Mary, affirming her purity and stating that Jesus’ conception was a miraculous act of God: by His command and by breathing of His spirit (understood as a special creative intervention, conveyed through the angel), God brought Jesus into being without a human father. The event vindicates Mary from slander and, together with her son, serves as a portent and proof of God’s absolute power, wisdom and mercy for all peoples and creatures.

translation: Indeed, this is your one community, and I am your Lord; so worship Me.
interpretation: God here affirms that the true vocation of humanity (and of believers) is unified: the prophets brought one fundamental call — recognition of One Lord — and therefore ultimate allegiance must be to Him alone. The command “so worship Me” makes exclusive devotion and obedience to God the criterion that overrides tribal, sectarian or political divisions; genuine religious life is measured by submission to God’s oneness (tawḥīd) and the rejection of rival authorities or deities.

translation: And their affairs will be severed among themselves; everyone will return to Us.
interpretation: The verse warns that on the Day of Reckoning all human plans, alliances and defenses will collapse and prove ineffective — people’s mutual supports will be torn apart — because ultimately every soul must come back to God for judgment; reliance on worldly ties cannot avert divine accountability.

translation: So whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer—there will be no denial of his effort; and indeed We are, of it, Recorders.
interpretation: The verse assures that when faith is genuine and is matched by righteous action, God will not let that striving be annulled or unacknowledged: every sincere good act is registered by God and will be recompensed. It underscores divine justice and encouragement to persist in humble, faith‑rooted service, trusting that even small, sincere efforts are preserved and rewarded by Him.

translation:
وحرام على قرية أهلكناها أنهم لا يرجعون
“And it is forbidden for a town which We destroyed that they should return.”
interpretation: The verse declares the irrevocability of divine punishment: when God decrees and executes the annihilation of a people because of persistent disbelief and corruption, they will not be restored to life or to their former state. It underscores God’s absolute power over life and death and serves as a stern warning to the living to heed guidance so as not to incur an irreversible fate.

translation: “Until, when Gog and Magog are released and they, from every elevation, rush forth.”
interpretation: The verse points to an eschatological reality: when God decrees their release, the forces called Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj will pour out from every ridge and pass, spreading uncontrollably across the land. The emphasis is less on the technical details of who they are than on the theological lessons — human barriers and plans cannot prevent what God wills, and this overwhelming surge is a clear sign of the nearness of the Hour. The picture serves as a warning to abandon complacency about worldly security, to turn back to God, and to remember that ultimate justice and deliverance rest with Him.

translation: And the True Promise drew near; and behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved were fixed [in terror]. “Woe to us!” they will say; “we were indeed heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The verse emphasizes the absolute certainty and suddenness of God’s promised Hour: when it comes its reality will be undeniable and will strike the disbelievers with stunned, paralysing fear. Their cry—“Woe to us; we were heedless; rather, we were wrongdoers”—is not merely surprise but a late admission that their own neglect of guidance and persistence in injustice brought about their ruin. The passage therefore functions as a moral and existential warning: denial or procrastination cannot avert divine judgment, and true salvation requires attentive submission and justice before the hour arrives, because belated regret cannot undo the consequences of having lived heedlessly and in wrongdoing.

translation: “Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be among its companions.”
interpretation: The verse employs the severe image of being ‘fuel’ for Hell to teach that turning worship to anything other than God binds one’s fate to those powerless objects or beings: they cannot intercede or save, and by choosing them the worshipper accepts humiliation and punishment alongside them. It is a theological and moral warning that misdirected devotion severs one’s reliance on God, establishes a shared destiny with what was worshipped, and thus makes the act of shirk the decisive cause of eternal loss and disgrace.

translation: If these were gods, they would not have approached it; indeed, each of them would abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse rejects the divinity of idols or false gods by pointing to their vulnerability: genuine divinity would prevent such beings from suffering, being overthrown, or entering punishment. Because these supposed deities share the fate of created beings—subject to loss, humiliation, or destruction—they cannot be true gods; their condition proves that ultimate sovereignty and protection belong only to Allah.

translation: For them therein is a sighing, and they therein do not hear.
interpretation: It depicts the fate of the punished: they will emit groans and gasps from their torment, yet be cut off from hearing any admonition, guidance, or consolation—their senses overwhelmed and they wholly unable to receive remedy or counsel, emphasizing their helpless isolation.

translation: Indeed, those for whom from Us the good has gone before — they are kept away from it.
interpretation: The verse indicates that when Allah grants certain people pleasing things and comforts of this present life in advance, those blessings can lead them to be satisfied with the worldly provision and to turn away from striving for the ultimate good of the Hereafter; as a result, they are kept distant from that final, lasting reward.

translation: They will not hear its hissing, and they will abide therein in whatever their souls desire, forever.
interpretation: The verse assures that the righteous dwellers of the Hereafter will be completely removed from the torment and reminders of punishment: they will not be disturbed even by the hissing of the Fire, and instead will enjoy an eternal, uninterrupted fulfilment of their deepest longings. “What their souls desire” indicates rewards fashioned to the innermost wishes and satisfaction of the soul, and “abiding forever” emphasizes the permanence and completeness of that blessings and security.

translation: لا يحزنهم الفزع الأكبر وتتلقاهم الملائكة هذا يومكم الذي كنتم توعدون
interpretation: الآية تشبّه ما يحدث للمتقين يوم القيامة بتحوّل كامل في حالتهم النفسية والوجودية: «الفزع الأكبر» هو الرعب الشامل الذي يملأ قلوب غير المستعدين أمام واقع الحساب، فأما المؤمنون الصادقون فذلك الرعب لا يمسهم لأن الملائكة تستقبلهم كعلامة على قبول الله وتكريمهم. استقبال الملائكة يعلن نهاية الخوف وبداية الظفر بالوعد الإلهي؛ عبارة «هذا يومكم الذي كنتم توعدون» تؤكد يقين وعد الله للداوم على الإيمان والعمل الصالح، وتبيّن أن الفرق بين أن يكون اليوم يوم رعب أو يوم فرح هو حالة القلب وأعماله، فالإيمان والصدق يحوّلان يوم الجزاء من محنة إلى مغفرة وثواب.

translation: The Day when We will fold up the heavens like the folding up of a scroll for the records. As We began the first creation, We will repeat it — a promise binding upon Us; indeed, We are going to do it.
interpretation: This verse declares God's absolute mastery over origin and end: the image of ‘‘folding the heavens’’ signifies the dissolution and contraction of the present cosmic order so that what is visible and expansive will be brought back under God’s control, as one closes a scroll. The parallel with the first creation stresses that resurrection and the re-creating of life are natural to God — He who originated creation can restore it — and the phrase ‘‘a promise binding upon Us; indeed, We are going to do it’’ affirms the certainty of that eschatological reversal and the ensuing accountability, leaving no room for doubt about God’s power or the inevitability of final judgment.

translation: And indeed We wrote in the Zabur, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants.
interpretation: The verse is a divine promise that history will culminate in the establishment and flourishing of those who are God‑fearing and morally upright. 'Inheriting the earth' does not merely mean acquiring land, but being granted rightful authority, peace, stability and provision under God's justice: corrupt power and oppression will be overturned and those who live by God’s guidance will be settled and honored. It is both consolation and incentive—assurance that worldly trials are temporary and a call to patient, principled conduct aimed at realizing a just and wholesome order appointed by God.

translation: Indeed in this is a clear message for a people who are worshippers.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the account just given is not mere narration but a decisive sign addressed to those whose orientation is toward God: it is meant to confirm divine truth for the sincere worshippers, to console them with the reality of God’s promise, and to prompt steadfastness and purity of intention in their devotion.

translation: And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.
interpretation: The verse states that the Prophet’s chief role is to manifest God’s mercy universally: his message, character, and law are meant to bring spiritual guidance, moral reform, compassion, healing of social ills, and reconciliation across all peoples and realms of creation (humanity, jinn, and the wider order). "Not except" emphasizes that mercy is the primary purpose that shapes every aspect of his mission—other functions (warning, legislation, community-building) serve this central aim of guiding, relieving, and restoring.

translation: Say, “It has been revealed to me that your God is only one God. Will you then submit?”
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to proclaim that revelation affirms the absolute oneness of God and to present this as a clear moral and existential choice: recognize and accept God’s exclusive sovereignty by sincerely submitting (becoming Muslim in the sense of wholehearted surrender), or reject it and remain accountable for that refusal. It functions both as a declarative truth delivered by revelation and as an invitation that shifts responsibility onto the listeners to respond.

translation: But if they turn away, then say, “I have warned you all alike; and I do not know whether that which you are promised is near or distant.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the messenger’s responsibility is to deliver the warning impartially and then leave the outcome to God. It affirms the prophet’s human limitation regarding the unseen — he has fulfilled his duty by warning, but he does not possess knowledge of the timing of God’s promise (punishment or recompense), which may be near or far. The passage thereby rejects any claim to control or foreknowledge of divine decree, enjoins humility about the limits of human knowledge, and comforts the messenger that accountability lies in conveying the truth, not in forcing its consequences.

translation: Indeed, He knows the loudness of speech and He knows what you conceal.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God’s knowledge fully encompasses both outward utterances and inward motives: nothing spoken aloud and nothing kept hidden escapes His awareness. The practical implication is moral accountability — one must cultivate sincere intentions and guard inner thoughts and private actions, for divine judgment attends not just visible deeds but the concealed realities of the heart; thus humility, honesty, and inner reform are required even when no human witnesses are present.

translation: وإِنْ أَدْرِي لَعَلَّهُ فِتْنَةٌ لَكُمْ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَى حِينٍ
interpretation: The speaker admits lack of certain knowledge and proposes that the matter may serve as a divine test for those who dispute it and as a short‑lived worldly diversion; the verse therefore warns that some curiosities function to try people’s faith and yield only temporary benefit, so they should not be made into grounds for vain contention or ultimate certainty.

translation: He said, “My Lord, judge with the truth.” And, “Our Lord — the Most Merciful — is the One from whom help is sought against what you attribute.”
interpretation: A plea of reliance on divine justice and mercy: the speaker entrusts the final judgment to God, asking Him to decide rightly, and affirms that vindication and help against false accusations or wrongful descriptions come only from the Most Merciful, not from human judgment or slander.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. O people, fear your Lord; indeed, the convulsion (quake) of the Hour is a mighty/awesome thing.
interpretation: The verse addresses all humanity to cultivate taqwa — a constant reverent awareness and obedience to God — because the ‘زلزلة الساعة’ (the shaking of the Hour) refers to the final, decisive upheaval that will overturn worldly certainties, expose inner realities, and bring absolute accountability. Calling it “شيء عظيم” emphasizes its unparalleled magnitude and consequences: therefore one must live in readiness through sincere faith and righteous conduct rather than complacency.

translation: The Day you will see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she was nursing, and every pregnant woman will drop her load; and you will see the people as if intoxicated, while they are not intoxicated — but the punishment of Allah is severe.
interpretation: The verse uses striking maternal and drunken imagery to convey the overwhelming, disorienting power of the Hour or of Allah’s manifest punishment: ordinary human bonds, instincts and states (nursing, pregnancy, clear reason) will be rendered powerless before Divine severity. What looks like intoxication is actually stupefaction from divine calamity, underscoring human helplessness, the suddenness and intensity of the coming judgment, and serving as a solemn warning to take the reality of accountability seriously and live accordingly.

translation: And among mankind are those who dispute concerning Allah without knowledge and follow every rebellious devil,
interpretation: The verse condemns the attitude of engaging in religious disputes driven by ignorance, conjecture, or personal desire rather than by sound knowledge and evidence. “Following every mureed (rebellious devil)” describes accepting whatever tempting or provocative argument comes along—whether from vain desires, malicious people, or false teachers—so one abandons true guidance and spreads error; the warning is to seek learning and evidence before debating or adopting claims about God.

translation:
كُتِبَ عَلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ مَن تَوَلَّاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يُضِلُّهُ وَيَهْدِيهِ إِلَى عَذَابِ السَّعِيرِ
"It is written about him that whoever takes him as a protector, he will surely lead him astray and will guide him to the torment of the Blaze."
interpretation: الآية تحذر من اتخاذ مَنْ يُضلِّ ويدلُّ إلى النار وليًا أو خليلاً؛ فقبول المرء لهذا المولي يعني سلوك طريق الضلال ونزع الحماية الإلهية عنه، والنتيجة الحتمية لذلك هي الهلاك في العذاب. المقصد أخلاقي واعتقادي: اختيار من نقتدي به يحمل مسؤولية، ومن يولي قلبه لمن يقوده إلى الباطل يحرمه هداية الله ويضع نفسه في طريق العذاب.

translation: O people, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clot, then from a lump — formed and unformed — so that We may make clear to you. And We place what We will in the wombs for an appointed term, then We bring you forth as infants, so that you may reach your maturity. And among you is he who is taken (in death), and among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit age, so that he knows nothing after having known anything. And you see the earth dead; then when We send down water upon it it stirs, swells, and brings forth every beautiful kind.
interpretation: The verse addresses skeptics of resurrection by pointing to the continuous and observable acts of divine creation — human embryonic development, the allotment of life spans, the variability of aging, and the revival of barren earth — as practical proofs that God already does what resurrection would require. By showing that life repeatedly emerges from inert or lowly beginnings and that God controls the timing and course of life and decline, the passage argues that returning people to life after death is not a new or impossible act but an extension of the same sovereign power; the reference to loss of knowledge in extreme old age underscores human fragility and the insufficiency of worldly certainty, urging recognition of divine authority and accountability rather than complacent doubt.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and that He gives life to the dead, and that He is over all things Powerful.
interpretation: The clause is asserting the foundational reasons why belief and submission to God are warranted: God’s identity as ultimate Reality (al‑Haqq) establishes the objective ground for faith; His power to resurrect the dead demonstrates His sovereignty over life and confirms His authority to judge and to fulfill His promises; and His encompassing might means nothing lies beyond His control. Together these truths undermine trust in false deities or worldly refuges and call people to orient their lives toward the One whose reality, creative power, and omnipotence justify obedience and reliance.

translation: And that the Hour is coming — there is no doubt about it — and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves.
interpretation: The verse affirms with finality that the Day of Reckoning will occur and that God, by His power over life and death, will raise the dead. Its purpose is to remove skepticism and to orient people’s minds and hearts toward accountability: awareness of inevitable resurrection should spur repentance, sincere worship, and just conduct in this life because every deed will be confronted in the hereafter.

translation:
وَمنَ النَّاسِ مَن يُجَادِلُ فِي اللَّهِ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ وَلَا هُدًى وَلَا كِتَابٍ مُنِيرٍ
"And among people are those who dispute about Allah without knowledge, without guidance, and without a clear, illuminating Book."
interpretation: The verse censures those who engage in debates about God on the basis of conjecture, prejudice, or rhetorical skill rather than on sound knowledge, prophetic guidance, or reference to the revealed, illuminating scripture. Such disputation is empty and misleading: it reflects ignorance or arrogance and risks drawing both the arguer and their audience away from truth; genuine theological inquiry must be rooted in learning, guidance, and the clear light of revelation.

translation: His repeated turning aside is to lead (others) astray from the way of Allah; for him in the world is disgrace, and We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the torment of blazing fire.
interpretation: The verse warns that when a person persistently departs from truth in a way that causes others to be misled, this is a grave moral offense with both immediate and ultimate consequences: it brings dishonor and humiliation in worldly life and exposes the wrongdoer to severe, fiery punishment in the Hereafter. Implicitly it places responsibility on those whose behavior or influence guides others—repeated, intentional misguidance is not mere private error but a public sin that merits disgrace now and divine retribution later.

translation: ذَٰلِكَ بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَيْسَ بِظَلَّامٍ لِّلْعَبِيدِ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد مبدأ الجزاء الجزائي والأخلاقي: ما أصاب بعض الناس من عذاب أو نقصان هو نتيجة أفعالهم وأسبابهم التي جلبوها بأيديهم، ولا يجوز نسب ذلك إلى ظلم من الله؛ فالله عادل لا يظلم عباده، وإنما يُجازي كل نفس بحسب ما قدمت من عمل واختيار، فالمسؤولية الإنسانية أمام حكم الله واضحة والجزاء قائم على الأسباب والأعمال.

translation: And among the people are those who worship Allah only partially/conditionally; when good befalls them they are reassured by it, but if a trial strikes them they turn on their faces — they have lost both this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.
interpretation: The verse warns against a shallow, transactional faith: “على حرف” describes worship that is provisional, motivated by benefit, comfort, or reputation rather than sincere devotion. Such people remain only while circumstances please them; when hardship or temptation tests their commitment they abandon worship and principle. Their faith therefore yields no true spiritual benefit and often brings worldly ruin as well — losing reward in the Hereafter and the guiding stability that secures well‑being in this life. The verse calls for steadfast, sincere faith that endures trials rather than conditional devotion that collapses at the first test.

translation: He calls upon besides Allah that which neither harms him nor benefits him; that is the most remote error.
interpretation: The verse judges the practice of invoking beings or things other than God as a profound misdirection: relying on entities that lack power to change one’s situation shows a fundamental failure in recognizing God’s sole sovereignty and in placing trust correctly. This error is both intellectual—accepting false notions of causation and divine agency—and spiritual, because it diverts one from seeking the true source of benefit, guidance, and mercy; therefore it constitutes the deepest form of deviation from the straight path.

translation: He calls upon one who will do him more harm than good. How wretched a protector, and how wretched a companion!
interpretation: The verse condemns turning for help to powerless or harmful sources—whether idols, vain desires, corrupt leaders, or misguided companions—whose support brings loss rather than benefit. It teaches that relying on such protectors is spiritually and practically disastrous: they are ‘wretched’ as guardians and companions, and true trust and refuge belong to God alone.

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate success in the hereafter is not a mere abstract hope but the outcome of a relationship between sincere faith, lived moral practice, and divine sovereignty: God’s promise of blissful reward encourages believers to embody their faith through virtuous action, while the closing clause reminds them that entrance to that reward is granted by God’s will and power—offering both assurance for those who strive rightly and humility in recognizing human dependence on divine mercy.

translation:
من يَظُنُّ أنَّ اللهَ لا يُنصِرهُ في الدنيا والآخرة فَلْيَمُدَّ حَبْلاً إلى السماء ثم ليَقصُهُ، فَلْينظُرْ هل يَذهبُ كيدُهُ ما يغيظُهُ؟

"Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter — let him stretch a rope up to the sky and then cut it off; then let him see whether his plot will remove that which enrages him."
interpretation: The verse challenges those who deny or despair of God’s assistance by exposing the futility of human schemes and desperate self-reliance: no matter how far someone tries to go or what contrivances he devises (even an absurd, extreme metaphor of reaching the heavens and severing the link), he cannot avert or undo what God has decreed. In short, God’s support and the outcome He wills cannot be frustrated by human anger, plots, or attempts to escape reality; such machinations will be exposed and frustrated, and true aid rests with God alone.

translation: And thus We have revealed it — clear signs — and Allah guides whom He wills.
interpretation: God affirms that He has provided unmistakable guidance, but being rightly guided is ultimately a gift of His will: the revelation makes the way known and removes excuses, yet true guidance comes by God’s mercy and choice, alongside the human responsibility to respond.

translation: Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Sabians and the Christians and the Magians and the polytheists — indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is, over all things, a Witness.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment God alone will determine the true standing of every group and person; earthly labels, sectarian claims or disputes will be resolved by God’s perfect knowledge and justice, for He observes both outward deeds and inner intentions—therefore ultimate accountability belongs to God, and humans should act with humility and awareness of that final adjudication.

translation: Do you not see that to Allah prostrate those in the heavens and those on the earth — the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals, and many people? And many are there for whom punishment is due; and whoever Allah humiliates, for him there is none to confer honor. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all creation, whether animate or inanimate, manifests submission to God — either by overt worship or by faithfully performing the role God decreed — and this universal obedience highlights His sole sovereignty. Human beings alone can choose acceptance or rejection of that authority; persistent denial or moral corruption leads to deserved humiliation and punishment, because divine honor and disgrace are ultimately determined by God and cannot be overturned by others. The passage thus warns against pride and reliance on worldly status, urging recognition that honor comes only from God and that His will governs who is elevated or abased.

translation: These two are adversaries who disputed about their Lord. As for those who disbelieved, garments of fire were cut out for them; boiling water will be poured over their heads.
interpretation: The verse teaches that denial of God’s truth does not remain a mere opinion but brings about an appropriate, divinely ordained consequence: the vivid images — garments of fire tailored for them and scalding water poured from above — signify both fitting retribution and the penetrating, inescapable nature of divine justice. It warns that persistent rejection and arrogance toward the truth will transform a person’s condition into one that reflects and suits their choices, serving as a moral deterrent and affirmation of cosmic accountability.

translation: بِهِ يُصَهِّرُ مَا فِي بُطُونِهِمْ وَالْجُلُودِ — By it He will melt what is in their bellies and their skins.
interpretation: The phrase emphasizes the absolute, penetrating effect of the appointed torment (or trial): it will not be superficial but will reach and liquefy both inner contents and outer coverings. Metaphorically and literally, nothing hidden or protected by the body will be spared; inward realities (intentions, sins, organs) and outward forms (skins) alike are exposed and consumed, underlining both the totality of God’s power in recompense and the futility of any concealment from divine judgment.

translation: And for them are iron maces.
interpretation: تُصوِّر الآية وسيلة عذاب في الآخرة — مقامع من حديد تُستعمل لضرب المعذبين — بهدف بيان شدة الجزاء وذلّة العقوبة لمن أصرّ على الكفر والعدوان على الحق. المقصود بها تذكير بواقع الجزاء العادل وعاقبة الإعراض عن البينة، وحثّ الناس على التوبة قبل أن يبلغهم ذلك المصير.

translation: Whenever they wished to emerge from it, in their anguish, they were driven back into it and tasted the torment of the blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse depicts the hopeless condition of those in Hell: every attempt to escape is frustrated and only increases their suffering. “From grief” signals the belated, futile remorse felt by the doomed, and being “returned” to the blaze shows the finality and inevitability of divine recompense for persistent rejection of guidance. It warns the living that repentance and obedience must occur before death, for remorse after the fact brings no deliverance.

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments therein will be silk.
interpretation: The verse portrays God’s promise of a transformed and dignified existence for believers who act righteously. The gardens and flowing rivers signify continuous, life-giving divine blessings and spiritual peace; the gold and pearl bracelets and silk garments signify honor, purity, and the complete removal of former hardship. These sensual images are not merely literal luxuries but symbols indicating that God’s reward perfects both outward condition and inner state: believers will receive enduring beauty, dignity, and closeness to God as an expression of divine grace rather than a fleeting worldly pleasure.

translation: and they were guided to the good of speech and were guided to the Praiseworthy Path.
interpretation: The phrase indicates a twofold divine guidance: first, shaping a person’s tongue and discourse so that they speak with truth, gentleness, wisdom and benefit (الطيب من القول); second, directing their life onto the way that is upright and honoured by God (صراط الحميد) — in other words, guidance that transforms both what one utters and how one conducts oneself, aligning speech and action with the path that merits God’s praise.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and who prevent (others) from the way of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque which We have made for the people — whether the one who stays there in devotion or the one who comes and departs — and whoever therein seeks to deviate with injustice, We will make him taste a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse asserts the sanctity and public purpose of al‑Masjid al‑Haram and condemns any who, out of disbelief or malice, obstruct people from the path of God or from access to the sacred precinct. By naming both the resident worshipper (al‑ʿākif) and the arriving visitor (al‑bād), it emphasizes equal rights of sanctuary and worship for all, rejecting claims of exclusive control. The phrase “seeks to deviate therein with injustice” (إلحاد بظلم) denotes willful perversion, oppression, or profanation of the holy place; such acts are treated not merely as social wrongs but as affronts to God’s ordained order and therefore draw severe divine recompense. The passage thus upholds protection of sacred space, freedom of worship, and stern accountability for those who use power to bar others from God’s way.

translation: And [remember] when We appointed the site of the House for Abraham, [saying], “Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate.”
interpretation: God’s commissioning of Abraham to establish the Kaʿbah is a divine injunction to dedicate that sanctuary exclusively to tawḥīd (unity of God) and to rid it of idolatry and corrupt practices; “purify My House” implies both the physical removal of objects of false worship and the spiritual preservation of sincere, regulated devotion so that the place remains fit for the essential acts of worship—tawāf (circumambulation), standing in prayer, bowing and prostration—across generations.

translation: And announce to the people the Pilgrimage: they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass.
interpretation: The verse frames Hajj as a divinely mandated, public summons that gathers humanity before God. The images of people arriving 'on foot and on every lean camel' and 'from every distant pass' stress that the ritual draws together all social strata and far‑flung communities — the poor and the rich, the near and the remote — into one collective act of submission, witness, and covenant. In this way the pilgrimage functions not merely as a set of rites but as a unifying, visible proof of God's sovereignty, a means of spiritual renewal, and a reinforcement of communal bonds and moral accountability among those who respond to the call.

translation: so that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on appointed days over what He has provided them of the cattle; so eat of them and feed the needy and the poor.
interpretation: The verse links ritual slaughter in specified pilgrimage days to concrete social and spiritual aims: the rite is meant not as empty formality but as a public affirmation of God’s provision, a communal sharing of sustenance, and an occasion for remembrance of God. By commanding that people eat of the sacrificed animals and feed the needy, the text makes clear that worship is inseparable from social responsibility — blessings from God are to be transformed into communal benefit, dignity for the poor, and a visible sign that faith is expressed through generosity and mutual care.

translation: Then let them complete their prescribed rites, and fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that ritual actions and vowed commitments are meant to be carried through to completion as tangible expressions of submission and gratitude to God; by faithfully finishing the prescribed rites and honoring vows the believer actualizes their covenant with God, sanctifying both communal worship and personal devotion.

translation: ذلك، ومن يُعظِّم حُرُماتِ اللهِ فهو خيرٌ له عند ربه. وأُحِلّت لكم الأنعامُ إلا ما يُتلى عليكم، فاجتنبوا الرجسَ من الأوثانِ واجتنبوا قولَ الزور.
interpretation: الآية تربط بين التقوى الحقيقية والاحترام لحدود الله: من يعظم ما حرَّمه أو أمر به الله ويُجل أحكامه سيُناله خيرٌ عند رّبه. ثم تؤكد أن الله أباح للناس بعض الرزق (الأنعام) مع استثناء ما صار تحريمه بالوحي، وتوجه تحذيراً عملياً — اجتناب طهرة الأوثان لا بمعنى مجرد البعد عن أصنامهم المادية فحسب، بل عن كل وسخ شركي وعباداتٍ تبدِّد وحدة الربوبية — واجتناب قول الزور، أي كل كلامٍ كاذب أو تزييف للدين (كالادعاء بأن شيئاً حلال هو حرام أو العكس، أو الشهادة بالباطل). الخلاصة: التزام حدود الله، والامتثال لنصوصه، والابتعاد عن الشرك والكذب هي ضوابط تحمي الإيمان وتكسب صاحبه خير ربه.

translation: حنفاء لله غير مشركين به ۚ ومن يشرك بالله فكأنما خر من السماء فتخطفه الطير أو تهوي به الريح في مكان سحيق
interpretation: الآية تضع مقابلًا بين الانحياز القلبي الخالص إلى الله (الحنيفة) والافتقار إليه بواسطة الشرك، مستخدمة صورة قوية للحالة التي ينتهي إليها مُذنِب الشرك: سقوط مفاجئ من العلو وافتقاره لكل ملاذ أو سند، مسلوب الكرامة محمولًا بلا رادع أو حماية. هذا التشبيه لا يهدف فقط إلى تصوير عقاب محسوس، بل ليبيّن أثر الشرك على وضع الإنسان الأخلاقي والروحي — إذ يحرم صاحبه من التوازن والطمأنينة والعلائق الحقيقية التي تستند إلى توحيد الله، فيصبح عُرضة للقهر والتيه والغياب عن رحمة وهداية الله. بالتالي التحذير يحث على الثبات على التوحيد كشرط للبقاء المعنوي والروحي والاعتبار الاجتماعي.

translation:
ذَٰلِكَ ۚ وَمَن يُعَظِّمْ شَعَائِرَ اللَّهِ فَإِنَّهَا مِن تَقْوَى الْقُلُوبِ
“That is so; and whoever honors the symbols (sacred rites) of Allah—indeed they are from the piety of the hearts.”
interpretation: Honoring God’s symbols and rituals is a concrete outward expression of inner God-consciousness: the reverence shown toward those sacred signs reveals sincerity, humility and moral seriousness in the heart. Observing and upholding these rites is therefore not mere formality but a manifestation and means of cultivating taqwa—purified intentions, discipline, and devotion that shape righteous conduct.

translation:
لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى ثُمَّ مَحِلُّهَا إِلَى الْبَيْتِ الْعَتِيقِ
"For you in it are benefits for a fixed term; then their place (or final return) is to the Ancient House."
interpretation: The verse indicates that certain lawful uses and provisions granted to people — especially in the context of the pilgrimage rites (e.g., the sacrificial animals and the sustenance made available during the sacred days) — are permitted only for a prescribed period; once that appointed time is over they are to be consecrated or returned to the Sacred House (al‑Bayt al‑Atīq, the Kaʿbah). It teaches that divine permissions come with limits and a divinely ordained timetable, and that these gifts are ultimately meant to culminate in worship and dedication to God at the sanctuary, reminding believers of submission to God’s ordinance and the sanctity of the House.

translation: And for every community We appointed a rite so that they may mention the name of Allah over the livestock He has provided them. Your God is One God; so to Him submit. And give glad tidings to the humble.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has instituted communal rites (like sacrificial remembrance) not as empty customs but as means to orient peoples toward gratitude and recognition of divine provision; by stressing the oneness of God and calling for submission, it reframes all particular rites under a single spiritual purpose — sincere surrender to God. The promised good news to the mukhbitin (the humble/those who abase themselves before God) indicates that true religiosity is measured not by external festivals alone but by humility, inner submission and attentiveness to God’s name and bounty.

translation: الَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَالصَّابِرِينَ عَلَىٰ مَا أَصَابَهُمْ وَالْمُقِيمِي الصَّلَاةِ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنفِقُونَ
interpretation: The verse portrays a spiritual condition in which remembrance of God produces genuine inner awe and humility rather than mere verbal profession. That trembling of the heart signifies a living consciousness of God’s majesty and accountability, which fosters moral restraint and sincerity. Patience regarding what befalls one reflects trust in God’s wisdom and perseverance under trial, not passive resignation. Establishing prayer indicates a regular, disciplined connection to God that orders the believer’s life, and spending from God’s provision shows that faith transforms attachment to wealth into generosity and social responsibility. Together these qualities mark a faith that is inwardly rooted and outwardly active: a faith whose awareness of God shapes character, worship, and conduct.

translation: And the camels — We have made them among the symbols of Allah; there is good for you in them. So mention the name of Allah over them when they stand in rows, and when their sides have fallen (i.e., when they are slaughtered) then eat of them and feed the contented and the one in need. Thus We have subjected them to you so that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that God’s prescribed rituals and the natural provisions He places at human disposal are not mere formalities or utilitarian resources, but means to cultivate divine consciousness and social responsibility. By requiring the invocation of God’s name over animals used in ritual and by commanding distribution of their meat to both those who need and those who are content, the law sanctifies provision, ties worship to ethical behavior, and frames God’s benevolence as a test: the proper response to God’s gifts is remembrance, restraint, sharing, and gratitude.

translation:
لن ينال الله لحومها ولا دماؤها ولكن يناله التقوى منكم ۚ كذلك سخرها لكم لتكبروا الله على ما هداكم ۗ وبشر المحسنين
"Neither their flesh nor their blood reaches Allah; but piety (taqwā) from you reaches Him. Thus He has subjected them to you so that you may glorify Allah for His guidance to you. And give glad tidings to the doers of good."
interpretation: The verse teaches that ritual acts and offerings are not valuable because they provide anything to God—He is free of need—but because of what they produce within the believer. Sacrificial rites and lawful provisions are means fashioned by God to train the heart: they are occasions for humility, obedience, gratitude, and care for others. What truly “reaches” God is taqwā—sincere God-consciousness, moral rectitude, and compassionate conduct. Therefore divine acceptance depends on the inward state that accompanies outward acts; the intended purpose of these permitted means is to prompt glorification of God and to shape people into muh'sinīn (those who do good), who are the ones promised glad tidings and reward.

translation: Indeed, Allah defends those who believe. Indeed, Allah does not love any treacherous, ungrateful person.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God actively upholds sincere believers—preserving their faith, rights, and community and thwarting the schemes and harms directed against them—while warning that treachery and persistent ingratitude are morally repugnant and forfeit divine favor, so those who betray trusts and persist in ungratefulness will be exposed to God’s disapproval and consequences.

translation: Permission to fight has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged. And indeed, Allah is Able to grant them victory.
interpretation: The verse enunciates a principle that armed struggle is permissible as a limited, defensive response when people are subjected to aggression and injustice. It does not authorize violence as a first resort or as retaliation for equal grievances, but legitimizes resistance aimed at ending oppression and restoring security and justice. The second clause reassures believers that God’s power supports the cause of the oppressed, framing legitimate defensive action within a moral and theological boundary rather than as an unrestricted license to fight.

translation: Those who were driven out of their homes unjustly — only because they would say, “Our Lord is Allah.” And had Allah not imposed some people upon others, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned would have been torn down. And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Exalted in Might.
interpretation: The verse affirms that believers who are persecuted solely for professing divine lordship are singled out for divine concern, and it explains that God’s allowing different peoples to check one another serves to preserve places of sincere worship across communities; it teaches that divine wisdom can permit human opposition as a means to protect religious institutions and remembrance, and reassures that those who stand for God and His cause will receive His support because He is omnipotent and exalted.

translation: Those who, if We grant them authority in the land, establish prayer, give zakāh, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong; and to Allah belongs the final outcome of all affairs.
interpretation: The verse sets the standard for legitimate and righteous authority: true success and rightful rule are shown by using power to organize communal worship, ensure social responsibility and charity, and to promote moral order while opposing corruption. At the same time it reminds believers that no matter the immediate results, the ultimate outcome of every enterprise rests with Allah, so actions must be taken with moral integrity and trust in His final judgment rather than for mere worldly gain or guaranteed triumph.

translation: And if they deny you, then indeed before them the people of Nuh, 'Aad, and Thamud denied (as well).
interpretation: The verse places the Prophet’s rejection within a recurring human pattern: earlier nations also rejected their messengers and suffered consequences. Its purpose is twofold—to console the Prophet that opposition is not a sign of failure but a historic response to truth, and to warn the listeners that persistent denial has real moral and eschatological consequences. The practical lesson is steadfastness in conveying the message for the messenger, and sober heed and self-examination for hearers so they do not follow the path that led previous peoples to ruin.

translation: and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot
interpretation: The phrase summons the historical communities attached to those prophets as moral examples: it highlights that when societies reject prophetic guidance or persist in corrupt, harmful ways, they invite divine scrutiny and consequence. By naming Abraham’s and Lot’s people, the text warns listeners to recognize the pattern—receptiveness to truth and reform leads to preservation, while obstinacy and immoral communal practice lead to loss—so believers should heed guidance, reform their conduct, and avoid the behaviors that brought ruin upon those earlier peoples.

translation: And the people of Madyan — they denied Moses; so I granted respite to the disbelievers, then I seized them. How severe was My retribution!
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s forbearance is not permissiveness: communities that rejected their messenger were given a temporary reprieve, which allowed disbelief to continue, but ultimately divine justice overtook them decisively. It is a warning that delay of punishment is a measured mercy or test, not a negation of accountability, and that the coming retribution for persistent denial can be sudden and severe.

translation: How many a town did We destroy while it was unjust — it now lies fallen upon its roofs, with a deserted well and a lofty palace.
interpretation: The verse warns that persistent communal injustice and rejection of God's guidance invite decisive punishment regardless of worldly prosperity; magnificent buildings and apparent security cannot shield a people from the consequences of their wrongdoing. The image of ruined houses, an abandoned well and an elevated palace serves as a reminder of the fragility of human power and a call to humility, moral reform and heedfulness of divine accountability.

translation: Have they not traveled through the land so that they may have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear? Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but blind are the hearts which are in the breasts.
interpretation: The verse urges people to observe and reflect on the world—through travel, history and contemplation—so that their inner faculties (the heart and hearing) may grasp truth. It distinguishes external perception (sight) from inner comprehension: one can see outwardly yet remain spiritually blind if the heart is closed by heedlessness, arrogance, or denial. True guidance is attained not by mere sensory experience but by a receptive, humble heart that recognizes and understands the signs and message of God.

translation: They urge you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will never fail His promise. And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.
interpretation: The verse warns against judging God by human impatience: those who demand immediate retribution misunderstand divine wisdom. God’s promises — whether of punishment or of recompense — are certain and will occur in His appointed time, which is measured on a scale unlike human time. The phrase “a day with your Lord is like a thousand years” emphasizes that apparent delay does not mean negation; what seems long to people may be brief or purposeful in God’s timing (for reasons such as mercy, testing, or completion of His decree), and ultimately all will be held to account when the Divine timetable unfolds.

translation: And how many a town did I grant respite to while it was unjust, then I seized it — and to Me is the return.
interpretation: إمهالُ الله لقرىٍ أو أممٍ ظالمةٍ لا يعني براءتهم أو أنَّ العقاب أُلغي، بل غالبًا هو فرصةٌ للتوبة أو امتحانٌ وبيانٌ للناس؛ فالاطمئنان لنعمةٍ أو طول أمدٍ لا يضمن النجاة، والعاقبة والمحاسبة بيد الله وحده.

translation: Say, “O mankind, I am only to you a clear warner.”
interpretation: The verse defines the prophet’s role as a universal, unambiguous admonisher: his duty is to present the truth plainly and warn of its consequences, not to coerce acceptance. By addressing all people and calling himself a “clear warner,” it transfers moral responsibility onto listeners—if they heed the warning, guidance and reform follow; if they reject it, accountability lies with them, not with the messenger.

translation: As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and a noble provision.
interpretation: The verse promises that sincere faith together with morally upright actions earns Allah’s pardon and a dignified provision: forgiveness meaning removal of sins and restoration of standing before God, and “rizq karīm” indicating sustenance granted with generosity and honor (which can include both honorable means and blessings in this life and reward in the Hereafter). Its intent is to link inner faith to outward conduct and to reassure believers that God rewards such combined devotion with both spiritual mercy and respectable, wholesome sustenance.

translation: And those who strove against Our signs, being helpless — those are the companions of the Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who, out of arrogance or hostility, actively oppose, mock, distort, or attempt to nullify God’s revelations will ultimately be powerless: their efforts cannot prevail against divine truth. The term “معاجزين” signals their real impotence and the futility of resisting guidance, and “أولئك أصحاب الجحيم” declares that such persistent rejection and obstruction of God’s signs leads to exclusion from mercy and to punishment in the Hereafter.

translation:
وما أرسلنا من قبلك من رسول ولا نبي إلا إذا تمنى ألقى الشيطان في أمنيته فينسخ الله ما يلقي الشيطان ثم يحكم الله آياته ۗ والله عليم حكيم
"We did not send any messenger or prophet before you except that, when he wished (or spoke) something, Satan cast into his wish; but Allah abolishes what Satan casts in, then Allah establishes His verses. And Allah is Knowing, Wise."
interpretation: The verse teaches that prophets, being human, could sometimes entertain personal desires or express things not from revelation; when Satan inserts such prompts, God removes or nullifies those satanic insertions and then clarifies and confirms the true divine guidance. The purpose is to reassure that the final, binding message delivered as God’s revelation is purified and preserved by Allah’s knowledge and wisdom, so what stands as God’s command and scripture remains authoritative and free of satanic corruption.

translation:
ليجعل ما يلقي الشيطان فتنة للذين في قلوبهم مرض والقاسية قلوبهم ۗ وإن الظالمين لفي شقاق بعيد
"That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and for those whose hearts are hardened; and indeed the wrongdoers are in a far schism."
interpretation: God allows the whisperings and provocations of Satan to function as a revealing test: such promptings expose the inner condition of people — those whose faith is weakened by a spiritual 'disease' or whose hearts are callous will be led into confusion or further hardness by these suggestions. In this way the trial distinguishes the susceptible and hypocritical from the sincere, and those who persist in following such impulses (the unjust) are thereby shown to be in a wide separation from guidance and truth.

translation: So that those who were given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord and so believe in it, and that the hearts of those who believe may humbly submit to it. And indeed, Allah is, for those who believe, the Guide to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true knowledge is meant to lead to recognition of divine revelation and to transform the knower into faith and inward humility—scholarship is validated only when it results in acceptance and softening of the heart before God. At the same time it reminds us that practical guidance to remain on the straight way is ultimately granted by Allah: knowledge and belief together open the heart to be guided, but the sustaining direction along the straight path is God’s gift.

translation: Those who disbelieve will remain in doubt about it until the Hour overtakes them suddenly, or the punishment of a barren day comes upon them.
interpretation: The verse warns that the unbelievers’ persistent skepticism is not resolved by argument but by their own stubbornness; it will continue until either the Last Hour surprises them with no chance to amend, or God sends an immediate, nullifying punishment — a 'barren' day in which no worldly gain, excuse, intercession or offspring will benefit them. Thus the verse emphasizes the futility and danger of clinging to doubt in the face of clear signs.

translation: الملك يومئذ لله؛ يحكم بينهم. فالذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات في جنات النعيم.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن في يوم القيامة تَصِير السلطة المطلقة لله وحده، وهو القاضي العادل الذي يفصل بين الخلق بالحقيقة؛ ومن ثم يُظهر القرآن أن النجاة لا تكون بالادعاء أو القوة الإنسانية بل بربط الإيمان الجوهري بالأعمال الصالحة، فإذا اجتمعت لدى الإنسان قناعة إيمانية وسلوك صالح فإن جزاء ذلك عند الله هو دار نعيم أبدية، مما يدل على مبدأ العدل الإلهي الذي يجازي الإنسان بحسب إيمانه وفعله.

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — for them is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that people who deliberately reject and call God’s revelations false will be met with degrading retribution: a loss of honor and dignity before God and, ultimately, a severe chastisement that strips them of standing. The phrase “humiliating punishment” emphasizes both the justice of God in holding willful rejection accountable and the moral consequence — spiritual and social abasement — that follows persistent denial of clear divine guidance.

translation: And those who emigrated in the cause of Allah and then were killed or died — Allah will surely provide for them a good provision. And indeed, Allah is the best of providers.
interpretation: The verse promises that sacrificial migration for God’s cause is not a loss: those who leave their homes and then die — whether slain in that cause or by other means afterward — will be granted a generous, honorable provision from God. “Rizqan ḥasanan” conveys both tangible care (for their families or dependents) and noble recompense in the Hereafter; the statement culminates by affirming God’s absolute ability to sustain and reward, reassuring believers that sincere sacrifice is met by divine provision and superior reward.

translation: He will admit them into an entrance that pleases them; and indeed Allah is All‑Knowing, Most‑Forbearing.
interpretation: The words assure that God will grant the believers a welcome and station that truly satisfies them — a divinely appointed outcome grounded in His complete knowledge of hearts and His patient mercy. By highlighting Allah’s being ‘All‑Knowing’ and ‘Forbearing’, the verse indicates that the pleasing entry is the result of God’s perfect awareness and His restraint: He knows people’s inner states, delays or withholds immediate retribution, accepts sincere repentance, and ultimately bestows the appropriate, merciful recompense in wisdom.

translation: That is [the ruling]. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, then is wronged (after that), Allah will surely grant him victory. Indeed, Allah is Most Forbearing, Most Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse teaches a balance between rightful retribution and the higher virtue of pardon: a person has legitimacy to respond proportionally to an injury and, if thereafter aggression is done against him, divine support will be given; yet this legal allowance does not negate the preferred ethical stance of forgiving, because Allah’s nature is forbearant and forgiving. In practice it means justice may be pursued within limits, but mercy and restraint are morally superior paths that reflect God’s own forgiving attribute.

translation: That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night; and indeed Allah is Hearing and Seeing.
interpretation: The verse points beyond the physical alternation of night and day to God’s absolute authority over changing states and events: the regular reversal of conditions reminds believers that nothing in creation is fixed apart from His will. Because Allah hears and sees all, every hardship, plea and hidden action falls within His knowledge and power to alter, so people are called to trust His timing, seek Him sincerely, and act righteously in the confidence that apparent darkness can be transformed by His will and that every deed is observed and will be accounted for.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is falsehood; and indeed Allah is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse asserts that ultimate reality and rightful object of worship is God alone: everything invoked or relied upon apart from Him has no true being or authority and is therefore vain. By naming Allah al‑Haqq and the others al‑Batil, and by calling Him al‑ʿAliyy al‑Kabir, the text emphasizes His absolute transcendence, permanence and supremacy over all apparent powers, directing believers to place their trust, obedience and hope solely in Him.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky and the earth becomes green? Indeed, Allah is Most Gentle (al-Latīf), All‑Aware (al-Khabīr).
interpretation: By pointing to a familiar, life‑giving process, the verse teaches that God's care operates both powerfully and through subtle, precise means: His 'latīf' is the tender, wise providence that brings revival and sustenance by ordinary causes, and His 'khabīr' means He knows outward circumstances and inward needs. Believers are thus urged to trust in God's intimate, intelligent care—recognizing that the same divine governance that renews the earth also sustains souls and will enact final restoration and judgment.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And indeed, Allah — He is the Self‑Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s possession of all things declares His absolute sovereignty while the attributes “al‑Ghani” (Self‑Sufficient) and “al‑Hamid” (Praiseworthy) stress His complete independence and intrinsic perfection: He neither needs creation nor is benefited by it, yet He alone deserves all praise. The intended practical lesson is to orient the believer’s reliance, gratitude and worship toward God alone, abandoning both arrogance born of false self‑sufficiency and despair born of misplaced dependence.

translation:
أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ سَخَّرَ لَكُم مَا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَالْفُلْكَ تَجْرِي فِي الْبَحْرِ بِأَمْرِهِ وَيُمْسِكُ السَّمَاءَ أَنْ تَقَعَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِ ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِالنَّاسِ لَرَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ

“Do you not see that Allah has made subservient to you whatever is on the earth and the ships that sail the sea by His command? And He restrains the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission. Indeed, Allah is to the people Most Kind, Most Merciful.”
interpretation: The verse points to God’s sovereign control over nature and the availability of creation’s resources as a deliberate, merciful provision for human life. That the earth’s goods and the movement of ships are “subjected” to us is a sign, not an entitlement: it calls for humble gratitude, responsible stewardship, and trust in God’s sustaining power. Likewise, the sky’s being held in place “except by His permission” emphasizes that the order of existence depends entirely on God’s will; His governance protects and sustains human life, and therefore we ought to recognize our dependence on Him, refrain from pride or idolizing what He has made useful, and respond with obedience, care for creation, and reliance on His mercy.

translation: And He is the One who gives you life, then causes you to die, then will bring you to life again; indeed, mankind is ever ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute sovereignty over the cycles of existence—our initial giving of life, the inevitable death, and the promised future revival—and uses that observable, repeated demonstration of divine power to expose a moral failing: despite experiencing these clear signs of dependence on God, people persist in ingratitude and denial. The intended lesson is ethical and spiritual: recognition of God’s control over life and death should engender humility, continual gratefulness, and readiness for resurrection and accountability; refusal to do so is portrayed as moral blindness and ingratitude.

translation:
لِكُلِّ أُمَّةٍ جَعَلْنَا مَنْسَكًا هُمْ نَاسِكُوهُ ۖ فَلَا يُنَازِعُنكَ فِي الْأَمْرِ ۚ وَادْعُ إِلَى رَبِّكَ ۖ إِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ هُدًى مُسْتَقِيمٍ
“For every people We have prescribed a way of worship which they observe; so do not let them dispute with you about the matter. Call to your Lord — you are indeed upon straight guidance.”
interpretation: God acknowledges that different communities have been given particular rites and ways of approaching the Divine; this verse instructs the Prophet (and by extension the believer) not to be drawn into fruitless disputation over those established practices. The priority is inviting people to God and remaining steadfast on the clear, upright guidance revealed to one’s mission, rather than being sidetracked by controversies about forms and customs that communities cling to. Thus the verse counsels focus on the central truth and patient calling, respecting that diversity of ritual histories does not negate the duty to proclaim the straight path.

translation: And if they argue with you, say, "Allah knows best what you do."
