interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to step back from petty disputes and to point out that ultimate knowledge and judgment of people's deeds belong to God; it teaches restraint and trust in divine wisdom, exposes the futility of mere verbal contest, and reminds both speaker and opponents that inner realities and true accountability are known only to Allah.

translation: Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that in which you used to differ.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the final resolution of disputes—especially over matters of truth, belief, and moral responsibility—belongs solely to God on the Day of Judgment; human arguments and claims will be laid bare and judged by divine knowledge and justice, so reliance on worldly victory or partisan certainty is misplaced and one must instead seek truth, humility, and accountability before God.

translation: Do you not know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth? Indeed that is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute, comprehensive knowledge of all realities—seen and unseen—and the certainty and permanence of that knowledge as recorded in His Book. Its purpose is to correct human presumption and complacency: nothing of intention, word, or deed escapes divine awareness, and therefore men and women must live with humility, sincerity, and responsibility before God. The phrase that this is “in a Book” reassures that events and deeds are preserved and will be brought to account, while “that is easy for Allah” comforts the believer that maintaining, recording, and executing divine knowledge and judgment requires no effort for the Almighty; His providence and justice are sure even when human affairs seem chaotic.

translation: They worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and concerning which they have no knowledge; and the wrongdoers have no helper.
interpretation: The verse condemns the practice of ascribing divinity or ultimate authority to other beings or things without any revealed warrant or reliable knowledge. “سلطان” here denotes a divinely sanctioned proof or mandate, and “ما ليس لهم به علم” points to worship based on conjecture, tradition, desires or imitation rather than evidence. Such objects of worship possess no real power to guide or defend, and those who persist in injustice—by replacing true worship with false objects or by acting unjustly in belief and deed—will find no protector or advocate for them before God. The passage therefore calls for worship grounded in true knowledge and warns that false refuges offer no help in this life or the hereafter.

translation: And when Our clear signs are recited to them, the faces of those who disbelieve reveal denial; they are almost about to seize those who recite Our verses to them. Say, “Shall I inform you of something worse than that? It is the Fire which Allah has promised to the disbelievers, and wretched is the destination.”
interpretation: The verse shows that evident truth inherently exposes the spiritual condition of its rejecters: when confronted with clear proof, their faces and actions betray inner denial and provoke hostile attempts to silence the truth. That outward aggression is a sign of moral blindness and unjust resistance, not a vindication of their position. God’s response—announcing a punishment far worse than their present threats—reframes temporal persecution as ultimately insignificant compared with final accountability. The practical lessons are twofold: for the believers, patience and trust in divine justice, since human hostility cannot overturn God’s judgment; for the rejecters, a warning that visible rage and suppression of truth only deepen their culpability and lead to a miserable end.

translation: O people, an example is set forth, so listen to it: indeed those whom you call upon besides Allah will not create even a fly, even if they were to gather together for it; and if the fly were to snatch away anything from them, they would not be able to reclaim it from it. Weak are both the seeker and the sought.
interpretation: The verse uses a stark parable to expose the impotence of all beings worshipped or invoked apart from God: they lack creative power and cannot even control or retrieve something as insignificant as a fly. By showing that the supposed auxiliaries are utterly powerless, the passage implies the futility of directing worship, fear or hope toward them and emphasizes that dependence and ultimate authority belong to God alone. It also turns the critique on human practice: those who seek aid from the powerless are themselves weak, thus the verse calls for right understanding of divine sovereignty and for directing reliance and worship to the One who alone has real power.

translation: They did not give Allah His due estimation. Indeed, Allah is Mighty, Exalted in Strength.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who underestimate or fail to recognize God’s true worth and authority; their misjudgment comes from arrogance and attachment to created things, but it neither diminishes God nor protects them — God’s attribute of being al‑Qawiyy (all‑powerful) and al‑ʿAzīz (invincibly honored) means He has absolute strength and sovereign authority to uphold truth, support His causes, and hold people accountable, and therefore right recognition of God demands humility, sincere submission, and worship.

translation: Allah selects from the angels messengers and from among the people; indeed, Allah is Hearing, Seeing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God, by His perfect knowledge and wisdom, appoints those who convey guidance in the way best suited to the task—sometimes through angelic intermediaries, sometimes through human prophets—so that the truth reaches creation effectively. This selection is not a matter of human preference but of divine insight into what each situation requires; therefore believers are called to trust and submit to the authority of God’s chosen messengers and to recognize that His hearing and sight encompass all circumstances and motives.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them; and to Allah all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute, encompassing knowledge of people’s past, present and future and of what is apparent and concealed, and that every affair ultimately comes back to Him for settlement; its practical meaning is to remind humans to live with humility and moral responsibility—trusting God’s wisdom, being conscious that nothing is hidden from Him, and knowing that final judgment and resolution belong to Allah alone.

translation: O you who have believed, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord and do good — that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine success (falah) arises from combining sincere, humble submission to God (expressed in bowing and prostration) with ongoing ethical action: worship is not an end in itself but a force that sanctifies the believer’s character and motivates concrete goodness toward others, and it is through this integrated life of devotion and right conduct that one attains true prosperity in this world and the Hereafter.

translation: And strive for the sake of Allah with the striving due to Him. He chose you and did not place upon you in the religion any hardship — the religion of your father Abraham. He named you Muslims before and in this [Book] — that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people. So establish prayer, give zakah, and hold fast to Allah; He is your Protector. Excellent is the Protector and excellent the Helper.
interpretation: This verse enjoins a sincere, measured striving (jihad) rooted in devotion to God and framed by the mercy of revelation: God has honored and chosen the community by restoring the straight, uncomplicated faith of Abraham and by calling them “Muslims,” thereby assigning them the responsibility to witness divine truth to humanity. The Prophet’s role as witness confirms and transmits the message, while the community’s role as witnesses requires moral witness through worship, charity and steadfast adherence to God. ‘No hardship’ signals that true religion is not a burdensome set of legalities but a practicable path of submission; therefore believers are to engage in struggle (spiritual, social, and, when rightly constrained, defensive) without excess, sustain communal rites (prayer, zakah), cling to God for unity and help, and take confidence in God’s protection and support as they represent and uphold justice and guidance among people.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Successful indeed are the believers.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that true success (falāḥ) is not merely worldly gain but spiritual and moral flourishing: those whose faith is genuine and is manifested in sincere worship, upright conduct, trustworthiness, humility, and self-restraint attain the pleasure of God, inner peace, and ultimate salvation — a success grounded in divine mercy rather than transient worldly achievements.

translation: Those who are humble and reverent in their prayers.
interpretation: The phrase points to believers whose ritual prayer embodies khushūʿ — an inward humility and full presence before God. It means their hearts are attentive, free from worldly distraction and show, experiencing awe, submission, and conscious awareness of standing in God’s presence; thus prayer for them is not mere bodily motions but a transforming inner communion that shapes their conduct and sincerity.

translation: And those who turn away from vain (idle) talk.
interpretation: This describes believers who deliberately refrain from all useless, frivolous, harmful or obscene speech — not merely silence for its own sake, but disciplined use of the tongue: avoiding gossip, slander, lies, empty disputes, crude joking and any talk that distracts from truth and remembrance of God. By turning away from ‘laghw’ they protect their dignity and relationships, prevent discord and sin, and keep their words focused on what is truthful, necessary and spiritually beneficial.

translation: And those who give the zakāh (alms).
interpretation: The phrase designates believers who faithfully fulfill the obligation of zakāh as an essential expression of their faith: they set aside the prescribed portion of wealth at its due time with sincerity and submission to God, thereby purifying themselves and their possessions, aiding the needy, and maintaining social justice. It encompasses not only the outward act of payment but the inner disposition of regularity, responsibility and trust in God — showing that true belief is manifested in concrete care for others and disciplined stewardship of one’s resources.

translation: And those who guard their private parts.
interpretation: This refers to believers who discipline and control their sexual impulses, refraining from fornication and adultery and preserving chastity and modest behavior within the limits God has set — protecting both their bodies and their moral integrity from illicit sexual relations and anything that would lead to them.

translation: Except concerning their wives or those their right hands possess; for they are not to be blamed.
interpretation: The clause limits a preceding prohibition by carving out an explicit, lawful exception: sexual relations and associated marital rights are permitted with one’s legally wedded wives and with those legitimately under one’s custody or ownership (classically understood as female slaves or concubines acquired by lawful means). The phrase “فَإِنَّهُمْ غَيْرُ مَلُومِينَ” (they are not to be blamed) signals that such relations, being sanctioned by the divine legal order, carry no moral or legal reproach so long as they occur within the bounds and responsibilities prescribed by the faith.

translation:
فَمَنِ ابْتَغَى وَرَاءَ ذَٰلِكَ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْعَادُونَ
“So whoever seeks beyond that, then those are the transgressors (the unjust).”
interpretation: The verse warns that deliberately going beyond the limits God has set — by seeking additional claims, conditions, rights, or advantages not permitted within the prescribed law — is an act of injustice. It condemns attempts to manipulate, oppress, or add burdens beyond divine ordinance and calls believers to respect the boundaries and fairness intended by God’s rulings.

translation: And those who are mindful of their trusts and their covenants.
interpretation: The verse describes true believers as those who safeguard whatever is entrusted to them—whether tangible property, positions of authority, confidential information, or moral responsibilities—and who fulfil their promises and covenants, whether made to God or to other people. Being “ra‘ūn” (careful guardians) means acting with integrity, not betraying trusts or breaking agreements; this ethical stance is presented as a defining quality of sincere faith and the foundation of social trust and justice.

translation: And those who guard (protect) their prayers.
interpretation: It describes believers who vigilantly preserve the prayer’s reality and effectiveness: they observe the five prayers at their appointed times, maintain the outward rites (wudu, proper postures and recitations) and the inward conditions (presence of heart, humility, and sincerity), resist neglect and worldly distractions, avoid corrupting innovations and ostentation, and thus keep prayer as a constant, discipline-forming bond with God that restrains them from sin and sustains their moral life.

translation: Those are the inheritors.
interpretation: The statement affirms that the people just described are the true heirs by God’s decree: they will receive the lasting inheritance — the final possession of what matters (ultimately the earth, God’s bounty and the rewards of the Hereafter) — showing that temporary worldly power and gains will pass away while God grants enduring sovereignty and reward to the righteous who believed and acted rightly.

translation: Those who inherit al‑Firdaws — they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The phrase presents Paradise (al‑Firdaws) as the divinely granted, ultimate portion for those who have lived in accordance with God’s guidance; to “inherit” it means it is bestowed as a rightful, lasting reward, and the description “they will abide therein forever” emphasizes that this state is not temporary but an eternal, consummate fulfillment of divine mercy and justice for the righteous.

translation: And indeed We created man from an extract of clay.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that human beings are purposefully fashioned by God from humble, earthly material; “sulalah min teen” implies an extract or refined substance rather than a random accretion, pointing to deliberate design. The statement underscores human dependence on the Creator, the humility of our origin, and the moral reminder that physical origin does not negate dignity or responsibility—rather it grounds human equality, fragility, and accountability before God.

translation: Then We made him a drop in a secure, firm resting place.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human life begins by God’s deliberate act from a seemingly insignificant origin and is placed into a protected, stable receptacle for its formation; by calling the womb a “secure, firm resting place,” it underscores God’s sovereign design, the intentionality and care in creation, and human dependence on divine power—calling for humility, gratitude, and recognition of the sanctity and vulnerability of early life.

translation: Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot; then We made the clot into a lump (of flesh); then We made the lump into bones, and We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the Best of creators.
interpretation: The verse points to a deliberate, staged process of human formation under God’s will: from a tiny germ to a clinging embryo, then a fleshy mass, then skeletal structure clothed with flesh, culminating in a distinct, fully formed human being. By outlining these successive, ordered phases the text emphasizes both God’s intimate control over biological development and the purposeful unity between matter and life. “Another creation” signals that through this process the being is transformed into a new, integrated creature with capacities and identity beyond the mere sum of its parts. The concluding phrase, “Blessed is Allah, the Best of creators,” affirms the perfection, wisdom, and uniqueness of divine creative power and invites reflection on human dependence on that transcendent design.

translation: Then indeed, after that you will surely be dead.
interpretation: An emphatic reminder of the inevitability of death: after the stages and events of life, human beings will unavoidably die. The clause stresses certainty and serves to awaken awareness of mortality, urging people to account for their deeds and prepare for what follows beyond worldly existence.

translation: ثم إنكم يوم القيامة تبعثون: Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection you will be raised.
interpretation: The verse affirms the inevitable, universal bodily resurrection and presentation before God for reckoning; the particle “ثم” stresses the sequence and certainty — after death and every preceding event, all people without exception will be brought forth to stand accountable, refuting any claim that death is the final end.

translation: And indeed We have created above you seven paths, and We were never unaware of the creation.
interpretation: “Seven paths” denotes an ordered, layered structure in the heavens or channels of divine governance through which provision, decree, and cosmic order operate; the phrase underscores God’s meticulous, purposeful arranging of creation and His complete, attentive knowledge of every affair—nothing is neglected or beyond His management.

translation: And We sent down water from the sky in due measure and caused it to settle in the earth; and indeed We are Able to take it away.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s sovereign mastery: the measured sending of rain and its lodging in the earth are signs that sustenance and the conditions of life are under His precise control. Because He can just as readily withhold what gives life, this reality is meant to awaken humility, gratitude and reliance on Him, and to remind people that the same power that governs provision also governs death and resurrection and therefore human accountability before God.

translation: So We caused, through it, gardens of date-palms and grapevines for you; therein are abundant fruits for you, and from them you eat.
interpretation: The phrase “by it” points to the means God mentioned earlier (e.g., rain, irrigation, or the earth’s fertility); through that means God brings forth organized, productive gardens of palms and vines to supply plentiful fruit. The verse emphasizes divine providence and wisdom in arranging natural processes to meet human needs, calling people to recognise their dependence on God’s sustaining power, to be grateful, and to see these provisions as signs pointing to His creative ability rather than as mere chance.

translation: And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, producing oil and a savoury condiment for those who eat.
interpretation: The image functions as a sign that God brings forth beneficial bounty and refinement from the very place of revelation: the “oil” connotes nourishment, healing and light, while the “condiment” connotes delight and refinement. Together they symbolize that divine guidance yields both material provision and inner good — God’s power to produce useful, pleasing gifts even from barren or sacred ground, intended to awaken gratitude, dependence on God, and recognition of His sustaining mercy.

translation: وَإِنَّ لَكُمْ فِي الْأَنْعَامِ لَعِبْرَةً ۖ نُسْقِيكُم مِّمَّا فِي بُطُونِهَا وَلَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ كَثِيرَةٌ وَمِنْهَا تَأْكُلُونَ
interpretation: The verse points to domestic animals as a sign of divine providence: their ability to yield drink (e.g., milk) and to provide numerous benefits (food, clothing, labor, transport) is meant to lead people to reflect on God’s wisdom and sustenance, to cultivate gratitude and trust in His care, and to adopt a responsible, grateful attitude toward the created resources entrusted to them.

translation: And upon it and upon the ships you are carried.
interpretation: The verse points to the divine provision and sovereignty evident in the means that sustain and move us: the earth that bears human life and the vessels that transport us over waters are deliberate signs of God’s power and mercy, calling humans to recognize their dependence on that provision, to trust His control over their journey, and to respond with gratitude and humility.

translation: And We certainly sent Nūḥ to his people, and he said, “O my people, worship Allāh; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then be mindful (fear Him)?”
interpretation: The verse functions as a moral and spiritual indictment: true faith requires exclusive devotion to God and an inner transformation — cultivating taqwa (God‑consciousness) so that belief changes conduct. By declaring that there is no deity besides Him it rejects all substitutes for ultimate trust and authority, and the rhetorical question “Will you not fear?” demands self‑examination and a practical turning away from corrupting attachments; without that inward fear and reform, mere words of profession cannot avert moral decay and the consequences that follow.

translation: And the notable ones who disbelieved among his people said, “He is nothing but a man like yourselves who wishes to gain superiority over you; if Allah had willed He would have sent down angels. We never heard of this among our forefathers.”
interpretation: The verse exposes how powerful, conservative leaders dismiss a true messenger by portraying him as an ambitious human rival and by demanding extraordinary, angelic proof as a precondition for belief; their appeal to ancestral precedent and refusal to accept a human prophet reveal a deeper unwillingness to submit to divine guidance and illustrate the common human tactics of privileging status quo, shifting the burden of proof impossibly, and rejecting God's sovereign choice of means for communicating revelation.

translation: He is nothing but a man possessed by a jinn; so wait for him for a while.
interpretation: The verse conveys how hostile opponents try to discredit a bearer of truth by branding him as ‘possessed’ and urging others to watch and wait—a tactic born of malice and fear that seeks to reduce divine message to insanity or trickery; it exposes the bad faith of deniers who prefer to stigmatize and delay judgment rather than engage with the message itself.

translation:
قَالَ رَبِّ انصُرني بِمَا كَذَّبُونِ
“He said, ‘My Lord, grant me victory against them because they deny [the truth].’”
interpretation: A petition that acknowledges God as the sole source of vindication: the speaker turns to Allah, renouncing reliance on his own power, and asks for decisive help so that the deniers’ falsehood is overcome and the truth is enabled to prevail. The verse teaches dependence on divine support in the face of rejection, patience under opposition, and trust that ultimate success against entrenched denial comes by God’s will and means (whether by clear signs, steadfastness, reform of hearts, or removal of the opposition).

translation: So We inspired him: “Construct the ark under Our watch and by Our revelation.” And when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, board it, taking into it of each pair two, and your family—except those about whom the decree has already gone forth among them. And do not plead with Me on behalf of those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned.
interpretation: God reassures and instructs the Prophet (Noah) to act on divine guidance—even when the task seems impossible—promising direct oversight and revelation. The command to take pairs and to bring one’s family except those already condemned emphasizes that deliverance depends on submission to God’s will, not on blood ties or human pleading. The phrase about not arguing on behalf of the wrongdoers teaches that persistent, unrepentant injustice removes one from the circle of divine mercy once judgment is decreed; intercession cannot override a just, established decree. Overall the verse stresses obedience to God’s command, the certainty of His judgment, and the principle that mercy is granted to those who follow divine guidance while culpable refusal brings inevitable consequence.

translation: So when you and those with you have settled on the ship, say: “All praise is due to Allah who has saved us from the unjust people.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that deliverance must be met with immediate gratitude to God: one should attribute salvation to divine mercy rather than personal skill, thereby cultivating humility, recognizing God’s sovereignty over fate, and affirming that rescue from oppression comes from Him alone.

translation: And say: “My Lord, cause me to be brought down to a blessed dwelling, and You are the best of those who grant dwellings.”
interpretation: This is a prayer that asks God to place the supplicant where true benefit and blessing (barakah) will accompany them—not merely a safe or comfortable spot, but one that fosters righteousness, wellbeing and divine favor. By ending with “You are the best of those who grant dwellings,” the verse affirms total reliance on God as the ultimate ordainer of one’s place and condition, turning the request from a mere desire for refuge into a submission to God’s wisdom about what dwelling will be truly good for one’s faith and destiny.

translation: Indeed in that are signs, and indeed We are surely testing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the events just related are intentional divine signs whose purpose is not merely to amaze but to put people to the test: God uses such signs and trials to reveal and distinguish true faith, patience and moral dispositions, to bring people to accountability, and to serve the larger wisdom of guidance and recompense.

translation: Then We produced after them another generation.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God, in His sovereign power, brings forth successive generations to replace previous peoples. This underscores God’s ability to renew life and societies, reminds that the rise and fall of communities is part of His testing and governance, and warns each generation that it too will be held accountable for accepting guidance rather than relying on the fate or deeds of those before them.

translation: So We sent among them a messenger from themselves, [saying], “Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear (Him)?”
interpretation: God often sends guidance through someone from within a community so the message cannot be dismissed as foreign; the command to worship only Allah cuts through all competing loyalties and idols — social, political or personal — and the rhetorical question “Will you not fear?” demands an inner reckoning: true acknowledgement of God must produce moral change, humility, and urgent preparation for accountability, otherwise stubbornness will lead to loss.

translation: وقال الملأ من قومه الذين كفروا وكذبوا بلقاء الآخرة وأترفناهم في الحياة الدنيا ما هذا إلا بشر مثلكم يأكل مما تأكلون منه ويشرب مما تشربون
interpretation: الآية تصوّر موقف زعماء قوم النبي الذين كفروا وتنكروا للآخرة مستندين إلى رفاهيتهم الدنيوية، فيخفضون من مقام النبي بتشبيهه لبشر عاديين يشاركونهم الطعام والشراب. التفسير أن اعتراضهم نابع من تكبّر مادي واستغلال لمنزلة دنيوية: إذ يرفضون الرسالة ليس لعيب منطقي فيها بل لأن اعترافهم بها يهدد مواقعهم ومتعهم. كما تُبيّن الآية بطلان الحجة القائمة على بشرية النبي؛ كونه إنسان لا يبطل كونه رسولا، وإنما يؤكد أن الدافع الحقيقي للرفض هو الهوى والمصلحة لا علة موضوعية.

translation: And if you were to obey a human like yourselves, then indeed you would surely be losers.
interpretation: The verse warns that yielding obedience to a mere mortal—one who does not represent or follow divine guidance—leads to true loss: spiritual ruin and failure in the ultimate reckoning. Success comes from following God’s guidance (and His Messenger), not from blindly submitting to fallible human authority or desires; placing human judgment above divine command results in being 'khāsirīn' (losers).

translation: Does He (truly) promise you that when you die and become dust and bones you will be brought forth?
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke of those who deny resurrection: the verse exposes the absurdity of basing belief on present appearances and asserts that God’s power to re-create is not limited by physical decay—therefore denial of being raised for judgment is unjustified and reflects a refusal to acknowledge divine authority over life and death.

translation:
هيهات هيهات لما توعدون
"هيهات، هيهات — بَعِيدٌ جداً ما عُدْتُم به"
interpretation: بيان تأكيدي يهدم آمال المكذبين: ما كانوا يرجون ـ سواء تأجيل العقوبة أو مَنْقِذٌ أو نصرٌ ـ لن يتحقق، فذلك الموعِد بعيدٌ عن أن يُنال ولن يُعطى لهم؛ توقعاتهم باطلة والعقاب أو الجزاء الموعود حتميّ لا مهلة فيه.

translation: «إنها إلا حياتنا الدنيا؛ نموت ونحيا وما نحن بمبعوثين» — “It is only our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected.”
interpretation: The phrase records a denial of the hereafter — reducing existence to the transient cycle of worldly living and dying and asserting that death is final. By quoting this claim the Qur'an exposes the limited, experience-bound outlook of those who reject resurrection: their conclusion arises from reliance on immediate observation and ignorance of God's power to revive, and it thus serves as a warning about the moral and existential consequences of denying ultimate accountability.

translation: إنه ليس إلا رجلاً افترى على الله كذباً، وما نحن له بمؤمنين.
interpretation: الآية تصوّر موقفَ المعارضين الذين يرفضون النبوّة بحصر النبي في حدود إنسانيّة واتهامه بابتداع الكلام على الله؛ في ذلك كشفٌ عن آلية إنكار الحقيقة: عندما يتصادم دعوة تتطلب تصحيحاً أخلاقياً أو تغييراً اجتماعياً، يلجأ البعض إلى تشويه الناقل واتهامه بالكذب بدلاً من محاججته بالمضمون. العبارة "وما نحن له بمؤمنين" تعبّر عن قرار قاطع بالبقاء على الكفر رغم الدلائل، فالنفي هنا ليس مجرد رأي بل التزام طوعي بالرفض وتحميل مسؤولية ذلك على الناصح.

translation: قال: «ربّ، انصرني بما كذبون» — “He said, ‘My Lord, help me against what they are falsely claiming.’”
interpretation: A prayer appealing to God as the ultimate helper and judge when one faces slander or false accusation: rather than relying on human defense, the speaker asks for divine support to vindicate the truth, to grant strength and patience, and to overturn falsehood by God’s power and justice.

translation: قال: «عما قليلٍ؛ ليَصْبِحَنَّ نادِمِينَ»
interpretation: The speaker declares that the opponents’ present triumph is only temporary: in a short time they will be seized by regret and loss. It conveys that apparent delay in punishment or accountability is not forgiveness but a brief respite before the inevitable consequence—those who persist in wrongdoing will soon realize their error and lament it, whether by sudden worldly reversal or by ultimate reckoning in the Hereafter.

translation: So the blast seized them in truth, and We made them like chaff. So woe to the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse depicts God’s decisive and just punishment: a single overwhelming strike (الصيحة بالحق) that comes with absolute truth and ends the lives of a corrupt people, reducing them to ‘ghithā’—worthless, scattered chaff with no lasting honor or benefit. The image stresses both the swiftness and the totality of divine retribution against persistent injustice, and the refrain ‘فبعدا للقوم الظالمين’ functions as a stern warning and moral judgment: those who persist in oppression and reject guidance will be stripped of dignity and remembered only as a lesson against wrongdoing.

translation: Then We produced, after them, other generations.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s continuous creative sovereignty: He did not end His work with earlier peoples but brought forth successive generations. It teaches that human societies are transient and that God renews communities to carry forward life, guidance and test; thus the fate of past nations stands as a warning and lesson for those who follow, since succession on earth depends on obedience to God and moral responsibility.

translation: No people can bring forward their appointed term, nor can they delay it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God has ordained fixed times for the course and outcome of peoples—a term for their endurance, rise, decline, punishment or deliverance—which human agency cannot hasten or postpone. It underlines the inevitability and justice of divine decree: efforts to escape, avert or accelerate what God has determined are ultimately futile, so one must recognize divine timing and be accountable for one’s deeds.

translation: Then We sent Our messengers in succession; whenever a messenger came to a people they denied him. So We let them follow one another, and We made them into tales (stories). So woe to a people who do not believe.
interpretation: The verse underscores God’s patient method of guidance—messengers are repeatedly sent out of mercy—but when communities persistently reject the truth, God permits them to go on in mutual imitation of error. Their fate, reduced to cautionary narratives, serves as a lesson for others: persistent denial results in the loss of guidance and exposes them to divine retribution. The warning (‘woe’) emphasizes that stubborn disbelief leads not only to moral ruin but to becoming an object of historical warning for succeeding generations.

translation: Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God equipped Moses and Aaron not only with miraculous signs to make truth evident, but also with a manifest, unequivocal authority (sulṭān mubīn) to carry out their mission. Together the signs and the clear authority validate their prophethood, remove excuses from opponents, and authorize them to confront oppression and establish God’s guidance among the people.

translation: (He was sent) to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they were arrogant — they were a people given to haughtiness.
interpretation: The verse points to pride as the decisive barrier to receiving guidance: Pharaoh and his court, insulated by power and self-exaltation, rejected the messenger not for lack of evidence but because their hauteur made them see themselves above accountability. “قوما عالين” thus characterizes a spiritual and moral elevation of self that blinds people to truth and leads to their ruin.

translation: فقالوا: «أنؤمنُ لبشرين مثلنا وقومُهما لنا عابدون» — They said, “Shall we believe in two men like ourselves while their people are worshippers (of false gods)?”
interpretation: The verse reproves the human tendency to dismiss truth because it comes from ordinary or socially marginal people and to favor the safety of majority opinion and established practices; it condemns prejudice and conformity that make people reject guidance when it threatens their social or religious status.

translation: But they denied them, so they became among the perishing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the rejection of God’s messengers and their guidance results in the rejectors’ own undoing: by refusing the truth they sever themselves from saving guidance and consequently are counted among the doomed—suffering ruin in moral status and, by God’s judgment, in outcome.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Book so that they might be guided.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the revelation given to Moses was a divinely granted means for leading people toward right belief and ethical conduct. The wording لعلهم (“that they might”) frames guidance as an invitation and possibility rather than compulsion: God provides clear teaching and law as an opportunity and responsibility, but guidance is realized only when people accept, understand, and act on it. Thus scripture’s purpose is remedial and directional—to illuminate the path—and the failure to be guided reflects human turning away, not a deficiency in the gift itself.

translation:
وَجَعَلْنَا ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ وَأُمَّهُ آيَةً، وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا إِلَى رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ
“And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We gave them refuge on a high place of firm rest and with a spring.”
interpretation: The verse presents Jesus and Mary as an āyah — a living proof of God’s power, wisdom and mercy. Their extraordinary circumstances (the miraculous birth, Mary’s purity, and the care they received) are meant to point people away from human attribution of divinity and toward God’s sole lordship: God alone creates, sustains, protects and honors whom He wills. The image of being sheltered on a settled, elevated place with a spring underscores that God’s support transforms precariousness into dignity and provision; it reassures believers that apparent weakness can be made a sign of divine capability and serves as a corrective against wrong beliefs or neglect of God’s signs.

translation: O messengers, eat of the pure (good) things and do righteous deeds; indeed, I am, of what you do, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those entrusted with guiding others must embody integrity in both means and actions: they are to accept lawful, wholesome provisions and to act righteously, for prophetic or moral authority neither sanctifies illicit gain nor absolves one of ethical responsibility—God’s full knowledge ensures that the purity of one’s sustenance and the sincerity of one’s deeds are integral to the legitimacy and acceptance of their mission.

translation: And indeed this is your one community, and I am your Lord—so fear Me.
interpretation: The verse declares the fundamental unity of the people addressed under a single Divine Lord and draws the practical consequence: recognizing that shared relationship to God should produce taqwa (God‑consciousness), obedience, and a turning away from factionalism or self‑assertion, because all stand answerable before the one Lord.

translation: So they divided their affair among themselves into factions; each faction rejoicing in what they had.
interpretation: The verse reproaches the tendency to break a unified truth or community into rival camps that cling to partial views and comforts. Each party takes pride in its own share of belief, practice or advantage, becoming self-satisfied and thus resisting correction or seeking the fuller guidance; that complacent attachment to a fragment sustains division, mutual isolation and error rather than humility, accountability and the pursuit of the whole truth.

translation: So leave them in their heedlessness for a time.
interpretation: The verse conveys that God, by His wisdom, delays immediate punishment and allows wrongdoers to remain absorbed in their false security or pleasures for a limited period; this postponement is purposeful — it provides an opportunity for guidance/repentance, exposes the transience of worldly ease, and ensures that justice will come at its appointed time.

translation: Do they imagine that what We grant them — of wealth and children...
interpretation: The verse warns that worldly provision (wealth and offspring) is not proof of God’s approval nor a shield against accountability; those who persist in wrongdoing or disbelief may be enjoying temporary favors or tests, but must not assume such blessings guarantee safety from divine judgment.

translation: نُسارع لهم في الخيرات، بل لا يشعرون — "We hasten upon them the good things, yet they do not perceive (or feel) it."
interpretation: The phrase means that God bestows blessings, opportunities and ease upon certain people swiftly and abundantly, but those people remain heedless and ungrateful: they neither recognize these favors as signs from God nor let them lead to thankfulness or guidance, so the divine grace passes without awakening them.

translation: Indeed, those who, out of fear of their Lord, are apprehensive.
interpretation: The phrase describes believers whose inner state is one of reverent awe and anxious watchfulness before God; this wholesome fear (خشية) is not mere terror but a humble consciousness of accountability that makes them cautious, restrains them from sin, prompts repentance and sincere obedience, and shapes their conduct with humility and carefulness while remaining balanced by hope in God’s mercy.

translation: And those who believe in the signs of their Lord.
interpretation: This describes people whose faith is grounded in recognizing and accepting God’s āyāt — both the revealed verses and the manifestations of His power and wisdom in creation. Their belief is a deep, considered conviction (not mere lip service) that shapes their understanding, trust, and behavior: they draw guidance and lessons from divine signs, submit to God’s authority, and let that conviction regulate their choices and moral conduct.

translation: And those who do not associate partners with their Lord.
interpretation: This describes believers whose relationship to God is founded on pure tawḥīd: they affirm and submit to Allah alone, directing worship, trust, obedience and seeking of help solely to Him, and rejecting any belief or practice that ascribes divine authority, attributes or independence to others. Such refusal of shirk shapes their creed, worship and conduct, marking true faith by exclusive devotion to the one Lord.

translation: And those who give of what they give, while their hearts are apprehensive that they will surely return to their Lord.
interpretation: The verse describes true believers whose acts of giving are marked by sincere humility and consciousness of accountability: they give not for show or out of complacency but with a trembling awareness of standing before God, so their charity and deeds are motivated by fear of God's judgment, hope for His mercy, and a deep inward humility that safeguards sincerity.

translation: Those are the ones who hasten to perform good deeds, and they are foremost in them.
interpretation: The verse speaks to a spiritual disposition: true believers cultivate a purposeful urgency toward righteous action — they do not delay or merely intend, but actively seize opportunities to worship, serve, and obey God. This ‘haste’ is disciplined and sincere, rooted in awareness of the hereafter and love and fear of God, producing consistent, exemplary conduct. Being “foremost” means they lead in practice and priority, prioritizing lasting moral gain over worldly procrastination or comfort, so their lives become models that draw others toward good.

translation: We do not burden any soul except to its capacity. And with Us is a Book that speaks with the truth, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: God affirms two guarantees: moral proportionality and perfect accountability. No person is held to obligations beyond what they can bear — responsibility is measured to individual capacity — and on the basis of a divinely preserved record (the Book) which will testify truthfully to each person’s deeds, every matter will be judged justly. Therefore no one will suffer injustice at God’s hands: obligations, rewards, and penalties will be exact, proportionate, and founded on incontrovertible testimony.

translation: بل قلوبهم في غمرة من هذا ولهم أعمال من دون ذلك هم لها عاملون
interpretation: الآية تُحكم أن قيمة العبادة والامتثال لا تُقاس بالأفعال الظاهرة وحدها، بل بوجه القلب ونظرته: قلوبهم مشتتة وغافلة عن المقصود الحقيقي، وهم منشغلون بأعمالٍ أخرى لا تتصل بهذه الحقيقة، فتبقى أعمالهم مكرسة لأغراض مغايرة ولا تجيب عن مطلب الحق. المعنى العملي: الاختلال بين داخل الإنسان وفعله يجعل العمل بلا جدوى فيما يُراد به من هداية أو إخلاص.

translation: حتى إذا أخذنا مترفيهم بالعذاب إذا هم يجأرون — "Then when We seized the affluent among them with punishment, behold, they cried out aloud."
interpretation: The verse conveys that those who lived in comfort and excess, having ignored warnings, only express loud fear and supplication when catastrophe strikes their privileged members; their outcry exposes the futility of belated panic and how worldly prosperity had blinded them to guidance, so their cries come too late to avert the consequences of persistent rejection.

translation: Do not raise your voices today; indeed you are of us — you will not be helped.
interpretation: This rebuke teaches that at a decisive moment (such as judgment or defeat) clamoring and appeals to one's affiliations are futile: being counted among a group or shouting for support will not secure assistance. It emphasizes the insufficiency of human alliances and loud protest when divine decree or overwhelming reality removes any prospect of help, calling for silent recognition of one’s lost standing rather than vain demands for aid.

translation: My signs were indeed recited to you, yet you turned back on your heels.
interpretation: The verse rebukes people who, despite repeatedly hearing clear divine guidance, respond by retreating into their former ways instead of embracing it; it highlights that mere exposure to revelation is insufficient—what matters is steadfast acceptance and moral courage, and turning away reflects fear, attachment to worldly comforts or hypocrisy that leads to moral failure and accountability.

translation: مستكبرين به سامرا تهجرون — Arrogant because of it, you forsake it and busy yourselves with nocturnal chatter.
interpretation: The phrase criticizes pride that leads people to abandon what is right or required—be it duty, guidance, or remembrance of God—and instead indulge in vain, late‑night social amusements and idle talk; such arrogance causes neglect of obligations and a turning away from moral and spiritual responsibility.

translation: Have they not then considered the Word? Or has that which did not come to their forefathers come to them?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who reject the revelation by pointing to two realities: either they have failed to ponder its clear reasoning, or they claim the message is unprecedented as a pretext for refusal. In either case their objection is not a legitimate intellectual barrier—warnings and truths were delivered to earlier peoples as well—so their denial reflects obstinacy, prejudice, and a refusal to use reflection, not any genuine novelty or impossibility in the message.

translation: Or do they not recognize their Messenger, and thus they deny him?
interpretation: The verse indicts a willful, culpable rejection: it implies that the messenger’s identity and message were sufficiently clear, so those who persist in denial do so from stubbornness, pride, or attachment to falsehood rather than true ignorance — making them morally responsible for their refusal.

translation: Or do they say, “It is a fabrication”? Nay, it has come to them with the truth, yet most of them are averse to the truth.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the revelation is genuine truth despite the accusation that it is mere invention or folly; it explains that the real reason most people reject it is not lack of evidence but an internal aversion—because the truth confronts their habits, privileges, or desires, they prefer to denounce it rather than submit to its demands.

translation: And if the Truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been ruined. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, yet they turn away from their reminder.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance, not human whims, sustains moral and cosmic balance: if God’s commands were bent to people's self‑serving desires, order and justice in creation would collapse. Therefore God sends revelation as a corrective reminder to restrain and orient human impulses; when people reject that reminder, the corruption is the consequence of their turning away, underscoring both divine wisdom in prescribing guidance and human responsibility for accepting or rejecting it.

translation: Or do you ask them for payment? But the provision from your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s gift and support transcend any human fee: true provision includes material sustenance, honor, protection and the unseen assistance that validates and sustains a prophetic or moral mission. By declaring that the Lord’s provision is superior, the text dissuades making spiritual guidance transactional and affirms reliance on God as the source of the highest and most fitting recompense—so that service offered without expectation of worldly payment remains pure and is ultimately upheld by the Best of Providers.

translation: And indeed you call them to a straight path.
interpretation: This affirms that the Prophet’s mission is to present and invite people to a divinely guided way of life that is upright, balanced and free from deviation. “Straight path” denotes the sound, clear course of belief and practice centered on tawḥīd, sincere worship, moral integrity and social justice — a middle way that avoids excess and deficiency. The verse underscores that the guidance offered is not a personal opinion but a revealed, coherent guidance for rightly ordered life; the Prophet’s role is to call clearly and persistently, while acceptance remains the responsibility of individuals.

translation: And as for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, they are surely turned away from the Path.
interpretation: Denial of the Last Day removes the moral and spiritual horizon that disciplines conduct; without belief in ultimate accountability people progressively abandon the straight guidance of God, chasing transient desires and thereby deviating from truth and right conduct.

translation: And if We had shown them mercy and removed from them the harm afflicting them, they would surely return to their insolence, wandering blindly.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God may withhold or allow hardship not out of cruelty but because removing it would only enable the stubborn to persist in arrogance and misguidance; allowing the harm exposes their true condition and can serve as a corrective or a consequence so that their corrupt pattern is not merely reinforced by easy relief.

translation: And indeed We seized them with punishment, but they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate [to Him].
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine chastisement can be a means to awaken hearts, but its effectiveness depends on people’s inner posture: if they remain proud and refuse sincere humility and prayer, punishment will not lead to reform but to deserved ruin. It underscores human responsibility — God provides warning and opportunity, yet arrogance and spiritual blindness can close one off from mercy and make punishment the final consequence.

translation: Until, when We open to them a gate of severe punishment, behold — they are bewildered therein.
interpretation: The phrase describes a moment when God, after warnings and the lapse of restraint, permits a chastisement to befall those who persisted in denial and wrongdoing; the image of a “gate” signifies that the means and conditions for punishment have been allowed to enter their situation. “Mablus” (bewildered) indicates not merely fear but utter disorientation, shame and powerlessness — they can neither avert the harm nor mount a credible defense. The verse thus teaches that divine punishment is a consequential response to persistent rejection and that, once God’s restraining mercy is withdrawn, those who ignored guidance will find themselves helpless and regretful.

translation: And He is the One who created for you hearing, sight and hearts; how seldom you give thanks.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has endowed human beings not only with external senses (hearing and sight) but with inner faculties (hearts) that enable understanding, reflection and moral choice. Because these gifts make recognition of truth and proper conduct possible, true gratitude is required — not mere words but using those faculties to reflect on God’s signs, to seek guidance, and to obey His commands. The rebuke “how seldom you give thanks” points to humanity’s habitual failure to acknowledge the divine source of these faculties and to repay the gift by rightly employing them in remembrance, contemplation and righteous action.

translation: And He is the One who scattered you across the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse asserts God's sovereign authorship of human placement and existence: the diversity of peoples and their dispersion across the world are by divine ordinance and serve a purposeful, testing life, and this worldly dispersal is temporary because ultimately all people will be brought back before God for reckoning—so earthly divisions and attachments are subordinate to the reality of divine unity, accountability, and final assembly.

translation: And He is the One who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of night and day; will you not then reason?
interpretation: The verse points to life, death and the regular cycle of night and day as observable signs that the world is governed by a single, wise Creator; it urges people to employ their intellect to recognize this divine sovereignty, abandon false assumptions about randomness or rival powers, and align their beliefs and conduct with the reality of God’s providence and moral accountability.

translation: بل قالوا مثل ما قال الأولون — Rather, they said the same as those before them had said.
interpretation: The verse condemns unreflective imitation: people opposing the message merely repeat the inherited objections and excuses of their predecessors instead of confronting the truth on its merits, demonstrating spiritual complacency and reliance on tradition and prejudice rather than sincere inquiry.

translation:
قَالُوا أَإِذَا مَتْنَا وَكُنَّا تُرَابًا وَعِظَامًا أَإِنَّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ
They said, “When we die and have become dust and bones, will we then truly be resurrected?”
interpretation: The verse records the scoffing objection of disbelievers who, seeing the body reduced to dust and bones, claim resurrection impossible; it exposes a narrow, materialist mindset and moral evasion—using physical decay as a pretext to deny God’s power and avoid accountability.

translation: We and our fathers were promised this before; indeed, this is nothing but the tales of the ancients.
interpretation: This utterance reflects a defensive rejection of a prophetic warning: people dismiss the message by appealing to inherited habit and collective memory, treating revelation as mere folklore. The phrase reveals a recurring psychological resistance—preferring the comfort of tradition, labeling inconvenient truth as 'old tales' to avoid moral accountability and change—so it exposes how societies can neutralize admonition by reducing it to familiar stories rather than confronting its demands.

translation: Say, "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?"
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge meant to expose human ignorance and to affirm divine sovereignty: the verse demands recognition that the earth and all its inhabitants are the possession and under the control of God alone; it refutes claims of independent power or rival deities, calls people to acknowledge their dependence on the One who sustains and disposes of creation, and points toward accountability before that sovereign Lord.

translation:
سَيَقُولُونَ لِلَّهِ ۚ قُلْ أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ
"They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then remember?’"
interpretation: This is a sober rebuke: when people casually ascribe things to God in words, the Prophet is commanded to press them to genuine inward recollection and accountability — to move beyond empty formulae and truly remember God’s signs, favors and warnings so that belief shapes their awareness and conduct.

translation: قُلْ: «مَنْ رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ السَّبْعِ وَرَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْعَظِيمِ» — Say, “Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?”
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question to expose and overturn false claims of multiple lords: by directing attention to the One who rules the seven heavens and the majestic Throne, it affirms Allah’s exclusive and supreme sovereignty, transcendence, and authority over all realms. It implies that true lordship—creation, sustaining, control, and ultimate judgment—belongs only to God, thereby nullifying the pretensions of idols or lesser powers and calling people to recognize and submit to Divine oneness and omnipotence.

translation: They will say, “To Allāh.” Say, “Will you not then be conscious (of Him)?”
interpretation: The verse rebukes those whose invocation of God is mere lip-service: when people defer matters or attribute outcomes to Allah with no corresponding fear, humility, or obedience, the Prophet is instructed to challenge them—asking whether they will cultivate true taqwa. It emphasizes that true faith requires inner God‑consciousness and righteous conduct, not just verbal formulae.

translation: Say, “Who is it in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and who grants protection while none can grant protection against Him—if you know?”
interpretation: The verse declares God’s exclusive sovereignty and absolute guardianship: all authority and control over existence belong to Him alone, He is the One who grants security and determines outcomes, and no being or idol can avert or oppose His will. Presented as a challenge to those who claim other protectors or deities, it exposes the ignorance of attributing divine power to anything besides God and calls people to recognize and submit to His sole lordship.

translation: They will say, “To Allah.” Say, “Then how are you being bewitched?”
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke directed at those who, confronted with clear signs of God, stubbornly refuse to accept them and instead dismiss them as sorcery; by asking “How then are you bewitched?” the Prophet is instructed to expose their inconsistency and self-deception, showing that calling divine action ‘magic’ only reveals their willful refusal to acknowledge the truth.

translation: Nay — We will bring them the truth, yet they are indeed liars.
interpretation: The verse asserts that God will make the reality — particularly the Resurrection and the coming judgment — manifest and incontrovertible to people; nevertheless those who persist in denial will be exposed as liars. It emphasizes that their rejection is not for want of evidence but stems from stubbornness, self-deception and desire, and that when the truth is fully presented God’s vindication will be decisive and their culpability clear.

translation: ما اتخذ الله من ولد، وما كان معه من إله. إذا لذهب كل إله بما خلق، ولَعلا بعضهم على بعض. سبحان الله عما يصفون.
interpretation: الآية تنفي نفياً قاطعاً أن يكون لله ولد أو شريك، وتُظهِر سُفَهية الاعتقاد بتعدد الآلهة بأن تلك «الآلهة» لو أخذت ما خلقت لَتَباعَت وتنافست وتغلّبت إحداها على الأخرى، أي أنها مخلوقات عاجزة تخضع للخلق لا خالقاً حَقّاً؛ ومن ثَمّ لا يجوز نسب الإلوهية أو النسب الإلهي إلى غير الله. خاتمة الآية «سبحان الله عما يصفون» تؤكد تنزيه الله عن هذه الأوصاف الباطلة وتثبت تفرده المطلق في الألوهية والكينونة.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the seen; so exalted is He above what they associate (with Him).
interpretation: This affirms that God alone possesses full knowledge of both hidden realities and all that appears, and by that very attribute He is wholly transcendent and beyond any partners people may invent. Because His knowledge and sovereignty are complete and unique, attributing equals or associates to Him is a manifestation of limited human perception and error; true recognition of God requires acknowledging His unmatched knowledge, lordship and transcendence, and rejecting any form of association with Him.

translation: Say, “My Lord, if what they are promised is true, then show me what they are promised.”
interpretation: The speaker appeals to God to make manifest, if the opponents’ warnings or claims are real, the outcome they assert—seeking a decisive, visible proof that distinguishes truth from falsehood. The prayer reflects both a longing for clarity and trust in God’s timing and wisdom: rather than relying on human speculation or taunts, the Prophet asks Allah to disclose the reality so that the empty assertions of the deniers are exposed and divine judgment and vindication become evident.

translation: My Lord, do not make me among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: A humble supplication asking God to be spared from being counted among the unjust—seeking protection from committing or being complicit in wrongdoing and asking for guidance and moral steadfastness so one will not share the fate or responsibility of transgressors.

translation: وَإِنَّا عَلَىٰٓ أَن نُّرِيَكَ مَا نَعِدُهُمْ لَقَٰدِرُونَ
interpretation: الله يطمئن النبي ﷺ بأنه قادر على تحقيق ما وعد به هؤلاء وإظهار وقوعه أمام نبيه؛ أي أن الوعد الإلهي — سواء كان جزاءً للعصاة أو بيّنة لحقّ الرسالة — لا محالة سيتحقق وسيجعله شاهداً على تجلي قدرته وعدله.

translation: Repel evil with that which is better; We are most knowing of what they describe.
interpretation: The verse commands responding to harm, insult, or injustice not with retaliation but with superior moral action — kindness, restraint, fair treatment — because such conduct has the power to transform hostility into reconciliation. At the same time it reminds the believer that God alone truly knows people’s inner motives and the reality behind their words, so one must act sincerely for God’s sake rather than seek merely to win appearances or be misled by outward claims.

translation: And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils."
interpretation: This injunction teaches that believers should actively seek God's protection against the subtle, persistent promptings and insinuations of Satan and his agents—those inner whispers that try to provoke doubt, distraction, despair, or inclination toward sin. By uttering this supplication one acknowledges human weakness before such corrosive influences and affirms reliance on God's exclusive power to guard the heart and mind; the phrase thus functions as both a spiritual defense and a practice of turning back to God whenever harmful inner promptings arise.

translation: وَأَعُوذُ بِكَ رَبِّ أَنْ يَحْضُرُونَ — “And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, from their coming (their presence).”
interpretation: The speaker appeals to God for protection from the arrival or presence of hostile people whose attendance would harm, intimidate, or overwhelm him and jeopardize his mission; he asks for divine shelter so that he will not be forced into danger, coercion, ridicule, or obstruction by those opponents.

translation: Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, return me."
interpretation: The verse warns that the moment of death exposes human regret and the finality of opportunities: asking to be sent back after life has ended will not restore the chance to repent and reform. It therefore stresses immediate responsibility — sincere faith and righteous action must be undertaken in this life, for accountability is real and Divine justice does not hinge on last‑minute pleas.

translation:
«لعلي أعمل صالحا فيما تركت» — «كلا — إنها كلمة هو قائلها — ومن ورائهم برزخ إلى يوم يبعثون.»
"‘Perhaps I will do some righteous deed from what I have left behind.’ — ‘No! Indeed, it is but a word he is saying; and behind them is a barrier until the Day they are raised.’
interpretation: The verse censures procrastination and empty verbal promises: when a person, faced with accountability, pledges to do good later, that claim—if not accompanied by present sincere action—is dismissed as mere talk. The phrase “a barrier” signifies a real separation (spiritual incapacity or cut-off from guidance and benefit) that results from persistent denial or insincerity, leaving such people confined by their excuses until the Day of Resurrection.

translation: When the Trumpet is blown, then on that Day there will be no kinship among them, nor will they ask one another.
interpretation: The verse teaches that at the Resurrection worldly ties and social protections—family, lineage, status—will be powerless; each person will be absorbed in their own reckoning and cannot rely on relatives or networks for help or intercession. It stresses personal accountability before God and that ultimate outcome depends on one’s deeds and God’s judgment, not on human connections.

translation: فَمَنْ ثَقُلَتْ مَوَازِينُهُ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ
interpretation: الآية تصف معيار النجاح الحقيقي يوم القيامة: حين تُوزَن أعمال الناس، الذين تثقل موازينهم بالأعمال الصالحة والعاملات الصالحة هم الفائزون المفلحون—أي الذين ينالون رضاء الله ونعيمه؛ لذلك تُشير إلى أن الفوز الأبدي مرتبط بجمع الصالح من الأعمال والنية الخالصة واعتماد الكريم الرحيم في الحساب.

translation: And whoever's scales are light — those are the ones who have lost their own selves; in Hell they will abide.
interpretation: The “scales” here signify the moral ledger of a person’s deeds on the Day of Judgment. If a person’s good deeds are few or insignificant—whether through neglect of duty, love of worldly things, hypocrisy, or lack of sincere faith—then they have effectively ruined their own best interest (خسروا أنفسهم): they have acted in a way that brings about their own loss. The statement that they will be “in Hell, abiding” underscores the seriousness and permanence of that outcome unless one turns to true repentance and cultivates weighty, sincere good works; the verse is therefore a stern reminder of personal responsibility and the need to live with inward sincerity and outward righteousness so that one’s deeds will carry weight on the scales.

translation: Their faces will be scorched by the Fire, and they will be therein downcast and wretched.
interpretation: The verse portrays the consequences for those who persist in rejection: the scorching of faces signifies not only physical burning but the loss of dignity and honor, while كَالِحُونَ describes a demeanour of humiliation—faces distorted, eyes averted, bowed in grief and regret. It emphasizes that their inner arrogance and defiance are transformed into visible abasement and despair in the punishment of the Fire.

translation: Were not My verses recited to you, yet you used to deny them?
interpretation: This is a divine reproach to people who received clear revelation yet willfully rejected it; the verse emphasizes that hearing God’s signs creates moral responsibility, and that persistent denial—rooted in arrogance, heedlessness, or attachment to worldly gains—is a culpable choice that removes excuses and justifies divine accountability and admonition.

translation: They said, “Our Lord, our misery has overcome us, and we were indeed a people gone astray.”
interpretation: The verse expresses a candid admission of responsibility: the people recognize that their suffering is the just consequence of their persistent misguidance, abandon excuses, and turn to God in humility. It teaches that genuine relief and reform begin when a community or individual acknowledges their error, seeks forgiveness, and resolves to be guided back to the right path.

translation: Our Lord, bring us out of it; and if we return (to it), then indeed we are wrongdoers.
interpretation: A humble plea that acknowledges human weakness and responsibility: asking God to remove them from the situation of sin or temptation and recognizing that a return to that state would be an act of injustice against themselves. It emphasizes dependence on divine help to avoid relapse, the moral weight of returning to disobedience, and the need for God’s protection and forgiveness.

translation: قَالَ: «اخسِئُوا فِيهَا وَلَا تَكَلَّمُونَ»
interpretation: الأمر هنا يصور الهزيمة المطلقة للمذنبين وحرمانهم من كل موقف دفاعي أو كرامة: يُؤمرون أن يسقطوا في ذلهم داخل العذاب ويُمنَعوا من الكلام، فالصمت المفروض يدل على إدراكهم لذنوبهم وقطع كل سبيل للاعتذار أو التفاوض، ويُبرز أن الحكم الإلهي نهائي لا يُجابه بالحجج أو التبريرات.

translation: Indeed, there was a party of My servants who said, "Our Lord, we have believed; so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith is paired with humility and continual turning to God: believers acknowledge their belief yet immediately seek pardon and compassion, recognizing their own shortcomings and dependence on Divine mercy. Calling God “the best of the merciful” frames hope in God’s unique capacity to forgive, so the proper spiritual posture is not complacency but sincere repentance and reliance on God’s mercy as the means by which faith is perfected and sustained.

translation:
فَاتَّخَذْتُمُوهُمْ سُخْرِيًّا حَتَّى أَنْسَوْكُمْ ذِكْرِي وَكُنْتُمْ مِنْهُمْ تَضْحَكُونَ
"So you made them an object of ridicule until they caused you to forget My remembrance, and you were laughing at them."
interpretation: The verse warns that by embracing mockery and aligning with those who turn God’s message into a joke, people become spiritually distracted: their attachment to ridicule and to companions who trivialize faith displaces remembrance of God, producing complacency and moral decline. In short, yielding to scornful companionship and laughter at sacred matters leads to forgetting God and losing guidance.

translation: Indeed I have rewarded them today for what they patiently endured; they are the successful.
interpretation: God's declaration here affirms that on the Day of Reckoning those who persevered—who kept faith, exercised self‑restraint, and bore trials without turning away—receive their full recompense. “Reward” is not merely relief from suffering but admission to God’s favor and the status of true success; “today” stresses that ultimate victory is realized in the final accounting, and “they are the successful” distinguishes lasting, moral‑spiritual triumph from temporary worldly gains.

translation: قَالَ: «كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ؟» — «عَدَدُ سِنِينٍ»
interpretation: The verse teaches that human reckoning of time is limited and ultimately subject to God's accounting: what people call “a number of years” is only a relative measure, and the Lord’s questioning reminds us that earthly stay is temporary, precisely measured by God, and will be judged — a warning against attachment, presumption, and forgetfulness of accountability.

translation:
قالوا لبثنا يوما أو بعض يوم فاسأل العادين
“They will say, ‘We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count [the days].’”
interpretation: The verse exposes a common human reaction at reckoning: people will try to minimize their responsibility and shift the truth by appealing to others’ testimony. It teaches that such self‑deception and bargaining are vain before God’s precise and absolute judgment — attempting to downplay one’s deeds or rely on others will not alter the ordained accountability.

translation: قال: «إن لبثتم إلا قليلا؛ لو أنكم كنتم تعلمون.»
interpretation: الآية تذكّر بأن العمر والفرصة في الدنيا قصيران، وأن غفلة الناس عن حقيقة هذا القصر هي سبب تضييعهم للفرصة؛ لو أدركوا حقًا قِصر المدة والعواقب اللاحقة لبادروا بالتوبة والاعتبار والإعداد للحساب.

translation: Did you think that We had created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the view that human life is meaningless: it asserts that creation is deliberate and purposeful, that our lives are a test and responsibility under God’s sovereignty, and therefore everyone will ultimately be brought back to God for account — so one must live with conscious purpose and moral accountability.

translation: So exalted is Allah, the Sovereign, the Truth — there is no god but He, Lord of the Glorious Throne.
interpretation: The verse asserts God's absolute transcendence and exclusive sovereignty: He alone is the true King whose reality and authority are the final measure, so all competing claims to divinity are null. By linking His uniqueness (“no god but He”) to being Lord of the Throne, it emphasizes that God’s rule is comprehensive and supreme, grounding the believer’s duty to single-minded worship, trust, and submission before an unassailable, all-encompassing divine authority.

translation: And whoever invokes besides Allah another deity for which he has no proof — then his reckoning is only with his Lord; indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse warns that calling on gods or intercessors without any valid proof (no revealed sign, sound argument, or just cause) is baseless shirk; such a person's matter is ultimately for God alone to judge — no created thing can justify or save him — and those who persist in that rejection of God’s truth will not attain true success in this world or the Hereafter.

translation: And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy; You are the best of the merciful."
interpretation: As a concise model supplication, the verse teaches humble reliance on God by coupling repentance with appeal for compassionate care: one turns to God to remove the burden of sin (forgiveness) and to receive ongoing compassion and support (mercy), while affirming that God’s mercy surpasses all. This affirmation both consoles the believer—encouraging sincere return to God—and frames mercy as the means by which God restores and elevates those who seek Him.

translation:
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَـٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ. سُورَةٌ أَنْزَلْنَاهَا وَفَرَضْنَاهَا وَأَنْزَلْنَا فِيهَا آيَاتٍ بَيِّنَاتٍ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ

"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. (This is) a chapter which We have revealed and enjoined, and in which We have sent down clear verses—so that you might remember."
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the chapter is of divine origin and carries a binding directive: its revelation is not incidental but meant to be observed. By describing its verses as clear, it frames the Qurʾān as a lucid guide whose purpose is to rouse remembrance and reflection, to orient hearts and actions toward God, and to compel the listener to internalize and live by its teachings rather than treat them as mere information.

translation: The female fornicator and the male fornicator—flog each one of them a hundred lashes, and let not compassion for them deter you from carrying out the judgment of God if you believe in God and the Last Day; and let a group of the believers witness their punishment.
interpretation: This verse prescribes a fixed corporal punishment for proven zina (fornication/adultery) as a means of protecting social morality and deterring sexual transgression. Its command to avoid letting compassion prevent implementation stresses obedience to God’s law once the strict conditions for proof are met (so that personal feelings do not override divine rulings). Requiring a party of believers to witness the punishment underscores the need for transparency, communal involvement, and safeguards against private or arbitrary enforcement; classical practice therefore couples this ruling with rigorous evidentiary standards (e.g., confession or reliable witnesses) to prevent wrongful punishment.

translation: A male fornicator shall not marry except a fornicator or a polytheist, and a female fornicator shall not be married except by a fornicator or a polytheist; and that has been forbidden to the believers.
interpretation: The verse functions as a legal‑ethical injunction: marriage among the faithful must not be used to legitimize or hide persistent illicit sexual behaviour. It bars believers from taking as spouses those who are known to commit zina, both to protect the moral integrity and trust of the Muslim community and to serve as a deterrent; the prohibition is understood to apply while the person remains unrepentant, and the verse thereby also encourages sincere repentance and moral reform as the means to restore full communal and marital acceptance.

translation: And those who accuse chaste women, and then do not produce four witnesses—flog them eighty lashes and never accept their testimony; and those are the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse establishes a legal and moral principle against slander: accusations as grave as adultery require the highest standard of proof, and making such a charge without the required witnesses is itself a punishable breach of justice. Its aim is to protect individual honor and social order by deterring false allegations, imposing a sanction on those who recklessly defame others, and denying the credibility of people who have demonstrated they will violate truth and trust. In short, it safeguards the community from the harm of unproven accusations by both punishing the slanderer and removing their standing as reliable witnesses.

translation: Except those who repent thereafter and make amends; for Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sincere tawbah — real remorse, stopping the wrongdoing, repairing any harm, and resolving not to return to it — removes spiritual culpability: such genuine moral reform places a person under Allah’s forgiveness and mercy. Its purpose is to give hope and to prioritize inner transformation and repair of wrongs as the path by which past faults are pardoned by a compassionate Lord.

translation: And those who accuse their wives, and they have no witnesses except themselves — then the testimony of one of them shall be four oaths by Allah; indeed, he is among the truthful.
interpretation: The verse establishes the procedure of liʿān: when a husband levels the grave charge of adultery against his wife but cannot produce witnesses, he is permitted to bind himself through four solemn oaths invoking God to assert his claim. Its purpose is twofold — to give legal weight to a serious accusation in the absence of external evidence, and to deter careless or malicious accusations by making the claimant swear repeatedly before God, thereby protecting marital integrity and individual honor by tying the outcome to the moral and spiritual responsibility of the oath-taker.

translation: And the fifth is: may the curse of Allah be upon him if he is among the liars.
interpretation: A solemn conditional imprecation declaring that if the person’s claim is false, then divine condemnation will follow; it underscores the seriousness of lying, invoking God’s judgement as the ultimate consequence and as a final arbiter where human certainty is lacking.

translation:
وَيُدْرَأُ عَنْهَا الْعَذَابُ أَنْ تَشْهَدَ أَرْبَعَ شَهَادَاتٍ بِاللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّهُ لِمِنَ الْكَاذِبِينَ
"What will avert the punishment for her is that she give four oaths by Allah; indeed he is among the liars."
interpretation: The verse prescribes a legal safeguard against unjust punishment: when a serious accusation lacks convincing proof, the accused may resort to a solemn oath procedure to avert penalty, while the text simultaneously condemns the false accuser by branding him a liar. The underlying principle is protection of the innocent and the requirement that claims be substantiated, with harsh moral disapproval and deterrence directed at those who fabricate charges.

translation:
والخامسة أن غضب الله عليها إن كان من الصادقين
“And the fifth: may the wrath of God be upon her, if he is among the truthful.”
