The phrase “everything will perish except His Face” teaches that all created things are transient, whereas God alone possesses everlasting being (the term “Face” signals His real, unending presence without implying physicality). Because sovereignty and final judgment belong to Him, human life must be lived in awareness of divine authority and ultimate accountability — worship, ethics, and hope are therefore to be oriented solely toward God in anticipation of the return to Him.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif Lam Mim.
interpretation: One interpretation is that the disjoined letters “Alif‑Lam‑Mim” are a deliberate, miraculous sign: though composed of ordinary letters they introduce a revelation no human can match, serving as a challenge to skeptics and an invitation to reflect on the Quran’s divine origin; their exact, esoteric meaning is known only to God.

translation: Do people think that they will be left to say, “We believe,” and they will not be tested?
interpretation: This verse warns that mere verbal profession of faith is insufficient; Allah subjects professed believers to trials (hardship, temptation, or ease) to reveal the reality of their iman, to purify and strengthen it, and to distinguish sincere believers from hypocrites — faith is proven and perfected through testing, not by unexamined assertion.

translation: And We did certainly test those before them; and Allah will surely make known those who are truthful and will surely make known the liars.
interpretation: Trials are a means God uses to reveal and refine inner realities: enduring hardship with patience and consistent righteous conduct confirms genuine faith and brings God’s recognition, while collapse or inconsistency under pressure exposes mere pretence. Because God alone knows the heart, believers are called to cultivate sincere trust and steadfast action rather than rely on outward professions.

translation: Or do those who do evil deeds think that they can outstrip Us? Evil is what they judge.
interpretation: This verse censures those who imagine they can evade or outrun God's decree — mistaking temporary worldly advantage or delayed consequence for ultimate success. Their judgment is corrupt because they measure outcomes by immediate gains and presume impunity, whereas divine justice and the timing of reward or punishment rest with God alone; in the end their calculation will be overturned and they will face the true consequences of their deeds.

translation: Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah—then indeed, Allah’s appointed time will surely come; and He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the eventual encounter with God is certain and comes only at the time He has decreed, so a believer who truly seeks that meeting must live in continual readiness—cultivating sincerity, righteous action, patience, and trust—because God hears and knows all intentions and circumstances; one cannot hasten or avoid His appointed decree, but must rely on His wisdom while preparing oneself morally and spiritually.

translation: And whoever strives, then indeed he strives only for his own soul; indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human striving — whether in worship, moral struggle, seeking knowledge, or endurance in hardship — primarily affects the doer’s own spiritual and moral standing: effort brings benefit or loss to oneself. It also affirms Allah’s complete independence and self-sufficiency, so our deeds do not add to or diminish His worth; rather, they determine our own accountability and reward by His justice and mercy.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will surely expiate for them their evil deeds and will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse affirms a divine principle: sincere faith joined with continual righteous action leads to spiritual purification and abundant recompense. "We will expiate for them their evil deeds" expresses Allah’s merciful removal or covering of their sins (either by forgiveness or by turning sins into lesser burden), and "reward them according to the best of what they used to do" indicates that their recompense will reflect the excellence and persistence of their good conduct—ultimately the highest good, often understood as admission to Paradise and intensified blessings beyond the mere tally of deeds. The promise is conditional and moral: genuine belief must be manifested in consistent, upright actions to attain this forgiveness and the superior reward.

translation: And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. And if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse establishes two related principles: filial devotion is a divinely mandated duty, but obedience to parents is not absolute—when they demand association of partners with God or require actions that contradict God’s instruction (claims “with no knowledge”), one must refuse their command. That refusal, however, does not annul the obligation of good treatment; the believer must still uphold respect and kindness while disobeying the sinful demand. The final clause reminds that ultimate adjudication belongs to God, who will hold each person accountable for their deeds, so one must follow God’s guidance even against parental pressure.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds — We will surely admit them among the righteous.
interpretation: It expresses God’s promise that true belief combined with morally upright action leads to being counted among the ṣāliḥīn (the righteous): a real elevation of status before God entailing acceptance, nearness to Him, and the reward reserved for the pious. The statement emphasizes that faith must be embodied in good deeds and that such believers will be granted membership in the company of the morally and spiritually upright in the hereafter (and thereby share their honor and reward).

translation: And among people are those who say, “We believe in Allah,” but when they are harmed for the sake of Allah they take the trial caused by people to be the punishment of Allah. And if there comes a victory from your Lord, they will surely say, “Indeed we were with you.” Is not Allah most knowing of what is within the breasts of all peoples?
interpretation: This verse exposes insincere faith and explains how trials reveal inner reality. Some profess belief outwardly, yet when facing hardship or persecution connected to standing for God, they treat the hostile reaction of people as if it were God’s punitive judgment and withdraw their support; their faith proves shallow and self-protective. Conversely, when success or divine help arrives, they opportunistically claim they were on the believers’ side. The warning is twofold: first, true faith is proven by patience and steadfastness under trial, not by words or by siding with the apparent winner; second, Allah fully knows intentions and inner states—no hypocrisy is hidden from Him—so one will be held to the reality of their heart, not their empty claims.

translation: That Allah may know those who believe, and that He may know the hypocrites.
interpretation: The words explain that God, through commands, obligations and the trials He permits, aims to disclose people’s inner realities: outward words or nominal affiliation cannot conceal true conviction. Tests and circumstances reveal who is steadfast in faith and who is insincere, for Allah’s knowledge of hearts is perfect; the sincere will be confirmed by their consistent obedience and trust, while hypocrisy will be exposed and dealt with justly.

translation:
وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا ٱتَّبِعُوا سَبِيلَنَا وَلَنَحْمِلَنَّ خَطَايَاكُمْ ۖ وَمَا هُمْ بِحَامِلِينَ مِن خَطَايَاهُمْ مِن شَيْءٍ ۖ إِنَّهُمْ لَكَٰذِبُونَ
“And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, ‘Follow our way and we will carry your sins.’ But they will not carry any of their sins at all; indeed they are liars.”
interpretation: The verse teaches the principle of individual moral responsibility and exposes the deceit of false leaders: sin and accountability cannot be shifted by human bargains or promises. Those who urge others to adopt their ways while offering to ‘bear’ their guilt are using a fraudulent tactic to recruit and excuse wrongdoing; ultimate judgment is personal, true relief comes through sincere repentance and right conduct, and anyone who promises otherwise is insincere and deceptive.

translation: And they will carry their burdens and additional burdens along with their own burdens; and they will surely be asked on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to invent.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who commit wrong and, worse, fabricate falsehoods (teachings, lies, slander, or innovations that mislead others) will not only be held responsible for their own sins but will also carry extra weight — the consequences of what they led others into. On the Day of Judgment every fabricated word and misguidance becomes an added burden for which one will be questioned; thus falsehood and misleading others intensify one’s accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah to his people; he remained among them a thousand years less fifty, and the Flood seized them while they were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse highlights the extraordinary patience and perseverance required of a prophet who calls a recalcitrant people for a protracted period; the phrase “a thousand years less fifty” stresses the long duration of his mission rather than serving as a mere chronological boast. It teaches that divine warning is given persistently and mercifully over time, but when a community persists in injustice and rejection despite repeated counsel, a decisive penalty may be enacted. Thus the passage warns listeners to heed sustained prophetic guidance, embrace reform, and recognize that persistence in wrongdoing ultimately brings accountability.

translation: So We saved him and the companions of the ship, and made it a sign for all peoples.
interpretation: By recounting the rescue, the verse conveys that God’s mercy delivers the obedient from destruction and that that deliverance itself—the ship and its salvation—serves as a permanent sign for humanity: a demonstration of God’s power and justice, a warning to those who deny His message, and a reassurance that submission to divine guidance leads to preservation.

translation: And [remember] Abraham when he said to his people, “Worship Allah and fear Him; that is better for you, if you only knew.”
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham’s call as a diagnosis of true human welfare: genuine benefit for individuals and society lies in turning wholly to God and cultivating taqwa (God‑consciousness and reverent restraint). By coupling worship with fear/respect of God, the guidance aims not merely at ritual acts but at an inner disposition that shapes right behavior; “that is better for you” affirms that this orientation secures lasting good beyond short‑term interests, while “if you only knew” reproves the people’s lack of insight—they fail to recognize what will truly prosper them. Thus the passage teaches that prophetic counsel prioritizes inward transformation that yields real, enduring benefit even when it is not immediately appreciated.

translation: You worship besides Allah only idols and invent a falsehood. Indeed, those whom you worship besides Allah do not possess provision for you. So seek provision from Allah and worship Him and be grateful to Him — to Him you will return.
interpretation: The verse rejects placing trust, worship, or hopes for livelihood in created things or fabricated deities, asserting that only God is the true source and disposer of sustenance. It calls believers to reorient both faith and practical dependence toward Allah alone — by seeking provision from Him, dedicating worship to Him, and cultivating gratitude — and reminds them that accountability before God (their ultimate return) is the moral foundation for abandoning false attachments and relying on the One who truly provides.

translation: And if you deny [it], then nations before you denied; and there is upon the Messenger only the clear conveyance.
interpretation: The verse reminds that rejection of prophetic truth has precedent and so does not negate its reality, while defining the Prophet’s role: he is charged solely with communicating God’s message plainly and faithfully; acceptance, guidance, and the moral consequences of belief or denial lie ultimately with individuals and God, not with the messenger.

translation:
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا كَيْفَ يُبْدِئُ اللَّهُ الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ ۚ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ يَسِيرٌ
“Do they not see how Allah begins creation and then brings it back? Indeed, that is easy for Allah.”
interpretation: The verse is a rebuttal to doubt about resurrection: because God has already brought things into existence, restoring them is within His power and therefore not difficult. It invites reflection on God’s absolute sovereignty over life and death, using His prior creative acts as decisive evidence that His promise of re-creation and final accountability is real and should shape human belief and conduct.

translation: Say, “Travel through the earth and observe how creation began. Then Allah will bring about the final creation. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.”
interpretation: The verse urges attentive, active observation of the natural world so that seeing how life and order arise from humble beginnings becomes evidence for God’s creative power. If God could originate the first creation—bringing order from nonexistence and producing living beings from simple beginnings—then He is fully capable of bringing about a later, final creation (the Resurrection and the life to come). The command to travel and observe promotes seeking understanding through reflection on signs in creation, and the concluding affirmation of God’s absolute power removes any doubt that what seems impossible to humans (re-creation after death) is entirely within Divine ability.

translation: He punishes whom He wills and He shows mercy to whom He wills; to Him you will return.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over judgment and mercy: ultimate consequences are determined by His wisdom and knowledge, not by human claims or temporary worldly conditions. That reality calls for humility, sincere ethical striving and turning to God for mercy, since every soul’s final fate is settled only when it returns to Him for reckoning.

translation: You are not able to cause anything to occur in the earth or in the heavens; and besides Allah you have no guardian nor helper.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute sovereignty of God and the powerlessness of all created beings: whatever influence seeming agents appear to have in heaven or earth is not independent of Allah’s will. Consequently those whom people worship or rely on besides God possess no real authority to protect, benefit, or avert harm. The passage therefore teaches tawḥīd in practice — true reliance, seeking help, and turning for protection belong only to Allah.

translation: And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and in the meeting with Him — those have despaired of My mercy, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse means that people who knowingly reject God's manifest signs and deny the reality of standing before Him on the Day of Return have, by their own persistent refusal, cut themselves off from hope in divine mercy. ‘Despaired of My mercy’ is God’s verdict that their deliberate unbelief and refusal to repent render them outside the reach of mercy in the afterlife; it is their choice and state of heart that produces that final outcome, which is followed by the just consequence of a painful punishment.

translation:
فما كان جواب قومه إلا أن قالوا اقتلوه أو حرقوه فأنجاه الله من النار ۚ إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يؤمنون
"Their only answer was, ‘Kill him or burn him.’ But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe."
interpretation: The verse teaches that when the message of truth meets violent rejection, God can overturn human schemes and visibly vindicate the righteous; such deliverance is not merely a rescue but a clear sign meant to strengthen believers’ trust in divine justice, to expose the impotence of persecutors, and to remind the faithful that steadfastness and reliance on God bring ultimate protection and confirmation of truth.

translation: And he will say, “You only took, besides Allah, idols as a mutual affection among you in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will deny one another and curse one another, and your abode will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that when people make something other than God the ultimate center of their loyalty—whether literal idols, wealth, honor, family ties, leaders, or worldly causes—those bonds are built on transient, self-interested affection. Such alliances may protect and comfort in this life, but they are conditional and will collapse under the test of final accountability: affiliations formed for worldly benefit will turn to denial, accusation and mutual condemnation when true justice is established. The moral and spiritual lesson is to root love and allegiance in God and in deeds pleasing to Him, so that relationships endure in the sight of the Real Judge; otherwise, the comforts of this world become sources of ruin when the true stakes are revealed.

translation: So Lot believed in him and said, “I will emigrate to my Lord; indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.”
interpretation: Facing imminent corruption and threat, Lot’s declaration to emigrate expresses a conscious act of faith and submission: he withdraws from a society that opposes God’s guidance, entrusts himself to Divine protection and judgment, and acknowledges that ultimate deliverance and wisdom rest with God alone.

translation: And We granted him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed prophethood and the Book among his offspring; and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God intentionally secured Abraham’s spiritual legacy by bestowing chosen descendants through whom revelation and guidance would continue. The gifts mentioned — children who carry prophethood and scripture — are both a worldly blessing and a sign of God’s ongoing plan for guidance; the phrase about receiving his reward in this life shows that God’s favors can include honor, progeny and visible blessings here, while the final clause affirms that true and lasting success is placement among the righteous in the Hereafter. In short, God’s promises are twofold: tangible blessing in this world and ultimate vindication and nearness to Him for the faithful, exemplified in Abraham’s station.

translation: And [remember] Lot, when he said to his people, “Do you indeed commit immorality such as no one among the peoples before you has committed?”
interpretation: The verse records Lūt’s stern rebuke of his community for openly practicing a gross sexual transgression (al‑fahsha) on a societal scale. He highlights that their behavior was unprecedented among peoples — not merely a private failing but a collective, normalized vice that violated the natural moral order and invited prophetic warning and divine reproof.

translation: أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الْرِّجَالَ وَتَقْطَعُونَ السَّبِيلَ وَتَأْتُونَ فِي نَادِيكُمْ الْمُنْكَرَ ۖ فَمَا كَانَ جَوَابَ قَوْمِهِ إِلَّا أَنْ قَالُوا ائْتِنَا بِعَذَابِ اللَّهِ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ
interpretation: The verse indicts a society whose private vice has become public wrongdoing and social disorder: the illicit sexual practices are coupled with brazen public display and the disruption of communal life ('cutting off the way'). When confronted by a prophetic rebuke, their single response is defiant incredulity — daring God to bring punishment rather than acknowledging fault. The deeper lesson is that moral corruption that is both practiced openly and defended with proud obstinacy undermines social order and invites divine accountability.

translation: He said, “My Lord, grant me victory over the people who are corrupt.”
interpretation: This utterance is a focused prayer for divine aid when facing entrenched injustice: it models turning to God as the source of real strength, asking not for mere personal vengeance but for God’s support to overcome corrupt power. It teaches that opposing widespread wrongdoing requires reliance on divine help, moral clarity in one’s cause, and submitting the outcome to God’s judgment rather than trusting only one’s own resources.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Abraham with the glad tidings, they said, “Indeed, we will destroy the people of this town; indeed, its people were wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The verse highlights the simultaneity of God’s mercy and His justice: a believer may receive divine good news while, at the same time, a corrupt community faces inevitable retribution. It teaches that messengers bring both reassurance to the righteous and warnings to the persistent wrongdoers, and that moral accountability is essential—divine favour does not exempt a people from consequences when their collective injustice reaches the point that punishment becomes necessary.

translation: قال أحدهم: "إن فيها لوطا". قالوا: "نحن أعلم بمن فيها. لننجينه وأهله إلا امرأته كانت من الغابرين".
interpretation: الآية تؤكّد أن النجاة رهن اليقين الإلهي والحالة الإيمانية الشخصية، لا بالرِّباط العائلي أو القرب من نبيّ. الملائكة -كأوصياء على تنفيذ أمر الله- تُبيّن علم الله بحال الناس وتصرّح بأن نجات لوط وأهله مضمونة لصدقهم وإيمانهم، بينما زوجته تُستثنى لأنها اختارت البقاء مع أهل الفساد أو رفضت الامتثال لله، فتبقى تحت حكم العدل الإلهي؛ منها يتضح أن المسؤولية الفردية والخيار الأخلاقي يقرران مصير الإنسان بغضّ النظر عن النسب أو المظاهر الخارجية.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was uneasy on their account and felt constrained for them. They said, “Do not fear and do not grieve; indeed, We will save you and your people, except your wife—she was of those who remained behind.”
interpretation: This verse highlights two theological points: first, the prophetic humaneness and the comforting role of divine messengers—when Lot’s natural anxiety arises, the messengers reassure him with God’s promise of deliverance; second, the principle that divine mercy and salvation are not conferred by blood ties but by moral and spiritual standing. The exclusion of Lot’s wife as “of those who remained behind” signals that persistent alignment with wrongdoing or hypocrisy—even within one’s household—renders a person liable to the general judgment, showing that inner assent to corruption nullifies familial privilege before God’s decree.

translation: Indeed, We will send down upon the people of this town a punishment from the heaven because they were defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a society's persistent, open rebellion against moral guidance can provoke a decisive, God‑willed chastisement. “A punishment from the heavens” indicates an overwhelming, sovereign response meant to halt widespread corruption, affirm divine justice, and serve as a stern warning that repentance and moral reform are required before consequences become unavoidable.

translation: And indeed We left of it a clear sign for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The phrase indicates that God preserved an unmistakable, enduring proof arising from an event or its consequences so that those who employ reason and reflection can recognize the truth; the sign is meant to awaken thoughtful scrutiny of history, consequences, and divine wisdom, distinguishing those who heed evident guidance from those who wilfully ignore it.

translation: And to Madyan We sent their brother Shuʿayb. He said, “O my people, worship Allah and expect the Last Day, and do not spread corruption on the earth as corrupters.”
interpretation: The verse links sincere monotheistic worship to an ethical horizon: belief must be accompanied by orientation toward the Hereafter, which governs conduct. Shuʿayb warns that hope in the Last Day should restrain short‑term greed and prevent social harms; “do not spread corruption” condemns forms of fasād such as economic fraud, oppression, and any action that destroys communal trust or the environment. In short, true faith manifests both inward devotion to God and outward justice in society.

translation: But they denied him, so the convulsion seized them, and they awoke in their homes crouching.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who stubbornly reject clear guidance and mock the messenger may be overtaken by sudden divine punishment that strips them of power and dignity; their waking “crouching” at home symbolizes humiliation and helplessness before God's judgment, a warning that disbelief leads not to impunity but to swift consequence and abasement.

translation: وَعَادًا وَثَمُودَ، وَقَدْ تَبَيَّنَ لَكُمْ مِن مَسَاكِنِهِمْ; وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ وَكَانُوا مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ
interpretation: الآية تحذر من حقيقة نفسية وروحية: حتى حين تكون الأدلة والعبر جلية، يستطيع الشيطان أن يزيّن الأعمال الخاطئة ويغري الناس بالتمادي فيها، فيقودهم عن سبيل الهداية. وصفهم بـ"مستبصرين" يفيد أنهم لم يفتقروا إلى براهين، بل كانوا في حالة انقياد مغلوط—رأوا أو بُسطت لهم الحقائق وظلّوا أعَمَّى عن تبنيها بسبب الكبر والهوى—فالتذكير هنا أن العلم بوجود الدليل وحده لا يكفي، بل تحتاج إليه استقامة القلب والقبول لله.

translation: وقارون وفرعون وهامان. ولقد جاءهم موسى بالبينات فاستكبروا في الأرض وما كانوا سابقين.
interpretation: الآية تشير إلى أن الثروة والسلطان لا يبرِّران تكبُّر الإنسان ورفضه للحق: فقد أُتي هؤلاء (قارون وفرعون وهامان) بآيات واضحة عبر موسى، فاختارتهم أهواؤهم وكبرياؤهم فتمسّكوا بالبغي والظلم. النتيجة أن الكبر عن قبول البيان الإلهي يقود إلى الهزيمة الأخروية والدونية الأخلاقية، فالمظهر القوي في الدنيا لا يقتضي الغلبة عند الله ولا النجاح الحقيقي.

translation: So each one We seized for his sin. Among them were some upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and some were seized by the (terrible) cry, and some We caused the earth to swallow, and some We drowned. And Allah would never wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine punishment in history is not arbitrary but a just consequence of persistent collective wrongdoing: nations were afflicted in different ways suited to their circumstances, and these afflictions are the outcome of their own choices and transgressions. The closing clause stresses God’s justice — He does not oppress His creatures; rather, people bring ruin upon themselves through rejection of guidance and continued injustice.

translation: مثل الذين اتخذوا من دون الله أولياء كمثل العنكبوت اتخذت بيتاً، وإن أوهن البيوت لبيت العنكبوت، لو كانوا يعلمون
interpretation: المثل يبيّن هشاشة الاعتماد على مخلوقات أو أصنام أو تقاليد بشرية بدلاً من الاعتماد على الله. مثل بيت العنكبوت يرمز إلى مأوى ضعيف زائل لا يقي ولا يحمي، فكل ما يتخذه الناس وليّاً أو ملجأ سوى الله فهو ضعيف وقابل للهدم، وعبارة «لو كانوا يعلمون» تشير إلى جهلهم بضعف ما اعتقدوا أنه سند لهم.

translation:
إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ مَا يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ مِن شَيْءٍ ۚ وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ
“Indeed Allah knows whatever they invoke besides Him of anything, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.”
interpretation: God’s awareness extends to the very things people call upon instead of Him—their names, supposed powers, and the realities behind those claims. By calling Him al-ʻAzīz (the All‑Mighty) and al‑Hakīm (the All‑Wise), the verse affirms that He alone possesses sovereign power to act and perfect wisdom to judge and govern affairs; therefore the alternative objects of worship are ultimately powerless and their invocation is known and measured by God’s wise, authoritative will.

translation: And these similitudes We set forth for mankind; but none will understand them except those endowed with knowledge.
interpretation: The verse indicates that Allah uses parables and signs to communicate deeper spiritual and moral truths, and genuine comprehension of these meanings is not attained by mere hearing or intellectual pride but by sincere knowledge — a combination of learned insight, heartfelt reflection, humility, and openness to guidance; thus true understanding is a gift granted to those who seek and reflect, not to the heedless or arrogant.

translation: Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth. Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers.
interpretation: The phrase “created… in truth” indicates that the cosmos was brought into being with deliberate wisdom, order and purpose rather than by accident; for the believer this ordered, meaningful creation functions as empirical and spiritual proof of God’s existence, power and governance, prompting reflection that strengthens faith, confirms the truth of revelation, and demands that one orient life and conduct according to that divine reality.

translation: Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer. Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater. And Allah knows what you do.
interpretation: The command to recite revelation and to establish prayer points to a twofold way of reforming the soul: disciplined ritual and continual God‑consciousness. Prayer serves as a regular, formative practice that restrains base impulses and wrongful deeds by habituating attention, humility, and accountability. Yet its moral effect depends on inner presence: “remembrance of Allah” is described as greater because sustained awareness of God — not mere mechanical performance — is what truly shapes character and governs conduct. The reminder that God knows what you do underscores that both outward acts and inner states are observed, so worship must be sincere and accompanied by ethical behavior rather than empty formality.

translation: And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in the best manner, except with those of them who commit injustice; and say, “We believe in that which has been revealed to us and that which has been revealed to you, and our God and your God is One, and to Him we submit.”
interpretation: The verse directs Muslims to conduct interfaith discussion with respect, reason, and good manners—avoiding harsh, mocking or aggressive dispute—and to seek common ground rather than escalate confrontation. The exception “except those who commit injustice” allows firm resistance against those who persistently persecute or act treacherously, not carte blanche for rude debate. Saying “We believe in that which was revealed to us and to you” is a conciliatory formula that affirms shared elements of revelation (and the oneness of God) as the basis for sincere dialog, while “our God and your God is One, and to Him we submit” emphasizes both theological unity and the ethical stance of humble submission to God. Overall the verse prescribes charitable, truthful engagement that preserves one’s own faith integrity yet seeks to build mutual recognition and reduce needless hostility.

translation: Thus We have revealed to you the Book. So those to whom We gave the Scripture believe in it; and among them are some who believe in it. And none deny Our signs except the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse asserts that the Qurʾān is a continuation of earlier revelation and that many among the People of the Book recognize and accept its truth; it answers objections by showing that acceptance exists even among those previously given scripture. By saying that only the disbelievers deny God’s signs, the verse emphasizes that rejection is a moral and spiritual choice (kufr) rather than a failure of evidence — distinguishing sincere responders from those whose hardened disbelief leads them to deny clear divine proofs.

translation: And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; if you had, the false claimants would have been in doubt.
interpretation: The verse asserts that the Prophet did not previously possess or read any revealed scripture nor did he author the Qur’an himself (symbolized by writing with his right hand). Its purpose is to remove the usual objections: opponents could have alleged he learned it from earlier books or forged it if he had been a learned scribe. By stating he was neither a prior reciter nor a writer, the text underscores that the Qur’an’s language, knowledge, and authority could not have come from the Prophet’s own study or craftsmanship, and it exposes the deniers’ disposition to invent causes for doubt rather than accept a divine origin.

translation: But rather, it is clear signs implanted in the breasts of those who were given knowledge; and none deny Our signs except the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse indicates that the Qur’an’s teachings are intrinsically clear and become convincingly present within the inner conscience of those granted true knowledge: such people perceive, accept and live by these signs because their hearts and intellects are rightly attuned. Rejection of these manifest signs is not an innocent difference of opinion but a morally culpable stance—born of injustice, arrogance, or self-interest—which harms the rejecter’s soul. Thus comprehension is both a God‑granted inner insight and a moral receptivity, while denial is an ethical fault rather than merely an intellectual error.

translation:
وقالوا لولا أنزل عليه آيات من ربه ۖ قل إنما الآيات عند الله وإنما أنا نذير مبين
"And they say, 'Why were not signs sent down to him from his Lord?' Say, 'The signs are only with Allah, and I am but a clear warner.'"
interpretation: The verse teaches that miraculous proofs belong to God's prerogative alone and are not at the prophet's disposal; the prophet’s role is to convey God’s message plainly and warn people—those who demand visible wonders are evading the moral responsibility to respond to clear guidance, and God may withhold or grant signs according to His wisdom and to test the sincerity of people’s hearts.

translation: Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them? Indeed in that is a mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’an’s continual recitation and clear message are themselves a sufficient, ongoing sign and provision: they function as mercy, guidance, and a warning for those willing to receive them. It implies that the Prophet’s primary duty is to deliver this Book and that acceptance depends on people’s inner readiness to heed its reminder, not on further extraordinary proofs.

translation: Say, “God is sufficient as a witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth.” And those who believe in falsehood and disbelieve in God—those are the losers.
interpretation: The verse asserts that Allah alone is the decisive, all‑knowing witness whose knowledge of inward states and outward realities makes human disputes ultimately irrelevant. It reassures the Messenger that divine testimony suffices in the face of opposition, and it condemns the posture of embracing falsehood while rejecting God: such a stance is self‑destructive, cutting one off from guidance, moral truth, and ultimate felicity. In short, the passage warns that deliberate attachment to error and denial of the Divine leads to real loss—spiritual ruin and accountability before God—while affirming reliance on God’s perfect knowledge and justice.

translation: They urge you to hasten the punishment. If it were not for an appointed term, the punishment would have come upon them; and it will come to them suddenly while they do not perceive.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God delays chastisement by His wise, merciful decree rather than because of weakness: there is an appointed term to allow the proof to be completed and people an opportunity to repent. Those who mock and demand immediate punishment reveal their insolence and misunderstanding, but they should not read delay as impunity—divine retribution can overtake the heedless unexpectedly. Thus the postponement is purposeful (mercy, testing, fulfillment of God’s plan) and serves as a warning against presumption and complacency.

translation: They urge you to hasten the punishment, while indeed Hell surrounds the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse answers those who demand immediate divine retribution by showing that their clamoring changes nothing: God will punish in His own time. Describing Hell as "surrounding" the disbelievers both affirms the inevitability and closeness of their doom and exposes the petitioners’ true condition—their taunts only reveal that they themselves stand within the compass of deserved punishment, not that they can force God’s decree.

translation: The Day the punishment will come over them from above them and from beneath their feet, and He will say, “Taste what you used to do.”
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Reckoning when divine punishment surrounds the wrongdoers so completely—above and beneath—that there is no refuge. The command “Taste what you used to do” means their suffering is the direct consequence of their own actions: the reality and full impact of their deeds will be imposed on them as just recompense. The imagery emphasises the inevitability and totality of God’s justice and serves as a warning that worldly choices have definite moral outcomes which will be experienced in full on that Day.

translation: O My servants who have believed, indeed My earth is vast; so worship Me alone.
interpretation: The verse asserts that God’s dominion and provision are so ample that there is no need to attach ultimate allegiance to anything or anyone else; believers are therefore commanded to direct their hearts, reliance and practices solely to God (tawḥīd), recognizing that His mercy and opportunities for obedience are broad and not confined to particular intermediaries, places or narrow imaginings.

translation: Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms that death is an inevitable, universal experience that all beings must undergo, and it places that event within a moral and eschatological framework: death is not an end in itself but a transition that leads back to God for reckoning and recompense. By linking the certainty of death to the return to God, the verse aims to reorient human priorities—reminding people that worldly life is transient, that actions have consequences beyond death, and that true success or failure is determined by how one stands before God after returning to Him.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds — We will surely admit them into gardens of Paradise, with chambers beneath which rivers flow; they will abide therein forever. Excellent is the reward of the workers.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s definite promise to those whose inner conviction (faith) is realized through righteous action: they will be granted permanent, elevated dwellings in Paradise. The image of “chambers” and “rivers flowing beneath” conveys continual, overflowing provision, purity, and tranquility — a private and honored habitation sustained by God’s bounty. “Abiding therein” stresses the eternal and secure nature of this recompense, and the closing phrase, “Excellent is the reward of the workers,” underscores both the justice and goodness of God’s recompense: sincere belief coupled with righteous effort merits a fitting, lasting reward.

translation: Those who are patient and who place their trust in their Lord.
interpretation: The phrase describes believers whose steadfast endurance in trials is joined to a sincere reliance on God: they persevere in obedience and good conduct, bear hardship without despair or complaint, take appropriate means, and then entrust the outcome to God’s wisdom and decree—this combined attitude brings inner calm, divine support, and ultimate reward.

translation: There are countless creatures that do not carry their provision; Allah provides for them and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches reliance on Divine providence: sustenance is ultimately granted by God, not solely by visible means or personal hoarding. Seeing that even creatures without stores are maintained, believers are urged to trust God, work responsibly without being consumed by anxiety or greed, and act with generosity and moral responsibility, confident that the One who hears and knows will provide for their true needs.

translation: And if you were to ask them, “Who created the heavens and the earth and made the sun and the moon subservient?” they would surely say, “Allah.” So how are they being turned away (from the truth)?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the inconsistency of people who, when questioned, acknowledge God as the Creator and Sovereign of the cosmos, yet in practice are diverted from true faith. By pointing to the clear signs of God’s lordship — the creation of heaven and earth and the ordered, subservient movements of sun and moon — it demands that intellectual assent be reflected in sincere submission; it asks how anyone can be led astray from guidance when the very facts of creation testify unmistakably to one divine authority.

translation: الله يوسع الرزق لمن يشاء من عباده ويقيدّه لمن يشاء؛ إن الله بكل شيء عليم.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن توزيع الرزق بيد الله وحده: هو من يوسع ويمنع ويقدر مقدار الرزق لكل عبد بحكمة ومعرفة مطلقة. هذا لا يلغي وسائط السعي والعمل والأسباب التي أمر بها، لكنه يذكّر بأن النتائج محفوظة بحكمته، فالتفاوت في النِعَم قد يكون ابتلاءً أو رحمة أو حكمة لا يدركها الإنسان، ولذا ينبغي أن يجمع المؤمن بين الاجتهاد في طلب الرزق والرضا والتوكل على علم الله وحكمته.

translation: And if you were to ask them, “Who sends down water from the sky and thereby brings the earth back to life after its death?” they would surely say, “Allah.” Say, “All praise is due to Allah.” But most of them do not reason.
interpretation: The verse criticizes a shallow faith that names God when confronted with obvious signs yet does not let that recognition penetrate the heart or guide conduct. The command “Say, ‘All praise is due to Allah’” instructs the Prophet to move beyond mere verbal identification toward grateful acknowledgment that implies dependence, worship, and moral responsiveness. The final clause — “most of them do not reason” — indicts those who fail to draw the logical and ethical consequences of God’s signs (His unity, providence, and sovereignty): they confess in words but neglect the reflective, thankful, and transforming response that true belief requires.

translation: And this worldly life is but play and amusement. And indeed the home of the Hereafter is the true life—if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the temporal pleasures, competitions and distractions of this world are essentially superficial and deceptive when measured against the enduring reality of the Hereafter; believers are urged to see through transient attractions, to reorient priorities toward deeds and intentions that secure the permanent, substantive life to come, and to realize that much of human striving here is misguided because people do not truly appreciate what is ultimately real and lasting.

translation: And when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincerely devoting their religion to Him; but when He delivers them to land, behold—they associate others (with Him).
interpretation: The verse reproaches a recurring human failing: in danger people turn to God with wholehearted devotion, but once delivered they lapse into forgetfulness and begin to ascribe their safety or benefit to others—idols, people, wealth, or chance—thereby committing shirk. It highlights that true faith is not situational worship confined to crises; sincere tawḥīd requires consistent recognition that both rescue and provision come from God, and ingratitude or returning to associating partners with Him reveals hypocrisy and a failure to appreciate Divine mercy.

translation:
لِيَكْفُرُوا بِمَا آتَيْنَاهُمْ وَلِيَتَمَتَّعُوا ۖ فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ
“So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will come to know.”
interpretation: God sometimes allows people to turn away from the guidance and blessings He has granted and to indulge in worldly pleasures for a time; this allowance is part of the unfolding of His wisdom and the test of choice, and ultimately those who chose denial will learn the reality and consequences of their choice — the truth will be made manifest and they will face the retribution or loss that proves their error.

translation: Do they not see that We have made the Sacred House (al‑Ḥaram) a place of security, while people are being snatched away all around them? So will they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?
interpretation: God points to the clear, tangible favor of preserving the Sacred Sanctuary as evidence of His care and power; yet many stubbornly place their trust in falsehoods and turn ungratefully away from that divine bounty. The contrast is meant to expose spiritual blindness: observable protection and blessing demand recognition and grateful submission, and refusing to acknowledge them—choosing vain beliefs instead—reveals ingratitude and misguidance that will be held to account.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it has come to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?
interpretation: The verse condemns, as the gravest form of injustice, both fabricating falsehoods about God and willfully rejecting the truth when it arrives; it frames such acts not as mere error but as moral culpability that inevitably draws divine judgment, using the image of Hell as a solemn warning to abandon arrogance or malice and to submit to the guidance revealed.

translation: And those who strive in Our cause — We will surely guide them to Our ways; and indeed, Allah is with the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse promises that sincere, sustained effort for God (not limited to armed struggle but including all earnest striving in faith, knowledge, worship, and moral action) will be met by divine guidance: Allah will open and direct individuals along paths appropriate to their situation so their efforts bear fruit. The plural “paths” signals tailored guidance (inner conviction, opportunities, means, protections). The assurance “Allah is with the muhsinīn” affirms that God’s nearness and support accompany those who act with excellence, sincerity and moral responsibility — human striving and divine assistance work together, not as automatic ease but as a real promise of guidance and support for the righteous doers of good.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Alif‑Lam‑Meem.
interpretation: The disjointed letters “Alif‑Lam‑Meem” are a divine sign placed at the opening of the surah to arrest the listener’s attention and to signify that the Qur’an’s language and message are of supernatural origin; their exact, literal meaning is known only to God, while their purpose is to highlight the miraculous, inimitable nature of the revelation and to challenge those who doubt it.

translation: The Romans have been defeated.
interpretation: The brief announcement functions as a theological reading of a historical event: it signals that apparent setbacks in worldly affairs occur within God’s sovereign plan and may be reversed by His will; the verse therefore reassures believers that divine knowledge and promise encompass the rise and fall of nations, serves as a test of faith in the truth of the revelation, and demonstrates that political outcomes ultimately testify to God’s control over history.

translation: غُلِبَتِ الرُّومُ فِي أَدْنَى الْأَرْضِ، وَهُمْ مِن بَعْدِ غَلَبِهِمْ سَيَغْلِبُونَ.
interpretation: نبوءة وتطمين مفادها أن الهزائم الظاهرية ليست نهاية المشهد التاريخي وأن الله يملك تبديل الأحوال؛ ما يبدو كغلبة وانهيار قد يعقبه انتصار بتقدير الله، وهذا يعزّز ثقة المؤمنين بوعد الله وحكمته في إدارة أمور الأمم والأحداث.

translation: Within a few years. To Allah belongs the command before and after. And on that day the believers will rejoice.
interpretation: The verse reassures that the present situation will be overturned within a short, divinely appointed span: God, sovereign over all time and events, will carry out His decree when He wills. The joy of the believers is not mere worldly pleasure but the deep vindication, deliverance, and reward that come when truth is established and injustice is removed, so they are called to patience and trust in God’s perfect timing.

translation: By the help of Allah — He grants victory to whom He wills; and He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that true support and triumph come solely from Allah; He bestows assistance according to His wisdom and mercy, choosing whom He wills for reasons known to Him. Invoking both His might (al‑ʻAzīz) and His compassion (ar‑Raḥīm) teaches that His power guarantees outcome while His mercy shapes how that power is applied—so what appears as success or failure in this world is ultimately subject to His wise and merciful decree, and believers should trust and seek His aid rather than rely solely on their own strength.

translation: “The promise of Allah—Allah does not fail His promise; but most people do not know.”
interpretation: This affirms that God’s commitments are absolutely certain: what He has decreed (for example resurrection, recompense, and the ultimate establishment of truth) will come to pass even if events appear delayed or contrary to expectation. Human doubt or denial springs from limited knowledge, heedlessness, or short‑sightedness; the proper response is trust in God’s timing, patience, and steadfastness in faith rather than being unsettled by apparent setbacks.

translation: They know only the outward aspects of the life of this world, while of the Hereafter they are, truly, heedless.
interpretation: The verse criticizes people whose understanding is limited to what is visible and immediately beneficial in this temporal life: they judge by outward appearances and short‑term gain and therefore fail to grasp the deeper, unseen realities, moral duties, and ultimate accountability that concern the Hereafter. This superficial, worldly focus leaves them spiritually negligent and ill‑prepared for the consequences that lie beyond what is apparent.

translation: Have they not reflected upon themselves? Allah created the heavens and the earth and what is between them only in truth and for an appointed term; and indeed many of the people are, concerning the meeting with their Lord, disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse urges inward reflection: by contemplating our own origin, fragility, and dependence and by observing the ordered, purposeful creation and its limited term, we are pointed to a meaningful design and an eventual meeting with God. Despite these clear signs, many remain spiritually blind—denying or ignoring accountability and the afterlife out of heedlessness, attachment to worldly life, or refusal to accept moral responsibility.

translation: أَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَيَنْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ ۚ كَانُوا أَشَدَّ مِنْهُمْ قُوَّةً وَأَثَارُوا الْأَرْضَ وَعَمَّرُوهَا أَكْثَرَ مِمَّا عَمَّرُوهَا وَجَاءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُهُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ ۖ فَمَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيَظْلِمَهُمْ وَلَـٰكِن كَانُوا أَنفُسَهُمْ يَظْلِمُونَ
interpretation: The verse urges people to reflect on history: past nations that were richer, stronger, and more populous nevertheless perished when they rejected divine guidance. Their worldly successes did not protect them because their ruin was the result of their own injustice — rejecting the clear proofs brought by the messengers — not divine unfairness. Thus the passage teaches that power and prosperity are no guarantee of salvation; moral responsibility and acceptance of guidance determine a people's fate, and punishment that befalls communities is portrayed as the consequence of their own choices rather than an injustice from God.

translation:
ثم كان عاقبة الذين أساءوا السوأى أن كذبوا بآيات الله وكانوا بها يستهزئون
"Then the end of those who did evil was nothing but that they denied the signs of Allah and mocked them."
interpretation: The verse indicates that persistent moral wrongdoing produces spiritual hardening: as people persist in evil they become prone to reject divine guidance and to ridicule the evidence and reminders that confront them. Their mockery is both an expression of arrogance and a defensive posture to avoid confronting guilt; it reflects an inner corruption that precedes and ensures their ruin—so the verse warns that immoral conduct not only brings external consequences but also corrupts the heart, making sincere acceptance of truth increasingly impossible and thereby increasing their responsibility before God.

translation:
الله يبدأ الخلق ثم يعيده ثم إليه ترجعون
"God begins creation, then He brings it back, and to Him you will be returned."
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute power over life and death: having originated all beings He is capable of resurrecting them, and ultimately every person will return to Him for judgment. It rebukes skepticism about resurrection, stresses the transience of worldly life, and calls for awareness of accountability by reminding people that their final return is to God.

translation: And on the Day when the Hour is established, the criminals will be in despair.
interpretation: The verse warns that when the Day of Judgment arrives the wrongdoers—those who denied or transgressed—will be utterly humiliated and hopeless. “Yablus” conveys being struck down, confounded and deprived of support: their excuses and allies will fail, their deeds will not avail them, and they will be seized by shame, terror and remorse as they face the just consequences of their choices.

translation:
وَلَمْ يَكُن لَهُمْ مِن شُرَكَائِهِم شُفَعَاءُ وَكَانُوا بِشُرَكَائِهِم كَافِرِينَ
"And none of their partners could intercede for them, and they were, with respect to their partners, disbelievers."
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning the very beings or idols people set up as partners with God will be powerless to help them; moreover, those who relied on them will themselves repudiate them when real need comes. It exposes shirk as a false reliance: the supposed partners have no authority or ability to intercede, and the worshippers’ professed alliance with them collapses, showing that placing trust in anything beside God brings no benefit in the hereafter.

translation: And the Day the Hour is established — on that Day they will be separated.
interpretation: When the Final Hour comes all social bonds and collective pretenses will break down and people will be decisively sorted according to their true standing before God: the righteous will be gathered toward mercy and reward, while the wrongdoers will be driven away toward punishment. The verse underscores that at resurrection each person’s reality and deeds are exposed, worldly ties and statuses will not avail, and everyone will be parted to their due outcome.

translation: As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a garden, rejoicing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that sincere faith together with morally upright action leads to a transformed, abiding state in the Hereafter: “a garden” conveys a living, flourishing realm of ease, refreshment and provision, and “rejoicing” indicates continual spiritual and emotional delight — freedom from fear, regret and want. It promises that the believer’s inner peace and external circumstances will both be restored and perfected as a direct consequence of faith made manifest in good deeds.

translation: As for those who disbelieve and deny Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, those will be brought forward into punishment.
interpretation: The phrase that they will be “brought forward into punishment” stresses that the consequence of persistent denial is neither accidental nor vague but preordained and publicly manifest. Denying God’s signs and the final meeting is here depicted as a moral stance that makes one culpable before Divine justice; on the Day of Gathering the retribution prepared for them will be set before them unmistakably, showing both the certainty of accountability and the overt, established nature of the punishment for deliberate rejection.

translation: So exalted is Allah when you come into the evening and when you come into the morning.
interpretation: A command to make the glorification of God a regular practice at the two daily turning points—evening and morning—affirming His absolute transcendence and perfection, acknowledging His sustaining care and sovereignty, and countering forgetfulness or attributing partners or flaws to Him; the repetition frames gratitude and dependence on God as the proper rhythm of ordinary life.

translation: وله الحمد في السماوات والأرض وعشيا وحين تظهرون
interpretation: الآية تثبت استحقاق الله تعالى للثناء المطلق والمستمر: فالحمد له في السماوات والأرض، وفي الأزمنة والحالات — «عشياً» وعند ظهور الناس — مما يدل أن تسبيح الحَق جامعة وعابرة للزمان والظرف، لا تنتظر اعتراف الخلق، وتربط بين مدارات الكون وحضور الإنسان في مقام المساء والظهور لتذكير الناس بواجبهم أن يلتزموا الاعتراف والامتنان لله في كل حال.

translation: He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living, and revives the earth after its death — and thus you will be brought forth.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute power to reverse states of being — to originate life where there seems to be none, to return living things to death and vice versa, and to restore a barren earth to life — using observable natural processes (e.g., germination, birth, death, seasonal renewal) as signs that the same sovereign power will effect the resurrection of humanity. It is meant to confront human doubts about life after death: if God can enact these profound transformations in creation, He can surely raise people on the Day of Judgment, so we should recognise His authority, prepare for accountability, and take comfort or warning in that reality.

translation: And among His signs is that He created you from dust; then — behold — you become human beings who spread abroad.
interpretation: The verse draws attention to the astonishing transformation from inert dust to social, multiplying human communities as a clear sign of God’s creative power and sustaining mercy. That humble origin paired with wide dispersion is meant to check human pride, awaken gratitude for the gift of life and development, and remind people that their flourishing carries responsibilities: stewardship of the earth, moral conduct, and accountability to the Creator whose power alone made and maintains them.

translation: And among His signs is that He created for you mates from yourselves so that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse teaches that marriage is a divinely willed social and spiritual institution: spouses are drawn from the same human essence so they can understand and comfort one another, and God has made love (mawadda) and compassion (rahma) the fundamental moral forces that hold families and communities together. By calling these features “signs,” the verse invites thoughtful reflection on how the mutual care, emotional intimacy, and ethical responsibilities found in marriage manifest God’s wisdom and purpose for human life—encouraging gratitude, responsible conduct, and the cultivation of mercy rather than seeing marriage as merely a legal or transactional arrangement.

translation:
وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ خَلْقُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَاخْتِلَافُ أَلْسِنَتِكُمْ وَأَلْوَانِكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ لِلْعَالَمِينَ
“And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the diversity of your tongues and your colors. Indeed in that are signs for the people of knowledge.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that human diversity — of language, appearance and the vast cosmos itself — is intentional and functions as evidence of God’s wisdom and power. Rather than being grounds for pride or division, these differences are meant to prompt reflection, learning and recognition of a common origin, to cultivate humility, mutual respect and the pursuit of knowledge about the Creator and His creation.

translation: And of His signs is your sleep by night and by day and your seeking of His bounty. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.
interpretation: The verse teaches that commonplace rhythms — the alternation of sleep and wakefulness and our striving to obtain sustenance — are intentional signs of God’s wisdom and care: sleep shows His power to withdraw and restore consciousness and to provide necessary rest for life, while the provision we seek and receive demonstrates human dependence on His bounty and the moral order linking effort with sustenance. Those who listen perceive these daily, ordinary facts as proof of divine design, which should lead them to humility, gratitude, reliance on God, and recognition of His authority over life’s needs.

translation: And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, inspiring both fear and hope; and He sends down water from the sky, by which He brings the earth to life after its death. Indeed in that are signs for people who reason.
interpretation: The verse points to natural phenomena—lightning and rain—as deliberate signs meant to awaken reflection: lightning, which provokes fear of danger and awe, also brings hope because it precedes beneficial rain; the rain’s revivification of barren land after apparent death illustrates God’s power to restore life. Together these events are meant to move rational people to recognize their dependence on God, to balance humility and trust, and to see in the cycles of nature an analogy for divine control over life, provision, and eventual resurrection.

translation: And of His signs is that the heavens and the earth are sustained by His command; then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come forth.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty in maintaining the cosmos and teaches the reality of bodily resurrection: when He summons from the earth (the graves) the dead will rise at His command for accounting. The image stresses the inevitability of the Day of Resurrection and serves as a warning to turn to God and live in awareness of ultimate judgment.

translation: And to Him belong whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth; all of them are devoutly submissive to Him.
interpretation: The verse declares God’s absolute ownership and sovereignty over every being and thing: everything in heaven and earth exists under His authority and, in different manners, submits to His will. The word “qānitūn” implies continual, reverent obedience — angels in perfect worship, righteous people by conscious faith and practice, and even created things by fulfilling their ordained roles — so the passage calls attention to the reality that true recognition of God consists in acknowledging His lordship and living in accordance with His guidance.

translation: And He is the One who begins the creation and then brings it back into existence; and for Him that is easy. To Him belongs the highest similitude in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Almighty, the All‑Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God, who alone originates life and being, has the power to re‑create or resurrect what He has created without difficulty; this capability is not a new feat but the same sovereign act repeated by One whose authority and pattern govern all that exists. “The highest similitude” points to God’s supreme, unchallenged reality and perfect ordering that underlies the heavens and the earth—so every return of creation (resurrection, renewal, restoration) occurs within His wise purpose and irresistible power.

translation: ضرب لكم مثلاً من أنفسكم: أَهَلْ لَكُم مِمَّا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ مِن شُرَكَاءَ فِي مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ فَأَنْتُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ؟ أَتَخَافُونَهُمْ كَخِيفَتِكُمْ أَنْفُسَكُمْ؟ كَذَٰلِكَ نُفَصِّلُ الآيَاتِ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ
interpretation: الآية تستخدم مثلًا من علاقات التملك البشري لتبيّن بديهيّة أنه لا وجود لشريك حقيقي في مصدر الرزق الإلهي: كما أن الإنسان لا يقبل أن يتقاسم سلطته التملكية أو يخشى مَنْ يَمْلكه كما يخشى نفسه، فكذلك لا معقول أن يجعَل الناس لِلَّه شركاء في التدبير والرزق والقدر. المقصود تنوير العقول على أن الخشية والاعتماد الحقيقيين يجب أن يكونا لله وحده، وأن نحوِلة الناس بأن يكونوا آلهة أو وسطاء مستقلين في الرزق هي عقلانية باطلة تُردّ على أهل الفهم.

translation: بل اتبع الذين ظلموا أهواءهم بغير علم ۖ فمن يهدي من أضل الله ۖ وما لهم من ناصرين
interpretation: The verse indicates that moral and spiritual error begins when people abandon knowledge and concrete guidance and instead follow their own desires; guidance is ultimately a gift from God, and when someone persistently chooses desire over truth God may leave them to that deviation—in that condition no human can truly guide them or rescue them, for they have cut themselves off from the source of guidance and support.

translation: So set your face toward the religion, inclining sincerely—[this is] the fitrah (natural disposition) with which Allah has created mankind. There is no changing the creation of Allah. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse instructs unwavering, sincere adherence to the original, God‑given orientation of the human soul—tawḥīd and moral uprightness—called fitrah. By affirming that Allah’s creative disposition cannot be altered, it teaches that the true religion is what corresponds to human nature as God designed it, and that deviations arise from ignorance, desire, or cultural distortion. The practical demand is therefore inner rectitude and faithful practice: return to the innate monotheistic and ethical framework, resist innovations that contravene fitrah, and recognize that popular error does not invalidate the divine way.

translation: Turn to Him in repentance and fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse calls for an integrated faith: a sustained, sincere turning to God (munībīn) that permeates heart and conduct, combined with God‑consciousness (taqwa) which governs choices; this inward orientation must be confirmed by outward regularity in prayer as the disciplined expression and safeguard of true devotion, and thereby one must reject any form of associating partners with God — for genuine repentance, reverent fear, and established worship together prevent the slipping back into beliefs or practices that compromise pure monotheism.

translation: Those who divided their religion and became sects — each party rejoicing in what it has.
interpretation: الانقسام الطائفي يُفضي إلى أن يكتفي كل فريق بموقفه ويحتفل به، فتغلق على نفسها آفاق التواضع والبحث عن الحق، ويولد عن ذلك التعصب والافتراق عن السنة المرادة من الله، فالفَرَحُ هنا فرحٌ مُضلّ ومُعيق للوحدة والإقرار بالهداية المطلقة.

translation: And when adversity touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance; then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold— a party of them set up partners with their Lord.
interpretation: The verse criticizes a recurring human inconsistency: in hardship people sincerely supplicate and return to God, but when God relieves them and grants blessing, some abandon that sincerity and revert to associating others with the Divine (through idolatry, reliance on created means as ultimate causes, or unequal devotion). This behavior reveals ingratitude and a fragile faith that is contingent on need rather than grounded in constant recognition of God’s lordship. The passage calls attention to the moral and spiritual test of prosperity: true response to God’s mercy should be steadfast gratitude and exclusive devotion, not a return to prior errors or social pressures that lead to shirk.

translation: (That) they might disbelieve in what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves; soon you will know.
interpretation: The verse warns that some are granted blessings or power yet choose to reject the divine guidance tied to those gifts; the address “so enjoy yourselves” is a terse, almost ironic allowance of temporary worldly pleasure, while “you will know” affirms the certainty that the true outcome — accountability, loss, or retribution — will ultimately be revealed. In other words, worldly enjoyment without faith is fleeting and will be shown in time to lead to a regrettable and unmistakable end.

translation: Or have We sent down upon them a manifest authority that speaks to them of what they used to associate [with Him]?
interpretation: The verse confronts the demand for a visible, speaking miracle as the only proof of prophethood: it implies that God did not have to send an externally speaking, irrefutable authority because the real obstacle was the people's attachment to their associations and stubbornness of heart. A dramatic, talking sign would not have resolved the deeper moral and spiritual resistance; divine guidance is conveyed primarily through revelation and the inward conviction it shapes, not merely by sensational outward displays.

translation: And when We give people a taste of mercy, they rejoice in it; but if an evil afflicts them because of what their hands have done, behold, they despair.
interpretation: The verse points to a common moral and spiritual failing: people welcome blessings as cause for pride or complacency but collapse into hopelessness when troubles—often the consequences of their own choices—overtake them. Rather than seeing both mercy and adversity as opportunities from God to be grateful, to correct course, and to seek forgiveness, they treat prosperity as entitlement and suffering as final condemnation. The intended lesson is to cultivate consistent faith: respond to mercy with gratitude and humility, and respond to hardship with patience, repentance, and effort to amend one’s actions, recognizing that both states can be means of guidance and reform.

translation: Do they not see that Allah expands provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]? Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the distribution of sustenance is ultimately governed by God’s wisdom rather than by mere worldly cause-and-effect or human merit. The widening or narrowing of provision is meant as a sign to awaken faith: for the prosperous it should inspire gratitude, humility and charitable responsibility; for the needy it should be a test that cultivates patience, reliance on God, and trust in His wisdom. Believers, seeing this divine pattern, are called to avoid arrogance or despair, to recognize wealth as a trust and poverty as not a condemnation of worth, and to respond morally—by working, giving, and submitting to God’s decree—so that material difference becomes an occasion for spiritual growth and communal solidarity.

translation: So give the relative his due, and the poor and the wayfarer. That is best for those who seek the Face of Allah; and those are the successful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that concrete acts of care for kin, the needy and travelers are not merely social obligations but spiritual means: when done with the intention of seeking God’s pleasure they purify wealth, protect family ties, and manifest true faith. Sincerity transforms charitable duty into the path of success, binding personal piety to communal justice and compassion.

translation: And whatever you give of interest so that it may increase in the wealth of people — it will not increase with Allah; and whatever you give of charity seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who will be multiplied.
interpretation: God distinguishes between worldly gain and divinely blessed giving: profits obtained by exploiting others (riba) may grow among people but carry no increase or blessing before God and therefore bring no true spiritual benefit, whereas sincere charitable giving done solely for Allah’s sake is accepted and multiplied by Him — in reward, blessing (barakah), and ultimately in the believer’s standing — so the moral and spiritual value of an act is determined by its intention and by God’s approval, not merely by its material outcome.

translation: Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, and then will give you life. Is there among your partners anyone who does any of that? Exalted and high is He above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s exclusive sovereignty over the fundamental stages of existence—bringing into being, sustaining, causing death, and restoring life—to demonstrate that no purported partner or idol shares in these essential powers. By posing the rhetorical question, it exposes the absurdity of associating others with God and calls for recognition of His unique authority and transcendence over all that people imagine or worship besides Him.

translation: Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned; so He will make them taste some of what they have done, that they might return (to righteousness).
interpretation: The verse teaches that the widespread disorder and harm we see—environmental devastation, social injustice, violence, and the breakdown of moral life—are not simply random misfortunes but consequences of human choices and sins. God permits these effects to manifest as a tangible ‘‘taste’’ of people’s own deeds so that suffering serves as a corrective and admonition, prompting awareness, remorse, and moral change. The purpose is not vindictive annihilation but to open a path toward accountability and repentance: recognition of responsibility should lead to sincere turning back to God and concrete reform in personal conduct and communal stewardship (ending oppression, restoring justice, caring for creation).

translation:
قُلْ سِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَانظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلُ ۚ كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُشْرِكِينَ
“Say, ‘Travel through the land and observe how was the end of those before; most of them were polytheists.’”
interpretation: The verse invites people to examine history and the world as evidence: by observing the fates of earlier peoples one can discern the moral and spiritual consequences of rejecting God and associating partners with Him. The command to “travel and look” stresses active, reflective inquiry rather than idle hearsay; it teaches that persistent disbelief and shirk tend to produce social decay and eventual ruin, and therefore serves both as a warning to avoid those errors and as corroboration of the Prophet’s call to return to God’s oneness.

translation:
فأقم وجهك للدين القيم من قبل أن يأتي يوم لا مرد له من الله ۖ يومئذ يصدعون
"So direct your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day from Allah from which there is no turning back; on that Day they will be cleaved/smitten."
interpretation: This verse exhorts immediate, resolute commitment to the straight path of God: turn wholeheartedly to true faith and conduct now, while there is opportunity, because the Day of Divine Reckoning is inevitable and irreversible. When that Day arrives people’s pretenses, excuses and divided loyalties will be torn away and they will be overwhelmed by the consequences of their choices — hence the urgency to submit and reform before it is too late.

translation:
منْ كَفَرَ فَعَلَيْهِ كُفْرُهُ ۖ وَمَنْ عَمِلَ صَالِحًا فَلِأَنفُسِهِمْ يَمْهَدُونَ
"Whoever disbelieves, then upon him is his disbelief; and whoever does righteous deeds, they prepare (benefit) for themselves."
interpretation: The verse affirms individual moral responsibility and divine justice: disbelief or faith, and the good or harm that follows, are essentially self-incurred. Rejection of truth primarily harms the rejecter, while sincere righteous actions build and secure one’s own path to God’s favor and reward. Thus outcomes correspond to personal choices—God neither wrongs nor is constrained; each person’s deeds prepare their own consequence.

translation:
لِيُجْزِيَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ مِن فَضْلِهِ ۚ إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الْكَافِرِينَ
“That He may recompense those who believe and do righteous deeds out of His bounty; indeed He does not love the disbelievers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s favors and rewards are granted by His generous grace to those who combine true faith with upright action — their recompense is not a transactional due but a manifestation of divine bounty. By contrast, the statement that He does not love the disbelievers emphasizes that rejection of God and persistent denial of guidance places a person outside the circle of His approving favor; it signals moral and spiritual consequence rather than merely emotional animus, underscoring the Qur’anic principle that acceptance of faith and righteous conduct are the paths through which one receives God’s mercy and honor.

translation:
وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَن يُرْسِلَ الرِّيَاحَ مُبَشِّرَاتٍ وَلِيُذِيقَكُمْ مِنْ رَحْمَتِهِ وَلِتَجْرِيَ الْفُلْكُ بِأَمْرِهِ وَلِتَبْتَغُوا مِنْ فَضْلِهِ وَلَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ
"And of His signs is that He sends the winds as glad tidings and that He lets you taste of His mercy; and that the ships run by His command, that you may seek of His bounty; and perhaps you will be grateful."
interpretation: The verse teaches that ordinary natural occurrences — winds, rain, and the ordered motion of ships — are purposeful signs of Divine providence intended to make human dependence on God evident. Winds bring the promise of rain and relief, rain and other mercies sustain life, and the control of the seas enables travel and commerce; these blessings are given so people may benefit materially but, more importantly, recognize their source. By describing these gifts as means to “taste” God’s mercy and to “seek” His bounty, the verse frames them both as merciful provisions and as tests: they invite gratitude, remind humans of their need for God’s sustaining power, and call for a moral response — acknowledgment, thankfulness, and rightful use of what is granted rather than heedless consumption.

translation: And We certainly sent messengers before you to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs; then We seized those who committed crimes. And it was, and is, incumbent upon Us to help the believers.
interpretation: This verse affirms a recurring divine pattern: God sends prophets with unmistakable signs and guidance, and when communities persist in transgression and injustice despite those clear proofs, divine punishment follows. The statement that helping the believers is a right upon God functions as a solemn assurance—God will vindicate the faithful and uphold justice, whether through deliverance from oppression, triumph in their affairs, or recompense in the hereafter.
