Believers are therefore called to trust in God’s promise, remain patient and steadfast in obedience, and recognize that clear evidence brings accountability for those who reject it.

translation: It is Allah who sends the winds, and they raise up the clouds; then He spreads them in the sky as He wills and makes them into fragments, and you see the rain emerge from within them. And when He causes it to fall upon whom He wills of His servants, behold, they rejoice.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s absolute sovereignty and wisdom in sustaining life: natural forces like wind and clouds are not autonomous but tools through which God dispenses mercy and provision. The description of clouds being stirred, arranged, and broken into pieces (kasf) until rain issues forth emphasizes purposeful divine orchestration rather than random weather. That He gives rain “to whom He wills of His servants” underscores that provision is distributed according to His wisdom and decree; the visible human response—joy and relief—highlights how material sustenance awakens gratitude, dependence, and recognition of God’s mercy. Implicitly the verse calls listeners to reflect on their vulnerability, to see rain as both a physical blessing and a sign requiring thankfulness and trust in God’s providence rather than pride in human control.

translation: And indeed, even before that they were already clearly misguided.
interpretation: The words point to a deep, preexisting spiritual blindness among the people: their rejection and error were not produced solely by the present messenger but had long been entrenched. Because their hearts were hardened and they had been led or remained astray beforehand, later warnings and reminders found little purchase — the verse emphasizes the prior, persistent nature of their misguidance rather than treating it as a new or accidental condition.

translation: So observe the signs of Allah’s mercy — how He gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, that (same) One is the Giver of life to the dead, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse points to the seasonal revival of dead-looking land as a deliberate, visible sign of God’s mercy and omnipotence: if He can awaken barren earth and produce life from what seemed lifeless, then He surely has the power to resurrect human beings on the Day of Return. The natural process of renewal is thus meant to draw people from heedlessness to reflection, to trust in God’s ability to restore and to submit to His justice and mercy.

translation: And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turning yellow, they would nevertheless remain thereafter unbelievers.
interpretation: The verse condemns a stubborn, self-willed rejection of clear divine signs: even an unmistakable, unusual wind (a visible, striking sign) would not turn their hearts toward faith. It teaches that refusal to believe is often a moral and spiritual choice—rooted in arrogance, hardness of heart, or wilful denial—so that miracles cannot compel true guidance; guidance comes from God and those who persist in rejecting it seal their own fate.

translation: Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away.
interpretation: The verse teaches that no human effort—including the Prophet’s preaching—can force spiritual receptivity: those whose hearts are ‘dead’ to guidance or who obstinately turn away like the ‘deaf’ will not receive the message. It consoles and limits the messenger’s responsibility (to convey the truth) and affirms that awakening, hearing, and acceptance are ultimately acts of God and a condition of the listener, not something that can be imposed by speech alone.

translation:
وما أنت بهاد العمي عن ضلالتهم ۖ إن تسمع إلا من يؤمن بآياتنا فهم مسلمون
"You are not, by any means, the guider of the blind out of their error; you hear only whoever believes in Our signs — they are the ones who submit (are Muslims)."
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Prophet’s role is to convey the message, not to compel inner guidance: spiritual sight and acceptance come from God, and only those whose hearts are receptive — who truly believe in God’s signs — will ‘hear’ and be counted as true believers (Muslims). The responsibility for guidance lies ultimately with God, while the messenger delivers the call and people respond according to their readiness and faith.

translation: Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then after weakness made [you] strength, then after strength made [you] weakness and gray hair. He creates what He wills; and He is the All‑Knowing, the All‑Powerful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human abilities and life-stages are not autonomous but bestowed and withdrawn by God’s will; strength is a temporary trust to be used responsibly, not a cause for pride, and the eventual return to frailty and old age reminds us of mortality and accountability. By adding that He “creates what He wills” and naming Himself All‑Knowing and All‑Powerful, the passage emphasizes God’s absolute sovereignty and wisdom in ordering life’s changes — He can reverse conditions, test or reform individuals, and nothing escapes His knowledge or power, so humans should live with humility, stewardship, and awareness of divine purpose.

translation: And on the Day when the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they did not remain except for an hour; thus they were deluded.
interpretation: The verse exposes the self-deception and evasions of the wrongdoers: at Judgment they will try to minimize their responsibility by claiming life was too short to be held accountable, the same way in this world they dismissed truth and excused their behavior. It teaches that temporal brevity cannot erase moral responsibility, that denial and trivializing of consequences are forms of being led astray, and it warns listeners not to adopt such excuses but to recognize that every deed is weighed and will be confronted.

translation: وقال الذين أوتوا العلم والإيمان: "لقد لبثتم في كتاب الله إلى يوم البعث؛ فهذا يوم البعث، ولكنكم كنتم لا تعلمون."
interpretation: القول هنا يبرز موقف المؤمنين المتمسّكين بالعلم واليقين: إن مصائر الناس مكتوبة وموقوتة في كتاب الله، وما حصل الآن هو تجلٍّ للموعد الذي كان مسجلاً — يوم البعث — وكشف لحقيقة قدرٍ لم يدركها الجاحدون. بمعنى آخر، المؤمنون يعلنون أن وقوع الأمر لم يكن مفاجأة عشوائية بل تحقيق لمرسوم ربّي سابق، وأن جهل المكذّبين كان سبباً في عدم إدراكهم لتلك الحقيقة الثابتة.

translation: On that Day the wrongdoers' excuses will not benefit them, nor will they be allowed to plead for respite.
interpretation: When the reality of people's deeds is laid bare before God, all attempts to excuse, rationalize, blame others, or bargain for more time will be powerless. “معذرتهم” denotes the justifications and defenses they relied upon in life, and “لا هم يستعتبون” means they will not be granted postponement, appeal, or mitigation—accountability will be immediate and final, so only sincere conduct and repentance before that Day truly matter.

translation: And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an from every [kind of] example. And if you were to bring them a sign, those who disbelieve would say, 'You are but falsifiers.'
interpretation: God has provided a wide variety of parables and examples in the Qur'an so the message can reach different minds and hearts; yet even if a manifest miracle were shown, those determined to reject the truth would still dismiss it as fabrication. The verse teaches that refusal often stems from stubbornness and ill intent rather than lack of evidence, and it reminds the Messenger and believers that their task is to convey clear guidance while God opens hearts to accept it.

translation: كَذَٰلِكَ يَطْبَعُ اللَّهُ عَلَى قُلُوبِ الَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ
interpretation: الآية تدل على أن الله يجعل قلوب بعض الناس مُغلقة عن إدراك الحق عندما يَثْبُت لديهم الجَحْد أو الغفلة أو الاعتراض المستمر على الهداية؛ فالختم هنا وصف لِنَتْجَة داخلية يَصِير فيها القلب عاجزًا عن استيعاب الحق، وهي نتيجة لازمة لتكرار الجهل أو الإنكار لا تدل بالضرورة على أمر عَرَضي عشوائي.

translation: So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And let not those who have no certainty discourage you.
interpretation: This verse calls the believer to steadfast patience rooted in trust: God’s promises of eventual vindication, justice and reward are certain, so one must endure trials without being shaken. It warns against yielding to the words or mockery of those who lack firm knowledge or faith—their doubt, ridicule or attempts to trivialize the cause do not negate Divine truth and should not divert one from perseverance and reliance on God’s timing.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif‑Lam‑Mim.
interpretation: The opening invocation places the revelation under the mercy and authority of God, while the disjointed letters “Alif‑Lam‑Mim” act as a deliberate, sacred sign whose full significance is known to Allah alone; they draw attention to the Qur’an’s miraculous, inimitable character by showing that its divine message is conveyed through ordinary Arabic letters yet carries a meaning and authority beyond human composition, humbling listeners and pointing them to God’s exclusive knowledge.

translation: Those are the verses of the Wise Book.
interpretation: This affirms that the statements just referred to belong to a single, divinely‑originated scripture characterized by perfect wisdom; calling it the “Wise Book” stresses that its words are purposeful, coherent, and reliable—meant to guide belief, conduct, and reflection—so one must take them seriously, ponder their meanings, and submit to their authority.

translation: Guidance and mercy for the doers of good.
interpretation: The phrase indicates that God’s direction and compassionate care are especially given to those who strive to excel in righteousness (al‑muhsinīn): by sincere faith and consistent moral action they become receptive to divine light and compassion, so that guidance shapes their conduct and God’s mercy accompanies and rewards their uprightness.

translation:
الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلَاةَ وَيُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ وَهُم بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ
"Those who establish the prayer and give the zakah (alms), and they, concerning the Hereafter, are certain."
interpretation: The verse characterizes true believers by the marriage of outward duty and inward conviction: regular, sincere worship (prayer) and fulfillment of social obligation (zakah) are grounded in a deep, unwavering certainty about the Hereafter. That inner certainty makes their actions accountable and purposeful — their rituals are not empty formality but expressions of moral responsibility shaped by awareness of ultimate judgment and reward.

translation: They are upon guidance from their Lord; and they are the successful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those who have accepted faith and acted accordingly are sustained by divine guidance: their hearts and conduct are aligned with God’s direction. Being “on guidance” is not merely having a correct belief once, but receiving and living by continuing guidance from the Lord, and therefore they attain true success (al‑mufliḥūn) — not merely worldly prosperity but the fulfillment of life’s purpose, moral rectitude, and ultimate salvation in the Hereafter.

translation: And among people are those who purchase idle talk to mislead from the way of Allah without knowledge and to take it as mockery. For them is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns the social practice of cultivating and sponsoring seductive but empty or false narratives—whether entertainment, rhetoric, or pseudo‑knowledge—whose purpose is to divert hearts from God's guidance and to ridicule what is sacred. It targets not merely casual amusement but the deliberate industry of distraction and mockery (including those who finance, popularize or exploit it), warning that profiting from or promoting spiritual corruption brings both loss of dignity in society and severe accountability before God.

translation: And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away in arrogance as though he had not heard them, as though there were a heaviness in his ears. So give him tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes people who, out of pride, deliberately shut themselves off from divine guidance: their rejection is not genuine ignorance but an act of arrogance that produces a self‑made ‘deafness’ to truth. By portraying their attitude as turning away and as if something blocks their ears, the text explains the inner mechanism—hardened hearts and willful refusal—and therefore affirms their culpability and warns of severe consequences for persistent, proud rejection.

translation: إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَهُمْ جَنَّاتُ النَّعِيمِ
interpretation: The verse affirms that genuine faith is inseparable from righteous conduct: those whose belief is manifested in moral, upright deeds are promised lasting, dignified bliss. 'جنات النعيم' signals not merely temporary pleasures but a comprehensive, enduring reward — spiritual fulfillment, honor, and peace — awarded to the integrity of inner conviction realized through outward action; thus the promise functions both as assurance for the faithful and as an ethical criterion distinguishing true Islam from mere profession.

translation: They will abide therein forever — the promise of Allah is true. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This statement affirms the absolute certainty and permanence of God’s decree: whatever recompense He has promised will be fulfilled without fail. The pairing of His attributes — al-‘Azīz (the All‑Mighty whose will cannot be resisted) and al‑Hakīm (the Perfectly Wise whose actions are just and purposeful) — stresses that the fulfillment is both inevitable and measured by divine wisdom. The implication for human conduct is twofold: it is a sober warning that outcomes are ultimately determined by an all‑powerful, just wisdom, and a reassurance that justice and reward are not arbitrary but rooted in God’s perfect knowledge and power.

translation: He created the heavens without any visible pillars that you can see, and He cast into the earth firm mountains so that it would not tremble with you, and He dispersed therein every living creature. And We sent down water from the sky and caused to grow in it every noble pair.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s lordship is manifest in both the unseen and the orderly provisions of creation: the heavens are upheld by His will rather than by visible supports, while mountains serve as stabilizing devices in the earth’s system and life is sustained through divinely ordained means (rain producing varied, paired life). Together these facts are signs of God’s wisdom, power, and care — they refute human self-sufficiency and call people to recognize their dependence, to reflect on divine order, and to respond with gratitude and submission.

translation: هذا خلق الله، فأروني ماذا خلق الذين من دونه؟ بل الظالمون في ضلال مبين.
interpretation: الآية توجه تحدّياً بلاغياً يُفضح عبثية الإشراك: إن الخلق من خصائص الله وحده، وطلب أن يُريْنَّا من يدعون الربوبية ما خلقوا يكشف عن غياب دليلٍ لديهم. بذلك تدين الآية الشرك ليس بوصفه مجرد خطأ عقائدي فحسب بل كزلّة فكرية وأخلاقية تُدخل صاحبها في ضلال واضح، وتهدف إلى ردّ الناس إلى إدراك توحيد الخالق والابتعاد عن عبادة المخلوقين.

translation: And We certainly gave Luqman wisdom: “Be grateful to Allah.” And whoever is grateful, then indeed he is grateful for the benefit of his own soul; and whoever is ungrateful—then indeed, Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse teaches that real wisdom is to recognize God’s gifts and respond with thankfulness, because gratitude primarily benefits the one who practices it: it sharpens awareness of dependence, cultivates humility and right conduct, and opens one to continued moral and spiritual growth. In contrast, ingratitude harms only the person who persists in it and does not affect God’s self-sufficiency or praise-worthiness, so the injunction is toward sincere, practical thankfulness that transforms the believer’s character rather than empty verbal expressions.

translation: And [remember] when Luqman said to his son, while he was advising him, “O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great injustice.”
interpretation: Luqman’s counsel points to the heart of faith: claiming partners with God is described as a supreme injustice because it wrongs God by denying His exclusive sovereignty and, simultaneously, wrongs the human being by diverting their worship, purpose and moral orientation. Framing shirk as 'great ظلم' (injustice) underscores that it is not merely a theoretical error but a corrosive act that corrupts spiritual truth, upends moral order, and leads to ultimate loss of guidance and accountability; therefore safeguarding pure monotheism is presented as the foundational ethical and spiritual duty from which true righteousness flows.

translation: And We have enjoined upon man to be dutiful to his parents. His mother carried him, bearing weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years. "Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final return."
interpretation: The verse grounds the moral obligation to honor and care for one's parents in both the real dependence and sacrifices involved in early life (most notably the mother's repeated weakness in pregnancy and nursing) and the theological fact of God’s provision. By linking gratitude to parents with gratitude to God and ending with “to Me is the final return,” it teaches that filial duty is a form of worship and accountability before God: one must respectfully and compassionately attend to parents as an obligation to God, while recognizing that this duty is framed and ultimately judged by divine command (so obedience to parents is required insofar as it accords with God’s guidance).

translation: And if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, then do not obey them; and be (kind and) companion to them in this world in a manner that is fitting, and follow the way of those who turn to Me. Then to Me will be your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches a clear hierarchy of loyalties: submission to God’s oneness overrides all human demands, even from one’s parents, when those demands require committing disbelief or innovation (associating partners with God). Yet it simultaneously commands maintaining respectful, compassionate treatment of parents in everyday life—remaining dutiful and gentle without complying in matters that contradict faith. Believers are also directed to follow the path of those who sincerely return to God (the righteous and repentant), recognizing that ultimate judgment and accountability rest with God alone, to whom everyone will return.

translation: “O my son, indeed — if it were (anything) the weight of a mustard seed and were (hidden) in a rock or in the heavens or in the earth — Allah would bring it forth. Indeed Allah is Subtle (Gentle), All‑Acquainted.”
interpretation: The verse asserts that God’s knowledge and power reach even the tiniest, most concealed things; nothing — no small deed, secret intention, or hidden trace — can remain beyond His awareness or ability to reveal. Calling God al‑Latif and al‑Khabir emphasizes that He notices the finest moral subtleties with compassionate, wise attention and will deal with them justly, so people should be mindful of even the smallest acts and motives while trusting in His nuanced knowledge and mercy.

translation: يا بني، أقم الصلاة، وأمر بالمعروف، وانهَ عن المنكر، واصبر على ما أصابك؛ إن ذلك من عزم الأمور.
interpretation: هذه وصية تربط العبادة الفردية بالمسؤولية الاجتماعية وبضرورة الثبات النفسي: إقامة الصلاة تُرسخ علاقة الإنسان بالله وتكوّن توازناً داخليّاً يجعل الإنسان قادراً على التمييز والعمل الصالح؛ الأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر يعبران عن واجب الإصلاح الاجتماعي والأخلاقي، لكنهما قد يثيران مقاومة أو فتورًا، لذلك يأتي التأكيد على الصبر عند البلاء والابتلاءات. وصف هذه الأوامر بأنها «من عزم الأمور» يعني أنها قرارات جوهرية تتطلّب عزيمة وشجاعة ومثابرة؛ ليست نصائح عرضية بل ركائز حياة مستقيمة تُمارَس بحكمة ولينٍ مع ثبات في المبدأ.

translation: And do not turn your cheek away from people in contempt, and do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like every arrogant boaster.
interpretation: This verse condemns pride both in expression and posture: showing disdain with your face or strutting proudly are outward signs of an arrogant heart. Such behavior disrupts social bonds, reflects ingratitude and self-deception, and is displeasing to God; true honor lies in humility, measured conduct, and sincere recognition of one’s dependence on Allah rather than in haughty display.

translation: Be moderate in your walking and lower your voice; indeed the most disagreeable of sounds is the braying of donkeys.
interpretation: The verse teaches an ethic of dignified restraint: walk with a measured, neither ostentatious nor slothful, bearing and keep your voice soft so as not to draw attention or insult others. Loudness and showy movement are likened to the crude braying of donkeys to stress that noisy, boastful, or coarse behavior degrades human dignity, damages social harmony, and betrays inner arrogance. Thus the injunction calls for humble, considerate conduct that reflects inner humility, self‑control, and respect for others.

translation: Do you not see that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and has bestowed His favors upon you outwardly and inwardly? And among the people are those who dispute concerning Allah without knowledge, without guidance, and without a luminous Book.
interpretation: The verse calls people to recognize and be grateful for God’s comprehensive providence — the ordering of the heavens and earth and the visible and inner blessings given to them — and warns that despite these clear favors some engage in vain disputes about God. To ‘argue without knowledge, guidance, or a luminous Book’ means to speak of the Divine from conjecture, passion, or empty rhetoric rather than from sound knowledge and revealed guidance; such disputation displays heedlessness and ingratitude and leads both the disputants and those who follow them away from true guidance.

translation: And when it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they say, “No; we will follow what we found our fathers following.” Would they then follow Satan, who calls them to the punishment of the Blaze?
interpretation: The verse censures the refusal to accept divine guidance on the basis of blind deference to ancestral custom: treating tradition as an unquestionable authority becomes an evasion of responsibility and a rejection of truth. By portraying such stubborn imitation as tantamount to heeding Satan’s call, the verse warns that clinging to inherited practices in opposition to God’s revelation is spiritually dangerous and leads one toward ruin and punishment.

translation: And whoever submits his face to Allah while he is a doer of good has certainly grasped the most trustworthy handhold; and to Allah is the final outcome of all affairs.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine surrender to God (orienting one’s whole life toward Him) combined with ihsān—active, upright conduct—constitutes the surest security a person can attain. “Grasping the most trustworthy handhold” pictures reliance on divine guidance and covenant rather than on worldly supports; it affirms that sincere faith must be lived through good deeds, and that those who do so gain a firm spiritual anchor. At the same time the reminder that “to Allah is the final outcome of all affairs” places every contingency under God’s wise management, calling the believer to trust in God’s ultimate judgment and provision while remaining morally responsible in this life.

translation: And as for whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you. To Us is their return; then We will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts.
interpretation: This verse consoles and directs the Prophet and the believers: they should not be dismayed by rejection or denial, because ultimate judgment and recompense belong to God alone. At the resurrection God will make plain both people's outward deeds and their inward motives, for He fully knows the hidden contents of the heart (ذات الصدور). Thus apparent success or rejection in this world does not overturn divine justice; believers are called to trust in God’s perfect knowledge, be steadfast in right action, and leave final accounting to Him.

translation: We will grant them enjoyment for a little while, then We will drive them into a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that apparent worldly ease given to those who reject guidance is temporary and often a deceptive respite; it serves either as a test or as a brief allowance before inevitable divine justice. The phrase “نضطرهم” emphasizes the compulsion and inevitability of their being turned over to overwhelming retribution — their short-lived prosperity does not avert the final, severe consequence of their persistent wrongdoing.

translation: And if you were to ask them, “Who created the heavens and the earth?” they would surely say, “Allah.” Say, “All praise is due to Allah.” Yet most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse highlights the gap between empty affirmation and true knowledge: many people will profess that God is the Creator, but that verbal assent often lacks the understanding, gratitude and moral transformation that such recognition demands. The Prophet’s rejoinder — to affirm praise to God — points to the need to move beyond mere words toward genuine awareness of God’s lordship, attributes and rights; most, however, remain ignorant of these deeper realities and therefore do not let belief shape their conduct or hearts.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed Allah is the Self‑Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty and complete independence: all that exists is His possession, while He Himself is free of need (al‑Ghani) and deserving of all praise (al‑Hamid). From this follows the call for humans to recognize their dependence on God alone, to refrain from placing ultimate trust in created things or beings, to direct worship and gratitude to Him, and to take solace in the fact that provision, authority and moral worth rest ultimately with One who neither needs creation nor is diminished by it.

translation: And if all that is on the earth were pens and the sea, replenished thereafter by seven [seas], were ink, the words of Allah would not be exhausted. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.
interpretation: By means of a deliberate hyperbole the verse teaches that God’s speech, knowledge, decrees and wisdom are infinite and cannot be fully recorded, described or limited by any created means. Even if all created things became instruments for writing and the oceans were multiplied, they would not suffice to contain the full scope of His words; this underlines human finitude, calls for humility before divine knowledge, and affirms God’s absolute power and perfect wisdom in His judgments and guidance.

translation: He did not create you, nor did He resurrect you, except as a single soul. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse asserts that creation and resurrection serve one unified purpose: to bring humanity into a single moral and spiritual accountability before God. It rejects any notion that people exist for multiple independent ends or can escape collective responsibility; ultimately everyone stands before the One who hears and sees all, so differences, self-exemptions, or rival claims to divine sanction are nullified in light of that single, God‑ordained aim.

translation: Do you not see that Allah causes the night to enter the day and causes the day to enter the night, and has made the sun and the moon subservient — each running its course to an appointed term — and that Allah is, of what you do, Acquainted?
interpretation: The verse points to the regular alternation and ordered motion of the heavens as a sign of God’s absolute sovereignty and precise governance: the same wisdom that measures cosmic rhythms also ordains limits and times for all things. From this it follows that human life is not random or beyond reckoning — our deeds occur within God’s knowledge and appointed order — so the proper response is humility, gratitude and conscious responsibility before One who both sustains the universe and is fully aware of every action.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is falsehood; and Allah is the Most High, the Great.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate reality and authority belong solely to God: calling God al-Ḥaqq (the Truth) affirms His exclusive, dependable existence and sovereignty, while labeling other objects of worship as bāṭil (false) stresses their lack of real efficacy or reality. By adding that Allah is al-ʿAliyy al-Kabīr (the Most High, the Great), the verse underscores His transcendence above creation and supreme greatness, so any reliance on or invocation of beings besides Him is ontologically misguided and spiritually misplaced.

translation: Have you not seen that the ships sail through the sea by the bounty of Allah, so that He may show you of His signs? Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful one.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the regular, beneficent workings of the world (here symbolized by ships moving safely across the sea) are not neutral occurrences but deliberate signs intended to awaken awareness of God’s providence. Those who combine patience in adversity and gratitude in ease are the ones who perceive these signs: they let such manifestations deepen trust in God, temper reliance on worldly means with humility, and transform everyday benefits into motives for steadfastness and thankfulness rather than complacency.

translation: And when a wave like a shadow covers them, they call upon Allah, sincerely devoting the religion to Him; but when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate. And none deny Our signs except every treacherous, ungrateful one.
interpretation: The verse exposes a common human pattern revealed by trials: in life-threatening danger people turn to God with utter sincerity, but once safety and comfort return many do not maintain that same devotion. The term “مقتصد” (moderate) indicates those who neither fully preserve the earlier fervent commitment nor openly reject it—they settle into a lukewarm, middle state—whereas “ختار كفور” describes those whose ingratitude and hardened obstinacy lead them to persistently deny God’s signs. The teaching is that true faith is shown by steady gratitude and consistent reliance on God, not only by temporary cries in distress; tests therefore distinguish between genuine believers, the lukewarm, and the brazenly ungrateful.

translation: O mankind, fear your Lord and be conscious of a Day when no father will avail his son, nor will a son avail his father at all. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true. So let not the life of this world deceive you, nor let the deceiver (Satan) deceive you concerning Allah.
interpretation: The verse stresses absolute personal responsibility before God: on the Day of Judgment neither family ties nor social status will secure anyone’s salvation, so one must live with God‑consciousness and prepare for that inevitable reckoning. It warns that transient worldly comforts and Satan’s deceptions can lull people into neglecting duty to Allah, and therefore one should not be misled by worldly allurements or false assurances but instead trust Allah’s promise and act rightly.

translation: Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour; He sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse asserts that knowledge of the unseen—when the final Hour will come, provision and natural phenomena, the hidden realities of conception, the outcomes of our deeds tomorrow, and the place and time of our death—belongs solely to God. Its purpose is to remind humans of their epistemic limits and to ground two responses: humility before Divine sovereignty (so one avoids false certainty about the future) and trustful responsibility (continually doing right, asking God, and relying on Him despite uncertainty). By ending with God’s names “Knowing” and “Acquainted,” the verse reassures believers that nothing escapes God’s intimate awareness, which is the basis for reliance, patience, and ethical vigilance in a life whose details remain hidden to us.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif‑Lam‑Meem.
interpretation: The invocation frames the revelation as bestowed through God’s mercy; the disconnected letters “Alif‑Lam‑Meem” remain a divine mystery whose specific signification God alone knows, and they function to arrest attention and point to the Qur’an’s miracle — that its unmatched guidance and eloquence arise from the same ordinary letters known to people, thereby challenging skeptics and strengthening the faith of believers.

translation: A revelation of the Book — in it there is no doubt — from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The statement affirms the Qur’an’s divine origin and absolute authority: its teachings and judgments are certain and trustworthy because they come from God, Sovereign of all existence. This certainty is meant to settle the heart, direct human conduct, and serve as the final criterion when people face uncertainty; any difficulty or apparent inconsistency lies in human misunderstanding or limited perspective, not in the revelation itself.

translation: Or do they say, “He fabricated it”? Nay — it is the truth from your Lord, sent to warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they might be guided.
interpretation: The verse answers the charge that the Prophet invented the Qur’an by affirming its divine origin and clarifying its purpose: it is a genuine revelation entrusted to the Prophet as a warning and invitation for a people who previously lacked a messenger. This frames the Prophet’s role as the truthful conveyor of God’s message rather than its author, and shows the scripture’s aim is not coercion but to present guidance and admonition so that, by receiving the warning, people may freely choose to be guided (لعلهم يهتدون), leaving ultimate acceptance to God’s will and human responsibility.

translation: It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days, then He established Himself above the Throne. You have no protector or intercessor besides Him. Will you not then remember?
interpretation: The verse affirms Allah’s exclusive, absolute sovereignty and governance over all existence: creation proceeded according to His wise plan, and His ‘establishment’ over the Throne denotes supreme authority and control (not a limitation or likeness). From this follows the practical lesson that no created being can truly replace Him as protector or intercessor, so people are urged to recognize their dependence on God alone, abandon reliance on false safeguards, and respond in mindful submission and trust.

translation: He directs the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a Day the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count.
interpretation: The verse affirms Allah’s absolute sovereignty and management of all events: He issues and administers decrees that extend through heaven and earth and ultimately return to Him for final reckoning. The expression “a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count” underscores that God’s timing and perspective transcend human measures of time—divine judgment and the unfolding of God’s plan occur on a scale beyond human reckoning, so human impatience or limited temporal understanding cannot confine or hasten God’s course.

translation: That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.
interpretation: God alone possesses complete knowledge of both hidden realities and outward events—He knows inner thoughts, intentions, and what will come, as well as everything manifest. His name al‑Aziz affirms absolute power and inviolable authority—nothing can oppose His will—while ar‑Rahim assures that His rule is suffused with compassion and mercy. The pairing teaches that divine governance is both omnipotent and benevolent: human actions and hearts are fully known and held to account, yet one may turn to Him in hope and trust because His power is exercised with mercy.

translation: He who has perfected everything He created, and began the creation of man from clay.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s absolute mastery and intentional order in creation: nothing is accidental or imperfect but fashioned with wisdom and measure. By stating that humanity’s beginning is clay, it teaches humility and dependence—our noble status before God does not come from a lofty material origin but from God’s deliberate act of forming and endowing life. Thus the created world, and the humble earthy origin of human beings, are signs meant to draw recognition of God’s sovereignty, wisdom, and the moral responsibility that flows from being deliberately formed and given life by Him.

translation: ثم جعل نسله من سلالة من ماء مهين — Then He made his offspring from a lineage of lowly (or despised) water.
interpretation: The verse highlights that human descent is formed from a humble, seemingly insignificant fluid; it teaches that all human status and lineage originate from a lowly substance by God’s creative will, calling people to humility and to recognize that nobility and continuity are granted by God rather than by the apparent worth of their material origin.

translation: Then He fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit; and He made for you hearing and sight and hearts. Little are you grateful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human existence and the inner faculties of perception and understanding are divine gifts that confer dignity and moral responsibility. Because life and the capacities to hear, see and comprehend are entrusted by God, they are meant to be used to recognize truth, choose rightly, and express thankfulness; the phrase “little are you grateful” is a rebuke pointing to the common failure to acknowledge or live up to that responsibility.

translation:
وَقَالُوا أَإِذَا ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ أَإِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ ۚ بَلْ هُمْ بِمِلَاقِ رَبِّهِمْ كَافِرُونَ
“And they say, ‘When we are dispersed in the earth, will we indeed be brought into a new creation?’ Nay — it is that they deny the meeting with their Lord.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring attitude: people dismiss the prospect of resurrection not through genuine intellectual inquiry but through scorn and evasive questioning. Their rhetorical doubt about being recreated after decay is less a technical objection and more a symptom of a deeper moral failure — an outright refusal to accept eventual accountability before God. The Qur’an thus reframes the issue: the impossibility they claim is irrelevant compared with their spiritual state; it is their denial of meeting the Lord that defines them as disbelievers, regardless of the physical details of how resurrection might occur.

translation: Say, “The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that death is not random but a divinely ordered transition carried out by an appointed agent; its purpose is to remind people of God’s absolute sovereignty over life and death, to ground moral responsibility in the certainty of an eventual return to God, and to both comfort believers with the orderliness of divine providence and warn everyone to live with accountability before the Final Meeting.

translation: And if you could see when the criminals lower their heads before their Lord, [saying], “Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us [to life] that we might do righteous deeds.” —“Indeed, we are certain.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true recognition and conviction after death are too late to change one’s fate: those who denied or neglected guidance will acknowledge the truth and beg for a second chance, proving they had the faculties and evidence in life but failed to act. It emphasizes that faith must be accompanied by timely righteous deeds; certainty without prior action cannot undo the consequences established by divine justice, and the scene is meant to warn the living to convert recognition into obedient practice before it is irrevocably too late.

translation: And if We willed, We would have guided every soul; but My word proved true: 'I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind together.'
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine power and human responsibility coexist: God affirms His ability to guide every being, yet He has willed a world in which guidance is offered and people freely respond. The certainty that Hell will be filled with some of jinn and humans is not a sign of impotence but of a purposeful moral order — many will knowingly reject guidance and thereby bring judgment upon themselves. Thus the statement functions as a solemn warning and affirmation of ultimate justice: guidance is a gift, choice has consequences, and God’s decree that the unjust will be punished will be fulfilled.

translation:
فَذُوقُوا بِمَا نَسِيتُمْ لِقَاءَ يَوْمِكُمْ هَذَا ۖ إِنَّا نَسِينَاكُمْ ۖ وَذُوقُوا عَذَابَ الْخَلِدِ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ
“So taste, for what you have forgotten of the meeting of this your Day — indeed We have forgotten you. And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do.”
interpretation: The verse is a denunciation of those who were heedless of or denied the inevitable meeting with God (the Day of Judgment). The phrase “We have forgotten you” should be understood not as a literal lapse of God’s knowledge but as a withdrawing of His protection, mercy and warnings: because they turned away from accountability, God leaves them to the consequences of their choices. Thus they are told to “taste” the long-lasting punishment that results from the persistent sins and rejection they willingly committed, underscoring human responsibility and that God’s patient admonitions can cease, after which the moral outcome of one’s deeds becomes manifest.

translation: Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration and glorify with the praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine faith is proved not merely by intellectual assent but by a humble, immediate bodily and spiritual response to God's revelations and signs: believers, upon being reminded of God, submit in prostration, utter praise and glorification of their Lord, and abandon pride. ‘آياتنا’ (Our signs) can mean the revelations or the manifest signs of God; the marked reaction — falling into sajdah and sincere tasbih — indicates an inner transformation and sincere devotion. By saying ‘إنما’ (only), the verse excludes a hollow or arrogant profession of belief and sets humility, submission, and heartfelt glorification as the distinguishing signs of true faith.

translation: تتجافى جنوبهم عن المضاجع؛ يدعون ربهم خوفًا وطمعًا؛ وممّا رزقناهم ينفقون
interpretation: يصف المشهد قلوب المؤمنين العملية: يتركون راحة النوم ليقوموا للعبادة والدعاء، متوازنين بين خشية الله ورغبة رحمته، ولا يقف إيمانهم عند العبارات بل يترجمونه إلى فعلٍ اجتماعي عبر إنفاق ما رزقهم الله — دالًّا على أن العبادة الحقيقية توأمُها الإخلاص في العبادة والتواضع بالاعتماد على الله والكرم تجاه الناس.

translation: No soul knows what delights of the eyes have been concealed for them as a reward for what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the joys and blessings of Paradise are beyond human imagination: “no soul knows” emphasizes that even the keenest awareness cannot fully grasp the hidden comforts (qurrat al-ʿuyūn) God has prepared. These concealed delights—spiritual contentment and outward pleasures—are promised as recompense for righteous deeds, showing both God’s generosity and the certainty that honest moral effort in this life will be rewarded in ways far greater than we can conceive, inspiring hope, humility, and continued striving for good.

translation:
أَفَمَنْ كَانَ مُؤْمِنًا كَمَنْ كَانَ فَاسِقًا؟ لَا يَسْتَوُونَ
“Is one who is a believer like one who is a transgressor? They are not equal.”
interpretation: The verse emphasizes a decisive moral and spiritual distinction: true faith influences a person’s inner disposition, choices, and relationship with God, producing guidance, righteous conduct, and hope for mercy, whereas persistent transgression reflects rejection of guidance and leads to estrangement and accountability. Consequently, believers and the defiantly sinful do not stand on the same level in rank, consequence, or proximity to God.

translation: As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are Gardens of refuge — a dwelling-place — as a recompense for what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that true faith is inseparable from sustained righteous action and that God’s reward is both secure and proportionate: “Gardens of refuge” implies a permanent, safe abiding in Paradise, while “نزلا بما كانوا يعملون” underscores that this gift is granted justly in accordance with the believers’ consistent deeds, highlighting divine justice and the practical, consequential nature of faith.

translation: As for those who transgressed, their refuge is the Fire. Whenever they desire to emerge from it they are returned to it, and it is said to them: “Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that deliberate transgression (فسق) and persistent denial of Divine warnings lead to irreversible accountability: Hell is presented not merely as a punishment but as a state from which any hope of escape is finally and repeatedly frustrated. The repeated attempts to leave and forcible return underline the permanence and certainty of divine justice and the loss of opportunity after death; the command “Taste” makes the retribution experiential, answering and exposing the falsehood of the deniers’ former scorn. The passage thus functions as both a theological affirmation of moral consequence and a stern warning to correct one’s course while life and opportunity remain.

translation: And We will surely make them taste of the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, perhaps they will repent.
interpretation: God’s measured afflictions in this life serve as a corrective warning and an opportunity: by permitting a limited, nearer punishment He aims to awaken conscience and provoke genuine return to obedience so as to avert the final, greater retribution. The wording emphasizes divine wisdom and restraint (the punishment is controlled and temporally prior), the reality of human responsibility (repentance remains a real possibility, not a certainty), and the moral purpose behind suffering — it can be both chastisement and mercy intended to reform rather than merely to destroy.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them? Indeed, We will surely take retribution upon the criminals.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who, despite being presented with clear divine guidance and moral reminders, deliberately avert their attention out of arrogance, indifference, or stubbornness. It diagnoses such turning-away as a profound injustice — not merely disbelief but a willful rejection of truth that one has been shown — and warns that this conscious rebuff of God's signs leads to inevitable accountability: God will punish those who persist in wrongdoing and refuse to respond to the guidance offered to them.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Book; so be not in doubt about his meeting. And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel.
interpretation: God here affirms the reality and authority of the revelation given to Moses and warns against doubting the truth of his encounter with the Divine. The Torah is presented as divinely appointed guidance for Bani Israel—a framework of law, ethics and direction intended to lead a people toward upright conduct. The verse thus stresses both the continuity and legitimacy of earlier revelation and the responsibility of the recipients: scriptures are genuine guidance, but their benefit depends on accepting and living by them rather than denying or distorting them.

translation: And We made from among them leaders who guided by Our command, because they were patient; and they used to be certain of Our signs.
interpretation: God raised certain steadfast believers to the rank of leaders and guides as a consequence of their patient perseverance and firm conviction in His signs. Their authority is portrayed as a divine commission: they direct others according to God’s ordinance rather than their own whims, and their patience and sure faith in the revealed signs made them reliable exemplars and transmitters of guidance for their communities.

translation: Indeed, your Lord — He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection regarding what they used to differ about.
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate adjudication belongs solely to God: the controversies and disagreements people argue over in this life (especially about creed, truth, and right conduct) will be finally and decisively settled by God on the Day of Judgment. Worldly disputes and temporary judgments will be shown as incomplete; God’s perfect knowledge and justice alone will determine the true outcome and assign recompense according to what people upheld and practiced.

translation: أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا كَمْ أَهْلَكْنَا مِن قَبْلِهِم مِّنَ الْقُرُونِ يَمْشُونَ فِي مَسَاكِنِهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ ۖ أَفَلَا يُسْمَعُونَ
interpretation: الآية تذكّر بأنّ أممًا سبقتهم كانت تعيش في مساكن ونعيم مماثلين ثم أَهْلَكَهُمُ اللَّه بسبب كفرهم وفسقهم؛ وهذه الحوادث والآثار المتبقية هي آيات تنبه إلى قدرة الله وحتمية الجزاء لمن يصرّ على تجاهل الحق. فالمطلوب من السامعين أن يتدبّروا وينقُصوا من غفلتهم: «السماع» هنا يعني الاستيعاب والقبول والعمل بما يقتضي تصحيح السلوك والابتعاد عن أسباب الهلاك.

translation: Do they not see that We drive water to the barren earth and thereby bring forth crops, of which their cattle and they themselves eat? Will they not then see?
interpretation: This verse points to the regular, observable miracle of God’s providence — sending water to apparently dead, arid land and causing it to yield sustenance — as a clear sign of divine power, mercy, and design. By highlighting that both people and their animals benefit from the revived land, the verse emphasizes humanity’s dependence on God’s gifts and uses the visible process of life-giving transformation as an analogical proof: if God can quicken sterile earth and provide for creation, He is fully capable of greater acts (including resurrection and judgment). The repeated rhetorical question (“Will they not then see?”) invites conscious reflection and demands that witnessing such signs lead to recognition, gratitude, and submission rather than heedless denial.

translation: And they say, 'When will this victory come, if you are truthful?','
interpretation: The verse conveys the scoffing demand of those who reject the Prophet’s message: they challenge the promised decisive outcome (al-fath), expressing impatience and mockery while trying to force a timetable on God’s decree. Their question exposes a hardened attitude that seeks immediate, visible proof despite signs already given; it implicitly reveals hypocrisy, for such taunting denies the sovereignty of God over when and how truth will be shown and often serves only to delay acceptance until after the clear vindication arrives.

translation: Say, “On the Day of Opening (the decisive Day), the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be granted a postponement.”
interpretation: The verse warns that the final, decisive Day of God is irreversible: professing belief after the reality of judgment has arrived — or only when confronted by evident punishment — cannot change one’s standing. What will be weighed there are the sincere convictions and deeds that were established before that hour; a last‑minute profession or request for delay will not avail those who persisted in disbelief, for the opportunity to repent and earn God’s acceptance ends before that Day.

translation: So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are waiting.
interpretation: This is a directive to cease fruitless engagement with those who persist in rejection: the Prophet (and believers) should refrain from further argument or pleading, adopt patient forbearance, and await the unfolding of God’s judgment or the consequences of people’s choices, since those people themselves are merely awaiting what will befall them.

translation: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. يا أيها النبي اتقِ اللهَ ولا تُطِعِ الكافِرينَ والمنافقينَ. إنَّ اللهَ كانَ عليمًا حكيمًا.
interpretation: الآية تأمر النبي أولاً بالالتزام بتقوى الله كأساس للقرار والعمل، وتحذّره من الانقياد لطلبات أو نصائح من يقفون ضد الرسالة أو يتظاهرون بالإيمان بينما يريدون الإضرار بها؛ المقصد أن لا تُبدّل مصلحة الدعوة بمخاوف من معارضةٍ ظاهرة أو إغراءات مصالح دنيوية. وتُطمئن الآية بأن الله عليم حكيم، أي أن ما يَجري من معارضة أو امتحان يقع تحت علم وحكمة إلهية، فلا يَحول ذلك دون الثبات على الحق، بل يدعو إلى التحلّي بالحكمة والصبر والثقة بأن الله سيتصرف بعلم وحكمة لا تدركها النظرة الآنية.

translation: And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Indeed, Allah is, concerning what you do, All-Aware.
interpretation: A directive to prioritize and act upon divine guidance rather than human opinion or desire; it reassures that God fully knows every action and intention, so sincere adherence to revelation is both the correct path and the basis for just accountability.

translation: And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse commands wholehearted trust in Allah, asserting that He alone is the ultimate Trustee and Manager of all matters; true tawakkul involves sincere reliance on Him while fulfiling one’s responsibilities, with confidence that Allah’s wisdom, power, and sufficiency will protect, provide for, and determine outcomes, freeing the heart from excessive fear of others or of worldly contingencies.

translation: Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his breast; and He has not made your wives whom you declare to be like your mothers (by zihār) your mothers; nor has He made your claimed sons your sons. That is but what you say with your mouths. And Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.
interpretation: This verse corrects mistaken social and legal assumptions: God emphasizes that inner reality and divine law cannot be overturned by mere words or customary practices. A person cannot possess two hearts so that outward declarations can hide true intention; saying a wife is ‘as my mother’ (zihār) does not change the marital bond, and calling an adopted child your blood son does not alter biological lineage and its legal consequences. Such formulas are human speech, but God affirms the objective truth and provides the right guidance — therefore legal rulings and moral accountability depend on reality and God’s guidance, not on evasive verbal declarations.

translation: ادعُوهم لآبائهم هو أقسط عند الله. فإن لم تعلموا آباءهم فإخوانكم في الدين ومواليكم. وليس عليكم جناح فيما أخطأتم به ولكن ما تعمدت قلوبكم. وكان الله غفوراً رحيماً.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد مبدأ عدالة الانتماء والشفافية في النسب: من الأفضل والأعدل أن تُنسب الناس إلى آبائهم الحقيقيين لا أن يُلبس عليهم نسبٌ غير صحي، لأن حفظ الحقيقـة يحفظ الحقوق والعلاقات الاجتماعية. وإذا عُيِّب النسب أو كان غير معلوم فالعلاقة الأخوية في الدين والولاء الاجتماعي تملأ فراغ النسب وتستمر بالعلاقات والتكليفات. كما تحدد الآية معيار المسئولية الأخلاقية: الأخطاء غير المقصودة تُعفى عنها، والمحاسبة تُقصر على ما قصده القلب من تعمد، وتذكّر أن الله يغفر ويتصف بالرحمة.

translation: The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves; and his wives are their mothers. And kinship ties are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah than the believers and the emigrants—except that you may do a kindness to your friends. That was written in the Book.
interpretation: The verse establishes a framework of communal order: it grounds a special moral and legal priority for the Prophet because his guidance preserves the true welfare of the community; it elevates the Prophet’s wives to a protective, maternal status that safeguards social boundaries and dignity; and it affirms that blood-relationships carry binding, Qur’anic obligations that normally take precedence in matters of mutual duty. At the same time the allowance to “do a kindness to your friends” preserves space for voluntary ties and political or social alliances beyond kin, so the verse balances fixed divine rulings that secure social stability with permitted human discretion to build non‑kin bonds.

translation: And when We took from the prophets their covenant — from you, and from Noah, and from Abraham, and from Moses, and from Jesus the son of Mary — and We took from them a solemn (firm) covenant.
interpretation: God is affirming that He bound the prophets to a grave, binding responsibility: to receive, preserve and faithfully convey His revelation, to uphold pure monotheism, and to bear witness to the truth even under trial. The description “a solemn/firm covenant” stresses the seriousness and accountability of that mission — the prophets were entrusted with a weighty duty whose fulfillment (or neglect) carries real consequences for them and for those they guided.

translation: ليُسأل الصادقون عن صدقهم؛ وأُعِد للكافرين عذابٌ أليم.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد مبدأ المحاسبة على الصدق الحقيقي: في الآخرة سيُستدعى أولئك الذين زُعم عنهم الإيمان ليُبتَحَن صدقهم ومقدار تجسيدهم للحقيقة في القول والعمل، فالمواقف الظاهرة أو الألقاب لا تكفي، بل تُقيّم النيات والأعمال. وفي المقابل تُذكّر بأن الذين جحدوا الحق وأصرّوا على الكفر قد أُعدّ لهم جزاء شديد؛ فهي دعوة للاعتبار والعمل بالصدق خشية الحساب.

translation: O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when forces came against you; We sent against them a wind and forces that you could not see, and Allah is, of what you do, Seeing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah’s help for the community can come through means beyond human perception—visible aid and unseen support alike—so believers must cultivate gratitude and trust in God’s providence in adversity, and live with awareness that Allah observes both their outward deeds and inward intentions, calling them to sincerity and accountability.

translation: “When they came at you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes went astray and the hearts reached the throats, and you were making assumptions about Allah (all kinds of suspicions).”
interpretation: The verse reproves the community’s panic when besieged: in acute fear their senses and composure failed and they began to imagine the worst about God’s help. Its meaning is ethical and spiritual — trials can drive even believers to doubt and despair, but such reactions expose a lack of firm reliance; the proper response is steadfastness, remembrance of God’s past favors, and trust that He will fulfill His promise rather than presuming abandonment.

translation: There the believers were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God subjects the faithful to intense trials that shake both outward circumstances and inner conviction; such severe disturbance serves to reveal and purify true faith by separating those who remain steadfast and reliant on God from those whose commitment falters, ultimately producing patience, reliance on God, and greater spiritual firmness in the believers who endure.

translation: وَإِذْ يَقُولُ الْمُنَافِقُونَ وَالَّذِينَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ مَا وَعَدَنَا اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ إِلَّا غُرُورًا
interpretation: الآية تكشف عن حالة نفسية وأخلاقية: من ينكرون وَعْدَ الله ورسوله ويدعونه 'غُرُورًا' يحاولون تبرير ضعف الإيمان أو الجبن بتقويض يقين الناس، وهذا إنكار نابع من مرض القلب (كالكبرياء أو الحسد أو الخوف)؛ القول يعمل كذريعة لنفاقهم ولا يغير حقيقة الوعد الإلهي، بل يدين نواياهم ويبيّن أنهم مسؤولون عن فساد ضمائرهم وسلوكهم.

translation: And when a party of them said, “O people of Yathrib, you have no stay here; go back,” and a party of them asked leave of the Prophet, saying, “Our houses are exposed” — while they were not exposed — they only wished to flee.
interpretation: The verse censures those who, when the community faced danger, cloaked their cowardice in excuses and sought to abandon collective responsibility. It distinguishes sincere commitment from hypocrisy: true faith requires standing firm with the community and its leadership in trial, whereas offering flimsy justifications (claiming one’s home is ‘exposed’) to escape duty reveals insincerity and an intent to flee rather than a genuine concern.

translation: وَلوْ دَخَلْتَ عَلَيهِمْ مِنْ أَقْطَارِهَا ثُمّ سُئِلُوا الفِتْنَةَ لَآَتُوهَا وَما تَلَبَّثُوا بِهَا إِلاّ يَسِيرًا
interpretation: The verse is warning about the superficial and fleeting nature of certain people's commitment: even if you confronted them from every side and put them to the test, they might appear to submit or accept the trial, but their endurance is weak—they will not remain steadfast in that state except for a short while. In other words, their conformity or faith under pressure is temporary and lacks deep steadiness.

translation: And indeed they had before made a covenant with Allah not to turn their backs; and the covenant of Allah is to be called to account.
interpretation: The verse censures those who, after solemnly swearing to God not to flee or betray the community, abandoned that pledge — teaching that vows made in God's name are morally and eschatologically binding. It warns that such broken commitments expose hypocrisy and will be rigorously examined by Allah, so one must take promises to God seriously and act in accordance with them.

translation: قل: لن ينفعكم الفرار إن فررتم من الموت أو من القتل؛ وإنما تُمتَعُون قليلاً.
interpretation: تحذير من عبثية الهروب من قدر الله: ليس في الفرار دفع لما قدره الله من موت أو عقوبة، والمتاع الدنيوي ما هو إلا نزرة زائلة لا تقي صاحبها حسابه أو مصيره، فالحكمة أن يتوقف الاعتماد على الهروب والملذات المؤقتة ويؤخذ بالاستعداد للقاء الله والالتزام بالمسؤولية الأخروية.

translation: Say, “Who is there that can protect you from Allah if He wills harm for you, or if He wills mercy for you?” They will find for themselves, besides Allah, no guardian nor helper.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over both calamity and blessing: nothing and no one can prevent what Allah decrees nor bestow what He intends except by His leave. It condemns reliance on other deities, allies, or means as ultimately futile—true protection, support and succor belong only to Allah—so people must recognize their dependence on Him, seek His aid, and orient their trust and supplication to Him alone.

translation: It may be that Allah will know those among you who lag behind and those who say to their brothers, “Come to us,” yet they do not come to the fighting except a little.
interpretation: God will expose the true state of people’s resolve and responsibility: some outwardly urge others to face hardship or danger while they themselves avoid it, contributing almost nothing. The verse warns that such posturing—calling others forward while remaining behind—reveals weakness or hypocrisy that only God can fully discern; one cannot shift communal duty onto others without being held accountable, and those who merely summon others will be shown to have offered only a small share of the burden.

translation: They are grudging toward you; yet when fear comes you see them looking to you, their eyes rolling as one fainting from death. Then when the fear has passed, they cut at you with the tongues of craftsmen, begrudging you good. Those — they did not truly believe, so Allah has rendered their deeds void; and that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a type of insincere, unstable faith: such people are outwardly connected but inwardly reluctant, showing a panic-driven attentiveness in danger while lacking steadfast conviction. Once safety returns they lash out with spiteful speech and envy, revealing that their apparent support was contingent and self-serving. Because their belief is not genuine — rooted in transient fear or advantage rather than sincere commitment — their actions carry no spiritual weight and are annulled by God. The passage therefore teaches that inner conviction, not mere outward show or temporary conformity, determines the moral and religious value of deeds, and that God can easily withhold His reward from those whose faith is hollow.

translation:
يَحْسَبُونَ الأَحْزَابَ لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا ۖ وَإِن يَأْتِ الأَحْزَابُ لَيُحِبُّونَ لَوْ أَنَّهُمْ بُدُّوا فِي الْأَعْرَابِ يَسْأَلُونَ عَنْ أَنبَائِكُمْ ۖ وَلَوْ كَانُوا فِيكُمْ مَا قَاتَلُوا إِلَّا قَلِيلاً
"They think that the confederates have not withdrawn; and if the confederates were to come, they would wish that they were in the deserts among the Bedouins, asking about your news; and if they had been with you, they would not have fought except for a little."
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke of hypocrites whose outward ties to the Muslim community hide a heart of self‑preservation. Faced with real danger they prefer absence, curiosity from safety, or token presence rather than genuine participation; their instinct is to avoid hardship and responsibility. This behavior shows weak faith and false allegiance: true commitment is measured by readiness to endure trials and stand with the community, not by mere words or proximity when it is convenient.

translation: There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example for anyone who hopes in Allah and the Last Day and remembers Allah often.
interpretation: The verse means that the Prophet’s life and behavior constitute the practical model for how a believer should live: his sincerity, worship, patience, humility, justice, social dealings and steadiness under trial show the concrete form of faith. But this exemplar effect is realized only by those whose inner orientation is toward God and the Hereafter and who cultivate constant remembrance of Allah—only such people will truly benefit from emulating his example in belief, character and practice.

translation:
وَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الْأَحْزَابَ قَالُوا هَٰذَا مَا وَعَدَنَا اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ ۚ وَصَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ ۚ وَمَا زَادَهُمْ إِلَّا إِيمَانًا وَتَسْلِيمًا
"And when the believers saw the confederate forces, they said, ‘This is what Allah and His Messenger had promised us.’ And Allah and His Messenger spoke the truth. And it only increased them in faith and submission."
interpretation: The verse teaches that encountering the fulfillment of a divine warning does not produce despair in the rooted believer but a deeper certainty. Recognition that God’s promise and the Prophet’s warning were true reinforces inner conviction (iman) and leads to a willing, peaceful surrender to God’s will (taslim). Thus apparent external threat becomes a means of spiritual confirmation and steadfastness rather than of doubt.

translation: Among the believers are men who were true to the covenant they made with Allah; some of them have fulfilled their pledge (by dying), and some are still waiting, and they did not change in the least.
interpretation: The verse honors those whose inward faith matches an outward, steadfast commitment to God — a covenant of belief, obedience and readiness to sacrifice. “Fulfilled their pledge” refers to those who completed that commitment (including by giving their lives in God’s cause) while “those who wait” are believers who remain patient and prepared for what comes. The phrase “they did not change” emphasizes constancy: despite trials, temptations, or the passage of time they did not abandon or dilute their devotion. The intended lesson is that true faith is proven by fidelity to one’s covenant with Allah, manifested in steadfastness, readiness to sacrifice, and unbroken trust.

translation: That Allah may recompense the truthful for their truth and punish the hypocrites — if He wills — or turn to them in mercy. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God judges by inner reality: those who are sincere in faith will receive reward proportionate to their truthfulness, while those whose outward profession conceals disbelief or treachery are liable to punishment. At the same time, punishment is not automatic or inevitable—God, in His wisdom, can choose to forgive and accept repentance. The passage therefore stresses the primacy of inner sincerity over mere outward conformity, warns against hypocrisy, and balances a warning of accountability with hope in God’s mercy for those who genuinely repent.

translation: Allah turned back those who disbelieved in their rage; they obtained no good. And Allah sufficed the believers in the fighting. And Allah is Strong, Exalted in Might.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God frustrates the plots and fury of hostile powers so their efforts come to nothing, and that true security and victory for the community lie in divine support: believers are to trust in God’s sufficiency and power rather than in their own strength when facing aggression.

translation:
وأنزل الذين ظاهروهم من أهل الكتاب من صياصيهم وقذف في قلوبهم الرعب فريقا تقتلون وتأسرون فريقا
"And He brought down those who backed them from among the People of the Book from their strongholds/ranks, and cast terror into their hearts; so that you would kill some and take some captive."
interpretation: The verse teaches that, in the context of a just military encounter, God can overturn the power and cohesion of opposing coalitions and place dread in their hearts so that victory comes to the believing community. Its point is theological and moral rather than a general license to violence: it affirms that success in such crises is ultimately a gift of God, that alliances opposed to the Messenger may be broken by divine intervention, and that the differing fates of the defeated (death for some, captivity for others) are consequences of that upheaval. The passage thus calls believers to trust in God’s support and serves as a warning about the consequences of siding against the prophetic cause while presupposing the event’s specific martial and historical context.

translation: And He caused to inherit you their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land which you had not trodden. And ever is Allah, over all things, competent.
interpretation: The verse affirms that outcomes of battles, conquests, and change in circumstances are ultimately determined by God’s sovereign will: He can transfer ownership and grant to a people what they did not acquire by their own footsteps. It teaches reliance on divine providence rather than solely on human effort, warns against taking credit for successes, and reminds believers that possessions and territory are granted or withheld by Allah’s power, so they should remain humble, grateful, and conscious that every gain occurs within His overarching capability and decree.

translation: O Prophet, say to your wives: “If you desire the life of this world and its adornments, then come — I will provide for you and release you with a gracious release.”
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to offer his wives a clear, dignified choice: if they prefer worldly comforts and status over the special moral and spiritual responsibilities of the Prophet’s household, he is to arrange for their material provision and effect an honorable separation. The ruling underscores that the Prophet’s wives are expected to accept a distinct, exemplary role; those who do not wish to live under that public, ascetic commitment may leave without disgrace, receiving fair support and a gracious, respectful release rather than coercion or humiliation.

translation: And if you (women) seek Allah and His Messenger and the Home of the Hereafter, then indeed Allah has prepared for the doers of good among you a great reward.
interpretation: The verse reassures those addressed that when their primary aim is to please God, follow His Messenger, and secure the Hereafter, God will grant abundant recompense to the truly righteous among them. It stresses that sincere intention and morally excellent action (المحسنات) — not merely social standing or worldly attachments — determine divine reward, validating sacrifices made for faith and promising a great spiritual return for upright conduct.

translation: O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, her punishment will be doubled; and that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the Prophet’s wives are held to a higher standard because of their public and exemplary role; if any of them commit an overt grave sin, the consequence is intensified (doubled) to reflect the greater breach of trust and the wider social harm their conduct could cause. The phrase “that is easy for Allah” underscores God’s authority and ability to enforce such increased accountability, not a legal technicality but a moral principle linking rank and responsibility.

translation: And whoever among you is devoutly obedient to Allah and His Messenger and does righteous deeds — We will give her her reward twice, and We have prepared for her a noble provision.
interpretation: The verse addresses believing women and affirms that sincere, consistent devotion to God and obedience to the Prophet, combined with righteous action, brings not merely ordinary recompense but a multiplied, emphatic reward. The term qunut denotes humble, steady submission inwardly and conformity to prophetic guidance outwardly; the promise of “reward twice” is a rhetorical assurance of abundant, multiplied blessing — classically understood either as reward here and in the Hereafter or as intensified recompense for deeds often enacted privately. The “noble provision” refers to an honorable, dignified sustenance and standing granted by God, encompassing spiritual favor and protected provision. Overall, the verse comforts and honors women believers: piety and good conduct yield generous, elevated returns from God, regardless of public role or gender.

translation: O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any [other] of the women. If you are conscious of Allah, do not be soft in speech so that one whose heart is sick might be tempted; and speak a fitting (honourable) word.
interpretation: Allah singles out the Prophet’s wives to remind them of their elevated role and the need for guarded dignity: they must avoid a soft, yielding, or flirtatious manner of speaking that could encourage those with impure intentions. The command teaches a general principle—speech can create temptation or misunderstanding—so those in positions of moral or public responsibility should set clear, respectful boundaries by speaking firmly yet courteously (‘a fitting word’), preserving both their honor and the community’s moral order.

translation: And remain in your houses and do not display yourselves as the display of the former ignorance; and establish prayer, give zakah and obey Allah and His Messenger. Indeed Allah intends only to remove from you the impurity, O People of the Household, and to purify you completely.
interpretation: The verse closes by declaring that God’s purpose in addressing the Prophet’s close household is to effect a comprehensive spiritual and moral cleansing: it marks them out for special sanctification and elevation in God’s sight so that they serve as exemplars of purity and integrity for the community. This purification is understood as divine removal of moral and social defilement (the faults and corrupting influences associated with ignorance) and the granting of a heightened status of righteousness and trustworthiness among the faithful.

translation:
واذكرن ما يتلى في بيوتكن من آيات الله والحكمة ۚ إن الله كان لطيفا خبيرا
“And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of Allah and the wisdom. Indeed Allah is ever Gentle (Subtle), All‑Aware.”
interpretation: This injunction emphasizes preserving and practicing Qurʾānic guidance and prophetic wisdom within the intimate sphere of the home: learning, recalling, transmitting and embodying that guidance in private life. By appending that Allah is لطيف (subtly kind/gentle) and خبير (fully aware), the verse reassures that these domestic acts of remembrance and instruction are seen with fine sensitivity by God—He knows inner intentions and circumstances—so what is quietly taught, lived, or nurtured in the household matters morally and spiritually and will be recognized and judged with divine subtlety and knowledge.

translation: Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the obedient men and obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their private parts and the women who do so, and the men who remember Allah often and the women who do so — for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine mercy and recompense are granted on the basis of moral and spiritual conduct, not gender. By pairing male and female forms across a range of inward virtues (sincerity, patience, humility, frequent remembrance) and outward actions (obedience, truthfulness, charity, fasting, chastity), it affirms that both inner devotion and corresponding ethical behavior together qualify a person for God’s forgiveness and a great reward; the criteria for God’s favor are universal and apply equally to men and women.

translation: It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice about their affair; and whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has indeed gone astray into manifest error.
interpretation: The verse affirms that genuine faith requires submitting to binding decisions that come from God and His Messenger: when a ruling or command has been established by revelation and prophetic guidance, believers must not set aside, delay, or replace it with personal preference. Obedience to those divinely sanctioned judgments is an integral part of iman, and deliberately rejecting them is not merely a private error but a clear deviation from the straight path; where no divine ruling exists, however, personal choice remains permissible, but not in matters already decided by Allah and His Messenger.
