interpretation: The verse affirms that God endowed Prophet Sulaiman with reinforced authority, profound insight for sound judgment, and a divinely given eloquence and communicative capacity; this combination empowered him to rule justly and to articulate, comprehend, and command across ordinary human boundaries (enabling clear judgment and interaction with other creatures), so his governance was both effective and divinely supported.

translation: Has the report of the adversary reached you, when they walled up the sanctuary?
interpretation: The verse rhetorically summons attention to an incident of covert cruelty performed under the guise of sacredness: those opposed to the victim used the very walls of the sanctuary to conceal and carry out injustice. Its lesson is moral and cautionary — outward piety or possession of holy places can be abused to hide malicious schemes, and God notices such hypocrisy and will expose and judge those who weaponize religion to harm the innocent.

translation: When they entered upon David, they were afraid of him. They said, “Do not be afraid. We are two disputants; one of us has transgressed against the other. Judge between us with truth, and do not be excessive [or partial], and guide us to the straight way.”
interpretation: The verse teaches the ethical essentials of adjudication and moral repair: parties come to a ruler not to grandstand but to have a wrong righted; they ask the judge to decide on the basis of objective truth, warning him against excess, bias or vindictiveness. It affirms that legitimate authority must dispel fear by administering fair, measured justice that corrects wrongdoing and restores people to the straight path, and it reminds both litigants and judge of mutual responsibility—the complainant admits transgression so the outcome is corrective, and the judge’s role is to balance firmness with restraint and to guide toward upright conduct.

translation:
إِنَّ هَذَا أَخِي لَهُ تِسْعٌ وَتِسْعُونَ نَعْجَةً وَلِي نَعْجَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ، فَقَالَ أَكْفِلْنِيهَا وَعَزَّنِي فِي الْخِطَابِ
"Indeed, this is my brother: he has ninety-nine ewes and I have only one. He said, 'Entrust her to me and support me in the argument.'"
interpretation: The verse reveals the behavior of a powerful, covetous person who seeks to absorb the weak’s sole possession by asking for custodianship as a pretext and demanding that others back him up in speech — an instance of greed, manipulation, and reliance on social influence rather than justice.

translation: He said, “Indeed he has wronged you by requesting your ewes to be added to his ewes. And indeed many of the created beings transgress one against another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds — and few are they.” And David perceived that We had tried him, so he sought forgiveness of his Lord and fell down in prostration and turned back (in repentance).
interpretation: The passage points to two intertwined truths: first, human (and created) nature is prone to injustice, rivalry and covetousness, so violations of rights often stem from selfish desire; only a small number — those whose faith is sincere and whose conduct is upright — resist that impulse. Second, trials that expose personal failing are not merely shameful incidents but opportunities for spiritual correction: recognizing a test, turning to God in repentance, and humbling oneself in worship (as David did) are the proper responses that restore moral balance and draw one nearer to God.

translation: So We forgave him that; and indeed for him with Us is nearness and a goodly return.
interpretation: The verse declares that God pardoned the person’s fault and, beyond mere forgiveness, bestowed upon him a high spiritual status: intimacy of nearness to God (zulfā) and a noble, pleasant dwelling as his ultimate recompense (hasan maʾb). It underscores that sincere repentance or God‑pleasing conduct can convert past failings into grounds for elevation — God’s mercy not only removes sin but may raise the repentant to privileged closeness and an honorable eternal abode.

translation: O David, indeed We have made you a vicegerent on the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who are led astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for forgetting the Day of Reckoning.
interpretation: God addresses David as a divinely appointed steward whose authority carries the duty of upright, impartial judgment; the command not to follow personal desires warns that leaders (and by extension every believer) must subordinate appetites and private interests to objective justice and divine guidance, because succumbing to whim corrupts decisions and distances one from God’s path, and those who lose sight of ultimate accountability—the Day of Reckoning—are liable to severe consequences. This verse therefore teaches that legitimate authority requires moral restraint, fear of God, and constant awareness of final accountability to prevent injustice and social harm.

translation: And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain; that is the conjecture of those who disbelieve. So woe to those who disbelieve because of the Fire.
interpretation: God affirms that the cosmos is purposeful and governed by wisdom and meaning, rejecting the claim held by some that existence is accidental or without design. The verse indicts the unbelievers’ assumption as a false outlook that severs creation from its Divine source and moral order; as a consequence it warns that rejecting this truth leads to ruin—symbolized by the Fire—because denial of God’s purpose brings moral responsibility and eventual accountability.

translation:
أَمْ نَجْعَلُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ كَالْمُفْسِدِينَ فِي الْأَرْضِ أَمْ نَجْعَلُ الْمَتَّقِينَ كَالْفُجَّارِ؟
"Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth? Or shall We make the pious like the wicked?"
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical affirmation of divine justice and moral distinction: God will not treat the faithful who perform good deeds as if they were corrupters, nor equate the God‑fearing with the God‑defying. It reassures that apparent worldly parity between good and evil does not negate ultimate moral discrimination — outcomes, recompense, and standing before God correspond to one’s faith and conduct, so the righteous will not be counted with the wicked.

translation: كتابٌ أنزلناه إليك مباركٌ ليدبروا آياته وليتذكّر أولو الألباب.
interpretation: الآية تُعلِن أن القرآن كتاب مُبارك مُنزَل لرسوله وللبشرية، وهدفه الأساسي أن يثير التفكُّر في آياته لا القراءة السطحية: التفكيرُ هنا يشمل التدبُّر في المعاني والأحكام والقصص والآثار الأخلاقية والكونية حتى تؤدي إلى هدايةٍ وتغيير في السلوك. وصفه بالمبارك يدلّ على أن في الالتزام به وبركته فوائد باقية، وأن مَنْ له عقلٌ وقلبٌ (أولو الألباب) سيستفيد منه حقًّا عبر التذكُّر والاعتبار وتحويل الفهم إلى عمل.

translation: And We granted Solomon to David — an excellent servant; indeed he was often returning [to Allah].
interpretation: The verse teaches that Solomon was bestowed upon David as a divinely given blessing linked to David’s exemplary servitude: David’s constant turning to God in worship, repentance and humility made him a ‘best’ servant whose devotion warranted the gift of a righteous successor. It emphasizes that God’s favors are granted to those who are sincere, humble, and continually return to Him.

translation: When, at dusk, the swift, coursing steeds were presented before him.
interpretation: The verse evokes a deliberate display of worldly power and splendor — symbolized by spirited, well-bred horses paraded in the evening — offered to a person as a form of temptation or intimidation; it warns that outward shows of strength and luxury can entangle the heart, testing one’s attachment to God and revealing whether one will be captivated by prestige or remain steadfast in humility and reliance on the Divine.

translation:
فقال: «إني أحببت حبّ الخير عن ذكر ربي حتى توارت بالحجاب»
"He said, ‘Truly I had become enamored with the love of worldly good, to the neglect of remembering my Lord, until I was hidden by a veil.'"
interpretation: The speaker confesses that an overpowering attachment to worldly benefits and comforts displaced God-consciousness; that attachment darkened his inner sight so that a spiritual veil fell between him and God, making him forgetful of remembrance and distant from guidance.

translation: «Return it to me!» — and he at once began to stroke (it) along the shanks and the necks.
interpretation: The verse depicts an impulsive, self‑assertive reaction: upon reclaiming what he thought was his, the person immediately begins to handle and caress the animals’ limbs and throats as a show of possession and control. The action symbolizes a superficial, outward display of dominance and enjoyment of material benefit without deeper awareness or humility — a critique of those who seize what they desire and indulge in it heedlessly, valuing appearance and ownership over conscience and true responsibility.

translation: And certainly We tested Solomon, and We placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (in repentance).
interpretation: The verse is understood to mean that Allah subjected Prophet Sulaiman to a humbling trial whereby his external authority and its trappings were taken away (symbolized by a lifeless body set upon his throne) to expose dependence on God rather than worldly power. The purpose of the trial was corrective: it brought Sulaiman to sincere return and repentance, showing that true dignity and kingship belong to God and that turning back to Him restores one’s spiritual standing.

translation: قَالَ رَبِّ اغْفِرْ لِي وَهَبْ لِي مُلْكًا لَا يَنْبَغِي لِأَحَدٍ مِنْ بَعْدِي ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْوَهَّابُ
interpretation: The speaker pairs sincere repentance with a request for a uniquely legitimate and enduring authority, implying that true rule is not merely a personal ambition but a trust granted by God to accomplish just and divinely intended purposes. By asking forgiveness first and then seeking a kingdom, and by invoking God as al‑Wahhâb (The Bestower), the utterance teaches that political power or distinction should be sought only through humility before God and reliant on His free bestowal, not by worldly means or pride; legitimate leadership is therefore a gift from God entrusted for service and responsibility rather than a self‑claimed right.

translation: And We subjected the wind to him, so it ran at his command, gently, wherever he directed.
interpretation: The verse signifies that God, by His will, can grant a righteous servant mastery over elements of creation as a practical sign of divine support and authority. The wind’s obedience symbolizes that any apparent power exercised by a prophet or chosen person is ultimately God’s doing; such gifts are instruments to facilitate the welfare and needs of the community (movement, labor, craft, defense) and therefore must be used responsibly and justly, affirming God’s sole sovereignty (tawḥīd) while demonstrating His favor.

translation: And the devils—every builder and every diver.
interpretation: The verse characterizes devils as both skillful fabricators and stealthy infiltrators: they “build” by devising lies, temptations and contrivances to mislead people, and they “dive” by secretly probing hidden realms — slipping into the depths of hearts, assemblies, or unseen places to seize or transmit corrupting influences. In short, it emphasizes their craftiness and covert methods in undermining faith and guiding people astray.

translation: And others, bound together in shackles.
interpretation: The phrase portrays the fate of those whose rejection of guidance has led to utter loss of freedom and dignity: being “muqarranīn” (tied together) in “al‑asfād” (fetters) emphasizes both physical restraint and collective humiliation — they are deprived of individual agency, forced to follow one another in captivity, and thereby shown as overwhelmed by the consequences of their choices, stripped of autonomy and honor.

translation: This is Our gift; so grant (as a favor) or withhold — without reckoning.
interpretation: God affirms His absolute sovereignty over provision: blessings are given or withheld by His will, not by human entitlement, and He is under no obligation to justify His distribution. The proper posture for people is trust and submission—accepting abundance or deprivation as part of divine wisdom, responding with gratitude and patience rather than demanding explanation.

translation: And indeed for him with Us is nearness and a good return.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the person described will be granted God’s special favor: intimate nearness to Him (لُزْفَىٰ) — a station of acceptance and closeness in Divine presence — and a beautiful final abode (حُسْنَ مَآبٍ) as his recompense in the Hereafter, indicating both spiritual elevation and an honored, pleasing destiny granted by Allah to the righteous.

translation: And remember Our servant Ayyūb when he called upon his Lord, “Indeed, Satan has afflicted me with hardship and torment.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true piety is shown not by the absence of suffering but by turning to God with humility when hardships overwhelm us. It indicates that trials can have a spiritual source and that rightly attributing harm — admitting human weakness rather than denying or despairing — leads one to sincere supplication, patience, and reliance on God's mercy as the way to relief and vindication.

translation: Run with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink.
interpretation: The verse urges immediate, decisive movement toward what God offers: a promised relief that both refreshes and cleanses. The command to “run” emphasizes urgent obedience and effort, while the “cool bath and drink” symbolize the tangible refreshment and spiritual purification and sustenance granted to those who hasten to God's mercy.

translation: And We granted him his family and others like them to be with them — a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s mercy can restore and even multiply what was lost: after the servant’s trial God returned his family (and provided their like to accompany them) as a deliberate act of compassion and reward. This restoration is not merely a reversal of misfortune but a sign meant to awaken reflection in thoughtful people — to show that perseverance and trust in God amid hardship lead to divine mercy, and to remind the prudent of God’s wisdom, justice, and bounty.

translation:
وَخُذْ بِيَدِكَ ضِغْثًا فَاضْرِبْ بِهِ وَلَا تَحِنَّثْ ۚ إِنَّا وَجَدْنَاهُ صَابِرًا ۚ نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ ۖ إِنَّهُ أَوَّابٌ
"Take in your hand a small tuft and strike with it, and do not break your oath. Indeed We found him patient — excellent the servant! Indeed he was ever-returning [to Allah]."
interpretation: The verse highlights that true healing and honor come through humble obedience and unwavering patience under trial: even a simple, seemingly powerless act (striking with a tuft) ordained by God can be the means of restoration when performed in trust, without abandoning one's solemn commitments. The praise that follows — calling him an exemplary servant who repeatedly turns back to God — teaches that steadfast patience combined with continual repentance and submission is the attitude that earns divine approbation and relief.

translation: And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, men of strong hands and keen sight.
interpretation: Calling them “men of strong hands and keen sight” signifies that these patriarchs united decisive, righteous action (strength, authority, struggle) with clear spiritual and moral perception (insight, vision); God commands their remembrance so believers hold them up as models of leadership and faith in which firm conduct and discerning understanding go together.

translation: Indeed, We have purified them by a sincere/pure remembrance of the Abode (the Home).
interpretation: The verse means that God has cleansed and made these people’s intentions and states genuine by instilling in them a deep, focused awareness of the eternal dwelling (the Hereafter). That remembrance removes worldly distractions and selfish motives, so their worship, choices and conduct become sincere and directed toward what endures—their actions are purified because their hearts live with the reality of the final Home.

translation:
وَإِنَّهُمْ عِندَنَا لَمِنَ الْمُصْطَفِينَ الْأَخْيَارِ
"And indeed, with Us they are among the chosen, the best."
interpretation: The phrase affirms that certain righteous people are singled out by divine choice for an honored, enduring station in God's presence: their inclusion among "المصطفين الأخيار" denotes God’s special favor and selection, signifying intimate nearness, elevated ranks and guaranteed reward in the hereafter—a status granted by God's grace rather than solely by worldly status or effort.

translation: “And remember Ismāʿīl and Al‑Yasāʿ and Dhū al‑Kifl — and all of them were among the best (the righteous).”
interpretation: The verse uses the remembrance of these named figures to teach a criterion of divine approval: true excellence is not fame or rank but steadfast faith, patience under trial, and faithful fulfilment of one’s responsibilities. By grouping well‑known exemplars with one about whom little is recorded (Dhu al‑Kifl), the text emphasizes that inner righteousness and just, persevering conduct — even when unnoticed — are what make a servant ‘among the best,’ and these qualities are the model believers should seek to imitate.

translation: This is a Reminder; and indeed for the righteous there is an excellent return.
interpretation: The statement promises that a life oriented by taqwa (God‑consciousness) culminates in a truly good outcome — not merely fleeting worldly success but restoration, honor and intimate acceptance in the final meeting with God. "Hassan maʾab" covers both the inner fruits of piety (peace, moral protection, freedom from regret) and the ultimate, enduring abode of reward; therefore the verse functions as both consolation for those who persevere in righteousness and a moral incentive to shape one’s conduct so that the present life coheres with that promised, beautiful end.

translation: Gardens of Eden, with their gates opened for them.
interpretation: The phrase portrays Paradise as a place of honored, effortless admission: the opened gates symbolize God’s welcome and the removal of all barriers so that the righteous enter freely into abundant, secure, and permanent blessings — an image of dignity, acceptance, and ready enjoyment rather than struggle or constraint.

translation: Reclining therein; therein they will be provided with abundant fruit and drink.
interpretation: The verse uses the images of ease and plentiful provision to signify the believers’ assured, dignified reward in the Hereafter: a state of permanent rest, sufficiency and honor granted by God without toil or want. The promised fruits and drink point both to real, pure pleasures and to symbolic blessings (spiritual nourishment, contentment, and closeness to God), emphasizing God’s generosity and the complete removal of earthly hardships and deficiency for those who attain His mercy.

translation:
وَعِندَهُمْ قَاصِرَاتُ الطَّرْفِ أَتْرَابٌ
“And with them will be companions of modest gaze, age‑mates.”
interpretation: The verse describes the companions allotted to the righteous in Paradise as possessing restrained, modest eyes and being peers of the same age. This emphasizes that the blessed companionship there is pure and respectful rather than objectifying or lustful; it is a relationship of equality, harmony and dignity perfectly suited to the believers’ spiritual state and reward, providing tranquil, appropriate fellowship rather than temptation.

translation: This is what you were promised for the Day of Reckoning.
interpretation: The verse affirms the fulfillment and certainty of the warnings about the Last Day: what was promised (or threatened) to people regarding recompense or punishment in the Day of Judgment has now come to pass. It underscores inevitability of divine justice and personal accountability—on that day each soul receives the consequences of its deeds and no excuse or denial will avert the appointed outcome.

translation: “Indeed, this is Our provision; it will never be exhausted.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that the blessing or sustenance in question is a gift from God whose supply is not constrained by human limitations; its purpose is to remind believers to trust in God’s inexhaustible bounty, to respond with gratitude and contentment rather than anxiety or hoarding, and to recognise that provision ultimately depends on Divine will rather than solely on worldly means.

translation: This — and indeed for the tyrants is surely an evil return.
interpretation: The verse conveys that those who transgress by arrogating power, rejecting God’s guidance, and committing injustice will inevitably face a disgraceful and ruinous outcome; their temporal strength and gains do not avert Divine judgment, so the passage functions as a solemn warning that arrogance and tyranny lead to destruction unless one turns back in repentance and submits to right conduct.

translation:
جَهَنَّمُ صَلَوْهَا ۖ فَبِئْسَ الْمِهِادُ
"They will enter Hell — what an evil resting‑place!"
interpretation: The verse declares the inevitable admission of the wrongdoers into Hell and uses the term “mihād” (resting‑place/cradle) ironically: what they will take as their final abode is not comfort but torment. It stresses both the certainty and the utter unsuitability of that destination, warning that worldly pride, schemes or temporary ease will not avert the permanent, painful recompense ordained for persistent rejection of truth.

translation: This — so let them taste it: scalding (boiling) water and ghisāq (foul, festering discharge).
interpretation: The phrase portrays the punishments awaiting the guilty as both excruciating and humiliating: “حميم” denotes burning, scalding liquid and “غساق” a nauseating, festering discharge associated with severe burns. Together they symbolize the real, corporeal agony and utter degradation that follow persistent rejection of truth — a stern warning that divine justice brings not only pain but abasement, intended to deter people from continuing in wrongdoing.

translation: And another of its likeness, in pairs.
interpretation: This phrase affirms that God creates things as corresponding counterparts—each species or phenomenon having a matching likeness or mate—so that creation is ordered, balanced, and complementary; the pairing (azwāj) points to divine wisdom and purposeful design rather than random assemblage.

translation: This is a band that has rushed in with you — no welcome for them; indeed, they will enter the Fire.
interpretation: The verse warns that some people who force themselves into the company of others—by arrogance, hypocrisy, or presumptuous claims to belonging—will find no acceptance before God. Their aggressive intrusion and wrong conduct do not earn greeting or admission to mercy; instead their way leads to punishment in the Fire. The passage emphasizes that true acceptance depends on sincere faith and righteous deeds, not on bold appearance or forcible association.

translation: They said, “No — rather you are not welcome; you yourselves have brought this upon us — what an evil resting‑place!”
interpretation: The verse conveys that the doomed will reject and reproach those who warned them, trying to shift blame, yet their ruin is actually the fruit of their own choices; it underlines personal responsibility for disbelief and wrongdoing and emphasizes that the final abode they preferred or caused is truly a wretched and deserved consequence.

translation: قالوا ربنا من قدم لنا هذا فزده عذابا ضعفا في النار
interpretation: They are pictured on the Day of Judgment as refusing responsibility and seeking vengeance: instead of repenting they ask God to increase the punishment of whoever brought them the warning (the messenger or the truth) — to double his torment in the Fire. The verse highlights their stubbornness, blame-shifting and malicious wish to punish the bearer of admonition, revealing moral corruption and the futility of their plea, for their vindictive request does not remove their own accountability.

translation:
وَقَالُوا مَا لَنَا لا نَرَى رِجَالًا كُنَّا نَعُدُّهُمْ مِنَ الْأَشْرَارِ
"And they will say, 'Why do we not see the men whom we used to count among the wicked?'"
interpretation: The verse cautions that human judgments based on worldly rank and appearance are fallible: those we hastily label as wicked or expect to be punished may not appear as we imagined when ultimate judgment comes. It teaches that true standing and accountability rest with God, not with our fleeting, superficial estimates, and thus warns against pride, envy, and premature condemnation.

translation: Have We made them a thing of mockery, or have their eyes gone astray?
interpretation: A rhetorical question denying that God has reduced certain people to mere objects of ridicule; rather, the verse points to the real cause of their rejection — their own distorted perception or turning away. “Eyes” here stands for insight and understanding, so the fault lies in their blinded or wayward vision (their inner disposition and choices), not in God making them contemptible.

translation: إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ لَحَقٌّ تَخَاصَمَ أَهْلُ النَّارِ
interpretation: The verse affirms that the scene described is an actual, decisive reality: in Hell the condemned will be consumed by mutual disputation and blaming one another. Their ties and defenses collapse into fruitless contention, exposing the certainty of the warning and the finality of their state — a moral and relational breakdown that shows the true consequences of having turned away from guidance.

translation: Say, "I am only a warner, and there is no god but Allah, the One, the Subduer."
interpretation: The verse defines the Prophet’s role as a messenger whose duty is to warn, while at the same time asserting the exclusive divinity and absolute sovereignty of Allah. Calling God al‑Wāḥid (the One) and al‑Qahhār (the Subduer) emphasizes that there is no partner or rival to Him and that He alone ultimately controls and overpowers all forces and outcomes; thus human claims to divine authority or reliance on false gods are untenable, and acceptance or rejection of the warning occurs under the dominion of the One who alone decides fate.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them — the Exalted in Might, the Oft‑Forgiving.
interpretation: The phrase affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over every realm and thing, while pairing two complementary attributes: al‑ʿAzīz (invincible, with power to enforce justice) and al‑Ghaffār (unceasingly forgiving). The intended lesson is theological and ethical: recognize Allah’s supreme authority and your accountability before Him, but also rely on His boundless readiness to forgive when you sincerely repent — thus balancing awe and hope in one’s relationship with God.

translation: Say: "It is a momentous tidings."
interpretation: The command to ‘say’ frames the report as a weighty, decisive announcement: it is not trivial or fictional but a serious revelation whose truth and consequences are immense, demanding sober attention, responsible response, and recognition that it can change destinies.

translation: You are turning away from it.
interpretation: A rebuke to those who deliberately avert their attention from the message or warning — they refuse to face the truth (the revelation, the admonition, or the reality of the Hereafter) out of heedlessness, pride, or love of worldly concerns, thereby rejecting guidance they ought to receive.

translation: I had no knowledge of the Highest Assembly when they disputed.
interpretation: The speaker denies any participation in or awareness of the deliberations of the exalted heavenly council, affirming that affairs decided in that august assembly — matters of the unseen and divine decree — were not known to him; his authority is limited to what God has revealed, and he distances himself from claiming insider knowledge of celestial decisions.

translation: ما يُوحَى إليَّ إلا أنَّما أنا نذيرٌ مبينٌ — لا يُنزل عليّ ما يزوِّدني معرفةٍ بالغيوب أو منفعةٍ دنيوية، بل ما يُوحَى إليّ هو أن أكون نذيرًا واضحًا.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد محدودية دور الرسول كنبي مفوَّض: الوحي لا يجعله صاحب أسرار مستقلة ولا تاجر مصالح، بل يمنحه مهمة واحدة مركزية هي تبليغ التحذير والهدى بصورة جلية. بذلك تُبرَز خُطورة الرسالة ووضوحها، وتُحمّل المكلفين مسؤولية الاستجابة أو الرفض لأن النبي لا يفرض الحقيقة بل يعرِّضها ببيان واضح.

translation: When your Lord said to the angels, “Indeed I will create a human being from clay.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that human beings are a deliberate, purposeful creation of God from humble, malleable matter. By announcing the act to the angels, God highlights the significance of humanity’s arrival: they are created not as accidental products but to be formed, educated and entrusted with a moral role in the world. The reference to clay stresses our physical origin and vulnerability while also implying potential for cultivation and moral growth under divine guidance; it underlines God’s sole authority over life and sets the stage for human responsibility, knowledge, and accountability before the Creator.

translation: When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit, then fall down to him in prostration.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God conferred a unique dignity on human beings by imparting to them of His “spirit” — a divine bestowal that brings life, consciousness, moral awareness, and the capacity for knowledge and relationship with God. The angels’ command to prostrate expresses recognition and honor of that God-given status and the trust of vicegerency; it signifies esteem for the qualities God placed in humanity, not worship of the human, and thereby emphasizes human responsibility to live up to the moral and spiritual capacities entrusted to them.

translation: So all the angels prostrated, every one of them.
interpretation: The verse signifies the angels’ immediate and unanimous submission to God’s command, expressing humility and recognition of the honor and knowledge God bestowed on Adam; their prostration is an act of obedience to Allah’s decree (not worship of Adam) and thereby exemplifies the right response to divine wisdom in contrast to prideful refusal.

translation: Except Iblis — he was arrogant and became one of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The phrase identifies pride as the decisive moral failure: Iblis’s refusal to obey God was a willful act of arrogance, not helplessness, and that choice placed him among those who reject God. The verse warns that pride leads to disobedience and spiritual estrangement, showing that moral accountability and freedom of choice, not one’s nature or origin, determine whether one remains within the community of the faithful or falls into disbelief.

translation: قال: «يا إبليس، ما منعك أن تسجد لما خلقت بيدي؟ أَستكبرت أم كنت من العالين؟»
interpretation: الله يوبّخ إبليس ويبرز سبب عصيانه: لم يكن الجدل لجهل بل لعُجب وتكبّر أو لادعاء نفوذ ومركزية. عبارة «بيدي» تدل على خصوصية صنع الله وبيان حقه في المطاع، فتُعرِّض الآية العُلوّ الزائف وتعلّم أن التكبر على أمر الربِّ هو أصل السقوط، وأن مكانةً مزعومة أو أصالة فطرية لا تبرر معصية أو رفض أمر الله.

translation: He said, “I am better than him: You created me from fire and created him from clay.”
interpretation: The verse exposes how arrogance based on a supposed superiority of origin corrupts the heart and leads to disobedience. It teaches that God’s assessment is not determined by one’s material origin or status but by righteousness and humility; claiming worth from one’s nature becomes the root of rebellion and spiritual ruin.

translation: He said, “Get out of it; indeed you are expelled.”
interpretation: God’s command to Iblis to leave the Garden is a declaration of his rejection and punishment for disobedience; the term “رجيم” conveys that he is cast out and accursed—removed from the presence and favor he once enjoyed—showing that pride and refusal to obey God result in disgrace, exile, and becoming an enemy to humanity’s guidance.

translation: And indeed My curse is upon you until the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: The phrase expresses God’s irrevocable condemnation of those who persist in grave unbelief or corruption: a withdrawal of divine mercy and protection, resulting in enduring disgrace and the effects of divine wrath both in this world and, finally, at the Day of Reckoning when ultimate justice is rendered.

translation: قال رب فأنظرني إلى يوم يبعثون — He said, “My Lord, then show me the Day when they will be resurrected.”
interpretation: The request expresses a malign, inquisitive resolve rather than repentance: the speaker asks to see the Day of Resurrection not to seek mercy but to behold and revel in the outcome of his opposition. It reveals an obstinate will to witness God’s judgment so he can gloat over those he misled and continue in his rebellion — a portrait of prideful enmity that seeks knowledge of the Last Day for spiteful ends rather than guidance or reform.

translation: He said, “Indeed, you are among those who are given respite.”
interpretation: This declares that the person addressed is being granted a postponement: their punishment or death is deferred and they are allowed time — whether as mercy to repent or as a delay until the appointed reckoning. It underscores that such reprieve is granted by divine will, is temporary, and carries the purpose of testing, warning, or allowing opportunity for change.

translation: Until the Day of the appointed time.
interpretation: The phrase points to persistence up to the divinely appointed Day of reckoning: a fixed, certain time known to God. It calls for living with awareness of eventual accountability — to remain steadfast in duty, patience, and righteousness because the outcome will be decided at that predetermined, unavoidable hour.

translation: He said, “By Your might, I will surely lead them all astray.”
interpretation: The words show Iblīs’s defiant resolve and method: by invoking God’s power he emphasizes his determination to wage a comprehensive campaign of temptation, not because he can overpower divine will but because he intends to exploit human weakness and choice. The verse alerts believers that misguidance is systematic and persistent—Satan promises to work on hearts and societies broadly—so guidance depends on human responsibility, vigilance, and seeking God’s protection rather than assuming temptation is occasional or negligible.

translation: Except, among them, Your sincere servants.
interpretation: The phrase indicates that God will make an exception for those within a people who are truly devoted and pure in faith; their genuine sincerity and devotion distinguish them so they are spared condemnation and are granted God’s protection and favor.

translation: قال: «فَالْحَقُّ وَالْحَقُّ أَقُولُ»
interpretation: توكيد حازم بأن ما يقوله المتكلم هو الحق المطلق؛ صيغة لتأكيد صدق ونزاهة القول ودعوة لسماعٍ وقبولٍ بلا ريب.

translation: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those of them who follow you, all together.
interpretation: The statement functions as a solemn divine judgment: those who persist in arrogant rejection and who lead or follow others into misguidance will, by their own choices, become the occupants of Hell. “Filling Hell” here expresses inevitability born of persistent disobedience, emphasizes the shared responsibility of leaders and their followers, and serves as a stern warning that pride and deliberate turning away from God’s guidance result not from God’s desire but from the actors’ own repeated choices and their consequences.

translation: قُلْ مَا أَسْأَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ أَجْرٍ وَمَا أَنَا مِنَ الْمُتَكَلِّفِينَ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد إخلاص النبي في تبليغ الوحي: أنه لا يطلب من الناس مقابل مادي أو أجر دنيوي على دعوته، ولا هو من الذين يتصنعون أو يختلقون الكلام لأجل مصلحة أو لرفع مكانة؛Message هي رسالة أمينة موكلة إليه من الله لا مدفوعة الأجر أو بدافع تفاخر.

translation: Indeed, it is nothing but a reminder for the worlds.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that the message’s essential role is to admonish and awaken conscience across all peoples and realms: it is a universal call to remembrance of God, moral rectitude and accountability. Its power lies not in coercion but in its capacity to stir inward reflection—becoming guidance and mercy for those who respond, and a warning and testimony for those who persist in rejection.

translation: وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ نَبَأَهُ بَعْدَ حِينٍ — "And you will surely learn his affair after a while."
interpretation: Allah warns that those who deny or overlook the matter (the prophet’s message or the outcome He has decreed) will come to know its reality in due course; truth and the consequences of people’s choices are not always immediate but will be revealed in God’s appointed time, bringing clarity, accountability, and often regret for having rejected the warning.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All‑Wise.
interpretation: By describing the Book as from al‑ʿAzīz (the Almighty) and al‑Ḥakīm (the All‑Wise), the verse signals that the Qurʾān’s authority rests on divine power and purposeful wisdom: its teachings are not arbitrary human opinion but expressions of irresistible, sovereign guidance crafted with measured wisdom. This implies believers should trust and submit to its rulings and guidance even when immediate benefit or full understanding is not apparent, because they form part of a coherent, wisdom‑filled plan that overturns falsehood and brings ultimate good.

translation: Indeed We have revealed to you the Book in truth. So worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur’an is a true, divinely sent guide, and from that source of truth flows the command to devote one’s life exclusively to God. ‘Sincere to Him the religion’ (mukhlisan lahu al-dīn) means purifying inner intention and outward practice from hypocrisy, ostentation, or any form of partnership with God, so that belief, worship, ethics and social conduct are consistently aligned with God’s guidance rather than personal gain, custom or show. Thus acknowledgment of the revealed Book becomes the basis for an integrated, single-minded commitment to God in both inward disposition and outward deeds.

translation: Unquestionably, to Allah belongs the pure religion. And those who take protectors besides Him say, "We do not worship them except that they may bring us nearer to Allah in status." Indeed, Allah will judge between them concerning that in which they differ; indeed Allah does not guide one who is a liar, a disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true, sincere worship is due to God alone and rejects the pretext of taking intermediaries or deities as a means to reach Him. Those who claim they venerate other beings merely to obtain nearness to God are deceiving themselves: nearness, acceptance, and authority belong to God and cannot be legitimately delegated to created beings. The statement that Allah will judge between them indicates that claims about intercession or authority will be settled by divine judgment, not by human fabrication. The closing warning — that God does not guide the one who is a liar and an unbeliever — points to the moral consequence of inventing false claims or persisting in denial: such obstinacy severs one from divine guidance. In sum, the verse calls for exclusive devotion to God, exposes the invalidity of using intermediaries as independent conduits to Him, and links deliberate falsehood and rejection with the loss of guidance.

translation: If Allah had wished to take a son, He would have chosen from among what He creates whatever He willed. Exalted is He; He is Allah, the One, the Subduer.
interpretation: The verse repudiates any literal claim that God has offspring by affirming His absolute sovereignty and transcendence: nothing about divine reality requires biological relations, and if God were to “choose” a son it would be by His free act of creation, not because He needs or resembles His creatures. The rhetorical conditional thus undercuts anthropomorphic ascriptions and emphasizes God’s unique oneness and overpowering dominion (al‑Wāḥid al‑Qahhār).

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He coils the night over the day and coils the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon — each running its course for an appointed term. Unquestionably, He is the Exalted in Might, the Oft-Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse reads the alternation of night and day and the regulated motion of sun and moon as intentional signs of divine governance: the cosmos is not random but unfolds according to fixed, appointed limits (ajl musammā). By describing these phenomena as ‘wrapped’ and ‘subdued,’ the text emphasizes God’s absolute control over natural order; by pairing His names ‘the Exalted in Might’ and ‘the Forgiver,’ it teaches that this sovereign control is exercised alongside mercy. The implication for the believer is to recognize that events occur within a purposeful timetable determined by God, to trust that order, and to turn to Him for forgiveness and reliance within that divinely ordained framework.

translation: He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate; and He sent down for you of the grazing livestock eight pairs. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers — creation after creation — within three layers of darkness. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. There is no deity except Him; so how are you being turned away?
interpretation: The verse connects three things to call for recognition of God’s sole lordship and the moral posture that follows. First, the affirmation that all people come from one soul and its mate grounds human kinship and invalidates pride based on lineage or tribe; it underwrites obligations of mutual dignity and justice. Second, the reference to God’s provision (the paired livestock) and to the successive, vulnerable stages of embryonic formation in “three darknesses” highlights God’s intimate, continuous sovereignty over origin, life and sustenance — realities that cannot be reduced to chance or human control. Third, the rhetorical question at the end reproves those who ignore these manifest signs: given such clear evidence of God’s creative power and mercy, to turn away in worship, gratitude, or ethical responsibility is irrational and blameworthy. Thus the verse moves from cosmology and embryology to an ethical summons: recognize God’s oneness and dominion, live in humility and mutual responsibility, and cannot legitimately evade accountability before Him.

translation: Indeed, if you disbelieve, then Allah is free from need of you. And He does not approve for His servants disbelief. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you. And no bearer of burden will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s self-sufficiency means human rejection harms only the rejecter; Allah neither needs worship nor is pleased by disbelief among His servants, while sincere gratitude draws His acceptance. It establishes individual moral responsibility—sins and merits cannot be transferred from one person to another—and warns that everyone will return to God who will make known both outward deeds and inward intentions. Thus true accountability is comprehensive: actions and the inner states behind them matter, and one’s ultimate standing depends on personal responsibility and sincere gratitude or rejection.

translation: And when adversity touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him; then when He bestows on him a favor from Himself, he forgets what he used to call upon Him for before and sets up for Allah equals to mislead [others] from His way. Say, “Enjoy your disbelief a little; indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire.”
interpretation: This verse exposes a steady human tendency: distress strips away self-sufficiency and drives people back to sincere reliance on God, but relief often breeds ingratitude and a return to trusting created causes or companions in place of the Creator. The verse condemns that fickleness and the implicit idolatry of attributing ultimate power to others, warning that worldly comfort falsely enjoyed through such disbelief is fleeting and will not avert the inevitable consequence—being counted among the companions of the Fire. The prophet’s command to proclaim this is both a rebuke and a reminder that steadfast faith and continual gratitude, not situational devotion, define true submission to God.

translation: Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, who fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord—equal to one who does not? Say: “Are those who know and those who do not know equal?” Indeed, only people of understanding take heed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine spiritual excellence is rooted in knowledge that shapes the heart and conduct: when knowledge awakens awareness of the Hereafter it produces humble, purposeful worship (even in the night), a sober fear of consequences, and a hopeful reliance on God's mercy. This inner transformation creates a real moral and spiritual difference between those guided by understanding and those who remain heedless; therefore seeking true knowledge and letting it guide one’s deeds is what yields real distinction before God.

translation:
قُلْ يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا رَبَّكُمْ ۚ لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا فِي هَٰذِهِ الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةٌ ۗ وَأَرْضُ اللَّهِ وَاسِعَةٌ ۗ إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى الصَّابِرُونَ أَجْرَهُمْ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ

“Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is a good (portion); and the earth of Allah is wide. Indeed the patient will be given their reward without measure.”
interpretation: This verse is a consoling command and promise: the Prophet is to address the believing servants and call them to God-consciousness (taqwa), because true piety shapes conduct and destiny. God assures that sincere, upright action does not go unrewarded even in this life—righteous people receive a real, good portion here, not only in the afterlife—so believers should not despair of worldly well‑being when they act rightly. “The earth of Allah is wide” widens the horizon of hope and lawful options: it reminds the oppressed or constrained that opportunities, refuge and provision are not confined to one place, and that moving, seeking, or expanding one’s effort can be a legitimate response. Finally, the promise for the patient (sâbirîn) is emphatic and transcendent: perseverance in faith and upright conduct will be rewarded beyond accounting, affirming both divine justice and the supreme worth of steadfastness. Together the elements urge active piety, practical trust, and hopeful endurance rather than passivity or despair.

translation: Say, “I have been commanded to worship Allah, devoting the religion purely to Him.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that the prophetic duty is single-minded, inward-and-outward devotion to God alone: one’s faith, worship and way of life must be purified from any partners, innovations or mixed loyalties so that every act, intention and allegiance is oriented exclusively toward Allah. “Mukhliṣan lahu al-dīn” therefore means sincere, undivided commitment—a unity of heart, words and deeds submitted to God’s guidance and sovereignty.

translation: And I was commanded to be the first of the Muslims.
interpretation: The statement signifies a divine injunction that the speaker should not only submit to God but occupy the position of precedence in that submission — to be a living exemplar who embodies sincere surrender before calling others to it, thereby leading by prior personal obedience and setting the standard of true faith.

translation:
قُلْ إِنِّي أَخَافُ إِنْ عَصَيْتُ رَبِّي عَذَابَ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ
"Say, ‘I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.’"
interpretation: The speaker expresses a humble, personal recognition that disobedience to God carries real, grave consequences on the Day of Judgment; by voicing this fear he underscores moral responsibility and accountability, showing that even one chosen to convey God's message remains mindful of ultimate divine justice and uses that awareness to deter wrongdoing and uphold obedience.

translation: Say, “I worship Allah, devoting my religion sincerely to Him.”
interpretation: A command to embrace and profess pure monotheism: one’s worship, belief and whole way of life (dīn) must be directed solely to Allah with ikhlāṣ — inner sincerity free from ostentation, personal desire, cultural accretion, or association of partners. True devotion here is not merely outward ritual but a unified inner intention that shapes conduct, making submission to God exclusive, consistent, and uncompromised.

translation: فَاعْبُدُوا مَا شِئْتُمْ مِن دُونِهِ ۖ قُلْ إِنَّ الْخَاسِرِينَ الَّذِينَ خَسِرُوا أَنفُسَهُمْ وَأَهْلِيهِمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ۚ أَلَا ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ الْخُسْرَانُ الْمُبِينُ
interpretation: The verse challenges those who worship other deities: do as you will, but know that true ruin is spiritual and ultimate — it befalls those who destroy their own chance of guidance and salvation and lead their families into the same error. ‘Loss’ here is not mere worldly setback but the irreversible loss on the Day of Resurrection: deprivation of God’s mercy and the consequences that make their ruin plain and manifest.

translation: Above them are shades of fire and beneath them are shades [of fire]. Thus Allah makes His servants fearful by it. O My servants, then fear [Me].
interpretation: The verse uses the powerful image of being surrounded above and below by fire to explain that God deliberately presents the reality of consequence in stark terms so people awaken from heedlessness. The frightening picture is not mere spectacle but a pedagogical tool: by making the danger vivid He urges believers to take their duties seriously, repent, and reform. The address “O My servants” shows that the ultimate aim of this warning is mercy and guidance—fear is meant to prompt accountability and return to God, not to satisfy arbitrary wrath.

translation: وَالَّذِينَ اجْتَنَبُوا الطَّاغُوتَ أَنْ يُعْبَدُوهُ وَأَنَابُوا إِلَى اللَّهِ لَهُمْ الْبُشْرَى ۚ فَبَشِّرْ عِبَادِي
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن طريق النجاة والقبول الإلهي لا يمرّ فقط بالإيمان اللفظي بل بقطع الولاء عن الطاغوت — أية قوة أو طاغوتٍ يدعو للعبادة أو الطاعة الباطلة (الأوثان، الطغاة، الأهواء والأنظمة الفاسدة) — والرجوع الصادق إلى الله. الوعدُ بـ«البشرى» هنا يشمل رحمة الله وغفرانه وهداه واطمئنان القلب وثواب الآخرة، والنداء بـ«بشر عبادي/فبشِّر عباد» يهدف لتحفيز الناس على التوبة العملية والإقلاع عن اتباع الباطل بإيمانٍ عملي وصادق.

translation: Those who listen to the Word and follow the best of it — those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.
interpretation: The verse commends those who receive guidance attentively, weigh and discern what they hear, and then act upon the most sound, beneficial meaning or ruling; such attentive listening combined with choosing and implementing the best course is the mark of true guidance from God and of people of sound intellect (أُولُو الْأَلْبَاب).

translation: Is then he upon whom the word of punishment has come to be spared? Will you then rescue those in the Fire?
interpretation: The verse emphasizes the finality of God’s judgment: when God’s decree of punishment has been established against someone for persistent rejection and wrongdoing, no human intervention can nullify it. It teaches that ultimate authority over salvation and punishment rests with God alone, warns against presuming protection from others or intercession apart from God’s will, and calls people to take the warning seriously before divine judgment becomes unavoidable.

translation: But those who feared their Lord — for them are chambers built above them, beneath which rivers flow. That is the promise of Allah; and Allah never fails in His promise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that sincere God‑fearing leads to exalted, enduring reward in the Hereafter: the ‘‘chambers’’ depict elevated ranks and comfortable abodes in Paradise, constructed one above another to signify increased stations, with rivers flowing beneath to indicate continuous, life‑giving blessing and tranquility. By calling this a promise and declaring that Allah never breaks His pledge, the verse assures believers of the certainty and justice of divine recompense for piety.

translation: أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ أَنزَلَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً فَسَلَكَهُ يَنْبُوعًا فِي الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ يُخْرِجُ بِهِ زَرْعًا مُخْتَلِفًا أَلْوَانُهُ ثُمَّ يَهِيجُ فَتَرَاهُ مُصْفَرًّا ثُمَّ يَجْعَلُهُ حُطَامًا ۗ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَذِكْرَىٰ لِأُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ
interpretation: The verse presents the natural cycle of rain, growth, withering and disintegration as a deliberate sign meant to awaken reflection: it demonstrates God’s sovereign power to give life, to withdraw it, and to provide and disperse provisions. For those of sound understanding, this visible pattern confirms the reality of divine governance (including the possibility of resurrection and recompense), calls for humility and gratitude, and demands that one let such insight shape one’s faith and ethical conduct.

translation: أفمن شرح الله صدره للإسلام فهو على نور من ربه ۚ فويل للقاسية قلوبهم من ذكر الله ۚ أولئك في ضلال مبين
interpretation: The verse teaches that true acceptance of faith follows an inner, God-given opening — a spiritual expansion of the heart that makes guidance clear and becomes a light from the Lord, directing belief and action. In contrast, a heart made hard by neglect of God’s remembrance becomes insensitive to truth; the pronounced ‘woe’ warns that such hardness leads to evident misguidance and its consequences in both one’s moral life and ultimate standing before God.

translation: Allah has sent down the best discourse — a Book whose verses are harmonious and oft-repeated; the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver because of it, then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah. That is the guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills, and whoever Allah sends astray — for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’an’s superior eloquence and inner coherence are not merely literary qualities but means of spiritual impact: its clear, recurring verses stir awe and trembling in the believer’s whole being, and that initial fear (a visceral opening) is transformed into gentleness and attentiveness of heart toward God’s remembrance. This movement — experiential conviction leading to inner receptivity and right action — is described as God’s guidance, a divine gift granted to some; conversely, persistent rejection or hardness produces a state in which God withdraws that guiding light, leaving the person without true guidance. Thus the passage links the Qur’an’s message, the soul’s embodied response, and the ultimate dependence of guidance on God’s will.

translation:
أفمن يتقي بوجهه سوء العذاب يوم القيامة ۚ وقيل للظالمين ذوقوا ما كنتم تكسبون
“Is then the one who is guarded from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection [to be regarded as the same]? And it will be said to the wrongdoers, ‘Taste what you used to earn.’”
interpretation: The verse uses a rhetorical contrast to affirm divine justice: deliverance on the Day of Resurrection belongs to those who truly guarded themselves—by sincere God‑fearing and avoidance of wrong—so they are spared the worst of chastisement, while those who oppressed or persisted in sin will be confronted with the direct consequences of their deeds. The command “taste what you used to earn” stresses moral responsibility and that punishment is the fitting outcome of one’s own actions, not an arbitrary fate.

translation: كَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ فَأَتَاهُمُ الْعَذَابُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ
interpretation: الآية تحذر أن الإصرار على إنكار الحق واغترار الناس بأمانهم يؤدي إلى هلاكٍ مفاجئ من جهات غير متوقعة؛ فما يظنّه المكذّبون أمانًا قد يخفي مقدماتٍ للعقاب. العبرة أنها دعوة للتواضع والتمحيص والتوبة قبل أن تأتي نتيجة الأفعال فجأة وبطرق لا يتصورونها.

translation:
فأذاقهم الله الخزي في الحياة الدنيا ۖ ولعذاب الآخرة أكبر ۚ لو كانوا يعلمون
"So Allah made them taste humiliation in the life of this world; and the punishment of the Hereafter is greater—if they only knew."
interpretation: The verse warns that those who persist in rejecting guidance or in following vain, self‑serving courses are permitted by God to suffer disgrace and loss in this world as a sign of His displeasure. That worldly humiliation is only a brief foretaste; the true and far more severe retribution awaits in the Hereafter. The phrase “if they only knew” reproaches their ignorance of reality—their failure to recognise the fleeting nature of worldly honour and the long‑term consequences of their choices; had they understood, they would abandon what leads to ruin and turn to what secures lasting success.

translation: And We have certainly presented for people in this Qur’an every kind of example, so that they might take heed.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah delivers His message through a variety of examples—stories, parables, legal illustrations and signs—so the guidance can speak to different minds and circumstances; the purpose is not mere information but to stir remembrance, reflection and moral change, prompting listeners to internalize the lessons and alter their beliefs and behavior toward God.

translation: An Arabic Qur'an, free of crookedness, that they might become righteous.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the revelation was given in the clear, familiar language of its initial audience and is composed without distortion or internal contradiction so that there remains no linguistic or rational excuse to miss its guidance; its primary aim is transformative—clearing away confusion so people can come to God‑consciousness (taqwa) and correct their conduct.

translation: ضرب الله مثلاً رجلاً فيه شركاء متشاكسون، ورجلًا سلِمًا لرجلٍ؛ هل يستويان مثلاً؟ الحمد لله، بل أكثرهم لا يعلمون.
interpretation: الآية تصوّر فرقًا جوهريًا بين حالة الانقسام والاختلاف في المعتقد والعمل من جهة، وحالة الانقياد والوحْدة في الولاء والاستقامة من جهة أخرى. الرجل «فيه شركاء متشاكسون» رمز لمن يشتت ولاءه بين آلهة أو قوى متنازعة فتنتج عنه تناقضات وضعف في الهداية، بينما «الرجل سلِمًا لرجل» يرمز لمن يسلم نفسه لرب واحد فيتصف بثبات ووضوح الطريق. المقارنة إذًا تبيّن أن توحيد العبادة والانقياد لله لا يقوم مقامه تشتت الشركاء، ومع ذلك كثير من الناس لا يدركون هذا البين.

translation: Indeed, you will die, and they will die.
interpretation: A divine reminder that death is the inevitable fate of every human being, including the Prophet and his adversaries; it equalizes worldly status and urges detachment from temporary disputes and consolations, directing attention instead to preparing for the Hereafter, where deeds and God’s judgment determine one’s ultimate outcome.

translation: ثم إنكم يوم القيامة عند ربكم تختصمون — "Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection you will dispute before your Lord."
interpretation: The verse warns that all people will be brought to stand directly before God to present their cases and make their claims; at that moment every worldly argument, reputation or alliance will be exposed and weighed by divine knowledge and justice, so efforts to evade responsibility, shift blame, or rely on mere words will fail. Its purpose is to awaken accountability: prepare now with sincere faith and righteous deeds, for final adjudication belongs solely to God and will render all disputes resolved by truth and proof rather than rhetoric.

translation: So who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah and denies the truth when it has come to him? Is there not in Hell a dwelling-place for the disbelievers?
interpretation: The verse denounces those who willfully fabricate falsehoods about God and reject clear guidance when it reaches them; such rejection is portrayed as the height of injustice because it knowingly repudiates truth and misleads others. By posing the rhetorical question and invoking Hell as the destined abode, the passage warns that persistent denial of divine truth—born of arrogance, malice, or self-interest—brings grave moral culpability and final, severe consequences, stressing the duty to receive guidance sincerely rather than to falsify or dismiss it.

translation:
وَالَّذِي جَاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ وَصَدَّقَهُ ۚ أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُتَّقُونَ
"And the one who brings the truth and believes in it — those are the righteous."
interpretation: The verse affirms that true piety consists in recognizing, affirming and living by the truth: those who either present the truth or accept it when it appears, and whose belief corresponds to that truth, are counted among the God‑fearing. Righteousness is therefore measured not by outward rituals alone but by sincere acceptance of and conformity to what is true.

translation: For them is whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the recompense of the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse affirms that those who live righteously will receive from God the fulfillment of their deepest legitimate longings in His presence: not merely transient worldly gains but complete gladness, satisfaction, and nearness to God, with every real need and desire met as a just and generous reward for their moral excellence.

translation: That Allah may blot out from them the worst of what they did and reward them their due for the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's transforming mercy: when people sincerely turn to Him and persist in good, Allah can erase their worst deeds from their record and treat them according to their best actions. It encourages hope and continual striving in righteousness, while implying that forgiveness is connected to genuine repentance and a commitment to improve rather than a license to persist in wrongdoing.

translation: Is Allah not sufficient for His servant? Yet they frighten you with those besides Him; and whoever Allah leads astray—there is for him no guide.
interpretation: The verse affirms that true sufficiency and protection belong to Allah alone: a sincere servant who relies on God need not be overwhelmed by threats or intimidation linked to other powers, idols, or influential people. Those who use scare tactics to divert trust away from God are offering nothing real; ultimate safety and guidance come only from Allah. Consequently, if a person persists in rejecting or opposing divine guidance and Allah withdraws His guiding light, no created being can substitute as a true guide—loss of God’s guidance brings spiritual misdirection and helplessness. The practical lesson is to place one’s trust in Allah rather than be intimidated by worldly authorities or false deities, and to seek and preserve the guidance that only He grants.

translation: And whoever Allah guides—there is none who can misguide him. Is not Allah Mighty, Owner of Retribution?
interpretation: The verse teaches that true guidance is granted by God alone and, once given, cannot ultimately be undone by people or forces that attempt to mislead. It emphasizes Allah’s absolute sovereignty and power: He decides who receives guidance and He has the strength and authority to enforce justice and requital. Believers are therefore invited to seek and trust divine guidance, confident that human opposition cannot prevail against what God has firmly set, while those who persist in misguidance are subject to His recompense.

translation: And if you were to ask them, ‘Who created the heavens and the earth?’ they would surely say, ‘God.’ Say, ‘Then have you considered those whom you invoke besides God? If God intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?’ Say, ‘God is sufficient for me.’ Upon Him the reliant put their trust.
interpretation: The verse exposes the contradiction of acknowledging God as Creator while relying on powerless idols or intermediaries: ultimate harm and mercy are determined solely by God, and no created being can avert His decree or seize His mercy. Hence the believer’s proper response is sincere tawakkul—declaring “Hasbiyallāh” and placing full trust in God alone, since He alone is truly capable of protecting and providing.

translation: قُلْ يَا قَوْمِ اعْمَلُوا عَلَى مَكَانَتِكُمْ إِنِّي عَامِلٌ ۖ فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ
interpretation: الآية تعبّر عن موقف حازم وواثق: النبي يخبر قومه بأنه لن يتخلى عن أداء رسالته ولا ينقيص من حقهم في التصرف، ويترك النتائج لتُظهرها الوقائع أو الحساب الإلهي. «اعملوا على مكانتكم» ليست مجرد استسلام بل تحدّ لتصرفاتهم وأسلوب حياتهم، و«إني عامل» إقرار بالوفاء بالواجب النبوي، أما «فسوف تعلمون» فتنبيه بأن الحق سيُبْنَى ويُبَيَّن عبر ما يترتب من آثار، فتنجلي تبعات الطاعة والمعصية، ويظهر جزاء كل قوم على ما كسبوا.

translation: Whoever is overtaken by a punishment, it will disgrace him, and upon him will befall an abiding (everlasting) punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that when God’s punishment comes upon a person — as a consequence of persistent rejection of guidance or sustained wrongdoing — it brings humiliation and loss of honor, and for those whose actions merit it the chastisement is lasting; 'disgrace' conveys both worldly abasement and spiritual ruin, while 'abiding punishment' indicates a permanent consequence in the Hereafter for those who remain obstinate.

translation: Indeed We have sent down to you the Book for the people in truth. So whoever is guided, he is guided for the benefit of his own soul; and whoever goes astray, then he only goes astray to its detriment. And you are not a guardian over them.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur’an is a truthful, universal message offered to humanity, but it makes clear that receiving its benefit depends on each person's response: guidance accrues to and benefits the individual who follows it, while misguidance harms the individual who rejects it. The phrase “and you are not a guardian over them” limits the Prophet’s (and by extension any teacher’s or leader’s) role to conveying the message—he cannot compel belief or bear the moral burden of others’ choices. The practical teaching is personal moral responsibility and accountability before God: guidance is provided, but each soul must choose and will be judged for that choice.

translation: Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die He takes during their sleep; then He withholds the one whose death He has decreed and sends the others back until an appointed term. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over life and death: sleep is a temporary withdrawal of the soul, while death is its final taking according to God’s decree. By retaining souls whose time has come and returning others until their appointed term, God demonstrates control, wisdom, and the reality of divinely ordained lifespan, calling people to reflect on their dependence, the certainty of resurrection and judgment, and to orient their lives in light of that accountability.

translation: Or have they taken, apart from Allah, intercessors? Say: “Even if they existed, they would possess nothing and would not be able to understand.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes the practice of setting up intermediaries or partners besides God: such supposed intercessors have no real power, ownership, or intellect to benefit or decide for others. By commanding the Prophet to say this, God exposes the futility of trusting beings or idols as sources of authority or mediation, reminding people that true control and judgment belong to God alone and that claims of independent intercession are baseless.

translation: Say, “To Allah belongs all intercession. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; then to Him you will be returned.”
interpretation: The verse asserts that any intercession on behalf of creatures is ultimately under God’s control and cannot occur independently of His will. By declaring His exclusive ownership of the heavens and the earth and the inevitable return to Him, it emphasizes divine sovereignty, the dependence of all created beings on God’s mercy and permission, and the futility of relying on any intermediary as having autonomous authority. The statement serves to direct hope, fear and ultimate accountability to God alone, reminding people that whatever role others may play in the hereafter is only what God grants.

translation: When Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink with aversion; but when those [beings or things] are mentioned besides Him, behold, they are joyful.
interpretation: The verse shows that people’s emotional responses reveal where their ultimate trust and hope lie: reminders of God alone and the reality of the Hereafter provoke disgust and repulsion in those whose allegiance is elsewhere, because such reminders confront their comforts, excuses and accountability; conversely, mention of other deities, authorities, or beloved worldly supports brings them pleasure because it affirms the false securities they prefer. Thus the reaction itself is a sign of a heart turned away from divine truth and attached to substitutes, exposing the moral and spiritual condition that will determine their standing before God.

translation: Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You will judge between Your servants concerning that in which they used to differ."
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone — as Creator and all‑knowing — is the ultimate arbiter of human disagreements; it urges surrender of partisan claims to divine judgment, reminding believers that their limited, contested views will be judged rightly by One who knows both the hidden realities and the outward facts.

translation: And if those who did wrong had all that is on earth and the like of it with it, they would indeed offer it as ransom to avert the worst of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection; but there will appear to them from Allah that which they did not reckon.
interpretation: The verse teaches that no amount of worldly wealth can save wrongdoers from God's judgment: even if they could pay with all the earth and twice as much, they would still be unable to avert the severe punishment of the Hereafter, for Allah will bring upon them an unexpected consequence—punishment, humiliation, or incontrovertible proof of their deeds—that they never anticipated, demonstrating that material means cannot buy forgiveness or escape accountability.

translation: And the evil of what they had earned became apparent to them, and that which they used to mock encompassed them.
interpretation: When people are held to account, the harmful consequences of their own deeds are made clear to them; the very warnings, signs, or punishments they once ridiculed now overtake and surround them, showing that derision of truth does not prevent the inevitable result of one's actions.

translation: When adversity touches man, he calls upon Us; then when We bestow on him a favor from Us, he says, “I was given it only because of knowledge.” Nay — it is but a trial, yet most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse warns that blessings themselves can be divine tests designed to reveal a person’s inner state: whether they remain humble and thankful or grow proud and attribute success solely to their own knowledge. Many fail to see favors as trials and become self‑sufficient and ungrateful; the intended lesson is to recognize dependence on God in both hardship and ease, respond with gratitude, and use gifts in ways that reflect faith and humility.

translation: Those before them had already said it, yet what they used to earn did not avail them.
interpretation: The verse warns that earlier nations likewise dismissed the warning and relied on their worldly gains, status, or deeds; those possessions and accomplishments did not protect them from God’s judgment, so worldly advantage and self‑assurance cannot avert the consequences of disbelief or wrongdoing.

translation: So the evils of what they had earned befell them. And those among these who were unjust — evils of what they had earned will strike them, and they will not be able to avert them.
interpretation: The verse asserts that suffering and punishment come as a direct consequence of people’s own wrongful deeds: the unjust among them will be overtaken by the harm their actions brought, and they will be powerless to avert God’s retribution, emphasizing personal moral responsibility and the inevitability of divine justice.

translation: Have they not known that Allah expands provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sustenance (rizq) is ultimately dispensed by God’s will: He widens it for some and limits it for others according to wisdom beyond human sight. This variability is not a reliable measure of a person’s moral worth or God’s favor but a means to test and refine hearts—to awaken gratitude, patience, trust in God, humility, and to stimulate social responsibility (charity and support for the needy). Believers who ponder this recognise Allah’s sovereignty over provision, avoid equating wealth with virtue, accept divine decree with contentment, and translate that acceptance into ethical action toward others.

translation: قُلْ يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَى أَنفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا مِن رَّحْمَةِ اللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا ۚ إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ
interpretation: الله هنا يخاطب بالخصوص من أساء إلى نفسه بالمعاصي أو بالغ في الباطل ليقطع عليهم طريق اليأس من رحمته: اليأس من رحمة الله مذموم لأن الله واسع المغفرة. تأكيد أن «يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا» يعني أن لا جرم مستثنى من قدرة الله على المسامحة إذا توافرت شروط التوبة الصادقة — الندم الحقيقي، الإقلاع عن الذنب، والعزم على عدم العودة، ومع مطلق رحمته لا يُستعمل هذا البيان كذريعة للإثم. أسماء الله «الغفور الرحيم» تبرز جانبي الصفح والعطف: يغفر الذنوب وينزل رحمته على التائبين، فالمقصود دعوة عملية للرجوع والإصلاح النفسي والعملي، وقطع طريق اليأس الذي يعيق التوبة.

translation: And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you; then you will not be helped.
interpretation: The verse urgently calls for sincere inner return to God and wholehearted submission now, warning that if one delays until divine punishment arrives there will be no possibility of rescue—so salvation depends on timely, genuine repentance and acceptance of God before consequences make change impossible.

translation: And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you are unaware.
interpretation: The verse urges immediate commitment to the most excellent, core guidance of revelation — morally and theologically sound teachings that lead to right belief and conduct — rather than clinging to partial, self‑serving readings or delaying reform. It warns that divine reproof can overtake people unexpectedly (بغتة) when they are heedless (لا تشعرون), so one must urgently adopt the highest principles of the message and enact them in life to avert sudden disaster.

translation: “That a soul should say, ‘O my regret for what I neglected in regard to Allah, and indeed I was among the mockers.’”
interpretation: The verse portrays the irreversible remorse of one who, having treated God’s guidance lightly and joined in mockery, realizes too late the loss that neglect and ridicule have brought; its point is ethical and soteriological—mocking or neglecting duties toward God leads to a final, inescapable regret on the Day of Reckoning, so sincere repentance and earnest observance must come now, not after the opportunity has passed.

translation: Or you might say, “If Allah had guided me, I would surely have been among the righteous.”
interpretation: The verse reports a common, self‑serving excuse of those who reject guidance: they pretend that lack of guidance, not their own choices, is the reason for their ungodliness. It exposes this as a form of self‑deception and blame‑shifting—true guidance is tied to sincere seeking, acceptance of clear signs and consequent righteous action, so one cannot legitimately claim hypothetical piety as a defense when one has rejected the means of guidance and persisted in wrongdoing.

translation: أو تقول حين ترى العذاب: «لَوْ أَنَّ لِي كَرَّةً فَأَكُونَ مِنَ المُحسِنِينَ»
interpretation: الآية تَحمل تحذيراً من المضي في المماطلة والتسويف في الطاعة؛ فهي تصف ندم المبطلين عند مواجهة الجزاء ورغبتهم بعودة زمنية ليصححوا ما فاتهم، وتُعلِم أن الأمل في «كرّة» بعد الموت باطل فعلاً؛ الفرصة للعمل الصالح موجودة الآن، ومن يؤجلها يفتقد الخلاص حين يبلغ الجزاء.

translation:
بلى قد جاءتك آياتي فكذبت بها واستكبرت وكنت من الكافرين
“Nay — My signs have indeed come to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers.”
interpretation: The verse asserts that clear divine evidence was presented to the addressee, so their failure to accept it was not due to absence of proof but a deliberate rejection born of pride; that combination of denial and arrogance defines their spiritual state as disbelief. It teaches that accountability rests on how one responds to manifest guidance — when a person willfully repudiates truth out of self-exaltation, that attitude itself constitutes disbelief and brings moral consequence.

translation: And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about Allah — their faces will be blackened. Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?
interpretation: The verse warns that those who deny, distort, or falsely accuse God out of pride will be publicly disgraced on the Day of Judgment: the “blackened faces” signify visible humiliation reflecting inner moral corruption. The rhetorical question emphasizes that Hell is the fitting and deserved dwelling for the arrogant — those whose pride prevented them from submitting to divine truth and led them to reject guidance.

translation:
وَيُنَجِّي اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا بِمَفَازَتِهِمْ ۚ لَا يُمَسُّهُمُ السُّوءُ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ
"And Allah will rescue those who are God‑conscious by granting them deliverance; no evil shall touch them, nor shall they grieve."
interpretation: The verse assures that true God‑consciousness (taqwa) results in divine rescue: 'mufazat' signifies decisive salvation and protection—both the inner security that preserves faith and hope, and the final deliverance on the Day of Reckoning.
