Because of their reverence and trust in God, such people are kept from ultimate harm and from enduring sorrow as a settled state; trials may occur, but they will not culminate in ruin or despair, for God safeguards their outcome and grants them peace.

translation: Allah is the Creator of all things; and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute sovereignty: He is the originator of every existence and the one who governs, sustains and executes outcomes. The word wakīl conveys both care and authoritative control — God arranges provisions, protection, and the course of events while holding creation accountable. Practically this calls for humble trust (tawakkul) in His wisdom and governance and for responsible action by humans within the framework of His comprehensive oversight.

translation: To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah — those are the losers.
interpretation: The verse stresses that ultimate authority and governance over the cosmos rest with God — the notion of “keys” denotes control over destiny, provision, life and death, and the laws that sustain existence. Rejecting God’s signs is therefore self-defeating: it severs one from the guidance, moral ordering, and means by which true well‑being and salvation are attained, so that the disbelievers incur a comprehensive loss both in this life (loss of guidance, blessings, and rightly ordered living) and most importantly in the Hereafter (deprivation of eternal success).

translation: Say, “Is it other than Allah that you would have me worship, O you ignorant ones?”
interpretation: This verse is a forceful, rhetorical repudiation of being obliged by people to worship anything or anyone besides God. By addressing the question to those who insist on such worship as “the ignorant,” it indicts the moral and intellectual error of substituting created beings, social conventions, or leaders for the Creator. The command thus affirms exclusive devotion to God (tawḥīd), insists that true obedience cannot be transferred to human demands that contradict divine guidance, and calls for courage and clarity of conscience in resisting communal pressure to adopt false objects of worship.

translation: And indeed it was revealed to you and to those before you: 'If you associate others with Allah, then surely your deeds will be rendered void, and you will surely be among the losers.'
interpretation: The verse warns that shirk (ascribing partners or ultimate objects of worship alongside God) fundamentally corrupts the acceptability of one’s actions: when the ultimate intention or devotion is divided, acts of worship and moral deeds lose their status before God and therefore no longer yield spiritual reward or success. By saying this was revealed to earlier prophets as well, the verse makes monotheism the essential condition for deeds to be accepted and for one to attain true success rather than spiritual loss.

translation: Nay — worship Allah and be among the grateful.
interpretation: This rebukes turning to false alternatives and emphasizes that true devotion to God must be exclusive and coupled with gratitude: being “among the grateful” is not mere lip‑service but an active stance of heart and deed that acknowledges God’s favors by obeying Him, using His blessings responsibly, giving thanks in prosperity and patience in trial, and thereby manifesting sincere worship.

translation: They have not estimated Allah at His true worth; indeed, on the Day of Resurrection the whole earth will be within His grasp, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Exalted is He and far above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the spiritual and intellectual failure to recognize God as He truly deserves—an error that has moral and eschatological consequences. The metaphors (the earth in His grip, the heavens folded in His right hand) stress absolute divine sovereignty and control at the Final Reckoning: nothing in creation is independent of His authority, and all will be brought into His presence for judgment. Reading these images correctly also affirms God’s transcendence (He is exalted beyond partners) and warns that any human attempts to liken, share, or diminish His lordship are vain and will be nullified when His full power is manifest.

translation: And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall dead, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and at once they will be standing, looking on.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate power over life and death belongs to God: the Trumpet’s blasts symbolize His ability to bring absolute cessation and then immediate restoration of creation so all may stand for reckoning. The exception “except whom Allah wills” highlights His sovereign choice and mercy in who is spared, and the whole scene is a solemn reminder of the certainty of resurrection and the necessity of living in readiness for divine judgment.

translation: And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, and the Record will be set down; and the prophets and the witnesses will be brought, and judgment will be passed between them in truth — and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Reckoning when God’s presence and truth become manifest: the world is illumined by divine light as a sign that all concealment and doubt are removed; the Book (the definitive register of deeds and arguments) is placed before creation as the incontestable basis for judgment; the Prophets and those called to witness are brought forward to attest to the truth and to settle disputes about guidance and responsibility. The judgment that follows is absolute and perfectly just — every claim is weighed by clear evidence, the truthful are vindicated, and no one suffers injustice. In short, it affirms that on the final day God’s light, the clear record, and authoritative witnesses ensure complete, equitable adjudication.

translation: Every soul will be fully recompensed for what it has done, and He is most knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse asserts that ultimate justice is inevitable: on the final accounting each person will receive recompense precisely according to their deeds. Because God’s knowledge encompasses outward acts, inward motives, and the contexts that shape actions, the settlement will be comprehensive and perfectly fair—no action is forgotten and no hidden intention escapes divine awareness, so reward or punishment will correspond to the true moral reality of each life.

translation: And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups. Until, when they come to it, its gates are opened and its keepers will say to them, “Did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?” They will say, “Yes, but the decree of punishment has come into effect upon the disbelievers.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s messengers had clearly conveyed guidance and warnings, so the ultimate punishment that unfolds is not arbitrary but the just consequence of willful rejection after being informed. The scene—people driven in groups, the gates opening, and the custodians’ question—serves to expose that the condemned themselves acknowledge receiving the message; their admission confirms the truth of the warning and removes any excuse. Thus the passage emphasizes moral responsibility, the certainty of accountability, and that enduring denial of guidance leads inevitably to the fulfillment of God’s just decree.

translation: It will be said, "Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein." Evil indeed is the abode of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse teaches that arrogance — the refusal to submit to God's truth, to recognize moral accountability, or to show humility toward others — leads to final and irreversible estrangement from divine mercy. The image of being ordered to enter the gates of Hell stresses complete exclusion and permanence, and the phrase "evil is the abode of the arrogant" underscores that pride, by blocking repentance and turning one away from guidance, brings ruin rather than honor.

translation: And those who feared their Lord will be led to Paradise in ranks. When they arrive and its gates are opened and its keepers say to them, “Peace be upon you; you have been well—enter it, abiding (therein),”
interpretation: The verse presents the reward for God‑consciousness (taqwa) as both communal honor and lasting peace. Being “led in ranks” (سِيقَ ... زَمْراً) emphasizes that the righteous enter together, with dignity and mutual support rather than isolated entry, reflecting the social dimension of salvation and the removal of envy or rivalry. The opening of the gates and the words of the keepers signify divine recognition: the inhabitants of Paradise are greeted with a formal benediction—“Peace be upon you”—which affirms the completion of their trials and the security of their state. طِبْتُمْ (“you have been well” / “you have become pure”) is an official attestation that their deeds and character have been accepted, and خَالِدِينَ denotes the permanence of the reward, not merely long life but an unending, settled felicity. Thus the verse teaches that sincere God‑consciousness leads to communal admission into an assured, honored, and eternal abode granted by God’s explicit felicitations.

translation:
وَقَالُوا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي صَدَقَنَا وَعْدَهُ وَأَوْرَثَنَا الْأَرْضَ نَتَبَوَّأُ مِنَ الْجَنَّةِ حَيْثُ نَشَاءُ ۖ فَنِعْمَ أَجْرُ الْعَامِلِينَ

"And they will say, ‘Praise be to Allah who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us heirs of the earth, so we may take up residence in Paradise wherever we wish. How excellent is the reward of those who worked.’"
interpretation: The verse teaches that in the hereafter the righteous will recognize God’s absolute faithfulness in granting them what He promised: not merely a transfer of possession but the settlement in a state of secure, dignified enjoyment and freedom within Paradise. “Inheriting the earth” signifies the reversal of worldly humiliation into lasting honor and established peace, and “the excellent reward of the workers” affirms that sincere, steadfast striving in obedience to God—despite hardship—is met with a perfectly fitting and abundant recompense.

translation: And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, praising the praise of their Lord; and judgment will be passed between them in truth, and it will be said, “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine governance is both majestic and perfectly just: the angels’ encirclement and perpetual glorification signify a cosmic order in which God’s decrees are enacted with full knowledge and wisdom. When matters are decided “بِالْحَقّ” (in truth), the appropriate, universal response is the declaration “Al‑hamdu lillāh rabb al‑‘ālamīn,” acknowledging that every judgment and outcome — even those beyond human understanding — rests within God’s wise, sovereign care and merits wholehearted praise.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ḥāʼ Mīm.
interpretation: The disconnected letters “Ḥāʼ Mīm” belong to the Qur’anic muqaṭṭaʿāt and their full, literal significance is known only to God; their presence functions as a divine sign that draws attention to the revelation and underscores the Qur’an’s miracle — that its inimitable meaning and power arise from the same ordinary letters of human speech, yet cannot be reproduced by human effort.

translation: A revelation of the Book from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the All‑Knowing.
interpretation: The phrase asserts that the Qur'an is a divine revelation whose source is God; calling Him al‑'Aziz emphasizes His sovereign power to establish and protect the truth, while calling Him al‑'Alim affirms that the message rests on perfect, comprehensive knowledge — together implying the scripture’s absolute authority, preservation from corruption, and suitability as wise guidance that rightly judges and corrects human beliefs and behavior.

translation: The Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of vastness; there is no deity except Him—unto Him is the final return.
interpretation: The verse teaches a single moral and spiritual lesson: God’s attributes of mercy and justice coexist and demand responsibility. Because He forgives and accepts sincere repentance, people are urged to turn back and reform; because He is also capable of severe punishment and is sovereign in enduring, far‑reaching power, one must not be complacent or presume upon His mercy. The affirmation of God’s uniqueness and that everyone ultimately returns to Him frames life as a moment to seek forgiveness, act righteously, and live with consciousness of accountability before the One who alone can pardon or judge.

translation:
ما يجادل في آيات الله إلا الذين كفروا؛ فلا يغرنك تقلبهم في البلاد.
"None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve; so let not their roaming about in the land deceive you."
interpretation: The verse teaches that arguing against God's clear signs comes from rejection, not from sincere pursuit of truth; the visible mobility, prosperity or influence of such people as they move through towns and countries is not a sign of divine approval. Believers should not be misled by their apparent ease or success—these are temporary worldly conditions and not proof of truth—so remain steadfast in faith and trust that ultimate judgment and recompense belong to God alone.

translation: قَـد كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ وَالأَحْزَابُ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ. وَهَمَّتْ كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ بِرَسُولِهَا لِيَأخُذُوهُ، وَجَادَلُوا بِالبَاطِلِ لِيُدْحِضُوا بِهِ الحَقَّ، فَأَخَذْنَاهُمْ. فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عِقَابُ (اللَّهِ)؟
interpretation: الآية تذكر في صورة تحذير أن تاريخ الأمم شهد أن الذين كفروا برسُلات الله ولم يكتفوا بالإنكار بل تآمروا على رسولهم وحاولوا إسكات الحق بالجدال الباطل انتهوا إلى أخذ الله لهم بعقابٍ جلاء. المقصود تفسيرًا واحدًا هو أن الآية تؤكد حتمية الجزاء الإلهي على من يرفض الرسالة ويستعمل الحيل والظلم لطمس الحق: محاولات الاستئصال والإقناع الباطل لن تنجح في الوقوف أمام الحقيقة، والنتيجة ستكون لقاء العقاب الذي أعدّه الله لمن يصرّ على العناد والظلم.

translation: And thus the word of your Lord has come true concerning those who disbelieved: that they are the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse affirms the certainty and fulfillment of God’s decree: those who persistently reject guidance bring upon themselves the consequences foretold by God, becoming inhabitants of Hell. It emphasizes divine justice and inevitability rather than caprice, serving both as a solemn warning to deter continued disbelief and as an assurance that God’s promises and punishments will be realized unless one repents and turns to Him.

translation: Those who bear the Throne and those around it exalt the praise of their Lord, and they believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believed: "Our Lord, Your mercy and knowledge encompass all things; so forgive those who have repented and followed Your way and protect them from the punishment of the Hellfire."
interpretation: The verse conveys that even the angels closest to God intercede for believers, appealing to God’s infinite mercy and perfect knowledge; it teaches that sincere repentance and following God’s path are the means by which people are brought within that mercy, so divine pardon and protection from Hell are both possible and to be hoped for for those who turn back to God and walk His way.

translation: Our Lord, admit them to the Gardens of ʻAdn which You have promised them and whoever among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring was righteous. Indeed You are the Almighty, the Wise.
interpretation: This is a supplication asking God to grant entry into the promised eternal paradise not only to the believers themselves but also to those of their close kin who were upright; it affirms that God’s mercy and promise extend to righteous family members while making clear that righteousness — not mere relation — is the condition, and by invoking God’s attributes “Al‑ʿAzīz” (the Mighty) and “al‑Hakīm” (the Wise) the prayer expresses trust that He has both the power and the perfect wisdom to fulfill His promise justly and beneficently.

translation:
وَيَقِهِمُ السَّيِّئَاتِ. وَمَنْ يُقْـهِ السَّيِّئَاتِ يَوْمَئِذٍ فَقَدْ رَحِمَتُهُ ۚ وَذَٰلِكَ هُوَ الْفَوْزُ الْعَظِيمُ

"And [may He] protect them from evils. And whoever is protected from the evils of that Day—then that is His mercy upon him—and that is the great attainment."
interpretation: The verse affirms that the ultimate good is God’s sparing a person from the harms and punishments of the Day of Reckoning. Salvation from those evils is presented as an act of divine mercy rather than merely a consequence of human effort; receiving that mercy—being shielded from chastisement and admitted to God’s favor—is the supreme success and true victory.

translation: إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنَادُونَ: «أَلَعَنَةُ اللَّهِ أَشَدُّ مِنْ مَقْتِكُمْ أَنْفُسَكُمْ إِذْ تَدْعُونَ إِلَى الْإِيمَانِ فَتُكَفِّرُونَ»
interpretation: الآية تصوّر لَفْظَ سُخريةٍ وادعاءٍ من جانب المكذبين: إنهم يتهمون الداعين إلى الإيمان بأنهم يَخْشُونُ عذابَ الله أكثر من حرصهم على مصلحتهم الشخصية، وكأن دعوة الإيمان تجلبُ لهم ضرراً في الدنيا. المقصود بالتفسير أن هذا الاتهام يكشف عن جهل وانقلابٍ في الرؤية لدى الكافرين: ما يظنّونه هلاكاً للمدعوين هو في الحقيقة خلاص لهم لو قبلوا الله، ومن يرفض الإيمان هو الذي يُهلك نفسه؛ وفي اتهامهم هذا يظهر تضليلهم وتبريرهم لعدم قبول الحق بوصفه "خطرًا" على مصالحهم الدنيوية.

translation: They will say, “Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice, and we confess our sins; is there any way of escape?”
interpretation: This verse depicts the remorse of wrongdoers confronted with divine judgment: their phrase “You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice” signals recognition of God’s control over the cycles of existence and the repeated chances they were granted. Their confession and plea for escape come too late — it exposes that they received opportunities and warnings in life but persisted in rejection, so belated acknowledgment cannot avert the prescribed consequences. The passage therefore warns that sincere repentance must come while opportunity remains, for posthumous regret offers no effective deliverance.

translation: That is because when Allah alone is invoked, you disbelieve; but if He is associated with others, you believe. So the judgment belongs to Allah, the Exalted, the Great.
interpretation: The verse censures a hypocritical response to religion: some reject pure, uncompromising monotheism yet accept a version of faith that mixes God with intermediaries or culturally acceptable partners. It exposes how social, political, or emotional attachments can lead people to favor a diluted faith that preserves their interests. The reminder that “the judgment belongs to Allah, the Exalted, the Great” stresses that ultimate authority and final reckoning are God's alone, so human attempts to relativize or redefine divine truth will not change His sovereignty and people will be held accountable for accepting or rejecting true tawhīd.

translation: He is the One who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the heaven; and none take heed except those who turn (to Him in repentance).
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s visible signs in creation and the sustenance that comes from heaven are meant as practical proofs and reminders of His lordship and mercy. Yet such external signs only become spiritually effective for those who inwardly return to God—who abandon self-sufficiency, humble themselves, repent, and seek closeness to Him; it is this turning (ninabah) that opens the heart to remembrance, gratitude, and rightly seeing those signs as evidence of the Divine.

translation: So call upon Allah, dedicating the religion to Him sincerely, even if the disbelievers dislike it.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to direct their worship, supplication, and way of life exclusively to God with inner sincerity (ikhlāṣ), making devotion and religious commitment purely for Him. It insists on steadfastness and moral courage: one must continue to pray, live, and invite others to the truth without compromising core belief or seeking the approval of opponents, because genuine intention and fidelity to God matter more than the dislike or rejection of disbelievers.

translation: High in ranks, Owner of the Throne — He casts the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting.
interpretation: The verse proclaims God’s supreme authority and that, by His will, He appoints and empowers chosen servants with the Spirit (understood here as the angel Gabriel or revelatory inspiration) so they can deliver His warning to humanity about the Day of Gathering; the sending of revelation and the mission to warn are therefore acts of divine ordinance and mercy, not human initiative.

translation: The Day when they will be exposed—nothing of them will be hidden from Allah. To whom belongs sovereignty today? To Allah, the One, the All‑Subduer.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that on the Day of Judgment every hidden deed, intention and pretence will be laid bare before God, who alone holds absolute and irresistible authority. By posing the rhetorical question about who truly owns dominion, it nullifies all human pretensions to power or secrecy and affirms that ultimate judgment, control and enforcement rest solely with Allah, the unique and overpowering Sovereign; thus it calls for humility, sincerity and awareness that worldly concealment and pride will avail nothing when divine justice is enacted.

translation: Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned. No injustice will be done this Day. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate, precise divine justice awaits: on the Resurrection each person will receive exactly the consequences of their deeds—no one will be denied their due nor wrongfully punished—and God’s accounting is immediate and exact. The implication is both a warning and a consolation: it warns against complacency and wrongdoing because no deed escapes reckoning, and it comforts those wronged in this life by assuring them that injustices will be rectified when God, who is swift and exact in judgment, administers the final account.

translation: And warn them of the approaching Day when hearts will be at the throats, choking. For the wrongdoers there will be no close protector and no intercessor who is obeyed.
interpretation: The verse uses stark imagery to teach that at the final reckoning human fear will expose the futility of worldly supports: neither intimate allies nor powerful mediators can avert the consequences of injustice. Its purpose is to underscore individual moral responsibility and the urgency of reform before death, since social ties, status, or promised intercession cannot substitute for just conduct or divine mercy at the decisive moment.

translation: He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that God’s knowledge is complete and penetrates both outward betrayals and inner secrets: the ‘treachery of the eyes’ denotes looks or glances that reveal desire, intent or disloyalty, while ‘what the breasts conceal’ refers to hidden thoughts, motives and feelings. The verse therefore warns against trusting that hidden gazes or secret intentions escape divine scrutiny, urging moral vigilance, sincerity of heart, and awareness that inner states will be judged even when outward actions are unseen.

translation: And Allah judges with the truth; and those they call upon besides Him do not judge anything. Indeed, Allah — He is the Hearing, the Seeing.
interpretation: The verse asserts the sole and absolute authority of God to decide what is right and to execute justice; other beings or idols that people appeal to have no real power to determine outcomes. Because God hears every word and sees every inner and outer deed, His judgments are fully informed and just, so believers are admonished to rely on Him for ultimate justice and not to place trust in powerless intermediaries or false deities.

translation: Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them? They were stronger than them in power and left more traces on the earth; so Allah seized them for their sins, and they had from Allah no protector.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly strength, prosperity, or visible achievements do not exempt a people from moral accountability: historical ruins and the fate of former nations are signs to be reflected upon. When a society persists in wrongdoing, its power and monuments cannot prevent divine retribution; thus the passage urges reflection, humility, and reform to avoid the same end.

translation: That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved; so Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Powerful, Severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches a principle of divine justice: when communities repeatedly reject the clear evidence and guidance brought by their messengers, God’s response is to remove His protection and bring about decisive consequence. “Seized them” denotes an inevitable, effective divine action—whether by immediate worldly chastisement or by final retribution—showing that Allah’s might assures that transgression and persistent denial of truth do not go unaccounted for; the closing attributes stress both His omnipotence and the seriousness of the penalty due to deliberate rejection.

translation: And indeed We sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: The phrase means that God commissioned Moses not merely as a messenger with miraculous proofs (the “signs”) to demonstrate divine backing, but also endowed him with a manifest mandate and legal-political standing (“clear authority”) to confront rulers, call people to submission, judge disputes and implement God’s will. Together the signs authenticate his prophethood; the clear authority makes his message binding and gives him the right and power to act decisively on God’s behalf.

translation: إلى فرعون وهامان وقارون فقالوا: «ساحر كذّاب»
interpretation: الآية توضح أسلوب ظلم الطبقات الحاكمة في تشويه رسالة الحق: بدل أن يردّوا على البينة والحجة، يلجؤون إلى تشويه صاحبها واتهامه بالتحايل والسحر والكذب ليتجنبوا محاسبة أنفسهم على ظلمهم ويحموا مصالحهم.

translation: So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, “Kill the sons of those who believed with him and spare their women.” And the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error.
interpretation: The verse teaches that opposition to divine truth often resorts to morally corrupt, expedient measures born of fear and injustice; such schemes—however forceful they seem—are rooted in misguidance and will lead to ruin, so believers should trust that plots against truth cannot ultimately prevail.

translation: وقال فرعون: "ذروني أقتل موسى وليدع ربه؛ إني أخاف أن يبدل دينكم أو أن يظهر في الأرض الفساد".
interpretation: الآية تكشف عن موقف الطاغية الذي يلبس دوافعه الشخصية لباس الحرص على النظام. حين يخاف فرعون من أن "يبدل دينكم" أو "يظهر في الأرض الفساد" لا يعني ذلك حرصًا على الدين أو الأمن، بل خوفًا من أن دعوة موسى ستهدم الأسس الأيديولوجية والاجتماعية التي تقوم عليها سلطته ومصالح طبقة الحاكمين. عبارة "ليدع ربه" تأتي كذريعة تسمح له بأن يقضي على المصلح الديني والسياسي بحجة حماية المجتمع، وهي صورة عامة لكيف يبرر الطواغيت القمع باعتباره دفاعًا عن النظام، بينما الحقيقة هي الخوف من فقدان السيطرة والفوائد.

translation: وقال موسى: إني أعوذ بربي وربكم من كل متكبر لا يؤمن بيوم الحساب.
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن الاستبداد والتكبّر ورفض مسؤولية الإنسان أمام الله (اليومِ الآتي للحساب) هما مصدر فساد وسلب الحق، وأن المواجهة الحقيقية لمثل هؤلاء لا تتم بالقدرة البشرية وحدها بل باللجوء إلى الله والحماية منه. بقول موسى «ربي وربكم» يذكّر بأن السلطة الحقيقية مشتركة ومتجاوزة لأي جبروتٍ بشري، وأن الاتكال على الله والاعتراف بيوم الجزاء هما صمام أمان أخلاقي ومجتمعي ضد الاستكبار والظلم.

translation: And a believing man from the people of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said: “Will you kill a man because he says, ‘My Lord is Allah,’ when he has come to you with clear proofs from your Lord? If he is a liar, then his falsehood will be upon him; but if he is truthful, some of that which he promises you will befall you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressing liar.”
interpretation: The verse upholds a principle of justice and evidence over prejudice: it reproaches rulers for persecuting someone who professes God when that person brings clear signs, reminding that responsibility for falsehood rests on the liar while the consequences of truth may still come upon the oppressors. It also asserts a moral–spiritual law: those who persist in arrogance, wrongdoing and deliberate falsehood lose divine guidance and thereby bring about their own undoing.

translation: “O my people, you possess sovereignty today and are manifestly dominant in the land — so who will help us against the might of Allah if it should come upon us?” Pharaoh said, “I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the way of right guidance.”
interpretation: This passage exposes the arrogance and self-deception of a tyrant who mistakes temporal power for immunity before God: having established dominance, he mocks the threat of divine might and seeks reassurance in worldly authority, then frames his personal judgments as objective truth and his self‑interest as ‘guidance.’ It warns that political dominance and confident rhetoric do not confer moral legitimacy or protect against divine justice, and that leaders who present their preferences as the only ‘right way’ are misleading their people.

translation: And the one who believed said, “O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the Day of the Confederates.”
interpretation: A faithful member of the community, alarmed by his people's rejection of truth and their perilous course, warns that their collective behavior may bring upon them a catastrophic, decisive judgment comparable to the ‘Day of the Confederates’ (the trench/Ahzab episode) — a moment when an opposing coalition was defeated by divine decree; he is urging them to repent and change direction to avoid similar ruin.

translation: Such was the way of the people of Noah, and of ‘Aad and Thamud and those who came after them. And Allah does not will injustice for the servants.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in history: successive communities heard clear warning and guidance, chose arrogance, disbelief and wrongdoing, and so experienced the consequences. Saying “Allah does not will injustice for the servants” affirms that divine punishment is not arbitrary oppression but a just response to persistent, freely chosen misdeeds after repeated warning; it also implies God’s patience and mercy in offering chances to repent before consequences follow. The mention of those past peoples serves as a warning and reminder that current listeners should not repeat the same course.

translation: O my people, I fear for you the Day of Calling.
interpretation: The prophet is warning his community about the coming Day of Judgment — a day when people will cry out and call to one another in terror and regret. He expresses heartfelt concern because their rejection of guidance will leave them exposed to overwhelming accountability and loss; the verse functions as an urgent admonition to repent and heed the message now, before the decisive day when mutual calls and worldly supports will avail nothing.

translation: The day you turn away as fugitives, there will be for you no protector from Allah; and whoever Allah leads astray—there is for him no guide.
interpretation: The verse warns that on the Day of Reckoning all human supports will fail: when people seek to flee or disown responsibility, no one can shield them from God’s judgment. Guidance and protection are ultimately granted or withheld by God’s will; persistent rejection of divine guidance risks being left to misguidance, and once God has withdrawn His guidance there remains no true guide to save that person. The passage thus emphasizes God’s absolute sovereignty over guidance and the urgent need to accept and seek His guidance and mercy before it is too late.

translation: And indeed Joseph came to you before with clear proofs, yet you remained in doubt about what he brought you; until when he died you said, 'Allah will not send a messenger after him.' Thus Allah leaves astray whom He wills — the excessive, the doubter.
interpretation: The verse reproves those who, despite having been shown unmistakable signs in earlier messengers, persist in skeptical stubbornness; their habitual rejection culminates in the false conclusion that revelation has ended, and as a consequence God allows such self-exceeding, doubting people to be left to the misguidance that their own obstinacy merits.

translation: Those who argue about the signs of Allah without any authority that has come to them — great is the detestation in the sight of Allah and of those who believe. Thus Allah seals the heart of every arrogant, tyrant.
interpretation: The verse teaches that combative rejection of God's signs out of pride, without rightful evidence or humble seeking, is deeply offensive to God and repulsive to true believers; as a consequence (and reflection) of persistent arrogance, Allah 'seals' such hearts — He withholds guidance and insight from those who stubbornly elevate themselves, so their capacity to perceive, accept, or repent is progressively closed off. This sealing is not a whimsical punishment but the logical spiritual outcome of sustained pride and obstinacy: the more one refuses truth from a position of arrogance, the more one becomes unable to receive it.

translation: And Pharaoh said, “O Haman, build for me a lofty tower so that I may reach the ways (or the sources).”
interpretation: The verse exposes Pharaoh’s proud, materialistic attempt to overcome his limits by commanding state power to build a monument that will extend his reach—literally to a high vantage and symbolically to the ‘sources’ of authority or knowledge. His order to Haman shows how tyrants use subordinates and grand constructions to satisfy vanity and to try to seize control of what belongs to the divine order; it highlights the futility of thinking worldly means can attain or replace true spiritual and moral authority.

translation: He said, “O Haman, build for me a tower so that I may reach the ways of the heavens and look upon the god of Moses; and indeed I think him a liar.” Thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed and he was turned away from the way; and Pharaoh’s plotting was only in ruin.
interpretation: The verse exposes how pride and envy deform judgment: Pharaoh’s imperial arrogance drives him to impossible, showy projects to challenge Divine truth, and God allows his delusion to be made appealing so that he departs further from guidance. The image of trying to “reach the heavens” underscores the futility of using worldly power to confront ultimate reality—such schemes flatter the planner but are self‑deceptive and inevitably collapse into ruin.

translation: And the one who believed said, “O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right guidance.”
interpretation: The verse presents the believer (typically a divinely guided leader or prophet) offering himself as a living exemplar of God’s guidance: true guidance is not abstract but embodied in the conduct and teaching of those who submit to God. It stresses that guidance must be actively followed — leaders can point out the straight path, but people must choose to follow it — and that the path of ‘rashada’ combines correct belief, moral rectitude, and practical reform aimed at the good of the community.

translation: O my people, this worldly life is but an enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the home of lasting settlement.
interpretation: The verse cautions that the pleasures and pursuits of this world are temporary and not the ultimate goal; true and enduring reality lies in the Hereafter, so one’s priorities, values, and actions should be oriented toward securing the permanent, final abode rather than being consumed by fleeting worldly gratification.

translation: Whoever does an evil will be recompensed only with its like; and whoever does a righteous deed — whether male or female — while he (or she) is a believer, those will enter Paradise and will be provided therein without account.
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s perfect justice and the moral logic of accountability: wrongdoing brings its due consequences and will not be met with an arbitrary or excessive punishment, while sincere righteous action combined with faith guarantees entry into Paradise and blessings there that are beyond ordinary reckoning. By explicitly including “male or female,” it emphasizes the equal responsibility and equal promise of reward for all believers, and by saying provision is given “without account” the text conveys both the plenitude of the reward and the relief from burdensome calculation — a final recompense that is generous, fitting, and administered with divine equity.

translation: O my people, why do I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?
interpretation: The speaker (a prophet) expresses astonishment and rejection of the moral inversion before him: he invites people to what leads to safety and eternal felicity (faith, obedience to God), yet they urge him toward destruction and punishment. The phrase "ما لي" conveys incredulity and refusal — he cannot accept being drawn into their error — and it highlights the irreconcilable split between guidance and misguidance: one cannot sincerely call others to salvation while submitting to pressure that would make one complicit in inviting one’s own ruin.

translation: تَدْعُونَنِي لأُكْفِرَ بِاللَّهِ وَأُشْرِكَ بِهِ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ، وَأَنَا أَدْعُوكُمْ إِلَى الْعَزِيزِ الْغَفَّارِ.
interpretation: النبي يُبين رفضه القاطع لما يطلبه منه معارضوه: هم يريدون منه ترك الإيمان بالله وإسناد أمور لا علم له بها — أي قبول شرك أو بدعٍ مبنية على روايات أو تخيلات بشرية — بينما دعوته هي إلى الإله القوي المتعزّز بقدْرته والذي يُظهر رحمته بالمغفرة. المعنى العملي: الحق لا يُبنى على الإذعان لِمطالبٍ باطلة أو افتراضاتٍ دون دليل؛ رسالة النبي تجمع بين الإقرار بقدرة الله وسلطانه وبين الدعوة إلى التوبة والرجاء في مغفرته.

translation: Indeed, what you call me to has no appeal in this world nor in the Hereafter. Our return is to Allah, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse warns that succumbing to false or immoral calls brings no real gain here or in the Hereafter; ultimate judgment belongs to God alone. Those who persistently exceed moral and divine limits—by wrongdoing, injustice, or rejection of truth—will be held accountable and consigned to punishment. It is an admonition to resist worldly temptations, remain within God’s bounds, and live with awareness of final accountability.

translation:
فستذكرون ما أقول لكم؛ وأفوض أمري إلى الله؛ إن الله بصير بالعباد
"You will remember what I say to you; and I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants."
interpretation: The speaker predicts that people will one day recognize the truth of his words but, instead of forcing the matter, he places his trust wholly in God’s wisdom and justice; by delegating his affairs to Allah and affirming God’s seeing of all servants he underscores reliance on divine oversight and the certainty that God observes actions and will ultimately hold people to account.

translation: But Allah saved him from the evil of what they plotted, and the terrible punishment of the people of Pharaoh overtook them.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God shields the righteous from the harmful results of others’ schemes, while the arrogance and plotting of tyrants ultimately lead to their undoing—serving as a reassurance of divine protection for the oppressed and a warning that oppressive plots bring about severe retribution.

translation: The Fire — they are exposed to it morning and evening; and on the Day when the Hour is established, (it will be said), “Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment.”
interpretation: The verse uses the image of repeated exposure to the Fire in this life and the final consigning on the Day of Judgment to teach that persistent denial, arrogance and oppression bring both immediate humiliation and inevitable ultimate retribution. ‘Morning and evening’ signals recurring chastisement and public disgrace as a sign and consequence of wrongdoing, while the command to admit the people of Pharaoh to the harshest torment holds up Pharaoh as the archetype of tyrants who rejected clear signs; their fate is presented as a warning that persistent rejection of truth and persecution of the oppressed will result in the most severe divine punishment.

translation: And when they quarrel in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant, “Indeed we were followers of you—so did you spare us any portion of the Fire?”
interpretation: The verse warns that relying on powerful or arrogant leaders as a substitute for one's own moral responsibility is futile: those who followed others into wrongdoing will reproach their leaders in the Hereafter, but leaders cannot avert or share the punishment. Accountability before God is personal, and following false authority does not excuse or protect one from divine justice.

translation: قال الذين استكبروا: "إنا كلٌّ فيها، إنَّ الله قد حَكَمَ بينَ العِبادِ".
interpretation: الآية تصوّر موقف المتكبّرين الذين يردّون على الإنذار بتبرير مبسط: يرون أن الجميع سيقع في الحال نفسها وأن الله قد فصل الأمور بين الناس بالفعل، فيستخدمون هذا الاعتقاد كذريعة لعدم التغيير أو التوبة. فالعبارة تكشف عن غطرستهم وتحمل استغلالاً خاطئاً لمفهوم القضاء والقدر — فهم يحولون حكم الله إلى مبرّر للفساد والتمرّد بدل أن تكون حافزاً للمسؤولية الخُلُقية، إذ أن حكم الله لا يعفي الإنسان من الدعوة إلى الحق ولا يبرّر الإعراض عن طاعةٍ أو محاسبةٍ أخلاقية.

translation: And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell, “Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment.”
interpretation: The verse portrays the desperate plea of the damned who, confronted with unbearable torment, implore the angels who guard Hell to intercede with God for temporary relief. It highlights human regret and the late recognition of Divine authority — they now hope for mercy they rejected in life — and teaches that pleading after the final reckoning is a manifestation of too-late repentance and the limits of intercession, for relief and judgment ultimately rest with God alone.

translation: They will say, “Did not your messengers come to you with clear proofs?” They will say, “Yes.” (It will be said), “Then call (upon those you used to call).” But the invocation of the disbelievers is only in error.
interpretation: The verse warns that mere late acknowledgment of truth brings no benefit: on the Day of Reckoning those who received clear signs but persisted in misguidance will vainly call upon the objects or leaders they trusted. Their supplications are a final symptom of their error—directing worship or hope away from God cannot avail when truth has already been rejected; sincere submission and rightly directed prayer in life are what truly matters.

translation: Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe — in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses are raised.
interpretation: The verse expresses a divine assurance that God will defend and vindicate His messengers and sincere believers both now and ultimately at the Final Reckoning. Practically, this means that apparent setbacks, persecution, or delay do not indicate abandonment: God’s support may come as protection, relief, moral or communal strengthening, or clear public vindication in this world, and will be perfectly realized and made manifest before all on the Day when witnesses stand. The promise therefore calls for patience, steadfastness, and trust that truth will prevail by God’s help.

translation: The Day when the wrongdoers' excuses will not benefit them; for them is the curse, and for them an evil abode.
interpretation: This verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning any pleas or justifications offered by those who lived unjustly will be rejected; the ‘curse’ signifies God’s decisive rejection of their deeds and any hope of mercy based on empty words, and the ‘evil abode’ denotes the dire, lasting consequence of their choices—emphasizing that moral responsibility is judged by one’s actions over time, not by belated excuses.

translation: And certainly We gave Moses guidance, and We made the Children of Israel inherit the Book.
interpretation: God granted Moses clear, divinely‑guided law and then entrusted the scripture to the Israelites as an inheritance; that ‘inheritance’ signifies a trust and responsibility to preserve, implement and transmit God's guidance—so possessing the Book is a duty to uphold its teachings and moral obligations, not merely a status or privilege.

translation:
هدى وذكرى لأولي الألباب
"[It is] guidance and a reminder for those of understanding."
interpretation: The phrase affirms that the Qur'an is intended to operate as both directional guidance and a warning whose full effect is realized by people who use their intellect and hearts to reflect. It means the text is not merely moral rhetoric; its truths become practical light for those who contemplate, weigh evidence, derive principles, and allow that reflection to reform their beliefs and conduct — whereas mere hearing without pondering will not yield its intended benefit.

translation: So be patient; indeed the promise of Allah is true. And ask forgiveness for your sin and glorify the praise of your Lord in the evening and the morning.
interpretation: The verse urges steadfast endurance in trials by affirming that God’s promise — of justice, help, or final recompense — will surely occur, so one must not despair at delay. It pairs that assurance with concrete spiritual practice: repent (seek forgiveness) to cleanse shortcomings and remain humble, and maintain regular remembrance and praise of God at both evening and morning. Together these actions—patience grounded in trust, continual repentance, and habitual worship—sustain the believer inwardly and align one’s life with God while awaiting the fulfillment of His promise.

translation:
إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُجَادِلُونَ فِي آَيَاتِ اللَّهِ بِغَيْرِ سُلْطَانٍ أَتَاهُمْ ۚ إِنَّ فِي صُدُورِهِمْ إِلَّا كِبْرًا مَا هُمْ بِبَالِغِيهِ ۚ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّهُ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ

“Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority that has come to them — there is nothing in their breasts except pride; they will not attain (the truth). So seek refuge in Allah; indeed He is the Hearing, the Seeing.”
interpretation: The verse indicts a posture of arrogant disputation: people who contend about God’s signs without sound proof, rightful knowledge, or legitimate authority are driven by pride, and that pride blinds them so they do not reach truth or guidance. The injunction to “seek refuge in Allah” is a remedial command — turn away from self‑assured argumentation, implore God’s protection from the corrupting influence of arrogance, and rely on the One who hears and sees all, for true understanding comes through humility, evidence, and sincere submission rather than boastful debate.

translation: Indeed, the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, yet most people do not know.
interpretation: The statement points to the disproportion between the vast, ordered, and wise fabric of the cosmos and the comparatively small, limited realm of human beings; this contrast is meant to humble people, direct them to recognize God’s supreme power and wisdom, and to warn that failing to perceive the universe as a sign of the Creator leads to arrogance, misplaced priorities, and spiritual heedlessness. The verse thus urges reflection on the heavens and earth as evidence calling for humility, submission, and correction of one’s understanding and conduct.

translation:
وما يستوي الأعمى والبصير والذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات ولا المسيء ۚ قليلا ما تتذكرون
"The blind and the one who sees are not equal, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds and the wrongdoer — how little you remember!"
interpretation: The verse teaches that true standing before God depends on inward sight and right conduct: spiritual vision (faith lived out in righteous action) is fundamentally different from spiritual blindness or persistent wrongdoing. It is a moral warning that people often fail to acknowledge this reality and seldom take it to heart, so they are reminded to wake from heedlessness and align belief with righteous deeds.

translation: Indeed, the Hour is surely coming; there is no doubt about it, but most people do not believe.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute inevitability of the Last Day as an objective reality that human skepticism cannot avert; by coupling that certainty with the observation that most people remain unbelieving, it diagnoses why moral and spiritual laxity persists—attachment to worldly comforts, pride, distraction, or stubborn rejection—and urges a practical response: live in conscious accountability, cultivate repentance and upright conduct, and persist in sincere invitation to the truth, since the eventual divine reckoning is certain even if many now deny it.

translation: وقال ربكم: ادعوني أَستجب لكم. إنَّ الَّذين يستكبرون عن عبادتي سيدخلون جهنم داخرين.
interpretation: الآية تُظهر أن الله مفتوح للدعاء ودعوة الناس إليه علامة على قربه ورحمته، ومع ذلك تحذر من حركة داخلية تقود إلى فقدان ذلك النعيم: الكبر عن العبادة — أي رفض الخضوع والامتنان والاعتراف بالاحتياج إلى الله — يقطع صلة الإنسان بمصدر النعمة ويؤدي إلى إذلاله في الآخرة. وعد الاستجابة ينبغي فهمه في سياق حكمة الله: الاستجابة قد تظهر بطرق مختلفة (إعطاء ما يُطلب، دفع مكروه، تأخير من أجل خير أعظم، أو منح ثبات ورضا)، لكن شرط حصول الخير فعليًا هو تواضع الداعي وإخلاصه، أما الغرور فَيُثمر ضياعًا وشقاءً وهوانًا.

translation: Allah is He who made the night for you, that you may rest therein, and the day, giving sight. Indeed Allah is the Possessor of bounty toward the people, yet most people do not give thanks.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the regular cycle of night and day is a purposeful mercy — a divine ordering that enables rest, perception, work and moral responsibility. Calling these basic conditions a ‘favor’ emphasizes they are gifts, not entitlements; true recognition of them should produce gratitude lived out in right conduct, mindful dependence on God, and proper use of one’s time and faculties. The reproach that “most people do not give thanks” warns that many remain heedless or fail to convert blessings into thankfulness and responsible action.

translation: That is Allah—your Lord, the Creator of everything; there is no deity except Him. So how are you being led astray?
interpretation: The verse confronts the moral absurdity of turning away from God: given the manifest reality of His exclusive lordship and creative sovereignty, anyone’s rejection cannot be excused as ignorance alone but points to willful heedlessness, attachment to passing desires, or following misleading authorities. The rhetorical question is meant to provoke self-examination and repentance, urging people to recognize the irrationality and culpability of denying or neglecting the One who sustains all things and to return to sincere acknowledgment and reliance on Him.

translation: Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of Allah.
interpretation: The verse conveys that persistent denial of God’s signs produces a real spiritual consequence: God allows such people to be diverted from guidance so that their perception and hearts are clouded. Their repeated rejection becomes self‑confirming — they grow preoccupied with falsehood and delusion, lose sensitivity to truth, and remain trapped in error as a direct outcome of their own refusal to acknowledge the signs.

translation: Allah is He who made the earth a resting-place for you and the heavens a structure, and fashioned you and made your formations excellent, and provided you with good things. That is Allah—your Lord; so blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s exclusive sovereignty and gracious care: by arranging the world as a fitting home, ordering the heavens, perfecting human form, and granting wholesome provision, God both dignifies humans and makes them dependent on Him. These visible favors are signs that call for recognition, gratitude, and submission to the One Lord; the term “tayyibat” (good things) emphasizes that true provision is not merely plentiful but lawful and pure, and the concluding blessing demands praise and moral responsibility in response to God’s mercy.

translation: He is the Ever‑Living; there is no deity except Him. So invoke Him, devoting the religion purely to Him. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute, self‑sustaining life and unique divinity as the basis for sincere monotheistic devotion: because God alone is truly alive and sovereign, worship and supplication must be directed to Him alone with wholehearted sincerity (ikhlāṣ), rejecting any partnership or divided allegiance. The closing phrase — praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds — reminds the believer that all gratitude and recognition rightly return to God, who alone deserves worship and on whom all creation depends.

translation: قُلْ إِنِّي نُهِيتُ أَنْ أَعْبُدَ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ ۖ لَمَّا جَاءَتْنِي الْبَيِّنَاتُ مِنْ رَبِّي وَأُمِرْتُ أَنْ أُسْلِمَ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
interpretation: The speaker (the Prophet) declares that divine revelation has forbidden him to worship any beings invoked besides God; because clear signs and guidance have been given by his Lord, his duty is to submit wholly to the one true Lord of all. The verse affirms that authentic guidance replaces inherited or popular religious practices, requiring exclusive monotheism and total surrender to God alone regardless of social pressure or the claims of intermediaries.

translation: He is the One who created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clot, then He brings you forth as a child; then so that you may reach your maturity, then so that you may become old — and among you are some who are taken (in death) before (that) — and that you may reach an appointed term; and perhaps you will understand.
interpretation: The verse is calling attention to the purposeful, staged nature of human existence under divine sovereignty: our origin, development, aging, and death are not random but ordained processes meant to prompt reflection and moral responsibility. By tracing life from dust to embryo to child to elder and reminding us that some die earlier and that all have an appointed term, the statement aims to awaken reason and humility — to recognize dependence on God, to value the time given, and to live with awareness of accountability and the need to use understanding wisely.

translation: He is the One who gives life and causes death; and when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and it is.
interpretation: The verse proclaims God’s absolute, effortless sovereignty: existence depends wholly on His will, so that when He ordains something its reality is instantly brought into being by a single divine command. This point is meant to unsettle human pretensions of control, cultivate humility and trust before God’s wisdom, and remind believers that ultimate outcomes rest with Him alone.

translation: ألم تر إلى الذين يجادلون في آيات الله أنى يصرفون
interpretation: الآية تشير إلى أن الذين يناقشون آيات الله بعناد أو بغرض الجدال لا يطلبون هدًى بل حكم عليهم بالابتعاد عن الحق: الله يصرفهم عن الهدى ويحول بين قلوبهم وإدراك الحقيقة، فتكون مجادلاتهم دليلًا على ضلالهم وسببًا في إزاحةهم عن نور الحق بدل أن تقربهم منه.

translation: Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers — soon they will know.
interpretation: The phrase warns that those who reject divine revelation and the messages brought by the prophets will inevitably be confronted with the truth and its consequences. “Soon they will know” expresses certainty and a coming disclosure — whether by events that make the truth undeniable, by loss and humiliation in this world, or by judgment in the Hereafter — so that their present denial will be shown to be wrong and will bring retribution or accountability when it can no longer be averted.

translation: When the shackles are upon their necks and the chains are being dragged,
interpretation: The verse uses the stark image of shackles and dragged chains to convey that on the Day of Reckoning the evildoers will be stripped of autonomy and dignity and will be forcibly conveyed to their inevitable punishment. It emphasizes the certainty and severity of divine justice — worldly power or denial will not avert accountability, and the visible restraint and procession symbolize both the inescapability of consequences and the public exposure of what their choices produced.

translation: Into scalding (boiling) water; then into the Fire they will be cast.
interpretation: The verse describes a two-stage, intensifying punishment for the transgressors: first they are subjected to scalding, searing liquid and then plunged into the blazing Fire—signifying the severity, certainty, and inexorable justice of divine retribution for persistent wrongdoing.

translation: Then it will be said to them, "Where are those [deities] which you used to associate [with Allah]?"
interpretation: This rhetorical question, posed on the Day of Recompense, exposes the absurdity and impotence of shirk: those whom the guilty relied on for help, protection, or intercession will be absent and powerless to respond. It forces the worshippers to confront that their supposed partners were either non-existent or incapable, underscoring that ultimate support and judgement belong to God alone and making clear the personal responsibility and consequence of having placed trust in anything besides Him.

translation: “Instead of Allah,” they said, “they have led us astray; no — we had never before been in the habit of calling upon anything.” Thus Allah causes the disbelievers to go astray.
interpretation: The verse depicts the stubborn self-justification of those who reject the divine message: when confronted with clear guidance they dismiss it and claim innocence or ignorance of prior error, and because of their persistent denial and refusal to seek truth, God leaves them to their misguidance — a consequence of their own obstinacy rather than a failure of the message.

translation: That is because you were rejoicing on the earth without right, and because you were frolicking.
interpretation: The verse attributes the ensuing consequence to a moral cause: people had treated worldly life as an illegitimate triumph and a playground. “Rejoicing in the earth without right” points to pride, unlawful gains, oppression or pretensions of security and ownership that have no moral or divine warrant; “frolicking” (tamruḥūn) denotes heedless, insolent revelry that ignores responsibility and warning. The meaning: when blessings and power are abused in arrogance and careless enjoyment, they become the very reasons for loss and retribution.

translation: Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein; evil indeed is the dwelling of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse teaches that prideful rejection of God and self-exaltation lead to an irrevocable, humiliating end: those whose arrogance caused them to deny guidance and oppress truth will be publicly cast into Hell and remain there. The strong imagery—being made to enter its gates and dwell permanently—underscores both the justice and finality of the outcome, turning worldly pride into eternal abasement and warning that humility and submission to divine truth are the remedies to avoid this fate.

translation: So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true. Whether We show you some of that which We threaten them with or take you in death, to Us they will all return.
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet to endure with trust in God’s timing: Allah’s promise of justice will certainly be fulfilled. It teaches that whether the Prophet lives to witness the consequences faced by the wrongdoers or dies before that happens, the decisive reality is the inevitable return of all people to God for judgment. The passage thus calls for patience, reliance on divine wisdom, and confidence that ultimate vindication and accountability rest with Allah alone.

translation: And indeed We sent messengers before you; of them some We have related to you, and of them some We have not related to you. And it is not for a messenger to bring a sign except by Allah’s permission. So when the command of Allah comes, it will be concluded in truth, and falsehood will perish thereupon.
interpretation: The verse teaches that prophethood is part of a continual divine plan: God sent many messengers, mentioning only some in the Qur’an for specific guidance while others remain within His knowledge. Miracles or signs are not independent proofs produced by a prophet’s will but are granted by God according to His wisdom, so demanding signs misunderstands how guidance is given. Ultimately God’s decisive decree will establish reality — truth will be vindicated and falsehood, along with those who relied on it, will be utterly destroyed — calling believers to trust God’s timing and authority rather than require immediate miraculous proof.

translation:
اللهُ الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَنْعَامَ لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنْهَا وَمِنْهَا تَأْكُلُونَ
"It is Allah who made the cattle for you — that you may ride some of them and from them you may eat."
interpretation: The verse points to God’s deliberate provision: He created domestic animals as practical means to sustain and serve humanity (transport, food), a manifestation of His wisdom and mercy. By highlighting these benefits the text invites recognition of human dependence on divine bounty, calls for gratitude rather than attributing independent power to creatures, and implies an ethical duty to use these blessings lawfully and compassionately — treating animals as trusts from God rather than mere instruments of exploitation.

translation:
وَلَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ وَلِتَبْلُغُوا عَلَيْهَا حَوَاجَّكُمْ ۚ وَعَلَيْهَا وَعَلَى الْفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ
“And for you in it are benefits, and that you may reach upon it what is in your breasts (your needs); and upon it—and on the ships—you are carried.”
interpretation: The verse indicates that the sea is a God‑willed means of provision and facilitation: it supplies benefits (food, resources, routes) and enables people to attain the needs and purposes they hold in their hearts (trade, travel, livelihood), since both people and their goods are borne upon the sea by ships—a sign of divine power and mercy providing for human needs.

translation:
وَيرِيكم آياته فَأَيَّ آياتِ اللَّهِ تَنكُرونَ
"And He shows you His signs; so which of Allah’s signs will you deny?"
interpretation: This is a pointed rebuke and call to reflection: God continually manifests unmistakable evidence of His power, wisdom and guidance—in the natural world, in the ordering of events, in revelation and in personal experience—so to persist in rejecting those signs is a willful, unjustified denial. The rhetorical question exposes the absurdity of refusal and summons people to acknowledge the divine realities that demand moral and spiritual response.

translation: Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength and left more traces on the earth, yet what they used to earn did not avail them.
interpretation: The verse warns that worldly power, size, and impressive achievements—monuments, wealth, influence—cannot protect a people from divine judgment when they persist in injustice or unbelief. By urging people to observe the fate of earlier nations, it calls for sober reflection and moral reform: the true measure of success is not temporal dominance or accumulated gains, but righteousness and accountability before God, for material accomplishments will be of no benefit at the moment of reckoning.

translation: But when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in the knowledge they possessed, and that which they used to mock overtook them.
interpretation: The verse criticizes those who, confronted by prophetic evidence, cling proudly to their own limited learning or inherited assumptions and treat the truth with scorn. Their self‑satisfaction — rejoicing in what little ‘knowledge’ they have — blinds them, so that the very reality they ridiculed (the messenger’s warning, the coming judgment) ultimately catches up with them. It warns against arrogance and false confidence in one's opinions when clear guidance and proofs are presented.

translation:
فَلمّا رَأوا بِأسنا قالوا آمَنّا باللهِ وَحدَهُ وكَفَرنا بما كُنّا بِهِ مُشرِكينَ
"So when they saw Our punishment, they said, ‘We believe in Allah alone and disbelieve in that which we used to associate (with Him).’"
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring human pattern: some people only profess true monotheism when confronted with evident divine punishment. Their declaration after witnessing chastisement may be borne of fear or compulsion and thus can be insincere or too late to avert consequence. The passage therefore warns that genuine faith and abandoning shirk must come sincerely and before punitive signs, not merely as a reactive utterance to escape suffering.

translation:
فلم يَكُنْ يَنْفَعُهُم إيمانُهُم لَمّا رأَوا بأسَنا ۖ سنتَ اللَّهِ الَّتي قَد خَلَتْ في عباده ۖ وخَسِرَ هُناكَ الكافرون
"But their faith did not avail them when they saw Our punishment. That is the way of Allah which has already passed among His servants; and there the disbelievers were the losers."
interpretation: The verse teaches that professing belief after divine punishment has overtaken people is futile: when rejection persists until the consequences manifest, a belated confession cannot undo what is decreed. This illustrates Allah’s established sunnah—past communities who persisted in denial experienced ruin—so the ethical demand is to accept guidance before warning turns into irrevocable consequence; persistence in disbelief leads to loss.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ha Mim.
interpretation: The letters “Ha Mim” are part of the Qur’anic muqaṭṭaʿāt; one interpretation is that they function as a divine sign and attention‑grabber—by beginning with simple, disjointed letters whose full significance is known only to God, the Qur’an announces its miraculous, inimitable nature and prepares the listener for the ensuing revelation, reminding us that the ultimate meaning of sacred speech rests with God rather than with human speculation.

translation: A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
interpretation: The phrase asserts that the message is divinely sent by God whose essential attribute is mercy, indicating that the guidance, laws, and admonitions in the revelation are grounded in compassion and aimed primarily at human welfare, guidance, and reform rather than arbitrary punishment.

translation: A Book whose verses are made explicit — an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse asserts that the Qur’an is composed of clear, carefully articulated signs in the Arabic tongue so that those endowed with knowledge and reflection can recognize its truth; its clarity and linguistic precision are both a means of guidance and a test—inviting thoughtful people to discern, accept, and be reformed by its message.

translation: (I have been sent) as a bringer of good tidings and a warner; yet most of them turned away — so they do not listen.
interpretation: The verse underscores the Prophet’s role as both encourager and cautioner, and points to an internal, moral refusal on the part of many listeners: their ‘turning away’ and ‘not hearing’ are not merely physical acts but indicate a closed heart and will. Despite clear guidance offered through hope and warning, pride, attachment to prior beliefs or worldly gains, and deliberate refusal prevent the message from being received and acted upon. The passage thus highlights human responsibility — the messenger’s duty is to deliver, while acceptance requires openness and sincere willingness to listen and change.

translation:
وَقَالُوا قُلُوبُنَا فِي أَكِنَّةٍ مِمَّا تَدْعُونَا إِلَيْهِ وَفِيٓ آذَانِنَا وَقْرٌ وَمِنْ بَيْنِنَا وَبَيْنِكَ حِجَابٌ فَاعْمَلْ إِنَّنَا عَامِلُونَ
“And they said, ‘Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a partition. So do [as you will]; indeed, we are doing [what we do].’”
interpretation: The verse exposes a posture of willful rejection disguised as incapacity. By claiming veiled hearts, deafened ears, and a barrier between them and the messenger, the opponents present their refusal as if it were inevitable or imposed; in reality these are self‑erected defenses against guidance. The phrase “So do; indeed, we are doing” conveys sarcastic defiance—an insistence on persisting in their own course despite the invitation—so the passage indicts them for deliberate stubbornness rather than excusing them for genuine inability.

translation: Say: “I am only a human being like you; it has been revealed to me that your God is one. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness. Woe to the polytheists.”
interpretation: The Prophet emphasizes his humanity to dispel claims of divinity and to show that his authority rests on revelation, not on personal exaltation. The core message revealed to him is pure monotheism, and the command “be upright toward Him” calls for a wholehearted, steadfast turning to God in belief, worship and moral conduct. Seeking God’s forgiveness is presented as the means to restore and maintain that relationship, because humans err; by contrast, persistent shirk—setting up partners with God—leads to decisive loss and divine woe because it perverts true devotion and moral orientation.

translation: الَّذِينَ لاَ يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ كَافِرُونَ
interpretation: امتناع المرء عن أداء الزكاة الواجب ليس مجرد إهمال مادي بل دليل على نقض الإيمان بالجزاء الآتي؛ بمنع ما فرضه الله عن الفقراء يتجلى لدى هؤلاء إنكار أو عدم اعترافهم بالمساءلة والجزاء في الآخرة، فتوصف حالتهم بأنهم كافرون بالنسبة للآخرة — أي أنهم يتصرفون كمن لا يؤمن بحقوق الله وبدود الحساب والجزاء الآتي.

translation: Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds will have a reward that is never cut off.
interpretation: The verse promises that true faith joined with righteous action merits from God an eternal, inexhaustible recompense: a lasting reward in the Hereafter that will not be diminished, ended, or withheld — bestowed by divine mercy rather than as a limited or grudging favor.

translation: Say, “Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days and set up for Him equals? That is the Lord of the worlds.”
interpretation: The verse confronts those who reject God despite the evident act of creation: by stressing that the One who fashioned the earth in two stages is none other than the sovereign Lord of all realms, it rebukes the irrationality of denying His oneness and assigning partners to Him — a stance that contradicts the clear testimony of God’s creative authority and universal lordship.

translation: And He placed on it firm mountains above it, and He blessed it and determined its provisions therein in four days—equal for those who ask.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the universe is purposefully ordered by God: the mountains function as stabilizing anchors, and the earth’s provision is arranged and apportioned in stages (here described as four days). By stating the provisions are “equal for those who ask,” it emphasizes divine impartiality and measured care—sustenance and the orderly conditions of life are dispensed by God’s wisdom to all seekers, so human beings should recognize God’s deliberate providence, trust in His provision, and avoid anxiety or claims of unfairness.

translation:
ثم استوى إلى السماء وهي دخان فقال لها وللأرض ائتيا طوعا أو كرها قالتا أتينا طائعين
"Then He directed Himself to the heaven while it was smoke, and He said to it and to the earth, ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly.’ They said, ‘We come, willingly.’"
interpretation: This verse describes God’s bringing the cosmos into ordered existence from an initial formless, smoky state and exercising sovereign command over it. “Istawa” indicates God’s assumption of authority and establishment of the created order (not a physical movement), and “smoke” points to an early, diffuse stage of the heavens and earth. By commanding the heavens and the earth to come — whether willingly or unwillingly — and their response “we come, willingly,” the verse emphasizes that all of creation instantaneously and completeley submits to Divine will and executes God’s decrees; it underlines God’s absolute power, the ease with which He enacts creation, and the inherent submission of the created realm to their Maker.

translation: So He completed them—seven heavens—in two days, and He revealed in every heaven its command. And We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and as a protection. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the All‑Knowing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the cosmos is the result of deliberate, sovereign design: God brought the seven heavens into ordered existence swiftly and purposefully, assigning to each its own laws and functions. The visible sky’s lights (stars, meteors) serve both as adornment and as a means of protection (preventing corrupting influences), underscoring that the universe is governed by precise, wise decree — a manifestation of God’s power, meticulous planning, and complete knowledge rather than random chance.

translation:
فإن أعرضوا فقل أنذرتكم صاعقة مثل صاعقة عاد وثمود
"But if they turn away, say: 'I have warned you of a sudden, overwhelming calamity — like the calamity that struck ʿĀd and Thamūd.'"
interpretation: The verse serves as a stern prophetic admonition: when people persistently reject God's message, the prophet's duty is to warn them that Divine retribution can come suddenly and decisively, comparable in severity to the destruction of earlier nations (ʿĀd and Thamūd). The term صاعقة conveys an overwhelming, swift, and incontestable act of God's power; the warning aims to awaken conscience and spur repentance, while emphasizing that judgment is ultimately God's prerogative and a real consequence of persistent disbelief and corruption.

translation: When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, [saying], “Do not worship except Allah,” they said, “If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels; indeed, we are disbelievers in what you have been sent with.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a habitual evasiveness and arrogance in people who, despite repeated calls to worship God alone, refuse to submit by inventing unattainable conditions (e.g., demanding angelic envoys). Their claim that God would have sent angels if He had willed is a rationalization: they use supposed divine prerogative as an excuse to dismiss human messengers and the truth they bring. The reference to messengers coming from “before” and “behind” underscores that guidance confronted them persistently, yet their rejection is rooted not in lack of evidence but in entrenched hostility and a willful avoidance of responsibility to believe.

translation: As for ʿĀd, they grew arrogant on the earth without right and said, “Who is more powerful than us?” Did they then not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than they? Yet they were denying Our signs.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses a common moral sickness: when a people confuse temporal strength and domination with legitimate authority, pride blinds them to their dependence on their Creator and leads them to reject divine guidance. Claiming invulnerability because of material power becomes a justification for injustice, but true sovereignty belongs to the One who gave them life; denying the signs of God is therefore both a symptom and a cause of their moral collapse and eventual divine reckoning.

translation: So We sent upon them a violent, howling wind in ill-fated days, that We might make them taste the humiliation of disgrace in this life; and the punishment of the Hereafter is more humiliating, and they will not be helped.
interpretation: The verse presents the wind as a form of divine retribution visited on a people whose persistent transgression and rejection of guidance brought about a sustained calamity that stripped them of worldly pride and security. 'Days of misfortune' signals that the punishment was neither trivial nor brief but a decisive, evident chastisement meant to expose and abase them. Emphasizing that the Hereafter’s torment is more humiliating underlines that temporal losses are only a precursor to an irreversible, greater accountability; and 'they will not be helped' stresses the finality of God’s judgment—neither power, allies, nor idols can avert the consequence. The passage thus warns that reliance on transient strength or status, and persistent denial of moral truth, leads first to public disgrace in life and ultimately to far worse loss in the hereafter.

translation: As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance; so the thunderbolt of a humiliating punishment seized them for what they used to earn.
interpretation: The verse illustrates a moral principle: divine guidance is offered, but human beings retain responsibility and can willfully choose to persist in error. “Choosing blindness” signifies deliberate stubbornness or love of sin that rejects clear light; that habitual rejection hardens one’s condition and brings about an abrupt, humiliating retribution that publicly exposes the moral consequences of their actions. Thus the passage warns that guidance does not nullify accountability—persistent, conscious refusal of truth leads to ruin proportionate to the deeds that produced it.

translation: And We saved those who believed and were conscious (of God).
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s deliverance is promised to people whose faith is lived out in taqwa — a sustained God‑consciousness manifesting in righteous conduct and avoidance of what displeases Him. Salvation here encompasses both being rescued from immediate danger or trial and ultimate protection from punishment in the Hereafter; it teaches that sincere belief coupled with piety elicits God’s mercy and intervention.

translation: And the Day when the enemies of Allah are driven to the Fire — then they will be distributed (to their places).
