interpretation: The verse speaks of the Day of Resurrection when those who made themselves enemies of God and His guidance — by persistent denial, hypocrisy, oppression or active hostility to truth — will be publicly mustered before punishment. The phrase “they will be distributed” denotes that their torment will be measured and assigned according to their deeds and ranks of guilt, underscoring both the certainty of accountability and God’s ordered, exact justice rather than chaotic retribution.

translation: Until, when they come to it, their hearing and their eyes and their skins will testify against them as to what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning God will make even the faculties and bodies by which people acted testify to the reality of their deeds. Nothing hidden — neither what was seen, heard, nor what was concealed beneath the skin (inclinations, touches, intentions) — will remain unrevealed, so excuses and denials will be impossible. The point is to affirm God’s perfect and comprehensive justice: accountability will be thorough and impartial, the very instruments that enabled actions will vindicate divine judgment, and believers are therefore urged to live with constant awareness that all acts and choices will ultimately be brought to light.

translation: And they will say to their skins, “Why did you testify against us?” They will say, “Allah has made us speak — He who makes everything speak — and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that on the Day of Judgment God will even empower the parts of a person that seemed lifeless to bear witness to their deeds, demonstrating that nothing in creation is beyond His authority to animate or to make testify; it affirms the certainty of resurrection and accountability, so that every attempt to evade responsibility is futile and all return ultimately to God.

translation: And you did not think that your hearing, your eyes, nor your skins would bear witness against you; but you thought that Allah did not know much of what you do.
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who imagine their sins and secret deeds are concealed. The rhetorical image — that even one’s hearing, sight and skin will testify — emphasizes that every faculty and aspect of a person, inward and outward, is known and will give evidence. The mistake is not merely underestimating human witnesses but denying God’s all-encompassing knowledge: nothing of intention, thought, sensation or action is hidden from Him, and therefore all will be held accountable.

translation: And that was your conjecture concerning your Lord — He turned you back, and so you became among the losers.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those whose complacent assumptions about God (that He would overlook their denial, negligence, or hypocrisy) replaced sincere submission and guidance. Because they relied on their own mistaken presumption instead of God’s revealed truth, God ‘returned’ them — withdrew His support and allowed them to fall back into ruin — and they thereby became among the real losers in consequence and accountability.

translation:
فإن يصبروا فالنار مثوى لهم ۖ وإن يستعتبوا فما هم من المعتبين
"So if they remain patient, then Fire will be their final abode; and if they beg for respite, they will not be among those who are granted respite."
interpretation: The verse teaches that obstinate persistence in rejection or sin cannot avert divine judgment: their continued 'patience' is not commendable endurance but stubbornness that only fixes them in Hell, and any plea for delay or reconsideration at the time of reckoning will be refused — mercy is not granted to those who knowingly persist in wrong and then seek to defer the consequence.

translation: And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them; and the word (i.e., the decree of punishment) has been justified against nations that passed away before them, of jinn and of mankind — indeed, they were losers.
interpretation: The verse warns that people are often provided with ‘companions’ — whether devils, misleading friends, or seductive false beliefs — that dress up error and desire so it appears desirable both in what they already possess and in what lies ahead. These companions do not merely accompany people; they reshape perception so that misguidance feels rightful. “The word” coming true against earlier nations shows that when communities persist in heeding such tempters and reject guidance, God’s warning is fulfilled in their destruction; punishment befell both jinn and human peoples who followed their inclinations. “They were losers” means ultimate loss: spiritual ruin and the forfeiture of lasting good, a fate avoided only by turning away from flattering falsehoods, reforming one’s companions and inclinations, and returning to sincere guidance.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, “Do not listen to this Qur'an and divert [others] from it, so that you might prevail.”
interpretation: The verse exposes a deliberate tactic of opponents: they seek to silence and distract people from the Qur'anic message—by preventing hearing, sowing confusion, or ridiculing it—in hopes of preserving their social or ideological dominance. It warns that resistance to truth often takes the form of suppression and manipulation, a temporary strategy rooted in fear of losing influence rather than in compelling argument.

translation: So We will make those who disbelieve taste a severe punishment, and We will recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse warns that persistent rejection of God and continued wrongdoing will meet with divine justice: the suffering inflicted on the disbelievers is a direct and proportionate recompense for the cumulative evil of their own actions (not an arbitrary cruelty). It serves both as a consequence for oppression and corrupt conduct and as a deterrent, affirming that ultimately God’s judgment corresponds to people’s deeds and the moral choices they persist in.

translation: That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is an abiding home — a recompense for that they were denying Our signs.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who consciously set themselves against God — by rejecting, denying, or actively opposing His revelations and leading others away — will meet a just and permanent consequence; ‘the Fire’ and ‘an abiding home’ speak to the certainty and permanence of that recompense, which is not arbitrary but a response to deliberate denial of clear signs, underscoring divine justice and the moral responsibility to heed what has been shown.

translation: And those who disbelieved said, “Our Lord, show us those who led us astray among the jinn and among mankind, so that we may put them under our feet and make them among the lowest.”
interpretation: The verse exposes the proud, evasive mindset of the disbelievers: confronted with ruin they refuse to acknowledge their own responsibility and demand visible scapegoats to punish. Their wish to humiliate and trample those they blame is a vain, vengeful attempt to reverse their humiliation; it manifests arrogance and moral blindness rather than repentance, and thus only confirms the degradation they seek to inflict.

translation: Indeed, those who say, “Our Lord is Allah,” and then remain steadfast — the angels descend upon them: “Do not fear and do not grieve, and give glad tidings of Paradise which you were promised.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that a sincere declaration of God’s lordship coupled with persistent uprightness (استقامة) brings concrete divine support: angels come to reassure such believers — especially at the approach of death and in severe trials — removing fear and sorrow and conveying the certain glad tidings of the promised Paradise. By emphasizing steadfastness, the verse makes clear that the promise is not for a mere verbal profession but for continued faith and right conduct; it therefore comforts the believer that God’s pledge of salvation is realized through His angelic assistance and the inner peace granted to those who persevere.

translation: We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter; therein you will have whatever your souls desire, and therein you will have whatever you call for.
interpretation: This phrase expresses a claim of absolute protection and unlimited provision made by false allies (whether misguided leaders, worshipped beings, or deceptive powers) who promise both worldly pleasures and guarantees in the next life to secure followers. The verse can be read as exposing the illusion of such claims: true sovereignty, provision, and the answering of supplication belong to God alone, so trusting in any earthly or fabricated patron for ultimate salvation and fulfillment is a dangerous delusion that diverts people from genuine faith and accountability.

translation: Sent down as a revelation from the Oft‑Forgiving, Most‑Merciful.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that the scripture is not from human origin but a divine gift rooted in God’s attributes of forgiveness and mercy; it frames all commands, warnings and judgments within a purpose of moral reform and restoration, assuring people that divine justice is exercised with compassion and that repentance and return are always possible.

translation: And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, “Indeed, I am of the Muslims.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that true excellence in speech is measured by its purpose and embodiment: the best words are those used to call people toward God when they are reinforced by upright behavior and a sincere, humble identification as a submitter to God. It insists that persuasion must be coherent—words must point to truth, actions must exemplify it, and the speaker’s declared belonging to the Muslim community signals both personal integrity and submission rather than mere rhetoric. Thus the ideal communicator is not merely eloquent but authentic, practicing what they preach and publicly aligning their life with the message they convey.

translation: Good and evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better; then he between you and whom there was enmity will be as a devoted friend.
interpretation: The verse enjoins moral superiority: do not meet wrongdoing with retaliation of the same kind but respond with what is better—forbearance, kindness, fair conduct or gentle speech. Such a response does not mean passivity toward injustice but a deliberate, principled stance that seeks to break cycles of hostility; by answering wrong with goodness you disarm the aggressor, diminish hatred, and create conditions for reconciliation so that an enemy can be transformed into a sincere ally. This guidance is both an ethical duty and a pragmatic strategy grounded in trust that higher moral action yields more lasting and righteous social harmony than tit-for-tat retaliation.

translation: And none will meet it except those who are patient; and none will meet it except a possessor of great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the good being promised (salvation, victory, divine favour or final recompense) is not for everyone but for those who endure with steadfast patience. The doubled expression stresses exclusivity: perseverance through trials and constancy in faith and conduct is the qualifying trait, and those who bear hardships with patience will obtain an immense share of blessing and reward.

translation: And if there comes to you from Satan an evil suggestion, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing.
interpretation: The verse instructs that when Satan plants a whisper or temptation in the heart — whether a fleeting suggestion or a repeated tug toward doubt, sin, or discouragement — the proper immediate response is to seek Allah’s protection (e.g., by saying A'ūdhu billāh, turning to remembrance, the Qurʾān, prayer, and righteous action). Calling on God is effective because He alone truly perceives and understands the inner state: He hears the request for refuge and knows the reality of the whisper, so relying on Him repels Satan’s influence and preserves the believer’s spiritual steadiness.

translation: And among His signs are the night and the day and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah who created them, if you truly worship Him.
interpretation: The verse uses the observable regularity and authority of night, day, sun and moon to confront the human tendency to venerate created things and to reorient worship toward the Creator. By forbidding prostration to celestial bodies and commanding prostration to Allah, it teaches that true devotion is judged by its object: outward acts of reverence must be directed to the One whose wisdom and power produced the order we behold. The phrase “if you truly worship Him” functions as a moral test of sincerity, calling believers to purify their faith from idolatry and to read the cosmos as signs pointing to God’s unique sovereignty and lordship.

translation: But if they are arrogant, then those near your Lord glorify Him by night and by day, and they never become weary.
interpretation: The phrase “those near your Lord” refers to the beings in God’s presence (traditionally understood as angels or purified servants) who continuously exalt Him. The verse teaches that human arrogance or rejection does not affect the reality of God’s majesty: around the Divine Presence praise and submission are constant and effortless, in contrast to human fatigue and resistance. It reassures that God’s praise, authority, and the work of His servants persist independently of people’s acceptance or refusal.

translation: And of His signs is that you see the earth humbled; then when We send down upon it water it quivers and swells. Indeed, He who has given it life is the Giver of life to the dead. Indeed, He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse invites reflection: the visible revival of barren earth by God’s rain is presented as a concrete sign of God’s exclusive power to give life. It teaches that natural cycles—creation’s humble submission and sudden reanimation—are evidence that the One who restores life to the land can likewise resurrect human beings; therefore witnessing such signs should strengthen trust in God’s sovereignty, awaken humility before Him, and reinforce belief in resurrection and accountability.

translation: Indeed, those who twist and turn away from Our signs will not escape Us. Is one who is cast into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? Do what you will; indeed, He is All‑Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse warns that anyone who distorts, denies, or deliberately turns aside from God's revelations cannot hide from His knowledge; their rejection has real consequences. The rhetorical question contrasts the fate of the wicked—cast into the Fire—with the blessed who will stand safe on the Day of Resurrection, making clear which outcome is preferable. The command “do what you will” is not permission to act without consequence but a challenge: continue in your ways if you insist, yet bear in mind that God observes both outward deeds and inward intentions and will hold people to account.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved in the Reminder when it came to them — and indeed it is a Mighty Book.
interpretation: The verse reproves those who, despite the message reaching them clearly, refused to accept it; their denial stems from arrogance, prejudice, or vested interests, not from any defect in the message itself. Calling the Book “ʿazīz” affirms its intrinsic strength, honor, and divine preservation — its truth is powerful, self-sustaining, and ultimately victorious — so human rejection only exposes moral failings and cannot undermine the Book’s authority or the consequences it brings.

translation: Falsehood cannot approach Him from before Him nor from behind Him; a revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute transcendence and perfection: no error, falsehood, or deficiency can originate with Him or reach Him, and therefore the revelation given (the Qur’an) is authentic, protected, and issued from perfect wisdom and praiseworthiness—warranting trust in its guidance and integrity.

translation: Nothing is said to you except what has been said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is Most Forgiving and Owner of a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse functions as a consoling and directive reminder: the opposition and accusations the Prophet meets are part of a recurring pattern experienced by earlier messengers, so he should not be swayed by novelty or despair. It highlights a theological balance—God’s wide mercy and readiness to forgive those who repent, alongside the real certainty of severe recompense for persistent, obstinate rejection—and so it counsels patient perseverance, measured firmness in calling people, and reliance on Divine justice and compassion rather than on personal retaliation or despondency.

translation: And if We had made it a non‑Arabic Qur’an, they would have said, “Why are its verses not made clear? Is it a foreign [book] and an Arabic [one]?” Say, “It is guidance and a cure for those who believe.” But those who do not believe — in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them; those are being called from a distant place.
interpretation: The verse answers a misplaced criticism about language by showing that acceptance depends on the inner state of people, not the tongue of revelation. For the receptive, the Qur’an functions as guidance and a healing — it corrects, comforts, and reforms hearts and lives. For the rejecters, metaphors of deafness and blindness describe spiritual insensitivity and self‑inflicted estrangement from truth: they hear yet do not internalize, and therefore remain distant from guidance (ultimately to be summoned from afar at reckoning). The passage thus shifts the focus from external form to moral receptivity and accountability.

translation: And indeed We gave Moses the Book, yet there was disagreement about it; and if not for a prior Word from your Lord, the matter would have been decided among them; and indeed they are in a perplexing doubt concerning it.
interpretation: The verse teaches that revealed guidance can be clear yet still be contested by human factions. The phrase “a prior Word” is best understood as God’s deliberate decree to defer immediate judgment — He allowed the dispute to continue as part of the test of free will and to reserve final adjudication for His appointed time. Thus the passage criticizes the persistent, self-interested wavering of people who, despite receiving decisive revelation, remain in misleading doubt because of desire, pride or factional interests rather than genuine uncertainty.

translation:
من عمل صالحا فلنفسه ۖ ومن أساء فعليها ۗ وما ربك بظلام للعبيد
"Whoever does a righteous deed does it for the benefit of his own soul, and whoever does evil does so to its detriment. And your Lord is never unjust to the servants."
interpretation: The verse affirms personal moral responsibility and the moral economy that binds actions to their rightful consequences: good deeds ultimately profit the doer’s soul (spiritual well‑being, reward, purification), while evil deeds rebound as harm upon the doer. At the same time it reassures that divine judgment is perfectly just—God neither wrongs anyone nor fails to give people what they deserve—so apparent injustices in this life will be set right by God’s fair reckoning. The practical thrust is individual accountability (no scapegoating for one’s sin), encouragement to pursue righteousness for one’s own true good, and trust in God’s ultimate justice.

translation: لَهُ يَعُودُ عِلْمُ السَّاعَةِ ۚ وَمَا تَخْرُجُ مِن ثَمَرَاتِ أَكْمَامِهَا وَمَا تَحْمِلُ مِن أُنثَىٰ وَلَا تَضَعُ إِلَّا بِعِلْمِهِ ۚ وَيَوْمَ يُنَادِيهِمْ أَيْنَ شُرَكَائِي قَالُوا آذَنَّاكَ مَا مِنَّا مِن شَهِيدٍ
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن العلم الحق بالساعة وبكل ما هو خفي —من دورات الطبيعة إلى أسرار الحمل والولادة— إنما هو من شأن الله وحده، وأن كل ظواهر الخلق علامة على تسلطه وقدرته. وبذلك تُفكك العقيدة الوثنية: الذين أُشركوا بالله لا يملكون علماً ولا قوة ولا قدرة على الشهادة لصالح أتباعهم يوم القيامة، بل ينكرونهم ويبرؤون، فتتكشف بطلان الاعتماد عليهم. الدلالة العملية: التوحيد الحقيقي يستلزم الاعتراف بألوهية الله في العلم والقدرة والرزق، وعدم الرجاء أو الخوف من شركاء لا يملكون نفعاً ولا ضراً.

translation: And that which they used to call upon before abandoned them, and they thought there was no refuge for them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that placing trust in false gods, idols, or transient worldly supports is finally exposed as vain: at the moment of death or divine reckoning those supports will offer no help, and the people who depended on them will find themselves utterly without escape. The lesson is theological and moral — true refuge and aid belong to God alone, and reliance on anything else will be revealed as betrayal when one most needs deliverance.

translation: A person does not grow weary of praying for good; yet if evil befalls him, he becomes despairing and hopeless.
interpretation: This cautions against a conditional, inconsistent relationship with God: many continually beg for blessings but, when tested by hardship, abandon hope and patience. True spiritual maturity requires steadfast reliance and persistent supplication in both ease and adversity, trusting that trials have purpose and not allowing them to extinguish hope.

translation: And if We were to let him taste mercy from Us after distress had touched him, he would surely say, “This is due to me, and I do not think the Hour will occur.” And “If I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best.” But We will certainly inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will make them taste a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse points to a spiritual sickness: when God relieves a person’s hardship and grants comfort, some become arrogant and assume that worldly ease proves their own merit and that there will be no final reckoning. Their self‑sufficiency leads them to deny the Last Day and to presume guaranteed reward. The warning is that temporal relief is not proof of eternal favor; God will, in the end, make clear the true nature of people’s deeds and hold the rejecters accountable, exposing their self‑deception and subjecting them to a severe consequence.

translation: When We bestow a favor upon man, he turns away and withdraws to one side; but when evil touches him, he is full of abundant supplication.
interpretation: The verse reproves the human tendency to be ungrateful and inconsistent: in prosperity people often distance themselves from God and neglect gratitude or obedience, yet when calamity strikes they return with loud, urgent pleas. “دعاء عريض” (abundant supplication) highlights how their invocation in hardship is intense and frequent but often lacks the steady trust, thankfulness and upright conduct that should accompany true faith.

translation: Say, “Have you considered: if it is from Allah and you then disbelieve in it, who is more misguided than one who is in manifest, distant schism?”
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical challenge to those who reject the revelation: if the message truly comes from God, then to persistently reject it is not mere error but a deliberate turning away that places one in the deepest level of misguidance. The phrase “in shiqaq ba‘īd” (manifest, distant schism) describes a stubborn, entrenched separation from God’s guidance — a willful, persistent rebellion rather than innocent mistake — and thus highlights the moral responsibility and grave consequences of rejecting clear divine guidance.

translation: We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth. And is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?
interpretation: The verse affirms that God will make the reality of revelation manifest both in the external world (the horizons — the cosmos, history, events) and in the inner world (people’s hearts, consciences, and personal experience), so that the truth of His message becomes unmistakable. This unfolding of signs is not merely intellectual proof but an experiential illumination that confronts people from without and within. The rhetorical question that follows reassures the Prophet and believers: even if many persist in denial, God’s continuous, comprehensive witnessing of every reality — His knowledge, justice, and presence — is in itself sufficient evidence and authority. In short, the verse teaches that ultimate proof lies in God’s manifest signs and His all-encompassing testimony, and that rejection does not diminish the objective truth already demonstrated to the world and the soul.

translation:
ألا إنهم في مرية من لقاء ربهم ۗ ألا إنه بكل شيء محيط
“Behold, they are indeed in doubt about meeting their Lord; surely He is, over all things, encompassing.”
interpretation: The verse addresses those who deny or doubt the coming together with God (the resurrection and final reckoning). Their skepticism does not render the event uncertain; rather it highlights human short-sightedness. God’s being “بكل شيء محيط” affirms His complete knowledge, power and authority: He is aware of hidden thoughts, controls every event, and can bring about the meeting He promised. Thus the passage warns that doubt will not avert accountability, because God’s encompassing attribute guarantees both the reality of the meeting and His just oversight of all people.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Ḥāʼ Mīm.
interpretation: The disconnected letters “Ḥāʼ Mīm” act as a divine sign that calls attention to the revelation and underscores the Qur’an’s miraculous nature: though made from the same Arabic letters known to people, its eloquence, depth, and impact cannot be produced by human skill. Their precise, inner meaning belongs to God, while their presence authenticates and solemnly introduces the message that follows.

translation: لم تُقدَّم آية كاملة — الكلمة المنفردة «عسق» غير كافية لترجمة دقيقة.
interpretation: هل تقصد هذه الكلمة وحدها أم تودُّ أن أترجم وأفسّر الآية الكاملة التي وردت فيها؟ أرسِل الآية كاملة لأقدّم ترجمة وتأويلاً دقيقين.

translation: Thus does Allah reveal to you and to those before you — the Almighty, the All‑Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qurʾanic revelation to the Prophet is of the same divine origin and mode as the messages given to earlier prophets; by naming God al‑ʿAzīz (Almighty/Invincible) and al‑Ḥakīm (All‑Wise) it stresses that this guidance carries God’s authoritative power and is shaped by perfect wisdom. Consequently the message is not a human invention but part of a continuous, purposeful divine plan whose truth, timing and effects rest on God’s might and wisdom, demanding acceptance and trust despite opposition or difficulty.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; and He is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty and exclusive ownership of all that exists: nothing in heaven or earth belongs to any other authority. Calling Him al-ʿAliyy (the Most High) emphasizes His transcendence above creation, while al-ʿAẓīm (the Most Great) stresses His unmatched majesty, power, and right to command and judge. This establishes the theological foundation of tawḥīd—that ultimate authority, provision and accountability rest solely with God—and summons believers to humility, dependence on Him, and recognition of His supreme authority.

translation: The heavens are almost about to burst from above them, and the angels exalt the praise of their Lord and ask forgiveness for those on earth. Indeed, Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the severity of the situation — symbolized by the heavens nearly cleaving under the weight of human corruption and denial — with the continual mercy that sustains creation: angels constantly glorify God and intercede by seeking forgiveness for people on earth. That juxtaposition teaches that although human wrongdoing invites grievous consequences, divine compassion is primary; God’s forgiveness and mercy remain available and can avert or temper punishment when people turn back to Him.

translation: And those who have taken guardians besides Him—Allah is, over them, a Guardian—and you are not a guardian over them.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when people put their trust in other gods, authorities, or intermediaries instead of God, God nonetheless remains the ultimate Keeper of their affairs: He permits them to follow their chosen protectors, preserves their situation, and will hold them to account in His time. It also reminds the Prophet (and by extension any messenger) that his role is to convey guidance, not to force belief or control others’ hearts—true guidance and guardianship belong to God alone.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you a Qur’an in Arabic so that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it, and warn of the Day of Gathering—there is no doubt about it—[that] a party [will be] in Paradise and a party in the Blaze.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God gave the message in the clear language of the Prophet so there would be no excuse for ignorance: the Qur’an’s clarity makes the warning immediate and accountable for its nearest audience (Mecca and its inhabitants). By linking the revelation to the inevitable Day of Gathering and the stark division of outcomes—some in Paradise, some in Hell—it stresses moral responsibility: individuals’ responses to the clear warning determine their final destiny. The emphasis on language and certainty underlines that guidance was presented plainly, leaving the choice and its real, eternal consequences to human free will.

translation:
وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً ۚ وَلَـٰكِن يُدْخِلُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ ۚ وَالظَّالِمُونَ لَهُم مَّا لَهُمْ مِن وَلِيٍّ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ

"And if Allah had willed, He would have made them a single community; but He admits into His mercy whom He wills. And the wrongdoers will have no protector or helper."
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty: He could have created uniform belief among people, yet by divine wisdom He allows moral freedom and diversity, granting His mercy to those He chooses (based on His knowledge, mercy and people’s response). This underlines that guidance and salvation are ultimately gifts from God, not automatic rights, while those who persist in injustice or rejection sever themselves from protection and will find no guardian or ally before God.

translation: Or have they taken, besides Him, protectors? Yet Allah is the Protector (al-Wali); He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things All‑Powerful.
interpretation: The verse denounces entrusting ultimate guardianship, trust or dependence to anyone other than God by asserting that true protection, authority over life and death, and sovereign power belong solely to Allah; therefore faith, reliance and ultimate submission are due to Him alone, since no created being can truly sustain, revive, or control affairs the way He can.

translation: And whatever you differ about, its judgement is with Allah. That is Allah — my Lord; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn in repentance.
interpretation: Disputes should be settled not by pride or partisanship but by submitting to divine criteria; genuine faith shows itself in entrusting outcomes to God while remaining ready to return to Him. Leadership and communal peace require humility before God's judgment, reliance (tawakkul) on His wisdom, and continual repentance (tawbah) to preserve moral integrity and unity.

translation: Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you from yourselves mates, and from the cattle pairs; He causes you to be multiplied through them. Nothing is like unto Him — and He is the All‑Hearing, the All‑Seeing.
interpretation: The verse presents two linked truths: God’s exclusive role as the real Originator of all existence, and the wisdom of His created order by which life continues. By creating human and animal pairs He established the means for reproduction, social bonds, provision and variety in creation; these observable arrangements are signs of His sustaining design. The phrase “there is nothing like Him” rejects any comparison or likeness with His essence, while “He is the Hearing, the Seeing” affirms His perfect, active knowledge of all affairs. Taken together the verse calls for recognition of God’s unmatched creative authority and attentiveness, and for understanding natural order as evidence of His power and mercy rather than as autonomous chance.

translation:
لَهُ مَقالِيدُ السَّماواتِ وَالأَرضِ ۖ يَبْسُطُ الرِّزقَ لِمَن يَشاءُ وَيَقْدِرُ ۚ إِنَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيءٍ عَلِيمٌ
To Him belong the keys (authority) of the heavens and the earth; He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it; indeed He is, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's sovereign control over the world includes the ordering of sustenance and circumstance according to His perfect knowledge. Differences in people’s wealth, status, and opportunity are not arbitrary but part of a wise, comprehensive divine plan: provisions may be increased or limited as tests, means for moral development, or instruments of mercy and wisdom beyond our sight. Therefore believers are called to combine sincere effort with trust and humility—working within the means God provides, using blessings responsibly, and refraining from judging God’s justice when the ultimate reasons lie within His all‑knowing wisdom.

translation: He has ordained for you the religion that He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus: that you establish the religion and do not be divided therein. Great is the aversion of the polytheists to what you call them to. Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills, and He guides to Himself whoever turns back [to Him].
interpretation: This verse affirms a single, continuous divine way running through the prophets: the core purpose of revelation is to establish a unified, God‑centered community that clings to essential truth rather than fracturing over secondary disputes. The charge to “establish the religion and not be divided” is a call to preserve the unity of faith and practice around submission to God, resisting sectarianism that erodes prophetic guidance. The noted hostility of polytheists explains why this call meets fierce rejection—because it threatens their attachments and interests. The statement that God “chooses whom He wills” stresses divine sovereignty in opening hearts, yet the clause about guiding “whoever turns” balances that sovereignty with human responsibility: sincere turning, repentance and orientation toward God dispose one to receive His guidance. Together the verse teaches continuity of revelation, the ethical necessity of communal unity on core principles, realism about opposition, and a theology that holds God’s elective will and human repentance in tension rather than contradiction.

translation: They only split into factions after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves. And if not for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord until an appointed term, their matter would have been settled among them; and indeed those who were given the Scripture after them are, concerning it, in grave doubt.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the fault lies not in lack of guidance but in human disposition: communities received clear truth yet allowed jealousy, pride and partisan passions to fracture that guidance into competing sects. God’s ‘word’ or decree — His timing and ultimate judgment — restrained immediate punishment, permitting a set term for testing and for His wisdom to unfold; otherwise He would have enacted decisive justice earlier. The reference to later inheritors of the Scripture being ‘in doubtful perplexity’ warns that when revelation is treated as tribal property, passed on by those who alter, dispute or neglect its meaning, its truth becomes obscured and followers fall into confusion. The practical lesson is that preserving sincere understanding, humility before the revelation, and submission to God’s timing are essential to prevent corrosive divisions and the corruption of transmitted guidance.

translation: So call (people) for that reason, and be steadfast as you have been commanded, and do not follow their desires. And say, "I believe in what Allah has sent down of the Book, and I am commanded to act justly among you." Allah is our Lord and your Lord; for us are our deeds and for you are your deeds; there is no argument between us and you. Allah will gather us together, and to Him is the return.
interpretation: The verse instructs the messenger to persistently convey the divine message while maintaining personal integrity and judicial impartiality regardless of popular pressure. It underscores that acknowledgment of a common Lord does not erase moral responsibility: each group will be judged by its own deeds, so the prophet’s role is not to seek worldly consensus but to uphold justice and truth. Ultimate reconciliation and judgment belong to God alone, so believers should focus on faithfully fulfilling their duties rather than conforming to desires or trying to manufacture agreement.

translation: And those who dispute about Allah after He has been responded to — their argument will be rejected before their Lord, and upon them is [His] wrath, and for them is a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that if people persist in arguing or denying the truth of God after clear proof, guidance, or a definitive response has been given, their disputes will be nullified in God’s presence; their reasoning will not avail them, and they will incur divine anger and a severe penalty. It emphasizes the futility and moral danger of stubbornly contesting settled divine guidance once the matter has been settled by God.

translation: Allah is He Who has sent down the Book in truth and the Measure (al-mīzān). And what will make you know? Perchance the Hour is near.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Qur’an is divinely revealed both as truthful guidance and as a ‘measure’—a criterion for justice, right conduct, and moral discernment. The rhetorical question “And what will make you know?” rebukes human complacency about the future and serves to unsettle any false assurance, while “perhaps the Hour is near” creates moral urgency: since final accountability may arrive at any time, people must apply the Book’s standards in their behavior, uphold justice, and live in constant readiness for judgment.

translation: Those who do not believe in it hasten toward it, while those who believe are apprehensive of it and know that it is the Truth. Verily, those who dispute concerning the Hour are in a far error.
interpretation: The verse diagnoses spiritual states: denial of the Last Day produces a reckless, impatient stance—people entrenched in unbelief rush headlong in life, seeking immediate ends and showing contempt for accountability—whereas true belief brings sober fear, readiness and acceptance of divine reality. The warning against disputing the Hour teaches that arguing about its reality is not a neutral intellectual exercise but a sign of profound misguidance: such disputation reflects pride and refusal to submit to truth, and it leads one away from moral responsibility and from the path of guidance.

translation: Allah is Gentle toward His servants; He provides for whom He wills, and He is the All‑Strong, the Almighty.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s attribute of Latīf denotes a nuanced, caring kindness that attends to people in ways that may be subtle, hidden, or finely tailored to their needs. Provision and relief are ultimately dispensed by divine will rather than solely by visible causes, so reliance on God and patience are called for when outward means seem lacking. The pairing with al‑Qawī and al‑ʿAzīz balances this tenderness with absolute power: God’s mercy is not weakness but is exercised from a position of sovereign might and justice, assuring that His subtle care is effective and authoritative.

translation:
من كان يريد حرث الآخرة نزد له في حرثه ۖ ومن كان يريد حرث الدنيا نؤته منها وما له في الآخرة من نصيب
"Whoever seeks the harvest of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his harvest; and whoever seeks the harvest of this world, We shall give him of it, and he will have no share in the Hereafter."
interpretation: The verse uses the image of sowing and harvest to contrast two life-orientations: those whose intentions and deeds are aimed at the eternal life (the Hereafter) will find their spiritual return multiplied by God, while those who single-mindedly pursue worldly gain may receive transient material benefits but forfeit any portion in the eternal reward. It emphasizes that God rewards sincere intention and prioritizing the everlasting over the temporary, and that worldly success alone cannot substitute for a share in the Hereafter.

translation: Or have they taken partners who have prescribed for them a religion which Allah did not authorize? And had it not been for a decisive word (a final decree), it would have been settled between them. And indeed the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who set up others as partners in authority who invent or impose religious rules aside from God's ordinance; such man‑made legislation is illegitimate. The phrase “كلمة الفصل” is understood as God’s decisive decree to withhold immediate retribution — a deliberate postponement so that people can be tested, warned, and given chance to respond — but that divine forbearance does not remove ultimate justice: persistent wrongdoers who persist in usurping divine guidance and oppressing others will face a painful, inevitable punishment.

translation: You will see the wrongdoers fearful for what they have earned, and it will befall them; but those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in gardens — for them is whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the inevitable self‑inflicted consequences of injustice with the comprehensive, fulfilling reward granted to the faithful. Wrongdoers are depicted as consumed by fear and remorse because their own actions bring about their punishment; by contrast, belief combined with righteous deeds leads to abiding felicity in lush gardens where God grants the true wants of the heart. Calling this outcome “the great bounty” emphasizes that the highest good is not merely material comfort but God’s generous favor, acceptance, and consummate satisfaction granted to those who acted rightly.

translation:
ذٰلِكَ الَّذِي يُبَشِّرُ اللَّهُ عِبَادَهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ ۚ قُلْ لَا أَسْأَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ أَجْرًا إِلَّا الْمَوَدَّةَ فِي الْقُرْبَىٰ ۗ وَمَنْ يَقْتَرِفْ حَسَنَةً نَّزِدْ لَهُ فِيهَا حَسَنًا ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ شَكُورٌ

“That is the glad tidings which Allah gives to His servants who believe and do righteous deeds. Say: I do not ask you any payment for it except love for the near of kin. And whoever does a good deed, We will increase for him its good; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Appreciative.”
interpretation: The verse sets a moral and communal priority: genuine faith must be accompanied by righteous action, and the Prophet’s mission imposes no worldly fee — his single request is that the community preserve and show sincere affection, support and duties toward those nearest in kinship (understood classically as both one’s own relatives and, by many readings, the Prophet’s close household). Framing ‘muwaddah fi’l-qurba’ as the lone demanded recompense teaches that sustaining family and close social bonds is an essential ethical responsibility in Islam; at the same time God assures that every sincere good is increased and that He forgives and rightly rewards people’s efforts, so love for kin together with concrete righteous deeds is the path to multiplied divine favor.

translation: Or do they say, “He has invented a lie against Allah”? If Allah had willed, He could have sealed your heart; and Allah wipes out falsehood and establishes the truth by His words. Indeed He is All‑Knower of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: This verse answers the charge that the Prophet fabricated revelation. It points out that acceptance or rejection of guidance lies in God’s sovereign will—He could have sealed the Prophet’s heart so he would not receive or convey the message, but He did not. Instead, by His decree and His speech (the revealed word and divine ordinance) God removes falsehood and causes truth to prevail. The reminder that He knows “what is within the breasts” underlines that outward accusations cannot overturn the divine reality: the origin, preservation and triumph of the message are determined by God alone, and inner motives and secret truths are fully known to Him.

translation: And He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons (or overlooks) their misdeeds, and He knows what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s mercy and His knowledge work together: He is ready to receive a sincere return to Him and to remove or forgive past wrongs, yet He remains fully aware of every action and intention. This both consoles and admonishes—the believer is encouraged to hope in God’s forgiveness and to turn back sincerely, while also being reminded that repentance must be real and accompanied by reform, because God’s all‑knowingness means deeds and motives are not hidden and will shape the moral reality of one’s relationship with Him.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds — He will respond to them and increase them out of His bounty; and for the disbelievers is a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true faith paired with righteous action elicits God’s accepting response: He answers, admits, and bestows blessings not merely as exact wage but multiplied by His generous grace. This divine increase shows mercy and favor toward sincere believers, while the warning of severe punishment for disbelievers underscores the moral seriousness and consequences of rejecting guidance.

translation: And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely transgress in the earth; but He sends it down in due measure as He wills. Indeed He is, concerning His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.
interpretation: The verse explains that God, in His wisdom, restrains limitless abundance because unchecked plenty would encourage human excess, injustice and corruption; by distributing provision “in measure” He preserves balance, creates conditions that call people to gratitude, responsibility and mutual support, and ensures that sustenance serves as a test and a means for moral behavior. His attributes “Acquainted and Seeing” reassure that this measured distribution is knowledgeable and purposeful: God is fully aware of people’s needs and actions and administers provision with just wisdom and oversight.

translation: And He is the One who sends down the rain after they had despaired and spreads His mercy; and He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine intervention can reverse situations that appear hopeless: God’s sending of relief (symbolized by rain) is an expression of His comprehensive mercy that renews life, provision and hope. Calling God al‑Wali (the Protector/Guardian) emphasizes that He is the real supporter and defender of those who turn to Him, and al‑Hamid (the Praiseworthy) reminds us that His actions are inherently worthy of gratitude and praise. The practical implication is a moral-spiritual lesson against despair and self-reliance: believers are urged to trust God’s timing, remain patient and seek His help, because apparent defeat can be transformed into deliverance by His mercy.

translation: And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and whatever living creatures He has scattered through them. And He is, over their gathering when He wills, All‑Capable.
interpretation: The verse points to the widespread variety of life in the heavens and on earth as deliberate signs of God’s wisdom and sovereignty; by stating that He can gather them whenever He wills, it affirms His absolute power to assemble and hold all creatures — a power that underwrites resurrection, accountability, and the moral order of creation — and invites reflection on God’s unity, providence, and the purposeful character of life.

translation: And whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your hands have earned; and He pardons much.
interpretation: The verse teaches that many difficulties that occur in life are consequences of human actions and moral failings, yet God’s mercy is vast and often refrains from requiting every fault; therefore such trials should lead to self-accounting, repentance and reform rather than despair, while recognizing that not every hardship is an exact punishment and that divine forgiveness remains abundant.

translation: And you will not be able to frustrate Us on the earth; and besides Allah you will have no protector or helper.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes Allah’s absolute sovereignty and the futility of relying on worldly powers or allies to thwart His decree: no human plan, force, or partnership can prevent what Allah wills, and whoever places ultimate trust in anything other than Allah will find no true guardian or aid when divine judgment or outcome comes.

translation:
وَمِنْ آيَٰتِهِ ٱلْجَوَارِ فِى ٱلْبَحْرِ كَٱلْأَعْلَـٰمِ
"And among His signs are the ships that sail in the sea, like banners."
interpretation: The verse calls attention to God’s sovereignty and providence: the fact that ships traverse vast, dangerous seas—moving visibly like standards—is a sign of His power and wisdom in making human enterprise, trade and travel possible and in subduing nature; it is meant to prompt reflection, gratitude and trust in God rather than reliance on mere human effort.

translation: If He wills, He makes the wind calm, and they would lie motionless upon its surface. Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one.
interpretation: The verse is teaching that God’s control over nature is intentionally manifest so as to prompt a spiritual response: reaching stillness in the face of forces beyond human control functions as a sign meant to be perceived by those who cultivate patience (sabr) and gratitude (shukr). Such people do not see these events merely as physical phenomena but as evidence of divine power and mercy—tests that refine trust in God and reminders to acknowledge His favors—so the calm and the storm both serve to distinguish and spiritually edify the steadfast and thankful.

translation: Or He destroys them for what they have earned, and pardons much.
interpretation: This juxtaposition highlights God’s balance of justice and mercy: He can punish people decisively for their culpable deeds, yet He often chooses to forgive and overlook many faults. The statement functions both as a sober warning about accountability and as an affirmation of the abundant clemency that accompanies divine judgment.

translation: And He will make those who dispute concerning Our signs know that for them there is no refuge.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who deny, contest, or mock God’s revelations will ultimately be forced to see that their arguments provide no escape from accountability. The word “محيص” denotes a hiding place or means of evasion; when the truth and its consequences are made manifest, their sophistry will be exposed, their excuses fail, and they will find no safe harbor from divine judgment. Thus the verse emphasizes the futility of resisting clear signs and the inevitability of being held to account.

translation: So whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the life of this world; and what is with Allah is better and more lasting — for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.
interpretation: This verse reminds believers that any possessions, status, or pleasures they receive here are temporary and secondary; the true good — the reward, justice, and permanence that come from God — surpasses worldly gains. It calls the faithful to prioritize the eternal over the ephemeral, to cultivate trust in God (tawakkul), and to avoid being attached or disheartened by loss or by the fleeting attractions of this life, since reliance on God and steadfast faith lead to what is better and abiding.

translation: And those who avoid the great sins and immoralities, and when they are angry they pardon.
interpretation: The verse commends a balanced moral nature: true believers deliberately shun grave transgressions and indecent behavior, and they exercise self-mastery over powerful emotions by choosing forgiveness instead of retaliation. This combination—vigilance against serious sin together with magnanimity in moments of provocation—marks spiritual maturity, preserves social harmony, and shows reliance on God’s justice rather than seeking personal vengeance.

translation: And those who respond to their Lord and establish prayer, and whose affair is by consultation among themselves, and from what We have provided them they spend.
interpretation: The verse presents a measure of true faith as a unity of inward surrender and outward responsibility: genuine responsiveness to God is manifested not only in ritual devotion (prayer) but in the ethical shape of communal life — decisions reached through mutual consultation (shūrā) and material provisions circulated for the welfare of others. In other words, authentic religion transforms private piety into participatory governance and social solidarity, making obedience to God the basis for just, consultative leadership and compassionate economic practice.

translation: And those who, when injustice befalls them, they defend themselves.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true believers do not passively accept oppression; when wrong or aggression touches them they rise to protect their dignity and rights, resisting injustice by lawful, measured means in order to restore justice while relying on God.

translation: The recompense for an evil is an evil like it; but whoever pardons and reforms, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse acknowledges the legitimacy of proportionate justice yet elevates mercy as the superior moral response: rather than perpetuating retaliation, a believer is urged to pardon and actively restore relations, trusting that God will grant the true recompense. This teaches self-restraint, the preference for reconciliation over revenge, and reliance on divine justice, while making clear that persistent oppression remains condemned.

translation: And whoever is avenged after having been wronged — then for them there is no blame.
interpretation: The verse affirms that when a person resists or seeks rightful redress after being subjected to injustice, their defensive response is morally and religiously permissible; God does not hold them culpable for defending their rights, while the guidance still implies restraint so that retaliation serves restoration of justice rather than excess or unlawful vengeance.

translation: The only course (of accountability) is against those who wrong people and transgress on the earth without right; for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse declares that divine accountability falls specifically on those who commit injustice and spread oppression or corruption on earth without justification. ‘‘السبيل’’ here denotes the rightful ground for retribution: it is the oppressors’ wrongful acts—usurping rights, abusing power, transgressing limits—that make them subject to severe punishment. The statement affirms moral responsibility and God's justice: victims are not blamed for the harms done to them, while perpetrators of unjust aggression will meet painful consequences.

translation: And whoever is patient and forgives — indeed, that is among matters of firm resolve.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true moral strength lies in enduring hardship with patience and responding to wrongs with forgiveness; such restraint and pardon are not signs of weakness but of determined character and deep trust in God’s justice, because choosing patience and forgiveness requires inner courage, discipline, and the firm resolve to rise above immediate anger or desire for retaliation.

translation:
وَمَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُ مِن وَلِيٍّ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ ۗ وَتَرَى الظَّالِمِينَ لَمَّا رَأَوْا الْعَذَابَ يَقُولُونَ هَلْ إِلَى مَرْدٍ مِنْ سَبِيلٍ
"And whoever Allah causes to stray—then he has no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers when they behold the punishment, saying, 'Is there any return by any way?'"
interpretation: This verse warns that guidance is ultimately a gift and a trust from God: those who persistently reject truth and choose wrongdoing may be left by God to their own misguided choices, so that no human guardian or intercessor can save them from the consequences. When the divine punishment becomes manifest, the wrongdoers will vainly ask if there is any way to turn back—whether to life for repentance or to escape the penalty—but their plea will come too late. The passage thus stresses personal responsibility to seek and accept guidance while it is still granted, and the finality of God’s judgment when He withdraws His protecting grace.

translation: And you will see them presented before it, submissive, humbled in abasement, casting furtive glances. And those who believed will say, “Indeed, the truly ruined are those who ruined themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection.” Verily, the wrongdoers will be in abiding punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate loss is not material failure but spiritual ruin—when a person’s choices lead both themselves and those under their influence away from guidance. The scene of the guilty humiliated before judgment illustrates divine justice and the irreversible consequences of turning to oppression or falsehood. The believers’ remark distinguishes fleeting worldly status from eternal outcome, warning that moral responsibility for oneself and one’s household carries immense weight, and that persistent injustice and misguidance result in a lasting, established penalty.

translation: And they had no allies who could help them besides Allah. And whoever Allah sends astray—then for him there is no way (to guidance).
interpretation: The verse teaches that ultimate protection and guidance belong solely to God: the idols, powers, or human supporters whom people rely on cannot intercede or secure salvation. When, because of persistent rejection or as a consequence of divine judgment, God allows a person to be led away from the truth, no created ally or path remains to restore them to guidance. Thus the passage warns that reliance on false protectors is futile and that access to the right path depends entirely on God’s guidance and mercy.

translation: Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from Allah from which there is no turning back; you will have no refuge that day, nor will you have anyone to deny (it) for you.
interpretation: The verse is a warning that demands urgent submission and reform now, because the Day of divine reckoning is inevitable and irreversible. It means that when that Day arrives, worldly shelters, excuses, defenders, or denials will be useless; therefore one must sincerely accept God’s guidance, repent, and act righteously before the chance to change one’s standing is gone.

translation: But if they turn away, then We did not send you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey [the message]. And whenever We cause a human to taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them for what their hands have sent before [them], then indeed man is ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse teaches two linked lessons: the Prophet’s role is limited to conveying God’s message—he is not responsible for forcing guidance or policing hearts—and human beings habitually fail in gratitude. When God grants mercy people celebrate yet often forget or claim credit; when misfortune comes, especially as a consequence of their own deeds, they complain or blame, exposing ingratitude (kufr). Thus mercy and trial alike are signs demanding recognition, accountability, and sincere thankfulness rather than self‑justification or reproach.

translation: To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He grants females to whom He wills, and He grants males to whom He wills.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over creation — including the most personal, contingent matters like the sex of offspring — and teaches that such outcomes are ultimately determined by His will. It calls believers to recognize children as gifts from God, to relinquish human pretensions of control, and to reject cultural favoritism (e.g., preferring sons) by accepting whatever God bestows with gratitude and trust in His wisdom.

translation: Or He appoints for them males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing, Able.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the gift of children, their sexes, and the state of fertility are governed solely by God’s wisdom and power. What people long for or lament — sons, daughters, or the absence of offspring — is not merely a product of chance or human effort but part of divine decree, serving purposes beyond our immediate understanding: tests, blessings, means of mercy, restraint, or social balance. The closing attributes, “Knowing, Able,” remind the believer to trust God’s perfect knowledge and capability rather than to resent, stigmatize, or ascribe blame to others; acceptance and reliance on God’s wisdom are the proper moral and spiritual responses to such matters.

translation: And it is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or He sends a messenger and He reveals, by His permission, what He wills. Indeed He is the Most High, the Most Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God's communication with humans is neither casual nor direct in ordinary terms but occurs by chosen, mediated means—inward revelation, concealed speech beyond human perception, or through a messenger/angel—and that this restraint reflects God’s transcendence and wise care: He discloses to whom, when, and by what method He wills, guarding human frailty and preventing arbitrary claims of hearing God while ensuring guidance is transmitted according to His wisdom.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed you will surely guide to a straight path.
interpretation: The phrase “a spirit from Our command” refers to the divine revelation brought by the angelic messenger — a communication originating entirely from God, not from the Prophet’s own invention. “You did not know what the Book nor faith” emphasizes the Prophet’s prior unfamiliarity with the revealed law and creed, underscoring that the scripture and the knowledge of true faith were bestowed upon him rather than self-derived. Describing the Book as a “light” teaches that the Qur’an illuminates hearts and minds, making moral and spiritual truth clear and enabling right action; this illumination effects real guidance in people’s lives, but it is given by God to those He chooses. The statement that the Prophet “will surely guide to a straight path” affirms his role as the faithful conveyor and exemplar who calls people to that illuminated way; yet the actual turning of hearts is ultimately God’s gracious gift. The verse therefore stresses both the divine origin and authority of revelation and the complementary roles: God grants guidance, and the Prophet faithfully transmits the light that leads to the straight path.

translation: The path of God — to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Know that all matters are returned to God.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute sovereignty and ultimate authority: true guidance is God’s way because everything in the heavens and earth is His possession and under His control. Every event, choice and outcome is ultimately subject to His will and will be brought back before Him for resolution and reckoning; therefore real security and proper direction come from recognizing His lordship, submitting to His guidance, and living with awareness of final accountability.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ḥāʼ Mīm.
interpretation: The letters Ḥāʼ Mīm are one of the muqaṭṭaʿāt (disjoined letters). They function as a purposeful, mysterious sign that draws attention to the Qurʾān’s divine origin and inimitability: by presenting simple, elemental sounds whose full significance is not openly explained, they simultaneously challenge human linguistic ability, invite reflection, and indicate that certain knowledge belongs ultimately to Allah.

translation: And the Clear (or Manifest) Book.
interpretation: This phrase presents the Qur'an as a divinely revealed scripture that is clear and self-evident in its core guidance: it makes God’s guidance, injunctions and distinctions between truth and falsehood manifest so that those who reflect can recognize, follow, or be held accountable by its unmistakable message.

translation: Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse asserts that God intentionally delivered the Qur’an in Arabic to make its meanings, eloquence and legal‑spiritual guidance clear and accessible to its primary audience; by saying “so that you may understand,” it calls for active reflection and moral reasoning rather than mere recital — the linguistic clarity removes a pretext of incomprehension and places responsibility on listeners to grasp, judge and respond to its guidance.

translation: And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us — exalted, wise.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qurʾān (its essence and decree) resides in the heavenly archetype — the ‘Umm al-Kitāb’ or Preserved Tablet — indicating it is part of God’s eternal, uncreated knowledge. Describing it as “ʿaliyyun” (exalted/high) stresses its supreme authority and rank above all human works, while “ḥakīm” (wise) affirms its perfect, deliberate wisdom: every pronouncement and ordinance serves a coherent, purposeful design. Taken together the terms assure that the text is divinely grounded, preserved, and intrinsically meaningful, warranting trust, submission, and study rather than being judged as mere human composition.

translation: Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, in neglect, while you are a people given to excess?
interpretation: This rhetorically rejects the idea that God would simply let His message pass without effect because people are sinful; He will not dismiss or withhold the reminder as if their transgression were inconsequential. Rather the verse underscores that God continues to present guidance and warnings and will confront persistent wrongdoing with appropriate response or accountability.

translation: And how many a prophet have We sent among the former peoples.
interpretation: The verse points to the recurring divine practice of sending guidance through messengers across different eras; its purpose is to show that the prophetic mission is continuous and universal, to warn that rejecting a prophet repeats a historical pattern that brought ruin on past communities, and to urge people to accept guidance and learn from the fate of earlier nations.

translation: And no messenger came to them but they ridiculed him.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring moral pattern: societies often meet divine guidance with scorn not for lack of evidence but out of pride, vested interests, and a desire to protect the status quo. Ridicule becomes a social mechanism to dismiss truth, harden hearts, and justify continued rejection, which in the prophetic narrative explains why warnings failed to reform them and why divine accountability followed.

translation: So We destroyed them with a mightier [punishment], and the example of the former peoples has passed away.
interpretation: The verse functions as a warning: when a community persists in denial, corruption, and rejection of guidance, God’s retribution may be intensified, not diminished. The clause about the “former peoples” makes these past destructions into a moral precedent — history provides clear, living examples that refusing prophetic guidance leads to ruin. The exhortation is practical and preventative: recognize the pattern of error in earlier nations, reform your conduct, and heed the warning so as not to invite a similar or greater consequence.

translation: And if you were to ask them, “Who created the heavens and the earth?” they would surely say, “They were created by the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing.”
interpretation: The verse shows that the recognition of a single, all-powerful and all-knowing Creator is deeply ingrained in human conscience: even those who persist in false beliefs cannot entirely escape admitting God’s supreme role in origin and governance. That innate acknowledgment, however, is distinguished from true submission—verbal or instinctive recognition points to God’s manifest signs, but requires heartfelt acceptance and righteous conduct to become genuine faith.

translation: He who made the earth a resting place for you and set up pathways in it so that you might be guided.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God has fashioned the world as an orderly, hospitable arena and provided means—literal roads, natural patterns, social arrangements, and signs of His wisdom—so that people can move, meet needs, and, through reflection on these provisions, be led toward moral and spiritual guidance. The emphasis is that guidance is facilitated by God’s design, yet requires human attention and choice: the created order is an open invitation to recognize, follow, and be guided, not an automatic guarantee of guidance.

translation: And He who sends down water from the sky in due measure, and by it We cause a dead land to come to life — thus will you be brought forth.
interpretation: The verse draws an explicit analogy: the same God who restores barren, lifeless earth to vitality by sending measured rain has the absolute power to resurrect human beings. It affirms divine sovereignty over life, death, and provision, using a natural, observable process to make the reality of resurrection and final accountability intelligible and inevitable.

translation: And He who created all pairs and made for you of the ships and the cattle what you ride.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s sovereign design and providence: by creating complementary pairs throughout existence and by providing means such as ships and beasts of burden for transport and livelihood, God demonstrates His wisdom, power and mercy. These signs are meant to remind people of their dependence on Him, to awaken gratitude and humility, and to oppose arrogance or the attribution of partners to God, since both the cosmic order and the everyday means of sustenance come from His will.

translation:
لِتَسْتَوُوا عَلَى ظُهُورِهَا ثُمَّ تَذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ رَبِّكُمْ إِذَا اسْتَوَيْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ وَتَقُولُوا سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لَهُ مُقْرِنِينَ
"So that you may sit upon their backs; then remember the favor of your Lord when you have mounted them, and say, ‘Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we were not able [to do it].’"
interpretation: The verse exhorts a spiritual posture: when God grants people mastery over means or comforts, the proper response is immediate remembrance and glorification of Him—an acknowledgment that such capacity is a bestowed favor, not an achievement of human power. By praising God at the moment of ease, one counters pride, cultivates gratitude and humility, and reaffirms human dependence on divine providence rather than self-sufficiency.

translation: And indeed, to our Lord we shall surely return.
interpretation: A succinct confession of the inevitable return to God that functions as a theological and ethical axiom: it affirms human transience and divine sovereignty, grounds patience and resignation in trials, and compels moral responsibility and repentance because all deeds and outcomes will be finally reckoned before the Lord.

translation: And they made for Him from among His servants a portion. Indeed, man is, toward his Lord, manifestly ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse reprimands the tendency to assign divine status, authority, or a share of God’s rights to other human beings (treating certain servants as partners or intermediaries); this behavior exemplifies humanity’s clear ingratitude to God, who alone deserves exclusive worship and recognition for His favors.

translation:
أَمِ اتَّخَذَ مِمَّا يَخْلُقُ بَنَاتٍ وَأَصْفَاكَ بِالْبَنِينَ
“Or has He taken daughters from among what He creates, while He has chosen you for sons?”
interpretation: The verse rebukes the pagan tendency to anthropomorphize God by ascribing female offspring to Him while privileging sons for themselves. It exposes the contradiction and moral bias of attributing human family roles to the Divine — a being who is utterly independent of procreation — and thereby rejects the idols and beliefs that project human social values (preference for males, lineage, honor) onto God. The statement affirms God’s transcendence and condemns the injustice and ignorance inherent in claiming He has daughters while men claim sons for their own status.

translation: And when one of them is given news of a parable concerning the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened and he is inwardly filled (with suppressed anger/anguish).
interpretation: The verse describes the reaction of those who reject or resent reminders of God’s mercy and guidance: when confronted with a clear example or truth that points to the Most Merciful, their outward countenance shows humiliation and hostility (a darkened face), while inwardly they choke back anger, shame or sorrow (kaẓīm). The physical change signals a hardening of the heart and an unwillingness to accept or be humbled by the truth; though the parable touches them, their pride, resentment, or fear of accountability causes them to reject it and to suppress the emotional turmoil it provokes.

translation:
أَمْنٍ يُنشَأُ فِي الْحِلْيَةِ وَهُوَ فِي الْخِصَامِ غَيْرُ مُبِينٍ
“Is one who is raised amid adornment, and when he is in dispute is not clear?”
interpretation: The verse critiques a person brought up in luxury and outward show whose conduct in conflict or accountability is evasive and obscure. Despite an attractive outward condition, such a person fails to make the truth plain—either through cowardice, hypocrisy, or deliberate ambiguity—so that when matters of right and wrong arise he does not clarify, defend, or accept what is just. The warning is that external adornment and comfort do not guarantee moral clarity; they can breed weakness or duplicity that prevents upright speech and responsibility in moments of judgment.

translation: And they assigned the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, as females. Have they borne witness to their creation? Their testimony will be written down, and they will be questioned.
interpretation: The verse condemns the human tendency to project familiar social categories—gender and family—onto the unseen realm, here by calling angels “daughters” of the Merciful. It exposes such claims as baseless: those who assert them have no real witness and their statements are liable and accountable. The warning is theological and moral alike: divine realities are not to be reduced to human familial roles, and unfounded attributions about God or His servants will be recorded and people will be called to answer for them on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: “And they say, ‘If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them.’ They have no knowledge of that; they do nothing but conjecture.”
interpretation: This rebukes the convenient excuse of attributing one’s idolatry to God’s will: claiming that God would have prevented their wrongdoing if He had wished is a self‑serving hypothetical that does not remove their responsibility. The statement exposes ignorance and mere guesswork — an attempt to evade accountability by speaking without knowledge and confusing divine omnipotence with a justification for one’s own choices.

translation: Or have We given them a Book before this, and they are firmly holding to it?
interpretation: The verse functions as a rhetorical refutation of claims that opponents are guided by prior revelations: genuine possession of a divine Book would be shown by faithful adherence to its guidance, so merely asserting an earlier scripture does not excuse rejection when their conduct and beliefs do not reflect true obedience to that revelation.

translation: بل قالوا: "إنا وجدنا آباءنا على أمة، وإنا على آثارهم مهتدون"
interpretation: الآية تكشف بوضوح حجة الناس الذين يستندون إلى تقاليد الأجداد لتبرير استمرارهم في ممارساتهم الدينية أو الأخلاقية، معتبرين أن الاتباع الأجدادي يعني هداية؛ والمعنى أن الوراثة ليست حجة على الحقّ، فالمعيار الحقيقي للهداية هو الدليل الشرعي والبرهان الصحيح، لا مجرد تبعية للآباء، وبالتالي يجب على الإنسان أن يراجع عقيدته وسلوكياته بالحقّ لا بالعرف فقط.

translation: وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِن قَبْلِكَ فِي قَرْيَةٍ مِّن نَّذِيرٍ إِلَّا قَالَ مُتَرَفُوهَا إِنَّا وَجَدْنَا آبَاءَنَا عَلَىٰ أُمَّةٍ وَإِنَّا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَارِهِمْ مُقْتَدُونَ
interpretation: الآية تبين نمطًا متكررًا في ردود الناس على الرسل: أصحاب الرفاهية والامتيازات يردون الدعوة بالتمسك بالتقليد و«آثار الآباء» ليبرروا بقاءهم على عاداتهم ومصالحهم. القول إنهم «مقتدون» بآبائهم ليس حجة عن صحة المنهج بل تعبير عن مقاومة للتغيير وخوف من فقدان المكانة؛ فالارتباط بالعادات يتحوّل إلى وسيلة لتبرير الظلم والجهل. المعنى العملي: الدعوة إلى الاسترشاد لا تُقبل لدى من يغلبهم التعلق بالميراث الاجتماعي والراحتين النفسية والمادية، فهذه مقاومة بشرية متوقعة للحق وليست دليلاً على بطلانه.

translation: He said, “Have I come to you with guidance more rightly guided than that upon which you found your fathers?” They said, “We disbelieve in what you have been sent with.”
interpretation: The verse highlights a recurring moral failing: a messenger offers a clearer, better guidance than the inherited practices of the people, yet those people, bound by tradition, pride, or vested interests, refuse it outright. The prophet’s question exposes that the new guidance is objectively superior, while their curt reply—declaring themselves disbelievers in the messenger’s revelation—reveals willful rejection rather than honest examination.
