If you had driven them away, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved with a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse explains that God, in His wisdom and mercy, withheld immediate collective retribution to prevent a greater wrong: because hidden faithful were present among the people, rash action by the believers could have harmed the innocent. It teaches that final judgment and punishment belong to God, who admits whom He wills into His mercy, and it cautions believers against taking violent, indiscriminate measures out of ignorance. The restraint shown is both a manifestation of divine mercy and a moral lesson for the community to exercise patience, avoid vigilantism, and trust God’s timing and justice rather than enforcing punishment themselves.

translation: When those who disbelieved had placed in their hearts arrogance—the arrogance of the Age of Ignorance—Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers and made them adhere to the word of piety; and they were more deserving of it and the people of it. And Allah is, over all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse explains that the opponents’ hostile pride—rooted in pre‑Islamic ignorance—threatened to dominate the situation, but God dispelled that danger by granting calmness and steadiness (sakīnah) to the Prophet and the faithful. That divine tranquility enabled them to act with restraint, unity, and moral firmness rather than with reactive zeal, and God required of them the guiding principle of taqwa (consciousness of God) as the rule that should govern their conduct. Because they genuinely embodied those qualities, they were the most entitled and fit to hold and apply that standard; ultimately, God alone knows the realities of hearts and situations and thus gives reassurance and obligations in wisdom.

translation: Indeed Allah has confirmed the vision of His Messenger in truth: ‘You will surely enter al‑Masjid al‑Haram, if Allah wills, in safety, with your heads shorn and shortened, without fearing.’ He knew what you did not know and He ordained besides that a near conquest.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God validated the Prophet’s visionary assurance and then brought it about by means beyond the companions’ expectation. Its core lesson is trust in divine knowledge and timing: what looked like a delay or setback was part of a wise plan that would culminate in peaceful restoration of the sacred sanctuary and public vindication of the community. The images of entering the Sacred Mosque ‘safe’ and with heads shorn/shortened signal both the completion of the pilgrim’s rites (humble submission and renewed communal order) and a visible, honor‑restoring outcome after hardship. ‘He knew what you did not know’ and ‘He made besides that a near conquest’ emphasize that God can convert unseen realities into immediate, practical victories, so believers should rely on prophetic guidance and divine decree even when circumstances seem adverse.

translation: He is the One who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He might make it prevail over all religion. And sufficient is Allah as a Witness.
interpretation: The verse means that God commissioned the Prophet to bring a universal, divinely‑guided way whose truth and justice would be revealed and ultimately vindicated above competing systems—its success coming through the clarity of its message, moral and social transformation, and eventual acceptance or divine vindication rather than mere coercion—and that God alone is the complete witness and guarantor of that promise.

translation: Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; and those who are with him are severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration. That is their likeness in the Torah; and their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed which sends forth its shoot, then strengthens it, and becomes firm on its stem, delighting the sowers — that He may enrage the disbelievers. Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds among them forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse sets a paradigm for a faithful community: genuine religion combines outward firmness against injustice with inward compassion and humility before God. Visible signs of worship (here symbolized by the mark of prostration) are not mere ritual marks but indicators of sustained devotion that shapes character and communal bonds. By linking the community’s reality to earlier scriptures and to the image of a thriving plant, the passage teaches that prophetic guidance, when received and nurtured, produces stable, beneficial growth that brings joy to the faithful and provokes opposition from those hostile to truth. The concluding promise grounds this social and spiritual ideal in divine justice: moral perseverance and righteous action will be met by forgiveness and an abundant reward, thereby encouraging steadfastness in both personal piety and communal integrity.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. O you who have believed, do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger; and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse warns believers not to presume priority over God’s command or the Prophet’s authority: do not act, speak, judge, or establish rules as if you know better than what Allah has revealed or before the Messenger’s guidance is given. It calls for restraint, humility and awaiting proper revelation or rulings, coupled with God‑consciousness (taqwa), since Allah hears all speech and knows all intentions and deeds.

translation: O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds be rendered void while you do not perceive.
interpretation: The verse enjoins respectful humility and proper etiquette before the Prophet: believers must moderate their tone and conduct in his presence rather than addressing him as they would their peers. Loudness or casual familiarity in that context indicates lack of reverence, disrupts communal order and sincere submission, and therefore can vitiate the moral and spiritual worth of one’s actions.

translation: Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah—those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety; for them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the outward act of softening one’s voice before the Prophet is a visible sign of an inward moral quality: humility and God-consciousness. Allah’s “testing” of their hearts means He has placed them in circumstances that reveal and refine their taqwa; their restraint reflects genuine reverence, self-discipline, and an avoidance of arrogance or disruption in a sacred setting. Because their manners spring from sincere inner faith, they are granted forgiveness and a lofty recompense — indicating that God prizes the formation of humble, reverent character and elevates those whose external conduct flows from an examined, pious heart.

translation: Indeed, those who call to you from behind the private rooms—most of them do not use reason.
interpretation: This verse reproaches people who shout or call out to the Prophet from behind private quarters—behaving with impatience, impropriety and lack of thought. It points to a broader moral: many who demand attention, issue accusations, or seek rulings impulsively and without proper respect, reflection or understanding reveal an immature, ill-considered mindset. The verse thus urges restraint, proper etiquette in addressing others (especially leaders or scholars), and thoughtful, respectful conduct rather than noisy, thoughtless interruption.

translation: And if only they had been patient until you had gone out to them, it would have been better for them; and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: The verse reproves rash, self-willed behavior and teaches that restraint and waiting for legitimate guidance (here represented by the Prophet’s appointed time and instruction) would have spared people harm and yielded a better outcome; at the same time, God’s forgiveness and mercy mean that failing through haste is not the final word—there remains space for correction and return to the right path if one repents and submits to rightful authority.

translation: O you who have believed, if a wicked person comes to you with information, then investigate/verify, lest you harm people in ignorance and become regretful for what you did.
interpretation: This verse enjoins a strict duty of verification: when a dubious or immoral source brings news, believers must not accept or act on it impulsively but should investigate before judging or harming others. Its purpose is to protect individuals and communities from false allegations, rash decisions, and the grave injustice of damaging reputations or rights on the basis of rumor. The command applies broadly — to private speech, social media, and to those in authority who adjudicate or punish — stressing that negligent acceptance of unverified reports leads to remorse and moral/accountability consequences. Practically, it requires checking the character of the informant, seeking corroborating evidence, consulting reliable witnesses or authorities, and withholding judgment until the facts are clear.

translation: And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he were to follow you in much of the matter, you would surely be harmed; but Allah has made faith beloved to you and has beautified it in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief, wickedness and disobedience. Those are the rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Prophet’s independence from popular opinion is a protective blessing: his refusal to yield to every communal desire prevents the community from being led into error. True guidance, the verse implies, is not simply majority approval but a divine reorientation of the heart—God makes faith attractive and sin repulsive so people will accept what is right even when it runs against their immediate inclinations. Those whose inner dispositions are thus set—who love faith, reject disbelief and refuse wickedness—are the ‘rightly guided.’

translation: فضلًا من الله ونعمة؛ والله عليم حكيم
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن النعم والفضائل ليست نتيجة للجهد البحت أو الاستحقاق البشري فحسب، بل هي منعٌ وكرم من الله؛ وما يُعطى أو يُدبَّر من أحوالٍ فهو مطابق لعلمه الكامل وحكمته البالغة، فتستلزم هذه الحقيقة تواضعًا وشكرًا والثقة بأن ما قضاه الله فيه حكمة بالغة قد لا تُدرك تفاصيلها من قِبلنا.

translation: If two groups of believers fight, reconcile between them; then if one of them transgresses against the other, fight the group that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah. And if it returns, reconcile between them with justice and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves the equitable.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principled procedure for resolving intra‑communal conflict: first, prioritize mediation to restore peace; if one party is the aggressor, limited coercion may be used only as a means to stop the wrongdoing and bring the party back to obedience to God’s law (i.e., to cease oppression and accept correction). The aim is not revenge but restoration: once the aggressor desists, full reconciliation must be achieved on the basis of fairness and equal treatment. The injunction stresses both the restraint of force—used only to halt transgression—and the moral duty of impartial justice in settlement, because God commends those who are evenhanded and just.

translation: The believers are but brothers; so reconcile between your brothers and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all true believers form a single moral family, obliging them to protect communal bonds by actively mediating disputes and restoring justice whenever conflicts arise. It makes reconciliation a collective duty—performed impartially and with concern for fairness—rooted in God‑consciousness (taqwa); cultivating this fear of God disciplines behavior, prevents factionalism, and opens the door to divine mercy, so social harmony becomes both an ethical responsibility and a means to spiritual well‑being.

translation: O you who have believed, let not a people mock another people; it may be that they are better than them. Nor let women mock other women; it may be that they are better than them. And do not insult one another, nor call one another by offensive nicknames. Wretched is the name of disobedience after [one’s] faith. And whoever does not repent — then those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to abstain from ridicule, derision and demeaning labels because true worth is known only to God; social mockery and insulting nicknames sow discord, assume false superiority, and violate the dignity faith demands. By warning that some mocked people may in fact be better, the verse teaches humility, prohibits prejudice based on tribe, status, gender or outward traits, and links persistence in such abusive behavior to moral perversity: refusing to repent of demeaning conduct makes one unjust. The practical aim is to preserve communal harmony, respect for individual dignity, and spiritual accountability before God.

translation: O you who have believed, avoid much suspicion; indeed some suspicion is a sin. And do not spy, nor backbite one another. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed Allah is ever Oft‑Returning, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse instructs that harmful inner attitudes and secret actions—unfounded suspicions, prying into others’ private affairs, and speaking ill behind their backs—undermine human dignity and communal trust; comparing backbiting to eating a dead brother’s flesh makes the moral horror vivid. The practical demand is ethical self‑restraint: verify before assuming, respect privacy, refuse gossip, and cultivate God‑consciousness so one avoids harming others. If one slips, turn to God’s forgiveness, since He accepts repentance and is merciful.

translation: O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may know one another. Indeed, the most honored of you with Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human diversity is purposeful and social categories (nations, tribes) exist to foster mutual recognition and relationship, not to establish superiority. True worth before God is not ancestry, race, or status but taqwa—consciousness of God expressed in uprightness, justice and moral responsibility. Because Allah is all‑knowing and fully aware of inward states as well as outward deeds, final honor and judgment depend on sincerity and righteousness rather than external distinctions.

translation: قَالَتِ الْأَعْرَابُ آمَنَّا ۖ قُل لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَٰكِن قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا وَلَمْ يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ ۖ وَإِن تُطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ لَا يَلِتْكُم مِّنْ أَعْمَالِكُمْ شَيْئًا ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ
interpretation: The verse distinguishes outward profession from inward conviction: some people claim “we have believed” while their hearts have not yet truly embraced iman. The Prophet is told to correct them—use the term “we have submitted” (aslamna) to indicate their external conformity—while emphasizing that genuine faith is an inner reality that grows through sincere obedience to God and His Messenger. Obedience and right practice safeguard and consummate one’s deeds rather than render them void, and because God is Forgiving and Merciful there is always room for spiritual growth and pardon as hearts move from mere submission to firm belief.

translation: The believers are only those who believed in Allah and His Messenger, then did not doubt, and strove with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah; those are the truthful.
interpretation: This verse defines true faith as more than verbal profession: it requires firm inner conviction (no wavering or hypocrisy) coupled with concrete commitment expressed through sacrifice and active striving for God’s purpose. ‘Then did not doubt’ indicates steadiness and sincerity after accepting the truth, and ‘strove with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah’ encompasses all earnest, self-giving efforts—material, physical, and moral—done sincerely for God’s sake. By calling such people ‘the truthful,’ the verse makes sincerity and consistent action the decisive signs of genuine belief.

translation: Say, “Do you inform Allah about your religion? And Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and Allah is Knowing of all things.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who presume to define, justify or validate religious positions as if God lacked knowledge or needed their counsel; it underscores that ultimate authority and full knowledge of belief, actions and inner states belong to Allah alone, so human arrogance in claiming exclusive religious truth or excluding others is wrongful and should be replaced by humility, sincere submission and reliance on God’s judgment.

translation: They boast to you that they have submitted. Say, “Do not boast to me of your submission; rather, Allah bestows favor upon you by guiding you to faith, if you are truthful.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who flaunt their profession of Islam as if it were their own achievement or a means to gain status, and it reminds both the Prophet and the community that true submission is a gift of God’s guidance, not a human boast. By saying “if you are truthful,” the speaker exposes the possibility of insincerity: genuine faith is recognized by God’s favor and inner reality, not by public claims. The proper response is humility and attributing guidance to Allah, while assessing people by the sincerity of their faith rather than their loud declarations.

translation: Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth; and Allah is All‑Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s knowledge is absolute and encompasses both hidden realities of the cosmos and every human thought and action. It calls for inner God‑consciousness: believers should take comfort that private struggles and sincere intentions are known and rewarded, and wrongdoers or boastful claimants of secret knowledge are warned that nothing is concealed from God and that He alone has authority over the unseen and final judgment.

translation: “Qāf. By the Glorious Qurʾān.”
interpretation: The disjoined letter and the subsequent oath serve to arrest attention and confer solemn certainty: God swears by His own majestic, glorious revelation to underline its divine authority and truth, to guarantee the seriousness of the message that follows, and to remind listeners that the Qurʾān is the decisive, honored criterion and source of guidance and warning for humanity.

translation: بل عجبوا أن جاءهم منذر منهم فقال الكافرون هذا شيء عجيب
interpretation: الآية تبيّن موقف النفوس المغلقة التي ترفض الهدي لا لأن الحجة ضعيفة بل لأنها ترفض أن تُنذر أو تُحاسب من داخل جماعتهم؛ يسخرون من الرسالة باعتبارها «غريبة» كحجة دفاعية لتبرير العناد الاجتماعي والغرور، فتتحوّل المعارضة إلى انكار مريح يهدف إلى الحفاظ على الوضع القائم بدلاً من استقبال الحق ومراجعته.

translation: “Is it that when we die and become dust — that would be a distant return.”
interpretation: The phrase expresses the objection of those who, seeing corporeal decay into dust, regard resurrection as absurd and remote; its deeper point is to expose human short‑sightedness about divine power — what seems impossible to creatures is entirely within God’s ability, so denying return reveals ignorance and rejection of God’s sovereignty.

translation: We already know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a Preserved Record.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God fully knows every loss or diminution that occurs on earth—whether lives, wealth, offspring, or support—and that nothing escapes His awareness; moreover, every such event is precisely inscribed in a guarded, unalterable Register with God, which reassures the oppressed that their losses are known and will be recompensed and warns wrongdoers that concealment is impossible and all will be accounted for.

translation: بل كذبوا بالحق لما جاءهم فهم في أمر مريج
interpretation: الآية تعني أن الذين واجهوا الحق ولم يقبلوه لم يرتكبوا مجرد إنكار لفظي، بل إن رفضهم للحق أدى إلى حالة من الارتباك والاضطراب الداخلي والخارجي. وصفُهُم بأنهم «في أمر مريج» يشير إلى أن أحوالهم وأفكارهم وسلوكهم مشتتة ومختلطة بلا ترتيب ولا يقين: لا استقرار في القول ولا صلاح في العمل، وهم لذلك عرضة للتيه والضلال ولفقدان قدرة العقل والضمير على الوصول إلى حكم سليم.

translation: Have they not looked at the heaven above them — how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no fissures?
interpretation: The verse calls people to reflect: the sky’s deliberate construction, its adornment (e.g., stars) and the phrase “no furooj” (no gaps, rifts, or breaks) indicate a single, orderly, secure cosmic fabric produced by one Wise Creator. This perfection and unity of the heavens are presented as evidence against chance, polytheism, or a disconnected universe, and as a sign that the same Sovereign who sustains such precise order is fully capable of resurrection and final judgment.

translation: وَالْأَرْضَ مَدَدْنَاهَا وَأَلْقَيْنَا فِيهَا رَوَاسِيَ وَأَنۢبَتْنَا فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍۢۚ بَهِيجٍ
interpretation: The verse presents the earth’s features as purposeful signs of divine wisdom and providence: its expanse made fit for habitation, its mountains functioning as stabilizing anchors, and the abundance of living things appearing in complementary ‘pairs’ that are pleasant and well-suited to life. Together these elements indicate an ordered, balanced system whose design points to God’s creative authority, sustaining care, and ability to give and restore life — a call to recognize that the universe is neither accidental nor aimless but structured for benefit and testimony to the Creator.

translation: A clear admonition and reminder for every servant who turns (in repentance) to God.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur’ān as an illuminating admonition whose real power is realized in the hearts of those who are humble and return to God; it is meant to awaken conscience, prompt sincere repentance and reform, and guide the responsive believer away from heedlessness—its benefits depend on a receptive, turning heart rather than mere exposure to the text.

translation: And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and by it We produced gardens and the grain of harvest.
interpretation: The verse indicates that rainfall is not merely a physical event but a divinely blessed means by which God sustains life and multiplies provision: the adjective mubārak (blessed) shows that the water’s effects—reviving the earth, yielding orchards and harvestable grain—are intentional manifestations of God’s mercy and power. Framing provision this way invites reflection that material abundance is a bestowed trust and a sign pointing to God’s care, deserving recognition, gratitude, and responsible use.

translation: And the lofty date-palms, with clustered fruit.
interpretation: The image of towering date-palms bearing compact, orderly bunches of fruit is presented as a sign of God’s deliberate, sustaining design: the regularity and abundance of their produce point to a wise Creator who provides for His creatures and who, having fashioned life in such an ordered way, is fully able to re-create and resurrect what has passed away.

translation: رزقًا للعباد، وأحيينا به بلدة ميتا؛ كذلك الخروج.
interpretation: الآية تصف إسهام الله في إنعاش ما كان ميتًا (مِن طبیعةٍ وزراعة) ليُظهِر بذلك مبدأً إلهيًا: ما يحيي الأرض بقدرة الله هو عين ما يؤكد قدرة الله على إحياء الناس بعد موتهم. الاستدلال بالرحمة الإلهية والرزق كدليل على حتمية الخروج (البعث) يجعل الإيمان بالقيامة متابعة طبيعية لإيماننا برعاية الله الدائمة وقدرته الفاعلة، فيدحض شبهات المستكبرين ويُنشئ مبررًا أخلاقيًا للمسؤولية والرجاء.

translation: Before them, the people of Noah, the people of al‑Rass, and Thamud rejected (their messengers).
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring historical pattern: successive communities have denied the clear message brought by their prophets and thus incurred divine consequence. Citing Noah, the people of al‑Rass, and Thamud serves both as a warning to those who are heedless — that rejection is followed by ruin — and as reassurance to the Prophet and his followers that opposition to the message is not new and does not nullify the truth of the revelation.

translation: And ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, and the brethren of Lot
interpretation: The grouping of these names functions as a warning: they are historical examples of nations that persisted in arrogance, disbelief and immoral behavior despite clear signs, and their destruction affirms that rejecting God's guidance leads to ruin—therefore their mention urges listeners to recognize the truth of the message and reform to avoid the same fate.

translation: And the companions of the Thicket and the people of Tubbaʿ — each one denied the messengers, so My warning proved true.
interpretation: This verse uses historical examples to teach that rejecting God's messengers brings inevitable consequences: the threats and warnings of God are not empty words but realities that were realized against past nations. It warns listeners to take the prophetic message seriously, reform their conduct, and believe, because the pattern of warning → rejection → divine retribution is a recurring and certain law of divine justice.

translation:
أفعيينا بالخلق الأول ۚ بل هم في لبس من خلق جديد
"Is Our having created them once a burden for Us? No — rather, they are in perplexity about a new creation."
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who deny resurrection: it is not that God found the first act of creating mankind so difficult that He could not recreate them, but that the deniers are confused, unwilling, or sceptical about the very idea of a renewed creation and life after death. The point is to underline God’s unlimited power and to expose the weakness of their objection — their problem is not Divine incapacity but human doubt, denial, and failure to accept accountability in the hereafter.

translation: And indeed We created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him; and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s knowledge and presence extend into the deepest inner life: He perceives the secret doubts, urges and intentions that a person may not even admit to themselves. Saying He is “nearer than the jugular vein” uses an intimate bodily image to indicate not physical proximity but an immediate, sustaining, and inescapable awareness—therefore every inward thought and moral inclination is within God’s purview, which calls the believer to conscientious responsibility, reliance on God’s support, and humility before divine knowledge.

translation: When the two receivers receive — seated on the right and on the left.
interpretation: The verse signifies that human deeds are unavoidably witnessed and recorded by appointed angels positioned at each side; their being “seated” conveys permanence, preparedness, and impartial witnessing, teaching that every action will be presented and judged, so one must live with consciousness of continuous accountability before God.

translation:
ما يلفظ من قول إلا لديه رقيب عتيد
"Not a word is uttered but with Him is an ever‑vigilant, ready watcher."
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah’s knowledge extends to every utterance and that angels stand ready to observe and record even the smallest speech; this is meant to produce moral restraint and sincerity—prompting one to guard the tongue, avoid slander and falsehood, and act righteously—while also comforting the oppressed with the assurance that nothing escapes Divine witnessing and that all speech will be accounted for before God.

translation: And the intoxication (swoon) of death came with the truth — that is what you were trying to avoid.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the overwhelming seizure of death is an inescapable, truthful reality that confronts every person; it rebukes those who sought to evade responsibility or deny the Hereafter by showing that death inevitably overtakes their attempts to escape, exposing the futility of their avoidance and precipitating the immediate transition to standing before God.

translation: And the Trumpet will be blown. That is the Day of the Warning.
interpretation: The verse signifies that a single, divine signal—the blowing of the Trumpet—will decisively usher in the Last Day, fulfilling God’s warning: it ends ordinary life, brings about resurrection and judgment, and exposes the truth so that every soul receives its due recompense under God’s promised justice.

translation: And every soul will come, accompanied by a driver and a witness.
interpretation: The verse signifies that on the Day of Judgment each person will be brought to account with two accompanying realities: a 'driver' (sā’iq) who compels or escorts the soul to its appointed place and a 'witness' (shāhid) who testifies to that person’s deeds. Together they underline the inevitability of the reckoning and the impossibility of escaping or concealing one’s actions—what a person did inwardly and outwardly will be presented and attested before God, confirming personal responsibility and the certainty of judgment.

translation: You were indeed heedless of this, so We removed from you your covering, and your sight today is piercing.
interpretation: God speaks to one who was heedless of the reality of resurrection and reckoning: the veil that sheltered him—whether ignorance, denial, or worldly distractions—has been taken away, so that on the Day of Judgment his eyes are made sharp and inescapable; he sees the truth and the consequences with stark, painful clarity, but that clear sight only confirms his loss and offers no respite.

translation: And his companion said, “This is what I have prepared.”
interpretation: The phrase represents the companion—understood in classical exegesis as the whispering ally (whether the soul’s inclinations or a satanic companion)—acknowledging that the misguidance, deeds, or consequences now confronting the person are exactly what he had laid ready. The passage points to moral responsibility and the clear outcome of following bad counsel: the paths one chooses (and the companions one heeds) bring about their own results, and on reckoning those hidden aids and intentions are exposed and shown to have been the cause of one’s ruin.

translation: Cast into Hell every obstinate disbeliever.
interpretation: The verse warns that those who, out of stubbornness and arrogance, persistently reject and refuse divine guidance despite clear evidence, will be consigned to Hell as the just consequence of their deliberate, hardened denial.

translation: مَنّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ مُعْتَدٍّ مُرِيبٍ — A withholder of good, transgressing and suspicious.
interpretation: The phrase characterizes a type of person whose selfishness and arrogance lead them to block acts of charity and right conduct, to overstep bounds toward others, and to foster mistrust; the warning is ethical — such a disposition undermines communal welfare and moral order and brings divine censure, so believers are urged to oppose stinginess, oppression, and suspicion and cultivate generosity, justice, and trust.

translation: Whoever sets up another god alongside Allah — they will be cast into severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse warns that associating partners with God (shirk) — by worshipping, obeying, or assigning divine status to anything or anyone besides Allah — is the gravest spiritual error and leads to exclusion from God’s mercy and final accountability: those who persist in such idolatry will face severe retribution on the Day of Judgment.

translation: His companion said, “Our Lord, I did not make him sin; rather he was far astray.”
interpretation: The statement reflects that evil influences try to deflect responsibility, but true culpability rests with the person who knowingly persists in deviation. Temptations and whisperings do not compel the will; when someone repeatedly turns away from guidance and chooses error, that settled, distant misguidance is what condemns them—so the devil’s denial cannot absolve the sinner before God.

translation: قال: «لا تختصموا لدي، وقد قدمت إليكم بالوعيد»
interpretation: المتكلم هنا يأمر النفوس أن تكف عن الجدال أمامه لأن رسالته قد أُكملت؛ قد بلغهم التحذير والتنبيه بالفعل، فالمجادلة المستمرة ليست سعيًا في الحق بل إصرارٌ على الباطل وإظهار تصلب القلوب. بالتالي التحذير يخلّص رسوله من مسؤولية الإقناع القسري ويُبيّن أن من يصرّ على الجدل بعد الوعد هو من يرفض الحق عن عمد.

translation: My word does not change, and I am not unjust to the servants.
interpretation: God is affirming that His decrees, promises and judgments are immutable and governed by perfect justice: He does not alter His word capriciously nor does He wrong people. What people receive—merit, punishment, mercy or delay—is consistent with His knowledge and justice, so apparent unfairness is due to our limited perspective, not to any deficiency in Divine judgment.

translation: The Day We will say to Hell, 'Have you been filled?' and it will say, 'Is there any more?'.
interpretation: The imagery conveys the inexorable and comprehensive character of divine justice: on the Last Day punishment will continue until every accountable wrongdoer is dealt with, and Hell’s reply, 'Is there any more?', functions as a rhetorical rebuke exposing human stubbornness and the gravity of persistent rejection of guidance—serving as a solemn warning to turn to God before that inevitable reckoning.

translation: And Paradise will be brought near for the God‑fearing, not far off.
interpretation: Allah promises that for al‑muttaqīn (those who are God‑conscious and righteous) the abode of bliss will be drawn close and made readily attainable: the nearness (أزلفت) denotes intimacy and immediacy of reward, and “not far” stresses that their piety has removed distance and difficulty, so the ultimate good is certain and within reach for those who lived in reverent obedience.

translation: This is what you were promised: for every one who repeatedly turns back (in repentance) there is a Guardian.
interpretation: The verse conveys that God’s promise is to place His protective care over those who persistently return to Him in repentance; such constant penitents are accepted and put under divine guardianship — their repentance is held, they are preserved from ruin, and their spiritual affairs are safeguarded by God.

translation: Whoever fears the Most Merciful in the unseen and comes with a heart turned in repentance.
interpretation: The verse defines true piety as an inner, private reverence for God — a moral consciousness that persists even when no one else observes — together with a sincere, humble turning of the heart back to Him. It teaches that authentic faith is not mere outward display but a persistent inward fear of God’s presence and a continual, contrite return (tawbah/tawajjuh) that reshapes conduct and opens one to divine mercy and guidance.

translation: Enter it in peace. That is the Day of Everlasting Abode.
interpretation: This verse conveys a divine assurance that the faithful will be received into Paradise with the greeting of peace, indicating the complete removal of fear, pain and anxiety and the onset of secure, untroubled existence; calling it “the Day of Everlasting Abode” stresses that this state is permanent and final — the consummation of God’s justice and mercy and the eternal reward for those who attained His pleasure.

translation: They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us there is yet more.
interpretation: This affirms that the blessings promised to the righteous in the Hereafter will fully satisfy their legitimate desires, and even that abundant fulfillment is only part of God’s generosity — He has additional, inexhaustible bounties beyond human expectation. The phrase emphasizes divine munificence and the limitless, qualitative surplus of the life to come: what people can imagine or ask for will be granted, and God’s provision transcends imagination, comforting believers that reward is complete and endlessly abundant.

translation: And how many a generation before them did We destroy who were mightier than them in strength, and they penetrated through the lands — is there any place of refuge?
interpretation: The verse warns that past peoples, though stronger and more powerful, were nonetheless destroyed for their corruption; their strength and roaming through the lands could not secure them a refuge from divine retribution. It teaches that worldly power, status, or escape routes do not protect against God’s judgment, so one should heed history’s examples, abandon arrogance and injustice, and turn to repentance and obedience before it is too late.

translation: Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is attentive (a witness).
interpretation: The verse means that the signs and admonitions just mentioned truly benefit only those who possess inward receptivity — a heart capable of understanding and conscience — or who listen with full attention and presence. ‘Heart’ denotes the faculty of insight and moral awareness, and ‘giving ear while he is a witness’ stresses active, conscious listening (not mere outward hearing). Thus the passage teaches that spiritual guidance requires both inner openness and deliberate, attentive reception for it to produce real conviction and change.

translation: And We certainly created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days, and no weariness of toil touched Us.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute power and transcendence: the cosmos was brought into existence in six successive stages by divine decree, but those “days” are measures determined by God and not indications of human limitation. By stating that no weariness touched Him, the text rejects any anthropomorphic notion that God labors or grows tired; creation is an effortless, sovereign act of God, and the ordered unfolding of the universe reflects His will and control rather than the constraints of created beings.

translation: So be patient with what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord before the sun rises and before it sets.
interpretation: The verse exhorts steadfastness in the face of hostile speech, paired with disciplined, daily remembrance of God at the bookends of the day; the morning and evening praises both anchor the believer’s heart in God’s sovereignty and renew resolve, so that passing slander or opposition does not uproot one’s faith or derail one’s mission.

translation: And during the night exalt Him, and (do so) after the prostrations.
interpretation: The verse commands ongoing remembrance of God beyond formulaic ritual: use the quiet, sincere hours of the night for glorifying Him, and continue that praise at the moment of rising from sujood — a point of special humility and closeness to God. It teaches that true worship is continuous and intimate, highlighting the night and the moments immediately after prostration as especially fitting times for heartfelt dhikr and supplication.

translation: And listen on the Day when the Caller will call from a near place.
interpretation: The verse warns that the Resurrection will be proclaimed by a single, compelling call—often understood as the trumpet blast or the angelic summons—issued from a “near place,” signifying its immediacy and inescapability. The command “listen” requires full spiritual attention and submission: when that moment comes no hiding or delay will be possible, every soul will be roused to stand before God, so one should live in readiness, heed the warning, and turn to God before the inevitable summons.

translation: The Day they will hear the blast (the Cry) with truth— that is the Day of Emergence (the coming forth).
interpretation: The verse points to the decisive, incontrovertible moment when the trumpet‑cry is sounded and the hidden reality of the Hereafter bursts into experience. “Hearing the Cry with truth” means that the event will be manifest and undeniable: all doubt and denial about resurrection will end, the dead will be drawn forth from their places, and every soul will confront the absolute reality of divine judgment. Calling it “the Day of al‑Khurūj” (the Day of Emergence) stresses both the literal emerging from graves and the moral exposing of hearts and deeds—an irrefutable turning point that separates pretension from truth and fixes final accountability.

translation: Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and to Us is the return.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s exclusive sovereignty over existence: births and deaths occur by His decree and wisdom, and every soul’s ultimate destination is to return to Him for reckoning and recompense. This truth reframes human life—temporal plans and attachments are provisional—calling for humility, moral responsibility, trust in divine timing, and readiness for the final meeting with the Creator.

translation: The Day the earth will split open for them in haste; that gathering is, for Us, easy.
interpretation: The verse uses the striking image of the earth violently parting to convey the sudden, inescapable arrival of the Resurrection; its purpose is theological rather than literal detail — to stress that bringing people forth and assembling them for judgment is effortless for God, so no hiding, delay, or escape can frustrate the Divine gathering.

translation: We are best aware of what they say; and you are not over them a tyrant. So remind, with the Qur'an, whoever fears a warning.
interpretation: God reassures the Messenger that He knows the secret words and objections of the opponents and that the Prophet is not meant to compel belief or dominate people ('jabbār'—an overbearing ruler). The Prophet’s duty is to present the Qur'anic reminder; it will reach and move those whose hearts are receptive—those who fear God’s warning—because guidance works through sincere admonition and God’s knowledge, not by force or the Messenger’s coercion.

translation: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. وَالذَّارِيَاتِ ذَرْوًا — In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. By those that scatter (the winds/agents that drive forth).
interpretation: The oath invokes powerful, dispersing forces (understood as winds or angelic agents) to point to God’s sovereign governance of the world: the visible, dynamic processes that distribute, separate and set events in motion are signs of divine control. By swearing on these scatterers, the verse asks the listener to recognize that the same sustaining power that organizes creation also administers moral consequence and will bring about what God intends — a call to awareness of providence, accountability, and the order behind apparent chaos.

translation: فَالْحَامِلَاتِ وَقَرًا — By those who bear (their burdens) with steadiness and dignity.
interpretation: An oath invoking creatures that carry weight or responsibility steadily and with composure, intended to draw attention to the disciplined, purposeful order in creation and to remind listeners of the seriousness of divine matters and the coming reckoning.

translation: By those that run swiftly and with ease.
interpretation: An oath invoking swift-running steeds (understood classically as war-horses) whose speed, discipline and power are summoned to stress the seriousness, swiftness and inevitability of what is being affirmed — the image of these horses running obediently and forcefully underlines the certitude and overwhelming nature of the divine reality being proclaimed.

translation: By those who apportion the affair.
interpretation: An oath invoking the agents who divide and carry out God’s decrees (classically understood as angels); it emphasizes that the unfolding of events and the coming judgment are precisely measured and administered—what God has ordained will be apportioned and executed with exactness, so the warning and promise that follow are certain and must be taken seriously.

translation: إِنَّمَا تُوعَدُونَ لَصَادِقٌ‎‎ — Indeed, what you are promised is true.
interpretation: The verse is a divine affirmation that the warnings and threats pronounced against the rejecters are not empty words but a certain reality: the promised retribution and the realities of the Hereafter will occur despite any delay or mockery. It rebukes those who doubt or ridicule the idea of divine accountability by stressing that God’s timing does not negate inevitability, and it consoles the faithful that divine justice and the Messenger’s message are reliable and will be fulfilled.

translation: And indeed, the Recompense is sure to come.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute certainty of divine accounting: there will come a moment of reckoning when every action is recompensed and justice is finally accomplished. Its purpose is to confront complacency and denial, to remind people that this-worldly life is transient and that moral choices have inevitable consequences, thus motivating responsibility, upright conduct, and trust that wrongs will be made right by God’s final judgment.

translation: And the heaven, perfectly woven.
interpretation: This phrase calls attention to the heavens’ meticulous, interlaced order — the harmonious, interconnected system of stars, orbits and pathways — as a sign of divine design and governance, inviting reflection on God’s wisdom, power and precise control over the cosmos.

translation: Indeed, you are in contradictory speech.
interpretation: The phrase accuses the addressed of inconsistency and self‑contradiction: their utterances conflict (with one another or with the truth), revealing confusion, lack of firm conviction, and an unreliable, incoherent stance rather than a clear, sincere claim.

translation: He turns away from it whoever is given to falsehood.
interpretation: It means that God lets the message (or its benefit) be lost on those who persist in inventions, fancies, and lies: by clinging to falsehood and conjecture they harden and distract their hearts and minds, so they become unable to receive, understand or act upon the truth.

translation: Perish the fabricators (of lies)!
interpretation: An emphatic denunciation of those who invent falsehoods about God and His message: it announces that such fabricators will be exposed and brought to ruin—their claims will be disproved, their influence destroyed, and they will face divine recompense for misleading others.

translation: Those who are in heedless immersion (in enjoyment).
interpretation: The phrase characterizes people utterly absorbed in worldly pleasures and distractions, so overwhelmed ('غمرة') that they are negligent and inattentive ('ساهون') to God’s guidance and the reality of the Hereafter; it warns that their engrossment leads them to neglect preparation for accountability.

translation: They ask, “When will the Day of Judgment be?”
interpretation: The question exposes a common human evasion: instead of responding to the moral demands before them, people fixate on the timing of the final reckoning. It reflects either mocking skepticism or anxious curiosity, but in either case it betrays ignorance—knowledge of the Hour belongs to God alone—and thus the question is irrelevant to the obligation to repent and act righteously now.

translation: The Day when they will be tested on the Fire.
interpretation: It points to the Day of Recompense when those who persisted in denial and wrongdoing will be subjected to the ordeal of Hell: their pretences and excuses will be stripped away, they will be brought to account, and the reality of their deeds and inner states will be exposed and vindicated by divine justice — “yuftanūn” conveying both the punitive suffering and the decisive testing that reveals truth.

translation: Taste your trial; this is what you were hastening toward.
interpretation: God is addressing those who pursued wrongdoing or denied His signs, declaring that the severe test or punishment they sought to provoke has now come upon them. “Taste your trial” commands them to experience the consequences—the humiliation, loss, or torment—that follow from their haste, arrogance, and rejection of truth; in short, the very outcome they rushed toward in their worldly pursuits is now realized as a divine retribution or chastisement.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs.
interpretation: Here “al‑muttaqīn” denotes those who live with God‑consciousness and moral restraint; “gardens and springs” function as both literal and symbolic descriptions of Paradise, signifying permanent, pure, overflowing blessings — inner peace, uninterrupted provision, and spiritual nearness to God. The verse promises that sincere piety will be rewarded by an enduring state of safety, satisfaction, and intimate felicity in the life to come, thereby encouraging steadfastness in worship and upright conduct in this life.

translation: Receiving what their Lord has given them; indeed, before that they were doers of good.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the blessed receive and continuously enjoy the gifts God grants them as a direct consequence of their prior, sustained righteousness. The present participle «آخذين» conveys active, ongoing acceptance and possession of divine bounty, while the clause about their earlier goodness locates the moral cause: consistent, sincere good conduct prepared them to be recipients of God’s generosity. It also subtly reminds that these favors are granted by God’s grace, not self-produced, and that true moral excellence leads to lasting divine reward.

translation: They used to sleep but little of the night.
interpretation: The verse highlights a hallmark of sincere devotion: believers willingly shorten their sleep to engage in night prayer and remembrance, showing disciplined self-denial, humility before God, and a prioritization of spiritual closeness, repentance, and earnest supplication over bodily comfort.

translation: And in the pre-dawn hours they used to seek forgiveness.
interpretation: The verse highlights a spiritual discipline: devoted servants, rising in the stillness before dawn, repeatedly turn to Allah in humble repentance. Their seeking forgiveness at that quiet hour signifies sincere reliance on Divine mercy, ongoing self-accounting, and a prioritized intimacy with God when distractions are few and the heart is most open to return.

translation: And in their wealth there was a due for the beggar and the deprived.
interpretation: The verse affirms that wealth is not absolute private property but carries a divinely established right for the needy: believers are obliged to set aside a portion of their resources to meet the claims of those who ask and those deprived, so that giving becomes a social and moral duty that purifies the giver and promotes justice and solidarity.

translation: And on the earth are signs for those who have certainty (al‑yaqīn).
interpretation: The verse teaches that the created world outwardly bears evidences of God's existence, wisdom and providence that become perceptible to hearts endowed with yaqīn—stable, reflective conviction. 'Those who have certainty' are not merely nominal believers but people whose inner clarity and sincere reflection allow them to see order, balance, life, provision and the consequences of actions as pointers to a wise Creator; these signs, contemplated with an upright heart, confirm and deepen their faith.

translation: And in yourselves — will you not then see?
interpretation: A call to inward reflection: the intricate order, faculties and moral awareness within each person are presented as clear signs of a wise, purposeful Creator; by looking into one’s own nature one should recognize that order and be moved toward acknowledgment, gratitude and moral responsibility rather than remaining heedless.

translation: And in the heaven is your provision and whatever you are promised.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sustenance and the fulfillment of divine promises originate in God's sovereign decree in the heavens; therefore provision and eventual outcomes are ultimately controlled by God, calling believers to trust His providence, strive lawfully without anxiety, and not ascribe their livelihood or destiny to chance or other powers, for what God has promised will be dispensed in wisdom and time.

translation:
فَوَرَبِ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ إِنَّهُ لَحَقٌّ مِثْلَ مَا أَنتُمْ تَنطِقُونَ
"By the Lord of the heavens and the earth: indeed it is the truth—just as you (speak)."
interpretation: This is a solemn divine oath affirming the absolute certainty of what has been proclaimed: God swears by the Lordship of heaven and earth that the announced reality (the message, the coming judgment/resurrection) is true and inevitable. Its truth is as plain and unavoidable as the words you utter; denial or mockery cannot alter its occurrence.

translation: Has the account of Abraham’s honored guests reached you?
interpretation: The verse functions as a rhetorical reminder: by pointing to Abraham’s encounter with his honored guests, God gives a precedent to reassure and instruct — showing that God’s support and glad tidings can come unexpectedly, that sincere hospitality and trust in God are met with divine favor, and that apparent distress can be transformed into consolation; the Prophet is thus urged to take comfort in God’s past dealings with the righteous, remain steadfast, and respond to God’s messengers and tests with generosity and faith.

translation: When they entered upon him they said, “Peace.” He said, “Peace.” — a people unaware.
interpretation: The brief exchange of salutations shows that the visitors brought divine reassurance and safety; the man’s immediate reply reflects his recognition and trust in that message, while the phrase “a people unaware” points to the surrounding folk who failed to perceive or accept the sign—ignorant or heedless of the mercy and truth carried by those guests.

translation:
فَـرَغَ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهِ فَجَاءَ بِعَجَلٍ سَمِينٍ
"He returned to his people and brought a fat (plump) calf."
interpretation: The phrase portrays an act of generous hospitality: the man, upon meeting the stranger, went back to his household to fetch a choice animal to serve him. It signals not merely provision of food but a social and moral readiness to honor, protect and integrate a guest—demonstrating communal responsibility, kindness, and the priority given to hospitality in the ethical life depicted by the text.

translation:
فَقَرَّبَهُ إِلَيْهِمْ قَالَ أَلَا تَأْكُلُونَ
"So he brought it near to them and said, 'Will you not eat?'"
interpretation: The phrase conveys more than a mere invitation; it reflects a deliberate provocation or test designed to elicit a response that would expose the true state of the listeners' hearts — whether shame, guilt, fear, or readiness to accept what is offered. The question functions simultaneously as an urging to dispel their hunger and as a subtle reproach, prompting them to reveal their inward condition by their action or hesitation.

translation: So he felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not be afraid; and give him glad tidings of a knowledgeable boy."
interpretation: The passage teaches that encounters with the transcendent naturally unsettle humans, yet God’s messengers bring calm and unexpected hope: the promised “knowledgeable boy” signifies not merely youthful age but a divinely granted spiritual maturity and insight. It emphasizes that God’s miraculous gifts answer human longing in ways that confer responsibility to use bestowed knowledge for guidance and righteousness.

translation: فأقبلت امرأته في صرة فصكت وجهها وقالت عجوز عقيم
interpretation: تعبّر العبارة عن ردة فعل إنسانية فورية من اليأس والدهشة: المرأة تصف نفسها بكلمات تحقير (عجوز عقيم) وتضرب وجهها تعبيرًا عن استحالة الظاهر — وهي بذلك تُبرز ميل البشر إلى حصر إمكاناتهم في قيود الجسد والسن، بينما تضع الآية هذا المشهد لتوضيح التباين بين شكّ الإنسان وامتداد قدرة الله فيما يبدو مستحيلاً.

translation: قالوا: «كذلك قال ربك؛ إنه هو الحكم العليم.»
interpretation: العبارة تعبّر عن اعتراف المتكلّم بأن ما وقع هو قول الله وتنفيذه، مع تأكيد صفتَي الحكمة والعلم لله؛ أي أن أحكامَ الله وأقداره تُنفَذ بعقلٍ وحكمة كاملة ومعرفة تامة، فالأحداث — مهما بدا بعضها غامضاً أو مُؤلِماً — جزء من تدبير ربّي حكيم وعليم يستوجب الثقة والقبول.

translation: He said, “So what is the matter with you, O messengers?”
interpretation: A pointed divine inquiry confronting the envoys for their hesitation or distress: it rebukes any failure to fulfill their appointed duty, demands they state their grievance or excuse, and underscores the expectation that those entrusted with a mission must act decisively and account for any impediment.

translation: They said, “Indeed, we were sent to a people who are criminals (wrongdoers).”
interpretation: The speakers (the messengers) are declaring that their mission is directed toward a community marked by persistent injustice and sin; describing them as 'mujrimīn' emphasizes the people's moral culpability and legitimizes the divine warning and corrective consequences that follow if they refuse to repent.

translation: We will send upon them stones of clay.
interpretation: The phrase signifies a divine, decisive punishment brought upon those who persist in denial and rebellion: the “stones of clay” are literal instruments of chastisement—created, unmistakable, and overwhelming—used by God to show His sovereignty and to make the consequences of persistent arrogance and rejection manifest and inescapable; the wording stresses the inevitability and seriousness of divine retribution as a deterrent to turning away from guidance.

translation: A punishment decreed with your Lord for the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse declares that God has appointed a specific, inevitable retribution for those who exceed bounds in wrongdoing, arrogance, or denial of His guidance. By saying it is “with your Lord,” it emphasizes that the measure, timing, and form of that recompense are under Divine wisdom and justice: the excesses of the مُسْرِفِين (those who transgress limits—whether by injustice, heedless indulgence, or rebellious denial) will not go unaccounted for, and their fate is determined by God’s righteous ordinance.

translation: So We brought out of it those among them who were believers.
interpretation: The phrase teaches that deliverance in the face of divine punishment is not a matter of lineage, tribe, or outward circumstance but of inner conviction: God, in His wisdom and mercy, distinguishes and saves those whose hearts truly believed. It emphasizes that salvation is granted by God’s will to the faithful, serving both as reassurance for sincere believers and a moral admonition that genuine faith, not mere social identity, is the criterion for divine protection.

translation: فما وجدنا فيها غير بيت من المسلمين — We found there nothing except a house of those who submit (Muslims).
interpretation: The verse highlights that the real value of a place lies in the presence of sincere believers: a household of those who submit to God constitutes a form of spiritual wealth, divine favor, and moral safety that outweighs material possessions. It teaches that true honor and protection come from faith and submission to God rather than from worldly goods or numbers.

translation: And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.
interpretation: God has placed a clear, purposeful proof so that those who are conscious of His severe recompense will recognize it; this sign is meant to awaken reverent fear, restrain from wrongdoing, and prompt sincere repentance and righteous conduct—serving both as a warning of accountability and as a mercy that guides the God-fearing back to obedience.

translation:
وَفِي مُوسَىٰٓ إِذْ أَرْسَلْنَٰهُ إِلَىٰ فِرْعَوْنَ بِسُلْطَٰنٍۢ مُبِينٍۢ
"And (remember) Moses when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority."
interpretation: The verse asserts that God equipped Moses with unmistakable, divinely granted authority—both miraculous signs and a legitimate mandate—so his confrontation with Pharaoh was not a mere human claim but backed by clear proof; therefore Pharaoh’s rejection was wilful arrogance, and the passage teaches that prophetic missions are validated by God’s signs and impose moral accountability on rulers.

translation: Then he turned to his seat and said, “A magician or a madman.”
interpretation: The verse shows how a proud, self‑interested leader reacts to confronting truth: rather than examine the evidence he retreats into contempt and seeks to neutralize the messenger by publicly branding him a sorcerer or insane. It illustrates the moral that arrogance and fear of losing power lead people to reject reasoned discourse, employ slander to preserve authority, and harden hearts against guidance.

translation: So We seized him and his hosts and cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy.
interpretation: The verse signifies that arrogant, oppressive rejection of God’s guidance brings about decisive and humiliating overthrow: worldly power and numbers cannot prevent divine justice, so tyrants who persist in wrongdoing will be disgraced and punished — a warning against pride and a reassurance that God ultimately vindicates the oppressed.

translation:
وَفِي عَادٍ إِذْ أَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمُ الرِّيحَ الْعَقِيمَ
“And [recall] 'Aad — when We sent upon them the barren (sterilizing) wind.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s retribution can be decisive and nullifying toward a people whose pride and persistent rejection of divine guidance make them culpable; calling the wind “العقيم” (barren) stresses that the punishment left no productive benefit and obliterated their power, serving as a moral and theological warning about the futility of relying on worldly might in opposition to God’s commandments.

translation: ما تذر من شيء أتت عليه إلا جعلته كالرميم — "There is nothing of anything that it comes upon which You do not make like scattered rubble/decayed debris."
interpretation: The verse affirms Allah’s absolute sovereignty over creation: whatever appears to endure or be established can be reduced to ruin by His will. Nothing persists independent of Divine power, so human possessions, works, and even apparent realities are ultimately transient and subject to God’s disposition.

translation: And [recall] Thamud, when it was said to them, “Enjoy yourselves for a while.”
interpretation: The verse recalls how the people of Thamud were told—whether as a taunt by opponents or as their own defiant counsel—to pursue fleeting worldly pleasures for a short time instead of heeding the prophetic warning. It highlights two things: the temporariness of that enjoyment and the moral error of postponing repentance. Granting a brief respite exposed their obstinacy and made their eventual punishment a just consequence of choosing transient comfort over submission to guidance.

translation: They rejected the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on.
interpretation: The verse warns that persistent rejection of God’s guidance and arrogant turning away from His command leads to a sudden, overwhelming divine chastisement (الصاعقة). That punishment comes decisively and publicly, leaving the transgressors powerless and humiliated as they witness its occurrence; it therefore serves to remind listeners of the certainty of accountability and the futility of denial when retribution arrives.

translation: So they could not rise up (in opposition), nor were they victorious.
interpretation: The verse teaches that those who oppose God’s command and truth ultimately lack the real power to stand against it; despite their efforts or bravado they fail to prevail. It underscores human impotence before divine will and serves as a warning that resistance rooted in pride or false security leads only to defeat, not success.

translation: And the people of Noah before [them]—indeed they were a people given to transgression.
interpretation: The verse invokes Noah’s community as an example of a society that habitually rejected divine guidance: their conduct was marked by persistent disobedience, moral corruption, and refusal to accept the prophet’s warning. The word “fasiqīn” stresses a settled, brazen breaking of God’s limits rather than occasional lapses. By citing that past nation, the text warns the present addressees that collective, entrenched rebellion against God and His messenger brings moral ruin and divine punishment, and therefore calls for sincere repentance, heedfulness of revelation, and reform to avoid the same outcome.

translation: And the heaven — We constructed it with power, and indeed We are [its] expander.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God brought the heavens into being by His sovereign power (the phrase “with hands” is a metaphor for strength, authority and creative agency) and that this creation is not static but subject to His ongoing will: He continues to expand and sustain the heavens. The statement underscores divine omnipotence and continuous creative activity, calling people to recognize their own limitation, to reflect on the signs in the universe, and to submit to the Creator whose work transcends human comprehension.

translation: And the earth — We have spread it out; how excellent are the spreaders.
interpretation: The verse declares that God has deliberately laid out and prepared the earth as a well-ordered, hospitable domain for life; by “spreading” the earth God’s creative skill is praised — He levels, furnishes and stabilizes the ground, provides its resources and passages, and thus manifests perfect wisdom and facilitation for human and living needs.

translation: And of everything We have created pairs, that you may remember.
interpretation: The verse indicates that creation is arranged in complementary pairs — not only biological sexes but opposing or matching elements and relationships throughout nature — as a deliberate sign of God’s wise, balanced order. These pairings reveal interdependence, harmony, and purposeful design intended to prompt human reflection, gratitude, and recognition of the Creator’s power and wisdom.

translation: So flee to Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner.
interpretation: The clause commands an urgent, decisive turning away from whatever binds one to destruction — idols, sinful habits, false securities — toward God alone as the only true refuge. Describing the speaker as “a clear warner from Him” stresses that this call carries divine authority and unmistakable clarity: it is meant to awaken people to imminent spiritual peril and to move them to sincere repentance, submission, and reliance on God for deliverance.

translation: And do not set up with Allah another god; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner.
interpretation: The verse functions as both a theological boundary and a moral summons: by forbidding any association with God it protects the unity of divine authority, and by identifying the Messenger as a 'clear warner' it makes the warning demonstrably authoritative and accountable. The effect is to transfer responsibility to the hearers — the message is unmistakable revelation, so refusing it is not ignorance but a moral choice with spiritual and social consequences; sincere response requires abandoning practices or beliefs that compromise God's uniqueness and heeding the guidance offered to reform one's creed and conduct.

translation: Thus it is; no messenger came to those before them but they said, “A sorcerer or a madman.”
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring human tactic: when people refuse a message that threatens their interests or worldview, they often attack the messenger’s character by branding him as a sorcerer or insane rather than engaging the evidence. Such accusations reveal the accusers’ unwillingness to confront the truth and serve to distract and delegitimize, so the verse warns believers not to be unsettled by personal slanders and to persist with patience, clear argument, and moral steadiness.

translation: They urged one another to it; but they are a people given to transgression.
interpretation: The verse warns that the gravest danger is not isolated wrongdoing but a social process that normalizes and promotes it: when people counsel and encourage one another toward error, this mutual reinforcement reveals their true character as ṭāghūn—those who overstep limits, act arrogantly against divine guidance and justice, and persist in rebellious, entrenched disobedience rather than repent or accept the truth.

translation: So turn away from them; for you are not to be blamed.
interpretation: This counsels the Prophet (and by extension any messenger) to withdraw from persistent rejection and abuse: his responsibility is to deliver the message, not to compel belief or be consumed by reproach. The phrase affirms his exoneration — he will not be held accountable for people’s obstinate refusal or for choosing to disengage from them to protect his mission and peace of mind; ultimate judgment of hearts belongs to God.

translation: So remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers.
interpretation: This injunction commands the Prophet (and by extension any righteous person) to continue offering admonition and counsel because such reminders awaken, strengthen and correct the hearts of those open to guidance. A reminder does not coerce belief but serves as a means of spiritual revival—prompting reflection, repentance, perseverance in faith, and rectification of conduct—and therefore bears real benefit for true believers even if some remain unmoved.

translation: And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they might worship Me.
interpretation: This verse states the fundamental purpose of human and jinn existence: to recognize, submit to, and live for God. “Worship” (ʿibādah) here is understood broadly — not limited to ritual acts like prayer and fasting but encompassing any belief, intention, words, and deeds done in sincere obedience to God and seeking His pleasure. Thus life’s proper orientation is to acknowledge God’s lordship, follow His guidance, act morally, and avoid associating partners with Him; through such devotion individuals fulfill their created purpose and will be accountable for how they lived in relation to that purpose.

translation: ما أريد منهم من رزق وما أريد أن يطعمون — I do not ask of them any provision, nor do I ask that they feed Me.
interpretation: The verse affirms divine (and prophetic) self-sufficiency and the purity of the mission: the Messenger does not seek material support or nourishment from people and is not motivated by worldly gain. Its point is to show that the call to God is sincere and not a demand for sustenance—worship and guidance are for people’s benefit, not because God needs anything from His creation.

translation: Indeed, Allah is the Provider, Possessor of Power, the Firm One.
interpretation: This affirms that ultimate provision and support belong to God alone: He is the source of sustenance, the one whose power is strong and unshakeable. The verse calls believers to trust in Him (tawakkul) and to act responsibly, knowing that while effort is required, the final outcome and lasting support come from God’s steadfast strength and care.

translation:
إِنَّ لِلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا ذُنُوبًا مِثْلَ ذُنُوبِ أَصْحَابِهِمْ فَلَا يَسْتَعْجِلُونَ
"Indeed, those who have wronged will have sins like the sins of their companions, so they will not be able to hasten (anything)."
interpretation: The verse warns that injustice multiplies liability: wrongdoers incur burdens comparable to the harms they brought upon others, and they cannot shortcut or hasten a different outcome before divine justice. In other words, one who oppresses or misleads others takes on culpability that mirrors the victims’ losses, and no human stratagem or pleading will accelerate forgiveness or avert the due recompense — accountability is inevitable and cannot be rushed.

translation: So woe to those who disbelieve on the Day they are promised.
interpretation: The verse warns that the appointed Day of Reckoning will bring unavoidable ruin and bitter regret specifically upon those who denied God and His message. “Woe” here denotes both severe punishment and the anguish of thwarted hopes; “their Day” signals that the hour of accounting is the destined moment when their rejection is exposed and its consequences enacted. The statement stresses the certainty and personal nature of divine retribution for persistent unbelief and serves as a stern admonition to heed guidance before that irreversible day arrives.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. By the Mount!
interpretation: The oath “By the Mount” invokes a concrete, sacred place of divine encounter (traditionally Sinai) as a witness to God’s presence and authority; by swearing on that manifest sign, the statement underscores the reality and gravity of God’s message, reminding people that God’s power and revelations are evident in history and that humans are accountable to that revealed truth.

translation: And a written (inscribed) Book.
interpretation: It denotes the divine, inscribed Record — a complete and preserved Book in which God has set down decrees, destinies and the revealed truth. The phrase emphasizes that these matters are fixed, recorded, and serve as incontrovertible testimony before God.

translation: في رق منشور — in an outstretched/opened neck
interpretation: The phrase portrays a scene of utter humiliation and exposure: the neck is laid bare and spread out, symbolizing the helplessness and subjugation of those subjected to punishment. “منشور” conveys being spread, opened or flattened so there is no cover or concealment; the image thus emphasizes total disgrace, vulnerability, and inability to resist or hide before God's judgment.

translation: And the much‑frequented House.
interpretation: It designates al‑Bayt al‑Maʿmūr, a celestial counterpart to the Kaʿbah that is continually visited by angels. The phrase points to a real, unseen locus of worship in the heavens—emphasizing the ongoing, universal act of devotion beyond the visible world and affirming the reality of the unseen order that undergirds earthly signs.

translation: By the raised roof
interpretation: This is an oath invoking the lofty, elevated canopy—understood as the heavens or high dome of creation—to draw attention to God’s majesty and power; the ‘raised roof’ serves as a visible sign and witness to divine sovereignty, underscoring the truth and seriousness of what is being affirmed.

translation: And the sea that is set ablaze.
interpretation: It refers to the Day of Resurrection when God will reverse the normal order of creation so that even the seas are made to burn or boil; this image underscores divine sovereignty to transform the elements and serves as a stark warning that the familiar world will be radically altered for the purpose of judgment and accountability.

translation: Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely coming.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that divine chastisement is not mere rhetoric but an inevitable reality for those who persist in denying truth and committing injustice; it functions to awaken urgency and moral seriousness, urging people to repent and reform because God’s justice and decrees will inevitably be realized even if their timing is concealed.

translation: He has no motive.
interpretation: The phrase indicates that the person lacks any valid reason, incentive, or justification for a particular action or stance; nothing drives or excuses his behavior, so the action appears baseless or culpable rather than warranted.

translation: On the Day when the heavens will convulse in turmoil.
interpretation: The phrase depicts the Day of Reckoning as a cosmic upheaval: the familiar order of the sky and universe is violently overturned to show God’s absolute power and the certainty of resurrection. Its purpose is to abolish human complacency and pride by reminding people that worldly stability is temporary and that all will be brought to account before their Creator.

translation: And you will see the mountains moving in procession.
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Resurrection’s cosmic upheaval: the mountains—symbols of permanence and security—are made to move like marching caravans, signifying God’s absolute power to overturn worldly stability, humiliate human certainties, and mobilize all creation toward reckoning; it teaches that what seems unshakable in this life is transient before divine judgment.

translation: So woe, that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This is a solemn warning that on the Day of Reckoning those who persistently denied God’s signs and the resurrection will experience utter ruin and remorse; the word “woe” denotes both unavoidable divine retribution and the complete loss—moral, existential, and eternal—that will overtake the deniers when the truth is unveiled, urging immediate repentance before that irreversible hour.

translation: Those who are immersed in vain talk and play.
interpretation: This refers to people who occupy themselves with frivolous, idle speech and amusements—mocking, trivializing, and neglecting serious duties—so that they lose sight of moral and spiritual responsibilities and waste their lives on vain distractions.

translation: The Day they will be called to the Fire of Hell.
interpretation: The phrase signifies the inevitable, public and decisive summons of divine judgment: on the Last Day those whose choices have severed them from guidance will be unmistakably summoned and driven toward their recompense. The language of being “called” emphasizes both the certainty and the finality of the outcome, the exposure of inner states before all, and serves as a stern admonition to take responsibility for one’s deeds now rather than face an inescapable destiny later.

translation: This is the Fire which you used to deny.
interpretation: A stern admonition confronting those who rejected warnings: it affirms the undeniable reality of divine retribution and exposes the folly of denying clear signs. Its purpose is moral and spiritual— to show that turning away from guidance leads to humiliation and consequence, to vindicate prophetic warning, and to urge reflection, repentance, and return to obedience before it is too late.

translation: Is this sorcery? Or are you not seeing?
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke: the speaker exposes the opponents' refusal to accept clear signs by saying that either they dismiss these manifest truths as mere magic, or they are willfully/spiritually blind. The verse shifts the burden onto the deniers—their rejection is not due to ambiguity in the sign but to their own inability or unwillingness to perceive reality.

translation: فَاصْبِرُوا أَوْ لَا تَصْبِرُوا سَوَاءٌ عَلَيْكُمْ ۖ إِنَّمَا تُجْزَوْنَ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ
