interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke aimed at both humans and jinn: it forces reflection on the countless, unmistakable blessings and signs of God's mercy and sovereignty in creation and provision, exposing ingratitude as an indefensible rejection of evident truth and calling the listener to acknowledge, be grateful for, and submit to the One who bestows those favors.

translation: He created human beings from sounding clay, like pottery.
interpretation: The verse affirms that humans originate from humble, fashioned material—clay—likening the Creator’s work to a potter shaping a vessel. This image teaches that our physical nature is contingent and crafted by God’s deliberate design, that we are malleable morally and spiritually (capable of formation or deformation), and that our dignity comes from being intentionally formed rather than from material superiority; it thus calls for humility, recognition of dependence on the Creator, and awareness of the potential for purposeful moral shaping.

translation: And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire.
interpretation: The verse indicates that jinn are a distinct created order made of a subtle, energetic, fiery reality (the word “marij” conveying a flashing, mixed or billowing flame) that differs in essence from human clay. This ontological difference explains their characteristic capacities — invisibility, swift movement, changeability — while not denying their moral agency: like humans they possess will and are accountable before God. Describing their origin as a ‘smokeless flame’ stresses their non-material, energetic constitution rather than implying mere metaphor, and serves to remind believers that creation encompasses diverse modes of being under divine sovereignty.

translation:
فَبِأَيِّ آلَاءِ رَبِّكُمَا تُكَذِّبَانِ
"Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?"
interpretation: This is a rhetorical rebuke addressed to both humans and jinn that aims to shatter complacency and ingratitude: by repeatedly asking which single blessing could be denied, the verse exposes the absurdity of rejecting God’s evident bounties—both outward (creation, provision, order) and inward (guidance, conscience)—and urges recognition, gratitude, and submission rather than denial or arrogance.

translation: Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests.
interpretation: A declaration of God’s absolute sovereignty over all horizons and cycles: every place or time of rising and setting, every apparent opposite or change of direction, falls under His rule—affirming that all beginnings and endings in creation are governed by one Lord.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge directed at both humans and jinn, meant to confront and shame persistent ingratitude: after enumerating God’s manifold blessings, the question forces reflection — there is no reasonable basis to reject or deny these clear favors and signs — and thus it urges recognition, gratitude, and submission to the One who bestowed them.

translation: He released the two seas, and they meet.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s act of setting two great bodies of water in contact yet maintaining their ordained limits; it is a sign of divine power and wisdom in establishing balance and boundaries in creation, inviting reflection on God’s sovereignty and the ordered harmony underlying the natural world.

translation: بينهما برزخٌ لا يبغيان — Between them is a barrier which they do not transgress.
interpretation: The phrase points to a divine law that sets fixed limits within creation: even mighty, opposing forces are held in measured balance and cannot overstep the boundary God has ordained. It teaches that God’s wisdom sustains order by restraining what would otherwise overwhelm or dissolve distinctions, and invites reflection on human responsibility to recognize and respect divinely set limits in nature, society, and personal conduct.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A pointed, repeated rhetorical challenge addressing both humans and jinn: it forces reflection on the countless, evident blessings and provisions that can only stem from God’s sovereign mercy and wisdom, exposing ingratitude and denial as unjustifiable and calling the listener to recognition, gratitude, and accountability before the Giver.

translation: From both of them come forth pearls and coral.
interpretation: The verse points to God’s wisdom and providence: even within distinct, contrasting realms He brings forth hidden, precious blessings that display beauty and benefit. Pearls and coral function as signs calling people to reflect on the Creator’s artistry, to recognize sustenance in unexpected places, and to respond with gratitude and awe at God’s power and generosity.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A forceful, rhetorical challenge directed at humankind (and jinn) that exposes and condemns ingratitude: by repeatedly asking this question the text compels listeners to confront the countless, evident blessings and provisions from their Lord, to recognize that denying or overlooking them is unreasonable in light of the clear signs of creation and care, and to understand that such denial carries moral consequence—thus the verse calls for acknowledgement, gratitude, and accountability.

translation:
وَلَهُ الْجَوَارُ الْمُنْشَآتُ فِي الْبَحْرِ كَالْأَعْلَامِ
"And to Him belong the ships that are set forth on the sea, like standards (or banners)."
interpretation: The verse uses the striking image of ships moving on the sea 'like standards' to point to God's sovereign lordship and sustaining power: the ordered, purposeful movement of vessels — enabling travel, commerce and human interaction — is a visible sign of divine control and provision, reminding the observer that such complex, beneficent arrangements in creation occur by God's will and testify to His authority.

translation: Which, then, of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A pointed, rhetorical rebuke addressed to people (and jinn): in view of the clear signs and countless blessings God has bestowed, it exposes the irrationality of rejecting or being ungrateful for those gifts and calls for recognition of God’s providence and the moral responsibility that follows such acknowledgement.

translation: كل من عليها فان — Everything on it is perishing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that all created things in this world are transient and dependent, and by contrast points to the sole permanence of God; its purpose is to reorient the believer’s priorities away from attachment to fleeting worldly goods and toward awareness of mortality, responsibility before God, and devotion to the One Who alone endures.

translation: And there will remain the Face of your Lord, full of Majesty and Honour.
interpretation: The verse affirms that all created things are transient while God alone endures eternally; the word “Face” signifies His real, uncreated Being and presence, and “Majesty and Honour” declare His absolute sovereignty and glory — thereby directing believers to focus devotion and trust on the everlasting Lord rather than on fleeting worldly realities.

translation: فبأي آلاء ربكما تكذبان — So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge addressed to the audience (human and jinn) that forces them to confront the innumerable blessings and signs bestowed by God; by repeatedly asking this question the verse exposes the inconsistency and ingratitude of denying divine favors, urging recognition, gratitude, and awareness of eventual accountability for rejecting what clearly evidences God’s mercy and power.

translation: Those in the heavens and on earth ask Him; every day He is engaged in an affair.
interpretation: All creatures in heaven and earth turn to God in need and in recognition of His authority, and God is continually and actively carrying out His decrees and sustaining creation. The phrase “every day He is engaged in an affair” emphasizes the permanence and constancy of His governance and activity — not that He undergoes change like created beings, but that His lordship and action are continuously exercised in ways beyond human comprehension.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge addressed to people and jinn that exposes ingratitude: it calls them to recognize and acknowledge the countless signs and mercies God has bestowed, warning that to deny or overlook these favors is a willful rejection of divine truth and sovereignty and urging grateful reflection and submission.

translation: سَنَفْرُغُ لَكُمْ أَيُّهَا الثَّقْلَانِ — We will give our full attention to you, O two weighty ones.
interpretation: Addressing the two great categories of creation (commonly understood as mankind and the jinn), the phrase promises that God will in due course turn His full and decisive attention to them: He will complete His dealings — bringing guidance, recompense and judgment — so that nothing of their accountability or destiny is left unresolved. It underlines Divine sovereignty, the certainty of a final reckoning, and that both groups will receive their due without omission.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A stern, rhetorical challenge addressed to the hearers that exposes and reproves ingratitude: by repeatedly asking which divine blessing they will deny, it forces self-examination, underscores the abundance and undeniability of God’s signs and mercies, and calls people (and jinn) to acknowledge, be grateful for, and submit to the Source of those favors rather than rejecting or taking them for granted.

translation: O company of jinn and mankind: if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass. You will not pass except with (clear) authority.
interpretation: The verse addresses both jinn and humans, challenging any presumption that they can escape God’s dominion by fleeing across the heavens and the earth. It asserts that such escape is impossible except by a granted power or permission (سلطان) — underscoring that all creatures remain under God’s sovereign control and cannot evade His knowledge, rule, or eventual accountability unless He wills to grant them a means; thus the passage is a reminder of human and jinn dependence and the certainty of divine authority and judgment.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge intended to confront human and jinn ingratitude: faced with the manifold, evident blessings and signs bestowed by God, the question exposes the absurdity of denying His favors, urging honest recognition, gratitude, and awareness that rejecting these signs is morally culpable and will be accounted for.

translation:
يُرسِلُ عَلَيْكُمَا شَوَاظًا مِنْ نَارٍ وَنُحَاسًا فَلَا تَنْتَصِرَانِ
"He will send upon you blazing flames of fire and molten copper, so you will not be able to defend yourselves."
interpretation: This verse portrays a decisive, irresistible divine punishment: the images of scorching flames and molten metal emphasize an overwhelming force that consumes and incapacitates the wrongdoers. The dual address underscores that neither power nor partnership will avail them — when God’s judgement comes, human defenses, pride, and weapons are rendered powerless and their fate is sealed.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: A pointed rhetorical challenge directed at both humans and jinn meant to pierce complacency and expose ingratitude: it forces inward reckoning by showing that blessings and sustenance ultimately come from God, that denying them is morally untenable, and that the only proper response is recognition, gratitude and submission—persistent denial is presented as a culpable rejection that will be accounted for.

translation: Then when the heaven is split apart and becomes like a rose, like molten oil.
interpretation: The image conveys the radical transformation of the cosmos at the Hour: the firmament is violently sundered and takes on a molten, blood‑red or oil‑like aspect, symbolizing overwhelming heat, disintegration of the familiar order, and the onset of divine reckoning — a vivid warning that what once sheltered and sustained life will be altered into something fierce and alien, announcing the immediacy and severity of the Day of Judgment.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge to humanity and jinn that exposes the absurdity and moral wrong of rejecting God’s obvious, continuous blessings; it is meant to awaken gratitude and responsible conduct by showing that ingratitude is unjustified in the face of clear signs and will be subject to moral and eschatological accountability.

translation: On that Day no human nor jinn will be asked about his sin.
interpretation: The verse stresses that on the Day of Resurrection every being’s true deeds will be manifest and judged directly: neither humans nor jinn can hide, make excuses, or be excused for another. Questioning in the ordinary sense will be redundant because God’s knowledge and the records will make each person’s responsibility plain, so every soul will be held individually to account for what it did.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A pointed, rhetorical challenge addressed to both humanity and the jinn that exposes the irrationality of ingratitude: by repeatedly asking which divine blessing could be rejected, the verse forces reflection on how every aspect of existence and provision is a gift from God and therefore grounds for recognition, gratitude, and moral responsibility rather than denial.

translation:
يُعْرَفُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ بِسِمَاهُمْ فَيُؤْخَذُ بِالنَّوَاصِي وَالْأَقْدَامِ
"The criminals will be recognized by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks and by the feet."
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Reckoning when wrongdoers will be unmistakably exposed — their outward ‘marks’ or signs will reveal their guilt — and they will be brought in utter humiliation to punishment, grasped by the hair/forehead (a symbol of control and disgrace) and by the feet (denying escape or dignity). The image emphasizes inevitable accountability, public exposure of inner corruption, and the complete loss of power and honor before divine justice.

translation:
فَبِأَيِّ آلَاءِ رَبِّكُمَا تُكَذِّبَانِ
"So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?"
interpretation: A rhetorical summons addressed to humans and jinn meant to jolt them into recognition and gratitude: by repeatedly asking which divine favors they will deny, the verse exposes the absurdity of ingratitude in the face of manifest blessings, points to those blessings as signs of God’s mercy and sovereignty, and urges humility, thankful acknowledgement, and awareness of moral accountability for persistent denial.

translation: This is Hell — which the criminals used to deny.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the torment of Hell is a real and imminent judgment that those who persisted in wrongdoing and disbelief had rejected as false or unimportant. Calling it "this" makes its reality immediate and unavoidable; the phrase criticizes the arrogance and heedlessness of the wrongdoers who dismissed the warnings, and functions as both condemnation of their denial and a warning to others to repent, abandon injustice, and take divine admonitions seriously.

translation: They will go round between it and a scalding (spring) for a while.
interpretation: The verse depicts a scene of punishment in the Hereafter: the doomed are made to move back and forth between two severe torments—the fiery place and scalding, boiling waters—for an appointed time, portraying the relentless, alternating nature of their suffering and the certainty of divine retribution.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A repeated, rhetorical challenge addressed to both humankind and jinn that exposes the impossibility of denying God’s manifold blessings: it calls attention to the countless signs and provisions of the Creator, condemns ingratitude and rejection, and urges recognition, thankfulness, and submission to God’s sovereignty.

translation: And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord there will be two gardens.
interpretation: A promise that genuine reverential fear of meeting God — understood as humble God‑consciousness and accountability that shapes one’s actions — will be met with a doubled, gracious reward in the Hereafter: two gardens symbolizing complete and abundant blessings granted to those whose awe of God leads them to righteousness.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge confronting humans and jinn with their habitual ingratitude: it highlights that the manifold blessings and signs from God are evident, and that to deny them is both irrational and morally culpable, meant to awaken conscience to recognize, be grateful for, and be accountable for those divine favors.

translation: (those) possessing spreading boughs
interpretation: The phrase depicts trees with abundant, outward-reaching branches as a sign of God’s generous provision and orderly, life-giving creation; the branching evokes fruitfulness, shelter and sustenance, directing the reader to reflect on divine care and blessings manifest in nature.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical challenge addressed to both humans and jinn, intended to expose and condemn ingratitude: in the face of the manifold, manifest signs of God's mercy, provision and power, denying those blessings is unreasonable and morally culpable; the verse presses the listener to pause, recognize the divine favors around them, respond with gratitude and humility, and remember that such denial will be accounted for.

translation: In both of them are two springs flowing.
interpretation: The mention of flowing springs symbolizes that the rewards of Paradise are permanent and self‑renewing: God’s mercy and provision there continuously refresh and sustain the dwellers without effort or decay, offering enduring spiritual and bodily fulfilment in contrast with the transient, labor‑bound gains of this world.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: This rhetorical question, repeated to both humans and jinn, is an admonition to recognize that the manifold blessings and signs described are unmistakable tokens of God’s mercy and sovereignty; to “deny” them is not merely to dispute facts but to refuse gratitude and responsibility, a moral failure that severs proper relationship with the Creator and blinds one to accountability.

translation: In both of them are pairs of every fruit.
interpretation: The verse signifies that Paradise is furnished with complete, harmonious provision: every blessing appears in complementary pairs, symbolizing God’s generosity, balance, and the perfected order of creation so that nothing is lacking and inhabitants enjoy abundance and mutual completeness.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A sharp, rhetorical challenge addressed to both humans and jinn that exposes persistent ingratitude: it repeatedly confronts the listener with the impossibility of denying God’s manifest blessings and calls for recognition, reflection, and repentance by making ingratitude morally and spiritually indefensible.

translation: Reclining on couches, the inner coverings of which are of brocade; and the fruits of the two gardens are near at hand.
interpretation: The verse pictures the reward of the righteous as secure, effortless, and dignified enjoyment: the sumptuous couches with brocaded linings signify honor, comfort, and permanence bestowed by God, while the nearby, low-hanging fruits of the two gardens signify abundant, varied blessings that are immediately accessible without toil—together emphasizing divine generosity and the guaranteed, untroubled fulfillment awaiting the faithful rather than mere transient or uncertain pleasures.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: A sharp, rhetorical challenge addressed to humans and jinn that exposes ingratitude: by repeatedly asking which of God’s countless blessings they would deny, the verse intends to jolt listeners into humble recognition of divine gifts, to show the denial as irrational and blameworthy, and to call them toward grateful acknowledgement and moral responsibility before the Giver.

translation:
فِيهِنَّ قَاصِرَاتُ الطَّرْفِ لَمْ يَطْمِثْهُنَّ إِنْسٌ قَبْلَهُمْ وَلَا جَانٌّ
"In them are modest (restraining-the-gaze) maidens, whom no human before them nor any jinn has touched."
interpretation: The verse promises that among the rewards of Paradise are companions whose chastity and modesty are preserved intact and reserved exclusively for the righteous; the phrase emphasizes both their inward purity (قاصرات الطرف — humility and modest gaze) and their untouched, unmarred status (لم يطمثهن) as a way to convey the unique, perfect, and divinely safeguarded nature of the joys prepared for the believers, signaling that the moral order and pleasures of the Hereafter are purified and distinct from worldly experience.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A repeated, emphatic rhetorical challenge addressed to humanity and jinn that confronts them with the manifold, undeniable blessings God has bestowed; it demands recognition and gratitude, exposing the irrationality of denying divine gifts and serving as a reminder of moral accountability for ingratitude.

translation: As though they were rubies and coral.
interpretation: The phrase uses a simile to convey extraordinary, otherworldly beauty and radiance: like precious gems, they are depicted as spotless, luminous, and of rare, lasting value—Emphasizing purity, brilliance, and an incomparable, exalted worth beyond ordinary human beauty.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge addressed to humankind and jinn that exposes ingratitude: by repeatedly asking which divine blessings they reject, it urges them to recognize the evident signs of God's mercy and provision, to cease denying His favors, and to respond with acknowledgement and gratefulness rather than denial.

translation: Is the reward for good anything but good?
interpretation: A rhetorical affirmation that those who practice ihsān (excellence, kindness, righteous conduct) will receive nothing other than fitting goodness in return from God — an assurance of divine justice and generosity that virtuous deeds will be met with corresponding blessings and ultimate reward (including mercy and Paradise).

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge to humans and jinn that reproaches their ingratitude: it emphasizes that God’s blessings are many and manifest, that denying or ignoring them is unreasonable, and thus calls for recognition, gratefulness, and submission to His lordship (with the implicit warning of accountability for persistent denial).

translation: And beneath them are two gardens.
interpretation: The phrase signals the abundance and multiplicity of the reward prepared for the righteous in Paradise: not just a single blessing but adjacent, layered gardens — ‘beneath them’ implying these blessings form a sustaining foundation and overflow beyond what is immediately apparent, emphasizing Allah’s generosity and the manifold, closely linked favors granted to the faithful.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke addressed to both humanity and the jinn, meant to confront their persistent ingratitude: by repeatedly posing this question the verse forces recognition that the countless blessings and signs of God are undeniable, and that refusing to acknowledge them is a willful moral failing that ought to lead to awareness, gratitude, and submission to God's sovereignty.

translation: Two dark, deep (seas).
interpretation: A reference to the two immense, dark-colored bodies of water — commonly understood as the meeting of two seas that remain distinct — presented as a sign of God’s power, wisdom and the divinely-established boundary between forces; it draws attention to the Creator’s control over nature and prompts humans to recognize and be grateful for His favors.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge addressed to both humans and jinn that highlights God’s abundant, manifest blessings and reproves ingratitude: by asking which specific blessing can be denied, it aims to awaken recognition and gratitude for every aspect of creation and provision, leaving no legitimate ground for rejecting Divine grace.

translation: In them are two gushing springs.
interpretation: The words point to permanent, life-giving provisions from God: the two springs symbolize abundant, paired blessings whose continuous gushing (نضاختان) emphasizes their inexhaustible, purifying and refreshing nature in the Hereafter, contrasting with transient worldly supplies.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: This repeated rhetorical challenge confronts people (and jinn) with the irrationality of rejecting the many manifest blessings bestowed by God; its purpose is to provoke inward reflection and gratitude, to expose ingratitude as a willful moral failing with consequences, and thereby to call the listener to acknowledge divine grace and live in humble submission and praise.

translation: In both of them are fruits, date‑palms and pomegranates.
interpretation: The verse points to the assured, abundant, and varied provision that God has prepared for the righteous: not merely food, but perfectly arranged blessings that signify nourishment, fertility, and delight. Mentioning specific, culturally prized produce (fruits, date‑palms, pomegranates) conveys completeness and ease — sustenance without hardship — and functions as a tangible sign of God’s generosity and the reality of the promised reward, calling the listener to trust the divine promise and to reflect with gratitude on God’s creative bounty.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A forceful rhetorical rebuke addressing humanity (and jinn): confronted with the clear, countless signs and provisions from God, the proper response is acknowledgement and gratitude; to “deny” these favors is not mere disbelief but a willful rejection of evident divine mercy and authority, a moral failure that leads away from thankfulness and right conduct.

translation: Therein are splendid, excellent bounties.
interpretation: It signifies that the dwellers of those abodes (understood as Paradise) will enjoy abundant, pure, and beautiful blessings—both outward delights and inward perfections—that are wholesome, perfected, and perfectly suited to their eternal happiness rather than the fleeting, corrupt pleasures of this world.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: A repeated rhetorical challenge directed at both humans and jinn that confronts ingrained ingratitude: by calling attention to the manifold, unmistakable blessings and signs of God, it exposes the irrationality of denial and aims to provoke recognition, gratefulness, humility, and submission to God's sovereignty.

translation: Houris confined in pavilions.
interpretation: The phrase describes a promised aspect of Paradise: pure, dignified companions who are preserved from worldly defilement and reserved for the believers in private, honorable dwellings. Their seclusion (mqoṣūrāt) underscores chastity and protection, conveying that God’s reward restores human intimacy to a sinless, dignified form—an expression of divine generosity and the believers’ spiritual and social fulfillment in the afterlife rather than merely physical indulgence.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge directed at human beings and jinn, calling attention to the innumerable blessings God has bestowed. By asking which single favor could be denied, the verse exposes the absurdity of ingratitude and invites recognition, reflection, and thankful submission, while implicitly warning that denying these gifts is spiritually culpable.

translation: No human had touched them before them, nor had any jinn.
interpretation: The verse affirms the exclusivity and purity of the companions promised in Paradise: they are preserved, untouched by any human or jinn, signifying a unique, unshared reward and the complete purity and perfection of the bliss reserved for the righteous, underscoring God’s just and special recompense for believers.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge to humans and jinn that forces reflection on God’s countless blessings: by repeatedly asking which single favor could plausibly be denied, the verse exposes the absurdity of ingratitude, calls for recognition and thankful submission to the Creator, and warns that rejecting these clear signs of divine mercy has moral and eschatological consequences.

translation: Reclining on green cushions and surrounded by fragrant, exquisite beauties.
interpretation: The phrase evokes the promised repose and dignified ease granted to the righteous in the afterlife: reclining signifies secure rest and honor, the green furnishings connote life, freshness and purity, and the fragrant, beautiful surroundings indicate refined, enduring pleasures beyond worldly toil — all metaphors for divine reward, serenity, and spiritual fulfillment bestowed by God.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: A recurrent rhetorical challenge addressed to both humans and jinn that exposes the absurdity of rejecting God’s evident bounties; it calls for humble recognition and gratitude for divine mercy and power, and warns that ingratitude and denial are unjustified in light of the manifest signs of God’s sovereignty.

translation: Blessed be the name of your Lord, Lord of Majesty and Honor.
interpretation: This is a doxology declaring that God’s name is inherently holy and exalted; it affirms His supreme dignity, authority and generosity (majestic power and gracious honor) and thus calls the reader to recognize and praise God as the ultimate source and exemplar of all glory and nobility.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. When the Inevitable (the Overwhelming Event) occurs.
interpretation: This opening announces the absolute certainty and transformative force of the Last Day: al‑Waqiʿah is a reality‑shattering, unavoidable event that will overturn worldly appearances and disclose people’s true states. It serves as a solemn reminder of divine sovereignty and mercy, calling for sober awareness of accountability and preparation through faith and righteous action.

translation: Its occurrence is not false.
interpretation: A declaration of the absolute certainty of the Overwhelming Event (the Day of Resurrection): its coming cannot be denied or made into a lie, and those who reject or ignore it will nonetheless confront its reality and be held to account.

translation: One that humbles, one that exalts.
interpretation: The two words signify God’s sovereign power to abase and to elevate: honor, rank, and condition are not intrinsic but are granted or withdrawn by divine will, so human status is transient and should inspire humility, gratitude, and reliance on God.

translation: When the earth is violently shaken.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the cataclysmic convulsion at the end of time: the earth will be violently shaken as a sign that the present order is overturned, hidden things are brought forth and people face the reckoning. It underscores God’s power, the reality of resurrection, and the certainty of accountability.

translation: And He spread out the mountains with mighty force.
interpretation: The phrase signifies that the mountains were placed by God through overwhelming power — they are not accidental features but deliberate, stabilizing signs of divine sovereignty intended to humble humans, demonstrate God’s control over creation, and remind people of the reality of divine judgment and their own dependence.

translation: فَكَانَتْ هَبَاءً مُنبَثًّا — "and it became scattered dust."
interpretation: The phrase conveys that whatever was trusted or relied upon (one’s plans, wealth, words or deeds when they lack true value before God) will be reduced to utter insignificance and dispersion — like dust driven apart by the wind — leaving no cohesion, benefit, or support on the Day of account.

translation: And you were three groups.
interpretation: The phrase signifies that people are classified into three distinct categories according to their response to divine guidance: sincere believers who accept and act upon it; outright rejecters who deny and oppose it; and those who are divided or hypocritical—externally appearing one way while inwardly another. The verse underscores that these differing dispositions determine moral responsibility and the different outcomes decreed for each group.

translation: فَأَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ
interpretation: عبارة تأملية تأكيدية تُبرز مكانة ومزية الذين يُوضعون على الميمنة يوم القيامة: هم المؤمنون الصالحون الذين نالوا رحمة الله ونعيمه، يعيشون الكرامة والراحة والقرب من الله كمكافأة على إيمانهم وعملهم الصالح، بغية تمييزهم عن أهل الشمال ومكانتهم الرفيعة لا تُقارن.

translation: And the companions of the Left—what are the companions of the Left?
interpretation: “The companions of the Left” denotes those who, by their disbelief, injustice, heedlessness, and pursuit of base desires, stand condemned on the Day of Reckoning and are consigned to humiliation and punishment. The rhetorical question “what are the companions of the Left?” intensifies their pitiable and shameful state, calling attention to the gravity of turning away from God’s guidance and warning listeners to reform their beliefs and deeds to avoid that fate.

translation: And the foremost, the foremost.
interpretation: An emphatic declaration referring to those who, by wholehearted faith and swift, selfless good works, advanced ahead of others in attaining closeness to God and thus are granted the highest ranks in the Hereafter; the repetition stresses their exceptional precedence and honor.

translation: Those are the ones brought near [to Allah].
interpretation: “Al‑Muqarrabūn” designates people whom God elevates to a position of intimate favor — not physical proximity but a relational status of acceptance, honor and closeness granted because of sincere faith, devotion and righteous conduct. It signifies that they enjoy special stations, mercy and nearness to their Lord as a result of their purification, constant remembrance and steadfast devotion.

translation: In the gardens of bliss.
interpretation: A portrayal of the afterlife as a permanent, honorable dwelling granted to the righteous, characterized by complete pleasure, ease, and dignity—both physical delights and spiritual contentment—free from hardship and sorrow as the recompense for obedience to God.

translation: a remnant of those who came before
interpretation: The phrase denotes a small remnant or handful from earlier generations—either the few survivors or the few who remained faithful—used to emphasize that only a small portion of former peoples persisted or were preserved, highlighting the transience of worldly strength and that God often leaves only a small group as witnesses or examples.

translation: and a few of the others
interpretation: It indicates that only a small minority among the remaining people share the described quality or fate — stressing rarity and exceptionality rather than a common occurrence.

translation: Upon couches arranged in rows.
interpretation: A depiction of the blessed in Paradise reclining in dignified, comfortable repose on orderly, well-appointed couches — signifying honor, ease, abundant and enduring reward, and the settled, dignified status granted to the righteous by God.

translation: Reclining upon it, facing one another.
interpretation: A depiction of the inhabitants of Paradise resting in complete ease on couches arranged opposite one another, indicating uninterrupted, honored companionship and mutual recognition — a restful, dignified fellowship free from fatigue, conflict, or concealment, reflecting the perfection and intimacy of the divine reward.

translation: Immortal youths will circulate among them.
interpretation: The phrase signifies that in Paradise there will be ever-youthful attendants who unobtrusively move among the inhabitants, providing service and refreshment without aging or fatigue; symbolically this underlines the permanence, ease, and continuous provision of divine blessings in the hereafter, and the removal of every worldly limitation on comfort and vigor.

translation: With goblets and ewers and a cup from a flowing spring.
interpretation: The phrase pictures Paradise’s refined and continuous provision: a variety of vessels and a cup drawn from a pure, bubbling source symbolize unending, dignified refreshment — both physical delight and spiritual renewal — bestowed by God’s pure, inexhaustible mercy.

translation: Do not beat your heads over it, nor let yourselves bleed.
interpretation: The verse forbids extreme mourning and self‑harm as a way of expressing grief — practices like striking one’s head or cutting oneself to show sorrow are not permitted. It teaches that grief must be contained within dignity and trust in God’s decree rather than enacted through injurious, excessive rites.

translation: And fruits of their choosing.
interpretation: The phrase signals that the rewards of the Hereafter are not generic provision but personalized, abundant bounty: inhabitants will be granted a variety of delights and the freedom to select what pleases them. It emphasizes God’s attentive generosity and justice — righteous people receive not only sufficiency but the fulfillment of their legitimate desires, a dignity and pleasure tailored to each person’s taste.

translation: And the flesh of birds — whatever they desire.
interpretation: This phrase signifies that in the hereafter righteous people will receive pure, delightful provisions exactly as they wish, without effort or limitation. The image of birds’ flesh emphasizes God’s generous, effortless provision of lawful pleasures: created things become fully available and tailored to the dwellers’ rightful longings, serving as a sign of divine mercy, the removal of worldly hardship, and the complete fulfillment of virtuous desire in Paradise.

translation: And wide-eyed maidens.
interpretation: The phrase refers to the pure, chaste companions of Paradise described with striking, large, lustrous eyes; it is an image meant to convey the dignity, beauty, and enduring delight of the heavenly reward bestowed upon the righteous.

translation: Like pearls kept hidden (treasured).
interpretation: The phrase likens the promised companions’ beauty and purity to precious pearls that are carefully stored and guarded, emphasizing their rarity, perfection, and protected, reserved status as an incomparable and enduring reward for the righteous in Paradise.

translation: a recompense for what they used to do
interpretation: It affirms that God will render a fitting recompense corresponding to the actions people habitually committed; their deeds determine their outcome, underscoring divine justice and personal accountability—no action goes without its due consequence.

translation: They will not hear therein any vain talk nor any sinful speech.
interpretation: The verse describes the inhabitants of Paradise as being entirely free from idle, frivolous, harmful, or blameworthy speech — no vain talk, slander, obscenity, or words that lead to sin will reach them. This absence of corrupt or hurtful speech signifies the complete moral and spiritual purity and peace of that realm, where conversation is dignified, beneficial, and oriented toward praise, truth, and tranquility.

translation: إلا قِيلًا: «سَلَامًا سَلَامًا»
interpretation: It means that what will be uttered to those whom God absolves or admits to bliss is nothing more than the concise, sovereign greeting “Peace, peace” — a declaration of safety, forgiveness, and entrance into repose; all fear, accusation and trial cease, and their final status is sealed by this affirmation of tranquility.

translation: And the Companions of the Right—what are the Companions of the Right?
interpretation: This is a rhetorical question intended to exalt and draw attention to those assigned to the “right” — i.e., the saved whose records are given to them in their right hands. By asking “what are the Companions of the Right?” the Qur’an signals that their rank, blessings and eternal felicity are sublime and largely beyond ordinary description, inviting reflection on the high status and sure reward reserved for the righteous who attain God’s mercy.

translation: In a lote-tree split open.
interpretation: This refers to the Sidrat al‑Muntahā — the extraordinary lote‑tree at the utmost boundary of the created heavens encountered in the Prophet’s vision. The adjective “makhḍūd” (split/opened) does not merely describe physical damage but signals an awe‑inspiring, transcendent reality: the tree appears in a state set apart from ordinary creation (as if rent or bowed by divine majesty), marking the limit of what created beings can approach and indicating the Prophet’s attainment of a unique, intimate station near the Divine Presence.

translation: And banana-trees arranged in clustered rows.
interpretation: The phrase pictures one of Paradise’s blessings: talḥ (understood as banana or similar fruit-bearing trees) set in orderly, closely packed clusters (munaddad). It emphasizes divine generosity and the perfected, deliberate arrangement of provisions in the Hereafter—beauty, abundance, and fruits made readily accessible to the blessed so that their enjoyment is effortless and complete.

translation: and an extended (spacious) shade
interpretation: A promise of a broad, enduring shade as a symbol of God’s mercy and protection — an expansive, continuous refuge granted to the righteous that conveys rest, comfort and relief from hardship (both physical and spiritual) rather than the fleeting relief of worldly comforts.

translation: and water poured forth
interpretation: A promise of abundant, freely flowing water as a divine gift — emphasizing effortless provision, refreshment and purity. In the context of the Qur'anic description of the hereafter it signifies God’s overflowing mercy and sustenance, a continual, untainted source of life and comfort (and metaphorically spiritual nourishment) made available to the blessed without labor or scarcity.

translation: and abundant fruits
interpretation: A promise of the gardens of Paradise: plentiful, diverse, and easily accessible fruits symbolizing God’s generous reward and the complete, effortless enjoyment of lawful blessings free from scarcity, spoilage, or labor.

translation: Neither cut off nor withheld.
interpretation: An affirmation that the matter in view continues to be available and is not severed or denied — signaling that divine provision/meracy/guidance (or the promised good) does not cease and is not barred, so one should not despair of receiving it.

translation: وَفُرُشٍ مَرْفُوعَةٍ — "and raised couches"
interpretation: This phrase depicts the honored and elevated state of the righteous in Paradise: they will recline on couches set high, symbolizing ease, dignity, distinction, and the special comfort and honor granted to them as their reward.

translation: Indeed, We created them by a deliberate act of creation.
interpretation: The phrase stresses that their existence is the result of God’s purposeful, sovereign action: He brought them into being in a particular, intended manner, showing divine power and design rather than accidental origin; it highlights God’s authority over how beings are formed and the wisdom behind their created nature.

translation: So We made them virgins.
interpretation: The verse conveys that God will provide the righteous with companions in Paradise who are preserved in purity and youth; this denotes not merely physical virginity but an idealized, unmarred state of companionship and fulfillment ordained by divine wisdom, emphasizing the sanctity, renewal, and perfection of relationships in the Hereafter rather than ordinary worldly imperfections.

translation: untouched, of the same age
interpretation: The phrase conveys that these companions are created in pristine, untouched freshness (عُرُبًا) and set as peers of equal years (أَتْرَابًا). Linguistically it stresses both purity/chastity and parity in age, evoking harmonious, balanced companionship and perpetual youthful vitality — an image of spiritual perfection and unchanging delight rather than a mere worldly description.

translation: For the companions of the right.
interpretation: It designates the group of the blessed on the Day of Judgment — those who are given their record in their right hand, a Quranic symbol of acceptance, honor, and reward; it points to the righteous who will receive God's favor, nearness, and entry into Paradise (in contrast to the companions of the left).

translation: a group (a remnant) of the former ones
interpretation: It refers to a small, select portion of earlier generations — a remnant among past peoples who either preserved the true way or whose example or fate is singled out as a witness or lesson for later people.

translation: and a group of others
interpretation: It points to additional, unspecified people included alongside those named, broadening the scope of the statement so that responsibility, participation, or reward applies not only to the explicitly mentioned individuals but also to their fellow companions — a reminder that the account embraces both the visible and the unmentioned.

translation:
وَأَصْحَابُ الشِّمَالِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الشِّمَالِ
“And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left?”
interpretation: The phrase “companions of the left” refers metaphorically to those destined for rejection and punishment on the Day of Judgment. The rhetorical question “what are the companions of the left?” draws attention to their wretched and ignominious state — a consequence of disbelief, ingratitude, and corrupt conduct — and prepares the listener for the description of the severe humiliation and torment that will befall them, in stark contrast to the fate of the saved.

translation: in poisonous (draughts) and scalding (boiling) water
interpretation: These words portray the severe, inescapable punishment prepared for the wrongdoers: a torment that is both spiritually corrosive (symbolized by 'poisonous draughts') and physically excruciating ('scalding water'). The pairing emphasizes the intensity and totality of divine retribution — it is meant to ward off complacency by showing that transgression leads to both moral ruin and acute suffering.

translation: and a shade of scorching wind
interpretation: The phrase conveys that what might be expected as relief—shade—will instead be itself a source of torment: a blistering, parching wind. It emphasizes a complete reversal of comfort into punishment in the hereafter, showing how even apparent shelter becomes painful for those deserving divine retribution.

translation: Neither cool nor generous.
interpretation: The phrase declares that what is being described offers no relief and no bounty: it will neither soothe nor confer honor or mercy, emphasizing its utter lack of comfort, benefit, or gracious recompense.

translation: Indeed, they had been, before that, living in luxury.
interpretation: The phrase warns that prior worldly ease and luxury often breeds complacency, arrogance, and forgetfulness of moral and religious obligations; prosperity is not definitive proof of divine approval but a test, and when blessings lead to ingratitude and heedlessness they can precede moral decline and eventual punishment.

translation: And they persisted in grievous perjury (the great breaking of oaths).
interpretation: This condemns a settled, willful habit of violating solemn oaths and promises: not a single lapse but stubborn, repeated perjury. The wording (‘يصرون’ and ‘الحنث العظيم’) stresses entrenched moral corruption—a deliberate contempt for the sanctity of vows and for truth, a sign of hypocrisy that brings spiritual culpability before God.

translation: And they used to say, “When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we truly be resurrected?”
interpretation: The verse records the scoffing objection of those who, seeing the body reduced to dust and bones, conclude that resurrection is impossible. Its meaning is to expose this limited, materialist assumption: physical decomposition is no proof against divine power. The point is theological and moral—human short-sightedness and reliance on apparent impossibilities do not negate God’s ability to re-create; thus the objection reflects arrogance and forgetfulness, not a valid argument against the reality of resurrection and accountability.

translation: Or our forefathers of old.
interpretation: The phrase reflects the common appeal to ancestral precedent as justification for beliefs or practices; its force in context is to show that simply following what earlier generations did does not prove truth, and that moral and religious claims must be tested by reason and divine guidance rather than accepted solely because ‘our forefathers did so.’

translation: Say, ‘Indeed, the former ones and the later ones.’
interpretation: This phrase underscores universality: the statement it introduces is meant to include all peoples across time—those who lived before and those who will come after—so the ruling, warning, promise, or truth being proclaimed is not confined to a single generation but applies equally to every age and to all human accountability before God.

translation: They will indeed be gathered to the appointed meeting on a known Day.
interpretation: The phrase asserts the inevitable, divinely‑ordained convocation of all people for resurrection and judgment: the word mīqāt conveys a fixed rendezvous beyond human control, and yawm ma‘lūm emphasizes that the time and nature of that Day are established in God's knowledge. Its purpose is to underline certainty of accountability and the futility of denying or escaping that final summons.

translation: Then indeed you are, O misguided and deniers,
interpretation: An emphatic rebuke addressing those who persist in error: it characterizes them as spiritually lost and as actively rejecting the truth, highlighting their culpable state and preparing the listener for the ensuing admonition or consequence—thus urging recognition of their condition (and implicitly the need to return to guidance).

translation: They will surely eat from a tree of Zaqqum.
interpretation: The phrase depicts how the punishment of the guilty in Hell is made manifest by forcing them to consume the repulsive fruit of the tree of Zaqqum: what sustains or comforts in this life is here inverted into a source of torment. It signifies divine justice and reversal—those who pursued corrupt, worldly ends receive nourishment that reflects their deeds (bitter, repulsive, and harmful), emphasising that their choices produce their own suffering and that true, life-giving provision is withheld from those who rejected guidance.

translation: So they filled their bellies with it.
interpretation: The phrase depicts people who greedily consume the provisions of this world, stuffing their bellies with what it offers — a symbol of selfish indulgence and heedlessness. It criticizes those who prioritize satisfying their appetites and material desires over moral responsibility, gratitude to God, and care for others.

translation: and they will drink therefrom of the scalding (boiling) water.
interpretation: The phrase conveys that the comforts of this life can be turned into instruments of punishment for those who persist in rejection and wrongdoing: thirst-quenching drink is perverted into burning torment. It functions as a moral and theological sign of divine justice—those who spurn guidance and misuse blessings will face an inevitable, humiliating suffering that is both physically painful (scalding internal burning) and emblematic of the reversal of earthly pleasures into retribution in the hereafter.

translation: So they will drink a scalding, seething draught.
interpretation: The phrase portrays a severe, relentless punishment: an intensely hot, foaming drink administered to the guilty. The wording (فشاربون) stresses repeated or continual drinking, so the image conveys both physical agony and ongoing humiliation — a vivid metaphor for the inescapable and lasting consequence of wrongdoing contrasted with the temporary nature of worldly pleasures.

translation: This is what has come upon them on the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: It declares that the suffering or recompense just described is the exact fate ordained for them at the Final Reckoning — what they now experience is their deserved outcome on the Day of Judgment.

translation: We created you — so why do you not believe?
interpretation: The verse reproaches people for refusing to acknowledge and affirm the Creator despite having been brought into existence by Him. It points to a moral and spiritual asymmetry: our very creation is a fundamental reason to recognize God's sovereignty, be grateful, and accept the truth revealed to us; to persist in denial or ingratitude is therefore unjust and accountable.

translation: Have you seen that which you wish for?
interpretation: A sharp, rhetorical rebuke aimed at those who deny or doubt the coming reality (such as the Hereafter or the Hour): it points out that their confident hopes and wishes are not the same as sight or proof. In other words, they base their stance on desire and wishful thinking, not on evidence, and their wishes cannot alter divine decree or avert what is certain to occur.

translation: Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge to human pretension: the verse denies any rightful claim by people to originate life or beings and affirms that absolute creative power belongs solely to God; what humans imagine as their making is nothing compared with God’s unique ability to create and to give life (and thus to resurrect).

translation: We have decreed death for you all, and We shall not be outstripped.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God has fixed a predetermined term of death for every person which cannot be hastened, postponed, or nullified by anyone; this reality is meant to humble human pretensions of ultimate control and to direct people to live responsibly and prepare for what follows, mindful that life’s span and its end are under divine wisdom and governance.

translation: (as though) that We would change your likenesses and recreate you in what you do not know.
interpretation: This expresses the absolute sovereignty of God to alter people’s condition and replace one form or generation with another beyond human anticipation. It warns that worldly status, lineage or accustomed ways offer no protection against divine decree: God can substitute peoples, create new circumstances or new lives in ways humans cannot foresee, as a means of enforcing justice, testing, or fulfilling His will.

translation: And you have already known the first creation; so will you not remember?
interpretation: The verse confronts human inconsistency: since everyone has experienced being brought into existence once from non‑existence, that first creation is evidence of God’s power to recreate — therefore refusing to accept resurrection or to take heed is unreasonable, and one should let the memory of the original creation inspire humility, reflection, and readiness for accountability.

translation: Have you considered what you sow?
interpretation: The verse urges reflection on human dependence: the seed you plant and the harvest you reap do not come from your independent power but from God’s sustaining creative agency. By pointing out that lifeless seeds and barren earth are made to produce life by divine will, it illustrates God’s ability to give life and provides an argument for His power to resurrect and to provide for His creatures.

translation: أأنتم تزرعونه أم نحن الزارعون؟ — Is it you who plant it, or are We the ones who cause it to grow?
interpretation: The verse confronts human pride and reminds that while people may sow and toil, the real power that produces life, growth, and provision belongs to God; human effort is a means, not the ultimate cause, so one must acknowledge dependence on divine will and sustenance.

translation: If We had willed, We would have made it rubble, and you would have remained to amuse yourselves.
interpretation: God is affirming His absolute power to obliterate whatever He wills — He could have turned it into ruins instantly — yet He withholds that destruction, allowing the wrongdoers to continue in their vain diversion. This postponement is not a sign of impunity but a measure of wisdom and testing: it serves as warning and an opportunity for repentance, while their present amusement is ultimately futile in the face of divine accountability.

translation: Indeed, we are surely in debt.
interpretation: A terse admission that the speaker is burdened with an unavoidable liability — not merely financial but moral and eschatological: their actions have left them obligated to recompense and therefore destined to suffer loss or punishment on account of their sins.

translation: Nay—rather, we are deprived.
interpretation: The speaker repudiates any expectation of share or favor and admits a state of exclusion: “محرومون” indicates being cut off from what others receive—guidance, mercy, provision, or reward—either as a consequence of their rejection and obstinacy or by divine withholding. The particle “بل” corrects a prior assumption and makes this a stark confession of spiritual and practical barrenness: they are denied the blessings they seek and are shut out from the bounty that comes from God.

translation: Have you seen (or considered) the water that you drink?
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge calling people to reflect: the water you drink is not your creation but a provision whose sending, measure and purity are controlled by God; recognizing this dependence is meant to awaken humility, reliance on Divine power, and thankfulness.

translation: Did you cause it to descend from the clouds, or are We the Ones who send it down?
interpretation: A rhetorical reminder that rain (and therefore sustenance and life-giving provision) is not the product of human power but a divine act; the verse calls people to recognize their dependence on God’s sovereignty over nature, to abandon claims of self-sufficiency, and to respond with humility and gratitude.

translation: If We willed, We could have made it bitter; so why do you not give thanks?
interpretation: God warns that the good and pleasant conditions people experience are by His will and mercy, and He could just as easily have turned them into bitterness; this is meant to spur recognition and gratefulness — ingratitude is unjustified because blessings depend solely on divine grace.

translation: Have you seen the Fire which you kindle?
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke: God draws attention to the small, human-made fire people take pride in (their possessions, deeds, power, or literal fires) to show its utter contingency and danger. What people kindle and rely upon in this life is not proof of safety or true strength; rather, those very acts and attachments can become the source of their humiliation and torment on the Day of Reckoning. The verse thus warns that worldly achievements and comforts are transient and may be turned against their makers, calling for humility and mindful accountability before God.

translation: أأنتم أنشأتم شجرتها أم نحن المنشئون؟ — Did you cause its tree to grow, or are We the Creators?
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke to those who arrogantly claim credit or deny divine agency: the verse affirms that bringing living things into existence and sustaining them is God’s prerogative alone, showing human powerlessness before creation and underscoring that if humans cannot produce a single tree by their own would, they have no grounds to deny God’s capacity to create or to resurrect.

translation: نحن جعلناها تذكرة ومتاعا للمقوين
interpretation: الآية تعني أن هذه الوحي أو الرسالة جُعلت تذكرة تحيّن الذاكرة وتذكّر الحق، وفي الوقت نفسه متاع ووقود دائم لمن يُقَوَّون بها — أي الذين تُقوّي قلوبهم بها وتثبتهم على الإيمان والعمل. فهي لمن يثبّتها في نفسه زاداً روحياً ومعيناً يعينهم على الثبات والصبر ومواجهة الابتلاءات حتى يبلغوا مقاصدهم.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
interpretation: An imperative that one must continuously acknowledge and proclaim God’s incomparable majesty—making His transcendence the center of one’s inner devotion and outward life, so that worship, speech, and actions reflect submission to His supreme authority.

translation: So I do not swear by the positions of the stars.
interpretation: The speaker refuses to give weight or authority to the fixed places of the stars, thereby rejecting astrological claims that celestial positions determine human fate; the verse points instead to the stars as created signs within God’s order, not objects worthy of oaths or ultimate reliance.

translation: And indeed it is a solemn oath — if you only knew — a mighty one.
interpretation: God is emphasizing the absolute truth and weight of what has just been mentioned by swearing an emphatic, solemn oath; the statement’s reality and consequences are immense, but people fail to appreciate their magnitude — were they to truly understand, they would recognize its certainty and the seriousness with which they must respond.

translation: Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an.
interpretation: The phrase affirms the Qur’an’s exalted, dignified status as a divinely revealed scripture—set apart from ordinary speech—whose purity, authority, and intrinsic worth demand reverent acceptance; it signals that the book is honorable, preserved, and a trustworthy source of guidance and moral illumination for humanity.

translation: في كتاب مكنون: In a well‑guarded (hidden) Book.
interpretation: The phrase indicates that the revelation and the deeper, ultimate realities it conveys are preserved in a protected divine register (al‑Lawh al‑Mahfuz). It affirms that God safeguards His Book and decrees from alteration or loss, and that certain knowledge rests securely with God beyond human access.

translation: لا يمسه إلا المطهرون — None may touch it except the purified.
interpretation: The verse asserts the Qur’an’s absolute sanctity and protection by stating that the heavenly, preserved Book is handled only by the “purified” — namely the sinless, ritually pure angels — thereby emphasizing that its origin, custody and transmission are from pure, incorruptible beings and that the scripture’s true reality is kept free from defilement.

translation: A revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that the text is not human invention but a divinely sent message: ‘تنزيل’ conveys a deliberate, preserved sending from above, and ‘ربّ العالمين’ stresses God’s sovereign authority over every realm of existence. Together they assert the scripture’s heavenly origin, universal scope, and binding authority as guidance and criterion for humanity, calling for submission and seriousness in receiving its teachings.

translation: Is it because of this statement that you are being conciliatory?
interpretation: A rebuke to those who treat the Divine message lightly: they answer with soft words, flattery or evasions to placate and delay rather than accept, repent or act. The term “مدهنون” pictures hypocritical, conciliatory behavior intended to avoid responsibility rather than sincere submission.

translation:
وَتَجْعَلُونَ رِزْقَكُمْ أَنَّكُمْ تُكذِّبُونَ
"And you make your provision a cause for denial."
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who treat the sustenance God has granted them (wealth, status, security) as a basis for rejecting Divine truth and accountability. Instead of recognizing provision as a trust from God that implies responsibility and dependence on Him, they interpret it as a shield or proof that they need not heed the message or fear judgment; thus their worldly means become an excuse for denial.

translation: فَلِمَـٰذَآ إِذَا بَلَغَتِ ٱلْحَلۡقُومَ
interpretation: It points to the harrowing, decisive moment of death — when what is within the body (often understood as the departing soul or the last breath/that which is swallowed) reaches the throat — highlighting human helplessness, the finality of that instant, and how afterwards one cannot avert the coming reckoning.

translation: And you will then be looking.
interpretation: The verse points to the Day of Reckoning when those addressed will be reduced to passive, helpless spectators: they will gaze in astonishment and dread as the consequences of their deeds and the events of that hour unfold before them, powerless to avert or alter what is coming — a reminder of human impotence before divine judgment and an exhortation to take present responsibility for one’s actions.

translation: And We are closer to him than you [are], yet you do not see.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's intimate, constant knowledge and presence with every human being—He is nearer to a person than anyone else (metaphorically closer than the jugular vein), so no whisper, motive, or secret of the heart is hidden from Him. People may live as if their inner states are concealed and act without fear or sincerity, but this divine proximity means every intention and action is observed and accountable; the statement therefore calls for inner mindfulness, sincerity, and humility before God’s omniscient presence.

translation: So why then, if you are not indebted?
interpretation: A rebuke aimed at those who make excuses to withhold what is due: if one genuinely has no financial constraint or legitimate reason, there is no justification for delaying help, repayment, or obligation; the verse urges prompt fulfillment of duties, sincerity, and refusal to hide behind false pretexts.

translation: Return it if you are truthful.
interpretation: هي دعوة لتقديم دليل عملي على الصدق: إن كنتم صادقين في مزاعمكم فلتردّوا الشيء أو لتظهروا الحقّ بالعمل. المقصود أن الصدق يُقاس بالأفعال لا بالأقوال، وأن إرجاع المطلوب أو إظهاره هو امتحان لصدق ادعاءات الأطراف وكشف لما في النفوس من حقيقة.

translation: But as for him who is among the ones brought near (to Allah).
interpretation: The phrase designates a distinct, honored category of the faithful who are granted intimate nearness to God as a bestowed rank: those whose faith, purification and deeds raise them to a special closeness and favor from Allah in the hereafter, signaling God’s mercy and honor rather than any self-attained entitlement.

translation: Coolness, sweet fragrance, and a Garden of Bliss.
interpretation: The three nouns depict Paradise as a complete restorative: “rouh” (a cool, refreshing breath or inner tranquillity) signals relief and spiritual calm; “rayḥān” (sweet-scented plants) signifies pure, pleasing delights and moral/ritual purity; and “jannat naʿīm” names the everlasting Garden of bliss. Together they convey that God’s reward heals and satisfies both the soul and the senses—an enduring gift of mercy and peace rather than merely transient pleasures.

translation: And as for him who is among the Companions of the Right,
interpretation: This phrase refers to those whom God counts among the ‘companions of the right’ — the righteous whose deeds are affirmed and who receive their record in the right hand at the Reckoning. It signifies a favorable, easy judgment and ultimate acceptance into God’s mercy and reward (Paradise), standing in contrast to those condemned on the left.

translation: So peace be upon you from the companions of the Right.
interpretation: This phrase is a benediction announcing that the addressee is greeted and confirmed by those who stand on God’s ‘right’ — the elect and blessed in the hereafter — signaling divine approval, honor, safety, and mutual recognition among the righteous as their journey culminates in tranquil acceptance and reward.

translation: As for the one who is among the deniers, the misguided—
interpretation: This phrase designates a settled spiritual condition: a person whose rejection of God’s message is not accidental but deliberate and rooted in moral misdirection. It implies that such denial involves a willful turning away from guidance—an obstinacy and preference for falsehood over truth—that leaves the individual estranged from divine mercy and subject to the consequences of that chosen deviation.

translation: ثم أَنزَلَ مِنْ حَمِيمٍ — So He sent down (poured out) from scalding/boiling water.
interpretation: The phrase conveys God’s manifestation of stern, purifying retribution: the ‘scalding water’ is a vivid image of immediate, overwhelming punishment poured upon wrongdoers who persisted in corruption or denial. It emphasizes divine power to exact fitting consequences and serves as a warning that rejecting guidance can bring direct and severe chastisement.

translation: وَتَصْلِيَةُ جَحِيمٍ — and the scorching of Hellfire
interpretation: This phrase signifies the intense, consuming punishment of Hell reserved for those who persist in rejection and injustice. It stresses not only physical torment but humiliation and loss — a purifying, retributive affliction from which there is no escape for the unrepentant — and serves as a stern warning intended to turn people away from sin and back toward God’s guidance.

translation: Indeed, this is the very truth of certainty.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that the matter just described (the Resurrection, God's judgment, or the Prophet’s message, depending on context) is not conjecture but an absolute, undeniable reality. “Haqq al‑yaqīn” denotes a truth that dispels all doubt — the objective, experiential reality that will be fully realized and witnessed — and the verse thus asserts the inevitability and certainty of what was announced, rejecting any skepticism.

translation: So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most Great.
interpretation: This imperative calls the believer to acknowledge and proclaim God’s absolute transcendence and greatness: to purify His name from any likeness, partnership or diminishment, and to express that recognition both in verbal praise (tasbih, remembrance) and in life — worship, moral conduct and humility that reflect awareness of His supreme majesty and authority.

translation: Bismillah ar‑Rahman ar‑Rahim. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah; and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all of creation—by its existence, order, and obedience to God’s laws—testifies to Allah’s sovereignty and perfect wisdom; this universal praise is evidence of His power and wisdom and calls humans to recognize His authority, trust His governance, and live in accordance with His guidance.

translation:
لَهُ مَلِكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۖ يُحْيِي وَيُمِيتُ ۖ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse proclaims God’s absolute sovereignty and power: all authority and existence belong to Him, and life and death occur by His will. Its purpose is to awaken awareness that human status and worldly control are temporary and contingent on divine will, to inspire humble submission and trust in God’s wisdom and justice, and to remind believers that ultimately nothing escapes His power—so hope, fear, responsibility, and reliance should be directed to Him alone.

translation: He is the First and the Last, the Apparent and the Hidden; and He is, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse declares God’s absolute transcendence and immanence: He exists before all things and endures after them (First and Last), He manifests through outward signs while encompassing unseen realities (Apparent and Hidden), and nothing—whether external events or inner intentions—escapes His knowledge. This grounds trust in His sovereign care, affirms that ultimate beginnings and endings belong to Him alone, and makes human accountability real since both deeds and inner states are fully known to Him.

translation: He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself over the Throne. He knows what enters into the earth and what comes forth from it, and what descends from the heaven and what ascends to it; and He is with you wherever you are. And Allah is All‑Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God’s absolute creative authority and comprehensive governance: the world was brought into being in an ordered, purposeful span and God’s establishment on the Throne signifies His supreme rule and sustaining dominion rather than a physical, humanlike posture. By enumerating what “enters” and “comes forth” of the earth and what “descends” and “ascends” in the heavens, the text affirms God’s knowledge and control over both hidden and manifest processes — from subterranean and earthly phenomena to celestial movements and spiritual realities — leaving nothing outside His awareness. The statement “He is with you wherever you are” underscores God’s immediate presence in the sense of knowledge, care, and governance (not spatial containment), meaning human beings are never beyond His vigilance or support. The final clause, that God is seeing of what you do, ties the cosmological claims to moral responsibility: because God knows and sustains all dimensions of existence, every action—open or concealed—falls under His sight and will be accounted for, calling believers to live with consciousness of divine sovereignty, presence, and accountability.

translation:
لَهُ مَلِكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۚ وَإِلَى اللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ الْأُمُورُ
“To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; and to Allah all affairs are returned.”
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over all creation and reminds that every event, decision and consequence ultimately comes back to Him for settling and judgment. Its practical import is to correct human pride and false security in power or wealth: while people should plan and act responsibly, they must do so with humility, justice and trust in God, knowing that outcomes are determined by divine wisdom and that they will be held accountable when matters return to Him.

translation:
يُولِجُ اللَّيْلَ فِي النَّهَارِ وَيُولِجُ النَّهَارَ فِي اللَّيْلِ ۚ وَهُوَ عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ
"He causes the night to enter the day and causes the day to enter the night; and He is Knowing of what is in the breasts (innermost hearts)."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the visible, orderly alternation of night and day is a sign of God's absolute sovereignty and precise governance over creation; the same Lord who controls these vast, observable cycles is also fully aware of hidden motives and inner states. Thus nothing inward or outward escapes His knowledge—what appears public and what is secret are both under His authority—so humans must cultivate sincerity, fear of God, and accountability, knowing that outward reversals or concealment do not obscure the heart from divine knowledge.

translation: Believe in Allah and His Messenger and spend out of that in which He has made you successors; and those of you who have believed and spent — for them is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse links inward faith to outward stewardship: God has entrusted people with wealth, authority, and resources, and true belief is manifested by using those trusts responsibly and charitably for God’s sake. Acting on faith through generous, accountable use of what one has been given both fulfills one’s role as God’s vicegerent and merits the promised great recompense.

translation: And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah, while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord, and He has taken your covenant, if you are indeed believers?
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who refuse faith despite the Prophet’s clear summons: it asks with astonishment why they will not believe in God when the Messenger calls them to affirm their Lord, pointing out that they (or their forebears) previously gave a solemn covenant to accept God’s guidance and the coming messengers. Their rejection is therefore a breach of their own pledged commitment and reveals inconsistency or hypocrisy; the Prophet’s invitation is simply a reminder to fulfill that divine obligation, and the verse stresses moral responsibility and accountability for breaking God’s covenant.

translation: He is the One who sends down clear signs to His Servant, so that He may bring you out from darkness into light. And indeed Allah is, toward you, Most Kind, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that revelation—the clear signs bestowed upon the Prophet—is a practical, transformative mercy: its purpose is to rescue people from spiritual ignorance, moral error, and social disorder (‘darkness’) and guide them into knowledge, upright conduct, and spiritual clarity (‘light’). This change is not coercive but an expression of God’s compassion and care, showing that guidance, patience, forgiveness, and support are central to God’s relationship with those who turn to His guidance.

translation: And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah? And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth. Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought — they are of greater rank than those who spent afterwards and fought. But to each Allah has promised the best [reward]. And Allah is, of what you do, Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse teaches that giving and striving for God’s cause are obligations rooted in the truth that all wealth ultimately belongs to God; it singles out the special moral worth of early, risk‑taking commitment (those who gave and fought before the decisive victory) because such acts involved greater sacrifice and tested faith under harder conditions. While Allah promises good to all who support His cause, He recognizes degrees of merit according to the risk, timing, and sincerity of one’s sacrifice, and He fully knows and will judge each person’s deeds.

translation: Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan? He will multiply it for him, and he will have a noble reward.
