interpretation: An exhortation to give sincerely for God’s sake: what looks like a sacrifice in this world is, by God’s promise, transformed into multiplied benefit and an honourable, enduring recompense. The phrase teaches trust in divine providence, urging believers to spend selflessly (in charity, support of the community, and other acts of obedience) because God rewards and increases what is given for His cause far beyond worldly calculation.

translation: The Day you will see the believing men and believing women— their light running before them and by their right hands— (it will be said), “Good tidings to you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein you will abide forever.” That is the great attainment.
interpretation: The “light” is a symbolic portrayal of faith and righteous deeds made manifest as both proof and honor before God: it illuminates, leads, and testifies on behalf of the believer. Its motion “before them and on their right hands” implies that those inner convictions and outward acts will go ahead of the person on the reckoning, guiding their way, distinguishing them from falsehood, and providing intercession or support in judgment. The promised eternal gardens therefore represent the ultimate outcome of a life shaped by sincere belief and consistent moral action: true and lasting success is not worldly gain but the spiritual vindication and nearness to God that such light brings. “That is the great attainment” stresses that this spiritual triumph—being validated and rewarded by God because one’s faith and deeds cohered—is the highest goal a person can achieve.

translation: On the Day the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say to the believing men and the believing women, “Wait for us; let us take some of your light.” It will be said, “Go back behind you and seek a light.” Then a wall will be set up between them with a gate; inside it is mercy, and on its outer side is punishment.
interpretation: The verse depicts the final separation between sincere believers and hypocrites: “light” symbolizes true faith, guidance and reward earned by sincere belief and deeds. On the Day of Judgment the hypocrites, having borrowed or feigned the appearance of faith in this life, will seek to share in the believers’ light, but they will be denied and told to turn back to their own state. Allah will place a barrier between the two groups with a gate whose interior contains mercy reserved for the genuinely faithful, while on the outside is torment for those whose hypocrisy and rejection barred them from genuine guidance. The image stresses that outward likeness to believers cannot transfer the inner reality of faith, and that divine mercy is granted to those who truly possessed it, not to those who only appeared to have it.

translation: ينادونهم: «ألم نكن معكم؟» فيقولون: «بلى، ولكنكم فتنتم أنفسكم، وتربصتم وارتبتم، وغرتكم الأماني، حتى جاء أمر الله، وغركم بالله الغرور.»
interpretation: الآية تُبيّن مسؤولية المكذبين والمتخاذلين عن عزلتهم: ليسوا ضحية عَدمِ نصرة من الآخرين بقدر ما أَضعفوا أنفسهم بإغواء الشك والتردد والأماني الفارغة. بُطْءُهم وارتيابهم وتعلقهم بمزاعم زائفة ركَّبوا لأنفسهم فِتنة وأبعدتهم عن الثبات حتى انقضى أمر الله، وبعد ذلك تبين أن من أغراهم وأوهمهم — سواء كان الشيطان أو خبث النفوس — قد خدعهم بشأن الحق. المقصد العملي: الثقة والطاعة واليقين مسؤولية فردية؛ التردد والأماني الباطلة والالتفات وراء وساوس تُفضي إلى الهلاك الروحي والعملي.

translation: So today no ransom will be accepted from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire — it is your protector, and what an evil destination!
interpretation: The verse declares that on the Day of Judgment all attempts to avert divine justice by payment, bargaining, or relying on worldly means—whether by the sinners themselves or by their fellow disbelievers—will be in vain. Those who persisted in rejection will find that the outcome of their choices has become their ‘wali’ or guardian: Hell is their final locus of protection and companionship, not out of mercy but as the inevitable consequence of their deeds and alliances. Thus the passage warns that relying on transient securities or false protectors in this life cannot reverse the moral reality established by one’s actions; the consequence is the worst possible outcome.

translation:
أَلَمْ يَأْنِ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَن تَخْشَعَ قُلُوبُهُمْ لِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَمَا نَزَلَ مِنَ الْحَقِّ ۚ وَلَا يَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ مِن قَبْلُ فَطَالَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْأَمَدُ فَقَسَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ ۖ وَكَثِيرٌ مِّنْهُمْ فَاسِقُونَ

“Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humbly submit to the remembrance of Allah and to what has been revealed of the truth, and that they not be like those who were given the Scripture before — for a long term passed over them and their hearts grew hard? Many of them are defiantly disobedient.”
interpretation: This verse is a solemn admonition urging believers to awaken spiritually: it calls for inner humility, sincere fear, and attentive obedience to God’s reminder and the revealed truth, rather than allowing spiritual lethargy, complacency, or worldly distraction to harden the heart. The reference to earlier “people of the Book” whose hearts hardened after a long period warns that prolonged delay, ease, or neglect of God’s guidance can erode sensitivity to truth and lead to disobedience. The practical lesson is to continually revive one’s faith through remembrance, reflection, and acting on revelation so that passage of time does not blunt conscience and devotion.

translation: Know that Allah brings the earth to life after its death. We have made Our signs clear to you so that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse urges a reasoned faith: the recurring renewal of the world is not presented merely as a natural curiosity but as deliberate evidence of God’s power and purpose. By drawing attention to these manifest signs and making them explicit in revelation, the text intends to move people from passive observation to active conviction—recognizing God’s ability to restore life, accepting moral accountability, and letting that understanding shape belief, humility, gratitude, and right conduct.

translation: Indeed, the believing men and believing women — and those who have lent to Allah a goodly loan — He will multiply [it] for them, and for them is a noble reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when men and women give sincerely in God’s way — described as ‘lending to Allah’ — their giving is treated as an investment with God: He increases its return beyond what they gave and grants them honoured recompense. It emphasizes equal spiritual recognition of both sexes, the overflowing, multiplied blessings (spiritual and often material) that accompany sincere charity, and the high status and reward awaiting such benefactors in the Hereafter.

translation: And those who believe in Allah and His messengers — those are the truthful. They are witnesses before their Lord; for them is their reward and their light. But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse declares that sincere acceptance of God and His messengers confers a moral and existential status—being among the ‘truthful’—which entails divine recognition: such believers stand as honored witnesses before God and are granted both their due recompense and a ‘light’ that signifies guidance, spiritual illumination, and manifest honor. Denying God’s clear signs, by contrast, cuts one off from that light and reward and places one among the destined occupants of Hellfire.

translation: Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement, and adornment, and mutual boasting among you, and competition in increase of wealth and children. It is like rain whose vegetation pleases the tillers; then it dries and you see it yellow; then it becomes chaff scattered by the wind. But in the Hereafter is a severe punishment and (also) forgiveness and pleasure from Allah. And the life of this world is only the enjoyment of deception.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly existence is ephemeral and deceptively attractive: its pleasures, honors and rivalries may dazzle people like lush vegetation after rain, yet they quickly wither and amount to nothing lasting. By juxtaposing fleeting worldly gains with the reality of a coming severe punishment as well as the possibility of Allah’s forgiveness and pleasure, the passage admonishes believers to not be seduced by transient pursuits but to orient their lives toward what endures—seeking God’s mercy, moral responsibility and the priorities of the Hereafter rather than mere accumulation and show.

translation: Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise whose width is like the width of the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who believed in Allah and His messengers. That is the bounty of Allah; He grants it to whom He wills. And Allah is the Owner of great bounty.
interpretation: The exhortation to ‘race’ is an imperative for urgent, proactive striving — not complacent hope — in repentance, faith, and righteous action; the vastness of the Garden is a metaphor for an immeasurable, comprehensive reward reserved for those whose belief is genuine and who follow the guidance brought by the messengers. By coupling this promise with the reminder that such bestowal is Allah’s gift given to whom He wills, the verse teaches that human effort in seeking forgiveness and obedience is essential, yet the final accession to mercy and the highest blessings depends on divine generosity and wisdom, so believers must combine zealous striving with reliance on God’s gracious will.

translation:
ما أصاب من مصيبة في الأرض ولا في أنفسكم إلا في كتاب من قبل أن نبرأها ۚ إن ذلك على الله يسير
"No calamity befalls on the earth or in yourselves except that it is recorded in a Book before We bring it into being; indeed that is easy for Allah."
interpretation: The verse teaches that every hardship or misfortune is encompassed by Allah’s knowledge and decree — it is already recorded in the divine Record before it comes to pass. This assures believers that trials are not random but take place within God’s wise and measured plan, and it is therefore a call to trust, patience, and reliance on Allah while still fulfilling one’s responsibilities; the phrase “that is easy for Allah” emphasizes His absolute power and effortless control over all events.

translation:
لِكَيْ لَا تَأْسَوْا عَلَىٰ مَا فَاتَكُمْ وَلَا تَفْرَحُوا بِمَا آتَاكُمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ kُلَّ مُخْتَالٍ فَخُورٍ
“So that you do not grieve for what has passed you by, nor exult over what He has given you. And Allah does not love any arrogant boaster.”
interpretation: The verse teaches a moral equilibrium: believers should not be consumed by sorrow over missed opportunities nor become proud and boastful over bestowed favors. Both excessive grief and boastful joy show excessive attachment to worldly outcomes and a failure to recognize Allah’s wisdom and testing. Instead one should respond with patient acceptance when deprived, grateful responsibility when blessed, and humility in success—since prideful self-exaltation (مختال فخور) is displeasing to God and undermines sincere faith, social harmony, and the proper use of blessings.

translation:
الَّذِينَ يُبْخِلُونَ وَيَأْمُرُونَ النَّاسَ بِالْبُخْلِ ۗ وَمَنْ يَتَوَلَّ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ الغَنِيُّ الْحَمِيدُ
"Those who are stingy and command people to be stingy; and whoever turns away — then indeed Allah is Free of need, the Praiseworthy."
interpretation: The verse censures those whose hearts are tied to worldly possessions so tightly that they not only withhold from others but promote withholding as a virtue. It assures that refusing to follow such counsel (turning away from their example and influence) does not harm God in any way, for He is entirely self-sufficient and worthy of all praise. Implicitly, the passage teaches that miserliness is a moral failing that benefits only the miser, whereas true moral worth lies in generosity and reliance on God, whose richness and praiseworthiness make human hoarding futile and spiritually misguided.

translation: Indeed, We sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and revealed with them the Book and the Balance so that people may establish justice. And We sent down iron in which is great military might and many benefits for the people, and so that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers even unseen. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Exalted in Might.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance comes with both normative authority (the Book and the Balance—principles of right and justice) and with concrete means (symbolized by iron) so that moral commands can be realized in society. Iron’s mention highlights that God provides tools and strength that can serve constructive purposes (benefits for people) or be a source of force; how they are used becomes a test revealing who truly stands with God and His messengers beyond mere words. Thus revelation and worldly means are paired to enable justice, to expose sincere commitment, and to make God’s promise of accountability effective, because He is all‑powerful and sovereign.

translation: And indeed We sent Noah and Abraham, and We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book; among them are those who are rightly guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine guidance — prophethood and scripture — can be a family heritage or communal trust, yet it is not coercive: possessing revelation or noble lineage does not ensure faith. Guidance remains an individual moral responsibility, so even among those given clear guidance some will accept and be rightly guided, while many will reject it and become rebellious. The passage thus explains both God’s bestowal of means to guide people and the human freedom to respond, offering reassurance to prophets that God’s plan includes both inheritors of guidance and those who turn away.

translation: Then We followed up after them with Our messengers, and We followed (in succession) with Jesus son of Mary, and We gave him the Gospel. And We put compassion and mercy in the hearts of those who followed him; yet they invented monasticism — which We had not prescribed for them — seeking thereby the pleasure of Allah; but they did not observe it with due observance. So We gave to those among them who believed their reward; and many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s guidance continued through successive messengers and that He endowed true followers with inward qualities — notably compassion and mercy. It criticizes religious innovations (here represented by monasticism) that originate from human initiative rather than divine prescription: even if begun with a desire for God’s pleasure, they can be corrupted when practiced outwardly without sincere, God‑ordained grounding. The underlying principle is that inner faith and genuine obedience determine God’s reward, while mere institutionalism or hypocrisy leads to deviation and accountability.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will grant you a double portion of His mercy, and will make for you a light by which you will walk, and will forgive you. And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The command to fear God and to believe in the Messenger is paired with a promise: God bestows a twofold mercy on those who respond—commonly understood as mercy in this life and in the Hereafter—which includes a ‘light’ of guidance and certainty that clarifies their path and empowers right action; alongside this illumination comes God’s forgiveness for their faults. The verse therefore teaches that sincere God-consciousness plus faith brings practical guidance, inner clarity, pardon, and the encompassing mercy of Allah, who is ever-forgiving and merciful.

translation: Lest the People of the Book should know that they have no power over any of Allah’s bounty; and that the bounty is in the hand of Allah — He grants it to whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God’s favors and spiritual privileges are not the possession or entitlement of any people by virtue of lineage, scripture, or social status; distribution of blessing rests solely with Allah, who gives to whom He wills according to His wisdom. It thereby warns against presumptuous claims of exclusive merit and calls believers to humility, reminding them that access to God’s grace depends on His will, not human privilege.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Allah has certainly heard the statement of the woman who argued with you about her husband and complained to Allah; and Allah hears the two of you in your conversation. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Seeing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God knows even private disputes and plaintive appeals, so divine hearing and sight guarantee that hidden wrongs and subtle details are not lost; this both consoles those who seek redress in God and reminds everyone that moral responsibility and justice rest on God’s complete awareness, calling people to trust Him, act truthfully, and refrain from hiding injustice.

translation: Those among you who pronounce zihār of their wives, saying, “You are to me as my mother’s back” — their mothers are none but those who gave them birth; and indeed they utter an abhorrent saying and a falsehood. And Allah is Ever‑Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse condemns the pre‑Islamic practice of zihār — a husband declaring his wife to be like his mother’s back to nullify marital rights — by ruling that kinship is not created by words: a mother is only the woman who bore one, so such declarations are legally and morally void. The text calls this statement odious and false, diagnosing it as an unjust, hurtful attempt to sever obligations; yet by ending with Allah’s attribute of forgiveness and mercy it indicates the door to repentance and restoration remains open for those who recognize their error and seek God’s pardon.

translation: والذين يظاهرون من نسائهم ثم يعودون لما قالوا فتحرير رقبة من قبل أن يتماسا ۚ ذلكم توعظون به ۚ والله بما تعملون خبير
interpretation: الآية تحكم على ممارسة «الظهار» — أن يسبغ الرجل على زوجته قطيعة بكلمات تشبهها بأمّه — بأنها فعل مضر له تبعات قانونية وأخلاقية: من يريد أن يتراجع عن قوله لا يجوز له استئناف العلاقة الزوجية إلا بعد أداء كفارة عملية، في النص تحرير رقبة (إطار للعدل والإصلاح العملي). المقصد أن الكلام الذي يقطع علاقة الزوجية ليس أمراً تافهاً بل يحمل مسؤولية ويجب تصحيحه بعمل يكفل حقوق الطرف المتضرر؛ والآية تختتم بتذكير أن هذا التشريع تنبيه للمؤمنين وأن الله عليم بأعمالهم ونواياهم.

translation: So whoever cannot find (the means), then (let him) fast two consecutive months before they touch each other; and whoever is unable — then (let him) feed sixty poor persons. That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. And those are the limits of Allah, and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse makes clear that God’s legal prescriptions combine firmness with practical accommodation: a missed or violated religious obligation must be repaired by a demanding act that demonstrates sincere resolve (fasting two continuous months) but, recognizing human incapacity, an alternative of collective charity (feeding sixty needy people) is permitted. The severity and specificity of these remedial measures are intended to cultivate genuine faith and obedience, to restore moral balance within the community, and to mark divine boundaries whose rejection places one outside the covenant and exposes one to severe consequences.

translation: Indeed, those who show enmity to Allah and His Messenger have been humiliated, just as those before them were humiliated. And We have sent down clear signs, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that deliberate hostility toward God and His Messenger—despite the clear, evident signs revealed—inevitably brings humiliation: a pattern seen in previous communities who rejected divine guidance. This humiliation can take the form of worldly defeat, loss of honour and coherence, and culminates in degrading retribution from God in the hereafter. Thus the passage functions as both historical precedent and moral deterrent: persistent rejection of God’s guidance leads to loss of dignity and severe punishment, while recognition and submission to the clear signs preserve honour and safety.

translation: The Day when Allah will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. Allah had counted it, yet they forgot it; and Allah is, over all things, Witness.
interpretation: This verse teaches that on the Day of Resurrection every person will be raised and confronted with an exact accounting of their deeds — an account that God has already recorded in full even though people, in heedlessness or denial, had ignored or forgotten it. Their forgetfulness does not erase what has been done; God’s comprehensive knowledge and witnessing guarantees that nothing is lost or unjustly overlooked. The passage thus stresses inevitable accountability and divine justice: human neglect or denial cannot avert the reckoning, and God alone authoritatively presents and attests to the true measure of each soul’s actions.

translation: أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ ۖ مَا يَكُونُ مِن نَّجْوَىٰ ثَلَاثَةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ رَابِعُهُمْ وَلَا خَمْسَةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ سَادِسُهُمْ وَلَا أَدْنَىٰ مِن ذَٰلِكَ وَلَا أَكْثَرَ إِلَّا هُوَ مَعَهُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كَانُوا۟ ۖ ثُمَّ يُنَبِّئُهُم بِمَا عَمِلُوا۟ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ
interpretation: The verse asserts that God’s knowledge and presence encompass every private conversation and gathering, so nothing is truly hidden from Him. Its purpose is both deterrent and consolation: a deterrent to those who plot injustice or hypocrisy—because secrecy offers no escape from divine awareness and eventual reckoning—and a consolation to the sincere believer, who may take comfort in God’s companionship and ultimate vindication. Theologically, it emphasizes God’s absolute, continuous knowledge without negating human responsibility: people choose and act, but their choices are fully known to God and will be disclosed and judged on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: Have you not seen those who were forbidden from private counsel, yet they return to that which they were forbidden, and they conspire in sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger? And when they come to you, they greet you with a greeting with which Allah has not greeted you, and they say within themselves, “Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?” Hell will suffice them — they will enter it; and how evil a destination.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who persist in secret plotting and sinful collusion despite being warned, revealing that outward politeness or ritual (even greeting the Prophet) can mask inner rebellion; their private counsel and mockery of divine authority show true hypocrisy, and they presume God’s patience means impunity. The passage teaches that hidden intent and continued disobedience determine spiritual accountability: mere external forms without sincere submission lead to divine punishment, and Hell is portrayed as the just outcome for such persistent hypocrisy.

translation: O you who have believed, when you converse privately, do not converse about sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger; but converse about righteousness and piety. And fear Allah—unto Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse forbids private consultations that plan or approve sinful, oppressive, or rebellious actions—especially those that undermine the Messenger’s guidance—and redirects intimate speech toward what builds virtue and God‑consciousness. It teaches that secrecy can be used to evade moral restraint, so believers must police their private discourse as well as their public acts: intimate counsel should promote justice, obedience to God’s guidance, and mutual good, not scheming, harm, or defiance. The reminder that all will be gathered before Allah reinforces accountability and serves as a deterrent against covert wrongdoing, emphasizing that true faith governs both words and hidden intentions.

translation: Secret counsels come only from Satan, to sadden those who believe; he will not harm them at all except by Allah’s permission. And upon Allah let the believers rely.
interpretation: The verse teaches that clandestine whispering, intrigue, or secret plotting that aims to demoralize the faithful is a tactic of Satan to weaken faith and communal solidarity. It at once limits Satan’s power—he can only affect people within the bounds Allah allows—so any sorrow or trial resulting from such machinations occurs under divine knowledge and with a purpose (testing, warning, or correction). The proper response, therefore, is not despair or spreading suspicion, but trust in God, seeking His protection, practicing patience and rectitude, exposing destructive covert schemes when necessary, and relying on Allah’s wisdom so that believers preserve inner steadiness and communal cohesion.

translation: O you who have believed, when you are told, “Make room” in assemblies, then make room; Allah will make room for you. And when you are told, “Rise up,” then rise; Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who were given knowledge by degrees. And Allah is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse enjoins courteous humility in social gatherings: when asked to give way or make space, believers should comply, because such outward deference reflects inner humility and trust in God. That attitude — readiness to yield, to honor others, and to defer for the sake of communal order — becomes a means by which Allah expands one’s opportunities, dignity, and rank. The promise of being “raised in degrees” singles out both sincere believers and those granted knowledge, indicating that faith together with learnedness earn increased standing and influence. The final clause, “Allah is Aware of what you do,” reminds that the worth of these actions depends on their intention and sincerity, and that God alone truly knows and rewards them.

translation: O you who have believed, when you confer privately with the Messenger, present before your private conference a charity. That is better for you and purer. But if you cannot find (the means), then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The command to give alms before a private audience with the Prophet functions as a moral and social safeguard: by requiring a voluntary gift prior to confidential access it deters selfish or worldly motives, purifies the intentions of the supplicants, and channels benefit to the needy rather than allowing private meetings to become avenues for favoritism or personal gain. Making charity the precondition cultivates sincerity and communal equity, while the final clause—Allah’s forgiveness and mercy—acknowledges genuine incapacity and emphasizes that the law’s aim is moral reform and compassion, not punitive exclusion.

translation: Did you fear — so that you might bring forward alms before your private consultations? When you did not do so — and Allah has accepted your repentance — then establish the prayer, give the zakah, and obey Allah and His Messenger. And Allah is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse corrects a misplaced concern about outward appearances that kept people from fulfilling duty: God rebukes those who let fear of how they would be perceived affect giving or obedience, and reminds them that sincere repentance is accepted. The essential requirement is steadfastness in core obligations — regular prayer, rightful almsgiving, and submission to God and His Messenger — because inner motive and actual deeds are fully known to God. In short, sincerity and consistent obedience matter more than social anxieties or show.

translation: Do you not see those who have taken as allies a people upon whom is the wrath of Allah? They are neither of you nor of them, yet they swear to falsehood while they know.
interpretation: The verse condemns the moral and spiritual duplicity of people who form outward alliances with a hostile, accursed group while belonging fully to neither side. Their oaths and professions of loyalty are deliberate deceptions: such bonds are insincere, revealing alienation from true communal and ethical belonging, and demonstrating that outward promises cannot hide inner betrayal; the passage therefore warns the community to recognize and reject such hypocritical allegiances and to judge by consistent faith and conduct rather than false declarations.

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment; indeed they were evil in what they used to do.
interpretation: الآية تحذر من عقاب إلهي مؤكد وشديد أُعِدّ لمن استمر في الكفر والظلم والمعاصي: لفظ «أعد» يدل على جاهزية وحتمية الجزاء بحكم عدل الله، و«ساء ما كانوا يعملون» تصف طابع أعمالهم الفاسدة التي استوجبت هذا الجزاء. المقصود تذكير بأن الاختيارات الظالمة والمخالفة للحق تترتب عليها محاسبة عادلة وعقوبة جزائية من قِبَل الله.

translation: They have taken their oaths as a screen and thus prevented [people] from the way of Allah; for them is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who treat solemn vows as a protective cloak or legal pretext—using words to justify themselves, conceal wrongdoing, or intimidate and divert others from following God’s path. It criticizes the hypocrisy of substituting formal oaths for true faith and righteous deeds; relying on such verbal shields to obstruct guidance earns them disgraceful retribution.

translation: Their wealth and their children will not avail them anything against Allah. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning neither material possessions nor family ties can protect a person from divine judgment; ultimate worth is determined by one’s faith and deeds, not by worldly status or offspring. It warns against trusting in riches or lineage as a substitute for sincere belief and righteous conduct, indicating that those who place their reliance on such transient things while rejecting guidance will suffer the consequences and remain in the punishment prescribed for them.

translation: The Day Allah will raise them all up; He will make them swear to Him as they make you swear, and they think that they are upon something. Nay — indeed they are the liars.
interpretation: The verse warns that on Resurrection Day the false confidence and manipulative oaths of those who opposed the believers will be exposed. What they relied on in this world — coerced pledges, status, or arguments that seemed to strengthen their position — will be turned back upon them: God will bring them to account and they will be compelled to swear as they once compelled others, showing that their worldly posturing carried no true weight. The point is that oaths and social power cannot change divine truth or escape judgment; in the end their claims will be proven false and they will be revealed as liars.

translation: Satan has prevailed over them and caused them to forget the remembrance of Allah; those are the party of Satan. Indeed, the party of Satan—they are the losers.
interpretation: The verse warns that yielding to satanic influence—through heedlessness, excessive attachment to worldly desires, pride, or deliberate turning away from God's guidance—erodes the practice of remembering and obeying Allah and thus binds people together as a collective allegiance opposed to divine guidance; this alignment produces moral and spiritual deterioration and leads ultimately to ruin and loss in this world and the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, those who are hostile to Allah and His Messenger — those are among the humiliated.
interpretation: The verse warns that deliberate enmity toward God and His Messenger brings real abasement: such opposition strips people of true honor and protection so that their schemes, status and inner dignity are overturned. Apparent power they may seem to have is temporary; ultimately they are placed in a state of weakness and disgrace both socially and before God. The passage therefore teaches that genuine honor comes through submission to divine guidance, while rebellion results in lasting humiliation.

translation:
كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَأُغْلِبَنَّ أَنَا وَرُسُلِي ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ قَوِيٌّ عَزِيزٌ
"Allah has decreed: ‘I and My messengers will surely prevail.’ Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Exalted in Might."
interpretation: The verse affirms that the triumph of divine truth is a settled, divinely ordained outcome: despite apparent setbacks or the temporary success of opposition, God’s purpose to establish His message through His messengers is certain. The language stresses that victory rests on God’s power and authority—not merely on human effort—so believers are reassured to remain steadfast and trust in the inevitability of God’s will; the pairing of “Powerful” and “Exalted in Might” underlines both the capability and the inviolable sovereignty by which that victory will be accomplished.

translation: You will not find any people who believe in Allah and the Last Day who take as intimate allies those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kinsfolk. Those — He has written faith on their hearts and supported them with a spirit from Him. He will admit them to Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever. Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. Those are the party of Allah — and certainly the party of Allah are the successful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that genuine faith inevitably reshapes loyalties: a true believer cannot cultivate deep affection or political alliance with those actively opposing God and His Messenger, even when such people are closest relatives. This is not a call to personal hatred but a moral boundary that places commitment to truth and divine guidance above family or tribal ties. The text also explains that such resolve is not merely human willpower but a transformation God inscribes in hearts, reinforced by His support (a “spirit” of guidance and strength), and it culminates in God’s pleasure and eternal reward. To belong to “the party of Allah” therefore means to stand with divine guidance in conviction and practice — a stance that brings inner conviction, divine assistance, divine approval, and ultimate success in the life to come.

translation:
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَـٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ
سَبَّحَ لِلَّهِ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ ۖ وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ
"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah; and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise."
interpretation: The verse teaches that all created things — angels, living beings, and even inanimate aspects of the cosmos — continually declare God’s praise by fulfilling the purpose and order He has given them. This universal glorification is not mere sound but an expression of inherent submission and testimony to God’s sovereignty; it points to His absolute power (al-ʿAzīz) in sustaining and governing the universe and to His perfect wisdom (al-Ḥakīm) in its design. By highlighting creation’s constant praise, the verse calls human beings to recognize that the cosmos itself witnesses to God’s authority and wisdom and therefore to align their intellect, worship, and conduct with that truth.

translation: He is the One Who expelled the disbelievers among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would leave, and they thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah; but Allah came to them from where they did not expect, and He cast terror into their hearts, so that they destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take heed, O people of insight.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human plans, power, and material fortifications cannot override divine decree: when God wills a change, it can overturn expectations, inspire fear, and lead to the collapse of apparent security. The proper response for those who understand ("people of sight") is to learn from this reality — to place ultimate trust in God, avoid reliance on worldly means alone, and reform one’s conduct so as not to be caught by the consequences of opposing God’s guidance.

translation: And if Allah had not ordained exile for them, He would have punished them in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God, by His wisdom and restraint, limited the immediate chastisement of certain wrongdoers by prescribing exile—a measured, lesser penalty—rather than allowing a fuller worldly punishment; nonetheless their persistent rejection guarantees severe recompense in the hereafter. The lesson: divine discipline can be tempered in this life out of wisdom or mercy, but final accountability remains inevitable.

translation: ذلك لأنهم عارضوا الله ورسوله؛ ومن يعارض الله فإن الله شديد العقاب.
interpretation: الآية تحذر من النتيجة المترتبة على المعارضة المتعمدة لأمر الله وسلطة رسوله: «شاقّوا» تعني العناد أو المعارضة المستمرة — سواء بانتهاك الأوامر، نقض العهود، التشكيك العلني في أحكام الشرع، أو العمل على تقويض الجماعة المسلمة. من يعمد إلى مثل هذا العناد لا يُعد مجرد مُخطئ عارض؛ بل هو متسبب في تهديد النظام الأخلاقي والاجتماعي الذي أراده الوحي، ولذلك تكون عقوبة الله ـ في الدنيا والآخرة بحسب مقتضى حكمته ـ شديدة كتحصيل لقدر خطورته ومرافعة للمسؤولية الأخلاقية.

translation: Whatever of a tree you cut down, or leave standing on its root — that is by the permission of Allah; and He will disgrace the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human actions toward creation—whether felling a tree or leaving it standing—take place within God’s sovereign will, yet this divine permission does not remove human moral responsibility. It warns that those who transgress God’s limits by abusing, wantonly destroying, or unjustly seizing what belongs to others (for example ravaging land, wasting resources, or acting defiantly) will ultimately be humiliated by God. In short: God permits human agency in the world, but holds accountable and will abase the rebellious who misuse that agency.

translation: And whatever Allah bestowed upon His Messenger from them — you did not urge horses or riders upon it — but Allah grants His messengers power over whom He wills. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse indicates that the gains the Prophet received in that incident were not achieved by Muslim military expedition or personal effort, but were granted by God’s will; it underscores that victory, authority, and the right to benefit rest ultimately with Allah, who empowers His messengers as He pleases, thereby grounding the Prophet’s possession and distribution of such spoils in divine sanction rather than human conquest and reminding believers of God’s absolute sovereignty and omnipotence.

translation: What Allah has bestowed upon His Messenger from the people of the towns is for Allah, for the Messenger, for the near relatives, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer — so that it will not be a means of circulating only among the rich among you. And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principled framework for public wealth and spoils: such gains are not private property but divinely designated resources to be distributed to specific vulnerable and communal categories so as to prevent concentration of wealth and protect social cohesion. By declaring the allocations binding and commanding acceptance of the Messenger’s decisions, the verse affirms that legitimate authority—when exercised in this public, divinely sanctioned manner—must be obeyed to secure justice. The exhortation to fear God and the warning of severe punishment underscore that mishandling communal resources or resisting the prescribed redistribution is a moral and spiritual wrongdoing with serious consequences, reinforcing accountability and the priority of collective welfare over private gain.

translation: For the poor emigrants who were driven out of their homes and their wealth, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and who help Allah and His Messenger — those are the truthful.
interpretation: The verse sets a moral test for authenticity in faith: truthfulness is shown by an inner orientation toward God’s pleasure and an outward commitment to His cause, even at personal cost. Those whose actions consistently prioritize the Divine over worldly attachments and who actively support the prophetic mission are to be recognized as genuinely sincere; the community therefore has a responsibility to honor, protect, and materially assist such people, for their sacrifices confirm their spiritual truthfulness.

translation: And those who had settled in the Home and in faith before [them] love those who emigrated to them; they do not feel any need in their breasts for what has been given to the emigrants, and they give them preference over themselves, even though they are in need. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul — those are the successful.
interpretation: The verse commends a moral ideal in which true faith is proven by an inner freedom from envy and by practical selflessness: people who are secure and faithful willingly prioritize the needs of newcomers despite their own scarcity, showing that spiritual wealth—trust in God and detachment from selfishness—matters more than material possession. ‘Not finding need in their breasts’ indicates the removal of jealous or resentful impulses, while ‘preferring others over themselves’ is an active ethic of altruism. The final clause teaches that moral success (salvation and real human flourishing) comes from overcoming the soul’s greed; protecting oneself from stinginess is the hallmark of those who truly prosper morally and spiritually.

translation: And those who came after them say, “Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not let there be in our hearts any resentment toward those who have believed. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind, Merciful.”
interpretation: This supplication models communal humility and spiritual solidarity: later generations recognize their dependence on earlier believers, seek God’s pardon for themselves and for those before them, and ask God to remove any ill will that would divide the community. The prayer implies that true faith requires inner purification — forgiveness for past faults and the eradication of rancor — and that maintaining unity and compassion among believers is a grace granted by God, who is ultimately the Merciful Source of reconciliation.

translation: Have you not seen those who are hypocrites who say to their brethren among the People of the Book, “If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you; we will never obey anyone against you ever; and if you are fought, we will surely aid you.” And Allah bears witness that they are certainly liars.
interpretation: The verse condemns a double allegiance: some pretend loyalty by promising solidarity with hostile outsiders while concealing their true motives. Their outward words are tactical deceptions aimed at securing favor or avoiding responsibility, not expressions of sincere commitment; God, who knows inner states, declares their claims false. The passage therefore warns that genuine faith demands truthful, consistent loyalties and that clandestine pacts with adversaries and hypocritical professions will be exposed and judged by God.

translation: If they are expelled, they will not go forth with them; and if they are met in battle, they will not aid them; and if they are aided, they will surely turn their backs — then they will not be helped.
interpretation: This verse diagnoses a kind of hollow, conditional allegiance: such people’s faith and commitment collapse under pressure — they will not stand with the community in exile, in conflict they refuse support, and even when superficially aided they will flee. The underlying lesson is a warning that insincere or self‑serving attachment cannot be relied upon, produces betrayal in trial, and forfeits real protection and solidarity.

translation: إِنَّكُمْ أَشَدُّ رَهْبَةً فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنَ اللَّهِ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ قَوْمٌ لَا يَفْقَهُونَ
interpretation: The verse indicts those whose primary motivation is fear of people rather than reverence for God: they give greater weight to human pressure, honor, or threats than to divine guidance. This misplaced fear reflects a lack of true understanding—spiritual myopia and moral cowardice—that leads them to reject or resist what is right because they are more concerned with worldly consequences and opinions than with accountability before God.

translation: They will not fight you all together except within fortified towns or from behind walls. Their ferocity is severe among themselves. You would think they are all together, but their hearts are scattered. That is because they are a people who do not reason.
interpretation: The verse is warning that apparent cohesion and outward boldness can hide inner weakness and moral/intellectual failure: those who avoid open confrontation and strike from protected positions, who seem united but whose hearts are divided, act out of fear, factionalism, and lack of sound judgment. Believers are thus cautioned not to be misled by surface displays of strength; true strength lies in sincere conviction, unity, and the use of reason, whereas reliance on walls, stratagems, and deceptive appearance exposes cowardice and an absence of right understanding.

translation:
كمثل الذين من قبلهم قريبا: ذاقوا وبال أمرهم ولهم عذاب أليم
"Like those before them — they tasted the evil consequence of their affair, and for them is a painful punishment."
interpretation: The verse teaches that communities who persist in rejecting guidance bring about their own ruin: the phrase “tasted the evil consequence of their affair” points to the social, moral and existential harms that result from collective wrongdoing, and the “painful punishment” denotes the inevitable divine reckoning that follows such persistent denial. It is thus a historical and moral warning — the calamities of past peoples were not arbitrary but consequences of their choices, and those who follow the same path risk the same outcome unless they repent and reform.

translation:
كمثل الشيطان إذ قال للإنسان اكفر فلما كفر قال إني بريء منك إني أخاف الله رب العالمين
“Like the example of Satan when he said to man, ‘Disbelieve.’ But when the man had disbelieved, Satan said, ‘Indeed I am clear of you; indeed I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”
interpretation: The verse highlights Satan’s duplicity: he lures people into denying God by promising or inciting transgression, yet when they follow him and suffer the consequences he disavows them and pretends piety. It teaches that the tempter’s counsel is deceitful — he seeks to corrupt and then absolve himself — so individuals must not be seduced by flattering whispers, must take responsibility for their choices, and discern true fear of God from hypocritical pretense.

translation: فَكَانَ عَاقِبَتُهُمَا أَنَّهُمَا فِي النَّارِ خَالِدَيْنِ_fīhā ۚ وَذَٰلِكَ جَزَاءُ الظَّالِمِينَ
interpretation: The verse affirms that persistent injustice and rejection of God's guidance lead to inevitable and lasting divine retribution: the wrongdoers’ choices result in an abiding punishment in Hell. Its purpose is not merely reportage but moral and theological: to confirm God’s perfect justice, to show that evil deeds have real, proportionate consequences, and to warn people to abandon oppression and turn to repentance before the final reckoning.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse urges believers to cultivate constant God‑consciousness and to practice regular self‑accounting: examine and reform your intentions and deeds now so that what you ‘send forward’ will stand you in good stead on the Day of Reckoning (and in the future generally). It is a warning against complacency and short‑termness — true piety requires both outward righteous actions and sincere inward intention, because Allah fully knows your inner states and outward acts; therefore prioritize enduring, beneficial deeds, repent and correct course immediately, and live with the accountability that will govern the final judgment.

translation: “And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that turning away from the remembrance and guidance of God results in an inner loss: when people neglect God, He allows them to become deprived of the moral self‑awareness and conscience that anchors right action. “He made them forget themselves” means they lose sight of their true purpose, judgment and restraint, becoming prone to self‑deception and excess; hence they are described as fāsiqūn — those who transgress the bounds of right conduct. The warning is practical: preserve continual remembrance and accountability to maintain inner integrity and avoid spiritual ruin.

translation: The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal. Indeed, the companions of Paradise — they are the successful.
interpretation: This verse asserts a fundamental moral and eschatological distinction: ultimate success is measured by attaining God’s pleasure and eternal well‑being in Paradise, not by worldly status. Those who secure Paradise have achieved the true, lasting victory because their faith and righteous conduct lead to reward; those doomed to the Fire suffer irrevocable loss. The statement functions both as reassurance for the obedient and as a clear warning that temporal gains cannot compensate for failure in what matters for the hereafter.

translation: If We had sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and splitting apart from the fear of Allah. And these examples We present to the people that perhaps they will reflect.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the Qur’an’s truth carries overwhelming spiritual gravity: its words are so weighty and manifest of God’s majesty that even the most inert, solid thing would be moved to awe and submission. By this stark image the text reproves human hardness of heart and calls for a deeper, transformative response — humility, conscious fear of God, and moral reform. The parable’s purpose is not mere rhetorical flourish but to provoke reflection and inward change, showing that hearing the revelation without being affected by it is a moral failing.

translation: He is Allah—there is no deity except Him; Knower of the unseen and the seen. He is the Most Merciful, Most Compassionate.
interpretation: The verse declares God’s exclusive divinity and sovereignty, asserting that no one shares His right to be worshipped. By calling Him the Knower of the unseen and the seen it emphasizes that nothing—hidden realities, future events, inner states, or outward occurrences—escapes His knowledge, so human uncertainty and ignorance are ultimately within His awareness and governance. Describing Him as the Most Merciful and Most Compassionate frames all divine management of creation (including guidance, tests, and judgment) as rooted in mercy, inviting trust, humility, and reliance on His wisdom rather than fear or despair.

translation: He is Allah — there is no deity except Him — the Sovereign, the Holy One, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Protector (Al-Muhaymin), the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supremely Great. Glory be to Allah above what they associate (with Him).
interpretation: By listing diverse divine names that combine absolute authority, sanctity, peace, trustworthiness, protection and irresistible power, the verse teaches that God’s reality transcends human categories and reconciles attributes that might seem opposite to us. Rather than permitting division of lordship or partnership, these names together demand exclusive recognition and reliance: His rulership is just and holy, His granting of peace and security grounds faith, and His overwhelming might prevents any true rival. The final phrase — exalted is He above what they ascribe — is not merely a polemic against idolatry but a theological statement that any attribution of partners distorts the unified, comprehensive nature of God described by these names, and so true devotion must flow from understanding and submitting to that unity.

translation: He is Allah — the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth proclaims His glory, and He is the Almighty, the All‑Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents a unified theological claim: God’s sovereignty is manifest in both the fact of existence and the specific ordered forms within it. The three creative names indicate complementary aspects of divine action — bringing things into being, originating distinct realities, and giving them particular shapes — which together show that the world is intentionally fashioned rather than accidental. Saying that the best names belong to Him affirms that every perfect attribute is found in God, and that human knowledge of Him is accessed through these attributes even though He transcends full comprehension. The continual glorification of heaven and earth means creation testifies to God by fulfilling its ordained roles, and the pairing of “Al‑Aziz” (Almighty) with “Al‑Hakim” (All‑Wise) assures that divine power is exercised with purpose and wisdom, grounding moral order, trust, and reverence toward God.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, exchanging affection with them while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, and they have driven out the Messenger and you because you believed in Allah, your Lord — if you went out striving in My cause and seeking My pleasure. You show them affection, while I know what you conceal and what you declare. And whoever among you does that has certainly gone astray from a clear way.
interpretation: The verse forbids making intimate, protective alliances with those who are openly hostile to God and the Muslim community — especially those who reject the truth and have persecuted or expelled the Prophet and the believers — under the appearance of friendship or political advantage. Its core warning is that loyalties that place such enemies above one’s duty to God and the community amount to hypocrisy: outward affection can hide treacherous intent, but God knows both what is hidden and what is declared. Thus anyone who makes an enemy of God and the community into a trusted protector or companion, thereby undermining communal obligation and faith, has strayed from the straight path. The injunction targets taking hostile opponents as protectors or primary allies, not routine just or civil relations with non‑believers.

translation: إن يمسكموكم (أو: إذا أمكنوكم) يكونون لكم أعداءً، ويبسطون إليكم أيديهم وألسنتهم بالشرّ، وودّوا لو تكفرون.
interpretation: الآية تحذر من خصومٍ يبدون العداوة تجاه المؤمنين ويستخدمون أفعالهم ('الأيدي') وكلامهم ('الألسنة') لإيذائهم ولإغراءهم بالابتعاد عن الإيمان؛ ومعنى ذلك أن بعض الناس قد يتعاطون مع المؤمنين بمظهرٍ أو معاملات تبدو طبيعية بينما في باطنها رغبةٌ في النيل منهم وإخراجهم من دينهم، فالمؤمن مطالب بالحذر من مثل هذه النوايا الخبيثة، والتمسّك بالإيمان والحكمة في التعامل وعدم الانخداع بالمظاهر.

translation: Your kin and your children will not avail you; on the Day of Resurrection He will separate between you. And Allah is, of what you do, Seeing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that in the final accounting personal relationships and lineage will not secure salvation; each person will be judged on their own beliefs and actions. On the Day of Resurrection God will distinguish and separate people according to their deeds, and because He fully observes everything, one must not rely on family ties but on sincere faith, righteous conduct, and seeking God’s mercy.

translation: There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, “Indeed, we disassociate ourselves from you and from whatever you worship other than Allah; we have rejected you, and there has arisen between us and you enmity and hatred forever—until you believe in Allah alone.” Except for Abraham’s saying to his father, “I will surely ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power to benefit you anything before Allah. Our Lord, in You we have placed our trust, and to You we have turned, and to You is the final return.”
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham and his companions as a paradigm for balancing principled separation from falsehood with personal mercy. It teaches that when close communities persist in idolatry or doctrines that threaten one’s commitment to God, believers are warranted to dissociate themselves publicly and break the bonds of ideological solidarity so as to protect the integrity of faith. At the same time, Abraham’s exception—his continued prayer and hoping for his father’s guidance despite recognizing he lacks power to change God’s decree—models compassion and humility: we may renounce error and refuse its partnership, yet still beseech God for guidance for those we love, rely wholly on God’s judgment, and acknowledge that ultimate return and verdict belong to Him alone.

translation: Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: A supplication asking God to prevent the believers’ weakness, faults, or suffering from becoming a pretext or temptation through which disbelievers are confirmed in their rejection, gloat, or are led into greater wrongdoing; it seeks God’s pardon and restoration while expressing trust that only the Almighty and All‑Wise can fairly adjudicate, protect the community from harm, and turn trials into mercy rather than cause for increased corruption.

translation: Indeed for you in them is an excellent example — for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true hope in God and the Hereafter naturally leads a person to adopt the conduct and character of the righteous as a guide for life: faith, patience, humility and steadfastness. Those who deliberately reject that guidance reveal their lack of sincere hope and bear the loss themselves; such turning away does not diminish God in any way, for He is self-sufficient and worthy of all praise. Thus the passage both urges personal responsibility in following worthy models and comforts believers with the reminder of God’s independence and perfect praise.

translation: Perhaps Allah will put between you and those of them with whom you were hostile affection. And Allah is Able; and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God can transform relationships by softening hearts and turning enmity into affection; this is both a hope and a moral incentive for the believer—one should behave justly, kindly, and patiently toward former adversaries and leave the outcome to Allah’s power and mercy, trusting that reconciliation may be part of His wise, forgiving plan.

translation:
لا ينهاكم الله عن الذين لم يقاتلوكم في الدين ولم يخرجوكم من دياركم أن تبروهم وتقسطوا إليهم ۚ إن الله يحب المقسطين
“Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who do not fight you because of your religion and have not expelled you from your homes; be good to them and deal equitably with them. Indeed Allah loves the equitable.”
interpretation: The verse establishes a moral principle that the duty to act with kindness and justice is not suspended by religious difference or by general conflict—only active aggression or expulsion removes that personal claim to trust. It obliges believers to distinguish between enemies and peaceful individuals, to honor treaties and fair treatment, and to respond to people on the basis of their conduct rather than their creed; justice and benevolence toward non-hostile others are commands grounded in God’s love for equity.

translation: Allah only forbids you concerning those who fought you for your faith, drove you out of your homes, and aided in your expulsion, that you take them as allies. And whoever takes them as allies—those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse limits a categorical prohibition on forming bonds of loyalty or alliance to a specific group: those who have actively persecuted believers—fighting them for their religion, expelling them from their homes, and assisting in that expulsion. It teaches a moral and practical boundary: while relations with non‑believers are not universally forbidden, one must not seek alliance or close support with people who have committed clear aggression and injustice against the community. Choosing to side with or protect such persecutors is itself an unjust act, because it endorses or enables their wrongdoing and betrays the rights and safety of the oppressed.

translation: O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them — Allah knows best their faith. If you recognize them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are the disbelievers lawful for them. Give the believing emigrant women what they spent. And there is no blame on you if you marry them when you give them their due compensation. And do not hold fast to the wives of disbelievers — ask what you have spent and let them ask what they have spent. That is Allah’s ruling; He judges between you. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes humane legal principles for cases where women who have embraced faith migrate from non‑Muslim households into the Muslim community. It requires careful, respectful assessment of their faith, and, once their belief is established, it protects them from being sent back to non‑believing spouses: the marital bond with a disbelieving husband cannot be used to compel a believing woman to return. The community must also settle financial rights fairly — refund or account for what was spent and ensure women receive their due bridal gifts — and there is no sin in entering marriage with such women after these obligations are discharged. At the same time, believers are forbidden from unlawfully detaining or exploiting the wives of disbelievers; mutual claims about expenditures should be openly settled. Overall the verse prioritizes the religious liberty and personal safety of believing emigrant women, insists on just financial settlement between parties, and underscores that these rules are a divinely mandated judgment grounded in wisdom and knowledge.

translation: And if any of your wives go over to the disbelievers and you have thereby suffered or taken action against them, then give to those whose wives have gone over the like of what they spent. And fear Allah, in Whom you are believers.
interpretation: The verse directs that when a marriage is broken because a spouse turns to disbelief, believers must settle the resulting financial and legal consequences with fairness: those who have lost wives through such rupture are to be compensated in proportion to what they spent on them, so that neither party suffers unjust loss. The injunction closes with a moral reminder to fear God and act justly in accordance with the faith.

translation: O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor will they steal, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse, nor kill their children, nor fabricate falsehood knowingly between their hands and their feet, nor disobey you in what is right—then accept their pledge and ask forgiveness for them of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to accept the sincere pledge of believing women who embrace tawḥīd and commit to a set of moral reforms as evidence of genuine conversion and repentance. The specific prohibitions name major social evils—idolatry, theft, sexual immorality, infanticide, and deliberate slander (the phrase about what is between their hands and feet is classically understood as inventing false accusations of sexual misconduct)—and the qualification “not disobey you in what is right” limits obedience to what is morally good. By telling the Prophet to take their bayʿah and to seek God’s forgiveness for them, the verse teaches that communal leaders should recognize and welcome sincere moral transformation, intercede on behalf of repentant believers, and rely on God’s mercy: acceptance into the Muslim community rests on sincere faith and reformed conduct, while ultimate forgiveness remains with God, who is compassionate.

translation:
يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تتولوا قوما غضب الله عليهم قد يئسوا من الآخرة كما يئس الكفار من أصحاب القبور
“O you who have believed, do not take as allies a people upon whom Allah’s wrath has fallen; they have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers despair of those in the graves.”
interpretation: The verse warns believers not to form intimate alliances or place their trust and guardianship in people whose hearts are closed to divine guidance and who are under God’s displeasure. Such people “have despaired of the Hereafter” — they have lost hope in resurrection and final accountability — so their values and aims are fundamentally at odds with faith. The injunction is to avoid making them protectors, leaders, or sources of decisive influence over the Muslim community in ways that would compromise obedience to God; it is a caution to preserve the community’s moral and spiritual integrity, not a blanket prohibition on ordinary social interactions.

translation:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. سبَّح لله ما في السماوات وما في الأرض، وهو العزيز الحكيم.
“In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah; and He is the Exalted in Might, the All‑Wise.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that the entire cosmos continuously manifests its praise of God by operating according to His ordained order and purpose; this cosmic glorification points to God’s absolute sovereignty and wise governance. For humans the lesson is practical: to acknowledge that events unfold under divine might and wisdom, to trust God amid trials, and to show true worship by consciously submitting one’s will and actions to the guidance that reflects that wisdom.

translation: O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?
interpretation: A direct rebuke against hypocrisy: believers must align their words with their actions. Making declarations, promises, or vows without intending or striving to fulfill them corrupts sincerity, breaks trust, and undermines the moral and social fabric of the community. True faith requires integrity — let your deeds confirm your speech, and avoid empty claims or token professions of belief.

translation: Most hateful in the sight of Allah is that you should say what you do not do.
interpretation: The verse condemns hypocrisy and calls for integrity: Allah strongly disapproves when people profess beliefs, make vows, or declare righteous intentions in words but fail to honor them in action. It teaches that speech has moral weight—promises, religious professions, and claims of virtue must be matched by corresponding conduct; otherwise trust, communal bonds, and genuine faith are undermined. True piety requires sincerity, fulfilling commitments, and aligning deeds with what one declares.

translation: Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in orderly ranks, as though they were a solidly-built edifice.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that what pleases God is not merely individual zeal but disciplined, collective effort: when people pursue a righteous cause in unity, order and mutual support — each person holding and being held by others like stones in a firm structure — their work becomes strong, resilient and effective. It therefore teaches the spiritual and practical importance of solidarity, organization, and steadfast cooperation in any sincere struggle for truth, justice and the preservation of faith.

translation: And when Moses said to his people, “O my people, why do you harm me while you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you?” But when they turned away, Allah caused their hearts to go astray. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse warns that deliberate rejection and ill-treatment of a divinely sent messenger—especially after recognizing his truth—is a moral choice that brings inner corruption: when a community persistently turns away from guidance, God allows their hearts to become further astray as a consequence of their own obstinacy. The statement that God “does not guide the fasiqīn” stresses that persistent rebellion and breach of covenant (fussūq) cut people off from guidance; divine misguidance here functions as a response to wilful rejection, underscoring human responsibility and the spiritual cost of hypocrisy, ingratitude, and recalcitrant sin.

translation: And when Jesus, son of Mary, said: “O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of Allah to you confirming what was before me of the Torah and bringing glad tidings of a messenger who will come after me whose name is Ahmad.” But when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, “This is obvious magic.”
interpretation: The verse is best read as asserting continuity in God’s guidance: Jesus affirms the Torah and foretells a future messenger called “Ahmad” (linguistically linked to Muhammad), signaling that revelation does not end with him. The hostile reaction—calling clear signs “obvious magic”—illustrates a recurring moral and sociological pattern in which people resist spiritual renewal and reject authentic prophetic evidence when it challenges established authority or expectations; thus the passage functions both as prophecy of a subsequent prophet and as a lesson about human obstinacy toward divine truth.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who, under the guise of religion, fabricate falsehoods about God or His message—whether by inventing doctrines, twisting teachings, or using the name of Islam to deceive and gain advantage. Such conduct is a profound injustice because it corrupts the truth that guides people; as a consequence, God withholds guidance from those who persist in this wrongdoing, leaving them to the moral consequences of their obstinacy and misguidance.

translation: They want to put out the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah will perfect His light, even if the disbelievers dislike it.
interpretation: The phrase depicts opponents trying to suppress divine guidance—through denial, slander, ridicule, or legal and social pressure (“with their mouths”)—but such human efforts cannot prevent God from establishing and manifesting His truth. “Allah will perfect His light” means He will ensure His guidance reaches its intended completion and effect (by protecting it, spreading it, or bringing its consequences), regardless of the hostility or displeasure of those who reject it. The verse affirms that the outcome is determined by God’s will, not by the attempts or objections of the disbelievers.

translation: He is the One who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth so that He might make it prevail over every religion, even if the polytheists dislike it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s sending of the Prophet was aimed at delivering a comprehensive, true way of life (guidance and the religion of truth) whose purpose is to be made manifest and dominant as the correct path for humanity. “To make it prevail” signifies the establishment and clear manifestation of its truth in hearts, laws and societies—not merely by coercion but by the power of its truth and God’s decree—so that its principles become authoritative despite resistance. The objection of the polytheists (‘even if they dislike it’) underscores that human opposition cannot frustrate God’s will for the truth to be recognized and to have moral and legal primacy.

translation: O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?
interpretation: The word “commerce” is used metaphorically: God offers believers an investment opportunity that, if accepted, yields eternal return. The terms of this ‘trade’ are sincere faith in God and His Messenger together with active sacrifice — striving in God’s cause with one’s wealth and life. Though it requires giving up immediate comforts and facing hardship, it transforms temporal losses into forgiveness and immense reward in the Hereafter. The verse therefore calls believers to prioritize a wholehearted, action‑bearing faith and readiness to struggle for God’s cause, trusting that such sacrifice will avert the painful punishment and secure lasting salvation.

translation: You believe in Allah and in His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives; that is better for you, if you but knew.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true benefit comes from the union of inner conviction and outward commitment: sincere faith must be expressed through costly, purposeful sacrifice for God's cause. Such giving of wealth and risking of life produces lasting good—spiritual growth, communal strength, and ultimate well‑being—far surpassing short‑term comforts; the phrase “if you but knew” cautions against short‑sightedness and calls people to recognize the unseen, long‑term advantages of wholehearted engagement in what is right.

translation: يغفر لكم ذنوبكم ويدخلكم جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار ومساكن طيبة في جنات عدن ۚ ذلك الفوز العظيم
interpretation: الآية تبيّن أن الفوز الحقيقي عند الله ليس في الامتلاك الدنيوي بل في مغفرة الذنوب ودخول الدائم في نعيم أخروي كامل: حدائق تجري من تحتها المياه ومساكن طاهرة ودائمة في جنات عدن. وصفُ الجنان بالمياه الجارية والمساكن الطيبة يؤكدان كمال النعمة واستمرارها وكونها مهيأة للراحة والصفاء الروحي والجسدي، وأن مغفرة الله هي المفتاح الذي يؤهل لبلوغ هذا المقام. بالتالي تُقدَّم الخاتمة الإلهية —مغفرة ورحمة وإقامة أبدية في حضرة الله— كأعظم نجاح يتجاوز كل مكاسب الحياة المؤقتة.

translation: وَأُخْرَىٰ تُحِبُّونَهَا ۖ نَصْرٌ مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَفَتْحٌ قَرِيبٌ ۗ وَبَشِّرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
interpretation: Allah is assuring the faithful that what they long for will come not merely by chance but through His direct support: a decisive divine aid and an imminent opening. This is meant to console and strengthen believers’ trust and perseverance—promising that their endurance and unity will be vindicated by tangible success, and therefore they should hold firm and receive the glad tidings with hope.

translation: O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples, “Who will be my helpers for Allah?” The disciples said, “We are the helpers of Allah.” A faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved; so We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to embody active, principled support for God’s cause: not merely private faith but public, united commitment to truth, justice, and the prophetic message, modeled by the disciples of Jesus. It teaches that when a sincere, cohesive minority stands for God—clearly identifying with His guidance, sacrificing personal interest, and acting with steadfastness and reliance on God—God grants them support and success against their opponents. The promise is moral and conditional: divine assistance follows genuine loyalty, unity, and perseverance in upholding what is right.

translation:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. يَسْبَحُ لِلَّهِ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ — الْمَلِكِ الْقُدُّوسِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَكِيمِ.
"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth proclaims the glory of Allah — the Sovereign, the Holy, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."
interpretation: This verse means that all creation, whether sentient or not, continually bears witness to God's reality by manifesting His attributes: sovereign rule (al‑Malik) in the order and governance of the universe, purity from defect (al‑Quddūs) in His perfect essence, irresistible power (al‑ʿAzīz) in His might, and purposeful wisdom (al‑Hakīm) in the fitting design and laws of existence. Their constant 'tasbih' is expressed through their ordained functions and harmony rather than only by human speech, and it calls people to recognize, trust and live in accordance with these divine realities.

translation: He is the One who sent among the unlettered a messenger from themselves, who recites to them His signs, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom — although before that they had been in manifest error.
interpretation: God deliberately chose a messenger from within the community so the message would be trusted and accessible; the three verbs describe a progressive method of guidance: first the public proclamation of divine signs (tilāwah) that opens hearts, then inner moral and spiritual purification (tazkiyah) that reforms character, and finally instruction in the revealed scripture and the practical wisdom (ḥikmah) by which that scripture is lived and applied. ‘Wisdom’ points to prophetic example, legal and ethical reasoning, and the habits of sound judgment that translate texts into righteous practice. The reference to their prior ‘clear error’ underscores the transformative purpose of the mission: to replace ignorance and disorder with knowledge, ethical integrity, and social order grounded in revelation.

translation: And others of them who will join them later; and He is the Almighty, the Wise.
interpretation: The clause points to a twofold reality within a community: some have already reached the destined state (of support, guidance, or recompense), while others remain to arrive later — not by chance but by God’s deliberate will. That delayed joining is part of divine governance: God’s might ensures that what He has decreed will occur, and His wisdom determines the timing and manner so that outcomes serve His just and wise plan. Thus apparent postponement is not neglect but purposeful arrangement under the power and wisdom of God.

translation: That is the bounty of Allah; He grants it to whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of immense bounty.
