interpretation: The verse teaches that blessings, honor, guidance, and favor are ultimately gifts from God, distributed according to His wisdom and purpose rather than merely by human effort, status, or claim. Because Allah alone is the source and owner of vast grace, believers are invited to respond with humility, gratitude, trust in His decree, and avoidance of envy or pride—recognizing that God gives and withholds for reasons beyond human view and that true success is measured by seeking His pleasure.

translation: The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah but then did not carry it is like the example of a donkey carrying books. Wretched is the example of the people who deny the signs of Allah; and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who possess divine scripture or religious authority yet fail to internalize, live by, or rightly convey its guidance. Like a donkey burdened with books, they may carry outward forms of knowledge but gain no benefit from it and cannot impart true understanding to others; their relationship to revelation is merely external and utilitarian. Because they reject or distort God’s signs through neglect, hypocrisy, or self-interest, their example is called ‘wretched,’ and by their persistent injustice they remove themselves from Allah’s guidance. The implied lesson: true bearing of revelation requires comprehension, moral transformation, and sincere transmission—without these, knowledge becomes a useless load and a cause of misguidance.

translation: Say, “O you who are Jews, if you claim that you are allies of Allah instead of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.”
interpretation: A rhetorical challenge aimed at exposing presumptuous claims of guaranteed divine favor: if a group truly believed themselves to be Allah’s exclusive friends and heirs of His nearness, they would not cling to worldly life but would be ready to meet God. The statement thereby rebukes self-assured, identity-based assurances of salvation, urging inner sincerity and reminding that genuine closeness to God is proved by readiness for the Last Meeting, while ultimate judgment and choice belong to God alone.

translation: And they will never long for it at all because of what their hands have sent before; and Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning those who committed injustice will find any wish to reverse or delay their fate futile—what they have brought upon themselves by their deeds cannot be undone by regret. It underscores divine omniscience: Allah fully knows the oppressors—their actions and intentions—and will judge them with perfect justice, so hidden harms and injustices cannot escape accountability.

translation: Say, “Indeed, the death which you flee from will surely meet you; then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the seen, and He will inform you of what you used to do.”
interpretation: The verse warns that death is unavoidable despite human attempts to escape it—whether by clinging to life, pursuing worldly safety, or ignoring accountability. After death every person is returned to God, Who perfectly knows both hidden inward realities and outward actions; He will make known and judge what one truly did. The practical lesson: concealment of intentions or deeds is futile, and one must live with consciousness of eventual return to God, cultivating sincere, righteous conduct in preparation for that encounter.

translation: O you who have believed, when the call is proclaimed for the prayer on the day of congregation (Friday), hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade. That is better for you if you only knew.
interpretation: The verse enjoins believers to suspend commercial concerns and promptly attend the communal remembrance of God on Friday, teaching that collective worship and spiritual discipline must take precedence over material interests. By ordering haste to the gathering and abandonment of trade, it emphasizes the moral and social goods of prioritizing Allah—strengthening communal bonds, correcting worldly preoccupation, and securing long‑term spiritual benefit that may not be immediately apparent (hence “that is better for you if you knew”).

translation: So when the prayer is concluded, then disperse through the land and seek of the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often so that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse teaches a balanced model of religious life: communal worship is not an end that isolates believers from society but a pause that empowers them to return to legitimate, active pursuit of sustenance and benefit for the community. ‘Disperse in the land’ authorizes work, trade and social engagement; ‘seek of the bounty of Allah’ frames provision as legitimate striving under divine providence; and ‘remember Allah often’ requires that this worldly striving be accompanied by continual God‑consciousness so that actions remain ethical and lead to true success.

translation: And when they see trade or amusement, they disperse to it and leave you standing. Say, “What is with Allah is better than amusement and than trade; and Allah is the best of providers.”
interpretation: The verse rebukes the tendency to abandon sacred responsibilities for fleeting worldly pursuits and affirms that the bounty and reward from God—both spiritual good and true provision—surpass any temporary profit or entertainment. It teaches believers to prioritize obedience, remembrance, and the promise of God over immediate material gain, trusting that reliance on Allah will not deprive them but is the truest and most sufficient source of sustenance.

translation: When the hypocrites come to you they say, “We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.” And Allah knows that you are His Messenger, and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars.
interpretation: The verse exposes the gap between outward profession and inner reality: some people will offer verbal assent to the Prophet for appearance’s sake, but their hearts do not accept it. By immediately reminding that Allah knows the truth and Himself testifies to the Prophet’s authenticity while declaring the hypocrites liars, the passage teaches that divine knowledge—not hypocritical declarations—determines reality. It reassures the Messenger and sincere believers that God’s witness validates true faith and that hypocritical pretense will be exposed and held to account; therefore genuine faith must be inward as well as outward, and one should beware of relying on mere words or seeking favor through insincere professions.

translation: They took their oaths as a covering, and thus turned people away from the way of Allah. Indeed, evil is what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who use solemn promises as a protective pretext—treating oaths as a shield to excuse neglect, hypocrisy, or refusal of duty—and by doing so they obstruct true obedience and guidance; elevating formal vows above sincere faith and compassion is condemned as a blameworthy, corrupt act.

translation: That is because they believed then disbelieved, so a seal was set upon their hearts; therefore they do not understand.
interpretation: The “seal upon their hearts” is a metaphor for spiritual hardening that results from knowingly accepting guidance and then turning away from it. After repeated or decisive rejection of truth, a person’s inner faculty for receiving and acting on guidance becomes closed—manifesting as stubbornness, insincerity, and moral blindness. This sealing is presented as the consequential state produced by their choices: because they abandoned belief, their capacity to comprehend and be guided is effectively blocked.

translation: And when you see them, their bodies please you; and if they speak you listen to their speech. They are like propped-up pieces of wood; they think every cry is against them. They are the enemy — so beware of them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded!
interpretation: This verse condemns hypocrisy: some people are outwardly attractive and speak in ways that win attention, but inwardly they are lifeless and impotent — like propped-up wood, impressive in appearance yet without real substance or guidance. Their constant fear and oversensitivity (thinking every alarm is aimed at them) reveal weakness and self‑deception rather than sincere commitment. The stern warning to ‘beware’ and the divine condemnation express that such hypocrisy is hostile to the community and dangerous; believers must not be beguiled by surface charm but must test for true faith and be vigilant against those whose speech masks disloyalty and moral emptiness.

translation: And when it is said to them, “Come, that the Messenger of Allah may ask forgiveness for you,” they turn their heads aside; and you see them turning away while they are arrogant.
interpretation: The verse indicts those whose pride keeps them from accepting the Prophet’s intercession and the call to repentance: their physical turning away is an outward sign of inner obstinacy and self‑righteousness. It teaches that the real barrier to forgiveness is not the absence of mercy but the person’s arrogance and refusal to humble themselves, which both blocks divine mercy and undermines communal guidance.

translation: It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or not; Allah will not forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse explains that in certain cases divine mercy is not unlocked by external intercession because of the moral state of the people involved: persistent, knowing rebellion and hypocrisy sever the conditions for forgiveness and guidance. Thus Allah’s withholding of pardon here is not arbitrariness but the consequence of their continued defiance — forgiveness and guidance are granted to those who sincerely turn from their wrongdoing, whereas those who insist in transgression place themselves outside that mercy until they genuinely repent.

translation: هُمْ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ لَا تُنفِقُوا عَلَى مَنْ عِندَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ حَتَّىٰ يَنْفَضُّوا ۚ وَلِلَّهِ خَزَائِنُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَلَٰكِنِ الْمُنَافِقِينَ لَا يَفْقَهُونَ
interpretation: الآية توبّخ من يستخدم الحرمان المالي كأداة للضغط السياسي والخصومة داخل الجماعة: المنافقون ينهجون سياسة أن لا تُنفق الأموال على من هم مع رسول الله بغرض إجبارهم على التنازل أو التشريد، وذلك انطلاقاً من بخل نفسي وعداوة، والنهي يذكّر بأن ملكية و provision الله لا تُعدُّ محصورة (خزائن السماوات والأرض) فلا معنى لأن تقرر مصالح الدعوة أو واجبات الجماعة بحسب حيل المتآمرين؛ فعلهم ناتج عن ضعف بصيرة وإسلام ناقص، والموقف المشروع هو الثبات في نصرة ودعم من يصنعون العمل النبوي بثقة في كفاية الله.

translation: They say, “If we return to al‑Madīnah, the stronger will surely drive out the weaker from it.” But to Allah belongs all honor, and to His Messenger, and to the believers; yet the hypocrites do not know.
interpretation: The verse indicts the hypocrites’ concealed ambition and false calculations: they measure influence by worldly strength and plan to oppress the weak when opportunity comes, failing to see that true authority and honor are rooted in divine support and the moral legitimacy of faith. It teaches that schemes based on arrogance and social dominance are futile because ultimate power belongs to God, His Messenger, and those united by sincere belief, and that hypocrites are blind to this deeper reality and its consequences.

translation: O you who have believed, let not your wealth nor your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that — those are the truly losing ones.
interpretation: The verse warns that worldly goods and family ties, though legitimate blessings, become spiritual liabilities when they replace or blunt a believer’s constant remembrance, worship, and moral duties toward God. It demands right prioritization: care for wealth and children is allowed, but if they cause neglect of prayer, gratitude, ethical obligations, and inward consciousness of Allah, the person suffers the real loss — failure in the sight of God and deprivation of what ultimately matters.

translation: And spend from that which We have provided you before there comes to any of you the death and he says, “My Lord, would that You would delay me for a short term so I would give charity and be among the righteous.”
interpretation: This verse admonishes against spiritual procrastination: it teaches that one must use the resources God has given now to do good and purify one’s life, because death can arrive suddenly and render last‑minute promises meaningless. The plea made at the point of dying — asking only for a brief reprieve to give charity and become righteous — exposes how habitual delay and attachment to worldly comfort can leave a person unprepared; true repentance and sincere righteous deeds require timely commitment and sustained practice, not desperate bargains at the door of death.

translation: And Allah will not delay a soul when its appointed term comes; and Allah is fully aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the timing of life and death is fixed by God’s decree and cannot be postponed by human effort, while reminding believers that God’s knowledge encompasses all actions. Its practical meaning is to cultivate readiness and moral responsibility: since death will come at its appointed time and nothing escapes God’s awareness, one should live deliberately—seeking righteousness, repentance, and good deeds—rather than relying on the illusion that one can indefinitely defer accountability.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth proclaims the glory of Allah. To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God’s sovereign authority and worthiness of praise are absolute and universal; all created things reflect His lordship. Its purpose is to reorient the believer: recognizing God’s sole ownership and praise should lead to sincere gratitude, humble submission to His will, reliance on His power in times of need, and confidence that ultimate justice and wisdom rest with Him.

translation: He is the One who created you; among you are disbelievers and among you are believers. And Allah is, regarding what you do, All‑Seeing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God, as Creator, has given human beings moral agency, and therefore their responses to guidance differ — some embrace faith and some reject it. This diversity is not a flaw in the divine plan but part of life’s test: actions and choices matter because Allah watches and knows them perfectly. The declaration that “Allah is All‑Seeing of what you do” underlines personal responsibility and the certainty of divine reckoning, calling people to sincere, conscious conduct while reminding them that God’s knowledge and justice encompass every deed and intention.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth, and fashioned you and perfected your forms; and to Him is the return.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the evident order and beauty of creation—and the deliberate excellence of the human form—point to a purposeful Creator, which grounds human dignity and moral obligation: our embodied life is a trust to be lived in awareness of God, fulfilling ethical responsibilities and stewardship, because ultimately every soul will return to God for reckoning.

translation: He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what you conceal and what you declare. And Allah is, concerning the innermost hearts, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute, intimate knowledge of both outer reality and inner intentions; nothing hidden in the mind or heart escapes Him. Practically, this means moral responsibility rests not only on outward deeds but on the sincerity and motives behind them—so one must purify intentions and remember that true recompense and accountability are based on what lies within, whether comfort for the sincere or warning for the hypocritical.

translation: ألم يأتكم نبأ الذين كفروا من قبل فذاقوا وبال أمرهم ولهم عذاب أليم
interpretation: الآية تذكّر بسابقة أقوام كفروا وواجهوا نتائج اختيارهم: خبرهم قد وصل، وقد ذاقوا عاقبة أمرهم السيئة، ولهم عذاب مؤلم. المقصود أن تجربة الأمم السابقة شهادة عملية على أن الإنكار والتمرد على هداية الله تؤدي إلى خراب الأمور في الدنيا وبلاء وعقاب في الآخرة؛ فالمستمعين يُنهاهم ذلك عن تكرار نفس السلوك ويحثّهم على التعقّل واستخلاص العبرة قبل أن يبلغهم ذات المصير.

translation: ذلك لأن رسلهم كانت تأتيهم بالبينات، فيقولون: “أبشر، يهدوننا”، فيكفرون ويتولّون. واستغنى الله، والله غني حميد.
interpretation: الآية تبيّن صورة النفاق والصلابة القلبية: أصحاب الرسالات كانوا يتلقون دلائل واضحة، فيبدون ترحيبًا أو استهزاءً بمظهر القول («أبشر يهدوننا») لكنهم في الباطن يرفضون الحق ويصرون على الضلال. النتيجة الأخروية ليست لأن الرسالة ضعيفة بل لأن قلوبهم عنيدة ومتكبِّرة، والمقابل إقرار بأن رفضهم لا ينقص من ذِكْر الله ولا من قدره — الله غني عن كل مخلوق، وحمده واجب، والهدى إنما يُمنَح بإرادة الله لا بقبول الناس الفارغ.

translation: Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be raised. Say, “Yes indeed — by my Lord — you will surely be raised; then you will be informed of what you did. And that is easy for Allah.”
interpretation: The verse confronts the denial of resurrection by asserting its certainty as a divine reality and warning of inevitable accountability: God will restore the dead and make every action manifest so each person will be confronted with the record of their deeds. By adding “that is easy for Allah” it teaches that resurrection is not a metaphysical problem but an expression of God’s sovereign power — what seems impossible to human reason is effortless for the Creator — and therefore human skepticism stems from ignorance or pride rather than from any real obstacle to God’s will. This is meant to awaken moral responsibility and humility before the coming judgment.

translation: So believe in Allah, His Messenger, and the Light which We have sent down. And Allah is, of what you do, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse commands wholehearted acceptance of God, His Messenger, and the “Light” — the revealed guidance that illuminates truth, moral clarity, and the way of life. Belief is not merely verbal assent but embracing and living by that divine guidance; the reminder that Allah is fully aware of your deeds stresses that inner faith must match outward conduct, warning against hypocrisy and calling for sincere, consistent obedience.

translation: The Day He will gather you — that is the Day of Gathering. That is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds — He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; that is the great attainment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Resurrection will disclose the true, eternal balance of loss and gain: worldly advantages can be revealed as loss if they were pursued without faith and righteousness, while sincere belief coupled with upright deeds secures mercy, the wiping away of sins, and admission to everlasting Paradise. ‘Taghabun’ therefore warns that what appears profitable in this life may ultimately be loss, and it reframes success as spiritual purification and eternal fellowship with God rather than transient worldly benefit.

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein. And wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse teaches that persistent refusal to acknowledge God’s clear revelations is not merely a factual verdict but a moral consequence: by willfully rejecting the signs, people place themselves outside the community of guidance and thereby become ‘companions of the Fire.’ The wording stresses permanence and the loss of divine mercy as the inevitable result of obstinate denial, warning that such a stance leads to an utterly ruinous end rather than a temporary chastisement.

translation: No affliction befalls except by the permission of Allah. And whoever believes in Allah—He will guide his heart. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse teaches that what we call disasters are not random catastrophes but events that occur within Allah’s sovereign decree and wisdom; for the sincere believer, faith is the means by which God steadies and directs the heart so that one finds inner guidance and tranquility amid trials. Knowing that Allah is fully aware of every reality should lead to trust and patience: believers are called to respond to adversity with reliance on God, seeking the guidance He grants to the heart rather than succumbing to despair or imagining that misfortune is meaningless.

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon Our Messenger is only the clear delivery.
interpretation: The statement limits the Prophet’s responsibility to faithfully and unmistakably conveying God’s guidance; while obedience to God and His messenger is commanded for the community, acceptance is ultimately the people’s choice. The verse therefore protects the messenger from blame for others’ rejection, emphasizes the primacy of clear proclamation over coercion, and locates moral accountability with individuals rather than with the one who delivers the message.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him. And upon Allah let the believers rely.
interpretation: By affirming God’s exclusive divinity and sovereignty, the verse makes reliance on Him the proper stance of the faithful: believers should entrust their affairs to Allah’s wisdom, power and decree. True tawakkul does not excuse effort or responsible action but frames human means as subordinate to God’s will; it yields inner peace, perseverance in hardship and contentment in success because ultimate control and provision rest with Him.

translation: O you who have believed, indeed among your wives and your children are enemies to you; so beware of them. But if you pardon, overlook, and forgive, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse warns that close family ties can become a source of spiritual danger when they lead a believer away from God—through pressure, temptation, or demanding loyalties that compromise obedience to divine guidance. It calls believers to be vigilant about priorities and boundaries: protect one’s faith even when that means resisting harmful influence from loved ones. At the same time it counsels moral restraint—if one can respond with pardon, forbearance, and forgiveness rather than hostility, that compassionate course is praiseworthy because Allah is forgiving and merciful.

translation: Indeed, your wealth and your children are only a trial; and Allah — with Him is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse teaches that material blessings and offspring are instruments of testing: they can either draw a person away from God through attachment, pride, fear, or negligence, or they can be means of spiritual success when used rightly (spent in charity, raised in righteousness, and kept in proper perspective). Thus true faith is shown not by the mere possession of wealth or children but by how one manages them in obedience to God; those who pass this trial by humility, responsible care, and generosity will find from Allah a mighty recompense.

translation: فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ ۖ وَاسْمَعُوا وَأَطِيعُوا وَأَنفِقُوا خَيْرًا لِأَنفُسِكُمْ ۗ وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ فَأُولَـٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ
interpretation: الدعوة هنا إلى تربية النفس على تقوى الله ضمن القدرة المتاحة: أن يكون المؤمن واعيًا بخشيته ومحافظًا على طاعته، مستمعًا إلى هدى الله ومطبقًا له، وأن يجعل الإنفاق عملاً في مصلحة نفسه لا هدرًا، لأن الصرف في طاعة الله هو استثمار روحي يعود بالنفع على صاحبه. والميزان الحاسم للنجاح ليس المال بحد ذاته بل التحرر من شح النفس؛ من يكسر قيود البخل ويجعل ماله وفعله طريقًا إلى مرضاة الله فهو الفائز الحقيقي — فالمفلحون هم الذين يغلبون نزعة الأنانية ويختارون الجود والطاعة فتتحقق لهم السعادة والنجاة.

translation: If you give Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you; and Allah is Appreciative, Forbearing.
interpretation: The phrase “loan to Allah” is a metaphor for sincere acts done purely for God's sake—charity, support for the community, sincere worship and sacrifice. The verse promises that such selfless giving is not lost: God will multiply its returns (in blessings, provision, spiritual gain and ultimate recompense) and will cleanse the giver by forgiving sins. Describing God as “Shakūr” (appreciative) emphasizes that even small sincere deeds are recognized and greatly recompensed; “Halīm” (forbearing) stresses His patience and mercy toward human shortcomings. The practical lesson is to give and serve without counting on immediate worldly profit, trusting that God, in His generosity and mercy, transforms such gifts into far greater and lasting good.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the seen; the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: تُشير العبارة إلى أن علم الله شاملٌ لكلِّ ما هو خفي وظاهر، وأن سلطانه وقدرته لا تُقهر، وأفعاله وتكاليفه متوائمة مع حكمٍ كاملةٍ لا يعتريها نقص. لذلك ينبغي للمؤمن أن يثق بحكمة الله وقضائه حتى في مصائب الحياة أو نوائبها، أن يسعى بالأسباب ملتزماً بالشرع، مستسلماً لقدرٍ تديره حكمةٌ وعزّةٌ إلهية تتجاوز فهمه المحدود.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their prescribed waiting period and reckon the waiting; and fear Allah, your Lord. Do not drive them out of their homes, nor should they themselves leave except in the case of obvious immorality. Those are the limits set by Allah; and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has indeed wronged himself. You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter.
interpretation: This verse instructs that divorce must be carried out with deliberation, justice and reverence for God: observe and count the prescribed ‘iddah so that rights, lineage and the possibility of reconciliation are preserved; keep divorced women in their homes during that period to protect their dignity and the welfare of any children and to prevent precipitous harm; allow them to leave only if there is clear, serious wrongdoing that justifies such a step. Framing these rules as Allah’s limits teaches that exceeding them is a moral and spiritual injury to oneself, and the warning “you do not know, perhaps Allah will bring about after that a matter” reminds believers that outcomes are ultimately in God’s hands (for example, reconciliation, a new decree, or unforeseen consequences), so decisions about separation must be made with restraint, fear of God and concern for justice.

translation:
فَإِذَا بَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ فَأَمْسِكُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ أَوْ سَرِّحُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ ۚ وَأَشْهِدُوا ذَوَيْ عَدْلٍ مِنكُمْ وَأَقِيمُوا الشَّهَادَةَ لِلَّهِ ۚ ذَٰلِكُمْ يُوعَظُ بِهِ مَن كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ ۚ وَمَن يَتَّقِ اللَّهَ يَجْعَل لَهُ مَخْرَجًا

"When they have completed their prescribed term, either retain them with kindness or release them with kindness. And call as witnesses two of you who are just, and establish the testimony for the sake of Allah. That is a reminder for whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever fears Allah—He will make for him a way out."
interpretation: This verse regulates what follows the end of a woman’s prescribed waiting period (’iddah) after separation or widowhood: the community must act with dignity, allowing either reconciliation (taking her back) or an honorable, amicable release. Requiring two just witnesses and the establishment of testimony stresses accountability and clear, truthful record-keeping so rights and obligations are protected and disputes or abuses are prevented. The injunctions are framed as moral guidance for believers—those who truly accept God and the Last Day are called to implement these rules sincerely. The promise that “whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out” links piety to practical relief: when people observe justice, honesty, and reverence for God in difficult personal and social situations, God facilitates lawful solutions, opens lawful means of relief and provision, and protects the community from the harms that arise from secrecy, injustice, or revenge.

translation: وَيَرْزُقْهُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَحْتَسِبُ. وَمَنْ يَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ فَهُوَ حَسْبُهُ. إِنَّ اللَّهَ بَالِغُ أَمْرِهِ. قَدْ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدْرًا.
interpretation: The verse assures that sincere trust in God brings provision and support from unexpected sources and that God Himself suffices for the one who truly relies on Him. It teaches that God’s plan inevitably comes to pass and that He has ordained precise measures for all things; therefore believers are invited to combine reliance with responsible effort, to find peace in God’s sufficiency, and to accept outcomes as part of a wise, divinely measured decree.

translation: And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation — if you have any doubt — their prescribed term is three months; and those who have not menstruated, and the pregnant women — their term is until they give birth to their burden. And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him an ease in his matter.
interpretation: This verse provides a practical legal ruling to remove doubt about the waiting period ('iddah) after a husband's death or divorce when the usual marker (menstrual cycles) is absent. By fixing three months for women who have passed the age of menstruation and for those who have not yet menstruated, and by making the term for pregnant women last until childbirth, the law secures clarity about lineage, rights and responsibilities (such as maintenance and inheritance) where biological signs cannot be used to calculate time. The final clause — that God, for the one who fears Him, will make his affairs easy — frames these rules within a moral assurance: adherence to God-consciousness leads to facilitation, so the legal prescriptions are meant to order life with justice and compassion rather than impose needless hardship.

translation: ذلك أمرُ اللهِ أنزلهُ إليكم؛ ومن يتقِ اللهَ يكفر عنه سيئاته ويعظّم له أجراً
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن ما نُزّل من أحكامٍ هو أمرٌ إلهي نافذ، وأن المفتاح لتحويل هذا الحكم إلى مغفرة وثواب هو التقوى — أي الخوف من الله والالتزام بما يرضيه بصدق. فمن كان خائفًا من الله ومجاهدًا لنفسه في الطاعة، فإن الله يمحو أو يغطي سيئاته ويزيد له جزاءً عظيماً؛ أي أن التقوى لا تُقتصر على أداء شعائر بل تثمر عفواً إلهياً وتكريماً وثوابًا متضاعفًا.

translation: Provide them (wives/ex-wives) with lodging in the place where you live, according to your means, and do not cause them harm so as to make life difficult for them. And if they are pregnant, then spend on them until they deliver their burden; and if they breastfeed for you, then give them their due wages. And consult between yourselves kindly; and if you find difficulty, then another woman shall nurse for him.
interpretation: The verse mandates humane, equitable responsibility toward women and children in family affairs: men must ensure suitable housing and maintenance according to their capacity, must not subject women to deliberate hardship, must continue support through pregnancy, must compensate those who nurse the child, and must make decisions by mutual consultation and kindness; where direct breastfeeding cannot be arranged, an alternative caregiver is to be provided. In short, the passage grounds family law in protection of dignity, economic responsibility, and compassionate cooperation.

translation: Let the one who has means spend according to his means; and whoever is constrained in his provision—let him spend out of what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden any soul except what He has bestowed upon it. Allah will surely, after hardship, grant ease.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of proportional responsibility and divine justice: moral and legal obligations (such as maintenance, support, or charity) are to be met in accordance with each person’s capacity. The wealthy are urged to give from their abundance, while those with limited means are required only to give from what Allah has provided them, for God does not impose duties beyond a person’s ability. Coupled with the promise that God will bring ease after hardship, the verse both tempers demands with mercy and enjoins social solidarity—encouraging compassion from those who can afford it and offering reassurance to those who are constrained.

translation: And how many a town defied the command of its Lord and His messengers; so We exacted from it a severe reckoning and afflicted it with a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse warns that when a community arrogantly rejects God’s guidance and the warnings brought by His messengers, divine justice will be comprehensive and decisive: their wrongful pride and persistent rebellion lead not merely to abstract blame but to tangible, often public, consequences that strip them of honor and security. The account and punishment described are meant both as a manifestation of God’s authority over social order and as a moral lesson — past destructions show that persistent collective disobedience carries communal ramifications that should prompt repentance and adherence to righteous conduct.

translation: So she tasted the calamity of her affair, and the end of her affair was loss.
interpretation: The verse warns that obstinacy in wrongdoing and rejection of guidance inevitably brings its own consequences: transient pleasures or power may be followed by immediate suffering (the ‘calamity’ tasted), and ultimately by definitive loss — spiritual failure, the forfeiture of lasting good, and the withdrawal of God’s mercy. It is a reminder that choices have moral and eschatological outcomes, so one must turn from error to avoid ruin.

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. So fear Allah, O people of understanding who have believed; indeed Allah has sent down to you a reminder.
interpretation: The verse connects a solemn warning about retribution for wrongdoers with an exhortation addressed specifically to thoughtful believers: because God has delivered clear guidance as a reminder, those who possess understanding bear the greater duty to respond with God‑consciousness. In other words, receiving revelation is not neutral knowledge but a charge—‘people of intellect’ are called to internalize the reminder, reform their conduct, and remain vigilant against the errors that brought punishment upon others, for awareness of the truth increases moral responsibility.

translation: A Messenger who recites to you the clear verses of Allah, to bring out those who believe and do righteous deeds from darkness into light. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds — He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. Indeed Allah has made for him excellent provision.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the purpose of revelation and the Prophet’s recitation is transformative: when people accept true faith and back it with righteous action, God delivers them from spiritual and moral darkness into His illuminating guidance. That union of faith and deed guarantees the ultimate, enduring reward (paradise) and is itself a completion of God’s bounty — a perfected provision that manifests both as final salvation and as the sufficiency/blessing granted along the way.

translation: It is Allah who created the seven heavens and, of the earth, the like of them. His command descends among them so that you may know that Allah is over all things competent, and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge.
interpretation: The verse stresses God’s absolute sovereignty and order in the cosmos: the ‘seven heavens’ and their counterparts on earth point to a structured, mirrored creation in which divine authority operates. The phrase that His “command descends among them” signifies that God’s laws, decrees and governance pervade every domain—natural processes, moral order and ultimate judgment—so that people may recognize that nothing lies beyond His power and nothing escapes His knowledge. The intended effect is to move human beings to acknowledge divine mastery, to trust the wisdom manifest in creation, and to live with humility and responsibility under God’s encompassing knowledge and authority.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: God is admonishing the Prophet to show that personal vows or concessions made to placate others must not override what Allah has permitted; one should not let family pressure or private motives turn lawful things into prohibited ones. The verse teaches that leaders and believers must uphold divine guidance above personal accommodations, and that if one errs in this way repentance is possible because Allah is forgiving and merciful.

translation: Allah has prescribed for you the expiation of your oaths; and Allah is your Protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.
interpretation: God is teaching that He has, out of His knowledge and wisdom, laid down clear, measured remedies to remove the moral and legal burden when people fail to keep oaths; by calling Himself your Mawla (guardian/protector) and naming His attributes of knowledge and wisdom, the verse reassures believers that the law is mercifully calibrated—holding people accountable while providing practical, equitable ways to repair wrongs and preserve communal justice and compassion.

translation: And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives and she informed [another] of it, and Allah made it known to him, he made known part of it and turned away from part. Then when he told her about it, she said, “Who told you this?” He said, “The All‑Knower, the All‑Aware informed me.”
interpretation: This verse teaches that breaches of trust and the spread of private talk produce harm and discord, and that divine guidance can uncover truth to protect the integrity of the Prophet and the community. It therefore enjoins honoring confidentiality, avoiding gossip and jealousy, and submitting to God’s clarification—recognizing Allah’s knowledge and wisdom as the ultimate source that rectifies human faults and restores justice.

translation: إن تتوبا إلى الله فقد صغت قلوبكما، وإن تظاهرا عليه فإن الله هو مولاه وجبريل وصالح المؤمنين، والملائكة بعد ذلك ظهير.
interpretation: الآية تظهر مبدأ أخلاقي و‑عقائدي: التوبة الصادقة علامة على استقامة القلب، بينما التآمر على مظلوم يوقظ نظام نصرة إلهي‑مؤسسي — فالله لا يترك من يُظلَم بل يهيئ له نصراً عبر وسائط معروفة: رسوليته (ممثلةً بجبرائيل)، جماعة المؤمنين الصالحين، ثم الدعم الملائكي. المقصود أن الاعتماد يجب أن يكون على إصلاح النفس والتوبة بدل المكائد، وأن المتآمرين يواجهون حكم التاريخ الإلهي الذي يعيد العدل بواسطة أدوات بشرية وسماوية.

translation:
عَسَىٰ رَبُّهُۥٓ إِن طَلَّقْكُنَّ أَن يُبْدِلَهُۥٓ أَزْوَٰجًا خَيْرًا مِّنكُنَّ مُّسْلِمَٰتٍۢ مُؤْمِنَٰتٍۢ قَٰنِتَٰتٍۢ تَٰٓئِبَٰتٍ عَٰبِدَٰتٍ سَٰئِحَٰتٍ ثَيِّبَٰتٍۢ وَأَبْكَٰرًا

"It may be that his Lord, if He divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you — Muslim, believing, devoutly submissive, repentant, worshipping, traveling about, mature (previously married), and virgins."
interpretation: The verse functions as a solemn admonition: divine favor and nearness to God's messenger are not guaranteed by status or privilege but by inner faith and righteous conduct. By listing virtues — submission to God, genuine belief, devoted obedience, sincere repentance, devoted worship, readiness to move or serve for God’s cause, and moral chastity whether mature or virgin — the verse teaches that Allah values spiritual qualities and service over social rank. It warns against complacency or misconduct and calls the addressed to self-examination and reform, reminding them that God can replace outward honor with people who embody true piety.

translation: O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones; over it are (appointed) angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.
interpretation: The verse is an urgent command that faith must be translated into active protection: believers are required not only to guard their own souls but to take responsibility for guiding and shielding their households from Hell. This guarding includes believing, doing righteous deeds, teaching and commanding good while forbidding evil, arranging a moral environment, and preventing behaviours that lead to disbelief and sin. The image of a Fire whose fuel is people and stones stresses the seriousness and reality of the punishment, and the description of obedient, severe angels emphasizes that divine judgment is certain and carried out without fail — so one must not be complacent but must take practical spiritual measures for oneself and one’s family.

translation: O you who have disbelieved, make no excuse this Day; you will only be recompensed for what you used to do.
interpretation: Addressing those who rejected faith, the verse warns that at the final reckoning all attempts at excuses will be futile: on the Day of Judgment reality and accountability will prevail, and each person will receive recompense strictly according to their deeds and choices. ‘Today’ signifies the moment when private rationalizations and worldly deceptions fall away, so that justice is exacted based on actual conduct and inner intentions reflected in those actions.

translation: O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow. On a Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him— their light will run ahead of them and by their right hands— they will say, “Our Lord, complete for us our light and forgive us; indeed, You are over all things competent.”
interpretation: This verse calls the believer to a radical, truthful return to God (tawbah nasuh) — repentance that is sincere, irreversible, and accompanied by abandoning the causes of sin and repairing its effects. Such repentance opens the door to divine pardon and the ultimate reward: entrance into gardens of eternal bliss. The image of “their light running before them and by their right hands” expresses both inner guidance and visible honor: faith and righteous deeds become a luminous, guiding reality that leads and testifies for the believer on the Day of Judgment, marking dignity and vindication (hence Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and the faithful). Even in that triumph the believers remain humble and seeking: they ask God to perfect and increase that light and to forgive them, acknowledging that final attainment depends solely on God’s power and mercy. Thus the verse teaches that genuine repentance transforms one’s moral condition, produces guiding light in this life and the next, and fosters continuous dependence on God’s mercy rather than complacency.

translation: O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites and be harsh with them; their refuge is Hell — and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to actively oppose both external opponents of the message and those within the community who feign belief while working against it. "جاهد" (strive/fight) here denotes determined resistance — by word, policy, and, where necessary, firm defensive measures — to prevent subversion of the community and its mission. "اغلظ عليهم" (be harsh with them) calls for resolute, uncompromising leadership rather than softness or appeasement toward forces that threaten the integrity of the faith. The warning that their abode is Hell and that it is a dreadful end stresses the moral and eschatological seriousness of hypocrisy and disbelief: it is both a communal danger to be checked and a spiritual error with dire consequences. Overall the verse is a call to principled firmness in defending the community and upholding the truth.

translation: ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلاً لِّلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا امْرَأَتَ نُوحٍ وَامْرَأَتَ لُوطٍ ۖ كَانَتَا تَحْتَ عَبْدَيْنِ مِنْ عِبَادِنَا صَالِحَيْنِ فَخَانَتَاهُمَا فَلَمْ يُغْنِيَا عَنْهُمَا مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيْئًا وَقِيلَ ادْخُلَا النَّارَ مَعَ الدَّاخِلِينَ
interpretation: The verse teaches that proximity to piety, authority or righteous people does not substitute for one’s own faith and moral choice. The word “betrayed” signals active treachery—rejecting, opposing, or undermining the truth they were privy to—so their relation to God’s servants could not avert divine judgment. The passage warns against relying on family ties, social status, or association with the righteous as guarantees of salvation; accountability is individual, and true protection is attained only through sincere belief and submission to God.

translation: And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, “My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds and save me from the unjust people.”
interpretation: This verse holds up the wife of Pharaoh as a paradigm of sincere faith and courageous reliance on God despite living amid oppression. Though surrounded by power and idolatry, she recognized that true security and reward are with Allah, so she petitioned for a dwelling ‘near You’ in Paradise rather than worldly protection. Her plea—asking deliverance not only from Pharaoh himself but from his actions and from the corrupt society around her—shows a comprehensive rejection of tyranny and a turning to God as the sole refuge. The example is meant to inspire believers to prioritize inner conviction, to seek closeness to God, and to trust in Him even when doing so entails personal risk within a hostile environment.

translation:
وَمَرْيَمُ ابْنَتُ عِمْرَانَ الَّتِي أَحْصَنَتْ فَرْجَهَا فَنَفَخْنَا فِيهَا مِن رُّوحِنَا وَصَدَّقَتْ بِكَلِمَاتِ رَبِّهَا وَكُتُبِهِ وَكَانَتْ مِنَ الْقَانِتِينَ
"And Mary, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity — so We breathed into her of Our Spirit — and she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devout."
interpretation: This verse elevates Mary as an exemplar of purity, sincere faith, and steadfast devotion. Her guarded chastity and wholehearted acceptance of God’s word made her the worthy recipient of a singular divine act: by God’s creative command He imparted life into the unborn child through His “spirit” (a designation of God’s life‑giving power), producing a miraculous birth without implying any partnership in God’s essence. The term qanitin (the devout) stresses her continual, humble obedience and worship — the moral and spiritual disposition that prepared her to receive and submit to this extraordinary mercy from God.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's complete and exclusive sovereignty and omnipotence as the framework for human life: it urges believers to anchor their trust and fear in Him alone, to understand that worldly power and outcomes are ultimately contingent on His will, and therefore to live with humility, moral responsibility, reliance on God, and consciousness of accountability before the One who governs all affairs.

translation: He who created death and life to test you — which of you is best in deed — and He is the Exalted in Might, the Oft-Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the existence of life and the certainty of death are deliberate means by which God assesses moral character: not merely who professes faith, but who actualizes it in righteous, persevering, and sincere conduct. “Best in deed” stresses the quality, consistency, and intention behind actions (including patience under trials, justice, charity, and repentance), showing that worldly life is an arena for moral development and accountability. Naming God al‑‘Azīz (Mighty) and al‑Ghafūr (Forgiving) balances His absolute power to enact judgment with His readiness to pardon those who turn back in sincere repentance, underscoring both responsibility and hope in the divine scheme of testing.

translation: He who created the seven heavens, layered one above another. You see no incongruity in the creation of the Most Merciful. So turn your sight again: do you see any rift?
interpretation: The verse urges contemplative re-examination of the cosmos: the ordered, seamless arrangement of the heavens is presented as evidence of a single, wise Creator. By insisting that no flaw or discontinuity is visible in the creation, it argues against ideas of chance, multiple gods, or imperfection in divine action, and calls the observer to recognize God’s unity, wisdom and providential control through attentive reflection.

translation: Then turn back your sight twice; your sight will return to you humbled and exhausted.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the arrogant denier: even if he scrutinizes the signs repeatedly, his eyes will be brought back defeated and powerless — repeated looking will not bolster his pride or prevent the humiliation that comes when faced with the truth of God's power and the reality of resurrection.

translation: And indeed We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them missiles for the devils; and We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the visible lights of the lowermost heaven — described as ‘lamps’ — are both an adornment and an active means by which God prevents rebellious jinn (the “devils”) from eavesdropping on the heavenly realm: burning projectiles or meteoric phenomena are portrayed as instruments that repel or punish those intruders. In this way the cosmic order manifests divine authority and protection, and the final clause warns that such disorderly, defiant beings who persist in rebellion will face a prepared, severe recompense (the Blaze), underscoring accountability for transgression against God’s command and the harmony He has established.

translation: And for those who disbelieved in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse asserts that persistent rejection of God brings an inevitable, just consequence: such people will receive the torment of Jahannam. Calling it a “wretched destination” stresses both the certainty and the utter misery of that end, conveying a moral and theological lesson about divine justice, accountability, and the grave spiritual cost of turning away from God’s guidance.

translation: When they are cast into it, they will hear it emit a convulsive cry while it seethes.
interpretation: The verse uses audible, violent imagery to show that the punishment of Hell is a concrete, overwhelming reality: the fire itself seems to convulse and roar and the inmates experience agonized, gasping cries as it continually boils. This emphasizes the intensity, relentlessness and inescapability of divine retribution—its effects are not merely physical pain but a public, unmistakable sign of utter humiliation and final loss for those within.

translation: It almost bursts with fury; whenever a company is thrown into it, its guardians ask them, “Did no warner come to you?”
interpretation: The verse portrays Hell as overflowing with rage and shows its keepers confronting each group cast into it with a question about whether a messenger or warning ever reached them. Its meaning is to emphasize moral responsibility: the condemned are not punished for mere ignorance but for having been warned — through prophets, clear signs, or admonitions — and yet persisting in denial or heedlessness. The rhetorical question underlines that the evidence against them is plain, making their accountability and the justice of the punishment unmistakable.

translation: They will say, “Yes — a warner did come to us, but we denied him, and we said, ‘Nothing has been revealed by Allah; you are only in great error.’”
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring moral pattern: people reject clear guidance out of pride, convenience, or social attachment and then rationalize that rejection by denying the possibility of divine revelation or by accusing the messenger of error. That self‑deception hardens the heart so that even a later admission of a “warner” is too late to undo the consequences. The passage thus warns that persistent denial born of arrogance or habit is itself a grave misguidance and that truthful recognition must be timely and sincere, not a retrospective excuse.

translation:
وَقَالُوا لَوْ كُنَّا نَسْمَعُ أَوْ نَعْقِلُ مَا كُنَّا فِي أَصْحَابِ السَّعِيرِ
“And they will say, ‘If only we had listened or used our reason, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze.’”
interpretation: The verse depicts the futile, belated remorse of the doomed: it teaches that guidance was offered through signs, admonitions and one’s own faculties, and that salvation requires actively attending (listening) and reflecting (using reason). Their complaint shows that neglect, heedlessness, or deliberate rejection of guidance during life—despite opportunities to hear and to think—brought them to punishment; recognition after the fact cannot alter the consequences of choices made when change was still possible.

translation: So they will confess to their sin; doomed are the companions of the Blaze.
interpretation: When the guilty stand before their Lord they will acknowledge their wrongdoing, and that confession shows both their responsibility and the righteousness and inevitability of their punishment in Hell—underscoring the certainty of divine justice.

translation: Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen — for them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: “Fearing their Lord in the unseen” means maintaining a sincere, inner God‑consciousness that shapes one’s private motives and conduct rather than performing piety for public recognition. This hidden reverence restrains one from wrongdoing, fosters humility and obedience, and reflects true accountability before God. Because such fear is genuine and not merely outward, God grants these people pardon for their faults and a vast recompense — a substantial divine reward in the hereafter and spiritual blessings in this life.

translation: Whether you conceal your speech or declare it openly, He is, truly, Aware of what lies in the inmost hearts.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's complete and intimate knowledge of both outward words and hidden intentions; because nothing inward escapes His sight, moral responsibility and divine judgement are tied not only to visible actions but to the motives and sincerity behind them. This teaching comforts those who suffer privately by assuring them their inner states are known and justly weighed, and it warns hypocrites and deceivers that outward appearances cannot hide corrupt or dishonest intentions from God.

translation:
أَلَا يَعْلَمُ مَنْ خَلَقَ وَهُوَ اللَّطِيفُ الْخَبِيرُ
"Does He who created not know? — and He is the Subtle, the All‑Aware."
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question to remind listeners that the Creator fully knows His creation in every detail. Calling God al‑Latif emphasizes His subtle care and the delicate, unseen manner in which He sustains, tests and guides beings; calling Him al‑Khabir affirms His perfect awareness of outward deeds and inner intentions. The implication is both warning and consolation: no action or hidden motive escapes Divine knowledge, so people should neither rely on concealment nor despair of God’s compassionate, discerning attention.

translation: He is the One who has made the earth subservient to you; so traverse its expanses and eat of His provision. And to Him is the Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God has made the earth available and manageable for human life—enabling movement, settlement and access to resources—and thus encourages seeking livelihood and benefit from creation. This facilitation carries moral weight: using the earth’s provisions should be done with gratitude, moderation and stewardship, mindful that provision is from God and that all will return to Him for judgment on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: Do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up — and behold, it trembles?
interpretation: The verse reproaches those who take their safety for granted and trust in worldly stability as if it were independent of God’s will. It asserts God’s absolute sovereignty over the earth: what seems firm and secure can be overturned at His command, whether by literal calamity (earthquakes, sinking) or by sudden social/political ruin. The warning is moral and existential — to abandon complacency, recognize human vulnerability, and return to humility, awareness of divine power, and upright conduct before a sudden overturning of one’s apparent security occurs.

translation: Or do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not send upon you a shower of stones? Soon you will know what sort of a warner We are.
interpretation: The verse warns against complacency and false security in the face of God’s absolute sovereignty over the heavens and the world. Those who dismiss divine warning and assume they are safe from God’s power are reminded that punishment can come suddenly and from unexpected means; when it occurs they will recognize the truth of the warning and regret their prior arrogance. The practical lesson is to heed the warnings of God and His messengers, cultivate humility before divine authority, and not rely on presumed protection from consequences one has earned.

translation: And indeed those before them denied — so how severe was My chastisement!
interpretation: The verse is a stern warning: by recalling that previous peoples who rejected their messengers were met with a decisive, grave divine response (نَكِير as severe chastisement or repudiation), it uses a rhetorical question to make clear that persistent denial brings inevitable ruin; meant to compel the listener to heed the warning, repent, and recognize the certainty of God’s justice manifesting in history.

translation: Do they not see the birds above them, spreading (in rows) and contracting? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed He is, of all things, Seeing.
interpretation: The verse points to a concrete sign in nature — the effortless balance and motion of birds — to teach a theological lesson: the order and sustenance of the world are not self-sustaining but depend continually on God’s sustaining mercy and power. What appears as natural habit or force is in reality upheld by Divine will, and because God is fully aware of every detail (“seeing” all things), this dependence calls people to humility, trust in divine providence, and awareness that nothing escapes God’s knowledge or care.

translation:
أَمِنْ هَذَا الَّذِي هُوَ جُنْدٌ لَّكُمْ يَنصُرُكُمْ مِنْ دُونِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ ۚ إِنَّ الْكَافِرِينَ إِلَّا فِي غُرُورٍ
“Is it this one — who is but a host for you — that will help you against the Most Merciful? Indeed the disbelievers are only in delusion.”
interpretation: The verse censures those who place their trust in created protectors (idols, leaders, or worldly forces) instead of God, by rhetorically asking whether any such 'host' can actually defend them against the power and decree of the All‑Merciful; it asserts that denying God’s sovereignty and relying on these substitutes is a self‑deceiving illusion that misleads the disbelievers.

translation: Is He — the One who provides for you — that if He were to withhold His provision from you? Rather, they have persisted in insolence and aversion.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, despite being sustained by God, behave as if they are independent and unaccountable. By posing the rhetorical question about God withholding provision, it highlights human dependence on divine sustenance and exposes the folly of ingratitude: instead of humbly recognizing this dependence or showing patience if tested, the wicked respond with ʿutuw (arrogant transgression) and nufūr (turning away or repulsion) — obstinate denial and fleeing from the truth.

translation: Is one who walks prostrate on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?
interpretation: The image of walking “prostrate on his face” stands for a person overcome by heedlessness, error, or slavish attachment to base desires—thus stumbling toward ruin—whereas walking “upright on a straight path” signifies someone guided by God’s revelation and moral clarity, moving steadily toward truth and salvation; the verse therefore asserts, rhetorically, that true guidance and success belong to those who follow the straight path, not to those consumed by misguidance.

translation: Say, “He is the One who produced you and made for you hearing, sight and hearts; little are you grateful.”
interpretation: This verse reproaches human ingratitude by pointing out that God is the originator who endowed people with the basic faculties needed to perceive, understand and choose. Hearing, sight and “hearts” stand for the means by which we receive information, reflect, form conscience and respond morally. The reminder is moral and existential: these gifts carry an obligation to seek truth, recognize God’s signs, live rightly and express gratitude—not merely by words but by rightly using our senses and intellect in obedience, justice and thankfulness. The phrase “little are you grateful” highlights how often people take these blessings for granted, misuse them, or fail to let them lead to sincere acknowledgment and responsible action.

translation: Say, “He is the One who produced you on the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.”
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s exclusive role as the Originator who brought humanity into existence and spread them across the earth, and it reminds that earthly life is transient: all people will ultimately be convened before God to account for their deeds, underscoring human dependence, divine sovereignty, and the certainty of return.

translation: And they say, “When will this promise be, if you are truthful?”
interpretation: عبارةٌ تُدلّ على سخريةِ المتكلمين واعتراضِهم، طلبُهم لميعادٍ محددٍ كشرطٍ لاختبار صدق النبيّ يكشف عن عنادهم وإنكارهم المتمّدد: يريدون تأجيل الحساب ورفع الشكّ عن أنفسهم بوضع شروطٍ ومواعيدٍ؛ فالكلام هنا يبيّن رفضهم للمسؤولية ورغبتهم في إبطال الإنذار بالتشكيك في مصداقية الرسول بدلاً من قبول الحقّ.

translation: Say: "Knowledge is only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."
interpretation: The verse affirms that ultimate and unseen knowledge belongs solely to God, while the messenger’s role is limited to conveying God’s guidance and warning people plainly; it teaches humility about human certainty, reliance on divine wisdom, and attentiveness to the Prophet’s clear admonition rather than expecting him to possess independent, hidden knowledge.

translation: So when they saw it drawing near, the faces of those who disbelieved were distressed, and it was said, "This is what you used to call for."
interpretation: When the promised reality (the Hour or the decisive punishment) actually approached, the disbelievers’ true dread and disgrace became plain to see; the very thing they had mocked, demanded as proof, or longed for in defiance of the truth has now come upon them, so their earlier scoffing and challenges are shown to have led only to their own ruin.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if Allah were to destroy me and those with me, or have mercy upon us, then who would protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?'
interpretation: This rhetorical challenge exposes the impotence of any power other than God: ultimate fate—destruction, mercy, and punishment—belongs to Allah alone, so those who trust in idols, allies, or worldly means are deluding themselves about their security. It calls people to recognize divine sovereignty, to abandon false assurances, and to understand that neither the removal nor the preservation of the Prophet and his followers would alter God’s just ability to hold the disbelievers to account.

translation: Say, “He is the Most Merciful. We have believed in Him and upon Him we have relied.” Soon you will know who is in manifest error.
interpretation: The verse is a confident declaration of faith and reliance: the believers affirm God’s attribute of Mercy, state their genuine acceptance of Him, and entrust their affairs to Him. It also contains a warning to opponents that truth will be vindicated by what follows — by outcomes, signs, and eventual accountability — so those who persist in denial will be exposed as being in obvious, unmistakable error.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if your water were to sink/vanish, then who will bring you a flowing (spring) water?'
interpretation: By posing a simple, imaginable contingency about the loss of water, the verse aims to expose human helplessness and overturn any presumption of self-sufficiency: control over the sources of life is not in human hands but in God's. It invites humility and recognition that provision and the workings of nature depend on the Divine will, serving as a warning to those who deny God’s power and a call to trust, gratitude, and submission to the One who sustains life.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Nun. By the pen and by what they write.
interpretation: God’s solemn oath by “the pen” and by what is inscribed elevates the written word and the faculty of recording as instruments of truth and accountability. The pen stands for human reason, learning and communication, while the writings—revelation, testimony, deeds—are lasting records that will be examined. By swearing on them God affirms the reliability and importance of preserved knowledge, vindicates the Prophet’s conveyed message against charges of fabrication, and warns that what is penned and transmitted carries moral and eschatological consequence.

translation: بنعمة ربك أنت لست بمجنون.
interpretation: الآية تقرّ صراحةً بأن الاتهام بالجنون باطل: النبي ليس مختلاً عقليًا بل ما ينطق به ويبلّغه من وحي وخلق حسن هو من فضائل الله عليه، فتصرفاته وكلامه مبنيان على هداية إلهية ومعيار صحيح، وأي تحميل له تهمة الجنون هو إنكار لهذه النعمة وادعاء باطل من خصومه.

translation: And indeed, for you is a reward that will never be cut off.
interpretation: God reassures the Prophet that he will receive a generous, continuous divine recompense—not a begrudged or limited favour of this world but an abundant, enduring reward from Allah (ultimately manifested in everlasting good in the hereafter and in the permanent honour and benefit of his mission). The phrase "غير ممنون" emphasizes that this gift is not withheld or grudgingly given but freely and perpetually bestowed.

translation: And indeed, you are of a great moral character.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Prophet’s personal conduct embodies the highest ethical standard—his truthfulness, patience, compassion, humility, and restraint are not accidental but integral to his mission. This exemplary character both validates the divine message he brings and serves as the practical model for believers: the faith is lived through noble behavior, not merely proclaimed in words.

translation: So you will see, and they will see.
interpretation: The phrase affirms that the reality of God’s message and its consequences will become manifest and undeniable: the Messenger (and the believing witness) will witness God’s vindication and the unfolding of His signs, and the rejecters will also behold the outcome—whether in clear worldly events or on the Day of Reckoning—so that the truth stands exposed and cannot be evaded.

translation: Which of you is to be the one tested?
interpretation: A warning that among people some will be singled out for trial, temptation or disgrace because of their rejection of guidance; it calls for sober self-examination and humility, reminding that outward status does not protect one from becoming 'al-maftūn'—the one who is led astray or exposed by his deeds.

translation: Indeed, your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best those who are rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse teaches that divine knowledge alone penetrates people’s inner states and true spiritual condition: outward behavior can deceive, but God alone knows who has genuinely gone astray and who is rightly guided. Consequently, human judgments about others’ salvation or failure are limited; believers are urged to act with humility and patience in inviting to truth, to avoid arrogance or despair, and to entrust ultimate judgment and the granting of guidance to God’s perfect wisdom and justice.

translation: فَلَا تُطِعِ الْمُكَذِّبِينَ — So do not obey the deniers.
interpretation: A command to refuse to follow, submit to, or be influenced by those who reject God’s message: do not let their denial, ridicule, or pressure divert you from proclaiming and adhering to the truth and carrying out God’s guidance.

translation: They wish that you would be conciliatory, so that they too would be conciliatory.
interpretation: This describes people who want the Prophet to relax or compromise the divine ruling; their hope is that if he softens, they can pretend to comply and thereby escape full accountability—their apparent willingness to follow is conditional and self-serving, not born of genuine submission.

translation: And do not obey every worthless, habitually oath‑swearing person.
interpretation: This is a moral and practical injunction not to be swayed by those who use profuse oaths, coarse language, or bluster to assert authority. Such people are described as low in character and unreliable; their loud swearing often masks vanity, deceit, or a readiness to coerce. The verse warns the Prophet and the community to judge leaders and advisors by honesty, wisdom, and integrity rather than by bombastic speech or ostentatious oaths, and to refuse compliance with demands or influences coming from those whose conduct and trustworthiness are contemptible.

translation: هَمَّازٍ مَّشَّاءٍ بِنَّمِيمٍ — A slanderer, one who goes about (to spread it), a gossip-monger.
interpretation: The phrase condemns the habitual defamer who moves from person to person spreading malicious talk and secrets; it indicts the moral vice of delighting in damaging others’ reputations and warns that such persistent backbiting and slander are morally corrupting actions that draw divine displeasure and eventual punishment.

translation: مَنِيعٌ لِلْخَيْرِ، مُعْتَدٍ، آثِمٌ
interpretation: يصف ثلاث سمات لواحد قلبه معطّل عن الإحسان: يمنع الخير عمداً أو يعيق التماس العون للناس، يتجاوز الحدود بالظلم أو الاعتداء، ويصرُّ على الذنب دون توبة. التركيب يشير إلى أن هذه ليست أخطاء عرضية بل مواقف متعمدة تقوّس عن الرحمة والعدالة وتُضعِف النسيج الاجتماعي، مما يجعل صاحبه مسؤولاً أخلاقياً ومرتكباً لاستحقاق العقاب الرباني.

translation: عَتِلٌ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ زَنِيمٌ — A wretched, contemptible person thereafter.
interpretation: The phrase singles out an individual whose true, ignoble character emerges after some turning point: someone who proves ungrateful, dishonorable and base despite prior appearances. The warning is ethical and social — outward rank or temporary advantage does not redeem inner corruption, and such moral failure exposes a person to disgrace and divine accountability.

translation: عندما كان ذا مالٍ وبنين.
interpretation: تشير العبارة إلى شخص اعتمد على ثراءه وذريته كمصدر للأمان والهيبة فاغترّ بالدنيا وغفل عن واجباته تجاه الله والآخرة — فالثروة والأبناء لا يغنيان عن حساب الله ولا يمنعان من عقاب أو جزاء الآخرة إذا صحبتهما الغفلة أو الباطل.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Legends of the former peoples."
interpretation: It indicts the reaction of hypocritical or hostile hearers who, confronted with divine revelation, contemptuously label it as mere ancient stories—a rhetorical move to dismiss and delegitimize God's message out of prejudice and stubborn refusal to accept guidance.

translation: We will brand him on the snout.
interpretation: The phrase conveys a promise of humiliating, unmistakable retribution: to be ‘‘branded on the snout’’ symbolizes a visible, permanent mark of guilt and disgrace that cannot be hidden. It emphasizes that the wrongdoer will be publicly exposed and punished, the reality and finality of divine accountability for persistent denial and transgression.

translation: Indeed We tested them just as We tested the companions of the Garden when they swore, “We will surely pluck from it in the morning.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that God uses apparent prosperity and certainty as a test to reveal people’s true inner states: whether they respond with gratitude and humble dependence on God or with boastful self-reliance and ingratitude. What seems like secure ownership or certain success can be withdrawn to expose character, so the verse warns against prideful trust in one’s own plans and calls for recognition of God as the ultimate source of provision and outcome.

translation: And they will not exempt anyone.
interpretation: It means that when divine judgment or a decisive decree arrives, no one will be able to claim special treatment or be spared by virtue of status, kinship, or influence; accountability will be universal and unavoidable.

translation: And a company from your Lord will circle it while they are asleep.
interpretation: It signifies that God dispatches groups of angels to attend and surround the inhabitants of that realm even during their sleep, showing that their rest is under continual divine care and honor: blessings, praise and mercy reach them without interruption, making their repose a state of perfect peace and dignity rather than neglect or fear.

translation: So she became like a consuming blaze.
interpretation: Here “الصريم” is understood as a fierce, rapidly devouring flame; the phrase therefore conveys that the one spoken of was transformed from a prior state of standing or pride into utter, swift destruction and humiliation — overwhelmed and consumed suddenly and completely, like something taken by a ravenous fire.

translation: So they called one another at dawn.
interpretation: The phrase signals deliberate postponement until daylight so that matters can be examined and decided with clarity and calm; calling at dawn here illustrates human prudence—seeking the light and cooler judgment of morning to settle disputes or to take action responsibly rather than acting hastily in darkness or passion.

translation: Go forth to your tillage in the morning, if you are resolute.
interpretation: A rhetorical dismissal to those who reject the message: if you insist on clinging to your worldly pursuits and obstinately deny the truth, then go and tend your fields — your stubbornness will not avert the coming judgment nor make your worldly labor a substitute for accepting guidance.

translation: So they set out, speaking softly among themselves.
interpretation: The phrase depicts a cautious, discreet departure: lowering their voices reflects fear, shame, or prudence to avoid detection or provocation. It teaches that in sensitive or dangerous situations people may act quietly and that discretion can be a wise response when openness would bring harm or escalate conflict.

translation: أن لا يدخلنها اليوم عليكم مسكين — that none of them, not even a poor person, will enter it for you today.
interpretation: The phrase conveys that on the Day of Reckoning no one can gain admittance or change another’s fate on someone else’s behalf; each person’s standing is determined by their own deeds, so neither poverty nor another’s plea will admit you or spare you from the consequence that is due.

translation: And they set out at dawn, enraged and able.
interpretation: The verse depicts people who, having been consumed by anger, go forth early with the power and readiness to carry out their intent; it warns that moral culpability is intensified when hostile passion is coupled with capacity for action, condemning the readiness to turn strength into aggression and oppression.

translation: So when they saw it, they said, “Indeed, we are surely astray.”
interpretation: Upon encountering the clear sign mentioned, the people recognize that their prior beliefs or conduct were wrong and openly admit they had departed from the right path — a belated confession of being misguided and in need of guidance.

translation: Nay — rather, we are deprived.
interpretation: A defensive declaration: the speakers deny the prior claim and insist that they themselves are cut off from good and divine favor, portraying themselves as bereft of blessings, comfort, or promised reward.

translation: قال أوسطهم: «ألم أقل لكم لِمَ لا تُسَبِّحُونَ؟» — “The one in their midst said, ‘Did I not tell you — why do you not glorify (Allah)?’”
interpretation: A central figure reproaches the others for failing to engage in tasbih (glorifying God), reminding them that he had warned them beforehand; the verse teaches that sincere faith involves continual remembrance of Allah, and that ignoring admonition to praise and sanctify Him—especially after being reminded—is a blameworthy lapse that reflects moral and spiritual neglect.

translation: They said, “Glory be to our Lord; indeed we were wrongdoers.”
interpretation: The phrase models sincere repentance: first glorifying God (declaring His purity from any defect or blame) and then openly admitting personal guilt. By putting God’s transcendence before confession, the speakers refuse to excuse their fault or shift blame, take full responsibility for their actions, and turn humbly to God for mercy. Thus the verse teaches that true return to God combines praise of Him with honest self-accounting and reliance on His forgiveness.

translation: Then some of them turned toward one another, reproaching each other.
interpretation: The verse shows that when people confront the consequences of their wrongdoing or denial, they break into mutual recrimination instead of taking responsibility; their blaming of one another reveals regret, confusion, and the collapse of solidarity that follows rejection of guidance, and it demonstrates that such mutual reproach neither undoes their harm nor saves them.

translation: They will say, “O woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors.”
interpretation: The verse captures the belated recognition of those who lived in arrogance and disobedience: confronted by divine judgment they confess their wrongdoing, admitting they exceeded bounds and oppressed themselves or others. The tone shows that such remorse, expressed only at the point of punishment, comes too late to avert consequences; thus the passage warns to abandon pride and turn back to God in time, for sincere, timely submission is what averts ruin rather than last‑minute regret.

translation: Perhaps our Lord will replace it for us with something better than it; indeed we are turned toward our Lord in longing.
