interpretation: The verse conveys that a righteous person who publicly appeals to God can provoke intense collective hostility to the point of imminent violence; it teaches that calling to the truth often exposes the caller to mob reaction, so patience, trust in God, and moral courage are required when facing communal opposition.

translation: Say, ‘I only call upon my Lord, and I associate no one with Him.’
interpretation: The verse is a firm affirmation of exclusive devotion: the speaker declares that his invocation, worship, and reliance are directed solely to God and that he refuses to attach any partners, mediators, or equals to Him. It functions as both theological repudiation of shirk and practical guidance for believers — modeling a pure monotheistic stance in prayer, trust, and religious life, and rejecting any practice that would place created beings alongside or between the believer and the Divine.

translation:
قُلْ إِنِّي لَا أَمْلِكُ لَكُمْ ضَرًّا وَلَا رُشْدًا
"Say: I do not possess for you harm nor right guidance."
interpretation: The speaker (the Prophet) is asserting his human limitation: he cannot inflict or avert harm for people nor can he by his own power confer true guidance; his role is to convey God’s message, while benefit, harm and true guidance rest with God and with people's acceptance or rejection of the truth.

translation: Say, “Indeed, no one can protect me from Allah, and I will not find any refuge besides Him.”
interpretation: A declaration of exclusive reliance on God: the speaker acknowledges that no person or being can avert Allah’s will or serve as a true protector, and that ultimate shelter, support, and recourse belong only to God—affirming tawḥīd, humility before divine decree, and the futility of seeking absolute security from anyone other than Allah.

translation: But it is only a conveyance from Allah and His messages; and whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger — for him is the fire of Hell, wherein he will abide forever.
interpretation: The verse delineates responsibility: the Prophet’s duty is to convey God’s guidance, not to compel belief or absorb its moral consequences; the real moral accountability rests with each person’s response. By framing deliberate rejection of God and His Messenger as a decisive, culpable act that brings everlasting punishment, the verse functions both as a theological boundary (affirming the authority of divine guidance) and an ethical warning intended to deter willful disobedience and underscore the seriousness of accepting or rejecting the message.

translation:
حتى إذا رأوا ما يوعدون فسيعلمون من أضعف ناصرا وأقل عددا
“Then when they see what they were promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.”
interpretation: The verse teaches that when the promised event (the punishment or the Hour) comes, those who trusted in worldly allies and numbers will recognize that such help was powerless and scant; apparent worldly strength will be exposed as insignificant before God’s decree, and the reality of who truly had support will be made clear.

translation: قُلْ إِنِّي أَدْرِي أَقْرِيبٌ مَا تُوعَدُونَ أَمْ يَجْعَلُ لَهُ رَبِّي أَمَداً
interpretation: The speaker affirms that he does not possess knowledge of the unseen timetable: the event promised to others may be immediate, or God may set for it a deferred term. The point is to convey prophetic honesty and to remind people that only God determines when promised things will occur, so one must abandon speculative certainty about timing, remain humble before the Divine decree, and live in readiness and trust rather than complacency or despair.

translation: Knower of the Unseen — and He does not disclose His knowledge of the Unseen to anyone.
interpretation: The statement emphasizes that full knowledge of hidden realities (future events, inner thoughts, the unseen realms) belongs solely to God; He does not entrust creatures with that complete knowledge. It therefore cautions against claims of certain knowledge about what only God knows, directs people to rely on revelation and prophetic guidance where God has chosen to inform them, and calls for humble trust in divine wisdom and decree when facing matters beyond human knowledge.

translation:
إلا من ارتضى من رسولٍ فإنه يسلك من بين يديه ومن خلفه رصداً
"Except those whom the Messenger approves; for he will place a watch before them and behind them."
interpretation: When the Prophet accepts or endorses certain people, they are granted comprehensive protection and guidance: a vigilant safeguard arranged on their front and rear. The Messenger’s approval means they will be guarded from harm and misguidance, guided on the right path, and supported by watchful care (understood as divine aid, angels, or the Prophet’s intercession), so that threats from every side are held back and their way forward is secured.

translation: ليُعلَمَ أنّهم قد أبلَغوا رسالاتِ ربِّهم، وأحاطَ بما لديهم، وأحصى كلَّ شيءٍ عدداً.
interpretation: الآية تؤكد أن البلاغ عن ربّهم كان واجبًا وقد أُديَ، وأن المسؤولية عن قبول أو ردّ الناس ليست على المبَلِّغين؛ وفي نفس الوقت تُبيّن كمال علم الله وحصره لكلّ ما في النفوس والهيئات، وأن جميع الأفعال والوقائع محسوبة ومسجلة بدقة، فليس للإنسان عذر عند الحِساب إذ كل شيء قد أُحاط به وأُحصي عدداً.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who are wrapped up (in garments)!
interpretation: The address calls the Prophet by the epithet “al‑Muzammil” — one enshrouded — evoking his state of seclusion, humility, and deep contemplation. By speaking to him in this intimate moment, God both recognizes his earnest devotion and summons him to take up the prophetic burden: to rise from private retreat into active worship, disciplined night prayer, and readiness for the heavy responsibility of delivering guidance. The form of address thus links inward devotion with the outward duties of mission and preparation for the challenges ahead.

translation: Stand (in prayer) during the night — except a little.
interpretation: A divine exhortation to set aside part of the night for prayer, recitation and remembrance: not demanding unbroken vigilance but urging a measured, regular night devotion that deepens one’s closeness to God, strengthens spiritual resolve and readies the believer for daytime duties while respecting human limits.

translation: نصفه أو انقص منه قليلا — "Half of it, or lessen it a little."
interpretation: An instruction toward moderation and leniency: when the full share or demand would be burdensome, allow taking half or a slightly reduced portion to relieve hardship and show compassion.

translation: Or add to it, and recite the Qur'an with measured, deliberate recitation.
interpretation: The verse is an injunction to deepen and refine one’s worship: not merely to increase the time devoted to prayer and Qur’anic reading when able, but to recite in a measured, attentive manner — observing proper pronunciation, pauses, and a contemplative pace so the words are understood and felt. It emphasizes quality and inner absorption of the message (reflection and tajwīd) over hurried or mechanical reading.

translation: Indeed, We will cast upon you a heavy message.
interpretation: God is assuring the Prophet that He will entrust him with a grave, weighty revelation—the Qurʾān—and with the profound responsibility and burden of receiving, preserving, embodying and conveying its guidance and judgments to humanity, a task requiring patience, strength and perseverance.

translation: Indeed, the hours of the night are more effective in impact and more fitting for speech.
interpretation: The verse indicates that worship, recitation and reflection carried out in the quiet of night produce a deeper spiritual effect and more sincere, concentrated utterance; night’s stillness better aligns heart and tongue, increases receptivity to guidance, and strengthens resolve, which is why rising at night for prayer and contemplation is recommended as especially beneficial.

translation: Indeed, for you by day is a long, continuous occupation.
interpretation: The verse promises that in the Hereafter the believers will enjoy extended, pleasant daytime leisure and engagement — a prolonged, untroubled occupation of joyful activities and repose, signifying enduring comfort and fulfillment free from worldly toil.

translation: And remember the name of your Lord, and turn to Him in complete devotion.
interpretation: The verse calls for more than occasional ritual; it enjoins sustained interior remembrance of God (dhikr) and a total, humble turning of the heart toward Him. "Tabtillahu tabtīlā" implies stripping away distractions, pretense and self‑concern so that worship and life are oriented by sincere reliance and intimate awareness of God — a disciplined, inward surrender that shapes both private worship and outward conduct.

translation: Lord of the East and the West; there is no deity except Him, so take Him as Guardian and Trustee.
interpretation: This affirms God’s absolute and indivisible sovereignty over all realms (the East and the West symbolizing the whole world) and commands total reliance on Him: one should entrust one’s affairs, protection and final recourse to God alone, rejecting any rival claims of authority or dependence on created powers, because only He is the true guardian, disposer and judge of affairs.

translation: And be patient concerning what they say, and leave them with gracious avoidance.
interpretation: This instructs the Prophet—and by extension the believer—to meet mockery, slander, and provocation not with retaliation but with forbearance and dignified withdrawal. One should not engage in heated dispute or return insult for insult; instead one distances oneself from harmful company and conversation in a calm, honorable way, maintaining moral integrity and kindness while protecting the mission and preventing further escalation.

translation:
فَذَرْنِي وَالْمُكَذِّبِينَ أُولِي النِّعْمَةِ وَمَهِّلْهُمْ قَلِيلًا
"So leave Me with the deniers—those who enjoy worldly ease—and grant them respite for a little."
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to leave the denunciation and ultimate reckoning of the powerful rejecters to God rather than becoming consumed with trying to force belief; the phrase “those of ease” points to people whose wealth, status or apparent comfort has made them dismissive of the message. God’s granting of a brief respite is not forgiveness but a measured delay: their present prosperity will not avert eventual divine accountability. The passage reassures the faithful to be patient, to trust God’s timing and justice, and not to judge truth by the temporary success or comfort of the deniers.

translation: Indeed, with Us are chains and a blazing Fire.
interpretation: God affirms His absolute power to restrain and punish: “ankāl” (chains) evokes confinement, helplessness and humiliation, while “jahīm” (a blazing Fire) denotes intense torment. Together the images signify ready, certain retribution for persistent injustice and denial, serving both as just recompense and as a deterrent that underscores divine sovereignty and moral accountability.

translation: And food that causes choking, and a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse depicts the recompense for the disobedient: they will be given sustenance that brings no comfort but causes choking and humiliation—a concrete expression of bodily torment that also symbolizes the inner bitterness and remorse of those who rejected guidance—followed by a severe, fitting punishment for their transgression.

translation: The Day the earth will tremble and the mountains will move, and the mountains will be like a scattered, crumbling heap.
interpretation: This verse conveys that on the Day of Reckoning the entire created order — even what seems most stable and permanent (the mountains) — will be utterly overturned and reduced to insignificance. That cosmic upheaval is meant to strip away all illusions of security and self-sufficiency, confronting every soul with the reality of Divine sovereignty and judgment, and thereby urging awareness, humility, and moral accountability in this life.

translation: Indeed We have sent to you a Messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh.
interpretation: God appoints prophets not merely to deliver guidance but to stand as objective witnesses to how people respond; the messenger records and embodies the truth presented, so that acceptance or rejection is not ambiguous — the reference to Pharaoh’s messenger reminds that clear signs and a witness were given before, yet people can still deny and thus bear responsibility, and the messenger’s testimony will be part of the account before God.

translation: But Pharaoh defied the messenger; so We seized him with a violent, crushing seizure.
interpretation: The verse conveys that persistent, willful rejection of God’s messenger provokes an inevitable and overwhelming divine response. “أخذا وبيلا” emphasizes a decisive, forceful and humiliating overthrow—both a fitting recompense for arrogance and a manifest lesson to others that opposing divine guidance leads to sudden, conclusive ruin.

translation: So how will you protect yourselves, if, when you disbelieve, a Day comes that will turn the young into grey-haired?
interpretation: The verse warns that the Hour will bring such overwhelming divine reckoning that it will strip away youth and vigor—what people rely on for security—and leave even the young aged and powerless; it is a rhetorical admonition that disbelief and reliance on worldly strength will be useless on that Day, so one must adopt faith and piety now because later protection will no longer be possible.

translation: The heaven will be split apart by it; His promise will indeed be fulfilled.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the cosmic event that ushers in the Hour: by the decisive blow (understood as the trumpet blast or God’s command) the sky will be violently cleaved, marking the onset of Resurrection and universal overturning. It affirms that God’s promise of final judgment and recompense is certain and will come to pass without fail.

translation: Indeed, this is a reminder; so whoever wills may take a way to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qurʾān as an open admonition and source of guidance, while stressing human freedom and responsibility. By saying “whoever wills,” it makes clear that accepting and following this reminder is a deliberate choice: one must intentionally orient belief and conduct toward God. “Taking a way to his Lord” means adopting a sustained direction of heart and action—repentance, sincere worship, moral conduct and seeking closeness to God—so the verse underscores divine outreach combined with the need for a conscious, ongoing response from the person.

translation: Indeed your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) for nearly two thirds of the night, and half of it, and a third of it, and a group of those with you. And Allah determines the night and the day. He knows that you will not be able to keep it (always), so He turned to you [in mercy]; so recite what is easy [for you] of the Qur'an. He knows that among you there will be the sick, and others traveling through the land seeking the bounty of Allah, and others fighting in the cause of Allah. So recite what is easy of it, and establish prayer and give zakah and lend to Allah a goodly loan. And whatever good you send forward for yourselves you will find it with Allah — it is better and greater in reward. And seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine commands are given with full awareness of human limitation and circumstance: God knows the sincere effort of night-worshippers and also knows that people cannot sustain extreme practices continuously, so He grants ease. Worship is therefore measured by capacity and sincerity rather than by rigid uniformity; different legitimate roles (the sick, travelers seeking livelihood, those fighting) are all recognized as part of the community’s service to God. The passage affirms a balanced religion: maintain core obligations (prayer, almsgiving), cultivate what is lasting (good deeds counted by God), and invest in the eternal through righteous acts, while relying on God’s mercy and seeking forgiveness. The underlying principle is that intention, proportion, and compassionate accommodation are central to divine guidance — God values varied forms of devotion and rewards what is done sincerely and within people’s ability.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. O you who are wrapped up (in garments)!
interpretation: A divine summons addressed to the Prophet at the moment of revelation—calling the one in inward seclusion (wrapped in his cloak) to rise from passivity and assume the outward duty of warning and guidance; symbolically, it teaches that God’s call can reach those withdrawn into themselves and turns private retreat into public responsibility to act on faith.

translation: Arise, then warn.
interpretation: A concise command to take initiative in conveying God's message: leave passivity or comfort and actively call people to awareness of the truth and the consequences of their choices. It emphasizes the urgency and personal responsibility of prophetic mission (and by extension the believer’s duty) to speak clearly and wake others from heedlessness, even when that requires effort or sacrifice.

translation: And magnify your Lord.
interpretation: A summons to exalt and glorify God — not as mere ritual words but by recognizing His absolute greatness and centering one’s life upon Him: to praise Him in heart and tongue, to submit in deeds, and to let that recognition displace attachment to transient things so that worship, conduct, and speech reflect His supremacy and worthiness of reverence.

translation: And purify your garments.
interpretation: This command calls for both literal and symbolic cleansing: literally to remove physical impurities from the Prophet’s clothes as a mark of ritual and social cleanliness, and symbolically to cleanse his outer conduct and inner state of moral defilement and corrupt associations so he is fit to worship, to receive revelation, and to present God’s message clearly and untainted.

translation:
وَٱلرِّجْزَ فَٱهْجُرْ
"And the defilement — then abandon it."
interpretation: A command to withdraw from all forms of spiritual and moral corruption: to renounce idolatry, falsehood, immoral behavior and the people or practices that propagate them, thereby preserving the purity of faith, worship and conduct by keeping away from their sources.

translation: وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ — And do not confer favors while expecting thereby to increase (your own advantage).
interpretation: The verse forbids insincere, calculating generosity: do not bestow benefits to show off, to make others indebted, or to seek greater worldly gain or social leverage. True giving must be free of ostentation, pride, and expectation of repayment or increased status.

translation: فَاصْبِرْ لِرَبِّكَ (So be patient for the sake of your Lord).
interpretation: A directive to adopt steadfast patience as an expression of devotion to God: it calls for enduring hardship, opposition, and delay not out of resignation but as active perseverance in carrying out God’s commands and mission, trusting His wisdom and timing, accepting trials as means of purification, and refraining from haste, resentment, or despair because ultimate justice and recompense rest with the Lord.

translation: Then, when the trumpet is blown.
interpretation: The phrase points to the single, decisive blast of the angel’s trumpet that heralds the Day of Resurrection: it shatters the present order, brings an end to current life, and initiates the process of raising people for final judgment.

translation: So that Day — on that day — will be a hard (difficult) day.
interpretation: The verse warns that the Day of Reckoning will be intensely severe for those who opposed the truth: a day of overwhelming distress and loss when all worldly aids and pretenses collapse, sins and realities are laid bare, and divine justice is executed so fully that the wrongdoers experience utter helplessness, remorse, and irrevocable consequence.

translation: For the disbelievers it will be no light matter.
interpretation: This warns that the consequences awaiting those who reject God’s message are severe and weighty rather than trivial—their denial brings grave retribution (in this life or the Hereafter) and should not be taken lightly.

translation: Leave me alone with the one whom I created alone.
interpretation: The phrase is read as Iblīs asking to be allowed access to the solitary human (Adam) so he can tempt and corrupt him. It exposes Iblīs’s arrogance and method—targeting human vulnerability in isolation—and teaches that solitude can make a person more susceptible to whisperings and moral failure. The verse therefore both reveals the enemy’s intent and warns believers to guard against isolation, seek God’s remembrance and righteous companionship, and rely on divine protection and chosen guidance to resist such temptation.

translation: And granted him abundant, outstretched wealth.
interpretation: It refers to someone who is endowed with plentiful, readily available riches and comes to rely on them as security and status; the verse warns that such wealth is a test that can breed arrogance and false self-sufficiency, not a guarantee of honor or protection from God's judgment.

translation: وَبَنِينَ شُهُودًا — "and (gave) sons as witnesses."
interpretation: It indicates that God provided offspring who would act as witnesses — bearing testimony to the man's character, preserving his legacy, and standing as living attestations to the blessings or truth associated with him.

translation: وَمَهَّدْتَ لَهُ تَمْهِيدًا — And You smoothed/prepared for him an easy way.
interpretation: The phrase expresses that God furnished that person or people with outward facilitation — making the land, means, and opportunities readily available so they could flourish and assert power. This divine smoothing is presented as a provision that tests how it is used: it can enable gratefulness and right conduct, or, if met with arrogance and injustice, become the very cause of their ruin.

translation: Then he hopes that I will increase [for him].
interpretation: A rebuke of presumptuous human expectation: it describes those who, despite ingratitude or wrongdoing, arrogantly assume God will continue to grant them more — blessings, respite, or provision — treating Divine mercy as unlimited and guaranteed; the phrase warns that such complacent presumption is unfounded and reflects arrogance rather than true trust.

translation: No indeed; he was, toward Our signs, defiantly obstinate.
interpretation: The verse explains that refusal of divine guidance is not accidental but stems from willful arrogance and stubbornness: the emphatic negation ('كلا') dismisses any excuse, showing the rejection was intentional and proud, and therefore morally culpable and leading to divine accountability.

translation: I will make him exhausted by the ascent.
interpretation: This phrase warns that the journey toward reckoning — the ascent to stand before God — will be an arduous, soul‑wearing ordeal for the wrongdoer: their sins, heedlessness and pride will make the climb heavy and exhausting, so that instead of ease they meet toil and weariness when facing divine judgment.

translation: Indeed, it is a thought and a measure.
interpretation: The phrase conveys that the matter referred to is the result of deliberate intention and precise determination: occurrences are not random but originate from considered planning and are apportioned with exact measure and wisdom (implying Divine will and order).

translation: So he was killed — as it had been decreed.
interpretation: The verse conveys that the killing occurred in accordance with God’s precise, preordained measure; it emphasizes divine sovereignty over life and death and that outcomes—including punishment for wrongdoing—unfold by God’s decree rather than by mere chance.

translation: ثُمَّ قُتِلَ كَيْفَ قَدَّرَ — Then he was killed; how he had schemed!
interpretation: The phrase warns that the very person who plotted or relied on his own measures met death as a result, illustrating that human scheming is futile before divine decree: people's plans may be reversed and frequently bring ruin upon their originator, so one should not be arrogant in trusting solely in one’s own plotting.

translation: Then he looked.
interpretation: The phrase marks a deliberate turning of attention — a moment of conscious reassessment in which the actor fixes his gaze, signaling a change in perception or intent that will determine what follows.

translation: Then he frowned and turned away.
interpretation: This phrase reproves an attitude of dismissiveness toward a sincere seeker: even a brief frown or turning aside is blameworthy when it discourages someone seeking guidance. It teaches that believers — and even the Prophet when corrected by revelation — must receive those who come for counsel with patience, humility, and respect, prioritizing the conveyance of guidance over social discomfort or prejudice.

translation: ثم أدبر واستكبر — Then he turned away and behaved arrogantly.
interpretation: The phrase depicts a person who, confronted with guidance or admonition, rejects it out of pride: his turning away is not merely physical withdrawal but a moral and spiritual refusal to humble himself before the truth, demonstrating stubborn self-sufficiency and contempt that closes him off from repentance and guidance.

translation: He said, “This is only sorcery that exerts an effect.”
interpretation: The words reflect the attitude of the rejecters who, confronted by the Prophet’s powerful speech and its visible impact on people, refuse to accept it as divine guidance and instead label it ‘sorcery’—‘يوثر’ emphasizing that they perceive a real emotional or persuasive influence, which they attribute to trickery rather than truth.

translation: Indeed, this is nothing but the speech of a human.
interpretation: A dismissal voiced by those who refuse to recognize the Qur'ān as revelation—reducing prophetic discourse to ordinary human words. It reflects a mindset that judges divine guidance by human standards and thereby rejects the Prophet’s authority and the moral/accountability implications of the message.

translation: I will burn him in Saqar.
interpretation: God here asserts the inevitable and severe retribution awaiting the unrepentant transgressor: “Saqar” is presented as a Quranic name for an intense, inescapable fire reserved for those who knowingly reject and corrupt guidance. The terse, forceful phrasing emphasizes both the certainty and the severity of divine justice, serving as a warning that persistent denial and moral arrogance lead to the withdrawal of mercy and entrance into punishment.

translation: And what can make you know what Saqar is?
interpretation: The phrase is a rhetorical challenge pointing to the utter severity and incomprehensibility of Saqar (a name for Hell). It emphasizes that the reality and intensity of that punishment exceed human imagination, serving to shock the listener into recognition of divine justice, awaken fear and seriousness about the consequences of rejection, and compel righteous conduct and repentance.

translation: Leave none remaining and leave none behind.
interpretation: An emphatic command to eradicate the enemy’s remaining strength or means of causing harm — to remove whatever would allow their mischief or power to persist so it cannot continue.

translation: A manifest sign for humankind.
interpretation: The phrase presents the thing referred to (for example a revelation, miracle or warning) as deliberately clear and evident so that all people can perceive it; its purpose is to rouse human conscience, guide them toward truth and moral reform, and to function as an unmistakable admonition that calls every person to recognize God’s message and be accountable for their response.

translation: Over it are nineteen.
interpretation: The verse indicates that nineteen angels are appointed as custodians over Hell; the mention of this precise number emphasizes the exacting, divinely ordered management of punishment and serves as a test and sign meant to prompt reflection and distinguish those who accept the revealed guidance from those who doubt.

translation: And We did not make the keepers of the Fire except angels, and We did not make their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve — that those who were given the Scripture may be certain and that those who believe may increase in faith — and that neither those who were given the Scripture nor the believers should doubt — and that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, “What did Allah intend by this as an example?” Thus Allah misleads whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is nothing but a reminder to mankind.
interpretation: The verse teaches that descriptions of the unseen (e.g. angels guarding the Fire and the cited number) are deliberate divine devices meant to sort and clarify people’s states of heart: they strengthen certainty for true recipients of revelation, increase sincere believers’ faith, remove groundless doubt among the People of the Book and the faithful, and at the same time expose the hypocritical and provoke objection in the hard‑hearted. By framing these facts as a test, the verse also emphasizes God’s absolute sovereignty over guidance and misguidance and His exclusive knowledge of the unseen; the proper response for the sincere is trust and humility before God’s wisdom, receiving such reports as admonition rather than demanding full human explanations.

translation: No — by the moon.
interpretation: A divine oath: God swears by the moon to reject human doubt and stress the certainty and seriousness of what follows; the moon’s clear, cyclical change is invoked as a visible sign of God’s power over time and a reminder that the coming judgment and divine decree are real and inevitable.

translation: By the night when it withdraws.
interpretation: The oath draws attention to the purposeful, regular turning of the night away toward dawn as a sign of God’s sovereign ordering: what is hidden or oppressive in darkness will not remain so forever but will be succeeded by light and clarity. It calls the listener to reflect on transience, divine control, and the coming of a moment of disclosure and reckoning, urging readiness and moral seriousness.

translation: And by the morning when it brightens.
interpretation: The phrase is an oath by the clearening of dawn, using the daily, unmistakable act of God bringing light from darkness to draw attention to His power and order in creation; it calls the listener to reflect that just as morning inevitably follows night and reveals what was hidden, so too God will bring about truth, expose deeds, and establish final accountability—the morning’s return is a sign of divine control, renewal, and the certainty of judgment.

translation: Indeed, it is one of the greatest (matters).
interpretation: The verse declares that the matter just spoken of is of immense gravity in God’s sight — a major, weighty reality (whether a great sin or a momentous truth) whose seriousness demands solemn attention and will bring decisive consequence, warning people to correct their stance accordingly.

translation: A warner to mankind.
interpretation: It declares that the message (or messenger) is meant to alert all human beings to the reality of divine guidance and impending consequences, calling every person to take heed, reform their conduct, and recognize their responsibility before God.

translation: For whoever among you wills to go forward or to stay behind.
interpretation: It affirms human choice: each person may choose to take the lead in obedience, effort, or devotion or to remain behind, and they will accordingly bear the consequences—those who advance will be rewarded for their striving while those who delay accept the outcome of their inaction.

translation: Every soul is held responsible for what it has earned.
interpretation: The verse affirms individual moral accountability: each person is bound to face the consequences of their own actions — they cannot shift that liability onto others. Being ‘held’ (rahīnah) denotes that one’s deeds determine one’s standing and fate until justice is finally settled, so reward or punishment corresponds to what one has earned.

translation: Except the companions of the right.
interpretation: A phrase denoting those who, at the Final Reckoning, are counted among the righteous — they receive their record in the right hand and are thereby affirmed as the fortunate, destined for salvation and admission to Paradise.

translation: In gardens, they will ask one another.
interpretation: The phrase portrays the inhabitants of Paradise conversing in blissful gardens out of wonder and reflection: their questions are not of distress but of amazement, gratitude and confirmation — probing how God’s promise came to pass, the fate of what they left behind, and the full reality of the reward. It emphasizes the communal recognition of God’s mercy and the lived certainty of the afterlife’s blessings.

translation: Concerning the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The phrase draws attention to those who commit injustice and transgress God’s limits, indicating that their deeds will be examined and they will be held accountable—their wrongdoing will not go unnoticed or unpunished.

translation: What brought you into Saqar?
interpretation: A rhetorical question that exposes the inmates' responsibility: they were cast into Saqar by their own sustained choices—persistent rejection of guidance, following vain desires, pride and injustice—so the verse stresses that Hell is the just outcome of continued moral and spiritual failure rather than a random fate.

translation: قَالُوا لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ — "They said, 'We were not among those who prayed.'"
interpretation: An admission by those brought to account that they neglected the prescribed prayers; the phrase highlights prayer as a defining sign of true submission and implies that their exclusion from mercy/results is tied to this failure of devotion.

translation: وَلَمْ نَكُنْ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ — “And we did not used to feed the poor.”
interpretation: This phrase criticizes a moral failing: it records the self-admission of people who, despite having means, neglected to show compassion and provide for the needy. Their refusal to feed the poor is presented as evidence of hardness of heart and social selfishness — a sign of moral and spiritual neglect that will be accounted for.

translation: And we used to join in the jesting with those who jested.
interpretation: It describes the stance of people who willingly allied themselves with scoffers and mockers—participating in derisive, frivolous talk and thus sharing moral responsibility for the denial and harm that resulted. The verse condemns such complicity: taking part in ridicule or falsehood places one alongside the wrongdoers and brings judgment for that alliance.

translation: And we used to deny the Day of Recompense.
interpretation: This expresses the mindset of people who, out of heedlessness, arrogance, or desire to continue in wrongful ways, reject the inevitability of final accountability; it serves as a rebuke and warning that such denial is a moral failing that facilitates injustice and will be overturned by the reality of divine judgment, urging a turn to responsibility and conscience before that day arrives.

translation: “Until certainty came to us.”
interpretation: It refers to the coming of death — the unavoidable, decisive reality that puts an end to opportunities and exposes the true outcome of one's deeds and choices.

translation: So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them.
interpretation: This verse teaches that on the Day of Reckoning no matter how powerful or esteemed the would‑be intercessors are, their pleas will avail those who persisted in denial and disobedience; ultimate judgment and pardon belong to God alone, so each person is accountable for their own deeds and cannot rely on others’ status to secure forgiveness unless God wills it.

translation: فما لهم عن التذكرة معرضين — So what is the matter with them that they turn away from the Reminder?
interpretation: A rhetorical rebuke: the verse points to people’s willful rejection of divine admonition — not mere ignorance but a deliberate turning away born of pride, attachment to worldly desires and self-sufficiency, which closes their hearts to guidance.

translation: كأنهم حمر مستنفرة — As though they were startled wild asses.
interpretation: The phrase uses a vivid simile: people are compared to startled, fleeing donkeys to convey frantic, unthinking haste and disarray. It emphasizes that they act out of fear or base impulse, scattering aimlessly without guidance, deliberation, or self-control — a picture of moral and spiritual confusion rather than calm, reasoned conduct.

translation: She fled from a harsh/unyielding one.
interpretation: The phrase portrays a person withdrawing from an oppressive or cruel presence; it emphasizes escaping a relationship or situation marked by hardness and injustice in order to protect one’s safety and dignity rather than endure subjugation.

translation: بل يريد كل امرئ منهم أن يؤتى صحفا منشرة
interpretation: يُشير إلى رغبة كل إنسان في يوم الجزاء أن يُعطى له كتبًا مبسوطَةً تُظهِرُ له ويثبتُ براءته أو حسناته — أي شَهَادةً او وثائق تُنقذه من العقاب. التعبير يبين يأسَهم وحلمَهم بوثيقة خارجة عن القضاء الإلهي لِتُغيّرَ نتيجة الحساب، وهو تأكيد على بطلانِ هذا الرجاء أمام حكم الله المُقدَّر.

translation: No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse rebukes a mistaken explanation for people's rejection of truth: it asserts that the core problem is not lack of evidence but spiritual indifference — they live without consciousness of divine accountability, so the prospect of the Hereafter fails to restrain them from denial and wrongful behavior.

translation: No! Indeed, it is a reminder.
interpretation: The verse rejects any dismissal of the revelation and affirms that its purpose is to awaken conscience and prompt inner reform: it functions as a corrective, admonishing message meant to make people reflect, turn back to God, and change their conduct, so to ignore it is to forfeit the opportunity for moral and spiritual reorientation.

translation: So whoever wills, let him remember Him.
interpretation: The phrase stresses that remembering God is an act of personal choice: divine invitation is offered but not coerced, and true spiritual engagement comes from a willing heart that turns to God’s names, favors and guidance—those who freely choose that remembrance draw benefit and reward, while the choice itself is part of human responsibility.

translation: And they remember (or call to mind) only as Allah wills. He is the Possessor of piety and the Possessor of forgiveness.
interpretation: The verse teaches that human turning to God—remembrance, recognition, or genuine repentance—happens only by Allah’s will; true God‑consciousness (taqwa) and the power to pardon belong to Him alone. Therefore believers must be humble about their own righteousness, rely on God for guidance and forgiveness, and understand that acceptance of repentance and inner reform are granted by Allah, not by human effort or claim.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I do solemnly swear by the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: By invoking an oath on the Day of Resurrection the speaker gives a solemn, irrefutable foundation for what follows: the reality of final judgment is presented as certain and morally urgent. This oath is meant to dispel doubt, confront those who deny accountability, and compel immediate ethical reflection and responsibility—reminding listeners that their deeds will be reckoned and that earthly denials and excuses will not avert the inevitable resurrection and judgment.

translation: No — I swear by the self that reproaches.
interpretation: God takes an oath by the nafs al‑lawwāmah — the inward, self‑reproaching conscience — to stress human moral awareness and responsibility. That inner voice which feels guilt and calls a person to account is presented as a witness to the reality of judgment: it proves that humans are morally accountable, will be called to account for their choices, and must answer for their deeds.

translation: Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?
interpretation: The verse confronts human skepticism about resurrection by stressing God’s absolute power to reconstitute the human body even from broken or scattered parts; it is meant to humble pride, negate the excuse that death makes returning to life impossible, and to remind people that divine ability and eventual accountability far exceed human imagination.

translation: Nay — We are able to make even his fingertips complete.
interpretation: The verse asserts God’s absolute power to recreate human beings down to the smallest, most identifying details. By invoking fingertips — uniquely individual and finely detailed — it stresses that nothing about a person is too negligible or lost for God to restore; thus resurrection and precise accountability on the Day of Recompense are entirely within His capability, and every distinguishing mark will be reconstituted and known.

translation: بل يريد الإنسان ليفجر أمامه — "Nay, man desires to rush headlong forward."
interpretation: The verse reproves a common human attitude of impatient urgency: people instinctively press forward to seize what they want, pursuing immediate gratification, advancement, or escape without proper restraint or regard for moral responsibility and the timing of God. It points to a selfish restlessness that leads one to push ahead heedlessly rather than remain patient, humble and accountable.

translation:
يَسْأَلُ أَيَّانَ يَوْمُ الْقِيَامَةِ
He asks, “When will be the Day of Resurrection?”
interpretation: The verse portrays the defiant, skeptical attitude of those who, confronted with accountability, demand the timing of the Last Day—not from sincere curiosity but as a way to dismiss responsibility and hope for delay so they may persist in their ways. It exposes human presumption and ignorance about divine timing and serves as a rebuke: the question reflects moral evasion, while knowledge of that Day belongs to God alone, so people should focus on preparing rather than bargaining over when judgment will come.

translation: When the sight is dazzled.
interpretation: This phrase points to the moment—commonly understood as the Day of Resurrection—when human vision is overwhelmed by an extraordinary, blinding manifestation (of light, terror, or divine reality), rendering people unable to perceive normally; it signifies the collapse of ordinary sensory certainty and the dawning of a terrible, unavoidable truth before which human faculties fail.

translation: And the moon was eclipsed.
interpretation: It signifies a divine, extraordinary disruption of the natural order — the moon’s being darkened or swallowed up — presented as a manifest sign of God’s sovereignty and a warning meant to humble the proud, confirm prophetic truth, and call people to reckon with the imminence of judgment.

translation: And when the sun and the moon are joined together.
interpretation: This phrase points to a decisive disruption of the cosmic order at the Hour: the sun and moon—symbols of the regular day–night cycle and temporal stability—will be gathered or brought together under God’s command (their normal functions ending), serving as a visible sign that ordinary time has ceased, the world’s order is overturned, and the Final Reckoning is at hand, thereby manifesting God’s absolute sovereignty over creation.

translation: On that Day the human will say, "Where can I flee?"
interpretation: The verse describes the moment of realization on the Day of Resurrection when a person, stripped of all worldly distractions and defenses, feels utter helplessness before God's judgement—recognizing that there is no refuge from accountability, that every supposed escape or advantage in this life is of no avail, and that only sincere remorse and God's mercy now matter.

translation: No! There is no burden.
interpretation: An emphatic denial asserting that no one will be held accountable for another’s sins or be weighed down by a burden that is not their own; responsibility and recompense are individual, so ultimate justice is preserved and each soul will answer only for its deeds.

translation: To your Lord on that Day will be the final resting‑place.
interpretation: The phrase asserts that on the Day of Reckoning every soul’s journey culminates in return and settlement before God: all worldly attachments and pretensions cease, accountability is established, and there is no other refuge or ultimate destination except the Lord — a reminder of divine sovereignty and the finality that should shape how one lives and prepares.

translation: On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he put off.
interpretation: The verse warns that on the Day of Resurrection every person’s record — both the deeds and preparations they advanced for the Hereafter and the acts or opportunities they delayed or neglected — will be made manifest and judged. It stresses that nothing (outward act or inner intention) escapes accountability, urging immediate, sincere investment in righteous deeds and warning against procrastination and hypocrisy.

translation: Nay! The human being is a clear witness against himself.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a person’s own conscience and the record of their intentions and actions constitute decisive testimony: in the sight of God and on the Day of Reckoning the self will reveal what it did and knew, so one cannot ultimately evade responsibility by outward excuses. It emphasizes inner moral awareness and personal accountability — the heart and deeds will convict or vindicate a person more truly than any external claim.

translation: وَلو ألقى معاذيره — "And even if he were to offer his excuses."
interpretation: It conveys that when the matter of judgment or consequence is settled, presenting excuses will not avail; human defenses and rationalizations cannot avert what is decreed, underscoring the futility of relying on excuses instead of sincere responsibility and preparation.

translation: لا تحرك به لسانك لتعجل به — Do not move your tongue with it so as to hasten it.
interpretation: A command to refrain from rushing, altering, or prematurely speaking about divine revelation: one must not try to speed up, distort, or anticipate God’s message with hasty words, but receive and convey it with patience, restraint, and fidelity to its proper timing and wording.

translation: Indeed, upon Us is its collection and [to] recite it.
interpretation: The verse declares that God Himself guarantees the preservation and proper assembly of the Qurʼān—He will gather its parts into the complete, protected Book and ensure its correct recitation and transmission; thus the integrity of the revelation is divinely entrusted and secured beyond human failure.

translation:
فَإِذَا قَرَأْنَاهُ فَاتَّبِعْ قُرْآنَهُ
"So when We recite it (the Qur'an), then follow its recitation."
interpretation: The verse instructs that when the Divine revelation is presented, one must accept and adhere to it: follow the Qur’an’s words in belief, conduct, and judgment, letting its guidance shape actions and decisions rather than personal desires or external influences.

translation: Then indeed, upon Us is its explanation.
interpretation: God asserts that He will Himself make the matter clear and manifest—removing confusion, revealing the true meaning and consequences so that people cannot plead ignorance; clarification of the affair rests with Divine authority and will be provided by Him.

translation: Nay — rather, you love the immediate (the fleeting things of this world).
interpretation: The verse censures the human inclination to prefer short‑term, tangible pleasures and gains over enduring, spiritual goods and the Hereafter; ‘al‑ʿājila’ denotes the transient worldly rewards that seduce people into neglecting duty, patience, and preparation for final accountability.

translation: and you abandon the Hereafter
interpretation: A warning against neglecting the eternal life by giving priority to fleeting worldly interests—urging that one must not forsake concern for accountability, righteous deeds, and preparation for the Hereafter in pursuit of temporary gains.

translation: And faces—on that Day—will be radiant.
interpretation: The phrase signifies that certain people on the Day of Judgment will show an outward brightness because of inner joy and God’s favor: their countenances will reflect relief, acceptance, and the light of Divine reward and proximity, free from sorrow, humiliation, or grief.

translation: Gazing toward her Lord.
interpretation: It portrays the human self on the Day of Gathering turning its full attention to God — a gaze of attentive expectation that combines awe before divine sovereignty, hope for mercy, and the realization of imminent accountability.

translation: And faces, that Day, will be downcast.
interpretation: The phrase describes the humbled, ashamed appearance of those who stand before God in disgrace on the Day of Judgment; their countenances will visibly betray despair, loss of honor and deprivation of God’s light and mercy as the consequence of their rejection or wrongdoing.

translation: تَظُنُّ أَن يَفْعَلَ بِهَا فَاقِرَةً — Do you think that He will leave her destitute?
interpretation: The phrase rebukes the presumption that God will abandon or neglect someone (or a people). It cautions against reading outward hardship as proof of divine forsakenness: God alone decides who is supported or withheld, and human assumptions about His treatment are mistaken. The verse therefore warns against complacent judgments and reminds listeners that apparent deprivation is not evidence that God has cast anyone off, for His wisdom and justice determine outcomes beyond our fleeting impressions.

translation: No! When the soul reaches the collar‑bones.
interpretation: This verse points to the decisive instant of death—the moment the soul rises to the throat/collarbones—when human self‑delusions and defenses collapse, power and excuses vanish, and the reality of accountability becomes unmistakable. It warns that what people pursue in life will then lose its meaning; what will matter is the soul’s state and the record of deeds, so one must heed the call to uprightness before that irreversible moment.

translation: And it will be said, “Who will deliver (us)?”
interpretation: The phrase depicts the moment of utter helplessness on the Day of Reckoning: people will cry out, asking who can save or protect them from the consequences they face. The question is rhetorical — it exposes the collapse of every false hope and dependence on anything other than God, and it signals recognition, too late, that deliverance lies only with Divine mercy and authority.

translation: وَظَنَّ أَنَّهُ الْفِرَاقُ — "And he thought that it was the parting (the final separation)."
interpretation: The phrase expresses a person's mistaken assumption that what is happening marks an absolute, irreversible severance — a final cutoff from what he values (life, mercy, guidance, companions). It highlights human tendency in moments of fear or distress to conclude hopeless finality, revealing both despair and lack of awareness of Divine wisdom, mercy, or later reconciliation; the statement therefore criticizes that premature, despairing judgment.

translation: And the leg will be wound round the leg.
interpretation: An image of the utter disarray and humiliation on the Day of Resurrection: people will be so overwhelmed by fear and turmoil that their bodies are twisted and intermixed, symbolizing helplessness, the collapse of ordinary order and dignity, and total subjection before God’s judgment.

translation: To your Lord, that Day, will be the journey.
interpretation: The verse declares the unavoidable return to God at the Final Reckoning: ‘al-masāq’ conveys being driven or led in haste and without choice, so on that Day every soul will be brought before its Lord in a solemn, irresistible procession to receive its due — emphasizing inevitability, accountability, and human inability to evade the divine meeting.

translation: فَلا صَدَّقَ وَلا صَلَّى — So he neither believed nor prayed.
interpretation: The phrase indicts a person cut off from faith both inwardly and outwardly: he lacks sincere conviction and also abandons the essential act of worship. It signals that without inner truthfulness, external rites are void, and the simultaneous absence of belief and prayer shows a complete estrangement from guidance and from being counted among the truly faithful.

translation: But he denied (it) and turned away.
interpretation: The verse characterizes the posture of someone who, when confronted with divine truth or a clear admonition, responds with conscious rejection and deliberate disengagement; 'kذّب' denotes willful denial, while 'tawalla' indicates an active turning of the heart and attention away from guidance, reflecting a moral choice to close oneself off from what one knows to be right.

translation: Then he went to his people, strutting (moving about with deliberate pride).
interpretation: The wording depicts a person who, after an extraordinary experience or elevation, returns to his community with measured, ostentatious gait — a posture of self-satisfaction and arrogance. The phrase criticizes the reaction of showing off and pride in the face of guidance or favor, implying that the proper response should be humility rather than boastful display.

translation: أولى لك فأولى — More appropriate for you, indeed more appropriate.
interpretation: An emphatic injunction that one choice is clearly more deserving of your attention and therefore must be preferred; the repetition intensifies the call to prioritize the nearer/better option (e.g., duty, closeness to God, or the superior course) and abandon what is less worthy.

translation:
ثم أولى لك فأولى
"Then it is nearer to you — nearer still."
interpretation: The wording stresses increasing immediacy and intensity: whatever was referred to is drawing progressively closer or becoming more incumbent upon you, so you must give it immediate attention, prioritize it, and prepare accordingly.

translation: Does man think that he will be left neglected?
interpretation: The verse rebukes human presumption that life ends without purpose or accountability; it warns that people are not abandoned to meaninglessness but are under God’s knowledge and will be called to account—therefore one must live with awareness of responsibility, moral consequence, and the coming Resurrection.

translation: Was he not a drop of sperm emitted?
interpretation: The verse reminds the listener that every human began from a humble, minute origin; by pointing to our creation from a mere drop of semen it rebukes arrogance and doubts about resurrection—if God can fashion a complete person from that tiny beginning, His power to raise the dead and judge them is self‑evident, calling people to humility and accountability before their Creator.

translation: Then it became a clinging clot; then He created (it) and proportioned (it).
interpretation: The words indicate two complementary divine acts: God first brings the embryo into existence as a fragile, clinging form and then immediately perfects and measures its limbs and structure — teaching that human life begins in a lowly, dependent state yet is formed by deliberate, precise divine design, a reminder of God’s sovereign power, wisdom, and purposeful ordering of creation.

translation:
فَجَعَلَ مِنْهُ الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنْثَىٰ
"So He made from it the two mates: the male and the female."
interpretation: The verse teaches that God brings living beings into existence as complementary pairs originating from a single source; this manifests divine wisdom and unity in creation, explaining sexual differentiation as purposeful and ordered to enable reproduction, social complementarity, and the balance of life.

translation: Is He not capable of giving life to the dead?
interpretation: A rhetorical affirmation that God’s absolute power, already manifest in creation, unquestionably extends to reviving the dead; it challenges doubt about the Hereafter by showing that denial of resurrection contradicts the same divine capacity that sustains and renews life, thereby grounding belief in resurrection and consequent moral accountability.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Has there not come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing to be mentioned?
interpretation: The verse calls attention to human beings’ original nothingness before God’s creative act; realizing that there was a time when we did not exist and were not noteworthy should humble us, make us conscious of our complete dependence on God’s will, and move us to gratitude, moral responsibility, and avoidance of pride.

translation: Indeed We created man from a mixed drop to test him, and We made him hearing and seeing.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes both the humble biological origin of human beings and the moral purpose of their existence: created from a small mixed fluid (underscoring dependence on God and the physical reality of conception), humans are placed in the world as subjects of trial (nabtalihi). God endows them with perceptive faculties—hearing and sight—not merely for sensation but so they can receive revelation, learn from signs, discern guidance from error, and thus be held morally responsible. In other words, our embodied senses are instruments by which we are tested in action and belief; how we use them to seek truth, obey God, and act ethically determines our success or failure in that test.

translation: إنا هديناه السبيل إما شاكرا وإما كفورا — We have guided him to the Way; he may be either grateful or ungrateful.
interpretation: God has provided a clear path of guidance and moral direction for humanity, but this facilitation does not override human freedom: each person faces the moral choice to respond with gratitude — inward acknowledgment and outward obedience, thankfulness shown in faith and righteous conduct — or with ingratitude — rejection, turning away, and resultant disobedience. The verse thus teaches that divine guidance and human responsibility coexist: God makes the way known, and individuals determine their fate by how they receive and live by that guidance.

translation: Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and fetters and a blazing fire.
interpretation: The verse presents a solemn warning that persistent rejection of divine guidance carries certain, severe consequences: the imagery of chains and fetters conveys humiliation, loss of freedom and restraint from honor, while the blazing fire denotes intense retributive suffering. Together they emphasize divine justice and accountability, intended to deter denial, awaken conscience, and urge turning back to God before it is too late.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a camphor‑mixed cup to signify the distinctive, purifying, and restorative nature of the reward reserved for the upright: camphor (kafūr) connotes coolness, fragrance, healing, and purity, so the gift promised is not merely sensual pleasure but a spiritually cleansing and ennobling provision that marks the blessedness and elevated status of the righteous in the hereafter.

translation: A spring from which the servants of Allah will drink, which they will make gush forth abundantly.
interpretation: The image indicates that the blessings of Paradise are dynamic and responsive: the righteous are granted access to an ever-flowing source of divine bounty, and by their honored status and devoted conduct these blessings are freely released and multiplied. “They make it gush forth” stresses that the servants’ purity and obedience do not merely receive a static reward but unlock and increase God’s generous provisions for them.

translation: They fulfill their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.
interpretation: The verse portrays a moral posture: true piety shows itself in keeping promises and vows (to God and to people) and in a sustained, reverent awareness of the Day of Reckoning. The image of a Day whose harm is 'spread about' conveys the vast, uncontrollable nature of that hour, and this awareness tempers behavior—producing humility, trustworthiness, self-restraint, and readiness to sacrifice for others—so that fear of ultimate accountability, far from causing despair, becomes the motive for steadfast righteousness and social responsibility.

translation: And they give food, though they themselves love it, to the poor, the orphan, and the captive.
interpretation: The verse praises sincere, selfless charity: true believers willingly share even what they cherish, prioritizing the needs of the most vulnerable (the needy, orphans, and captives) out of devotion to God rather than for pride or gain, thereby showing inner piety and trust in God's provision.

translation: We feed you only for the sake of Allah; we seek from you neither reward nor thanks.
interpretation: The phrase affirms an intentionally pure act of worship: the givers direct their charity solely to win God’s pleasure (lillah) and deliberately renounce any expectation of worldly compensation or human praise. It teaches that true righteousness lies in correcting the heart’s intention—doing good free from desire for recognition or return—trusting that ultimate recompense is with God, and thereby guarding one’s action from ostentation, hypocrisy, and attachment to social reward.

translation: Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day that is stern and stormy.
interpretation: The speaker conveys dread of the Day of Reckoning when God’s displeasure will be openly manifest; the description “frowning and stormy” evokes an uncompromising, overwhelming divine judgment and palpable gloom, stressing that on that Day severity and punishment will dominate rather than consolation—thus serving as a warning to recognize accountability and turn from wrongdoing.

translation: Allah protected them from the evil of that Day, and He greeted them with radiance and joy.
interpretation: It signifies that those whom God shields from the terrors and punishment of the Day of Judgment will be received into His mercy and favor: their faces and spirits will be renewed and luminous (‘nadhra’) and they will feel inner gladness and delight (‘suroor’)—so salvation is portrayed both as deliverance from doom and as an immediate experience of Divine acceptance and bliss.

translation: And He will reward them for what they patiently endured with a Garden and silk.
interpretation: Patience in hardship is not merely tolerated by God but transforms the sufferer’s status: the promised ‘Garden’ signifies abiding nearness, peace, and spiritual fulfillment, while ‘silk’ signifies honor, refinement, and dignified enjoyment. Thus endurance refines the soul and is met by divine mercy with an everlasting, elevated reward that dignifies and comforts beyond worldly trials.

translation: Reclining therein on couches; they will not see therein any sun nor any piercing cold.
interpretation: The verse describes the residents of Paradise enjoying constant, dignified ease—reclining on couches and completely shielded from extremes of heat and cold. By saying they will not see “sun” or “zamharir,” the text signals more than mere physical comfort: it signifies the removal of all hardships, discomforts and trials, offering a state of enduring tranquility, balance and divine protection.

translation: And its shade will be close to them, and its fruit will be made low and easy to reach.
interpretation: The verse describes how, in Paradise, God arranges creation to serve the righteous: shade draws near to give restful protection and the fruits are humbled and brought within reach so that enjoyment requires no effort. The term تذليلا stresses that the blessings are rendered submissive and accessible — a sign of divine mercy, abundance, and the removal of hardship for those granted these favors.

translation: And vessels of silver will be passed around them and goblets which were crystal.
interpretation: The imagery conveys that the righteous will receive honourable, refined and pure rewards in Paradise: silver signifies dignity and worth, crystal signifies clarity and unblemished purity, together portraying pleasant, wholesome comforts befitting their inner purity and patient righteousness rather than the coarse or corrupt pleasures of this world.

translation:
قوارير من فضة قدروها تقديرا
"Silver goblets, measured out with precise measure."
interpretation: The verse portrays the vessels of Paradise as exquisitely fashioned from silver and allotted with exact measure, signifying that heavenly provision is both beautiful and perfectly ordered — every blessing apportioned with Divine wisdom and justice so that rewards are fitting, neither wasteful nor deficient.

translation: And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is of ginger.
interpretation: The verse depicts one of Paradise’s delights: a carefully prepared, ginger‑mixed drink offered to the righteous. By naming “zanjabīl” (ginger) the text conveys a beverage that is fragrant, refreshing and invigorating—pleasant to the senses yet wholesome and harmless—emphasizing that the rewards in the Hereafter are refined, intentionally prepared to revive and satisfy, and distinct from worldly intoxicants.

translation: A spring therein called Salsabīl.
interpretation: The phrase names a particular spring of Paradise whose chief meaning is spiritual and experiential: Salsabīl signifies a uniquely pure, gentle and delight-giving flow — God’s special provision that wholly refreshes body and soul. It stresses that what awaits the righteous is not ordinary water but an effortless, immaculate source of nourishment and consolation, symbolizing divine bounty that permanently satisfies thirst and longing without harm or toil.

translation:
وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدَانٌ مُّخَلَّدُونَ ۝ إِذَا رَأَيْتَهُمْ حَسِبْتَهُمْ لُؤْلُؤًا مَنْثُورًا
"And young boys, made everlasting, will circulate among them; when you see them you would think them scattered pearls."
interpretation: The verse conveys that the pleasures of Paradise are enduringly preserved and presented with flawless beauty: the term 'mukhalladun' stresses permanence and freedom from aging or decline, while the simile of 'scattered pearls' evokes luminosity, purity, variety and meticulous order. Together these images signify that the blessings and attendants of the hereafter are not only constant but also perfectly harmonious and aesthetically sublime, reflecting the unblemished and everlasting nature of divine reward.

translation: And when you look, then you will see bliss and a great kingdom.
interpretation: Addressing the Prophet (and by extension the believers), the verse promises that on the Day of Reckoning they will behold two overwhelming realities: the pleasant, abiding rewards (the bliss) prepared for the righteous, and alongside that the vast, absolute sovereignty and majesty of God (a great kingdom). The vision of reward is inseparable from the recognition of Divine authority — the felicity granted is both a gift and a manifestation of God’s supreme dominion.

translation: Upon them will be green garments of fine silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver; and their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink.
interpretation: The verse uses images of luxurious robes, silver bracelets, and a purifying drink to convey that God will dignify and sanctify the righteous—elevating their status, cleansing them from earthly stains, and personally bestowing intimate, unmediated blessings. These worldly symbols point beyond material pleasure to spiritual honor, moral purification, and the closeness to their Lord that constitutes the true reward in Paradise.

translation: Indeed, this is a recompense for you, and your striving has been appreciated.
interpretation: The verse reassures that God gives what is due: the benefits received are the rightful reward for the believers’ actions, and importantly their effort — not only visible results but the sincerity and diligence behind them — is recognized and accepted by God; thus one should take comfort that honest striving will not be wasted even if its fruits are not immediately obvious.

translation: Indeed, it is We who have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages.
interpretation: The verse asserts that the Qur'an is a divine revelation and that it came gradually rather than all at once; this gradual descent served a wise, practical purpose—allowing the Prophet and the community to receive, learn, apply, and preserve guidance step by step, and enabling revelation to address changing circumstances and human capacity over time.

translation:
فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلَا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِمًا أَوْ كَفُورًا
"So be patient with the judgment (decree/command) of your Lord, and do not obey any of them who is a sinner or an ingrate."
interpretation: The verse instructs steadfastness in submission to God's ruling and guidance: patience here means enduring trials, implementing divine commandments, and awaiting God's judgment without yielding to pressure. It warns against taking as models or following the counsel of those whose character is corrupt—those who openly transgress (آثِم) or who deny or show ingratitude for God's favors (كفور). In practice this teaches prioritizing fidelity to God's guidance over popular opinion or the influence of immoral or ungrateful people, because obeying them would lead away from the truth and harm the community and mission; patience combined with refusal to follow the sinful or ungrateful preserves integrity and trust in God's wisdom and timing.

translation: And remember the name of your Lord morning and evening.
interpretation: This command calls the believer to regular, disciplined remembrance of God at the decisive points of the day — morning and evening — not as empty repetition but as conscious, heartfelt orientation toward God. Fixing remembrance at these times sanctifies the day’s threshold moments, cultivates gratitude and trust, prevents heedlessness, and ensures that one’s intentions and actions are continually checked and guided by awareness of God, so that devotion shapes both the beginning and the close of daily life.

translation: And during the night prostrate to Him and glorify Him long into the night.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to use the quiet of night for intimate, sustained worship as a means to draw near to God. Nightly prostration and prolonged glorification are not merely ritual acts but spiritual disciplines: they cultivate humility and sincerity, detach the heart from worldly distractions, sharpen moral resolve, and open the believer to repentance, guidance, and inner tranquility. By prescribing devotion in the solitary hours, the verse highlights the importance of private communion with God as the wellspring of strength and steadfastness for life’s public duties.

translation: Indeed, these people love the immediate [worldly life] and leave behind for themselves a heavy Day.
interpretation: It warns that preferring fleeting, worldly pleasures and neglecting duties for the Hereafter results in a burdensome Day of reckoning: because they abandoned what earns lasting good, they will face severe accountability, regret and loss when their short‑term gains cannot avail them.

translation: We created them and made their bonds firm; and if We willed, We could replace them with others like them, in exchange.
interpretation: The verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over people and social orders: He fashioned those individuals and fixed the ties, conditions, or positions that keep them as they are, yet none are indispensable. If God so chooses, He can substitute them with others of similar standing. The point is to humble human pride in lineage, power, or continuity and to remind that the composition and occupants of communities are contingent on divine will, so moral responsibility and readiness for change are essential.

translation: Indeed, this is a reminder; so whoever wills may take a way to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse presents the revelation as an open, merciful invitation rather than compulsion: acceptance depends on individual will. To “take a way to his Lord” signifies a deliberate, ongoing turning—inner transformation, sincere submission, and consistent righteous practice following God’s guidance. Thus guidance is granted, but entry onto the path to God requires a conscious choice and sustained effort, with personal responsibility for that choice.

translation: And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is Ever‑Knowing, Ever‑Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that human intention and effort operate within the framework of divine sovereignty: people form desires and make choices, but their ability to bring those choices to fruition ultimately depends on God's decree and permission. This does not remove moral responsibility—humans are accountable for their intentions and actions—but it locates final causal power with God, whose perfect knowledge and wisdom govern outcomes. The purpose of this reminder is to cultivate humility about our limited control, trust in God’s wise ordering when things differ from our plans, and a balanced stance of sincere striving combined with submission to God’s will.

translation: He admits into His mercy whom He wills; but for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Divine mercy is given according to God’s sovereign wisdom rather than as an automatic right; mercy is an act of grace toward those He chooses, while persistent injustice and wrongdoing remove one from that protective scope and bring God’s just retribution. Its practical lesson is to seek God’s mercy through humility, repentance and righteous conduct, recognizing both hope in God’s compassion and warning of accountability.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. By those sent forth in succession.
interpretation: The oath refers to winds (or similar forces) sent out one after another; their disciplined, purposeful motion under divine command is invoked as a visible sign of Allah’s sovereign control and as a warning of the coming reckoning—these ordered phenomena attest to God’s power and remind humanity of accountability.

translation: By those that blow violently, scattering with force.
interpretation: The phrase is an oath invoking fierce driving winds (or the angelic agents likened to them) to stress that overwhelming, seemingly uncontrollable forces serve God’s purpose; it highlights divine sovereignty and the certainty and inevitability of God’s decree — a warning that the powerful events to come (not the winds themselves) are intentional acts of God and will accomplish His judgment.

translation: By those who scatter, scattering.
interpretation: The phrase is an oath invoking powerful agents—understood in classical readings as angels, winds, or forces of God—that disperse and distribute by His command. Their relentless, purposeful scattering is cited to draw attention to God’s sovereign control and to underscore the certainty and inevitability of what follows (the Day of Reckoning): just as these agents carry out their tasks without fail, so too will God’s judgment and the events of resurrection occur as He decrees.

translation: By those that cleave apart, separating.
interpretation: An oath referring to the angels or forces that decisively separate souls from bodies at death; it emphasizes the absolute power and finality of that separation as a sign of God’s control over life, death and the ensuing accountability on the Day of Judgment.

translation: By those who are cast forth, carrying a reminder.
interpretation: An oath invoking those whom God sends forth to deliver reminders—understood as angels or divinely appointed messengers—signifying that reminders and warnings are intentionally dispatched to mankind; this stresses the reality and seriousness of God’s message and the corresponding responsibility of people to heed it.

translation: عذرا أو نذرا — as an excuse or as a warning
interpretation: The phrase draws a distinction between two types of rationale behind an action: one is mitigation or allowance granted because of a legitimate excuse (leniency for a vulnerable or constrained party), and the other is a measure taken to warn, deter, or admonish (a punitive or preventive response). It signals that responses and rulings depend on whether the circumstance calls for compassion and exemption or for warning and deterrence.

translation: ما يُوعَدُكم به سيقع لا محالة.
interpretation: تأكيد حاسم على حتمية وعد الله: ما أبلغه من جزاء أو عذاب أو وقوع للآخرة ليس تهديدًا افتراضيًا بل واقع محتوم، لا ترده شكوك الناس ولا تؤخّره مرافعاتهم. النتيجة العملية لذلك هي وجوب التعامل مع الحياة بوَعْيٍ بالمسؤولية والاحتساب — التوبة والصدق والعمل الصالح — لأن الجزاء الموعود سيتحقق بلا هروب من تبعاته.

translation: When the stars are extinguished.
interpretation: It signifies that at the Hour the ordered heavens will be upheaved and the stars will be extinguished, removing the familiar signs and guidance of creation as a dramatic display of God’s power and the imminence of final accountability.

translation: When the heaven is split open.
interpretation: This verse points to a decisive, eschatological event: the sky’s normal ordered state will be violently undone and the protective, familiar canopy of creation will be rent, manifesting God’s absolute power and bringing into clear view realities now hidden. It signals the end of the present cosmic order and the onset of the final reckoning, stirring awe and certainty in those who witness it.

translation: And when the mountains are blown away.
interpretation: The phrase points beyond a literal upheaval to a theological truth: what seems most fixed and secure in this world will be undone by God’s command on the Day of Recompense, thereby demonstrating His absolute power, exposing human vulnerability, and compelling people to recognize the transient nature of worldly anchors and prepare for accountability.

translation: And when the messengers fought among themselves.
interpretation: The line is best read as a warning: when those who claim or are entrusted with a divine message descend into rivalry and bloodshed, it betrays the falsity or corruption of their cause. True prophetic guidance leads to moral coherence and communal guidance; internecine conflict among leaders reveals worldly ambition, undermines the truth they claim to serve, and foreshadows divine judgment and the dispersal of their followers.

translation: To what day have you been deferred?
